text: To require the Czech authorities: to take corrective measures as regards observed deficiencies in particular the Czech approval procedure for meat product export establishments and its implementation, and to approve the establishments for export to the Member States of the Community accordingly;
To require the Czech authorities to inform the Commission's service of these corrective measures;
To list the Czech meat product establishments proposed by the Czech authorities on the basis of the above mentioned;
To require the Czech authorities to inform the Commission about full implementation of the HACCP system;
To perform a follow up mission in the Czech Republic after receiving the information on implementation of the HACCP system.

The system laid down in the Decision can not function, as long as the separation of lots already from the beginning onwards is not ensured. Numbered labels and colour codes facilitate significantly the identification of bags and therefore the work of the inspectors, but the lots must in any event be kept separately already by the exporting country.

In the present case of imports to Portugal it is highly recommended to try to find out the real number of bags imported and also the number of bags and the respective lots sold to the agricultural co-operatives.

As a third vessel is still expected for the next weeks, it should be taken into account, to carry out an inspection at the arrival of it. If it shown, that the lots are not loaded separately, a refusal of the consignment is recommended. Only such a stringent measure taken already at the beginning of the chain of trade can force the exporter to follow the prescriptions precisely.

It is obvious, that the loading and shipment in Canada are the bottlenecks of the whole procedure. Therefore, future inspections should be carried out with priority on these aspects. With a second priority, the unloading procedure in the relevant Member State should be another key point for inspections.
A suggested solution could be the shipment of each separated lot in a separate container. 3

Resources should be used first of all to improve working conditions in the laboratories and district departments. Every laboratory must have basic equipment. It is absolutely essential to purchase equipment, in particular for laboratories. Where resources are limited, these should be targeted, i.e. a reduction in the number of laboratories should be considered.
Technical training of staff should be carried out only if the laboratories are suitably equipped.
Training in general management/administrative tasks should also be given alongside technical training.
A register of persons and firms subject to phytosanitary instructions is urgently required. This is the only way of guaranteeing that the whole system is monitored by the SPA's inspectors.

Comments from the Finnish authorities: the instructions sent by EELA and MAF with the exception of on-line sampling of meat at slaughterhouses refer to targeted sampling. The targeting criteria were decided on the central level. There are few targeting criteria used which are the amount and type of livestock production and the results of the residue control programs of previous years.

Comments from the Finnish authorities: the veterinary drugs chosen for analysis are substances most commonly used in Finland and thus the most probable to be found. No illegal use of veterinary medicines has been discovered in our country. The use of organophosphate insecticides for animals is small in Finland. In the past years, no positive results were found concerning organophosphates.
Comments from the Finnish authorities: the bovines mentioned in the table for examinations of meat includes both young animals and culled cows.

Comments from the Finnish authorities: concerning the poultry, there is a mistake in the table of the 1998 plan: the "5% of the poultry samples" should be read as "one fifth (20%) of the poultry samples".
Comments from the Finnish authorities: phenoxymethylpenicillin is almost the only antibacterial drug which is today used in poultry.
Comments from the Finnish authorities: all the methods have been finalized, except the method for xylasin.

Comments from the Finnish authorities: the detection limit for azaperon (40 µg/kg) is lower than the MRL for the substance (100 µg/kg). -Page 7 of 11- 6. SAMPLING 6.1. On livestock holdings As a rule, sampling performed by municipal vets on livestock holdings under the supervision of provincial vets is carried out by motivated, competent staff. However, some shortcomings were apparent, in particular: · the possible conflict of interests referred to above; · improper use of blood sampling equipment for cattle: use of unsuitable needles, vacuum opening of the sampling tubes leading to subsequent improper closure with a risk of overturning; deplorable conditions of hygiene during sampling; · an individual sampling form was not filled in for each sample; · there was no sealing of samples and improper packaging. 6.2. In abattoirs Although outside the scope of this mission, attention should be drawn to the inadequate hygiene facilities at the abattoir visited, in particular the lack of suitable material for the effective cleaning of boots (rotating brushes) and the overlapping of clean and contaminated areas. The central authorities issue annual instructions to abattoirs and these are respected by the officials. On the whole, sampling is carried out in accordance with the provisions of Directive 96/23/EC and Decision 98/179/EC, though some inadequacies were observed, in particular: · the refrigerator for storing samples was also used for storing laboratory reagents used for analyses carried out on-site; · official samples were not sealed as required in point 2.6 of Decision 98/179/EC and were placed in an unsealed isothermal box placed outside the establishment pending collection by an official from the municipal laboratory; · the laboratory had no global data processing system, which made traceability difficult. 6.3. In milk plants Sampling at the milk plant provided no guarantee that the milk samples taken actually came from the respective tanker, since they were taken at the level of the control station, contrary to the provisions of Decision 97/747/EC. -Page 8 of 11- 7. LABORATORIES 7.1. National reference laboratory The national reference laboratory for all substances is the National Veterinary and Food Research Institute (EELA). This is an efficient, well-equipped laboratory with competent, motivated staff. Besides performing the tasks of a national reference laboratory, it also carries out all routine chemical analyses. This centralisation has a certain number of advantages, in particular for the comparison of results and organisation of the transport of samples, but in these circumstances confirmation is always carried out in the same place as the initial analysis, and the time allowed for the development of analytical methods is reduced8. In the case of inhibiting substances, the national reference laboratory does not carry out routine analyses and devotes itself entirely to the development of methods and the organisation of interlaboratory proficiency testing. The EELA also decides in which locations samples are to be taken at central level, with no criteria for targeting sampling and without taking into account regional problems which would enable the sampling to be targeted9. 7.2. Network of public laboratories The only analyses carried out at local laboratory level under the residue control plan are those to detect inhibiting substances using the microbiological method. There are 54 municipal laboratories (34 of which are accredited) and laboratories within large abattoirs. The analytical method applied used 2 Petri dishes, whereas the method recommended by the Community reference laboratory concerned used 410. It was noted that tests for inhibitors were performed in muscle and renal tissue, though the residue plan refers only to the testing of renal tissue11.
Comments from the Finnish authorities: in Finland, with small population, it would not be reasonable nor economically possible to maintain more than one laboratory.
Comments from the Finnish authorities: the few known local problems have been included in the targeting criteria (ex.: arsenic in certain areas in Finland).

Comments from the Finnish authorities: During the past years, research work on the microbiological method has been done at EELA. The results show that no essential differences in the results can be found using the recommended 4-plate test compared with 2-plate test.

Comments from the Finnish authorities: the official test is made of renal tissue, which contains higher concentrations of inhibitorsd than meat. -Page 9 of 11- 8. MEASURES TAKEN BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITIES AFTER DETECTION OF POSITIVE CASES The Finnish authorities have very little experience of the subject since the number of positive cases detected is very low. This stage is carried out by municipal authority veterinarians supervised by provincial veterinarians. All the procedures to be followed are set out in the Ministry of Agriculture's decision on residues. 9. CONTROL OF THE DISTRIBUTION OF VETERINARY MEDICINAL PRODUCTS The National Agency of Medicines is responsible for controlling the various levels of the distribution chain of veterinary medicinal products, with the exception of practising veterinarians who are controlled by the Ministry of Agriculture. In order to carry out their trade, wholesalers-distributors and pharmacies must be in possession of a licence issued by the National Agency of Medicines. Practising veterinarians may buy their medicinal products from wholesalers- distributors, but they are not allowed to make a profit when they re-sell them to their clients. Veterinarians may also prescribe medicinal products, which are then dispensed by a pharmacy. It is acceptable for the contents of a prescription to be communicated by telephone, but if in any doubt, the pharmacist is obliged to ascertain the identity of the prescriber. No clinical test for bovine somatotropin has been introduced on Finnish territory. 10. CONCLUSIONS (1) The central body responsible for coordination within the meaning of Article 4 of Directive 96/23/EC (National Veterinary and Food Research Institute) is capable of carrying out its functions correctly. (2) In some cases there may be a conflict of interest for the veterinarian responsible for treating animals who may be required to take samples from the same animals. (3) Community legislation concerning residues has been transposed into Finnish national law. (4) The residue control plan was approved by the Commission in its Decision (98/154 of 10 February 1998). However, sampling is not sufficiently targeted and the testing of certain groups is inadequate. (5) Shortcomings have been detected with regard to the practical procedures for the taking of samples on livestock holdings and establishments. (6) The national reference laboratory carries out its duties correctly. (7) There is proper control of the distribution of veterinary medicinal products. -Page 10 of 11- 11. RECOMMENDATIONS 11.1. For the Member State (1) The possibility of a conflict of interests on the part of officials responsible for sampling must be eliminated before the end of a period of 6 months starting when receiving the final version of this document, in particular by requesting veterinarians not to take samples from livestock holdings where they are responsible for treating the animals (request other colleagues). Appropriate provisions should be contained in the control plan for 1999. (2) The residue control plan for 1999 must remedy the deficiencies and inaccuracies contained in the plan for 1998. (3) The shortcomings observed with regard to the practical procedures for the taking of samples must be remedied before the end of a period of 6 months starting when receiving the final version of this document. 11.2. For the European Commission Services (1) Monitor the amendments to the residue control plan proposed by Finland for 1999. (2) Monitor the correction of deficiencies observed in the sampling of live animals by carrying out an interim on-site mission. -Page 11 of 11-

A general view of the deficiencies seen during the previous visit and of the significant improvements since last visit is given for each plant. The detected minor deficiencies not impinging the approval given by the veterinary authority to the plants were mentioned on the spot. 4 7.3. Establishment n°3. Deficiencies seen during previous visit The slaughterhouse/cutting plant complex showed especially in the slaughterhouse section, very serious lack of equipment and working hygiene. Current situation during the visit Almost a complete new slaughterhouse has been build, including the slaughterline, amenities, stables, blast chiller, detention chiller, red and green offal rooms. Staff at slaughter has received training on slaughter hygiene. This establishment has made a great effort to rectify all the deficiencies found during previous inspections and presents acceptable structures, maintenance and operational practices. 7.4. Establishment n°4. Main deficiencies seen during previous visit The plant showed still some deficiencies in regard to structures (protection against entrance of pests, amenities), installation, maintenance and cleanliness. The training to improve the hygienic practices of the personnel should be implemented as soon as possible. Current situation during the visit. Most of the observations mentioned in the previous report have been rectified The departments of the plant which had shown severe deficiencies not in compliance with the Directive (expedition, amenities, emergency slaughter facilities, red and green offal rooms) have been renovated in accordance to the requirements of the Directive. Proper slaughter hygiene has been achieved by an educational training of the staff on operational hygiene practices and by improvement of technical equipment for slaughter. This establishment has made a great effort to rectify the deficiencies found during previous inspections but still presents some deficiencies regarding slaughter hygiene, veterinary supervision on the slaughter hygiene, ante and post-mortem inspection. Most of the non-compliances can easily be rectified 7.5. Establishment n°5. Main deficiencies seen during previous visit The plant showed severe deficiencies in regard to structures, installations, maintenance and cleanliness and operational practices. Severe deficiencies were found in the slaughter so that faecal material and hair contaminated many carcasses. Current situation during the visit 5 This establishment has made some effort to rectify the deficiencies found during previous inspections. · A new expedition / loading bay has been build. · New amenities, emergency slaughter facilities, red and green offal rooms have been installed. · Training has been organised to improve the hygienic practices of the personnel · Slaughter activities have reorganised and concentrated. · Floors have been repaired. An important number of the observations mentioned in the previous report have not been rectified. The establishment still presents some deficiencies regarding slaughter hygiene, veterinary supervision on the slaughter hygiene, ante and post-mortem inspection. Some operational practices inside the slaughter room need improvement. Action taken by the French authorities after the visit to this plant: The French authorities have informed the Commission of the action taken. · The central competent Authorities have requested the Prefect of the Département concerned to suspend the approval. This suspension has been published the 10/12/98 in the "Official Journal of the French Republique". · All corrective actions other than the important big alterations (p.e. cleaning and disinfection of the premises, maintenance, training of personnel on hygiene and it's control) have been applied immediately. · A working programme for finalisation of the important big alterations has been transmitted to the French Veterinary Service and are programmed for the first semester of 1999. 8. CONCLUSIONS In four out of five plants visited, the deficiencies seen during the previous visit have been rectified. The approval requirements mentioned in the Chapters I and II as well as the hygienic conditions laid down in the Chapters V and VII of the Directive 64/433/EEC are met. Minor deficiencies were detected in the plants during the visit; they do not impinge on the approval given by the veterinary authority to the plants. In the fifth plant visited, major non-compliances have been noticed although some improvements can not be ignored. The French Competent Authority has suspended the approval pending rectification of the remaining deficiencies. The provisions of Art. 10 of Counsil Directive 64/433/EEC requiring that the competent authority should not approve the establishments unless the requirements are fulfilled, are met. 6 9. RECOMMENDATIONS 9.1 Recommendations for the Commission services : Having verified that the veterinary authorities have acted in a satisfactory way by improving the four establishments to the required standard, and that action is taken to suspend the approval of the fifth establishment, consideration should be given to suspending the infringement proceedings opened by Commission (reference A/96/2022) against France while waiting for further guarantees from the French authorities. 9.2 Recommendations for the French authorities : Further information on the follow-up of the fifth establishment and its supervision should be provided by the French Authority by August 1999 and eventually verified on the spot. 7

Ministerial Decree No 358 of 2 May 1996 on leucosis. - Decree No 429 of 12 August 1997 makes a number of amendments to the decrees on brucellosis and leucosis to standardise a number of procedures, 6 particularly with reference to compensation for farmers, the possibility of slaughtering entire herds, and the non-availability of funding to farmers who do not subject their own livestock to sanitisation operations; this bring the decrees into line with the decree on tuberculosis. 5.3. Financial considerations 5.3.1. Animal disease eradication programmes are funded from the National Health Fund. It is said that veterinary activities receive about 1% of this fund. A budgetary year is 12 months and each of the 20 regions receive an agreed amount. The regional authorities may decide on priority spending (this may extend to non-veterinary actions), this procedure has a bearing on the efficiency of implementation of the animal disease eradication programmes - see Chapters 5.5.5 and 5.5.6. 5.3.2. The Ministry each year issues a decree updating the rates. The amount of compensation to animal owners is not a set amount, but may vary depending on the animal category, the number of animals on the farm, and whether or not there is a possibility of using the meat. The Ministry each year issues a decree updating the rates. It is usual for the owner of a reactor animal to sell it to a dealer, who then delivers it to a slaughterhouse and receives the salvage value of the meat. The owner may deliver the reactor direct to the slaughterhouse. For 1999 the Italian authorities will receive from the E.U. a maximum of 1.7 million for the slaughter of brucellosis reactor animals, 0.8 million for the slaughter of tuberculin reacting animals and 2.5 million for the slaughter of E.B.L. reactors. 5.4. Laboratory Service The regional laboratories and their sub-laboratories carry out all blood testing in relation to the eradication programmes. Well-documented blood samples arrive at the reception area and are subjected to the following tests: ­ For brucellosis all samples are subjected to a rose bengal plate test and if positive the sample is retested with a complement fixation test (C.F.T.). If the sample is positive to the C.F.T. the reaction is deemed positive. If the reaction is negative to the C.F.T. than it is deemed inconclusive and the animal is retested in six weeks; ­ For E.B.L. the AGIPT test is normally employed, occasionally the ELISA test is used. 5.4.1. Positive results are faxed to the relevant D.V.O. 5.4.2. Abortion material is always subjected to microbiological culture in the regional laboratories. 7 5.4.3. The laboratory which was visited was well equipped and staffed and was capable of efficiently dealing with the number of received samples. 5.5. Live animal controls A number of procedures are common to the three diseases in question. 5.5.1. All herds are registered and all animals are individually identified. Double tagging with plastic tags is currently being implemented and will be completed within the time scales as laid down by E.U. laws (Council Directive 92/102/EEC and Council Regulation 820/97). The system is numeric allowing the animal to be identified by Member State, region, D.V.O. and herd as well as an individual number. A computerised database is being generated to cover these aspects of registration, identification and disease status. 5.5.2. Control procedures vis-à-vis testing are only applied to herds which contain breeding animals. Fattening and slaughter herds are not subjected to routine testing and may only source their animals from officially free herds for the three diseases in question. Animals are not allowed to move out of non- status or reactor herds except for direct slaughter. Cattle moving to a fattening herd must originate from establishments which are officially tuberculosis-free, brucellosis-free or leucosis-free. If such animals are over the age of 12 months, they must be subjected to serological tests for brucellosis and leucosis (within 30 days preceding their departure). If they are aged under 12 months, they are not subjected to tests and, as regards leucosis, they may also be exempted from the obligation concerning origin from an officially free herd. A post-movement test for tuberculosis carried out 15-42 days after arrival is applied. The animals are isolated during the waiting period, these animals are accompanied by a veterinary certificate signed by an official veterinarian. If the animals are moving to a fattening or slaughter herd than no pre-movement testing of any description is applied. They are accompanied by a travel document (Model 4) signed by the owner in this instance. The veterinary certificate previously alluded to is the last section of the Model 4 document and is only signed by an official veterinarian in the described circumstances. In all instances the D.V.O. in the receiving area receives a copy of the Model 4 document. 5.5.3. Each owner receives the first page of a herd register in which all relevant data relating to births, deaths, treatments, tests and movements are recorded, this must be kept up to date.In addition and on request to the D.V.O., the owner is provided with an individual "passport" which records all relevant details concerning the animal as well as the disease status of the herd. This "passport" accompanies the animal if it moves. 5.5.4. Each officially free herd receives two blood tests per year for brucellosis (not less than 3 months or more than 6 months apart), one tuberculin test and E.B.L. test per year, regarding E.B.L. calves from reacting mothers must be slaughtered in the case of singleton reactors. Dogs are tested for brucellosis in positive herds. All female bovines over 12 months of age and bulls are included in the testing programme for brucellosis and E.B.L. animals over six weeks of age are tested for T.B. Vaccination against brucellosis was forbidden in 1994. All testing and blood sampling is carried 8 out by official veterinarians permanently attached to the D.V.O.s, and veterinary practitioners who are contracted to carry out testing. 5.5.5. In one D.V.O. it was found that the planned annual round of testing was not completed in the 1998 year. There was a shortfall of 105 herds out of 3245 herds for T.B., 22 herds out of 3209 herds for brucellosis and 22 herds out of 3209 for E.B.L., thus losing their status. When asked for an explanation it was explained that due to a lack of resources (personnel and finance) and the inaccessibility of some of the herds (mountain area) it was not possible to complete the round of testing on time. 5.5.6. In one bovine herd visited it was found that an E.B.L. reactor was found and the farmer officially notified by the local mayor to this effect in March 1998. The reacting animal was slaughtered in March 1998. On the day of the teams visit to the farm on 14 April 1999 the farmer had still not received the slaughter compensation, i.e. a delay, to-date, of over a year. 5.6. Disease Eradication Programmes 5.6.1. In 1997 there were 6.5 million breeding animals contained in 208,000 herds, i.e. animals and herds controllable for the three diseases. It is estimated that at any one time there are about 1.5 million animals in an unknown number of herds which are intended for fattening or slaughter i.e. animals not subject to control for the three diseases. No exact figures are currently available for the latter figure until the system is fully computerised, it being considered too laborious to calculate due to the amount of movement into fattening and slaughter herds both from outside and within Italy. 5.6.2. In general, for the three diseases under consideration the long-term trend is downward in relation to discovery of reactors and upward in relation to herds under testing control. However, in recent years it is noticeable that there are upward spikes in the two parameters. This phenomenon can be attributed to a number of factors including the following: ­ The application of regulations on milk represented by M.D. 54/97 which transposes EC Directives 92/46/EC and 92/47/EC, which makes it compulsory to possess the health status in order to supply raw milk for human consumption; ­ The increasingly comprehensive implementation of the system of herd registration and individual animal identification, made law by M.D. 317/96 which transposes Council Directive 92/102/EEC; ­ The full application of M.D. 429/97 which prevents holdings which do not subject their own livestock to disease eradication measures from accessing any form of financial benefits and loans, and from marketing dairy products for human consumption; ­ The carrying out of crosschecks on livestock registered for health purposes and on livestock registered for the purposes of EU premiums. 9 5.6.3. The evaluation of the bovine brucellosis eradication programme is given in Tables 1 to 6 annexed. The programme is compulsory. Table 6 gives the areas which are officially free and free of bovine brucellosis, this status is defined as having 99.8% of the eligible herds as officially free or free of bovine brucellosis (as defined in Council Directive 64/432/EEC). It should be noted that the North of the country is more advanced than the South. 5.6.4. The evaluation of the bovine tuberculosis eradication programme is given in Tables 7 to 12 annexed. The programme is compulsory. Table 12 gives the areas which are officially free of bovine tuberculosis, this status is defined as having 99.9% of the eligible herds as officially free of tuberculosis (as defined in Council Directive 64/432/EEC). It should also be noted that the North of the country is more advanced than the South. 5.6.5. The evolution of the E.B.L. eradication programme is given in Tables 13 to 18 annexed. The programme became compulsory in 1997. Table 18 gives the areas which are officially free of E.B.L., this status is defined as having 99.8% of the eligible herds as free of E.B.L. (as defined in Council Directive 64/432/EEC). 5.7. Buffaloes (Bubalis bubalis) There are a total of about 160,000 buffaloes in Italy; all are females except for a small number of bulls. There are about 120,000 head in Campania, 20,000 in Lazio and 3,000 in Lombardia. 5.7.1. They are kept in closed herds and are used for production of milk, which is used to manufacture the world famous mozzarella cheese. In all cases the milk is pasteurised prior to cheese manufacture. Gestation lasts for 310 days and they produce about 2000 litres of milk per lactation, which lasts for 270 days. The milk has a butterfat content of 9% average and a protein content of 4.2% average. 5.7.2. They arrived in Italy over 2,000 years ago and have over the centuries been selectively bred for milk production. They are entered on the list of rare breeds. 5.7.3. Legislatively they are equated with bovines, although they are a different species and from a disease point of view are covered by Council Directives 64/432/EEC regarding official freedom from brucellosis, TB and E.B.L. They are also covered by the EU law relating to technical aspects 10 concerning disease eradication programmes as mentioned in Annex 1 to Council Decision 90/638/EEC. They are part of the 1999 Italian programmes for bovine brucellosis, TB and E.B.L. 5.7.4. Disease eradication programmes. In general terms, with some notable exceptions the rules and procedures that are applicable to the bovine programmes are applied to buffaloes. The mission has been informed that disease does not appear to be a problem in buffalo herds in Lazio, Puglia and Lombardia but brucellosis is a greater problem in Campania. Only about 60% of the herds are registered and of these only about half are controlled for the three diseases. In Campania about 20% of the controlled herds are infected with brucellosis and they have a high within herd incidence. In Campania the mission has been informed of problems on the validity of the diagnostic tests for brucellosis in buffaloes. Due also to the animal husbandry practices applied, none of all the buffalo herds identified as infected during the last year has been cleared using the test and slaughter policy. The compulsory nature of action to eradicate brucellosis in buffaloes was confirmed by a ministerial decree of 1989, which laid down identical health measures for both cattle and buffaloes. To ensure that the operations in the local laboratories of the IZ are properly controlled by the ISS in the shortest time possible.

To consider the problems reported by the farmers in eliminating the reactors and to inform the Commission Services of the possible solutions as soon as possible. 7.2. If these guarantees appear to be satisfactory, the Commission services should consider to propose to Member States that Croatia be placed on list I of the Annex to the amended Commission Decision 97/296/EC, and that a Commission Decision laying down the health conditions for the importation of fishery products originating in Croatia be adopted. ­ With regard to bivalve molluscs, the Commission services should not consider to propose including Croatia in any of the lists of third countries contained in the Annex to Commission Decision 97/20/EC, prior to receiving from the Croatian Authorities information concerning the actions they have undertaken to address to point 7.1.7. of recommendations and before a follow-up mission has been carried out to verify the conditions of bivalve molluscs production and the surveillance programme of the production areas. 11
The reorganisation of the inspection system should be completed by implementing the remaining steps.
The Competent Authority should monitor the use of certificates more rigorously and verify the consistency and effectiveness of the certification system.

The Competent Authority should request the inspection bodies to take samples for residue analysis wherever it is suspected that unauthorised products are used, equivalent to the provision of point 6 of Annex III A and point 4 of Annex III B of Council Regulation 2092/91.

Both the inspection body and Competent Authority should make sure that the inspection of farms with both organic and conventional production is documented in a more complete way in order to obtain more guarantees that conventional products are not sold as organic.
Compliance with certain administrative EN 45011 or ISO 65 requirements needs to be improved.

The Competent Authority should inform the Commission of the steps taken to implement the recommendations contained in this report by 1 December 1999 at the latest. 7.2. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: ·Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States. ·Council Directive 92/46/EEC of 16 June 1992 laying down the health rules for the production and placing on the market of raw milk, heat-treated milk and milk based products. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Production and trade information 4.1.1. The milk production in Belgium The number of production holdings and cows has been continuously decreasing during the period 1987-1997 (from 38.021 to 19.186 holdings and from 919.800 to 637.364 cows). The mean production per cow has however increased in the same period (from 4.107 to 5.041 litres). The milk quota given to Belgium in 1997 was of 3,31 millions of tonnes (3,21 litres). The actual production was close to this amount. Approximately 11% of the milk is processed directly by the farms. Seventy-seven percent of the production is concentrated in 5 of the 10 Belgian provinces. Three of these provinces were visited by the inspection team: West Flanders (22 % of the total production holdings and 18% of the total national production), East Flanders (18 % of the holdings and 16% of the production) and Hainaut (14 % of the holdings and 11% of the production). The total number of sheep and goats in Belgium in 1997 was of 154.700 and 12.276 respectively. The CCA declared that although there is no sheep milk production in Belgium, there is some production of goat milk. However, no figures were available at central level about goat dairy herds, holdings or production. 4.1.2. The dairy industry The production of dairy products in Belgium in 1998, according to the statistics given by the CCA, is given in the following table (figures x1000): Liquid milk 669.137 l 03/02/00 - 42161 Milk powder 135 Tn 35,2 Tn Butter 90.218 l Cream 215.897 l Fermented milk 72,7 Tn Cheese 5 Buttermilk 25.189 l Serum powder 9,9 Tn Frozen cream 99.246 l Belgium is self-sufficient in its production of dairy products, except for cheese. It is an important exporter of fresh dairy products such as milk, yoghurt and milk drinks, and melted cheese. However, it is a significant importer of milk and serum as primary materials, and cheeses. 4.2. Health information 4.2.1. Animal health situation - Bovine diseases The herd incidence of bovine brucellosis has decreased from 1,13% in 1987 and 0,46% in 1990 to less than 0,01% in 1998. Respectively, 12 and 2 outbreaks were declared in 1997 and 1998. The herd prevalence at the end of 1998 was zero. With regards to tuberculosis, 6 and 4 outbreaks were declared in 1997 and 1998, respectively. (herd incidence of 0,01% and 0,007%, respectively). Collection and treatment of milk from farms suspected to have tuberculosis are forbidden. The last case of foot and mouth disease was recorded in Belgium in 1976. There are no systematic controls on Q fever although, voluntarily, an investigation of abortion causes is carried out in certain centres of prevention and veterinary guidance. - Ovine and caprine diseases Belgium has a status of officially free of Brucella melitensis in both sheep and goat. 4.2.2. Public health situation regarding milk products The Belgian authorities have declared that no food-borne diseases and zoonoses caused by Belgian milk and milk products have been registered in 1997 and 1998. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent authority 5.1.1. Description of responsibilities The competent authority regarding milk and milk products health rules in Belgium is the Ministère des classes moyennes et de l'agriculture, Direction générale 5 (DG 5). The section responsible is the Inspection générale de la Qualité des produits animaux. They are in charge of the legislation and co-ordination of the controls over the whole territory. However, some related activities such as additives or residues are dealt i0n3/02/00 - 42161 6 collaboration with the Ministère de la Santé (Ministry of Health). The Rapid Alert System is managed by the Ministère de la Santé. The Belgian authorities remarked that plans for creation of a Food Security Agency are being drafted. This would imply merging of some of these activities dealt by the two ministries. The Belgian territory is divided into 10 provinces. The powers for application of the milk and milk products legislation have been delegated to the local (provincial) authorities (Bureaux Provinciaux). 5.1.2. Belgian milk and milk products health rules These are the main legal texts on milk and milk products health rules that have been given to the inspection team: · Arrêté Royal (A.R.) of 6.10.93 regarding the apposition of the health mark to milk and milk products, amended by the A.R. of 14.9.95. · A.R. of 3.3.94 regarding the approval of interprofessional organisms for quality and composition determination of the milk. · A.R. of 7.3.94 regarding the approval of milk establishments, amended by the A.R. of 29.5.95 and the A.R. of 8.8.97. · A.R. of 17.3.94 regarding milk production and creating the official control of raw milk, amended by the A.R. of 11.7.96. · Arrêté Ministériel (A.M.) of 17.3.94 regarding the official control of raw milk quality and composition, amended by A.M. of 11.7.96. · A.M. of 14.10.94 regarding the analytical methods for the official control of raw milk, amended by A.M. of 26.8.97. · A.R. of 15.12.94 regarding the production and place in the market of milk and milk products, amended by A.R. of 14.9.95. Some items of the reviewed rules are different from the requirements laid down in Directive 92/46/EEC: - The animal health requirements for raw milk coming from sheep and goats of Chapter I, Annex A of Directive 92/46/EEC have not been included in the Belgian legislation. - The method of analysis for detection of sulphonamides described in Decision 91/180/EEC has been differently transposed into the Belgian legislation. The staff of National Reference Laboratory (DG6) of Melle has declared that their method for sulphonamides has been improved (see section 5.1.4 for further details). - The list of pharmacologically active substances included both in the A.M. of 17.3.94 and the A.R. of 15.12.94 have not been updated. Th0e3/02/00 - 42161 7 CCA were aware of this deficiency but pointed out that procedures to modify an A.R. or an A.M. take some time1. - Some of the microbiological criteria for sheep and goat raw milk are stricter than in Directive 92/46/EEC. 5.1.3. Co-ordination of the services in charge of application of Directive 92/46/EEC 5.1.3.1. The CCA · Description As already pointed out, the Inspection générale de la Qualité des produits animaux is in charge of the application of Directive 92/46/EEC at central level. There, seven people (2 academics and 5 administrative staff) deal with raw milk as primary material and 7 more people (3 academics and 4 administrative staff) do so with milk products. · Responsibilities The CCA have legislative powers at national level. In general, when new legislation is proposed, a co-ordination group meets consisting of representatives of the Ministère des classes moyennes et de l'agriculture, the Ministère de la Santé, the dairy industry, the milk producers and the research and controlling laboratories. Moreover, they are in charge of the approval and suspension of approval of milk processing establishments. The CCA have coercive power* on the local (provincial) competent authorities (LCA). The CCA is also responsible for the training of the LCA. The inspection team has received information about the courses organised during the last three years; i.e. the last training about HACCP for the inspectors consisted of a one-day seminar in 1996 for the Dutch speaking inspectors and another day in 1998 for the French speakers. Recently, a handbook about HACCP principles in the milk industry has been published by the CCA. · Exchange of information with the LCA There are regular meetings (approximately once every month) with the heads of the provincial bureaux, in which different matters are dealt. However, no system of audits of the LCA has been put in place. The 1 See comments of the Belgian competent authorities (5.1.2). 03/02/00 - 42161 * Meaning that the CCA has the power to direct and sanction, if necessary, the LCA. 8 visits of the CCA to the LCA are only made when a problem arises and not on a regular basis. The CCA have published a number of "Technical Circulars" and "Operational Instructions", such as the control of the quality of the raw milk delivered to the dairy industry, the control of the prohibition of delivery of milk, the approval of dairy farms, or the approval of milk processing establishments. The inspection team has however noted the lack of clear instructions regarding the type and number of samples to be taken during the official inspections and the setting of the frequency of these inspections in accordance with the size of the plant and/or the risk of the production. In addition, monthly notes are written from the Head of the Province to the CCA on diverse matters and both authorities keep informal contacts. However, no annual reports on inspections performed, type and number of samples taken, type of problems encountered during the visits or in the results of the samples, etc are sent by the LCA to the CCA. · Prioritisation/Risk Analysis Through a computerised system, the CCA receive prompt information from the provincial bureaux about the farm's approval and the farms that have been forbidden to deliver raw milk. However, the CCA does not have information about food-borne diseases and zoonoses caused by milk and milk products in Belgium, nor do they have statistics about the microbiological results in final products resulting from the official controls performed by the LCA. According to the CCA, this situation may improve when a new computerised system called "Sanimilk", which is currently being developed, will be in place. Since 1993, no official surveys have been organised at national level for specific microbiological pathogens in the final milk products. No data could be either found at central level about the frequency of official visits to the milk and milk products establishments. As a result of this lack of information, no evaluation of the risk has been done to define the priorities regarding the milk and milk products establishments. 5.1.3.2.The LCA (Provincial Bureaux) · Description The Belgian territory is divided in ten provinces. The team visited the central offices in two of them: West Flanders and Hainaut. In addition, the LCA of East Flanders were met during the visit of the establishments situated in that province. The Provincial Bureaux visited consist of 5 or 6 inspectors, 2 or 3 administrative staff and one head of the bureau. They are generally 03/02/00 - 42161 9 officials. The majority of the inspectors have a secondary school degree and they are usually not specialised in the milk sector. The motivation of the inspectors was generally good and their level of knowledge varied according to the individuals met. · Training and responsibilities The training, as already seen, is organised by the CCA. The LCA of one of the provinces visited declared that inspectors usually learn in the field. The last HACCP course was given in 1998 (including the latter a total of 6 hours). Therefore, the knowledge of the HACCP principles of most of the inspectors met during this mission was poor. They are in charge of the implementation of the milk and milk-based products health rules, as well as those of the egg products. Thus, they carry out inspections and sampling in the milk establishments, they inspect and approve the dairy farms and they also ensure that the prohibition of delivery of milk exceeding the limits for total plate count (TPC), total cell count (TCC) or antibiotic residues is observed (see section 5.3.4 for further details). It is important to point out that they also take a large number of samples of butter and milk powder for quality analyses purposes. In fact, in one big establishment visited the job description of the inspector was basically related to sampling for composition quality purposes and not for hygienic quality purposes. · Reports According to the observations made by the inspection team, very often no written reports are made after the inspections of the establishments. In one province, it was noticed that reports on inspections are only made when temporary approvals have to be renewed. On the other hand, many of the visits are for sampling purposes only and the actual number of complete inspections is therefore low. · Official sampling The official sampling of the final products in some cases did not cover all the criteria laid down in Annex C, Chapter II of Directive 92/46/EEC (i.e. Salmonella and Listeria spp. were missed in two of the three establishments visited). No official control of the water was carried out in any of the establishments visited by the inspection group. · Prioritisation/risk analyses No planning of the inspections or visits to the establishments are made at provincial level according to the risk and the staff available in order to 03/02/00 - 42161 10 make a prioritisation of the inspections. No follow-ups of the problems encountered were either found. · Documentation Moreover, in one of the Provincial Bureaux visited, the documents were incomplete, disorganised and very difficult to find. The inspection team observed that in one case the documentation of the approval of one establishment producing two types of products had not been amended although they had abandoned the production of one of the products. · Inspections of the milk farms The situation is slightly different when it comes to inspections of milk farms. The provincial bureau of Hainaut is more focussed on inspection of the farms since no large processing establishments are found in the province. It was noticed that reports with deadlines for the requested changes or improvements are usually made after the inspection to the farm. Moreover, farms under prohibition of delivery of the milk, due to exceeding of the limits for TPC, SCC or antibiotic residues, are visited and thus prioritised. However, those exploitations included in the national residue plan and showing adverse results seem not to be prioritised by the LCA. 5.1.4. Official laboratory network The official laboratory network consists of four laboratories that belong to the Ministry of Agriculture: the two laboratories of DG5, in Melle and in Gembloux, and the two laboratories of DG6 (Recherche et Développement), also in Melle and in Gembloux. The four laboratories have been nominated as National Reference Laboratories for Belgium. Due to the number of laboratories to be visited by the inspection team, the premises of the four laboratories could not be visited in detail after the meetings with their staff. The team could determine however that the staff seems to be well motivated in all the laboratories. The methods used by the laboratories are usually IDF and ISO methods. As previously pointed out, the official method for detection of sulphonamides used in Belgium does not comply with that described in Decision 91/180/EEC. The staff of National Reference Laboratory (DG6) of Melle has declared that the improved agar diffusion method (Vermunt et al., 1993)* is used as screening method. According to them, the detection limits for sulphonamides come closer to the MRL values (100 µg/l). * Vermunt AEM, Stadhouders J, Loeffen GJM, Bakker R. Improvements of the tube diffusion method for detection of antibiotics and sulfonamides in raw milk. Neth Milk Dairy J (1993) 47: 31-40 03/02/00 - 42161 11 5.1.4.1. The two laboratories of DG5 The two laboratories of DG5 mainly process official samples (dairy and egg products) and participate in ring tests organised by other laboratories and organisations such as Cecalait but they do not co-ordinate the official network or conduct ring tests themselves. Results of the official analyses carried out in the laboratories are not studied and, thus, neither global statistics nor annual reports of the results are sent to the competent authorities. The laboratory of Melle carries out analyses of the final product (19.000 per year). The laboratory of Gembloux performs both analyses of the final product (12.648) and of raw milk (3.181), being the latter in the frame of control of performance of the interprofessional laboratories (see section 5.3.3)2. None of these laboratories are accredited, although they will try to be accredited by the end of year 2000. 5.1.4.2.The two laboratories of DG6 One of the main tasks of the two laboratories is research. Both laboratories collaborate since last year in the organisation of monthly ring tests (TPC, SCC, coliforms, antibiotics and disinfectants) for the 5 interprofessional laboratories performing the analyses of raw milk quality. They make annual reports on the performance of the interprofessional laboratories. Furthermore, both laboratories take part in the meetings, training and comparative tests organised by the Community Reference Laboratory and other organisations. The laboratory in Melle is also in charge of third party analyses and official counter analyses for most of the analyses required in Directive 92/46/EEC. On the other hand, the laboratory in Gembloux does not perform analyses of pathogen microorganisms and, therefore, does not participate and/or organise ring tests on this subject. Finally, the laboratory in Melle is accredited since 1995 by BELTEST according to the rules EN 45001. The one in Gembloux is working in the accreditation procedure and expects to be accredited by the end of year 2000. 5.1.5. Imports of milk and milk products Imports from third countries for human consumption must be accompanied by the certifications regarded in Decision 95/343/EC. The EUROSTAT statistics of 1998 show that some milk and milk products have been introduced in Belgium from non-authorised third countries (countries not authorised by the Annex of Decision 95/340/EC)

Commission Decision 98/140/EC laying certain rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries. 3 Background 3.1 Summary of previous animal health missions finding Several missions (animal & public health) have been undertaken in the past to Croatia and include animal health missions in 1996 and 1997 (see Doc.VI/8099/96 and Doc. XXIV/2034/97 respectively). The last animal health mission report (June 1997) concluded that the performance of the veterinary services was adequate and that the whole Croatian territory was under their effective control. Furthermore, the animal health situation was good. The report made the following recommendations: (a) To the Commission: To lift the regionalisation of Croatia as per Decision 93/242/EEC and to withdraw from Croatia their officially free status for Bovine Tuberculosis and Brucellosis. This recommendation was made because of the re-integration into the Republic of the districts of Osjecko-baranjska and Istarska where tests had not been undertaken for the duration of the war. (b) To the Croatian authority: To designate a Reference Laboratory (to meet their public and animal health obligations) and to establish validation procedures for the regional laboratories. In response to the recommendations detailed above, Decision 98/372/EC was amended by Decision 98/505/EC. This revised decision removed the regionalisation of Croatia so that the districts of Osjecko-baranjska and Istarska could be included and the certificates were amended, requesting additional guarantees for Bovine for breeding and production. 3 3.2 Live animal imports from Croatia Croatia is on the list of third countries from which Member States are authorised to import live animals and products (Council Directive 72/462/EEC and Council Decision 79/542/EEC). · The specific animal health conditions and veterinary certification requirements for the importation of live animals of bovine and porcine species from Croatia are laid down in Decision 98/372/EC as amended by Decision 98/505/EC. This Decision authorises the importation into the EU of bovines for breeding and production, and slaughter from anywhere within Croatia. Bovines destined for breeding, however, must be accompanied by a guarantee that they come from a registered herd free from Tuberculosis, Brucellosis and Leucosis. No export of swine into the EU (for breeding or slaughter) is authorised. · The specific animal health conditions and veterinary certification requirements for the importation of live ovine and caprine species for breeding, fattening and slaughter are laid down in Decision 93/198/EEC as last amended by Decision 97/231/EC. For equidae - Croatia is included in the list of countries (group B), from which imports are authorised, of the annex I of Council Decision 93/197/EEC. At present most equidae imported from Croatia are destined for human consumption in Italy. The list of laboratories approved by the member states for the importation of equidae from Eastern Europe was distributed at the SVC in April 1999 (Doc VI/3058/1999). The "Croatian Veterinary Institute at Savska cesta, 143 Zagreb", has been approved by the Competent Authority (C.A.) of Germany, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands and the "Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Heinzelova, 55 Zagreb", has been approved by Italy. 4 Observations 4.1 General Veterinary Administration The veterinary services in Croatia belong to the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (Ministarstvo Poljoprivrede i Sumarstva). A description of the Croatian veterinary services was given in Doc. XXIV/2034/97. A good description can also be found on the web-site: www.veterinarstvo.hr. Only complementary or more in-depth information will be given in this report. 4.1.1 National Veterinary Administration (Uprava za veterinarstvo) The National Veterinary Act was published in the Croatian Official Journal on the 7th of July 1997. It is a comprehensive document, which defines the area of responsibility of the public, and private veterinary services and includes the list of notifiable diseases. 4 The veterinary administration is responsible for the adoption and enforcement of the legislation on animal health protection, control of zoonotic diseases, safety of products of animal origin, promotion of animal reproduction and veterinary environmental protection. 4.1.2 Field services The country is divided in 20 districts (Zupanija) and the City of Zagreb, having the status of a district), including district 14 (Osjecko-baranjska) and 18 (Istarska), which have been recently re-integrated into the Republic. During the war and especially during periods of occupation, animal health (intensive surveillance and monitoring programmes) was not totally under the control of the Croatian veterinary service. In each district there is a District State Inspector in charge of supervising activities in the animal and public health sectors. 4.1.3 Veterinary stations and Authorised Veterinarians The Local veterinary services have been totally privatised. The different types of private practice are classified according to the size and type of work. A typical "veterinary station" group contains 10-30 veterinarians - it may have branches in the area covered and provide the livestock owners of the area with all livestock related services (treatments, fertility work, prophylaxis, animal feed and drugs sales etc). Some veterinarians are also "Authorised Veterinarians" (AV). These veterinarians are 'authorised' by the Central C.A. to perform some official duties, such as taking samples for national surveillance programmes, vaccinating pigs against CSF, etc. Included in the authorised veterinarians' work are slaughterhouses and other establishments. Approximately 50% of the work and the income of a veterinary station are derived from private practice and 50% from " public health activities" though the proportion of each varies throughout the year. · One of the tasks of the authorised veterinarian is to sign certificates. At present the veterinarian providing clinical services to the farmer and export certification belongs to the same organisation (possible non-compliance with Council Directive 96/93/EC, Art 4a: certifying officers should be impartial and have no commercial interest in the animals or products being certified). 5 In total there are 107 "veterinary stations" and 25 outpatient clinics, each covering one or more Municipalities or "epidemiological unit". No serological surveillance for FMD in indigenous animals is carried out. Classical Swine Fever (CSF): During the mission there was the first outbreak this year (1999), the previous outbreak occurring in October 1997. There is a CSF vaccination policy. In 1996 and in preceding years there were several outbreaks of CSF during which time vaccination was compulsory and the costs borne by the farmer. The Croatian veterinary services estimate that there was incomplete vaccination cover of the swine population. In 1998 the government introduced (free of charge) compulsory vaccination, resulting in almost complete vaccination cover (98%). In 1999 the Government will subsidise the vaccine and the farmer will have to pay the veterinary fees ­ good vaccination cover is anticipated. A private company manufactures the vaccine in Croatia. Details of vaccination strategy change slightly from year to year but in general - all pigs older than 60 days must be vaccinated. An independent consultant (funded by the World Bank) will carry out an evaluation of the different vaccination options later in 1999. This may or may not lead to a change in Croatian vaccination policy. 6 The veterinary services representatives told the mission that the farming community is in favour of a non-vaccination policy because they wish to export pig meat-products. The outbreak which occurred during the mission involved 2 smallholdings where 5 sick animals and 5 "in contact" animals were destroyed. A movement ban was implemented (20km radius). The area is hilly, there are few animals (350 pigs) and no industrial holdings. The affected animals had been on the farm for three months and no other animals had been introduced to the farm. An epidemiological investigation was ongoing. Contingency plan: There is a contingency plan and an operations manual for List A diseases. The veterinary services have the legal power to enter any holding. 4.2.2 List B diseases Bovine Tuberculosis (TB): in 1997 there were 10 out breaks and 38 animals were slaughtered, no more outbreaks were reported between January and October 1998. Farms with more than 10 head of cattle are tested every year. Furthermore, each year in selected districts all animals are tested. Practically all animals in small farms are tested every three years. Leucosis is present in 5 districts with 32 outbreaks recorded in 1998 (January ­ October). The testing programme adopted for TB applies also to Leucosis. Bovine Brucellosis: in holding with more than 5 head of cattle, 20% of breeding cows and heifers are tested annually. Bulls used for reproduction are tested twice a year. No positive cases have been recorded in Croatia since 1965. In small herds (less than 5 heads) all cattle are tested within a group of districts, once every three years. All cases of abortion are to be investigated and samples sent to the regional laboratory. Porcine Brucellosis: the porcine (including sows) populations are systematically tested for brucella suis. From January to October 1998 there were 8 outbreaks of Porcine Brucellosis, all in the districts of Osjecko ­baranjska and Istarska. All cases of abortion are to be investigated and samples sent to the regional laboratory. Small ruminants brucellosis: 10% of imported animals are tested. The last case occurred in 1990, requiring the destruction of 2500 sheep imported from Macedonia. Rams are tested for Brucella Ovis. Rabies is present, the eradication of which is a priority for the state veterinary services. XXIV/2034/97 respectively). The last animal health mission report (June 1997) concluded that the performance of the veterinary services was adequate and that the whole Croatian territory was under their effective control. Furthermore, the animal health situation was good. The report made the following recommendations: (a) To the Commission: To lift the regionalisation of Croatia as per Decision 93/242/EEC and to withdraw from Croatia their officially free status for Bovine Tuberculosis and Brucellosis. This recommendation was made because of the re-integration into the Republic of the districts of Osjecko-baranjska and Istarska where tests had not been undertaken for the duration of the war. (b) To the Croatian authority: To designate a Reference Laboratory (to meet their public and animal health obligations) and to establish validation procedures for the regional laboratories. In response to the recommendations detailed above, Decision 98/372/EC was amended by Decision 98/505/EC. This revised decision removed the regionalisation of Croatia so that the districts of Osjecko-baranjska and Istarska could be included and the certificates were amended, requesting additional guarantees for Bovine for breeding and production. 3 3.2 Live animal imports from Croatia Croatia is on the list of third countries from which Member States are authorised to import live animals and products (Council Directive 72/462/EEC and Council Decision 79/542/EEC). · The specific animal health conditions and veterinary certification requirements for the importation of live animals of bovine and porcine species from Croatia are laid down in Decision 98/372/EC as amended by Decision 98/505/EC. This Decision authorises the importation into the EU of bovines for breeding and production, and slaughter from anywhere within Croatia. Bovines destined for breeding, however, must be accompanied by a guarantee that they come from a registered herd free from Tuberculosis, Brucellosis and Leucosis. No export of swine into the EU (for breeding or slaughter) is authorised. · The specific animal health conditions and veterinary certification requirements for the importation of live ovine and caprine species for breeding, fattening and slaughter are laid down in Decision 93/198/EEC as last amended by Decision 97/231/EC. For equidae - Croatia is included in the list of countries (group B), from which imports are authorised, of the annex I of Council Decision 93/197/EEC. At present most equidae imported from Croatia are destined for human consumption in Italy. A description of the Croatian veterinary services was given in Doc. XXIV/2034/97. A good description can also be found on the web-site: www.veterinarstvo.hr. Only complementary or more in-depth information will be given in this report. 4.1.1 National Veterinary Administration (Uprava za veterinarstvo) The National Veterinary Act was published in the Croatian Official Journal on the 7th of July 1997. It is a comprehensive document, which defines the area of responsibility of the public, and private veterinary services and includes the list of notifiable diseases. 4 The veterinary administration is responsible for the adoption and enforcement of the legislation on animal health protection, control of zoonotic diseases, safety of products of animal origin, promotion of animal reproduction and veterinary environmental protection. 4.1.2 Field services The country is divided in 20 districts (Zupanija) and the City of Zagreb, having the status of a district), including district 14 (Osjecko-baranjska) and 18 (Istarska), which have been recently re-integrated into the Republic. During the war and especially during periods of occupation, animal health (intensive surveillance and monitoring programmes) was not totally under the control of the Croatian veterinary service. In each district there is a District State Inspector in charge of supervising activities in the animal and public health sectors. 4.1.3 Veterinary stations and Authorised Veterinarians The Local veterinary services have been totally privatised. The different types of private practice are classified according to the size and type of work. A typical "veterinary station" group contains 10-30 veterinarians - it may have branches in the area covered and provide the livestock owners of the area with all livestock related services (treatments, fertility work, prophylaxis, animal feed and drugs sales etc). Some veterinarians are also "Authorised Veterinarians" (AV). These veterinarians are 'authorised' by the Central C.A. to perform some official duties, such as taking samples for national surveillance programmes, vaccinating pigs against CSF, etc. Included in the authorised veterinarians' work are slaughterhouses and other establishments. Approximately 50% of the work and the income of a veterinary station are derived from private practice and 50% from " public health activities" though the proportion of each varies throughout the year. · One of the tasks of the authorised veterinarian is to sign certificates. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation governing the performance of on-the-spot checks in third countries and in particular: Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries and Commission Decision 86/474/EEC of 11 September 1986 on the implementation of the on-the-spot inspections to be carried out in respect of the importation of bovine animals and swine and fresh meat from non-member countries Council Decision 95/408/EC of 22 June 1995 on the conditions for drawing up, for an interim period, provisional lists of third country establishments from which Member States are authorised to import certain products of animal origin, fishery products or live bivalve molluscs. 4. BACKGROUND This mission was part of a series of missions to Eastern European applicant States provided for in the mission programme of the FVO (DG SANCO) and covering the same issues. Various public health (fresh meat) missions have been carried out in Slovenia in the past, the most recent having been undertaken in 1998 (Document XXIV/1390/98). The report of this mission made recommendations with regard to: · Improvement of the documentation relating to veterinary supervision of establishments. Page 4 of 16 · Definition, improvement and enforcement of the approval procedures for establishments. · Reassessment of the layout, maintenance and cleanliness of meat products establishments. · Improvement in the hygiene of operations and the associated technical equipment. · Improvement of the operation and documentation of establishment own check systems. · Approval of establishment own check systems by the competent authority. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Structure of the Competent Authority The competent authority comprises two component organisations ­ the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia (VARS) and the Animal Health Centre (AHC). The Central Competent Authority in Slovenia is the (VARS) which forms part of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food. The structure and responsibilities of the VARS are outlined below. It should be noted that the VARS is not responsible for the provision of day to day supervision in establishments (see section 5.1.2. below)2. 5.1.1. Structure and responsibilities of the VARS The central office of the VARS is based in Ljubljana under the responsibility of the Chief Veterinary Officer. The VARS has 12 regional offices. The central office of the VARS is responsible for the following: · Policy in the veterinary field. · Drafting and proposing legislation in the veterinary field; · Approval of establishments for the Slovenian market; · Proposing (to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food) the approval of establishments for export markets (including the EC market); · Control of imports of products of animal origin. This includes the issuing of specific import licenses for such products and direct responsibility for Border Inspection Posts. · Drafting and approval of veterinary export certificates.
