VARS does not have the power to insist on changes to the AHC plan. Authority for approval of the plan rests with the Minister and the Government. · Organising and delivery of training of VARS staff (a number of workshops are held in conjunction with the AHC). The regional offices of the VARS are responsible for the following · Monitoring of the approval conditions is establishments. This is carried out by regional inspectors of the VARS on a regular basis (monitoring visits in the past were carried out monthly, however this is being amended to an inspection every two months). · The taking of appropriate action where establishments are found not to be in compliance with requirements. Such action may include suspension of export certification, reduction of the rate of production or interruption of the production process until the deficiencies detected are rectified. The regional inspectors of the VARS may propose, to the Minister via the central office, the suspension or revocation of the approval of an establishment. · Initial stages of the establishment approval process (see below). Neither the central nor the regional offices of the VARS have the powers to directly control the implementation of veterinary legislation by the AHC. 5.1.2. Structure and responsibilities of the AHC: The AHC was established as an independent body by the Government of Slovenia. The AHC has a central office based in Ljubljana and is made up of nine organisational units. The AHC is responsible for the day to day delivery of veterinary services throughout Slovenia, including the supervision of the production of fresh meat, game meat and meat products. Other sections of the AHC provide, inter alia, disease control and laboratory diagnostic services. AHC staff have the power to control or stop production. They may also report deficiencies to the regional VARS inspector so that appropriate action may be taken at that level. 5.2. Controls in establishments In relation to controls in establishments, the mission team focused on approval of establishments, veterinary supervision (including traceability and certification of meat and meat products and establishments' own checks), supervision by the regional veterinary authorities and slaughter hygiene. Page 6 of 16 5.2.1. Approval of establishments The system in place until this year may be summarised as follows: · Establishments are required to apply to the local municipality for approval to erect a factory or to modify an existing establishment (this is a general requirement which applies to all types of enterprise and not merely to food producing establishments). The application must be accompanied by detailed plans. · The municipality circulates the plans to the relevant authorities (environment, medical, etc.). In the case of the veterinary authorities, the regional office of the VARS was required to comment on and approve plans ­ conditional approval could be given subject to stated modifications to the plans being made. · Having received the comments of all the authorities consulted, the municipality grants approval for building to commence. The comments received are attached to the approval documentation. Where conditions have been set by any of the authorities consulted these should be incorporated into the plans. · When building is completed, the relevant authorities (including the regional VARS office) are asked to visit the premises and confirm that the building is in compliance with the plans approved, including any modifications stipulated. · At this stage, the operator may apply for temporary approval pending a final decision. · Assuming the building has been deemed to be satisfactory, the regional VARS office informs the central VARS office and national approval is granted. · At this time the operator may apply to the regional AHC for the provision of an inspection service. · Should the operator wish to gain approval for export, he is required to apply to VARS. Following a satisfactory VARS inspection, export approval is proposed to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food who may then grant such approval. Earlier in 1999, VARS introduced a revised system for the inspection of establishments prior to approval whereby this is undertaken by a team of three experts appointed from a central list of such persons however this system was not in place in relation to any of the establishments visited during the mission. Page 7 of 16 Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 13 During an FVO mission to Slovenia in 1998, the mission team found that an integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment (all parts approved for export to EC) and a separate meat products and meat preparations establishment (approved for export of meat products to EC) shared the same approval number (both establishments were owned by the same company). The separate meat products establishment was found not to be in compliance with Community requirements and, as a consequence, the Slovenian authorities were requested to delete the separate meat products establishment and the products section of the integrated establishment from the EC approval list. This was done. Subsequently the Slovenian authorities re-approved, for export to the EC, a section of the detached meat products establishment and assigned a new approval number to this part of the establishment. The products section of the integrated establishment remained unapproved for export to the EC. The procedures for approval of establishments, as outlined above, were not followed in the case and no documentation relating to the process was available. This year the mission team re-visited both the integrated and the detached establishments. In relation to the integrated establishment the mission team was asked to assess the products section to determine whether it could be recommended for approval for export to the EC. In relation to the detached establishment, the mission team was asked to confirm approval for that section to which the Slovenian authorities had granted approval for the export of meat products to the EC. The mission team discovered that the unapproved section of the detached establishment continued to be approved for the Slovenian market with its old approval number which was the same as that used by the integrated establishment for which meat products approval was being sought. Prior to the inspection of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment, the mission team was assured by the Slovenian authorities that this section of the establishment had been completely segregated from other, unapproved parts of the establishment and a plan of the establishment was shown to illustrate this. This assurance was found to be false ­ two rooms for storage and weighing/mixing of spices for an unapproved meat products section were discovered within the approved section (the door from the intake area of the approved section to these rooms was not shown on the plan; the mission team were assured, prior to the door being opened, that the door was permanently locked, however, the rooms were in constant use and the only access to them was via the approved section of the establishment); It was also discovered that part of the EC

The Slovenian commentary on the draft report states that the establishment was ordered to ensure complete physical separation between the EC approved and non-EC approved sections of the establishment. It is clear from the commentary that approval was subsequently granted without the performance of any verification that this order had been followed. No changes to the text have been made. Page 8 of 16 approved meat products establishment was utilised for the production of raw meat preparations for the local market ­ production of raw meat preparations took place in an area adjacent to the area used for wrapping and packaging of cooked meat products. The mission team also found a new door between the approved section and the unapproved section (where cooked sausages were produced for the local market); raw carton packed meat and cooked sausages were found behind this door proving that it was in regular use and that the EC approved section of the establishment was not adequately separated from the sausage section. The layout of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment was not in compliance with EC requirements: there was no logical product flow with many cross-overs of cooked and raw meat and packaged and exposed meat and meat products; routes for evacuation of soiled cardboard were not acceptable. Approval of the meat products section of the integrated slaughter establishment would have led to a situation where it shared an approval number with an unapproved meat products and thus given rise to the potential for fraudulent exports of meat products from the non-approved establishment to the EC. Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 2 The team also visited an unapproved integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment which was at an advanced stage of the approval process. The Slovenian authorities adjudged the establishment to be in compliance with EC requirements and they wanted to add it to the list of approved export establishments. The construction of the meat products section of this establishment had completed in late 1998. While some of the initial aspects of the approval procedure described above had been followed, the process had not been completed and, in any case, was demonstrably ineffective. Documentation was available which showed that plans had been submitted to the municipality prior to commencement of the project and that these plans had been examined by a regional VARS veterinarian who had approved the plans providing four stipulated alterations were made. Approval for building to commence had been issued by the municipality. Building work had been completed in November 1998 and production commenced at that time however the municipality had not issued a request for an inspection to verify that the establishment had been constructed in accordance with the plans received until mid 1999 and this inspection had not been completed at the time of the FVO visit even though, by that time, the establishment had been in production for approximately 10 months. Documentation was available which showed that the establishment had applied to the regional AHC office for the provision of an inspection service. This request had been complied with by the AHC. Documentation was available which showed that a provisional approval, valid until the end of 1998 had been granted by the VARS. No documentation illustrating the basis on which this decision had been taken was available. Page 9 of 16 No documentation extending this provisional approval was available and the establishment was, therefore, operating in contravention of Slovenian regulations. The plans approved contained many deficiencies in layout with many cross- flows with the potential to cause hygiene problems. One very serious deficiency entailed raw meat being prepared beside the cooker doors. Cooked meat was removed form the cookers by the operatives who handled raw meat. Cooked meat emerging from the cookers comes into close proximity with raw meat. These processes, therefore, constitute a serious public health risk. Only two of the conditions imposed by the regional VARS had been complied with however it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. The building had not been constructed in accordance with the plans submitted ­ again it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. 5.2.2. Official Veterinary supervision in establishments: The numbers of veterinarians assigned to establishments were satisfactory in all cases. However, as detailed below, the effectiveness of veterinary supervision was unsatisfactory in virtually all establishments visited. On a number of occasions during the mission, the mission team was given information which subsequently was found to be false (e.g. in one establishment the team were told that a locked room was empty when it, in fact, contained ingredients, packaging material and building materials). Training of Official Veterinarians : The VARS has established a training programme for its staff. AHC personnel receive some training from the VARS. The AHC does not have a training programme for the official veterinarians. Documentation containing instructions for the official veterinarians has been issued by the VARS over a number of years. This documentation is quite comprehensive, however, many of the official veterinarians in the establishments appeared to be unaware of the existence of part or all of these instructions. In relation to many of the aspects of supervision detailed below, the official veterinarians did not appear to understand their significance or the underlying principles. Water quality: · Plans of the water distribution systems were not always up-to-date. · All establishments had good systems for the rotation of water sampling points. · In one establishment, the regional AHC laboratory had unilaterally reduced the range of tests carried out on water samples. This problem had not Page 10 of 16 been identified by the official veterinarian or by the regional VARS inspector. Medical certification of workers: · A comprehensive system for medical examination and certification of workers was in place throughout Slovenia. · Checking of the operation of this system (by both the establishment and the official veterinarian) was insufficient in all establishments visited ­ many documents were not signed and/or dated. Scrutiny of establishments'own check programmes: · A major effort was in progress to introduce own check systems in meat product establishments with application of HACCP principles. The legal basis requiring the development of own checks is not yet in place however this is scheduled for September 1999. · In some establishments, the official veterinarian was involved in the development of own check systems, however, the own checks systems were not always comprehensive. · In one establishment it was found that the annual programme of the AHC was not being respected in that the programme specified that 40 bacteriological samples per month should be taken by the official veterinarian and analysed by the official service (AHC). The official veterinarian collected 40 samples per month, however, only 10 of these were analysed by the AHC laboratory ­ the remaining samples were analysed in the establishment's own laboratory. No differentiation was made between establishment results and AHC results and it was therefore not possible for the official veterinarian to verify the accuracy of the establishment sampling programme. Pest control: · Pest control programmes were in place in all establishments, however, these programmes were not sufficiently comprehensive and were not systematically supervised

A meeting was held at the farm with the management, the farm veterinarian and the Veterinary Director from the County Animal Health and Food Control Station. The required information regarding controls at farm level was received at the meeting and is included in the findings of this report. Page 3 of 14 3. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Council Directive 72/462/EEC of 12 December 1972 on health and veterinary inspection problems upon importation of bovine, ovine and caprine animals and swine, fresh meat or meat products from third countries. · Council Directive 77/96/EEC of 21 December 1976 on the examination for trichinae (trichinella spiralis) upon importation from third countries of fresh meat derived from domestic swine. · Council Directive 93/119/EC of 22 December 1993 concerning the protection of animals at slaughter. · Council Directive 96/93/EC of 17 December 1996 on the certification of animals and animal products. · Commission Decision 86/474/EEC of 11 September 1986 on the implementation of the on-the-spot inspections to be carried out in respect of the importation of bovine animals and swine and fresh meat from non-member countries. · Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Summary of previous mission results Various public health (fresh meat) missions comprising individual reviews of fresh meat establishments have been carried out in Hungary in the past, the most recent having been undertaken in 1996 (Document VI/8401/96). Furthermore a public health mission concerning meat product establishments was carried out in Hungary on 2 - 6 March 1998 (Document XXIV/1345/98 MR-Final). The reports of these missions were in general very positive and only recommended minor improvements in a few areas in regard to structure/layout, own checks and the veterinary supervision. 4.2. Production and trade information Pigmeat is Hungary's principle meat. Hungary exported 26,339.4 tons of pigmeat and 49.9 tons of pig offals to the EU in 1998. Page 4 of 14 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authority 5.1.1. Legislation in force The general structure of the veterinary services is outlined in the Act No. XCI of 1995 on Veterinary Rules. Other relevant legislation for this mission is Act No. XC of 1995 on Foods, Act No. XXVIII of 1998 on Animal Welfare, Decree No. 41/1997 laying down the Veterinary Regulations and Decree No. 17/1999 on the Sanitary Requirements for the Production and Distribution of Foodstuffs. 5.1.2. The Central Competent Authority The central competent authority is the Animal Health and Food Control Department (the Department) under the Ministry of Agriculture and Regional Development. The minister has the power to issue secondary legislation in the veterinary field. The Department is headed by the Chief Veterinary Officer (CVO) and is divided into three sections. The section for epizootology deals with transmissible diseases and animal welfare. The administrative section deals with international relations, import and transit of live animals and products of animal and plant origin as well as animal welfare during transport. The food control section has overall responsibility for food hygiene and quality control activities of the service. The Department has no legislative powers but can propose secondary legislation and issue instructions to the regional competent authorities. Under the Department the National Food Investigation Institute (the Institute) provides technical support. The Institute interprets the requirements of EC Directives and issues instructions to field staff, inspect slaughterhouses and processing plants approved for export every six months and make recommendations to the Department on their acceptance or otherwise for international trade. 5.1.3. The Regional and Local Competent Authority The 19 County Animal Health and Food Control Stations (the County Stations) represent the regional level. The County Station is managed by a Veterinary Director who is appointed by the Minister and has around 120-150 staff on average under his direct control. The County Stations cover both the animal health and public health fields and have their own laboratories. The County Stations collect statistical data regarding for example slaughter and post-mortem findings that are submitted to the Department in a yearly report. Each County Station has a Food Hygiene Specialist. These specialists meet regularly at central level for co-ordination and exchange of information. Food producing establishments approved for export to the EU are inspected at least every three months by the County Stations and every six months the inspection is carried out together with experts from the Institute to secure a uniform approach. The results from these inspections are recorded in a written report to the establishment and the Official Veterinarian. Page 5 of 14 The County Stations can issue instructions to the staff working at local level and are also issuing animal health and public health certificates for export. At local level there are Food Hygiene Offices at all the export-approved establishments and 110 Veterinary Districts with State Veterinarians in the Field. These are official veterinarians and are employed by the County Stations. The County Station charges fees from the farmers and the various establishments for the necessary official services. These fees are the greater part of the yearly budget for the County Station. 5.2. Veterinary supervision 5.2.1. Approval procedures The legal basis for approval of establishments is outlined in The Food Act XC of 1995. The producer must notify the County Station and submit plans and documentation for approval if a new establishment is built or if a reconstruction is carried out that means substantial changes. This in order to obtain the compulsory operational license. The County Station reviews the documentation, submit its written opinion on the documentation in relation to the requirements to be fulfilled and makes an inspection on the spot. After this review and after receiving the opinion from the municipality and other concerned parties the County Station can, if no doubts are still at hand, issue an operational license to the establishment. The County Station can withdraw or suspend an operational license if the conditions are no longer provided for, in agreement with the expert authorities concerned. Only the export-approved establishments receive an approval number after application to the Department. The Department issues the approval number after receiving the comments from the County Station. In most cases (EU and US approvals) experts from the Institute carry out an inspection on the spot prior to the final decision. The approval procedure was reviewed in the establishments visited by the mission team and the documentation found showed that the procedure in general had been followed. However the following observations were made: · Two establishments were found with activities (cold storage) that were not recorded in the national or EU lists of approved establishments. 5.2.2. Controls in establishments Veterinary supervision The veterinary staff in the Food Hygiene Offices in EU approved establishments comprise veterinarians and auxiliaries employed by the County Stations. The official veterinarians were present full time in all EU approved slaughterhouses as well as in cutting plants and cold stores. Page 6 of 14 The veterinary supervision was in general considered satisfactory, however written documentation of the supervisory activities were not always available and in particular: · The official veterinarians did not keep detailed records of the results of ante- mortem examination (only records of emergency slaughtered animals were compulsory). · The official veterinarians did not keep detailed records of the results of post- mortem examination (only records of the number of animals slaughtered and the number and findings of totally condemned carcasses were compulsory). Reports from the supervisions from the County Station and the Institute were available and documented corrective action taken. However the supervision had not exposed the non-compliances found by the mission team. Hygiene control of the production The slaughter hygiene as well as the operational hygiene in the establishments visited was in general of a high standard. However a number of minor problems were identified: · The splitting saws on the slaughter lines were not properly cleaned and sterilised between each carcass due to a faulty design of the sterilising cabinets. · Excessive condensation, which could lead to contamination of exposed meat, was observed in several areas of one establishment. Health marking and labelling Health marks and labels were kept by the official veterinarian in the Food Hygiene Office. Carcasses weighing more than 65 kilograms were clearly marked with 5 oval health marks (HUNGARIA XXX INSPECTED) on each half-carcass and the "T" in circle mark indicating that the carcasses had been examined for trichinae in accordance with Directive 77/96/EEC with a negative result. However the following discrepancies were found: · The health marking was not always applied on the external surface of the thigh, loin, back, breast and shoulder as required in the EC legislation. · In one independent cutting plant visited carcasses received from one EU approved slaughterhouse only bore 3 oval health marks on each half-carcass although some of them clearly weighed more than 65 kilograms. · In one slaughterhouse visited the "T" in circle mark did not bear the three letters indicating the Community and the marking took place immediately after the sampling and before the examination was performed. However tracing back to the individual carcasses was possible due to the clear marking with slaughter number. Page 7 of 14 · In the other slaughterhouse visited the "T" in circle mark was applied on the outside of the thighs instead of the inside as required by Directive 77/96/EEC. This was corrected immediately by the official veterinarian. Porcine livers were not branded with the health mark in any of the slaughterhouses visited. It was explained that the branding of livers only would take place if the livers were intended for export to the EU and that no livers at present were exported to the EU. The labels used to seal packed meat were individually numbered and bore the oval health mark as well as the "T" in circle. These seals were applied in such a way that cartons could not be opened without breaking the seals. In connection with labelling of packed meat the following was observed: · Packed fresh meat that had been frozen was found in the cold stores visited without indication of the month and year in which it was frozen. It was explained that this information was applied at the time of loading for export to the EU. The information was only available on a document loosely attached to the shelves or pallets holding the packed meat. · Packed fresh meat was found in one independent cold stores visited without information on the nature of the cuts applied to the individual cartons. Only one carton on each pallet bore this information and it was explained that at the time of the visit none of the meat held in this cold store was intended or approved for export to the EU. Certification Copies of issued export certificates and received certificates were available on file in the official veterinarians' offices. However the following problems were identified during the visits: · In one establishment the original certificates had been typed out on bad photocopies and the printed text on these and the copies on file were often illegible. Furthermore as the copies of the certificate held the original signature and health stamps, and no "DUPLICATE" or "COPY" stamps these could be mistaken for original certificates. · In one cutting plant visited it was found that export certificates for the EU held information of the slaughterhouse of origin which was different to the slaughterhouse from where the meat had been received. The meat had been received packed for freezing and the incoming national meat transfer certificate did not hold any information on the slaughterhouse of origin. The approval No. of the cutting plant was recorded on the export certificate for EU despite the fact that this establishment is not approved for EU as a cold store. It was explained that there is no legal obligation to supply information concerning slaughterhouse(s) of origin or information about which marked the meat is approved for on the national meat transfer certificate. Page 8 of 14 Product traceability Pigs received for slaughter were marked with a tattooed number on the shoulders or hindquarters, with ear-cut numbers or with ear tags referring to the farm of origin. The accompanying animal passports (covering maximum 25 animals), the certificates from the farm veterinarians and the certificate from the official veterinarian approving the transport made reference to this identification. The systems for animal identification and the registers kept in the slaughterhouses were found to have the following weaknesses: · The marking systems in use did not make specific and unique reference to the farms of origin (e.g. holding number) and other markings than the tattooed numbers were lost during the slaughter process. · As one consignment of pigs could contain animals from several farms and the register at the ante-mortem examination could only link the slaughter number to the groups of animals received and not to the individual farms the tracing back was lost after the post-mortem examination had been performed. Only pigs with the tattooed numbers could be traced back to the farm of origin after the trichinae examination had been completed. Due to the lack of information concerning slaughterhouse(s) of origin and information about which marked the meat is approved for on the national meat transfer certificate there was no clear documentation in place allowing tracing back product through the production. 5.2.3. Trichinae controls The rules for trichinae examination in Hungary is laid down in Annex 1, Article 694, of Decree No.41/1997 laying down the Veterinary Regulations. In Hungary there is a general obligation to examine fresh meat of pigs and horses for the presence of trichina larvae. When the meat is intended for export into the EU, the examination must be carried out according to the requirements and methods of the EU (Directive 77/96/EEC). The laboratories carrying out trichinae examination in EU approved slaughterhouses are situated inside the slaughterhouse. The collection of specimens and the examination of samples are carried out by trained auxiliaries employed by the County Animal Health and Food Control Station and under the supervision of the official veterinarian. All specimens taken could clearly be traced back to individual carcass numbers and samples from one day's slaughter were kept on numbered trays in refrigerators in the trichinae laboratories until all had been examined. The most commonly used method for trichinae examination in EU approved slaughterhouses is "III. METHOD USING THE ARTIFICIAL DIGESTION OF COLLECTIVE SAMPLES". Page 9 of 14 However in one visited establishment the method used was "VI. THE MAGNETIC STIRRER METHOD FOR POOLED SAMPLE DIGESTION", and in this case the following discrepancies from Directive 77/96/EEC, Annex I, was observed: · Instead of using 16 ml of 25% hydrochloric acid the laboratory used 10.8 ml of 37% hydrochloric acid, · A double strength hydrochloric acid solution was produced the day before use, and 1000 ml of this double strength solution was initially added to the meat samples together with the pepsin during the blending procedure and finally 1000 ml of preheated water was added. Official records of the results from the trichinae examinations were kept by the official veterinarians in the EU approved pig slaughterhouses and these documented that the examinations had been carried out as required. Furthermore the official veterinarians were regularly (once or twice annually) checking the performance of the trichinae examination staff using positive samples (infected mice). This evaluation was documented in the official records. The mission team was informed that trichinae have not been found in domestic pigs in Hungary since 1971. 5.3. Producer controls Water controls In all the establishments visited water sampling and testing programmes were found to be satisfactory and in accordance with the EC requirements. However the plans of the water distribution systems were not always comprehensive and up-to-date. Medical certification for workers A comprehensive system for medical examination and certification of workers were in place in all the establishments visited. Medical certificates were required prior to employment and there was an obligation to report any symptom of sickness. The medical certificates were renewed once or twice every year. The requirements for medical certification of workers are laid down in Decree No. 17/1999 on the Sanitary Requirements for the Production and Distribution of Foodstuffs. Staff training programmes A staff training programme for workers were available in all the establishments visited. The programme contained 3-8 hours of initial training for new staff. In some cases the official veterinarian was involved in the planning and carrying out of these courses, in other cases the training course took place in a special technical school. Furthermore the staff received 1-4 follow-up courses annually and the official veterinarians were involved in the planning and carrying out of these courses. Page 10 of 14 The requirements for the initial staff training programmes are laid down in Decree No. 17/1999 on the Sanitary Requirements for the Production and Distribution of Foodstuffs. Temperature controls Satisfactory computerised systems for recording the temperature in production and storage areas with graphic presentation was available in all the establishments visited. Cleaning programmes Comprehensive cleaning programmes were in place in all the establishments visited. These had been developed in connection with the establishments' SSOP or HACCP programmes. The official veterinarians were performing bacteriological testing and supplying written results and comments as regard unsatisfactory levels to the establishments. Detergents used were all approved. Pest controls Satisfactory programmes with numbered bait stations and planned supervision were available for rodent control. In most establishments UV flytraps were also available for protection against flying insects. 5.4. Animal welfare Council Directive 93/119/EC of 22 December 1993 concerning the protection of animals at slaughter had been copied into national legislation by Decree No. 9/1999 (IV. 1.) of the Minister of Agriculture and Regional Development concerning the protection of animals at slaughter. Before transporting pigs for slaughter the animals must be examined by the farmer's veterinarian who signs a certificate stating that none of the animals have been treated with either illegal substances or approved medicine within the withdrawal period and that the animals are fit for transport. Furthermore before transport can take place an official veterinarian employed by the County Station must sign another certificate stating that there are no animal health reason prohibiting the transport and that the animals are fit for transport. It was explained that most small-scale farmers would transport their own pigs to a collection point from where they were transported to the slaughterhouse. The official veterinarian would examine the animals and issue a joint animal health certificate to accompany the transport at this collection point. Laboratory service 5.4.1. Structure of the laboratory service The structure of the laboratory service is described in the circular of 06.01.00 from the IEV/IVK. According to this circular laboratories must be approved by IEV/IVK to perform bacteriological or chemical analysis of official samples. A condition for this approval is that the laboratory must be accredited by an independent accreditation organisation. It was noted that there is no obligation for the laboratories in Belgian legislation to inform the official veterinarian of the results of samples taken in the framework of own check programmes. There is a requirement to report the results in relation to PCB, dioxin and hormones immediately to the IEV/IVK. 5.4.2. National reference laboratory for trichinae The Trichinella Reference Laboratory is a part of the Veterinary Department of the Prince Leopold Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. The reference laboratory was established in 1996. Apart from trichinosis the institute also deals with cysticercosis. The laboratories for trichina testing, situated inside the slaughterhouses or the independent laboratories, must be recognised by the central competent authority IEV/IVK. For this inspection a representative of the national reference laboratory for trichina accompanies the IEV/IVK. The procedure foresees a revisit of the recognised laboratories at an unspecified interval. Only laboratories in which a re-inspection audit was performed with a favourable result may remain on the list of recognised laboratories. A ring test is planned for April this year. Training of technicians took place last year and training of the remainder of the technicians is planned for this year. The duration of the training is half a day. The mission team made the following observations: · For budget reasons the auditing of laboratories has only been operational during one year employing one part time veterinarian. The whole operation is foreseen to be finalised within three years. · Until now seventeen laboratories have been audited. · Negative outcome of an inspection did not result in an unfavourable conclusion regarding the approval of the laboratory. · The French summary of one audit report did not reflect the severe findings in the Flemish original version. 9 5.5. Trichina control The instructions concerning trichina testing are described in the circular of 17.01.00 from the IEV/IVK. As a general rule, all pigs slaughtered in Belgium and intended for intra-community market must be tested for trichina. In the case of pork meat exported to third countries, which have no specific requirements for certification of this examination, the obligation does not exist. Animal health situation Germany profits from a favourable animal health situation for bovines, sheep and goats: Ø Foot and mouth disease: freedom since 1989 Ø Bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis: Germany is officially free from bovine tuberculosis (Commission Decisions 99/467/EC and 2000/69/EEC) and brucellosis (Commission Decisions 99/466/EC and 2000/69/EEC) and also free from Brucella melitensis (Commission Decision 93/52/EEC). The monitoring of bovine Brucellosis is based on testing of the tank milks every second year with ELISA and of Brucella melitensis on random testing of 5 % of the animals annually. The screening for bovine tuberculosis is based mostly on the post mortem controls. 4.2.2. Food poisonings and zoonoses In 1993-1997, 4,7 % of food poisoning outbreaks were caused by milk and milk products (33/782 outbreaks). Of these outbreaks, 7 were caused by Campylobacter sp.. In 1998, one outbreak (source cheese made from raw milk) was caused by S. aureus. No milk and milk product related data on salmonellosis was available, but the total number of persons with enteritis infections caused by Salmonella serovars in 1999 was 85,015. The number of human brucellosis cases in 1999 was 21, of Q fever 276 and of newborn listeriosis 31 (data published by the federal authority Robert-Koch- Institute). In 1999 there were 2 microbiological alerts for German milk products (both Listeria monocytogenes in cheeses). 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. General structure of the German CA At the federal level, the veterinary services responsible for the co-ordination of all the activities concerning the policy and the implementation of Council Directive 92/46/EEC fall under the responsibility of 2 Ministries, BMG and BML. BMG is in general responsible for the transposition of the Directive 92/46/EEC and has issued the primary legislation for this purpose. BML is responsible for the transposition of the legislation concerning raw milk quality control and has issued primary legislation for this purpose. The application of Council Directive 92/46/EEC is under the responsibility of the Federal States (Länder) (total number 16), each of which has its own Government (Landesregierung). The local CAs are formed by the Districts (Kreise). The total number of Kreises in Germany is 439. In some Federal States an intermediate level, "Bezirksregierung or Regierungspräsidium", exists between the Federal State and the Kreis level (total number 32). The SVUs (total number 36), operating under the supervision of the Federal States, form a part of the veterinary administration. Within BMG 4 veterinary officers work in Division 422, of whom 1.5 work mostly with milk hygiene matters. Division 422 is also responsible for the co-ordination of the Rapid Alert System and receives and transmits the messages between the Commission and the responsible CA in the Federal State. Responsibilities for the official control of drinking water and of residue monitoring are in the same Ministry but fall under the responsibility of other Divisions. Ø BML The BML and its Directorate Market Policy, Division 423 (General and special aspects of the milk market) is, inter alia, responsible for legislative activities on the raw milk quality at the farm level. The number of staff working within the unit for milk market is 7, of which 1 deals half-time with raw milk quality aspects. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legal requirements for exports to the European Union The Czech Republic is an EU associated member country as a result of the Europe Agreement of 19931. It is also an EU candidate country belonging to the "Luxembourg group". The target date of accession of this group was fixed at the Helsinki Summit as 1 January 2003. Council Decision 98/250/EC lays down the protocol concerning sanitary, phytosanitary and animal welfare measures in relation to trade between the European Communities and their Member States, on the one part, and the Czech Republic, on the other part. According to this protocol, in particular Article 6 and Annex V.A, equivalency of sanitary measures is recognised concerning raw milk, raw milk products, heat-treated milk and milk products from heat treated milk for human consumption. Nevertheless for export to the EU, certificates on the basis of Commission Decision 95/343/EC have to be provided and the requirements laid down by Council Directive 92/46/EEC have to be fulfilled. Import requirements for imports to the Czech Republic The requirements for import of milk and milk products are not equivalent to the requirements of European legislation. The Czech Republic has concluded bilateral agreements with countries that are not on the list of authorised countries for the export to the European Union or that have no list of authorised establishments (e.g. Ukraine). The import certificates of the Czech Republic set up less stringent provisions for the quality of the processed raw milk than European legislation does. Official control plan on water An official control plan on water does not exist. The Swedish authorities pointed out, in their comments of 4 July 2000 on the draft version of this report, that district veterinary officers, employed by the SBA monitor some animal welfare provisions during inspections of milk production holdings and if a district veterinary officer has reason to criticise animal welfare and no remedial action is taken, he must report the matter to the municipality. The reports of their inspections are also sent to the municipality concerned, which can use it as a basis for its priority work on animal welfare surveillance. 9 5.3.7. Taking animals into care and prohibitions on the keeping of animals In cases where there was a failure to provide basic care for animals, the county administrative boards have used their powers under the Swedish Animal Welfare Act to seize animals and to prohibit farmers from keeping animals. At both meetings with representatives from the county boards it was explained that the municipality usually applies to the county board to make a decision to take animals on a farm into care, but will make such decisions themselves if the case has to be urgently addressed or in cases involving individual animals (e.g. pets). In one county it was explained that their adopted procedure involved one vet giving assistance to the municipalities in order to help them make decisions and a second vet was involved in hearing any appeals against such decisions. In another county one vet was responsible for both providing advice and hearing appeals on decisions made by the municipalities. It was stressed however in both counties that in any event the regional level has not the power to tell the local level what to decide. In the previous 12 months two cattle farms in one county were the subject of a taking into care order and one of these cases also resulted in a prohibition on the farmer from keeping animals. In this county, the first procedure for reaching this decision was to hold a meeting to hear all the opinions relating to the case. This included the farmer in question, who could also bring a legal representative. After the proceedings of this meeting were considered, a further visit was made to the farm and finally the county board would make its decision. A prohibition could be appealed but it was not possible for someone who was closely related to the farmer to take over the running of the farm in his or her name, for instance the farmer's wife. Such a move was considered a deception and any animals involved would be seized. It was reported that it is up to each county to devise a mechanism for reaching decisions on prohibitions. 5.3.8. National inspection strategies The SBA launches a national enforcement strategy on animal welfare (Projekts) once every two years. One such project in 1995 looked at the keeping of sows and involved the inspection of 1000 pig holdings. Sows were found to be confined for a period of between 8 and 60 days on 4% of holdings at this time. Such findings are the subject of enforcement actions by the supervising authority. The most recent Projekt involved inspections of animal transport and although the municipalities visited were very positive about taking part, some municipalities have chosen not to participate. 5.4. Field visits carried out by the mission team 5.4.1. Inspections of pig holdings The mission team observed the inspection of three pig holdings. Each inspection was carried out by one of three local inspectors, each of whom was from a different municipality and who was accompanied by representatives from both the central and regional authorities. One birth to finisher and two weaner producing units were visited. It was reported that the inspector would normally have inspected other farm activities, such as manure handling and use of chemicals on farm. 10 5.4.1.1 Space allowances and provision of bedding With the exception of one group of recently served sows, sows on all the farms visited were not confined in crates or stalls. On the farm where sows were confined, the inspector concluded that this practice complied with the Swedish legislation, which allows single sows to be confined for up to one week around the time of service or farrowing. He also reported that it was common practice to confine sows in this way. The county vet did not agree with this interpretation and explained that only problem sows could be confined in this manner. The county vet would not normally have been present during an inspection carried out by the local inspector. Although no measurements were made of any of the pens, none of the pens for growing pigs were overcrowded. Several inspectors cited the Swedish requirement for prior approval of buildings by the county board as sufficient evidence that the pens met the legislative requirements. The majority of local inspectors were satisfied with the amount of bedding provided for all categories of pigs on the farms visited, apart from one inspector who required a mat or more bedding to be provided for small piglets, several of which had knee abrasions. On a large pig unit a small amount of bedding was provided for growing pigs and the local inspector explained that he had to reconcile the requirement for bedding with the farmer's need to handle the manure effectively. 5.4.1.2 Surgical mutilations In compliance with Swedish legislation, tail docking was not practised on any of the farms visited. However, tooth clipping was carried out routinely on two out of the three farms visited. The inspectors did not ask for any justification for this practice. Swedish legislation allows routine tooth clipping provided it is carried out in the first week of life. 5.4.1.3 Unfit and injured pigs The majority of local inspectors recommended that a veterinarian should be involved where unfit or injured pigs were seen. However, on one farm a group of 30 group housed dry sows had a large number of skin injuries and there were two sows in the farrowing house which had savaged their piglets. No remarks were made on these issues. The farmer reported that a veterinarian from the Swedish Animal Health Service had visited the previous week but that such issues were not discussed during these visits. On another farm, the farmer reported that he would carry out the euthanasia of all categories of pigs himself. 5.4.1.4 Ventilation and alarms Several inspectors commented on the air quality on two of the farms visited. Swedish legislation requires that the ammonia level should not be greater than 10 PPM and several inspectors considered that this was exceeded if the smell of ammonia was detectable. It was not clear what steps the farmer was being asked to take in order to improve the air quality on the farms where this requirement was not met. None of the inspectors made any remarks about alarms for automatic ventilation systems. Swedish law requires a contingency plan in the event of a failure of such systems and recommends that an alarm is installed (see point 5.2). However, 11 the existence of such a contingency plan was not directly raised by any of the inspectors but only at the instigation of the mission team. 5.4.2. Inspections of calf holdings Six cattle holdings were inspected during the mission. In each case a local inspector from the municipality carried out the inspection and in addition to the mission team, representatives from both the central and regional authorities were also present. The inspector reported that normally all animals present on the farm would have been inspected as well as environmental aspects of farm activities. Five of the six farms were dairy farms and the sixth farm was a suckler beef herd. Most of the accommodation for calves had been in use before Council Directive 91/629/EEC (as amended) entered into force and so did not yet have to meet all the requirements. The calf accommodation on the sixth cattle holding was constructed in 1998 and this holding was added to the itinerary at the request of the mission team. 5.4.2.1 Construction and provisions of calf pens Measurements of pens were only made when doubts were raised as to whether pens for group reared calves were in compliance or not and in some cases pens for individual calves were measured. Several inspectors cited the Swedish requirement for buildings to be pre-examined prior to being built as proof that the pens met the legislative requirements. On one farm the farmer had not applied for this approval before constructing calving boxes and the inspector did not make any remarks on this issue. The farmer was a member of the committee responsible for animal welfare. On another farm a pen to accommodate sick calves was indicated on the plan for the calf accommodation but this had not yet been constructed and the inspector did not make any remarks on this issue. The transitional periods for the various space allowances in the legislation caused confusion for several inspectors. These inspectors did not have sufficient information with them or were not sufficiently informed to conclude on-the-spot as to whether the requirements were met on several farms inspected and deferred judgement. On the last farm visited the pens were constructed in 1998. The dividing wall between calf pens was solid up to a height of 80 cm and above this height neighbouring calves could see and touch each other through the bars which formed the remainder of the wall. Recommendations to the Member State 10.2.1. Disease control measures A number of improvements or corrective actions need to be taken without any delay in order to increase the efficacy of the disease control measures and, thus, considerably decrease the risk of further spread. The Italian authorities should inform the Commission, within 5 days of receipt of the draft of this report, of the action taken in this respect. (1) Italy should put a stronger emphasis on thorough epidemiological inquiries. For this purpose, the relevant epidemiological units should be reinforced (with human and other resources). Intensive contacts between the different units should be developed or, even better, a single unit should be created in view of the multiple contacts between the two regions. The epidemiologists need to have access to all relevant information without delay and report clearly back to the authorities with possible recommendations for measures to be taken. (2) The Italian authorities should carry out preventive slaughter of poultry flocks, which as a result of the epidemiological inquiries or in view of their location, are clearly at risk of infection. (3) Permanent contact between the affected contiguous regions involved should be reinforced or, where necessary, put in place. Clear information on the results of such contacts should be available. 19 Mission report Italy - avian influenza (03 - 05.01.2000) DG(SANCO)/1112/2000-MR FINAL (4) The control measures in the different controlled zones should be reinforced. For this purpose, clear information to the public should be in place to indicate the borders of the different zones. The veterinary authorities should have close collaboration with enforcement authorities such as the "carabinieri" and the municipal police in order to increase the level and quality of surveillance and install road blocks or other means for enforcement of movement bans. (5) Intensive contacts with farmers and their organisations should be organised in order to increase their awareness of the seriousness of the situation and to improve their knowledge of the applicable control measures. As far as possible, press releases should be complemented with on-the-spot information meetings.

The organisation and functioning of the crisis centres at different levels should be more clearly specified. 10.2.2. Reporting and notification The notification of outbreaks to the Commission and the other Member States, as well as the reporting in general, need to be improved without any delay in order to decrease the risk of any spread to other countries and to allow the relevant authorities to decide whether additional safeguard measures are needed. The Italian authorities should inform the Commission, within 5 days of receipt of the draft of this report, of the action taken in this respect. (1) Italy should endeavour to centralise all information on the outbreaks in the different regions, and to constitute a list with a national numbering system. (2) The Italian CCA should follow the ADNS system (codes) in accordance with Council Directive 82/894/EEC for reporting outbreaks to the Commission and the other Member States, even when not all numerical details are completely available at the time of reporting. 10.2.3. BACKGROUND 4.1. Overview of previous missions regarding aflatoxin contamination in groundnuts The European Commission carried out a mission to Greece with the objective to evaluate in general the official foodstuffs control system in Greece. In addition, missions to Egypt with similar objectives were carried out. The reports of both missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection Internet site (at http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/) under Report from the Commission on the second series of visits by Commission Representatives to the Member States [reference number: COM(1999) 751 final] and Report of a mission to Egypt for the purpose of the control of aflatoxin in groundnuts intended for export to the EU [reference number: SANCO/1216/1999­MR­final]. 4.2. Background to present mission Further to the mission carried out in Egypt, the mission to Greece was undertaken as a consequence of the recommendation that the Commission Services should consider the designation of entry ports through which imported groundnuts will pass the required import control measures. This mission forms part of a series of missions with the same objectives. 4.3. Product and trade information In 1999 the Food and Veterinary Office received 17 Rapid Alert Messages from Greece indicating that the aflatoxin levels in groundnuts were exceeding the specified limits laid down in the Annex to Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, 2 OJ L 37 of 13 February 1993 3 OJ L 201 of 17 July 1998 4 OJ L 290 of 24 November 1993 5 OJ L 372 of 31 December 1985 6 OJ L 186 of 30 June 1989 7 OJ L 201 of 17 July 1998 5 as amended. The lowest aflatoxin levels exceeding the maximum permitted limits were 3.9 µg/kg for aflatoxin B1 and 4.4 µg/kg for the total aflatoxin. However, in most cases the aflatoxin contamination in groundnuts detected was much higher, exceptionally reaching 1225 µg/kg in one case. The Competent Authority of Greece submitted the highest number of Rapid Alert Messages to the European Commission per Member State, which reflects their enormous efforts to determine aflatoxin levels in the big volumes of groundnuts imported to the European Union through Greece. 4.4. Public health information Aflatoxins are mycotoxins produced by certain species of Aspergillus, which develop at high temperatures and humidity levels and may be present in a large number of foods. The aflatoxins group includes a number of compounds of varying toxicity and frequency in food. Aflatoxin B1 is the most toxic compound. For safety reasons, it is advisable to limit both the total aflatoxin content compounds B1, B2, G1 and G2 of food and the aflatoxin B1 content. Maximum limits for aflatoxins in food were fixed taking into account the known possible effects of sorting or other physical treatment methods to reduce the aflatoxin content of the peanuts. In accordance with the Annex to Council Regulation (EC) No 194/97, the aflatoxin maximum admissible levels in various groundnuts and products thereof intended for human consumption are as follows: a) Groundnuts and processed products: 2 µg/kg aflatoxin B1 content, and 4 µg/kg total aflatoxin content b) Groundnuts subject to sorting or other physical treatment: 8 µg/kg aflatoxin B1 content, and 15 µg/kg total aflatoxin content In addition sampling plays a crucial part in the precision of the determination of the levels of the aflatoxins, which are very heterogeneously distributed in a consignment of groundnuts. Therefore, in Commission Directive 98/53/EC a sampling procedure and general criteria were fixed to ensure that laboratories, in charge of the control, use methods of analysis with comparable levels of performance. 5. MAIN OBSERVATIONS 5.1. Legislation Import control for aflatoxins in groundnuts is carried out at authorised points of entry in co-operation with the Customs services (Ministry of Finance), the Regional Centre of Plant Protection and Quality Control (Ministry of Agriculture) and the Regional Chemical Laboratories (Ministry of Finance) in accordance with the Customs Code law 1165/1918. Based on Ministerial Decision 14871/363 on sampling and the examination of imported foodstuffs, sampling of groundnuts for aflatoxin analysis is carried out in ports, before importation, by authorised personnel of the Ministry of Agriculture. 6 Currently, inspectors of the Regional Centre of Plant Protection and Quality Control apply the sampling method described in Presidential Decree 236429, which is in accordance with Commission Directive 79/700/EEC8 of 24 July 1979, as amended, regarding establishing Community methods of sampling for the official control of pesticide residues in and on fruit and vegetables. 5.2. Import control procedures for aflatoxin levels in groundnuts 5.2.1. Import control procedure The inspection of imported groundnuts is carried out mainly at authorised points of entrance, where custom inspection is conducted. In some cases the inspection of imported groundnuts may also be carried out at the importer's premises. The Ministry of Agriculture has advised customs officers that all imported groundnuts be subject to Quality and Phytosanitary Inspection. No groundnut imports are allowed to enter Greece before the Inspectors of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control have seen these groundnut consignments and have confirmed the conformity of these consignments with the relevant legislation on food quality and safety. Customs officers, inspectors of the corresponding Offices of the Regional Centre of Plant Protection and Quality Control and the Regional Chemical Laboratories in Piraeus and Thessaloniki co-operate closely in terms of import controls for aflatoxin levels in groundnuts. The importer needs to submit an application for each import of groundnuts or an official customs document to the Offices of the Regional Centre of Plant Protection and Quality Control prior to the opening of the container by customs officers. Customs officers identify and verify all consignments of groundnuts on basis of their accompanying documents, including aflatoxin certificates issued by the exporting Third Country Competent Authority. Inspectors of the Offices of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control continue the inspection of each groundnut consignments, which comprise at least the following: - means of transport of groundnuts, - appearance of groundnuts, - materials and articles intended to come into contact with the groundnuts, - labelling and presentation of groundnuts, - reading of values recorded by measuring instruments installed by the importer (e.g. moisture of groundnuts during transport, if available) - taking samples from all consignments of groundnuts for aflatoxin analysis and sending these to the Regional Chemical Laboratories in Piraeus or Thessaloniki, which are empowered to carry out aflatoxin control in groundnuts. 8 OJ L 207 of 15 August 1979 7 5.2.2. Sampling procedure Sampling of groundnuts for aflatoxin analysis is only performed by inspectors of the Offices of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control. The place of sampling of imported groundnuts is carried out mostly at the authorised points of entrance, otherwise at the importer's premises, where the inspection of groundnuts is conducted. These inspectors follow a sampling procedure, which is based on the requirements of Commission Directive 79/700/EEC. During the period of January to November 1999 a total of 757 groundnut samples were taken. The analytical results of these samples showed that, in 59 cases the maximum allowed aflatoxin levels were exceeded. The results of the second analysis confirmed that 33 out of these 59 samples were above the maximum allowed limits. Those consignments, from which the 33 samples were taken, had been finally rejected. Most of the groundnut imports pass the harbour in Piraeus. The main countries from where groundnuts are imported to Greece are Argentina, Egypt, China, India and the USA. During the same year, the percentage of groundnut samples exceeding the maximum allowed limits were 12.2% in groundnuts originated in Egypt, followed by 8.9% in groundnuts originated in China and 4.9% in groundnuts originated in Argentina. No such figures on groundnuts from India exceeding the limits were available. Based on national requirements, each lot of groundnuts, which is to be imported, is sampled separately. As far as possible inspectors take samples at various places throughout the lot. Inspectors of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control explained that they usually take incremental samples from 20 different points within a container, which are easily accessible to them without unloading the container. They use sampling spears of different sizes when taking the incremental samples from various bags filled with groundnuts. The combined total amount of the incremental samples is around 2 ­ 3 kg sample weight, which is required for the preparation of 2 laboratory samples. Uniting and mixing the 20 incremental samples in coloured plastic bags makes up the aggregate sample or final sample. The inspectors prepare 2 sub- samples from the final sample as required by national rules. The 2 sub- samples are used as 1st and 2nd laboratory samples, whereby each weight is between 1 ­ 1.5 kg. Inspectors place each laboratory sample in a clean, inert paper bag. These paper bags are labelled and sealed by the inspectors in such a manner that these cannot be opened or the labels removed without damaging the seals. The inspectors keep records of each sampling, permitting each lot to be identified unambiguously and giving the date and place of sampling together with additional information likely to be of assistance to the analyst at the laboratories. Finally, the inspectors prepare a sampling protocol and forward a analysis request form to the Regional Chemical Laboratories empowered to carry out aflatoxin analysis in groundnuts, containing information on 8 container and sampling necessary for the analysts. Copies of both documents are kept in the Offices of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control. The importers or their representatives usually take both laboratory samples of a lot to the laboratory in question for analysis. 5.2.3. Notification of analysis results and follow up actions The containers from which samples have been taken are under custody of the responsible customs office until the final results of the aflatoxin analysis have been provided to the inspectors of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control. The maximal time elapsed between taking samples and receiving the results of the aflatoxin analysis is 1 week. § If the 1st laboratory samples examined are found to contain aflatoxin levels below the defined limits laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, as amended, the inspectors notify the Customs to proceed the applications for importation of that lots of groundnuts. Additionally, under the provision that other national and/or community qualitative and phytosanitary conditions are fulfilled, the customs officers allow the import of those lots. § If the 1st laboratory samples examined are exceeding the aflatoxin levels as laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, as amended, the importers may object to these results. They may request that the Regional Chemical Laboratory carry out an analysis in the 2nd laboratory samples taken from the same lots. § If the 2nd laboratory samples examined are found to contain aflatoxin levels below the defined limits laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, as amended, the customs officers may allow the import of that lots. § If the 2nd laboratory samples examined are exceeding the aflatoxin levels as laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, as amended, the inspectors notify the Customs not to proceed the applications for importation of that lots. These lots may be returned to the country of origin, delivered to other third countries or destroyed under the presence of an inspector of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control. In these cases the inspectors notify the General Chemical State Laboratory that specific lots of groundnuts are exceeding the aflatoxin levels fixed in Commission Regulation (EC) No 194/97, as amended. Representatives of the General Chemical State Laboratory forward these messages to the European Commission as Rapid Alert Messages. 9 5.3. Competent authorities performance in connection with the import control of groundnuts for aflatoxin contamination 5.3.1. The General Chemical State Laboratory The General Chemical State Laboratory is a scientific service based within the Ministry of Finance. It was founded in 1929 and is responsible for the protection of public health, consumers and the environment. In addition, it provides scientific support to the state authorities in Greece, such as customs, juridical and police authorities. Furthermore, the General Chemical State Laboratory is responsible for the fulfilment of national and Community requirements related to its work responsibilities. The General Chemical State Laboratory is divided in Divisions of Food, Alcohol and Alcoholic Beverages, Wine and Beer, Technical Tarification, Raw Materials and Industrial Products, Petrochemicals, Personnel and Administration and Environment, of which the latter has a laboratory dealing with the determination of aflatoxins. Further details of this laboratory of the Division Environment within the General Chemical State Laboratory are described in section 5.4.1 of this report. The General Chemical State Laboratory has several peripheral Regional Chemical Services all over Greece. The Regional Chemical Laboratories in Piraeus and Thessaloniki are empowered to carry out routine analysis of aflatoxins in groundnuts. Further details of these regional laboratories are described in sections 5.4.2 and 5.4.3 of this report. The General Chemical State Laboratory has set up a Quality Management System for all its services to achieve and maintain high standards of quality in all aspects of the laboratory work performed. Approximately 500 staff in total, of which 350 are scientists, mainly graduated chemists, are employed at the services of the General Chemical State Laboratory, which is committed to provide regular scientific training and specialisation to its staff to constantly improve work performance. The General Chemical State Laboratory has adopted for all its laboratories a laboratory quality system according to the criteria laid down by the United Kingdom Accreditation Service. These criteria include the requirements of the European Standard EN 45001. The Section Planning and Technical Support within the Division Personnel and Administration is co-ordinating and monitoring the uniform implementation of the quality system applied in all services of the General Chemical State Laboratory. The General Chemical State Laboratory operates an information technology system connecting all its services throughout Greece. It comprises food sample applications, internal market inspections, food business operators within every prefecture and the food codex. Every analyst receiving samples of imported foodstuffs for chemical analysis needs to fill in a specific form in the data system containing necessary information on the sample, the origin of the sample and the consignment from which the sample is taken. Representatives of the General Chemical State Laboratory explained that the 10 tasks of this data system would soon be extended to include also the results of the chemical analysis performed in each sample of foodstuffs. 5.3.2. Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control of Piraeus and Thessaloniki The Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control are peripheral services of the Ministry of Agriculture. In total there are 8 Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control9. Each of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control has a Phytosanitary and a Quality Control Section. To each of these Sections a laboratory is attached responsible for phytosanitary inspection of imported plants and plant products and qualitative laboratory inspection respectively. Inspectors of the Phytosanitary Section within each of the Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control usually inspect imported plant and plant products, including sampling of all groundnut consignments, at authorised entry points10. Samples of imported groundnuts taken at entry points in the Regions of Kavala, Thessaloniki and Volos are analysed for aflatoxin levels at the Regional Chemical Laboratory in Thessaloniki. Samples of imported groundnuts taken at all other entry points are analysed for aflatoxin levels in the Regional Chemical Laboratory in Piraeus. The inspectors of both Regional Centres of Plant Protection and Quality Control co-operate with the Customs services located at the harbour. The services have persons working permanently and persons working under limited time contracts. Persons of the permanent staff are agronomists, specialised in either Phytosanitary Inspection, Plant Protection or in Quality Inspection. The non-scientific staff is occupied with secretarial and financial activities. The non-permanent staff is occupied at the laboratory and does not carry out inspections. The Dutch authorities had already assured the Commission services that the Dutch government has no doubt about the quality of milk and beef produced in the Netherlands. In addition, the Dutch authorities had clarified that the NZO had commissioned the Animal Health Service (GD) to carry out an investigation into the veterinary problem on the farms concerned. The farm inspections will be carried out following a government-approved protocol. At the same time the authorities had declared that in spite of the media reports on this matter, which suggest a possible risk to public health, there is absolutely no reason to assume that this might be the case. They stated that milk produced by sick animals may not be sold for human consumption and is not accepted by dairy factories. Moreover, they stated that these factories run an extensive quality system that complies with Council Directive 92/46/EEC. Raw milk samples are thoroughly analysed in the laboratory. According to this communication to the Commission, routine government checks have produced no evidence of any danger to public health. The authorities further stated that milk factories had not at any time indicated that the quality of milk concerned might in some way be compromised. Legal requirements for exports to the European Union For export to the EU, certificates on the basis of Commission Decision 95/343/EC have to be provided, and the requirements laid down by Council Directive 92/46/EEC have to be fulfilled. National legislation corresponding to Council Directive 92/46/EEC, is formed by: · Food (Control and Sale) Law 54 (1) 96, · The "Milk and Milk Products Hygiene (Production and Processing) and Control of Cowsheds, Sheep and Goat Sheds and Dairies Regulations 86/95 (hereafter named Regulation 86/95). The sanitary measures that are taken in the establishments authorised for export to the European Union are based on the above mentioned national legislation. However, it does not contain all provisions of European legislation in the framework of Council Directive 92/46/EEC. For example, the national limit for the Total Plate Count (TPC) is 500 000 TPC/ml instead of 100 000 TPC/ml, as given in Annex A, Chapter IV, of Directive 92/46/EEC. The Regional CA (RCA) comprises 4 District Veterinary Offices (DVOs), responsible for 5 Districts. The official veterinary laboratories are also under the direct supervision of the CCA. The Director of the VS has the legal power to plan, supervise and co-ordinate the activities of the DVOs and RVS and the official veterinary laboratories. The CCA also prepares legislation and carries out inspections and sampling under certain circumstances. Responsibility for Council Directive 92/46/EEC within the CCA lies with the Division of Veterinary Public Health, where one Veterinary Officer is in charge of milk and milk products. The Veterinary Officers at the DVOs are in charge of the supervision and inspection of milk-processing establishments and dairy farms. They also supervise the LCA. The Veterinary Officers and Inspectors at the Rural Veterinary Stations are subordinate to the DVOs.
