text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Summary of previous mission results A mission was undertaken to France from 6 to 10 July 1998 (XXIV/1415/98) on the handling and trade of animal waste. In this report the national French measures as regards SRM are described. The last mission to France as regards BSE was carried out from 31 May to 4 June 1999. It was part of a series of missions in Member States to evaluate the implementation of Commission Decision 98/272/EC (epidemiosurveillance of Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies). The report of this mission is available under reference number: DG(SANCO)/1058/1999 ­ MR ­ final on the Commission's internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/france/index_en.html The report made a number of recommendations for action to the competent authorities. These recommendations are outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of part 5 of this report. 4.2. Actions undertaken/announced by the CCA following the report In their response to mission report DG(SANCO)1058/99 from June 2000, the CCA informed the Commission services of a number of actions (hereafter referred to as the "Action Plan") that had been/would be undertaken to address certain recommendations made. In a letter from July 2000 the FVO asked for clarification on some of the actions foreseen but has not received an answer. These actions concerned both the feed ban, and epidemio-surveillance, and are outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of part 5 of this report. (9) OJ L 38, 12/02/1998 p. 10. 6 5. MAIN FINDINGS For ease of reference, the recommendations concerning the feed ban, and epidemio-surveillance as set out in report DG(SANCO) /1058/99 are indicated under the appropriate section headings, in italics and preceded by a "bullet" point. 5.1. Feed ban Meat and bone meal (MBM) is the generic term for both mammalian meat and bone meal (MMBM) and poultry offal meal (POM). 5.1.1. Evolution of the feed ban in France Ø 24 July 1990: prohibition of feeding of MMBM to cattle Ø 20 December 1994: prohibition of feeding of MMBM to all ruminants Ø 8 July 1996: prohibition to use all kinds of animal protein (including poultry offal meal and fish meal) for the feeding of ruminants, with the exception of milk and egg proteins and certain other products (amino acids, calcium phosphate from bones) Ø 14 November 2000: prohibition to use all kinds of animal proteins to any farmed animals (total feed ban) with the exemption of milk and egg proteins and certain other products (gelatine derived from pig skin). In addition, bone fat from gelatine production and fat from MBM production is forbidden. A recall of feed already delivered to farms is not foreseen. According to the CA the following measures are considered to have had a positive effect on MBM safety: Ø Since 28 June and 17 September 1996 respectively: cadavers, animal tissues condemned and declared unfit for human or animal consumption and SRM are excluded from the feed chain. Ø Since 6 February 1998: MBM for feeding purposes has to be compulsorily pressure treated (133°C, 20 min, 3 bars, maximum size 50 mm). 5.1.2. Co-ordination of control activities Feed mills are controlled by departmental offices of DGCCRF and SVD, which belong to DGAL. DGCCRF is responsible for checking of ingredients and labelling provisions. Veterinary services are in charge of checking the production machinery, hygiene and medicated feeding stuffs. On farm controls (including on farm mixers) are normally performed by veterinary services. However, DGCCRF is also visiting farms if a suspicion arises during the control of a feed mill. Samples on farm are taken mainly to check post production cross-contamination. The co-ordination of controls in the field of animal nutrition is laid down in a written procedure (Note de Service) issued by DGAL and DGCCRF. An updated version was distributed to all DVSs and "Departemental" DGCCRF offices in 7 September 1999. It was explained that the written procedure has existed already since the mid 1990s. 5.1.2.1. Uniformity of official controls and instructions for inspectors · The extent and content of official controls on feed-plants in the framework of feed-ban should be reviewed by French authorities to ensure uniform application by departmental services. An annual programme concerning BSE protective measures was issued by DGCCRF for 1998. Inspectors were at this time asked to check critical points in the feed mills and highlighted the need to check the production sequence of feed batches. In addition, it was mentioned that all feed producers have to be checked. In the National sampling plan 2000 the critical points (see 5.1.2.2.) to be checked in feed mills are summarised. A standard protocol for the samples taken is provided. Information on the method of sampling (targeted/random) of ruminant feed samples is not included. On the spot DGCCRF inspectors stated that they normally take random samples. They also explained that follow-up samples are taken targeted (batch to be sampled after studying of production sequence) if possible. During the visits to feed mills discussions with DGCCRF inspectors revealed that during their inspections in the feed mills they address all relevant aspects as regards the feed ban (check of production records, check of working instructions, check of raw material reception, production line and loading area). 5.1.2.2. National sampling plan · A national sampling plan should provide the basis for samplings within each department. Emphasis should be given to the targeting of samplings and including a fixed number of on-farm mixers, farms and transport vehicles in the sampling plan. A National sampling plan was issued for the year 2000. This lays down the number of feed samples to be taken by region (21 regions). The number of samples is fixed according to the amount of cattle and sheep/goat feed produced in feed mills in the different regions (tonnage principle). This sampling plan foresees 900 cattle feed samples and 103 for small ruminants to be taken in 2000. Additionally, non-ruminant feed containing MBM had to be sampled in 2000 in the different regions (204 samples). These samples were checked for appropriate heat treatment of the MBM used. Most of the samples taken were taken in feed mills. Sampling of on-farm mixers was considered not to be relevant as this number in France is low. It was explained that although it was foreseen sampling on farms did not start at the time of the mission. The responsible DGCCRF inspectors decide how often the feed mills in their territory have to be checked. It was explained that they carry out their own "risk analysis" mainly based on their experience with the individual feed producers. 8 5.1.3. Analytical method used The detection limit of the method used is a single bone fragment. The quantification limit is set at 0,01 % bone fragments. To express the content of MBM the percentage of bone fragments found is multiplied by 3. 5.1.4. Consequences of positive samples Samples with a bone content of 0,01 % (=0,03 % MBM) but less than 0,1 % (< 0,3 % MBM) have to be followed up (a suivre), whereas samples with a bone content of 0,1 % (0,3 % MBM) and more are not conforming (non conforme), which implies legal proceedings. The procedure to be followed in case positive feed samples are found is set out in an instruction that the DGCCRF (central administration) sent to all "Departemental" directorates of the CCRF in November 2000: If positive samples (bone content 0,01 % or more) are found a warning letter is sent to the feed mill. In addition, the DGCCRF inspector has to visit the feed mill again, block the remaining feed of the examined batch and take further samples. The contaminated consignment is condemned. The other consignments are blocked and may not be released until the sample taken turns out negative. Further measures are: Ø If two samples show a bone content of 0,01 % but less than 0,1 % (a suivre) legal proceedings have to be started. Ø If a sample is not conforming (bone content 0,1 % or more) legal proceedings have to be started immediately. It was explained by staff from DGCCRF headquarters that positive samples have been treated in a similar way as explained above since 1998. 5.1.5. Number of samples taken and sampling results · The number of annual samples should be increased considerably. The mission team was provided with preliminary results of the sampling activities in 2000. According to this information, the number of samples taken increased considerably: until 24 November 2000, approximately 900 samples were taken of which 657 samples have been examined by the DGCCRF laboratory. The table below provides information on the number of samples taken and analysed by DGCCRF throughout France during the last years: Year Number of Bone fragments from Bone fragments from samples 0,01 % to < 0,1 % 0,1 % and more 1997 307 45 (14,7 %) 10 (3,3 %) 1998 454 21 (4,6 %) 4 (0,9 %) 1999 380 15 (3,9 %) 5 (1,3 %) 2000* 657 32 (4,9 %) 0 * as of 24 November 2000 9 5.1.6. Measures to avoid cross-contamination of ruminant feed with MBM · Clear instructions should be distributed to the industry on how to avoid and control cross-contamination. This can be achieved by elaborating and approving the manual of good practice already drafted by the industry. Measures aimed at avoiding cross-contamination of ruminant feed samples are laid down in a guide of good manufacturing practice. This guide has been elaborated by two associations of compound feed producers together with DGAL and DGCCRF and was approved by these. It is attached to the National sampling plan 2000. This guide highlights in particular the obligation to record the production sequence of feed batches and the need to flush the production line before the production of ruminant feed. In the introduction of the National sampling plan for 2000, the inspectors are asked to verify that the feed producers are aware of the critical points in feed mills as regards cross-contamination (e.g. reception of raw materials, cleansing of intake bins or pipes, recycling of returned feed etc.) and that they take appropriate action in order to avoid cross-contamination. 5.1.7. Implementation in practice To verify the approach used by DGCCRF inspectors used for feed ban controls, three feed mills were visited and discussions were held with the feed mill management and the responsible DGCCRF staff. The issues discussed were the following: Ø measures taken by feed producers to avoid cross-contamination of ruminant feed with MBM on production lines, where MBM was used for the production of monogastric feed and where ruminant feed was also produced; Ø activities of DGCCRF as regards the feed ban and follow-up action by DGCCRF in case of breaches. All three feed mills were producing ruminant feed on production lines on which feed for monogastric animals was also produced using MBM. § One of these feed mills where ruminant feed was also produced was producing dog feed using up to 20 % MBM on the same production line up to summer 1999. Since ownership changed in 1998 the cooperation with DGCCRF has improved which is reflected in a lower number of positive feed samples. The feed mill used the same intake line for the reception of MBM and other raw materials in the past. Cleansing procedures were in place until a separate intake line for MBM was installed. Records on the cleansing of the intake line were kept and provided to the mission team. In addition, some production records from the last years were checked by the mission team. According to these flushing batches were used to cleanse the production line before the production of ruminant feed. The size of the flushing batches used seemed to be reasonable (minimum two production runs). In order to control efficiency of flushing auto- control samples were taken randomly by the feed mill and were examined in a private laboratory. So far no positive samples were found. 10 § During discussions in another feed mill it turned out that the production line was not always flushed before the production of ruminant feed although MBM was used in the previous run. The manager explained that this was not necessary because French MBM is very safe due to the fact that fallen stock and SRM were not allowed as raw material for the production of MBM for feeding purposes. The feed mill provided figures, which demonstrated that the tonnage of MBM used by the feed mill was too large in comparison to the total amount of ruminant feed and MBM free monogastric feed produced. To flush the system with raw materials or to abandon MBM at least for a part of the produced monogastric feed would have increased the cost of the feed produced. DGCCRF confirmed that flushing batches were not always used for economic reasons rather than because of a lack of awareness of staff. DGCCRF checked production records in November 1999 and found that approximately 25 % of the ruminant feed batches produced were produced directly after a production run using MBM without flushing in between. This feed mill has been monitored closely by DGCCRF since summer 1998. Legal proceedings were initiated in November 1999 when a ruminant feed sample containing 0,4 % MBM was found. However, the state attorney decided not to take the case up. DGCCRF staff told the mission team that they do not have the power to force a feed mill to avoid cross-contamination. DGCCRF forced the feed mill to sample each ruminant feed batch produced and allowed delivery of the feed only if the feed mill could prove that MBM was absent. § The third feed mill visited is one of the biggest in France. The procedures in place for the unit where ruminant feed is produced was flushing after the use of MBM. This feed mill was taking auto-control samples to be checked for MBM presence in ruminant feed. Trucks for delivery of ruminant feed were dedicated for 3 days per week. After delivery of MBM containing feed they were cleaned following a written procedure. No positive samples have been found since 1998. The DGCCRF inspectors met have a technical or scientific background and seemed to be well trained. 5.1.8. The farms are inspected in conjunction with other controls (mainly the sampling in the context of the National Residues Plan) and the feed mills are sampled for the detection of MBM once per year. It was unclear if and to what extent a risk assessment approach (level of production, number of lines of production, animal feed destined to different animal species) was in place to better target the controls and the sampling in the feed mills. Producers are, in general, well aware of the EU rules concerning the feed ban, due to information/awareness available at Feed-mill Industry Association level. As regards the implementation of feed ban in practice, during the visit in a feed mill (Castilla y Leon) it was observed that: In general there are no controls on risk ingredients (e.g:fishmeal); No obligation exists in the auto-control system to inform the competent authority where problems occur; (e.g: cross-contamination) Pre-production cross contamination is not completely addressed (no direct controls/guarantees on the ingredients of vegetable origin -Soya, sun-flower, etc;- transported previously with the same truck) During production, prevention of cross contamination is ensured by the rotation of production (no ruminant feed can be produced after feed where MBM has been incorporated); the informatic system governing the composition of the recipes is providing the staff of the plant with the information concerning this prohibition but this warning can not stop the production; 12 Post production cross contamination is not completely addressed (a certain number of silos are available to store ruminant feed but they are not dedicated); Incoming materials are accompanied by commercial documentation where the declaration is not completely complying with Council Directive 97/47/EC. INTRODUCTION Estonia is on the provisional list of third countries allowed to export milk and milk-based products to the European Union (Commission Decision 95/340/EC). The mission took place from 28 May to 1 June 2001. The mission team comprised three inspectors from the Food and Veterinary Office (FVO) and one national expert. The mission was undertaken as part of the FVO's planned mission programme, and was the first mission in Estonia specifically on the dairy sector. The inspection team was accompanied during the whole mission by several representatives from the Veterinary and Food Board, the central competent authority (CCA). An opening meeting was held on 28 May 2001 with the CCA. At this meeting, the objectives of, and itinerary for, the mission were confirmed by the inspection team, and additional information required for the satisfactory completion of the mission requested. 2. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objective of the mission was to carry out an evaluation of the performance of the official services to guarantee that the health rules for the production and placing on the market of milk and milk-based products intended for export to the EU are at least equivalent to those laid down in Chapter II of Directive 92/46/EEC for Community production. In order to assess the system put in place by the Estonian CA, visits to the different levels of the CA, some of the establishments approved for export to the EU, as well as related official laboratories and dairy farms were performed. In pursuit of this objective, the following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Comments 1 Competent Central 1 authority Regional 4 milk plant laboratories LABORATORY VISITS 3 Private Public 1 LIVE ANIMAL CONTROL SITES Farms FOOD PROCESSING 4 ESTABLISHMENTS - there are no milk collection centres in Estonia Milk processing premises Collection centre 7 3. LEGAL BASES The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries1. · Council Directive 92/46/EEC of 16 June 1992 laying down the health rules for the production and placing on the market of raw milk, heat-treated milk and milk based products2. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Previous related missions to Estonia There were two previous OICVP/FVO missions to Estonia, related to milk and milk products. The first (XXIV/2241/97) was carried out in October 1997. While the animal health situation in relation to milk and milk products was considered satisfactory, the public health inspection of the establishments proposed by the Estonian CCA was unsatisfactory. The second mission (XXIV/1412/98) was carried out from 9 to 12 June 1998 as follow-up to the previous one. During this mission, the performance of the CCA was assessed, and one dairy plant, visited previously in 1997, was inspected, as well as one integrated slaughterhouse, cutting and meat processing plant. The outcome of the visits was satisfactory for the dairy plant but unsatisfactory for the meat plant. The report of this mission is available under its specific reference number on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html 4.2. General The main legal acts in Estonian legislation, relevant for this mission, are the following: 10 · Food Act of 25 February 19993, as amended · Veterinary Act ( Veterinaarkorralduse seadus) of 16 June 19994 · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No. 28 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for the Production of Milk and Milk Products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.30 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for Producing Raw Milk in a Dairy Farm · Veterinary and Food Inspectorate Directive No. 35 of 15th November 2000 on requirements for veterinary certificates and certification · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.44 of 24th December 1999 on veterinary requirements for importation of animals and animal products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.12 of 16th of March 5 ("Statutes of the Veterinary and Food Board") An extensive list of Estonian legal acts, corresponding to EC legal acts relevant for this mission is attached after the table of content. The mission team noted that amongst the large number of recently (1995- 2001) adopted Estonian legal acts related to the objective of the mission, two ­ Raw Milk Hygiene Regulation no 30 of 1999, and Milk and Milk Products Hygiene Regulation, no 28 of 1999 ­ refer officially to the relevant EC legislation (Council Directives 92/46/EEC, 89/362/EEC, 89/384/EEC, 94/71/EEC and 95/165/EEC). 5.1.2. Equivalence of Estonian legislation An initial assessment of the Estonian legislation revealed that certain provisions of the Community legislation relevant for the current mission had no equivalent in the Estonian legislation: · no approval required for heat treatment equipment · no formal requirement for official recognition of laboratories carrying out analysis about own-check samples · no official registration of farms supplying milk to EU-premises. 3 RT (= Riigi Teataja, State Gazette) I 1999, 30, 415 4 RT I 1999, 58, 608 5 RTL 2000, 38, 535 11 · no procedure for the withdrawal of farms supplying milk not fulfilling EC requirements In addition, there were no administrative measures in place to ensure that EU exports met these requirements. With regard to quality of raw milk, the current Estonian legislation requires a plate count of 500,000/ml or less, and a somatic cell count of 500,000/ml or less, in raw cow's milk (c.f. chapter 5.4.2). One standard of milk is officially acknowledged. However, in one EC approved plant, the mission team was told by the management that the old system based on the Soviet GOST is still used "internally"- for domestic production. This system comprises three standards of milk: superior, first and unclassified (out ­of-standard). 5.2. CA structure and organisation The Central Competent Authority for matters related to the production, collection and processing of milk in Estonia is the Veterinary and Food Board, Veterinaar- ja Toiduamet (formerly Veterinary And Food Inspection Service, the name changed in 2000). The VFB is working under the Ministry of Agriculture and the Chief Veterinary Officer reports to the Minister of Agriculture. 5.2.1. Management structure The structure of the CCA is described in details in the report XXIV/1412/98 and has not changed since that time. It is a pyramidal structure with direct line of command. 5.2.2. Independence All the officials responsible for the performance of inspections and supervision of establishments enjoy an employment status that guarantees their independence from the establishments for which they are responsible. The staff are paid by the Ministry of Agriculture, but the budget is allocated by the Parliament and cannot be changed by the Ministry. No other occupations for the staff are authorised, unless permitted by the Director (CVO for the CCA and the Director of the Regional Veterinary Centre for the provincial staff). 5.2.3. Resources The budget of the VFB is currently 64 000 000 EEK (ca 11 636 363 ). It is 30 % tax-funded, allocated by the Parliament through the Ministry of Agriculture, together with supervision fees from the food industry, import fees and meat inspection fees. The staff of the VFB is 334 in total, 32 of them in the HQ in Tallinn (20 veterinarians and 12 administrative staff including central bookkeeping). This also includes 118 staff of the Border Inspection Service, 15 of them 12 in the HQ in Tallinn. There are currently vacancies within the VFB, but this is not considered as a problem. The CVO finds the staffing situation satisfactory. 5.2.4. Recruitment & training 5.2.4.1.Recruitment Staff are recruited on the basis of public competition, as required by the Law on Public Service of the 25 January 1995. A yearly accreditation (review) is carried out of all staff members by the Director (and of the Director by a governmental commission). The mission team was told that in one case, accreditation was delayed for six months for one regional VFB director. In addition to officials, there are a number of authorised veterinarians, i.e. private practitioners employed by the VFB on a contract basis. They may be contracted by the CCA for the performance of some official tasks, e.g. TB testing, vaccination or monitoring of hygiene on the farms. The contract is for 1 year, but may be extended for up to 5 years, depending upon the budget situation. There are currently 209 authorised veterinarians in Estonia. All veterinary practitioners in Estonia have to be licensed by the Veterinary and Food Board. To obtain a licence, the following is required: a veterinary diploma, a certificate from the regional VFB and evidence of additional training. A licence is valid for 5 years, and a list of licensed veterinarians is kept by the CCA. Currently, there are 852 licensed veterinarians in Estonia. SUMMARY Brucellosis The eradication of Brucella melitensis in small ruminants has made little progress in the year 1999, and the performance targets were missed. In buffaloes, the level of official farm controls is low in the region of Campania, which holds the major part of the Italian buffalo population. The effectiveness of the eradication scheme is severely limited by the failure of the official services to visit and control the disease situation on farms, and the retention of brucellosis positive animals on farms with a prevalence of disease higher than 5 % for periods of up to five years. Delays in the payment of compensation within the target interval for a high proportion of small ruminants, and the failure of compensation for buffaloes to reflect their market value, both reduce the level of support for the programmes within the farming community. Milk and milk-based products The Italian central authorities have responded positively to a number of the recommendations made in the previous mission reports (ref. no. XXIV/1099/99 and DG(SANCO)/1073/2000). However improvements at regional and local level have not been achieved as many of the changes required have not been implemented. 43 9. RECOMMENDATIONS 9.1. (2) ensure that milk from buffalo holdings that do not receive such regular veterinary inspections is not processed in approved milk-processing establishments. 9.1.2. to transmit to the Commission within three months of receiving the translated copy of the final report an action plan with a timetable, indicating how they will: (1) set up and implement procedures to allow the central services to monitor and, where necessary, improve, the operation of the eradication programmes at regional and local levels (2) improve co-operation between departments at the central level and ensure that there are sufficient staff resources available to address the issues raised in this report. The immediate consequence of this approach is that the Greek version of the monitoring programme consists of the expectation of the sampling of a certain number of animals (50/60 bovines and 14 In their response to the draft report the Greek Authorities (GA) give more details on this statement. 15 In their response to the draft report the GA highlight that these two texts are the backbones of the TSEs surveillance in Greece. 16 These texts were subsequently available to the mission team in a translated form. 17 In their response to the draft report the GA confirmed the delegation of training competence from the central to the local level. 18 In their response to the draft report the GA state that a Ministerial decision is not really the proper instrument to introduce such an obligation and that the Presidential decrees (133/92 for BSE and 35/1995 for Scrapie) are more relevant and still in force for the notification of cases. 8 330/350 small ruminants, according to the annex of the CD 98/272/EC) to be examined on the basis of a clinical suspicion of TSE, without taking into consideration the other sub populations. No specific mention is given in the Decision of the Ministry of Agriculture in terms of the competent authority responsible for verifying the use of TSE diagnostic methods and protocols in the laboratories approved20. 5.1.2. Awareness and training According to the CCA, the Prefectures Veterinary Services (PVS) are responsible for providing training activities related to each level involved in TSE surveillance. · Awareness: the specific documentation (leaflet, guideline, etc.) issued by the CCA to be used in the PVS to ensure a similar level of intervention throughout Greece (taking into account that according to Art. 1 of Commission Decision 98/272/EC the competent authorities have to ensure the awareness of all the parties involved) was not provided to the mission team and was not available in the Prefectoral Veterinary Services visited. The CCA stated that they had organised a one day seminar with the responsible veterinarian for animal health of each PVS, but the date, the agenda and the list of participants were not available. During the meetings the PVS, the actions presented to the mission team were limited to press releases and articles recently published in local newspapers and concerning the new set of legislation, as well as the transmission of the legal decisions to the LVS21. · As regards the awareness of the farmers, the competent authorities rely mainly on the frequent visits of the official veterinarians of the Local Veterinary Services (LVS) to the farms where they are mainly acting as practitioners (free service). However, the absence of documentation specifically produced for this target result in a major difficulty in demonstrating the effectiveness and the harmonisation of these actions. This was confirmed in the visit on the spot, where the farmer, manager of a very high genetical quality dairy cow herd and very well informed of all subject linked to livestock farming, stated that he had received information mainly from TV news rather than directly from the LVS8. · Training of the official veterinarians: no training courses were organised to take into account the different specific task of the staff (slaughterhouse, farms, etc.). In the slaughterhouses visited, it was noted that the veterinarians are only aware of the existence of "typical symptoms" of TSEs, and on this basis, exclude the possibility of considering other symptoms in the ante mortem inspection. On the 19 In their response to the draft report the GA confirm their different interpretation of annex of CD 98/272/EC. 20 In their response to the draft report the GA are satisfied that the NRL is operating effective TSE diagnosis methods and protocols as it is located in the Veterinary Faculty of the University of Thessaloniki. The CCA do not consider that their senior administrators have the background or the technical expertise to carry out the verifications foreseen in the CD 98/272/EC. 21 In their response to the draft report the GA give more details on the intra-service awareness and training (circular letters, seminars, video tape) and on what has been done to increase the awareness of the farmers. 9 other hand, some courses have been recently organised to specifically address the "active" surveillance system and the use of rapid post mortem tests. · Training of the PVP: according to the Greek Authorities (CCA and PVS), the PVPs are not playing an important role in the fight against TSEs, because they are mainly involved with pet animals and the supply of veterinary drugs. The official staff are also requested to cover the demand of the farmers to treat their animals (mainly bovines and small ruminants) and, more generally, to provide the necessary interventions concerning pathological conditions, tasks usually provided by the PVPs. This is resulting however in direct sanitary control of the farms present in Greece by the LVS, which is requested to provide this "public" service to the farmers, to register each visit, and to report to the PVS in a monthly overview the clinical interventions and the treatments provided as well as their results. According to the competent authorities, the lack of interest of the few PVPs dealing with ruminants is the main reason for the poor involvement of the PVPs in the flow of information concerning TSEs to the CA22. · No clear and harmonised procedure has been transmitted to the PVPs and the official veterinarians of the LVS to describe in practical terms what to do in cases of TSE suspicion in a farm or in a slaughterhouse e.g. movement restriction, clinical and epidemiological investigation, use of treatment and/or laboratory examination, sampling (fixation, accompanying documents, sending)23. 5.1.3. Compulsory notification According to the competent authorities BSE has been notifiable for the general public, including farmers and PVPs since 1992 (Presidential Decree 133/92, transposition of Commission Decision 92/450/EC, as repealed by Commission Decision 98/12/EC) and Scrapie is notifiable since 1995 (Presidential Decree 35/95, transposition of Council Directive 91/68/EC). As the Presidential Decree 133/92 does not give more specification on the time of the compulsory notification (at the time of the suspicion or at the time of the confirmation) it is not clear to the mission team if there is a legal basis to notify the suspicion of TSEs according to art.2 of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. In one Prefecture, the PVS did not receive any official notification concerning a sample of a bovine from the area sent to the NRL by a PVP. No suspect cases of BSE/Scrapie have been officially notified so far24. 5.1.4. Procedure to rule out TSEs According to the Greek Authorities, no instructions are in place to ensure a proper ruling out of TSE25. In particular: 22 In their response to the draft report the GA give more details on the training provided to the private veterinary practitioners. 23 In their response to the draft report the GA declare that the TSEs surveillance programme 99 and 2000 provide all relevant information. 24 In their response to the draft report the GA declare that the suspicions are notified to the regional and local veterinary services. 10 1. During the visits in the Prefectures it became clear that the flow of information from the LVS concerning the control of the health status of the farms (registration of the pathological conditions, registration of the treatments, etc...) is simply not considered and processed as an indicator of hypothetically suspect conditions, suggestive of TSE. For instance, the repeated treatments provided to the same animals, the thorough examination of recurrent clinical conditions in the farms or a failure in the treatment are not taken into account at all. 2. In one of the Prefectures visited, small ruminants displaying behavioural changes/ neurological disorders were sampled by the LVS to investigate the reasons for these pathological conditions. Despite the vast majority of samples being confirmed negative (mainly for the detection of Listeria), no samples have been forwarded to the NRL to exclude TSE and no immediate actions have been taken in terms of notification of TSE official suspect26. A negative result concerning examination for one of the possible conditions (Listeria) can not result in the definitive diagnosis of the pathological condition of the animals sampled. In this case, according to art.3 of CD 98/272/EC the animals must be notified as suspect, pending the confirmation/exclusion of TSEs performed by the Laboratory concerned. No instructions have been provided to the mission team to demonstrate that in the case of inconclusive results the procedure always includes the official notification of a TSE suspect and the further examination of the same sample for different pathologies. Moreover, according to the CCA, the flock is supposed to be subject to further examination and sampling by the LVS, but on different animals, which can not bring any additional information to clarify the above mentioned inconclusive result27. No evidence has been found in the two PVS visited that bovine samples are sent to the RVLs. 3. In the farm visited, high production dairy cows are reared and regular hypocalcaemiae are observed; the farmer buys the medicine at the PVP practice and applies the treatment himself. The PVP and the official vet of the LVS of the farm, who were present at the time of the mission visit stated that they were not aware of any cases of such a disease in this farm. The farmer stated that sometimes the treatment does not work and the cow finally dies without any further examination. The steps 1, 2 and 3 described in the annual report on the monitoring programme of the Greek authorities to rule out TSE is not complying with what really happens. 5.1.5. Movement restrictions in case of suspicion · The specific investigations as foreseen in art.3 of CD 98/272/EC are not performed in the case of suspects, but only in the case of TSE confirmed animals. 25 See foot note n°23 26 In their response to the draft report the GA confirm that the regional veterinary laboratories should refer all inconclusive samples to the TSE reference laboratory. 27 In their response to the draft report the GA confirm this procedure based on a flock-basis approach; the replacement animals should preferably present clinical signs or be linked with the animal previously sampled (progeny, cohorts) to be sampled. 11 5.1.6. Monitoring programme 5.1.6.1.Sample size · According to the information provided by the Greek authorities, around 250,000 cattle aged over two years are present in Greece. As regards the sample size, 30 samples should be taken per year according to the part A of the annex of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. · The discussion on the monitoring programme performed in 1999 and 2000 was mainly held in the NRL, where all the files concerning the samples taken were made available after some practical difficulties (see below)28. According to the Greek annual report of the monitoring programme notified to EU Commission in relation to art.4 (2) of Commission Decision 98/272/EC, 20 and 22 samples from bovines have been examined in the NRL during 1999 and 2000, respectively. According to the information gathered during the discussion, several discrepancies were observed, at least for the samples concerning the examination for BSE (bovine). As regards 1999, only one animal out of the 20 sampled can be considered eligible for the monitoring programme: as regards the other animals, they came from MCF outbreaks and different tissues (tonsils, spleen and lymph nodes) were tested but not the brainstem. As regards 2000, only four animals out of the 22 sampled can be considered eligible for the monitoring programme: all the other samples were unfit to be tested (autolysed samples) or belonged to non relevant sub-populations (no clinical signs compatible with TSE, age). Many of the samples were delivered to the NRL by private companies (Insurance), one directly by a farmer29, or analysed for the training of the laboratory staff. Two samples out of the four considered eligible for the monitoring programme came from animals where TSE was not excluded by the veterinarians (LVS and private practitioner); however, no official declaration of a suspect has been notified to the CCA and to PVS. 5.1.6.2. text: BACKGROUND 4.1.Summary of previous mission results The previous mission was undertaken from 24 to 27 August 1998. It was one of the first missions in Member States to evaluate the implementation of Commission Decision 98/272/EC (epidemiosurveillance of Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies). The report of this mission is available under reference number: XXIV/1436/98/MR ­ Final on the Commission's Internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/sweden/index_en.html At the time of the previous mission, due to the early stage of the implementation of Commission Decision 98/272/EC, mainly the legal transposition and the initial phases of the monitoring programme for 1998 could be assessed. The recommendations made in the previous report are outlined in section 5 under the appropriate section headings in italics. All recommendations were judged to have been properly addressed on the basis of the response of the competent authorities to the draft report. Two earlier missions carried out in October 1996 (doc. VI/8077/96a) and November 1997 (doc. XXIV/1003/98) focussed on the feed ban of mammalian derived proteins to ruminants, although the microscopic examination of ruminant feed for the presence of MBM was not implemented at that time. 4.2.Background to present mission Although the E.U. legislation concerning BSE epidemio-surveillance and the feed ban has been amended since 1st January 2001, this mission concentrated mainly on the evaluation of those issues until the end of 2000. Only general information concerning the implementation of the new amendments have been collected and put into the present report when considered appropriate.

Responsibilities Three official Bodies belonging to the Ministry of Agriculture are mainly responsible for the implementation of Commission Decision 98/272/EC: The Swedish Board of Agriculture (SBA), which is in charge of co- ordination at central level and practical implementation through the District veterinary offices; The National Food Administration (NFA) responsible for the controls in slaughterhouses and cutting plants; The National Veterinary Institute (NVI) in charge of planning and managing of the monitoring programme and laboratory examinations; The County Boards (regional level), which must comply with both SBA and NFA regulations, are in charge of ensuring co-ordination and supervision at district veterinary office and slaughterhouse level within a region. 5.1.2. Administrative framework The legal transposition of Commission Decision 98/272/EC and the national measures foreseen in case of a BSE suspicion are described in detail in the previous mission report (XXIV/1436/1998). Since the last mission the national legislation was amended in 1999 to include all TSE(s) of animals in the Swedish Act on epizootic diseases (all TSE(s) were compulsory notifiable since 1995 following a SBA regulation). Following another amendment to the SBA regulation in 1999, farmers will now receive full compensation (100 %) for losses caused by the application of restrictive measures applied in case of BSE suspicion or/and confirmation11. 5.1.3. Awareness and training · "The mission recommended to convene a meeting of the "information working group" comprising the different bodies involved in TSE control, to inform on the different aspects of the provisions of Commission Decision 98/272/EC". Since the last mission several meetings of the "Information working group" were held. All the different bodies responsible for TSE control were involved in these meetings including the breeding associations. During these meetings all control bodies involved in TSE epidemio- 11 In their response to the draft report the Swedish competent authorities noted that a full compensation for farmers was already foreseen in the previous legislation. 8 surveillance were informed of the different aspects related to Commission Decision 98/272/EC. Before the previous mission NVI had already distributed a leaflet (A5- size, nine pages) containing information about BSE to all veterinarians. This leaflet described amongst other things, the clinical symptoms, ruling out and differential diagnoses for BSE. As regards the clinical signs, ruling out and the need to suspect BSE, the instructions were as follows: "Clinical picture is variable and two cases are seldom clinically identical." "If, after clinical examination, you can not rule out the possibility that the animal could have BSE, you should notify it to the competent authorities." "An animal with central nervous symptoms shall not, under any circumstances, be slaughtered or transported from the holding unless a definite alternative diagnosis has been established." The Vet@ system was used to find a bovine animal, which was diagnosed as having neurological symptoms during 2000 and resided in one of the areas covered by the mission. The mission team visited the veterinarian, who had examined this animal to evaluate the ruling out procedure. The veterinarian explained that the animal had convulsions on 1 October 2000 and was treated with vitamin B, corticosteroids, Calcium and Magnesium. In addition, he took a blood sample, which was sent to a laboratory. Magnesium levels turned out to be low. The animal recovered and according to the veterinarian is still alive. This holding had similar cases in the past and in fact, one such case was sent for BSE examination. The problem was assumed to be mainly nutritional and after dietary changes no additional cases have occurred. A brochure concerning scrapie was sent to all keepers of small ruminants and all veterinarians in spring 1999, and another brochure concerning BSE was sent in autumn 1999 to all registered keepers of bovines, hauliers and veterinarians. This brochure contains information about BSE symptoms and epidemio-surveillance of BSE. In particular keepers were informed about the monitoring programme and asked to report old cattle affected by progressive diseases to the veterinarian, who has to judge if the animal has to be sampled and included in the monitoring programme. The brochure also provides information on the legal obligation of keepers to report suspect BSE cases to a veterinarian. A new brochure on BSE has been drafted. According to the competent authorities the brochure will be sent to all parties involved by the end of February 200112. 12 In their response to the draft report (dated 14 June 2001) the Swedish competent authorities noted that the brochure has already been sent to all bovine keepers, veterinarians and registered hauliers. 9 · "The mission recommended collecting information on the different aspects relating to awareness and training on TSEs, as this was part of the annual report to be presented to the Commission, under article 4 of the Decision". All activities relating to awareness and training have been included in the annual reports sent to the Commission in 1998 and 1999, following Article 4 of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. 5.1.4. Surveillance on farm The bovines examined for BSE in Sweden between 1998 and 2000 can be split into two broad categories: animals notified because of central nervous symptoms and other animals sampled in the framework of the monitoring programme without specific suspicion of BSE. Activities in relation to the first category are described in this section and section "surveillance at slaughterhouses" below, whereas the second category is described under "monitoring programme" later in the report. Until January 2001, all BSE suspects and all cattle included in the monitoring programme originated from farms. The district veterinary offices played a key role in this exercise, because of their close connection to farmers and frequent visits to holdings. During 1998, 19 cattle were notified to the competent authorities because of central nervous disorders. As a result of the clinical and epidemiological examinations, two cases were handled as official suspects, whereas in four cases BSE was ruled out on the basis of response to treatment (the animals recovered). The remaining 13 animals were sampled and included in the monitoring programme. 21 and 20 cattle were notified in 1999 and 2000, respectively. One case was handled as an official suspect in 1999 and the remaining animals were included in the monitoring programme. 5.1.5. Surveillance at slaughterhouses So far no bovines were declared as BSE suspects from slaughterhouses. Four animals in 1998 and two animals in 1999 were sent for examination from slaughterhouses in the framework of the monitoring programme. The inspection team visited a slaughterhouse approved for emergency slaughter. Most of the animals arriving in this slaughterhouse were already killed on farm and brought to the plant accompanied by a veterinary certificate of ante-mortem inspection (carried out on farm). The other slaughterhouses visited were approved for normal slaughter only but one of these had a special unit carrying out so called "feed slaughter" (slaughtering 10 of animals not fit for human consumption and intended for feeding to zoo animals). On inspection of the records of the last half of 2000 in these slaughterhouses, the mission team made the following findings: Bovines that died or were found recumbent either during transport or after arrival were not examined for BSE even in the absence of a definite alternative diagnosis. Some of these animals had not responded to repeated treatments for hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia. Bovines suffering from progressive conditions were not sampled and examined for BSE. For example: one animal was presented for normal slaughter although it was emaciated, in poor general condition, apathetic, salivating, grinding its teeth and had difficulties in standing up. The carcass was condemned because of emaciation, abnormal colour and smell but not examined for BSE in the framework of the monitoring programme. One animal arrived at the emergency slaughter unit in November 2000 accompanied by a Veterinary Certificate indicating that the animal was: sensitive to light, touch, voice, had convulsions, twitchy eyes, could not stand up and did not respond to Calcium and Magnesium therapy13. This animal was neither suspected for BSE nor sampled in the framework of the monitoring programme but was instead approved in post mortem inspection except partial condemnation of 71 kilograms from the left front quarter (pressure injuries and oedema). 5.1.6. Monitoring programme (Annex A of Commission Decision 98/272/EC before being amended) · The existing data on the number of nervous disorder in cattle and sheep should be double-checked for accuracy. After the last mission the computerised veterinary database has been reviewed and the number of diagnoses considerably increased. Moreover a working group has been established to issue guidelines for veterinarians to standardise the different diagnoses. However due to technical problems (slow connection to the server) the team did not have the opportunity to query the database. · In the framework of the monitoring on certain cattle displaying clinical signs compatible with BSE, the mission team recommended that the choice should be more targeted on cattle with progressive disease conditions. 13 In their response to the draft report the Swedish competent authorities noted that the animal had responded to treatment with calcium and magnesium, but did not recover completely and had been sent for emergency slaughter for welfare reasons. 11 Instructions were sent in 1998 and 1999 to 10 district veterinary offices (out of 70) asking them to sample at least 5 bovines to be included in the monitoring programme. The aim of those instructions was to reach the minimum number of bovines examined annually in the framework of the monitoring programme. The approach was changed in autumn 1999, when detailed information, about the necessity to sample animals showing "signs of chronic illness" or "marked decrease in production" or "moribund animals without signs of infection or trauma", was sent to all farmers and veterinarians. In 1998, all of the 41 cattle included in the monitoring programme did not fit into the sub-categories as laid down in annex A of Commission Decision 98/272/EC (e.g. "moribund animals without signs of infectious or traumatic illness" or "animals displaying other progressive conditions"). A large proportion (17/41) of samples was taken from animals suffering traumatic or infectious conditions such as: post-operative peritonitis, septicaemia, mastitis, arthritis, gastritis, endometritis or pneumonia.14 In 1999, 39 bovines were sampled in the framework of the monitoring programme. From this total of 39 animals, 26 were suffering from conditions like mastitis/septicaemia, endocarditis, traumatic peritonitis, abomasal displacement (also post-operative peritonitis), laryngitis, tympany, trauma, higroma, pneumonia.14 The results of 2000 were similar: out of 36 animals sampled in the framework of the monitoring programme the majority were suffering from arthritis, septicaemia, gastric ulcer, mastitis, endocarditis, foot lesions, traumatic peritonitis, tympany, abomasal displacement, ketosis or pneumonia.14 According to the data provided by the competent authorities, in 1999 tetanus was suspected in 8 cattle, none of them was either suspected of BSE or included in the monitoring programme. Moreover, 6 brains were received in the reference laboratory in 2000 because of listeriosis suspicion, however none of them was declared as a BSE suspect or included in the monitoring programme. The mission team had the opportunity to discuss the monitoring programme with officers of a district veterinary service. The district was one of the 10 districts involved in 1998 and 1999 in the monitoring activities. According to the officers, as animals displaying behavioural or neurological signs are compulsory notifiable in Sweden, in the framework of the monitoring programme they were concentrating on moribund animals without signs of infectious or traumatic illness and animals displaying other progressive 14 In their response to the draft report the Swedish competent authorities noted that the anamnestic data of the above animals justified their inclusion in the monitoring programme as they would fit the animal categories as foreseen in Annex A of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. 12 disease conditions. In this district one animal in 1999 and 2 animals in 2000 were sampled after developing post-operational peritonitis. This district office is also in charge of a rendering plant where autopsies of fallen stock are performed but no samples have been taken from there before the beginning of the new monitoring programme (January 2001)15. The competent authority should take measures to ensure that requirements as laid down in Article 6 (e) of the Council Directive 64/433/EC are met. 26 With regard to the approval procedures of the premises slaughtering on the farm:

The competent authority should enforce controls on the feed mills, in the intermediaries and at the farm level as already recommended in the previous report DG (XXIV/1506/1998).

The competent authority should include risk assessment in targeting official feed samples for the possible presence of bone fragments in compound feed and take measures to comply with the requirements for labelling of final samples as laid down in Commission Directive 76/371/EEC.

The competent authority should ensure appropriate corrective actions in cases of MMBM contamination. The time delay associated with laboratory results should be reduced or some other solution provided. With regard to epidemio-surveillance of BSE:
The competent authority should produce clear guidelines for the destruction of BSE contaminated carcasses and internal organs as already recommended in the previous report DG (XXIV/1506/1998).

The competent authority should ensure that information is collected on each sampled bovine, as regards the clinical history, signs and age of the animal in addition to the service, which has requested sampling. This information should be available to the Commission Services on request.
The competent authority should fulfil all requirements as regards the contents of the annual report as laid down in Annex II of 98/272/EC, as amended. With regard to SRM:

The competent authority should set up a system to ensure and check that SRM is removed and destroyed in accordance with Annex I, points 2 to 5 of Commission Decision 2000/418/EC. Departmental level Description of the system France is administratively divided into 100 Departments. Each department has decentralised veterinary services under the responsibility of a Director of Veterinary Services. The Director of Veterinary Services has the responsibility to define the organisation of its services according to the specificities of its department. These services are responsible for the implementation of health regulations concerning the protection of animal health, food hygiene and the protection of the environment. They are under the direct authority of the Prefect of the Department, who represents the State authority at departmental level. At departmental level, the DPMA is represented by 26 DDAM (Departmental Directorate of Maritime Affairs). The DDAM ensures the implementation of measures in the field: classification and management of production areas, suspension/closure and issuing of transport registration documents. For the classification and monitoring of production areas which involves closing and opening, samples are analysed in the coastal laboratories of IFREMER. These laboratories are situated along the French coast and provide the monitoring of microbiological, chemical and phytoplankton quality of shellfish water. The DDAM are also consulted for approval/suspension of purification and dispatching establishments. Verification In the first department visited there are 415 purification and dispatch centres for live bivalve molluscs, 33 fishery product establishments and 2 auction halls. A veterinary inspector and a part time technical assistant are in charge of the inspection and supervision of these establishments. In 2000, 154 out of the 415 centres have been inspected and all 33 fishery product establishments have been visited. There was no clear yearly planning for inspection visits and a checklist for inspection was drafted by the DSV but not used routinely. In the second department visited there are 350 purification and dispatch centres and 70 fishery product establishments. Two veterinary inspectors are responsible for fishery products and for live bivalve molluscs establishments. They are assisted by 20 technicians of the veterinary service who cover all activities of the departmental veterinary service. A detailed programme is available, specifying that the 350 purification/dispatch centres are inspected once a year and the 70 fishery product establishments are inspected every 3 months or once a year depending on the size of the establishment. 11 The practical organisation of the veterinary inspections is done at departmental level and therefore planning, use of checklists, frequency of inspection visits and sampling differ from department to department. 5.2.3. Training Description of the system The veterinary inspectors after their degree in veterinary sciences have a specialised training of 1 or 2 years at the national school of veterinary services. The auxiliary veterinary staff is trained by the agents of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fishery specifically for the tasks that they have to carry out. The technicians of veterinary services are specially trained by the State for two years after their high school diploma at the National Training Institute of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (INFOMA). The DGAL has a continuous training programme, organising courses of 1 week dealing with certain subjects as for instance in the field of fishery products, aquaculture and shellfish. Verification Training for fishery products, aquaculture and shellfish was organised in 2000, but not in 1999 or 2001. A planning for 2002 has been presented to the mission team. 5.3. Other Authorities The General Directorate of Health and the departmental directions of social and sanitary matters under the Ministry of Health are in charge of the control of public potable water and of the health of workers. The General Directorate of competition, consumer goods and repression of frauds and the DDCCRF at the Department level of the Ministry of Economy and Finance are interalia in charge of the control of additives and labelling. Accreditation of laboratories in France is done by COFRAC, the French committee for accreditation. COFRAC is a member of EA (European co-operation for Accreditation), the organisation of European accreditation bodies. 5.4. Laboratories 5.4.1. National Reference Laboratories 5.4.1.1. Marine Biotoxins Description of the system For the detection of marine biotoxins in shellfish, the AFSSA ­ LERQHA has been designated as national reference laboratory according to Council Decision 93/383/EEC. The laboratory reports to 3 Ministries: the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Consumption. 12 Verification The AFSSA-LERHQA laboratory has a good quality system in place and is currently accredited by COFRAC for PSP detection analysis since 1996 according to the norm NF EN 45001. Steps have been taken to remind the control services (instructions dated 20 November 2001) of the obligations on the industry as regards denaturing SRM. In addition, the risks of superficial contamination of carcasses by spinal 31 cords on their removal have also been identified by the health authorities. This gave rise to an amendment to the Order of 17 March 1992 concerning the requirements to be met by slaughterhouses for the production and placing on the market of fresh meat and laying down the conditions for the health inspection of such establishments (amendment introduced by the Order of 19 July 2001); it requires removal of the spinal cord of bovines aged 12 months and over prior to cutting the carcass into halves by splitting the vertebral column. This requirement, which entered into force on 1 January 2002 in all bovine slaughterhouses, now precludes, on the one hand, the risk of nervous tissue spreading onto the carcass after splitting and, on the other, contamination of the muscle masses next to the vertebral column when the cord is removed manually both by the operators and by the equipment used. 2. As far as the rules are concerned, the requirement to incinerate the vertebral columns of bovines aged 12 months and over was introduced by the Order of 2 October 2001. The formal classification as SRM was officialised by the Order of 4 January 2002. (These two Orders are amendments to the Order of 17 March 1992.) 3. The French authorities ensure that all "low-risk" meal and fats are incinerated. Although, pending establishment of specific collection in the so-called "high- risk" channel of vertebral columns of bovines aged 12 months and over, notably collection from butchers, these products were treated with "low-risk" waste, the Community requirement, that is the incineration of vertebral columns, will be complied with. The French authorities authorise only two types of disposal for the meal produced, direct incineration or storage pending incineration. No processing, including into so-called technical products, is permitted. Furthermore bearing in mind the special requirement in France for a specific dedicated procedure for the production of processed animal protein intended for petfood (as meal from ruminants is prohibited to ensure that there is no cross- contamination resulting from the existence of several channels) and the ban on the use of meal from ruminants in fertiliser production, the only type of disposal for all meal (high and low risk) is incineration. 4. Retaining two channels, high and low risk, could be unwarranted in so far as all products are disposed of by incineration. However, given the limited incineration capacity, the French authorities wanted to retain this separation to ensure priority for just-in-time incineration of TSE risk products and to store only the others. For the special case of the vertebral column, inclusion in the high-risk sector without preparation, notably as regards setting in place new logistics and the selective sorting of bones in the cutting plant, might have resulted in a requirement to store meal also containing dead animals and all SRM. It therefore appeared preferable to store meal containing only bovine vertebral columns, rather than meal containing all SRM, naturally requiring in all cases ultimate incineration 32

Operational procedures 5.6.1. Description of the system of supervision The CCA has issued checklists for the inspections of calf, pig, laying hen and fur animal holdings. These include instructions and guidelines for the completion of the inspection. The checklists were used by all inspectors during the mission and in all previous inspections checked by the mission team. While the checklist for the laying hens was complete, the checklists for the pigs and calves did not include all aspects of the Council Directive 98/98/EC e.g. concerning the staff requirements and the requirements for record keeping of medicinal treatment and mortalities. 9 During the mission some inspectors did not check all criteria mentioned on the checklist but completed some of them on presumption. There were cases where the inspector did not give the correct answer because he did not read the questions on the checklist exactly. In the beginning of each year the CCA sends a list of holdings to be inspected to the regional services, which forward this list to the corresponding municipalities. There is no date set2 for the inspection and the time period in which the inspections had been carried out in previous years depended on the municipality inspectors. The veterinarians normally perform 4 to 6 EU inspections per year. There are four copies of the inspection checklist which is signed by the inspector only: the original is given to the farmer, one copy is for the inspector himself and two copies are sent to the regional office which forwards one of the copies to the CCA. For infringement cases the CCA has drafted a special report form in which the inspector documents the deficiencies detected and gives either advice notices in the case of minor deficiencies or orders in the case of infractions. It was observed by the mission team that the inspectors preferred to give advice notices rather than orders even in cases where orders would have been more appropriate. The inspector sets a deadline on the order for remedying the deficiencies. There are no instructions concerning the appropriate length of deadlines. On one occasion a deadline of one year was set for modifying the housing system of calves older than 8 weeks from individual pens to group housing. While most revisits were done shortly after the deadline there were some revisits done several months after. The mission team observed cases where there were several revisits on a farm and at no time were any sanctions imposed. The veterinary service understands its role mainly in remedying the deficiencies and not in sanctioning. The orders have to be signed by the farmer and the inspector. The farmer receives the original, one copy is for the inspector, one copy for the police and one copy for the regional veterinary service. If an official veterinarian at a slaughterhouse has reason to believe that there has been an animal welfare infringement in an animal unit delivering the animals, he is expected to report this to the corresponding provincial office. The mission team was shown such a case. There is close co-operation between the veterinary services and the police (see chapter 5.6.3 Sanctions). The police act in all cases whereas the veterinary service is responsible for the follow-up for minor deficiencies. In court cases the inspecting veterinarians are often consulted for professional advice.

The CCA has instructed the regional and local authorities that the inspections ordered must be done within the calendar year and during all seasons. 10 Although there are guidelines laid down in the Finnish legislation to describe the norms of some specific technical requirements such as air quality, floor characteristics and light, clear guidelines are missing for the assessment of the need for artificial ventilation or the isolation of sick and injured animals. In addition there were no guidelines for formulating action plans for farmers. Staff personnel Except for the personnel in the CCA, the supervision of animal welfare issues is only a part of the tasks of the veterinary service personnel. The local (municipal) veterinarians reported that the time spent for official administrative tasks including animal welfare amounts to 10-30 % and the rest is curative practice. No income comes from the sale of veterinary drugs. The municipal veterinarians are engaged by the Municipal Health Board which requires that there is always a veterinarian on duty in the municipality. Several municipal veterinarians work together in order to achieve a permanent duty representation. The municipality gives a fixed salary for this task which represents only a part of the income of the veterinarian. The other part of the income is the payment for the administrative tasks based on the number of official inspections or the inspection time and the curative practice. The municipal board has set a price range for each veterinary treatment on the farms. All inspectors during the mission stated that they only followed the instructions from the veterinary service without interference of the municipal board.3 Number of official veterinarians in the veterinary service Region 1 Region 2 Whole Whole District Whole District Finland region visited region visited 52¹ 2 56 3 498 ¹ The number includes the veterinarian officials in the regional and municipal service, the slaughterhouses and the border inspection service. There were indications that there was a certain conflict of interest for the local municipal veterinarians related to the double function as officials and curative practice. On some occasions the municipal veterinarian issued recommendations (advice) as a follow-up after an inspection although the deficiencies detected were non-compliant with legislation and an order would have been more appropriate. One inspector who worked for 15-20 years in one municipality reported that he personally has difficulty imposing official orders to farmers whom he visits regularly. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION. The objective of the mission was to examine the legislation, structures and procedures which have been introduced in France to give effect, in the event of one or more outbreaks of either disease, to the contingency plans. This mission was the first carried out in France in this context by the FVO, following the approval of the national contingency plan for the control of CSF by Commission Decision 1999/246/EC of 30 March 19991. In addition, this was the first visit to examine the plan submitted by the French authorities for the control of FMD, approved under Commission Decision 93/455/EEC2. This mission formed part of a wider series of missions to all Member States evaluating control systems and operational standards in these sectors. 1 Official Journal L 093 , 08/04/1999 p. 0024 - 0025 2 Official Journal L 213, 24/08/1993 p. 0020 4 3. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Council Directive 64/432/EEC3 of 26 June 1964 on animal health problems affecting intra-Community trade in bovine animals and swine · Council Directive 80/217/EEC4 of 22 January 1980 introducing Community measures for the control of classical swine fever. · Council Directive 90/423/EEC5 of 26 June 1990 amending Directive 85/511/EEC6 of 18 November 1985, introducing Community measures for the control of FMD. · Commission Decision 98/139/EC7 of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in Member States. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. History The FMD and CSF non-vaccination policy adopted by the EU together with increasing trade, reduction in border controls and the illegal movements of animals have increased the risks of an outbreak and have highlighted the importance of developing suitable contingency plans. As a consequence, Community legislation has been introduced which requires each Member State to draw up a contingency plan and a manual of operations for the two diseases. The annex to Commission Decision 91/42/EEC8 sets out the criteria for FMD contingency plans and forms the basis for this evaluation. Commission Decision 1999/246/EEC9 establishes that these criteria will be applied mutatis mutandis when drawing up contingency plans for the control of CSF. Furthermore, the following Commission documents set out detailed guidelines for the preparation of contingency plans: · Contingency plans for epidemic diseases, VI/5211/95; 3 Official Journal B 121 , 29/07/1964 p. 1977 - 2012 4 Official Journal L 047, 21/02/1980 p. 0011 - 0023 5 Official Journal L 224, 18/08/1990 p. 0013 - 0018 6 Official Journal L 315 , 26/11/1985 p.0011 -0018 7 Official Journal L 038, 12/02/1998 p. 0010 - 0013 8 Official Journal L 023 , 29/01/1991 p. 0029 - 0030 9 Official Journal L 093 , 08/04/1999 p. 0024 - 0025 5 · Guidelines for FMD contingency plans in non-vaccinating countries, VI/6319/98 Rev 1. The last outbreak of CSF in France was in 1993 and remained restricted to one département. The last outbreaks of FMD were in the first half of 2001 in two départements. Based on the experiences from these FMD outbreaks, the French authorities re-evaluated their contingency plans, which are currently being amended. There will be one contingency plan common for the major epizootic diseases, with a separate manual for each disease containing details specific to the disease. 4.2.
