This national legislation is supplemented by "notes des services" sent to the départements. 5.2. Competent authority control system 5.2.1. Management structure and responsibilities The Central Competent Authority (CCA) is the Direction Générale de L'Alimentation -( DGAL) , Ministère de l'Agriculture et de la Pêche (MAP). A description of its organisation and responsibilities has previously been provided in mission reports XXIV/1112/1999, DG SANCO 1118/1999 and DG SANCO 3180/2001, which are available on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) Internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/. Details about the organisational structure can also be found on the Internet site of the French Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (http://www.agriculture.gouv.fr/.) The unit responsible within the DGAL for the preparation/implementation of the contingency plans is the Bureau de Santé Animale under the sous direction de la santé et de la protection animales (SDSPA). For special interventions going beyond the geographical limits of the département, there is the brigade nationale d'enquêtes vétérinaires et sanitaires, (BNEV), acting under the direct authority of the DGAL. Their actions in the implementation of contingency plans (CP) would be to organise movement control of live animals and/or assist in juridical investigations. Regional Veterinary Services France metropolitan is divided administratively in 96 départements, which are regrouped under 22 régions. Development of the CP within the various départements is the responsibility of the Services Vétérinaires Départementales (DSV) under the Direction de L'Agriculture et de la Foret (DDA). There will be a change as from January 2002 by which the DSV will be a separate entity (direction) separate from the DDA. The DSV, amongst the other state services, is under the direct authority of the Préfet, who is the representative of the government at the level of the département. The Vétérinaires Correspondants Régionaux (VCR) are veterinary inspectors (VI) who are based at the DSV, but have additional responsibility for their region concerning development and updating of contingency plans, organisation of simulation exercises and training courses of personnel for that purpose. On a more general level, the activities and policies of the départemental veterinary services are monitored and audited by the Contrôleur Général Interrégionaux (CGIR). The role of the CGIR at regional level will be reinforced as from January 2002. Non-official services Private practitioners who have a sanitary mandate (Vétérinaires Sanitaires, VS) are obliged, inter alia, to inform the DSV in the case of suspicion of notifiable diseases and to promote vigilance among their farming clients. 8 Farmer co-operatives known as Groupements de Défense Sanitaire (GDS) have various responsibilities in relation to cleaning/disinfection of premises, provision of identification tags in some départements (as a delegated task from the Etablissement Départemental d'Elevages (EDE)), farmer education/information, complementary compensation in case of major disease outbreaks and financial contributions for voluntary disease eradication programmes (IBR, BVD, Aujeszky's Disease). Farmers pay a yearly contribution based on the number of their animals. La Féderation Nationale des Groupements de Défense (FNGDS) co-ordinates their activities on a national level and liases with the MAP. In the regions with a high density of industrial pig farmers, there is also the Union des Groupements des Producteurs, with activities in the field of training of farmers and financial compensation for disease control programmes. 5.2.2. Resources For the year 2001, the global budget for the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries was 1.3 billion FF, from which 10 million FF is allocated outside times of crises for the preparation of the contingency plans. Following the FMD outbreaks in 2001, an estimated 110 million FF was spent to eradicate the disease. 5.2.3. Personnel The DGAL employs about 190 agents, including 52 VIs, 7 agricultural engineers, and 22 technicians. For all DSVs, about 400 VIs, 69 agricultural technical engineers, 1665 veterinary technicians, and 796 technicians (préposés sanitaires) are employed. 5.2.4. Independence The staff of the official services, both at central and départemental level, are full time employees and are independent of the industry. The VS work either as independent private practitioners or may be employed by a GDS or a Union des Groupements des Producteurs 5.2.5. Legal/enforcement powers The legal powers for all agents of the DSV are fixed in the Code Rural. For some controls (depending on the time and/or place) it is necessary to be accompanied by members of the customs, police or gendarmerie. 5.2.6. Prioritisation of controls The CGIR perform audits of the DSV on an annual basis, during which they review the contingency plans. They also have a co-ordination role at interregional level. 5.2.7. Documentation of controls The DVSs have to transmit a monthly epidemiological report as well as a yearly report to the DGAL. More specifically for the CP, the DSV have to report by means of questionnaires that are sent at regular intervals by the DGAL. The results of the audits that the CGIR perform are also reported to the DGAL. 9 5.2.8. Laboratory service (general) The National Reference Laboratory both for FMD and CSF is the Agence Française de Sécurité Sanitaire des Aliments (AFSSA). For FMD, AFSSA has two sites that can perform diagnostic analysis, one in Maison-Alfort, the other in Lyon. For CSF, AFSSA has two sites that participate in diagnostic analysis, one in Maison-Alfort for virology and one in Ploufagran for serology. AFSSA is a government agency, which provides services to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, Ministry of Health, as well as to the Ministry of Economics/Finance. AFSSA has in total 13 laboratories at 10 different sites. Funding derives mainly from the State but also from the charging of fees for work carried out. Its overall budget for the year 2000 was 474 million FF. Laboratories in the départements are under the responsibility of the Conseil Général of the département. There are 14 départemental laboratories approved for serology for CSF (Elisa and/or VN) by the Minister of Agriculture, based on recommendations from AFSSA who perform compulsory proficiency testing (blind ring tests), training of laboratory staff and audits of the départemental laboratories. Two other organisations are involved in the regulation of the laboratories: COFRAC (Comité Français d'Accréditation) is responsible for the quality accreditation of laboratories by means of audits carried out according to ISO 17025 AFNOR (Association Française de Normalisation) is responsible for the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for the performance of the various laboratory tests, sample handling, etc. 5.3. Farm registration 5.3.1. General Farm registration is compulsory and is laid down in various parts of the national legislation (see 5.1). For small ruminants, there is no derogation foreseen for farmers with less than 3 animals. Registration of bovine, porcine, ovine and caprine holdings is managed by the EDE. EDEs are bodies established under national legislation, and which operate in virtually all départements. A number of EDEs operate in two or more départements. Regardless of the species, a holding number is allocated, comprising the country code, followed by 2 digits for the département, 3 digits for the commune, and a 3- digit serial number for the holding. The EDEs visited during this mission had computer-based lists of registered farms for the different species available, with holding numbers allocated in compliance with national requirements. The same information was also available at the DSV within the département. The DSVs visited consider registration coverage complete for cattle and pigs, but recognised the difficulty of registration of small backyard- holdings keeping 1 or 2 sheep/goats 10 5.3.2. Ruminants EDEs keep data on registered holdings on local databases, and are connected to the central national database in Toulouse (BDN)10, for transferring data on bovine holdings. There is no national database for sheep and goat holdings yet, except for mixed holdings which have sheep/goats in addition to cattle. At the EDEs visited, the procedure for herd registration was satisfactorily explained and demonstrated to the mission team. The national list for bovine holdings is kept in the central database which was shown to the mission team at the DGAL.. 5.3.3. Pigs Most départements have their own computer-based register of pig holdings and this was shown to the team during one of the visits to the DSVs. The DGAL has requested, in a note sent on 22/12/2000, that all EDEs send data from their local database to the central national database in order to complete the national register of pig holdings, in order to comply with the requirement of Directive 97/12/EC, art 18b. To date, this has not been accomplished. It was explained by the CCA that for pig holdings, there is an additional entry foreseen in the national database to record the slapmark number of the farmer or 'indicatif de marquage', which is the number which is used in practice to identify the pigs, since the herd registration number is too long to be used as slapmark. A pig farmer can have more than one slapmark number because a number is attributed to sub-units of the farm more than 500 meters apart. It was noted during the visit to the pig farm, that in practice, farmers use their slapmark number rather than their official holding registration number. 5.4. Animal identification 5.4.1. General Animal identification is compulsory and the relevant directives are transposed into national legislation (see 5.1). EDEs are responsible for recording and distribution ear tags for cattle and small ruminants, although these tasks may sometimes be delegated to the GDS. Farmers are responsible for identifying their animals (cattle, small ruminants, pigs) 5.4.2. Bovines Bovine animals are identified by double ear tags bearing a unique number. Births have to be notified to the EDE and the calf has to be tagged within 7 days. The farmer signs an agreement to act as the identifier. In case of tag losses, he orders and replaces the tag as soon as possible. When a bovine has lost both of its tags, it is the agent of the EDE who has to replace the tags, at the expense of the farmer, after thoroughly establishing the identity of the animal. In case of doubt, the animal is destroyed. 10 Commission Decision 2001/399/EC approved the national database for bovine animals under certain conditions. 11 During the visits to the EDEs, it was said that such cases do occur, but are rare. It was stated by the DSV that the requirement for annual checks on the identification of 10% of the bovine holdings (EC 2630/97, modified by 1898/2000), are partly biased towards holdings with a higher frequency of tag losses and/or other non- compliances. A farmer can lose the right to act as identifier and, in such cases, an agent of the EDE will become responsible for all tagging, with an increased cost to the farmer. During the visits to the bovine farms, it could be seen that all animals were properly identified according to the requirements. 5.4.3. Small ruminants A detailed description of sheep/goat identification can be found in a recent FVO report on the French Brucella melitensis eradication programme (see report DG SANCO 3180/2001). The EDE is the distributor of the eartags and each year the farmer has to order a required number of tags. There is no official procedure for official controls on identification of small ruminants although it is indirectly done at the time of brucellosis prophylactic testing. Replacement of tags in case of loss is the responsibility of the farmer. There is a proposal for new legislation on identification of small ruminants linked to the future creation of the national database. Ther

Potato trade in Poland 4.1.1. General Exports and imports comprise less than 1% of the total crop supply. Potatoes are mainly processed to produce starch and alcohol, although there is a growing food processing sector. In 1997, 43.5% of the national crop was used for animal feed, 23% for direct human consumption, 5.3% for processing and 13.8% for planting. Post-harvest losses accounted for 14.4%9. Plant health situation in Poland Poland is considered free from brown rot and Globodera pallida. The root knot nematodes Meloidogyne chitwoodi and M. fallax have also not been detected in the country. The Polish authorities report that no case of potato spindle tuber viroid has been found in field crops for at least a decade. There were a total of 2,088 cases of ring rot confirmed in Poland between 1998 and 2000. The disease has been found in all 16 voivodships (equivalent to a region). Globodera rostochiensis (Ro1) is found throughout Poland, although there are some areas in the south-east that are still free of this nematode. Three foci of Globodera pallida (Pa3) have been detected in one village in the north of the country. One focus has been eradicated and the other two are under eradication. Potato wart disease, pathotype 1(D1) was common during the 1950s. Since then, in an effort to eradicate the disease, only resistant varieties have been planted. Despite this, viable resting sporangia are still found in the soil. Pathotypes 2 and 3 are known to occur in the south of the country. Ditylenchus destructor has a restricted distribution in Poland, in the last five years, the highest incidence has been in eastern and central regions; no cases have been found in the western regions. D. destructor is regarded as a quarantine pest on certain propagating material, including seed potatoes. 7 Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) is considered to be a quarantine pest in Poland. It is found in glasshouse crops throughout the country and in the south, in tobacco crops. Potato stolbur phytoplasma occurs sporadically; 34 cases were confirmed between 1998 and 2000. Quarantine measures were imposed. Beet necrotic yellow vein virus (BNYVV) has a quarantine status in Poland. The pathogen occurs in some regions of the country. The Colorado beetle is present in all regions of Poland. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Plant health system in Poland 5.1.1. Structure of the plant health system The duties of the Plant Protection Inspection Service are implemented by the structure consisting of the Main Inspectorate of Plant Protection and Voievodeship Inspectorate of Plant Protection. 5.1.1.1. The Main Inspectorate of the Plant Protection Inspection Service The Main Inspectorate of the Plant Protection Inspection Service (MIPP) is the "single and central authority" for plant health within the meaning of Article 1 of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. It is based in Warsaw and is part of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) reporting directly to the Minister or to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. The MIPP is responsible for directing, supervising and controlling the various institutions involved in plant protection, including the Central Laboratory in Toru, the 16 Voivodeship Inspectorates and for co-operation with other Ministries. It is also responsible for the introduction and supervision of regulations for the protection of crop plants. The responsibilities are implemented by: ­ issuing instructions for inspectors in field units; ­ organising and conducting training for inspectors and producers; ­ inspection of plants, fields, stored plants and plant products for the presence of harmful organisms; ­ phytosanitary inspection of plants, plant products and objects imported to Poland at BIPs; ­ export inspections and issue of phytosanitary certificates; ­ supervising the marketing, storage and use of pesticides; ­ supervising the technical condition of equipment for plant protection treatments etc. The MIPP may order national control operations in the case of quarantine pests by issuing administrative decisions. 5.1.1.2. The Voivodship Inspectorates There are 16 voivodes (equivalent to regions) in Poland. The Voivodeship Inspector of Plant Protection (VIPP) conducts on behalf of the voivode, the tasks and competencies of the MIPP. The VIPP is appointed or dismissed at the request of the Main Inspector of MIPP. The VIPP is responsible for the supervision of the potato sector, in particular: 8 ­ surveillance of potato cultivation areas and storage facilities, for harmful organisms, including the sampling and testing of potatoes and soil for potato wart disease, potato cyst nematodes and other quarantine pests. They also carry out visual inspection of crops for quarantine diseases. ­ evaluation of the threat to potatoes from harmful organisms ­ keeping records of occurrences (included suspected occurrences) of harmful organisms, as well as the area infested by such organisms, ­ in the event that harmful organisms are found, determination of infested and safety zones and supervision of eradication, disinfection and other treatments. ­ phytosanitary inspection of potatoes and means of conveyance at BIPs and inland, ­ carrying out pre-export inspections and issuing phytosanitary certificates, ­ notifying plant protection organisations of the exporting country of detention or destruction of infested potatoes. Structure of the NFA 'HVFULSWLRQ RI WKH V\VWHP The Director General and the Executive Committee are responsible for the day-to-day running of the NFA, which has a staff of about 290 at its headquarters in Uppsala. The organisation of the NFA consists of five departments, responsible for research and development, regulations, control, information and 8 administration. The departments co-operate in their daily work, in special projects and in intradepartmental working groups. The Food Control Department is responsible for all activities involving the implementation of regulations and the exercise of public authority in the administration's area of responsibility. Within the Department there are three Divisions ­ the Meat Inspection Division, the Inspection and Co-ordination Division and the Implementation Division. NFA supervision activities 'HVFULSWLRQ RI WKH V\VWHP The NFA carries out "normative inspections", in accordance with article 46a of the Food Decree. These are used by the NFA to supervise the local authorities and are intended to ensure that the obligations related to the national/EU regulations are followed. The NFA may comment on any deficiencies in the local official control and according to Article 46 of the Food Decree the NFA may take over the responsibility of the control and the approval of an establishment from the municipality. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: - Council Directive 91/492/EEC of 22 July 1991 laying down the health conditions for the production and placing on the market of live bivalve molluscs; - Council Directive 91/493/EEC of 22 July 1991 laying down the health conditions for the production and placing on the market of fishery products; - Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Production and trade information 4.1.1. Fishery products At present there are 1912 approved establishments, wholesale fish markets, auction facilities and factory vessels. Production and marketing establishments are concentrated primarily in Lombardia, Veneto, Emilia Romagna, Toscana and Sicilia. Fishing activity is concentrated in the Adriatic Sea and in Sicilia. 4.1.2. Bivalve molluscs There are currently 231 approved establishments, 79 of which are purification centres, and 231 dispatch centres (14 of which are floating centres). National production is concentrated on the Adriatic coast (Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Veneto, Emilia-Romagna and Puglia) with some local production areas (Taranto, Gaeta, La Spezia, Olbia, Oristano). Mussels (120 000 tonnes) are the most important product, followed by clams (Tapes semidecussatus) (50 000 tonnes) and Venus gallinae (30 000 tonnes)). Other products include other clams (Callista chione), scallops and oysters. 4.2. Previous missions 4.2.1. Summary of previous mission findings and conclusions The report of the previous mission carried out from 11 to 15 May 1998 for bivalve molluscs is available at the following Internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/index_en.html 4.2.2. Follow up by the competent authority Following the Food and Veterinary Office mission between 11-15 May 1998 concerning live bivalve molluscs, a series of guidance and co-ordination notes has been drawn up, by the Ministry of Health, on: -the official control plan; -marking of live bivalve molluscs; -relaying of live bivalve molluscs; 7 - biotoxins; -microbiological checks. -A Decree was also published on 14 October 1998 amending the annex to the D. Leg. of 30 December 1992 (N° 530 and subsequent amendments) implementing Directive 97/61/EC. Some of the recommendations listed in the mission report have been only partially addressed: monitoring programme for shellfish waters in accordance with Directive 79/923/EEC, setting up of an intercalibration network for laboratories. Furthermore, no actions have been taken on the recommendation concerning: re- immersion and setting up of a system for purification of small batches, role of the CCA in the approval of classification systems. Finally with respect to the recommendation for the Ministry of Health to have a role in the approval of the classification system and of the monitoring programme, the approach chosen at national level was in the opposite direction, that is an even more devolved delegation of competencies and powers to the regional level. 5. Description of the system 5.1.2.1.1. General The CCA is the Ministry of Health (Ministero della salute): - Dipartimento Alimenti e Nutrizione e Sanità Pubblica Veterinaria. It has the legislative power and co- ordinates the measures put in place in the regions. The Ministry of Health acts by means of application instructions under the form of explicative notes or circolari addressed to the Assessorati alla sanità. Regional/local level The regional authorities, the Assessorati alla sanità are in charge of the implementation of the legislation in the field. They co-ordinate the tasks of the Aziende Sanitarie Locali which are the bodies with implementation and enforcement duties and powers. The regions are responsible for the official controls of establishments and vessels, the controls on the products put into circulation and the classification and monitoring of the production areas for bivalve molluscs. 5.1.2.2. The staff were highly motivated, well informed and familiar with EU and international developments in this area. Official laboratories 5.1.3.2.1. Description of the system Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali 10 IZS are spread in the national territory. These centres are sometimes interregional and possess a centre in each region. The IZS is competent for the chemical and microbiological routine analyses of foodstuffs, biotoxins and phytoplankton, with the exception of the Po River delta, where the analyses are carried out by the CRM. 10 ARPA laboratories These laboratories are responsible for environment monitoring, including carrying out the analyses related to Directive 79/923/EEC for the quality of shellfish waters. 5.1.3.2.2. Verification The Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale laboratories were visited in Ferrara, Padova and Palermo. All of the laboratories were found to have adequate/good facilities with well- trained and motivated staff. All laboratories were using the prescribed official methods for both microbiological and biotoxin (where performed) determinations. All laboratories were accredited for these determinations by SINAL, the national accreditation body for Italy. A satisfactory SINAL audit report was inspected for the laboratory in Ferrara. The organisation of inter-laboratory comparison exercises is part of the remit of the NRL and is an important aspect of quality assurance procedures. International external quality assurance schemes for determination of E.coli and Salmonella in shellfish are available but none of the laboratories visited were participants. However, the Istituto Superiore di Sanità, has given scientific advice on the establishment of the relevant analyses methods. Where checked all laboratories were found to have good standard operating procedure documentation for methods. 5.1.3.3. Laboratories responsible for the own checks 5.1.3.3.1. As far as the outbreak of Ralstonia solanacearum is concerned Portugal states that "Given the characteristics of the farms and production systems in the areas where outbreaks of infection with the bacteria were detected, it was not always possible, despite the great efforts made, to precisely identify the origin of the contamination and, therefore, to successfully carry out all the surveys that were needed. Whenever infected potato fields were found, the quarantine measures required under the Directive were taken. In the case of fields that were probably contaminated, it was decided to subject them to more intensive official checks, stepping up inspection of the crops growing there. As regards contaminated irrigation water, the fact that laboratory tests on samples collected from the same watercourse at different dates often produced both positive and negative results made it difficult to have a clear overview of the situation and to take the radical step of banning irrigation. However, the Authorities kept the situation under control, issuing circulars drawing attention to the risk to plants and recommending that the water not be used to irrigate solanacea crops".
Portugal will devise a contingency plan by the end of this year to deal with any future outbreak of Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus. A copy of the plan will then be sent to the Commission.

Taking account of existing laboratory capacity, Portugal will make an attempt this year to adapt the control plan by increasing the number of tests carried out on Portuguese ware potatoes in order to detect Ralstonia solanacearum.
An attempt will be made to increase the official supervision of the PCN tests processed by the accredited body. 25

LEGAL BASIS/BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation governing the performance of on-the-spot checks in Member States and in particular: Council Directive 91/495/EEC concerning public health and animal health problems affecting the production and placing on the market of rabbit meat and farmed game meat, 6 Council Directive 92/45/EEC on public health and animal health problems relating to the killing of wild game and placing on the market of wild game meat, and Commission Decision 98/139/EEC laying down detailed rules concerning the on- spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Previous missions The following missions with special interest for this mission have been carried out by the FVO in Greece: · February-March 2000; Poultry (DG(SANCO)/1133/2000 - MR final) · September 2000; Fresh porcine meat (DG(SANCO)/1192/2000 - MR final) · February 2001; Meat products, meat preparations, minced meat and processed casings (DG(SANCO)/3159/2001 - MR final) · March 2001; Milk and milk products (DG(SANCO)/3352/2001 - MR final) Reports of these missions are available under their specific reference number on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/ In the reports of the previous missions, a number of deficiencies were identified, of which the following have special relevance for this mission: · Lack of co-ordination/co-operation between official bodies at central and regional level · Lack of veterinary resources employed by the CA · Insufficient further training organised for the official veterinarians · Problems with approval/licensing of smaller establishments in several production sectors · Lack of adequate supervision in the processing plants and on farms. 4.2. Production and trade information The Greek CCA were not able to provide the mission team with information on the annual hunting statistics, nor the number of rabbits, farmed and wild game processed annually in Greece, nor the import statistics for rabbit, farmed and wild game meat. Once a year the Greek Forestry Service issues hunting rules, in which the species covered and the hunting seasons are specified. Wild swine, rabbit, hare, and fox can be hunted without special conditions. Deer species, wild goat, wild sheep and Cretan wild goat may be hunted only under special 7 conditions. The hunting of wolves and bears is prohibited (protected species). Hunters must be registered annually. The number of registered hunters in 2000 was 193 597. The Greek CCA were not able to provide the mission team with summary statistics on the number of rabbit and farmed game holdings in the different Prefectures, although they had received raw data on the situation in 50 of 54 Prefectures before the start of the mission. The Greek CCA undertook to send the latter two data sets with their comments on the draft report. A gross overview of the number of holdings is presented in the following table: Number of Prefectures* with Rabbit farms Farmed wild swine Hare farms Deer farms 6 12 6 5 *(except Halkidiki, Agio Oros, Preveza, Trikala, which did not answer to the questionnaire of the CCA before the FVO mission). The residue control plan for 2001 included a figure of 4453 tonnes for rabbit meat production. However, according to the CCA, this figure is not up to date. 4.3. Information on animal health and zoonoses 4.3.1. OIE List A diseases Greece has in recent years had outbreaks of OIE list A diseases which could also affect wild and farmed game: OIE List A Disease Last outbreak/s Area of outbreak Current status Foot and Mouth disease 2000 Evros and Xanthi Free Sheep Pox 2000 Evros Free Bluetongue 2001 several 13 Prefectures affected Not free outbreaks Greece has a special epidemiological surveillance programme called EVROS for bluetongue, peste des petits ruminants, foot and mouth disease and sheep and goat pox in the prefectures of Evros, Rodopi, Lesbos, Xios, Samos and Dodekanisa. However, no targeted sampling for these diseases is carried out in farmed or wild game. 4.3.2. OIE list B diseases List B diseases which can also be present in the wild game, e.g. bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis (both Brucella abortus and melitensis) are present in some areas in Greece. Farmed and wild game is not examined for these diseases. 8 Under Greek legislation, it is compulsory to examine all swine (including wild swine) for trichinae. According to the Report on Trends and Sources of Zoonotic Agents in animals, feedingstuffs, food and man in Greece, in 2000, the number of wild swine analysed for trichinae was 14 and all were found negative. Trichinae were not detected in the 262 291 domestic swine investigated for this parasite. No wildlife has been examined for Echinococcus sp. The total number of positive cases in bovines, sheep and goats and pigs in year 2000 was 54488 (of 2766213 animals examined). 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Transposition of legislation Council Directives 91/495/EEC and 92/45/EEC have been transposed into Greek law by means of the following national legislation: · Presidential Decree No 11 of 14 January 1995 on public health measures affecting the production and placing on the market of rabbit meat and farmed game meat, and the killing of wild game and the placing on the market of wild game meat, in compliance with Council Directives 91/495/EEC and 92/45/EEC. The transposition is generally correct, except for Art. 17 of Directive 91/495/EEC, which has not been transposed into Greek national legislation. Separate Greek national rules on imports of rabbits and game have existed since 1990. These rules allow the imports of rabbit and farmed and wild game meat from some countries, which are not on the list of approved countries, from which Member States are allowed to import this meat according to Art. 16 of Council Directive 92/45/EEC or Art. 17 of Council Directive 91/495/EEC. However, according to the CCA, Article 15 of Council Directive 92/45/EEC (import conditions of wild game meat) has been transposed into national legislation and overrules the provisions of earlier national legislation. The CCA claimed that in practice they follow the EU rules and not the national legislation. 5.2. Competent Authority 5.2.1. Management structure No significant changes have occurred in the structure of the CA since the previous FVO mission (details in mission report DG(SANCO)/1133/2000 - MR final). At the time of the mission the Interministerial Decision describing the division of responsibilities between the Hellenic Food Authority (EFET) and the MA had not been signed. 5.2.2. Independence Official veterinarians are not allowed to pursue any additional activities, which might lead to a conflict of interest with their official duties. For taking up other work, they need the permission of the RCA. 9 5.2.3. Staff resources The number of official veterinarians employed by the CCA and the RCA has increased. The MA received 51 new posts in 2001, and 15 veterinarians recruited for these posts started in principle their new jobs on 1 March 2002. However, as the Greek VS were on strike on that day the OVs were not on duty. The CVO stated that 144 new veterinarians had started to work in the Prefectures in 2001. For 2002, the CCA have requested 70 new veterinarians for the central services, border inspection posts and official laboratories. An additional 435 temporary staff (8-month contracts) will be employed in May 2002. Of these staff, two-thirds will consist of technical and support staff. In the visited Prefectures the increase in veterinary staff could be verified except in Thessaloniki, which had lost some staff to EFET. However, the number of additional technical and support staff has not increased in the MA, nor in the visited Prefectures. For example, in the Prefecture of East Attiki, only one of the four FVS has administrative staff. The central office of this Prefecture has no administrative/support staff. 5.2.4. Recruitment and training The recruitment of the staff is organised via the central Higher Council of Selection of Personnel. The staff have a probation period of two years after which the RCA write a report on their performance to the central office, and can thus at this stage influence whether the "new" staff member stays in the Prefecture. Neither the CCA, nor the RCA in the prefectures visited, have organised special training on wild or farmed game or rabbit meat. However, the CCA stated that in April 2002 two seminars of one-week duration (one week on animal, and the other on public, health subjects) would be held for all veterinary staff of the CCA and RCA in the Institute of Lifelong Learning. Legislation on game meat will be included in the programme. The CCA stated that some Prefectures have organised training on trichinae testing. However, in two of the visited Prefectures, the veterinary staff had not participated in training courses on this subject. The CCA stated that they would organise training on trichinae for the new recruits. 5.2.5. Co-ordination of activities and prioritisation of controls The CA in Greece have not co-ordinated their activities on rabbit, farmed and wild game meat, nor have their prioritised the controls over these sectors. The rabbit, farmed and wild game meat industries have started to develop only recently and the number of producers is relatively low. The CCA have send a circular to the Prefectures in November 2001 asking them for basic information (number of approved wild game collection centres and processing houses, number of approved slaughterhouses for rabbits and farmed game, number and type of farms (rabbits, farmed and wild game)). In Thessaloniki and Pieria the RCA have recently sent out instructions to the FVS on legislative requirements for wild game (killing, processing). The RCA of Pieria have also distributed instructions on the rules applicable to farmed game to the producers. 10 Prioritisation of control activities between the visited Prefectures varied greatly. No prioritisation was noted in the visited Prefectures in respect of controls in rabbit, farmed and wild game meat production. 5.2.6. Application of definitions and derogations The Greek CA had experienced difficulties in deciding whether to classify animals as wild or farmed game. For example, in one case wild swine, which were living within an enclosed area under conditions of freedom similar to those enjoyed by wild game, were classified as farmed game, and stamped with the oval health mark (the owner of the animals had complained about this as the price received for wild game was much higher than for farmed game). Farmed wild swine were generally correctly classified, and either slaughtered in establishments approved according to Council Directive 91/497/EEC, or killed by shooting on the farm, bled and transported to the slaughterhouse for further processing. The Greek CA has not specified the production or hunting volumes (rabbit or wild game meat, respectively) under which derogations may be granted for direct sale or local markets. The whole rabbit meat production sector in Greece operates under derogations provided for in Art. 4 of Council Directive 91/495/EEC. However, derogations had not been formally given to rabbit producers in the Prefectures visited. The RCA wait for instructions from the CCA concerning the definitions of small-scale production and small quantities. 5.3. Official controls 5.3.1. Supervision of farms The supervision of the rabbit, hare and farmed wild swine farms was in general not well documented by the OV of the FVS responsible for farm supervision. The OVs stated they visited the farms for wild swine 1-2 times/year and the rabbit farms 2-4 times/month. In one FVS a logbook was kept of the visits to the rabbit farms. 5.3.2. Approval procedures The Greek CA have only recently started to give separate approvals to slaughterhouses and processing plants for rabbit and farmed game or wild game, respectively. The CCA had no lists available for the approved premises for wild and farmed game and rabbit meat. No slaughterhouses have been approved for rabbits. According to the CCA, two plants are under construction. No wild game collection centres or separate wild game processing houses have been approved. Some slaughterhouses are, however, also approved for processing wild game. These approvals had been given recently. Not all slaughterhouses, where farmed large game is slaughtered or processed, have been given an approval for this purpose. No separate authorisations have been given by the CA for the killing of the animals on the farm in the visited Prefectures. The operational licences given by the RCA, and the approvals given by the CCA, were available in the visited establishments. Some slaughterhouses 11 had also received an approval for temporary slaughter of wild swine (for Christmas season). In the Prefecture of East Attiki, it was stated that no pigs are slaughtered in the municipal slaughterhouse. However, according to the monthly report of activities of the FVS, 4-10 pigs were slaughtered monthly in this plant. The information on the official list of slaughterhouses approved for intra- Community trade is not always up to date. For example, the mission team visited a slaughterhouse which, on the list, was approved only for pigs. However, the plant had recently installed a new sheep slaughter line, which was already in use. 5.3.3. Controls in the establishments The veterinary presence in the visited slaughterhouses was sufficient. Ante and post mortem controls, and the use of the health mark, could not be verified in situ, as the plants were not in operation during the visits. The documentation of ante and post mortem records in the three slaughterhouses visited was uniform and generally satisfactory, except that no records were kept for examinations for trichinae. The OVs kept the stamps used for health marking in lockable rooms or cupboards. No pentagonal stamp for wild game meat as described in Directive 92/45/EEC was available in the one establishment, which had also been approved for wild game. The OV responsible for the supervision of the slaughterhouse with serious hygiene deficiencies (see point 5.8.) had noted them in his inspection report in October 2000, and asked for immediate rectification of the situation. The requested actions had not been taken. The RCA claimed that the slaughterhouse had been temporarily closed a few times after that, but was unable to present any evidence of further actions/sanctions taken on this matter to the mission team. 5.3.4. Trichina examination The trichinoscopic method was used for the detection of trichinae in all three visited slaughterhouses. It was also used for farmed wild swine, although Art. 6 of Council Directive 91/495/EEC states that meat from farmed wild pigs or other species sensitive to trichinae infestation shall be subjected to examination by digestion according to Council Directive 77/96/EEC. A stereomicroscope was used for the trichinoscopic examination at one of the abattoirs. In one abattoir, the team was informed that piglets were not being examined for trichinae. No positive control for trichinae was available in any of the abattoirs inspected by the team, and only in one slaughterhouse were photographs of positive cases available as reference material. A different room for the preparation of samples only existed in one of the inspected premises. In another abattoir the basin in the toilet was used to clean the tools recommended for the preparation of samples obtained from carcasses. 12 The meat which had been tested negative for trichinae was stamped using a national, rectangular stamp in two of the visited slaughterhouses, instead of the "T" stamp described in Council Directive 77/96/EEC. BACKGROUND 4.1. Introduction Those MS in which bovine brucellosis eradication programmes are approved for Community co-financing (EL, ESP, FR, IRL, IT, PT, UK/NIRL), have, in general, reached a very low prevalence (i.e number of positive herds or animals in a population) of the disease. Efforts to eradicate bovine brucellosis in Spain started in the early 1950s (principally in dairy cattle), although the present programme was started in the early 1990s. The BBEP, in addition to current requirements for herd registration and individual cattle identification, requires specific movement controls, testing, marking and removal of reactors, disinfection and slaughter compensation. Vaccination has been reduced and is now confined to small areas with a particularly high disease prevalence. In describing the epidemiological situation of the disease, the Spanish CA refer to the Livestock Health Improvement Campaigns carried out since 1990. These point to a favourable development in the disease over the past decade in that there has been a gradual reduction in the number of infected herds and animals. The figures for 1999 and 2000, however, are static10 (see annex 1). Measures, in regions where disease prevalence is low, include - stamping out, detailed epidemiological enquiries and bacteriology. 4.2. Summary of previous mission findings and follow up The previous mission to Spain to evaluate the BBEP took place from 22 to 26 November 1999. The report of this mission is available under reference number DG(SANCO)/1165/1999 MR final (web-site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/). The revised figures for the year 2000 now show a reduction from 98.6% to 98.5% of herds free from bovine brucellosis. 6 · The execution of the eradication programme complies with the approved plans. Although there are variations between the 17 AC, the sanitary status of brucella abortus in cattle is generally good and satisfactory progress is being made. The disease situation in the two ACs visited (Galacia and Asturias) had improved as a result of the efforts made in previous years. · In areas where the pre-final stage of the disease eradication has been reached (herd prevalence below 1%), the eradication strategy needs to be adapted to this new circumstance with a view to speeding up the eradication process. · The last amendments of Council Directive 64/432/EEC had not been transposed into national law. This had direct consequences for the re-qualification procedures of the animal health status of herds with reactor animals. Epidemiological situation The number of herds free from the disease has risen from 98.09% in 1998 to 98.72% in 1999, reducing slightly in 2000 to 98.61%. The number of animals testing positive has fallen from 0.41% in 1998 to 0.26% in 2000. Nonetheless, significant differences do exist between Autonomous Communities for 2000. High herd prevalence can still be observed in Andalucia (6,14%). At present, no part of the Spanish territory is officially declared Brucella abortus free in accordance with Annex A of Council Directive 64/432/EEC. 4.4. MISSION OUTCOME Note to reader: Under each of the following key point headings, the conclusions (italic type) of the inspection team are given first, followed by the main findings (normal type) that led to these conclusions. 6.1. Legislation Conclusions No major differences were observed between EU and French legislation. However, minor points of inconsistency were noticed. The French authorities have a particular interpretation of the labelling provisions of Regulation 1760/2000/EC, whereby retail outlets and butchers' establishments are not required to register the quantities of meat processed.(18) The definition of final consumer in the French legislation is more open than that in EU legislation. (18) In their reply to the draft report, the French competent authority confirmed their view that this is not a requirement of this legislation. 8 Findings During 1999, a Decree was adopted to define the responsibilities of the private sector at different points along the meat production chain (99/260 of 2 April 1999, concerning labelling and traceability of beef meat). For the implementation of Regulations (CE) n° 1760/2000 and n° 1825/2000, the CCA (DGCCRF and DGAL) have produced several "notes de services" in order to explain their provisions in more detail to the départemental authorities (DDSV and DDCCRF) and to define the delegation of responsibilities to the authorities concerned: · Note de Service DGAL/SDRRC/N2000-8031 (and Note de service DGCCRF 2000/13) relating to the labelling and traceability of beef meat · Note d'information DGAL of 28 December 2000 relating to labelling of beef meat (and Note d'information DGCCRF N2000/174) · Note TP 84 Z, which defines the programme of beef meat control activities for DGCCRF during 2002 The following elements of French legislation were noted not to be in accordance with EU legislation: ­ a label on meat must only contain information on the cutting establishment where de-boning takes place. Establishments where subsequent cutting activities take place do not have to be recorded.(19) ­ for some beef meat production (sautés and bourguignon) the information contained on the label may mention several abattoirs and several cutting establishments where the meat was processed. ­ concerning minced meat, the term "origin: France " is being used on the label instead of "prepared in France".(20) ­ retail shops and supermarkets are not forced to include registration of the quantity of meat received or delivered. The French authorities include in their national legislation (Arrêté of 8 September 1994 fixing conditions for derogation of some establishments delivering meat or meat products and not obliged to obtain sanitary approval) a general derogation for butchers selling beef. This allows the (19) In their reply to the draft report, the French competent authority stated their view that Regulation (EC) no 1760/2000 only requires recording of the establishment approval number where the meat was deboned. (20) In their reply to the draft report, the French competent authority indicated that, where the minced meat came from animals reared and slaughtered in France, and where it had been prepared exclusively in France, this approach was used to increase the legibility of the labelling for consumers. 9 sale of beef to retailers or restaurants as "collective" final consumers. This legislation allows beef meat to be sold at farm level under certain conditions. 6.2. Competent authority controls Conclusions There are no major changes in the CA structure since the last FVO mission in France. There are two authorities involved in controls over traceability: DGAL and DGCCRF. DGAL is in charge of traceability controls from the farm to the abattoirs (as well as labelling control in abattoirs). DGCCRF is in charge of traceability and labelling controls from the abattoir to the retailer. There is an annual programme of controls over traceability and labelling of beef and beef products within the food processing chain and through the retail distribution, storage and sale chain. Findings Responsibilities are shared between DGAL and DGCCRF. No major structural changes have occurred in the CA since the last mission by the FVO in November 2001, apart from the creation, within DGAL, of "Directions Départementales des Services Vétérinaires" (laid down in Décret N° 2002-234 of 20th February 2002). These Directions co-ordinate the actions of the responsible services in the implementation of public health and veterinary controls, improve collaboration between the département authorities on health policy and provide technical support. The administrative head of the département will answer to the head of the Direction. These Directions will be under the authority of the Préfet. More information concerning the structure of, and controls performed by, DGAL is available in report DG(SANCO)/3381/2001-MR final. For DGCCRF, there is national programme in place to control both traceability and labelling in the meat industry (abattoir, cutting, minced meat, meat preparations establishments, retailer, restaurants, markets, butchers and supermarkets). The frequency and the number of visits is fixed at département level. These follow minimum requirements set by the central services, which fix the minimum number of establishments to be controlled per département. In some départements a fixed number of hours of inspection per month is set in an annual programme. In most départements visited, reports with information on planning of inspections, number of premises inspected and results of these inspections (in some cases with detailed information on legal actions taken following infringements) were available. This information was collected nationally and was available at central level. There is a potential over-lapping of responsibilities since both DGAL and DGCCRF share competences in abattoirs. The outline of the national 10 control and surveillance programme is set at central level. This programme is subsequently adapted and implemented in each département by the responsible authorities. In some départements, "pôle de compétences" have been created in order to co-ordinate the performance of controls by the services concerned and the generation of results of these controls. The creation of these "pôle de compétences" was an initiative of the central services.(21) 6.3. Holding registration and animal identification Conclusions Registration of animal movements is properly implemented in farms. However, serious failures in the registration of animal movements was observed in the case of traders, collection centres and live animal markets. Findings At the farms visited, registration records were properly kept. The information matched the number of passports (containing animal health and identification information) with the animals actually present. The permitted delay in notification/registration of animal movement onto/off the farm and for notification/registration of new-born is seven days, and application of new passports is 14 days. Some inconsistencies were observed during one visit where major delays were observed in obtaining passports for young animals. Animal identification was in place on the farms visited. When an animal loses one ear-tag, the farmer may apply, following a detailed, official, procedure, either directly to the private supplying company (all recognised by the Ministry of Agriculture) or to EDE (or GDS, if delegated). This, may result in a lack of information being recorded in the data-base (see section 6.4). Checks on animal identification in farms are carried out by DGAL and DPEI (Directions des Politiques Economique et Internationale), both being Departments within the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. DPEI operates these checks in the field via DDAF (Direction Départementale de l'Agriculture et la Forêt). The planning of these checks is set out in "Circulaire" DGAL/SDSPA/C2000-8004, of 29 December 2000. At least 10% of all holdings in each département must be checked. 50% of these holdings will be inspected in conjunction with premium/animal identification checks by the DDAF. The other 50% will be inspected only for animal identification purposes by the DGAL. For this latter group, 40% will be chosen randomly and 60% following a risk analysis. During all visits, the same official standard form is used whether for premium or animal identification checks. Depending on the département, results of these inspections performed by different services (DGAL and (21) In their reply to the draft report, the competent French authority stated that the limits of competence between the two services involved are defined in the "notes de service". 11 DDAF) are collected in départemental centres in order to co-ordinate the information obtained from different sources. Special procedures are in place for the identification of bull-fight bovines born in France (Arrêté of 27 June 2000 amending arrêté of 3 September 1998 regarding identification of bovine holdings). Animals must be hot-branded as well as having two metallic ear-tags showing an individual identification number. The animal must be identified before six months of age or before leaving the holding within six months of birth, and be accompanied by a passport. Bull-fight bovine meat is allowed in France for human consumption. Traders and live animal markets are not obliged to notify animal movements to the data-base.(22) They should, however, register entry/exit of all animal movements. However, it was found that no information on animal movements is registered by traders, collecting centre or markets, and the authorities did not appear to have tried to enforce these rules. These movements are never recorded in the animal passport. More information on the CA structure and controls, holding registration and animal identification is available in report DG(SANCO)/3381/2001-MR- final. 6.4. Tracing of bovine animal movements Conclusions No major deficiencies were observed in the tracing of bovine animal movements between farms. However, problems were detected in respect of animal movements for transhumance, and where traders, collecting centres, markets and abattoirs were involved, such that many animals intended for slaughter could not be reliably traced. The database is not kept fully up-to- date due to delays in the submission of the necessary information. Findings All bovine animal movements are registered in a national database system (More information is available in report DG(SANCO)/3381/2001-MR final). Animal movements between holdings, new born and dead animals were properly registered in the database. However, some deficiencies were observed in the database operation which might adversely affect traceability of animal movement: (22) In their reply to the draft report, the competent French authority described the action taken, and planned to improve the existing system. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION. The objective of the mission was to examine the legislation, structures and procedures which have been introduced in the Netherlands to give effect, in the event of one or more outbreaks of either disease, to the contingency plans for Foot- and-Mouth Disease (FMD) and Classical Swine Fever (CSF). This was the first mission undertaken to the Netherlands for this purpose. This mission formed part of a wider series of missions to all Member States evaluating control systems and operational standards in these sectors.

text: BACKGROUND 4.1. History The Annex to Commission Decision 91/42/EEC sets out the criteria for FMD contingency plans and forms the basis for this evaluation. Commission Decision 1999/246/EEC7 establishes that these criteria will be applied mutatis mutandis when drawing up contingency plans for the control of CSF. The FMD and CSF contingency plans of the Netherlands were approved by Commission Decisions 93/455/EEC8 and 99/246/EEC respectively. The following Commission documents set out detailed guidelines for the preparation of contingency plans: · Contingency plans for epidemic diseases, VI/5211/95; · Guidelines for FMD contingency plans in non-vaccinating countries, VI/6319/98 Rev 1. 1 OJ L 121 , 29/07/1964 p. 1977 - 2012 2 OJ L 047, 21/02/1980 p. 0011 - 0023 3 OJ L 224, 18/08/1990 p. 0013 - 0018 4 OJ L 315 , 26/11/1985 p.0011 -0018 5 OJ L 023, 29/01/1991 p. 0029 - 0030 6 OJ L 038, 12/02/1998 p. 0010 - 0013 7 OJ L 093 , 08/04/1999 p. 0024 - 0025 8 OJ L 213 , 24/08/1993 pp. 0020 - 0020 5 In February 1997, CSF was diagnosed on a farm in the Southern part of the Netherlands, one of the most densely populated pig areas in the world. In this area there were between 2,500 and 2,900 pigs per Km2 and approximately 1000 pigs per farm. The last case of infection was recorded on a farm in March 1998, and a total of 429 farms were infected from February 1997 to March 1998. During the epidemic, almost 11 million pigs were destroyed. The first case during the last outbreak of FMD was officially recorded on a cattle farm in Olst on 21 March 2001 in a herd of goats in Oene, Gelderland (north of the city of Apeldorn) and was linked to the FMD outbreak in Mayenne (France). The causal agent was identified by the ID-Lelystad (now the CIDC Lelystad) as being virus type O. Following the outbreak of FMD there was an FVO mission, DG(SANCO)/3324/2001, to review and evaluate the measures taken by the NL authorities (which included suppressive vaccination with inactivated vaccine of FMD virus type O1-Manisa) to eradicate FMD and to prevent further outbreaks. The report of this mission is available on the Health and Consumer Protection Directorate General Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html. 4.2. FINDINGS 5.1. Transposition of EU legislation and national legislation. The prevention and control of animal diseases is laid down in the 1992 Animal Health and Welfare Act (GWWD). The section of the Act on animal disease control "dierziektebestrijding" provides either explicit instruction or a framework for the implementation of European legislation on veterinary 6 disease control, such as Council Directive 80/217/EEC and Council Directive 85/511/EEC. Article 31 of the GWWD authorises the Minister to take additional control measures, thus avoiding the need to follow the normal procedure, in which regulations do not come in to force until officially published in the Dutch Official Gazette (Staatscourant). Legislation can also be adopted quickly by using models that exist for many measures (transport ban, breeding ban etc). Further controls are applied through the Veterinary Practice Act (WUD), the 1957 Dry Rendering Act (Destructiewet) and the Meat Inspection Act. Council Directive 92/102/EEC is mainly transposed by I&R regulations (Regeling identificatie en registratie van dieren 2002) and the GWWD. 5.2. Competent authority control system 5.2.1. Management structure and responsibilities The veterinary service in the Netherlands involve two Ministries directly. The Ministry of Agriculture, Nature Management and Fisheries (MLNV) and the Ministry of Public Health, Welfare and Sports (MVWS). These Ministries comprise policy directorates and executive directorates/ departments. The MLNV Department of Veterinary and Food Policy Affairs (VVA), is responsible for policy and strategy. It gives directives for the execution of disease prevention and eradication. The CVO operates within this directorate. The National Inspection Service for Livestock and Meat (RVV) undertakes executive tasks for both ministries and in relation to contingency plans, is the main department dealing with the eradication of OIE list A diseases. The RVV has had a central office since 1999 and 5 regional (kring) offices. There are 3-4 districts per region (each run by a district director) each of which comprise 3-4 veterinary teams. Detailed information on the structure of the veterinary services in the Netherlands can be found in recent reports. Updated information is available on the official government web-site (http://www.minlnv.nl). 5.2.2. Resources Money voted to the Ministry each year cover operational expenses and the cost of staff employed by the MLNV. If additional personnel are required on a temporary basis due to a disease outbreak the cost is borne by the Emergency Fund for the Control of Contagious Diseases (see chapter 5.6.2). The RVV has a current annual operating cost of 91 million Euro. 5.2.3. Personnel The RVV has 1600 employees of which 1000 are inspectors, 350 are veterinarians and 250 support staff. The central organisation based in Voorburg employs 25 veterinarians and 50 non-veterinarians in 8 staff departments. In addition, 400 private practitioners have been contracted on a 7 part-time basis to perform specific official duties (e.g. OVS slaughterhouse duties). 5.2.4. Recruitment and training See Chapter 5.6.11 Independence The RVV does not permit staff to engage in work that could give rise to a conflict of interest. 5.2.5. Legal/enforcement powers Under Article 114 of the GWWD, officials designated by the Minister are responsible for compliance with disease control as established in accordance with this Act. Detection of punishable offences is the responsibility of the officials designated under the Criminal Code. Violations of Article 3 of the GWWD are punishable under the Economic Offences Act. 5.2.6. Prioritisation of controls During a disease outbreak, the prioritisation of controls is ultimately decided at Cabinet (Government) level, taking into account proposals made by the MLNV. Contingency plans have been given a high priority and funding is in place for the next five years to maintain the response capability of the RVV (e.g. service contracts, training and equipment). 5.2.7. Documentation of controls In "peace-time", the RVV undertakes a continual risk assessment of animal health taking account of the disease situation world-wide. The mission team was provided with examples of how this assessment is used to advise the MLNV policy department (VVM) and advise other departments as to the most suitable control strategies (e.g. extra BIP checks, import restrictions and luggage inspection). The mission team was also provided with data arising from the routine serological controls performed in pigs. 5.2.8. Laboratory service (general) The CIDC (NRL) was separated from ID-Lelystad from 1/1/2002. It retains the responsibility for the prevention and control of notifiable diseases and control of the registration of animal products. 8 It works for, and is directly controlled by government. The GD now has a centralised laboratory service at Deventer, however, it has no direct role in the event of a disease outbreak other than to submit samples from suspicious cases in a timely fashion to the CIDC9. 5.2.9. Import controls The Netherlands performs a non-discriminatory check on 10% of all cattle imports notified by the EU animal movement system - ANIMO. At present there is also a 100% check on even-toed ungulates from Great Britain and pigs from Belgium, Luxembourg, France and Germany. In one instance, at the district office visited, the documents confirming that an inspection had taken place on a consignment of pigs from Belgium could not be located. Animals imported from "Third Countries" are re-tagged with a Dutch identification number. 5.3. Farm registration 5.3.1. Description of system Prior to January 2002, animal identification and farm registration (I&R) was operated at a national level in co-operation between the MLNV, GD and the agricultural product boards (PVE). Since January 2002, a new I&R Bureau MLNV has been established (located in Deventer), with separate offices dealing with cattle (including the Dutch Central Database Database I&R), pigs, and sheep/goats. Changes are still in progress however, and for example the GD will remain largely responsible for I&R sheep/goats until the end of 2002 and from January, on-farm controls conducted by the I&R Bureau LNV will pass to the AID. The location of each farm (and type of activity) is identified by its unique enterprise number Uniek Bedrijfs Nummer (UBN) issued by the animal health service (GD). 5.3.2. Operation of system Some small holdings (typically described as "hobby farms") were identified during patrols carried out in response to the FMD outbreaks in 2001. These were estimated at 1% of total holdings and are believed to have now been registered by the I&R Bureau MLNV. 9 In response to the draft report, the Dutch authorities stated that, the GD has a central dissection room and a central laboratory in Deventer to analyse material sent in by cattle farmers, the authorities, production chains and other clients. The authorities give instructions to monitor etc. a number of animal diseases. In the case of classical swine fever, samples are taken from all the material received for dissection; the samples taken (tonsils etc) are forwarded to the CIDC for examination. If the RVV expresses any "suspicions" the GD, acting under the RVV's instructions, organises transport to the dissection room. The carcases are then dissected and samples taken for examination by the CIDC. A report of GD-activities under the instruction of the authorities is sent (depending on the client) to the RVV and VVA. The RVV's quality management department carries out inspections to monitor the quality of the service provided; the laboratory is also accredited by Sterlab (national accreditation body). 9 5.4. Animal identification Bovines Bovines are double ear-tagged within 3 working days of their birth. Ear tags contain the country code (NL), a unique 9 digit identification code (ID code), with check digit, and a bar code corresponding to the ID code. A version number is also included to know the number of replacement ear tags. Imported cattle from other MS keep their original ID code and the CDB notified within 3 working days of arrival on the farm. Cattle imported from "third countries" must be identified within 3 working days of arrival on the farm. Small ruminants Small ruminants are ear-tagged (UBN number, individual number optional) within one month of birth or prior to transport when leaving the farm. Imported small ruminants must be tagged within 3 working days after arrival on the farm, unless slaughtered within 30 days. There is no central database for sheep and goats, however, holders of sheep and goats must be registered with the GD (in the process of being taken over by the I&R Bureau MLNV), which assigns a UBN to the approved holding. The GD records the following data: name, address, veterinarian, species, number of animals and nature of the establishment. Each year a form is sent to farmers who enter any changes on the farm situation and number of animals. The GD processes the data and updates the register. After changes have been entered the annual contribution has been paid, the GD sends an order form with which the farmers can order new ear tags. All sheep inspected at the market/collection centre were properly identified. Pigs Pigs are to be ear tagged within 1 week of weaning, or prior to transport when leaving the farm. Pigs imported from a "third country" should be ear- tagged within 3 working days of arrival on the farm, unless slaughtered within 30 days. There has been a central database since 1996, with the registration of herds (UBN number) and the issue of ear tags with UBN (unique individual numbers optional). The CCA explained that to their knowledge nearly 100% of producers use unique individual numbers. The pigs inspected at the abattoir were individually and uniquely identified (by plastic and metal tag) and this was recorded in movement certificates. 5.5. Movement controls 5.5.1. Description of the system Bovine The Dutch CDB is recognised as fully operational (Commission Decision 1999/546/EC). Cattle movements within the Netherlands do not have to be 10 accompanied by a passport and those for export are issued with a passport by the I&R Bureau MLNV. When moving animals, the keeper can update the CDB on-line, by letter/fax or via the phone using the numbered keys. The CCA is trying to discourage letter/fax communication, as there is a three-day time period for notifying the system of departure and arrival. On arrival, the holding is placed under movement restrictions for 30 days. This also applies to veterinary clinics and the veterinary school at Utrecht. On reviewing the system it was noted that there were a lot of "floating cattle10". Due to the numbers, the system was set up to list those animals for which a notification had been outstanding for 7 days. In the final meeting, the CCA stated that in the last month alone the numbers had been reduced from 500,000 to 50,000. Furthermore there are plans to modify the system so that rendering plants update the CDB when animals are collected. Spurious errors such as arrival dates preceding departure dates were evident on checking a few holding records. When errors are detected (for example the system generates an error message for certain types of implausible entry), the farmer is sent a letter requiring amended details and a small administrative charge is made. During the market visit, animals from the intake register were selected at random and a check made on the CDB from a remote terminal. There was a "transit" notification for those animals selected. Small ruminants Animal keepers must keep a farm register recording movements on and off the holding, although these were not inspected on-the-spot by the FVO team. Dealers are obliged to keep a weekly trading register that must be retained for a minimum of three years containing: date of purchase and sale, name and address of purchaser/seller, number of animals purchased/sold, address of collection centre for purchase/sale and loss of tags. For animals in their possession for more than 5 working days, dealers may come under the I&R regulation of 2002 (Regeling identificatie en registratie van dieren 2002). There is a thirty-day standstill on farms following the introduction of a
