BACKGROUND 4.1. Introduction European Union (EU) funding for the bovine brucellosis eradication programme in Portugal commenced in 1987 under Commission Decision 87/270/EEC and has been continued every year. In 1989, 86% of animals were positive (as determined by serology), but by 1998 this had fallen to 0.22% (c. 0.52% of herds infected). The BBEP, in addition to current requirements for herd registration and individual cattle identification, requires specific movement controls, testing, branding and removal of reactors, disinfection and slaughter compensation. Vaccination was discontinued in continental Portugal in 1992. 2 Official Journal L 145, 13/06/1977 pp. 44-47 3 Official Journal L 038, 12/02/1998 pp. 10 ­ 13 4 Official Journal L 347, 12/12/1990 pp. 27 ­ 29 5 Official Journal L 224, 18/08/1990, pp. 19 - 28 6 Official Journal L268, 14/09/1992, pp. 1 - 32 7 Official Journal L 355 , 05/12/1992 pp. 32 - 36 8 Official Journal L 204 , 11/08/2000 pp. 1 - 10 5 4.2. Summary of previous mission findings and follow up The previous mission to Portugal to evaluate the BBEP took place from 20 ­ 29 October 1999. The report of this mission is available under reference number DG(SANCO)/1162/1999 MR final (web-site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/). Results of follow-up/actions by the CCA General assurances were received in letters from the CCA that the recommendations contained in the report would be implemented in 2000. In particular: · The Regional Veterinary Services were instructed to fully implement Decreto Lei No 157/989 (the transposition of Council Directive 64/432/EEC) from February from February 2000. · Instructions were given in the first semester of 2000 to reinforce procedures and measures in high-risk areas (the Açores). · The LNIV will put in place a blind ring-testing procedure for controlling regional laboratories as from the second semester of 2000. · Increased testing in high risk Regions of the Azores has been in force since the beginning of 2000 and infected animals are isolated as soon as the diagnosis results are confirmed. · Farm dogs will be tested in reactor herds and, if positive, treated after the publication of the new legislation in the Official Journal. · The Açores is preparing a dossier in order to submit an application under article 8 of Council Directive 91/68/EEC, to request declaration of official freedom from Brucella Melitensis. At the time of the current mission, no part of Portugal has been accorded the status of officially brucellosis (BM) free. Details of action since this response are given in the text of this report. 4.3. Epidemiological situation The DGV has observed that few animals show clinical signs to indicate the presence of disease and the incidence of aborted calves is low. In such circumstances the DGV states there are inherent difficulties in reducing infection rates when these are at a low level (in the order of 0.75% of herds infected and 0.18% of animals testing positive in 1999). Its task has been further complicated by such factors as the illegal movement of animals and poor disease awareness in many producers. The DGV has forecast an animal prevalence of 0.05% for 2001 (this figure was revised in the 2002 eradication plan to 0.16%). 9 updated by Decreto Lei No 378/99 6 There has been a reduction in the herd prevalence of bovine brucellosis in cattle from 0.75% in 1999 to 0.42% in 2001. There has also been a reduction in animal prevalence from 0.35% in 1999 to 0.18% in 2000. The figures rise slightly to 0.24% in 2001, largely due to increases in Ribatejo e Oeste. 4.4. Duration of the eradication programme The plan for the eradication of bovine brucellosis in 2000 ran for one year. For a three-year period from 2001-2003 a marked reduction in the prevalence and incidence of the disease is forecast to achieve a disease-free status in the medium term. The 2001 programme ran for one year and was renewed for 2002. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authority 5.1.1. Legislation and geographical area covered by the plan Relevant legislation introduced since mission DG(SANCO)/1162/1999 · Portaria No 205/2000 ­ on the collection and transport of reactor cattle to the slaughterhouse and the commercialisation of the meat fit for human consumption. · Despacho conjunto No 530/2000 ­ setting out the amount of compensation to be paid to the owners of slaughtered animals. · Despacho No 11 371/2000 ­ 2nd sérle ­ approved list of slaughterhouses for reactor cattle. · Decreto-Lei No 338/99 updated by Decreto-Lei No 99/2002 ­ on matters relating to the identification, registration and movement of animals (in particular the requirements of EC Regulation No 820/97) and the approval of assembly centres. All animal movements (bovine) may be checked on SNIRB. · Decreto-Lei No 244/2000 ­technical rules for brucellosis eradication including the revised system of herd classification. · EC Regulation No. 1760/2000 and No. 1825/2000 have been the object of a consolidated publication (Decreto-Lei No 323-F/2000), which contains practical measures for the implementation of the legislation. Bovine brucellosis has been a notifiable disease since 1953. It is listed in the Schedule of Diseases annexed to Decreto-Lei No 39/209 of 1953. The treatment of this disease is prohibited. In the 2002 bovine brucellosis eradication plan, it is obligatory for the owner to give notification of abortions. The National Eradication Programme is implemented throughout Continental Portugal and the Açores by means of plans adapted to their special features. 7 5.1.2. Management structure Detailed information on the structure of the veterinary services in Portugal (DGV) can be found in documents DG(SANCO)/1162/1999 and DG(SANCO)/3166/2001, on the DG SANCO web-site: (http://europa.eu.int/comm/dg24/). There have been no significant changes since 1999. Further information can be found on the web-site of the Ministry of Agriculture, Rural Development and Fisheries (Ministério da Agricultura, do Desenvolvimento Rural e das Pescas): www.min- agricultura.pt/. 5.1.3. Independence Full time staff in the official services are independent of the farming industry. However, they are permitted to conduct private veterinary practice outside official working hours, subject to authorisation from the Minister of Agriculture. The "semi-private" veterinarians contracted by the OPPs, who do most of the on-farm testing, must demonstrate an absence of conflict of interest between official tasks and private activity. 5.1.4. Resources The annual budget allocated for veterinary measures by the Ministry of Economics and Finance in 2001 was 5.3 billion PTE (26 500 000 Euro). Approximately 40% of this amount is spent on TB, brucellosis and EBL eradication in cattle. 5.1.5. Personnel The personnel within the veterinary services is described in report DG(SANCO)/3166/2001. More specifically, at the central level there are 3 permanent staff dealing with animal health matters, of which 1 spends 80% of this time on bovine brucellosis, TB and EBL. There is one audit team with 2 veterinarians and an IT specialist who have been responsible for audits on 51 of the 118 OPPs. There were originally 2 teams when the processed was initiated in July 2001, but the members of the second team have not had their contracts renewed. There are staff at regional (DSV) and DIV level dedicated to the BBEP but not dealing exclusively with the programme. The CCA acknowledge that budgetary constraints limit staff recruitment at all levels. There has been an increase from 90 to 99% of the farmers associated with OPPs. The DGV has encouraged this development, thus reducing some of the workload on the official services. 5.1.6. Recruitment & training There is, at present, limited staff recruitment due to severe budgetary restrictions throughout the civil service. Training is as described in report DG(SANCO)/3166/2001 for BM, although there is no specific guideline for further training requirements. There has been no training organised at the DGV level this year. 8 5.1.7. Legal/enforcement powers The national legislation entitles the veterinary services to impose sanctions on farmers who do not adhere to their legal obligations and do not co- operate with the programme. For example, · In 2001, 3 actions were taken with regard to legislation on the bovine eradication programmes (Decreto-Lei 244/00 de 27.09.2000). This increased to 12 in the 1st semester of 2002. · In 2001, a total of 215 actions were taken in response to animal movement/identification irregularities (Decreto-Lei 245/96 de 1996 and 338/99 de 1999). 5.1.8. Prioritisation of controls At the central level, the DGV has identified problem herds by analysing the information held on the PISA system (no such measures have been taken over the last 12 months at the regional level). A circular (09505) was sent by the DGV to the DRA on 3 September 2002, giving guidance on how to ensure compliance with the ovine, caprine and bovine brucellosis eradication programmes including the legal steps to be taken if necessary. The DGV is preparing a handbook to guide the regions in the prioritisation of their controls (including the use of data held on PISA). 5.1.9. Documentation of controls Quarterly technical reports on the eradication programmes are requested from the regions. This reporting frequency will be retained after the introduction of twice/yearly reporting to the Commission Services from 1 January 2003 (see Commission Decision 2002/677/EC10). The OPPs submit an "annual sanitary programme" in the autumn each year, to the DGV for approval. This programme includes their proposals for the following year and summary of the work done to-date (presented as a % of the target for the year). 5.1.10. Laboratory service (general) The Laboratorio Nacional de Investigação Veterinária (LNIV) of Benefica, Lisbon and the Delegação do Porto form the national reference laboratory (regulated by Decreto Regulamentar 23/97). The LNIV works according to GLP principles and is seeking accreditation (EN 17025) from the Portuguese Institute for Quality. The first audit is to take place in December 2002. Standard Operating Procedures have been developed and these formed the basis of a manual (controlled document) supplied to the regional laboratories. The LNIV is responsible for the certification of all the authorised laboratories, comprising 10 public laboratories and 7 private laboratories (all regulated by Decreto-Lei No 241/90). The laboratories are licensed by 10 Official Journal L 229, 27/8/2002, p.24 9 the LNIV to participate in the eradication programmes. The LNIV is responsible for the production and quality control of RBT and CFT antigens and control sera. It is the only authorised body for the distribution of such reagents to the Portuguese Laboratory Network. The LNIV aims to audit laboratories twice/year. However, due to staff constraints, only 1 audit/year takes place. Additionally, sera samples and antigen are collected, for re-testing at the LNIV. These audits have identified deficiencies in methods, structure and equipment and 6 public laboratories are currently suspended (non-certified). However, these laboratories continue to work without restriction or correction of the shortcomings identified. In practice, they are given guidance, and staff are asked to come to the LNIV for further training (although it is at their discretion when this takes place). The laboratories were also required to participate in ring tests (RBT, CFT). These were organised by the LNIV in April/May 2001 and it is planned to carry out further tests every other year. Around half of the laboratories recorded at least one false positive result in the RBT. From the DGV viewpoint, false positives do not unduly undermine the animal health controls. From January 1998, it became compulsory to collect material removed during post-mortem examinations (retromammary, suprainguinal and retropharyngeal ganglions) of animals from herds classified as B2.2, B3 and B4, with a view to identifying the link between serum-positive and the presence of disease (i.e. bacterial isolation). 67 samples were tested in 1998, 2,648 in 1999 and 877 in 2000. Brucella melitensis made up nearly 50% of the 84 brucella isolates in 2000. Despite it being compulsory to submit material from abortions, only 5 samples of placenta/foetus were submitted to the LNIV (from the 7 regions) in 2001 for bacteriology (no organisms isolated). 5.1.11. Liaison with Public Health Services In the past, the DGV was sent updated information in monthly bulletins. There are no formal means by which co-ordination takes place between the Ministries of Agriculture and Health. There has been a gradual reduction in the number of human cases of brucellosis, although no distinction is drawn between the serotype/biovar. System for notification for suspected/confirmed outbreaks Bovine brucellosis is subject to compulsory notification. 5.1.13. Food safety controls Milk and milk products Milk is marketed through centralised dairy treatment plants and the farmers have been made aware of bovine brucellosis (information booklets from the DGV to farmers and the transport industry). In the establishment visited, all milk was pasteurised. A list of suppliers was maintained by the establishment. There was a column in which the classification of the herd could be recorded. It was noted that a) some producers had no classification recorded, and b) in one case a farm was recorded as B2.1, although communication between the dairy establishment and the DRA/DSV confirmed that the herd had been subject to re-tests and was now considered BOF (B4). The establishment representative stated that they were aware of the status of their suppliers. However, they relied on the veterinary services for official confirmation of the herd status. The DRA (Ribantejo e Oeste) notifies dairy establishments of farms with animals testing positive to brucellosis, although this was not the case for the B2.1 farm cited above which was located in the DRA of Alentejo. The form sent by the DRA of Ribantejo e Oeste requires that the milk of (negative) animals in contact with infected animals must be subject to heat treatment ­ Portaria No 861/84 of 15/11 and Portaria No 533/93.The milk of non-infected animals to be used for producing cheese on the holding must undergo suitable heat treatment before it is processed. The establishment visited had procedures in place for "non-conforming milk". This required that it was subject to a UHT treatment. 5.2. Farm Registration 5.2.1. Farm and herd registration system The system of farm and herd registration has been described in report DG(SANCO)/1162/1999 and more recently in DG(SANCO)/8526/2002. Only additional observations are reported here. Animal identification, registration and movement, particularly as regards accompanying documentation, are regulated by Decreto-Lei No 338/99, which came into force on 24 August 1999. The herds visited had a herd registration number (marca) and, where checked, the animal registers were up-to-date. In some cases, births were not reported to the competent authority for more than 20 days. It was stated that in Portugal, farmers had up to 24 working days to notify a birth, which differs from the requirement in the eradication plan for the farmer to inform SNIRD of the birth of any animal within no more than 7 days. 11 5.3. Animal Identification 5.3.1. Description of system The system of animal identification has been described in report DG(SANCO)/1162/1999 and more recently in DG(SANCO)/8526/2002. Only additional observations are reported here. Identification of cattle is obligatory before 20 days old. It is done by making two identical marks, one in each ear. After identification the competent authority should issue the respective passport within no more than 14 days (though this sometimes took longer). Most animals were found to be identified correctly. In a few cases, animals were found with one ear tag. When the register was inspected, these were typically found to be cattle born and identified before January 1998. In addition to the information identifying the animals, the passport also has a section for indicating the various health measures taken and the classification of the herd. BACKGROUND 4.1. History The Annex to Commission Decision 91/42/EEC6 sets out the criteria for FMD contingency plans and forms the basis for this evaluation. Commission Decision 1999/246/EEC7 establishes that these criteria will be applied mutatis mutandis when drawing up contingency plans for the control of CSF. The FMD and CSF contingency plans of Greece were approved by Commission Decisions 93/455/EEC8 and 99/246/EEC respectively. The following Commission documents set out detailed guidelines for the preparation of contingency plans: · Contingency plans for epidemic diseases, VI/5211/95; · Guidelines for FMD contingency plans in non-vaccinating countries, VI/6319/98 Rev 1. The last outbreak of CSF in Greece was in Halkida in 1986. The last outbreak of FMD was confirmed on 11 July 2000 in the prefecture of Evros, in the Delta of the river Evros. The causal agent was identified by the Institute for Foot-and-Mouth Disease and Exotic Diseases in Athens as being virus type Asia 1. Following the outbreak of FMD there was an FVO mission, DG(SANCO)/1280/2000, to review and evaluate the measures taken by the Greek authorities to eradicate FMD and to prevent further outbreaks. The report of this mission is available on the Health and Consumer Protection Directorate General Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html. 2 OJ L 047, 21/02/1980 p. 0011 - 0023 3 OJ L 224, 18/08/1990 p. 0013 - 0018 4 OJ L 315 , 26/11/1985 p.0011 -0018 5 OJ L 038, 12/02/1998 p. 0010 - 0013 6 OJ L 023 , 29/01/1991 p. 0029 - 0030 7 OJ L 093 , 08/04/1999 p. 0024 - 0025 8 OJ L 213 , 24/08/1993 pp. 0020 - 0020 5 4.2. Disease surveillance The EVROS programme was introduced to provide early detection of disease. It was partially financed by the EU on the basis of Commission Decision 2000/71/EC9 of 20 December 1999 concerning specific financial contribution by the Community relating to epidemiological surveillance of certain animal diseases in areas at risk in Greece. It was based on regular serological screening, movement controls and regular contact with farmers. 4.3. FINDINGS 5.1. Transposition of EU legislation and national legislation. 5.1.1. Foot and Mouth Disease. Act 3196/1995 (A98/23-4-1955) describes measures to combat foot-and- mouth disease whilst Presidential Decree 133/1992 deals with the compulsory notification of animal diseases. Presidential Decree 36/1987 (A10) on measures to combat foot-and-mouth disease, as amended by Presidential Decree 49/1992 (A21) implements Council Directives 85/511/EEC and 90/423/EEC. Article 3 of Presidential Decree 36/1987 (A10) prescribes the immediate notification of any suspected or actual outbreak of FMD by the Prefectural Veterinary Authorities to the responsible Directorate of Veterinary Matters at the Ministry of Agriculture, which in turn informs the European Commission in accordance with Ministerial Decision 329364 of 1 April 1994 (B223) transposing Council Directive 82/894/EEC10. 9 OJ No L 024, 29/01/2000, p53 10 OJ No L 378/82, p58 6 5.1.2. Classical Swine Fever. Council Directive 80/217/EEC is transposed by Presidential Decree 707/82 (A97) as amended. There is no provision to prohibit swill feeding, although in practice no permit has ever been issued for this purpose. 5.1.3. Animal identification and farm registration. Council Directive 92/102/EEC is transposed by Presidential Decree (PD) 84/1995. Holdings with less than 5 small ruminants are not registered. No request (Council Directive 92/102/EEC, art 3.2) for approval of this derogation has been submitted to the Commission.11 5.2. Competent authority control system 5.2.1. Management structure and responsibilities Detailed information on the structure of the veterinary services in Greece can be found in the previous report DG SANCO/1035/1999, and in English on the internet web-site of the Ministry of Agriculture at http//www.minagric.gr. The Directorate of Animal Health (within the GDVS) is responsible for the preparation of the FMD and CSF contingency plans and for ensuring that necessary legislation, structures and procedures are in place to give effect to these plans. The department for control and preparedness in the 54 prefectures ("nomos") is the Prefectural Veterinary Service (PVS). Activity is directed through approximately 30012 active Field Veterinary Stations. The official veterinarians working at both these levels are not accountable to the CCA but to the Prefect (Ministry of Internal Affairs). In the event of a disease outbreak, however, the PVS relies on the CCA for additional finance, laboratory support and technical assistance/co-ordination. A draft Presidential Decree foresees the re-establishment of Regional Veterinary Inspectorates, to act as a liaison and to develop a more direct line of command between the CCA and the prefecture or 'nomos' level. There has been further delay in progress with this proposal, as the Ministry of the Interior may reduce the proposed number of regional administrative units from 13 to 7. These changes affect the public administration as a whole and not only the veterinary services. 11 In their response to report DG(SANCO)/3352/2001, the Greek authorities stated that they intend to apply immediately to the Commission Services for such derogation. No such application had been made at the time of this mission. 12 This is an estimated figure as the number of FVSs continue to fall due to amalgamation, and some were found on-the-spot to be listed but not in operation. 7 There is also a proposal to create a fourth Directorate (an executive body) responsible for inspection and control to monitor and guide the activities of the PVS. 5.2.2. Resources The budget for the Animal Health Directorate is 15.5 million Euro. In the past the department has funded disease control costs from within this budget. This year, a request has been made for further funds to cover costs associated with BSE controls (principally laboratory costs). 5.2.3. Personnel There are approximately 40 permanent, full-time veterinarians, in the CCA and 6 staff in the Department of Infectious Diseases. On the basis of the 2002 census (by nomos), there are 621 permanent veterinarians in the Ministry of Interior Affairs (comprising both public and animal health duties), 108 veterinarians on 12 month contracts and 44 veterinarians on 8 month contracts (total: 773). 5.2.4. Recruitment and training The CCA has recruited 51 veterinarians, 15 destined for the head office in Athens, 30 for the 17 official laboratories and 6 for the BIPs. In particular, a veterinarian with postgraduate qualifications in epidemiology is to join the Department of Infectious Diseases. The Ministry of the Interior has 143 appointments approved. It is the intention of the CCA to arrange seminars on a monthly basis. The first seminar, which included talks on crisis management, was held from 1 to 5 April 2002. Fifty veterinary officers had participated from all levels of the veterinary service13. 5.2.5. Independence Civil servants are not permitted to undertake other activities unless special permission is granted. The veterinary staff at the central level, BIPs, and those with temporary contracts, are paid directly by the Ministry of Agriculture. The veterinary staff of the prefectures (nomi) are paid by the Ministry of the Interior. The veterinary services are obliged to treat animals, if requested, free of charge. 13 In their response to the draft report, the Greek Competent Authorities stated that, since the mission, a second seminar was organized from 25 to 28 June which was attended by 22 veterinarians working in Regional and Local Veterinary Services. This seminar also addressed relevant topics such as practical implementation of contingency plans and crisis management. From September onwards it is intended that these seminars will be continued at an accelerated pace. 8 5.2.6. Legal/enforcement powers General legislation on animal health and, in particular, the control of FMD and CSF is in place in Greece, and EU legislation has been transposed into national law. The prefectural veterinary services are empowered to take whatever measures are necessary to eradicate and/or control epizootic disease. Any costs arising are recouped from the central budget of the veterinary service. In the penal code there are horizontal provisions for failure of individuals to comply with veterinary legislation, which could lead to criminal prosecution. 5.2.7. Prioritisation of controls There is no formal system for the prioritisation of controls within the CCA. In practice the service responds to the demands placed upon it as these occur. 5.2.8. Documentation of controls The CCA carry out systematic checks on the PVS to ensure proper implementation of the relevant legislation (see report DG(SANCO)/3352/2001, Chapter 5.1.3). For animal health purposes, monthly returns are provided by the PVS to the CCA, documenting the disease situation throughout Greece at the municipality level and the pharmaceutical product dispensed/used. 5.2.9. Laboratory service (general) There are 17 official laboratories and a National Reference Laboratory for FMD (the FMD Institute) and CSF (Veterinary Centre of Athens ­ laboratory for pig pathology) under the supervision of the CCA. CSF serology (within the framework of the surveillance programme) for the north of Greece is undertaken at the official laboratory in Thessaloniki. At present there has been no consideration given to using the official laboratories to provide additional capacity in the event of an outbreak of either disease. 5.3. Farm registration 5.3.1. Description of system There are plans to introduce a national farm database for sheep and goats. However, the software has not been developed and no decision has been reached on the ear tag code system (which will comprise a holding code and unique animal number). This system will not be operational in the near future. Cattle holdings have been issued with a 9 digit alphanumeric code (the first 2 letters (EL) are for Greece, the next 2 numbers represent the nomos, and the final 5 numbers are used to provide a unique farm holding number). This date is now being recorded in an OSDE (Integrated Animal Management and Control System) database, part of a pilot project in 7 nomos. There is a new computerised system for the national registration of pig herds though this is not yet fully operational (the alphanumeric farm code is as described for cattle). 9 5.3.2. Operation of system In the nomos visited, a farm register (with serial numbers), is maintained by the FVS. The holdings are grouped by village, and this information is used in the event of a disease outbreak to impose restrictions (i.e. all holdings within one village would be included within a protection/surveillance zone). In Evros the mission team was shown how the FVS farm register was used to impose restrictions during the 2000 FMD crisis and to identify all relevant holdings. At the slaughterhouse visited, both old and new pig holding codes were in use and both were shown to identify the farm of origin. The OSDE system was seen in operation at the Prefectural Veterinary Services in Alexandroupoli. The number of cattle holdings did not match the most recent census data. It was explained that the veterinary services were in the process of entering data on the remaining 20 - 30% of holdings. 5.4. Animal identification 5.4.1. Description of system An account of the small ruminant animal identification system (including operation) has been given in report DG(SANCO)/3352/2001. The problem remains that until a harmonised system is developed for the ear tags, effective tracing of animals will not be possible. All bovine animals must be tagged at birth with double plastic tags with a unique 14 digit alphanumeric code. The code is as for farm registration, except there are another 5 digits for the individual animal. Breeding pigs are identified with the holding registration number either by ear-tag or by ear tattoo. 5.4.2. Operation of system The level of identification in small ruminants varies throughout Greece. In areas of increased surveillance (e.g. Evros) the level may be in excess of 50%, whereas the estimated average for the country is between 30 ­ 40%. All cattle observed by the mission team (free ranging animals in the Evros delta) were all ear tagged correctly. At the slaughterhouse visited, none of the pigs were identified by any mark or tag to show the farm of origin. This concurred with the findings of a specific mission on pig-meat in 2000 (report DG(SANCO)/1192/2000). It was explained that only breeding animals were required to be identified on an individual basis. 5.5. Movement controls 5.5.1. Description of the system The procedures for movement have not changed since the previous mission in 1999 (report DG(SANCO/1035/99)). For the whole of Greece, all animal movements should be subject to FVS authorisation by issuing an official movement permit. However, no veterinary permit is required if livestock movements are within the area covered by the local veterinary station. 10 The vast majority of movements are related to transhumance of flocks (60% of the flocks on the mainland), which is described in detail in report DG(SANCO)/3352/2001. 5.5.2. Operation of system Permits were demonstrated for movements (slaughter/transhumance) outside the FVS-area. This information concurred with that held on the EVROS database (now due to be phased out). Cattle movement records were also held on the OSDE system, although it was not possible to verify the information in the time available. At the slaughterhouse, ante-mortem records did not always identify the farm of origin. Further information was requested in a number of these cases. It was noted that a consignment of pigs could contain animals with and without a movement permit. The movement permit did not always specify the animal destination. 5.6. The FMD and CSF contingency plans The contingency plans for classical swine fever (CSF) and foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) have been approved by the Commission Services. The CSF plan was updated in September 1999 and the FMD plan in 2000 in response to recommendations made in report DG(SANCO)/1280/2000. Copies of these plans were available at all levels of the veterinary service. 5.6.1. Legal powers General legislation concerning animal health and, in particular, the control of CSF and FMD is in place in Greece, and EU legislation has been transposed into national law. The CCA are empowered to take whatever measures to eradicate and/or control epizootic diseases it deems necessary. Failure to implement decisions adopted by the prefect can lead to prosecution under Article 285 of the penal code. 5.6.2. Financial provisions There are no emergency funds, and the CCA is responsible for meeting the costs of a disease outbreak from the annual budget approved by the Inter- ministerial Decision of the Ministers for Agriculture and Finance. At the level of the nomos, a tendering exercise is performed when special equipment or external contractors are required. The invoices are submitted to the DGVS for reimbursement. The valuation of slaughtered animals and contaminated material, the supporting documents required for compensation and the procedure for submitting these documents is set out in Decision 325473 of 18 June 1998. Animals for slaughter and destruction (on the basis of a prefectural decision) are valued by a committee comprising a veterinarian, an agronomist and a representative of local government. Payment should not exceed market value and be made within 90 days. 11 5.6.3. Chain of command and National Disease Control Centre (NDCC) The responsibility for FMD and CSF control rests with the Minister for Agriculture. The relevant decisions are issued by the Director-General for veterinary matters and responsibility for implementation is delegated to the Director of the NDCC. While the Director of the NDCC is responsible for supervising the activities of the operational LDCCs, the LDCC is responsible for control of disease in its territory and is directly accountable to the Prefect.

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent authority Organisation of the Central Veterinary Service The Ministry of Agriculture, Food, Fishery and Rural Affairs and particularly the sub Directorate for Animal Health and Animal Welfare within the General Directorate for Food (Direction Général de l'Alimentation - DGAL) is in charge of issuing regulations and instructions and co-ordinating and supervising the activity of the local offices. Organisation of the local offices France is divided into 100 administrative départements (96 on the continent and 4 overseas). In each département, the local Veterinary Services (Direction Départementale des Services Vétérinaires ­ DDSV) are under direct responsibility of a Director and under direct authority of the Prefect. A delegation of legal powers is granted to the Director. The departmental Veterinary Services are in charge of the implementation, according to the DGAL instructions. Particularly, the checks on animal welfare are carried out by the Service for Animal Health and Animal Welfare and, in the abattoirs, by the Service for Food Hygiene. The Director is assisted by the agents of the veterinary services, described as follows: - veterinary inspectors of Public Veterinary Health, both permanent official veterinarians (OVs) and contracted veterinary surgeons; the contracted veterinarians are private practitioners performing official tasks of animal health (vétérinaires sanitaires) or working for a certain amount of hours as official veterinary inspectors (vétérinaires vacataires). - agricultural engineers (ingénieurs des travaux agricoles), full time civil servants with a specific three-year training; - technicians of the veterinary services, full time civil servants with a specific two-year training. 5.2. Applicable legislation Since the previous mission in 1999, the French legislation, which transposes EU legislation on the welfare of animal during transport, has been amended with the transposition of Council Directive 95/29/EC. 7 The applicable legislation on animal welfare during transport and at slaughter in France is as follows: EU legislation French legislation Transport Council Directive 91/628/EEC as amended Décret n. 95-1285 of 13 December 1995, by Council Directive 95/29/EC amended by Décret 99-961 of 24 November 1999; Arrêté 5 November 1996, amended by Arrêté Ministeriale 24 November 1999; Décret 12 February 2001, on the approval of the standard contract for public transport of livestock. Article L. 214-12 of Code Rural, regarding authorisation of transporters Slaughtering Council Directive 93/119/EC Décret n. 97-903 of 1 October 1997 Arrêté 12 November 1997 The transposition of Council Directive 95/29/EC became effective at the end of 1999. It should have entered into force on 31.12.1996. Although a comprehensive check of the above legislation was not carried out, the following points were noted: ­ there is an obligation for vehicles to be inspected by the Veterinary Services as part of the procedure for the authorisation of the transporter and for drivers with less than 5 years experience to complete a training course validated by the CA. The driver is also obliged to carry a copy of his authorisation when transporting animals. These requirements are additional to Council Directive 91/628/EEC; ­ Article 3 of Décret 12.02.2002 does not fulfil the requirements of Article 4 of Council Directive 91/628/EEC. It only applies to professionally contracted transporters and indicates that time of departure is only required "if necessary"; ­ there is no obligation to give notice of the existence of the route plan through the ANIMO system (Article 5(A)(2)(c) of Council Directive 91/628/EEC); ­ a market is considered as a place of departure in French legislation, when it is less than 50 km from the first place of loading, or if more than 50 km distant, where the animals are rested for a period for them to be watered and fed if necessary. Article 2(e) of Council Directive 91/628/EEC (as amended) states that the latter category of animals are watered and fed before being reloaded and does not indicate that this is only "if necessary". Another piece of legislation, which was introduced as part of the measures to reduce the risk of TSE or scrapie infected animals entering the food chain, concerns the slaughtering of casualty animals (Arrêté 09.06.2000, last 8 amended on 04.02.2002). This prohibits the following animals from arriving at slaughterhouses: ­ casualty ovine and caprine animals; ­ casualty bovine animals more than 24 month old; ­ any animal which is ill or in state of physiological weakness. This legislation does not prohibit the transport of other casualty animals, where the accident has occurred in the previous 48 hours5. 5.3. Each DDSV is requested to carry out 100 controls each year on the means of transport. Moreover it detailed the performance of the inspections, provided a checklist for this purpose and gave instructions in case of detection of infringements; ­ an instruction of 22.06.2001, aiming to establish the checks for the year 2001, gave further details on the inspections to be performed. Controls at markets According to a representative of the CA at the first market visited - where the trade was only within France - agents from the DDSV were present once every three to six months. A private practitioner came to treat each sick or injured animal and, once a month, for a private control. In the second market two technicians from the DDSV were present each market day throughout the time when the market was operational. Moreover, the official veterinarian of the Animal Health and Protection Service alternated with the Director of the DDSV to ensure an OV was present on 2- 3 market days out of 4. This presence of OVs was necessary in this market, in order to certify animals for export and to validate route plans. Controls at slaughterhouses With regard to animal welfare at slaughter, an instruction of 24.06.1998 was distributed to all DDSVs, which explained the new regulation on this subject. It dealt particularly with staff training, the conformity of the equipment for stunning, ritual slaughter and sanctions in case of infringements. Two of the three départements visited had surpassed the target of 100 checks per year. In the third département records 47 vehicles had been inspected at road side checks in collaboration with the police, but checks at other locations were not systematically recorded. 5.4. Fitness for transport An evaluation is made of the checks for fitness to transport based on both the checks conducted by the CA on the spot during the mission and documentation of previous checks. Animals were present in all the sites for live animals visited except in the staging point. Fitness for transport to market The overall fitness for transport of the animals seen was satisfactory but the fitness of a few animals was questionable: ­ in both markets three ruminants with hoof problems were noticed by the CA, who proposed as corrective action a written warning to the dealers and to the farmers; 10 ­ an adult cow, which leaked milk and whose udder had weak suspensory ligaments, had probably not been milked since the previous evening; ­ in the second market a ewe had 3 big safety pins in its vulva, which had been carried out to prevent the prolapse of the uterus. The OVs considered this animal fit for the intended journey which had involved transport to the market and further transport to a slaughterhouse6. In the past veterinarians in both markets had carried out euthanasia on the few occasions when severely unfit animals had been presented. In the second market 21 cases of infringements of animal welfare requirements, particularly related to fitness for transport, had been recorded in 2000, of which 19 had been followed by written warnings and 3 followed by procès-verbaux (PV). It was reported that two of these cases had resulted in fines of 76 and 182. In 2001 there were no infringements recorded. A representative of the CA explained that this improvement was partly a result of the regulation of 09.06.2000 on casualty animals and partly due to the closure of the market for several months in 2001 during the FMD crisis. Fitness for transport to slaughter In both slaughterhouses visited, each unloading of animals was checked by the CA. In the bovine abattoir the veterinarian ­ appointed by the DDSV - performing the ante-mortem inspection had been chosen for his practical experience in cattle practice. Although after the implementation of the regulation for casualty animals the number of seriously injured animals transported to slaughterhouse was reduced, certain seriously ill and injured animals were still transported. In an area outside the slaughterhouse, there were 4 carcasses of animals euthanised because their condition on arrival was in violation of the regulation of 9.6.2000. Records indicated that approximately 0.75% of animals arriving at this slaughterhouse were in a similar condition. The OV sent monthly summaries to the DSV of his département, who in turn sent the information to the DDSV of the farm of origin of the euthanised animal. One warning letter had been issued to one farmer following one such incident. There was also a category of animals (approximately 0.1%), such as younger cattle with a broken leg, which were slaughtered in the designated area for emergency slaughter. No follow-up action was taken following the transport of any animals in this category. Several representatives of the CA were of the opinion that this transport was legal as this category of animal had not been excluded by the regulation of 09.06.2000 on casualty animals. 6 In their response to the draft report the French Authorities noted that this procedure is carried out to prevent complications such a prolapse and that the presence of safety pins does not prejudice the fitness of the animals for transport. 11 Among the pigs isolated in the casualty pen, were some which were visibly suffering and they potentially had to wait for several hours before being killed. Point 6 of Annex A of Council Directive 93/119/EC requires that such animals are either killed immediately on the spot or at the latest within two hours from unloading. It also requires that any movement to the point of killing does not entail unnecessary suffering. The loading of animals with fractures onto a trolley in order to bring them to this pen does not comply with this latter requirement. During the visit, about 35 to 40 pigs were in this sick pen. The OV in this slaughterhouse had developed a strategy to reduce the number of unfit animals arriving and stated that the severely unfit animals were killed in the shortest possible delay. In the first three months of 2002, 66 written warnings had been addressed to assemblers of pigs and to DDSVs of origin. The OV, together with a technician, had also prepared an internal instruction for staff in the slaughterhouse in relation to ante mortem inspection and the channelling of sub-optimal animals within the slaughterhouse. The OV pointed out that he had written this instruction without the assistance of the other levels of the CA and had difficulty to define the minimum standard regarding fitness for transport. 5.5. Means of transport On the basis of the information received in the three offices visited, it is estimated that 32% to 40% vehicles have been approved. Regarding the checks of vehicles performed during the mission the vehicles seen in the slaughterhouses were in good general condition and fulfilled the minimum requirements. Although the overall situation at the market was satisfactory, the following points were noted: ­ checks on the vehicles in the first market were not performed on a routine basis; the only one transporter to whom the CA asked for the agreement had not been approved. The overall condition of the trucks was good although one trailer, which had been designed for transporting horses, was used to transport a cow and a calf and did not have a ramp; ­ in the second market, vehicles were again of a generally satisfactory standard but one vehicle, which had been approved, had a ramp with an inclination of 75%. A small vehicle had a second level for transporting small ruminants but this compartment did not possess a ramp for unloading, which may give rise to mishandling of animals during unloading; ­ adult bovine animals with horns, were loaded onto the upper deck of a two-deck vehicle and could not stand in a natural position because of the low level of the roof of the second deck. Action was taken by the CA after this observation made by the mission team. One OV indicated that similar corrective action had been taken in the past; ­ a Spanish truck, loaded with young bovine animals destined for Spain, was not adequately equipped for watering the animals and one compartment provided inadequate headspace. During one office visit, in another département, it was also found that vehicles were used to 12 transport animals from a market to Spain on journeys of up to 18 hours without being equipped for connection to a water supply; ­ the main problem in the second market was related to the cleaning and disinfecting of the vehicles. OVERALL CONCLUSION The system in place for surveillance is largely satisfactory. However, the lack of verification that all eligible animals are sampled implies that there is no possibility for timely correction and therefore, that positive cases might be missed. The current system of controls on the feedban, whilst on paper quite comprehensive and demonstrating relatively low numbers of positive samples, does not ensure that all positive cases followed up, nor that all users of derogated PAP are captured. Moreover, there is little in place to ensure that controls are targeted and inspectors carry out controls as required, nor to initiate corrective action where necessary. The high number of BAB-cases without explanation is a matter of concern. SRM controls have been reinforced by occasionally substantial administrative measures, but are affected by a lack of resources and of co-ordination of activities. 7. BACKGROUND 4.1. EC measures in place The main difference compared to the legal situation during previous missions was the introduction, since 1 January 2002, of an active surveillance programme for TSEs in small ruminants. This programme concerned animals slaughtered for human consumption as well as fallen stock. Modifications to this programme require from 1 April 2002 a considerable increase of random sampling in small ruminants. Since the last BSE mission to the Netherlands, mesentery from bovines of all ages was added to the list of SRM. 4.2. Summary of previous mission results The previous mission to the Netherlands concerning the epidemio-surveillance, feed ban and SRM was undertaken from 24 to 28 September 2001. The report of this mission is available under reference number: DG SANCO/3305/2001 ­ MR ­ Final (hereafter: report 3305/2001) on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/netherlands/index_en.html . The report made a number of recommendations for action to the CCA. In relation to the epidemio-surveillance, the recommendations focused on: · A more formal and documented monitoring system on the performance of the active and passive surveillance and the installation of an official procedure for the detention of sampled animals awaiting the laboratory results In relation to the feed ban, the recommendations focused on: · The setting up of the channelling system for derogated processed animal proteins (PAP), shortening the delay when lab results of routine tests for feed ban have been obtained and establishing the risk assessment for the control of feed ban. In relation to SRM, the recommendations focused on: · The evaluation of the proper staining, the correct channelling of SRM to final incineration and the reconciliation at every stage of the chain and the official control of the purification of ruminant fat. In relation to Establishments recommendations were issued on correction of deficiencies in establishments and the prevention of meat destined for the local market was put into intra community trade. (9) OJ L 38, 12.02.1998, p. 10. 6 These recommendations are outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of Part 5. of this report. 4.3. Actions undertaken/announced by the CCA following the previous report In their response to mission report 3305/2001, the CCA informed the Commission services of a number of actions that had been/would be undertaken to address certain recommendations made. The main points are reflected in the Addendum to that report and outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of Part 5. of this report In addition, the CCA provided the Commission services in June 2002 with further information concerning actions aimed at addressing the recommendations made in the report (hereafter referred to as the "Action Plan"). These actions are, where appropriate, outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of Part 5. of this report.

MAIN FINDINGS AND OBSERVATIONS For ease of reference, and where appropriate, relevant recommendations as set out in report 3305/2001 are indicated under the appropriate section headings, in italics and preceded by a "bullet". 5.1. Epidemio-surveillance in Bovine Animals 5.1.1. Competent authorities For a description of the authorities involved and their tasks, reference is made to mission report 3305/2001. 5.1.2. Passive Surveillance The CCA informed the Commission services that the awareness of the disease is kept up by keeping on providing information and training to veterinary practitioners. The mission team noted that: 57 cattle in 2000 and 145 cattle in 2001 were notified as official suspects. During 2002 until the month of June 33 cattle have been notified as official suspects. 1457 cattle were culled as a consequence of the BSE cases in 2002 until the month of June (birth cohorts, offspring and co-habitants) 5.1.3. Active Surveillance (follow up) The relevant recommendations concerned: · The Dutch authorities should consider a more formal and documented monitoring system of control by the central and regional level on the performance of the active and passive surveillance. In response to this recommendation the Dutch authorities informed the Commission services that: 7 The Audit Department (AD) of the Ministry of Agriculture began in the spring 2002 a process analysis of the different elements of the surveillance programme for BSE (selection of animals, sampling strategy analysis of tests, etc.). The AD looked at the various steps in the monitoring and management of the BSE surveillance programme and how the various agencies and departments were involved in these tasks. Per section, a risk analysis was carried out and additional internal controls and measures as necessary were identified. The implementation of the additional measures awaits the result of an audit of the system actually in place. The mission team noted that: The sampling procedure of fallen stock, the quality control of samples for BSE testing, the reporting of samples taken to the management of the system (RVV and LASER), the culling of positive herds, and the approval of private laboratories for the BSE rapid test have been identified as the high risk areas. Figures concerning the number of animals tested, sampled and notified to the central bovine database are already available within the Ministry of Agriculture (the division named LASER) for the financing of the system. According to the CCA, these figures could be used for an overall monitoring and management of the BSE surveillance system by the CCA. · The Dutch authorities must install an official procedure in the slaughterhouse to ensure that no parts of examined animals bearing the health mark can leave the slaughterhouse until a negative result to the rapid test has been obtained. In response to this recommendation the Dutch authorities informed the Commission services that: An official instruction lays down the requirements for ensuring that no parts of slaughtered animals leave the slaughterhouse before the result is received. Stamping of carcasses before the result of the BSE rapid test is known can take place only if the plant is under full-time RVV supervision. A protocol approved by the RVV district office must describe the method used to demonstrate that the relevant carcasses, their organs and offals cannot leave the slaughterhouse or are disposed of as SRM. At plants without full-time RVV supervision stamping is not allowed before the result of the BSE rapid test is known. Release of carcasses, its organs and offals, when the result is negative can only take place in the physical presence of the RVV. The mission team noted that: In the two slaughterhouses visited with full-time RVV supervision protocols were available describing instruments to control that no parts of the slaughtered animals could leave the slaughterhouse before the BSE test result was known. It could be verified that no parts could be released without the presence of the RVV. In the slaughterhouse without full-time RVV supervision the available protocol laid down that no parts of the slaughtered animals could be stamped before the BSE test result was known. It was verified that carcasses sampled for BSE testing awaiting the test result were detained without being stamped. 8 5.2. TSE controls in ovine and caprine animals (EC Reg. 999/2001) 5.2.1. Identification and registration of ovine/caprine animals. 5.2.3.1. Legal basis for identification and registration (I&R) of small ruminants The requirements concerning I&R of small ruminants are laid down in Council Directive 92/102/EEC10, and should have been applied no later than 1 January 1995. The CCA provided two national regulations in Dutch. However, the evaluation of this documentation was not done due to time constraints. A new Regulation concerning the I&R of animals was issued by the LNV in December last year and entered into force last 1st January 2002 (Regeling identificatie en registratie van dieren 2002). On reviewing this regulation the mission team noted that: ­ The responsibility for the implementation of I&R of animals, including small ruminants, will be taken over by the Dutch office of I&R of animals from the GD (Animal Health Service (Gezondheistdienst for Dieren)) as from 1 October 2002. ­ The tags to be used for sheep and goats must include apart from the indicatives NL and LNV, a UBN number (the holding number) and an individual serial number. ­ On farm checks for premium purposes are carried out each year by a different department of the LNV on an scheduled number of farms, but these visits are mainly focused on the number of ewes kept in the holding. ­ No system of regular specific controls has been set up by the CA as regards the enforcement of identification and registration requirements in small ruminants. The mission team was informed that as a result of the 2001 emergency caused by Foot and Mouth Disease, AID (General Inspection Service (Algemene Inspectie Dienst)) has been visiting sheep farms to check all the elements of the I&R. Information on the outcome of the project were not provided to the mission team. The CCA has recognised that with the current legislation in place, it is difficult if not impossible to trace e.g. parents, progeny or cohort animals to a given animal. However, CCA is considering issuing additional legal instruments on I&R of small ruminants which should improve the traceability of the animals. (10) OJ L 355, 05.12.1992, p. 32 10 5.2.4. Identification and registration of holdings (holding register) A computerized register of all holdings with small ruminants is kept at the Dutch Office of I&R. Each holding is identified by a unique number (UBN). The information on the holding must be kept in the database for up to three years after the date the keeper notifies the discontinuation of husbandry practices. The computerised database contains data for each registered holding on the single holding number (UBN), location of the holding, name and address of the keeper and the species of animals kept in the holding. It was noted that: The farmers will be entitled to ask a number of eartags up to three times the number of animals declared in this annual census. 5.2.4.1.Identification and registration of animals The system in place for the identification of small ruminants requires: ­ Sheep and goats born on a holding shall be marked within a month of birth or if they are removed from the holding. ­ If the establishment is an approved assembly centre for small ruminants the keeper shall mark the incoming animals immediately after arrival with a metallic orange slaughter tag. Once earmarked these animals can only be conducted to a slaughterhouse and not returned to a holding. ­ An animal which looses its ear tag, must be re-tagged immediately with a new printed ear tag showing the UBN of the herd where it is present. The mission team noted: According to the keepers visited, a link was not always established between the new and the original ear tag when re-tagging an animal. 5.2.4.2.Registration of movements and holding inventory The system in place requires that the keeper of small ruminants maintain a herd inventory which contains up-dated information on: ­ Lost eartags, the new eartag number and the date, ­ the number of animals in the herd, ­ for an animal leaving or entering the herd, the UBN of the holding of origin or the holding of destination, or if no UBN is given, the name, address and domicile, the eartag number, the date, and in case of animals imported from third countries an special RVV registration number. ­ the accommodation of sheep or goats placed elsewhere, including number of animals, UBN of the holding of accommodation, dates, births and deaths, ­ the copies of the transport document intended for the keeper. 11 1st January each year, the keeper shall notify the number of female animals over 12 months of age or which gave birth , and the total number of sheep and goats. The mission team noted: Both holdings visited kept a herd inventory fulfilling the legal requirements. Sheep and goats shall be accompanied by a transport document when they are removed from a holding to another one, to an assembly centre or to the slaughterhouse. The animals that loose their eartags in the assembly centres are usually retagged with the UBN of the assembly centre. 5.2.5. The report of this mission is available under reference number DG SANCO/3307/2001 ­MR Final 7 OJ L 224, 18.08.1990, p.29 8 OJ L 395, 30.12.1989, p.13 9 OJ L 38, 12.02.1998, p.10 2 (hereafter: report 3307/2001) on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/greece/index_en.html The report made a number of recommendations for action to the CCA. In relation to epidemio-surveillance, the recommendations focused on: · Bringing national legislation in line with EC requirements, particularly for the definition of a BSE clinical suspect and the procedure in case of positive rapid test, and to improve the detection of BSE clinical suspects. · Inclusions of sick animals as a sub-population in the monitoring programme. · Improved declaration, collection and sampling of fallen stock, · Monitoring the inclusion and sampling of bovines over 30 months, · Improved supervision of regional laboratories by the national reference laboratory (NRL), · Monitoring the performance of all the parties involved in TSEs controls and ensuring an equivalent level of epidemio-surveillance throughout the country. · Improvement of the bovine Identification and Registration System (I&R) and its control. In relation to the feed ban, the recommendations focused on: · Implementing sufficient levels of control in all types of establishments concerned and provision of instructions for action when prohibited PAP are detected. · The inclusion of risk assessment in targeting official feed controls and sampling procedures, and adoption of measures to ensure that official samples are taken in compliance with EU requirements. Collaboration between different services should be improved. · Provision of instructions for practical implementation of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC, and implementation of Commission Decision 2001/165/EC. · Ensuring that rendered ruminant fats used in the feed mills are purified or treated in accordance to Commission Decision 99/534/EC, · Ensuring that the certificates accompanying fishmeal meet the EU requirements. In relation to the SRM, the recommendations focused on: · The establishment of a properly documented system for the official control along the SRM chain, including instructions as regards controls on the removal and disposal of SRM, · Measures ensuring the proper removal of the vertebral column, and the effective destruction of SRM. Where necessary; destruction capacity should be increased. · Ensuring collection and destruction of fallen stock in line with EU requirements. These recommendations are outlined in more detail in the relevant sections of Part 5. 4.2. These actions are, where appropriate, outlined in more detail in Part 5 of this report. 3 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. EPIDEMIO-SURVEILLANCE IN BOVINE ANIMALS (FOLLOW-UP) 5.1.1. Competent authorities The Greek Veterinary Services are an integrated part of the Ministry of Agriculture and their competence covers all aspects of animal health, public health and animal welfare. Directorates of the Central Service pursue their particular set of activities in close co-operation with appropriate de-centralised, regional and local services, while overall co-ordination is assured by the Director General and senior officers. In recent years regional and local veterinary services passed to the authority of Prefects for practical implementation of veterinary activities and organisation of delivering veterinary services. There are 54 PVS and 323 Local Veterinary Stations (LVS). At central level the BSE epidemio-surveillance is under the responsibility of the Communicable and Parasitic Diseases Department in the Animal Health Directorate of the Directorate General of Veterinary Services. Its tasks include the co-ordination and management of the programme throughout the country and are done in co-operation with the PVS, the NRL and the RVLs. Regarding responsibilities of the CCA as regards general co-ordination and management of BSE epidemio-surveillance the recommendations of report 3307/2001 concerned: · CCA should ensure an equivalent level of epidemio-surveillance by the PVS throughout the country (detection of clinical suspects, sampling of fallen stock). · CCA should ensure that the NRL carries out all necessary procedures to improve its level of routine supervision on RVLs as defined in Annex X-A-1 to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. · CCA should implement a system to monitor the performance of all the parties involved in TSEs controls (training activities, the monitoring programme, TSEs suspicions and the laboratories' activities) using the information already available from the PVS, LVS and private veterinary practitioners (PVPs). · CCA should take measures to improve the bovine I&R and its control. CCA advised that spatial and temporal distribution of the samples indicates a uniform mobilisation of all PVS and LVS and reflects both the geographical distribution of the bovine population and a uniform general increase of awareness and co-operation of the farmers. It also emphasised the non-homogeneous geographical distribution of cattle herds and the absence of approved slaughterhouses for the slaughter of bovine animals over 30 months in certain Greek prefectures, which means that the animals are finally registered in the prefecture of sampling. The mission team reviewed data provided by the CCA on the geographical distribution of the Greek bovine population and the number of bovines sampled so far in 2002. It noted that: The number of fallen stock sampled in certain prefectures with an important adult bovine population (e.g. Ilia, Karditsa, Drama, Pella or Florina) is too low for a period of eight months. In some prefectures (e.g.Larissa, Kozani and Xanthi), the numbers provide clear evidence of a persistent underreporting of fallen stock. The number of animals over 30 months sampled in some prefectures (e.g. Larissa, Kilkis, Kozani, Florina , Kyklades) is below that normally expected 4 considering the adult bovine population, particularly dairy cattle, present in these areas. The temporal distribution of the bovine sampled population so far shows that the ongoing monitoring programme is performing evenly all through 2002. CCA also indicated that the NRL has satisfied itself, either by on the spot visits or by recalling experts working in the RVLs, that diagnostic methods and protocols are efficiently and correctly implemented. Inter-laboratory ring tests for both Biorad and Prionics tests were organised since November 2001. The mission team noted: The ring tests offered satisfactory results. Experts of the parent companies providing reagents for rapid tests repeatedly visited all RVLs. However, the NRL has not advised them of the necessity of actively seeking independent accreditation of their testing functions within one year of commencing commercial operations as regards TSEs. NRL carries out a permanent re-examination of inconclusive results. NRL has neither advised nor monitors if the RVLs have established an in-house quality control of the day-to-day performance of the rapid tests, particularly in the case of Biorad test. The NRL does not check regularly enough the performance of the daily indicators of the tests, either. Consequently, and in spite of having sufficient information available, consistency of the analytical results of the positive and negative controls in Biorad test or the results of the assessment of reproducibility and repeatability that the RVLs should be frequently carrying out with both tests are not being assessed. CCA indicated that the establishment of an interprefectural network of Veterinary Inspectorates aimed at facilitating the co-ordination of the implementation of national policies by PVS and LVS should have been in place since the end of 2001. There should be 13 of such interprefectural services now. Nevertheless, CCA explained that they supervise and control actions both by having issued Circular Letters to further update and clarify the implementation of the national monitoring programme of TSEs in 2002 (5 such circulars so far). They have set up as well a new purpose-designed database operational since last 1st January 2002 that co- relates and assesses epidemiological data pertaining to TSEs surveillance coming from the field. CCA also highlighted the importance of confidence and good faith in the daily operation of the Greek veterinary services. The mission team noted progress concerning training and updating activities for official veterinarians (OV), the existence of the database for the control of the number, traceability and quality of the samples analysed in RVLs, and the initiatives put in place to monitor the role of the NRL as supervisor of RVLs. However, as stated, there is an evident lack of supervision of the monitoring programme when it comes to ensuring the sampling of all eligible animals in the sub-populations concerned by Regulation (EC) 999/2001 (see also points 5.1.2. and 5.1.3). The reasons would appear to be the absence of an operational and reliable bovine I&R database as well as an established programme of I&R inspections and controls at farm level. Within this context, CCA indicated that it considers the definitive set-up of a fully operational and reliable database for the bovine I&R.an urgent priority. Given its wider importance, this task is being addressed in an horizontal manner by another department within the Directorate General of Veterinary Services. CCA indicated that the database should be established by the end of 2002. 5 CCA provided the mission team with the following data regarding the sampling programme of the different sub-populations included in Regulation (EC) 999/2001, as it concerns passive and active surveillance. The relevant recommendations made in report 3307/2001 concerned: · The Greek Authorities should modify the current national legislation in order to comply with the EU legislation, particularly for the definition of a BSE clinical suspect and the procedure in case of positive rapid test. Regulation (EC) 999/2001 should be used as the legal basis. · The Greek Authorities should take additional actions to improve the detection of BSE clinical suspects (farmers and official veterinarians' knowledge of clinical signs, systematic procedure to rule out alternative diagnosis). The response from the CCA and the evaluation during the inspection by the mission team of legal instruments, instructions and measures concerning the above mentioned recommendations can be summarised as follows: By Ministerial Decision No 425605 of 28.12.01, the definition of a BSE suspect was brought in line with EC legislation. CCA issued Circular Letters to inform all official partners of the monitoring programme about this updating. CCA emphasised that, from the very beginning, all suspect cases of TSEs have to be notified to the LVS and PVS which are legally responsible and have all the administrative and technical resources required to implement the necessary measures with a view to confirm or rule out the suspicion. It stressed that, given the existing measures and procedures (such as information and sensitisation of veterinarians and livestock-keepers, regular visits to the farms by OVs, movement license following individual clinical examination of the animals or stringent ante-mortem inspection), the risk of an animal with clinical BSE- symptoms going unnoticed is in practice non-existent. The mission team noted: CCA have prepared a new leaflet addressed specifically at farmers in order to raise their awareness and co-operation in detecting BSE clinical suspects. There is no specific training programme focused on raising the awareness, technical capability or co-operation of private veterinary practitioners (PVPs). CCA consider that as OVs are largely replacing them, their theoretical role in the frontline of the passive surveillance in cattle farms is no longer important. There has not been any notification of a BSE clinical suspect either from farmers or PVPs so far in 2002. 6 CCA have organised several training seminars for OVs. So far in 2002, three seminars have taken place. This training includes use and handling of official forms to record all the information pertinent to the diagnosis of a BSE clinical suspicion. The training programme is scheduled to cover all officials, before the end of 2003. Both representatives of the CCA as well as OVs from PVS and LVS met during the on-the-spot visits insisted on the capability of the latter to rule out the presence of the disease in most cases (80% of the disorders initially roughly compatible with TSEs). Additionally, regional laboratories would be able to confirm the ruling out in almost all of the remaining cases (15%); the remaining 5% would need further investigation by NRL to rule out the presence of a TSE. It remains unclear when an animal would be considered an "official" clinical suspect of BSE. There has not been any clinical suspect so far in 2002. CCA have reminded regional laboratories of their obligation to transmit samples of animals suspected of TSEs infection to the NRL. They should also record and transmit data including, inter alia, the results of all tests performed on samples of animals possibly infected by TSEs. None of such samples from a suspect clinical case of TSEs considered officially as such has been sent to the NRL so far in 2002, neither has any of the data submitted to the NRL or the CCA raised suspicion of an underreported clinical suspect. CCA recognised the absence of practical experience amongst officials, PVPs, and the farming community with regard to the clinical symptoms of BSE. This would, at least initially, lead to a passive surveillance with an overreporting of clinical suspects, even if all of these would eventually give a negative result ("false positive suspicion"). 5.1.3. BACKGROUND INFORMATION The figures contained in the Annex under this section were provided by SBA, and are based on producers' statistics as reported to SBA. 4.1. PRODUCTION AND TRADE OF FEEDINGTUFFS Sweden produced or imported a total of 2,462,400 tonnes of feedingstuffs. Of this total, 2,305,200 tonnes (94 %) were intended for food producing animals, and 157,200 tonnes (6 %) for pets (Table 1). Domestic production accounts for 96 % of the compound feedingstuffs (CFS) consumed by all animal species. As regards food-producing animals, 99 % of the CFS consumed are produced domestically. Imports of CFS intended for food-producing animals are largely from the EU (93 %). Most of the imported petfood comes from Europe (86 %). With regard to feed materials, 68 % are produced in Sweden;. 99 % of proteins is of vegetable origin, the remaining 1 % is fish meal produced domestically. Most protein feed materials are imported (67 %). The meat and bone meal are used mainly in feed for pet (98%) and for non-food-producing animals (2%).(Table 2) The mission team noted that: Ø The central data base used contains only data from commercial producers; data from operators that mix cereal with complementary feedingstuffs are not included. Ø There are no details regarding type, origin and targeted animal species for additives and pre-mixtures used by producers of CFS7 The vast majority of feed additives used are imported, primarily from other EU countries. With the exception of CFS for fish, all CFS containing active substances for all species of animals are produced domestically (Table 3). Table 4 shows the quantity of zootechnical additives incorporated in feed for different species and categories of animals; the data is based on manufacturers' and home mixer's reports to SBA. 4.2. STRUCTURE OF THE FEED INDUSTRY Commercial plants, located mainly in the southern part of Sweden, produce 40-45% of CFS consumed, the balance being produced on-farm. The production of complete feed, pre-mixtures and complementary feedingstuffs is dominated by two large companies which supply 72.5% and 17.5% of the market, respectively. 6 OJ L 38, 12.2.1998, p. 10. 7 In their response to the draft report the Swedish authorities stated that all information is available in their register and in the database "Feedbase", but not all the information is published. In some cases the target species is not specified, when the product is aimed for all species. 15/10/03 - 44958 2 There are two associations, the "Foreingen Foder & Spannmal" and "Svenska Lantmannens", which represent 97% of the CFS production and 37 plants. Table 5 provides a breakdown of the feed businesses. Five plants are approved for the production of pre-mixtures and three plants are approved for the production of feed additives (micro-organisms). Out of the 40 manufacturers producing feedingstuffs intended for food producing animals, 34 have a permit to produce CFS containing medicinal products. Three plants manufacture feedingstuffs exclusively for fur animals, and one plant only produces CFS for fish. Operators that mix cereal with complementary feedingstuffs are not included in the table. The 98 home mixers are approved for the production of CFS containing medicinal products. There are 50 importers mostly of petfood. The SBA stated that the use of probiotics is marginal, whereas the use of enzymes in feed production is common. 5. MAIN FINDINGS AND OBSERVATIONS 5.1. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.1.1. Organisation Within the SBA, the "Animal Production and Management Division" deals with feed quality, use of medicinal products and animal by-products. The District Veterinary Division within the District Veterinary Department co-ordinates the activities of the + 80 district veterinary stations, which perform official veterinary tasks. The district veterinarians perform official feed controls at farm level to verify respect of the prohibition to administer processed animal protein (PAP) to food-producing animals (the "feed ban") and the approval of the mixing of medicated feedingstuffs on farms. The National Veterinary Institute (Statens Veterinärmedicinska Anstalt, (SVA) is the accredited laboratory for feedingstuffs. The County Administrative Boards (CAB) are the regional authorities, in which the "Veterinary Section" is involved in feed controls.8 Ø The three bodies are independent9. It was noted that the SBA consider the SVA to be acting under its instructions, whereas the SVA considers itself independent, but with the undertaking to handle SBA requests with a certain priority. 5.1.2. Responsibilities The responsibilities in respect of official feed controls are as follows: 8 In their response to the draft report the Swedish authorities stated that in Sweden one region is covered by inspection personnel located at SBA and other regions are inspected in the field by personnel located at four (out of 21) CABs. The inspectors from CAB are employed by SBA during the inspection missions and perform inspection on behalf of SBA i.e. the field control is centralised from administrative, responsibilities etc. points of view, but some personnel are located regionally. 9 In their response to the draft report the Swedish authorities stated that SVA and inspectors located at CAB report directly to SBA. The CCA stated that the feed control plan focuses on three aspects: basic control, safety checks and data collection: ü Basic control consists of the control of nutrients in CFS.
