To continue training of official veterinarians, including simulation exercises; 6 (4) To ensure that private practitioners working in the field of pig husbandry receive adequate training on relevant aspects of CSF, including in particular, early recognition, notification and control, and that all relevant information laid down in the permanent instructions of the contingency plan is distributed; (5) To officially appoint members of the expert group; (6) To ensure that in the event of an emergency killing of pigs complies with the provisions of Directive 93/119/EC; (7) To ensure that the national reference laboratory for CSF organises diagnostic intercalibration test at national level; (8) To establish written contracts between the veterinary services and the rendering industry to ensure proper destruction of pigs in the event of a CSF outbreak; The mission report is available at the DG(SANCO) website: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html Recommendation no. 7 had been fully addressed. Recommendation no. 3 was partly addressed: some training of OVs had been carried out in the regions and/or by the national reference laboratories, but there had been no simulation exercises since 1998. Some work had been undertaken in respect of recommendation no. 6, in that plans were in hand to create mobile emergency slaughter units. The remaining recommendations were not satisfactorily addressed, despite a letter, dated 20 June 2000, from the Italian authorities, indicating the actions taken. In particular, the mission team found, during this mission, that: ­ the National Disease Control Centre was not operational, ­ there was no evidence of central supervision of Regional and Local Disease Control Centres, ­ no simulation exercises had been held since 1998, ­ the evidence of training provided to private veterinary practitioners, and the distribution of instructions, was limited, ­ no members of expert groups had been appointed at any level, ­ no written contracts between the veterinary services and the rendering industry had been established. 7. OUTCOME OF THE MISSION 7.1. Competent Authorities Conclusions Certain elements of relevant EU legislation have not yet been transposed. 7 The CCA has no authority to audit the implementation of the contingency plans at regional/local level, nor to enforce the application of EU requirements at regional level. The Regions have full powers to develop and implement their own policy in respect of the contingency plans. Findings Council Directives 2000/75/EC and 2001/89/EC are not yet transposed into Italian legislation1. The structure and organisation of the Italian competent authorities have been described in detail in previous FVO reports (XXIV/1011/1999 and DG(SANCO)/3199/2001). During the initial meeting with the CCA, the mission team was informed that the structure of the CA remained unchanged since the last FVO mission. However, whilst the CCA can give guidelines to the Regions, it cannot give formal instructions for actions to be taken. This situation is still in a state of flux, and the relationship between central and regional services continues to evolve. It was noted that the bluetongue and ND control & eradication programmes continue to be centrally managed. This difference in treatment of OIE list A diseases was partly attributed to the application of the national Legislative Decree 112/19982, and partly to the excellent relations between the CCA and the National Reference Centre for the Exotic diseases in Teramo. The Italian authorities suggested that a similar approach to CSF or FMD might be possible in the event of outbreaks of these diseases. 7.2. Holding registration and animal identification The rules for holding registration and animal identification are described in detail in mission report DG(SANCO)/3199/2001. Conclusions The situation was considered to be satisfactory in respect of these issues. Findings The mission team visited one pig farm, one ovine farm and one animal dealer's premises. No deficiencies were found during these visits. It was noted that the farms/premises were frequently visited by the OV from the ASL and that documentation of these visits was kept. 7.3. Movement controls The rules for animal movement controls are described in detail in mission reports DG(SANCO)/1143/99, DG(SANCO)/3199/2001 and 1 The Commission's services have already taken formal action to address these failings. 2 Decreto Legislativo n.112 - 31/03/1998 Conferimento di funzioni e compiti amministrativi dello Stato alle regioni e agli enti locali. 8 DG(SANCO)/8547/2002. These rules require, inter alia, that sheep are identified with eartags or tattoos when leaving the holding. Conclusions The national rules for the control of animal movements are not always respected. Findings During the visit to a slaughterhouse in Lazio, the mission team found 50 lambs with no identity marks present in the lairage, awaiting slaughter. They came from an area in which all animals were vaccinated against Bluetongue. The animals were accepted for slaughter by the OV of the slaughterhouse. 7.4. Contingency Plans Conclusions There are contingency plans for FMD and CSF in place, approved under Commission Decisions 93/455/EC and 99/246/EEC. These are supported by operational manuals. These plans were not implemented uniformly in the regions visited (Lazio, Umbria, Abruzzo). They have not been updated since their approval. There are different regional plans and manuals in place, but these have neither been approved by the competent central authority, nor notified to the Commission. The contingency plan for FMD does not address a number of issues identified in the guidelines provided by the European Commission. The Italian authorities have not yet finalised, nor submitted for approval, a contingency plan for bluetongue. There is no agreed operational manual for bluetongue. Instead, there are working drafts, which are adapted to changing circumstances because of the current disease situation in Italy. Operational manuals had been prepared in respect of FMD and CSF. However, there was a lack of consistency in their preparation and availability, and uncertainty as to the status of some of the manuals in use. There was only limited evidence to indicate that staff at local level and in establishments were aware of the provisions of the manuals. The level of preparedness for, and awareness of, the action required to respond effectively to disease emergencies was limited and inconsistent between regions. Resources available to respond rapidly to emergencies were generally insufficient, or it was unclear how they could be obtained. The action necessary to plan for Regional and Local Disease Control Centres had not been undertaken. A mobile emergency slaughter system was under development. Only limited simulation exercises had been undertaken (the last being in 1998). 9 7.4.1. Plan Documentation Findings The CSF contingency plan is approved under Commission Decision 99/246/EEC, whilst that for FMD is approved under Commission Decision 93/455/EEC. There is no approved contingency plan for bluetongue, as required by Article 18, Council Directive 2000/75/EC. The CCA indicated that the plan and manual had been drafted, but were not yet finalised, due to ongoing amendments in light of the disease situation in Italy. The CSF plan was described in mission report DG(SANCO)/1143/99. The FMD plan was drafted on 5 November 1991 and entered into force in August 1993. It provides a description of the structure of the central, regional and local authorities, the role of the veterinary laboratory network and of the national reference centres, and the organisation and facilities of the local veterinary services. However, in the light of the provisions of the "Guidelines for FMD contingency plans in non-vaccinating countries" (VI/6319/98, rev 1) and the guidelines on "Contingency plans for epidemic diseases" (VI/5211/95), there are a number of apparent gaps in the coverage of the plan: - there is no reference either to the legal powers available to the authorities or to the financial aspects of the plan; - the description of the National Disease Control Centre is non-specific. Although it refers to the Standing Committee for Emergencies, which must be equipped with fax, phones, list of experts, lists of phone numbers, addresses, maps, etc, there is no indication of its location, co-ordination of tasks, etc.; - the description of the Local Disease Control Centres is non-specific; - information on the existence of updated expert groups is not provided; - personnel, laboratories, equipment and facilities must be available, but no details of staff resources, contact points etc. are given; - there is no reference to emergency vaccination procedures; - there is no reference to training in relation to disease preparedness/awareness. The mission team received both the approved plans and the FMD manual from the CCA during the initial meeting in Rome. The CSF manual was available on CD-ROM, distributed by the CSF National Reference Centre in Perugia. A draft new Contingency Plan, common to all OIE list "A" 10 diseases, with separate manuals for each relevant disease is in preparation. This draft has not yet been approved by the national authorities or the European Commission. There was no indication that the original Contingency Plans and Manuals had been updated since they were first approved. 7.4.2. National legal powers The main legal texts relevant for control of CSF and FMD in Italy are the following: Decree of the President of the Republic of 17 May 1996, no 3633 transposing Council Directive 80/217/EEC, as amended by Directive 91/685/EEC. Decree of the President of the Republic of 1 March 1992, no 2294 transposing Council Directive 85/511/CEE as amended by Directive 90/423/EEC. In case of an outbreak of an infectious disease, the Minister of Health can impose animal movement restrictions and request help from the police. The Minister has delegated this power to the General Director of Office VIII (Sanità Animale e Anagrafe del bestiame) of the Directorate General of Veterinary Public Health, Food and Nutrition. 7.4.3. Financial provisions - eradication, compensation Details concerning financial provisions for responding to disease outbreaks are provided in mission report DG(SANCO)/1143/99. The CCA stated that the Decree of 3 January 2001 provided additional resources of 50 000 000 for all emergency purposes, and that these funds are available for outbreaks of infectious diseases. The compensation system is based on the principle of 100% compensation of the market value within 60 days for animals killed in the event of an infectious disease. The legal bases include Act 218 of 2 June 1988 and Decree 298 of 20 July 1989. The prices of animals of different categories in all Regions are indicated in a periodical publication "Prezzi degli animali da vita e riproduzione, dei prodotti dell'acquacoltura e dell'apicoltura" issued by Istituto per studi, ricerche e informazioni sul mercato agricolo. 7.4.4. Organisation and chain of command There is a chain of command established in the contingency plans from the central authority (Director General of the Department of Food, Nutrition and Veterinary Public Health of the Ministry of Health) through the Director of 3 D.P.R. 17 maggio 1996, n. 363 Regolamento recante norme per l'attuazione della direttiva 91/685/CEE, del Consiglio dell'11 dicembre 1991, recante modifica della direttiva 80/217/CEE che stabilisce misure comunitarie di lotta contro la peste suina classica

DPR 1 marzo 1992, n.229 Regolamento di attuazione della direttiva 85/511/CEE che stabilisce misure di lotta contro l'afta epizootica, tenuto conto delle modifiche dalla direttiva 90/423/CEE 11 the Office VII of the Department to the regional veterinary service and the ASLs. However, as has been indicated in previous missions, in practice the CCA can provide guidance to the Regions, but has no enforcement powers. During visits to the Regions it was made clear that they regard themselves as responsible for their own actions, and that they are not obliged to follow the CCA's instructions, even in an emergency. They can, however, seek the support of the central authorities if the situation is considered sufficiently serious or delicate. An example was given on the basis of the recent vaccination campaign against bluetongue. As the Regions could not agree whether to vaccinate or not, the Consiglio Superiore di Sanità (which is a technical consultative body serving the Minister of Health) was consulted, and decided that all susceptible animals should be vaccinated. In "peace time" a body called the Standing Emergency Committee (Comitato permanente per le emergenze) has been set up at central level. At regional level, there are Comitati Regionali per la Zooprofilassi, and at local level, the ASL. These bodies have specific control functions, and the number of officials (but not individual names or tasks) is indicated. No confirmation, e.g. minutes of meetings, of the outcome of the activities of these bodies was available. The mission team was advised that frequent contacts take place between the officials concerned. In case of an emergency (notification of an infectious disease) these "peacetime" bodies should be transformed into Crisis Units at central, regional and local level. The National Crisis Unit would act as the decision- making body, whilst the implementation of its decisions would be co- ordinated at regional, and implemented at local, level. 7.4.5. National Disease Control Centre In an emergency, the National Disease Control Centre will be located in the Ministry of Health in Rome, and would be under responsibility of Office VI (Ufficio VI, Sistema di allerta, Unità di crisi ed emergenze). In "peace time", the Standing Emergency Committee has this role, and the contingency plans require certain facilities to be provided. The mission tea

SUMMARY OF PREVIOUS MISSIONS 6.1. Response to previous mission A previous mission, DG(SANCO)/1215/1999, to review the FMD and CSF contingency plans, took place in December 1999. The report of that mission, and of others mentioned in this report, are available at the DG SANCO website: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html That report made a number of recommendations, most of which were satisfactorily addressed by the CCA in their response to the mission. However, by the time of the current mission, no training exercise for staff likely to be involved in an outbreak had taken place (c.f. 7.3.12) and the NRL had not yet achieved accreditation (c.f. 7.3.11). 7. OUTCOME OF THE MISSION 7.1. Competent Authorities Conclusions The structure and organisation of the CA allows a clear allocation of responsibilities and a co-ordinated approach. The relevant EU legislation has been transposed into Danish Law. Findings A detailed description of the structure of the veterinary services in Denmark is given in documents DG(SANCO)/3282/2001, DG(SANCO)/3369/2001 and DG(SANCO)/3356/2001, which can be found at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html. Further information regarding the CCA can be found on their web-site at http://www.fdir.dk/. The DVFA of the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries is responsible for the transposition of EU legislation on animal health into national law, and the organisation of a harmonised implementation in the different regions. Within the DVFA the Division for Domestic Animal Diseases is responsible for contingency planning activities. The eleven Regional Veterinary and Food Control Authorities (Fødevareregion ­ RVFCA) are 6 responsible for implementation and enforcement of the legislation, as well as disease preparedness in their regions. For co-ordination purposes, meetings are regularly organised between the DVFA and the RVFCA. Relevant EU legislation has been transposed into Danish law. Most recently, Council Directive 2001/89/EC has been transposed by Bekendtgørelse om bekæmpelse af klassisk svinepest, reference: Bekendtgørelse n° 212 of 27/03/2003. 7.2. Holding registration, animal identification and movement controls Conclusions Holding registration, animal identification and movement controls for cattle, pigs, sheep and goats were found to be satisfactory for the purpose of epizootic disease control. Findings The rules for bovine holding registration and identification are described in detail in mission report DG(SANCO)/8671/2002. Holdings with cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, deer or commercial poultry are registered on the Central Holding Register (CHR) operated by the Danish Agricultural Advisory Centre. Details of the owner and location of the holding, herd details, the private veterinary practitioner and veterinary events are recorded. All holdings must be registered - there is no derogation for small holdings. Movements of animals (individual animals in the case of cattle and batches in the case of pigs, sheep and goats) must be notified to CHR. Local offices issue movement documents, based on the animal health status shown in CHR. Individual animal identification, based on the holding number, is required for cattle, pigs, sheep and goats. However exemptions are allowed for slaughter pigs (a slap mark is acceptable) and piglets moving once within an approved `piglet ring', i.e. a piglet supply chain authorised by the CA. Cattle have to be identified within 20 days of birth. Pigs, sheep and goats must be identified before leaving the holding of birth, or in the case of sheep, within 60 days of birth. Owners are required to keep holding registers, showing movements and additional data on identification, births and deaths, according to the species. Herd inventories are sent out from CHR at regular intervals to allow owners to check data. During visits to farms, a collection centre for intra-Community trade, a slaughterhouse and regional offices, the examples seen by the team of animal identification, herd registers and movement documents were correct and would have allowed tracing of animals back to herds of origin. Official controls on identification and movement documentation were satisfactory. 7 7.3. Contingency Plans Conclusions In general the contingency planning arrangements in place would allow the competent authorities (CA) to respond appropriately to one or more outbreaks of epizootic disease. The further work on-going in this area should increase the effectiveness of any such response. There are national contingency plans for CSF, FMD, ND/AVI and other epizootic diseases. The CSF plan was up-dated in April 2003 to reflect the requirements of Council Directive 2001/89/EC. The FMD plan was last up- dated in 2003, following a project reviewing FMD contingency planning in 2001. A further up-date is planned following the adoption of the new FMD Directive. The contingency plans and operations manuals are generally in compliance with the requirements of EU legislation and guidelines. The Danish legal powers and financial provisions are generally sufficient to allow the services to respond to an outbreak of epizootic disease. There is a clear chain of command. Plans are in place for the operation of the NDCC and the establishment of LDCCs. A new Regional Contingency Group for Epizootic Diseases, with responsibilities for contingency planning has been created and has started work on a number of new initiatives in relation to training and preparedness, including assisting the Regions with the development of their local arrangements. Many of the required elements of contingency plans are in place, e.g. access to the holding registration and movement control database, an expert group and valuation, compensation and carcass disposal procedures. Possible sources of the additional staff, facilities, equipment and materials had been identified, although arrangements for obtaining these resources were not always formalised. The procedure and time required for the changes of approvals for rendering plants that would be required for carcass disposal during an outbreak needs further clarification. The NRL for CSF and FMD has sufficient diagnostic capacity to respond to outbreaks. Work to achieve accreditation is still in progress and procedures for responding to outbreaks have not been formalised. An agreement describing the services that the NRL will provide to the DVFA is currently being drawn up. No real-time alert exercises have taken place to date, although an exercise is being planned at present. Although the level of disease awareness was found to be high, very few suspicions of epizootic disease were notified to the competent authorities. 8 7.3.1. Plan Documentation Findings The national contingency plans for CSF and FMD have been approved by Commission Decisions 99/246/EC and 93/455/EEC, respectively. The CSF plan was up-dated in April 2003 to reflect the requirements of Council Directive 2001/89/EC. The revised CSF plan has been submitted to the Commission for approval as required by that Directive. This plan has a revised format, consisting of a "Strategy and Resource Plan", with general procedures for responding to an outbreak and a detailed operations manual with disease-specific instructions for official veterinarians. It is expected that all future revised plans will follow this format. The plan foresees different alert levels based on the risk of outbreaks and describes actions to be taken at each level. Targets are set for response times for clinical inspection of suspect cases, completion of culling of infected herds, culling of in-contact herds and cleaning and disinfection. The FMD plan was last up-dated in 2003 following a project, commissioned by the veterinary services in 2001, reviewing FMD contingency planning. This project involved consultation with industry representatives, veterinary associations and the veterinary services. Some, but not all, of the recommendations in this project have been implemented or taken into account in the revised plans. Changes already implemented include amendment of the Animal Health Act, tighter rules for trade in live animals, the introduction of a national standstill for all species in the event of an outbreak and the possibility of carrying out preventive culling. A further revision of the FMD contingency plan is planned in 2003/4 following adoption of the new FMD Directive. The plans are generally drawn up in accordance with Commission Decision 91/42/EC and Annex VII of Council Directive 2001/89/EC. In addition, the plans generally address the requirements of the Commission's guidelines on "Contingency plans for epidemic diseases" (VI/5211/95) and "Guidelines for FMD contingency plans in non-vaccinating countries" (VI/6319/98, rev 1). The requirements of Commission Decision 2002/106/EC are reflected in the revised CSF contingency plan. The contingency plan for ASF is due to be completed in June 2003 and submitted to the Commission for approval. The plan for `other epizootic diseases', i.e. general procedures for list A diseases not covered by a specific plan, has been revised in 2003. The CCA plans to carry out a review of the response to the Newcastle Disease outbreak is planned for June/July 2003 in the regions affected. A revision of the ND/AI plan is planned for 2004. Regional offices have been provided with a model for preparation of local contingency arrangements. They have been asked to submit the completed plans to the CCA for approval. 9 7.3.2. National legal powers General provisions relating to the control of epizootic diseases are laid down in the Animal Health Act (Lov nr. 351 af 2. juni 1999 om sygdomme og infektioner hos dyr as amended by Lov nr. 966 af 4. december 2002). The relevant EU legislation has been transposed into Danish legislation by a number of disease specific orders, as well as orders relating to aspects of the management of outbreaks, e.g. slaughter and killing, compensation, cleaning and disinfection etc. In addition, a number of instructions have been issued regarding notification of cases of suspicion of exotic disease and measures for persons having contact with cloven-hoofed animals outside Denmark. The Danish legislation gives powers, inter alia, to require notification of suspicion of disease, carry out diagnostic and epidemiological investigations, impose movement restrictions, create protection and surveillance zones, control movements within these zones, take samples, slaughter infected and in-contact animals, pay compensation, destroy carcasses and potentially infective materials, carry out cleaning and disinfection and, where necessary, carry out emergency vaccination. Areas with a high density of pigs have been identified, as required by Directive 2001/89/EC. At present no particular measures for disease awareness promotion are foreseen for such areas (c.f. 7.3.13). 7.3.3. Financial provisions A specific `peacetime' budget has been allocated for contingency planning activities at Regional level and a further amount has been allocated for the `Veterinary Alarm Service', which provides an out-of-hours on-call service. A budget is immediately available for payment of compensation and costs associated with controlling an outbreak and further funds can be obtained on submission of a request to the Finance Committee. There are clearly defined procedures for valuation of animals slaughtered for disease control purposes. The Ministry for Food, Agriculture and Fisheries pays compensation for animals killed on infected and in-contact premises and for 20% of the owners' operating losses. Private emergency funds for, inter alia, disease control, cover the remaining 80% of the farmers' operating losses. For pig farms these losses are covered by the swine industry fund (Svineafgiftsfonden). Losses in dairy farms are covered by the "Maelkeafgiftsfonden" and losses in meat producing cattle farms are covered by the "Kvaegafgiftsfonden". The poultry industry does not have a formal arrangement for a private emergency fund for disease control. On a case by case basis, they may decide to compensate farmers from the "Fjerkraeafgiftsfonden". During the Newcastle disease outbreak in 10 2002, they decided to compensate farms that were subject to area-restrictions and consequential losses. No maximum time for payment of compensation is specified in Danish legislation or Ministry procedures. During the ND outbreak in 2002, compensation was generally paid within 30 days. 7.3.4. Chain of command The chain of command is clearly defined, direct and was clearly understood by persons met during the mission. The CVO has overall responsibility for responding to an outbreak. Under the CVO, the Division for Domestic Animal Diseases is responsible for running the NDCC and co-ordinating activities nationally. The Veterinary Services in the Regions are responsible for running the LDCC, carrying out control actions within their Region and reporting to the NDCC. In addition a Regional Contingency Group has been established, which has responsibilities for co-ordinating `peacetime' contingency planning activities, although its exact role in the event of an outbreak has not yet been fully defined. The national Strategy and Resource plan for CSF describes a CVO Crisis Management Group, meeting daily, made up of representatives from major stakeholders: industry organisations, the Veterinary Association, the NRL, disease experts, the Agricultural Council, Police, Army and Danish Emergency Management Agency. Individual task forces with responsibilities for specific issues, such as epidemiology and eradication, and movement restrictions, have been defined and the heads of these task forces have been identified, although additional staff likely to be involved in each unit have not. Similarly, task forces to operate at regional level have been identified and Regions have been asked to identify staff responsible for each group. 7.3.5. National Disease Control Centre In the event of an outbreak the NDCC would initially be staffed by the personnel of the Division for Domestic Animal Diseases and would use their offices for accommodation. Other offices and rooms, equipped with necessary IT and telephone/fax connections, could be made available within the same building if it was necessary to increase the size of the NDCC. The NDCC has access to the CHR and GIS, as well as the DVFA intra-net and the internet. There is no specific computer-based system for managing data on disease control tasks during an outbreak, although the creation of such a system is under discussion. It was stated that additional administrative staff could be obtained from other parts of the Ministry if required, although no formal agreement regarding the release of such staff has been made and staff likely to be called upon have 11 not been identified, precluding any possibility of providing them with training. 7.3.6. Local Disease Control Centres RVFCAs have been provided with a model to complete describing their arrangements for setting up and staffing the LDCC. In the first instance the LDCC would be in the Regional Office. RVFCAs have been asked to identify other sites, which could be used as LDCCs if the capacity of the office is exceeded. In the Regions visited, possible sites had been identified but no discussions had taken place nor agreements made with the owners of these sites regarding their availability in the event of an outbreak. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objective of the mission was to assess: · the phytosanitary situation of Phytophthora ramorum Werres, De Cock & Man in't Veld sp. Nov. (Phytophthora ramorum ) on the territory of Germany; · the implementation of Commission Decision 2002/757/EC1 of 19 September 2002 on provisional emergency phytosanitary measures to prevent the introduction into and the spread within the Community of Phytophthora ramorum. This was the first mission undertaken to Germany for this purpose. 1 OJ No. L 252, 20.09.2002, p.37 5 In pursuit of this objective, the following sites were visited: AUTHORITIES Comments 1 BBA Department for Plant Health Single and Central Central 3 Schleswig - Holstein Authority Regional Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Agriculture Responsible Official Amt für Ländliche Räume Lübeck Bodies Lower Saxony Landwirtschaftskammer Weser -Ems Baden - Würtemberg Ministry for Agriculture, Food and Rural areas Landesanstalt für Pflanzenschutz Regierungspräsidien Stuttgart, Karlsruhe LABORATORIES Comments Regional 2 Lower Saxony (Oldenburg) Research centres Baden - Würtemberg (Stuttgart) 1 BBA (Braunschweig), Institute of Plant Protection in Horticulture PLANT HEALTH CONTROL SITES Comments Nurseries (producers and /or traders) 7 Of which: 3 in Schleswig - Holstein, 3 Private green sites in Lower Saxony and 1 in Baden- Württemberg 1 In Baden - Württemberg

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular, Art. 21 of Council Directive 2000/29/EC2. 2 Council Directive 2000/29/EC of 8 May 2000 on protective measures against the introduction into the Community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the Community (as amended) - OJ No. L 169, 10.07.2000, p.1 6 3. BACKGROUND 3.1. Background to the present mission BBA officially informed the European Commission (EC) on 12 March 2001 about the presence of an unknown Phytophthora on its territory, isolated from Rhododenron sp. and Viburnum sp. . In October 2001, P. ramorum was described in a joint scientific publication by German and Dutch scientists, as a new Phytophthora species. According to the results of the 2002 survey, sent by Member States (MS) to the EC, samples of Rododendron and Viburnum plants from Germany were found infected by P. ramorum in Denmark, Sweden and the United Kingdom (respectively 5, 3 and 2 samples/findings). From 1 November 2002, the date of the implementation of Commission Decision 2002/757/EC, up to the time of the mission, no interception of consignments of German Viburnum and Rhododendron plants have been officially notified by MS3 to the EC. 3.2. Production and trade information Plant species, which are susceptible to P. ramorum and present in Germany are: Rhododendron spp., Viburnum spp. and Quercus spp. In Germany, there are at least 2,000 registered nurseries under the Plant Inspection Order (Pflanzenbeschauverordnung)4, which was issued on the basis of the plant Protection Act (Pflanzenschtzgesetz)5. The production of Rhododendron plants in Germany is concentrated in northern Lower Saxony where there is a stock of around 8 million plants, with 1,5 to 2 million traded each year. The total amount of Viburnum plants is estimated at approximately 100,000 plants, with 30,000 plants produced and traded annually. Lower Saxony has the majority of traded consignments involving almost all EU Member States, as well as third countries and other Länder in Germany. In Schleswig-Holstein the estimated production of Rhododendron plants is localised on 20 ha. Baden-Württemberg has mainly trade in plants, but little production. Rhododendron plants are mainly found in private and public green sites. Viburnum plants are found on the edges of woods and at roadsides. Quercus rubra can be found in private gardens. In Lower Saxony, Rhododendron plants are widespread in private and public green sites. 35 % of the land in Germany is covered with forest. Oak accounts for around 5-10 % and beech is 30 %. Most oaks in the forest are Q. robur and Q. petraea. In some areas, Q. rubra is also present.

German competent authorities The Federal Ministry for Consumer Protection, Food and Agriculture (Bundesministerium für Verbraucherschutz, Ernahrung und Landwirtschaft=BMVEL) is the Federal Authority in the field of plant health. It represents Germany at the international level and is in charge of plant health legislation. BBA is a governmental organization subordinate to BMVEL. BBA Department for National and International Plant Health is the Authority in charge of co-ordination and contact, as referred to in Art. 1 (4) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. The implementation of EU and Federal legislation on plant health is carried out at Länder level. The Plant Protection Services of the Federal Länder are the Responsible Official Bodies as referred to Art. 2 (1), (g) of the same Directive. Their activities are supervised by the competent ministries in the Länder. In Germany, there are 16 Länder and 18 Plant Protection Services. The Services are technically and hierarchically under the competent ministries in the Länder. In Lower Saxony, the Plant Protection Service is attached to the respective Chambers of Agriculture - Landwirtschaftskammern -, which have been authorised by the Länder Ministry to perform tasks according to plant health legislation in their geographical areas. There are two Landwirtschaftskammern: Weser-Ems and Hannover. In Baden-Würtemberg, the Ministry of Agriculture of the Land has delegated the technical co-ordination of the activities, to a governmental organization, Landesanstalt fur Pflanzenschutz. In Baden-Würtemberg, there are 4 local branches of the Plant Protection Service, namely in the Regierungspräsidien of Stuttgart, Karlsruhe, Freiburg, Tübingen. In Schleswig -Holstein, the regional offices of the Plant Protection Service are called Amt für Ländliche Räume (ALR). There are 3 ALR: Husum, Kiel and Lübeck. 4.2. Legislation The duties of the Länder and of BBA are described in the national primary legislation pertaining to plant health, the Plant Protection Act -Pflanzenschutzgesetz, as amended (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The secondary legislation, implementing Council Directive 2000/29/EC, is the Plant Inspection Order Pflanzenbeschauverordnung as amended (hereinafter referred to as the Order) . Commission Decision 2002/757/EC has been officially notified from BMVEL to the Ministries of the Federal Länder and published on the BBA web site. Under the current legislation, the producers of the registered nurseries are obliged to report occurrences of harmful organisms listed in Annex I and II of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. There is no obligation to report the occurrence of harmful organisms not listed in the above mentioned Annexes, which is the case of P. 8 ramorum6. Private and public green owners are not obliged to report occurrences of P. ramorum. Some doubts on the interpretation of the words "signs of European isolates ", "infected plants" and "finding" used in Commission Decision 2002/757/EC were raised by the responsible official body in Lower Saxony and BBA. In particular, it was not clear if the retention at the place of production for the "10 m radius" plants and the three month period starts at the moment where symptoms are found on the plants or when a positive result from the laboratory is obtained. 4.3. Co-ordination, work planning and policy The technical co-ordination role assumed by BBA is based on provisions in the Act and the Order, as amended, and on an internal agreement between BMVEL and BBA, existing since 1995. BBA co-ordinates the inspection activity of the Länder mainly through the elaboration of specific guidance. For P. ramorum, BBA Plant Health Department has developed, in 2002, specific forms as a basis for monitoring and reporting activities of the Plant Protection Services7. In this form, all the steps of the inspection have been included: first finding of symptoms, laboratory diagnosis and contacts with the Plant Protection Services of another Land from where the infected plants were obtained. At the annual meeting of BBA and Plant Protection Services in May 2003, the new strategy for the P. ramorum campaign will be reviewed and discussed. It is planned to discuss several topics e.g. monitoring intensity, survey in green sites (private and public) and in the forests, co-operation with forest services and measures in case of findings, diagnostic network, polymerase chain reaction method (PCR) and use of fungicides. In the visited Länder, the services are waiting for this meeting before organising their campaign on P. ramorum. No specific instruction on how to carry out inspections and/or how to manage outbreaks, were found in the visited Länder. Some internal training for inspectors has been carried out8. BBA does not always receive relevant information from all the Länder (e.g. data requested for the pre-mission questionnaire were not available for Hessen, Hamburg, Northrhine-Westphalia). Inspection of the nurseries and survey campaign In 2001, a survey was carried out at around 230 sites (nurseries and green sites); Phytophthora ramorum was found in 13 nurseries and 2 private green sites. In 2002, the number of sites inspected was increased to a total of 624 nurseries and 48 green sites; P. ramorum was found in 36 nurseries and in 2 private green sites. During both years, infections at nurseries were found in the following Länder: Baden-Württemberg, Lower Saxony, Northrhine-Westphalia and Schleswig- Holstein. In addition, outbreaks were reported also from Bavaria and Saxony in 2001 and from Hessen in 2002. In 2002, Baden-Württemberg and Hessen each reported one outbreak case in private green sites. In one of those, the eradication was carried out by the supplier of the plants, while in the other case the trace-back to the owner of the garden was not possible. During both years, the disease was found on Viburnum and Rhododendron plants. NURSERIES In Schleswig-Holstein, there are 390 nurseries registered under the plant passport regime. During 2002, in the area under the control of the ALR Lübeck, 194 nurseries producing Rhododendron and/or Viburnum plants were inspected from July to September. P. ramorum was found in 8 nurseries on both species. 87 nurseries, already under the plant passport regime, were inspected during 2002. Some of these have been authorised to issue plant passports for Viburnum plants although, up to now, they have still not been inspected. In Lower Saxony Weser-Ems area, there are 563 registered nurseries under the plant passport regime. In 2002, the survey was carried out from July to September on 217 nurseries. P. ramorum was found in 17 nurseries. At the Plant Protection Service in Weser-Ems, 40 nurseries have been recently registered and authorised to issue plant passports for Rhododendron and Viburnum plants, but two-thirds of them have not been subject to any official preliminary control. In Baden-Würtemberg, 448 nurseries are registered. In 2002, 21 nurseries were inspected during July -August and 8 outbreaks were found. There are only few nurseries (around 10) involved in the production of Viburnum plants and trade of Rhododendron plants (in the latter case, plants are sold to the final consumer). In particular in the Karlsruhe and Stuttgart areas, the nurseries have been controlled during 2002, but have still not been authorised to issue the plant passports. The FVO 10 team was informed that this is the case also in the other Regierungspräsidien of this Land9. In Rhineland-Palatinate the work to extend the plant passport scheme to include Rhododendron and Viburnum plants in the registered nurseries was not yet completed. In the Länder visited, it was reported to the team that there is a lack of personnel and an increase in tasks in the plant health field, which does not enable them to cope properly with the requirements of Commission Decision 2002/757/EC. BBA and the Responsible Official Bodies representatives stressed that, up until the issuing of Commission Decision 2002/757/EC, there was no legal basis to apply the measures referred to therein, during the 2002 campaign. Traceback and traceforward in the outbreaks nurseries are usually carried out. FORESTRY, PUBLIC and PRIVATE GREEN SITES During 2002, in Schleswig-Holstein checks of the oak forests by the ALR Lübeck around the outbreak nurseries were carried out. In the other Länder visited, no specific survey out of the nurseries was undertaken. In Baden-Würtemberg, an indirect survey of the private green sites informing Associations of Landscapers and of Nursery Producers, is planned for the next campaign. In Lower Saxony Weser- Ems area, some hundreds of points in public green sites will be observed in 2003. In general, the planning for the 2003 public and private green sites survey is expected to be done after the yearly meeting of the Services and BBA in May. In the Länder visited, co-operation between the Plant Protection and the Forestry Services on monitoring P. ramorum is not yet foreseen, although first contacts for collaboration have been taken. Similar co-operation has already been carried out in the past (i.e. Bursaphelenchus xylophilus survey). Up to now, the surveys have been carried out by the Foresty Research Stations, in some Länder. The Forestry Research Station in Lower Saxony carried out a survey of the occurrence of Phytophthora spp. in beech trees in the north-west, centre and south of Germany, and in oak trees in Lower Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein and North Rhine- Westphalia. A specific survey on Phytophthora quercina has also been carried out in Bavaria. Symptoms of bleeding canker found in Lower Saxony have been associated with the presence of xylophagous insects (Coleoptera: Buprestidae)10.

No cases of non-compliance for documentary or phytosanitary reasons were found. 4.5. Identification In the Länder, each Plant Protection Service has its own laboratory. Identification of P. ramorum is carried out with culture grown on various media (e.g. selective, carrot agar medium) and morphological diagnosis. Literature and comparative cultures are available for the identification of P. ramorum. In cases of doubt, samples can be sent to the BBA's Institute for Plant Protection in Horticulture. PCR analysis is currently being developed in Lower Saxony and at the Institute for Plant Protection in Horticulture in BBA. The time of response from the laboratories of the Länder visited varied from 10 days to 4 weeks, partly resulting from the different procedures followed. According to data provided in the pre-mission questionnaire the time response varies from one week to 6 weeks, although in most cases the result of the test is available within 14 days. The Plant Protection Services do not have experience in isolating P. ramorum from wood. However, as a result of its experiments, the BBA's Institute for Plant Protection in Horticulture is able to isolate the pathogen from artificially inoculated and naturally infected wood. The personnel met had the required knowledge to identify P. ramorum. In the visited laboratory, the samples are registered and coded. Confidentiality is also ensured. In general, the laboratories report the results to the regional Plant Protection Services. From these a letter is sent to the owner with the results of the test, together with the measures to be applied. In Lower Saxony, this letter also clearly indicates the follow-up inspection date. OUTCOME OF THE MISSION 7.1. Competent Authorities Conclusions Council Directive 92/102/ECC and Council Directive 64/432/EEC as amended are still not completely transposed into Luxembourg law. There is no legal basis for a swine registration database. There is still no list of officially approved disinfectants in Luxembourg. Control measures, regarding the swill feeding ban, animal transporters and dealers, and the medical register on farms, are missing. 7 Staff were competent and motivated, and there was a spirit of collaboration and co-operation. However, there is no regular control procedure regarding the different levels of the veterinary service in place. Due to the lack of appreciation of the scale of response required, the Luxembourg authorities are not sufficiently prepared to deal with a major disease outbreak of FMD. The contract with the rendering plant company does not reflect the needs in the event of a large scale outbreak of an OIE list A disease. Findings The recent EU legislation regarding epizootic diseases is completely transposed into Luxembourg legislation. However, parts of Council Directive 92/102/EEC on identification and registration are still not transposed, although the Luxembourg CCA has given a commitment in their response to the draft report of the previous mission regarding CPs to Luxembourg (DG(SANCO)/8655/2002), that "necessary measures have been undertaken to complete the transposition of Council Directive 92/102/EEC". No clear mention is made of the need to identify pigs and small ruminants with an eartag or tattoo, enabling the holding from which they have come to be determined. There is no legal basis for a swine database as foreseen in Article 18 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC as amended. A list of disinfectants approved by the CCA is still not available as foreseen in Article 12 of Council Directive 2001/89/EC, although, in the response to the draft report to the previous CP mission to Luxembourg (DG(SANCO)/8655/2002), the CCA noted that a list of officially approved disinfectants is under preparation4. The mission team identified one disinfectant, used at a cleaning and desinfection facility, which is not listed in the CP for CSF. Concerning the implementation of national legislation, it was noted that there is no procedure in place regarding: Ø the control of swill feeding at farm and at catering level (swill feeding ban was imposed in 1987); Ø the control of animal transporters and livestock dealers. However, a checklist for the means of transport is available; Ø the control of the medical records at farm level (identification of treated animals, records of all kind of medicines); Ø the control of approved veterinarians as foreseen in Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC as amended. 4 In their response to the draft report, the Luxembourg authorities stated that, since the veterinary services have no experts on evaluation of disinfectants and the Pharmaceuticals and Medicines Division of the Ministry of Health was unable to bring work on this question to a conclusion, the official list of disinfectants approved in Germany and Belgium have been used. 8 At central level of the veterinary service, there are five veterinarians in charge, supported by four veterinary inspectors at regional level. The total number of veterinarians in Luxembourg is about one hundred, from which about 30 veterinarians are working in the production animal area. These veterinarians are all officially approved in accordance with Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC as amended. However, there is no regular control procedure in place in order to monitor the performance of the different levels of the veterinary service. The organisation of the Luxembourg veterinary service and the facility of communication within the services itself, and to the different parties, represents an important positive impact in the event of an outbreak of an OIE list A disease. However, during discussions of possible disease outbreak scenarios, it was apparent that the level of risk envisaged was low. This does not correspond to the reality encountered in Member States during outbreaks of FMD in 2001. As a consequence, the CP for FMD is designed to cope with best case rather than worst case scenario. The mission team also noted a high level of willingness and preparation by the police and customs to provide every assistance to the veterinary authorities in emergency situations, movement control of vehicles and road blockages. The police and custom services have not been consulted in the drawing up of the CPs, but during the FMD crisis in 2001, they participated in meetings organised by the CVO. No suitable rendering plant exists in Luxembourg. However, a contract exists with a rendering facility in Belgium. In the case of disease eradication, the rendering plant collects and transports cadavers and waste directly from the holding to the rendering plant. However, the contract does not provide sufficient guarantees in the case of a large-scale outbreak. The CCA provided the mission team with a map of Luxembourg indicating water protection zones. However, no suitable areas for burning of infected cadavers have been drawn in. 7.2. Monitoring programme for OIE list A diseases Conclusions There are monitoring and vaccination programmes for CSF in wild boars in place. The monitoring programme for CSF in domestic pigs is based on movement control and serological testing at farm and slaughterhouse level. Findings Concerning wild boars, monitoring and vaccination programmes for CSF are in place. Dead wild boars, which are delivered to one of the 15 collection centres, have to be serologically tested. If the meat of a delivered and negatively tested wild boar is not fit for human consumption, the hunter will get compensation of 100 for each cadaver. In 2003, three vaccination campaigns were carried out, with the result that the seroprevalence of CSF antibodies in wild boars, has increased from 30% in February 2003 to 60% in October 2003. 9 Concerning domestic pigs there is a monitoring programme for CSF in place, which is based on extensive movement control and on serological testing of domestic pigs: Ø on farm before transport from holding to holding and, Ø monthly sampling of domestic pigs at slaughterhouse where the following random selection criteria are applied: all of the first ten pigs, 10% of the next 340 and 5% of all the rest. No other monitoring programmes for OIE list A diseases are in place. 7.3. Outbreaks and suspect cases of OIE list A diseases Conclusions The lack of reporting of suspect clinical cases of FMD during the last two years raises doubts about the level of awareness and vigilance in Luxembourg. The actions taken in relation to the outbreak of CSF in August 2003 and the suspicion of CSF in September 2003, illustrate deficiencies in the CP for CSF, as well as in its implementation (actions not always appropriate or consistent). There is a lack of appreciation of the importance of taking prompt action in response to suspicions or outbreak of disease. This has resulted in delays in initiating eradication procedures. Delays in receiving results from the Belgian reference laboratory CERVA have contributed to this. With regard to tackling a suspect case of CSF, the provisions laid down in Chapters III and IV of the Annex of Commission Decision 2002/106/EC5 were not sufficiently taken into account. Bio-security measures are not always applied in a satisfactory manner. Findings In February 2001, there was one suspect case of FMD. The Luxembourg CCA applied a general ban on the movement of all susceptible animals, but no further measures were taken. No clinical suspicion of FMD has been reported since. In 2003, three outbreaks of CSF occurred in wild boars (January and February) and in domestic pigs (August). In September 2003, there was one suspect case of CSF in domestic pigs. On 5 August, during screening at a slaughterhouse, two out of three blood samples returned a serological positive result (ELISA Ab and AG) and were sent to CERVA for confirmation on 6 August. From 6 August, increasingly clinical symptoms occurred at the farm of origin. By 12 August, 9 pigs had 5 Official Journal L 39, 09/02/2002 p. 71 10 died. On 11 August, CERVA finalised the serum neutralisation test (1:160). On 13 August, the CCA visited the infected farm for the first time. On the night of 14 August, the entire pig herd was killed and a protection and surveillance zone established. On 18 August, the test results of the virus isolation and serum neutralisation were positive. The mission team noted that: Ø on 6 August 2003, the CCA did not inform the farmer or the approved veterinarian about the suspicion of CSF, expressed by the LMV, based on two positive serological test results. The CCA explained that there was an indirect movement ban in place for all pig holdings with serological positive test results, and they would not stamp the transport certificates of those farms concerned. This procedure is insufficient and is not in compliance with the EU requirements with regards to a suspected case of CSF. Ø on 7 August 2003, the approved veterinarian failed to notify the CCA of clinical symptoms of the pigs concerned, although he took blood samples for CSF. This caused a delay of at least five days in taking appropriate action. Ø on 11 August 2003, CERVA finalised the serum neutralisation test (1:160) and the result was sent to the Luxembourg CCA on 12 August. However, the appropriate time-span for carrying out the serum neutralisation test is two days maximum, resulting in a delay of four days to take appropriate action to tackle the outbreak as laid down in Article 5 of Council Directive 2001/89/EC. Ø on 14 August, in the notification to the Commission Services, the date of suspicion was specified as 12 August. However, in accordance with Luxembourg law, the date of suspicion, should have been 6 August. In September 2003, during screening of all holdings within the surveillance zone, pigs were detected with positive serological test results. The blood samples were sent to the CERVA for confirmation. The result of the serum neutralisation test of one pig was inconclusive (1:15). The CCA, however, did not place the holding involved under official control. The CCA decided that all pigs on this farm had to be sent to a slaughterhouse, and slaughtered by the end of the day. Following this, the slaughterhouse was cleaned and disinfected. The farmer transported the animals in his own lorry, which was normally used for the transport of sheep. The final result of the tests carried out by CERVA was Border Disease6. text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Background to present mission This mission formed part of a planned series to Member States in order to evaluate their systems for import controls for plant health. The FVO had previously carried out several missions to Italy on a variety of topics including: October 2001, Eradication programme for Diabrotica virgifera virgifera Le Conte; February 2001, Pinewood nematode; July 1999, Erwinia amylovora; October 1998, Pilot phase of the Vademecum; April 2000, The Plant Health System in the Potato Sector. FVO Mission reports are available on their web-site: www.europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html 4.2. Information on trade 4.2.1. Sources of Information Information on imports is held at regional level in the form of inspection records and copies of the Phytosanitary Import Certificate, which the RPS issues after completion of each plant health check. Information on inspection activity is recorded at local level using EXCEL datasheets and an annual summary is sent to the Regional office. The four regions visited provided data on the number of consignments of regulated and non-regulated plant material that were imported and inspected in 2002; this showed that all consignments of regulated and non-regulated material were inspected. However, this data was derived from inspection records, and as such, only relates to consignments that have actually been inspected. The mission team found (see 5.4.2.6. below) that only a small proportion of the total number of consignments of non-regulated material, was inspected. 2 OJ L 126, 28.04.1998, p.26 3 OJ L 032, 05.02.1994, p.37 4 OJ L 205, 17.08.1993, p.22

OJ L 184, 03.08.1995, p.34 3 Italy imported 87,799 tonnes of Egyptian potatoes between 2001 - 2002. Gioia Tauro reported that in 2002 they received 112 consignments of Egyptian potatoes; the port is authorised for this purpose. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Official responsible bodies 5.1.1. Structure, reporting relationships and responsibilities The Plant Protection Service (PPS) in Italy consists of the Central Phytosanitary Service (CPS) and 19 Regional and 2 Provincial Plant Protection Services (RPS). The CPS (Unita' Dirigenziale XI ­ Settore fitosanitario e dei fertilizzanti, of the Dipartimento della Qualita' dei Prodotti Agroalimentari), which is part of the Ministero per le Politiche Agricole e Forestali (Mi.P.A.F.), acts as the Single, Central Authority as defined in Article 1.4 of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. The staff of the PPS are all civil servants; the salaries of CPS staff are paid directly by Mi.P.A.F, while the salaries of the regional and provincial staff are paid by the relevant Regional Administration. The powers and responsibilities of the CPS are laid down in Law (L.) 987/1931 and Ministerial Decree (D.M.) 536/92; these include the transposition of Community legislation, issuing Decrees for the compulsory control of specific pests and parasites, and co-ordinating the work of the various RPS. The CPS is also responsible for international relations and it represents Italy at the Standing Committee for Plant Health in Brussels. The CPS also maintains the national register of phytosanitary inspectors and organises training courses for inspectors at national level. It is important to note that the competence and responsibility for agricultural matters, including plant health, has been transferred to the 19 regions and 2 autonomous provinces. As a result, the Central Phytosanitary Service cannot act directly in plant health matters (although it does have the legal authority to do so, in the event that the RPS do not comply with national and European provisions). Each of the RPS has its own diagnostic laboratory. In addition, two laboratories act as reference laboratories; the Istituto Sperimentale per la Patologia Vegetale (I.S.Pa.Ve.) in Rome, and the Istituto Sperimentale per la Zoologia Agraria in Florence. University laboratories can provide additional capacity or expertise if required. 5.1.2. Human resources Data was on the total number of inspectors employed nationally was requested but was not provided. However, the relevant data was provided by the regions visited during the mission and is summarised in table 5.1. below. The CPS itself consists of three specialists and one administrator. The minimum entry requirement for inspectors is currently a degree or diploma in agricultural sciences; in addition, they must successfully complete a specific training course before joining the service. The duties of inspectors and their locations is determined by each RPS, but generally, inspectors are responsible for a range of duties, other than just import inspections. These include the inspection of nurseries for plant passport purposes, conducting specific surveys (based on Ministerial Decrees) and performing pre-export inspections. The percentage of time spent by inspectors on each of these duties varies by location, but import controls are usually their main duty. The mission team was informed that inspectors based at Malpensa Airport spend 70% of their time on import controls. 4 TABLE 5.1: NUMBER OF INSPECTORS IN EACH OF THE VISITED REGIONS Region Total number Total number carrying out import controls of inspectors Lombardia 32 11, (including 6 at Malpensa airport) Liguria 15 5 (3 at Genova Port, 1 at Savona Port and 1 at La Spezia Port) Calabria 6 3 (plus 2) Gioia Tauro Port Lazio 25 12 (covering Fiumicino airport, Ciampino airport, and Civitavecchia port with at least 3 inspectors present at the same times each day) 5.1.3. Training The CPS provides training courses for inspectors at national level. These are either general in nature, for example inspection procedures and sampling techniques, or specific, such as courses on the identification and control of specific quarantine pests, fruit cooling and solid wood treatment. The RPS plays the main role in training inspectors; they arrange basic and refresher type courses on specific topics. All of the staff met during the mission appeared to be well-informed and trained on plant health matters. 5.1.4. Financial resources The financial resources for each of the RPS are provided by their Regional Administration, as laid down in the Regional Finance Laws. The Regional Administrations may also provide additional funds for specific activities; for example, in 2003, the Lombardy Administration allocated an additional 500.000 for quarantine measures in the region. 5.1.5. Record keeping and work planning Records of activities are maintained at regional level, usually in Excel format. There is no national database; if the CPS require information, they must first request it from each of the RPS, who will then provide it in the format that they use. This makes the collection, collation and monitoring of data difficult for the CPS. Meetings are held between the Central and Regional Phytosanitary Services at least once each month, in order to discuss progress and exchange information. In addition, several working groups have been set up to deal with specific issues such as import controls, imports for research purposes and control measures for specific pests. The RPS issue instructions for inspectors, usually in the form of circulars, which take into account any advice or instructions given by the CPS. The circulars are usually also sent to other stakeholders, and are updated as necessary. Inspectors have access to other technical information including the EU Vademecums. The Lombardia Region has also developed its own website for use by inspectors. 5.1.6. Legislation and legal powers of inspectors The CPS is responsible for transposing Community legislation, either by Ministerial Decree (D.M.), which are published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale della Repubblica Italiana (Italian Official Journal), or following consultation with the RPS, by Circulars. 5 The system of import controls is based on D.M. of 31.01.19966 as amended, which transposed Council Directive 77/93/EEC. Subsequent Community phytosanitary legislation amending this Directive and Council Directive 2000/29/EC, have been transposed by amendment to this Ministerial Decree. Commission Directive 98/22/EC laying down the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks at inspection posts other than at place of destination, has been transposed by D.M. of 19.10.19987. This places the responsibility for provision of the necessary facilities and equipment on the RPS. Inspectors' powers are established in D.M. 536/92; these include powers to enter premises, to inspect and to take samples, and to require the detention, treatment, destruction or re-export of consignments. 5.2. Co-operation between the Plant Protection Service and other administrations All of the RPS visited maintain contact with other administrations involved in import controls, including the Customs and Veterinary Services. In the case of Customs, their co-operation is based on a legally binding convention. The Customs service will not allow the clearance of regulated consignments or the use of Community transit procedures until permission is given by the RPS (in the form of a Phytosanitary Import Certificate (PIC) ­ see below). They identify regulated consignments by comparing the declared botanical name with those on a list of regulated articles provided by the RPS, or by the presence of a phytosanitary certificate with the entry documents. The Customs service also assists the RPS by identifying and notifying them of consignments suspected of containing wood packing that might not comply with the provisions of Commission Decision 2001/219/EC8. In Genova, consignments are held by the Customs service for 48 hours, pending action or reply by the RPS. If a reply is not received within 48 hours, the consignment will be released and is free to enter. The RPS in Genova told the team that `applying the controls in question posed serious problems, essentially because of the very high number of imports of such material and the extreme difficulty of knowing the type of material imported (coniferous wood or other). Hence, the controls have been sporadic and limited in number'. The mission team met representatives of the Customs service at each point of entry ­ in general, they appeared to be informed about plant health matters, and with the exception of Fiumicino, had access to a list of regulated material. Officers at Fiumicino said that they had a database with the list of regulated articles, as well as the paper version, which automatically alerts officers to the need for a PIC. However, when they were asked to demonstrate this, it was not possible for them to find the information on the database and neither could they produce the paper copies of the list or the relevant customs instructions. All of the Customs officers met by the team said that they had good contact with local RPS staff, although they complained that there did not appear to be sufficient collaboration and communication between the two services at national level. RPS staff

"Gazzetta Ufficiale" del 15.12.1998 Serie Generale, n. 292 8 OJ L 081, 21.03.2001, p.39 6 from Genova and Milano said that this is important because the Customs service is a national service and not regionalised like the PPS. 5.3. Co-operation between the Plant Protection Service and Forwarding agents All of the RPS visited maintain regular contact with forwarding agents, helping to ensure good co-operation. The agents are kept up-to-date via newsletters. Forwarding agents are not registered by the RPS. 5.4. Import Procedures 5.4.1. Customs entry procedures relating to plant health The RPS must issue a Phytosanitary Import Certificate (see Figure 5.2 below) before Customs can permit clearance or use of Community Transit procedures (such as `T1'). Customs identify regulated consignments by comparing the declared botanical name with a list provided by the regional service; their computer system does not automatically alert officers to the need for a PIC. Although a customs officer does not have to be present while a plant health check is being carried out, they must be present in order to break the seal and if necessary, re-seal the containers. 5.4.2. Plant Protection Service import procedures 5.4.2.1. Registration of importers All importers of regulated plants and plant products are registered by the RPS. Records are kept at regional level, usually in a log-book, and/or in Excel format. These records are copied to the Central Phytosanitary Service on an annual basis. 5.4.2.2. Notification of import Due to the need for a Phytosanitary Import Certificate to be issued before Customs clearance may be permitted, the RPS is always notified of the arrival of regulated items. At all of the ports visited, this notification must be in writing, although only Fiumicino used a standard form for this. Importers should notify the RPS at least 24 hours in advance of arrival of consignments, but in practice, the amount of notification varies. At the two sea-ports visited by the mission team, it was not usual practice for import agents to provide the RPS with copies of ships manifests. The team met two forwarding agents in Genova; they explained that all of the administrations involved in import controls have to be notified separately of the arrival of a consignment. This requires the use and hand-delivery of different forms. The agents also complained that after notification, poor co-operation between the administrations often resulted in considerable delays, while each carries out a separate inspection. As a result, a number of agents and shipping companies are developing a computer network at their own cost, to link them with the various government agencies. In an attempt to simplify the notification procedure, increase co-operation and reduce delays in clearing consignments, The importers and shippers also plan to purchase all of the computer equipment for themselves and the government agencies. They explained that this would 7 not replace the need to hand-deliver the entry documents, but it would allow real-time notification of arrival to be sent and they were optimistic that it should result in a reduction in the clearance times. The importer and a representative of the Customs service said that the same problem existed in other ports, and that developments at Genova were being closely followed; the trade would probably provide similar networks at other posts if this project is successful. The Customs representative confirmed that there was no facility for importers to make electronic entries (Direct Trader Input) to them; entries will still have to be paper-based and hand-delivered. 5.4.2.3. General procedures Import checks for plant health are carried out only by the RPS, and only at the place where the consignment first lands, which in Italy, is the `place of entry'. The checks must be completed prior to customs clearance or approval for the use of Community transit procedures. Having received a written application for an import check from the importer or his agent, the RPS carries out the documentary, identity and plant health checks. Checks are carried out on all consignments of regulated material and some non-regulated consignments too. Following completion of the identity and plant health checks, a Phytosanitary Import Certificate is issued (see Fig. 5.2 below). Each PIC has a unique number and contains similar details to those contained in the original phytosanitary certificate that accompanied the consignment. The PIC issued by the different regional services are identical except for the regional emblem. The PIC must be included with the other relevant documents in the customs entry; it replaces the original phytosanitary certificate, which is retained by the R

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of the Treaty of the European Community (in particular Articles 10, 152, 153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation and, specifically: · Council Directive 93/99/EEC on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, in particular Article 5. 4. BACKGROUND Three previous missions carried out in Finland by the FVO and the former DG XXIV to evaluate the national food control system should be considered: · The first mission was carried out from 30 September to 4 October 1996. Its main objective was the monitoring and evaluation of the equivalence and effectiveness of official food control systems operated by the competent authorities of the Member States. · The second mission was carried out from 28 September to 2 October 1998. The objective was to follow up the first report on the official food control systems and to study the system for controlling imported foods of non-animal origin. · The third mission was carried out from 25 to 29 October 1999. The objective was to follow up on the previous missions and to assess controls on food of non- animal origin in the retail sector. The reports on the third series of missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/food_hygiene/index_en. html 8 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities Finland has four-levels of administration for food control, which comprises of ministries, central administration, the provincial governments and the municipalities. It is the responsibility of the ministries to develop legislation. Central administration is in charge of co-ordinating national food control. The National Food Agency (NFA) directs food control throughout Finland and the National board of customs check goods at import point. The provincial governments through the 6 State Provincial Offices (SPO) are responsible for developing regional control in every field covered by the ministries, while at local level the municipalities conduct the actual food control via the Municipal Food Control Authorities (MFCA). Since the time of the last mission (SANCO 1218/1999) in October 1999 the NFA has been placed in charge of all aspects of food control (from March 2001). The merger of the former National Food Agency and the Department of Control of Food of Animal Origin formed the NFA, which was part of the National Veterinary and Food Research Institute. The original agency was subordinated to the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and the new NFA operates in the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry's (MAF) administrative sector. However two other ministries MTI and Ministry of Social Affairs and Health (MSAH) are still involved in other aspects of food control. The structure and responsibilities of these organisations within the scope of this report are summarised in table 2 (page 11). 5.1.1. National Food Agency (NFA) The NFA is subordinate to the MAF and is responsible for planning, developing and directing food control in Finland. Its tasks include supervising and monitoring regional and local authorities, participating in many EU and other international projects as an expert body, producing and publishing research reports and addressing the needs of industry, commerce and consumers. The NFA does not participate in local inspections except where it is directly involved in the surveillance of high capacity slaughterhouses and establishments connected to them (production, processing and importing foodstuffs of animal origin). The Competent Authorities in these establishments are the official veterinarians, who work in NFA's service. The NFA has no auditing function within the scope of this mission. The National Food Agency is responsible for the supervision of the legislation mentioned in the objectives of the mission. The organisation of NFA and how it relates to the relevant ministries is available at the following site: http://www.elintarvikevirasto.fi/english/p1958.pdf 9 The NFA meets with the 3 ministries annually and an agreement is reached which sets out performance targets for the year. Based on this agreement and feedback from regional and local level the NFA sets out the National Food Control Programme. The NFA agree performance targets with the State Provincial Offices (SPO) each year. There are 74 people employed in the NFA at Helsinki and a further 101 in slaughterhouses in the regions. The state is responsible for funding the NFA. The latter makes a budget proposal to MAF, which is submitted to the Ministry of Finance and voted on in parliament. There is regular communication between the NFA at central level, the SPOs at regional level and MFCAs at local level by e-mail, monthly newsletters and the NFA web site on legislative changes and relevant publications. The NFA issued detailed instructions and guidelines to the SPO and MFCA for the organisation of local food control, in June 2003 with a date of enforcement of September 2003. This document provides an update on previous instructions and combines various elements of Finnish legislation. It gives basic information on the preparation of food control plans, inspection visits, autocontrol plans, sampling, penalties and training. It lacks detail, in particular for guidelines on risk assessment of premises. However the NFA informed the mission team that more detailed instructions on risk assessment is planned for 2004. The NFA provided information to the mission team on the National Food Control programme for 2004. The performance targets of this programme include the assessment of food operators' readiness to implement autocontrol systems based on HACCP, the preparation of instructions and enforcement of new hygiene laws and plans to provide more information to consumers on foodstuffs. It also includes control programmes for Salmonella and residues along with several research projects concerned with food safety. 5.1.2. Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (MAF) MAF's scope of activity includes agriculture, horticulture and forestry, fisheries, game and reindeer farming. MAF is responsible for the implementation of Council Directives on meat and meat products mentioned in the objectives of the mission, in particular the implementation of; Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 laying down rules for the prevention, control and eradication of certain transmissible spongiform encephalopaties; Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 establishing system for the identification and registration of bovine animals and regarding the labelling of beef and beef products and repealing Council Regulation (EC) No 820/97; Regulation (EC) No 1825/2000 laying down detailed rules for the application of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 as regards the labelling of beef and beef products. 10 Table 2 Authorities Levels Central Regional Local Competencies Institutions National Food Responsible for planning, Agency developing and directing Ministerial food control, subordinated to MAF. Ministry of Agriculture and Responsible for safety and Forestry quality of food of animal origin.
