The customs authorities are competent authorities in food control at import point and are part of the Ministry of Finance. Regional 6 State Planning and directing of Provincial food control regionally and provide support to Offices municipalities. Local 276 Municipal Provision of practical food Food Control control including Authorities inspections and advising businesses. 5.1.3. Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) Food issues are the responsibility of the Competition, Consumer and Food Policy Division of MTI. Its function is to guarantee the health-related quality of foodstuffs, to protect consumer health from foodstuffs unfit for human consumption and from economic losses due to non-conforming foodstuffs. MTI issues more detailed provisions on food labels and packaging materials, contaminants, pesticide residues, food additives, flavourings, and food control. MTI is further responsible for drafting of policy on foodstuffs at national level issued under the Finnish Food Act (361/1995) and for Finnish opinions to be presented to EU institutions. MTI is responsible for Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and for Council Directives 93/99/EEC and 89/397/EEC on the official control of foodstuffs, the application of which is discharged to the local authorities through the NFA. 5.1.4. Ministry of Social Affairs and Health (MSAH) The responsibilities of the MSAH include the health aspects of the quality and hygiene of foodstuffs, the implementation of Council Directive 93/43/EEC on the 11 hygiene of foodstuffs and thus the implementation of autocontrol systems based on HACCP principles and the rules on the hygiene of foodstuffs. 5.1.5. Provincial Governments There are six State Provincial Offices (SPO) in Finland which are under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior. They have a co-ordinating and supervisory role for the municipalities in their region. The regions are Southern Finland, Western Finland, Eastern Finland, Oulu, Lapland and Åland. The mission team met with a representative of the SPO of Southern Finland. In this region there are 8 departments and food control is the responsibility of the Department of Social Affairs and Health. The NFA discusses the National Food Control Programme with the SPO and sets performance targets for its achievement with SPO. These targets can take the form of official control projects. Local food control plans produced annually by the municipalities are required to be submitted to the relevant SPO. There is no formal or informal communication on food control between the six SPOs. Each SPO guides and directs food control in the municipalities within its region according to the guidance from the NFA. The SPO of Southern Finland assesses local food control activities through the number of inspections carried out, number of samples taken, participation in training and projects and calculation of "work effort". The latter is a calculation of the number of man-hours worked per year based on number of inspectors and number of inspections undertaken. The SPOs have offices in 12 cities and have 12 food control officials and 21 veterinarians. The state is responsible for funding of food control at both provincial government levels. 5.1.6. Municipal Food Control Authorities (MFCA) At local level there are 276 Food Control Units through out the municipalities or municipal federations in Finland. Each municipal authority is largely autonomous in the organisation of its activities including official control of foodstuffs. The MFCA have a total of 261 veterinarians, 65 food control officials, 436 inspectors and 97 assistant personnel. The Municipal Food Control is financed mainly by tax revenue. The municipalities decide themselves how much they can allocate to the control. The authorities can levy charges for licenses, inspection of notifications and taking of samples. 5.1.7. The National Board of Customs The customs authorities are competent authorities in food control at import and are subordinated to the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry has no actual responsibilities concerning food legislation. The Finnish Customs consists of the National Board of Customs, five customs districts, and the Customs Laboratory. Both the District Customs Offices and the Customs Laboratory are subordinated to the National Board of Customs. Customs check at import point (specifically, in the importer's warehouse) the goods that have not yet entered the market place and, in case of non-compliance, the 12 necessary measures can be directed at the entire consignment before it reaches any consumer by the customs officials. 5.2. Legislation In Finland the parliament prescribes the constitution and Acts, decrees are produced at ministerial level. Each Ministry is responsible for drafting legislation in its relevant sector and has the power to produce regulations on the basis of the Acts. EFET has regional offices established in 4 of the 13 regions in Greece, i.e. Attica, Central Macedonia, Crete and Western Greece. At regional level, it is organised into four sections (Industry control, Laboratory control, Appraisal Licences and Administrative Support) and a Consumer Services Office. As mentioned in the last report, the Agency is still in a transition stage and plans to operate in 13 regional offices. Although the opening of a fifth regional office is planned very shortly, the timetable for the Agency to become fully operational was not made clear during the mission. Within these four regions, EFET's responsibilities range from post-primary production to the retail level as laid down in Joint Ministerial Decision (JMD) B3-32/2003 between EFET and the Ministry of Agriculture. At prefecture level, the Trade Directorates have limited responsibility within the scope of this mission. It employs 180 veterinarians at the Central Service and 700 veterinarians in the prefectural directorates. A third of these (290) are involved in the control of food of animal origin. The Directorate-General for Animal Production is responsible for implementing the labelling of bovine meat. As regards the objectives of this mission, the veterinary directorates at prefecture level are responsible for official control of food of animal origin, whether produced in processing facilities or in the retail sector. 5.1.3 Ministry of Health Within the Ministry of Health, there are four central services: the Directorate for Public Health, Primary Healthcare, Environmental Hygiene and the Public Health Laboratory Service. The Directorate-General for Public Health has responsibility for legislation and implementation of policy in the control of foodstuffs and food establishments. At prefecture level, the health directorates employ 250 public health inspectors. 5.1.4 Ministry of Economy and Finance The General State Chemical Laboratory (GSCL) is the main body that deals with laboratory analyses of foodstuffs. Legislation Official control The EU legislation within the scope of this mission has been transposed. Of the four Ministries with responsibilities for official control, only the regional Directorates of EFET are currently enforcing Council Directive 93/43/EEC, and then only in 4 of the 13 Greek regions in which they are currently operational. Existing Greek legislation on the official control of foodstuffs A large body of older existing national legislation concerning the official control of foodstuffs is still implemented by the Health, Trade and Veterinary Directorates at prefecture level; this legislation includes the following: · Presidential Decree 40/77 and Act No 2538/97 concerning the Veterinary Directorate; · hygiene provisions ALB 8577/83, as amended, concerning the Health Directorate. · Act No 1401/83 concerning the prefectural services of the Ministry of Trade. This older national legislation does not require the implementation of HACCP. 5.3. Good Hygiene Practice Guides. The preparation of GHP Guides is carried out by the representative bodies of the specific food sectors involved. This is followed by an evaluation of the guidelines by a scientific committee which consists of EFET representatives, representatives of the sector involved and consumers' representatives, as well as representatives of the Greek Standardisation Organisation (ELOT) and the Organisation for the Standardisation of Agricultural Products (OPEGEP). LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of the Treaty of the European Community (in particular Articles 10, 152, 153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation and, specifically: · Council Directive 93/99/EEC of 29 October 1993 on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, in particular Article 5. 4. BACKGROUND Three previous missions carried out in Spain by the FVO and the former DG XXIV to evaluate the national food control system should be considered: · The first mission was carried out from 3 to 7 February 1997. Its main objective was the monitoring and evaluation of the equivalence and effectiveness of official food control systems operated by the competent authorities of the Member States based on Article 5 of the Council Directive 93/99/EEC. · The second mission was carried out from 23 to 27 February 1998. The objective was to follow up the first report on the official food control systems and to study the system for controlling imported foods of non-animal origin. · The third mission was carried out from 19 to 23 March 2001. The objective was to follow up on the previous missions and to assess controls on foodstuffs, and in particular the implementation of safety procedures based on HACCP principles and the rules on the hygiene of foodstuffs at the retail sector level. 7 The reports on the third series of missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/food_hygiene/index_en. html 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities Responsibility for official control within the scope of this mission is divided between Spanish Food Safety Agency and the 17 Autonomous Communities `Comunidades Autónomas' (AC's), and the Municipal Authorities of the AC's. The main change since the last mission has been the transfer of responsibility from the Ministry of Health and Consumer Affairs `Ministerio de Sanidad y Consumo' (MISACO) to the AESA. The AESA is now responsible for most of the functions formally implemented by MISACO with the notable exception of import controls at borders, international relations and agreements. At regional level the 17 AC's have sole responsibility for the organisation and implementation of official control requirements in respect of foodstuffs. Within municipalities of more than 50 000 inhabitants there is also the provision for the local municipal administration to carry out official control of foodstuffs, in respect of inspection and sampling. The structure and responsibilities of these organisations within the scope of this report are summarised in Table 1. 5.1.1. Ministry of Health and Consumer Affairs (MISACO) As indicated above the responsibilities of MISACO have changed since the last mission with several of its former functions, such as drafting legislation, co-ordination of the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), and co-ordination of the co-operation between the AC's now transferred to the AESA. MISACO continues to have inter alia the following tasks: · International relations and agreements · Direct health control at borders 8 Table1. Central Regional Local Competencies ------------ Levels Institutions MISACO ---------- Import Control Ministerial International relations and agreements Autonomous AESA ------------ ------------ Transposition of Communities --------------- community legislation 17 Peripheral and preparation of Autonomous services and national legislation Communities Health Units Co-ordination of food safety at all stages of the food chain Co-ordination of co- operation between CA Risk assessment Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed Regional legislation Co-ordination and conducting inspection and control Issuing guidance Regional laboratories Municipalities --------------- --------------- Municipal Inspection of food Health establishments in Authorities municipality. 5.1.2. Spanish Food Safety Agency (AESA) The AESA is an independent body attached to the Ministry of Health and Consumer Affairs, set up by Law No.11 of 5 July 2001. Its broad aim is to promote food safety, and to provide objective information to consumers and operators in the Spanish agri-food industry. The Agency has no legal powers of enforcement but has several functions relating to its core tasks including: · Administration of the work of competent bodies to promote co-ordination on food issues; · Acting as a reference body to deal with food safety issues and food crises; · Co-ordination of the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed in Spain; · Drafting legislation on foodstuffs; 9 · Risk assessment (through the AESA's Scientific Committee); · Operation of a central register of food premises (RGSA). The management board of the AESA comprises several different appointments from the Ministries of Health and Consumer Affairs, Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, Environment, and Science and Technology. In addition, each of the Autonomous Communities appoints a member to the board. Membership is also drawn from other bodies including most of the economic organisations in the agri-food sectors, including, production, processing, distribution and catering. This board co-operates with the Chairman of the AESA in issuing advice and reports and dealing with opinions requested by central /regional government within the framework of the Agency's goals. Interregional co-ordination between the AESA and the Health Authorities of the AC's is organised through the Institutional Committee of the AESA. This body is responsible for the former functions of the Food Safety Co- operation and Co-ordination Committee (CO.CO.CO.SA). The committee normally meets twice a year; special meetings may be organised on the chairman's initiative or at the request of a third of its members. However, there was very little evidence presented during the mission as to how the current co-ordination impacts on the organisation of official controls in the AC's within the scope of this mission, in particular with regard to enforcement policy, training, official control laboratories or the RASFF. In addition to the above there are also specific ad hoc groups which meet every two months, and have responsibility for such topics as co-ordination of laboratories, ratio of inspectors to establishments, risk assessment, contaminants, salmonella, among others. No further information was available concerning the work of these groups. 5.1.3. Autonomous Communities (AC's) There are 17 AC 's, some consisting of one province, others of a number of provinces. The mission team visited the AC's of Aragón (1 province) and Extremadura (2 provinces). The AC's have responsibility for their own organisational structures and resources and are solely responsible for co- ordinating and implementing food safety controls within their own geographical area. In general the AC Services for Hygiene Control of foodstuffs are organised as follows: · Central Services: (Central Services of the Directorate-General for Public Health and/or Consumer Affairs) which normally issue instructions/technical programmes/guidelines to other provincial services or districts. · Provincial district services: these services normally cover a whole province. The provincial services in turn are normally organised into smaller more basic areas (health areas, district services, etc) covering one or more municipalities. They are responsible for carrying out official 10 control of foodstuffs and have a degree of autonomy, within the guidelines issued by the central services, for organising the resources available. 5.1.4. Municipalities (local government) In addition to the organisational structure at AC level, municipalities with more than 50 000 inhabitants may take over responsibility for implementing the official control of foodstuffs in retailing and in wholesaling (carried out mainly in "MERCAS" wholesale markets for retail). They are known as "special municipalities" (for example, Madrid, Barcelona, Seville, Zaragoza). The mission team visited the Municipal Authorities (MA) in Zaragoza who have taken responsibility for official control, and in particular for the issuing of municipal licenses. The service has 3 inspectors with responsibility for this role, and 4 auxiliary staff with responsibility for sampling foodstuffs. Regular meetings were organised between the MA and the provincial services of the AC's with the objective of minimising overlap in official control activities. The MA in Extremadura has not taken responsibility for official control of foodstuffs. 5.2. Legislation The drafting of legislation is now the responsibility of the AESA through an Inter-Ministerial Committee on Food Regulations. This committee is a collegial body, which includes central government departments holding powers relating to foodstuffs and is headed by the Director of the AESA. It also co-ordinates activities with committees of experts from specialist international organisations and in particular with the Codex Alimentarius Commission and the Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Programme. All relevant legislation within the scope of this mission has been transposed into national legislation. Of particular note, a new Royal Decree No.1376/2003 has been recently enacted detailing the storage and production conditions for retail shops selling fresh meat and meat products. This Decree transposes Council Directive 93/43/EEC, whereas formally older existing national legislation on hygiene applied to such premises. Art. 4 of the Decree makes provision for the sale of meat from the butcher's shop to authorised catering establishments provided that: · the establishment has facilities and suitable equipment for the hygienic preparation of volume of production; · they are limited to fresh meats, meat products and meat preparations, with the exception of mince meat; · the establishments are not subject to inclusion in the `Registro General Sanitario de Alimentos' (General Health Register on foodstuffs),i.e. mass catering operations (see section 5.5.5); · its distribution is within the municipality's geographical area. 11 The AC's may also enact additional detailed legislation, provided that this is within the framework of national legislation. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of the Treaty of the European Community (in particular Articles 10, 152, 153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation and, specifically: · Council Directive 93/99/EEC of 29 October 1993 on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, in particular Article 5. 4. BACKGROUND Three previous missions carried out in Italy by the FVO and the former DG XXIV to evaluate the national food control system should be considered: · The first mission was carried out from 5 to 10 May 1995. Its main objective was the monitoring and evaluation of the equivalence and effectiveness of official food control systems operated by the competent authoritiesof the Member States based on Article 5 of the Council Directive 93/99/EEC. · The second mission was carried out from 11 to 15 May 1998. The objective was to follow up the first report on the official food control systems and to study the system for controlling imported foods of non- animal origin. 7 · The third mission was carried out from 18 to 22 September 2000. The objective was to follow up on the previous missions and to assess controls on foodstuffs, and in particular the implementation of safety procedures based on HACCP principles and the rules on the hygiene of foodstuffs at the retail sector level. The reports on the third series of missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/food_hygiene/index_en. html 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities The competencies of those organisations with responsibility for the official control within the scope of this mission are summarised in the following table: Levels Central Regional Local Competencies Institutions Directorate --------- --------- -Production of legislation General for -Policy Ministerial Veterinary Assessorati --------- -Guidance of control Health and Food alla Sanità / Regions (19) (DANSPV) Direzioni Local Health activities and Sanità Units (ASL) - Co-ordination of import Autonomous --------- Pubblica Provinces -------------- control for foodstuffs of (2) --------- --------- non-animal origin Local Health --------- -Co-ordination of food alerts Authorities --------- - Consumer information Maritime Central -Production of regional Frontier Command Anti legislation Health Office adulteration -Guidance on control (USMA) and Health activities Carabinieri body of the -Co-ordinating role military police -Training co-ordination (NAS) -Planning of official control activities -Enforcement -Control of imports Specific controls of multiregional/national significance and/or required by the Ministry of Health. 5.1.1. Central competent authority At central level the Directorate General for Veterinary Health and Food (DANSPV), a department of the Ministry of Health has responsibility for official control, and consists 8 of 14 separate offices, of which office V, VI and VII, XIV play the most significant role within the scope of this mission. The responsibilities of office V concern policy issues in relation to food safety, drafting national legislation, implementation of coordinated programmes of EU official controls, and collating information relating to the official control of foodstuffs returned from the regions. The department also plays a role in promoting scientific research and consumer information, and the staff can also control food premises in occasional situations of serious national significance. Office VI, which was set up in October 2002, has responsibility for the operation of the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF). Office XIV is responsible for co-ordinating import control for foodstuffs of non-animal origin. Ministerial Decree 12.09.2003 established office VII within the DANSPV. This office carries out audits on the veterinary and food safety prevention systems, both with a view to verifying the proper implementation of national legislation and compliance with operational procedures. However, the office currently has a staff of three, and has no plans in the foreseeable future to evaluate the implementation of Community legislation within the scope of this mission. The DANSPV is also responsible for co-ordination of the regions by means of the "Inter- regional co-ordination group ­ Prevention Group ­ Subgroup on Food Safety". This is a technical body consisting of representatives from the Regions and the Ministry. The group holds periodical meetings to discuss draft technical provisions, as well as the implementation plans of the annual EU co-ordinated programs for official control of foodstuffs. Attendance at these meetings is voluntary, and not all regions participate. 5.1.2. Regional authorities There are 20 Regions within Italy one of which, Trentino Alto Adige, is subdivided in two Autonomous Provinces. At regional level Public Health Directorates have responsibility for the official control of foodstuffs. The main role of the regional authorities is in the provision of guidance for official control activities at local level. The regional authorities also have the power to produce regional legislation so long as it does not supersede National legislation. The regions also have responsibility for the provision of staff training. 5.1.3. Local authorities Official control is carried out at local level by the 250 Local Health Units (ASLs). The number of ASLs varies in each region according to their geographical size. Each ASL is further divided in terms of responsibility into separate services; the Hygiene and Nutrition of Foodstuffs (SIAN), and the Local Veterinary Services (SV). Within the SIAN some staff are trained as medical doctors, but the majority (70 to 80%) are technicians with a high school diploma. The majority of inspectors in the SV are veterinarians. The responsibilities of both the SIAN and SV were clearly defined in both regions visited. In addition, in the region of Sardegna the ASL visited has produced a protocol for joint inspections in cases were there was common responsibility. The USMA are peripheral offices of the Ministry of Health and report directly to DANSPV concerning import control on foodstuffs of plant origin coming from Third 9 Countries. They have similar powers and duties to those of the local inspectors, but operate only within the boundaries of the relevant marine port or airport. The report on the last import control mission to Italy (Ref. 9131-2003) is now available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/contaminants/italy/index _en.html 5.1.4. Anti adulteration and Health Body of the Military police The Anti adulteration and Health Body of the Military police (NAS) are regional departments of the police corps `Carabinieiri'. The service comprises a Central Command based in Rome, three anti-adulteration and health groups based in Milan, Rome and Naples and 35 anti-adulteration and health units located throughout the country. They have, among others, competence for monitoring hygiene measures and carrying out health inspections in a wide range of areas, including water, beverages, meat, processed food, dairy products, catering etc. In practice they can be requested to perform control activities in situations of multiregional or national significance that require co-ordinated action, or in support of the Ministry of Health. 5.2. Legislation All relevant legislation within the scope of this mission has been transposed into national legislation. The main legislation transposing Council Directive 93/43/EEC is Legislative Decree No. 155, of 26 May 1997, which has been subsequently amended. Most of the provisions of the legislation came into force on 26 May 1998. With regard to official controls, Legislative Decree of the 14 July 1995 provides guidance to the regions on the minimum inspection and sampling frequencies and on the analytical priorities for different foodstuffs. This Decree specifies that catering operators must be inspected once every 6 months, supermarkets every 9 months, while restaurants and retail shops once a year. The role of the enforcement bodies and the powers given to authorised officers are laid down in the Legislative Decree No. 123 of 3 March 1993. Under constitutional law No.3 of 18 October 2001, amending the Italian constitution, the regions also have powers to legislate in the food sector, without prejudice to the basic principles laid out in National legislation. With regard to the implementation of the above Legislative Decree 155, the regional authority of Toscana indicated that there were occasional conflicts between an older existing Act 283/62 on food hygiene (which is still in force), in particular with regard to one case regarding the imposition of sanctions for non implementation of HACCP. The Legislative Decree 155 also contains a number of important additional requirements concerning food businesses. The first relates to the requirement that food business have a documented HACCP system in place identifying the critical steps, the control procedures, and the results of monitoring of the critical control points. Additionally, all personnel linked to a food establishment must have an individual health certificate issued annually by the local health authority. 10 In addition to the above there is also a detailed list of legislation concerning temperature and microbiological criteria applying to certain types of foodstuffs. The regional authorities visited all had drafted guidelines on the requirements for the implementation of HACCP by food businesses, indicated as `simplified procedures for HACCP' Legislation is published in the Official Bulletin of the Italian Republic, and further guidance is provided through letters/circulars addressed to the Regions, and to the trade associations and other concerned stakeholders. 5.3. These guides are produced by trade organisations, in consultation with the competent authorities. On completion of the consultation process the guides are sent to the DANSPV for assessment prior to publication. Responsibility for the promotion and dissemination of the guides rests with the organisations that produced the guides. The use of the guides was not evident in all of the premises visited, and it was noted that the guides are not normally used as part of routine official control. Those guides which were examined by the mission team complied with the requirements of Article 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. 5.4. Laboratory Services 5.4.1. General organisation Since the last mission the planned reorganisation of public health laboratories has continued, with most food control and environmental monitoring combined at regional level under a single Regional Agency for Environment Protection (ARPA). Federal Public Health Service, Food Chain Safety and Environment Since the last FVO evaluation in November 2001 (Ref. SANCO 3388/2001) there have been a number of changes in the organisational structure of official control in Belgium. Firstly the new Federal Governmental Service for Public Health, Safety of the Food Chain and Environment (FPS) replaces the former Ministry of Health and Environment. Secondly the former services within this Ministry, that were responsible for the framing of policy and the drafting of legislation concerning animal health, plants and foodstuffs, have been brought together within the Directorate General 4 (DG4) of the FPS. Within DG4 Division 3 is responsible for legislation within the scope of this mission. With regard to its responsibilities the FPS has mainly a legislative function and has its own advisory board: the supreme Health Council. The FPS does not have a role in the implementation of official control; this is the responsibility of the FASFC. 5.1.2. Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain Under the Act of 4th February 2000 the Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain (FASFC) was created. This agency has primary responsibility for official control within the scope of this mission. Since the last FVO evaluation the integration of the official control activities of four former departments and institutes listed below is almost complete: · The Institute of Veterinary Inspection (IVK); · The General Food Inspection (AEWI); · The Directorate for the quality of raw materials and the plant sector (DG4); · The Directorate of Animal Health and Quality of Animal Production (DG5). This agency reports to the Minister of Health and has as its core tasks the: ­ Control, investigation and certification of all feed and food and their components throughout the food chain; ­ Control and surveillance of production, treatment, storage, transport, trade, import and export of foodstuffs; ­ Approval and registration of activities in the food chain; ­ Controlling implementation and control of traceability and identification systems for animal feed and foodstuffs. In addition, FASFC is responsible for legislation on control measures, such as sampling, recognition of laboratories, and other areas, which directly affect the control services. The agency is composed of four departments including control policy, control, laboratories and corporate services, plus some staff units (e.g. communication, and crisis management). 9 The control policy department is responsible for the design and integration of control procedures and programmes relating to public health, animal and plant health. The co-ordination of the 11 Provincial Control Units (PCUs) is done by the Control Department. Provincial Control Units Official control is now organised in Belgium on a provincial basis with the control department of the FASFC co-ordinating the implementation of official control by the 11 PCUs. Within the 11 PCUs all controllers and inspectors are grouped under three categories which include primary production, processing, and distribution. Municipal City services The Municipal cities of Brussels, Antwerp, Ghent, Mons, Brugge and Leuven are also responsible for official control within the scope of this mission. The legal powers for the Food Agency officers are fixed by 2 Decrees: o Royal Decree of 9 January 1992 on the official control of foodstuffs: this is the transposition in Belgian law of directive 89/397/EC of 14 June 1989.This Royal Decree is modified by the Royal Decree of 14 September 1995, which is the transposition of Council Directive 93/99/EC on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs. o Royal Decree of 21 February 2001 on the organisation of controls by the Food Agency In addition to Royal Decree of 7 February 1997 which transposes Council Directive 93/43/EEC Belgium has adopted a Royal Decree on self-checking, compulsory notification requirement and traceability in the food chain. This Decree was published on 14 November 2003, and is based mainly on Regulation 178/2002 with the exception that Article 3 of Chapter II of the Decree provides that food operators should introduce a self-checking system based upon the 7 HACCP principles. An 8th principle was added which provides for the defining of a sampling and analysing plan that makes it possible to check the validity of the self-checking system, if necessary. The Decree will come into effect on 1 January 2005 for the section concerning self- checking and traceability. Compulsory notification has been in force since 1 March 2004. Official orders and instructions concerning new legislation, policy decision and interpretation of the legislation are sent to the 11 PCUs and to all Officers via post, e- mail, and intranet. Similar orders dealing with general or specific matters of the legislation or with specific requirements concerning measures or corrective actions that have to be taken are also sent from the central level to the representatives of the food sectors by circular, by post or via the website of the Agency. If there are no microbiological criteria specified in national legislation, the agency uses standards described in the draft Commission regulation on microbiological criteria for foodstuffs (SANCO/4198/2001 Rev 9) or DG Control Policy determines the limit of action in collaboration with the Federal Public Service of Public Health, Food Chain Safety & Environment. 11 5.3. Good Hygiene Practice Guides. There are currently 8 Good Hygiene Practice Guides, which comply with the requirements of Art 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. These apply mainly to the hotel and catering and mass catering sectors, but also to the potato processing sector. Within the framework of the new Royal Decree on self-checking (auto-control) of 14 November 2003 a team was set up within the FASFC, which consists of staff members from the DG for Control Policy, as well as other competent staff of the Agency. This team will evaluate whether guides are compliant with legislation in force. Procedures have been drafted concerning this evaluation and validation process and are available at the Agency's website. http://www.favv-afsca.fgov.be Following approval of the guide, the co-ordinator of the team sends a letter to the applicant (respresentative organisation/ institution submitting guide, e.g. hotel and catering federation) to inform him of the validation. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of the Treaty of the European Community (in particular Articles 10, 152, 153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation and, specifically: · Council Directive 93/99/EEC on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, in particular Article 5. 4. BACKGROUND Three previous missions carried out in Luxembourg by the FVO and the former DG XXIV to evaluate the national food control system should be considered: · The first mission was carried out from 11 to 13 June 1996. Its main objective was the monitoring and evaluation of the equivalence and effectiveness of official food control systems operated by the competent authorities of the Member States based on Article 5 of the Council Directive 93/99/EEC. · The second mission was carried out from 29 June to 2 July 1998. The objective was to follow up the first report on the official food control systems and to study the system for controlling imported foods of non-animal origin. · The third mission was carried out from 16 to 19 October 2001. The objective was to follow up on the previous missions and to assess controls on food of non- animal origin in the retail sector. 8 In addition this report follows up on outstanding recommendations from a mission to evaluate control systems for the placing on the market and use plant protection products and residues in foodstuffs of plant origin carried out from 26 to 28 March 2001. The reports on the third series of missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/food_hygiene/index_e n.html 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities There are several competent authorities charged with the official control of foodstuffs in Luxembourg. These include the Health Inspection Division (Division de l'Inspection Sanitaire (DIS)) within the Health Directorate (Direction de la Santé) under the umbrella of the Ministry of Health. The Veterinary Service (Administration des Services Vétérinaires (ASV)) falls within the remit of the Ministry of Agriculture in its work on animal health, animal welfare and animal identification. However, as regards its activities in the field of public health, it works under the supervision of the Ministry of Health. There is some change since the time of the last mission SANCO 3394/2001 in so far as there is now an inspection division in the National Health Laboratory (Laboratoire National de Santé (LNS)) which is also charged with official control activities. The ASV was not included in the competent authorities at the time of the last mission. Other bodies concerned with the official control of foodstuffs are the customs authorities (Administration des Douanes et Accises) and the police service. The structure and responsibilities of these organisations within the scope of this report are summarised in table 2 (page 9). 5.1.1. Health Inspection Division (Division de l'Inspection Sanitaire) The Health Inspection Division (DIS) is one of several divisions within the Health Directorate in the Ministry of Health. There is one head of division (a medical doctor), two engineers (agronomy and chemistry) and six health inspectors (agent sanitaires) in DIS. The engineers and health inspectors are both authorised to carry out official control activities. The DIS meets once a week to plan activities and discuss any problems that arise. The DIS is responsible for ensuring the protection of public health both with regard to environmental hygiene and the monitoring and combating of communicable diseases. 5.1.2. The Veterinary Service (Administration des Services Vétérinaire) The Veterinary Service (ASV) is placed under the responsibility of the Ministry of Agriculture and under the supervision of the Ministry of Health for matters relating to public health. The ASV consists of two departments, veterinary 9 inspections and the Veterinary Medicine Laboratory. The ASV is concerned with inspection of butchers shops within the scope of this mission. In Luxembourg butchers shops sell meat only to the final consumer. The ASV also carry out some combined inspections with inspectors from DIS. There are 16 veterinarians in the Veterinary Inspection Division, including official veterinarians assigned to approved establishments and the Veterinary Medicine Laboratory has two. Table 2 Authorities Levels Central Local Competencies Institutions Policy development making food legislation Ministry of Health Division de - Food hygiene inspection l'inspection sanitaire Official sampling GHPG Laboratoire - National sampling plan, analysis National de Sante (LNS) and results Inspections and official sampling Ministry of Administration des - Inspections of butchers shops and Agriculture Services Vétérinaires official sampling Veterinary Service activities Administration des - Food hygiene inspections of cafes Douanes et Accises and small restaurants Customs and excise duties Police Service - Participate in food hygiene inspections as requested by DIS Police duties 5.1.3. National Health Laboratory (Laboratoire National de Santé) The LNS is an administrative body within the Ministry of Health. It has a number of divisions of which the division for control of foodstuffs is of most relevance. Since 5 April 2003 there have been three control divisions, the analytical laboratory, the inspection service and the QA department. 10 The inspection control division consists of two inspectors and one sampler. It is in the process of accreditation to ISO 17020 at the time of the mission15. This division is responsible for inspection and sampling activities for the official control of foodstuffs and for collation of data for the official control programmes (returns data). There is a contract between the inspection division and the analytical laboratory division for planned sampling activities. Official control activities are planned annually with monthly meetings to verify if objectives are being met. 5.1.4. Customs Authorities (Administration des Douanes et Accises) Within the customs authority's administration there is one director and two assistant directors one for internal services and the other for external services. Within the internal service the Security Division (Division Attibutions Securitaires) provides technical support to four divisional inspectorates and eleven motorised units. Each unit comprises of two inspectors who have received basic training in the control of foodstuffs. The customs officers are responsible for controlling all premises licensed to sell alcohol for consumption and carry out hygiene inspections in cafes and restaurants. The officials of the Customs Authority have the status of judicial police officers in all the implementing laws and regulations concerning food hygiene. 5.1.5. Police Service Police officers are authorised to carry out inspections for the official control of foodstuffs. However, since the time of the last mission SANCO 3394/2001 the police only participate in food inspections at the request of the DIS. They verify the authorisation of the proprietor to set up the premises, the commercial licence. 5.1.6. Communication and co-ordination Since the last mission (SANCO 3394/2001), a health-agriculture co-ordination unit ("cellule de concertation") has been set up and holds meetings approximately 10 times per year to discuss official control activities. The participants include high rank officials from DIS, ASV, LNS, the Agricultural Technical Service and representatives of the two ministries involved: the Ministy of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture. Representatives of other authorities can be invited as the need arises. In addition to the co-ordination unit there have been three meetings between DIS, ASV and the customs authorities in since October 2003 to discuss official control activities. 15 In their response to the draft report the Luxembourg Authorities noted that the Inspection Control Division has been accredited in accordance with standard ISO 17020 since September 2004. 11 5.2. Legislation All relevant EU legislation within the scope of this mission has been transposed into national legislation with the exception of Council Directive 93/99/EEC. The mission team was informed that there is no legal document transposing this Directive. Parts of this Directive are already provided for in the Act of 25 September 1953. In addition the Law of 22 March 2000 provides for the creation of a national laboratory accreditation body. Council Directive 93/43/EEC is transposed by Règlement grand-ducal of 27 July 1997 and the requirements of Council Directive 89/397/EEC are transposed by Règlement grand-ducal of 28 February 1994. The EU legislation specified in section 2, has been transposed into national legislation. With regard to the beef labelling Regulations, the ASV have circulated all sectors of the business and official veterinarians with guidelines on these Regulations. Approximately 50% of butchers' shops are registered and approved to remove Specific Risk Material (SRM) in accordance with the derogation in point 6 of the annex to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 5.3. Good Hygiene Practice Guides. There are eight guides to Good Hygiene Practice (GHP) for industry sectors in accordance with article 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. The guides are validated by the Ministry of Health in line with the opinion of its administrative departments and are distributed to food businesses by the Chamber of Trades (Chambre des Métiers). At the time of the mission six of the eight had been notified to the Commission services. The mission team was informed that the remaining two guides will be notified to the Commission shortly. The mission team assessed two GHP guides and found them adequate to meet the requirements of Article 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. In addition the guides provide generic HACCP tables. There was some evidence of circulation of guides at site visits and inspectors recommend their use to food businesses. 5.4. Laboratory Services 5.4.1. General organisation There are several approved laboratories in Luxembourg which are involved in the official control of foodstuffs, one of which, the LNS, is accredited for the control of foodstuffs within the scope of this mission. The State Veterinary Medicine Laboratory (not visited by mission team) analyses meat-based foodsftuffs and certain fisheries products is in the process of being accredited to ISO 17025. The LNS is accredited to ISO 17025 by the Luxembourg accreditation body OLAS since May 2003. This was notified to the Commission services in June 12 2003. The accreditation covers a range of chemical and microbiological methods. As it is the only laboratory in this sector the range of pathogen microbiological methods is somewhat limited. For example, the scope does not yet include Listeria, Campylobactor or E. coli O157. 5.4.2. Laboratory visited Analytical Laboratory Division: The LNS exhibited a good QA system including staff training records, traceability, internal quality audits, proficiency tests and corrective action procedures. There is one head of laboratory, one scientist (both have doctorates) and 6.5 technicians in this division. The new building structure in place since the time of the last mission is adequate with a designated sample reception area. The condition and temperature of samples arriving at the sample reception area is well monitored. The laboratory receives 78% of its samples from its own inspection service, 8% from private samples and the rest from DIS and ASV. 5.5. Competent Authority Controls 5.5.1. Organisation of Controls The national priorities of the DIS and the ASV are set annually based on the past years inspection reports. All competent authorities concerned with the official control of foodstuffs plan their inspection priorities independently and they each have a separate filing system and database of food premises. Through the newly set up co-ordination unit there is now some co-operation in the planning of inspection activities between ASV and DIS including some joint inspections. The DIS and LNS inspection division met in 2003 to avoid overlap in inspection activities. The DIS focus on large canteens in hospitals, retirement homes, schools, crèches, mineral water companies, flour works, breweries, nut importers and supermarkets. The DIS estimate that approximately ninety percent of large food businesses have auto-control systems based on HACCP principles in place. The LNS inspection control division has no definitive list of premises for which it is responsible, or a clear number. Following the agreement reached in 2003 with DIS, it concentrates on certain premises; namely bakeries, delicatessens, chocolate manufacturers and dairies (in co-operation with veterinary inspectors). Prior to this unofficial division of premises between DIS and the LNS inspection division both bodies inspected all these types of food businesses. Inspection activities concentrate on larger premises which are inspected once per year The LNS inspection division take samples from small premises once every two years. They also take samples from premises where they do not routinely carry out inspections such as supermarkets. They only inspect small premises if there is a problem identified following sampling. 13

text: The competent authorities in Austria should consider amending the existing Guides to Good Hygiene Practice in order to allow food business operators to receive sufficient guidance for the implementation of all HACCP principles as required by Article 5.1 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC.

The competent authorities in Austria should consider taking measures to ensure, that official foodstuffs hygiene inspections assess the potential food safety hazards associated with the businesses and that the evaluation of CCP's and their related controls are performed in accordance with Article 8.2 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC.
The competent authorities in Austria should consider providing specific training programmes with regard to the assessment of HACCP systems to all foodstuffs inspectors.

The competent authorities in Austria should consider taking measures in order to achieve the level of enforcement, especially with regard to the service sector, as laid down in annual inspection plans. 18 In their response to the draft report the Austrian Authorities noted that in their view products sold only locally do not represent a serious risk for consumers outside Austria, nor are rapid actions outside Austria required. Additionally the Austrian Authorities noted that notification of such test results would overload the network. 22 A programme in response to these recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission Services within a period of two months after the dispatch of the final report. 10. ADDENDUM In their response to the recommendations made in the draft report, the Austrian CA indicated that work on the amendment of one specific GGHP has already started and other guides will be revised in due course. Furthermore, the CA replied that they have started preparations to provide HACCP training to all food inspectors, covering the assessment of critical control points and the related controls pursuant to Article 8.2 of Council Directive 93/43/EC. Finally, regarding the level of enforcement, the Austrian CA stated, that in the course of introduction of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules19, a sampling working party is seeking to optimise the auditing and sampling plan. 19 OJ L 165; 30/04/2004, p. 1 - 141 23

Take into consideration potential limitations on the current "fourth item approach" to reduce the risk of routine inspections not properly assessing all areas of the Annex I to Council Directive 93/43/EEC in all premises.

Proceed with the implementation plan for HACCP principles to ensure that Article 3 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC is adequately enforced. A programme in response to these recommendations should be produced by the Competent Authority, which should provide detailed information of the actions that will be taken and proposed deadlines by which these actions will be completed within 2 months of receipt of the final report. 10. ADDENDUM Regarding the recommendations made in the draft report an action plan has been provided by the Danish authorities during the preparation of the final report. With regard to the recommendation (1) the Danish authorities noted that there is already an action plan to secure that all areas of the annex I of Council Directive 93/43/EEC is covered. Concerning the recommendation (2), the Danish authorities noted that they have an implementation plan for HACCP based own check at retail level that will be fulfilled by the end of 2005. At that time every food operator at retail level will have an HACCP based own check program approved by the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration. 20

Ensure that food premises are inspected at a frequency which has regard to the risk associated with those premises, as provided for in Article 8(2) of Council Directive 93/43/EEC 21 (2) Address the low level of auto control systems based on HACCP principles in small businesses. (3) Encourage the development of Guides to Good Hygiene Practices and ensure their proper assessment. (4) Ensure that all aspects of Council Directive 93/43/EEC are covered during inspections. (5) Enhance communication with the local authorities, in particular with regard to the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed. The reports on the third series of missions are available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/food_hygiene/index_en. html 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities The competencies of those organisations with responsibility for the official control within the scope of this mission are summarised in the following table: 7 Table 2: Structure and responsibilities of organisations within the scope of the mission Levels Institutions Central Regional Competencies Central Ministry of - Holds main political Agriculture, Nature responsibility for the and Food Quality Authority Ministry of Health, - Production of Legislation Welfare and Sports (Policy Unit) and funding -------------------- -------------------------------- Food and Consumer - Policy advising Product Safety - Co-ordination and Authority supervision of the enforcement of legislation -------------------- - Production of standard National Institute for operating procedures to guide Health and enforcement agents Environment - Co-ordination of training - Risk assessment and Regional 5 Regional communication Health - Co-ordination of research Inspectorates -------------------------------- (including Research laboratories) - Enforcement of foodstuff legislation - Co-ordination of specified inspection activities and related work throughout the country - Research/monitoring (special sector designated) 5.1.1. Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (VWA) The Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority is an independent agency in the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality (LNV) but is also a delivery agency for the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (VWS). The Authority is responsible for policy advising, co-ordination and supervision of inspection activities, co-ordination of training for food inspectors, risk assessment and communication and co-ordination of research. The VWA consists of a central co-ordinating unit ­ the Directorate of Inspection - and two delivery units: the Inspectorate for Health Protection and Veterinary Public Health (KvW) and the National Inspection Service for Livestock and Animal Health (RVV), but only the KvW has responsibilities within the scope of this mission. Since mission SANCO 1260/2000 the KvW and the RVV amalgamated into the VWA and it is planned to merge the two units before 01/01/2006. The central Inspectorate for Health Protection provides administrative support regarding legal advice, IT, personnel, 8 handling of information and complaints, finance, quality control and issuing of administrative fines. The VWS finances the activities of the VWA. The policy department of the VWS is preparing legislation within the scope of the mission, which is sent for consultation to an advisory committee, consisting of relevant stakeholders. The Minister of Health then finally approves new legislation. The National Institute of Public Health and the Environment belonging to the VWS plays a minor role in the enforcement of food safety legislation in that it provides specific advice in case of new risks to public health. 5.1.2. Regional Inspectorates Beside the central co-ordinating unit of the VWA in The Hague there are 5 regional inspectorates, enforcing foodstuff legislation throughout the country. Each of the regions has its own laboratory, carrying out the most common analysis necessary. In addition the regional inspectorates dedicate part of their capacity to a specific area of competence as follows: · Region North-West: Primary agricultural and horticultural products · Region North: Non-food chemistry · Region East: Veterinary products · Region South: Composite food products · Region South-West: Non-food product safety This includes for example drafting of annual inspection plans or inspection protocols in co-operation with the other regions or providing specialised analytical capabilities or research capacities. Regional inspectorates have a common structure each divided into enforcement and research/monitoring departments. Within the enforcement departments a number of "Food Teams (FT)" and "Veterinary/Technology Teams (VT)" were set up. Inspectors of food teams have in general a professional education in food technology or related professions, like butcher, baker etc. Inspectors of the VT teams are required to have a high professional education or a relevant University degree. In the Netherlands there are 220 inspectors (FTE) employed working either in the Food teams or the VT teams. Local inspection units are integrated within the regional inspectorates. 5.1.3. Communication and co-ordination An Intranet application created for the VWA is the main tool regarding communication from top-to-bottom and vice versa for all levels involved. It provides a comprehensive database regarding food establishments and previous inspection activities, dissemination of new or amended legislation, inspection plans and protocols, recommendations on sampling procedures etc and is accessible by every inspector. Furthermore the regions prepare and submit quarterly activity and performance reports to the central level showing the level of compliance against standards agreed upon before. 9 Horizontal communication between the regions involved with regard to reporting and planning of activities, harmonisation of inspections and other activities take place on different occasion throughout the year, at least quarterly. Meetings on regional level are organised by the regions, which have a lead role with regard to the areas of competence mentioned earlier. 5.2. Legislation In the Netherlands the "Warenwet" forms the framework piece of legislation on which the secondary legislation called "Warenwetbesluit" is based upon. Concerning the hygiene of foodstuffs of non-animal origin the "Warenwetbesluit Bereiding en behandeling van levensmiddelen" (Stb. Nr. 678, 10-12-1992) is the major piece of legislation. On basis of Article 3, paragraph 3 of the "Warenwetbesluit" the Minister of Health has adopted the "Warenwetregeling Hygiene van levensmiddelen" of 12 December 1994 (nr. DGVgz/VVP/L942587, Stcrt. 245), which requires by article 30 the application of all HACCP principles including documentation by food establishments. According to Article 31 of the "Warenwetregeling" food establishments have the choice between setting up their own auto-control system based on the HACCP principles as described in Article 30 or they apply a branch specific Guide to Good Hygiene Practice (GGHP). Thus in theory legislation allows every food establishment to apply the branch specific GGHP independently from the size of the business or the risks associated. Microbiological and temperature criteria are laid down in the "Warenwetbesluit Bereiding en behandeling van levensmiddelen" and in the "Kokswarenbesluit". The microbiological criteria refer to pathogenic and indicator organisms like Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, Enterobacteriaceae etc. 5.3. Good Hygiene Practice Guides The "Bekendmaking, betekenis, inhoud en opstelling hygienecodes" of 15 Juli 1996 (GZB/VVB/962326, Stcrt. 136) describes the formal procedure and the stakeholders involved in producing GGHP. Draft guides are assessed by the "Adviescommissie Warenwet" (ROW) and after receiving a favourable opinion they are approved by the Ministry of Health. The "Mededeling opstellen en aanpassen hygienecodes" of 16 February 1999 required owners of already approved GGHP to re-assess the guides in order to introduce necessary changes, e.g. with regard to microbiological criteria, and parameters like mycotoxins and further contaminants. Microbiological reference values as for total aerobic count, Enterobacteriaceae and other species are laid down in the GGHP where applicable. Values for indicator organisms like Enterbacteriaceae are primarily seen as reference values to evaluate the effectiveness of the process controls. To date most GGHP, of which 8 include microbiological reference values, are fulfilling the requirements set by the "Mededeling opstellen en aanpassen hygienecodes". In total 33 guides were approved since 1996 and notified to the European Commission, all are in compliance with Article 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. 10 As required by law, guides are based on the HACCP principles and have to incorporate · a branch specific hazard analysis, · the identification of Critical Control Points (CCP's) and · setting of critical limits in order to maintain proper process control and/or to meet legal requirements. After assessment by the ROW they are officially approved by the Ministry of Health. By applying the guides, food establishments are no longer obliged to perform the aforementioned points, but have to establish a monitoring system based on the guide and have to document all related activities. In case individual operations are not included in the branch specific guide, companies are allowed to use the relevant parts of other applicable guides, if available. 5.4. Laboratory Services 5.4.1. General organisation No major changes were observed in comparison to mission report SANCO 1260/2000. Each region is equipped with its own laboratory, performing chemical and microbiological analysis as well as working in the specific area of competence. All laboratories are accredited according to ISO 17025 by the "Rad voor Accreditatie", the national accreditation body. In addition internal audits were performed by staff of the regional and central quality departments of the VWA. 5.4.2. Laboratory visited The mission team visited the laboratory of the Region East, located in Zutphen. It employs 30.5 FTE and is generally well equipped, the laboratory design should prevent cross-contamination during handling of samples. It participated regularly in proficiency tests organised by FAPAS for the chemical sector and by PHLS for the microbiological sector with acceptable results. Samples are received temperature controlled, the laboratory applied an automated sample identification scheme and Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) were available for the analysis to be carried out. The overall impression of the laboratory was positive with an adequate quality management system in place. 5.5. Competent Authority Controls 5.5.1. Organisation of Controls The KvW is producing 3-year "visions" (multi-annual policy programmes) which serve as basis for annual inspection and sampling plans. They undergo annual reviews taking into account results of the previous year. The latest vision comprises the period 2003-2005 and describes roughly the main subjects to be followed by foodstuff inspections, like imports, labelling, viral or parasitic contamination of products and others. The review process is facilitated by regular communication in the form of quarterly and annual reports on inspection results and performance, sent 11 from the regional inspectorates to the central inspectorate who produces the annual report of the VWA. Preparatory work for the plan of the following year begins every April. The Regional Inspectorate South of the VWA is responsible to prepare inspection and sampling plans within the scope of the mission. In general, two types of inspections are performed, namely target related inspections and inspections at industrial food producers. Inspections with the same target and scope are summarised in one project and the annual plan for 2004 consists of 130 projects to be executed. Inspection frequency is based upon number and type of businesses and associated risks, as well as inspection capacity available. As an indicator, the VWA estimated, that 75% of the inspection capacity is in general spent on target related inspections and 25% on inspections at industrial food producers. Target related enforcement started in 2001 as an attempt to increase the frequency and effectiveness of foodstuff inspections as well as to increase the information dissemination to stakeholders. The term "target related enforcement" describes different activities like inspections with different scope and depth/length, sampling, monitoring (no enforcement) and survey. BACKGROUND 6.1. Previous mission reports The last mission to Italy, which included Brucella melitensis in its scope was carried out in May 2001 (ref. DG(SANCO)/3199/2001). The last mission with regard to bovine and buffalo brucellosis, was carried out in March 2002 (ref. DG(SANCO)/8533/2002). These reports are available on the Health and Consumer Protection Directorate General internet site at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html. In mission report DG(SANCO)/8533/2002 the following conclusions were drawn with regard to the buffalo eradication programme: The approved national eradication programme is not being correctly applied in the case of buffalo in the province of Caserta. The current situation, where seropositive animals are retained on farm, with inadequate isolation from seronegative animals, is likely to lead to an increase in the prevalence of disease within the herd. The special plan for buffalo in Caserta province is a control, rather than an eradication plan. It is not clear that the plan will reduce prevalence within herds. In addition, milk from seropositive buffalo continues to be used for the manufacture of milk products intended for human consumption and for intra-Community trade, contrary to EU legislation. In this respect the following recommendations were made: Action should be taken to ensure the respect of EU legislation laying down controls over the handling and processing of milk in the region of Campania, notably for milk from seropositive animals. Urgent action is needed to limit the spread of disease within buffalo herds in Campania, particularly in respect of the isolation and removal of positive animals. The response of the Italian CA with regard to above recommendations had been evaluated as not satisfactory at the time as the relevant issues had not been addressed. 6.2. Approval of eradication programmes The Italian programmes for the eradication and monitoring of animal diseases and for the prevention of zoonoses 2002, 2003 and 2004 respectively had been approved by Commission Decisions 2001/729/EC11, 2002/943/EC12 and 2003/849/EC respectively. MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 7.1. Competent authority structure and responsibilities Conclusions No significant changes to management structure and responsibilities have been made since the last mission in this sector. The central competent authority does not have the necessary powers to alter the actions of the regional and local veterinary services, even when these are contrary to Italian national legislation and EU requirements. In the two regions visited enforcement powers of the CA are insufficient to fully implement the relevant measures of the eradication programmes. No effective system has yet been put in place by the CCA to co-ordinate and audit activities at regional level in the sector of eradication programmes. Prioritisation of controls is decided locally. Documentation of controls was found deficient in both of the regions visited. In one ASL the filing system in place partially accounts for significant deficiencies with regard to control activities and disease management. The number of brucellosis cases in humans dropped during recent years, however, in the regions of Puglia, Campania and Sicily the number of human cases is significantly higher than in other regions of Italy. Findings 7.1.1. Management structure of the services involved in the eradication programmes The Italian competent authority has been described in detail in previous reports. Further information on the Ministry of Health can be obtained from their website: http://www.sanita.it. No significant changes to management structure and responsibilities have been made since the last mission in this sector. The CCA provides guidance and direction, and is responsible for drawing up the national eradication programme. The regional eradication plans are drafted by the regions and collated at the CCA. Responsibility for applying the programmes rests with the regional authorities. In their response to previous mission reports the Italian Authorities stated that Office VII of the Directorate General for Veterinary Public Health and Nutrition was established in 2001 to monitor operations in the regions. Three regions were to be visited in 2003 to review the eradication programmes. These visits have not taken place and are now scheduled for 2004. Within the region of Campania, regional authorities have started to audit the ASLs 8 and to verify data transmitted in the framework of the eradication of buffalo brucellosis. 7.1.2. Resources Financial resources for the implementation of the eradication programmes have been made available at national level and in the case of Campania also at regional level for the eradication of buffalo brucellosis. In addition, other regions have made regional funds available for the implementation of eradication programmes, in particular for compensation purposes. EU co-finance payment to Italy for compensation of slaughter of positive reactors, the purchase of vaccines and the costs of laboratory tests may be up to 3.500,000 Euro for brucellosis in small ruminants and 1.200,000 Euro for bovine brucellosis in 2004. 7.1.3. Personnel There is no indication that lack of veterinary staff is a problem in the context of the eradication programmes. 7.1.4. Legal and enforcement powers Presidential Decree 320 of 8 February 1954, as amended, lays down basic principles and general procedures for notifiable diseases, including legal and enforcement powers. The CCA does not have the necessary powers to alter the actions of the regional and local veterinary services, even when these are contrary to Italian national legislation and EU requirements. Significant differences in the progress with eradication of Brucella melitensis within the area of one ASL in Sicily were explained by the difficulties of the veterinary services to enforce the measures of the eradication programme. For the enforcement of measures in the framework of the eradication programmes, in certain instances the support of police is required. (See section 7.2.4 for further details). In Campania legal and enforcement powers of the veterinary service are not sufficient to overcome the hindering effects of legislation introduced by the regional parliament. The reluctance of the mayors to sign orders to the farmers, containing the official transmission of measures to be taken on brucellosis infected holdings is not overcome by the CA. (See section 7.3.6 for further details). 7.1.5. Prioritisation and documentation of controls Each Region prioritises controls according to its regional policy. In Campania the regional CA had not given any direction to the ASL, however, holdings with `unknown' status were to be targeted first. The % of holdings with `unknown' status has been reduced, in particular, in the ASL of Caserta 9 2 in recent years. In this ASL priority was thereafter given to the testing of officially brucellosis free (OBF) farms in the year 2004.13 Documentation of controls in the two regions visited was done on paper. The visited ASL in Sicily had difficulties producing the relevant control documents. The filing system in place partially accounts for significant deficiencies with regard to control activities and disease management as the CA could not easily determine from the files the dates for pending controls.14 In the two ASL and in the slaughterhouse visited, no documentation regarding disinfection measures carried out on infected farms or for transport vehicles was available. 7.1.6. Laboratory service The laboratory network for the diagnostic duties in the framework of the Brucellosis Eradication Programmes has been described in a number of previous mission reports. The IZS for Abruzzo and Molise, in Teramo has been designated the National Reference Centre (NRC) for Brucellosis since 1999. The laboratory network is partially accredited according to EN-17025 for the performance of the official brucellosis tests. The number of accredited laboratories (57) has not changed since March 2002, when the Bovine Brucellosis Eradication Programme was last evaluated by the FVO. According to information provided by the NRC, which co-ordinates inter- laboratory proficiency tests for brucellosis serology, in the 2003 inter- laboratory test trial, 72 official laboratories participated for the Rose Bengal Test and 60 official laboratories for the Complement Fixation Test. The NRC had evaluated the results of the individual laboratories, which were broadly satisfactory. Private laboratories are not authorised to carry out tests within the framework of the Brucellosis Eradication Programmes. 7.1.7. Liaison with human health authorities Liaison with human health authorities has been described in detail in report reference DG(SANCO)/8533/2002. The following table provides the number of human Brucellosis cases over the years: 13 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities of Italy noted that in the district of Caserta 2 inspection of holdings, which had not been checked for at least two years had been a priority when the special plan entered into force. In 2004, priority was given to farms, which had not been checked the previous year. 14 See addendum. 10 Year 2000 2001 2002 2003* Number of human cases 1064 923 813 528* of Brucellosis in total Worst affected regions Sicily 544 557 445 380 Campania 262 117 147 89* Puglia 149 128 111 59* * data not complete No information on the causative Brucella species was available. In the year 2002, for which the information given was broken up per age group, 102 of the 813 national cases (12.5%) were recorded in the age group of the under 14 year old children for which the risk factor `direct animal contact' is less relevant. 7.1.8. Food Safety controls According to national legislation implementing Council Directive 92/46/EEC, only milk from OBF and Brucellosis Free (BF) herds is to be used for the manufacture of milk products for human consumption in approved premises. Milk from healthy animals on infected farms may also be used for human consumption, provided that it undergoes heat treatment under official control. Italian national legislation and the approved national eradication plan require that milk from animals which are infected or suspected of being infected be collected separately and used exclusively for animal feed, following heat treatment. Milk processing establishments should receive a health attestation for each herd supplying milk following each herd test for brucellosis every six months. See section 7.3.9. with regard to the implementation of these controls. 7.2. National eradication programme for sheep and goat brucellosis, in particular, with regard to the region of Sicily Conclusions Italian legislation with regard to the eradication of brucellosis in small ruminants transposes the provisions of relevant Community legislation. The data provided confirms that further progress has been made throughout Italy with the eradication of Brucella melitensis in sheep and goats. Progress has also been made in Sicily as regards herd testing coverage and herd prevalence. Animal prevalence remained stable in Sicily over the last two years. Systems for holding registration, animal identification and movement controls have been established. Movement controls are mainly based on the compulsory use of transport documents including the Model 4 health certificate. In the province of Sicily visited, certain deficiencies with regard to registration of holdings with no more than three small ruminants, animal identification and movement controls were encountered. Contrary to the 11 provisions of the national eradication plan, transhumance in Sicily is also authorised for herds of small ruminants not OBF. In Sicily, preparations for the introduction of vaccination in infected holdings as provided for in the special plan for Sicily are at an initial stage. The supplier of the vaccine has recently been identified, the number of vaccine doses, details of the vaccination programme and procedures for its implementation have yet to be defined. In the Sicilian province visited, implementation of the current eradication programme is deficient with regard to granting and maintaining the `officially free' status, timely elimination of reactors and disinfecting practices. 7.2.1.
