LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: ­ Art. 9 of Directive 1999/74/EC; ­ Art. 10 of Council Directive 91/628/EEC of 19 November 1991 on the protection of animals during transport and amending Directives 90/425/EEC and 91/496/EEC (hereafter: Directive 91/628/EEC)5; ­ Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States6. 4. BACKGROUND INFORMATION The previous FVO mission in Spain to evaluate checks of laying hens was carried out from 10 to 14 September 2001 as part of a mission on animal welfare on farms (reference number: DG SANCO3344/2001). At this time, only battery cage systems were covered by specific EU animal welfare requirements for laying hens, as set out in Council Directive 88/166/EEC7. The report concluded that battery cage systems for laying hens were satisfactorily inspected, but that there was a lack of follow-up when infringements were detected. Other previous FVO missions concerning poultry meat (ref: DG SANCO 1213/1999 and 1198/2000), and animal welfare during transport and at slaughter (DG SANCO 8553/2002 and 9215/2003) are also relevant. Reports 3344/2001, 8553/2002 and 9215/2003 highlighted the shortcomings in the enforcement of animal welfare legislation, as a consequence of a lack of legal basis in a number of autonomous regions. The reports of these missions are available under their reference number on the DG Health and Consumer Protection website, at: http://www.europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/spain/index_en.html

Co-ordination meetings on animal welfare issues are held between the CCA and the CA of the ARs about every three months. These meetings have the aim of informing and updating on EU matters such as proposals for new legislation and results of the FVO inspections. Guidelines can be proposed and discussed at these meetings, although ARs are not obliged to follow them. 5.2. Legislation The requirements of Directives 1999/74/EC and 2002/4/EC have been transposed (Real Decreto 3/2002 and Real Decreto 372/2003) and entered into force within the required deadlines. Although a comprehensive check of the national legislation was not carried out by the FVO mission team, it was noted that: ¾ the provision for sanctioning infringements of Royal Decree 3/2002 refers to a law on consumer protection and to a Royal Decree on epizootic diseases. The CCA explained that these would be applicable in a case where an infringement involves both consumer protection and animal welfare aspects or both animal health and animal welfare aspects. In case of infringements purely on animal welfare, only the regional legislation for sanctioning would apply. A representative of the CCA indicated that the legal departments of the ARs had been consulted on the procedure for sanctioning infringements regarding animal welfare and hoped to clarify the issue fully in a short delay. · The CA in Andalucía clarified that Ley 11/2003, entered into force in December 2003, although intended mainly for pets, does not exclude explicitly farm animals9 and gives the competency for imposing sanctions for infringements regarding farm animals to the Agriculture Department. This legislation is considered as a framework that needs further specific regulations. For the time being it may be applied but the administrative procedure may not be accepted by the Courts. · In contrast, Ley 6/2003 of March 2003 of the AR of Valencia clearly includes animal welfare on farm and during transport. A representative of the CA explained that as it only provides general requirements, it needs to be developed through more detailed regulations. If a deficiency were detected during an inspection, an order to correct it within a certain 8 Commission Regulation (EC) No. 2295/2003 of 23 December 2003 introducing detailed rules for implementing Council Regulation (EEC) No. 1907/90 on certain marketing standards for eggs, OJ L 340 of 24.12.2003, p. 16 (hereafter: Regulation 2295/2003) 9 In their response to the draft report, the CA for Andalusia noted that farm animals fall within the scope of its legislation and all the infringements and penalties apply. 3 deadline would be issued by the provincial CA, on the basis of the inspection report. Information was provided also at agriculture fairs and at conferences. · A meeting is planned for 2004 in the region of Andalucía with the Agriculture Department, the Veterinary Faculty of Cordoba and the regional federation of egg producers. The farmers also received direct information from the association. · In the region of Valencia meetings are held quarterly with the regional association of poultry farmers, that signed a co-operation agreement with the Agriculture Department. Marketing standards EU marketing requirements provide a means whereby the consumer is informed of the farming method for all purchases of eggs. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7231/2004 In their initial reaction to the recommendations, the central competent authority indicated that: In relation to recommendation (1) that exchange of information is already taking place, both formally and informally and is encouraged. Training will be organised at regional and inter-regional levels, in particular to standardise the practises used by field officials on certain complex technical points. In relation to recommendation (2), that they agreed with the DDSV concerned, who considered that it would not be appropriate to block the installation of cages where works were in progress on 1.1.2003. The regulations on the protection of laying hens are currently applied and monitored. BACKGROUND Following the previous, pre-accession mission, a number of recommendations were made and the Hungarian CA undertook the implementation of an action plan to address these. 4. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: 1 ­ Article 9 of Council Directive 99/74/EC; 1 ­ Article 14 of Council Directive 93/119/EC;2 ­ Article 10 of Council Directive 91/628/EEC;3 ­ Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States4. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authority The Ministry of Agriculture and Regional Development (CCA) is responsible for transposition and implementation of the EU requirements covered by the scope of this mission. Below the national level, the first administrative level is the county. There are 19 counties and one metropolitan region (Budapest), both operating control stations (hereafter: Stations). Although the legislative framework for animal welfare during transport is shared with The Ministry of Economy and Transport, the Animal Health and Food Control Department of the CCA is solely responsible for its implementation. There is a unit within the Animal Health and Food Control Department dedicated to animal welfare issues. There are 36 separate issues where the CCA receive information on checks carried out by the counties on animal welfare. Two members of staff analyse this information and co-ordinate these tasks. They rely on holding meetings to convey information on many of these issues as they do not have sufficient resources to provide written guidance. In each county, there is an inspector in charge of disseminating information, organizing training and coordinating inspections on animal welfare. The CCA has used these inspectors in the development of check lists. 5.2. Legislation Although a comprehensive check of the legislation was not carried out, the inspection team noted that certain gaps between national and EU legislation, which had been previously identified, had been closed. It was also noted that the format 1 Council Directive 1999/74/EC of 19 July 1999, laying down minimum standards for the protection of laying hens, OJ L 203, 3.8.1999, p. 53 (hereafter: Directive 99/74/EC).

In the course of investigating the practical implantation of EU requirements, a small number of transposition problems were identified: ¾ Legislation transposing Directive 91/628/EEC (Joint Decree 52/2003) does not provide a minimum resting time following a journey of more than 50 km to an assembly centre. Directive 91/628/EEC states that a 24 hour rest must be provided. However, a further decision at EU level on this issue which was foreseen in second indent of Article 2e of Directive 91/628/EEC has not yet been taken. ¾ Chapter I, section C (16) of Council Directive 91/628/EEC lays down that vehicles shall carry suitable equipment complying with the requirements of paragraph 4, whereas Joint Decree No.52/2003, section 22 (3) request in the vehicle the equipment suitable for loading and unloading of the livestock only if necessary. ¾ Spare equipment for stunning is not required at the place of slaughter, as foreseen in Directive 93/119/EC, but within the slaughterhouse. This arose as a consequence of the wording in the Hungarian text of this Directive, on which national legislation was subsequently drafted. 5.3. Checks of holdings with laying hens In order to ensure compliance with Directive 99/74/EC, the CCA indicated that: · The national control plan foresees an annual inspection with the use of a check list. · Written instructions had been sent to the Stations and training provided, which emphasised the daily inspection and removal of birds from cages (point 6 of the Annex of Directive 99/74/EC). The inspection team noted that: ¾ The registration of farms had been completed, but information was not recorded to distinguish between keeper and owner, nor on other establishments under the same management, as required. ¾ Training on inspection of laying hen farms was provided in the County visited. The general method for inspection was satisfactory. The CA had detected deficiencies in relation to inspection devices and imposed deadlines for their correction. ¾ The method, approved by the CCA, to calculate the maximum capacity of the farms overestimates the maximum number of birds allowed. As a result, the farm visited was around 25% overstocked, whereas the inspecting veterinarian had come to the conclusion that it was 10% overstocked. 3 5.4. Registration of transporters A system of registration is in place. The code attributed to each transporter indicates the county of registration and enables rapid identification when necessary. However it was noted that: ¾ As this register is maintained at county level it allows a transporter to register in more than one county. ¾ Transporters from third countries have not yet been registered as required by Article 5, 1(a) of Directive 91/628/EEC. Although billboards at BIPs indicate several animal welfare requirements which must be met, the necessity to be registered by a MS is not one of those mentioned. This would indicate that this requirement may have been overlooked. 5.5. Checks of animal transport To comply with the provisions of Article 8 of Directive 91/628/EEC, the CCA indicated that: · Control is mostly focused on places of departure and destination, where veterinarians are already present to carry out animal health or public health checks. Checks are carried out on 100% of consignments at these locations and 306,231 checks were carried out in 2003. Compliance is achieved as the vehicle is not allowed to leave the place of departure if there are deficiencies. · Check lists and inspection protocols have been sent to the county offices and a reporting system has been set up. · Transport documents for journeys of more than 50 km indicate the time of departure. · Route plans for journeys of more than eight hours would be verified. Regarding checks at departure, the inspection team noted: ¾ Check lists are exhaustive in terms of detailing the legal requirements for all types of transport, with most requirements irrelevant to the inspection seen at a place of departure. The inspecting veterinarian indicated that this format would not encourage the use of the check list. ¾ Measures were taken to ensure that only animals fit for the intended journey are loaded. ¾ Regarding a truck which had already part loaded at another location, it was indicated that the animals would be rested on the vehicle to avoid unnecessary unloading/ reloading. However, the animals were unloaded in the assembly centre after waiting on the truck for some five hours. ¾ A four decks vehicle, considered acceptable by CA, provided insufficient head space for sheep. 4 ¾ There is no system to ensure that route plans are verified or that they are returned. Copies of issued route plans were not kept; incomplete route plans had been approved and in most cases, they had not been returned after the completion of the journey. Regarding checks during transport, the CCA indicated that: · Regarding checks at Nagylak BIP, which have been the subject of complaints from NGOs, it is planned to roof the parking area, where documentary checks are carried out, by 31.4.05. Procedures have been revised to give priority to the transit of consignments of live animals and to provide a minimum of 30 minutes after the last animal is unloaded for feed and water before reloading at the installation where physical checks are carried out. · At Zahony BIP, the unloading and inspection facilities are roofed and further pens would be roofed by 1.12.04. · In relation to both facilities, the CVO indicated that fines collected from sanctions imposed for infringements of animal and public health requirements would be diverted to carry out this work, as there was insufficient EU funding available. · At staging points, a register would be maintained as required by Annex C.7 of Council Regulation (EC) No. 1255/975. · Mobile teams carried out checks at 12 other locations since 1.5.04. 14 deficiencies were detected and verbal warnings were given as the findings were not considered serious. At the sites visited, the inspection team noted: ¾ Separate registers were maintained at the staging point, one providing details of consignments of animals which made a one hour mid-journey rest and the other details of consignments which were unloaded for a 24 hour rest. However, this double use of the staging point, including mid-journey rests for species for which it did not have approval, was not notified to the Commission as required by Article 1.1 of Council Regulation (EC) No. 1040/20036. ¾ In the absence of guidance from central or county authorities, there had been insufficient checking of the details of the registers. As a result insufficient rest periods had not been detected by the CA. Although the check list used for inspecting the staging point focused on the facilities provided, the pen approved by the CA for sick or injured animals was inappropriate.
Council regulation (EC) No. 1255/97 of 25 June 1997 concerning Community criteria for staging points, OJL 174 of 02.07.1997 p.1.

Council regulation (EC) No. 1040/2003 of 11 June 2003 amending Regulation (EC) No. 1255/97 as regards the use of staging points, OJL 151 of 19.6.2003 p. 21. 5 ¾ Although action was taken to care for a recumbent horse on board a vehicle, the CA did not investigate the transport conditions and it was the mission team, who pointed out that there were two horses too many, which were tied in the opposite direction to the seven other horses in this compartment. ¾ A previous case of overcrowding had been detected on a vehicle using the staging point. In this case, apart from removing the nine dead sheep, no further action had been taken. The CA did not consider such a mortality rate significant (9 in a consignment of 700), whereas it is considerable. ¾ The number of consignments using the staging point is six times lower than before accession, which indicates that there is probably a high level of non- compliance with journey time requirements for those animals transiting Hungary. Regarding checks at destination, the CCA indicated that action regarding transport inspections at slaughterhouses was established as follows: · According to the CCA a check list should be completed annually. · County level required check lists to be completed four times a year for large slaughterhouses. The inspection team noted that: ¾ None of the documents, which accompanied consignments of animals, indicated the time of departure, as required. ¾ The number of checks is limited compared with the number of consignments. ¾ In one slaughterhouse, neither vehicle seen had suitable unloading equipment. The OV had not detected that a gap between the truck and the unloading ramp could give rise to serious injury. 5.6. Animal welfare within the slaughterhouse Check lists had been provided and training of the county animal welfare inspectors had been carried out to ensure that the requirements of Directive 93/119/EC were respected, in particular emphasising: · The appropriate handling of animals (Annex A.II.9 Directive 93/119/EC); · Appropriate back-up equipment is available at the place of stunning (Article 6 Directive 93/119/EC); · Bleeding should commence not later than 15 seconds after stunning. The inspection team noted that: ¾ Handling of animals was not adequate in the larger of the two slaughterhouses visited, as electric prods were used inappropriately. 6 ¾ Back-up equipment was not at the place of slaughter, but was kept elsewhere in the slaughterhouse. ¾ In the smaller slaughterhouse visited, the OV was aware that bleeding did not commence within 15 seconds after stunning and was trying to solve this through the up-grading of the establishment. 6. CONCLUSIONS 6.1. Competent Authority 1. There is an effective system for the exchange of information between the CCA and the counties. 2. As a result of the inadequate resources at central level, written instructions are often inadequate to ensure a correct application of animal welfare requirements. 3. The delegation of tasks to county animal welfare officers compensates to a certain degree for the lack of staff at central level. However, check lists, developed by the counties and distributed by the CCA, are of variable usefulness. 6.2. Legislation 1. The adoption into national legislation of the format proposed by the Commission for reporting results of transport checks (Article 8 of Directive 91/628/EEC), could ensure that this is followed in a uniform way throughout the country. 2. Gaps previously identified in the legislation have been amended, however, three further areas of non-transposition were identified: spare equipment for stunning at the place of slaughter, which arose due to a problem with the Hungarian translation of Article 6.2 of Directive 93/119/EC; vehicles shall carry suitable loading and unloading equipment (Chapter I, section C (16) of Council Directive 91/628/EEC) and rest time at assembly centres (second indent of Article 2e, Directive 91/628/EEC). Directive 91/628/EEC foreseen the adoption at EU level of further requirements to address the third issue. 6.3. Checks of holdings with laying hens. 1. Although the legal basis corresponds to Directive 2002/4/EC, the format used for the practical registration of laying hen holdings does not contain all the information required. 2. Although the general method for inspection of laying hen farms was satisfactory, overstocking may be a greater problem than reported, as the authorised maximum capacity of birds in the farms is systematically overestimated in the CA´s calculations. 6.4. Registration of transporters A system of registration of transporters is in place, except for third country transporters. 7 6.5. Checks of animal transport 1. The inspection programme over-relies on checks at places of departure, the main focus of which is not animal welfare. As a result certain deficiencies are not detected. Documents were not checked sufficiently, with the result that journey times could not be established or were not verified and measures were not taken to ensure requirements for head space were respected. 2. The CCA has not yet developed an enforcement strategy and as a result appropriate follow-up actions are not initiated when deficiencies are found. 3. Although steps have been taken to develop a system for checks during transport, the effectiveness and number of checks are insufficient to ensure a higher level of compliance for consignments transiting Hungary. 4. Checks at destination are insufficient, as the OV at the slaughterhouse considers that all requirements have been checked at the place of departure. 6.6. Animal welfare within the slaughterhouse 1. Although the check list allowed inspectors to identify problematic areas, inappropriate handling was tolerated by the OV when there were more tasks and time constraints, which is the case in a high throughput rather than a low throughput slaughterhouse. 2. The CA are taking steps to minimise the possible recovery of animals after stunning, which is problematic in certain low through-put establishments. 6.7. Overall conclusion Although most requirements of EU law have been transposed into national legislation a small number of gaps were identified. Staff at central level is insufficient, with the result that insufficient guidance and instruction has been given. Although the CA has set up a basic framework for exchange of information and there is an adequate system for carrying out farm checks, the lack of an enforcement strategy means that systematic overstocking in laying hen farms is accepted. Transport checks over rely on full compliance at the place of departure which were not fully adequate. Although check lists have been provided to assist inspectors carrying out their duties at various locations, an enforcement strategy has not been developed. The system for checking requirements at slaughter is satisfactory, with deficiencies arising when there is a lack of day to day supervision.

text: CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 17 September 2004 with the CCA. At this meeting the main findings and conclusions of the mission were presented by the inspection team. The CCA did not express any major disagreement with these, but pointed out that the lack of resources at central level contributed to the difficulties in establishing more effective controls. 8 8. RECOMMENDATIONS To the competent authorities of Hungary 1) To ensure that there are adequate resources at central level, to ensure the practical implementation of EU requirements on animal welfare. 2) To transpose the following requirements into national legislation: a. Spare equipment for stunning is available at the place of slaughter Article 6.2 of Directive 93/119/EC; b. Vehicles shall carry suitable loading and unloading equipment (Chapter I, section C (16) of Directive 91/628/EEC). 3) Regarding holdings with laying hens, to ensure: a. That the calculation of maximum capacity respects the minimum space requirement per hen (Article 5.1.1 of Directive 99/74/EC). b. Stocking rates are re-evaluated and actions are taken to address problems of overstocking. 4) Regarding animal welfare during transport: a. To include third country transporters in the system of authorisation (Article 5, 1(a) of Directive 91/628/EEC). b. To develop an inspection programme and enforcement strategy to comply with Article 8 of Directive 91/628/EEC. c. To ensure that documents that accompany animals during transport are in compliance with Article 4 of Directive 91/628/EEC. d. To put in place a system for the control of route plans (Article 5 of Directive 91/628/EEC). e. To ensure that appropriate action is taken where checks at staging points indicate inappropriate resting periods and that the outcome is subsequently communicated to the MS of departure (Article 18 of Directive 91/628/EEC). f. To communicate to the Commission the double use of staging points (Article 1.1 of Council Regulation (EC) No. 1040/2003). 5) Regarding slaughterhouses: To ensure that handling of animals is appropriate (Annex A.II.3 of Directive 93/119/EC) through guidelines and instructions to slaughterhouse staff and their subsequent supervision. 9 9. BACKGROUND 4.1. Background to present mission In May 2003, one Member State sent initial information through the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed relating to discovery of an adulterant dye, Sudan I, in hot chilli products originating from India. In response to the level of alerts and public health concerns Commission Decision 2003/460/EC on emergency measures regarding hot chilli and hot chilli products was adopted by the Commission on June 2003, and subsequently was updated by Commission Decision 2004/92/EC, which was adopted in January 2004. Following the adoption of Commission Decision 2003/460/EC, Member States (MS) are required to check consignments of chilli and chilli products presented for importation. Such consignments must be accompanied by an analytical report demonstrating the absence of Sudan I, and in the absence of such a report the importer shall have the product tested to demonstrate that it does not contain one or more of the adulterants Sudan I-IV. Pending availability of the analytical report, the product shall be detained under official supervision. The original measures set out in Commission Decision 2003/460/EC were subsequently extended by Commission Decision 2004/92/EC to include curry powder and other adulterants Sudan II, III and IV. There have been 119 RASFF notifications for Sudan I in 2003 and 31 in 2004. Implicated products include crushed chillies, chilli powder, spice mixes, curry powder, different kinds of sauces, spicy pasta, meat products and snacks. A report on a mission concerning an evaluation of import controls to Italy (Ref. 9131-2003) is now available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection's Internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/contaminants/italy/index _en.html 4.2. Public health information Sudan I is an industrial dye that is used for colouring solvents, oils, waxes, petrol, and shoe and floor polishes. It is prohibited as a food ingredient in the EU. Sudan I-IV have been classified as category 3 carcinogens by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities Table 2. Ministry of Health (Ministero della Salute) The central authority with responsibility for the controls over foodstuffs of non- animal origin and of general consumer safety and protection is the Ministry of Health (`Ministero della Salute'). This Ministry has responsibilities in the following: 8 · Producing legislation, and disseminating directly applicable Community legislation · Co-ordination of national control activities and collation of data By Decree of 12th September 2003 the Ministry has two Directorates-General with responsibility for import controls of food of plant origin into the EU, The DGSVA (Directorate General for Veterinary Public Health, Food and Nutrition) (Direzione Generale della Sanità Veterinaria e degli Alimenti') and the DGP (Directorate General for Prevention)('Direzione Generale Della Prevenzione'). Both of these belong to the Department for Prevention and Communication. The DGSVA is divided into 16 offices of which: Office 4 ` Hygiene and Food Technologies, Additives and Contaminants, Material in contact with food' has six units. Office 4 produces the transposition of relevant community legislation. Office 5 is responsible for official control of foodstuffs. Office 6 was established in October 2002 and is the contact point for the Commission RASFF system. Office 14 ` Food of Plant Origin' deals with all issues related to safety of products of plant origin, and is responsible for the development of policy in this area, including on import controls for food of plant origin. The DGP consists of 9 offices. The most relevant to the scope of this mission is Office III `Co-ordination office of the USMA's'. This office employs 7 staff of whom 4 are medical doctors and 3 administration staff. This office is responsible for the co-ordination of operational procedures and administration of the USMA. Unlike official control of food premises within the community the responsibilities for safety of products imported into Italy are not devolved to the regions but are retained at central level. Following a Ministerial Decree and subsequent reorganisation, control of goods imported is now undertaken by 12 Principal offices of the USMA (Port, Airport and Border Health Offices) ( 'Uffici di Sanita marittima, aerea e di frontiere '). These offices are directly responsible to the Office 2 of the DGP. The USMA have 34 territorial units at the main points of entry and exit (ports, borders and airports). The staff are predominately health technicians under the control of medical doctors. The responsibilities of USMA include a range of activities including inter alia, health checks on products of plant origin, health checks on individuals, granting of free circulation at landing points, and health checks on transport. The ISS is a central institute of the Ministry of Health based in Rome. It has responsibility for the development of methods and the training of regional laboratory staff. In some situations it performs second instance analysis. It is also designated as an accreditation body for the official control laboratories. 9 5.1.2. Customs Authorities ( Dogane) The customs authority comes under the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance. There are 14 Regional Offices (although some have responsibility for more than one region), 48 Customs Districts and 7 recently established Customs Offices. These districts include customs offices and 15 chemical analysis laboratories. The primary responsibility of customs within the scope of this mission is to ensure that products submitted for import are accompanied by a health approval certificate issued by the USMA. No list of products that require a health certificate is issued centrally to the customs offices. 5.1.3. Other Competent Authorities There are 20 Regions within Italy one of which, Trentino Alto Adige, is subdivided in two Autonomous Provinces. At regional level Public Health Directorates have responsibility for the official control of foodstuffs, but enforcement is carried out at local level by 250 Local Health Units (ASLs). The Anti adulteration and Health Body of the Military police (NAS) are regional departments of the police corps `Carabinieri'. The headquarters of this body is in Rome and it performs its tasks through the N.A.S. (Anti-adulteration and Health Bodies) which consists of 34 offices located in different regional centres. They have competence for monitoring hygiene measures and carrying out health inspections. In practice they can be requested to perform control activities in situations of multi regional or national significance that require co-ordinated action, or in support of the Ministry of Health. Within the scope of this mission they have carried out a substantial sampling program on the market for foodstuffs adulterated with Sudan I. The Central Inspectorate for repression of fraud within the Ministry of Agriculture also play a role within the scope of this mission and provided data on sampling and seizure of foodstuffs in two separate instances. 5.2. Legislation The Ministry of Health produces legislation within the context of this mission. Commission Decisions are disseminated to all the relevant offices (including the USMA) and to relevant trade and industry federations by fax with a cover note. In the files provided, it was shown that Decisions 2003/460/EC and 2004/92/EC were disseminated with an explanatory note shortly after the Decisions were published in the EU Official Journal. The powers of official control are held in transpositions of the Official Control Directives (Council Directives 89/397/EEC and 93/99/EEC) in Legislative Decree No 123 of March 1993 and Legislative Decree No 156 of May 1997. This legislation includes the powers of inspectors to gain access to premises, powers to seize non- conforming products and powers to initiate legal proceedings and impose corrective measures. 10 5.3. Competent Authority controls on Sudan I-IV 5.3.1. Organisation of controls Import control Import procedures are in general the responsibility of the customs officials. Goods imported must be declared to customs in the form of a general entry declaration, in line with Community customs rules. The customs staff enters this data on their computer system at the point when a submission for import is made. However, the owner of the goods (the importer) also requires a health approval certificate from the Maritime Frontier Health Office (USMA) for all products of plant origin, and submits relevant documentation to the USMA in advance of importation. This office examines this documentation (bill of lading, invoice, health certificates from the country of origin) and makes a decision as to whether a documentary/physical check, or sampling is required. Decisions are made at local level by the medical staff of the USMA, based on experience, RASFF data that is received at the USMA, and on EU Commission Decisions communicated from the DGSVA. With regard to the scope of this mission Art.2 of Commission Decision 2004/92/EC provides that the competent authorities shall check that each consignment of chilli and chilli products presented for importation is accompanied by an analytical report showing the absence of Sudan I-IV. In the absence of such an analytical report the importer shall have the product tested. Furthermore, in accordance with Article 3 of Decision 2004/92/EC, the competent Italian authorities carry out random sampling and analysis. Pending availability of the analytical report, the product is detained under official supervision. If the documentary and analytical results are satisfactory the USMA issues a health approval certificate, which is then presented with other documents to customs to allow clearance of the goods onto the marketplace. Provision can also be made for the product to be sent by T1 transfer for control by another customs office within Europe. Where routine analysis is required the ARPA laboratories run at a regional level undertake this. In the event of non-compliance (document and/ or analysis) the products are usually rejected at entry. This rejection is notified to the central offices (including the RASFF office), to customs and to the other USMAs to reduce risk of the product being presented as another customs point. The Mission team visited one of the 12 principal USMA offices, which was located in Livorno. The office was staffed by 3 medical doctors, 6 technicians, and 3 administrative support staff. The office had taken the initiative to develop its own well structured protocols for sampling and reporting on Sudan I. This has recently been expanded to include the additional requirements of Commission Decision 2004/92/EC, in particular concerning the analysis for Sudan II, III, and IV, and sampling for curry powder CN 0910 50. It is not known if the other 11 USMA offices have developed similar protocols. NATIONAL RESIDUE CONTROL PLAN AND OTHER RESIDUE MONITORING PROGRAMMES 5.3.1. National Residue Control Plan 5.3.1.1. Planning of NRCP The NRCP is formulated centrally by the NFA in collaboration with the National Veterinary and Food Research Institute (EELA) and MAF for meat, aquaculture animals, milk, eggs, game and honey. Live animal sampling (including aquaculture animals) is planned by MAF in collaboration with the PG. A first meeting between NFA, MAF and EELA starts in September for the planning of the NRCP for the coming year. The mission team noted that: ¾ sampling instructions are clear and are in line with the provisions of Directive 96/23/EC, Commission Decisions 97/747/EC and 98/179/EC; ¾ the PG is not directly involved in the yearly planning of the NRCP; ¾ the design of the NRCP is in general in line with the EU requirements, and all required commodities (apart from rabbit meat) and mandatory substance groups listed in Council Directive 96/23/EC are tested for. The CA stated that the production of rabbit meat in Finland is minimal; ¾ some substances which are known to have been (ab)used in food animal production in the EU are not included in the NRCP for certain commodities, e.g. phenylbutazone in live bovine animals and milk; nitrofurans, bromopropylate, chlorobenzilate and chlorodimeform in honey; nicarbazin in poultry and eggs; chloramphenicol (CAP) and all nitroimidazoles with the exception of dimetridazole in poultry, nitroimidazoles in pigs and eggs; corticosteroids in milk; ¾ the spectrum of several substance groups is limited (e.g. Group A5, B2a, B2c, B2d and nitroimidazoles); ¾ for several analyte/matrix combinations, only one or two substances are tested for, despite the fact that multiresidue methods are available in the laboratory (See section 5.5.3). 3 5.3.1.2. Implementation and supervision of NRCP For live animals, sampling is performed according to the instructions given by MAF. The PG designates MVPs, communicate this data to MAF who in turn contacts the MVPs directly to request sampling on the farms. In order to avoid a conflict of interest (MVPs sampling their own clients), MVPs so-designated are meant to take on farm samples in a neighbouring municipality (3). The NFA is responsible for organising the sampling of the other commodities. The annual sampling programmes and instructions for sampling are sent to the PG, MVPs and MFCA. In addition the staff of the NFA are directly responsible for some sampling. EELA immediately reports all non-compliant results to the NFA, which notifies the relevant PG. Until recently, the compliant results were reported once a year, however EELA now sends all results to NFA on a monthly basis. With the exception of non-compliant results, the local laboratories (carrying out screening tests for Group B1 substances) send a summary of all compliant results to NFA once a year (see also section 5.5.1.). The mission team observed that: ¾ sampling is organised in such a way that an equal distribution of sampling throughout the year is guaranteed for most of the substances covered by the NRCP; ¾ the written instructions for NRCP sampling issued by the CCA were effectively communicated to the local units; ¾ the visited PG has several general meetings with MAF and NFA during the year. In addition, the visited PG stated that a meeting is held two times a year with the MVPs, however, the issue of residues has not been highlighted yet; ¾ annual publication of the results of the NRCP is established, in accordance with Art. 8(3) of Council Directive 96/23/EC; ¾ samples are sent as soon as possible to the laboratory. There is an agreement between NFA and EELA to analyse samples within 4 weeks. Compliance with this agreement is not monitored by either NFA or MAF (4); ¾ the order to take samples was in several cases not immediately acted upon the municipal level. In several cases there were delays of several months before the sample was taken. Moreover, neither the PG nor the CA has up-to-date information about any time delays in sampling. Concerning the potential conflict of interest arising from the use of MVPs who primarily function as VPs, the PG stated that they could not exclude that MVPs could also take samples from the farm on which he/she acts as the VP. With regard to the implementation of targeted sampling as required by Community legislation, the mission team noted that: ¾ whilst there is an element of targeting by the CA (those farms with the biggest production volumes are selected centrally for sampling), the MVP is not informed about the substances that will be analysed and therefore is not in a position to target individual animals; ¾ EELA decides about the substance to be analysed mainly based on the laboratory capacity without having sufficient information about the nature of the sampled live animals. A specific section in the sample form is foreseen to note and describe specific information about the animal sampled. It was observed that this section was completed in only a few cases; ¾ cluster sampling for live animals was observed in several cases (up to 5 samples per farm on the same day). The CA stated that although the targeting principle and instructions for sampling are given in the annual sampling programme, they have no supervisory procedures in place to ensure that the sampling is unforeseen and unexpected, or indeed, whether targeting is based on valid criteria. 5.3.2. Other residue controls The CA stated that, in addition to the minimum number of milk samples taken under the NRCP, in 2003 a further 2000 milk samples were tested for the presence of inhibitors by a microbiological growth inhibition screening test. These results were reported in the NRCP. The dairy industry also test for residues of antimicrobial substances under their in-house control programmes, which have been approved by MFCA. The number and results of in-house collection tanker control are reported annually to the NFA. Non-compliant results are immediately communicated to the relevant CA. 5.4. FOLLOW-UP INVESTIGATION(S) AND ACTIONS If a non-compliant residue result is detected, EELA immediately informs the NFA of the case and the follow-up action is carried out in co-operation between the PG, MFCA, NFA and MAF. If there is reason to suspect that the residue found could have any connection with animal feedingstuffs, the KTTK is also informed and co- operates with the other authorities in taking feed samples. The results of the investigations are sent to NFA and MAF. The CA possesses the enforcement power to act upon in case of a non- compliant result as foreseen in the relevant EU legislation (e.g. movement restrictions, destruction). Several non-compliant results were found in 2002 and 2003, e.g. malachite green (MG) (5) was found in April 2004 in samples which were part of 2003 follow-up samples from one fish farm, leucomalachite green in fish (2 fish samples in 2002, 4 fish samples in 2003, 1 follow-up fish sample in 2002), and antimicrobial

MG is an unauthorised VMP within the EU. This substance was officially banned as VMP in Finland in October 2001. Leucomalachite green is a major stable metabolite of MG. 5 residues in honey (1 sulphonamide in 2002; 2 sulphonamides and 1 tetracycline in 2003 (6). The mission team noted that: ¾ there was a good standard of record keeping at both central and provincial level for the follow-up investigations examined; ¾ no detailed standardised action procedure or staff instructions for dealing with follow up investigations were available (7); ¾ there were lengthy delays in initiating re-sampling, carrying out on-farm investigations and sometimes long turnaround times at laboratory level could be seen. In several of the non-compliant cases studied, the investigation was either not sufficiently thorough or too late to establish the source of the residue violation; ¾ the action taken following the detection of residues of an unauthorised substance (MG) was limited to further sampling. The CA stated that they could find no evidence of illegal treatment with MG. Consequently, measures foreseen in Art. 17 and 23 of Council Directive 96/23/EC (movement restriction and destruction) were not implemented in the majority of the files examined by the mission team (8); ¾ in contrast, for some of the cases of non-compliant results in honey, movement control and destruction of the product was stated by the PG to have been performed. However, no documentary evidence of these actions was available as the PG did not verify the implementation of the order. Furthermore, in all of the non-compliant honey cases studied by the mission team, the on farm investigation was performed by the MVP. The CA stated that it could not been excluded that he was investigating his own private client. 5.5. LABORATORIES 5.5.1. Laboratory network. EELA operates under the control of the MAF and is the national reference laboratory (NRL) for all commodities and all substance groups listed in Annex I to Council Directive 96/23/EC. It analyses the majority of all NRCP samples. EELA also sends milk (for Group B3b) and honey samples (for Group B3a and B3b) for analysis to the Customs Laboratory, which resorts under the Ministry of Finance. A further 25 local laboratories (municipal, private and slaughterhouse laboratories) screen milk and meat samples for antibacterial substances (Group B1). All of the laboratories involved in testing NRCP samples are approved by the NFA. All non-compliant results (EELA and local laboratories) are communicated to NFA immediately after the analysis. NFA in turn informs the PG in whose region the offending farm or production site is situated.

The use of sulfonamides or tetracyclines is not authorised in honey production in the EU. Sulfonamides or tetracyclines could be used in bee-keeping only in exceptional cases and specific conditions according to Article 10 (2) of Directive 2001/82/EC. However, the prolonged withdrawal time is to be respected and should provide that there are no residues in the honey put on the market.

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation, in particular: · Art 21 of Council Directive 96/23/EC; · Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998, laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States. BACKGROUND A previous residues mission to Spain was undertaken from 27 September to 1 October 1999, the report of which (XXIV/1142/1999), has been published on the DG SANCO website at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/vi/reports/spain/vi_rep_spai_1142- 1999_en.pdf 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legislation A list of the Spanish national legal instruments transposing the Community legislation on residue controls is provided in Annex 2. The main relevant provisions of Community law are transposed. Autonomous Communities (ACs) can adopt specific legal instruments for the implementation of national legislation in their territory. The mission team noted that: ¾ in one AC visited, the authorities were unable to authorise or carry out specific control visits to pharmacies and dispensaries (centros dispensadores) dealing with VMPs or feed mills producing medicated feedingstuffs, due to a lack of legislation designating the competent authority for these activities at the regional level. 5.2. The National Residue Control Plan 5.2.1. Planning According to the Royal Decree (RD) 1749/1998, the competent authorities with regard to controls on residues in live animals and animal products are: · The competent authorities of the Autonomous Communities (CA ­ Órganos Competentes de las Comunidades Autónomas), with regard to the internal market; and 2 · The Ministry of Health and Consumer Affairs (MSC ­ Ministerio de Sanidad y Consumo) and Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (MAPA - Ministerio de Agricultura, Pesca y Alimentación), for trade with third countries and for communication with the European Commission and other Member States. RD 1749/1998 also established a co-ordination body, the National Commission for Co-ordination of the Investigation and Control of Residues or Substances in Live Animals and their Products (NCC - Comisión Nacional de Coordinación de la Investigación, Control de Residuos o Sustancias en animales vivos y sus productos). The NCC is made up of representatives from the relevant competent authorities, the Spanish Agency for Food Safety (AESA ­ Agencia Española de Seguridad Alimentaría, an agency of MSC), MAPA and each AC. It is assisted in its work by the National Reference Laboratories (NRLs) and representatives from the Ministries of the Interior and Justice. Each CA is responsible for drawing up residue control plans for their AC, following the suggestions of the NCC. Within each AC, the CA designates one co-ordinator to be responsible for the preparation of the residues monitoring plan. The NCC is responsible for preparing the National Residues Control Plan (NRCP), based on the information provided by each CA, and communicating this plan to the services of the European Commission. The NCC can also propose amendments to improve the effectiveness of the NRCP. With regard to planning of the NRCP, the mission team noted the following points. ¾ A procedure is in place for the elaboration of the NRCP, including participation of relevant departments within the CCA, the CA and the NRLs, through the NCC. ¾ In general the number of samples foreseen in the NRCP is in excess of the minimum number of samples required by Directive 96/23/EC. ¾ The information in the NRCP does not accurately reflect the plans being implemented at AC level2. In particular: - limits of detection (LODs) used in the routine control laboratories (RCLs) are, in some cases, different to those quoted in the NRCP. For example in one AC visited, the LODs noted for group A2 (thyrostats) and A4 (resorcylic acid lactones) compounds were 200 and 4 µg/kg, while the LODs given in the NRCP were 100 and 2 µg/kg respectively; - different ranges of substances are analysed. For example, the NRL was confirming a larger range of antibiotics than was indicated on the NRCP, and in one AC visited, one of the RCLs was able to detect and confirm a larger range of beta-agonists than was indicated in the plan, while another RCL was only able to detect and confirm a much narrower range.

Follow-up of non-compliant results 5.2.4.1. Non-compliant results for authorised and unauthorised substances In the case of suspicion of use of unauthorised substances or products, or when residues of authorised substances or products at a concentration exceeding the Maximum Residue Limit (MRL) are detected, the procedures for investigation and follow-up are laid down in Royal Decree 1749/1998. These procedures are in accordance with the requirements laid down in Council Directive 96/23/EC. RD 1749/1998 foresees the possibility of imposing administrative sanctions (fines, movement restrictions, destruction of animals, etc.). Penal sanctions can also be imposed under the "Ley Orgánica 10/1995, del Código Penal" and RD 1945/1983. During visits to the ACs, the mission team noted the following points. ¾ A working group has drawn up draft guidelines at the request of the NCC in order to better harmonise the approach taken to follow up within the ACs. ¾ In the results reported for 2003, in a case related to a group of animals sampled as suspects at an animal market, clenbuterol (5 animals), testosterone (1 animal) and 17-oestradiol (1 animal) were found. In relation to the recommendations above, the response can be summarised as follows: NRCP Recommendation 1: It is planned to submit samples to the control laboratories more frequently, to extend the sampling period during the year, and to sample honey both in late spring and in autumn. The laboratories have also been requested to provide information on the stability of substances tested for and this information will be attached to the contracts for 2005. Recommendation 3: Discussions with the control laboratories have been initiated with the aim to increase the substance groups tested per species. Information has also been requested from the laboratories concerning the relevance of research into incidents and to provide an update in the NRCP of the methods, preferred matrices and detection levels. Laboratories Recommendation 4: The LMVE intends to include testing for inhibitors in their scope of accreditation for 2006 and will take part in ring tests from 2005. VMPs Recommendation 7: The DPM intends to obtain information on imported medicinal products on a regular basis and report to the NRCP co-ordinator. Recommendation 8: The DPM intends to reassess its interpretation of the rules that it is possible to sometimes authorise the same VMP as both a medicated premix and an oral powder and to clarify the legal status of each product so that VMPs authorised as oral powders in the country of origin must not be allowed to become medicated premixes at national level in Luxembourg under the mutual recognition procedure. The DPM adds that this will lead to fewer products being nationally authorised as medicated premixes and an increased import of medicinal products not authorised in Luxemburg. _______________

text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Previous Missions In the context of the enlargement process, a mission was undertaken from 11 to 15 March 2002 in order to assist and monitor progress with the adoption of the relevant EU requirements. 4.2. Statistics on potato production Statistical data in this and the following sections were provided by the authorities of the Republic of Bulgaria on the pre-mission questionnaire or during the mission, unless stated otherwise. In 2003, 606 000 tons of potatoes were produced on a total potato cropping area of 55 000 ha. Certified seed potatoes were produced on a cropping area of 247.25 ha., accounting for 50 registered producers. 1 OJ L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 1 2 OJ L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 3 3 OJ L 259, 18.10.1993, p. 1 4 OJ L 235, 21.8.1998, p. 1 5 OJ L 205, 17.8.1993, p. 22 6 OJ L 169, 10.7.2000, p. 1 6 There are few cooperatives in the Republic of Bulgaria, and only in the seed potato production sector. Only a few larger potato producers grow seed on an area of over 10 ha. The normal size is 0.1-0.5 ha. Whilst potato production is widespread in almost every region, there is only one processing plant for potatoes, producing crisps. At the moment, the Government is pursuing a policy of restoring properties to their previous owners. In addition, restructuring of production is also taking place. Statistics on the size of the producers were not available. 4.3. Potato trade in the Republic of Bulgaria In 2003, Bulgaria exported 45 tonnes of potatoes for consumption to Serbia and Montenegro. In the same year, 2,700 tonnes of seed potatoes from the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, France and Slovakia, and around 28,000 tonnes of ware potatoes from Greece, Macedonia, Turkey, Poland, Serbia and Montenegro, Slovenia, Germany and Belgium were also imported. An import ban of potatoes (ware and seed) from Central and South America is in place. 4.4. Potato plant health situation in the Republic of Bulgaria The data is based on both the official controls and on information from the research institutions. The potato cyst nematode Globodera rostochiensis (PCN) was detected in Bulgaria in 1978 on the State seed production farm in Govedartsi, Samokov region. It is slowly spreading and at the moment it is found in the potato production areas in the Sofia, Smolian, Pazardjik and Plovdiv regions. Globodera pallida, Ralstonia solanacearum (R.s.), Clavibacter michiganensis spp. sepedonicus (C.m.s.), potato spindle tuber viroid (PSTV), potato wart disease (PWD), Meloidogyne chitwoodi and M. fallax, have never been detected in Bulgaria. Dytilenchus destructor occurs sporadically. In 2002, one case of contamination of ware potatoes was found. Potato stolbur phytoplasma has a limited distribution in the high mountain regions of Sofia and Smolian. Beet necrotic yellow vein virus (BNYVV) has not been detected in the mountain regions where seed potato production is located. The virus has spread in the northern regions of Bulgaria, where there is intensive production of beet, (Veliko Tarnovo and Russe regions) and southern Bulgaria (Stara Zagora). Beet is not cultivated in the potato production areas. Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) is widespread throughout the country, except in the mountain regions. It has not been found in tested seed potato production, which generally takes place at an altitude of over 800 m. Leptinotarsa decemlineata is widespread in Bulgaria. 7 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Plant health system in the Republic of Bulgaria 5.1.1. Structure of the plant health system The National Service for Plant Protection (NSPP) is a governmental organisation which performs its tasks under the supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry. The NSPP is responsible for official controls in the areas of plant health, plant protection products and fertilisers, plant protection machinery, contaminants, organic production and integrated pest management. The NSPP structure could be described as a three-tier administration. The first level is represented by the Director-General and the Director of the Plant Protection Directorate. At the second level, there are the following Directorates (or bodies with equivalent status): financing and control of property, legal activities and human resources, the Plant Protection Directorate and the two central laboratories, one for plant quarantine (CLPQ) and another for the control of pesticides residues, nitrates, heavy metals and fertilisers. At the third level are the Regional Services for Plant Protection (RSPPs) which also comprise the departments of phytosanitary control, prognosis, book-keeping and accountancy. Each RSPP is run by a Director. They also have laboratories available. NSPP headquarters are located in Sofia, to which 14 regional services for plant protection (RSPP) plus 13 district units are directly subordinated. The CLPQ is located in Sofia, with a branch in Somokov. 5.1.1.1. NSPP Headquarters Within the Plant Protection Directorate, the Phytosanitary Control Department (PCD) is in charge of coordination of the RSPPs on plant quarantine-related issues. However, the technical coordination of the regional inspectors and the laboratories' activities (inspection and analysis) is mainly delegated to the CLPQ. The Phytosanitary Control Department operates in the field of harmful organism (HOs) controls, and its responsibilities include: ¾ planning of on-site inspections and surveys; ¾ coordination of inspections and surveys, staff training and issuing of orders and guidelines for the regional inspectors; ¾ supervising regional activities; ¾ drafting of the relevant legislation. The Central Laboratory is, among other things, responsible for: ¾ phytosanitary tests on imported and domestic plants, plant products, soil and other objects; ¾ coordinating regional-level activities, issuing methodological guidelines for inspections, and drafting of monitoring programmes; 8 ¾ supervising regional offices and border inspection posts (BIPs) laboratories, validating of positive and doubtful results, and issuing of instructions on methods of analysis; ¾ training and instructing staff on diagnostics and identification of pests. It is planned that the NSPP will have a consulting council including representatives from universities, plant protection associations and other experts to provide technical expertise on specific issues on request. In addition, the NSPP will have a section of the National Research Institute, namely Plant Protection Institute, attached to each of the Departments within the Plant Protection Directorate, in order to provide them with technical and scientific support. 5.1.1.2. Regional Services for Plant Protection The RSPPs are in charge of applying and enforcing legislation. In particular, they are responsible for: ¾ on-site inspections and surveys; ¾ import and export certification; ¾ routine analyses of harmful organisms; ¾ running the alert system for producers regarding identification of pests and use of plant protection products (prognosis). 5.1.2. Human and financial resources 5.1.2.1. HUMAN RESOURCES The NSPP employs a total of 521 staff, including 499 inspectors and specialists and 20 administrative staff. All are civil servants. Data on staff in the field of harmful organism (HOs) are shown in the following table. Table 5.1: Staff in the harmful organisms control field Phytosanitary Control Department (PCD) 5* Central Laboratory for Plant Quarantine (CLPQ) 20* specialists Regional Plant Protection Services (RSPPs) 179 inspectors TOTAL 204 * includes the Head of the Department and the Head of the Laboratory At the CLPQ, 20 persons are employed, of which 14 are specialists with higher-level training in the field of agriculture, four are specialists with secondary education qualifications. In each of the following regional laboratories, Plovdiv, V. Tarnovo, Burgas and Varna, one laboratory specialist with higher-level agricultural training is in charge of analyses. In the other nine regional laboratories, tests are carried out by the inspectors. 9 Inspectors and analysts are educated to degree level (bachelor's or master's degree in plant protection). They work full-time on plant health issues. The inspectors carry out import/export activities, check on domestic production and also implement the monitoring programmes. There is a division of tasks among inspectors, with some of them carrying out import activities at BIPs and others carrying out plant passport control, surveys and other activities. They have the necessary powers to enter premises where plant health control has to be carried out (private property included) and they do not need to be assisted by other governmental officers (such as customs or police officers). The team was informed that the current resources allow the NSPP to carry out its duties. A global assessment of the resource requirements following accession has been carried out and, as result, the number of the staff will not be reduced. At the time of accession, a number of BIPs will cease to operate, and plans are under way to reorganize the relevant regional services. It is intended that some inspectors will change their field of activity from import controls to internal controls, although there are no exact figures on this yet. In the short term, staff numbers at the CLPQ will increase by four, and it is planned to recruit some laboratory specialists for the regional services. The headquarters prepare an annual training programme. Refresher training is provided on technical issues by the CLPQ and, on administrative and legislative issues, by the headquarters. In particular, a number of courses for RSPP inspectors on import control issues and laboratory expertise were provided in the course of 2003. At least 40 hours of training every three years is compulsory for inspectors. Training is also provided within the twinning light projects with France for both inspectors and laboratory staff. In particular, training programmes for CLPQ personnel have also included training at laboratories in the Member States. 5.1.2.2. FINANCIAL RESOURCES The financial resources used in the plant health sector come from fees collected for import, export, transit and plant passport activities, and for laboratory analysis not related to plant health procedures (i.e. soil quality and pest analysis). The regional services prepare draft budgets, and the headquarters then prepares the national draft budget, which the NSPP submits to the Minister of Agriculture and Forests. The State Budget defines the amount that NSPP can use. Approximately 70­80% of all the resources coming from fees are transferred back to the NSPP. A request to adapt the budget to post-accession needs has been made by the NSPP to the Ministry of Finance. 5.1.3. Compensation of affected growers Financing for eradication campaigns and for recovering damages comes from the NSPP's budget. In case of emergencies, provision can be made for extra resources, although the mission team was informed that this was not a straightforward procedure. 10 5.1.4. Working procedures and internal communication The activities are based on a general monitoring programme, which is prepared every year by headquarters (PCD and CLPQ) with the collaboration of the inspectors at regional level. It includes the list of harmful organisms for which the surveillance of the territory is required, the best period to carry out the checks, main symptoms, sampling procedures, relevant forms etc. . During the year, this programme can be amended by the headquarters according to contingencies. The CLPQ organises meetings with the inspectors at least twice a year. During these meetings, proposals can be made for changing the programme. Specific monitoring programmes are also prepared (e.g. for potato diseases). Weekly and half-yearly activity reports are sent by each RSPP to the Director-General. Each month, the CLPQ sends the results of the analyses to the Director-General, who is notified directly in the event of positive findings. The Phytosanitary Control Department compiles the information received in an annual report which is then sent to the CLPQ and the RSPPs. The annual report is used as a tool to assess and review the monitoring programme. It also contains a list of interceptions at all the BIPs. Since 2003, four employees have been designated as national reporters with responsibility for drafting final reports on specific subjects (e.g. fire-blight, potato diseases, etc.). Administrative and technical methodological guidelines, orders and documents related to the implementation of plant health legislation are available to the inspectors. At the moment, these are not set out in a single handbook, but there are plans for this to be done. In case of outbreaks or interceptions of quarantine organisms, the inspectors have the power to apply measures directly, although in case of initial outbreaks specific orders are issued by the headquarters (PCD and CLPQ). In the event of positive findings, trace-back is carried out by the inspector on the spot and the results are sent to the headquarters which can, if necessary, inform other regional services of the need to carry out targeted inspections. Coordination also includes follow-up to the activities undertaken by the regional services. Where samples are taken for analysis, a form including all the relevant information always accompanies the samples. Where an analysis is required for an imported consignment, the CLPQ sends the results to the BIP and RSPP concerned and, in the event of a positive finding, to the Director- General. Where an outbreak is suspected, the inspector must place the production/batch under quarantine. Samples are taken and sent to the CLPQ. If the CLPQ confirms the finding, the Director-General and the RSPP are notified. The CLPQ sends the inspector suggestions for measures to be implemented accordingly. 11 In 2004, the NSPP prepared an annual work plan for the first time. It will be reviewed in June with a view to possible adjustments, and assessed at the end of the year. It is detailed and targeted on the activities carried out by each department. A five-year plan is in preparation at the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Agriculture for the period until 2009. The NSPP is subject to administrative and financial auditing by the Ministry of Agriculture. An electronic information system has been in place since 1991. It contains registration details on importers and exporters, statistics and geographical maps showing the distribution of HOs within the country. However, the system is outdated and used only at regional level, for statistical purposes. Data on testing and sampling activities for the whole country are kept at the CLPQ and the PCD, although these are not standardised or always consistent; for example, the CLPQ does not have any tables showing amounts and analyses performed on ware potatoes imported, while this information is kept at the RSPP, which reports this to the Phytosanitary Control Department. A data network is being developed to link the CLPQ, RSPPs, BIPs and PCD. This will allow the headquarters to have a unified collection of data and also on-line access to the regional registers of importers/traders and producers. Communication within the NSPP is achieved through meetings (at least twice a year), phone, fax, e-mail. Representatives from the headquarters, CLPQ and regional services meet regularly. However, no minutes of these meetings are kept. Inspectors from all of Bulgaria meet once a year. The inspectors within visited RSPPs meet every month. The inspectors are well-equipped. 5.1.5. Communication to the public Laws and ordinances are promulgated in the Bulgarian Official Journal. Stakeholders are kept informed through leaflets, meetings, media etc. During the on-the-spot inspections, the mission team examined some brochures issued by the NSPP and generally found them to be outdated. Where necessary, the NSPP organises meetings and consultations with different branch organisations, producers and importers. In December 2003, an information meeting on potato diseases was held for the producers in an area near a seed potato production site. 45 producers (both seed and ware potato producers) participated in the meeting, which was advertised through letters addressed to the producers, the media and also with the help of the municipal authorities. Other meetings were organised to coincide with fairs ("potato harvest"). The NSPP has also provided producers with pictures of potatoes with symptoms of ring rot. A report of the inspection findings is always left with the undertaking concerned and signed by the owner. If a sample is taken for analysis, the owner is also informed of the result. 12 5.1.6. Legislation The framework legislation for plant quarantine is the "Plant Protection Act" of 10 October 19977 and its amendments. Ordinance No 1 of 27 May 1998 on Phytosanitary Control8 and its amendments transposes the Council Directive 2000/29/EC, and the Commission Directive 93/50/EEC, Commission Directives 95/44/EC9, and 97/46/EC10 are transposed with Ordinance No 1 dated 4 January 2002. Council Directive 93/85/EEC on the control of potato ring rot has been transposed by Ordinance No 1911 of 2 July 2001, Council Directive 98/57/EC on the control of brown rot by Ordinance No 1112 of 10 April 2001, Council Directive 69/464/EEC on the control of potato wart disease is transposed by Ordinance No 20 of 2 July 200113 and Council Directive 69/465/EEC on control of potato cyst eelworm is transposed by Ordinance No 3914 of 20 November 2001. The Ordinances are accompanied by specific methodological instructions designed to help the inspectors in implementing the relevant legislation. A detailed check of the legislation was not an objective of the mission, but some observations were made. The national legislation reflects, in general, the relevant EU legislation. The control measures to be implemented within the demarcated zone according to Council Directives 93/85/EEC and 98/57/EC are included in the relevant Ordinances and are consistent with those in the EU legislation. However, some inconsistencies were noted in the text of the relevant national legislation. For example, in Annex 5 to Ordinance No 1 of 27 May 1998, the list of plants, plant products and other objects that have to be accompanied by a domestic plant passport includes the general wording "tubers of Solanum tuberosum". ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7306/2004 In their comments on a draft version of this report, the CCA provided the following initial reaction to the recommendations: (1) Routine tail docking of pigs is not permitted, except in cases when this procedure is needed for animal health reasons. (3) By the Order of the Director of SFVS of 10 June 2004 all subjects, including animal transporters are currently undergoing veterinary approval procedure and will be included into the Register, which is available at the web site of SFVS. (4) County and district SFVS are obliged to approve the route plans only if they are appropriately completed. In the case of non return, a letter has to be sent to the transporter and, if necessary, further export shall be prohibited. SFVS is strengthening the control under the management of route plans. Food and Veterinary Audit Service on the regular basis performs controls on all activities (including approval of route plans) of SFVS. (5) Regarding surveillance in slaughterhouses: (a) The SFVS is monitoring the proper restraint of animals before stunning. (b) By the Order of SFVS of 5 July 2004 inappropriate devices for electrical stunning of cattle were prohibited. The new questionnaires for the inspections of slaughterhouses approved by the Order of SFVS of 31 August 2004, ensures that inappropriate devices for electrical stunning of cattle are not used. 9

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation, (the Treaty of the European Community, in particular Articles 10, 152,153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation, specifically: - Council Directive 89/397/EEC2 of 14 June 1989 on the official control of foodstuffs, - Council Directive 93/99/EEC3 of 29 October 1993 on additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Overview of previous missions regarding import controls. This report is the 14th in a series of missions to Member States with similar objectives. The final reports of these missions are or will be available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection Internet site: (http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/fnaoi/reports/contaminants/index_en. html) This is the first FVO mission concerning import controls on products of plant origin since the accession of Lithuania to the EU. Prior to accession the FVO carried out a number of missions in the framework of the accession preparations, in order to assist and monitor progress with the adoption of the relevant EU legislation. 4.2. Background to present mission There have been an increasing number of rapid alert messages notified in the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) within the European Union related to products containing mycotoxins, pesticide residues and 3-MCPD. 2 OJ L 186 of 30 June 1989, p. 23 3 OJ L 290 of 24 November 1993, p. 14 6 In 2003 there were over 500 RASFF messages for mycotoxins. In 2002 there were over 250 RASFF messages for mycotoxins, and in 2001 a total of 186. Implicated products included peanuts and peanut products, pistachios, hazelnuts, Brazil nuts, almonds, dried fruits (figs, apricots), spices, coffee products and cereals. As well as a general obligation for Member States to undertake random analysis of products, there are specific conditions imposed in Commission Decisions over products from certain third countries where the risk is considered greater. These specific conditions relate to mycotoxin contamination. There is an additional Commission Decision imposing conditions over the import of hot chilli and chilli products following the presence of the unauthorised colorant sudan I-IV. In 1999 the Commission received the first notification of excessive levels of 3- MCPD in soy sauce imported from third countries, particularly Asia. This was followed by a large number of alerts in 2000, 15 in 2001, 10 in 2002 and 20 in 2003. There are only a small number of rapid alerts related to pesticide residues in products imported to the Community, predominately in dried products such as teas and herbs. However the extent of monitoring of these products is unknown, and there are very large quantities of these products entering through European ports. At present the import of irradiated foodstuffs into the EU is only allowed from five irradiation plants approved for export to the EU in the context of Directive 1999/2/EC. The level of imported products is not known. Between the adoption of the Commission Decision on sudan I in June 2003 and the date of the mission, there had been over 200 alerts and additional information notifications pertaining to the finding of sudan dyes in a wide range of products. 4.3. Public health information Mycotoxins Mycotoxins are naturally occurring metabolites produced by certain species of moulds (e.g. Aspergillus spp, Fusarium spp) which develop at high temperatures and humidity levels and may be present in a large number of foods. This group of toxins includes a number of compounds of varying toxicity and frequency in food. The mould may occur on the growing crop or after harvesting during storage or processing. Whilst the moulds can be considered plant infection the ingestion of the toxin can result in disease in animals or humans. Some of the mycotoxins are known to be carcinogenic. In addition sampling plays a crucial part in the precision of the determination of the levels of mycotoxins, which are very heterogeneously distributed in a consignment. Therefore, in Commission Directives, a sampling procedure and general criteria were fixed to ensure that laboratories in charge of the analysis use methods of analysis with comparable levels of performance. 7 3-MCPD 3-MCPD is one of a group of chemical contaminants known as chloropropanols. It is known to be carcinogenic in animals at relatively low levels. For safety reasons it is recommended that 3-MCPD should be limited in foods to ensure that this threshold of intake is not exceeded and furthermore be limited to levels which are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). 3-MCPD is a contaminant, which is known to be formed during the industrial processing of foodstuffs, in particular during the acid hydrolysis of vegetable protein (to produce acid-HVP) using concentrated hydrochloric acid. The contaminant was originally identified in acid-HVP; which is used as an ingredient to flavour savoury products such as soups, stock cubes, snacks and sauces. It was then identified in soy sauce and similar savoury sauces that are produced with the addition of HVP as a flavour enhancer to shorten the traditional fermentation process: "compound" sauces. Particular problems were identified in imported sauces from a number of Asian countries, including China, Hong Kong, Vietnam and Thailand. The maximum level for 3-MCPD in soy sauce is established in Commission Regulation (EC) No 466/20014, as 0.02 mg/kg. Sampling methods and methods of analysis are established in Commission Directive 2001/22/EC5. Pesticides A pesticide is any substance intended to be active in the control or elimination of pests, which are all organisms affecting plant health, including competitive weeds. The term also sees wider use and incorporates plant growth regulators. Their use generally may result in the presence of residues in the crop or subsequently produced products. To limit this risk of food being contaminated a number of MRL (Maximum Residue Levels) are established in European legislation. More than 17000 of these levels have been established in various commodities for a total of 133 pesticide active substances. In addition where there is no harmonised Community MRL, Member States may set MRL at a national level to protect consumer's health. Member States must establish national monitoring programmes to ensure that food conforms to these MRL. In addition to these national programmes co-ordinated European monitoring has been established. It requires the facility irradiating such products to be approved by the Community and to appear on an official list. There are currently five Community approved premises in third countries. The Directive also requires Member States to report yearly to the Commission results of controls carried out in their approved irradiation facilities (for list of approved facilities in the Member States see OJ, C 38/17, 12.2.2002) and at the product marketing stage.
