In May 2003 notification was received from France of the colorant in imported chilli products indicating adulteration that could constitute a serious health risk. This resulted in Commission Decision 2003/460/EC8 in June 2003 requiring all consignments of chilli to be received with an analysis certificate demonstrating the absence of Sudan I. This Decision was then updated by Commission Decision 2004/92/EC9. The original measures were extended to curry powder and to additional controls on Sudan II, III and IV. Member States are required to check consignments of chilli and chilli products presented for importation. Such consignments must be accompanied by an analytical report demonstrating the absence of Sudan I-IV. Where such reports are not available, Member States must detain the consignment. They shall also include random sampling and analysis of these products, for importation or already on the market, in order to verify the absence of the chemical substances mentioned. 5. State Food and Veterinary Service The main competent authority for import controls of products of plant origin is the State Food and Veterinary Service (SFVS). It is under the direct control of the government and the director reports directly to the prime minister. The SFVS is the sole institution responsible for food control in Lithuania and for developing policy, enforcement and communicating with international bodies and also the Commission. Within the central administration of the SFVS (headquarters) there are 7 departments, the Food Department and the Risk and Quality Management Department being the most relevant to the scope of this mission. The food inspection activities are under the Food Department and the Risk and Quality Management Department is responsible for risk assessment and for the management of the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF). 11 The central administration of the SFVS is organised in 5 subordinate institutions: State Inspection of Veterinary Preparations, Food and Veterinary Audit Service, National Veterinary Laboratory (NVL), Border and Transport State Veterinary Service (BTSVS) and the County State Food and Veterinary services (CSFVS). The subordinate institutions of direct relevance are the NVL, the BTSVS, and the CSFVS. The BTSVS is in charge of the management of the 12 Border Inspection Posts (BIPs) ensuring that all foodstuffs coming from third countries are checked according to the procedure for the control of the safety and quality of non-animal origin foods imported into Lithuania (Order No.B1-411 of 30 April 2004). The NVL is responsible for carrying out foodstuff analysis. Its involvement and functions are described in chapter 5.6.2. Lithuania is divided by 10 counties and 4 cities and the counties are also divided by 34 districts. The CSFVS covers from three to six districts or cities. They are responsible for the co-ordination and analysis performed by the districts in their area of competence. The cities are at the same level as the counties. The District and the City SFVS, which employ together 182 inspectors, implement the inspection programmes and are responsible for the regular control of relevant foodstuffs. 5.3.2. Ministry of Health The National Nutritional Centre of the Department of Health is responsible for drafting legislation. 5.3.3. Ministry of Finance- Department of Customs The Department of Customs is subordinate to the Ministry of Finance. It is divided into 10 regional customs offices and is responsible for applying the customs procedures for imported goods. They decide which goods require further checks at BIPs before they could be cleared to the market and they also have the final responsibility of the products detained by the local inspectors (from the City or District SFVS). Communication In general, there is good communication between the services of the SFVS. Communication is mainly via electronic mail and there are also periodical meetings and working groups with the participation of all levels of responsibility. All SFVS officers have access to an intranet including legislation and RASFF information. Communication between customs and the BIPs takes place basically by means of documents. The local inspectors have also contact with customs in relation to the detained consignments before releasing them onto the market. However, no further communication exists and there is no connection between the database systems of the two organisations. 12 5.4. BACKGROUND Since January 2001, several missions have been carried out in Romania to evaluate the export certification procedures. Reports of those missions included recommendations to the CCA on improvements needed in the export certification of live animals. During 2003, the FVO performed two missions on this issue in Romania. 5.1. Production and trade information According to the information received during the mission, there are 7,157,626 sheep and 840,143 horses in Romania. During 2003, Romania imported 355 sheep for breeding, all of them from EU countries. Also 18 working horses and 77 sport horses were introduced into from EU countries, Moldova, Serbia and Bulgaria. During the first five months of 2004, the number of horses exported to the EU was 18 registered horses, 750 for production or breeding and 7,749 intended for slaughter. Romania also exported 1,036 donkeys for breeding or production and 80 intended for slaughter to the EU during that period. For sheep, 433,348 animals for fattening and 143,113 for slaughter were exported to the EU from January to May 2004. There are 53 approved quarantine stations for sheep and goats, 49 of which exported animals to the EU during 2003 and 39 did so in 2004. For horses, there are 8 quarantine stations, 4 of which exported live animals to the EU during 2004. 5.2. Health information According to data from the OIE, no list A sheep or horse diseases have been reported in recent years. The country is also recognised as officially free of Brucella melitensis (Commission Decision 2003/736/EC)4. 6. MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Competent authority organisation and performance Conclusions The CCA for veterinary matters is now the National Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Authority whose competencies include supervision, prevention, risk analysis, 3 OJ No. L038 , 12.02.1998, p. 14 4 Commission Decision 2003/736/EC of 13 October 2003 amending Decision 97/232/EC drawing up lists of third countries from which the Member States authorise imports of sheep and goats (OJ No. L 266 16.10.2003, p.1) 6 control, inspection and authorisation in the fields of animal health and welfare, food safety and border inspection posts (BIPs). Although the CCA has issued instructions and provided training to improve the certification procedures, certifying officers met were not acting in accordance with the principles of veterinary certification laid down in Council Directive 96/93/EC5. The system in place to detect and correct failures in the procedure is not sufficient to guarantee correct certification. Findings The Romanian Food Safety Agency, the Sanitary Veterinary Agency and certain other services in the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Rural Development have been reorganised to create the NSVFSA whose competencies includes supervision, prevention, risk analysis, control, inspection and authorisation in the fields of animal health and welfare, food safety and BIPs. The Authority is an independent body with its own budget and is managed by a President (ranked as State Secretary), assigned by and reporting directly to the Prime Minister. The NSVFSA is organised in four directorates: 1-Veterinary, 2-General Food Safety, 3-Inspection, Control, BIPs and Co-ordination of Veterinary Institutes and 4- Economical-administrative, Juridical and International Relations. Two consultative bodies to assist the Authority (Scientific Council and Consultative Council) and an audit department are foreseen but are not yet operational. The Authority is responsible for the State veterinary network (with 3,800 staff) now organised in a single pyramidal system based on a territorial principle (with local, district and central levels). It is also in charge of the authorised veterinarians, formerly known as "concessionaires" (around 2,500 private practitioners authorised to carry out official activities), who can be hired on the base of one, seven or fifteen- year contracts which may be cancelled by the CA if necessary. After mission DG(SANCO)/9279/2003 the CCA elaborated a training programme for 2004, containing training for veterinarians who certify the export of live animals and for those controlling the quarantine stations, based on the requirements of Council Directive 96/93/EEC and the internal procedures. At the beginning of 2004, the CCA sent out a Service Note to the Districts about the necessary controls before issuing export certificates. According to the documentation received, 218 courses were provided during 2003 and 62 are planned for 2004 in the whole country. The three veterinarians who signed the certificates in the quarantine stations visited had recently attended a training meeting in their District offices on the new service note. 5 Council Directive 96/93/EC of 17 December 1996 on the certification of animals and animal products. (OJ No. L 013 16.1.1997, p.28) 7 During the mission, one out of fifty-three ovine and two out of eight equine quarantine stations were visited. The mission team saw evidence that the Districts were performing frequent inspections in the three quarantine stations visited. According to the documentation reviewed, the District in charge found some deficiencies during 2003 and 2004 in the equine quarantine station visited in Covasna County. Evidence of financial penalties for the official veterinarians and the owner of the quarantine station was seen, but despite the fines imposed, the deficiencies were not corrected and severe irregularities have been occurring since last year. A number of irregularities were observed: · Animals were accepted arriving without the certificate for transport or with an expired one. · Some animals exported to the EU did not appear on the farm register. · Animals had been accepted from other counties without the compulsory inter- county agreement. · Some animals had been accepted arriving without identity papers. · Some tests were not performed within the period specified in the certificate. · Two animals present on the quarantine station for at least ten days had not been identified by microchip upon their arrival. No effective corrective actions were taken in this quarantine station and exports have continued with the same shortcomings under the responsibility of the same veterinarians. The second equine quarantine station visited, in Braov County, had been closed for export during different periods in 2003 and 2004 due to the deficiencies found by the District inspections. The CA of Braov had not up-dated their procedures after October 2003 and the quarantine period of 30 days was still not respected. 6.2. Animal health controls 6.2.1. Animal identification and movement controls Conclusions Animal identification is not fully implemented in the country and although provisions for sheep and horses intended for export have been adopted to permit tracing back the animals, they are not always followed. No significant improvement was seen in the implementation of sheep and horse identification since the last mission in October 2003. Findings The requirements for animal movements are described in the report DG(SANCO)/9226/2003. 8 Equidae identification and movement controls The identification of horses using microchips is partially implemented. All horses sero-positive to Equine Infectious Anaemia (EIA) are identified, but the percentage of healthy horses identified varied between 10 and 20% in the three counties visited. The CCA informed the mission team that due to commercial problems (importation) there are difficulties to obtain the microchips in Romania. Equines consigned to a quarantine station should be marked, at the place of origin, either by numbers clipped in the hair and accompanied by an identity paper or by microchip. The procedures establish that the former have to be identified by a microchip on entry to the quarantine station and its number should be correlated with the incoming documentation. In the quarantine station visited in Covasna, 40 donkeys arrived without any number clipped and without any identity papers. The documentation showed that some animals arriving without identity papers were exported to the EU. There were two animals which had been there for ten days. The official veterinarians stated that only one had been identified by microchip, but they were not able to read it and the microchip number was not recorded in the documentation. In the other quarantine station, the documentation for animal identification was complete, and the two animals present in the facilities bore microchips. Sheep identification and movement controls: The identification of ovine and caprine animals by official means has not yet started. The system of blocking the farms in case of disease allowed the CA to fulfil the EU import requirements without a quarantine period. This means that sheep quarantine stations are, in fact, used as assembly centres. In the quarantine station visited, the animals were identified before entering the farm (at the farm of origin or on arrival) by unofficial ear-tags, and the numbers appeared in the certificates for transport and/or on the register kept by the owner. The individual numbers were also annexed to the export certificates. A large majority of animals present in the facilities (about 5000) were identified. The CA explained that a small number of animals lost their ear-tags on the quarantine station and that those were sold to different markets (local or Arabic markets), but the documentation showed that all animals which entered the farm during 2004 were exported to EU or Hungary (before 1 May 2004) or died on the premises. There was no procedure in place to ensure that animals which lost eartags remained at least 40 days in the holding specified in the certificate. Some animals were seen wearing two ear-tags with different numbers. 6.2.2. National disease surveillance programme Conclusions There is a complete national surveillance programme covering a large number of diseases. In the counties visited, the programme including sampling was being applied. 9 In relation to Equine Infectious Anaemia, all horses above 6 months of age are tested annually. The elimination of sero-positive horses has not started due to delays in the availability of money for compensation. Findings A national programme is in place to monitor most of the list A and B diseases and the sampling is decided according to the animal population. In relation to EIA, all horses over 6 months are annually tested and all sero-positives are identified with a microchip. Those animals are not allowed to move outside the village. In one District, the team found long delays in the identification of positive horses and the restriction of movements. A Service note from the CCA (No. 222489 of 17.02.2004) was sent to the Districts informing them of the availability of funds to compensate owners for the slaughter of sero-positive animals to EIA in 14 counties. However, due to the reorganisation of the CCA, the money is not yet available, and the slaughter of positive horses has not started. The CCA stated that this problem would be solved within one month. 6.2.3. Certification for export of live sheep and horses Conclusions National legislation requires the 30-day pre-export quarantine period for horses, as required by the Commission Decision 93/196/CEE6 and Commission Decision 93/197/CEE7. If the legislation and approved procedures are followed, animals intended for export are identified and can be linked to the movement documents, so the certifying officer can confirm that the guarantees given in the export certificate are valid. However, in practice this is not always the case, and the serious deficiencies found indicate that the certification of live horses for export to the EU is not reliable. Due to mixing of horses which had undergone pre-test with untested horses, the health status of exported horses could not be guaranteed. Findings According to the Order of the Ministry of Agriculture MAFWE No. 710/24.10.2003, the quarantine period for equines intended for export is now 30 days. In one equine quarantine station visited, the animals did not stay for the prescribed 30 days. From the documents seen in the equine stations, large groups of equidae were kept together in the quarantine farms visited, but only some were tested for EIA and 6 Commission Decision 93/196/EEC of 5 February 1993 on animal health conditions and veterinary certification for imports of equidae for slaughter (OJ L086, 6.4.1993, p.7) 7 Commission Decision 93/197/EEC of 5 February 1993 on animal health conditions and veterinary certification for imports of registered equidae and equidae for breeding and production (OJ L086,6.4.1993, p.16) 10 exported, while the rest were not sampled until after the consignment of the first group. This type of situation had been pointed out as a problem during mission SANCO/9279/2003 in October 2003. It means that no guarantee can be given that animals at the export station have only been in contact with animals of equivalent health status for the previous 30 days. However, in the equine quarantine station visited in Braov County, the CA stated that based on the annual testing of horses, the results of the surveillance programme for the previous years and because this facility is only receiving animals from the neighbouring localities, it is possible to support the veracity of the certification even if not all the results for EIA were available when signing. In the sheep quarantine station, the current models of the certificates for export of live sheep were not those foreseen in Commission Decision 2004/212/EC. The CCA explained that the new models would be in place from 1 July 2004, because that was their understanding of Article 5 of that Decision. The veterinarian signing the certificates for sheep did not always invalidate the non- applicable options (relating to scrapie). 6.2.4. Export quarantine facilities Conclusions The equine quarantine stations visited were approved without fulfilling all the national requirements. Findings The two equine stations visited did not have facilities which are easy to clean and disinfect or an adequate system for the collection of waste water, all of which are required for approval. 7. CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 11 June 2004 with the central competent authority, the Romanian National Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Authority. At this meeting, the main findings and conclusions of the mission were presented by the inspection team; the CCA were also informed those had been communicated to the responsible Commission services, and were advised that a recommendation for additional Community measures might be made. The CCA assured the mission team that immediate actions to correct the deficiencies found would be implemented and sent to the Commission services for their information.8 8 On 18/06/2004, the Commission services received information on the measures taken in respect of the equine quarantine station in Covasna. 11 8. RECOMMENDATIONS 8.1. To the competent authorities of Romania (1) To ensure that the 30 day quarantine period for horses to be exported to the EU is rigorously enforced (2) To ensure that certifying officials act fully in accordance with the principles of veterinary certification
To implement an effective control system to detect and correct failures in the certification procedures and in the approval of quarantine stations.
To implement, as soon as possible, the official identification of sheep, goats and horses.
To proceed to eliminate horses sero-positive to EIA.
To ensure that the correct certificate model for sheep is appropriately completed.

To inspect all quarantine facilities and procedures to ensure that they meet all conditions for certification of live animals for export to the EU. To submit within one month of receiving this draft report an action plan with the actions planned, or already taken, to address these recommendations. This plan should include deadlines by which the planned actions will be completed. 9. ADDENDUM On 23 August 2004 the Romanian CCA provided the FVO with the immediate actions taken and an action plan to address the recommendations made. The operating licence of the farm visited during the mission in Covasna County has been withdrawn and disciplinary measures were taken against the official veterinarians responsible for its control. Training for veterinarians with responsibilities in the export of live animals took place between 5 July and 10 August 2004. Only veterinarians achieving high marks in the final test are permitted to certify exports of live animals. The CCA sent instructions to the counties about the models of certificate to be used and their completion, according to Commission Decision 2004/212/EC. The CCA stated that the correct models are in use since 7 July 2004. 12

LEGAL BASIS The mission was carried out under the general mandate of Article 21 of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Background to present mission This mission was the ninth in a series of missions to all Member States evaluating control systems and operational standards in this sector, and the third mission undertaken to Portugal addressing the issue of plant passports. The Phytosanitary Inspectorate (OICVP - 3 = Office CE d' Inspections et de Contrôles Vétérinaires et Phytosanitaires, Unité 3) carried out a mission to Portugal in July 1993 on "registration, plant passports and inspections of third country produce". Another mission took place in February 1995 on "inspections concerning the plant passport issuing by different kinds of professional producers". These missions focused on discussion on the way the plant passport system was implemented, the experience gained, and on possible amendments to the relevant directives. s to the competent authority were made. Missions concerning the pine wood nematode have briefly addressed the plant passport regime applied to wood from the zone, affected by this pest, e.g. DG(SANCO)/8597/20026. No major problems were encountered. This mission focused on the functioning of the plant passport system for non- forestry material. 2 OJ L 344, 26.11.1992, p.38 3 OJ L 004, 08.01.1993, p.22 4 OJ L 205, 17.08.1993, p.24 5 OJ L 252, 20.09.2002, p.37 6 http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm 6 4.2. Data on the amounts traded to other Member States or to protected zones were not available. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legislation Council Directive 2000/29/EC and the Commission Directives on registration, plant passports and protected zones are transposed by Decreto-Lei no. 517/99 of 4th December 1999 and its amendments. The transposition of Commission Directive 2004/70/EC of 28 April 2004 was published in July 2004 and the latest amendment to Council Directive 2000/29/EC at the time of the mission, Commission Directive 2004/102/EC of 5 October 2004 is being transposed. Article 6 of the Decreto-Lei no. 517/99 provides inspectors with the legal power to enter premises and to carry out the necessary plant health inspections, documentary checks, sample taking etc. 5.2. Competent authority performance 5.2.1. Structure and responsibilities The Direcção-Geral de Protecção das Culturas (DGPC) of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry is the single and central authority in Portugal within the meaning of Article 1 (4) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. It represents Portugal at international level, is in charge of policy and is responsible for transposing the relevant EU legislation, drawing up proposals for the approval of the Ministry of Agriculture. The DGPC has a specific Directorate for Phytosanitary Services (DSF) with a Division for Phytosanitary Inspections (DIF) in charge of implementing the plant passport system. The field inspectors in mainland Portugal are attached to 7 Regional Agricultural Directorates in their Divisions for Phytosanitary Control. Phytosanitary matters in the forestry sector, including plant passport related inspections of forestry nurseries are the responsibility of the Direcção-Geral dos Recursos Florestais (DGRF) under the same Ministry, but with its own State Secretary. Figure 5.1, below shows the organisation of the Portuguese plant health system (including the two autonomous regions, Azores and Madeira). 7 Figure 5.1 Organisation of the Plant Health Service in Portugal (source: DGPC) Ministério da Agricultura Pescas e Florestas Secretaria de Estado das Florestas Secretaria de Estado da Agricultura e Alimentação DGRF DGPC ­ DSF - DIF Inspectores Direcções Regionais de Agricultura Fitossanitários Divisão de Controlo Fitossanitário Entre-Douro e Minho Inspectores Direcção de Serviços de Protecção Trás-os-Montes Fitossanitários das Culturas dos Açores Beira Litoral Direcção de Serviços de Beira Interior Inspectores Investigação Agrícola da Madeira Ribatejo e Oeste Fitossanitários Alentejo Algarve 5.2.2. Human resources There are four employees + one administrative staff allocated at the DGPC for plant quarantine matters. In the regions (including the two autonomous regions, Azores and Madeira) there are a total of 65 inspectors and 10 administrative staff. All personnel are civil servants. Inspectors are normally graduates (Licenciatura) or under graduates (Bacharelato) in agriculture, horticulture or similar. Inspectors are usually responsible for a geographical area or a group of local farmers, growers or traders and appeared to have a good overview of establishments present in their area, whether or not authorised to issue plant passports. In addition the plant passport related work, inspectors carry out a number of other tasks, such as, pest surveys, import-export controls and monitoring under the propagating material legislation. In practice, inspectors often spend less than half of their time on plant quarantine issues and the total human resources allocation for this work is therefore quite limited in some regions. In Algarve, where the nursery sector (especially of ornamentals) is expanding, one of the two inspectors there spend about 50% of his time on plant quarantine matters, while it for the second inspector is much less. Inspectors receive a training course upon recruitment. In addition, there are occasional training courses on specific topics. For instance, in 2003, 24 inspectors 8 were trained on forestry issues and 25 in Diabrotica surveying. However, some of the inspectors met had not received any training since their recruitment some 6-9 years ago. When asked by the team during visits to nurseries for vegetable plants and fruit trees, the local inspectors did not appear well informed of the specific requirements for these plant species, laid down in Annex IV to Council Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.2.3. Financial resources Most of the funding for the plant health service' activities is Government finance, 75% from the state budget and 5% from research funds. In emergency situations, such as a new outbreak of a serious pest, these allocations can be increased. The remaining 20% of the budget, approximately 250,000 comes from fees charged for registrations, inspections, laboratory analyses and certification. 5.2.4. Working relationships and procedures Priorities for the work are established at general co-ordination meetings held once or twice a year with participation of all the regional offices. The Regional Directorates for Agriculture come under the Ministry of Agriculture; the plant health inspectors answer directly to the Regional Director, and therefore have to follow the plant health policy guidelines laid down by the Central coordination services (DGPC). There is not a specific inspectors' manual, but a range of material on how to recognise the major pests and diseases and carry out surveys has been prepared and written instructions on current topics are from time to time sent out to the inspectors. There is also a plant health web-site with information on current legislation, surveys etc. All officials, however, do not yet have convenient internet access; only in 5 of the 9 Regional Agricultural Directorates do the employees have direct (personal) internet access. A set of standardised forms is used, e.g. for registration of operators and for the annual updates of their data. 5.2.5. External communication and co-operation The above mentioned web-site is accessible to the general public. In addition to the plant health legislation (list is not quite up-to-date), this contains general information on the EU plant health regime and requirements for operators. It provides the necessary forms to apply for registration and the list of registered operators. It also lists the plants that need plant passports (albeit not yet updated with Phytophthora ramorum hosts). A number of pamphlets have been produced to inform the stakeholders about plant quarantine matters, especially individual quarantine organisms. Material was produced specifically on the plant passport system when this entered into force, but it is no longer in print. Technical information is also given directly by the inspectors, which was what most operators referred to when asked by the mission team about their sources of plant health information. In general, the working relationship between the inspectors and the operators appeared good. 9 5.3. The Plant Passport System Portugal has protected zones for several quarantine organisms: Bemisia tabaci (Alentejo, Azores, Beira Interior, Beira Litoral, Entre Douro e Minho, Madeira, Ribatejo e Oeste and Trás-os-Montes), Gonipterus scutellatus (Azores), Leptinotarsa decemlineata (Azores and Madeira), Curtobacterium flaccumfaciens pv flaccumfaciens, Erwinia amylovora, Beet necrotic yellow vein virus (Azores), Sternochetus magifera (Alentejo, Algarve and Madeira).") and Citrus tristeza virus. 5.3.1. Registration and authorisation to issue plant passports Establishments apply for registration to the relevant Regional Agricultural Directorate (for forestry, DGRF) using a standard form. The application is followed up by an inspection of the premises and if the results of this are favourable, a registration number is issued. There is no separate inspection for the subsequent authorisation to issue plant passports. This authorisation is given to registered establishments, which apply by approving the format of the plant passport to be used. The registration and authorisation do not need renewal, but remain valid as long as the operator complies with the rules. On the application form, the applicant must indicate whether he is a producer, exporter, importer or trader and give information, such as, the location of the site(s) where he operates and the type of plant material he processes. There is a general requirement in the Decreto-Lei no. 517/99 (Art. 11) that any changes in the information given for the registration must be notified to the plant health service. In addition, under the implementation of the marketing directives, producers are required to submit annual plans (by May) and reports (in November) on species and amounts produced. Such plans, of which examples were shown to the mission team, follow a standard format and help to plan inspections for compliance also under the plant quarantine legislation. The total number of registered entities in Portugal in 2004 is around 1,800 with DGPC and 1,200 with the DGRF. Of these, 306 are authorised to issue plant passports. Table 5.1 breaks this down into the categories of registration. There is a national electronic database with all the registered establishments. The data are kept up-to-date by the DGPC, based on information provided from the Regional Agricultural Directorates. The latter, however, do not themselves have access to this database and although some extracts are sent out to the regions, the inspectors do not base the planning of their work on it. The inspectors met had a good overview of the relevant establishments in their geographical area. Table 5.1 Registered establishments authorised to issue plant passports, 2004 Producers Traders Exporters Importers Total 253 273 39 59 306 Note: some are listed in more than one category, hence the total is not the sum of the 4 categories Obligations for the registered companies are stated in Article 12 of the Decreto-Lei no. 517/99. They include the requirement to have a current map over the premises, to keep a register of in and outgoing and produced material and keep relevant 10 documentation for two years, to carry out plant health inspections as directed by the plant health service and to provide access for the latter to carry out inspections, sampling and documentary checks. There is no specific requirement for availability or designation of a technically experienced person to liaise with the plant health service, although, as mentioned above, indication of a contact person is requested on the registration form. Several of the operators met were not well informed of the purpose and workings of the plant passport system. Thus, some did not know which species needed plant passports and generally issued passports for all material. Garden centres and similar establishments are generally authorised to issue plant passports because of their need for replacement passports when consignments are combined or split up, however the individuals met in this category knew very little about which plant species needed passports and why. One of the trader/small producers met did not know what the "RP" (Replacement Passport) or "ZP" (Protected Zone) indication on the passport meant. At some establishments it was not clear who were in charge for the liaison with the plant health service. None of the establishments visited had an updated plan of the premises or guideline instructions for visual inspections from the plant health service Most had a reasonable record keeping, allowing tracing of in- and outgoing material. 5.3.2. Use of Plant passport In Portugal, the plant passport most often consists of a stamp or a pre-printed section on the delivery note. In this case, it does not contain an individual number, the botanical name or the quantity, since this is presumed given on the delivery note itself. However, often the delivery note gives the Portuguese common name only, in which case the Latin name is left out all together. Figure 5.2, below shows an example of a stamped plant passport. Figure 5.2 A plant passport in the form of a stamp For small sales from garden centres and retailers, delivery notes are normally not issued and the plants are consequently sold without plant passports. The team visited two such establishments and observed Viburnum, Camellia, Malus, Pyrus, Sorbus, Crataegus and Eriobotrya in the sales area without plant passports fixed to them. In some cases the delivery note format plant passport is supplemented by a label. At a Vitis nursery, the plant passport was combined with the certification label. At a fruit tree nursery, the plant passport was always included on the delivery 11 note/invoice, but also a tie-around label containing all the 10 items of the Commission Directive 92/105/EEC annex was sometimes used. At an ornamental citrus nursery, some of the production, when furnished with the company's own label, had some plant passport details on the label: "EEC Phytosanitary Passport Citrus", "DGPC Portugal", the company registration number and month/year indication. When customers' own labels were used, plant passport details were not included. 5.3.2.1. Specific cases (replacement passport, protected zones passport) The Portuguese replacement passport does not have a specific format. The standard passport includes the letters "RP:" followed by an empty field and it becomes a replacement passport by filling in this field. However, at the establishments visited by the team, this field is rarely filled in when passports are replaced ­ as mentioned above, one did not even know what "RP" meant. When applying for registration/authorisation, there is no specification of whether protected zone designation is needed for any products. The authorisation automatically includes issuance of plant passports for protected zones where needed. 5.3.2.2.Import from third countries An estimated 80-90% of imports are inspected at the point of entry. After clearance, the inspector issues a plant passport for products where this is needed. The remaining 10-20% are inspected at the place of destination, and thus not moving from the place of entry in free circulation. 5.3.3. Internal market checks In 2003, a total of 11,358 inspections were carried out at registered establishments, including inspections for export certifications, inspections as part of surveillance programmes, occasional checks etc. Table 5.2 shows the distribution on two main categories. Table 5.2 Number of inspections at registered establishments, 2003 Producers and traders Exporters and importers Total 4,262 7,096 11,358 5.3.3.1. Official examination The authorised establishments are inspected at least once a year. In addition some are visited in connection with surveys for specific organisms, e.g. Phytophthora ramorum or organisms for which Portugal has a protected zone, e.g. Erwinia amylovora, and Citrus tristeza virus. Depending on the production range, nurseries can also routinely be visited more often. One of the nurseries visited by the team, which produces Begonia sp. and Euphorbia pulcherrima cuttings for protected zones is inspected up to once a month. Other producers stated that they are visited several times a year. The vegetable plant producer visited stated that he receives 12 inspectors each 2-3 months. The responsible inspectors mentioned that in addition to the visual inspection of plants, traps are deployed for monitoring of Bemisia sp. (nursery is located in the part of Portugal that is a protected zone for B. tabaci) and samples had been taken for Pepino mosaic virus. Although the production range included tomato and other solanaceous species, the inspectors appeared inattentive to Ralstonia solanacearum. Records and related documents are checked at least once a year. The inspectors have minor equipment at their disposal, such as magnifying glass, scalpel and bags for samples. 5.3.3.2.Protected zones The team observed checks carried out in a nursery on Euphorbia pulcherrima cuttings grown for movement to protected zones. The total production area is 3.6 ha in 8-9 glasshouses. The inspectors' checks were focused on ascertaining the presence of relevant quarantine organisms indicated in Annex IV to Council Directive 2000/29/EC and Bemisia tabaci in particular. He stated that he spends about an hour of inspection on each of his monthly visits, including checks that the window screens are intact. To support the monitoring, yellow sticky traps are placed at regular intervals

text: To fully implement Council Directive 96/43/EC without delay;
To take action to ensure that the annual NRCP and the results of the previous year's NRCP are submitted to the Commission Services within the deadlines specified in Council decision 96/23/EC;
To take data on VMP usage into account when planning the NRCP;
To ensure a more even spread of sample collection for each analyte throughout the year;
To take action to reduce the times between sample collection and availability of confirmed results in order to facilitate effective follow-up of non- complaint results;
To ensure that the targeted approach is used for collection of samples under the NRCP and that all sampling is unforeseen and unexpected;

To ensure that staff carrying out sampling are instructed to take suspect samples when appropriate; 21 (8) To ensure that all samples collected under the NRCP are stored, sealed and transported in such a way as to ensure sample security at all stages between collection and receipt at the laboratory; (9) To improve the system of central monitoring and control over the sampling activities carried out by the Prefectural Veterinary Directorates; (10) To provide sufficient staff and appropriate equipment to ensure that all analytes included in the NRCP are analysed as planned; (11) To ensure that the consumables necessary for the laboratories to carry out analyses under the NRCP can be obtained as required; (12) To ensure that all laboratories carrying out analyses for the NRCP become accredited to ISO 17025 within the shortest possible timeframe; (13) To validate all methods of analyses for A Group substances to the standards required in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC within the shortest possible timeframe; (14) To develop an action plan to ensure that all analyses for B Group substances will be validated to the standards required in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC within the deadlines specified in that Decision; (15) To ensure that all laboratories carrying out analyses under the NRCP implement quality assurance measures necessary to ensure the reliability of analytical results, as foreseen in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC; (16) To provide sufficient resources to ensure that the NRLs can fulfil all requirements as laid out in Article 14 of Council Directive 96/23/EC; (17) To ensure that sufficient finance is available to allow laboratory staff to receive adequate training and, in particular, to ensure that NRL staff can always participate in relevant CRL workshops; (18) To ensure that only VMPs with active substances included in either Annexes I, II or III of Council Regulation (EEC) No 2377/90 are authorised for use in food producing animals; (19) To ensure that an updated list of all authorised VMPs is available to the relevant competent authorities and all persons involved in distribution, prescription or dispensing of VMPs; (20) To ensure that manufacturing of medicated feedingstuffs takes place in accordance with the requirements of Council Directive 90/167/EC. 9. The CA has stated that the LOD (limit of detection) for monensin in the official screening method is 50 µg/kg, whereas the LODs for narasin and salinomycin are 200 µg/kg. It will draw this discrepancy to the attention of the approved laboratories and, assisted by the NRL, check their ability to meet this criterion. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to top-dressing of VMPs: The CA has stated that these are old marketing authorisations for orally administered powders. The national agency for veterinary medicinal products will therefore revise the references on the labels and the instructions for all of these marketing authorisations. 17 Recommendation 1 The CA has stated that the number of samples will be increased for the year 2006. 100% of the samples required by Directive 96/23 for growth promoters and thyrostatic substances on farms and in slaughterhouses will be scheduled in the control plans for 2006. Account should also be taken of the difficulty in sampling urine on farms, particularly in the case of suckling, animals due to the problem of animal containment and the inherent occupational safety risks for the agents taking the samples. The CA has stated that the Directorate-General for International Affairs has decided to incorporate the management of the residue control plans in 2006 into its computer system (SIGAL). Using the SIGAL database, a system to monitor the rate of plan implementation during the year will be established together with schedules to make it easier to follow the sampling carried out by the DDSVs and the observance of their submission and analysis deadlines. This tool will keep us informed on the progress of the control plans and the DGAL will be able to organise follow-up as needed with the DDSVs. Recommendation 2 Regarding the scope of testing and the inclusion of all necessary substance groups, the CA points out that it relies on the National Reference Laboratory and the National Agency for Veterinary Medicinal Products to advise on issues such as method availability, analysis feasibility and the relevance of this research in France, in view of the use made of veterinary medicinal products for these species. In the case of nitroimidazoles these may be tested for in sheep using the LC-MS-MS method, which is already widespread as a confirmatory method and that TLC could be discontinued as a screening method to increase the performance of the control plan. For coccidiostats (B2b), work is under way to develop an LC-MS-MS method to monitor ionophores. This method will be tested in 2006 on study protocols for chicken livers and eggs. The aim of the method development plan is to establish a multi-family method or several methods covering the majority of molecules for 2008. For coccidiostats used in lambs and kids, a method derived from the one which is currently under development for poultry will be finalised in 2007. For coccidiostats, the LERMVD assumed responsibility for additives just a few years ago. The methodological developments (work by the CRL and other NRLs) in this field of activity, which covers various substance families of different chemical makeup, are being followed very closely by the NRL, as are the MRL proposals made by EFSA. Over the next two years, the NRL will able to improve monitoring in this field under its work plan. Considering the substances authorised within the country but which are currently not tested for (e.g. lasalocid and nicarbazin (poultry and eggs), benzimidazoles (pigs), sulphonamides (horses); quinolones (pigs and bovine) and phenylbutazone (milk and pigs), the CA has stated that the same factors (as described above) need to be considered and they are studying the possibility of including these substances in the 2006 NRCP. Specifically the existing methods for benzimidazoles, sulphonamides and quinolones will also be used for the specified species in 2006. The method under development for ionophore coccidiostats will be used as part of the 2006 NRCP. The use of phenylbutazone in muscle is currently being validated and will be widespread by 2006. Its extension to milk will be tested under a study protocol and introduced in 2006. 18 A detection method for avermectins is being developed and will be used for milk under a study protocol in 2006. Regarding the analysis of nitroimidazoles, the NRL proposes reviewing its position (for example, the discontinuation of TLC screening) once an MRPL has been published for nitroimidazoles (so far, an MRPL of 3µg/kg has been proposed by the CRL in Berlin). Metronidazole will be added to the list of molecules in the nitroimidazole family at the time of the request to reopen the 2005 session of the Residue Application. An LC-MS-MS method for the detection and confirmation of nitroimidazoles was used within the framework of the NRL work plan and validated in accordance with Regulation 2002/657. This method will be introduced and possibly replace the current screening method upon publication of the MRPL for these molecules. Tests for sulphonamides and tylosin in honey are currently being developed. For nitrofurans in honey, the NRL is waiting for the results of work ongoing in the UK before adapting the method. For nitrofurans in milk, the method can be adapted for the purposes of monitoring total residues. An addition to the method will be proposed. A new method for analysis of beta-agonists has been developed using Molecular Imprinting Polymer purification with LC-MS-MS in electrospray positive mode. This will allow CRL-recommended limits to be met whilst maintaining broad spectrum screening of numerous beta-agonists. Although a comprehensive check of the legislation was not carried out, it was noted that: · Decree 135/2003, which transposes Directive 91/630/EC, applies to intensive breeding and fattening of pigs instead of confined pigs (as laid down in Article 1 of 91/630/EEC). "Intensivo" is the word in the Portuguese translation of Directive 91/630/EEC and consequently holdings with less than 20 sows or less than 200 fattening pigs are excluded from the scope of national requirements. The English version of Directive 91/630/EEC applies to pigs confined for rearing and fattening and does not restrict this to intensive production systems. · Decree 135/2003 provides space allowances only for holdings built or rebuilt after 28.6.2003, whereas Article 3, 1(a) of 91/630/EC provides requirements applicable to all holdings.

The CCA organised seminars with egg producer associations in 1999 and 2002 on the new legislation for laying hens and the registration of farms. A protocol for co-operation between the CCA, the National Institute of Agriculture Research and the National Association of Egg Producers for a study on laying hens in enriched cages is in preparation. The CCA indicated that if the outcome is positive, something similar will be started in relation to pigs, with the aim of producing an integrated management system. Although the CAA instructed the regional inspectors to assess the extent of training undertaken by farmers, this was not emphasised during the visits. In addition, the inspection team noted that structured training courses for stock persons (Article 5a of 61/630/EC) were not available. In Beira Litoral the regional CA provided information on pig welfare through articles published in sector association magazines in 2000 and 2001. A further publication is foreseen on the impact of the new requirements in the pig breeding sector, in particular the group housing of sows. A leaflet on handling of free range pigs was also published and two seminars, partially concerned with animal welfare, were held in 2001 and 2002. In Ribatejo Oeste a representative indicated that they have not provided any information to farmers. A representative of the CCA indicated that, as the sector producers association did not recommended it, no pig farms were built or rebuilt after 1.1.2003. However, there was no system of surveillance to ensure that this deadline was respected. A representative of the regional CA was not clear that stalls cannot be brought into service on refurbished holdings.

Commission Directive 2002/4/EC of 30 January 2002 on the registration of establishments keeping laying hens covered by Directive 99/74/EC: OJ L 30, 31.1.2002, p.44. 3 A CCA representative indicated that egg producers were informed that the installation of unenriched cages after the deadline is not permitted; the check list also mentions that installation after 14.04.2003, which is the date in national legislation, is prohibited. 5.4. Inspection programme In response to recommendations in report 9039/2003, the CCA indicated that they will carry out quality controls of the work of veterinary inspectors (VIs) and technicians and that the outcome of this assessment would be submitted quarterly to the Co-ordination Committee and to the regional CAs. A CCA representative indicated that they supervise the checks in the regions, performing inspections on their own or jointly with the regional CA. Although quarterly reports were not made, the outcome of inspections are discussed at the Co-ordination Committee meetings and included in their yearly reports. The target for inspections, which is set in national legislation, is 5% for pig farms and 10% for laying hen farms. Following agreement from the Co-ordination Committee, guidelines and checklists have been provided and the holdings to be inspected are selected by this Committee every year. Farms are mostly chosen on a random basis but are also targeted on the basis of previous problems or suspicion of non-compliance. A new computerised database to record the outcome of inspections is not fully in place due to budgetary restrictions, but computer compatible check lists have been produced and should be in use in 2005. Except for checks of pig farms in Ribatejo Oeste, targets were achieved in both regions in 2003 and 2004. The shortfall arose as staff had to deal with controls on nitrofurans and confirm herd records following the death of animals in forest fires. The inspection team noted that: · Quality control of the work of VIs and technicians, which was the action indicated in response to a recommendation in report 9039/2003, has not taken place. · As national legislation only applies to pig farms which are considered to operate intensive production systems, the smaller pig farms are not included for a possible inspection. The selection for inspection is therefore based on 15% of farms in Ribatejo Oeste and 10% of farms in Beira Litoral, whereas the requirements of Directive 91/630/EC are applicable to all holdings where pigs are confined for rearing and fattening 5.5. Checks of holdings with pigs The CCA indicated that a new check list form (in accordance with Decree 135/2003) is in use since the end of 2003 and an instruction summarising the issues to be checked was issued in 2005. The current check list and instruction sets limits for environmental conditions such as levels of ammonia and humidity. The inspection team noted that: · In Ribatejo Oeste deficiencies were found in four out of nine farms inspected in 2003 and warning letters were issued but no sanctions imposed. Only one report 4 of these four farms with deficiencies was available at the regional office. Contributions from this region to the report required by Decision 2000/50/EC9 were not available. In Beira Litoral 25 farms were inspected in 2004. Deficiencies found mostly related to mortality records, medical treatment books, back-up system for ventilation and general state of repair and cleaning. · An inadequate previous check list, which did not include recent requirements, was used on several occasions at the end of 2004. Although the amended check list allows recording of dates of construction or reconstruction, which is essential information in relation to which requirements apply, in most cases this was not filled in. · On one farm the CA indicated that before 1.1.2006 sows tethered in single stalls must be relocated into new stalls or group housing. · In all pig farms visited there were some improvements in relation to the previous year's visit, although some deficiencies remain to be corrected as this was still within the deadline imposed by the CA. On the three farms, two overstocked pens were detected and a third pen, although overstocked, was not noticed by the local inspector. Restriction of some sows, in particular with movable bars at the back of the farrowing crate, was similarly not detected. Point 7 of the Annex of Directive 98/58/EC requires that the movement of the animals must not be restricted in such as way as to give rise to unnecessary suffering or injury. · The openings and slats of new concrete floors of a farm were not measured to check if they complied with the new requirements (Article 3, (2)(b) of 91/630/EEC) as the CA considered that the new requirements did not apply. · The CCA did not respond to a recommendation in report 1022/1999 asking them to actively encourage farmers to find ways of reducing the need to tail dock piglets. Although the guidance from 2005 asked for an investigation of this issue, there were no further details on the requirements surrounding this issue and the farmer was consequently not asked to provide a justification for this practice during the inspections (Directive 91/630/EEC, Annex, Chapter I, 8). · Although the checklist does refer to the provision of enrichment material, deficiencies in relation to this were not pointed out to the farmer. The CCA representative indicated that this is difficult to implement, due to hygiene and economic considerations. The provision of fibrous food for dry sows was similarly included in the checklist but not raised with the farmer. · Presence of bedding in sick pens was not routinely checked and in one particular was not sought as a measure to reduce aggression between pigs, which were not fully healthy and which had been grouped together in a sick pen (point 3 of Chapter II, D of Directive 91/630).

Commission Decision 2000/50/EC of 17 December 1999 concerning minimum requirements for the inspection of holdings on which animals are kept for farming purposes: OJ L 19, 25.01.2000, p. 51 5 5.6. Checks of holdings with laying hens To complete the registration of holdings (Directive 2002/4/EC), farmers provided the necessary information, including the maximum capacity, in a self declaration to the Animal Health Section of the DGV. The CA verifies the stocking density when the holding is inspected. Although the CCA indicated that 95% of the 200 registered holdings in Portugal have been inspected at least once, the number inspected according to 99/74/EC requirements was unavailable. The Co-ordination Committee issued guidelines for inspections according to 99/74/EC in 2004, including drawing of technical requirements for cages. The CCA indicated that they have performed 101 inspections of laying hen holdings on their own or together with the regional services in 2003 and 2004. Most deficiencies in 2004 concerned overstocking of cages, lack of records of mortalities and medical treatment, and lack of claw shortening devices. The inspection team noted that: · A holding in Ribatejo Oeste installed non enriched cages after both the EU and the national deadline. Due to several problems including overstocking, which were detected in August 2003, legal proceedings had already been initiated against this farmer, but not yet concluded. Subsequent to this infringement, a new and a rebuilt house were brought into operation without a licence and unenriched cages had been installed. Another infringement procedure was launched. A representative of the CA indicated that no other punitive measure (e.g. withdrawal from register, refusal of permission to repopulate) is possible until such legal procedures are finished. · At the end of 2004 a check list with only the old space requirement was used. Another check list was also used which indicated both new (550 cm2) and old (450 cm2) space allowances10. In Ribatejo Oeste overstocking was found in 28% of farms inspected in 2003 and in Beira Litoral overstocking was found in 11% of farms in 2004. Overstocking was a repeated finding in inspection reports for one particular holding in both 2002 and 2004. On the farm visited, overstocking had been previously detected, but the farmer had not been notified of this deficiency. During the inspection marginal overstocking was found, but the CCA accepted the justification that this surplus of 1.1% was to make up for deaths in transport. Obstacles in the cages were not taken into account in measuring cage height. · Forced moulting was performed in one farm visited. The flock-keeper explained that the procedure takes 30 days in total: feed is removed for 15 days and is given back gradually; no water is given for the first three days and is again gradually re- introduced. Light is also reduced until the birds stop laying and the dark period extends for a few days. When eggs production resumes, light is increased gradually and high energy feed is given until normal production is achieved.

In their comments on the draft report, the CA indicated that these checklists were prepared during a period of transition in legislative requirements and there were some flocks had been in production for more than one year when it was permissible for birds to be provided with 450 cm2 each. 6 5.7. Checks on sea transport Regarding transport by sea, some progress was seen between mission 3311/2001 and 9039/2003. At the time of the last mission certain deficiencies persisted, particularly concerning provision of adequate water and foodstuffs, protection against the weather, and that containers were clean and adequately bedded. In response to the recommendations in report 9039/2003 the CA indicated that: · They organised training sessions for the CA from the Azores islands and the transporters in March 2004. Farmers there also undertook a course, which is mandatory in order to get subsidies, and included a module on animal welfare. · They issued instructions and check lists, of which a new electronic format is under test. They maintain a list of licensed containers with identity number, date of authorisation and species allowed. · CA technicians are always present at the place of departure and check the fitness of the animals for transport, documents and loading densities of containers. · The most common deficiencies were wet bedding and sporadic cases of slight overstocking. Deficiencies are notified to the Azores CA, who collect the information and send this to the CCA for a decision on the appropriateness of a sanction. The inspection team noted that: In 2003, 71% of the inspections were documented and 18% of inspections had deficiencies, whereas in 2004, 32% of inspections were documented and 20% had deficiencies. Although the incidence of documented inspections was lower in 2004 than in 2003, the CA indicated that every ship was checked and in most cases it is possible to correct the deficiency immediately. No sanctions were imposed. There was systematic communication from the CAs of departure to the CA of destination so that the latter are aware of the details of arriving consignments. Official controls in place of departure have been enhanced with the use of standard inspection procedures indicating clearly the criteria to be checked. Provisions for feed (straw and hay) are recorded in the journey plan ("plan de viagem") signed by the captain. Although the provision of feed and water was adequate, the time of departure and the total number of animals were not indicated in this document. During the visit, the VI found that not all the 21 containers were adequately protected from the weather, two containers had insufficient bedding and in another animals of different ages were mixed together. A representative of the CA explained that the captain would decide on the positioning of containers to take account of weather conditions. This was seen to be insufficient to ensure adequate protection for animals placed in containers facing the sea. 7 Although the instrument for emergency slaughter was not on board the vessel, the captain indicated that such a device was already ordered. During unloading, containers were handled with care and trucks for bringing animals to their final destination were already at the port to avoid unnecessary delays. 6. CONCLUSIONS 6.1. Legislation 1) Although this has arisen from an error in the Portuguese version of Directive 91/630/EEC, the exclusion of holdings with less than 20 sows or less than 200 fattening pigs from the scope of national legislation does not comply with the English version of Directive 91/630/EEC. 2) Due to errors in the transposition of Directive 91/630/EEC space allowances are not applicable to holdings built before 28.6.2003, whereas certain requirements should apply to such holdings. 6.2. Competent Authority 1) Initiatives by the CCA such as their involvement in studies on new technologies and the development of guidance for farmers, demonstrate a commitment to achieve better compliance. However, the CA has not ensured that appropriate training courses are available to farmers, which is a requirement in relation to pig stockpersons (Article 5a of 61/630/EC). 2) The methodology for inspections has improved significantly from the time of report 1022/1999, with all levels involved in their development and execution. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of the Treaty of the European Community (in particular Articles 10, 152, 153 and 211) and other general provisions of Community legislation and, specifically: · Council Directive 93/99/EEC on the subject of additional measures concerning the official control of foodstuffs, in particular Article 5. 4. BACKGROUND This report is the 18th in a series of missions to Member States with similar objectives concerning official foodstuffs control system. The final reports of these missions are or will be available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection Internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fvo/index_en.htm This is the first FVO mission concerning official foodstuffs control system since the accession of Hungary to the EU. Prior to accession, the FVO carried out a number of missions in the framework of the accession preparations, in order to assist and monitor progress with the adoption of the relevant EU legislation. 7 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities The competencies and authorities remain substantively unchanged since previous missions carried out during the process of accession. There have been changes to the Ministry to which the HFSO and GICP report, but no changes in their roles. Table 2 Authorities Levels Central Regional Local ------- -------- Institutions Ministry of Health HFSO ------- -------- National Public 20 Regional 137 Local Offices Health and Medical Offices -------- -------- Officers' Service District Offices National Institute for ------ -------- Food Safety and Nutrition -------- Ministry of ------ Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Animal Health and 20 County Animal Food Control Health and Food Department Control Stations National Food ------ Investigation Institute Ministry of Youth, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities General Inspectorate 20 Regional for Consumer Inspectorates Protection 8 5.1.1. The Hungarian Food Safety Office (Ministry of Health) The HFSO was established by statute in Decree 66/2003, as a body dependant on the Ministry of Health but with its own legal entity and budget. Its stated roles include liaison with EFSA and other external bodies, contribution to relevant policy, national contact point for the RASFF system in Hungary, development of risk assessment procedures gathering of results from control bodies, and the co-ordination of food control activities of other bodies. It does not have powers of official control itself and thus does not carry out inspections. The office employs at present 21 staff, with 4 posts unfilled. The HFSO was involved in the production of amended legislation in the area of food safety. Central to this was the allocation of responsibilities between the different control bodies. At the time of the mission the office had begun co-ordination activities, but these are considered to be in their early stages. Some examples were given of arranged combined visits, and data on official controls in 2004 was awaited. 5.1.2. The National Public Health and Medical Officers' Service (Ministry of Health) The NPHMOS reports to the central National Office of the Chief Medical Officers. The central office supervises the 20 County offices (19 Counties and the capital), who in turn are responsible for a total of 137 municipal institutes. The NPHMOS employs 362 staff, mainly medical doctors and public health inspectors, with one doctor located at the national office, 15 doctors and 40 public health inspectors at County offices, and 38 doctors and 268 public health inspectors at a municipal level directly involved in inspections. The NPHMOS is responsible for public health (including investigation of food borne infections) and for food hygiene in all premises, although mainly in catering and retail facilities. The County level offices also have a number of official control laboratories. These have recently been rationalised from 20 to 6 operational laboratories covering more than one county. The central NIFSN (National Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition) now reports directly to the central `National Office of the Chief Medical Officers', and thus is now a separate entity to the NPHMOS. It runs a number of analytical laboratories and plays a central role in the co- ordination of regional laboratory activities. 9 5.1.3. The Animal Health and Food Control Authority (Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development) The AHFCA consists of a central department of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD); The Animal Health and Food Control Department (AHFCD), 20 County Animal Health and Food Control Stations and a central `National Food Investigation Institute'. The AHFCA Food Safety Unit employs 6 staff centrally, with approximately 1170 other staff employed at a regional level. The majority of these are veterinarians, controlling production of food of animal origin, and mainly premises where vertical product specific legislation applies. Additional `food engineer' staff are employed, controlling mainly food of plant origin premises and the retail and catering sector. Official veterinarians control the retail and catering sector aswell. The National Food Investigation Institute is a central laboratory under the direct supervision of the AHFCD. It is responsible for routine analysis in relation to food safety and for the co-ordination of regional laboratory activities. 5.1.4. The General Inspectorate for Consumer Protection (Ministry of Youth, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities The GICP is now part of a new Ministry, following division of the Ministry of Health, Family and Social Affairs in October 2004. The provided organigram identifies that centrally located there is a Market Inspection and Surveillance Directorate (comprising 30 staff), within which there is a Food Safety Department divided into `Food Safety Group' and `Catering Inspection Group'. There is also a central Laboratory of Foodstuffs and Chemicals, employing 24 staff. The laboratory carries out a range of quality and safety related food analyses (7800 for 2004), of which around 50% (4012) can be classed as safety related, including microbiological analyses, heavy metals, additives, toxins, irradiation and radioactive contamination. There are then 20 County level inspectorates subordinated to the competent public administration offices of the Ministry of the Interior. These offices have responsibility for all product safety including food. Their activities include sampling, inspection and investigation of consumer complaints. In 2004 they carried out 18767 related inspections, of which nearly 6000 were targeted inspections of caterers. Other inspections included inspections regarding paprika and market surveillance of milk products. As with the other inspection bodies the GICP have official control powers and are able to issue fines for non-compliance. 5.2. Legislation All relevant EU legislation within the scope of this mission has been transposed into national legislation. 10 The powers of the HFSO are provided for in Decree 66/2003 amended by the Government Decree 333/2004. Most of the horizontal requirements of food hygiene, including the application of HACCP principles are in Joint Decree 90/2003 and official control powers are held in Joint Decree 92/2004. An amendment to legislation (specifically Act No LXXXII of 2003 and Joint Decree 92/2004) is proposed, but not yet finalised, that will allocate responsibilities to the different control bodies, and allocate official control powers to the Plant and Soil Protection Service (of the MARD), which were apparently omitted in the earlier legislation. Butchers' shops in Hungary are not permitted to remove Specific Risk Material (SRM) and there are no derogations granted in accordance with point 6 of the annex to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. The national interpretation of the definition of the `final consumer' with regard to butchers' shops permits the sale of fresh meat to catering establishments, but not to other shops. 5.3. Good Hygiene Practice Guides. There are now 14 operational industry guides to Good Hygiene Practice (GHP) published in Hungary. These guides cover a range of food sectors and include more general guides such as for the retail sector and the catering sector. Most of these had been produced using PHARE funding by a private company in conjunction with relevant industry sector bodies, and then approved jointly by the AHFCA and the NPHMOS. Two guides were assessed by the mission team and were found to be in accordance with Article 5 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. They included the application of HACCP principles and one included models and templates for monitoring of critical control points. The guides are published and disseminated by the Ministry of Health, The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural development and the Ministry of Economic Affairs. The guides are relatively recent and they were not widely used in the visited premises or by the assessed inspectors. 5.4. Laboratory Services 5.4.1. General organisation There are official control laboratories within the AHFCA, NPHMOS and GICP. Within the context of this mission all would have some responsibility for official control, with the AHFCA laboratories concentrating on food of animal origin and the NPHMOS and GICP laboratories covering a cross section of food hygiene related physical, chemical and microbiological analyses. Since the last mission the number of NPHMOS laboratories has been rationalised with 6 instead of 20 county level laboratories. Each of the 6 operational county level laboratories is responsible for a number of counties. A central National Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition acts both as an official control laboratory and as a central laboratory with responsibility for co-ordination and training, including organising ring tests. 11 There are currently also 20 laboratories run by the AHFCA, with an additional central laboratory in the National Food Investigation Institute. There are further proposals to rationalise the number of AHFCA laboratories. Laboratories are funded by respective control authorities but also receive significant funding from conducting private analyses. In the visited laboratory 30% of analysis was from samples submitted by private clients, although the contract with these clients now states that non-conformances will be notified to the control authorities, which is a recent change. 5.4.2. Laboratory visited The mission team visited the microbiology section of the Budapest municipal NPHMOS. As with the other laboratories it carries out a range of routine microbiological analyses. The laboratory is accredited by the Hungarian Accreditation Board to ISO 17025. It received initial accreditation to EN 45000 in 1994 and reaccredidation to ISO 17025 in 2002. The laboratory is situated in an old building and was first established in this building as a food laboratory in 1970. Samples are received from either inspectors or couriers and logged in a sample book and allocated a unique number. There is no Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) in use. Temperatures are recorded at delivery and if a product for microbiological analysis is above 4oC then this is recorded on the analytical certificate. The number is transferred to a work sheet with the required analysis. Unless specifically stated as a request by the private company or sampling authority the scope of analysis is based on a Ministry of Health Decree of 1998. This includes analysis for routine pathogens (Salmonella spp, Staphylococcus aureus, E. coli, Clostridium perfringens), for Coliforms and for TVC. Traceability was demonstrated between sample delivery and the issuing of analytical certificates. The laboratory took part four times a year in proficiency tests, usually those run by the NIFSN. Results for those tests checked were satisfactory. All accredited methods were recorded as SOP's within the laboratories quality system. Described procedures were in line with SOP's and were acceptable. The staff had undergone some training but the budget for training was described as limited. Where not possible externally the laboratory had run internal training courses. The records of staff training and of allocated competence were fragmented and only found in separate and unlinked files. The preparation and disposal of agar plates takes place in a separate laboratory that serves the three microbiological laboratories within the building. Examination of the equipment quality control files indicated that internal calibration of weighing scales used for series dilutions (using calibrated weights) was not recorded. It was stated that only non-conformances would be recorded. 5.5. Competent Authority Controls 5.5.1. Organisation of Controls At the time of the mission the extent of co-ordination bet

As a result, measurements of floor slope were not reliable. Although measurements of cage area were adequately performed, in neither region was either the system of farm approval or information provided on birds delivered, adequately used to ensure that stocking densities were respected.

In tolerating the practice of forced moulting, the CA does not take account of points 11, 14, 15 and 16 of the Annex to Directive 98/58/EC and Article 3 of Directive 99/74/EC, which makes such a practice contrary to EU law.

The CA does not independently evaluate travelling times for species such as poultry, for which no route plan has to be submitted, and as a result the maximum journey time laid down in Chapter II of the Annex to Directive 91/628/EEC is not respected. 6.6. Overall conclusion Although central level has acted in a constructive way to deal with FVO recommendations, actions to address deficiencies detected during previous FVO missions have been slow and inadequate. In those regions where an adequate legal basis exists to impose sanctions, there is a very low level of enforcement, indicating a general lack of will at regional level to ensure that EU animal welfare requirements are respected. BACKGROUND 4.1. Background to present mission Significant amendments have been made to Council Directive 88/407/EEC by Council Directive 2003/43/EC5 concerning: ­ new animal health conditions applying to entry of bulls into artificial insemination centres; in particular, but not exclusively, concerning infectious bovine rhinotracheitis/infectious pustular vulvovaginitis (IBR/IPV) and bovine diarrhoea/mucosal disease (BVD/MD); ­ requirements for storage applying to all establishments whether or not they are associated with a production unit; including the definition of semen storage centres. Legislation Council Directive 88/407/EEC has been transposed into national legislation through Decree DPR 226/92 (01/03/1992); Council Directive 89/556/EEC has been transposed through Decree DPR 241/94 (11/02/1994).
