In their comments to the draft report, the CCA stated that Council Directive 2004/43/EC was transposed into Italian legislation by Legislative Decree No 132 of 27 May 2005, published in Official Gazette of the Italian Republic No 163 of 15 July 2005. 6 Regional legislation may be adopted within the frame of the national legislation. In case of the absence of national transposition of European Directives, the regions may also transpose them directly. However, this possibility was not used for Council Directive 2003/43/EC in any of the three regions visited. To the specific question about their knowledge and actions in relation to Council Directive 2003/43/EC, the regional competent authorities (RCA) gave different answers. One region stated that they had no particular knowledge, another one provided the mission team with a document prepared by the region for the conference of State and Regions, and the third region told the mission team that at the beginning of 2005 they informed the official veterinarians (OVs) in charge of the supervision of the SCCs of this new Directive; however, no documentation could be provided on the content of this information. 5.2. Competent Authority control system Organisation At central level, two Ministries are involved with activities related to animal reproduction: ­ The Ministry of Health (Ministerio della Salute), which is in charge of animal health aspects; ­ The Ministry of Agriculture (Ministero delle Politiche Agricole e Forestali), which is responsible for zootechnical aspects. The CCA in charge of the aspects within the scope of the mission is therefore the Ministry of Health. The competent authority (CA) system is decentralised; the role of the CCA is to define objectives and to ensure good coordination with the regions. It is also the contact point for exchanges of information with the European Commission. The service in charge of animal reproduction within the CCA is Office X (Ufficio X), of the General Directorate for Food and Veterinary Health. The Istituti Zooprofilattici Sperimentali (IZSs) are public diagnostic laboratories which work on technical/scientific matters for the CCA and RCAs. The CCA coordinates their research activities, through a National Scientific Committee. For other activities, the IZSs are at the service of the RCAs. There are 10 main laboratories and 90 peripheral diagnosis stations. The RCAs are directly in charge of implementation of the legislation. Although the regions are responsible for defining the structures of their services, the organisation pattern of services involved in the scope of the mission is similar across the regions, and reflects that at central level. A regional veterinary department, reporting to a regional Directorate for Health, is in charge of animal health aspects (and therefore represents the RCA for the scope of the mission), whereas a regional Directorate for Agriculture is responsible for zootechnical aspects. In order to implement the supervision, control and certification activities in the field, the RCAs are assisted by a network of local veterinary services, organised within entities called Azienda Sanitaria Locale (ASL). Each ASL controls several 7 districts. The veterinary department in each ASL is usually organised according to three different sectors: hygiene of food of animal origin, animal health, and hygiene of holdings. The OVs in charge of the supervision of activities related to the production and trade of bovine semen or embryos are officials from one of the last two sectors, located at the district level. The general organisation of the CA can be consulted at the following web address: http://www.ministerosalute.it Training, information, control The CCA has no role in ensuring training at regional or local level. It may perform audits in the regions through a dedicated Office (Ufficio IX), which has been operational since the second semester of 2003. According to the CCA, sectoral audits have so far not included topics related to the scope of the present mission. The RCA also have control systems in place. The implementation of these controls as observed during the mission varied widely according to the region: ­ one region had a system of audits of the ASL in place, according to a prioritisation list. Topics related to the scope of the mission had not been included so far; ­ one region had performed audits on animal reproduction in 2003/2004, and realised that further training was needed. A first (general) one-day training course was organised for a selection of people from the ASLs, and the RCA stated that further training would be provided; ­ one region was controlling the work of the ASLs through the compilation of all reports from official supervisions performed during the year, and was publishing an annual report. 5.3. Approval/Authorisation Until the transfer of competencies from the central government to the regions in October 2000, the CCA was responsible for approvals of SCCs and ECTs for intra- community trade (ICT). The regions were responsible for the approvals of the centres and teams operating only at national level. Since then, all approvals are managed by the regions. As approvals are given according to compliance with animal health and zootechnical criteria, both regional directions (of agriculture and of health) are involved in the approval and supervision process. The regional entity responsible for Health is ultimately responsible for issuing the approvals of centres and teams for ICT. The procedure for approval of centres and teams for ICT was the same in the three regions visited: following a request from an operator, the local OV inspects the premises and issues a report and an opinion, on which the RCA decides whether or not to grant the approval. If it decides in favour, the RCA will then contact the CCA who attributes the approval number, which is included in the publication by the region of the approval certificate. 8 The mission team noted the following points related to approvals: ­ In addition to the EU approval number, the SCCs and ECTs are granted a national approval number, attributed directly by the regions8; ­ The procedure is not followed in all regions, and approvals for ICT have been granted by regions using national approval numbers, and not informing the CCA; ­ One SCC visited was split into two different operational places; each of these places had one national approval number, but there was only one EU approval number, which was used for ICT of semen from either origin; ­ The ECT/EPT visited was operating with an approval as an ECT only; The regions are also responsible for the suspension and withdrawal of approvals. The mission team noted that a SCC which decided a decade ago no longer to trade semen, and was no longer under supervision, was still on the list of the EU approved SCCs. As some regions have not informed the CCA of the approval of SCCs or ECTs for ICT, the list available at central level was not updated. This list was not accurate and did not contain all details as published on the website of the European Commission at: http://forum.europa.eu.int/irc/sanco/vets/info/data/semen/semen.html However, it contained additional approved centres, which were not notified to the relevant services of the European Commission. 5.4. SSCs Of the two SSCs visited, one presented only minor defects, whereas the other one was not acceptable with regard to the structural requirements set out in Annex A of Council Directive 2003/43/EC (facilities not in a condition to be readily cleaned and disinfected, isolation not sufficient, premises not set aside for the purpose). 5.4.3. ECT/EPT Structural deficiencies were noted in facilities for embryo collection and production. The ECT visited had no separate room for manipulation of embryos (no entry door and no separation from the cleaning and sterilising area). This ECT also had a mobile laboratory, with two sections, but with a common section for storing material used for manipulation of embryos and equipment and material in contact with donor animals. The ECT/EPT presented all required facilities. However, they were clearly not adapted to the level of activity performed by the team. The laboratory was packed with equipment and material, making it difficult to maintain a high standard of hygiene; there was not enough space available, and although laminar-flow facilities were present, not all operations involving penetration of the zona pellucida were performed using these facilities; at the time of the visit, a window without any protection was open to the outside. The team veterinarian of the ECT/EPT mentioned that in case of collection in a holding, he would install a "campaign" laboratory in a clean section of the holding, which is not provided for by Council Directive 89/556/EC (Annex A, Chapter II.1(c))10. 5.5. Animal health status of bulls in semen collection centres An animal health testing regime was in place in all SCCs visited. All incoming bulls were accompanied by an official certificate authorising the movement of animals. These certificates indicate that the herd of dispatch is officially free from tuberculosis, brucellosis and EBL, and that the animal had been recently tested with negative results. However, no certificate was seen, either for bulls from Italy or from other Member States, stating that the animal had never been kept in a herd of a lower status. Testing results for IBR/IPV or BVD/MD virus and antibodies were not always available in the files of the incoming bulls. However, in one region, evidence was presented to the mission team, related to a case of prevention of movement of bovine animals into a SCC following positive IBR/IPV test results identified in their farm of origin.

In their comments to the draft report, the CCA indicated that the only activity which ECT/EPT carries out on the ground is collection ­ and not embryo testing and manipulation ­ and that the subsequent phases take place in the embryo production centre. 10 Pre-quarantine testing of bulls and quarantine testing of bulls Two SCCs visited received most of their bulls from "genetic centres". The operators explained that these genetic centres are defined in the national legislation, and are considered to have the same health status as the SCCs. For this reason, the bulls could be directly introduced into the SCC, without quarantine. Regarding the genetic centres, the mission team noted: ­ that the national legislation states that these genetic centres must comply with the national animal health requirements and test regimes, which differ from those described in Council Directive 88/407/EC; ­ that no historical health file is transferred together with the bulls entering the SCCs, and no certificate is issued to confirm that the health status of the genetic centre is equal to the SCC11; ­ that one genetic centre applied for EU approval as SCC, so as to guarantee an equal animal health status to the producing SCCs. This approach has not been followed by the other genetic centres. The genetic centre which applied for EU approval as an SCC was visited by the mission team. Some of the pre-quarantine and quarantine animal health tests which were applied in this centre were carried out at a higher frequency than required by Council Directive 2003/43/EC. However, the timeframe for testing brucellosis and leucosis was not in accordance with Annex B, Chapter I.1(e) of the Directive. The other SCCs visited also received some bulls directly from holdings. One of these SCCs had a quarantine station in another location; the testing regime presented as being applied in this quarantine station did not completely conform to the requirements of Council Directive 2003/43/EC, with no systematic testing for both virus and antibody for BVD/MD. The other SCC did not apply any quarantine health tests to these incoming bulls. BVD/MD Virus isolation tests in semen of antibody seropositive bulls were performed since the first of January 2005 in one of the SCCs visited. These tests were not yet performed or had just started in the other two SCCs. Routine testing of bulls within SCCs The frequency of routine health checks was at least equal to that specified in Council Directive 88/407/EC. Compulsory sampling and tuberculosis tests were in most cases performed by the OVs. In one centre, the centre veterinarian was performing the sampling12.

BACKGROUND This mission was the first FVO mission concerning BSE and Animal Nutrition since the accession of Hungary to the EU. Prior to accession, the FVO carried out missions in the framework of the accession preparations of Hungary, in order to assist and monitor progress with the adoption of the relevant EU requirements. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. BSE CONTROLS 5.1.1. Competent authorities The relevant recommendations made following pre-accession missions referred to: - ensuring that there were sufficient staff to carry out BSE and other work; - improving supervision of implementation of BSE controls. In their action plan produced in response to previous FVO missions (hereafter: action plan), the CCA undertook: - to organise use of staff efficiently so that several tasks could be carried out at the one farm visit; - to carry out supervision in line with the national Contingency Plan for Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE). The comprehensive Contingency Plan (CP) for the control of TSE was drawn up in 2003 in accordance with the provisions of Hungarian Decree 69/2003 on the prevention control and eradication of TSE. This plan is issued to all official veterinarians (OVs) involved in the control of TSE and contains detailed information on all aspects of TSE controls including the controls on SRM. The requirements for active surveillance for TSE are set out in an action guide which is annexed to the CP. The CP details the supervisory checks that must be carried out by the AHFCD to ensure that required TSE controls are implemented. The mission team noted that: ¾ in the counties visited, farm visit check lists for veterinary staff covered many different work areas to be checked at the same farm visit; ¾ there were sufficient staff present to carry out on-farm inspections in the counties visited. 5.1.2. Legislative provisions On accession the TSE Regulation became directly applicable in Hungary. However, Hungarian Decree 69/2003 which transposed the TSE Regulation before accession is still in force as an implementing rule. As the TSE Regulation has subsequently been amended there are some differences between the TSE Regulation and Decree 69/2003. The fact that the TSE Regulation has primacy over Decree 69/2003 has been published as a signed announcement by the Chief Veterinary Officer (CVO) in April 2004. Decree 69/2003 is currently being amended to bring it into line with the TSE Regulation. 3 5.1.3. Epidemio-surveillance in bovine animals The relevant recommendations made following pre-accession missions referred to: - supervision of the epidemio-surveillance system to ensure that all animals requiring to be tested for BSE are tested; - distribution of samples between the National Reference laboratory and the regional veterinary institutes and ensuring uniform testing and reporting procedures throughout Hungary. In their action plan, the CCA undertook to: - supervise the County Animal Health and Food Control Stations (hereafter: Stations) in accordance with the requirements of the CP; - increase the amount of samples tested by the regional laboratories and to supervise the testing of samples and reporting of results to ensure that procedures are in line with the action guide for implementation of rules for control of TSE (this is the annex to the CP referred to in section 5.1.1 above). In addition the CCA stated that both the regional veterinary laboratories that carry out BSE testing would be supervised by the Central Veterinary Institute during 2004. The mission team noted that: ¾ the legal and administrative provisions with respect to the epidemio-surveillance system for BSE in bovine animals are in line with the requirements of Annex III of the TSE regulation; ¾ in 2004 four Stations have been supervised by staff from the AHFCD in accordance with the requirements of the CP. Documentary evidence of these supervisions was available for inspection; ¾ following a reorganisation the two regional veterinary laboratories are now considered to be an integral part of the Central Veterinary Institute (CVI). Staff in the regional laboratory visited stated that they were directly trained in the CVI. However the requirements of Annex X Chapter A of the TSE Regulation are not fully met e.g. no ring trial has been organised by the CVI to assess the reliability of BSE testing in the regional laboratories and no on-site supervision by the CVI of BSE testing in the regional laboratory visited had taken place. ¾ in 2004 there were 62 clinical BSE suspects. All tested negative for BSE; ¾ data from the ENAR system with respect to epidemio-surveillance presented to the mission team prior to the mission was inconsistent particularly in respect of the emergency slaughter category e.g. in two counties visited ENAR data provided showed that 80 and 295 bovines were recorded as having been sampled as in the emergency slaughter category while the figures provided during the mission by stations visited were 4 and 552; ¾ in 2004 3.83% (16,687) of the bovine population over 24 months (435,668) were recorded as having died on farm. However, 4,423 of these bovines were not tested for BSE. It is unclear how much of the shortfall is due to inaccuracies in the data and how much is due to actual failure to test dead bovines. In one of the Stations visited it was not possible to easily evaluate data on bovines having died on farm during the first quarter of 2005 using the bovine identification 4 database (ENAR system)(8). However, information was provided at the closing meeting that indicated the situation appears to be improving; ¾ bovines aged over 30 months slaughtered on farm for home consumption are not tested for BSE. Currently it is not a national legal requirement to officially notify such bovines for BSE sampling. The CCA stated that they have recently started to capture data on on-farm slaughtering in ENAR system and that national legislation would be changed to make notifications of bovines slaughtered on farm obligatory. This will enable BSE sampling of these animals to take place. Information provided at the closing meeting and after the mission showed that there were 148 over 30 month animals out of 599 animals slaughtered from January to May 2005; ¾ in the high throughput slaughterhouse visited normal slaughter bovines over 30 months old were sampled in accordance with the TSE Regulation. However, health marks were applied to carcases prior to negative BSE test results being available in contravention of the requirements of Annex III Chapter A I 6.1 of the TSE Regulation(9). In addition, evidence that all bovines slaughtered had been routinely subjected to ante-mortem inspection could not be provided and only 2 animals had been sampled in the "animals found sick at ante-mortem" category in 2005 until the date of the mission; ¾ review of documents and information provided by the OV and County staff responsible for a low throughput slaughterhouse indicated that bovines slaughtered in the emergency slaughter category were less urgent cases than would be covered by the definition of emergency slaughter in Directive 64/433/EEC(10). The mission team were informed by the CA that many bovines slaughtered as emergency slaughter cases were slaughtered for economic reasons rather than being true emergencies. Full reliance was placed on the information in the passport accompanying the animal. The data on one animal selected at random by the mission team was checked. It had been slaughtered as a 23 month old emergency slaughter case (not BSE tested). It was subsequently found on the ENAR system to have been older than 24 months of age at slaughter and, accordingly, should have been BSE tested; ¾ an examination of the ENAR system in one of the counties visited showed that it was potentially a useful tool for implementing BSE controls e.g. the progeny of one animal selected as a hypothetical BSE case could be identified on the ENAR system. However, a random check on traceability showed that there are gaps in the information e.g. some movements were not notified to the system. 5.1.4. Specified Risk Materials (SRM) The relevant recommendations made following pre-accession missions referred to: - ensuring that all SRM, including dead ruminants under 50kg, are disposed of in accordance with EU requirements; (8) In their response to the Draft report the Hungarian authorities noted that the programme used for the query of dead bovines is based on internet and the time of the visit was during the busiest period of the day. In response to the above recommendations, the CCA undertook to: - fully implement EU legislation including the ABP Regulation from the date of accession; - supervise the system for removal and disposal of SRM in accordance with the provisions of the CP; - procure funds to pay for the incineration of the stored backlog of Meat and Bone Meal (MBM) resulting from the processing of SRM. An announcement issued by the CVO in April 2004 advising that EU legislation had primacy over national Hungarian legislation stated that the burial of ruminants is only allowed in remote areas as defined in the TSE Regulation. Five such remote areas have been notified to the Commission. The mission team noted that: ¾ the legal and administrative provisions for dealing with SRM were in line with EU requirements; ¾ in 2004 four Stations were supervised by staff from the AHFCD in accordance with the requirements of the CP. These supervisions included checks on removal and disposal of SRM; ¾ with respect to the stored backlog of SRM MBM, in 2004 5425 tonnes of Category 1 MBM were exported to Slovakia for disposal. At present there is more than sufficient capacity for disposal of MBM within Hungary and, according to the CA, the backlog should be eliminated by mid-2006. text: OJ L 38, 12.02.1998, p.10. 2 4. BACKGROUND This mission was the first FVO mission concerning BSE and Animal Nutrition since the accession of Latvia to the EU. Prior to accession, the FVO carried out missions in the framework of the accession preparations of Latvia, in order to assist and monitor progress with the adoption of the relevant EU requirements. Following pre-accession missions, a number of recommendations were made and, in response, the competent authorities (CA) undertook to take a number of corrective actions. Where appropriate, both the recommendations and the corrective actions are outlined in the relevant parts of Section 5. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. BSE CONTROLS 5.1.1. Competent authorities The relevant recommendations made following pre-accession missions referred to: - Developing detailed instructions for the work areas that are covered by the mission. These instructions should cover how and what to control at the various levels of supervision in the system. In their action plan produced in response to previous FVO missions (hereafter: action plan), the CCA indicated that: - Relevant instructions were in force from May 2004. The mission team noted that: ¾ Adequate procedures and instructions are in place for dealing with collection and disposal of SRM and covering the implementation of Directive 95/53 and 95/69. ¾ There is no Contingency Plan for BSE in place as required by Article 14 of the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001(8). It is planned to draft instructions for dealing with any BSE cases that may arise. Representatives of the CCA advised the mission team that these instructions will be included later on in the BSE Contingency plan but its is not of the highest priority in the service at present. 5.1.2. Epidemio-surveillance in bovine animals The relevant recommendations made following pre-accession missions referred to: - Ensuring that all bovines were registered in the bovine identification and registration system (hereafter: I&R system) in order to be better able to monitor the BSE epidemio-surveillance system; - Ensuring the all BSE clinical suspects are reported; - Ensuring that animals found sick at ante-mortem inspection are sampled for BSE as a separate category as required by EU legislation; (7) Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 October 2002 laying down health rules concerning animal by-products not intended for human consumption; OJ L 273, 10.10.2002, p. 1. In their action plan, the CCA indicated that: - Bovine I&R requirements had entered into force in January 2004; - It is a legal requirement to report any suspicions of BSE in Latvia, compensation for BSE suspect and confirmed cases had been put in place, and information leaflets on BSE had been distributed to farmers; - Animals found sick at ante-mortem inspection are now tested for BSE as a separate sub-population as required by the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; - From May 2004 all cattle over 30 months slaughtered for human consumption are tested for BSE and public education is leading to a progressive increase in the numbers of fallen cattle notified for sampling; - Training of laboratory staff in immuno-blotting and immunocytochemistry methods had taken place and these confirmatory tests would gradually be introduced. Until the confirmatory techniques are in place any confirmatory analysis needed will be carried out in the Community Reference Laboratory in Weybridge, UK; - Measures were being put in place in order to compare information between the cattle I&R system and the BSE surveillance database to monitor sampling and testing of fallen animals. The mission team noted that: ¾ The bovine I&R system is now in place and is used to monitor BSE epidemio- surveillance. In the event that a BSE case would be confirmed the I&R system would be a useful tool for identification of at risk animals that would need to be killed in accordance with Article 13 of the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. ¾ With respect to BSE, publicity and information had been issued to farmers, veterinarians and other stakeholders. Both government and private veterinarians have received training in recognising and dealing with BSE should it arise. However, since January 2004 there was only one official clinical suspect notified in one imported animal and none in the domestic population. There is a reluctance to consider animals that display nervous signs to be possible BSE cases because of the existence of rabies. In 2004 there were 52 cases of suspect rabies in cattle. Twenty-five of these suspect rabies cases were confirmed as rabies leaving 27 cases not confirmed as rabies. All cases suspect of rabies are tested in line with EU provisions for BSE clinical suspects (histopathological examination) and with a BSE rapid test, but insufficient evidence was present to explain why these non confirmed rabies cases had not been considered official BSE suspects at any moment. The CCA advised the mission team that only if a positive BSE rapid test result is received the animal would then be considered as an official clinical suspect. 4 ¾ Since May 2003 there is a separate category to record BSE tests of animals over 24 months of age found sick at ante-mortem inspection. However, no animals have been tested in this category. Before July 2004 all animals sent for slaughtering were accompanied by a veterinary certificate ­ in effect ante mortem examination was taking place on farm and animals that were "sick" were sent for slaughter as "emergency slaughter animals". Since August 2004 animals for slaughter are only accompanied by a movement document completed by the owner. The ante-mortem inspection now only takes place in the slaughter house and animals that are found sick at this stage are slaughtered in the special emergency slaughter category in accordance with the definition in Article 2(n) of Council Directive 64/433/EEC(9). 169 emergency slaughter animals over 24 months old were tested for BSE in 2004 and 86 animals were tested in this category in the first semester of 2005. ¾ A system is in place to take the required BSE samples from fallen cattle over 24 months old. However, the number of fallen cattle sampled is less than expected at 0.6% of the adult cattle population although this figure has increased since the last pre-accession BSE mission. The CA stated that this low figure is not unexpected as there is a low average herd size in Latvia and farmers take great care that cattle do not die on farm. They also stated that the numbers of fallen cattle tested continues to increase in 2005. ¾ Since accession a system is in place to take BSE samples from all healthy slaughtered cattle over 30 months old. The practical implementation of the system was verified at the slaughter house visited. Data provided by the CA confirmed that the sampling system is in place throughout Latvia. In the slaughter house visited it was noted that 2 carcasses in a batch detained pending the receipt of BSE test results had already been health marked. The official veterinarian explained that this was a mistake and confirmed that the carcasses would not be released until negative BSE test results were received. ¾ Immuno-blotting and immunocytochemistry have been introduced as confirmatory BSE tests in the National Reference Laboratory (NRL). ¾ Currently, there is no direct link between the bovine I&R system and the laboratory BSE testing database. At the NRL, it was possible to cross check results of BSE tests on specific animals by cross reference to paper files. The mission team was informed that a new laboratory database is under development which will allow easy interrogation of data based on the animals identification number registered in the bovine I&R system. 5.1.3. OJ L 121, 29.7.1994, p.2012. 5 - ensuring that ABP processing plants are validated in accordance with EU legislation; - ensuring that all animal waste is collected; - ensuring that all animal waste is correctly disposed of; In response to the above recommendations, the CCA indicated that: - on accession that Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 would be directly applicable; - training of staff in the correct removal of SRM had taken place; - they would introduce a system of supervision and reports to ensure that all SRM is correctly disposed of ; - the legislation on ABP in Latvia had been brought in line with EU legislation; - a centralised system for collecting animal waste had been established; - existing ABP processing establishments would be upgraded in line with EU requirements. The mission team noted that: ¾ Since accession the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 is fully applicable in Latvia and the State Chief Food and Veterinary inspectors order no. 87 of 22 April 2004 confirms that the definition of SRM used in practice in Latvia complies with Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 requirements. ¾ In the slaughter house visited SRM were correctly removed. The data are then reconciled at the regions and verified at the slaughterhouse on a quarterly basis. However, in the slaughter house visited there was not sufficient evidence that the amounts of SRM produced by the slaughter house could be correlated to the numbers of animals slaughtered and that this correlation was carried out on a regular basis. ¾ There is an organised collection system for fallen stock and SRM. There is the intention to build an incinerator to dispose of processed product. There is currently sufficient capacity in Latvia to deal with all Category 1 material. SCRAPIE EPIDEMIO-SURVEILLANCE 5.2.1. Animal identification and registration The system of identification in small ruminants in place prior to 9 July 2005 has been described in report 8630/2002. A new system of identification, based on a compulsory individual and unique identification of all animals, was introduced on 9 July 2005. There is also an obligation for all keepers of small ruminants to have a register of animals which must be kept for five years. The register must contain information on the address of the holding, the type of production, a record of animals on the holding and information on animals that enter and leave the holding. It is also compulsory for animals moving between holdings to be accompanied by a transport document which contains the following information: the name of the transporter, vehicle details, details of holding of origin, details of holding of destination, date and time of loading and unloading and the total number of animals at departure and arrival. There is also a national database that holds details of all holdings, census details, and identification details of small ruminants. The population of small ruminants that were subject to epidemio-surveillance for TSEs at the time of the mission was identified according to the rules in place before the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 on 9 July 2005. Figures supplied to the mission team indicate that there is a total sheep population of approximately nine million sheep and 1.2 million goats in France. Passive surveillance The relevant recommendation of report 8630/2002 concerned compensation for killing and destruction of Scrapie positive animals as required by the TSE regulation. In response to the above recommendations, the CA undertook to consider reviewing the national rules applicable to the payment of compensation to owners of animals impounded at abattoirs after testing positive for Scrapie. Clinical suspicion of Scrapie on farms and abattoirs relies on a network of clinical surveillance which has been in place since 1997. It is the responsibility of the Directors of Departmental Veterinary Services (DDSV) to coordinate all those involved such as farmers, veterinary surgeons and Departmental Veterinary laboratories. Small ruminants (alive, slaughtered or having died) which present or had presented neurological or behavioural symptoms or a progressive general deterioration in condition related to a disease of the central nervous system and for which an alternative diagnosis cannot be established are considered as scrapie suspects. Scrapie suspects must be reported to DDSVs. Compensation is paid for Scrapie positive animals that are detected on farm. However compensation is not paid for positive animals detected as a result of abattoir surveillance. The CCA stated that this was to deter owners from sending potential Scrapie cases for routine slaughter rather than reporting them as suspects as required. The number of cases detected in recent years by passive surveillance is as follows: Suspicions 2003 2004 2005 (to October) Confirmed cases 59 36 38 42 18 20 4 The mission team noted that: ¾ On farms visited there was no evidence provided of any recent general advisory campaign with respect to the clinical signs of Scrapie. ¾ The most recent general awareness programme for Scrapie was described in report 8630/2002. There is a network of official organisations which conduct awareness campaigns but there is little co-ordination amongst them in this respect. Not all farmers belong to these organisations leading to the possibility that some may not receive information. 5.2.3. Active surveillance The relevant recommendations of report 8630/2002 concerned: - the sampling of fallen stock. - the monitoring and adjustment of the sampling programme in order to avoid over-representation of any particular category of animals. In response to the above recommendations, the CA undertook to: - Consider continuing to sample high numbers of fallen stock. - Review the operation of the Scrapie monitoring programme so that over- representation of any group of animals would be avoided. For a description of the system of TSE surveillance in both animals slaughtered for human consumption and animals not slaughtered for human consumption reference is made to report 8630/2002. At the end of each year a comprehensive sampling plan is established by the CCA setting out the sampling that to be performed in the following year. In this plan each abattoir and rendering plant is allocated a number of animals that must be sampled based on the number of animals that were processed at each establishment during the previous year. All abattoirs slaughtering small ruminants and all the Category 1 ABP processing plants that receive fallen small ruminants are included in the sampling programme even if low numbers of stock are received. DDSV are instructed to ensure that the rate of sampling reflects the rate of slaughtering throughout the year. With respect to sheep, the sampling programme is designed to be fully representative in terms of geographical location and season. In the case of goats, all over 18 month animals normally slaughtered or that die on farm are required to be tested for TSEs. Laboratory network Rapid tests used in the TSEs surveillance programme must be carried out in one of 48 Departmental laboratories approved for this purpose. Approved laboratories must initially be accredited by the French institute for accrediting laboratories (Comité français pour l'accréditation) and perform successfully in a ring trial carried out by the National Reference Laboratory (NRL). Approval is granted by DGAL and must be renewed on an annual basis. A number of different rapid tests are used in different rapid testing laboratories: Prionics-Check Western, Enfer, Bio-Rad TeSeE, Prionics-Check LIA. The InPro CDI-5 test is also currently being assessed for use. Rapid test results are electronically transmitted to a central database of TSE results managed by DGAL. The remaining tissue from any samples giving non-negative results is sent to the NRL for confirmation of the result and the associated portion of ear is sent to another laboratory approved for genotyping. Confirmation at the NRL is carried out using Western blot and, if necessary, immunocytochemistry. Tests to discriminate Scrapie from BSE are also carried out using a Western blot technique developed in the NRL and approved by the Community Reference Laboratory. This discriminatory testing detected a case of BSE in a goat slaughtered in 2002, a result subsequently confirmed by the CRL in 2005 using mouse bio-assay testing. 6 The mission team noted that: ¾ There is adequate laboratory capacity and arrangements in place to conduct the required rapid, confirmatory and discriminatory tests for TSE control in small ruminants. ¾ There is quick reporting of results to the central TSE results database and to abattoirs when slaughtered sheep and goats are sampled (in the laboratory visited samples from slaughtered animals are given priority). ¾ In the rapid testing laboratory visited, extensive documentation was seen to demonstrate the effectiveness of supervision by the NRL and the written approval from DGAL was seen. ¾ The laboratory visited was a well equipped, modern unit and demonstrated a high degree of competence in carrying out the Prionics-Check Western blot test. ¾ With respect to atypical Scrapie cases, 61 have been diagnosed in France from 2002 to 2004. These were all initially detected using the BioRad TeSe ELISA test on standard brainstem samples. No atypical cases have been detected using other rapid tests The atypical cases are generally positive in immunocytochemistry tests and have all been confirmed by the OIE Western blot method. Seven of the 61 cases were of the ARR homozygous genotype. 5.3. MEASURES FOLLOWING SUSPICION/CONFIRMATION OF TSEs Once a suspicion of Scrapie is established (by clinical suspicion in a live animal or a non-negative post mortem rapid test result) an epidemiological enquiry is immediately launched. This enquiry will identify those holdings potentially at risk which must be restricted in the event of confirmation of a positive Scrapie case by the NRL. These at-risk holdings are defined as those where the affected animal was born or those where it has given birth during its lifetime. Movements of animals onto or off at-risk holdings are prohibited, the identification of animals is checked and a census of all animals on the holding is taken. When Scrapie is confirmed in an animal that has lived on only one farm for most of its lifetime the sanitary measures taken are as described in report 8630/2002. In summary, in sheep flocks all the animals are genotyped and those with susceptible and very susceptible genotypes are removed. For a period of three years following removal of these animals, restocking can only take place with resistant rams and ewes that are not susceptible or very susceptible. In affected goat herds all goats must be culled and restocking can only take place after the premises has been thoroughly cleaned and disinfected. In case of both sheep and goats, a number of culled animals aged over 12 months are tested for TSEs. The number tested is sufficient to give a 95% probability of detecting at least one positive TSE case in the event of there being a minimum prevalence of 2%. When Scrapie is confirmed in an animal that has been in several flocks all the at-risk flocks as defined above are subjected to the following measures for three years: animals over 12 months of age destined for human consumption must have a specific authorisation to move directly to an abattoir where they are tested for TSEs, all animals over 12 months of age that are euthanized or die on farm must also be tested for TSEs. In addition, five goat holdings where only one case of Scrapie has been detected are being subjected to an experimental research protocol as follows: a TSE test is carried out on tonsil biopsies from all goats over 12 months old and a second test is repeated 30 months after the first one. All dead goats or culled goats over 12 months old are 7 destroyed after being rapid tested for TSEs (tests carried out on obex, tonsils and other tissues). No goats can leave these holdings subject to the experimental research protocol with the exception of goats less than 45 days sent to slaughter and in that event all viscera and the heads of the carcases must be destroyed. In the event that a subsequent case of Scrapie is detected in these experimental holdings then all goats on the affected holding are destroyed according to standard procedures. Movement restrictions and testing in these experimental holdings are maintained for three years. For further information on this experimental protocol see http://www.afssa.fr/Ftp/Afssa/28807-28808.pdf. The mission team noted that: ¾ From January 2002 to October 2005, there have been 304 outbreaks of Scrapie in sheep holdings, 25 outbreaks in goat holdings and eight outbreaks in holdings with both sheep and goats. ¾ DDSV staff met in the displayed a high degree of competence and were fully aware of the procedures in place for dealing with Scrapie infection in small ruminants. Comprehensive documentation was available to demonstrate the measures taken in Scrapie affected flocks. ¾ In the flock visited which had recently been affected by Scrapie, it was confirmed that the measures taken were in line with the procedures as described by the CCA. ¾ Milk from the goat holdings subject to the experimental protocol for eradication of Scrapie is used for human consumption. 5.4. BACKGROUND 4.1. DIOXINS IN BALTIC SEA FISH In collaboration with the Member States, the European Commission has been proactive in tackling the problem of dioxin contamination of foodstuffs and animal feedingstuffs. Comprehensive Community legislation has been put in place with the aim of reducing dioxin contamination and consumer exposure to these chemicals. Dioxin contamination in the Baltic region has been recognised for years. Pursuant to Commission Regulation (EC) No 466/2001 establishing maximum levels (MLs) for the 17 most toxic congeners of polychlorinated dioxins and furans in foodstuffs including, inter alia, fish and fishery products, Sweden and Finland have been granted a derogation (Council Regulation (EC) No 2375/2001) allowing marketing of fish from the Baltic region containing concentrations of dioxins exceeding the Community ML. Such fish may only be marketed within the national territories of Sweden and Finland. Other Member States fishing in the Baltic region are required to comply with Community law and must not place on the market foodstuffs, including inter alia fish and fishery products exceeding Community MLs. Member States may export to third countries such foodstuffs, provided that third countries have given their express approval to receive products exceeding Community MLs (Article 12, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002). Commission Regulation (EC) No 199/2006 set MLs for the sum of dioxins and dioxin-like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs)3 in foodstuffs; this legislation is applicable from 4 November 2006. 4.2. FISHING ACTIVITIES IN THE BALTIC REGION All commercial fishing vessels, irrespective of size, must be registered by the Department of Fisheries (DF) in the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD). In total 949 vessel were registered in 2005, most of them (576 vessels) were below 10 meters. Each fishing vessel must also hold a permanent sea fishery licence and a special fishing permit, issued for one year, specifying type of fish, catch area, fishing quota, fishing time, and fishing gears. There are 4 factory vessels registered in Poland, which do not run fishery activities on the Baltic Sea. The total catch of Baltic Sea fish for Poland in 2005 was approximately 120,411 tonnes comprising inter alia herring (21,957 tonnes), sprat (74,452 tonnes), cod (12,778 tonnes), and eel (76 tonnes). In addition, 21,816 salmon and 141,464 trout were caught. Almost all catches were from the ICES sub areas 24, 25 and 26; 3 "dioxin-like PCBs" are 12 non-ortho or mono-ortho PCBs which exhibit toxicological properties sim1il3a/r09/06 - 37133 to dioxins. 2 however some small amounts of cod and sprat originated additionally from sub area 27 and some sprat from sub area 28. Most of catch is used for human consumption and, according to the CA; approximately 40 % of the sprat catch is for industrial use (feed production). There are 74 landing points registered. For the landing of big cod catches, specific registered landing points are assigned. In 2005, a small number of vessels from other Member States (mainly from Denmark and Finland) landed fish (mainly cod and flounder) in Polish ports and no vessels from third countries landed fish in Polish ports. Polish vessels landed also Baltic Sea fish (mainly cod, herring and sprat) in Russian, Danish, Swedish and German ports. In 2005 there were also transhipments from Polish vessels to Russian and Danish vessels (sprat and herring). There are no aquaculture activities at the Polish Baltic Sea coast. There are no registered establishments for the production of fish oil for human consumption. 4.3. PREVIOUS MISSIONS In May 2005 a mission was performed by the European Commission's Directorate- General for Fisheries and Maritime Affairs on common grading marketing standards and consumer information in order to evaluate inter alia the application of Council Regulation (EC) No 104/2000 and Commission Regulation (EC) No 2065/2001. Lack of consumer information (i.e. labelling) at retail level was observed. As a follow-up to that mission the CA had prepared a leaflet for establishments with information inter alia about identification and labelling of fish and fishery products. The General Veterinary Inspectorate (GVI) is responsible for the implementation and supervision of this dioxin monitoring programme. Research programmes on dioxin in Baltic Sea fish Several disparate research projects on dioxins in Baltic Sea fish have been organised by the Sea Fisheries Institute (SFI) in Gdynia, initiated by the DF in MARD. This research was financed at the beginning by the Norwegian Ministry of Fisheries and later on by the Polish MARD. Fish samples originated from Polish coastal waters and were taken by research vessels and at landing points. In addition, also canned fish was analysed. Samples were analysed in 2002 and 2003 by the National Institute of Nutrition and Seafood Research (NIFES) in Bergen, Norway and in 2004 and 2005 in the Institute of Public Health in Ostrava, Czech Republic. A written agreement is in place with the Ostrava Institute. Both laboratories are accredited according to ISO 17025. In the Ostrava laboratory sample preparation and dioxin analysis had been performed according to Commission Directive 5 In their response to the draft report the Polish authorities stated that in 2006/2007 there are planned tests on dioxins and dioxin-like compounds in 36 samples of fish products (smoked fish, salted f1i3s/h09/06 - 37133 and pickled fish). 4 2002/69/EC. For analysis the skinless filets of herring and salmon were used, for sprats the filets were taken with skin. In 2006 it is planned to analyse 50 fish samples from the Baltic Sea, a tender for the dioxin analysis had been prepared. No data were communicated to the Commission6; ¾ no actions were taken or initiated on the basis of these results by the CAs. 5.2.2. Other organochlorinated contaminants Aquaculture products (e.g. carp, trout) are regularly tested for organochlorinated substances (e.g. DDT, HCH, HCB, indicator PCBs) in the scope of the NRCP, in accordance with Council Directive 96/23/EC. In 2005, 66 samples were analysed7, the same number of samples is planned for 2006. The results of these analyses are reported annually to the Commission. In 1995-2003 the SFI conducted a research project on the contamination of fish and fishery products from the Baltic Sea, including the analysis of organochlorinated pesticides and the seven indicator PCBs. The fish samples were taken from the Polish fishing zone. In total 1731 fish samples and 1095 fish products were analysed. The most commonly fished species were analysed: sprat, herring, cod, flounder, and salmon. The results from 2001-2003 were studied by the mission team. The CA plans a monitoring system which will probably start in summer 2006. The analysis will be performed by the NVRI Pulawy. The mission team noted that: ¾ beside relatively low levels in the fish muscle samples cod liver had high levels of sum DDT and indicator PCBs. 5.3. LABORATORIES The National Veterinary Research Institute (NVRI) in Pulawy is designated by the GVI as national dioxin laboratory for food and feedingstuffs. NVRI purchased a high resolution mass spectrometer for dioxin analysis two years ago. NVRI plans to apply for accreditation in April 2006, in order to have the accreditation audit in autumn 2006, after the movement of the dioxin laboratory into a new building. Thus, the final accreditation is foreseen for the end of 2006. This accreditation will include all relevant analytical methods for food (screening and confirmatory methods). The mission team noted that: ¾ up to now the NVRI has not participated in proficiency tests in regard to dioxin analysis in foodstuffs; ¾ scientific contacts have been established with other European and USA dioxin laboratories, a budget for training of staff is in place; 6 In their response to the draft report the Polish authorities stated that by the time of Polish accession, Poland was not obliged to inform the European Commission (the tests were started in 2002), moreover the tests are of scientific project nature and they are not the national monitoring (the DF is not entitled to carry out such measures). 7 In their response to the draft report the Polish authorities stated that in 2005 66 samples were plann13e/d09/06 - 37133 to be examined for organochlorinated and PCB pesticides, but in fact 77 samples were tested. 6 ¾ NVRI is involved in a European research project concerning a dioxin screening method (the CALUX test). 5.4. ACTIONS TAKEN TO REDUCE CONSUMER EXPOSURE TO DIOXINS The mission team noted that: ¾ despite research data indicating a proportion of Baltic Sea fish contain concentrations of dioxins exceeding Community MLs, no measures have been taken by the CAs (GVI and DF) in order to ban or limit fishing and marketing of fish from the Baltic Sea for human consumption; ¾ no environmental monitoring data were available. Further more, no measures regarding the reduction of dioxin emission and exposure were presented to the mission team; ¾ studies on human exposure to dioxins and PCBs via foodstuffs and estimations of the daily exposure, including fish, are not available; ¾ general dietary advice on fish consumption has been provided in leaflets drawn up by the DF. However, no information on dioxins and other contaminants in Baltic Sea fish is included, not even for commonly consumed fish with higher dioxin levels such as herring, sprat and salmon. In addition, no dietary recommendations have been given to sensitive consumer groups e.g. children, young people, people at fertile age and pregnant women. The CA stated that due to the lack of reliable monitoring data there is no sound basis for such consumer information or legal/administrative measures. 5.5. OFFICIAL CONTROL 5.5.1. Roles of the Competent Authorities Fishery control The DF under the MARD is responsible for the management of fishery resources (EU's Common fisheries policy) and for administration and control of fishing activities up to and including the first sale of the fresh fish. The Polish coast line is divided into three District Fishery Inspectorates and several Local Fishery Inspectorates (LFIs). The controls on sea and at landing points are performed by the LFIs. All fishery data is recorded by the Fishing Monitoring Centre which is part of the DF. Food control The three main bodies controlling foodstuffs are the General Veterinary Inspectorate (GVI) and the Inspectorate of Agricultural and Food Quality, both under the MARD, and the State Sanitary Inspection (SSI) under the MoH. The GVI is the CCA responsible for the hygiene control of food of animal origin up to the wholesale and retail level. As regards fresh fish the GVI is responsible also for the hygiene control of fishing vessels and wholesalers. Controls are coordinated by the GVI at central level and regional (voivodship) level, while the district (poviat) veterinary inspectorates (PVI) carry out the controls. The PVIs are also responsible for the control of requirements on traceability in the establishments. 13/09/06 - 37133 7 The Inspectorate o

LEGISLATION The main national provisions referring to the relevant EU legislation are the Veterinary Activity Law of 1991, the Law on Pharmaceuticals of 1996, and several Orders of the State Food and Veterinary Service (SFVS) and Orders of the Health Minister. NATIONAL RESIDUE CONTROL PLAN 5.2.1. Planning The SFVS is the CCA in accordance with Article 4 of Council Directive 96/23/EC. Several bodies are involved in the design of the National Residue Control Plan (NRCP) - The Lithuanian State Inspection on Veterinary Preparations (LSIVP), the Risk and Quality Management Department (RAQA) (both residing under the SFVS) and the National Veterinary Laboratory (NVL) which is designated as the National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for residues.

Official Journal L 038, 12/02/1998 p. 10. 2 The planning cycle starts in February and the NRCP is approved by the SFVS in March after which the plan is sent to the Commission Services. On the basis of the animal population and production data, the LSIVP allocates a proportional number of samples in the NRCP to each of the ten County Food and Veterinary Services (CFVS) residing under the SFVS. In turn each CFVS allocates samples to those District Food and Veterinary Services (DFVS) for which they are responsible ­ there are 34 in all. The allocation includes the species, matrix, analyte and temporal sampling requirements. Regarding the 2005 NRCP the mission team noted that: ¾ all responsible authorities are involved in the planning of the NRCP; ¾ the NRCP is planned to run from March to December each year which is not in accordance with Commission Decision 98/179/EC as monitoring should take place throughout the entire year; ¾ with some exceptions (listed below), the design and coverage of the NRCP is in general in line with the EU requirements. Whilst the plan includes data on the number of active marketing authorisations for each therapeutic category of VMP, and the CCA states that these data are taken into account in the planning process, the primary criterion for analyte selection is laboratory analytical capability. According to the CCA the VMP usage pattern/volume will be taken into account for the 2006 NRCP; ¾ problems with the 2005 NRCP included: o no confirmatory methods in place in the NRL for Group A substances (though there are arrangements made with other laboratories to confirm putative screening non-compliant results); o within Group A6, nitroimidazoles are not tested for (though method validation is ongoing in 2006); o limited scope of testing for Group A5 (three beta-agonists are screened for) and, inter alia, Group A3 (no gestagens or corticosteroids included for cattle and the androgens tested exclude important compounds such as methyltestosterone and stanozolol); o no testing of sheep for Groups A1, A2, A3, A4 and A5. Similarly a limited testing of rabbits; o no sampling for Group B substances in horses, although a small number of horses was slaughtered in 2005; o for poultry, on-farm sampling was restricted to drinking water and animal feedingstuffs. Community law requires live animals to be sampled (Chapter 2 of Annex IV to Council Directive 96/23/EC); o the limit of detection for thyrostats is much greater than that proposed by the relevant Community Reference Laboratory (CRL) (500 µg/kg vs. 100 µg/kg); o within Group B2b (coccidiostats), chemical anticoccidials are not monitored for (e.g. nicarbazin); ¾ with regard to the deficiencies listed for the 2005 plan, the CA has already addressed many of the criticisms made and has indicated that the scope of testing will be increased for the 2006 plan, in the context of a twinning project between Germany and Lithuania to improve laboratory capability (see also section 5.3. on laboratories). With regard to sampling of sheep and rabbits, the 3 CCA has justified the decision to omit certain Groups due to the small number of animals slaughtered annually. Horses will be sampled for Group B substances in the 2006 NRCP. 5.2.2. Implementation All samples are taken by officials employed by the SFVS (at CFVS and DFVS level). The mission team noted that: ¾ all sampling is unforeseen and taken at no fixed time as required by Commission Decision 98/179/EC. A uniform sample submission form is used throughout the whole country and was observed in the DFVS and slaughterhouse visited. All sampling materials and equipment are supplied by the NRL and appropriate sampling equipment was seen in the DFVS and slaughterhouse visited even though the 2006 NRCP has not commenced yet; ¾ sampling instructions are issued as a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in the Quality Management System of the SFVS. These include targeting criteria for the selection of animals for sampling. However, no suspect samples were recorded in the results of the 2005 NRCP although follow-up samples were actually taken after non-compliant results. These were not marked as suspect samples as there was no such option on the sample submission form. The CA agreed that this omission could be rectified easily; ¾ in 2005 there was over- and under-sampling for certain therapeutic categories For example, in live pigs, 10% of the samples for Group A compounds had been taken. For cattle, there was a seven-fold increase in the numbers of samples for thyrostats (A2), and approximately a 30% shortfall in the number of samples tested for Group A5 (beta-agonists). However, in the CFVS and DFVS visited, all samples in 2005 had been taken according to the plan. The CFVS hold monthly meetings with officials of the DFVSs where, inter alia, sampling is discussed; ¾ each DFVS selects farms from which live animal samples and milk samples are to be taken as well as establishments for sampling of products. The DFVS takes into account production data and previous non-compliant results. In the DFVSs visited sampling is targeted to bigger farms; ¾ in the NRCP 25% of raw milk is sampled directly from farms, 50% from dairies and 25% from milk collection points; ¾ data studied at the laboratory and the CFVS visited showed that samples had been submitted promptly from the DFVSs/CFVSs to the laboratory and had been analysed quickly. 5.2.3. Supervision of implementation The responsibility for the overall supervision of the implementation of NRCP lies with RAQA. Every six months each DFVS is obliged to send a report on the implementation of the NRCP to their respective CFVS which collates these data and sends a report to LSIVP and RAQA. In addition, the NVL sends each quarter a cumulative report of sampling progress to all CFVSs, the LSIVP and RAQA. Each CFVS is responsible for the supervision of the implementation of the NRCP in its area. RAQA stated that it analyses the six-monthly reports received from CFVSs and that their analysis is available in the website of the SFVS. The mission team noted that: 4 ¾ the quarterly reports of the NVL which detail the cumulative progress of implementation are not analysed by the CCA. The format of the reports of the NVL and the CFVS is such that it is not easy for RAQA to analyse whether there has been over- or under-sampling in a certain analyte group. The CCA recognised the need to improve the format of these reports and had already discussed this with the NVL; ¾ RAQA received the data on the 2005 NRCP implementation in late January 2006. Those CFVSs not performing according to the NRCP were written to (during the course of the mission) and were asked for explanations as to the discrepancies in their performance. Answers had already been received; ¾ the NVL stated that if the NRCP samples were not received, the NVL would contact the respective CFVS to resolve the issue. A letter was sent by the NVL in November 2005 to all of the CFVSs indicating shortfalls in sampling for each ­ this letter was also sent to LSIVP and RAQA; ¾ in the CFVS visited, six-monthly reports from the DFVSs had been received, the data had been analysed and summary data had been submitted to RAQA and the LSIVP. In addition, the CFVS had compiled an internal report of the performance of the individual DFVSs under their command which had been sent to each DFVS, clearly indicating their respective performance and pinpointing sampling deficiencies for each substance group. According to the CA, a similar reporting system is used in all CFVSs. However, these data (i.e. the internal reports) were not sent to RAQA (as there is no requirement to do so) ­ had they been sent, this would have facilitated RAQA's task of analysing sampling performance; ¾ in the CFVS visited, all sampling had been performed according to the plan. The CFVS stated that in the event of a DFVS under-performing, the CFVS would contact the DFVS directly. Only if problems could not be resolved would a formal letter be sent to SFVS. 5.2.4. Follow-up of non-compliant results Instructions for the follow-up of non-compliant results are published as SOPs. According to the CCA, there were a total of 20 non-compliant results in the 2005 NRCP. Of these, 18 were antimicrobials in milk (all unconfirmed by chemical confirmatory tests) and in two cases, residues of cadmium were detected in bovine kidney in excess of Community Maximum Limits (MLs). The CCA stated that the NVL reports all non-compliant results to RAQA, LSIVP, the CFVS and the DFVS in question. Each CFVS and DFVS is responsible for the follow-up of non-compliant results in their area (farms, veterinarians, establishments). When necessary, LSIVP carries out inspections at veterinary medicine manufacturers, wholesalers and veterinary pharmacies. Reports are sent to RAQA which keeps a record of the initial non-compliant result and the associated investigation activities. The mission team noted that: ¾ Details of non-compliant samples (screening and confirmatory) are sent from the NVL to the DFVS but not to the CFVS; ¾ according to national rules, investigations are required in the event of a `screening' non-compliant result for antimicrobial residues; ¾ the follow-up files examined at the RAQA and the CFVS were in order and all the requisite follow-up actions had been carried out promptly; 5 ¾ in the event of non-compliant results in pooled milk samples (taken at dairies or at milk collection points, en route to the dairy), the CA formally requests the respective dairy (by letter) to identify the origin of the non-compliant sample in order for further follow-up actions to be taken. In the case of samples taken from milk collection points, identification of the `non-compliant' farmer can take some time as the dairy has to resample each of the farmers supplying that milk collection point (usually several days after the initial result) test the samples and write to the CA with the results. 5.2.5. Other residue control programmes Since 2004 there has been an additional chloramphenicol prevention programme which included raw milk and milk powder in 2004 and raw milk in 2005. Programme is financed by the Ministry of Agriculture but the SFVS is responsible for sampling and follow-up. Laboratory screening by commercial ELISA kits is performed in an accredited Government milk laboratory and confirmation by LC- MS-MS is performed at the NVL. In addition, as a service to industry, the NVL also performs chloramphenicol analysis for own-check samples of raw milk and milk powder. This testing is voluntary and no target number of these samples is set by the CA. The NVL annually supplies the SFVS with summary data on the results of own check samples. Establishments are obliged under national law and Community law (Article 19.4 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Counil) to inform the DFVS of non-compliant results. The mission team noted that: ¾ the results of the chloramphenicol prevention programme are not included in the annual report of the NRCP furnished to the Commission Services (under `other' sampling). This is not in compliance with Article 4 2. (d) and Article 8, 3. of Council Directive 96/23/EC; ¾ although the NVL is a government-funded public laboratory, it does not reveal ownership details of non-compliant results from commercial/private samples to the SFVS. It does however present collated data to the SFVS. Whilst the national law is clear in obliging the owners to report such non-compliant results to the DFVS, it is difficult for the SFVS (especially at central level) to know whether this has in fact occurred. However, in the CFVS visited, the affected establishments had informed their DFVS of the non-compliant results; ¾ in 2004 a total of 4183 samples of raw milk and milk powder were analysed for chloramphenicol under the prevention programme and own-check testing.
