text: BACKGROUND Two missions concerning ABP have been carried out in Greece. The first, took place from 15 to 19 March 2004, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/7015/2004 ­ MR Final). The second mission was carried out from 13 to 23 September 2005, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/7516/2005 ­ MR Final (hereafter: report 7516/2005). These reports are accessible at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm Following report 7516/2005 a number of recommendations were made to the CCA, which subsequently informed the Commission of actions that had been or would be taken aimed at addressing the recommendations made (hereafter: action plan). Where appropriate, both the relevant recommendations and the action plan are outlined under Section 5.

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. STRUCTURE IN PLACE FOR THE HANDLING OF ABP The relevant recommendation of report 7516/2005 concerned: ­ Ensuring that adequate arrangements are in place and there is sufficient infrastructure to enable compliance with the requirements of the ABP Regulation. (3) OJ L 165, 30.04.2004, p.1 corrected and re-published in OJ L 191, 28.05.2004, p. 1. (4) OJ L 38, 12.02.1998, p. 10. 6 In response to this recommendation, the CA noted that: ­ A political decision had been taken to reject the tender process for private bids to assume responsibility for the management of ABP throughout the country, in favour of promoting investment in the development of infrastructure for the handling and processing of ABP through the third Community Support Framework (CSF3) and the Development Act of the Ministry of Economics and Finance, respectively. ­ The proposals submitted under these two programmes had been prioritised. Some of the plants were already operating and the others were expected to commence operations at the end of June 2006. According to the CCA, the Minister of Rural Development and Food had decided to forward 36 proposals for funding under the CSF3, accompanied by a letter stressing the need to give priority to supporting the development of ABP plants. The proposals concern the development or upgrading of 35 processing plants, including three stand alone plants, and one biogas plant, which will bring the total processing capacity to approximately 250,000 tonnes per year. This is estimated to be sufficient to process ABP of all categories, except hides and fallen stock, while also enabling any existing processing plants which do not meet the relevant requirements of the ABP Regulation to be closed down. The CCA stated that the processing needs for each category of ABP would be assessed once it is known which proposals the management committee of the CSF3 had agreed to support. The beneficiaries of funds would then be informed what category of ABP they should process. According to the Solid Waste Management Department of the Directorate General for the Environment (DGE) of the Ministry of the Environment, Regional Planning and Public Works (MERPPW), there is a general plan to put in place a sufficient number of `sanitary' landfills (XYTAs) approved according to Council Directive 1999/31/EC(5) to enable the unauthorised landfills (XADAs), sometimes also referred to as `municipal' landfills, to be phased out by 2008. The DGE stated that there are currently 46 XYTAs, of which 42 are in operation. A further 60 new XYTAs are being constructed, of which 12 are extensions to existing XYTAs. The DGE noted that no unprocessed ABP can be accepted by these XYTAs. The mission team noted that: ¾ The infrastructure and arrangements in place remain largely as described in report 7516/2005. ¾ According to figures provided by the CCA, there is theoretically sufficient capacity to process all Category 3 ABP and 72% of Category 2 materials produced, excluding fallen stock and hides. However, there is wide variation between regions in this respect: a) nine of the 13 regions which produce approximately 37,680 tonnes of Category 2 ABP currently have no capacity to process these materials, b) five of the 13 regions have no capacity to process Category 3 ABP, c) none of the regions has surplus processing capacity for Category 2 ABP, and d) four regions have surplus processing capacity for Category 3 ABP. (5) Council Directive 1999/31/EC of 26 April 1999 on the landfill of waste; OJ L 182, 16.07.1999, p. 1. 7 ¾ There has been no significant increase in processing capacity since the previous mission, although two of the processing plants visited had been recently constructed and were operating while awaiting a decision on their proposals submitted for funding under the CSF3. ¾ The extent to which the current processing capacity can be utilised is dependent on the willingness of private operators to accept ABP from other businesses at a reasonable cost. In this regard, the situation was similar to that seen before, where some processing plant operators were reluctant to accept ABP from other premises, owing to the additional wear and tear on the machinery and difficulties of marketing or disposing of the MBM and fat produced. ¾ According to the CCA, the possibility of obliging the operators of processing plants receiving funding under the CSF3 to accept ABP from other sources was being considered. However, it was not clear if the legal framework in place would enable such obligations to be enforced. The CCA stated that a feasibility study should be conducted at the level of the Prefectural Veterinary Service (PVS) in order to assess the most appropriate options. ¾ According to the CCA and the processing plants visited, there is a limited market for Category 3 MBM and fat which is mainly used in petfood. There is little demand for organic fertilisers and soil improvers made from these materials. ¾ The developments foreseen under the CSF3 do not include the processing of fallen stock or any collection system for ABP. The CCA confirmed that all producers of ABP will be responsible for making their own arrangements to deliver ABP to the processing plants. ¾ According to data provided by the DGE, 1071 decisions have been made by the Prefectures to stop operations at 1122 XADAs. Ten XADA have actually closed and funding has been arranged to replace a further 429 XADA. 5.2. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES The relevant recommendations of report 7516/2005 concerned: ­ Continuing efforts to ensure that sufficient staff are available to enable the system of official controls to be implemented effectively ­ Increasing the level of awareness of the ABP Regulation amongst officials. ­ Increasing the level of co-ordination and co-operation between all official services involved in the ABP chain. In response to the above recommendations, the CA undertook to: ­ Continue the recruitment of new staff through the on-going competitions and other initiatives already in place, which are expected to result in a net increase of 196 permanent veterinarians in the CA. 43 veterinarians are expected to retire by the end of 2006. ­ Provide training on the ABP Regulation to at least one designated official from each PVS and border inspection post (BIP) by March 2006, so that all veterinary directorates have staff specialised in the handling and monitoring of ABP. There are a number of different CA with roles in the ABP chain, which are described in detail in report 7516/2005; a summary of the main functions of each is provided here to aid understanding of the situation. The Veterinary Directorate General (VDG) of the MRDF acts as the CCA with three of its four directorates 8 having responsibility for co-ordinating and monitoring the implementation of the ABP Regulation. The Prefectural Veterinary Services (PVSs) within each of the 54 Prefectures are part of the Ministry of Interior and are under the control of the Prefects. They are responsible for the implementation of the ABP Regulation, including issuing approvals, applying sanctions and controlling the handling of ABP and processed products in food establishments, ABP plants, farms and transporters. At local level, the PVS is assisted by the Veterinary Field Stations. In the framework of its competencies, the DGE within the MERPPW is responsible for issuing environmental permits to incinerators, according to Directive 2000/76/EC (6), and to XYTAs, in accordance with Directive 1999/31/EC, which serve a population equivalent of 200,000 and above. Environmental services at regional and Prefectural levels, which are separate from MERPPW, are responsible for approving XYTAs serving population equivalents less than 200,000 according to Directive 1999/31/EC. As regards incinerators, the regional authorities are responsible for issuing environmental permits, in accordance with Directive 2000/76/EC, to incinerators operating at slaughterhouses with a capacity of less than 200 tonnes/day, while the Prefectural services may authorise very low capacity incinerators and for ensuring that the requirements of the relevant Directives are implemented. The Prefectural environmental, health and veterinary services are also responsible for issuing permits for businesses to operate, which take account of factors relating to ABP. An Environmental Inspectorate (EI) investigates complaints regarding, amongst others, XADAs. A number of initiatives have been taken to recruit additional staff at central and Prefectural levels. Notice 27/23K/2003, published on 18 November 2003, advertised vacancies for 75 veterinarians to staff the PVS. Notice 18/13K/2004, published on 16 September 2004, advertised vacancies for 28 veterinarians and 15 other multi-disciplinary staff; according to the CCA, 17 of these staff have already been recruited, with a further four expected to start shortly. In addition, a further 64 permanent veterinarians have been recruited as a result of another notice, 27/21K/2004. In addition to these procedures, permission had been granted for the PVS to recruit 100 veterinarians directly by way of exception. The CCA stated that progress made in recruiting these staff varied between Prefectures and no clear overview was provided. Approval had also been given to recruit 443 seasonal staff to carry out a range of activities. As regards steps taken to increase awareness of the ABP Regulation among officials, in a letter of 10 October 2005, the CCA requested all PVS to appoint at least one official to learn about the legislation and correct management of ABP. Once trained, these staff would be expected to transfer this knowledge to other officials and establishments and to monitor all premises involved in the ABP chain at regular intervals. According to the DGE, the MERPPW has created an official website with a view to informing interested parties of the ABP Regulation, other relevant legislation, and administrative provisions. The mission team noted that:

Directive 2000/76/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 December 2000 on the incineration of waste; OJ L 332, 28.12.2000, p. 91. 9 ¾ The situation regarding the recruitment of new staff was not clearly explained by the CCA but, data provided showed that at the time of the mission approximately 75% of the allocated posts were actually occupied. ¾ In most prefectures visited, the Director of the PVS complained of being unable to perform all of the tasks relating to ABP owing to a shortage of staff and a lack of other resources including vehicles. In one Prefecture, only 27 out of 40 permanent posts were occupied and letters were provided showing that this issue had been raised with CCA; in some cases, notification had been received that new staff would be provided. While the Directors welcomed the prospect of new staff they stated that the numbers allocated would not be sufficient to meet the needs. ¾ In one Prefecture visited, three new staff were due to take up employment with the PVS by the end of 2006. However, according to the Director of the PVS, in the same period five permanent officials were due to retire, resulting in a net decrease in staff levels. ¾ The Directors of the PVS met acknowledged the value of temporary staff in helping to boost staff numbers, but also commented that the posts were of limited duration (typically eight months), so that by the time they were familiar with the tasks to be performed the contracts were nearly finished and could not be extended. ¾ The EI has a broad remit which includes, amongst others, competencies for the inspection and monitoring of compliance with EU and national environmental legislation and the conditions of environmental permits as they relate to projects in the public and private sectors, and for proposing sanctions where deficiencies are identified. According to the inspectors met, there are three inspectors based in northern Greece with responsibility for six regions (20 Prefectures) and a further 25 based in Athens are responsible for the other seven regions. ¾ The EI Inspectors met stated that owing to lack of resources they could only respond to complaints in order of priority. Inspections had been carried out in slaughterhouses and landfills and sanctions applied where non-compliances were found but these did not include ABP specifically. ¾ According to the CCA, between December 2005 and March 2006, 110 officials from the 54 Prefectures and BIPs were provided with comprehensive training on the ABP Regulation in a series of courses lasting four days each which were held at different locations throughout the country. Further training was provided to a limited number of officials from the CCA and PVS through workshops organised by the Commission held in Athens in May 2006. ¾ The officials met in the PVS who had received training were aware of the requirements of the ABP Regulation and the procedures and protocols put in place by the central level. However, this knowledge was rarely used when performing official controls of ABP plants and food producing establishments (see sections 5.4.2. and 5.5.2.). The CCA stated that it cannot oblige the PVS to follow its instructions and use its inspection protocols concerning ABP as the PVSs are under the authority of the Ministry of Interior. ¾ The officials met from the EI were aware of the requirements of the ABP Regulation and had received copies of the guidance and protocols concerning its implementation. Copies of circulars showed that instructions prepared by the CCA regarding certain ABP had been sent to the Prefectural services for the 10 environment and health. However, these had not always been followed in practice (see section 5.5.2.). 5.3. LEGAL PROVISIONS A draft Presidential Decree containing complementary measures for the implementation of the ABP Regulation has, according to the CCA, been agreed by the relevant Ministries and has received a positive opinion from the Council of State. It was estimated that it will enter into force by September 2006(7). The mission team noted that: ¾ According to the CCA, the consequences of the entry into force of the draft Presidential Decree will be that the temporary approvals issued to ABP plants (see below) will need to be made permanent and that there will be more legal clarity regarding implementing measures for the ABP Regulation. 5.4. APPROVAL OF ABP PLANTS AND OTHER PREMISES 5.4.1. Administrative provisions The relevant recommendation of report 7516/2005 concerned: ­ Establishing an approval system which will ensure that all sites involved in the ABP chain can be approved according to the relevant provisions of the ABP Regulation. In response to this recommendation, the CCA undertook to: ­ Issue temporary approvals pending the publication of the draft Presidential Decree. A procedure for the approval of ABP plants according to the ABP Regulation is laid down in the draft Presidential Decree described above. This foresees the establishment of a committee within each Prefecture to consider applications for approval. Approvals will only be issued if a favourable opinion is given following an inspection of ABP plants. According to the CCA, the new Presidential Decree requires that all ABP plants be approved within three months of its entry into force; those which do not fulfil the relevant requirements will be closed. The CCA took steps to mitigate the effects of the delay in publishing this Presidential Decree by introducing a system for issuing temporary approvals. Details of the procedure to be followed were circulated to the PVS on 4 November 2004, followed on 11 February 2005 by a detailed description of the requirements for plants and activities covered by the ABP Regulation. 5.4.2. Approval process The relevant recommendation of report 7516/2005 concerned: ­ Ensuring that ABP plants approved according to the ABP Regulation meet all the relevant requirements. In response to this recommendation, the CCA undertook to: ­ Address this issue in the training courses provided to officials.

In their response to the draft report the Greek Authorities noted that the Presidential Decree entered into force when it was published in the Greek Government Gazette, Vol. A, No 211 on 5 October 2006.

(7) The competent authorities should ensure that analytical methods with the required sensitivity are used to enforce MRLs specified by Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. ADDENDUM Regarding the recommendations made in the draft report, initial comments were provided in relation to actions that have been or will be taken. With regard to recommendation (1), the competent authorities stated that the amendments to Directive 91/414/EEC have now been transposed up to 2006. With regard to recommendation (2), the Customs provided an action plan with details regarding training of inspectors, and regarding planning, performance and reporting of controls. With regard to recommendation (4), the competent authorities provided an action plan in order to fully comply with Directive 2002/63/EC.

BACKGROUND 5.1. Summary of previous mission series results Prior to this mission, the FVO carried out a number of missions to Member States in order to evaluate the implementation of previous EU legislation on GMO products. The final reports of these missions can be found on the DG Health and Consumer Protection Internet site: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fvo/index_en.htm Overall, it was found that the level and scope of enforcement in Member States varied and analytical activities, if carried out, were impeded by the lack of quantitative GMO detection methods and certified reference materials. Prior to the entry into force of current Regulations, imported GMO raw materials such as grains and milling products were not covered by EU legislation and the findings of the mission series indicated that these commodities were infrequently inspected and/or sampled. 5.2. Background to present mission series This report is part of a series of missions to Member States, with similar objectives concerning the evaluation of the implementation of new EU Regulations on official controls for GMOs in food, feed and seed. The final reports of these missions will be made available on the DG Health and Consumer Protection Internet site. 6 According to the report "Global Status of Commercialized Biotech/GM crops 2005"2 the cultivation area of biotech crops increased from 1.7 million hectares in 1996 to 90 million hectares in 2005. The main producers of biotech crops are outside Europe, led by the USA and followed by Argentina, Canada, Brazil and China. The most important crops are soy beans, maize, cotton and rapeseed. It is estimated that GM crops cover almost 4% of total global arable land.3 Several authorisations for placing on the market and for deliberate release into environment of GM plants have been granted under previous and current legislation. The current situation is shown on the following website: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/food/biotechnology/authorisation/index_en.htm 6. MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. The sampling plans and control activities are coordinated by the RVFA in 8 regions. Inspections of GM food are conducted by inspectors of the DVFA in 40 districts. The VFA has 2 inspectors at central level, 8 at regional level and 161 at district level. In the DVFAs in Bratislava and Zvolen, visited during the mission, 9 and 6 staff respectively are responsible for controls of food of plant origin. Only a minor portion of their working time is dedicated to controls and sampling within the scope of this mission, with inspection and sampling for GMOs being carried out in parallel with other official control responsibilities. In the years 2004, 2005 and 2006 staff of the SVFA, sometimes in cooperation with TAIEX, provided 25, 9 and 6 workshops, training courses or consultations in the food field (mostly with a duration of 2 days) for 20 to 60 participants from the districts. In 7 of these meetings single lectures dealt with GMO food or feed but with no specific training on Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 and 1830/2003. The PHA is structured at central and local level and is responsible for carrying out inspections for GMO food at catering services. The headquarters of the PHA 10 coordinate the inspection activities of the local offices. As with the VFA above the inspection and sampling for GMOs is carried out in the normal course of other official control responsibilities. 6.3.2. Communication among the central, regional and local authorities and with other relevant ministries For the coordination of activities and the distribution of information within the VFA regular monthly meetings at regional level attended by the directors and heads of departments and divisions are organised. To ensure communication between services responsible for food, feed and seed controls, the MA or the Ministry of Environment (ME) convene meetings. Representatives of the MA and the ME, the Academy of Science, the SVFA, the headquarters of CCTIA, the Food Research Institute, the Public Health Institute and occasionally of consumer organisations and NGOs are invited. 6.3.3. Planning of controls on GM (Inspection and sampling) The annual sampling plan of the VFA is set up on the basis of a sampling guideline prepared at central level. Each DVFA drafts a sampling plan for its own district based on this guideline document. These sub-plans are coordinated by the RVFAs and the SVFA and they are finally compiled to a national plan. The regional plans specify numbers of samples and commodities to be taken. Results from the previous year are taken into account for planning. Controls at imports are not covered by the annual regional plans, but are carried out as the need arises. The frequency for the sampling of imported consignments for GMO analysis is laid down in Methodological Instruction 1/2004. A sampling frequency of 50% for soy, 30% for soy products, 50% for maize, 20% for canned maize, 3% for maize products and 3% for pasta from maize flour, extruded maize products and bakery maize products is specified. Inspectors of the DVFA in Zvolen stated that they reduce the sampling frequency when produce of the same suppliers has been shown to be compliant on previous consignments. Structure and organisation of responsible authorities The Ministry of Health is responsible for policy making and legislation for GM food and is the responsible authority as mentioned under Article 5.2 of 1829/2003. At central level, HIRS, which is a constituent part of the MH, is responsible for drafting inspection and sampling plans, reporting, methodological guidelines and for organisation of training in relation to official food control. In their response to the draft report the competent authorities noted that "Initial document control at point of import, release for free circulation after approvals of imports have been issued by competent inspectorates, such as approval of HIRS in case of food, of IRSAFF (agricultural inspectorate) in case of feed and of IRSAFF (phytosanitary inspectorate) in case of seed." 10 6.4.2. Communication among the central, regional and local authorities and with other relevant ministries To ensure coordination of activities, regular monthly meetings between central and regional staff take place. In addition, written instructions, guidelines, SOPs and notifications are issued by the central authorities to the regional units. The regional units are required to report to the central authorities on a monthly basis. An IT system is in place to facilitate communication and proper planning of activities. Training for inspectors is provided by headquarters on various issues relating to food control. Specific training for GMO controls took place at seminars and workshops, particularly provided by MESP. Also, liaison between HIRS and other bodies, such as the Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Craft, Chamber of Agriculture and Forestry, Consumer Association, other inspection services and professional bodies, takes place. 6.4.3. Planning of controls on GM (Inspection and sampling) Priorities for the routine control activities are based on a number of factors, such as risk assessment and categorisation of the various enterprises into high, medium or low risk, observations from previous controls or legislative obligations. Where special control activities are triggered additional factors, such as results of inspections and analyses, notifications through the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), information from other inspection services or other sources and complaints received, are taken into account. Annual plans for inspections and sampling are circulated to each regional unit. The inspection plan specifies the number of inspections to be conducted by each regional unit. It was explained by the CA that the inspection plan does not specify controls for GMOs, and such controls do not form part of the normal inspection routine unless the inspector is conducting controls at premises where GMOs may be present, such as importers or food processors. The sampling plan specifies the number of samples to be taken in each regional unit, the commodity to be sampled, the week of sampling and the laboratory to which the sample should be sent. The sampling is co-ordinated by a mentor in each regional unit who decides on the sampling officer and the date of sampling and the sampling officer decides on the location of sampling. In 2005, the plan for GMO control involved 70 inspections and the taking of 213 samples. The plan for GMO control for 2006 foresees 60 inspections and the taking of 208 samples from mainly soy and maize products, being 148 samples at retail level, with a further 60 samples taken at import level. 11 Table 4: Overview of controls on GM Food planned for 2005 & 2006 No. of Controls Import Processing Retail 2005 2006 2005 2006 2005 2006 Inspections 2 15 5 15 63 30 Sampling 95 30 15 30 103 148 6.4.4. Performance of inspection and sampling The mission team observed the inspection for traceability and sampling at a food processor. The food processor had been inspected in October 2005, but not for GMO or traceability. However, evidence was provided by the CA to demonstrate that the central purchasing company of the food processor had been inspected for GMO and traceability in December 2005. The inspection was confined to those areas relevant to the scope of this mission and was carried out by an inspector from the region of Ljubljana. The inspection began with an evaluation of the company's internal control system for soy meal. The inspector stated that an evaluation of traceability in the company is conducted by tracing a raw material through the production lines. An inspection report form, which includes a check-list, is completed in triplicate and signed by a representative of the food processor and the HIRS inspector. The sampling procedure observed was a demonstration which followed the provisions of Commission Recommendation 2004/787/EC, including file increment samples. The inspector was equipped with the necessary equipment for sampling and for protection against cross-contamination. This was the first time this sampling procedure was followed by the inspector. It was explained that a simplified sampling procedure is used for sampling food on the national market, particularly at retail level, whereby 1 sample of 3 - 5 kg is taken from 1 bag for monitoring purposes. A sampling report form was completed, with 1 copy being provided to the person in charge, one copy to the laboratory and one copy retained by the inspector. The inspector transports the sample to one of the 2 Public Health Institute (PHI) laboratories in Slovenia. 6.4.5. Results of controls on GM (Inspection and sampling) The finalising of analytical results takes 3-4 weeks, especially in cases where the presence of GM material is detected by the PHI, because the samples are forwarded to the NIB for quantitative analysis. The quantitative results are reported to the PHI who assesses the analytical result for compliance with the legislation and informs the sampling inspector of the outcome who, in turn, informs the central CA. In 2004, 183 samples of mostly soy and maize products were analysed for content of GMOs. One sample of texturised soy steaks, labelled as GM-free, was taken in a retail shop and shown to contain 1.6 % RR soy with a measurement uncertainty of 0.5%. Extraction of DNA was not possible in the case of 18 samples. 12 In 2005, 213 food samples were taken and 3 samples, labelled as GM-free, were shown to contain RR soy. Structure and organisation of responsible authorities Performance of GMO food monitoring is the responsibility of the regional (Länder) authorities. In Hamburg the Department for Food Safety and Veterinary Affairs of the BWG is responsible for the monitoring GM food under Regulations (EC) No 1829/2003 and No 1830/2003. It supervises the control activities of the Offices for Consumer Protection (Verbraucherschutzämter) of the 7 District Administrations (Bezirksämter), with 60 posts for food inspectors and the laboratory of the Institute 11 for Hygiene and Environment (Institut für Hygiene und Umwelt IHU) regarding official surveillance of GM food. Training for food inspectors in Hamburg for the monitoring of GM food is provided by the IHU and the BWG. The Veterinary Office for Border Services (Veterinäramt Grenzdienst) with 55 employees, is part of the Department for Food Safety and Veterinary Affairs of the BWG. It is responsible for GM foods of animal and non-animal origin which are subject to obligatory checks at import (Vorführpflicht). The Authority for Urban Development and Environment (Behörde für Stadtent- wicklung und Umwelt, BSU) is resonsible for inspections, including sampling, under the Genetic Engineering Act (Gentechnikgesetz). In this function it also samples food and feed for the analysis of non-authorised GMOs. In Saxony-Anhalt under the supervision of the MS (2 food chemists an 1 administrator) the Regional Administration Office (Landesverwaltungsamt, LVwA, 3 technical and 1 administrative staff) is responsible for the coordination of controls of GMO food. The controls are carried out by 95 food inspectors of the Local Veterinary and Food Monitoring Offices (Veterinär- und Lebensmittelüberwachungsämter der Landkreise und kreisfreien Städte). Food inspectors in Saxony-Anhalt receive training, among other things, for controls of GM food during the initial two-year-training period, which includes laboratory work, during regular training (every two years) and during meetings (1-2 times a year). 6.4.2. They noted their disagreement with the FVO's assessment that KDS is a control body as defined in Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, article 5. The Dutch Authorities stated that KDS has no control over the way in which its employees and contracted workers carry out their work as official auxiliaries. BACKGROUND TO PRESENT MISSION This mission was the 16th in a series of missions to Member States in order to evaluate control systems and operational standards in the plant passport sector. Previous missions carried out in the Slovak Republic by the FVO include DG(SANCO)/7769/2005, on plant health in the potato sector, and DG(SANCO)/7771/2005, to evaluate the current situation of Erwinia amylovora. They were combined and took place from 7 to 11 November 2005. The reports can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm. Commission Directive 2006/36/EC of 24 March 2006 amending Directive 2001/32/EC recognising protected zones exposed to particular plant health risks in the Community and repealing Directive 92/76/EEC10, recognises the territory of the Slovak Republic as a Protected Zone for Erwinia amylovora, except the communes of Blahová, Horné Mýto and Okoc (Dunajská Streda County), Hronovce and Hronské Kacany (Levice County), Veké Ripany(Topocany County), Málinec (Poltár County), Hrhov (Rozava County), Kazimír, Luhya, Malý Hores, Svätuse and Zatín (Trebisov County). 6. MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Legislation CCTIA provides the mission team with the following information about national legislation. Act 193/2005 of 16 March 2005 of the National Council of the Slovak Republic is the main legal act governing Plant Health, and provides legal power to the responsible official bodies to conduct their duties. It transposes one part of Directive 2000/29/EC. Ordinances issued by the Government of the Slovak Republic transpose Directives regulating the plant passport area. Ordinance 199/2005 of 4 May 2005 (with further amendments) on protective measures against the introduction and spread of organisms harmful to plant or plant products, transposes the rest of Directive 2000/29/EC, Directive 92/90/EEC, Directive 92/105/EEC, and Directive 93/50/EEC. Ordinance 64/2004 of 21 January 2005 (with further amendments) on protected zones, transposes Directive 93/51/EEC and Directive 2001/32/EC. Decision 2002/757/EC on phytosanitary measures against Phytophthora ramorum is implemented by way of "Protective Measures to contain the spread of Phytophthora ramorum Werres et al. within the territory of the Slovak Republic" of the CCTIA on 20 June 2006. The mission team was informed that the Decision was directly implemented prior to the adoption of the protective measures. Article 5 of Act 193/2005 gives the inspector legal power to enter establishments and to carry out checks. Article 8 of Ordinance 199/2005 and Article 4 of Act 193/2005 allow CCTIA to take measures in the event of non-compliance. 10OJ L 88, 25.03.2006, p.13 7 6.2. Competent authority performance 6.2.1. Structure and responsibilities The Ministry of Agriculture ­ Department of Plant Commodities ­ of the Slovak Republic is the Single Authority, within the meaning of Article 1(4) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, responsible for co-ordination and contact with the Commission and the other Member States. The Central Testing Institute of Agriculture (CCTIA), is the Responsible Official Body for the protection of the territory against the introduction and spread of harmful organisms, and in particular for the Plant Passport System. CCTIA operates at three levels: -the national headquarters in Bratislava; -the regional headquarters in Zvolen and Kosice for the central and eastern parts of the Slovak Republic respectively; the western part is managed directly from Bratislava; -local units set up for a county or a group of counties, under the direct supervision of the national or the regional headquarters. The Plant Protection Section of CCTIA (SPP) is responsible for the Plant Passport System. However, it has completely delegated to the Section of Seeds and Planting Materials of CCTIA (SSPM) its authority to conduct controls for the issuing of Plant Passports for beet and hops and on seeds of potato, alfalfa, sunflower, tomato, bean, shallot, onion and chives. The SSPM co-operates with SPP for the registration of producers and importers of the same crops, plus grape and fruit plants. SPP has also delegated controls on forest plants to the National Forestry Centre, which is a part of the Ministry of Agriculture of the Slovak Republic. The CCTIA Diagnostics Section is responsible for official laboratory testing. 6.2.2. Human resources There are 84 inspectors in charge of internal market checks: 59 are agents of SPP, 25 are agents of SSPM. The proportion of working time spent on internal market checks is estimated at 20%. The total number of officials in SSP is 87. In addition to the inspectors in charge of internal market checks, there are 12 inspectors in charge of controls at the points of entry into the customs territory of the European Community. The rest of the officials are employed at headquarters or have other special tasks. The total number of officials involved in plant health matters in SSPM is 30. The minimum educational requirement for all the inspectors is an university degree in agriculture. Training on the Plant Passport System was given to all the inspectors of SPP prior to accession to the European Community, under a twinning programme with Germany. Since accession, these inspectors have attended 1 to 3 days training a year, on the Plant Passport System and diagnosis of harmful organisms. Inspectors of SSPM spend 3 training days each year on legislation and the inspection process. The Diagnostics Section participates in SPP and SSPM training measures. 8 6.2.3. Financial resources and fees The financial resources of all responsible bodies come from the Government. Fees are charged for the registration and issuing of Plant Passports. All revenues are transferred to the National Budget, which allocates 10% to the CCTIA. 6.2.4. Co-ordination, work planning and policy Inspections are carried out according to the objectives defined each year by the CCTIA headquarters. For each kind of production, CCTIA specifies the number and the periodicity of inspections to be carried out. Local inspectors are issued with a copy of this plan at the beginning of each year and have to apply it to the establishments in their area. Declared priorities are seed potatoes, fruit crops, grape vine, and all host plants of fireblight (Erwinia amylovora) and powdery mildew (Mycosphaerella dearnessii and Mycosphaerella pini). Inspectors of SPP attend monthly meetings at their regional headquarters. Four to five times a year, representatives of national headquarters are also present. Once a year, there is a meeting with representatives of the national and regional headquarters. Inspectors of SSPM also attend monthly meetings at their regional headquarters. All the local units are connected to the CCTIA intranet. This gives inspectors easy access to legislative, administrative and technical information. Technical guidance for the main cultivated species has been issued to inspectors, who can also refer to illustrated books and brochures describing plant pests and diseases. Inspection reports are filed in the local units and at national level. 6.2.5. External Communication and co-operation The mission team noted a close co-operation between inspectors and establishments. For this reason, communication of new official or technical information to stakeholders is facilitated. Usually, this takes place during inspections. General information on the Plant Passport System is circulated by articles in newspapers at the beginning of each year, and the legislation can be found on the website of CCTIA (www.uksup.sk). CCTIA organise training for stakeholders. In 2006, one 2-day course was organised by SSPM and SPP. It concerned legislation on seed production and codes of good practice. Inspection on the spot also enables stakeholders to communicate information to the inspectors, although there is no obligation for stakeholders to notify the arrival of regulated articles which are not in line with the Plant Passport System. 6.3. The Plant Passport System 6.3.1. Registration SPP is responsible for registration of importers and producers, in close co-operation with SSPM. The headquarters of CCTIA handle a common Registration Information System, using computer software. An applicant for registration must submit an official application to the headquarters of CCTIA with, among other documents, an inspection report issued by the local 9 phytosanitary inspector. The applicant must pay a fee of 500 SKK (approximately 14.50 on 20/12/2006). If the dossier is complete CCTIA headquarters enter the producer or the importer in the Registration Information System and send him/her a certificate. Each establishment has a unique number. In the event of a change in the scope of his/her activities the applicant must submit a special application for updating his/her registration. The validity of registration is not time-limited. A visit, carried out on site by the local inspector, is compulsory prior to registration. Following the visit, the local inspector draws up a report describing the premises and the production of the establishment. If the establishment is split over several sites, there is a separate report for each site. Local inspectors have access to the registration dossier of the establishments of their area, via the CCTIA intranet. The number of registered establishments is 2122 (538 producers, 864 producers/traders, 422 traders, 298 importers), of which 956 deal with regulated articles. CCTIA explained that the substantial difference between these two figures comes, first, from the large number of establishments which were registered according to the national rule in force prior to accession, but do not now deal with regulated products, and second, from some others which have ceased activity without cancelling their registration. The mission team found that some dispatching centres of seed potatoes were not registered. Also some registered establishments said that all or part of their production was bought from contractors which are not individually registered. This was the case of a Lucerne seed distributor, a grapevine plant multiplier and a seed potato producer. However, these contractors are regularly checked by inspectors of CCTIA. 6.3.2. Plant passport 6.3.3.1. Authorisation to issue plant passports CCTIA does not issue Plant Passports directly. It delegates the issuing of Plant Passport to registered establishments which have submitted an application for authorisation to issue Plant passport. Each year, authorised establishments have to ask for a Systematic Phytosanitary Control before a specified deadline (e.g. 15 May for non-forest crops in open air, 31 August for forest crops) to SPP, SSPM or the National Forestry Centre, which then forward a copy to the local inspectors, who in turn carry out controls according to the work plan (see 6.2.4). Any establishment which does not apply for a Systematic Phytosanitary Control is not allowed to issue Plant Passports that year. CCTIA stated that because the inspectors have a good knowledge of the situation within their area, it is unlikely that an establishment can issue Plant Passports without asking for the Systematic Phytosanitary Control. The authorisation does not expire, but CCTIA can withdraw the authorisation in the event of repeated infringements. In 2006, 208 establishments have been authorised to issue Plant Passports. 6.3.3.2. Issuing plant passports The Plant Passports are produced, printed and stored by the authorised establishments. They take the form of a label attached to the plants or homogenous group of plants. 10 The mission team noted that labels were printed on suitable material. The mention "Rastlinný Pas", which means Plant Passport in Slovak, was sometimes abbreviated to "RP". In one situation, "EC-Plant passport" was not clearly indicated: at the top of the label was the acronym "ES", which means European Community, at the bottom was "Cislo RP", which means number of Plant passport. 6.3.3.3. Replacement plant passports Replacement Plant Passports can theoretically be issued, but this does not happen in practice. In the situations where a Replacement Plant Passport is necessary, the mission team noted that CCTIA allows authorised establishments to issue new plant passports, provided they keep a record of the origin of each commodity, for the purposes of traceability. 6.3.3.4. Protected zones plant passport Any person applying for authorisation to issue Plant Passports must specify in the application form his/her intention to issue Plant Passports for Protected Zones. Most of the Plant Passports are used for movements within the Slovak Republic, the whole territory of which is a Protected Zone for Globodera pallida, and almost all of which is a Protected Zone for Erwinia amylovora. All the Plant Passports issued by the establishments visited by the team lacked the mark "ZP" and the special code for Globodera pallida. Also, some Plant Passports on host plants of Erwinia amylovora, as described in point 2 (b) of part B, Annex II of Council Directive 2000/29 EC, lacked the mark "ZP" and the specific code for this disease. The mission team noted that some plant passports received by establishments from other Member States lacked the mark "ZP" for Globodera pallida. 6.3.3. Imports from third countries The Single Authority stated that there have been no imports of regulated articles which require a plant passport to enter the internal market. 6.3.4. Internal market checks 6.3.4.1. Official examinations All establishments authorised to issue Plant Passport are inspected at least once a year, and in some cases more often, depending on the work plan (see 6.2.4). A report is produced for every inspection and is signed by the inspector and the contact person for the establishment. In 2005, CCTIA conducted 1223 inspections (669 at producers, 313 at producers/traders, 101 at traders, 140 at importers). During their visits to the local offices, the mission team observed that the inspectors have technical guidance available for control and sampling, and also adequate equipment. By using the CCTIA intranet, inspectors have easy access to the basic data of the authorised establishments they deal with, like the type of production or the name of the contact person. Inspectors were found to be well aware of the characteristics of Phytophtora ramorum and the phytosanitary measures against this disease, in particular recent national measures (see 6.1). 11 During their visits to the establishments, the mission team observed that the number of inspections per year is at least one. In some of the largest establishments it is far beyond that: more than 30 per year. Records of activities were kept and maps were present, so that it is possible to trace back the specific location of a perennial plant from its Plant Passport. The mission team noted also that some irregularities had not been spoted by the local inspector: some Plant Passports were received or issued without the relevant "ZP" marking, and in one case Plant Passport labels were received by mail separately from the plants. Samples are taken during the inspection. On some cultures they are taken systematically each year (e.g. lucerne seeds, seed potatoes). In all cases, the inspector takes a sample if suspicious symptoms are found. 6.3.4.2. Occasional checks Non-registered establishments are also checked occasionally, e.g. potato ware producers, for the presence of harmful organisms. These checks are unscheduled. 6.4. Exemptions from the system 6.4.1. Small quantities, small producers or processors and local movement These establishments are not registered. 6.4.2. Plants, plant products and other objects prepared and ready for sale to the final consumer CTIA stated that producers of plants, plant products and other objects listed in Annex V, Part A, Section I, points 2 and 3 of Council Directive 2000/29/EC are very few, and that they are all inspected. 6.5. Enforcement of the system In the event of sampling, the plants under investigation cannot be sold pending the receipt of results from the laboratory. In the event of a harmful organism being found, CCTIA headquarters are informed, decide on official measures and send instruction to the grower with a copy to the local inspector. The local inspector is responsible for verifying execution of these measures on site. In 2006, two samples of mother plant of Prunus were positive for the Plum Pox Virus (PPV) in one establishment visited. Previous missions The FVO has previously carried out several missions to Italy. There are available on the web-site: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm This was the third mission undertaken in Italy for this purpose. The last mission with the same objective was undertaken in 2001. The report DG(SANCO)/3402/2001 recommended in particular carrying out intensive monitoring in Veneto, Lombardy, Piedmont and in the regions where Diabrotica had not been found, to continue the eradication programme in Veneto and to determine appropriate measures in Lombardy and Piedmont to contain or eradicate the pest. 5.2. Diabrotica virgifera Diabrotica virgifera is a quarantine pest of maize listed in Council Directive 2000/29/EC, Annex I, Part A, Section I. There are two subspecies of Diabrotica virgifera in America affecting maize: Diabrotica virgifera virgifera Le Conte, and Diabrotica virgifera zeae Kryzan & Smith. Only the first subspecies is present in Europe, and in this report hereafter will be referred as "Diabrotica". Diabrotica was first detected in Europe in former Yugoslavia in July 1992 and has since spread within Eastern Europe and the European Union (EU). It was found for the first time within the EU in Italy in 1998 nearly Venice airport. Its main means of spread are: flight of the adult forms and transport by plane, road and rail. Transport of fresh maize could also provoke its dispersal. As of 1 January 2006, the situation in the European Union is as follows: - in Belgium the insect was detected in 2003 and 2004 but was not found in 2005; - in France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Poland, Diabrotica is present in the form of isolated outbreaks and the population is still low;

Both adults and larvae of Diabrotica attack maize, but it is larval feeding that damages the roots, causes weakening of plants and makes them more susceptible to lodging (which is the main reason of economic losses). Adults feed on the pollen of flowering cobs, and on the silks, leaves and developing kernels, thereby hampering seed set in sweet corn and grain maize. The female adults can migrate over long distances, more than 40 km a year. There is an ecotype in North America of which the female lays eggs not only in maize fields but also in soybean fields. This complicates the best mean of control, which is crop rotation. On 24 October 2003, the specific Commission Decision 2003/766/EC was issued, detailing emergency measures for outbreaks in areas where Diabrotica had not occurred before. Later, Commission Decision 2006/564/EC4 of 11 August 2006 amending Commission Decision 2003/766/EC on emergency measures to prevent the spread within the Community of Diabrotica virgifera Le Conte was issued. This Decision lays down measures to limit the spread of the insect from the "infested areas", where the pest is established (including areas where Diabrotica occurred before 24 October 2003), to the areas free of the organism. 5.3. Legislation As early as 21 August 2001, the Ministry for Agricultural and Forestry Policy (Ministero delle Politiche Agricole e Forestali) issued a national decree declaring the control of Diabrotica compulsory throughout the Italian territory (Lotta Obligatoria Contro la Diabrotica Del Mais). This decree instructed the SFRs to organise a systematic survey, made it compulsory to notify outbreaks and, in Article 5, laid down measures to eradicate outbreaks. However, Article 7 already foresaw the possibility that Diabrotica might become established, and in that event required the SFRs concerned to take appropriate measures in order not to eradicate but to contain the spread of the insect, without specifying those measures. The Single Authority stated that the procedure followed in Italy for applying the Commission Decisions requires a transposition into a national rule. This results in a delay in application. Commission Decision 2003/766/EC of 24 October 2003 was transposed by a decree on 30 June 2004, and Commission Decision 2006/564/EC of 11 August 2006, which amends the preceding Decision, has not yet been transposed and is thus not applied yet either. In other words, the decrees of 21 August 2001 and 30 June 2004 are the only legislation in force. The SFC has also issued notes spelling out the way in which the decree of 21 August 2001 is to be applied. The last one was drawn up on 30 June 2004. It concerns the areas where Diabrotica is established, providing technical details concerning the methods of survey and the measures to be taken. There is no similar note for the areas still being free from the organism. National legislation is usually supplemented at regional level by regional implementing decrees. In Piedmont, Determinazione (Decision) 206 of 7 October 2005, issued by the SFR, designates some areas, according to the results of the survey, and specifies compulsory measures to be taken in those areas. Any infringement of these measures can involve legal consequences. In Lombardy, regional decree 18000 of 20 October 2004 approved a guideline (Linee guida) and was subsequently published in the Regional Official Gazette No. 45 of 2 November 2004. The aim of the guideline was to pursue the containment and control of the insect in order to avoid economic losses. It described the situation and gave recommendations concerning the survey and advices on the measures, taking into account the situation in different provinces. In Veneto, decree 01 of 1 February 2006 identifies some outbreak sites (focolaii), according to the results of the survey, and specifies compulsory measures to be taken in those areas. Any infringement of these measures can involve legal consequences. In Lazio, no regional rules have been issued. The mission team was informed that, following the Italian procedure, it is not necessary due to an absence of the insect in this region (see6.4). 9 6.1.2. Competent authorities The structure and responsibilities of the Plant Health Service in Italy has already been described in detail in previous mission reports. Additional information is available in the FVO country profile (http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/CP_italy.pdf). In summary, the Central Phytosanitary Service (Servizio Fitosanitario Centrale), which is part of the Ministry of Agricultural and Forestry Policies (Ministero delle Politiche Agricole e Forestali), acts as the Single Authority as defined in Article 1.4 of Directive 2000/29/EC. Plant health controls are implemented by the SFR of each of the 19 Regions and 2 autonomous Provinces. 6.1.3. Human and financial resources In Piedmont the inspector-specialist in entomology in the SFR, supported by two colleagues, manages all activities concerning Diabrotica. Under his supervision, and with the collaboration of the administrations of the 8 provinces belonging to this region, the survey is performed in the field by 77 technicians employed by farmer associations. The SFR has drawn up agreements with these associations. Identification of the insect is not considered to be difficult, but where necessary, the SFR can rely on university experts, on the basis of informal agreements. The cost of the survey is financed by the SFR. In 2006, about 30,000 was spent for this purpose, including communication activities. In Lombardy, the inspector-specialist in the SFR, supported by one colleague, manages all activities concerning Diabrotica. He is assisted by the provincial administrations and various associations of farmers through 74 technicians who perform the survey, under official agreements. The cost of the survey is financed by the SFR. In 2006, it amounted to 98,000. Further 62,000 was spent on other tasks, in particular works in order to improve the effectiveness of the control measures. In Veneto, the survey is carried out by 10 operators recruited by the SFR under contract. In each of the region's provinces, their work is supervised by an inspector, and a regional inspector-specialist is in charge of the coordination of all the activities concerning Diabrotica. The cost of the survey is financed by the SFR from special regional funds. It amounted to 110,000 in 2006. In Lazio, all inspectors at the SFR in Rome are in charge of the survey. There are no inspector-specialists. They have been trained by the University of Tuscia and have the necessary technical documentation, such as pest description, available. Where a suspected insect is captured, the University of Tuscia would confirm the identification. The cost of the survey is financed by the SFR. In the regions visited, there is no compensation scheme in place for measures to be taken by the farmer where Diabrotica is present (see6.4). Compensation is not required by relevant EC legislation, but is considered as a factor conducing control. 6.2. Coordination and work planning 6.2.1. Role of the Comitato Fitosanitario Nationale and the working group The Comitato Fitosanitario Nationale (CFN) is an official national committee for plant health, which brings together representatives of the SFC and the heads of all 10 the SFRs. It is responsible for putting forward official proposals with a view to drawing up national rules or instructions. Its meetings take place on monthly basis. There are also working groups for several specific subjects, and one of them deals with Diabrotica. Their role is to provide scientific and technical advice to the CFN. They are composed of specialists either working for the SFRs or coming from technical or research institutes. On behalf of the SFC, the working group for Diabrotica has the particular task to notify by 31 December of each year the Commission and other Member States of the results of the annual survey carried out in Italy, in order to comply with Article 2(2) of Commission Decision 2003/766/EC. 6.2.2. Working procedures In the four regions visited, Diabrotica survey and control is part of the SFR's work programme. Operators in charge of observations in the fields have detailed working instructions and brochures about the insect. In Lombardy, the guideline of 2 November 2004 is the basis of these instructions. In Piedmont and Lombardy, operators meet frequently the inspectors of SFR during meetings or joint observations in the fields. In Piedmont they send their results to the SFR by E-mail with the use of e-mail immediately after their checks, with a copy to the provincial administration. In Lombardy, results are sent at the end of the survey period. In Veneto, when the operators find insects in a trap, they have to notify the SFR immediately and send a sample for confirmation. Each year, data are collected by the SFR at the end of the survey period. Every year, each region sends the results of the survey to the SFC with a copy to the coordinator of the national working group, who is responsible for drawing up an annual report and sending it to the Commission. However, in 2005 Lazio sent its results only to the SFC and thus the annual report sent to the Commission did not take this region into account (see6.2.1). 6.2.3. Communication and co-operation among SFRs The national working group for Diabrotica provides a forum for general communication among the SFRs. Generally, the global results of the survey carried out by an SFR are communicated to other SFRs in this way. However, not all regions are represented in this working group. The regions that are most affected by the pest are most interested in participating, while regions not yet affected by the pest are not always attending and consequently have a significantly lower level of awareness. It was not the impression of the mission team that co-ordinated procedures of communication were in place. In addition, SFC does not play the role of a main coordinating body that shares the information and encourages regions to closer cooperation. At the moment, informal and sporadic exchanges, concerning the specific situation close to the respective border, exist between SFR Piedmont and SFR Lombardy, between SFR Lombardy and SFR Veneto, and between SFR Veneto and SFR Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Close and organised cooperation existed in 2004 between SRF Lombardy and SFR Veneto in order to avoid the spread of the insect from Lombardy to Veneto. It has not been renewed in the subsequent years, and at the moment there is no organised cooperation between bordering regions, either for the survey or for the control measures. 11 6.2.4. The competent authorities for the control of pesticide residues in domestic and imported produce of plant origin are clearly identified.

Horizontal communication between competent authorities involved in the control of pesticide residues is deficient, particularly in the areas of planning of controls and reporting of results and does not comply with Article 4 (3) of Regulation 882/2004. 6.3. Implementation of controls 6.3.1. Control activities regarding pesticide residues on domestic produce

The annual national plan by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries & Food for control of pesticide residues 'at source' provides useful control on use of pesticides by growers but, because the controls are taken before the produce is put into circulation, the plan does not allow enforcement of the Maximum Residue Level legislation. The plan for 2007 is not yet in place.

The controls conducted by the Autonomous Community health authorities are not co-ordinated but the Multi-Annual National Control Plan, required for compliance with Articles 41 and 42 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, is expected to address these deficiencies once it has been adopted.

Overall conclusion The control system in place for pesticide residues in foodstuffs of plant origin is developing but further progress is required, particularly in the areas of co-ordination, co- operation and performance of controls, the communication of results, assessment of consumer risk and in the laboratories. Some progress, since the last mission, in the control system for pesticide residues is acknowledged. The residue controls introduced for the illegal pesticide, isofenphos-methyl, appear to be working well. However, the means of introduction of the pesticide into Spain is not clear and a risk of further illegal pesticides being introduced continues.

CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 23 February 2007 with representatives of the Spanish Food Safety and Nutrition Agency, the Ministry of Health and Consumer Affairs (DGSP), the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food and a number of Autonomous Communities. At this meeting, the initial findings and conclusions of the mission were presented by the inspection team. The representatives provided some clarifications to the initial findings and conclusions presented. 10 In their response to the draft report the Spanish authorities noted that "the range of pesticides tested for during analysis is being extended as far as the instrumental resources available on the market allow." 22 8. RECOMMENDATIONS TO THE COMPETENT AUTHORITIES OF SPAIN In making the following recommendations, it is emphasised that recommendations (4) and (12) are repeated from the 2004 mission on pesticides, while recommendations (1), (2), (5), (6), (7), (9), (10) and (11) also relate to deficiencies from the 2004 mission but have been revised to take account of progress made since the last mission and to take new legislation into account. (1) The competent authorities should ensure that amendments to Council Directives 86/362/EEC, 86/363/EEC and 90/642/EEC as regards maximum residue levels are transposed and national legislation providing for coordination of control measures under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 is introduced without undue delay. (2) The competent authorities should ensure that efficient and effective co- ordination takes place between all competent authorities carrying out official controls for pesticide residues, in accordance with Article 4 (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. (3) The competent authorities should ensure that all monitoring results, including follow-up, are routinely reported to the Commission as required by Articles 4(3) and 7(3) of Council Directives 90/642/EEC and 86/362/EEC respectively. (4) The competent authorities should consider taking into account the draft "Guidance document on notification criteria for pesticide residues findings to the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF)" (SANCO/3346/2001, rev 7), including systematic consumer risk assessments for adults and children. (5) The competent authorities should ensure that (i) all laboratories involved in the official control of pesticide residues are designated in accordance with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and (ii) all designated laboratories comply with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, or are availing of the derogation foreseen in Article 18 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2076/2005. The quality control system in the laboratories availing of Article 18 should be based on the SANCO guidelines for 'Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residue Analysis' (Document No SANCO/10232/2006). (6) In cases where monitoring shows non-compliance, the competent authorities should ensure that appropriate enforcement actions are taken in accordance with Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and should consider taking into account the analytical uncertainty, established in accordance with the SANCO guidelines for 'Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residue Analysis' (Document No SANCO/10232/2006). (7) In accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the competent authorities should ensure that staff receive appropriate training so that samples are taken in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC.

The competent authorities should consider substantially increasing the range of validated analytical methods for detection of pesticide residues and metabolites being sought, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and used. 23 (9) The competent authorities should ensure the introduction of co-ordinated and comprehensive inspection and enforcement procedures for controlling the marketing of plant protection products, including follow-up, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC and clarify the competencies and procedures for importation of plant protection products. (10) The competent authorities should ensure the introduction of co-ordinated and comprehensive inspection and enforcement procedures for controlling the use of plant protection products, including the use of illegal products and follow-up, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC. (11) The competent authorities should ensure that the annual report to the Commission in the framework of Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC includes results from all Autonomous Communities. The CA of Spain is invited to send to the Commission, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan in response to the recommendations. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation.

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION AND OTHER RELEVANT LEGISLATION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: ­ Art. 21 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; ­ Art. 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules (3); ­ Commission Decision 98/139/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States (4). Other legislation, including implementing measures, was considered during the mission, in particular, Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002 (5), Decision 2003/100/EC (6) and Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 (7). Harmonised rules with regards to intracommunity trade and imports into the territory of the Community of live ovine and caprine animals and their genetic material were also considered insofar as they might have an impact on control measures on TSEs in sheep and goats. 4. BACKGROUND The mission was carried out as part of a series of missions to assess control measures on TSEs in small ruminants in Member States. It was the first FVO mission to Hungary specifically concerning control measures on TSEs in small ruminants. Previous FVO missions to Hungary considered, as part of their scope, TSEs controls in cattle (DG(SANCO) 7688/2005), the system of identification of small ruminants (DG(SANCO) 7619/2005) and the implementation of health rules on animal by- products not intended for human consumption (DG(SANCO) 7517/2005). These reports are accessible at http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm. Community legislation requires specific controls in respect of TSEs infected flocks and provides for on monitoring of TSEs in sheep and goats. A requirement for breeding programmes for resistance of sheep to TSEs and a system for the identification and registration of small ruminants is also required. (3) OJ L 191, 28.05.2004, p. 1. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Competent Authorities Information on the competent authorities (CAs) can be found in the country profile for Hungary which is accessible at http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/CP_hungary.pdf There have been some recent changes in the organisational structure of the CAs. On 1 January 2007 the Central Agricultural Office (CAO) of MARD has been established. In respect of the scope of this mission the CAO is the legal successor to, and has taken over the work of, the former County Offices for Agriculture, County Animal Health and Food Control Stations and the National Veterinary institute. The aim of the reorganisation is to set up a smaller and more service orientated public administration. MARD remains responsible for legislation, international relations and interfacing with the government. The mission team noted that: ¾ Organisational change is currently underway and staff met were not fully aware of the consequences for implementation of work required for control of TSEs. ¾ The CCA informed the mission team that there has been insufficient staff to deal with TSEs work at central level in recent years, and that this situation should improve in the near future. 5.2. Legislative provisions On accession Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 became directly applicable in Hungary. However, Decree 69/2003 which transposed Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 before accession is still in force as an implementing rule. The fact that Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 has primacy over Decree 69/2003 has been published as a signed announcement by the Chief Veterinary Officer (CVO) in April 2004. The mission team noted that: ¾ Hungarian Decree 69/2003 has not been amended since 2004 and it does not reflect changes in Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 since. 5.3. Scrapie epidemio-surveillance 5.3.1. Animal identification and registration The system of identification in small ruminants has previously been described in report DG(SANCO) 7619/2005. Figures supplied to the mission team indicate that there is a total sheep population of approximately 1.45 million (of which 1.14 million are ewes over 12 months old) and approximately 32,000 goats in Hungary. The mission team noted that: ¾ Small ruminants seen during on-the-spot visits were identified as required. ¾ At the time of the mission approximately 32,000 goats were registered. The CA estimate that the adult goat population is approximately 50,000 and work is ongoing to ensure that all goats are registered. ¾ Tracing of parents or offspring of TSEs positive sheep and goats can be carried out in pedigree flocks by the use of on farm records (approximately 300 out of 7800 sheep flocks). 3 5.3.2. Passive surveillance No cases of Scrapie have been detected by passive surveillance in Hungary. The number of clinical suspects reported over the last 3 years is as set out in the following table: YEAR Animals showing neurological signs and tested for TSEs 2004 Sheep Goats 2005 2006 35 12 34 10 20 7 The mission team noted that: ¾ During 2004 in the framework of TSEs twinning projects related to accession of Hungary to the EU several training sessions for officials on TSEs issues took place. These focused mainly on BSE in cattle. ¾ There was no evidence provided of any education or awareness campaign for farmers with respect to the clinical signs of Scrapie. However, farmers met during the on-the-spot visits were aware of the clinical signs of Scrapie. 5.3.3. Active surveillance In slaughtered and dead on farm small ruminants the TSEs sampling system is carried out by the entire head of the animal being removed and sent to a Veterinary Diagnostic Directorate laboratory for TSEs testing. Since the accession of Hungary to the EU in May 2004 there have been several changes in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 with respect to the numbers of small ruminants that should be tested for TSEs. Currently Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 requires that all over 18 month small ruminants slaughtered for human consumption and 20 000 dead on farm sheep and 1000 dead on farm goats must be tested for TSEs. In the case of the dead on farm sheep and goats each county is set a target number to be tested throughout the year. The results of the TSEs testing programmes in Hungary can be found in DG SANCO reports on the monitoring and testing of ruminants for the presence of TSEs in the EU accessible at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/food/biosafety/bse/annual_reps_en.htm The mission team noted that: ¾ The official veterinarian in the slaughterhouse visited was fully aware of the sampling requirements. Heads sent for testing were accompanied by appropriate documentation. ¾ Private veterinarians of the farms visited were also aware of the sampling requirements. In one county visited each veterinarian had been allocated a specific number of fallen small ruminants to be tested for TSEs. In another of the Counties visited the mission team were informed that quotas of fallen small ruminants to be sampled had been allocated by the district CA to each of the larger farms. 5 ¾ The CA reported that the majority of small ruminants over the age of 18 months are slaughtered on farm for own consumption. It is a national requirement that the slaughter of these animals on farm is reported to the CA but very few are actually reported and many animals that should be tested for TSEs are not tested. To illustrate the problem, in 2006 there were 5,448 adult sheep slaughtered in slaughterhouses while the population of adult sheep is greater than 1.1 million. With a breeding ewe replacement rate of 10% per year one would expect a slaughtering rate of approximately 100,000 per year. 5.3.4. Laboratory network The national reference laboratory (NRL) for TSEs is the Veterinary Diagnostic Directorate of the Central Agricultural Office. Confirmatory and discriminatory tests for TSEs are carried out at the NRL. Rapid tests (Bio-Rad TeSeE) for TSEs are carried out at the NRL and also at two regional TSEs laboratories which are organised as departments of the NRL. The regional laboratories can also carry out histopathology in cases of clinical suspicion of TSEs. Laboratories receive the entire heads of sheep and goats to be TSEs tested. Laboratory staff remove a sample of brainstem and cerebellum through the foramen magnum. These samples are tested using the Bio-Rad TeSeE rapid test. In the case of a non-negative rapid test result samples are submitted to the NRL for confirmatory tests (histopathology, immunocytochemistry and immuno-blotting). Positive Scrapie samples are subjected to a discriminatory test (CEA Western Blot) to rule out BSE. A sample of buccal mucosa is also retained from each head subjected to a rapid test. This sample is used for genotyping in the case of a positive TSEs result. The mission team noted that: ¾ There is adequate laboratory capacity and arrangements in place to conduct the required rapid, confirmatory and discriminatory tests in small ruminants. ¾ There is quick reporting of results to the central TSEs results database and to abattoirs when slaughtered sheep and goats are sampled. ¾ Five atypical Scrapie cases have been diagnosed in 2006 and 2007. These were all initially detected using the BioRad TeSe rapid test on standard brainstem samples. They were confirmed as atypical cases using CEA Western Blot tests. ¾ No comparative tests have been organised by the NRL to assess the reliability of TSEs testing in the regional laboratories. No on-site supervision by the NRL of TSEs testing had taken place in the regional laboratory visited. 5.4. Measures following suspicion/confirmation of TSEs Apart from one positive case in a Romanian cull ewe imported for direct slaughter in 2004, no Scrapie had been recorded in Hungary until June 2006. From June 2006 until January 2007 there have been seven cases of Scrapie recorded in sheep flocks. No cases of Scrapie have been identified in goat herds. All positive cases have been identified by active surveillance (four in dead-on-farm stock and three in healthy slaughter sheep). Five of the cases have been identified as being atypical Scrapie. The usual method of control in infected flocks is the killing and complete destruction of all small ruminants on the holding. Parents and offspring of infected animals are also to be identified and destroyed. In exceptional cases (flocks of indigenous breeds of high genetic merit) it is possible to genotype and retains the following: - animals of the ARR/ARR genotype, - animals with at least one ARR allele (but not carrying a VRQ allele, 6 - animals with at least one ARR allele which are intended solely for slaughter. Two of the infected flocks have opted for the genotyping option. The mission team noted that: ¾ The Scrapie affected flock visited (an indigenous breed of high genetic merit) had chosen to genotype and retain resistant sheep. The mission team confirmed that only those genotypes permitted by Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 had been retained in the flock, ¾ County staff met on the sheep farm visited displayed a high degree of competence and were fully aware of the procedures in place for dealing with Scrapie infection in small ruminants. ¾ Sheep movements off the farm were restricted in line with Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 5.5. Breeding programmes for resistance to TSEs A breeding programme with the objective of increasing the resistance of sheep flocks to Scrapie has been in place since 2004. The programme is managed by the Hungarian Sheep Breeders association and is targeted at flocks of high genetic merit. Based on the results of a survey carried out in 2004 sheep breeds were divided into two groups, breeds with an ARR allele frequency above 25% and breeds with an ARR frequency below 25 %.
