R3 Low risk in case of tested animal, but ARR/ARH, ARR/ARQ there is a risk in case of its offspring AHQ/ARH AHQ/ARQ depending on the genotype of the other parents R4 ARH/ARH ARH/ARQ ARQ/ARQ There is a high risk in case of tested ARR/VRQ AHQ/VRQ animal and offspring as well. R5 ARH/VRQ ARQ/VRQ The highest risk VRQ/VRQ In breeds where the frequency of the ARR allele is less than 25% it is highly recommended to use rams of the R1, R2 or R3 risk groups. In breeds where the frequency of the ARR allele is greater than 25% only R1, R2 or R3 rams may be used for breeding (use of the R3 ARR/ARQ genotype rams is not recommended. It is intended to assess the effectiveness of the breeding programme in December 2007 when modifications to the programme may be made on the basis of experience gained at that time. Council Directive 95/53/EC of 25 October 1995 fixing the principles governing the organization of official inspections in the field of animal nutrition; OJ L 265, 8. 11. 1995, p. 17. 1 The mission itinerary included the following: COMPETENT AUTHORITIES VISITS Comments Competent Central Opening and closing (de-briefing) meeting authority Regional 2 Meetings in the two regions visited SITES Feed control laboratory Managerial staff of the National Diagnostic Centre met during initial and final meetings Feed mills approved/registered as traders and importers, using food by-products and producing Animal feed processors/manufacturers 2 compound feedingstuffs and pre-mixtures using additives and pre-mixtures, of which one produced also medicated feedingstuffs and was using banned substances for export. On-farm mixer/primary producer 1 Large scale poultry farm with on-farm mixer and supplying food by-products for feed purposes Food operator supplying feed operators 1 One food operator supplying by-products of the milling process to feed operators BIP 1 One Border inspection post where feedingstuffs are imported into the EU 3. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: - Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. - Commission Decision 98/139/EC laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in the Member States (6). 4. BACKGROUND One mission concerning animal nutrition was carried out in Latvia from 19 to 23 September 2005, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/7694/2005 ­ MR Final (hereafter: report 7694/2005). This report is accessible at: http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm The report made a number of recommendations to the CCA, which subsequently informed the Commission of actions that had been or would be taken aimed at addressing the recommendations. Since the previous mission, the relevant EU legislation concerning feed safety has been modified significantly. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 has introduced a harmonised framework of general rules for the organisation of official controls on food and feed so as to integrate them at all stages of production and sectors, using the "farm to fork" principle. Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 recognised the need to ensure feed safety starting with primary production of feed and comprising also the transport, storage and handling of feed; moreover, procedures based on the principles of hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) should be in place for feed business operators (FBOs) (except at the level of primary production of feed and (6) OJ L 38, 12. 02. 1998, p. 10. 2 certain associated operations), and the compulsory registration of all FBOs was introduced. 5. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. INFORMATION ON THE FEED SECTOR At the time of the mission 17 feed mills were in activity, which during 2006 produced approximately 208,000 tons of feedingstuffs. In addition two approved mobile mixers processed during the same period about 10,400 tons of feed. These figures show an increase of 25% over those from 2005. At the time of the mission the CCA did not have figures on amounts of feedingstuffs produced by on-farm mixers. 5.2. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.2.1. Organisation and responsibilities The main features of the organisation of the competent authorities in the context of the scope of this mission can be found in the country profile for Latvia; which is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/LV_latvia.pdf Three authorities are involved in the feed chain: ­ The Ministry of Agriculture (MA), responsible for determination of State policy and development of national normative acts. ­ The Food and Veterinary Service (FVS), organises and performs official surveillance and controls over the feed chain. It can impose penalties according to Code of Administrative Offences. The Veterinary Surveillance Department and its divisions are responsibles for feed controls. At local level the FVS is represented by 27 Territorial Structural Units (TSU), implementing the different control programmes. ­ State agency ,,Agricultural Data Centre" (ADC) will maintain the register of operators involved in the feed chain. Currently it is in charge of maintaining the register of animal holdings Inspections on primary producers of vegetal products are carried out by the Food Surveillance Department, another service in the FVS. 5.2.2. Resources and training Each TSU has designated one official inspector (OI) in charge of the feed sector in the region. This official carries out the inspections in the feed operators together with other responsibilities. The FVS informed the mission team that topics for training courses are planned taking into account new legal requirements, findings from supervisory activities, questions arisen during meetings/courses, test results from the annual qualification courses for inspectors and feed back from the training courses. Communications on new requirements and changes in legislation are forwarded to the TSU on ad-hoc basis (e. g. banned antibiotics). 3 Observations: ¾ The FVS provided the mission team with comprehensive information on the veterinary inspectors' and experts' training in 2006 and 2007 in relation with general fields of responsibility as well as specific training related to feed hygiene. ¾ The OIs met explained that for solving technical problems they contact the FVS Central Office. They attended monthly meetings and insisted on the efficacy of this tool for keeping updated. ¾ Awareness of the OIs on feed hygiene requirements was satisfactory. Staff met were fully aware of the new requirements under the feed law. Documents used during the supervisory activity were updated and correctly filled. ¾ Guidelines had been provided to the OI in order to interpret the requirements of feed hygiene and to guarantee harmonisation on the outcome of the reports. Those guidelines were in use and the OIs met were fully aware of their content. ¾ The CCA stated that, when OIs attend training, the standard requirement is that information will be afterwards passed to the rest of the staff in charge of feed controls. The effectiveness of this activity could not be evaluated during the mission. ¾ Feed and food business operators visited expressed their satisfaction with the information provided to them by the OIs in order to comply with the new legislation. 5.2.3. Internal supervision The system in place to supervise the official controls involves a first step of checks of the performance of the OIs by the Chiefs of the TSU with a subsequent review of both OIs and Chiefs of TSU by specialised staff of the FVS Animals Feed Surveillance Division at central level. The Internal Auditing Division, Quality Department of the FVS, verifies the work of those specialists at central level. Each level of supervision is based on written procedures. The controls are regularly summarized and analyzed during the management meetings of TSU every six months and, in case of need, during monthly meetings. Observations: ¾ The FVS presented examples of supervisory activities. They included report assessments from the Chief of TSU and the central level, where some deficiencies (e.g. incomplete reports) were found and the OI received feedback. ¾ When needed (e.g. new/rare activities for which the OI could be not fully updated) inspections were carried out together with staff from the central level. When major discrepancies appear during an inspection the inspectors of FVS Internal Auditing and Control Division can carry out extraordinary inspections. ¾ In the two regions visited, the Chiefs of TSU met, who are in charge of supervising OIs, had a limited knowledge of the feed sector in their regions (in one case they were not aware of the feed activity of a food operator visited; in the other case, of the activities in the feed mills in the region). 5.3. OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON FEED A programme for inspections is elaborated by the Veterinary Surveillance Department of the FVS. It establishes the minimum frequencies of visits for each 4 group/type of establishments, based on risk analysis. The programme leaves room for increasing the frequency of the visits based on inspector's opinion, experience, or specific targeted situations. A separate programme for sampling is designed at national level, setting down for each TSU a monthly calendar with the type and number of samples. It takes into account the type of establishments in each TSU and previous results obtained and allows for additional sampling (after suspicion or following information from the Rapid Alert System for food and feed (RASFF). Observations: ¾ The inspection programme is largely complied with. At the establishments visited the frequency was at least the prescribed one, and in some cases extra follow up had been carried out. Increasing the frequency was based on OI experience and availability. ¾ The sampling programme was fully complied with in 2006 and during 2007 up to the date of the mission. Verification of compliance with the target is done in the central office; feed back is given to the TSU at least once per quarter or when needed once per month in the meetings. All the results during 2006 were compliant with legal requirements 5.4. LABORATORIES CARRYING OUT OFFICIAL ANALYSES The laboratory network in charge of feed safety consists of three central laboratories and four regional laboratories (RL). The FVS stated that the National Diagnostic Centre (NDC) carries out most of the analysis on feedingstuffs according to the "Feed surveillance programme and Sampling plan". In the RL only microbiological testing is carried out. The analysis of the dioxins (PCDD and PCDF) and dioxin-like PCB are carried out by a delegated body, a private laboratory located in another Member State. The NDC explained that all laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025 by the Latvian accreditation body LATAK. Observations: ¾ NDC has the capability to analyse the following tests in feedingstuffs according to Commission Recommendation 2005/925/EC(7): ochratoxin A, zearalenone, T-2 toxin, deoxynivalenol, nicarbazin, narasin, salinomycin, lasalocid, tetracyclin, copper and zinc. During the final meeting, representatives of the NDC explained that, when additional testing is needed, they require the services of external laboratories, as it is the case for dioxins. ¾ In order to obtain initial information regarding the presence of antibiotic residues in feed, antimicrobial growth inhibition screening tests are used. If a screening test indicates the presence of a drug residue, the identity and the quantity of the residue must be confirmed by other methods. No such case occurred in 2006 and 2007. (7) Commission Recommendation of 14 December 2005 on the coordinated inspection programme in the field of animal nutrition for the year 2006 in accordance with Council Directive 95/53/EC. (O. J. L 337, 22.12.2005, p. 51) 5 5.5. COMPLIANCE WITH REQUIREMENTS FOR FEED HYGIENE 5.5.1. Scope Observations: ¾ The CCA declared that presently there are no derogations in the national legislation according to Art. 28 of Regulation (EC) 183/2005. According to the representative of the Ministry of Agriculture, there is no intention to define rules governing the activities described by Art. 2 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2004, which would be exempted from the requirements for feed hygiene (8). ¾ Production of feed for horses is included in the official feed controls for production animals. ¾ National rules require that retailers where pet food is sold from opened packages shall be registered. ¾ National rules require that operators handling medicated feed shall be approved. 5.5.2. Registration and approval of feed business operators 5.5.2.1.Implementation of the requirements Regulation of the Cabinet of Ministries No 102, from 13 February 2007 puts in place the framework for implementing Regulation (EC) No. 183/2005. National guides to good practice as laid down in Art. 21 of Regulation (EC) No. 183/2005 have not been developed. The procedure for approval/registration of FBO is laid down by Regulation of the Cabinet of Ministries No 102. FBO already approved/registered under Directive 95/68/EC should, within three month since entering into force of this Regulation, submit an application to FVS in order to obtain an updated approval/ registration. The application form is provided by the Annex to the same Regulation. Operators not required to be registered/approved under the previous legal framework shall indicate type of activity/ies within three months and attach a complete dossier on the activity. They are requested to confirm their awareness concerning provisions of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and other national and Community requirements for animal feed before 1 January 2008. Before registering the operator is inspected by the OI. FBO to be approved are assessed by a specialist of FVS Animal Feed Surveillance Division from the central office. Observations: ¾ Despite the delayed start of implementation of the feed hygiene requirements, 94% of the establishments already approved/registered under Directive 95/68/EC have been re-approved/registered. The CCA was aware of the situations of the remaining ones, most of them being in one TSU. ¾ As regards food business operators supplying feed materials, they were already subject to official controls and the process for registration is ongoing. The CCA explained that some food operators requested such registration already at the beginning of 2006, having been informed of the requirements by their clients in the feed chain or by professional associations. (8) This refers notably to the definition of small quantities of primary production of feed which are directly supplied to local farms for use on those farms. 6 ¾ As regards the operators involved in grain drying and storage, they were already registered by FVS as food operators. As of May 2007 there were 279 grain drying operators and 267 grain storage operators listed. ¾ Primary producers keeping livestock are already registered by the ADC. In the current register there is no indication of the presence of on-farm mixers. The CCA stated that this information is being gathered and will be reflected in the future in the database. ¾ During the mission the CCA expressed their concerns about the problems of identifying and registering transporters and traders. 5.5.2.2. Transitional measures Observations: ¾ The procedure in place for registering new activities that were not approved/registered under 95/68/EC is in line with that laid down in Art. 18 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The CCA is applying the transitional measures laid down in this article: - for establishments and intermediaries requiring neither registration nor approval in accordance to Directive 95/68/EC, where they apply the deadline of 1 January 2008 to present the declaration of compliance with requirements of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and - the CA has taken into account systems already in place for the collection of data (e.g. food business operators lists, animal holdings register. 5.5.2.3. List of establishments Regulation of the Cabinet of Ministries No 102 establishes the Agricultural Data Centre as the CA for maintenance of the register of approved/registered FBOs. Until the register is not fully operational, the register of operators that are not primary producers is maintained by the FVS, which has established a list of feed operators, involved in all stages of food circulation. Any operator registered by FVS is in the list. The list is permanently updated. Information on registered and listed grain drying and storage operators is also publicly available on FVS home-page at: http://www.pvd.gov.lv/ 5.5.2.4.Amendments to statuses, including their suspension or revocation Observations: ¾ FBOs have the obligation to notify the CCA within ten working days of any change in the activity for which they have been approved/registered. ¾ The CCA stated that the feed law gives the right to the official services to revoke or cancel temporarily the approval and registration of establishments. This measure has not yet been used. 7 5.5.3. Specific obligations of primary producers 5.5.3.1. Hygiene provisions Observations: ¾ The FVS stated that hygiene requirements for primary producers of feed materials are, since January 2006, those set in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs (9). 5.5.3.2.Record-keeping Observations: ¾ In the feed mills visited the HACCP system included requirements for the primary producers supplying raw materials, which included records of use of plant protection products. At present, those records are under the official control of the State Plant Protection Service. The CCA expressed their intention to use the same records in the future for the purpose of feed controls. 5.5.3.3. Official inspections As regards control and supervision activities performed by FVS, grain drying and storage operators are inspected once a year. Observations: ¾ During 2006 approximately five percent of the total of animal holdings registered underwent an inspection. The CA informed that those inspections will be used to locate on-farm mixers and include some general questions on animal feeding. The CCA foresees to increase the animal holdings visited up to ten percent in 2007. ¾ During the mission the CCA expressed their concerns about the difficulties in the implementation of an own control system in all the primary producers. 5.5.4. Specific obligations of feed operators other than primary producers 5.5.4.1. Facilities and equipments Observations: ¾ The feed operators visited had adequate facilities to guarantee hygienic handling of feed materials and feedingstuffs. Maintenance programmes were in place and routine calibration was carried out. 5.5.4.2. Quality control and HACCP Observations: ¾ FBOs visited had put in place, implemented and maintained own control systems based on the principles of the HACCP system. Procedures were recorded and reviewed. Documents checked were up-to-date and records were complete. Comprehensive testing for hygiene parameters was carried out as part of their own control system in the feed mills and the food business operator visited. ¾ In the operator visited producing medicated feedingstuffs and coccidiostats, carry-over was included in the HACCP system, flushing was carried out routinely (9) Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs (OJ L 139, 30.4.2004, p. 1 ) 8 and contaminated material was adequately stored and labelled to be used in the next suitable batch. 5.5.4.3.Record-keeping and product recall Observations: ¾ All establishments visited had a recall system based on the traceability provided by production records. In the checks done during the visits the traceability of the batches forwards and backwards was successful. 5.5.4.4. Official inspections Observations: ¾ During 2006 a total of 4283 inspections were carried out, of which 139 were in feed mills. This figure is expected to increase during 2007. ¾ Food operators supplying feed materials are controlled by the FVS according to their activity in the food chain. LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general mandate of Articles 21 and 27a of Council Directive 2000/29/EC of 8 May 2000 on protective measures against the introduction into the Community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the Community. 4. RELEVANT COMMUNITY LEGISLATION Community legislation cited in this report refers, where applicable, to the version as last amended. The following legislation was of particular relevance for this mission: ­ Council Directive 2000/29/EC of 8 May 2000 on protective measures against the introduction into the Community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the Community; ­ Commission Directive 92/90/EEC4 of 3 November 1992 establishing obligations to which producers and importers of plants, plant products or other objects are subject and establishing details for their registration; ­ Commission Directive 93/50/EEC5 of 24 June 1993 specifying certain plants not listed in Annex V, part A to Council Directive 77/93/EEC, the producers of which, or the warehouses, dispatching centres in the production zones of such plants, shall be listed in an official register; ­ Commission Directive 98/22/EC of 15 April 1998 laying down the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks in the Community, at inspection posts other than those at the place of destination, of plants, plant products and other objects coming from third countries; ­ Commission Directive 94/3/EC6 of 21 January 1994 establishing a procedure for notification of interception of a consignment or a harmful organism from third countries and presenting an imminent phytosanitary danger; ­ Commission Regulation (EC) No 1756/20047 of 11 October 2004 specifying the detailed conditions for the evidence required and the criteria for the type and level of the reduction of the plant health checks of certain plants, plant products or other objects listed in Part B of Annex V to Council Directive 2000/29/EC; Previous missions to Denmark on import control This was the first mission on import control carried out by the FVO. The last mission carried out in Denmark concerned the plant passport system. The report can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm. 5.2. Import data There are 165 registered importers, among which 28 have been approved for control at the place of destination. In 2005, 2 348 consignments were checked. The distribution by categories was given to the mission team by lots; several lots can be gathered in a sole consignment. MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Single Authority and Responsible Official Bodies 6.1.1. Structure of the plant health system The Single Authority is the Department of Plants and Plant Health of the Danish plant Directorate (DPD-DPPH), which is one of the six departments of the Danish Plant Directorate (DPD). The DPD itself is part of the Danish Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries (DMFAF). Its headquarters is in Lyngby. Import inspections for plant health are carried out by staff in six district offices. This staff is in charge of tasks for DPD-DPPH, but also for other Departments of DPD, within a geographically delimited area. The sole official laboratory in charge of analysing samples taken during import inspections is part of the DPD and situated in Lyngby. 6.1.2. Human resources There are 25 inspectors in DPD involved, fully or partially, in performing phytosanitary inspections. Among them, the number involved by import inspections is 12. No inspector is fully employed in import inspections. He/she carries out other controls for plant health (inspections for export, surveys), for implementing the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and for checking conformity with the marketing standards applicable to fresh fruits and vegetables. 6.1.3. Training and working instructions A minimum of two days of training is given to all inspectors every year. The programme concerns the regulations, internal procedures and harmful organisms. It is organised by the DPD-DPPH, with the participation of the laboratory for the description of the harmful organisms and their symptoms. Furthermore, certain inspectors collaborate directly with specialist researchers on specific subjects. At all of the inspection posts and district offices visited by the team, books describing pests and diseases were present, and the inspectors demonstrated they had easy access to updated and illustrated data sheets on harmful organisms via the intranet of the DMFAF. Each inspector has a manual, the latest version of which was issued in November 2006. It describes the legislation, the importer's obligations, the performance of documentary, identity and plant health checks, and how to complete reports, take samples and reject consignments. There is no specific guideline describing methods for sampling on lots without symptoms, for example on plants intending for planting. 6.1.4. Internal communication Exchanges of information and experience takes place during the two-day courses, between headquarters and inspectors, and among the inspectors themselves. The inspectors at the DPD district office in Roskilde play a major role because they are in charge of Copenhagen airport which is the most important point of entry (see 6.5.1., 8 Table 3 ). Other informal meetings are held, bringing together the officials interested by a specific subject. The intranet is another important means of communication. Through this medium, headquarters promptly inform the inspectors of the latest news. In particular, headquarters inform the inspectors of interceptions made in the EU, providing an overview of the data provided by the EU information system EUROPHYT. Also, inspectors can ask questions or transmit their observations to headquarters or to their colleagues via a "forum". Specialised officials coordinate work nationally at headquarters, and they can be contacted directly by inspectors. 6.1.5. Financial resources and fees All of the costs of import inspections, including salaries and administrative tasks, are covered by the import fees. Fees are charged on a full-cost recovery basis. Registered importers are charged a registration fee once a year. In addition, they are charged for each consignment inspected; to that end, an invoice is issued on a monthly basis. The level of the fee was set on the basis of a specific cost calculation, but no evidence that a report specifying the method used or that such a report had been sent to the Commission was shown to the mission team. Details of the fees currently charged appear in the DPD Order No 1 720 of 21 December 2006. The income from fees for 2006 was estimated to be 2 600 000 Danish crowns, equivalent to around 348 400 euros. 6.1.6. Work planning and record keeping All consignments are checked at the time of their arrival. Inspection reports are kept for one year at the inspection posts and five years at headquarters. They are subsequently destroyed. The headquarters is responsible for collecting the data concerning the number of consignments inspected per year and per district. More detailed statistics concerning the lots imported are published on the public part of the DMFAF's website. They mention the countries of origin and the type of goods. However, since a number of lots can be grouped together in a single consignment, these statistics do not reflect the exact situation regarding consignments. The website also gives details of the number of lots refused. 6.2. National legislation and legal powers of inspectors EU directives are transposed by means of DPD Orders (Bekendtgørelsere). The rules on import controls laid down in Council Directive 2000/29/EC and in other EU implementing legislation on this subject, in particular Commission Directive 2004/103/EC, are provided in DPD Order No 100 of 17 February 2005 on the importation of plants and plant products. This Order allows the inspectors to access a consignment and possibly to intercept it before release. Furthermore, in any situation where harmful organisms are present or suspected to be present, DPD Order No 186 of 20 March 2003 on harmful organisms authorises inspectors to enter private property and to take appropriate measures. 9 6.3. Cooperation with customs and importers 6.3.1. Customs A formal general agreement between the DPD and the Danish customs authority is scheduled to be concluded before the end of the first quarter of 2007, but a special section of the customs instruction manual regarding plants and plant products has already been drawn up by the DPD-DPPH. This customs manual has been distributed to the local customs offices. The DPD-DPPH and Danish customs are currently involved in discussions with their Swedish counterparts with a view to concluding an agreement dealing with cases where the point of entry is in one of the two Member States and control at the place of destination is in the other. Customs officials at the local offices were found by the mission team to be fully aware of the phytosanitary part of the import control procedure. Both customs officials and DPD inspectors stated that they were satisfied with their collaboration Furthermore, each week, customs offices send the DPD's district offices a list of all the latest imported consignments containing plants or plant products. This gives the DPD inspectors an opportunity to carry out post entry checks on targeted non-regulated products. 6.3.2. Importers Two lists are available at the headquarters of DPD-DPPH: the list of registered importers, and the list of approved places of inspection. Importers met by the team were aware of their obligations under the import procedure. These obligations are listed in Annex 6 to DPD Order No 100 and take into account the obligations specified in Article 2(2) of Commission Directive 92/90/EEC and Article 13c(1) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. Whenever DPD Order No 100 is amended, the updated version is sent to all registered importers. Furthermore, the public part of the DMFAF's website presents the import control system and gives access to the current version of DPD Order No 100. However, the importers stressed that they obtain regular information chiefly through direct contact with the DPD inspectors, since they have plenty of occasions to meet them not only for import control but for various other reasons, e.g. export controls or control under marketing regulations. The importers therefore declared themselves satisfied with their collaboration with DPD inspectors. 6.4. Import procedures 6.4.1. General overview Importers have to be registered by the Single Authority. Advance notification has to be given at the latest 24 hours before arrival of the goods. It has to be sent preferably by fax to a single address operated in the DPD district of Roskilde. The form to be used (GA 140 (16)) is available on the DMFAF's website. The notification must be accompanied by a copy of the phytosanitary certificate. In a second step, all of these documents are forwarded to the customs office at the relevant point of entry and, if necessary, to the DPD's district office responsible for the point of entry. The goods are cleared through customs only when a copy of the notification and the inspection report, both signed by the DPD inspector with the DPD stamp, is submitted to customs, mentioning that the import check has been completed successfully. Then, if necessary, a plant passport is issued by the importers who are also authorised for this purpose. The inspectors take 10 advantage of the possibility to follow up the products, particularly plants intended for planting, by further survey in the fields, taking the occasion of other regular controls to be carried out (see 6.1.2.). The customs tariff identifies the products for which a plant health check is necessary. The customs officials are therefore able to verify whether the procedure has actually been initiated by the importers. If not, they warn the DPD inspectors. 6.4.2. Control at places other than point of entry Article 10 of DPD Order No 100 allows the possibility of the identity and plant health checks being carried out inside an approved place of inspection. The importer has to fill in and sign a plant health movement document. This document contains the required information in accordance with the model in the Annex to Commission Directive 2004/103/EC. It is faxed with the advance notification and with the phytosanitary certificate to the DPD district of Roskilde. Inspectors at Roskilde sign box 7 on the plant health movement document to certify that the documentary check has been performed and forward it, together with the other documents, to the customs office at the relevant point of entry and, if necessary, to the other DPD district office responsible for the approved place of inspection. The customs office then allows the goods to be moved to the approved place of inspection for identity and plant health checks. However, at one point of entry, the mission team found one case where a consignment was authorised by customs to be moved to the approved place of inspection despite the fact that customs had received a plant health movement document without the signature in box 7. The original certificate is received and verified at the DPD district office responsible for the approved place of inspection. The goods can be officially customs cleared only when the customs office at the point of entry receives a copy of the plant health movement document signed and stamped in boxes 8 and 9, certifying that the identity and plant health checks have been completed, in addition to the other documents as mentioned in point 6.4.1.. Agreements have been concluded with Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands to allow the possibility of a documentary check being carried out at one of the points of entry in these Member States, followed by the rest of the checks in an approved place of inspection in Denmark. The Single Authority stated that a list of the approved places has been provided to these Member States. In such cases, the plant health movement document and the phytosanitary certificate are transmitted to both the customs office and the DPD district office responsible for the approved place of inspection. After completion of the inspection, the relevant documents are signed and copies are sent for clearance to the customs office responsible for the approved place of inspection. Goods are currently imported by Sweden through points of entry in Denmark. In this case, the import controls are carried out entirely in Sweden. Goods are transferred from Denmark to Sweden without being opened and are accompanied by a T1 customs document. The Danish Single Authority is not aware of these transfers. In 2007, the Danish and Swedish Single Authorities have officially started discussions with a view to changing this situation (see point 6.3.1). Representatives of headquarters and DPD inspectors consider that cooperation between, on the one hand, customs and the departments in charge of import control in the points of 11 entry (in Denmark or in another Member State), and, on the other hand, their counterparts where the approved places of inspection are located, is satisfactory. 6.5. text: RELEVANT COMMUNITY LEGISLATION The following legislation4 was of particular relevance for this mission: ­ Council Directive 2000/29/EC of 8 May 2000 on protective measures against the introduction into the Community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the Community; ­ Commission Directive 92/90/EEC5 of 3 November 1992 establishing obligations to which producers and importers of plants, plant products or other objects are subject and establishing details for their registration; ­ Commission Directive 93/50/EEC6 of 24 June 1993 specifying certain plants not listed in Annex V, part A to Council Directive 77/93/EEC, the producers of which, or the warehouses, dispatching centres in the production zones of such plants, shall be listed in an official register; ­ Commission Directive 98/22/EC of 15 April 1998 laying down the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks in the Community, at inspection posts other than those at the place of destination, of plants, plant products and other objects coming from third countries; ­ Commission Directive 94/3/EC7 of 21 January 1994 establishing a procedure for notification of interception of a consignment or a harmful organism from third countries and presenting an imminent phytosanitary danger; BACKGROUND Unless otherwise stated, statistical data in this and the following chapters were provided by the Belgian authorities. 5.1. Previous missions The FVO had previously carried out a mission in 2003 in order to evaluate the system of import controls for plant health (ref: DG(SANCO)/9117/2003-MR). In the intervening time since this mission, the Community legislation relating to import controls has been revised, with a view to clarifying and harmonising import controls across the Community. Mission reports are available on the FVO website: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/index_en.htm . 5.2. Import data Approximately 18,000 consignments of regulated material, principally fruit and cut flowers, were imported into Belgium from Third Countries in 2006. Of these, 6,700 cleared customs controls in Belgium; the remainder were moved in transit to other Member States or Third Countries. In 2006, Belgium also received 951 consignments which entered the Community via the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Germany (see section 6.4.2 below). The majority of imports are through Antwerp, Bierset, Ghent, Ostende, Zaventem and Zeebrugge. 5.3. Interception data According to EUROPHYT, the Community's notification system for interceptions for plant health reasons, Belgium has notified a total of 654 interceptions of imported consignments between 2004 and 2006. These were for a variety of reasons as detailed in the following table: Table 5.1: Interceptions notified by Belgium (source: EUROPHYT) Reason 2004 2005 2006 Total 84 303 267 56 50 45 Presence of harmful organisms 19 103 68 Non-compliant wood packaging material

MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Single Authority and Responsible Official Bodies The structure of the plant health service in Belgium was described in detail in the previous mission report on this subject (DG(SANCO)/9117/2003). In summary: The responsibility for plant health is shared between the Plant Protection Division of the Federal Public Service for Health, Food Chain safety and Environment (FPS) and the Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain (FASFC). 7 The tasks and responsibilities of each of these entities have been defined in a common protocol signed on 22 October 2003. The FPS acts as the Single Authority in the sense of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The Plant Protection Division is part of the recently formed Sanitary Policy of Animals and Plants Service of the FPS. It is responsible for establishing national plant health policy, transposition of Community legislation and representing Belgium at Council. FASFC is responsible for establishing control policy and performing the official controls, including import checks. The FASFC consists of four Departments, two of which - the Control Policy Department and the Control Department ­ have responsibilities relating to import controls for plant health. ­ The Control Policy Department is responsible for developing control programs and related legislation. It also performs pest risk assessments in collaboration with an independent Scientific Committee. ­ The Control Department consists of the Central Service and 11 Provincial Control Units. The Central Service is responsible for planning and coordinating the work of the Provincial Control Units, which include the Border Inspection Posts (BIPs). 6.1.1. Human resources The Plant Protection Division of the FPS employs 4 full time equivalent (f.t.e.) specialist staff (compared to 2 f.t.e. reported in 2003). FASFC employs a total 1,290 staff covering all areas of their activity, including 162 staff based in the laboratories. 696 of these staff are based in the Provincial Control Units, 80 of which are inspectors and 115 are control officers in the primary production sector. 15 of these inspectors and 64 of the control officers have responsibilities for plant health, quality and pesticide residues (79 f.t.e. compared to a total of 75.5 reported in 2003). The number of inspectors in the BIPs has increased since the last mission to 26.05 f.t.e., mainly through the use of independent veterinary specialists. These are effectively retained staff and are called in as needed. Their contracts, which are signed by the head of the Provincial Control Unit, include a clause to prevent potential conflicts of interest. There is one plant health specialist in each Provincial Control Unit who acts as a co- ordination and reference point for the independent vets with regards to plant health issues. ¾ The independent vets met by the mission team had been trained in plant health and appeared to be fully familiar and competent regarding plant health matters. They work in rotation. (2) * API = Approved Place of Inspection 6.1.2. Training and working instructions FASFC has established training programmes for plant health, at central and regional level. Two training courses have been held in 2007; a five-day training course on the recognition of symptoms and harmful organisms, and a one-day course on phytosanitary legislation. New colleagues are trained "on the job" by experienced colleagues; there are no specific training courses on plant health arranged for newcomers. In addition, consultative meetings are held between the central Service of DG Control and the Provincial Control Units every two months in order to facilitate an exchange of experience. Changes in regard to import legislation, procedures or sampling methods are communicated to inspectors through instructions which are sent by e-mail to the heads of the Provincial units and are also available to inspectors on the FASFC intranet. Inspection guidelines and technical information have also been issued to inspectors. ¾ The inspectors met by the mission team appeared to be familiar with relevant legislation and technical information however in one case, the inspector was not fully aware of the guidelines issued by the FASFC. 6.1.3. Financial resources and fees FASFC is funded from the State Budget (45%) and operators (53%). Fees are payable for the plant health import checks and are the same as those established in Annex VIIIa to Directive 2000/29/EC. In 2007, the European Community will contribute the equivalent of 2% of the total budget, in the form of a financial contribution to strengthen inspection infrastructures, in line with the Commission Decision 2007/100/EC10. A reduced frequency of checks is applied at Antwerp. In such cases, the full fee established in Annex VIIIa of Directive 2000/29/EC is charged for those consignments that are inspected. FASFC informed the mission team that they had been advised by their 10 Commission Decision of 14 February 2007 on a Community financial contribution for Belgium for its programme for strengthening in 2007 inspection infrastructures for plant health checks on plants and plant products coming from third countries; O.J L 43, 15.02.2007, pg 37. 9 legal service that it is not lawful in Belgium for a fee to be charged unless a check has been performed and therefore, a proportionally reduced fee is not levied. 6.1.4. Work planning and record keeping FASFC's Control Policy Department establishes an annual control programme, which applies to the whole of Belgium. DG Control converts this into control plans on provincial level. Data relating to these plans as well as other control activities is recorded in FASFC's computer database 'Foodnet'. 6.2. National legislation and legal powers of inspectors Relevant Community legislation, including amendments to the Annexes to Directive 2000/29/EC, adopted since the mission in 2003, had been transposed into national legislation. ­ Directives 2000/29/EC, 92/90/EEC and 93/50/EC have been transposed by Royal Decree of 10 August 2005, which replaces the Royal Decree of 3 May 199411, as the primary legislation relating to plant health. ­ Directive 95/44/EC has been transposed by Ministerial Decree of 4 July 1996. ­ Directive 2004/103/EC has been transposed by Ministerial Decree of 23 December 2004. The Royal Decree of 10 August 2005 establishes the powers of inspectors, which include provisions to enter property, take samples, treat, destroy or refuse entry to consignments and to impose fines or seize material. 6.3. Cooperation with Customs, importers and agents 6.3.1. Customs A formal protocol was signed between FASCF and the Customs Service on 13 March 2007, and an updated version of the Customs instruction on Plant Health (D.I. 594.20/2) has been issued. This is available on the Customs Service website: www.fisconet.fgov.be A permanent coordination group, which includes representatives of the FASFC and Customs Service, has been established in order to discuss policy initiatives, increase cooperation and facilitate the flow of information. text: BACKGROUND At the time of accession in 2004, Cyprus was recognised as a protected zone for three 2 harmful organisms: Daktulosphaira vitifoliae (Fitch) (grapevive phylloxera), Ips sexdentatus Börner (six-toothed bark beetle), and Leptinotarsa decemlineata Say (Colorado beetle). The recognition was granted until 31 March 2006 and then subsequently extended until 31 March 2008, when the status will be evaluated again. By this date, Cyprus is expected to have submitted proof that its territory is appropriately surveyed and free from these harmful organisms. Cyprus has requested that it be recognised as a protected zone for Seiridium cardinale (W.W. Wagener) B. Sutton & I. Gibson, the fungus that causes Cypress canker. This request was considered by the Standing Committee on Plant Health in March 2006 (http://ec.europa.eu/food/fs/rc/scph/rap91_en.pdf), and the "Working Group on revision of the Annexes" was asked for technical examination. Further information on this subject was requested by both bodies. The FVO has previously carried out two missions to Cyprus. The reports from these are available on the FVO web-site: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm. The mission related to protected zones' status was the first one on this topic carried out by the FVO in Cyprus.

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1 SINGLE AUTHORITY AND RESPONSIBLE OFFICIAL BODIES Legal requirements Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC states that each Member State shall establish or designate a single authority, which shall be responsible for matters covered by this Directive. Article 1(3)(b) of Directive 92/70/EEC requires that regular and systematic official surveys on the presence of organisms in respect of which the protected zone has been recognised shall be carried out by persons entitled to act for the responsible official bodies in a Member State. Findings 5.1.1 Structure of the plant health system The structure and responsibilities of the plant health services in Cyprus have already been described in previous mission reports. Additional information is available in the FVO country profile (http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/CP_cyprus.pdf). In summary, the Department of Agriculture (DA) of the Ministry of Agriculture, Natural Resources and Environment acts as the Single Authority within the meaning of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC. Following a recent internal reorganisation, the DA has separated its control and advisory functions. The newly formed Plant Health and Quality Control Service (PHQCS) has become responsible for the implementation of the legislation and all plant health activities. The advisory work is carried out by the Plant Protection Service. The PHQCS head office, which is situated in Nicosia (which also services the Nicosia 3 and Pistislia districts), consists of several sectors, of which the Plant Health Sector (PHS) is the main unit involved in plant health issues. There are also district offices in Larnaca port, Larnaca airport (servicing the airport and both the Larnaca and Famagusta districts), Limassol (servicing the Limassol district and the port) and Paphos (servicing the Paphos district and airport). The PHQCS is responsible for transposing EU plant health legislation and other legislative work, preparation of annual control programs, coordination of the activities of the regional offices and points of entry, reporting, cooperation with the EC and international bodies. Local inspectors are responsible for a wide range of duties related to plant health control, and are also involved in seed and propagating material production, quality aspects and pesticide use control. Some are involved in import control. With regard to forestry issues, the PHQCS closely cooperates with the Forestry Department (FD), which is structured within the same Ministry. The Director of the DA has authorised FD officers to carry out inland phytosanitary controls of plant and plant products. 5.1.2 Human and financial resources In total, there are 38 officials in the PHQCS. Of these, 22 are agronomists (at least BSc degree in agriculture). There are in total 19 officials employed in the PHS: 15 agricultural and produce inspection officers, 3 agricultural supervisors, and 1 technician. In total, 18 inspectors are involved in surveys: 15 inspectors of the PHS (7 in the Nicosia district, 3 in Limassol, 2 in Larnaca, and 3 inspectors in the Paphos district), and 5 inspectors of the FD. In addition, officers from the Plant Propagating Material Sector and Quality Control Sector may also be involved in the surveys if needed. There are no special funds reserved for work in the surveys for harmful organisms. Funds are allocated to the general activities of the PHQCS and used according to the needs. The Director of the DA stated that the funds are sufficient enough to carry out the surveys in an unhampered way. Conclusions There is a clear structure and division of responsibilities among authorities involved in plant health control and surveys performance. All persons involved in surveys are duly entitled to act as required by the relevant EC legislation. 5.2 NATIONAL LEGISLATION AND LEGAL POWERS OF INSPECTORS Legal requirements Article 2(1) of Directive 92/70/EEC requires that Member States shall adopt necessary legislation at national level to comply with the relevant EC legislation. Article 1(3)(b) of the same Directive requires that surveys shall be carried out by persons who have the power to have access to all relevant grounds and to draw samples. Findings 4 The transposition of EU Directives is done in the form of Laws, Regulations and Orders. EU Decisions are implemented by way of Circulars, signed by the Director of the DA. The Law 147(I)/2003 is the primary legislation for plant health, approved by the Cypriot Parliament; it transposes most of the provisions of Directive 2000/29/EC and specifies the role, responsibilities and powers of the particular bodies involved. Community legislation relevant to the protected zones has been transposed into national legislation by way of regulations. Thus, Regulation ('! 760/2003 transposes Directive 92/70/EEC, ('! 768/2003 ­ 2001/32/EC, and ('! 755/2003 ­ 93/51/EEC. All legal acts are regularly amended if needed. The national legislation is published in the Official Journal of Republic of Cyprus. Conclusions Relevant Community legislation has been transposed into the national legislation and inspectors have adequate powers to enable them to carry out their tasks. 5.3 GENERAL ORGANISATION OF THE SURVEYS Article 2(1)(h) of Directive 2000/29/EC states that the Member State concerned shall conduct regular and systematic official surveys on the presence of organisms in respect of which the protected zone has been recognised. 5.3.1 National coordination and work planning Legal requirements Article 1(2)(b) of Directive 92/70/EEC requires that surveys programme shall be monitored by persons entitled to act for the responsible official bodies in a Member State. Findings All surveys are carried out at national level. The PHQCS is the sole body responsible for development, planning and coordination of survey activities. With regard to forestry pests, it strictly cooperates with the FD. For each survey a specific person has been designated as a national coordinator. All coordinators have to respond to the main coordinator in the head office in Nicosia. Each coordinator drafts annual reports and forwards them to the main coordinator. The main coordinator finalises the report and sends it to the Commission and other Member States. The main coordinator is informed of any problems that may arise during the surveys performance. An annual program is prepared each year with the number of establishments to visit, based on data kept in the Plant Health Official Register used for plant passporting purposes (see also section 5.4), and other sources of information. Cadastral maps are used for exact location of plots selected. In the case of forestry, coordinates of designated points are registered. Conclusions Surveys programmes are monitored in line with the relevant EC provisions. 5.3.2 Establishment of surveys methodology Legal requirements 5 Article 1(2)(a) of Directive 92/70/EEC requires that an official action programme shall be established which aims to seek confirmation that the relevant harmful organism of concern is not endemic or established in the protected zone concerned. Article 1(3)(a) of the same Directive, first indent, requires that a survey shall be based on understanding of the biology of the harmful organism of concern and of the agronomy and environment of the relevant zone using appropriate methods of analysis. Findings Survey programmes have been established at the head office level and are coordinated by survey coordinators. Various sources of information are used for this, including statistics on cultivation/growth, biology of the harmful organism of concern, meteorological data, environment, cultivation practices, data from import and EU internal movement. Detailed instructions have been issued for each type of surveys, available for inspectors in charge of surveys conduct. Details of surveys programmes for relevant harmful organisms of concern are provided in section 5.5. The mission team noted that: · In general, specialists from other bodies involved in production/growth of specific plant species (such as producers associations, private experts) and from laboratories were not consulted during programme establishment or revision. · In the case of surveys for Seiridium cardinale, no particular statistical principle and other criteria (such as host species, vector density) were used for designation of observation points. Conclusions The surveys methodologies for Daktulosphaira vitifoliae, Ips sexdentatus and Leptinotarsa decemlineata were established in line with the relevant EU requirements. The survey methodology for Seiridium cardinale is not fully adequate. See section 5.5 for details. Specialists from other bodies involved in the production or control of the relevant plant species were not involved either in the surveys establishment or in their review, which is not the optimal use of resources available in the country. 5.3.3 Training and working instructions Legal requirements Article 1(3)(b) of Directive 92/70/EEC requires that persons entitled to carry out the surveys shall have the qualifications necessary for the proper operation of the surveys. Findings The PHQCS has issued a number of general manuals dealing with all sorts of inspection activities and setting up the general rules of coordination and performance. In addition, specific guidelines for surveys, describing the surveys methodology, inspection procedures and providing some information on the harmful organisms of concern, such as symptom descriptions and images, have been issued. Since each point of entry and a district office of the PHQCS keeps at least one copy of such manual or guideline, every inspector has an easy access to these documents. The materials are regularly updated. 6 Specific technical training courses on the surveys and identification of the harmful organisms of concern that are targeted at all persons involved in the surveys are rare. At least twice a year (preferably in June and December) all persons responsible for surveys meet at the head office and discuss the relevant issues and problems encountered. The mission team visited some district offices and met several inspectors and noted that: · In the offices visited, relevant legislation, technical literature, manuals and other materials describing pests and diseases were present. Operational guidelines and instructions covering a wide range of aspects of plant health control were also available. There was also access to the Internet. · The PHQCS inspectors met appeared familiar with the harmful organisms of concern and competent to perform survey activities. · The FD officers met were not aware of all symptoms that may be produced by Seiridium cardinale (see section 5.5.4 for details). Conclusions The PHQCS inspectors have qualifications to carry out the relevant surveys. The FD officers are competent to carry out surveys for Ips sexdentatus, but are not fully prepared to carry out surveys for S. cardinale. 5.3.4 Contingency plans Legal requirements Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC requires that a Member State shall take all necessary measures to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the harmful organisms concerned. Findings No specific contingency plans have been prepared for the harmful organisms of concern. However, the PHQCS has established a general instruction to manage findings. There is also a national plan, although at early stage of its preparation, that in a case of finding of D. vitifoliae, Vitis crops would be replanted with the use of new seedlings grafted on resistant rootstock. Conclusions There is a general instruction on eradication of findings. This fulfills the requirement, but the specific instructions would guarantee an immediate and effective eradication of outbreaks of the harmful organisms of concern due to their specific features. 5.3.5 Diagnostic support and research Legal requirements Article 1(3)(a) of Directive 92/70/EEC, first indent, requires that surveys should be carried out using appropriate methods of analysis including growing medium and crop inspection and, if necessary, laboratory testing. Article 1(4)(e) of the same Directive requires that a survey shall comprise, in cases of doubt, laboratory testing of samples. 7 Findings Whenever possible, local inspectors can preliminary examine captured insects or samples of plant material. For this, basic laboratory equipment is used, such as microscopes (available in some district offices). Nevertheless, suspected samples are always sent to specialised laboratories for final confirmation. The Plant Protection Laboratory (PPL) operating within the DA is the main diagnostic unit for the plant health services. The laboratory of the Agricultural Research Institute (ARI) is mainly involved in research, but provides an additional diagnostic support and also serves as a reference laboratory. In some cases, samples may be sent abroad, e.g. to laboratories in Greece or to the Central Science Laboratory in the United Kingdom. The mission team visited both PPL and the laboratory of ARI and noted that: · PPL has basic equipment and facilities for detection and identification of bacteria, fungi, nematodes and insects. At present, the staff consist of 2 specialists with higher education and 6 technicians covering all main disciplines. Staff appeared to be trained and motivated and had developed some international contacts. Identification of fungi is generally based on plating methods and/or morphological examination of isolates under microscopes. Microscopy (both binocular and compound) is a basic method for identification of insects. Updated bibliography on symptoms and microscopic features of Seiridium and other fungi responsible of resinaceous cankers on Cupressaceae, and reference colonies of S. cupressi were lacking. · The laboratory of the ARI also has staff and good facilities, including molecular techniques, to detect and identify a wide range of harmful organisms. It also has special quarantine facilities to carry out research on living insects. Nevertheless, no particular research with the use of harmful organisms of concern was carried out at the time of the mission. · In both laboratories, samples for the presence of harmful organisms of concern are very rare. The 2007 case of examination of plant material suspected to be infected with Seiridium cardinale was eventually confirmed in a laboratory in Greece. Conclusions The laboratory operating within the DA provides the basic diagnostic support, and can be supported by the laboratory of the ARI and laboratories from other Member States. Therefore, this specific legal requirement is fulfilled. 5.3.6 Internal communication and record keeping Legal requirements Article 1(3)(a) of Directive 92/70/EEC, third indent, requires that survey programmes should comprise a system of keeping records of the results. Findings There are internal communication procedures that provide easy and instant communication between all the staff involved in the surveys on various levels. For these, meetings, consultations, telephones, faxes, postal and electronic mail are used. The 8 PHQCS has not established a central computerised database, therefore any information and reports are prepared and sent with the use of commonly accessible software, such as word processors and spreadsheets. All surveys activities are adequately registered and every inspection is documented. For this, specific forms are used, different for each type of crop or pest species involved. They include particulars related to a producer, observation point location, inspection outcome, etc. All data and statistics are recorded as both hard copies and in electronic form. Official registers are also saved as backup on CDs. The PHQCS is responsible for collection and synthesis of data from surveys. All records are collected by the coordinators in charge of the relevant harmful organism and notified to the PHQCS head office. The final report is drafted by the main coordinator. Copies of the forms completed for each harmful organism by inspectors are collected and sent to the head office in Nicosia by the end of the year. Before that date, data may be sent to the head office either electronically or by fax, if need be. · The mission team saw the relevant records and registers both in the head office and the district offices visited. Conclusions There is a good internal communication and system of record keeping in place that meets this specific requirement of the EC legislation. 5.4 COOPERATION WITH PRODUCERS AND STAKEHOLDERS Legal requirements Article 6(5) of Directive 2000/29/EC requires that all producers of products, which must be accompanied by a plant passport when moved within the EU, must be officially registered.
