All legal references relevant for this mission are listed in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND The previous mission concerning feed safety in Lithuania was carried out from 10 to 14 October 2005, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/7692/2005 ­ MR Final (hereafter: report 7692/2005). This report is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/comm/food/index_en.htm The report made a number of recommendations to the CCA, which subsequently informed the Commission of actions that had been/would be taken aimed at addressing the recommendations made (hereafter: action plan). Where appropriate, both the relevant recommendations and the action plan are outlined under Section 5. Since the previous mission, the relevant EU legislation concerning feed safety has been modified significantly. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 has introduced a harmonised framework of general rules for the organisation of official controls on food and feed so as to integrate them at all stages of production and sectors, using the "farm to fork" principle. Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 recognised the need to ensure feed safety starting with primary production of feed and comprising also the transport, storage and handling of feed; moreover, procedures based on the principles of hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) should be in place for feed business operators (FeBOs) (except at the level of primary production of feed and certain associated operations), and the compulsory registration of all FeBOs was introduced. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 INFORMATION ON THE FEED SECTOR According to CCA, 35 commercial feed mills and 74,000 farmers mixing exclusively for the requirements of their holdings (hereafter: on-farm mixers), produced approximately 3 850,000 tonnes of compound feedingstuffs (CFS) in 2008. The Lithuanian production of premixtures was ensured by four operators and amounted to 2,300 tonnes. In 2008, the national production of CFS was mainly destined to the feeding of fur animals (42%), pigs (33%) and cattle (12%). These figures are based on data provided by FeBOs, which, under national legislation, must communicate their annual production to SFVS territorial services. There are two main industry organisations whose members manufacture or place on the market most of CFS and pet food produced: · The Lithuanian Grain Industry Association. The members of this organisation (nine operators) cover around 90 % of the total production of CFS. · The Baltic Petfood Association. The members of this organisation (three operators) account for approximately 98% of pet food production. According to the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), several guides to good practice have been developed by the grain production sector. However, none of them have been yet submitted to MoA for being assessed according to the provisions of Art. 21 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and, therefore, they are not considered as official national guides to good practice for the production of feed. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.2.1 Organisation and responsibilities Legal Requirements Art. 4.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires Member States to designate the competent authorities (CAs) responsible for official controls. Findings The relevant recommendation of report 7692/2005 concerned the distribution of responsibilities between CAs in charge of feed controls. In response to this recommendation, the CCA undertook to draft a control programme that would better define the distribution of tasks between central and local services. SFVS, a governmental agency whose director is accountable to the Prime Minister, is the CCA responsible for the organisation of official controls on feed. At central level, the Animal Health and Welfare Department (AHWD) of SFVS is mainly involved in planning, guidance preparation, instructions drafting and coordination activities. SFVS territorial services (ten counties, five cities and 34 districts) ensure the implementation of official controls on feed. MoA is responsible for drafting feed legislation and, through the State Seed and Grain Service (SSGS), ensures the registration and approval of FeBOs. SSGS is also in charge of keeping the list of FeBOs up to date. The State Plant and Protection Service (SPPS), placed under the remit of MoA, in involved in controls over the use of plant protection products, including on crops intended for feed production. In July 2008, important changes occurred in SFVS structure. In particular, the Lithuanian State Inspectorate for Veterinary Preparation (LSIVP), CA formerly in charge of certain 4 tasks related to feed controls, ceased to exist. After the reorganisation, LSIVP tasks were distributed as follows: · Inspections of all FeBOs, controls on the use of medicated feed and the implementation of the national monitoring programme for feed (NMPF ­ official sampling and analyses for undesirable substances, antibiotics and coccidiostats) were attributed to SFVS territorial services. · The design of the NMPF was transferred to the National Food and Veterinary Risk Assessment Institute (NFVRAI). · The overall coordination and supervision of feed controls carried out by SFVS territorial services were given to AHWD. NFVRAI was established in July 2008 and placed under the authority of SFVS director. As part of its responsibility for risk assessment, NFVRAI participated in the drafting of the NMPF for 2009. According to the CCA, NFVRAI was also consulted in the process which led to the design of the new risk-based approach to inspections in FeBOs (see 5.3). The CCA stated that these changes were prompted by the need to clarify the distribution of responsibilities for feed controls and also to set up a risk assessment process in line with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. The mission team noted that: · At central level and in all SFVS territorial services visited, there was a good understanding of the distribution of responsibilities as regards feed controls. No overlaps between tasks performed by different CAs were identified. · No CA has been designated for the implementation of official controls in primary producers of feed that do not keep animals. Consequently, this verification is not performed. According to the CCA, there is a legal loophole that does not allow SFVS to verify compliance with Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 in such FeBOs. Conclusions A redistribution of responsibilities within the CCA has recently taken place. This new organisation has resulted in a clearer attribution of control tasks and it is well understood by SFVS staff. However, no CA has been designated for implementing controls in certain operators at the level of primary production of feed. This is not in line with the requirements of Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2 Cooperation and coordination Legal Requirements Art. 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 provides for efficient and effective coordination and cooperation between CAs. Art. 4.5 of the said Regulation requires that, when, within a CA, more than one unit is competent to carry out official controls, efficient and effective coordination and cooperation shall be ensured between the different units. 5 Findings Within SFVS, territorial services are in charge of the implementation of feed controls. Depending on the territorial level (county, district or city), responsibilities vary: · County and city services are in charge of all approved and registered FeBOs in their territory, with the exception of registered on-farm mixers. · District services are responsible for inspections to on-farm mixers and farmers using feed that are located in their territory. · County services are responsible for border inspection posts (BIPs) in which are notably performed controls on imported feed. · County, district and city services are in charge of implementing the NMPF and taking samples on imported feed when BIP inspectors have requested such samples. At territorial level, inspectors in charge of feed controls are usually assigned to the animal health and welfare divisions while inspectors in charge of food operators are posted in the food safety divisions. According to the CCA, cooperation arrangements are in place between competent authorities involved in controls over the feed chain. In particular, an inter-institutional working group has been set up to facilitate the exchange of information between SFVS, SSGS and SPPS. There are also several cooperation agreements signed between Customs services, SPPS and SFVS in relation to import of feed. The mission team noted that: · Shortcomings related to incomplete or inaccurate records on the use of pesticides by primary producers of feed, including on-farm mixers, are not communicated to SFVS when they are identified by SPPS inspections. SPPS only liaises with SFVS when the use of non-registered plant protection products is detected or when indications for use are not followed, as in such cases samples must be taken by SFVS for the detection of residues. · Many FeBOs are approved or registered for activities they do no carry out. This information was known by the SFVS inspectors met but was not communicated to SSGS, which, therefore, could not ensure that the national list of FeBOs was kept up to date (see 5.5.2.3). · SSGS received applications for registration of food operators as part of the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. These applications contained information about food operators supplying feed as co-products of their main activity. This information has not been communicated to the CCA, resulting in some SFVS territorial services which were not always aware of the existence of such FeBOs. In order to improve this situation, the CCA recently requested all territorial services to investigate such activities. · Food inspectors from a city SFVS visited had identified that a large brewery was supplying co-products used as feed by several farms. The inspector responsible for feed controls in the same city SFVS was not aware of this activity as he had not been informed about it. Consequently, this brewery was not included in the planning of feed inspections. 6 · Feed inspectors in charge of an approved intermediary had identified that this operator was supplying several FeBOs with a feed additive not authorised under Community legislation. These inspectors had not informed the SFVS territorial services responsible for the feed operators to which this non-authorised additive was dispatched for the production of feed intended to be placed on the market in third countries. During the mission, immediate action was taken in order to pass on the information to all concerned SFVS services. Conclusions Arrangements for cooperation and coordination between CAs involved in feed controls have been put in place. However, the level of co-operation remains limited and adversely affects the organisation of official controls and the updating of the list of feed operators. Similarly, in some cases, limited communication between SFVS territorial services can also affect the implementation of official controls. This does not ensure that the efficient and effective cooperation required by Artt. 4.3 and 4.5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 is achieved. 5.2.3 Resources and training Legal Requirements Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the CA to ensure that they have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff; that appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment are available. Art. 6 of the said Regulation requires CAs to ensure that staff receive appropriate training, and are kept up-to-date in their competencies. Findings The relevant recommendation of report 7692/2005 concerned the training of inspectors in charge of feed controls. In response to this recommendation, the CCA undertook to organise training courses on feed hygiene requirements. Within SFVS territorial services, 53 inspectors were involved in feed controls in 2008. They are not dedicated feed inspectors as they also perform other controls tasks, in particular in the area of animal health and animal welfare. In 2008, it was estimated that the annual number of inspections performed per inspector ranged between 20 and 168. According to the CCA, 190 inspections per year and per inspector would be the maximum achievable. Every year, a training programme for SFVS staff is drafted. According to the CCA, the evaluation of SFVS officials that is performed every four years is used as the main basis for determining the areas for which further training is required. The evaluation forms filled in on completion of training courses are also used to identify additional training needs. The mission team noted that: · In all SFVS territorial services visited, resources were present to allow for regular inspections to FeBOs and for samples on feed to be taken and analysed. In 2007 and 2008, 1,100 and 1,300 inspections were respectively carried out. In 2009, according 7 to the new risk-categorisation, and based on the number of feed operators registered in the national database, a minimum number of 9,000 inspections could be planned. According to the CCA, such an increase in the number of inspections is achievable as the verification of compliance with feed hygiene requirements in farms could be performed during animal identification checks. Indeed, 90% of registered FeBOs are on-farm mixers. · In 2006 and 2007, several training courses concerning official controls on feed were organised by the CCA. In 2009, additional training on that topic has been planned but only for a limited duration (four hours). · Food and Veterinary Internal Audit Service (FVIAS) auditors are invited to all training courses organised by SFVS. In 2009, training courses on audit techniques are planned and will cover the organisation and performance of audits, drafting of reports and implementation of follow-up activities. · The feed inspectors met had participated in training courses on feed controls and feed hygiene requirements. However, most of them had still a limited knowledge about very basic requirements of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. This resulted in important shortcomings being overlooked during official controls (see 5.5.4.2) Conclusions The CCA can avail of the sufficient and adequate resources referred to in Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in order to organise official controls on feed. In the future, the new prioritisation of official controls, if applied as currently designed, will result in a significant increase in the number of inspections to be carried out (at least seven time as much as in 2008) and will mobilise much more resources than those presently available. Arrangements are in place to identify training needs and organise training courses when required. However, given that official controls on feed can overlook basic feed hygiene requirements, training arrangements on feed hygiene rules are insufficient to ensure that SFVS staff performing official controls carry out their tasks competently and in the consistent manner required by Art. 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.4 Internal supervision Legal Requirements Art. 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that the CCA must have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls, to ensure effectiveness of corrective action and to update documentation where needed. Findings The relevant recommendation of report 7692/2005 concerned the implementation of an internal supervision system. In response to this recommendation the CCA undertook to draft a procedure for the evaluation of the effectiveness of official controls on feed. According to SFVS, the verification of the effectiveness of official controls on feed is performed in two different ways: · Territorial SFVS must report to AHWD about the number of inspections carried out 8 and their outcome as well as the number of samples taken and the result of the analyses performed. This information is subsequently analysed by the CCA and used as indicators to follow the implementation of official controls on feed. In 2009, the CCA issued a new set of instructions to improve the flow of information from territorial SFVS, in particular new templates for submitting data to AHWD. For import controls, databases are in place and contain information on the nature of the feed imported through BIPs, and the analyses planned and performed as part of physical checks. The CCA has recently set up a new database that unifies the information contained in different computerised systems and that aims at facilitating the supervision of import controls by AHWD. · All county, city and district SFVS officials performing controls are evaluated every four years. This assessment is carried out by the Strategic Planning and Quality Department (SPQD) of SFVS and comprises the evaluation of the inspectors' professional skills through various tests and joint inspections. Until July 2008, LSIVP was carrying out joint inspections with territorial feed inspectors. According to LSIVP, one of the objectives was to evaluate the performance of territorial inspectors. text: BACKGROUND 2 The total feed ban is one important tool in the package of measures to control transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSE). It aims at ensuring that possible TSE agents can not (re)circulate in susceptible species via feeding practices. Its effective application is therefore of paramount importance in preventing future BSE cases. Implementing measures pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002 as regards OF/SI entered into force in April 2006, in the form of Regulation (EC) No 181/2006. Both Regulations established rules to allow placing on the market of OF/SI under conditions which prevent their misuse, in particular that the material is not fed to animals. The previous mission where the total feed ban was covered was carried out from 27 February to 10 March 2006, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/2006/8068 - MR Final (hereafter: report 2007/8068). Another mission carried out from 27 February to 10 March 2006 evaluated the implementation of health rules on ABP, the results of which are described in report DG(SANCO)/8087/2006 - MR Final (hereafter: report 8087/2006). These reports together with previous reports covering the same scope are accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm In response, the CCA provided the FVO with the actions planned and/or undertaken to address the recommendations contained in report 2006/8068 (hereafter: action plan). Where appropriate, relevant recommendations are indicated under the appropriate section headings in Chapter 5 below. The corresponding actions as announced in the action plan are outlined thereafter.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES The main features of the organisation of the CA in the context of the scope of this mission can be found in the country profile for Germany; which is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/CP_germany.pdf 5.1.1 Organisation and responsibilities Legal requirements Art. 4.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires Member States to designate the competent authorities (CAs) responsible for official controls. Findings The mission team noted that: The CCA for the topics covered by this mission is BMELV. The implementation and control of the total feed ban and the use of OF/SI lies with the Länder: a) in Lower 3 Saxony the Ländesamt für Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit (State office for consumer protection and food safety ­ LAVES) is responsible for total feed ban controls while the Ländwirtschaftkammer (Agricultural Chamber) is responsible for controls on use of fertilisers (including OF/SI); b) in Schleswig-Holstein total feed ban controls are the responsibility of the Amtliche Futtermitteluberwachung Ländeslabor Schleswig-Holstein (Schleswig-Holstein state laboratory for the supervision of feeding stuffs ­ AFLSH), while the Landesamt für Landwirtschaft, Umwelt und ländliche Räume (Land Office for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Areas) implements controls on use of OF/SI on farms. Official controls on the production of OF/SI are the responsibility of the Ministerium für Ländwirtschaft Umwelt und ländliche Raume des Landes Schelswig-Holstein (Schleswig-Holstein Ministry for agriculture, the environment and rural spaces) and are carried out under their instruction by the Agricultural Chamber. Conclusion In both Länder visited the responsibilities of the CAs for total feed ban control and controls of OF/SI were well defined, as required by Art. 4.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.2 Cooperation and coordination Legal Requirements Art. 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 provides for efficient and effective coordination and cooperation between CAs. Art. 4.5 of the said Regulation requires that, when, within a CA, more than one unit is competent to carry out official controls, efficient and effective coordination and cooperation shall be ensured between the different units. Findings The mission team noted that: · There is no system for routine communication of information on which farms are using OF/SI from the CAs responsible for controlling the use of OF/SI to the CAs responsible for controlling the total feed ban. Therefore, the latter CAs do not know in which farms OF/SI are being used, and they are unable to target their controls accordingly. · Checks on the use of OF/SI on farms did not focus on the possible illegal feeding of OF/SI to animals. However, the mission team was informed that if if there were suspicions of illegal use of OF/SI for feeding animals the information would be passed to the CAs responsible for total feed ban control for further investigation. Conclusion In both Länder visited there was insufficient communication and coordination between the CAs responsible for control of the total feed ban and the CAs responsible for controlling the use of OF/SI. This, which affects the targeting of on farm controls to verify implementation of the total the feed ban, is not in compliance with Art. 4.3 of 4 Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.3 Resources and training Legal Requirements Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the CA to ensure that they have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff; that appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment are available. Art. 6 of the said Regulation requires CAs to ensure that staff receive appropriate training, and are kept up-to-date in their competencies. Findings The mission team noted that: · In both Länder visited the mission team met staff at all organisational levels that were suitably qualified and trained to carry out work related to the implementation of the total feed ban and controlling the use of ABP as OF/SI. · In the Länder visited sufficient staff were available to carry out controls in respect of the implementation of the total feed ban and on the production of OF/SI and its use on farms. · In the Länder visited, the 2007 targets for sampling to detect the illegal use of animal protein in animal feeds, set out in the national framework plan for control activities in the feed sector, (see section 5.2.2 below) were not reached. In particular there was a shortfall of samples taken in Lower Saxony due to staff being diverted to deal with a dioxin contamination incident. However, the numbers samples taken were in line with the latest recommendations in Commission Recommendation 2005/925 on the coordinated inspection programme in the field of animal nutrition. Conclusion Staff met in the Länder visited are suitably qualified and experienced. Commission Decision 2003/766/EC, Article 2(1), states that Member States shall each year conduct official surveys for the presence of Diabrotica virgifera in areas in their territory, where maize is grown. Article 2(2) of the same Decision requires the results of these surveys be notified to the Commission and to the other Member States by 31 December of each year. Commission Decision 2004/200/EC, Article 4, states that Member States shall conduct official surveys on premises involved in the production of tomato plants and tomato fruits, for the presence of Pepino mosaic virus, the results of which shall be notified to the Commission and to the other Member States. Commission Decision 2006/464/EC, Article 5(1), requires Member States to conduct official annual surveys for the presence of Dryocosmus kuriphilus in their territory. The results of those surveys shall be notified to the Commission and to the other Member States by 31 December of each year. Commission Decision 2007/410/EC, Article 3(1), requires Member States to conduct official surveys, and where appropriate, testing, for the presence of Potato spindle tuber viroid on host plants or evidence of infection by this harmful organism in their territory. The results of those surveys shall be notified to the Commission and the other Member States. Commission Decision 2007/433/EC, Article 5(1), requires Member States to conduct official annual surveys for the presence of Gibberella circinata in their territory. The results of those surveys shall be notified to the Commission and to the other Member States by 15 December of each year. 37 All above mentioned legal acts lay down that Member States should, if necessary, adapt their legislation in order to comply with the Decisions. Audit findings The SA stated that above mentioned decisions are directly applicable in Greece and that no transposition is needed. They also stated that the relevant susceptible plants, i.e. host plants of the concerned harmful organisms, grow on the Greece territory. The SA informed regional and local units in due time of the requirements of the Decisions and, as in the case of other activities, left it at their discretion to organise the specific surveys. The SA could not provide any details on the subject, such as numbers of inspections or their results. Therefore, the mission team addressed this issue during its visits in the RCPPQCs and RDDPs and found that: ¾ Officials from the RCPPQCs and RDDPs visited were generally aware that the above mentioned decisions are in force and that surveys should be carried out. ¾ No co-ordination of specific surveys had been established and specific instructions, guidelines or programmes had been developed either. Specific training courses on these subjects had never been delivered to plant health inspectors. ¾ None of the officials met by the mission team could state that there had been any kind of activity as regards surveying of their territories for the presence of the above mentioned harmful organisms (such as inspections or, where relevant, deployment of pheromone traps). ¾ The SA stated that, to their knowledge, the situation in other regions and prefectures is the same, i.e. none of these specific surveys are carried out. The SA stated that, similar to the surveys required for protected zones' recognition, they had taken considerable steps to improve the situation and to start conducting official surveys as required by EC legislation. To this end detailed survey protocols had been drafted by the BPI and they are in the final stage of their development and approval. The Forest Service is, in cases where it concerns sylvan areas, also expected to participate in these surveys. ¾ The mission team saw drafts of the relevant survey protocols, both in the SA seat and in the BPI. Conclusions All EC emergency decisions are directly applied in Greece and no additional national legislation has been issued. However, systematic surveys for the following harmful organisms regulated by the EC emergency decisions are not carried out: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pine wood nematode), Diabrotica virgifera, Dryocosmus kuriphilus, Gibberella circinata, Pepino mosaic virus, Phytophthora ramorum, Potato spindle tuber viroid. Since no surveys are carried out, no data can be recorded and reported to the Commission. 5.5.3. General conclusions for the EC Emergency Decisions The territory of Greece has never been systematically surveyed for the presence of harmful organisms regulated by relevant EC emergency decisions, and the status of the country with regard to the presence or absence of these organisms is not known. Therefore, with the exception of Rhynchophorus ferrugineus, Greece does not fulfil their requirements with regard to conducting regular and systematic official surveys required by relevant EC emergency measures. 38 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION Not all activities and controls required by EC plant health regime have been implemented in Greece. Some of the official controls, particularly those related to imports, are largely in line with the requirements of Community legislation. However, there are many areas which have remained unaddressed. This in particular concerns surveys required for protected zones and those required by EC emergency measures. There has also been no adequate response to the previous FVO mission related to the potato sector, and measures imposed in case of potato ring rot or brown rot are not in line with EC legislation. Detailed conclusions are included in the relevant sections in Chapter 5. The SA is aware of the weaknesses and there are plans to improve the situation, in particular with regard to the official surveys, amongst others by involvement of the Forest Service in the plant health controls system, and development of survey programmes. 7. NRL Centre for Animal Health, Sofia VACCINE DISTRIBUTOR 1 Subcontractor responsible for the aerial vaccination programme 3 LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Union legislation and, in particular, Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules. Full legal references are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND The Community-funded rabies eradication programmes have been approved since 2007 and include biannual oral vaccination campaigns in wildlife reservoirs, and controls to monitor the efficacy of these campaigns. However, for financial reasons, implementation of these multi-annual plans only began in January 2009. At the time of the mission, the independent subcontractor (responsible for the aerial distribution of vaccine bait) was awaiting the transfer of funds to begin the autumn campaign. The annual plans for 2009 and 2010 were approved by Commission Decisions 2008/897/EC and 2009/883/EC respectively. 1 Data The CCA provided details of confirmed cases of rabies and the total number of investigations (in brackets), which are summarised as follows: Domestic Other domestic animals Wild animals Total carnivores Year 6 49 59 (417) 2009 4 6 (141) 2010 0 2 4 Initially, the vaccination area covered the entire Bulgarian territory north of the Balkan range, as these mountains have provided a natural barrier to the spread of rabies from north to south. Following a number of outbreaks south of the Balkan range in 2007 (South West Bulgaria) and 2008 (Burgas), the NVS extended the programme to cover the relevant regions/municipalities. Historically, the incidence of rabies has fluctuated significantly over time. While a recent peak was noted between 2007 to 2009, the incidence of the disease in domestic and wild animals appears to be declining once again. There have been no cases of human rabies since 2001. The objective of the programme in 2011 is to ensure eradication of rabies on the territory of Republic of Bulgaria. This vaccination is to be performed for a further period of at least 5 years (i.e. 2011 - 2016), twice per year in spring and autumn (April-May and September-October). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5 RABIES ERADICATION PROGRAMME 5.1 Legal requirements Prior to 24 May 2009, Article 24 of Council Decision 90/424/EEC empowered the Commission to reimburse from Community funds the expenditure incurred by MSs in the course of implementing national programmes for the eradication, control and monitoring of certain animal diseases and zoonoses, including rabies. From that date, Articles 25, 26 and 27 of Council Decision 2009/470/EC provide equivalent powers.

BCP Riga - port Establishments Food producers ­ users of FCM 2 Dairy, brewery Supermarket 1 User and seller of FCM 1 3 LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION 3.1.1 Legal basis for the audit The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation, in particular: · Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Full references to the acts quoted in this report are given in Annex 1. 3.1.2 Relevant legislation The audit was carried out under the following EU legislation: · Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2002 laying down the general principles and requirements of food law, establishing the European Food Safety Authority and laying down procedures in matters of food safety; · Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules; · Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 October 2004 on materials and articles intended to come into contact with food and repealing Directives 80/590/EEC and 89/109/EEC; Further relevant legislation is listed in Annex. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 Audit Series Between 2007 and 2010, the FVO carried out a series of audits to 19 Member States (MSs) of the EU to examine controls for FCM. As part of this series, the FVO carried out a mission to Latvia in November 2009 report DG(SANCO)8174/2009. The report of this mission can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/ir_search_en.cfm In the mission report DG(SANCO)8174/2009 a number of shortcomings were identified, related to the implementation of EC legislation on FCM especially the lack of official controls of FCM business operators and the incomplete assessment of the declaration of compliance(DoC) for FCM. 2 4.2 COUNTRY PROFILE The FVO has published a country profile for Latvia, which describes in summary form the control systems for food and feed safety, animal health, animal welfare, and plant health, and gives an overview of the state of play regarding the recommendations from previous FVO missions. The country profile for Latvia can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles_en.cfm 4.3 ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND As regards FCM, 1000 notifications, mainly concerning materials from Third Countries (TCs) and to a lesser extent from MSs, have been notified through the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) in the last four years. These break down as follows: 192 notifications in 2006, 172 in 2007, 206 in 2008, 197 in 2009 and 233 in 2010. The following hazards were reported: primary aromatic amines, semicarbazide, Di-2- ethylhexyl-adipate, formaldehyde, heavy metals (lead, cadmium, chromium, nickel, iron, manganese and zinc), excessive total migration, organoleptic properties, isopropyl thioxanthone, benzophenone, 4-methylbenzophenone and phthalates e.g. Di-2-ethyl hexyl phthalate, Di-n-butyl phthalate. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements The EU legislation requiring transposition is listed in Annex1. Findings The main legislation establishing the responsibilities of the Competent Authorities (CAs) is the Law On Supervision of the Handling of Food. To address the first recommendation from report DG(SANCO)8174/2009 (to carry out official controls in FCM manufacturing, processing and distributing establishments), the Law On The Supervision of the Handling of Food was amended in November 2010 and responsibilities were clearly defined. The amendment will come into force on 1 January 2012. The audit team was informed that the legislation to implement the changes in the Law On the Supervision of the Handling of Food is being drafted. The CAs stated that it would be adopted by the end of 2011. The CAs stated that there had been no changes in national FCM legislation not covered at EU level. 3 Conclusions The amended national legislation provides legal powers for FCM controls. The amendment will enter into force on 1 January 2012. The first recommendation from mission DG(SANCO)8174/2009 has been addressed. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.2.1 Designation of Competent Authorities Legal requirements Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires MSs to designate the CAs responsible for official controls. Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 sets out the scope of possible delegation to control bodies, the criteria for delegation, and the minimum criteria which must be met by control bodies Findings Since the last mission there have been done following changes in desigantion of the CAs : · According to the changes in the Law On the Supervision of the Handling of Food from 2012 the Food and Veterinary Service (FVS) is the only CA with responsibility for official controls of FCM (FCM operators and FCM users). · In September 2010 there was a reorganisation of The Food Surveillance Department within the FVS and four divisions were created. They are: the Products of Plant Origin, Beverages and Organic Farming Surveillance Division (6 staff members), the Products of Animal Origin, Production Surveillance Division (9 staff members), the Food Distribution Surveillance Division (5 staff members) and the Food Surveillance, Planning, Analysis and Establishment Approval Division (5 staff members). All these divisions have responsibilities for the official controls of FCM. Since the last mission there have been no changes in Territorial Structural Units (TSUs) structure. Border control administration within the FVS consist from the administrative block on the central level with 10 officers and 11 Border Controls Posts (BCP) with 57 staff involved in FCM controls. The CA responsible for receiving the applications for authorisations, as referred to in Articles 9 - 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004, was renamed as the FVS Assessment and Registration Agency on 1 January 2011. Conclusions The CAs in the context of this audit have been designated. 4 5.2.2 Resources for Performance of Controls Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the CA to ensure that they have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff; that appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment are available. Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires CAs to ensure that staff receive appropriate training, and are kept up-to-date in their competencies. Findings The CAs informed the audit team that there was no reduction in the number of staff since the last audit. The annual training plan is established in September and is prepared by the planning division in consultation with the other departments dealing with food safety controls. In 2010 seven persons participated in Better Training for Safer Food on FCM, one of whom was an inspector from TSU. There was no specific training provided to inspectors on the assessment of the DoC. All inspectors met stated that they received limited or no specific FCM training and that they need such specific training see point 5.3.4. In Tucums and Jelgava TSUs, the audit team was informed, that in May and June 2010 all staff of the TSUs responsible for official controls of FCM participated in the compulsory annual training course, which included one lecture on FCM legislation. In November and December 2010 training was organised for all inspectors from the BCPs which included two lectures on FCM legislation. In December 2010 training was organised for inspectors from TSU Riga on the amended FCM methodology instructions, that entered into force on 3rd January 2011. The audit team was informed, that each TSU will receive this training by September 2011. Conclusions The CAs have qualified and experienced staff available. There were numerous trainings since the last mission on legislation, but training on the assessment of the DoC was inappropriate. 5.3 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Registration / approval of food business operators Legal requirements Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires MSs to establish procedures for the 5 registration / approval of food and feed business operators, for reviewing compliance with conditions of registration and for the withdrawal of approvals. Findings Currently the FCM operators are not subject of official control by FVS. However, the changes made in the Law On the Supervision of the Handling of Food will provide the legal basis for the registration of FCM operators from 2012. Conclusions The registration of FCM operators is still not in place and will be obligatory from 2012. 5.3.2 Prioritisation of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, taking account of (a) identified risks; (b) the food business operators' past record as regards compliance; (c) the reliability of any own checks that have already been carried out; and (d) any information that might indicate non-compliance. Findings The official controls of FCM are carried out as part of food safety checks. There is a food establishments risk categorisation system in place which is described in the report from the last mission DG(SANCO)8174/2009. According to the instructions in the 2010 sampling plan, ten samples were taken at the BCPs. For 2011 it is planned to take ten samples from the market and 21 from the BCPs which will be tested for overal migration, PAAs and formaldehyde. The sampling plan is based on the type of FCM, the country of origin, availability in food establishments and RASFF notifications. The plan is linked to the budgetary resources. The BCPs of the FVS perform documentary and identification checks of all FCM consignments imported into Latvia. Physical checks are generally done according to the plan but also in cases of suspicion or in response to RASFF notifications received. Conclusions The official FCM controls in food establishments are carried out regularly, the inspection frequency is based on risk. All consignments of imported FCM are checked. The whole FCM chain will be covered with the official controls by 2012. 6 5.3.3 Controls at visited premises including traceability, labelling Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 establishes traceability requirements in FCM. Article 15 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 establishes labelling requirements for FCM. Findings The audit team visited a number of food premises namely one supermarket, and food producers in the dairy and brewery sectors, in which inspection procedures for FCM were observed. The inspections were carried out by three inspectors from two TSUs. All premises visited were categorised based on risk and had been inspected according to the stated targets. All inspections performed by TSU inspectors were well structured. Labelling and traceability of FCM were included in all inspections and were assessed adequately. The inspectors traced the FCM using the labelling and other supporting documents like invoices, production notebooks or sheets. During all inspections a general check list and the recently issued methodology guidelines for controls of FCM (3 January 2011) were followed. Conclusions All inspections performed were well structured and followed the methodology guidelines. The assessment of the labelling and traceability requirements for FCM was adequate. 5.3.4 Declaration of Compliance Legal requirements Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 on materials and articles intended to come into contact with food requires that FCM shall be accompanied by a written declaration stating that they comply with the rules applicable to them. Article 9 of Commission Directive 2002/72/EC as amended relating to plastic materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs requires that at the marketing stages other than the retail stage, plastic materials and articles as well as the substances intended for the manufacturing of those materials and articles, shall be accompanied by a written declaration in accordance with Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004. Article 2(a) of Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended relating to ceramic articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs requires that at the marketing stages up to and including the retail stage, ceramic articles which are not yet in contact with foodstuffs shall be accompanied by a written declaration in accordance with Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004. 7 Findings The documentary check of imported FCM included an assessment of the DoC. During the visit to the BCP Riga, the inspectors informed the audit team, that they have never found a non compliant DoC. However, two out of three DoCs checked by the audit team were not fully compliant with the legal requirements. One of the DoCs was issued by a TC manufacturer and the date of the DoC, the specification of type of food with which it is intended to be put in contact and the ratio of food contact surface area to volume used to establish the compliance of the article were missing. In another DoC for ceramics which was issued by the importer the identity and the address of the manufacturer were missing. To address the second recommendation from mission DG(SANCO)8174/2009 (ensure that official controls adequately include the examination of written material) the FVS issued in January 2011 an amended version of methodology instructions for control of FCM which include instructions for the assessment of the DoC. All inspectors met in the visited establishments used this instructions. The audit team noted that in general the DoCs presented for assessment were in English. The inspectors met, with the exception of one were not fluent in English, therefore they were not able to adequately carry out the assessment of the DoC. Conclusions The second recommendation from audit DG(SANCO)8174/2009 has been addressed. There were shortcomings in relation to the assessment of the DoC. 5.3.5 Good Manufacturing Practice for Food Contact Materials Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 requires that FCM shall be manufactured in compliance with good manufacturing practice (GMP). Commission Regulation (EC) No 2023/2006 on GMP for materials and articles intended to come into contact with food. Findings To address Recommendations No 4 and No 5 from the mission No DG(SANCO)8174/2009 (implementation and official control of GMP in FCM manufacturing establishments) the national Law On the Supervision of the Handling of Food was amended and the implementation of GMP in FCM manufacturing establishments will be obligatory from 2012. The amendment provides the legal powers to FVS inspectors to control FCM producers, including the controls of GMP. Conclusions From 2012 official controls will include assessment of the implementation of the requirements of GMP Regulation (EC) No 2023/2006. Recommendations No 4 and No 5 from the report No DG(SANCO)8174/2009 were addressed. 8 5.3.6 Sampling Legal requirements Article 11 of the Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 establishes requirements for sampling. Findings The central administration provides sampling instructions annually to the TSUs. According to the instructions the samples are delivered to the State Research Institute, the Food Safety, Animal Health and Environment Research Institute (BIOR). In emergencies, when it is necessary to take supplementary samples not envisaged in the plan, the inspector is required to get specific authorisation from the central administration which is based on budgetary possibilities. Since 2008 the budget for sampling has been halved. Conclusions The sampling methods used in the context of official control of FCM comply with relevant rules. 5.3.7 Laboratory performance Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that analytical methods used in the scope of official controls shall comply with relevant EU rules. Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that CAs only designate laboratories that operate and are assessed and accredited in accordance with the standards EN ISO/IEC 17025 and EN ISO/IEC 17011. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires MSs to designate a National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for each European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) referred to in Article 32. The NRL shall collaborate with the EURL, coordinate activities, organise comparative tests, ensure dissemination of information, and provide scientific and technical assistance. Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 on materials and articles intended to come into contact with food requires the EURL for FCM and NRL established as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 to assist MSs with a high quality and uniformity of analytical results. Findings National Reference Laboratories The BIOR, formerly the National Diagnostic Centre, was designated as the NRL for FCM by Cabinet of Ministers regulation No 714 from 19 October 2009. The Laboratory has participated in five meetings organised by the EURL (one in December 2009 and four during 2010). 9 However, only the BIOR and not the MS has communicated its nomination as NRL to the EURL for FCM and MSs. Laboratories visited The audit team was informed that no official tests of FCM are carried out in Latvia therefore no laboratory was visited. However, the audit team noted that testing protocols were issued for tests performed by BIOR in September 2010 for ceramics imported in to Latvia. None of the methods used by BIOR for official analysis of FCM is accredited. The audit team noted, that the samples taken during the investigation of RASFF notification 1597: 2010 in December 2010 were analysed in an accredited laboratory in Estonia. The analyses undertaken in this laboratory are ordered by phone or by e-mail. No agreement was signed between laboratories. To address recommendations No 7 and 8 (Continue expanding the range of validated and accredited methods in the areas of plastic FCMs and ensure that the migration conditions for determination of formaldehyde migration from kitchenware applied in the official laboratory is in line with the Commission Reference Laboratory/National Reference Laboratory Guidelines) from mission DG(SANCO)8174/2009, the FVS stated in the action plan, that there is an agreement between BIOR and a laboratory in Germany to carry out laboratory tests for plastics. However the audit team was not provided with that agreement. Furthermore the audit team was informed by BIOR that the tender procedure has not started yet. The BIOR representatives stated that the order for analysis from BIOR serves like an agreement between them and the German laboratory. The only criteria to choose the laboratories in the other MSs was the scope of accreditation. Conclusions The nomination of BIOR as NRL in October 2009 was not officially communicated by Latvia to the Commission, the relevant EURL and other MSs in accordance with requirements of Article 33 (4) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. The laboratories used for official analysis of FCM are accredited as required by Article 12 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. Recommendations No 7 and No 8 from the report No DG(SANCO)8174/2009 were addressed. 5.3.8 Procedures for performance and reporting of control activities Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that CAs carry out their official controls in accordance with documented procedures, containing information and instructions for staff performing official controls. Article 9 of the above Regulation requires CAs to draw up reports on the official controls carried out, including a description of the purpose of official controls, the methods applied, the results obtained and any action to be taken by the business operator concerned. 10 Findings Since the last audit, there have been no changes to the food control system operated by FVS. The central administration issued on 3 January 2010 amended methodology instructions for official control of FCM performed by TSU staff. The BCP staff use the methodology instructions for controls on materials and articles coming into contact with food (August 2010) and the procedure for action with samples taken at BCP (June 2010) for the official controls of FCM. Conclusion CAs carry out official controls on the basis of documented procedures. 5.3.9 Co-operation between and within CAs Legal requirements Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 provides for efficient and effective co-ordination and co-operation between CAs. Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that, when, within a CA, more than one unit is competent to carry out official controls, efficient and effective co-ordination and co- operation shall be ensured between the different units. The Food Act (OG 81/13) is the legislative framework on food and feed safety, providing for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council.
The Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Health are the competent authorities responsible for the policy in the food safety area and for carrying out official controls on food and feed.

BVIITS is responsible for import and transit controls of live animals and products of animal origin. The Border Veterinary Inspection Section supports the seven BIPs, drafts the procedures and prepares guidelines and information for border veterinary inspectors. The International Trade Department drafts legislation and models of health certificates and issues import permissions and import bans and is responsible for conducting risk analysis of international trade.

Article 4(5) requires that, when more than one unit within the same competent authority is competent to carry out official controls, efficient and effective coordination and cooperation is ensured between those units. Findings

The Ministry of Agriculture is responsible for ensuring effective cooperation and coordination of activities of official controls, as well as for communication and reporting system on official controls. It is also the contact point for the European Commission.

An agreement on "Integrated Border Management" was signed in 2006 between the competent authorities involved in import controls (e.g. Ministry of Health, Customs). The agreement stipulates meetings between competent authorities at both central level (every 2-3 months) and local level (usually monthly) to discuss import issues. It also facilitates access by BIPs to relevant information in the Customs information systems and access for Customs to instructions from the veterinary services. The agreement is updated regularly with the latest version dated 2012.

The Ministry of Health cooperates with the Ministry of Agriculture as regards the preparation of control plans and reports, implementation of official controls, authorisation of official laboratories and registration/approval of establishments. The respective responsibilities for official controls are set out in Article 7-10 of the Food Act (OG 81/13).

There were records available during the audit related to meetings at both central and local level between the Ministry of Agriculture and Customs which referred to discussions on import controls. Conclusions on competent authorities

As the basis for an effective import control system, Croatia has designated the competent authorities responsible for the control system on imports and transits and there is a framework for cooperation and/or communication between competent authorities. 5.2 RESOURCES FOR PERFORMING OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Provision of staff and facilities Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authorities to ensure that they have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff and that appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment are available. Findings

The BVIITS has four veterinarians and one administrator in the Border Veterinary Inspection Section. There is a Head of Service, three veterinarians and one administrator in the International Trade Department. Twenty two veterinary inspectors perform veterinary controls at BIPs and the audit team did not note any evidence of shortcomings in the controls audited which could be linked to inadequate allocation of human resources. 3 11. The seven approved BIPs largely comply with EU legal requirements in relation to equipment and facilities and there is a procedure in place at each BIP to maintain this compliance (see findings 75-83 annd conclusion 84). 5.2.2 Staff qualifications and training Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires competent authorities to ensure that staff receive appropriate training, and are kept up-to-date in their competencies. Findings 12. The competent authority supplied the audit team with information on a wide range of training related to import controls on products of animal origin that had been provided in the build up and during the period post-accession. The training was provided by TAIEX, BTSF (Better Training for Safer Food) program and by the Croatian competent authority both at central and local level. Experts from other Member States were available at Croatian BIPs in the immediate period post-accession to assist with implementation of EU requirements. 13. Training plans are created at the beginning of each year based on training needs identified via the verification procedures described in findings 24-30. 14. Training records for individual officials were available at all BIPs and all staff met during the audit had a good knowledge of EU import rules relevant to their work. 5.2.3 Procedures for performance and reporting of control activities Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that the competent authorities carry out their official controls in accordance with documented procedures, containing information and instructions for staff performing official controls. Article 9 of the above Regulation requires the competent authorities to draw up reports on the official controls carried out, including a description of the purpose of official controls, the methods applied, the results obtained and any action to be taken by the business operator concerned. Findings 15. The central competent authority has provided a wide range of procedures/instructions to officials working at BIPs including: · A BIP Manual (first drafted in 2009, last updated in July 2013). · Procedures for taking samples. · Instructions for using TRACES. · Translations of guidance documents issued by the Commission, e.g. re-enforced checks. · A check list for official controls of individual consignments The competent authority stated that these instructions will be reviewed in response to experience gained with their implementation, the results of verification activities and changes in legislation. 16. There are some areas for which instructions have not been provided or require more detail e.g. instructions on.: clarifying to BIP staff what Customs have to check if they check exiting transit consignments on behalf of a BIP (linked to finding 43); 4 sampling horses, related to Commission Decision 79/794/EC (linked to finding 27); approved bodies as referred to in Council Directive 92/65/EC (linked to finding 30); follow-up when confirmation of receipt at destination is not received by the BIP for consignments so requiring (e.g. channelled, re-imports) (linked to finding 32); approved quarantines for certain imported birds as per Commission Regulation (EC) No 318/2007, and for live aquaculture animals as per Commission Decision 2008/946/EC (linked to finding 69). 17. The list of CITES points of entry is not the same as the list of BIPs. Even thought this is not a requirement, this could cause problems if a live animal or product of animal origin is presented at a CITES entry point but it also requires a BIP check and there is no BIP at that entry point. Conclusions on resources for performance of controls 18. The effectiveness of the controls is ensured by, amongst others, a sufficient number of experienced staff, the provision of appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment, the level of training provided pre and post-accession. Although a wide range of procedures and instructions have been provided to BIP staff, there are some areas for which instructions have not been provided or require more detail. 5.3 ENFORCEMENT MEASURES Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires a competent authority which identifies a non- compliance to take appropriate action to ensure that the operator remedies the situation. Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that Member States shall lay down the rules on sanctions applicable to infringements of feed and food law and other Union provisions relating to the protection of animal health and welfare and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented. The sanctions provided for must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive Findings 19. Section V of the Veterinary Act (OG 82/13) covers "Administrative supervision and inspection". Article 152 in particular includes measures which can be taken when non- compliances are suspected or identified. Sections 14 and 15 of the BIP Manual also deal with measures to be taken by officials at BIPs in the case of illegal imports. 20. Section VI of the Veterinary Act covers "Penal provisions" and Articles 165 and 166 relate to "Entry of consignments" and set out various fines for a range of non-compliances. 21. There were records on file at BIPs of verbal or written warnings issued following non- compliances, e.g. late notification of the arrival of a consignment to a BIP. 22. There were records of fines issued related to non-compliances, e.g. late and no notification to a BIP. 5 Conclusions on enforcement measures 23. Croatia has provided an administrative framework which enables officials to take appropriate action, including sanctions, to ensure that operators remedy non-compliances when detected, contributing to the overall effectiveness of the import control system. 5.4 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS AND PROCEDURES Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authorities to ensure the impartiality, consistency and quality of official controls at all levels and to guarantee the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls. Article 8 states that they must have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls, to ensure effectiveness of corrective action and to update documentation where needed. Under Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 competent authorities are required to carry out internal audits, or have external audits carried out. These must be subject to independent scrutiny and carried out in a transparent manner. Findings 24. The supervision of BIPs includes supervisions by the central competent authority twice per year and by the head of each BIP four times per year. These supervisory checks are carried out based on a check list which covers documentation, training, procedures, certification, completion of the CVED, facilities and equipment. The reports issued by the central office to BIPs may include recommendations and the BIPs have to agree an Action Plan with deadlines with the central office who then monitor its implementation. The heads of BIPs have to forward copies of their supervision reports to central office. 25. In addition to the above, the head of each BIP is responsible for carrying out regular supervisory checks. This involves a spot-check of individual import files and discussions with staff on any issues noted. It also involves a spot-check of Customs records for all consignments that entered the border at road BIPs. 26. The audit team were provided with copies of the most recent local and central supervision reports for all BIPs. The reports were comprehensive and all lead to the issuing of recommendations. There was evidence on file that a system existed to follow-up the recommendations via action plans and deadlines and that corrective actions had been implemented. 27. The supervision reports did not refer to all the issues identified by the audit team. This is mainly due to the fact that the supervision uses the national procedures (e.g. BIP Manual) as the reference standard and checks its implementation but does not assess whether the procedures provide instructions/comply with all relevant EU requirements, e.g. findings 9, 28, 30 and 32. The supervision reports did not refer to issues which are covered by national procedures such as findings 24 and 32. 28. Article 14 of the Food Act (OG 81/13) requires that audits shall be conducted in line with Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. According to the Act on Public Internal Financial Control in the Public Sector (OG 141/2006), the Internal Audit Service within the Ministry of Agriculture reports directly to the Minister and is functionally independent from all other directorates and departments. Article 24 of this Act also obliges Internal Auditors to apply the Internal Auditors' Charter, Internal Auditors' Professional Code of Ethics and Internal 6 Auditors' Manual prepared by the Central Harmonisation Unit within the Ministry of Finance. 29. The main tasks of the Internal Audit Service are to assess the organisation of the Ministry of Agriculture and its relation with other control bodies, the performance and effectiveness of planned arrangements and the implementation of follow-up measures. 30. Audits of the import control system for products of animal origin are planned by the Internal Audit Service for the fourth quarter of 2014. Conclusions on verification procedures 31. The verification of BIPs is based on supervision by central staff and by the heads of each BIP, which is implemented as planned, has a comprehensive scope and reports are followed-up and lead to improvement. 5.5 CONTROLS OF CONSIGNMENTS AT ENTRY BIPS 5.5.1 System to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks Legal requirements Article 4 (1) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Article 3 of Directive 97/78/EC require that Member State shall ensure that no consignment from a third country is introduced into EU territory without having been subjected to the veterinary checks at a BIP and being notified in advance to the BIP and also gives the Member States the possibility to check manifests. Additionally, Article 7 of Directive 2002/99/EC stipulates that products of animal origin intended for human consumption are introduced only if they comply with the EU requirements for animal health. Article 2 (1) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 requires notification of consignments of products of animal origin before their physical arrival on Union territory to the BIP staff and Article 1 (1) of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 specifies the same for live animals at least one working day before their physical arrival on Union territory. In order to ensure that all animal products and live animals undergo veterinary checks, Articles 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 require the Member States to gather all pertinent intelligence from Customs, manifests and other information sources and to have access to the information in relevant databases held by Customs. Findings 32. Section 5 of the BIP Manual deals with notification of consignments at BIPs. Notification is submitted via part 1 of the CVED in TRACES in the vast majority of cases and the competent authority stated that the compliance rate with this procedure was very high. 33. The Customs database flags the positive list so that consignments presented for free circulation will only be released on presentation of an appropriate CVED. The flagging does not apply to consignments presented for transit and Customs stated that they check all these consignments to identify those that require BIP checks based on their CN codes and descriptions. Customs stated that they contact the BIPs if they have a query but there were no written records available to demonstrate this. 34. The two port BIPs and the one airport BIP monitor incoming consignments via a combination of manifest checks, checks of operator databases and checks of information supplied by operators. 7 35. The BIPs at both Ploce Port and Zagreb Airport have agreements in place with Customs that unloading cannot take place without the agreement of the BIP. 36. The entire port in Rijeka is a free zone.
