The BMEL is responsible for compiling legal provisions at national level and is involved in their implementation; in this, it is supported by BVL. The federal states are responsible for official controls on ABP/DP. The senior competent authorities in the federal states visited are: a. In Bavaria: Bayerisches Staatsministerium für Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz (the Bavarian Ministry of Environment and Consumer Protection ­ StMUV). For the execution of official controls on ABP/DP, Bavaria has a three level structure, a central authority (StMUV), a middle authority (seven provinces) and lower authorities (rural and urban districts). b. In North Rhine ­ Westphalia (NW): Ministerium für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz (Ministry of Nature, Environment and Consumer Protection). There is a three-tier structure in North-Rhine Westphalia for official checks on ABP/DP: a central authority (MKULNV), a higher authority (LANUV) and lower authorities (district authorities). In NW, LANUV and the district authorities are responsible for the approval of ABP plants. The rural and urban district authorities are responsible for performing official controls on the ABP/DP chain. Officers from the competent authorities of the federal states visited had a clear understanding of their roles within their field of competence and of their responsibilities concerning ABP/DP. 3 3. According to representatives from the federal states visited, the exchange of information and co-operation between the federal states normally takes place in the framework of the Working Group for Animal Diseases and Animal Health of the Länder Working Group on Consumer Protection, but ABP/DP is not always on the agenda of these meetings. 5.1.2 Registration and approval 4. As required by Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, lists of approved and registered ABP/DP plants and operators are compiled and kept updated and published on its website by BMEL based on information provided periodically by the federal states. All the plants visited were approved and listed. 5. Representatives of BMEL informed the audit team that traders which are shown in the commercial documents as being the final destination for ABP/DP even though they do not actually receive the goods (hereafter: paper traders) have not been registered in accordance with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 as this activity is considered to be outside the scope of the ABP Regulations. In the federal states visited, such traders were not included in the scope of official controls on the ABP/DP chain. 6. In all plants visited, operators were aware of the requirements relating to the registration or approval of their suppliers or customers. The inspectors carrying out official controls in the plants visited were actively cross-checking that the operators and plants shown on commercial documents (including those located in other Member States) were approved or registered as required. The audit team checked the registration/approval status of several operators appearing on commercial documents and noted that all but the paper traders were registered or approved in accordance with Articles 23 or 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, respectively. 7. Transporters of ABP/DP which are also active in the feed chain are also registered according to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 5.1.3 Organisation, planning and execution of official controls 8. The organisation of official controls remains largely as described in the country profile (see section 4.1). Within their territories, each of the 16 federal states has exclusive competence for the organisation, planning and execution of the official controls and supervision of ABP/DP required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 9. There were a number of important differences in the approach taken in the two federal states in the organisation, planning and performance of official controls on the ABP/DP chain and so these are covered separately: The following was observed in Bavaria: a. A system of risk-based official controls for ABP/DP plants and operators has been put in place, as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which takes into account a number of criteria to determine the basic frequency of official controls (above a set minimum) to be carried out. With the exception of one transporter, all 4 plants and operators visited by the audit team in Bavaria had been inspected at least as often as established in the risk-based control plan. b. This federal state has put in place relevant checklists and guidance, which help to ensure that points relating to traceability and commercial documents are taken into account during the routine official controls carried out in the ABP/DP chain, in accordance with Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. These documents were being used in practice in the plants visited. c. Staff met by the audit team were aware of the relevant requirements for documentation and traceability of ABP/DP and the reports of the inspections performed were sufficiently detailed to show that the requirements regarding commercial documents and traceability set down in Articles 21 and 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, respectively, had been checked. The results of these inspections were entered into a database which, according to the competent authority, provides a means to monitor that the official controls are carried out regularly in accordance with the risk-based programme, set down in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The following was noted in NW: d. In contrast to the situation seen in Bavaria, the district authorities, rather than the federal state, are responsible for planning the official controls. The audit team noted that insufficient measures have been put in place by the federal state which could help ensure that each of the district authorities carried out this task consistently and appropriately, in accordance with the criteria set down in Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Deficiencies in this respect were evident, as neither the transporter of ABP/DP nor the storage facility for derived products visited by the audit team had been subject to official controls as the district authority had not established an inspection frequency for these operators. In another case, a district authority had classified traders and transporters as being a low-risk activity irrespective of the categories and volumes of ABP/DP which they were handling, or if any risk of cross- contamination were present. As a result, it cannot ensure that official controls of the ABP/DP chain in NW are carried out in accordance with the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. e. Similarly, in the absence of any measures, such as checklists or guidance, being put in place at the federal state level, the district authorities are also responsible for deciding what should be checked during official controls. A lack of relevant checklists for transporters of ABP/DP and producers of OF/SI at district level was given as one of the reasons why the operators referred to in point (d) above were not subject to official controls. f. Information provided by the competent authorities prior to the audit showed no non- compliances relating to traceability of ABP/DP were identified in the last two years in the establishments to be visited in NW. However, given the range of shortcomings identified by the audit team in the ABP plants visited which were overlooked during 5 official controls (see points 16, 17, 18) this raises doubts about the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that the correct handling of ABP/DP, including requirements for traceability and commercial documents, are verified regularly in NW, as set down in Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. g. According to the representatives of NW met, an initiative was started several years ago with the aim of establishing a quality management system, but it is not known when this could be expected to be in place(1). Conclusions on official control systems 10. The system in place for the organisation, planning and implementation of official controls of the ABP/DP chain relies largely on the federal states putting in place adequate measures to ensure the relevant EU requirements are fulfilled. However, in the absence of measures to encourage a harmonised approach to these tasks, substantial differences were seen in the two federal states visited. While one (Bavaria) had put in place a mostly satisfactory system of risk-based controls for most operators in the ABP/DP chain, many deficiencies were identified in the effectiveness of the systems put in place by the districts authorities in the other federal state visited (NW) and there were insufficient measures in place to enable these to be identified and corrected either by the federal state or by the competent authorities. This issue, combined with the fact that paper traders of ABP/DP are neither registered nor subject to official controls, undermines the ability of Germany to ensure that all relevant operators in the country are subject to regular official controls, carried out in accordance with EU requirements, to verify compliance with the traceability requirements for ABP/DP. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Articles 17(1), 32 and Chapter II of Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Articles 1, 2 and 3 of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC; and Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. 1 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that each of the district authorities in NW has installed its own QM system. A state-wide QM framework strategy was established in 2014 to ensure that official controls were more consistent, transparent and logical in their implementation. The state-wide QM framework strategy includes a state-wide documentation system. This consists of the purely formal state-wide procedural instructions laid down by the Länder Working Group on Consumer Protection and any other necessary procedures for official checks. The state-wide QM documentation system is currently in the process of being created. 6 Findings and observations 5.2.1 Imports, exports and intra-EU trade 11. Each of the federal states has an officer responsible for TRACES and the Friedrich Loeffler Institut acts as the national coordinator. This body has provided some guidelines on its TRACES-specific website, but no instructions have been given to the inspectors in the federal states to help them decide the nature and frequency of checks to be carried out on consignments of ABP/DP before confirming their arrival in TRACES in accordance with Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 12. In both federal states visited, the officials met provided evidence that the importers of the vast majority of consignments of ABP/DP subject to the channelling requirements which enter the EU through Border Inspection Posts located in the territory of the federal states concerned, are research facilities and universities which have arrangements in place to ensure the traceability of channelled goods, including confirmation of their arrival. The requirements of Article 3(c) of Decision 2004/292/EC were mostly fulfilled for a number of such consignments checked by the audit team. 13. In a pet food manufacturer visited in Bavaria, the arrival of all consignments of ABP/DP traded from other Member States which were recorded in TRACES had been confirmed as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, the inspector met stated that a large number of consignments of PAP are dispatched from another Member State to the plant in question without being notified in TRACES. The audit team saw evidence that BMEL had been informed of this issue and that it had contacted the relevant authorities of the Member State concerned. 14. In a processing plant visited in Bavaria, the audit team noted that the inspector informed the StMUV which had subsequently notified BMEL that two Member States receiving consignments of PAP notified through TRACES do not confirm their arrival, contrary to the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The BMEL had contacted the Member States concerned which had confirmed in writing that the consignments were received. 15. In a processing plant visited in NW, the audit team noted that consignments of PAP containing ruminant material declared in TRACES as being pet food were dispatched to a trader(2) in another Member State. It was not known if these consignments were subsequently exported from the EU. 16. In the same processing plant, the audit team noted that consignments of PAP containing ruminant material were dispatched to a trader in another Member State but the associated notifications of their dispatch were generated in TRACES up to four weeks later, contrary to what is required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. This could hamper 2 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that these consignments were dispatched to a retailer and there was a declaration error which resulted from older versions of TRACES and which had not been corrected by the processing plant when newer versions of TRACES were adopted. 7 the ability of the competent authorities in the Member State receiving these consignments to carry out checks to confirm their arrival at the intended destination. 17. At a storage plant for derived products visited in NW, the audit team noted that several consignments of horn chips which, according to the operator, originated in a third country, were received without being accompanied by a commercial document. These consignments were found to have been imported by a trader based in a federal state other than the ones visited in this audit, and then stored in a different federal state before being dispatched to the plant in NW without commercial documents. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Annex XIV, Chapter II, Section 12 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. This issue had not been identified during the official controls performed in the federal states involved. 18. According to data extracted from TRACES by the audit team, in 2013 approximately 8,570 commercial documents notifications were sent to Germany from several Member States and the arrival of around 5,470 (64%) of these consignments was confirmed. Consignments entering Germany via traders were not confirmed in TRACES as traders are not registered and not subject to official controls. In 2014, data extracted from TRACES show that approximately 3,000 (30%) out of 10,000 consignments arriving in Germany were confirmed. In their response to the draft report the CA stated that the Act on the supervision of organic production (294/2015), the Act on amending the Food Act (295/2015) and the Decree of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry on organic production (454/2015) had come into force on 1 May 2015. 6 Article 27(14) provides that CtrlAs and CBs shall transmit to the CAs each year by 31 January a list of the operators which were subject to their controls on the 31 of December of the previous year and by 31 March a summary report of the control activities carried out during the previous year. Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 provides for the exchange of information between CtrlAs, CBs and CAs. Findings According to the provisions laid down in MD No 846/2008, MAF is responsible for the overall regulation of the organic food sector. The MAF keeps the legislative power of organic production, establishes general objectives for the planning of official controls and reports on the results of these controls to the COM. According to MD No 846/2008, the competencies of planning, organisation and implementation of organic production controls have been conferred by MAF on EVIRA which is CA for organic production control according to Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. EVIRA is under the auspices of MAF and is responsible in particular for: ­ The supervision/audit of CtrlAs for organic production ­ The collection of annual data on organic production by the CtrlAs and reporting to MAF ­ The issuing of technical guidance to the CtrlAs and the evaluation of industry standards (private) for animal species referred to in Article 42 of Regulation (834/2007/EC) for possible application in Finland ­ The training of inspectors and official personnel of CtrlAs ­ Granting derogations on feeding stuff referred to Article 47 c of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 ­ The supervision of imports of organic products, the notification to OFIS2 (Organic Farming Production Information System) and the reporting to Eurostat. Under the same act, the implementation of controls in the organic sector has also been conferred to CtrlAs, as follows: 1. 15 ELY-centres responsible, at regional level, for controls on organic farms. ELY-centres are also responsible for the regional implementation and the development tasks of the Ministry of Employment and Economy.
EVIRA's Organic production control unit (that acts as CtrlA) and is responsible for: Controls on organic products at wholesalers. Controls on establishments processing organic products

VALVIRA which is responsible for the controls of organic alcoholic beverages. VALVIRA is a centralised body operating under the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health. 2 OFIS is a telematics network that supports the implementation of organic production policies. It provides a system that allows for the electronic exchange of organic production data between the EU Member States and the COM and supports the management of related business procedures. OFIS also facilitates the dissemination of information to European citizens and operators through the provision of public data on the EUROPA website 7 These CtrlAs are responsible for the inspection and certification of registered operators in the field of organic production and the verification of compliance with the organic production rules. Each of these CtrlAs has a unique code number based on the following template: FI ­ EKO ­ XXX. According to MD 846/2008, the NBC is the authority responsible of the controls for releasing for free circulation of products imported in accordance with Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Official controls on organic products at retail level are performed by the Hygiene Services of the Municipal Food Control Authorities (MFCAs), within the framework of food safety controls. An information system (named as KUTI) is being implemented for the food safety controls sector in order to improve coordination and cooperation within and between the CAs responsible for food safety as well as to improve the monitoring of controls at central level. The KUTI system currently in place contains only limited information on controls of organic products in the retail sector as it only identifies whether organic products are sold in a specific market point (see also Chapter 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability of Organic Products at Retail Level). In the autonomous island of Aland there are separate authorities, responsible for the control of the whole organic sector, under the own government of Aland. The audit team was informed in the opening meeting by the representatives of the government of Aland that the reports of these controls are directly sent to the COM. The structure and organisation of the Finnish Authorities are described in the country profile of Finland. This profile can be found in the website: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/controlsystems_en.cfm?co_id=FI On-the-spot inspections of operators in the field of organic production are carried out by private inspectors who are authorised centrally by EVIRA. A list of authorised inspectors is maintained by Evira. The authorised inspectors (101 inspectors at the time the FVO audit) are assigned by the CtrlAs to carry out inspections. Authorised inspectors are specialised in the different categories of organic production such as plant production, livestock production, food production and food processing, beekeeping, collection of organic products, seed packing and feed. EVIRA has a written procedure for the authorisation of these inspectors based on legislative act No 6799/0439/2012 on qualifications of organic production auditors. This procedure includes written examinations, participation in training courses for new inspectors and initially compulsory participation in inspections led by an experienced inspector - four to five times - before independently carrying out such inspections. Specific guidelines have been prepared for inspectors by EVIRA (handbook for inspector and guidance on organic production rules). According to the qualification criteria, an inspector of primary production may apply for qualification to carry out inspections in other sectors only after working as an inspector for at least two years. Inspectors of processing plants must have received basic training in the food sector or have long experience in carrying out primary production inspections. The authorisation is valid for one to three years and renewed by EVIRA.The same inspector cannot perform more than two consecutive inspections in the same organic production operator. The audit team found evidence of these procedures being followed in all the CtrlAs visited. The supervision and evaluation of the performance of authorised inspectors by EVIRA is based on: ­ At least one witness audit of new inspectors in the year after the first authorisation, and ­ One witness audit every 5 years afterwards. 8 The audit team reviewed reports on witness audits carried out by EVIRA on inspectors. No specific problems on the performance of the inspectors were revealed. ELY-centres do not currently perform any supervision or witness audits on the authorised inspectors. There are provisions concerning conflict of interest defined in national legislation. Inspectors are required to sign a declaration of absence of conflict of interest before their authorisation. They are excluded in cases of family links or financial dependency. The audit team was informed by EVIRA that audits of ELY-centres are organised by its personnel under a five year cycle plan, covering three ELY-centres per year. These audits are focused on one special control topic and include a general performance review of the centre. The audit team reviewed the audit report for one centre and noted that no non-compliances were detected. In case deficiencies are found during such audits they are communicated to the MAF. There is however no legal obligation for ELY-centres to follow up on recommendations made by EVIRA. EVIRA has no legal power to take remedial actions.3 This is not in line with the requirements of Article 4 (6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which requires that when audits are carried out, appropriate measures shall be taken in the light of their results, to ensure that the objectives of the Regulation are achieved. In order to harmonise the system EVIRA has issued to the ELY-centres several control guidelines and a list of non-compliances and enforcement measures. However, the audit team noted that control guidelines are not always implemented by the ELY-centres with regard to. risk planning of controls, sampling in cases of suspicions, and corrective measures to be taken in cases of non-compliances (see also Chapter 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of controls, Chapter 5.2.6 Sampling and Laboratory Analysis and Chapter 5.2.9 Measures in Cases of Irregularities and Infringements). As regards the controls at retail level, Evira has provided MFCAs with guidelines on the supervision of organic production. These were updated in summer 2014. At the time of the FVO audit no training had yet been given regarding their application. The audit team noted that there are no regular communication channels established between the ELY-centres. It was also noted that there are no procedures in place to ensure the exchange of information between CtrlAs which is not in line with Article 92(5) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Furthermore, ELY-centres are not required to notify EVIRA when non-compliances affecting the organic status of a product are detected and it is not ensures that the information is communicated to other CtrlAs and CAs as required under Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Evira and the regional competent authorities collect data on controls with regard to organic production in the ELMO (Information Management System Laboratory & Control) database. Findings Verification of Compliance prior to placing the product on the market A new producer of an agricultural product or foodstuff shall apply either to the CB that has been designated for the certification of the foodstuff in question, or to a PG. In both cases, certification is granted by the relevant CB. The PG shall conduct an internal control of the new producer. Where the new producer has been found compliant with the Product Specifications, the CB shall be notified thereof, which in turn shall accordingly amend the Annex to the certification document. Where the new producer submits the certification application directly to the designated CB, the latter shall undertake the verification of compliance of the new producer with the registered Product Specifications and, based on favourable findings, issue the relevant certificate to the new producer. The certification is valid for three years in both cases. In the case of non-compliances being found and the product not being in line with the Product Specification, the CB issues a decision refusing the issuance of a certificate. Official controls of processors / producers of PDO/PGI/TSG A producer of a PDO/PGI/TSG may be part of a PG, in which case the certification documents are held by the PG and the names of all members of the PG are listed on the annex of the certificate. In these situations, the CB deals directly with the president of the PG. A producer may decide not to become a member of a PG and can be certified individually. In these situations the CB always deals directly with the FBO on all issues relating to the annual control. The designated CBs are required to control each PDO/PGI/TSG certificate holder on a regular basis. Where a PG exists, the process involves the CB initially carrying out an audit of documents at the office of the PG once per year. For each particular PDO/PGI/TSG, a number of producers are randomly selected to be inspected during that year. The selection is calculated using the square root of the number of producers / processors registered. A report of the complete process is prepared by the CB and given to the president of the PG. The president of the PG is required to respond to any issues raised in the report and to deal directly with the FBOs to resolve any non-compliances detected by the CB. The CB is required to inform the CA when they withdraw certification, which is the only sanction available to the CB. 7 The PG itself is required to inspect each of its members once per year. This inspection is announced and comprises a documentary check, organoleptic testing, observing the production process as well as laboratory analysis in some cases. The audit team was informed that the prescribed frequency of official controls is never reduced even with a good inspection history, however an increased frequency may be introduced if non-compliances are detected. Each FBO producing / processing PDO/PGI/TSG is obliged to inform the MAE of the quantities of PDO/PGI/TSG produced each year. In practice, if the producer / processor is a member of a PG, the data may be collected and submitted by the PG. In addition to controls by CBs, regional offices of the AFSVSPP may carry out controls in the framework of regular controls planned in advance and as extraordinary, unplanned controls triggered by any information on suspected non-compliances. Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market are primarily carried out by the regional offices of the AFSVSPP. These controls can be undertaken as part of the normal control plan, in response to consumer complaints and non-compliant results of laboratory analysis. The audit team was informed that CBs may also undertake market controls, including the taking of samples for the products which they certify. Some PGs also undertake market controls. Conclusions Official controls on PDO/PGI/TSG are carried out regularly, are in part risk based and are in line with Articles 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 and 3 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Article 36 (3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 requires that official controls cover (a) verification that a product complies with the corresponding Product Specification: and (b) monitoring of the use of the registered names to describe product placed on the market in conformity with Articles 13 and 24 as appropriate. PGI covers agricultural products and foodstuffs closely linked to the geographical area. At least one of the stages of production, processing or preparation takes place in the area. TSG highlights traditional character, either in the raw materials, composition or means of production. Further details on the quality schemes are available on the following website: http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/quality/schemes/index_en.htm 4.3 STATUS OF REGISTERED PRODUCTS IN THE NETHERLANDS. There are five PDO, three PGI and two TSG registered from the Netherlands on the Database of Origin and Registration. Four registered names were selected to form part of this audit as a sample, in order to evaluate how the system of official controls works in the Netherlands. The criteria used by DG AGRI for selection were, inter alia, the economic value and production volume, potential risks factors, the assessment of the multi-annual national control plan and annual reports, a good mix of PDO/PGI/TSG and the vicinity of geographical locations. At the time of the FVO audit, there were around 370 producers/processors of products of animal origin and 29 producers of products of non-animal origin in the Netherlands. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal Requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU establishes that MSs shall adopt all measures of national law necessary to implement legally binding EU acts. As described in page 5 of the CP, the main CAs on the context of this audit are as follows: The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (Nederlandse Voedsel-en Warenautoriteit, NVWA) is an independent agency in the MEA and a delivery agency for the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport. It is the CA responsible for surveillance of the use of the registered names in the market place. The Netherlands Controlling Authority for Milk and Milk Products (Centraal Orgaan voor Kwaliteitsaangelegenheden in de Zuivel (COKZ)) is an independent body which only performs public duties. KCB is the designated CA for official controls for PDO/PGI/TSG for products of food of non-animal origin.

All of the abovementioned CAs involved in official controls are fully competent within their own fields of activity. They are responsible from the planning and implementation of official controls, including decision-taking on enforcement measures to be applied when non-compliances are found.

The audit team was informed by the CCA that no formal communication has been established among all CAs involved in official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. The CCA stated that such communication had not been necessary as no market controls had been undertaken to date (see finding No 15 and conclusion No 16).

There is no reference to official controls related to PDO/PGI/TSG in the country profile for the Netherlands. The FVO audit team was informed by the CCA that there is also no specific sections or references to the activities concerning official controls on PDO/PGI/TSG within the multi-annual national control plan. This is not in compliance with Article 40(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The CCA stated during the opening meeting that a specific section to this regard is under preparation and it is expected to be included in the 2015 National Control Plan. Resources for the performance of controls

The FVO audit team was informed that two NVWA inspectors followed training on PDO/PGI/TSG in the framework of the "Better training for safer food" courses. In 5 addition, two employees from the department of enforcement policy will follow the same training in December 2014.

Eight COKZ inspectors are assigned to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. Theoretical and on-the-spot training is provided and regular supervision is implemented through witness audits carried out by COKZ at least once a year. Findings Verification of Compliance prior to placing the product on the market

The FVO audit team requested the CAs to provide the reports issued for the verification of compliance in the establishments visited. COKZ representatives stated that reports in the case of products of animal origin were no longer available as they had been issued with respect of the national rules in force before EU registrations had taken place. NVWA representative stated that no verification of compliance had been carried out for products of non-animal origin prior to placing products of non-animal origin on the market. The FVO audit team visited one producer who had placed products in the market labelled as PGI for the first time in 2003. NVWA had only carried out the first official control in 2008. This is not in line with Article 37 of Regulation 1151/2012, which establishes that verification of compliance with the product specification before placing the product on the market shall be carried out. 6 Official controls of processors/producers of PDO/PGI/TSG

Official controls are currently undertaken at cheese processing establishments, which account for the most economically valuable products in the Netherlands. The FVO audit team noted that official controls were risk-based, taking into account the inspection history, self-checks carried out by the operators and the risks associated with the nature of the products. Inspections are carried out monthly at all operators and are always unannounced. A key part of the official control is related to extensive sampling to test the composition of the products. The level of sampling can be reduced if the operator is compliant over a period of time. Self-checks carried out by operators are also taken into account to decrease the number of official samples taken. Samples for analytical tests and organoleptic tests are taken at each site visit. The additional requirements of the Product Specification other than those tested through sampling are checked at least twice a year.

COKZ representatives stated that there are no specific official controls for PDO/PGI/TSG undertaken at farms except when processing also takes place at that site. This is not adequate as some of the requirements of the Product Specifications may only be checked at farm level. This is also the case for the legal requirement on the use of feed for PDOs of animal origin (Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 664/2014 establishes that, in respect of PDOs of animal origin, feed must be sourced from within the defined geographical area).

The FVO audit team was informed that a number of products with lower economic value were not currently subject to official controls. KCB stated that such controls will commence in 2015. In one establishment visited, the FVO audit team observed a pilot audit undertaken by the NVWA for the purpose of demonstrating how controls had been carried out. The last inspection had taken place in 2008 and no other controls on PDO/PGI/TSG had been undertaken since that date. The CA stated that the lack of such official controls was due to the small and local production. This is not in compliance with Article 36(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, which establishes that official controls shall cover the verification that a product complies with the corresponding Product Specification. Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market

NVWA representatives confirmed that at the time of the audit there were no market controls on PDO/PGI/TSG. This is not in compliance with Article 36(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, which establishes that official controls shall cover the monitoring of the use of registered names to describe product placed on the market. For the purpose of discussion and illustration on the different issues that might occur at market level, the FVO audit team along with NVWA visited a large supermarket. Some examples of non- compliances related to labelling were detected. Conclusions

The FVO audit team witnessed four inspections carried out at producers and processors of PDG/PGI/TSG products. Three of them were routine inspections carried out by COKZ. The remaining one was a pilot inspection carried out by NVWA in a producer of PDO/PGI/TSG of non-animal origin. The NVWA was the CA to inspect that establishment in 2008. The inspection was also witnessed by a KCB representative, as this CA will be responsible for controls as from January 2015.

COKZ inspectors stated that all inspections are unannounced, in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In all establishments visited, inspections are carried out regularly with appropriate frequency. The main object of the visits is sample-taking, with a large number of samples taken for the purpose of organoleptic and laboratory testing. Although sampling is undertaken in every inspection, two inspections per year are also dedicated to examining other requirements contained in the product specifications.

There are documented procedures in place giving instructions and information to the inspectors. These procedures, which require approval by the MEA, include checklists used by inspectors, which are specific for each Product Specification. The FVO audit team noted that this inspection list is the basis for the inspection. During the visits, all inspectors checked the requirements contained in the checklists. However, checklists do not contain in all cases all the requirements of the product specification. In addition the requirements related to identification and correlation between inputs and outputs, as referred to in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 668/2014 were not included to date. Inspectors confirmed that they do not perform mass-balance calculations. Inspectors did not check documentary evidence recorded by operators in any of the sites visited.

After each inspection, a debriefing with operators takes place to communicate the outcome of the visit. DG(SANCO)/2014/7152) was carried out from 9 September to 18 September 2014 in Belgium covering the official controls performed at farm level by the CA. The report of that audit has been published on the SANTE Directorate- General Internet site at:- http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3478 7 At the time of that audit, farms were found by the audit team appropriately registered and under regular official supervision. Controls were in place at farm level to prevent Salmonella contamination. However, some shortcomings concerning official controls on biosecurity standards were detected. 5.3.2 Approval procedures Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 31 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings The PCUs are responsible for the approval of establishments located in the area under their control. Approval is granted following favourable result of the assessments carried by PCU officials to verify FBO compliance with EU requirements. The CA has established comprehensive procedures for the approval, withdrawal and suspension of food business establishments. The approval procedures require official staff to use the same checklists used during routine official inspections. An FBO who wishes to start an activity requiring approval has to submit an application form to the PCU. Under national legislation the FBO is also obliged to provide to the PCU a plan of the establishment indicating facilities and process flows. If the review of this documentation is satisfactory, the PCU carries out an on-site visit to verify infrastructural conditions and to take a decision as regards the granting of conditional approval. A second visit takes place after three months to verify operational conditions and to decide whether to either grant definitive approval or to extend the conditional approval for a further three months. The approval procedures indicate that definitive approval cannot be granted if establishments do not comply with EU legislative requirements. This was confirmed during examination of the approval process through documentary reviews carried out by the audit team at establishment level and in the PCU office visited. All documents reviewed were found satisfactory as regards timeliness and procedures applied. In one establishment the audit team noted that after the initial approval visit the FBO was told by the PCU he could start operating prior to receiving the official letter which was sent ten days later than the given date to start operations. All establishments visited were approved by the CA for activities carried out on-site and the approval documents were provided to the audit team. The updated list of approved poultry establishments are publicly available on the CA website. Conclusions Establishment approval procedures are in place and aligned with relevant EU requirements. 8 5.3.3 Controls in slaughterhouses: Ante-mortem inspection and post-mortem inspection Legal requirements Article 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Findings Ante-mortem inspection (AMI) : AMI is carried out by a DMO at slaughterhouse level. The MD of 20 September 2010 lays down the model form and the contents of the Food Chain Information (FCI). In all slaughterhouses visited the FCI was received by the DMO 24 hours before the arrival of the poultry flock at the premises. In all cases reviewed, poultry flocks were accompanied by the FCI which included, among others, production data, veterinary treatments and Salmonella test result. The FCI was always signed by the farmer and checked by the slaughterhouse FBO before being submitted to the DMO. The AMI consisted of:- documentary check covering the examination of the FCI; identification of the consignment; check on animal welfare; clinical examination of the birds, including check on dead birds. In all the slaughterhouses visited the AMI was performed as required. All relevant information, including the outcome of the AMI, was entered in a CA database known as Sanitrace, which is also accessible to the FBO as regards its own data. PMI: PMI is carried out either by the DMO or slaughterhouse staff under his/her supervision. The poultry slaughterhouses can use their own slaughterhouse staff to perform PMI if conditions set by relevant national legislation (RD of 25 January 2011 laying down rules for the organisation of involvement of slaughterhouse staff in poultry slaughterhouses) are met, namely:- the possession of a CA validated own-check system, which must be under the responsi

Royal Decree of 03/08/2012 on the approval of laboratories performing analysis in relation with the safety of the food chain. 4 The control bodies have prepared instructions on official sampling for their relevant staff. Clear guidelines for the poultry holders known as Salmonella Action Plan, which are mandatory for broiler and fattening turkey farms Salmonella positive for the same serotype on three consecutive occasions, can be found on the CA's website. FASFC validated auto-control guidelines for primary production covering, among others, hygiene and biosecurity in the poultry sector and several circulars concerning general conditions for poultry farms, Salmonella in various poultry populations and in feed are published on the same website. Training The CA informed the audit team that official staff has received training when the Salmonella baseline studies were implemented (2004-2005). Between 2012 and 2014 the NRL has organised training for its laboratory staff, those of the control bodies and other designated laboratories via communication groups. Topics covered include e.g. Salmonella Typhimurium (ST) monophasic strains. Contents and list of attendance were available to the audit team. DGZ and ARSIA staff undergo an education programme which includes induction training and is regularly kept updated. Evidence of this was noted in the laboratory visited. The audit team was informed by FACSF that the own-check sampling procedures had been explained to private veterinarians on various occasions by DGZ, which has been appointed by FASFC as responsible for guidance at farm level in the framework of SNCPs. FBOs and their veterinarians attended training sessions organised by both DGZ and ARSIA and presentations prepared by ARSIA for these events were provided to the audit team. Furthermore, FASFC informed the audit team that DGZ and ARSIA inform poultry holders and private veterinarians through newsletters and leaflets during events concerning Salmonella control in poultry. In general officials, laboratory staff and FBOs interviewed during the audit were familiar with relevant EU legislative requirements and had adequate knowledge of the implementation of SNCPs, in particular sampling frequency and sampling protocols to be applied. However, despite information on this subject being available on the CA's website, shortcomings in biosecurity were detected by the audit team in many farms visited which had not been noted during official controls (see also Chapter 5.2). Audit In 2012 an internal audit was carried out by the CA internal audit section AIQP (Internal Audit and Quality Management Services) in one of the eleven PCUs. The scope of this audit was to evaluate if official controls implemented in the egg sector were in compliance with legal requirements and related procedures. The resulting audit report was available to the FVO audit team. No major problems were observed by AIQP in relation to inspection and sampling in the laying hen farm visited during the internal audit. The FVO audit team noted that one of the shortcomings identified in that report is related to biosecurity conditions. Conclusions The CA responsible for official controls within the scope of this audit is clearly designated in compliance with EU requirements. The CA is not in compliance with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in that it cannot guarantee that the bodies to which official control tasks have been delegated and individuals involved are impartial and free from any conflict of interest. Furthermore, to date, the CA has not performed any audit/inspection of such bodies to verify their performance in relation to the 5 implementation of these tasks in the framework of Salmonella control, contrary to Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In general relevant training has been provided by the CA to official staff involved with the implementation of the programmes and they had adequate knowledge of the requirements to be applied. However, some weaknesses exist as regards the identification of shortcomings related to biosecurity measures to be applied by the FBO on farms. 5.2 CONTROL AT FARMS LEVEL Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires Member States to carry out regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency controls on feed or food businesses.

Denmark has adopted national legislation to further develop obligations contained in EU regulations with regard to the organisation of the control system for organic production. The Law on organic production No 416 of 03/05/2011 issued by the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries contains the legal basis for the Danish organic control system in respect of EU regulations on organic production and labelling of organic products.
legal_basis: for the Danish organic control system in respect of EU regulations on organic production and labelling of organic products.

text: Based on this law DVFA has issued Order No 49 of 22 of January 2013 on organic food and aquaculture. This order lays down the DVFA control system including control in respect of processing, labelling, import and marketing of organic food and organic aquaculture.

DAFA also drafted national legislation to implement EU regulations as follows: Order No 488 of 8 May 2014 on the production of organic poultry; of 27 of June 2012 on organic agricultural production; Order No 956 of 7 December 2013 amended Order No 716; Order No 1053 of 6 September 2010 on the use of organic control label in agricultural products; Order No 1112 of 21 November 2011 on the production and marketing of organic pullets.

DAFA and DVFA also issued several guidelines and manuals to help organic inspectors carry out official controls and to ensure a harmonised implementation of the legislation. Both CAs have detailed instructions for inspectors to carry out inspections in the different types of premises and have comprehensive checklists. 3 Conclusions on legislation

All measures of national law necessary to implement legally binding Union acts relevant to this audit have been adopted by the CA. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities, Control Authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 27(1), 27(4), 27(4)(a) and 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Organic production in Denmark is under the control of DAFA and DVFA under the aegis of the Danish Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries. Both DAFA and DVFA are designated as CAs to control organic production. These two CAs do not confer control tasks to any control authority. The control system for organic production in Denmark is based on CAs.
SKAT is the Customs authority in charge of control of imports including organic products.

The distribution of tasks between DVFA and DAFA in the area of organic production is clearly divided and is described in cooperation agreements between the two entities. DVFA deals with the rules on importing, marketing, processing, labelling and production in aquaculture farms and in organic food establishments, while DAFA deals with rules on organic production for organic agricultural farms and associated supply operators. In addition, DAFA deals with tasks concerning area-based subsidies for organic farming and project and market aid schemes, including the organic production promotion scheme.
DAFA and DVFA are well structured, documented procedures are in place, and internal supervision of inspectors takes place.

Cooperation between DAFA and DVFA has been formalised in a principal cooperation agreement and in three sub-agreements. Cooperation agreements have also been signed between DAFA and DVFA and SKAT for official control on imported products including organic products.

DAFA, DVFA and SKAT exchange information when necessary, and as prescribed in the agreements. Good communication and co-operation, in line with Article 31 of 4 Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 is in place. The FVO audit team was provided with examples of the exchange of information between the two CAs when non-compliances were found during inspections.

Regular meetings are held between the CAs. Two annual meetings are held between DAFA and DVFA in the "Dialogue Forum on Organic Production" to discuss specific issues relating to organic production. Other channels of communication are established, such as letters and the frequent exchange of e-mails.

The DVFA's Chemistry and Food Quality Division is responsible for organic controls at central level. DVFA has six regional offices involved in organic production control. These offices carry out the organic controls and also the general food control.

Coordination and cooperation within DVFA is done through experience groups called ERFA. There is an ERFA group specifically dealing with organic. The group members are inspectors from DVFA's regional offices as well as specialists from the Chemistry and Food Quality Division. The ERFA group meets twice a year to discuss issues related to organic control and to ensure that there is continuous control coordination and mutual knowledge sharing across DVFA. Participants of these groups should later disseminate the information to the other colleagues in the relevant regional offices. Intranet is also a useful tool for coordination and cooperation between central level and regional offices. Agenda and minutes of the ERFA meetings were provided to the audit team.
The Organic Farming and Fertilizers Team within DAFA is responsible for organic controls. DAFA local offices carry out the on-the-spot visits at organic operators.

Cooperation between the central Organic Farming and Fertilizers Team and the local offices has been formalised in the 2015 monitoring agreements on controls in the organic sector. The agreement stipulated that the Organic Farming and Fertilizers Team must, among other things, hold four ERFA meetings per year with the local offices. The meeting must ensure the sharing of knowledge. Agenda and minutes of the ERFA meetings were provided to the audit team.
Regular supervision of inspectors is in place in DAFA and DVFA. Witness audits are carried out on inspectors.

DAFA carries out supervision of all inspectors in a five year period. Staff from the central office accompanies the inspector during an inspection visit to assess the inspector's performance. A report is produced of this supervision. DAFA provided to the FVO audit team supervision reports carried out on inspectors.

Internal audits are carried out on DAFA by the internal audit service. The organic control system was audited in 2014. The FVO audit team reviewed the audit report where two recommendations were made. Corrective actions had been taken in response to these recommendations. 5 20. DVFA carries out supervision of all inspectors at least once every three years, and each new inspector during the first year. In total, at least half of the inspectors are supervised every year based on a needs assessment. 21. There is an internal audit programme where control of organic food is part of the audit universe. DVFA has not been audited yet for organic production. 22. Training and regular evaluation of inspectors is organised by the two designated CAs. 23. DVFA control offices must ensure that the inspectors have the necessary competences to carry out organic controls. Training is organised by DVFA to ensure inspectors have knowledge on organic production. There are three types of courses organised. Course level one for general matters (one day), course level two (two days) specifically focusing on control documents, input-output balances and course level three that is more specialised and intended for key persons that should later disseminate the knowledge to other colleges in the relevant regional offices. At least one inspector in each regional office should follow course level three. DVFA inspectors met during inspection visits had participated in the above-mentioned courses. 24. DAFA also organises training sessions for organic inspectors. Instruction courses are organised once a year. Two types of these courses are organised: one for inspection of farms and the other for inspection of suppliers (feed mills). 25. Records of training activities organised by DAFA and DVFA were provided to the FVO audit team. Conclusions on competent authorities 26. A system of controls is in place in accordance with EU provisions. The CAs are designated and the tasks clearly distributed. Exchange of information between CAs, included SKAT, is carried out and good communication and cooperation is in place in line with Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1), 28(2) and 28(5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings 27. DVFA requires operators to apply for registration on-line in order to undertake organic activities. A set of documents have to be provided (description of premises, production plan, precautionary measures, etc). DVFA assesses the documentation submitted by the 6 operator and if the evaluation is satisfactory, an on-the-spot visit is normally carried out. If the visit is satisfactory the operator is approved to carry out new organic activities and market organic products and the documentary evidence (Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) is issued. It is valid for one calendar year. The list of approved operators is published containing updated documentary evidence related to each operator. The level of detail of the information provided on the activities and production of each operator allows for the public to be adequately informed. 28. DVFA does not use the model of the documentary evidence set up in Annex XII of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which is not in line with Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The date of control is missing. 29. DAFA also have a detailed procedure for registration of organic operators. In case of organic farmers, applications have to be signed by a consultant approved by DAFA. If the assessment of the application and accompanying documents are satisfactory an inspection visit is organised within the next six months. If the result of the inspection is satisfactory the operator is approved for conversion. In case of agricultural operators, documentary evidence is issued during the summer period and is valid until next year. A procedure for registration of suppliers is also in place. 30. DAFA keeps and publishes on the Internet a list of organic operators under their control. The list is updated every month. However, documentary evidence related to each operator is not published with this list, which is not in line with Article 92b of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 31. Denmark has made use of the exemption provided for in Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Retailers who only sell pre-packaged and labelled products directly to the final consumer or user are exempted from the requirement of registration. DVFA is the CA in charge of the control on general food hygiene in food establishments, included retailers. More than 200 retailers that do not meet the conditions to be exempted from the control system are under organic control. DVFA stated that those exempted are still under control for food hygiene requirements so DVFA is able to check that they fulfil the conditions to be exempted when those establishments are inspected for food hygiene. For example, in 2014, 22 exempted retailers were checked for organic labelling and no irregularities were found. 7 Conclusions on registration of operators 32. There is an adequate system in place for the registration of operators and overall it is effectively implemented. The CAs publish and keep an updated list of operators, in line with EU legislation. However, DAFA does not publish the documentary evidence and the documentary evidence issued by DVFA to the operators does not follow the model of Annex XII of Regulation (EC) No 899/2008. 33. Operators who only sell products directly to the final consumer or user and do not prepare or import these products are exempted from the organic farming control system in line with Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 65(4), 92c(2) and 92f of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 3 and 41 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 34. DVFA carries out inspections of organic operators as part of the general food control. The general food control is risk-based in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. After a risk assessment is carried out, all food establishments are classified in five risk groups and the frequency of inspection visits is based on this risk categorisation. The ordinary inspection frequencies range from five inspections per year to as and when required. In addition, organic operators are visited for follow-up inspections and extra campaign visits. 35. Additional visits are also planned and are risk-based and unannounced. DVFA have a manual on inspection of organic food where criteria for additional visits are established as follows: follow-up of non-compliances, size of establishments, parallel production, and regular inspection campaigns. According with this manual additional visits are follow-up inspections ordinary inspections and extra inspections. 36. DVFA informed the FVO audit team that, in 2014, more than 2464 inspection visits were carried out at the organic operators registered (i.e. 1165 organic operators registered the full calendar year and the 458 new/discontinued organic operators). Around 800 of the total visits were considered additional visits in compliance with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 37. As a general rule, organic operators are visited by DAFA at least once a year. Additional risk based visits are carried out. However, there are 110 registered small farmers that are not visited annually. DAFA indicated that these operators do not sell organic products. 8 DAFA carries out an annual organic control only on 10% of these operators as long as they do not place any organic products on the market. This is not in compliance with Article 65(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 38. In 2015 DAFA had planned to carry out around 250 additional unannounced visits. 75 of these additional visits are reserved to be selected by inspectors, for example in cases of suspicion. The organisation of additional visits to farmer operators is mainly based on previous non-compliances. This means that farmers without previous non-compliances are not selected for additional visits. This is not in line with organic regulations as the nature and frequency of the additional visits are not based on an assessment of the risk of occurrence of irregularities and infringements (Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007), the size of the operator or the risk of exchange of products as established in Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 39. Different types of farmers are selected for additional visits based on the evaluation of the totality of irregularities found the previous year to ensure that all types of potential non- compliances are covered. DAFA additional visits are only focused on one pre-selected aspect of the organic production (e.g. animal welfare, use of non- organic seeds, etc). In 2015 additional visits will be focused on: animal welfare in housing for cattle, pigs and poultry, access to grazing for cattle, use of fertilizers or plant protection products, production of fruits and vegetables and production records. 40. DAFA risk assessment for additional visits to suppliers of organic products takes into account previous non-compliances, size and parallel production which is in line with the organic regulation. 41. In the initial meeting DAFA informed the FVO audit team that the risk assessment process was being reviewed for 2016. Conclusions on planning and prioritisation of controls 42. Controls on organic operators are in most cases annually carried out in line with Article 65(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the frequency of control on a defined group of small farmers that do not place products on the market is not in line with the above-mentioned article. 43. Additional visits are primarily unannounced and based in most cases on risk assessment as established in Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the risk assessment carried out to select additional visits to organic farms is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 5.2.4 Controls of Operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 9 Titles II and IV and Article 65(1) and 65(3) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 44. DAFA has procedures in place to ensure that inspectors verify the precautionary measures when visiting operators. DAFA guidance on organic production for operators clearly specifies the type of precautionary measures operators should put in place to avoid potential contamination of crops, products or animals. Operators should ensure clear boundaries between organic fields and non- organic ones (buffer zones, fence, bare soil strip), separation of non-organic animals and organic ones (for grazing and housing), clear separation of organic products (crops, feed, seeds, etc) and non-organic products during transport, production and storage. 45. The FVO audit team noted that inspectors verified precautionary measures in place during the inspections to organic operators. Examples of cases with irregularities related to precautionary measures were shown to the FVO audit team. 46. The FVO audit team witnessed three inspections carried out by DAFA inspectors. It was noted that they have available plenty of information for the preparation of the visit. The inspectors check national databases related to registration and identification of animals, medical treatments, agricultural production, etc. All this information is a very useful tool for the inspector prior the inspection visit. It helps the inspector to focus the inspection in certain areas. Inspectors make a good preparatory work prior the inspections. 47. Overall, the three inspections witnessed by the FVO audit team were considered satisfactory. During the inspections the FVO audit team noted that: Inspectors visited all the premises and visually checked the conditions and identification of animals; Precautionary measures were verified; Calculations to demonstrate the balance between the inputs and outputs were made; Calculations of the feed consumption by animals were carried out in the farm visited. Calculation of manure produced by the animal was made; Veterinary treatment records and the withdrawal period for treated animals were checked; Animal welfare and husbandry were checked. 48. If there are no irregularities arising from the inspection an "OK report" is produced and sent to the organic operator. If irregularities are identified, the inspector gives 14 days to the operator to make comments. After this period, the inspector sends the report together with the organic operator's comments to the central level where a decision is made. 49. DVFA carries out annual inspection visits to all operators under their control (retailers, wholesalers, processing establishments, importers, aquaculture farms).
