Lithuania has adopted national legislation to further develop obligations contained in EU regulations with regard to the organisation of the control system for organic production. These rules include: Order No 375 of 28 December 2000 on the approval of the rules for organic agriculture; Order No 3D-341 of 8 May 2013 governing the tasks, functions, rights and work organisation of the CA ­ the Agri-Environment and Organic Farming Division within the Agricultural Production and Food Industry Department of the Ministry of Agriculture; Order No 3D-78 of 3 March 2006 on the approval of the rules for granting authorisation to certify production, processing and placing on the market of organic products; Order No 3D-2 of 6 January 2009 on the approval of the procedure for labelling of organic agricultural products and foodstuffs and for the use of the logo for organic agricultural products and foodstuffs; Order No 3D-352 of 17 May 2012 on the approval of the procedure for documentary checks on imported organic agricultural products and foodstuffs; Order No B1-255 of 28 March 2013 approving the list of imported foodstuffs of non-animal origin that are subject to more rigorous state food control; Order No 3D-873 of 19 December 2013 approving the committee for the evaluation of information on non-compliances with and infringements of the requirements for organic production and approving its rules of procedure; 3 Order No 3D-370 of 22 May 2009 on the provision of information by institutions and bodies that have found the infringements of the European legal acts regulating organic production. Conclusions

All measures of national law necessary to implement legally binding Union acts relevant to this audit have been adopted in Lithuania. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities, Control Authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 27(1), 27(4) and 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The CtrlA is accredited according to ISO standard EN 17065 and is responsible for: Certification and control of operators; Enforcement of the legislation; Evaluating requests for derogations under Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and providing a technical opinion to the CCA (see also Section 5.2.7).

The CtrlA has one central office and two branch offices. Controls on organic operators involved in primary production are distributed, by area, amongst these three offices. Controls on importers and processors are carried out by inspectors from the central office.
The SFVS is responsible for import controls (see also Section 5.2.8) and for the control of organic products on the market including labelling.

The distribution of tasks between the CtrlA and the SFVS in the area of organic production is clearly divided and is described in the cooperation agreement between these two entities, as required by Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Good cooperation is in place including for the regular exchange of information regarding inspections, non-compliances and follow-up investigations, and other relevant data on operators as required by Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The CtrlA has signed similar cooperation agreements with the State Plant Service ­ Valstybin augalininkysts tarnyba ­ and the National Paying Agency ­ Valstybin augalininkysts tarnyba (NPA). Representatives of the NPA indicated that this cooperation agreement 4 was also necessary for the purposes of payments of EU funds to organic operators since these were only made once the certification was granted.

The CtrlA employs staff on a full-time basis. Selection of staff is based on their qualifications and work experience. The CtrlA may allow inspectors to carry out private work on condition that prior authorisation is requested and after verifying that there is no conflict of interest, as required by Article 4(4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Newly employed staff of the CtrlA undergo a provisional 3-month period which satisfies the requirements of Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and includes: training on EU and national requirements on organic production; shadowing experienced inspectors while carrying out controls; carrying out controls under the supervision of experienced inspectors. The supervisors then have to write an evaluation report on the performance of the trainee; a final test on organic production requirement and a final evaluation by the branch manager.

The CtrlA carries out annual supervision of all inspectors. This includes an evaluation of the quality of reports produced, an assessment of the preparation of controls and an annual test. Witness inspections are carried out at least once every three years for each inspector.

The CCA carries out audits on the CtrlA. This includes office audits and witnessed inspections. As part of the audit the CCA: ensures that the inspectors of the CtrlA are free from conflicts of interest; verifies that written procedures are properly followed; verifies that inspections cover all the criteria included in the checklist; ensures that appropriate corrective actions are taken when non-compliances are detected; evaluates whether the amount of time dedicated to the inspection is adequate to the size and type of activity of the operator; evaluates the behaviour and conduct of the inspectors of the CtrlA. Conclusions

A system of controls is in place in accordance with EU provisions. The designation of the CAs and CtrlA is in place and distribution of tasks is clear. In addition, a system for the cooperation between the authorities carrying out controls on organic products is in place and ensures the exchange of relevant information. 5 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1), 28(2) and 28(5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

Operators wishing to undertake organic activities have to submit an application to the CtrlA. In the case of primary production these applications have to be submitted by 15 June of the year. The information to be provided in the application includes those indicated in Article 63(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 including a description of the envisaged precautionary measures. The application also includes a list of commitments the applicant has to undertake, as listed in Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.
The CtrlA informs the CCA of all applications received, and decisions taken to grant or refuse a certification, or withdraw or suspend an existing certification.

The list of certified operators and their relevant documentary evidence is managed and updated by the CtrlA, as envisaged by Article 28(5) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, and is accessible from the websites of the CCA and of the CtrlA, as required by Article 92b of Regulation (EC) No 882/2008.

The documentary evidence issued by the CtrlA includes the information required by Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and is compliant with the model in Annex XII of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The expiry date of the documentary evidence is the end of December of the year following the year of inspection. The CtrlA indicated that: annual inspections are carried out after the deadline for submission of farming land to the NPA as this information is used to determine the most critical period at which to carry out these inspections; although the maximum validity of these documents is more than one year, new documentary evidence annulling the previous document is issued after each full annual control. In general the lifetime of the documentary evidence is therefore between 10 and 14 months.

Lithuania has made use of the exemption provided for in Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Retailers who only sell pre-packaged and labelled products directly to the final consumer or user are exempted from the requirement of registration as indicated by Points 24 to 26 of Order No 375 of 28 December 2000. The SFVS is the CA in charge of general food hygiene in food establishments, included retailers. When carrying out controls at retailers the SFVS inspectors also verify that the retailers fulfil the conditions for exemption under the said Article. In 2014, 315 retailers were inspected and 14 non-compliances to Article 28(2) were detected and notified to the CtrlA. In addition, the SFVS requests the non-compliant operators to take corrective action (either to become a registered organic operator or to stop the activity) and carries out follow-up inspections. A representative of the SFVS indicated that in most cases this non-compliance was detected at small retailers who sold small quantities of loose products. These small retailers generally opted to stop selling the organic products. 6 Conclusions

There is an adequate system in place for the registration of operators and overall it is effectively implemented. The CtrlA publishes and keeps an updated list of operators, in line with EU legislation.

Operators who only sell pre-packaged and labelled products directly to the final consumer or user are exempted from the organic farming control system in line with Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Article 27(3) of Regulation 834/2007. Articles 65(4), 92c(2) and 92f of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 3 and 41 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

In 2014, the CtrlA carried out annual inspections on all the organic operators, as required by Article 65(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Data provided by the CtrlA for 2015 indicated that until 1 September 2015 62% of annual inspections had been carried out. 20. 451 additional inspections were carried out in 2014. This amounts to 17% of all organic operators and widely exceeded the minimum target of 10% indicated in Article 32 of Order No 375 of 28 December 2000. However 71% of these additional inspections were announced although Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 requires that additional inspections are to be primarily unannounced. Furthermore, the number of unannounced inspections totals 5% of organic operators and does not meet the minimum target of 10% laid down in Article 32 of Order No 375 of 28 December 2000. 21. Additional inspections are carried out on operators based on risk assessment. In the case of primary producers: there are four risk-based categories; several risk criteria are used to categorise these operators including past non- compliances (previous two years), the quantity of products concerned and the risk for exchange of products, as required by Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and storage facilities, origin of the animals, type of fertiliser used and presence of multiple organic operators in the same household. 22. Regarding the risk assessment in the case of processors: there are three risk-based categories; the risk categorisation of these operators is based on several criteria including past non-compliances (previous two years) and the risk for exchange of products but it does not include the quantity of products concerned although this is a requirement of Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This omission is clearly reflected in 7 the results of the risk categorisation wherein only 15 of 116 processors are classified in the highest risk category for 2015. 23. According to the procedures of the CtrlA the proportion of operators subjected to additional checks are: 100% in the highest risk category; 50% in the second risk category; 10% in the third risk category; 2% in the lowest risk category. 24. Areas to be checked by the CtrlA inspectors when carrying out the additional visits include previous non-compliances and the areas of high risk identified by the risk assessment. Conclusions 25. Controls on organic operators are carried out annually in line with Article 65(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 26. A high number of additional visits are carried out but these are not primarily unannounced although this is a requirement of Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Furthermore, the risk assessment carried out to select additional visits to organic processors is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 as it does not take into consideration the production quantities resulting in a reduced number of additional checks at processors handling large quantities of products. 5.2.4 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Titles II and IV and Article 65(1) and 65(3) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 27. The CtrlA and SFVS have detailed procedures in place, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to ensure that inspectors verify all requirements of EU organic Regulations. These procedures include checklists with legal references for each field and a relevant set of instructions. The audit team also noted that all inspectors had copies of relevant legislation with them when carrying out the inspections. 28. The CtrlA requires organic operators to regularly provide it with information on the activities carried out. Such information includes: medical treatment of animals whenever this is carried out; a yearly summary of crop production; a monthly summary from each processor of the incoming organic raw materials and relevant details of the organic supplier. 8 This has been identified as a good practice by the audit team as it allows the CtrlA to better supervise the activities of organic operators. 29. The audit team witnessed four inspections carried out by the CtrlA. It was noted that the inspectors have plenty of information available for the preparation of the visit which includes the information regularly provided by the operators, information obtained from past inspections and information from the NPA. 30. During the four inspections witnessed by the audit team: All inspectors were aware of the critical points of the holding/establishment that was being inspected; All inspectors paid particular attention to the calculation between the input and the output of the organic products (Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) and to the traceability of these products; Precautionary measures (Article 63(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) were checked by the inspectors at all operators. The inspector at the cereal farm paid particular attention to the buffer zones around the parcels of land that were in the first year of conversion; Animal welfare, husbandry and identification were checked in the dairy farm. The farmer visited had de-horned all adult bovines without requesting a derogation, contrarily to Article 18(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and this was noted by the inspector. Furthermore, the inspector noted that veterinary medicinal products had been administered to the animals at the time of de-horning but the farmer had failed to respect the withdrawal period (see also paragraph 57). Conclusions 31. Controls carried out on organic operators in general follow the instructions and other documented procedures. Controls of operators are effective and are carried out largely in line with organic regulations. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Articles 23, 24 and 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Title III of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings 32. Samples of labels used for organic products by registered operators have to be submitted to the CtrlA for approval. The CtrlA keeps these samples, bearing an approval stamp, in the operator's file. 33. Checks on labelling of organic products are included in the controls carried out by the SFVS at retailers (see also paragraph 16). During controls carried in 2014 the SFVS detected 22 non-compliances with labelling requirements. 9 34. During the visit to the retailer the SFVS inspectors: checked the labels of organic products against EU and national organic labelling requirements; carried out a traceability check of an organic product against its accompanying documents. 35. During the visit to the importer and processor the CtrlA: checked the traceability of the organic products from point of entry to point of dispatch; checked labels of the final product against labelling requirements at the importer, as processing operations (cleaning and re-packaging) were also being carried out. 36. Checklists used by both SFVS and CtrlA inspectors include a field for compliance against organic labelling requirements (see also paragraph 27). 37. Between March 2015 and May 2015 the CAs organised a training exercise on the traceability of organic products. This exercise involved representatives of the CCA, the SFVS and the CtrlA. A traceability exercise was also carried out by the CtrlA together with the SFVS during the audit. Two processed products were collected from a supermarket. The outcome of the exercise was overall good, and all ingredients selected could be traced back to the producers. Conclusions 38. Labelling and traceability checks are regularly performed by the CA and CtrlA during inspections. There is an appropriate system in place to ensure traceability of products at all stages and to ensure that the labelling of the products complies with EU provisions. 5.2.6 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 65 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 39. Sampling by the CtrlA is carried out at operators that are in the highest risk category and that are therefore selected for additional controls (see also paragraphs 21, 22 and 23). Samples may be collected during either the annual or additional inspection. Based on this risk-categorisation the CtrlA plans to collect a total of 154 samples

In the framework of PDO/PGI/TSG, the relevant national legislation for official controls of product specification in the context of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 is implemented through a series of legal instruments at national level. The most relevant pieces of legislation governing the official control system in place for PDO/PGI/TSG are the Rural and Maritime Fishing Code and the Consumer Code. These provisions are implemented by the two CAs designated in France to control quality schemes: the National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO) and the Directorate-General for Competition, Consumer Affairs and Fraud Prevention (DGCCRF).

The relevant provisions for the controls performed under the responsibility of INAO are mainly contained in Titre IV of Book VI of the Rural and Maritime Fishing Code. INAO also adopted instructions to help in the organisation of the controls in the format of Directives and Circulars.

The relevant provisions for the controls performed under DGCCRF are contained also in Title IV of Book VI of the Rural and Maritime Fishing Code and in the Books I and II of the Consumer Code. 3 Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation

Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG products. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 36 (1), 36(2), 37(1) and (3) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular Articles 4 and 6. Findings

The French 2011-2013 Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) has been extended for 2014. The MANCP for 2015 is currently being drafted. Official controls related to PDO/PGI/TSG are described in a separate section of the MANCP. The Annual Report on the implementation of the MANCP in 2014 was submitted to the COM, including a specific section on PDO/PGI/TSG. This is in line with Article 40 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The main Authorities in the context of this audit are described in the MANCP and in the Country Profile and are as follows:

The CCA within the scope of this audit is the Ministry of Agriculture, Agro-Food, and Forestry (MAAF). In particular, the Directorate General of Economic Performance and Environment of Enterprises (DGPE) is responsible for the definition of the quality system policy, to ensure the tutelage of INAO, to approve together with DGCCRF the PDO/PGI/TSG product specifications and is the French contact point for the DG AGRI Unit in charge of quality scheme. In addition, the Directorate General for Food (DGAL) of the MAFF is tasked to participate in defining and monitoring the INAO policy on official controls.

INAO which is a public administrative body under the auspices of the MAAF is the CCA responsible for verification of compliance with the product specification prior to placing PDO/PGI/TSG products produced in France on the market. INAO delegates control tasks to Control Bodies (CBs) pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

INAO is also responsible for protecting registered PDO/PGI/TSG names. INAO verifies the trademark applications with the National Institute of Industrial Property (INPI). If there is an infringement regarding one of these marks, INAO sends its observations to the INPI. Within the scope of these duties, it may also send letters to those operators that do not respect the rules protecting the registered PDO/PGI/TSG or initiate proceedings in civil courts. 4 9. INAO is responsible for the approval, the suspension and withdrawal of CBs. It is also responsible for the supervision of delegated CBs and for the approval of control plans prepared by CBs for each PDO/PGI/TSG product specification. 10. INAO has eight regional offices. 11. The DGCCRF is a Directorate of the Ministry of Economic Affairs. It is the CCA for labelling. It is responsible for checking labelling and the product specifications at the market as well as to protect the use of registered names to describe PDO/PGI/TSG products. The checks carried out under the responsibility of the DGCCRF may take place at any stage in the production chain (production, processing, wholesale, retail, distribution, markets, restaurants, internet sites, etc). They are mainly carried out at departmental level by the Departmental Directorates for the Protection of the Population (DDPP) or the Directorates for Social Cohesion and Protection of the Population (DDCSPP). The Regional Directorates for Enterprises, Competition, Consumer Affairs and Employment (DIRECCTE) play a coordinating role. 12. There is good coordination and cooperation between the CAs involved in the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. The audit team was provided with examples of good cooperation and coordination between INAO and DGCCRF. There is a cooperation protocol signed on 2009. The cooperation coordination procedure includes a "fiche de liaison" where INAO inform DGCCRF in cases where serious non-compliances in operators visited are identified and vice versa. 13. There is also good exchange of information between the CAs and COFRAC. There is an agreement with INAO to exchange information through regular meetings and a yearly meeting at director level. DGAL and DGCCRF are part of the COFRAC board. Conclusions on Competent Authorities 14. CAs are designated for the verification of compliance of product specification prior to placing on the market of PDO/PGI/TSG products and for the monitoring of the use of registered names to describe PDO/PGI/TSG products on the market in line with Article 36 of Regulation (EC) No 1151/2012. There is a good cooperation and coordination between the two CAs involved on official controls. 5.2.2 Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 39(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 5(2) (e) and (f) and 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5 Findings 15. Official controls to verify compliance with the product specification are delegated to CBs accredited to ISO Standard 17065. This is in line with the requirements of Article 39 (2) of the Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Accreditation is issued by COFRAC for a specific category of products. Then, the CB is approved by INAO to carry out delegated official control tasks on PDO/PGI/TSG products. 16. At the time of the audit, seven CBs are approved to carry out official controls on PDO/PGI/TSG products. One product specification can be controlled by more than one CB. 17. INAO has documented procedures in place for the approval of the CBs. These describe the criteria to be fulfilled to obtain the approval, the most relevant being the requirements related to accreditation. This is in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 18. CBs are regularly evaluated by COFRAC every 15 months. Evaluation includes office and witness audits. The COFRAC evaluation is based on the control plans produced by the CBs for each product specification. These plans have to be approved by INAO. The audit team saw an example where CB accreditation was withdrawn by COFRAC as a result of a supervision audit. As a result, INAO withdrew the approval of the CB and requested the relevant Producer Group (PG) to engage a new CB. The control plan prepared by the new CB was approved by INAO. 19. CBs are also regularly supervised by INAO. Supervision includes office and witness audits. INAO has procedures in place to supervise CBs. Checklists are used and a report is produced after the audit. A normal supervision audit could be carried out in two to four days. Supervision is carried out every year during the first four years after approval. Afterwards supervision audits are carried out every 12 to 18 months. 20. The audit team reviewed INAO supervision reports during the visits to two CBs. It was noted that regular supervision of CBs was carried out by INAO. When deficiencies were noted, an action plan was required and follow-up was carried out. The audit team checked supervision reports issued by INAO and noted that they were comprehensive and detailed, including recommendations and specific deadlines for the CBs to remedy the non-compliances. 21. There is a good exchange of information between the CBs and INAO, in particular, serious non-compliances must be notified to INAO in seven working days. Communication between the CA and CBs is regularly established. The audit team noted that INAO requires the CBs to submit reports on official controls quarterly and annually. 22. CBs have procedures in place to train new inspectors. The performance of the inspectors is regularly assessed by the CB. 6 23. As an example of good practice, the audit team considers that having a control plan approved by INAO for every single product is a good tool for CBs to carry out consistent official controls and to harmonise the controls at national levels (e.g. two CBs carrying out controls on the same product follow the same control plan). It also serves as guidance and facilitates the work of the relevant inspectors. It could also serve to allow INAO to harmonise the controls for the same type of products at national level. 24. The procedure for supervision sets out the basic principles to follow. The means of verification may include the review by INAO of control reports issued by the CBs on the inspections carried out at operators, visits on the spot to witness the performance of the CBs inspectors, checking that inspectors have the right tools and procedures available, impartiality, staff resources, etc. Conclusions on Control Bodies 25. The CA ensures that CBs fulfil all requirements for approval, including accreditation to ISO 17065. The delegation of official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG products to CBs is adequately supervised by the CA as required in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings Verification of Compliance Prior to Placing the Products on the Market 26. Control procedures implemented by INAO require new operators to notify the relevant PG of their intention to produce PDO/PGI/TSG products. The PG carries out a documentary check and informs the relevant CB. The new operators cannot place products on the market under the PDO/PGI/TSG scheme until they are included in the CB list of operators authorised to produce under the relevant quality scheme. 27. Approval/authorisation of new operators by CBs may be given without the CB carrying out an inspection of the new operator. This is not in line with Article 36 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 as verification of compliance with the product specification can only be checked/assessed by carrying out a physical visit to the operator. This is also not in line with Article 10(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which establishes that official controls shall be carried out using appropriate control techniques. 7 Official Controls at Producers/Processors 28. CBs plan and prioritise official controls based on the relevant control plan approved by INAO for every product specification. The organisation and planning of sampling is also based on the control plan. This was considered by the audit team as an example of good practice. Control plans cover operators own-checks and internal controls carried out by the PGs. The internal controls are supervised by the relevant CB. 29. The methodology, the procedure and the checklists used to carry out internal controls are the same as those used by CBs for official control which may facilitate the supervision of the CB of the tasks carried out by the PGs. This was also considered as an example of good practice. 30. However, control plans lack harmonization as regards risk assessment, methodology used (e.g. sampling of feed) for the same type of product and same nature of the visits (in some cases visits are unannounced and in other cases announced). 31. For some products, the volume of production and past records were used as risk criteria to decide on the frequency of visits. However, for most of the PDO/PGI products selected for the audit, an effective risk assessment was not carried out to determine the frequency of controls. The audit team noted that the control frequency is set up in order to ensure that all operators with the same activities (producers, dryers of products, processors, etc) are visited in a stipulated period of time, regardless of specific criteria such as size, volume of production, parallel production of conventional and PDO/PGI/TSG products, etc. The number and relevance of the different requirements of the product specification is not taken into account when deciding the frequency of visits to operators at each stage of the food chain. As an example, the control plan for a product of animal origin had around 40 points of control that can only be checked at farm level. Nine of them could lead to grave or major non-compliances. However, these control points are only checked by the CB in 3% of the operators each year. This is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 32. Internal controls are taken into account to reduce the frequency of visits, which is in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, for several PDO/PGI/TSG products official controls are carried out on a very low number of operators, especially at producer level. Therefore, it cannot be considered that operators are visited regularly as established in Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. As an example, in the case of the product of animal origin mentioned in paragraph 31, it can be the case that some operators in the group will never receive an official control visit to check their compliance with the product specification, which is not in line with Article 36 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Moreover, in some cases the frequency of visits is reduced even if internal controls are only carried out on a small number of operators. This was the case for a product of non-animal origin, for which the control plan set up a percentage of 20% of producers to be visited each year, even if internal controls only covered 5% of the producers annually. 8 33. All of the visits witnessed by the audit team were inspections, according to the definition of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Most control plans stipulated that official controls shall be announced, contrary to Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In other cases, control plans state that official controls shall be unannounced. However, during the visit to one producer of a product of animal origin, the audit team was informed by the CB that in principle official controls are announced, which is not in line with the approved control plan. Official Controls on the Market 34. There is a national and a regional programme for official controls carried out by DGCCRF on the market. 35. The national plan for controls of the DGCCRF is biannual. The audit team reviewed the report produced relating to the previous control plan for 2012-2013. At the time of the audit DGCCRF still was working on the 2014-2105 plan. 36. The official control is based on risk analysis to select products to be audited. During inspection at market level, inspectors have an updated list of products already inspected. The list is updated after every inspection to include new products inspected. The same procedures are followed for sampling. The audit team consider this as an example of good practice. 37. Controls on the market are carried out for national, EU and third country products. 38. DGCCRF controls may include a visit to processor responsible for placing the product on the market. The audit team were accompanied by officials of DGCCRF during the visits to some operators, who explained the purpose and methodology of their visits. 39. When DGCCRF identify non-compliances on the label at market level, a follow-up of the non-compliances is ensured (visit, warning letter, etc) to the relevant operator responsible for placing the product on the market. When labels are correct, no traceability exercise is carried out. 9 Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 40. CBs may grant authorisation to new operators joining the production scheme without an inspection visit being carried out by the relevant CB to verify compliance with the product specification. 41. Official controls for verification of compliance with the product specification prior to placing on the market of PDO/PGI/TSG products are not always adequately planned and implemented as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In particular, the selection of operators to be visited is not always based on risk assessment and the frequency of visits does not always ensure that all operators are regularly inspected. Moreover, inspections are not always carried out without prior warning. 42. Official controls for t

The import monitoring plan (hereafter ­ IMP) is developed and updated by the Länder working group for import and transit (Arbeitsgruppe Ein- und Durchfuhr der Länderarbeitsgemeinschaft ) in co-operation with representatives of the BMEL and the BVL. The IMP is published together with the national residue control plan. This working group considers the information on previous IMP results, RASFF notifications, the applicable EU legislation, results of studies provided by other authorities, information from EU working groups (i.e. residue controls, veterinary checks), training, and other relevant risk factors, in accordance with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The risk-based approach is applicable for all products of animal origin imported via German BIPs, ensuring that products intended for release into free circulation in another Member State are also controlled, in compliance with Article 3(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The IMP covers residues of veterinary medicines, pathogens, contaminants, hormones and other substances dangerous for humans, animals or the environment, in compliance with Annex II to Regulation (EC) 136/2004.

The IMP is adopted by the Länder working group for import and transit of the Länder joint operations body on consumer protection (Länderarbeitsgemeinschaft Verbraucherschutz Arbeitsgruppe Ein- und Durchfuhr der Länderarbeitsgemeinschaft) 4 and then it is forwarded to the BIPs, which are responsible for its implementation. The plan is implemented throughout the calendar year.

The BIP follows the general rule of 5% sampling of all different origin and types of products of animal origin without being prescriptive in how to achieve this. Analytes considered for testing are based on information available in the database and the BIP takes a flexible approach to the selection of consignments for sampling. The audit team noted that the system in place allows BIP staff to take samples in line with the IMP. Hamburg and Bremen: Hamburg port and Bremerhaven BIPs prepare the annual plan indicating the number of samples to be taken for different types of products of animal origin and analytes for laboratory tests. The annual IMP is split into monthly plans ensuring the sampling is spread throughout the year. In Hamburg, the IMP includes the possibility of sampling in case of new hazards and samples are selected ensuring that different origins are covered.

An annual budget for the implementation of the IMPs is allocated by the Länder competent authorities in accordance with Article 26 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Länder competent authorities indicated that BIPs can re-allocate the finances for the different tests within the annual budget for implementation of the import monitoring plan.

All BIPs visited have instructions on which laboratories are to be used for different laboratory tests. Official laboratories are used for testing samples taken under the import monitoring plan, re-enforced checks or in case of suspicion, as required by Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. After consultation with the official laboratories, BIPs can send samples to private laboratories if the methods for testing are not within the scope of accreditation of official laboratories.

Training covering official import controls including physical checks and sampling has been provided to BIP staff, in accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. During the visit to Hamburg port BIP, BIP staff demonstrated appropriate knowledge on practical sampling.

In accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the official controls on physical checks including sampling are carried out in accordance with documented procedures contained in the BIP manual (Handbuch).

The IMP is only for official use and the import monitoring plans developed by the Länder are not made available to the public/operators. text: BACKGROUND Information on the existence of direct or indirect risks to human health deriving from food or feed is disseminated via notifications through the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) to all Member States (MSs) and to the exporting country. From 2011 until 2014, there were 370 notifications concerning pathogenic micro-organisms in fruit and vegetables. During this period, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) adopted a number of scientific opinions on the risk posed by FNAO: http://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/publications.htm The EFSA noted that FNAO is consumed in a variety of forms, and is a major component of almost all meals. These food types have the potential of being associated with large outbreaks, as seen in 2011, of Verocytotoxin Producing Escherichia Coli (VTEC) O104. A comparison of the incidence of human cases linked to consumption of FNAO and of food of animal origin was carried out to provide an indication of the relative incidence between these two groups of foods. Using data from 2007 to 2011, FNAO was associated with 10% of outbreaks, 26% of cases, 35% of hospitalisations and 46% of deaths. If the data from the 2 2011 VTEC O104 outbreak is excluded, FNAO was associated with 10% of outbreaks, 18% of cases, but only 8% of hospitalisations and 5% of deaths. From 2008 to 2011 there was an increase in the number of reported outbreaks, cases, hospitalisations and deaths associated with FNAO. In order to identify and rank specific food/pathogen combinations most often linked to human cases originating from FNAO in the EU, a model was developed using seven criteria: strength of associations between food and pathogen based on the food-borne outbreak data from EU Zoonoses Monitoring (2007- 2011), incidence of illness, burden of disease, dose-response relationship, consumption, prevalence of contamination and pathogen growth potential during shelf life. The top ranking food/pathogen combinations were: leafy greens eaten raw as salads/Salmonella spp. and norovirus; bulb and stem vegetables; tomatoes; melons; sprouts/Salmonella spp; fresh pods, legumes or grains/pathogenic Escherichia coli. EFSA adopted several scientific Opinions on the public health risk posed by pathogens that may contaminate FNAO. In general, as regards specific mitigating options to reduce the risk for humans posed by pathogens in FNAO, EFSA concluded that: appropriate implementation of food safety management systems including Good Agricultural Practices (GAP), Good Hygiene Practices (GHP) and Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) should be the primary objective of operators producing the relevant crops. These food safety management systems should be implemented along the farm to fork continuum and should aim at the control of a range of microbiological hazards. The risk factors for the contamination of the crops assessed at primary production with different pathogens at growing stages are likely to include the following: Environmental factors, in particular climatic conditions (e.g. heavy rainfall) which may increase the transfer of pathogens from sewage or sewage effluents to irrigation water sources or fields; Use of untreated or insufficiently treated manure or compost; Use of sewage-contaminated agricultural water, either for irrigation or for application of agricultural chemicals such as fungicides; Contact with animal reservoirs (domestic or wild life) gaining access to fields, and Contamination and cross-contamination by harvesters, food handlers and equipment at harvest or post-harvest. EFSA adopted a scientific opinion on the risk posed by Shigatoxin Producing Escherichia coli (STEC) and other pathogenic bacteria in seeds and sprouts, after the outbreaks of STEC in May 2011 in the EU. The EFSA report can be found at: http://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/2424.htm Consumption of sprouts was identified as the most likely origin of the outbreaks. Over 4000 human cases were reported and 55 people died. In its opinion EFSA concluded that the 3 contamination of seeds with bacterial pathogens was the most likely initial source of sprout- associated outbreaks. Due to the high humidity and the favourable temperature during sprouting, bacterial pathogens present on dry seeds can multiply on the sprouts. In view of the number of large outbreaks and the high number of RASFF notifications concerning primary products of non-animal origin, the FVO decided to undertake an audit series of MSs on primary production of FNAO.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Findings 1. Section 22 of the Food Act, which entered into force on 1 March 2006, establishes the obligation of places of primary production to notify the activity carried out to the municipal food supervisory authority. Amendment 365/2013, which entered into force on 1 June 2013, provides for the approval required by places of primary production of sprouts. Prior to this, sprout production was legally defined as operation in a food establishment and had to be notified to the municipal food supervisory authority under Section 13 of the Food Act. The original version of the Finnish Food Act, without later amendments, can be read online at the following address: http://www.finlex.fi/fi/laki/alkup/2006/20060023 2. Section 22a of the Amendment 365/2013 requires that a FBO "shall obtain approval for the primary place of production from the municipal supervisory authority". However, "in the case of a minimum risk-activity a notification must be made instead of an application for approval". There is no further clarification of "minimum risk-activity".2 3. Government Decree 1258/2011 on Operations Considered Minor as regards the Risks to Food Safety (which entered into force on 01/01/2012 and was notified to the Commission by notification 2001/132/FIN of 21/03/2011) defines the types of supply of primary products directly to the consumer and delivery of primary products to local retail sale, which can be exempted from requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 as referred to in Article 1(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. i.e. this Regulation does not apply to "the direct supply, by the producer, of small quantities of primary products to the final consumer or to local retail establishments directly 2 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that:" The phrase 'Operations considered minor as regards the risks to food safety' has been clarified by provisions in Government Decree 1258/2011 on Operations Considered Minor as regards the Risks to Food Safety." 4 supplying the final consumer". Article 1(3) of this Regulation sets out that MSs "shall establish, under national law, rules governing the activities referred to in paragraph 2(c). Such national rules shall ensure the achievement of the objectives of this Regulation". This exemption is applied in Finland to producers of fresh leafy vegetables with an annual volume of no more than 5 000 kg. The threshold for other primary products of plant origin is 10 000 kg per annum. Since there are no specific provisions for producers of sprouts, sprout-producing FBO avail of the exemption from EU hygiene rules laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 if their annual production volume is not more than 10 000 kg. As a consequence of this exemption, such FBOs are not obliged to follow Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 on microbiological criteria for foodstuffs and Commission Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 on the approval of establishments producing sprouts, since those legislative acts are implementing Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Likewise, because of this exemption, sprout-producing FBOs with an annual production below 10 000 kg, although subject to official controls as regards the requirements laid down in national legislation, do not have to comply with all requirements laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Commission Regulation (EU) No 210/2013, in particular the requirements concerning the testing of the seeds for sprouting and the sprouts (see also paragraph 31).3 4. Taking into account the size of a normal serving portion of sprouts (ca 50 g), at least 200 000 serving portions per producer could reach the market without complying with all requirements laid down in Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Commission Regulation (EU) No 210/2013. 5. Procedures for registration and approval of FBO are comprehensively described in the Country profile for Denmark.

According to the information provided by DVFA, ice factories producing ice to be used for lowering the temperature of fishery products do not have to be registered or approved (only ice factories supplying ice to be used as an ingredient in the production of food are registered by DVFA). According to the information provided by DVFA to the audit team, in order to respect the requirements of Annex II, Chapter VII. 4 to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 (i.e. ice is to be made, handled and stored under conditions that protect it from contamination), DVFA requires that FBOs using this ice have in place procedures to ensure that it is safe. The audit team noted that all FBO visited requested from their ice supplier microbiological and physic-chemical laboratory analyses results for water and ice, and some of these FBOs took additional samples of water and ice. 4 9. According to the information provided by DVFA, establishments using recycled or recirculated water have to be specifically approved for that purpose. This practice is only authorised to be carried, as required by Annex II, Chapter VII. 3 to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004) where the water does not represent a risk of contamination for the food product. The audit team visited an establishment which was approved to use recirculated water. The DVFA inspector responsible for this establishment agreed that recycling of water was a potential source of contamination that had to be handled in the own-check system of the establishment. The CA added that neither analysis done by the establishment nor audits and analysis done by the DVFA indicated that the recycling of water constituted a risk. 10. The audit team noted that all establishments visited had been approved by DVFA for activities carried out on-site and the approval documents were available to the audit team. Approval documents were found to be adequate and contained all elements prescribed in national procedures except in one case. In this case the activities allowed to be carried out were not updated (i.e. provider of services) and a situation in place for the previous months was not reflected (i.e. a new establishment was approved in a separated area located on the site of its premises, with part of the premises being shared by both establishments). Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings Official control system in place 12. The official control systems in place by DAFA and DVFA are described in the Country Profile for Denmark. The following paragraphs provide additional detail on the systems as they impact on the fishery products sector. a) Official control system put in place by DAFA at primary production, landing operations, first sale and facilities handling fishery products 13. The official control system put in place by DAFA is limited to its area of competences (i.e. fresh fishery products until the point of first sale), and it includes hygiene controls of fresh fishery products at sea, on vessels and during landing; and at sorting and grading establishments, auctions halls and other establishments handling fresh fishery 5 products until the point of first sale. The target for DAFA is to carry out hygiene controls on 10% of the total quantity of landed amounts in the country, both for Danish and non-Danish vessels. The hygiene control of fresh fishery products is carried out simultaneously with other control tasks including controls related to quota management. These controls are prioritised adapting the "traffic light system"3 used for fish quota controls together with the evaluation of the non-conformities detected in previous controls. 14. Controls on vessels and during landing comprise checks on hygiene on board, hygiene of the catch, hygiene of boxes, crates, etc. and the suitability of the fishery products for human consumption. Controls at first buyers and establishments on land comprise checks of hygiene of fishery products, hygiene during transportation and the suitability of the fishery products for human consumption. An inspection report is completed after each control. 15. The audit team noted that DAFA inspectors carried out official controls according to the system described above and that inspection reports were completed in the IT system after each visit. Reports of official controls carried out in non-Danish vessels were also transmitted to the flag country of the vessels, via the DAFA Central Office in Copenhagen in cases of Member States' vessels or directly in case of third countries vessels. b) Official control system in place by DVFA at facilities, including vessels, handling fishery products 16. The official control system in place for fishery products by DVFA is part of the general official control system for food and feed. In the general system, each food sector is placed in one of five risk groups based on seven risk factors covering microbiological, chemical and consumer-based risks to food safety. In particular, the establishments under the scope of this audit are classified as very high (e.g. establishments producing salted or smoked fishery products) or high risk (e.g. freezer and factory vessels). Each risk group has a standard inspection frequency which is five times per year for "very high" risk establishments and three times per year for "high risk "establishments. There is also an evaluation for individual establishments and those establishments with inspection reports with no remarks on the previous four inspections and no remarks for all inspection reports for the last 12 months are classified as Elite-establishments. Elite- establishments are subject to fewer inspections, meaning that frequencies are reduced in nominally "very high risk" establishments to three per year (in case of Elite 1) or two per year (in case of Elite 2) and in high risk establishments to one per year (Elite 1 as these establishments cannot be Elite 2). 17. Findings

In accordance with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the DGAV is clearly designated as the CCA responsible for the development, co-ordination, evaluation and implementation of official control plans on the primary production of FNAO during the pre-harvest, harvest and post-harvest stages. DGAV was established in April 2012 by taking over the competencies of the former Directorate-General for Veterinary Health and, partly, those of the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development and the Policy and Planning Office.

In DGAV, there are three relevant directorates in the context of this audit: the Directorate for Food Safety (DSSA) responsible for development, co-ordination and implementation of official controls on hygiene (including microbial safety) in primary production of FNAO and for co-ordination of approval and control of sprouting establishments; the Directorate for Food and Nutrition (DSNA) responsible for implementation of legislative acts and policies applicable to agricultural, industrial and environmental food contaminants and for registration in a database of all the operators involved in the marketing of fruit and vegetables according to Article 10 of Regulation (EU) No 543/2011 and Portuguese Order No 246/94; and the Directorate for Strategy, Communication and International Affairs (DSECI) ­ which includes the National Contact Point (NCP) for RASFF ­ responsible for co-ordination of border inspection controls and risk management actions related to food imports and of Multiannual National Control Plan (MANCP) related activities.

At regional level, five Regional Directorates for Agriculture and Fisheries (DRAPs) and the control services in both Autonomous Regions (Azores and Madeira) are responsible for implementing controls, following instructions issued by DGAV.

DRAPs are responsible for performing official controls prior, during and post-harvest, which includes general hygiene provisions for primary production of FNAO and associated operations, as laid down in Article 4 and in Annex I, Part A of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. In addition, DRAPs are responsible for carrying out controls of imported FNAO.

The ASAE is responsible for law enforcement on food safety and economic activities in general. The ASAE deals with risk assessment, risk communication and risk management in the whole food chain. 6 11. At the time of the audit, there were adequate resources in place to undertake the official controls within the scope of this audit in accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 13. The Institute for Financing, Agriculture and Fisheries (IFAP) carries out registration of growers of FNAO applying for subsidies. The registration includes information on the crop production volumes and location. There are approximately 180,000 registered growers of FNAO. The audit team was informed that this register is normally not used for the purpose of planning of official controls due to lack of information necessary for risk-based approach in the system of official controls (no information about the crops cultivated). 14. All operators involved in the marketing of fruit and vegetables are registered in a database administered by DGAV. The CA stated that this database can be used for the purpose of planning of official controls. There are 130,153 registered FBOs in that database. Each registered FBO is assigned a unique number called HF. The audit team was informed that only FBOs involved in the marketing of fruit and vegetables are registered in this database, meaning that not all primary producers of FNAO are registered in this specific database. 15. The audit team was informed that the majority of primary producers of FNAO, mainly larger producers, are members of producers organisations (POs), recognised by DRAPs or by the designated authorities in the Autonomous Regions. According to national legislation, POs must submit information from their affiliates to the CAs on an annual basis, including, among other things, the types of crop produced, production volumes and the crops' production area. It is not mandatory to be a PO member. 7 16. The audit team noted that there are no procedures in place for some primary producers of FNAO to apply for the registration of their establishments in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 contrary to what is required in Article 31.1(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Consequently these FBOs are not registered by DGAV/DRAPs and thus cannot be considered for relevant official controls; the selection of FBOs for official controls in 2015 was done using other information sources (see findings under 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls). 17. There is no requirement to register importers and retailers of seeds intended for sprouting. None of the databases observed by the audit team contained information on importers and retailers of seeds intended for sprouting. DGAV informed the audit team that their interpretation is that seeds used for sprouting are not covered by Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and in general do not meet the definition of food, which is not in compliance with requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 208/2013. The audit team emphasised the importance of correct designation of business operators dealing with seeds intended for sprouting as FBOs with consequent inclusion in the system of official controls. 18. During 2014-2015, DGAV developed the Control Plan for Primary Production of FNAO 2015 (PCPP), which outlines the general procedures for official controls carried out on primary production of FNAO. The PCPP is based on a risk assessment, which takes into account the type and intended use of the produce and production volume in Portugal. To categorise the primary produce in risk groups, EFSA's opinions (which mainly address microbial risks) were taken into account. Currently, there are four risk groups of primary produce: Group 1 (highest risk) includes leafy green vegetables and fruits intended to be eaten raw, carrots, onion, garlic, tomato, melon, watermelon and berries. Group 2 includes other vegetables and fruits intended to be eaten raw but not listed in Group 1. Group 3 includes mushrooms and horticultural crops intended to be eaten cooked. Group 4 (lowest risk) includes cereals, potatoes, oilseeds, tomatoes for processing, olives and grapes for processing. Organisation of Official Controls Legal Requirements Article 75(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on designation of CAs Article 75(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Article 4(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on the qualification and experience of staff who carry out official controls Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on the monitoring and controls, in particular, annual reports to the Commission on the scope and the results of controls Chapter I of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on the general obligations with regard to the organisation of official controls of PPPs used at all stages of production of food Chapter II of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on CAs and, in particular, designation of CAs, staff performing official controls, control procedures and reporting Findings Designation of Competent Authorities:
A number of CAs are responsible for controls on PPPs - FPS-HSFCE, FASFC, Customs and Regional Agricultural Authorities.

Directorate General (DG) 4 of FPS-HSFCE is the CA for granting authorisations and parallel trade permits and maintaining the register of PPPs. DG5 of FPS-HSFCE is responsible for controls on non-food producing PPP users e.g. growers of flowers/ornamental crops and municipalities. They are also the CA for the safe storage of PPPs, but FASFC include storage conditions in their controls and cross report any infringements. DG5 of FPS-HSFCE are the CA responsible for the labelling of treated seed. FASFC and DG5 of FPS-HSFCE share competence for controls on seed treatment operators, relating to the safe use of PPPs. Customs are the CA for controls on PPPs at the point of import and for counterfeit PPPs.

FASFC are the CA for controls on manufacturers, re-packers, distributors of both professional and amateur use PPPs and food-producing PPP end users. There are 4 DGs within FASFC ­ DG Control Policy, DG Control, DG Laboratories and DG Corporate Services. DG Control Policy is responsible for drawing up the annual risk-based control programme on marketing and use of PPPs. DG Control oversees the 11 PCUs and the National Investigation Unit (NIU). The PCUs conduct routine controls, whereas the NIU conducts targeted controls on both distributors and users. PCUs comprise three sectors, covering primary production, processing and distribution. Controls on users fall under the primary production sector, with the processing sector responsible for controls relating to marketing. Finally, FASFC is responsible for the formulation analysis programme.

Regional Agricultural Authorities are the paying agencies under cross compliance (CC). They can access FASFC inspection results of end users to satisfy Statutory Management Requirement 9 under CC. The Regional Agricultural Authorities are responsible for IPM. 4 Resources for Performance Controls

There is one full-time equivalent (FTE) in DG Control Policy and two in DG Control responsible for all aspects of controls on PPPs. PCU staff responsible for PPPs carry out a range of other tasks, making it difficult to determine the amount of time dedicated to PPPs. It is estimated that there are 22 FTE dealing with controls on PPPs in all PCUs, 16 dealing with controls on users and six dealing with controls on marketing. In West Flanders PCU, there are 2.5 FTE in the primary production sector and 0.75 FTE in the processing sector, while in Hainaut PCU, the allocation is around 1 FTE and 0.5 FTE respectively. There is half of one FTE in the NIU dealing with PPPs. One chemist and two technicians, equating to one FTE, work on formulation analysis.

All FASFC staff have a relevant educational background ranging from primary degrees to doctorate level qualifications. On-the-job training is provided for new recruits until they are deemed competent, usually after six months. On-going training is provided on an ad- hoc basis at regular internal sector meetings and when there are major changes in legislation or procedures. The most recent PPP specific training took place in October 2014 at six different centres throughout the country. The one-day agenda covered a broad range of relevant issues. Staff participate in BTSF training on PPPs and the training material is provided to colleagues via an intranet. Prioritisation of Controls

Under a Royal Decree of 2006, all operators involved in the distribution and use of PPPs must be approved, registered or authorised by FASFC. A list of these operators is publicly available at http://www.favv-afsca.fgov.be/foodweb-fr/. FASFC controls are based on multi-annual control programmes, with the current programme running from 2015-2017. All approved, registered and authorised operators fall under the scope of controls, with the exception of seed treatment operators. Operators are scheduled for inspection based on a pre-determined frequency linked to their type of activity. The standard inspection frequency is once every eight years for professional users of PPPs exclusively for their own use, once every six years for retailers of amateur use PPPs and every second year for all other operators. Where validated own-control systems are in operation, the inspection frequency is adjusted to once every 12 years in the case of users, once every eight years for retailers of amateur use PPPs and once every four years for all other operators. Serious non-compliances, resulting in administrative fines, or more severe penalties, lead to follow-up inspections in all cases. Ten per cent of all non-compliant operators, who have had a favourable follow-up inspection, are inspected in the year following the non- compliance.
The NIU have no programme of routine controls, but conduct investigations on a targeted basis.

Customs conduct risk-based documentary controls on approximately 10 % of PPP imports through sea ports. Consignments destined for operators previously found to be non-compliant are examined in all cases, whereas other consignments are selected for controls on a random basis. 5 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities

FASFC inspectors use detailed checklists/inspection reports for controls on both marketing and use of PPPs. Up to six individual checklists can be used at a single inspection, each covering a different subject, such as storage conditions, packaging/labelling, records and own-control systems. All checklists are publicly available at http://www.afsca.be/checklists-fr/. Reports are drawn up following all inspections and a copy provided to the operator.

The 2013 Annual report on the scope, and results, of official controls under Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 was provided to the Commission in June 2014. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within Competent Authorities

Within FASFC, there is clear evidence of co-ordination between central level and the PCUs. This manifests itself in, inter alia, harmonised checklists used throughout the country and the use of common IT platforms to monitor implementation and compliance levels under the national control programme.

There is an agreed protocol in place between FASFC and DG5 of FPS-HSFCE, the two authorities primarily responsible for controls on PPPs, since 2008. This protocol clarifies the scope of competence of both organisations. Furthermore, there is an annual meeting to discuss issues of mutual concern, in addition to on-going informal contacts. There is a protocol in place between FASFC and the Regional Agricultural Authorities on the sharing of inspection results.
There is close co-operation between the NIU and Customs, and CAs in other MS, involved in controls on imports of PPPs and illegal PPPs. Conclusions
CAs are designated and their roles clearly defined, as required by Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Staff are competent to perform their tasks based on their qualifications, initial and on- going training and experience, as required by Articles 6(a) and (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

CAs perform regular, risk-based controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, covering all categories of operators, in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, except in the case of seed treatment plants.
Documented procedures for the performance and reporting of controls comply with Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Annual reports on controls are provided to the Commission in a timely manner, as required by Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Co-ordination and co-operation between and within competent authorities is excellent, leading to a system of efficient and effective controls, as required by Articles 4(3) and (5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 6 5.3. The official register of PPPs, located at www.fytoweb.fgov.be, is freely available and updated daily. There are approximately 1 400 PPPs, comprising about 1 180 professional use PPPs and 220 amateur use PPPs that can be marketed and used in Belgium. The professional use products comprise 1 100 authorised products and 80 parallel trade permit products. One hundred parallel trade permit products, granted prior to 2011, do not appear on the product register. Artwork versions of product labels are not approved as part of the product approval process, and hence don't appear on fytoweb. The authorisation/parallel trade permit certificate is available for all PPPs on fytoweb showing the product classification and instructions for use. A list of revoked PPPs, including the final dates for their sale and use, is available. Authorisation numbers do not change at re-authorisation, even when significant changes are made to the conditions of use.

There are 22 manufacturers, 15 re-packers, 26 third party manufacturers/re-packers, 1 600 retailers of amateur use PPPs and 630 distributors of professional use PPPs. Of these 630, 100 are involved in the import and export of PPPs. Operators are subject to unannounced inspections in accordance with the pre-determined frequency. Checklists are used and the operator receives a copy in all cases. 7 26. In 2013 and 2014, FASFC carried out 422 and 468 inspections on operators placing PPPs on the market. Inspectors typically conduct four types of controls per inspection. Storage conditions, the authorisation status of PPPs in store, own-control systems and records are checked in 90 % of inspections. Packaging/labelling is checked in about 75 % of inspections, with 348 detailed label checks in 2014. In both years, over 80 % of operators were found to be compliant in the areas of storage conditions, the products in store and own-control systems, while virtually all operators were compliant regarding records and packaging/labelling. The most common infringement is the marketing of PPPs revoked more than six months. 27. In accordance with procedures, inspectors check the authorisation status of at least 25 % (minimum of five) of the PPPs present, intended for placing on the Belgian market, and conduct a detailed label check on one randomly chosen Belgian product. As inspectors don't have internet access, this detailed label check is typically done upon returning to the office, using the product's authorisation information on fytoweb. All details on the label are checked, including name, active substance level, formulation type, classification, risk and safety phrases, authorisation number, authorisation holder, approved crops, rates of use and pre-harvest interval. 28. Controls are only conducted on products destined for marketing in Belgium. There are no controls done on products being stored, produced or moved, intended for use in other EU MS or third countries. Furthermore, FASFC consider that PPP active substances are outside the scope of their controls. 29. DG Control Policy draws up the annual formulation analysis programme, PCU inspectors take the samples from distributors and the accredited FASFC laboratory in Liege conducts the analysis. In both 2013 and 2014, approximately 80 samples were analysed for the level of active substance, physical-chemical properties and some impurities. Compliance rates were 96 % and 91 %. There is no product profiling or analysis of co- formulants in the programme. Non-compliant products are selected for sampling and analysis the following year. 30. FASFC highlighted some aspects of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 which they believe hamper controls. These include the definitions of PPPs "as products, in the form in which they are supplied to the user" under Article 2 and "placing on the market" under Article 3. They consider that PPPs in large containers e.g. 1000 l, do not fall under the scope of the Regulation, as product is typically supplied to users in smaller pack sizes. Controls on products in transit, stated to be destined for placing on the market in other countries, is difficult. Customs stated that vague descriptions of PPPs, and the practise of declaring PPPs under incorrect names and CN codes, hinders controls at the point of import. They also stated that there can be difficulties in controlling consignments in transit, where products enter the EU through one MS for Customs clearance in another MS. 31. The NIU provided specific examples of targeted controls. In March 2013, six containers declared as containing two different PPP active substances were imported into Antwerp for forwarding to Germany. Customs alerted the NIU based on inconsistencies in the documentation. These were part of a larger consignment of over 100 000 l, with an estimated retail value of over 2 m , destined for marketing in France. The counterfeit PPP was sourced at a quarter of the price of 8 legitimate product. The last case involved a container of counterfeit oxamyl, tebuconazole, folpet, prochloraz and esfenvalerate containing PPPs, with the Netherlands stated to be the final destination. The estimated retail value of these PPPs was 100 000 . In all cases, the products have been seized and the cases are on-going. Controls observed by the audit team: 32.
