ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal Requirements Article 75(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on designation of CAs Article 75(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Article 4(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on the qualification and experience of staff who carry out official controls Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on the monitoring and controls, in particular, annual reports to the Commission on the scope and the results of controls Chapter I of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on the general obligations with regard to the organisation of official controls of PPPs used at all stages of production of food Chapter II of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on CAs and, in particular, designation of CAs, staff performing official controls, control procedures and reporting 4 Findings Designation of Competent Authorities:

Within the Directorate-General of Sustainable Plant Production (DGSPP) of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food (MRDF) (former Ministry of Reconstruction of Production, Environment and Energy), the Directorate of Plant Produce Protection and Biocides (DPPPB) is the Coordinating National Authority (CNA) for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Directive 2009/128/EC. DPPPB is responsible for authorisation of PPPs and the Directorate maintains the register of authorised PPPs http://wwww.minagric.gr/syspest/.

At regional level, the CAs are the eight Regional Centres for Plant Protection and Quality Control (RCPPQC) of the MRDF. Their responsibilities are to implement controls on the marketing and use of PPPs; controls on sustainable use of PPPs; to manage the Early Warning System for pests and the internal audit system.

The local government structure is established by the Kallikratis Law (3652/2010). The Decentralised Administration is supervised by the Ministry of Interior and thirteen regions were established where Governors of the Regions are elected in regional elections. Within the General Directorates of Regional Agriculture and Veterinary of each region, there are a total of 59 Directorates of Agriculture Economy and Veterinary Regional Units (DREVs) which conduct controls on marketing and use of PPPs.

The Laboratory of Chemical Control of Pesticides of Benaki Phytopathological Institute (BPI) is responsible for formulation analyses of PPPs in the country. Two other official laboratories at Thessaloniki and Piraeus also carry out some formulation analyses.
The Customs is the CA responsible for conducting controls on imports of PPPs and active substances for use in PPPs in Greece.

The Greek Payment and Control Agency for Guidance and Guarantee Community Aid (OPEKEPE) is responsible for controls on farmers receiving payments under the EU basic payment scheme (BPS). Resources for Performance Controls

The assessment of applications for authorisation of PPPs is conducted in the BPI where 30 people are involved. Within the DGSPP, the DPPPB has 4.2 full time equivalents (FTE) dealing with authorisation of PPPs. DPPPB has 5 FTE dealing with controls and for the management of the PPP website. Three DREVs were visited during the audit where controls on PPPs were conducted by 2 FTE in Thessaloniki, 1.5 FTE in Xanthi and 1.6 FTE in Attika. In all DREVs visited the inspectors conducted a wide range of activities in addition to controls on PPPs. RCPPQC staff conduct specific ad-hoc investigation tasks on the use and marketing of PPPs as requested by the CNA.

DREV inspectors are required to be agronomists with University degrees or have technical third level qualifications in agriculture. There is no system for initial PPP- specific training for staff, despite the very technical nature of the area and the plan for 5 on-going training for inspectors designed by the CNA was not fully implemented in the last year due to the recent economic restrictions.

Controls on users are conducted in teams with two or three inspectors involved. This facilitates the specific on-the-job training for new entrants. However, no training has been arranged before staff start to conduct inspections on PPP in cases where new staff were allocated to DREVs where no experienced inspectors were on duty and supervision activities have not highlighted the needs for training. This situation has occurred more frequently in recent years due to the high number of staff retirements. This lack of training is not in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Due to economic restrictions, the number of trips for inspections has been limited. For the next year 2016, a maximum of 220 Km per month will be allocated to each inspector. Responsible staff for the visited DREVs highlighted that this would require a significant reorganisation of the works in order to be able to conduct the same number of inspections.

The Presidential decree 159/2013 states that inspections to retailers of PPPs shall be conducted by commissions of three inspectors. Other inspections to users are usually conducted by two inspectors, although there is no legal requirement for that. This practice decreases the time available for conducting inspections. Evidence was provided that the numbers of inspections planned in all 3 DREVs is dictated by staff resources plus working practices, rather than identified risks. This is not in line with Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. Prioritisation of Controls

The CNA defines the scope of the official controls. The risk assessment for 2015, and consequently, the official control plan did not cover routine inspections to packers, re- packers and producers of PPPs or to seed treatment plants. This is not in line with Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The 2015 control plan adopted by the CNA covered marketing and use of PPPs including official controls to professional users on farms, retailers of PPPs (i.e. sale to end users), specific controls on parallel trade packagers and producers of PPPs for other MS or TC, when such PPPs are not authorised in Greece. There is an annual monitoring plan for formulation analysis of PPPs.

From the 750 000 farms claiming funds for the BPS, controls cover only the applicants receiving more than 1 200. OPEKEPE stated that 3 900 farms were inspected in 2014. However, these controls are not reported by the Greek CNA as official controls to enforce compliance with Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Prioritisation of the controls in the regions is conducted by the DREVs in line with the instructions established by the CNA. For the controls on users, the risk assessment takes into consideration the type of crop and its relevance within the region, previous maximum residue level (MRL) exceedances, information from pesticide residue monitoring programme, previous non compliances (non-compliant operators are always inspected within a year of the infringement) and the size of the farms. 6 17. There is no information available on the number of farms not claiming funds under the BPS or on users of PPPs other than farms. This compromises the organisation of official controls accordingly to an appropriate risk basis as required by Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 18. For controls conducted by the DREVs on professional users, a minimum frequency or annual inspection rate has not been established. The CNA does not prescribe the number of planned controls to be conducted in each region. The number of inspections is determined by economic resources available and not the outcome of the risk assessment. This is not in line with Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. It was noted that in some important agricultural areas such as Larissa and Kavala no inspections on marketing and use of PPPs were conducted by DREVs in 2014. 19. Ad-hoc inspections are arranged for 100 % of cases where the residue analysis programme detects the use of authorised PPPs not approved for the specific crop or the use of non-authorised PPPs in Greece. Under the residue analysis programme, approximately 2 300 samples are taken each year. 20. In 2014, the DPPPB launched a specific survey of professional users of PPP. This survey is anonymous and 2 815 answers were collected. Information on the use of illegal pesticides, implementation of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and other questions on PPP have been taken into consideration for risk assessment. 21. The DREVs are responsible for planning and conducting the official controls on operators placing PPPs in the market. The frequency of inspection of PPP retailers has been increased from 25 % annual inspection to 33% in 2015 onwards. Therefore, the CA stated that every retailer is to be inspected at least once every 3 years. All Retailers are registered on a website operated by DPPPB http://www.minagric.gr/index.php/el/for- farmer-2/crop-production/fytoprostasiamenu/elenxoifitoprostateytikonmenu/529-mhtroa. 22. Since 1 January 2014, retailers must record electronically every sale of PPP to end users. The specific products sold and the customer details are recorded. This data is only accessible to DPPPB staff. The CNA informed the FVO audit team that the data will be used to monitor trends in PPP use and to identify emerging risks, which DREVs can incorporate into their control programmes. 23. The absence of risk based controls at manufacturers, packers and re-packers of authorised PPPs means that the system to ensure that authorised PPPs for use in Greece comply with their conditions of authorisation under Articles 29(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 is not effective. Although there is not a programmed plan for the control of manufacturers, packers and re-packers of PPPs, targeted inspections are conducted based on intelligence provided by other CAs, other MS and PPP industry. 24. For companies manufacturing, packing or re-packing PPPs which are not authorised in Greece but destined to be delivered to other MS or exported to third countries (TC), the CAs have established a comprehensive control system conducted on 100% of deliveries. The same comprehensive control system is in place for producers granted with a parallel trade permit (PTP). This system provides assurances that these products comply with their conditions of marketing. 25. There is a formulation analysis program in place. The BPI conducts the majority of the analyses. There are two other laboratories conducting official formulation analyses with 7 a reduced scope of substances that can be analysed. An annual risk assessment is conducted for the selection of the active substances to be included within the annual plan taking into consideration previous infringements, parallel trade authorisations and the most used PPPs in the country. The decision of the CA to allocate a certain number of analyses to the two laboratories which can only analyses a very limited scope of formulated PPPs compromises the risk assessment process for the annual plan. This is not in line with Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities 26. For the inspections conducted by DREV under the annual control plan at retailers and users of PPPs, the CNA has issued several internal circulars with instructions for conducting the controls and specific checklists are in place for the inspections. A report form is used and a copy is provided to the operator, either on site, or by post, when the inspection report is finalised at the office. The same checklist and report forms are used for non-planned inspections such as visits triggered by results of the residue monitoring plan. 27. For ad-hoc inspections at formulators, packers holding parallel trade permits, packers and re-packers, there are no specific checklists in place but general report forms. Operators are always provided with a copy of the report. 28. Article 8 of the National Law 4036/2012 lays down the obligation of operators to co- operate and supply any requested information during controls. This addresses recommendation No 7 of the previous audit 2012-6285. 29. The annual report on the scope, and results, of official controls under Article 68 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 is provided to the Commission by the due date. The FVO audit team reviewed the compliance with the submission deadlines for the years 2013 and 2014. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within Competent Authorities 30. There is active, ongoing co-operation between the control and the authorisation unit within the DPPPB, responsible for co-ordinating the enforcement and authorisation of PPPs respectively. Co-ordination and co-operation between the DPPPB and the DREVs, Customs and laboratories is excellent. There is continuous two-way exchange of information between these services. The annual control programme is devised taking the views of all authorities into account. High priority work can be undertaken at short notice, e.g. targeted controls on suspected use of illegal PPPs in cotton, involving the CCA, DREVs and the BPI, due to this close working relationship. 31. There is limited co-operation with OPEKEPE, and while the DPPPB cross reports the outcomes of inspections to OPEKEPE, this is not reciprocated since DPPPB has not access to information relevant to the use of PPPs and IPM implementation issues such as type of infringement. DPPPB have not access to a format allowing the data to be useful for prioritising controls. 8 32. There are numerous examples of co-operation between the DPPPB, other MS, TCs and industry for example controls on imports are targeted based on intelligence provided by other MS. Conclusions on the Organisation of Official Controls 33. Although there is nominally training programme for official controls on marketing and use of PPPs, the lack of implementation of the programme and the absence of systematic initial PPP-specific training for inspectors is not in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and compromises the effectiveness of the controls. 34. The absence of defined lists of all professional users of PPPs, the risk assessment which does not cover all types of users and the absence of a defined risk based inspection frequency on users is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and compromises the effectiveness of the official controls. 35. The absence of regular inspections of manufacturers, packers and re-packers of PPPs limits the effectiveness of the control system to ensure that authorised PPPs for marketing in Greece comply with their conditions of authorisation. 36. There is a comprehensive control system in place for manufacturers, packers or re- packers of PTP PPPs, and for operators producing PPPs not authorised in Greece but intended for use in another Member State (MS) or Third Country (TC). These controls coupled with the excellent co-ordination and co-operation between the CNA and Customs enhances the effectiveness of controls of PPPs traded within the EU. 37. The BPI provides analytical services to give assurances that PPPs placed on the market comply with their conditions of authorisation/parallel trade permit as required by Articles 29(1) and 52 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. However, the formulation analysis programme is weakened, in both its risk based planning and execution, by the use of two laboratories with very limited analytical scope. 38. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within competent authorities and between the CAs and relevant external stakeholders is excellent, which contributes greatly to the efficiency and effectiveness of controls, as required by Articles 4(3) and (5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, with the exception of co-ordination and co-operation with OPEKEPE. 39. The audit team was informed by DGAL that for the egg production and processing sector, the CAs follow the relevant EU and national legislation.
DGAL has issued several guidance documents and "Note de service" (Official instruction) related to the official controls of foodstuffs and also related specifically to egg and egg products sector.

Implementation of the official control system is based mainly on:- Decree No 2003-1275 of 23 December 2003 on the identification of establishments rearing laying hens. Official instruction DGAL/SDSSA/L2008-0796 of 4 September 2008: Identification of poultry establishments and units. Method for recording in SIGAL. Order of 26 June 2013 establishing the health inspection of poultry farms. Official instruction DGAL/SDSPA/2014-621 of 23 July 2014 on Poultry health inspection: 2015. Order of 28 August 2014 on the marketing standards for eggs. Technical instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2015-365 Marketing standards for eggs and related controls. Order of 18 December 2009 on the health rules applicable to products of animal origin and to foodstuffs containing them. Order of 8 June 2006, as amended, concerning the approval of establishments placing on the market products of animal origin or foodstuffs containing products of animal origin. Official instruction DGAL/SDSSA/N2012-8119 of 12 June 2012 on the approval procedure and the composition of the approval file. Technical instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2014-920 of 20 November 2014 on the calculation of the risk rating and the scheduling of inspections in food safety fields 1 and 2, on the basis of three approaches: prevention, improvement and elimination. Technical instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2014-912 of 19 November 2014 on inspection strategy and frequency in establishments in the food safety sector over the period 2011 to 2015. 4 Official instruction DGAL/SDSSA/N2012-8156 of 24 July 2012 concerning the inspection of procedures based on the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) principles in the context of the official control of the health control plan of a food business establishment, excluding primary production. Official instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2005-8205 of 17 August 2005 on the monitoring of traceability pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 ­ Provisions on foodstuffs (excluding primary production). In addition, DGAL issued inspection checklists ("inspection grid") and inspection manuals ("vade-mecum") to be used during official controls in farms, in egg packing centres, egg products establishments and food transport vehicles.

Regarding Food Business Operators' (FBOs) compliance with temperature requirements related to eggs during storage and transport, the audit team was informed that no national legislation has been issued. Temperature requirements are contained in "Technical instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2015-365 on marketing standards for eggs and related controls" which refers to the requirements contained in Article 2(3) of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008.

While a comprehensive review of the French legislation was not carried out by the audit team, the national laws and implementing measures (including guidelines), seen by the audit team during the current audit were in line with EU requirements related to the audit scope. Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
France has issued national legislation and guidelines necessary to implement EU requirements relevant to eggs and egg products and, from a summary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation.

National temperature requirements for storage facilities and for vehicles transporting eggs, in the context of Point 2 of Chapter I, Section X, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, have not been fixed in national legislation. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5 Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Findings Structure and organisation

Competencies are distributed as follows between the CAs responsible for the official controls carried out in the egg/egg products production chain:- DGAL under the Ministry in charge of Agriculture, at central level ­ amongst other things ­ is responsible for transposition of relevant legislation, and for co-ordination of supervision of approved food establishments (including issuing technical instructions and guidance for the official staff at local level); Generally, DGAL is responsible for matters relating to product safety (e.g. hygiene, risk of Salmonella contamination). DGAL is also the CA responsible for official controls on animal welfare. A more detailed description of the control system for animal welfare can be found in the FVO report DG(SANCO) 2012-6446 which is available on the following webpage: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3068 DGCCRF under the Ministry in charge of Economy is responsible for official controls over food labelling, its ingredients and for fair trading (e.g. consumer information, fair advertising, etc.), DGCCRF responsibilities also include controls regarding organic production (especially on requirements related to labelling, traceability and laboratory analyses).
Responsibilities related to the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008 (marketing standards applicable to eggs) and official controls on food additives are shared by DGAL and DGCCRF.

Official controls at departmental (local) level are implemented by the Departmental Directorates. The directorates names depend on the organisation of the administrative services at "département" level: DDPP, or Departmental Directorate for Social Cohesion and Protection of the Population (DDSCPP). These directorates are under the co- ordination of the regional authority (Regional Directorates of Food and Feed, Agriculture and Forestry for DGAL staff and Regional Directorates for Enterprise, Competition, Consumers and Employment for DGCCRF staff).
There is a direct chain of command between central and departmental level.

Private Control Bodies (CBs) are responsible for regular controls on organic production. They are subject to approval by the "Institut National des Appellations d'Origine" (National Institute for Quality and Origin ­ INAO ­an institution under the supervision of Ministry in charge of Agriculture) and to accreditation by the French Committee for Accreditation (COFRAC). The audit team was informed that at present there are eight such approved CBs. 6 14. The structure of the CAs and the allocation of responsibilities are described in the country profile1 of France available in DG SANTE webpage at:- http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=FR Training 15. The audit team noted that DGAL has a system of providing training to officials under their supervision. The audit team saw evidence in one of the egg products establishment visited that a new official inspector had to follow an induction training in order to acquire the necessary theoretical knowledge and experience (through on-the spot training and mentoring by senior inspectors). The audit team also noted that each year DGAL through the "National Institute for training of Ministry in charge of Agriculture personnel" (INFOMA) organises training on official controls of egg packing centres and on the egg marketing regulations. The audit team was provided with the training programme for 2014 and 2015 and saw evidence of staff participation in such training. 16. In addition the audit team saw evidence of local CA staff participation in general training courses on HACCP. 17. DGCCRF provides training to their staff through annual meetings (e.g. "Egg and egg products network" meeting). During these meetings outside speakers (e.g. from universities, technical institutes, etc.) present various topics relevant to the sector and the staff has the opportunity to exchange relevant information. Evidence of such meetings was provided to the audit team. Audit and verification 18. The FVO audit team was informed by DGAL that three types of internal audits are carried out (a new system from 2015): 1. Internal Ministerial Audits; 2. Local (Departmental) level audits; 3. Specific (thematic) audits. 19. The local level audits are planned based on risk analysis, and are carried out by regional CA staff or by local CA staff from another department. The scope of these audits is e.g. confidentiality and impartiality, planning, equipment, management of procedures, or any specific subject (e.g. animal welfare). The objective is to carry out at least three such internal audits within a five year period for each local CA. 20. Objective of the specific audits is to verify the performance of official controls in specific areas of concern (e.g. slaughterhouse, border inspection posts, implementation of Salmonella National Control Programmes (SNCPs)). 21. The audit team was informed that no internal audits covering the egg and egg products sector had been carried out so far. 1 French language version only 7 22. In addition to internal audits, supervision of inspectors takes place in line with ISO/IEC 17020 standard (as a part of quality management system). It comprises documentation review and on-site visits. The procedures are set out in a national quality plan document. The audit team saw evidence of such supervision in an egg packing centre visited. The audit team noted that the performance of an official inspector was assessed by her supervisor during the official inspection in this establishment. Conclusions on competent authorities 23. The CAs responsible for the official control system over the production of eggs and egg products are clearly designated. The CAs' structure and organisation are adequate for the performance of their tasks. 24. A training system aimed to ensure that official staff can execute its tasks effectively is in place. 25. France complies with the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 as an audit system has been established. 5.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 31 (1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Article 28 and Title V of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 7 of Council Directive 1999/74/EC and Article 1 of Directive 2002/4/EC. Findings Registration of laying farms (Gallus gallus) 26. DGAL informed the audit team that all FBOs keeping laying hens have to declare their activity to the DDPPs/DDSCPPs in order to be able to send eggs to egg packing centres or egg products establishments. The laying hen holdings are registered and the FBOs receive for each poultry house/building a unique national identification code (INUAV). 27. Holdings and individual poultry houses are registered by the DDPPs/ DDSCPPs in DGAL's centralised information system (SIGAL). 8 28. In order to comply with egg marketing rules (Regulation (EC) No 589/2008) the FBOs have to obtain a producer's code which will be used for marking eggs whenever required by the legislation. This code is granted by the Farming Agency (Etablissement Départemental d'Elevages - EDE) when applied for by an FBO. (The code is composed of four sections: the first indicates the method of production, then the second is FR (ISO code for France), the third which is a unique three letter code and the fourth section refers to the identification of the building within the holding.) Once a code has been allotted to an FBO, the Farming Agency informs the local CAs on the codes issued. These codes are then introduced into SIGAL by the local CA. The audit team was informed that FBOs are required to notify the CAs in case of any change related to their method of production. 29. The audit team also noted that for each poultry house, both numbers INUAV and the producers' codes are stored in SIGAL which allows the CAs to identify farms based on method of production. 30. As regards compliance with animal welfare requirements for laying hens, newly built poultry houses are inspected by the CAs. 1% of all houses are subject to an animal welfare inspection each year. 31. In order to be registered as an organic producer, an FBO has to be inspected and certified by one of the CBs (see also structure and organisation chapter). Registration of laying farms of poultry species different from Gallus gallus 32. The audit team was informed by DGAL, that FBOs keeping laying poultry other than Gallus gallus (e.g. ducks, quails, etc.) and placing their eggs on the market are required to notify the local CA about their activities by using a declaration form. The registration procedure is the same as for laying hens (Gallus gallus) with the exception that no code for marking the eggs is required. 33. The audit team was provided with evidence of such registration. Registration of egg collectors 34. Collectors, defined as any establishment registered in accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 to collect eggs from a producer for delivery to a packing centre, to a market selling exclusively to wholesalers whose undertakings are approved as packing centres, or to the food or non-food industry (Article 1(c) of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008), must be registered as a FBO with the local CA under the egg marketing legislation. The audit team was informed by DGAL that in France this type of activity is usually carried out as complementary to the main activity of laying farms, egg packing centres or egg products establishments. The audit team was informed by DGAL that in total there are 136 such registered egg collectors in France out of which seven are stand- alone (i.e. not attached to any other establishment). 9 Approval of establishments 35. Ministerial Order of 8 June 2006 lays down requirements on the approval of establishments that place on the market products of animal origin. The administrative procedure used by the CA for approval of establishments is laid down in Official instruction DGAL/SDSSA/N2012-8119 of 12 June 2012 on the approval procedure and the composition of the approval file. 36. In accordance with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the competent authorities responsible for the import control system for live animals and food of animal origin have been designated: the FCCD in the Ministry of Agriculture (Inspection and Audit Division) and the DAHAW and Department for Live Animal Trade Supervision 3 and Traceability within the NFCSO. The CGOs are responsible for the provision of facilities and staff at BIPs.

In accordance with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the detailed roles of the NFCSO and Customs outlining their cooperation and coordination are set out in a cooperation agreement (latest version 2012). This is complemented by local agreements between BIPs and Customs at all locations visited. The audit team saw reports of meetings between BIP staff and Customs at several locations. Conclusions on the designation and cooperation between competent authorities

The arrangements in place in relation to the allocation of responsibilities support the correct implementation of the import controls. 5.2 RESOURCES FOR PERFORMING OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 3 of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC. Findings

In accordance with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, appropriate facilities and equipment (with some exceptions detailed in Section 5.5) have been provided at the five approved BIPs to enable official import controls to be carried out efficiently and effectively.

In accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, training to enable staff to carry out official import controls competently and in a consistent manner has been provided via a range of mechanisms including on-the-job training, local meetings/training, annual training for BIP staff organised by the central competent authority and some BIP staff attending Better Training for Safer Food courses on import controls and sharing the knowledge gained upon their return.
At Kelebia BIP, which has never received any consignments, staff are not sufficiently knowledgeable about import controls as they are not regularly exposed to this area of official controls.

In accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, official controls are carried out in accordance with a wide range of documented procedures. Most of these procedures/instructions are provided by the central competent authority, e.g. the BIP Manual and the national monitoring plan. More are provided at individual BIP level, e.g. further details on the implementation of the national monitoring plan. There are some areas for which instructions have not been provided or require more detail e.g. instructions related to the implementation of physical checks, ensuring that equipment at 4 BIPs is calibrated as required, and implementing systems that ensure effective cleaning and disinfection at BIPs (see section 5.5 for more details). Conclusions on the resources for performance of controls

The effectiveness of the import control system is supported by the provision of a sufficient number of staff, appropriate facilities, relevant training and a wide range of procedures/instructions. Some of these instructions, however, could go into more detail. 5.3 CONTROL OF CONSIGNMENTS AT BIPS 5.3.1 System to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks Legal requirements Articles 2, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Articles 1, 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. Findings

BIPs receive pre-notification as required by Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 via part 1 of the CVED before the physical arrival of consignments on Union territory. The majority of consignments are not pre-notified electronically via TRACES (all BIPs stated that they check for TRACES notifications at least daily and according to the competent authority, about 10% are notified via TRACES at Budapest-Liszt Ferenc and Röszke and up to 50% at Záhony). Part I of the CVED is usually received in hard copy or via a scan attached to an e-mail, and BIP staff enter the information into TRACES. As reported in audit report DG(SANCO) 2014-7012, the competent authority is continuing its efforts to encourage economic operators to use TRACES directly but progress is slow in the absence of a legal requirement.

The Customs database flags the positive list so that consignments presented for free circulation will only be released on presentation of a CVED. The flagging does not apply to consignments presented for transit and Customs stated that they check all these consignments to identify those that require BIP checks based on their CN codes and descriptions. Customs stated that they contact the BIPs if they have a query (usually by phone).

All BIPs implement cross-checks with data available from Customs in accordance with the local agreement. BIPs verify if consignments were not presented for controls by cross-checking data available from Customs as required by Articles 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. Both road BIPs carry out monthly retrospective examinations of Customs files. The airport BIP has direct access to the Customs database and according to the competent authority checks it daily. BIP Kelebia aims to check Customs files twice annually 5 although no records were kept from the 2014 checks and no check had been carried out during 2015.

There were four transhipment consignments of products during 2015 which were destined for the Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. This BIP had not detected the relevant TRACES notification sent from the first EU BIP although staff stated that TRACES notifications are checked twice per day. The competent authority contacted Customs who confirmed that all four consignments had been released for free circulation as they had CVEDs (see finding 10). A similar finding was reported in report DG(SANTE) 2014-7012 but corrective actions have not been implemented. Conclusions on the system to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks

There is a system is in place to ensure that no consignment from a non-EU country is introduced into EU territory without being subjected to veterinary checks, although the system did not work for consignments transhipped via other Member States during 2015 at Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. 5.3.2 Veterinary checks and the decision on the consignment Legal requirements Articles 4, 8, 15 and Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC, Article 4(1) of Directive 91/496/EEC, Article 27(2) of Commission Regulation 142/2011, 4(2)(d) of Commission Decision 2001/812/EC, Annex II of Commission Decision 97/794/EC and Commission Decision 94/360. Findings

BIP staff check the information in part 1 of the CVED submitted by the economic operator against the relevant EU health certificate which accompanies the consignment as required by Article 4(3)(a) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 4(1) of Directive 91/496/EEC. If problems are detected with part 1, it is returned to the economic operator for correction.

In relation to the implementation of identity checks on consignments (products), the audit team noted that: Staff at Záhony BIP stated that the full identity check was carried out on a representative sample of products from each consignment and would involve unloading. Staff at Röszke BIP stated that no unloading took place during normal identity checks. The BIP Manual (and Article 4(4)(a) of Directive 97/78/EC on which it is based) does not specifically require unloading. However, identity checks limited to the back row of products in a means of transport could fail to detect non- compliances especially where operators become aware that this approach is standard practice. 6 Seal checks were sometimes performed on seals which were not included in the health certificate (Budapest-Liszt Ferenc) or the seal number was not included in part 1 of the CVED (Röszke).

In relation to the implementation of physical checks on consignments (products), the audit team noted that: Röszke BIP received 82% of consignments presented at Hungarian BIPs in 2014. Staff at Röszke BIP stated that physical checks are often carried out without unloading any of the consignment from the means of transport and can be based on only a visual examination of the boxes. This approach does not comply with the requirements of Section 3.4 of the BIP Manual. It also does not comply with Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC which describes the aim and types of physical checks to be conducted at BIPs. This also means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs. Finding 22 from report DG SANCO/2014-7008 reported on the lack of unloading for physical checks at Röszke BIP and the situation has not changed. Contrary to the requirements of Decision 94/360/EC Röszke BIP does not implement the reduced physical checks regime. The excessive number of controls is not based on suspicion or a documented risk assessment. The BIP implemented physical checks in 905 out of 1,237 consignments destined for import during 2014.

The competent authority stated that the identity checks of live animals always involve a visual examination of some of the animals in a consignment (e.g. ornamental fish) or confirming a match with identity papers (horses or dog passports) as required by Article 4 of Directive 91/496/EC.

Both Röszke and Záhony check horses and take blood samples based on a local risk assessment in line with Annex II of Decision 97/794/EC. Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP has taken samples from canines in the past.
The decisions on consignments were generally correct but Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP should have channelled some consignments under Article 8(4) of Directive 97/78/EC, e.g. eggs for technical use.

Registers of consignments which required confirmation of receipt at destination are maintained by all BIPs and were monitored to ensure that the notification complied with the relevant deadlines. See also findings 38 to 40.

The audit team examined a range of import/transit files at each BIP which included CVEDs selected from the TRACES database before the audit (7 to 20 files per BIP) and other files randomly selected during the visit to the BIP (about 15 per BIP). The files selected from the TRACES database had a range of issues which were discussed with BIP staff. The randomly selected files did not include any significant non-compliances. 7 Conclusions on veterinary checks and the decision on the consignment

In general, veterinary checks and decisions on consignments are correct but there are several issues which undermine the effectiveness of the system. The most significant of these is at Röszke BIP where the system to implement physical checks does not comply with national or EU requirements. Appropriate corrective action was not implemented in response to a related finding in report DG(SANCO) 2014-7008. This means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs and the competent authority does not ensure that corrective action is taken when needed.

Röszke BIP does not implement the reduced physical checks regime which leads to the incorrect application of the risk based approach established for import of certain goods in the EU. 5.3.3 Use of TRACES Legal requirements Article 3 of Decision 2004/292/EC. Findings

As required by Article 3 of Decision 2004/292/EC, TRACES is being used for recording the outcome of official import controls, communication between authorities and issuing CVEDs at BIPs. BIP staff screen notifications via TRACES for part 1 CVEDs submitted by economic operators and notifications for exiting transits.

Both Röszke and Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIPs use the cloning function in TRACES for certificates from non-EU countries. According to central supervision reports from May 2015 for Röszke and February 2015 for Budapest-Liszt Ferenc, the cloning rate is about 75% at both locations and is rising. Röszke BIP stated that the cloning function in TRACES cannot be used in cases when, due to the short distances and time involved for transportation, some consignments from non-EU countries arrive at the BIP before the health certificate has been entered into TRACES by the competent authority in the non- EU country.

The following issues were noted by the audit team in relation to the use of TRACES: Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP includes multiple CN codes in CVEDs issued for ornamental fish which is not in line with point 5.3 of the "Guidance document on the animal health requirements for placing on the market, import and transit of aquaculture animals according to Council Directive 2006/88/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1251/2008" ( SANCO 4788/2009/rev 5); 9 out of 13 results for blood samples taken from horses at Röszke BIP during 2014 were entered into TRACES during November 2015. 8 Conclusions on the use of TRACES

In general, TRACES is used correctly for recording the veterinary checks implemented at the BIPs and issuing related CVEDs although there is room for improvement as regards transhipments, indirect transits, communication between competent authorities and the traceability of the consignments. 5.3.4 Monitoring plans for sampling imported consignments Legal requirements Points 1 and 4 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. Findings
As required by point 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, DAHAW develops a risk based national monitoring plan in collaboration with FFCD for food of animal origin.

The monitoring plan consists of 13 food categories divided into 3 sub-categories ­ high- risk, medium-risk, low-risk and a minimum target for the number of consignments sampled and tested per month/commodity/year. It also includes a list of accredited laboratories to which samples should be sent for testing. The plan is amended when the central competent authority considers it appropriate, with the last amendment being in June 2015.

The national monitoring plan is further developed and implemented at each BIP on an annual basis taking into account hazards identified in the plan and the flow of consignments during the previous year. Samples are not always taken at BIPs from relevant consignments in accordance with the planned arrangements under the national plan, e.g. salmon at Röszke between May - September 2015. The main CAs responsible for the SNCPs are: At Federal level: · BMEL, which is the CCA for food of animal origin, for feed safety and animal health and is responsible for policy and legislation at federal level. BMEL drafts and overall coordinates SNCP implementation and reports the data to the European Commission (EC). · BVL, with responsibilities for the co-ordination of development and implementation of monitoring programmes and the drafting and reporting to BMEL for the zoonoses annual report (which is published and includes data on Salmonella but not on SNCP). · BfR (epidemiological unit) collects SNCP data from the Länder authorities and analyses it before transmitting it to the BMEL. It also sends the relevant data to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The NRL is is located within the BfR and carries out testing and analysis of official samples collected under the SNCPs (serotyping of all salmonella isolated from samples taken from the Lander 3 within SNCP). BfR provides risk assessment and advice to BMEL, BVL and to the Länder in the fields of food safety and animal health. At Länder level The Länder are responsible for the implementation of official controls to comply with food safety and animal health legislation. In the Länder visited by the audit team the CAs under the scope of this mission were: · the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Consumer protection in NI, and MLU-ST, are the supreme authorities at Länder level in the Länder visited. Their competencies comprise control, planning, steering, coordination and instructions on the lower veterinary administrations of their respective Land. · In NI LAVES and in ST LAV LSA . These are higher specialist authorities whose main mandate is to offer technical advice to ministerial and district authorities. They include also the official laboratories of the Länder. · LVwA in ST, represents the intermediate Land authorities in ST in the areas of food and feed safety, animal health and animal welfare technically supervising the local authorities1. · the local (district or municipal) authorities (veterinary units). These are responsible for the implementation of the SNCPs and the official controls on the relevant poultry holdings (inspections, official sampling, application and supervision of restrictive measures).
There are several channels for coordination and communication between Federal and Länder level. BMEL regularly organises federal/ Länder officer meetings to discuss legislative issues.

Furthermore, with a view to coordinate and harmonise implementation across all Länder, and serving as an interface between the federal and Länder level, the Länder have themselves developed coordination and communication structures known as working groups (AG). Each Land is represented in these AGs. In the sector covered by this audit the primary AGs are the Länder Working Groups for Consumer Health Protection (LAV). The heads of the Departments for Consumer Protection in the Länder administration are responsible for this co-ordination. The resolutions issued by LAV are binding for all Länder.

In order to achieve its goals LAVs are supported by other specific AGs (LAV AG). In the field of this audit the most important of these groups at Länder level are: · the Animal Diseases and Animal Health Working Group (AG TT) ­ it is the leading group dealing with SNCPs · the meat and poultry meat hygiene and specific matters relating to food of animal origin (AFFL), · the Working Group on Quality Management (AG QM) - which establishes the framework for Quality Management Systems (QMS) to be implemented in the 1 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that in Saxony-Anhalt, the competence of the highest authority at Land level covers the administrative and specialist supervision of the Land Administrative Authority (Landesverwaltungsamt (LVwA)) which is authorised to issue instructions to the subordinate veterinary authorities. 4 Länder · the Animal feed AG (AFU) Legislation

Within Germany, the Ministry is responsible for drawing up legislative initiatives and General Administrative Regulations (AVVs), as well as for issuing related statutory regulations (Rechtsverordnungen).

Important legislative provisions relevant to the scope of this audit are: the Framework Control Regulation of 2004 (AVV RÜb), as amended, lays down general administrative provisions on the principles of how to carry out official controls in compliance with legislation the General Administrative Regulation on the collection, analysis and publication of data on the occurrence of zoonoses and zoonotic agents along the food chain (AVV ZL), published in 2008, known also as AVV Zoonosen Lebensmittelkette. It contains the definition of an outbreak and detailed rules on zoonoses monitoring and reporting, the Act to prevent and combat animal diseases (Tiergesundheitsgesetz (TierGesG))2, the Animal Disease Pathogens Ordinance, providing for public or private laboratories to work with animal disease pathogens The Animal Transport Ordinance and Avian Influenza Ordinance, providing, among others, for the registration of poultry farms

The legal powers to carry out official controls under the scope of this mission and take measures are laid down in the Animal Health Act (TierGesG). Responsibility for implementation lies with the competent authorities in the Länder. The Länder have also the legislative competence where the Federal level has not adopted laws on the topic concerned. The division of competences has its origin in the Federal Constitution.

In the context of this audit the federal Regulation to protect against certain Salmonella infections in domestic poultry and turkeys (Geflügel-Salmonellen-Verordnung (GflSalmoV)), which came into force on 16 April 2009 is particularly important. This Regulation incorporates the relevant EU requirements and establishes more comprehensive provisions for the implementation of SNCPs at Länder level. It was amended in January 2014, mainly in order to include the new EU requirements of the SNCP for turkey populations.

The audit team reviewed this Regulation and noted that: According to its § 1, par. 2 (1) a Salmonella infection exists only if it has been ascertained by an official test. In all kinds of poultry populations a confirmatory sample has to be taken by the CA in order to verify a positive own-check result. This routine practice is not line with current EU legislation (see also paragraphs 62,81,96,115,127 and 134). 2 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that this Act contains rules on protection against animal diseases and efforts to with combat these and to improve their monitoring 5 Regarding FBO notification of Salmonella positive test results to the CA there are additional requirements: § 4 requires immediate notification of any suspicion of relevant Salmonella while § 8(3) requires FBOs to inform the positive results in a timeline of 14 days.3. The latter provision is not in line with the requirements of EU legislation, in particular with Point 2.1.1, of Annex of Regulation (EU) No 200/2010 for breeding flocks, Point 4.2. of Annex of Regulation (EU) No 200/2012 for broilers and Point 4.2.3. of Annex of Regulation (EU) No 1190/2012 for turkeys, which require FBOs to notify the CAs without undue delay. However, in all the cases reviewed by the audit team it was observed that when FBO samples resulted positive for Salmonella, the notification to the CA was done immediately either by the laboratories or by the FBO. The federal CAs explained to the audit team that "..§ 4 of GflSalmoV applies and that § 8 requires further specific information connected to the initial notification to be provided to the competent authority. The audit team noted during its visits that this legislative provision was not always clear for authorities met at Land and district level. § 11 Paragraph 2(1) provides that in cases of breeding hen holdings found positive for Salmonella hadar, Salmonella virchow and Salmonella infantis the FBO has to take specific actions in the holding affected. These actions could be the treatment, vaccination or killing of the infected flock. According to Point 2(c), of Article 2, Regulation (EC) No 1177/2006 antimicrobials to control Salmonella in poultry can be used only in exceptional situations and under specific requirements. However, the audit team noted in all the cases examined that the routine FBO actions in such cases include the killing of the infected flock in line with current EU legislation.

At Länder level additional legislation on the application of animal health controls and the implementation of the programmes has been issued. Several instructions, quality management documents, etc have been issued by the Länder authorities.

In NI, the audit team noted that specific instructions relevant for the scope of this audit have been issued, inter alia for official controls and inspection of poultry establishments for Salmonella, for official sampling and sampling protocols applied, for filling of submission forms, disinfection procedures at farm level, hygienic management of farms, courses of actions to be applied when dealing with Salmonella contaminated flocks and for the assessment of quality systems applied in smaller laying hen farms. These instructions were available to relevant staff via the Länder CA intranet.

In ST, the audit team noted that specific instructions for official controls and official sampling protocols, for the assessment of biosecurity measures at farm level, for the specific requirements applied in smaller laying hen farms, for the assessment of the food chain information (FCI) and for the specific requirements applied for the authorization and supervision of certain poultry farms implicated in intra-Community trade have been issued. 3 § 8(3) refers to breeding populations. However, a reference to it is further made for all the poultry populations in the regulation. 6 14. Guidelines for good hygiene practices for FBOs have been prepared and published by the CAs in both Länder on their websites. 15. Legal provisions grant to the inspectors the necessary right of access to the premises and to the documentation kept by FBOs. With regard to official controls and appropriate measures these rights are governed by Länder laws implementing the corresponding federal laws (i.e. Animal Health Act and LFGB). 16. It is mandatory for the veterinary authorities in all the Länder to have a QMS pursuant to Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In practice, QMS are being introduced for all sectors covered by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Sector specific procedures are prepared by the relevant LAV working group. Such a system is applied in both Länder visited by the audit team covering horizontal areas. Sanctions 17. The GflSalmoV (§ 37) provides for the specific FBO actions related to the implementation of SNCPs that are considered as administrative offences. Depending of the offence committed, different categories of sanctions are established in § 32 of Section 9 of the TierGesG. As examples it is considered an administrative offence, in breach of § 4 or § 8(3) of the GflSalmoV (see also paragraph 10 of this report), for FBOs to fail to keep the results of SNCP tests, to fail to issue a notification or to do so incorrectly or in full or in good time, to fail to vaccinate chicks or pullets, to fail to take appropriate actions after positive infections, etc. Training 18. A training plan is implemented at Länder level as a part of QMS4. This includes regular service meetings between authorities of different levels as well as formal training activities (seminars, workshops) organised by the Länder authorities or by veterinary associations. According to the information provided by the CAs, in both Länder visited, several trainings have been organised for officials at different levels that comprised issues relevant to the scope of this audit. 19. As part of the QMS, steps are taken to monitor whether every veterinarian who undertakes official duties complies with the further training requirements laid down in the codes of professional conduct of the chambers of veterinarians. 20. The official laboratory of each Land provides additional specific training to officials regarding the implementation of SNCPs (sampling protocols, collection and transport of samples, interpretation of test results). Evidence of these training initiatives was seen by the audit team in some of the districts visited. 21. Furthermore the audit team reviewed in one of the districts visited a specific training plan for every employee which had been developed as part of QMS. It included both internal and external training for officials organised for example by LAVES and the University of Hanover. 22. In general officials, laboratory staff and FBOs interviewed during the audit were familiar with the relevant EU legislative requirements and had adequate knowledge of 4 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that a training plan is implemented at the level of every authority as part of QMS and through the codes of professional conduct of the chambers of veterinarians. 7 the implementation of SNCPs, in particular regarding sampling frequency and sampling protocols to be applied. Audit 23. Responsibility for carrying out audits according Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 lies within Länder. Each Länder decides on the type of audits to be conducted, the planning cycle, follow-up, transparency and other principles laid down in Commission Decision 2006/677/EC. 24. Systems for internal audit were in place in the Länder visited as part of the QMS applied. The internal audits reports are independently assessed by a Quality Management Committee. The internal audits started in 2008 and at the end of 2013 all local and intermediary CAs had been covered in the Länder visited. 25. In both Länder visited, no specific audits have to-date been organised regarding the implementation of the SNCPs. The CAs informed the audit team that some elements of SNCP were included in animal health audits but with no specific findings as regards the SNCPs were made. Conclusions on competent authorities 26. Council Directive 92/65/EC was transposed into Dutch legislation by "Regeling handel levende dieren en levende producten" (Regulation for the trade of live animals and live animal products), in particular by Chapter 8 of this regulation. Article 8.6 of this regulation directly refers to Annex C of Council Directive 92/65/EC. This article stipulates that ABICs are required to meet the requirements of point 1 and 2 of Annex C to the Council Directive. However, no reference has been made to points 3 and 4 of the Annex C leading to some legal uncertainty on the enforceable requirements. 2 2. As regards of list of notifiable diseases the CA confirm that it is through this Regulation that animal keepers must notify the CA of suspicion of Annex A to Directive 92/65/EEC diseases. 3. The CA stated that the Netherlands has no national programmes for diseases listed at

The Federal Regulation on Internal Movements and Import of Animals and Goods transposes Council Directive 92/65/EEC. The Federal Regulation requires ABICs to meet the requirements of Annex C to Directive 92/65/EEC. CA confirmed that Section 7 of the Federal Regulation required any establishment taking part in intra-community 2 trade to be approved by CA. This goes beyond the requirements of Directive 92/65/EEC.

The Federal Regulation on Notifiable Animal Diseases lists the diseases which are notifiable in Germany. CA confirmed that it is through this Regulation that animal keepers must notify CA of suspicion of Annex A to Directive 92/65/EEC diseases. This list does not include psitacosis which is listed in Annex A to Directive 92/65/EEC as a notifiable disease. The Law for the Prevention and Control of Animal Diseases (Animal Health Law), section 4, requires keepers of an animal suspected of a notifiable disease to immediately inform CA.

The CA confirmed: Psittacosis was a reportable disease and any laboratory isolating it had to report finding to CA; Germany has no national programmes for diseases listed at Annex B to Directive 92/65/EEC. 5.1.2 Competent authorities

The full structure and organisation of the CA, as well as the control system for animal health is described in the country profile for Germany at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=DE At national level, the Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture (BMEL) has responsibility for policy and Federal legislation relating to animal health. The Länder are responsible for the implementation of official controls to comply with the animal health legislation and the administration can consist of up to three levels: Ministry level ­ is the supreme Länd authority. Intermediate Länd level ­ some Länder e.g. Hessen are subdivided into provinces which have an intermediate administrative level between supreme Länd authority and District authorities. District authorities ­ constitute third administrative level of the Länder and are responsible for delivery of official controls.

Responsibility for approval of ABICs varied between Länder visited. District authorities were responsible for the approval procedure in Berlin (Mitte and Lichtenberg Districts). In Hessen (Frankfurt), Intermediate Länd level was responsible for initial approval while in Mecklenburg Vorpommern (MV), the Ministry was responsible for the approval procedure. Following approval, District authorities were responsible for delivery of official controls in ABICs in all cases.

In one Länd visited (MV), documented procedures (instructions / guidance) relating to official controls in ABICs were in place and were part of a quality management system (QMS). CA confirmed no documented procedures, which are required by Article 3 (8)(1) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004, had been issued for official controls performed in ABICs in Frankfurt, Berlin Liectenberg and Berlin Mitte (see also paragraphs 12 and 13) .

There is a working group (LAV) for animal health and animal diseases established to facilitate cooperation between Länder - this is an effective mechanism for coordination in line with Article 4(3) to Regulation 882/2004. The minutes reviewed from 2010 and 2011 confirmed that ABICs are sometimes discussed at these meetings, but not often. These minutes solely made reference to a Q fever outbreak in a zoo and the need to have one official check to zoos per annum.

A mechanism does exist for the supervision of work performed at District level but there was little evidence of this supervision covering official controls at ABICs which is not in line with Article 8(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 requiring CA to verify the effectiveness of official controls. In Berlin (Mitte), CA confirmed they could not supervise / audit Districts but did receive quantitative reports recording number of inspections and findings carried out by District1. Conclusions on legislation and competent authorities

There is a framework for delivering official controls in ABICs which are delivered mainly at District level. The absence of documented procedures and limited supervision, in two out of the three Länd visited, leads to a variation in the quality and consistency of official controls delivered in ABICs. The fact that Districts have responsibility for this area and each District has a relatively small number of ABICs makes it difficult for them to build up expertise in this area.

The fact that psittacosis is not a notifiable disease in Germany will likely result in a delay in suspending approval of an ABIC should there be a case because there is no obligation to report a suspicion of the disease, only an obligation by laboratory to report a confirmed case. 1 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that in Berlin, monitoring of the districts' supervisory tasks is not carried out by means of technical supervision, but is implemented through a notification obligation, the power to intervene, administrative provisions (currently not covering the area concerned by Directive 92/65/EEC) and the Länd 's common QMS, including a related audit system (currently not covering the area concerned by Directive 92/65/EEC).The number of controls and their outcome are listed by district in the statistical reports. 4 5.2 APPROVAL OF BODIES, INSTITUTES AND CENTRES Legal requirements Article 13 of Directive 92/65/EEC; Annex C to Directive 92/65/EEC. 5.2.1 Procedures and conditions for approval

CA confirmed all ABICs in Germany were allocated a unique approval number in accordance with Article 13(2)(d) of Directive 92/65/EEC. Federal level have responsibility for the allocation of these numbers and updating the publicly available list of ABICs. All ABICs visited were approved and documents were made available to FVO team confirming approval status.

In one ABIC visited, the CA (Hessen) confirmed they had not made an on-site visit to assess compliance with requirements of Directive 92/65/EEC prior to issuing approval. Instead, they had reviewed documentation e.g. types of animals to be kept, quarantine facilities and how animal by-products were going to be handled and consulted with veterinary colleagues who visited the establishment for other reasons e.g. good laboratory practice. No report was available to record the extent of documentary checks carried out to fulfil the requirements of Annex C to Directive 92/65/EEC. In another ABIC, the CA(MV) confirmed they had approved the establishment for simiae and prosimiae only and the most recent approval document dated 14 May 1997- reviewed by the FVO team- indicated approval for primates only.
