The CCA updated arrangements for contingency planning for a number of major exotic animal diseases, including FMD and AI, which is in line with requirements laid down in Council Directives 2003/85/EC (Art. 72) and 2005/94/EC (Art. 62). Inadequate arrangements were in place in relation to other diseases, which is not in line with provisions laid down in Council Directive 92/119/EEC (Art. 20). · Before 2014, the contingency plan system was based on individual plans for a number of exotic animal diseases. As a result of a review, from 2010, the CCA developed a unique generic national contingency plan that can be used for all those diseases. The CCA's intention is to complete the plan with specific operational manuals for each disease, as required by EU legislation. The reviewing process is carried out in cooperation with a specific standing strategic committee where all 21 RVS in the country are represented. · The generic plan covers a description of the chain of command and general aspects such as management of suspicions and confirmations, financial arrangements, options for animal depopulation, etc. It also has a number of technical annexes and pre-set harmonised documents and forms that can be used in the event of any disease outbreak.

At the time of the audit, the CCA had prepared specific operational manuals for FMD, AI, classical and African swine fever, African horse sickness, Newcastle disease and bluetongue. These manuals incorporate tailor-made tools adapted to each disease (e.g. epidemiological enquiries, diagnostic criteria, specific provisions on cleaning and disinfection and options for the setting out of restriction zones and vaccination). The generic national contingency plan and the specific operational manuals are available on the CCA official webpage to all staff of the CAs and to the general public.

The specific operational manuals for FMD and AI were updated in cooperation with the respective national reference laboratories (NRLs), which also play the role of national reference centres for their epidemiology and control. The manual for AI is under continuous review to adapt it to the lessons learned during outbreaks of the disease. The audit team saw examples of updates done according to that policy. 4 4. Manuals for other diseases included in Council Directive 92/119/EEC were not available. The CCA stated its intention to develop specific manuals for other diseases required by EU legislation in the near future. The RVS and the ASLs developed their own contingency plans and operational manuals following the principles and measures contained in the national one. These plans were available in the regions and ASLs visited. In general, they were adapted to the local conditions and, in some cases, there were considerable additional details that go beyond the baseline documents in the national plans. In particular, these plans included specific details on the structure and composition of the local disease control centres (LDCCs), and the allocation of staff 5. According to all representatives of the RVS and the ASLs met, the CCA had a limited involvement in coordinating and verifying the level of preparedness of the RVS and the ASLs (e.g. they do not facilitate or encourage the sharing of experience and expertise gained from this exercise between the RVS and the ASLs). As a consequence, the CCA is not sufficiently aware of whether those plans are fully fit for purpose and applicable. This is not in line with general EU requirements for the preparation of contingency plans (see Appendix 2 section 5.1.1) and with provisions laid down in Article 4 (2)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In the regions visited, the RVS have also paid insufficient attention to those responsibilities with respect to the ASLs. One of the regions visited acknowledged that gap and the RVS had incorporated that task as a major priority for the next few years. · In the Lombardy region more attention had been paid to the coordination of the levels of preparedness in the ASLs, whilst in Veneto and Tuscany coordination in that area has been largely neglected. · The CCA informed that no specific verification activity has been carried out on the RVS and the ASLs in recent years in relation to their level of emergency preparedness, including on the availability of adequate contingency plans and staff operation manuals. However, their internal audit service carried out some targeted audits to verify the response of some RVS to outbreaks of exotic diseases (e.g. in 2007, including Veneto and Tuscany). 5.1.2 Addressing the main EU criteria and requirements for contingency plans Findings 6. In accordance with EU legislation, the generic national contingency plan includes a well-defined chain of command for the national disease control centre (NDCC) aimed at guaranteeing a rapid and effective decision-making process in the event of an outbreak of an exotic disease. In addition, it incorporates similar guidance for the deployment and operation of disease control centres by the regions (RDCCs) and the ASLs (LDCCs). · A national crisis management centre for animal diseases was created at the end of 2005 (by the same Law that set out the structure of the CCA). This centre is operational in "peace time" (when no outbreaks are present) and when an exotic disease outbreak occurs (as the NDCC). The distribution of tasks and responsibilities 5 is based on a well-defined structure and instructions that are laid down in the generic national contingency plan. The activities of the centre are ensured by a dedicated unit within the structure of the CCA that has permanent staff and it is operational permanently. · The RVS and the ASLs visited had developed detailed chains of command to adapt the requirements of the generic national contingency plan to their local conditions. 7. The national contingency plan includes references to the options available to cooperate with many other CAs (e.g. the police, civil protection services, the fire brigade, etc.) and underlines the importance of the general crisis management systems established at local, regional and national level, which could be availed of easily by the RVS and the ASLs in case of necessity. · All contingency plans seen in the regions and ASLs visited had arrangements in this respect and staff from these CAs had been nominated, and participated regularly in a activities carried out in the context of those regional and local crisis management systems. · The CCA and the RVS were preparing national and regional general crisis management plans which, amongst other areas will incorporate specific arrangements to improve the level of preparedness for animal health crisis. 8. The RVS and the ASLs visited have drawn up a variety of staff operation manuals that describe the actions, procedures, instructions and control measures to be employed in handling outbreaks of exotic animal diseases, with the exception of those covered by Directive 92/119/EEC. This last point is not in line with provisions laid down in Annex IV to that Directive. · In general, the staff operation manuals drafted by the RVS and further developed and adapted by each ASL, cover all basic practical arrangements needed to deploy an early response to an exotic disease. They include a clear indication of who must do what, while providing details on the human resources and specific equipment available at local level. · In all cases, CAs have put high emphasis on preparing practical arrangements to respond to an outbreak of AI, as they had frequent and recent experiences with the disease, but more limited arrangements were in place for FMD and other exotic diseases. · Those staff operation manuals had taken into account, in most cases and mainly for AI, the details included in the national specific operational manuals prepared by the CCA. Thus, in most ASLs visited there were no specific arrangements in place to adapt the staff operation manuals to the specific epidemiological conditions derived from outbreaks of the diseases included in Directive 92/119/EEC (such as lumpy skin disease or sheep and goats pox), despite the increased risk associated with the recent incursions of those diseases in the EU. 6 9. The generic national contingency plan and the specific operational manuals include templates and forms that can be used in the outbreak scenario (e.g. templates for epidemiological investigations adapted to each disease, forms to be used for sampling purposes, forms to communicate within the CAs or to stakeholders, measures to be taken). The audit team observed that those tools were available to staff of the ASLs and, in some cases, they have been incorporated as annexes in the regional and local staff operation manuals. 10. Operations manuals available to ASLs staff included instructions on how to perform a number of tasks and activities related to the investigation of the suspicion of exotic diseases. Those for AI and FMD have been updated recently, and in the case of AI, they include all relevant provisions of the current EU Diagnostic Manual for the disease: · The specific operational manuals developed by the CCA for FMD and AI with the technical support of the national reference centres included a clear description of the responsibilities for staff of the RVS and the ASLs in case of suspicion and confirmation of either disease. · For AI, the new specific operational manual that has been used for the update of the staff operation manuals makes specific reference to the procedures described in the current EU Diagnostic Manual for this disease. · In general, the manuals seen for FMD contain adequate information for staff of the ASLs to investigate a suspicion of the disease, including extensive details on how to evaluate the ageing of lesions and on specific sampling procedures to optimise the diagnostic activities of the NRL. 11. The generic national contingency plan and the specific operational manuals for AI and FMD include instructions on application of control and restriction measures once the outbreak has been confirmed in order to accelerate eradication of the diseases. In general they are in line with EU requirements and they have been incorporated in the staff operation manuals present in the ASLs visited. · The documents propose adequate measures to apply movement restrictions for the affected holding(s) and in the protection and surveillance zones. They also have options for granting derogations in surveillance zones to allow movement of animals to slaughter for animal welfare reasons. · Specific provisions underline the importance of collaborating with other crisis management services (e.g. police, civil protection services) to apply measures in the protection and surveillance zones (e.g. installation of signs and roadside warnings to demarcate those zones visibly, setting up checkpoints for road controls). · The specific operational manuals prepared by the CCA include guidelines on how cleansing and disinfection of vehicles in the restricted zones should be checked. These were translated into staff instructions by some RVS and ASLs, on how, when and by whom those would be done. 7 12. There is an extensive network of laboratories and associated diagnostic centres which includes NRLs for all the exotic diseases covered by EU legislation. They are under regional administration but operationally coordinated by the Ministry of Health. The laboratory in Veneto (Padova) has been designated as NRL for AI and the one in Lombardy (Brescia) and NRL for FMD. The national contingency plan and specific operational manuals for both diseases include provisions for them to fulfil their role in accordance with EU legislation, in particular with regard to: a) the confirmatory diagnosis of AI and FMD, b) coordination of other laboratories involved in the serological and virological diagnosis of those diseases, and c) regular cooperation with the relevant EU reference laboratories. 13. The generic national contingency plan has a specific chapter containing measures to safeguard animal welfare when killing of animals is performed for the purpose of depopulation. They are in line with the requirements of Article 18 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. · The guidance on animal welfare in the generic national contingency plan was drawn up with the national reference centre for animal welfare and with representatives of the RVS. ASLs, under coordination of the relevant RVS, have to use the standard depopulation procedures contained therein to develop action plans taking into account the specific regional conditions and their available resources. · The guidance contains extensive criteria for selection of the most appropriate method for stunning and killing and, on the basis of that, the staff operation manuals seen in the ASLs visited contained details on the key parameters for those methods and options for adapting them to the size and location of suspected outbreaks. 14. The information given on the methods provides guidance on their estimated maximum kill rates. This would provide support for granting possible derogations to some provisions envisaged in Article 18 (3) to the said Regulation under exceptional circumstances. However, neither the generic national contingency plan, nor the staff operation manuals seen in the regions and ASLs visited contained details on the way CAs could evaluate the exceptional circumstances that would permit derogation from certain provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. 15. The generic national contingency plan includes rules for disposal of animals killed for disease control purposes in order to prevent and minimise risks to public and animal health in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and with Article 72 of Directive 2003/85/EC (with respect to FMD). Staff operation manuals developed by the RVS and the ASLs have identified undertakings for the treatment of animal carcasses and animal waste in the event of a disease outbreak in the geographical areas under their responsibility, and in some cases have evaluated the options for the use of burial sites for that purpose. · The generic national contingency plan indicates

The Directorate General for Health of Agricultural Production of MAFF remains the single plant health authority. Its Sub-directorate General for Plant and Forestry Health and Hygiene (SDPFHH) acts as the single official body in the field of plant health. It is responsible for the transposition of the European Union (EU) legislation and represents Spain at international level in this area. It is responsible for policy relating to plant health under Council Directive 2000/29/EC.

The regional body concerned with agricultural matters is the DALFF, which is responsible for planning, implementing, supervising and enforcing legislation for Pomacea sp. eradication. Within this body, responsibilities for plant health matters are covered by the DGAL in particular the Plant Health Services which coordinates the Pomacea sp. eradication action plan.

Concerning the actions to be taken against Pomacea sp. in the Ebro river, several central bodies are involved, especially in matters related to water availability, as well as management and movement of boats. The water course from the mouth of the river upstream to Tortosa is under the responsibility of the Harbour Master Authority. The Ebro Hydrographic Federation has responsibility upstream from Tortosa.

An Emergency Management Team, acting as a wider coordination group amongst the various relevant entities from both the central and regional administrations exists. Co- chaired by the General Directors/Deputy Directors of the MAFF and Catalonian counterparts, its function is to provide a coordinated, overarching technical review of measures towards addressing overall eradication.
It was noted that the Pomacea sp. eradication action plan, along with other prominent pests and their associated eradication action plans, is included as part of a wider National Contingency Plan.

Given the Pomacea sp. infested and buffer zones span both agricultural (intensively managed) and conserved natural park lands, DGAL acts jointly with the Directorate- General of the Natural Environment and Biodiversity (DGNEB), responsible for natural 3 parks, and the Directorate General Rural Development. This is important as some of the area affected by Pomacea sp. lies partially within designated natural park land (primarily along the entire Ebro delta's sea fringe).

The region of Catalonia is divided into five sub-regions which mirrors the structure of the regional services in Barcelona. One of the sub-regions is the Terres de l'Ebre Territorial Directorate which coordinates and applies the eradication measures at local level. Six staff are permanently involved in Pomacea sp. eradication in the Ebro delta area. Similarly in Pals, the Girona Territorial Directorate has local responsibility for the co-ordination and application of eradication measures. 5.1.2 National and regional legislation 8. The EU Decision 2012/697/EU is directly applicable. 9. Apart from the general plant health national legislation, including Order AAM/63/2013 of 16 April 2013 (modifying Order AAR/404/2010 for the adoption of 2012/697/EU) the national legislation remains the same as described in the previous report. 10. Two additional DGAL annual resolutions, namely Resolution AAM/2529/2014 of 7 November 2014 establishing control measures, as modified by Resolution ARP/1457/2015 of 25 June 2015, have since been enacted and a further Order with respect to the recent outbreak in Pals is currently in preparation. 5.1.3 Guidelines and training 11. The audit team noted that DALFF maintains an accessible intranet database of protocols and operating procedures for the control of Pomacea sp. (available in both Spanish and Catalan). This includes guidelines, protocols and procedures for surveillance, treatments and cleaning of machinery, etc. The intranet database is updated as and when new information becomes available. 12. The CA stated that meetings and training courses are frequent. These are aimed primarily at inspectors and rural agents, but also include other important actors such as local administrators, etc. 13. The audit team viewed a wide variety of detailed technical leaflets, brochures and information sheets detailing the morphology, biology and epidemiology, as well as the control of the pest (used in both training and public awareness raising efforts). 14. The audit team noted that all staff, technical, as well as administrative, including law enforcement personnel (e.g. local police and Rural Agents), met during the audit were fully familiar with the organism and had specific guidelines and procedures to follow with respect to their respective function and remit. 4 5.1.4 Communication with stakeholders and awareness 15. During the previous audit a number of concerns and issues regarding the scope and effectiveness of the awareness raising approach and target actors were raised and formed the basis of Recommendation 5, which stated; Ensure that the awareness programme is extended and covers information to be provided to the general public and tourists visiting the river Ebro delta, in line with Art. 5 (2) of Decision 2012/697/EU. 16. During the course of the current audit the auditors found/noted that; Communication with stakeholders and awareness raising is co-ordinated by a spokesperson appointed by the Emergency Management Team. In general, a high awareness of the presence, on-going threat and economic significance of Pomacea sp. exists across the Ebro delta region, both with the general public and with associated stakeholders, in particular producers and associated actors with respect to rice production (those spoken with by the audit team were found to be fully familiar with the eradication and control of Pomacea sp.). This was the same with regards to the situation in Pals. Producers are directly communicated with by letter and via community and industry focused meetings. With regards the general public, awareness raising has been largely achieved through an active information dissemination and communication programme, in particular via numerous press articles, radio reports and dedicated television documentaries (both regional and national), of which the audit team was shown evidence. In addition to the provision of more technically orientated guidelines for use by their own staff and associated responsible bodies, the DALFF also produces a wide range of publicity and technical information for dissemination to the general public as well as maintaining a range of technical information on its website. In addition to this, a wide range of publicity and technical information, available in various languages and targeted at various groups of stakeholders, including the general public, tourists and visitors, anglers, boaters and those involved in rice production in the delta, exists (and was viewed by the audit team). Public awareness of the significance of the presence and impact of Pomacea sp. to the local economy and environment to be high, although the message to certain targeted high risk actors, in particular leisure boat users and anglers, including tourists, with regards the risk of spread and necessary control/mitigation approaches, was found to be less so. 5 On-going efforts to actively involve as wide a spectrum of relevant stakeholders as possible, particularly sector representatives such as rice production associations, regional official services, research and conservation/environmental groups (most of whom constitute and are involved in the 'Technical commission for Island apple snail' towards the effective application of the eradication action plan). Communication between the regional services and stakeholders continues to operate well. During visits to the delta, with the exception of one sign by a river mooring facility near the main left-right access point (although not prominently positioned), the audit team noted that no posters or signs are in place to alert the general public and tourists to the presence of the pest, the demarcated area or to the risk of spreading Pomacea sp. to new areas. No public signs alerting other growers, or the general public, to the presence of the pest in or around the Pals demarcated area, or to the risk of spreading Pomacea sp. to new areas. 5.1.5 Research and Laboratories 17. During the course of the current audit the auditors found/noted that; An integrated programme of basic and applied research activities towards control and eradication of Pomacea sp., spanning a range of statutory, research, university and non-governmental organisations is on-going. During the opening meeting the audit team was presented with an overview of completed, on-going, and planned research activities to support control and guide the on-going development and evolution of the eradication action plan. Although not visited on this occasion, the mollusc laboratory, within the 'Fauna recuperation centre', operating under the auspices of DGNEB, remains active, including provision of the facility for freeze destroying live snails collected in the fields. 6 Conclusions 18. Organised within a legal framework, there is a clear structure and division of responsibilities between the competent authorities responsible for developing and implementing eradication measures against Pomacea sp. in Spain. 19. There is a good awareness of the pest amongst central competent and regional official staff with the message of the risks and impacts reaching the general public and those directly involved in rice production. However, the situation with respect to informing specific, high risk Ebro river users, such as leisure boat owners and anglers, is inadequate which could inadvertently contribute to the spreading the pest to new area. Furthermore, public signs aimed at raising the awareness and alerting other growers, as well as the general public, to the presence of the pest in or around the demarcated areas remain absent. This is not fully in line with point 2 of Article 5 of Commission Decision 2012/697/EU, and as such Recommendation 5 of the previous audit remains partially addressed. 20. In addition to outputs already realised, on-going research continues to provide support and contributes to the development of strategies aimed at better control, and ultimate eradication of Pomacea sp. 5.2 IMPORT OF POMACEA SP. AND OF PLANTS Legal requirements Article 1 of Decision 2012/697/EU. Article 2 of Decision 2012/697/EU. Findings 5.2.1 Import and trade of snails 21. The SDPFHH stated to the audit team that, as found in the previous audit, the import of live Pomacea sp. snails is prohibited under Decision 2012/697/EU and the national legislation for exotic invasive species. 22. Article 5 of Decision 2012/697/EU. Findings 5.3.1 Survey in Spain 26. A detailed national survey protocol for Pomacea sp. remains in place to harmonise surveys at national level and is updated as and when further information or new findings come to light (the most up to date version can be found via the DALFF intranet database of protocols and operating procedures). 27. Application at national level continues to be coordinated by SDPFHH. 5.3.2 Demarcation of the areas 28. Following the notification of the most recent outbreak of Pomacea sp. in the municipality of Pals, Girona Province on 21 August 2015, a second demarcated area, in line with Article 5 of Implementing Decision 2012/697/EU, was established, bringing the total number of established demarcated areas in Spain for Pomacea sp. to two (both restricted to Catalonia only). 5.3.2.1 The Ebro delta 29. The infested zone incudes the entire rice production area within the left part of the Lower Ebro delta (including infested irrigation channels) covering the municipalities of Camarles, Deltebre, L'Aldea and L'Ampolla. 30. The CA stated that the right delta is considered free of Pomacea sp., despite on-going reports of small, isolated incidences (approximately 10 per annum) which the CA considers as intentional introductions. The CA qualified this view based on both the 8 isolated sporadic pattern of incidences and physiological age of individual snails found (which tend to be mature adults (commonly estimated at 3-4 years old minimum)). 31. The CA stated that each intentional introduction encountered in the right delta is subjected to intense eradication efforts. 32. Irrespective of the on-going situation and status in the right delta, the buffer zone covers the remaining area of the Lower Ebro district. The demarcated area is established as the entire districts (Comarcas) of Baix Ebra and Montsià (representing approximately 1738 Km2), but is practically focused on both sides of the delta (both fields and irrigation/drainage channels) and the Ebro river, upstream to Tortosa (as described in the previous audit report). 33. Fundamentally, surveys are based on the visual check for egg clutches and adult snails and are conducted by DALFF staff in cooperation with irrigation associations, natural park staff and farmers. 34. One lagoon, and the final stretches of the river Ebro (downstream), under the responsibility of the DGNEB, remains infested. The DGNEB cooperates in the on-going surveying and overall eradication effort. 35. During the course of the current audit; The audit team received technical information and an explanation of survey approaches, including river surveys as conducted from boats (normally out-sourced contractors with training) as co-ordinated by the DALFF, as well as those conducted by the DGNEB. The audit team observed the presence of snails and egg clutches across various sites and locations in the left delta area, both in fields and irrigation/drainage channels, as well as clutches, and remnants of clutches, in lower parts of the Ebro river (downstream from the town of Amposta at the location of the river mooring facility as mentioned in Finding 16). The CA stated that incidences of random, sporadic intentional introductions to various rice fields in the right delta have each been eradicated following the application of intense measures (with the audit team taking the opportunity to visit several such locations as part of the audit). The CA stated that some 520 rural agents, under the control of DGNEB are responsible for surveillance, law enforcement and control activities of the natural environment. In addition to regular, on-going field inspections, the CA stated that 600 Km of irrigation/drainage channels were surveyed in 2014 with the aim of inspecting the entire irrigation/drainage network of the right delta by the end of 2015. 9 The CA stated that the distribution of the pest in the Ebro delta has not extended beyond that as reported during the previous audit in 2013. The demarcated area remains much larger than required under the Implementing Decision 2012/697/EC. 5.3.2.2 Pals municipality 36. Following receipt of the official notification of the presence of Pomacea sp. from the municipality of Pals, Girona Province, on 21 August 2015, a second demarcated area, in line with Article 5 of Implementing Decision 2012/697/EU, was established in Catalonia. Pals is approximately 300 Km NE from the Ebro delta, situated in undulating arable and forested land (as mentioned in point 4.4). 37. According to the Girona Territorial Directorate, adults and egg clutches found were destroyed as and when encountered during the course of the bi-weekly survey regime and that the infection zone was further subjected to saponin treatment (evidence of which was apparent to the audit team from the widespread presence of dead crayfish carcases across the infested zone). According to the Girona Territorial Directorate, a wider intensive survey, particularly across the buffer zone, was not conducted, nor beyond to the source of the irrigation water (river Ter). 10 Conclusions 38. Demarcated areas around the Ebro delta, and the most recent Pals outbreak site, were established in accordance with the provisions of EU legislation. 39. The pest remains widespread in the original Ebro delta infested zone, particularly across the left delta, with sporadic random intentional introductions across the right delta (which are subjected to intense eradication measures). 40. The structure and organisation of the competent authority, as well as the control system for animal health is described in the 2015 audit report and in the Country Profile of Estonia. The Ministry of Agriculture became the Ministry of Rural Affairs on 1st September 2015 but the structure and organisation of the services responsible for official controls related to ASF remain largely as described in the Country Profile available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=EE
The National Reference Laboratory for ASF is the Central Veterinary and Food Laboratory in Tartu and is the only institution authorised to examine epizootic infectious animal diseases including ASF.

There is a range of national legislation in place in order to provide appropriate legal basis to the competent authority to implement animal health controls relating to ASF, e.g. : Directive 2002/60/EC is transposed into national legislation by the Regulation of the Ministry of Agriculture, No 179 of 2004 and the last amendment was in August 2015. (Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU is directly applicable in Estonia). The Infectious Animal Disease Control Act of 1999 provides the necessary powers for enforcement and penalties. text: There are numerous instructions and procedures issued by the competent authority with the aim of controlling and eradicating ASF. They are known by staff and updated. E.g.: 4 ASF Contingency Manual: continuously updated, e.g. deadlines of 30/06/16 and 31/12/16 for updates in response to recommendations from internal audit see finding 50, instructions for carrying out biosecurity inspection on holdings including check-lists and inspection reports templates (recently updated via Decree 130 of 18/10/16), instructions for the application of various articles of Decision 2014/709/EU.

Staff performing official control duties received training in line with Article 6 to Regulation (EC) 882/2004. The competent authority arranged several training sessions relating to ASF throughout the country for official and authorised veterinarians from 2014 onwards, e.g. ASF training held in Tallinn during September 2016 and attended by over 50 official and authorised veterinarians.
Estonia has an eradication plan for ASF in wild boars, which has been approved via Commission Implementing Decision 2015/570/EU.

The competent authority has established an expert group as required by Article 15 (2)(a) of Council Directive 2002/60/EC. Membership is drawn from the Veterinary and Food Board, Veterinary Food Laboratory, hunters association and the Environment Board with the possibility to include police and border staff if required.

The competent authority's website (http://www.agri.ee/et/seakatk) contains instructions and guidance for hunters and farmers. Topics covered include details on diseases, biosecurity, details of the regions affected by the Annex to Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU and recommended disinfectants. The VFB organises meetings with veterinarians, staff of Environment Inspectorate, hunters and representatives of local administrations to discuss the ASF situation and necessary eradication measures in defined infected and risk areas. The VFB also performs information campaigns through press, radio and television ­ for public about the ASF situation and necessary eradication measures, e.g. provision of 15,000 A2 posters on biosecurity to be displayed in forests. In addition, several information campaigns were organised by Estonian Association of Pig Keepers and by Union of Estonian Hunters and by Association of Estonian Hunters.

The Environment Board and Environment Inspectorate are government authorities under the Ministry of the Environment with responsibility for hunting activities in Estonia. Responsibilities include hunting quota, census of wild animals and licensing of hunters. There is no formal agreement between the Environment Board and the VFB but there are frequent contacts between both at central and regional levels.

Out of an estimated 15,000 hunters in Estonia, about 11,000 are members of the Estonian Hunters' Society (http://www.ejs.ee). In 2015, there was a single national contract in place between the Hunters' Society and the VFB related to activities linked to ASF. In 2016, this has been replaced by 130 contracts at local level between VFB and hunting clubs, many of which are members of the Society. The contract includes the possibility for hunters to take samples from both wild boar (both hunted and found dead), disposal of wild boar carcases and offal that tested positive for the disease, the use of disinfectants 5 and financial incentives for hunters to hunt female boar and dispose of wild boar carcases.

The VFB meets the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 through the Internal Audit Department in the Ministry of Rural Affairs (see paragraph 45). Conclusions on organisation of official controls

The structure and organisation of the competent authority enables sufficient and trained staff to perform ASF-related official controls. The training and written procedures that are available for staff help to ensure consistency and quality in the controls and the continuous information campaigns for hunters and farmers help to raise awareness.

The existing legal gap for biosecurity requirements in hunting grounds means that certain important measures to prevent the spreading of the disease cannot be enforced and that there is no objective information on their implementation currently available. The new legislation and subsequent official controls that Estonia plans to introduce within weeks will address the mentioned gap. 5.2 HOLDING REGISTRATION, ANIMAL IDENTIFICATION, MOVEMENT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 18 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC; Articles 4 and 18 of Council Directive 2008/71/EC; Article 15 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC; Article 1 of Commission Decision 2000/678/EC and Article 7 and the Annex to Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU. 5.2.1 System in place

The database kept by the Agricultural Registers and Information Board (ARIB) provides the competent authority with an up-to-date list of all the holdings which keep pigs, in line with Article 3 to Directive 2008/71/EC, including the keeping of a single animal. The competent authority has direct access to that database.

The information in ARIB database contains all the information required by Article 1(1) to Commission Decision 2000/678/EC. For pigs, data recorded included holding number, keeper name and address, date holding registered, geographic coordinates and the number of pigs recorded at last annual census.

Pig keepers must provide census information on numbers of pigs kept on an annual basis (1st May). There is a requirement for both the seller and the buyer to notify the database within 7 days when pigs move between holdings. There is no requirement for notification when pigs move from a holding to an abattoir which does not comply with the requirements of Article 18(c) of Council Directive 64/432/EEC. 6 19. Between September 2014 and September 2016, there was a 30% decrease in the pig population and 80% decrease in the number of holdings keeping pigs. Most of the 80% was made up of small holdings. There are two farms keeping wild boars in Estonia. 20. National legislation does not provide specific definition of commercial and non- commercial/back-yard holdings and all holdings must comply with all biosecurity rules. Wild boars are kept in two farms, both have less than ten pigs. 21. The Regulation of the Ministry of Agriculture governing animal identification (No 128 of 2009) requires pigs to be identified with a tattoo or a plastic ear tag identifying holding of birth. Pigs sent for slaughter must have a mark identifying the holding from where they have been despatched. When pigs move from a holding other than the holding of birth to another holding, they are identified via the holding of birth identification. 22. National legislation requires holdings to keep records (paper or electronic) with the information set out in Article 4 to Council Directive 2008/71/EC, but there is no prescribed format for herd registers in Estonia. Officials check this part of the biosecurity controls. The audit team confirmed that both holdings visited during this audit had acceptable records. 23. There are no markets for pigs in Estonia. There are two approved assembly centres although neither has been used for several years. There are two semen and one embryo collection centres located in Part II of Annex to Decision 2014/709/EU. The last consignment that moved to another Member State from any of these was in August 2015 when they were in ASF free territory. 24. All animal by-products from porcine animals go to two processing establishments which are both situated in Part III. Therefore, implementing Article 7 of Decision 2014/709/EU is unnecessary. Neither establishment sends porcine by-products to other Member States. 5.2.2 Official controls 25. In case of a disease outbreak or case, the VFB uses the database to get a list of holdings within the protection and surveillance zones or infected area in order to apply relevant controls. 7 ASF in domestic pigs ­ locations of outbreaks during 2015 and 2016 26. Following the detection of ASF in wild boar or in a pig holding, the competent authority implements the measures required by Directive 2002/60/EC including epidemiological investigation, depopulation, cleaning and disinfection, establishment of infected areas or protection/surveillance zones, census and restriction of pig movements. The file for one outbreak was examined by the audit team and the measures foreseen in legislation were applied. 27. There was evidence that official controls on biosecurity and identification and traceability on pig holdings have been carried out according to the central instruction. The frequency of the controls varies depending on location of the pig holding: once a month in infected areas (93% of holdings), twice a year in Parts I, II and III (7% of holdings). 28. Of the 181 holdings with pigs currently in Estonia: 90 holdings do not move pigs to other holdings or abattoirs and carry out home slaughter. 62 are listed as complying with the requirements of either Article 3, 3a or 4 of Decision 2014/709/EU. Compliance is based on twice annual blood sampling of the holding pre-certification checks on 30 day rules for residency/no new animal introduced from Parts II/III, compliance with biosecurity rules etc. 29 holdings are subject to sampling of all animals in each departing consignment at least 15 days pre-movement and other relevant rules as above. 8 29. All holdings in Part II or III that send pigs to either an abattoir or to another holding have to obtain a certificate for the movement, usually issued by an authorised veterinarian, i.e. a "9T" in the case of animals moving from a holding to an abattoir or a "7E" in the case of animals moving between holdings. Both certificates are used to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of various Articles in Decision 2014/709/EU, e.g. articles 3 or 4. These certificates provide information on the ASF testing history (either on a holding or consignment basis) and confirmation of the clinical health of the animals in the consignment. However, there is no certification of compliance with other relevant rules such as 30 day residency of animals, no introduction of new animals on to the holding within 30 days prior to certification or respect of biosecurity rules. 30. The competent authority has provided training for official veterinarians which included information on conditions for derogations for dispatch of live pigs (Article 3 of Decision 2014/709/EU). Officials were in charge of forwarding the information to the authorised veterinarians. At a holding visited by the audit team, the authorised veterinarian was not applying the criteria for selection of pigs to be sampled as foreseen in Part A of Chapter IV of Annex to Decision 2003/422/EC (required by Article 3.3 (ii) of Decision 2014/709/EU), and it was evidence that pigs had been moved. Moreover, the introduction of 1,000 pigs from areas listed in Part II/III into the holding did not trigger a suspension of a weekly certification for movement of live pigs from this holding by the authorised veterinarian. 31. The competent authority verifies the certification issued by authorised veterinarians through documentary review. The verification does not involve on-site supervision on a relevant holding, where the herd register and medicine records can be checked (in order to verify the conditions for certification). Conclusions on holding registration, animal identification, movement controls and official controls 32. The very significant reduction in the number of holdings keeping pigs and in the total number of pigs has decreased the overall workload of the competent authority which should facilitate the availability of more resources to ensure compliance. 33. In general, the national system for holding registration, animal identification and movement controls provides a solid basis to support ASF-related controls. The fact that movements of pigs to abattoirs do not have to be notified to the national database decreases the amount of information in the database available to the competent authority and makes the forward tracing of pigs difficult. 34. The pre-movement certification of all live pigs provides, in principle, guarantees of compliance with movement rules and thus reduces the risk of disease spread between holdings. However, as authorised veterinarians do not perform pre-certification checks correctly (i.e. sampling procedures and verification of residency periods) and the verification system does not pick-up failures in the system, the measure is not very effective, which hinders this reduction of risk. 5.3 BIOSECURITY MEASURES Legal requirements 9 Article 8 of Directive 2002/60/EC. 5.3.1 Biosecurity in relation to wild boar 35. The hunting season for wild boar in Estonia runs from 1st March to the last day of February the following year. At the time of the audit, Estonia was divided into 327 hunting grounds. Hunting increased by nearly 55% between 2014 and 2016 and there was about a 40% decrease in the Spring census over the same period as shown in the following figures related to wild boar: Spring census 2016 2015 2014 Hunting quota 12,220 20,600 19,710 17,580 29,608 27,909 Effective hunting Season 2015/2016 Season 2014/2015 32,580 24,909 Season 2013/2014 20,885 36. Decree of Environmental Board No 1-4.1 /15/365 sets out a number of measures for wild boar, including: Selective hunting from sub-adults and adults, 60% of wild boar shot must be females; (plus a financial incentive of 100 per female is available). Additional feeding is forbidden all year around, except for baiting and all feeding places must be registered. Driven hunts are allowed subject to certain restrictions. 37. As stated in paragraphs 6 and 7, only guidance exists for many of the biosecurity requirements during hunting and there is no national legal basis. There are no official controls in hunting areas to check compliance with guidance or the requirements for which a legal basis exists via the Environmental Board. 38. EU legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the most recently amended version. Full references to the EU acts quoted in this report are given in Annex 1. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 COUNTRY PROFILE DG Health and Food Safety has published a Country Profile for Greece, which describes in summary the control systems for food and feed, animal health, animal welfare and plant health as well as quality labelling gives an overview of the state of play concerning recommendations from previous audits. The country profile for Greece can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=GR 2 4.2 GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS OF WINE Through the EU quality schemes, PDO/PGI wines are promoted and their names are protected from, inter alia, misuse, evocation and imitation. The scheme also helps consumers by providing information concerning the specific character of the products: PDO wines are denominated by the name of a region, a specific place or, in exceptional cases, a country. Their quality and characteristics are essentially or exclusively linked to a geographical environment. All production steps take place in the geographical area and 100% of the grape variety must originate from the geographical area. PGI wines are denominated by the name referring to a region, a specific place, or, in exceptional cases, a country. They possess a given quality, reputation or other characteristics, attributable to a given geographical origin. All production steps must take place in the geographical area and at least 85% of the grape variety must originate in the geographical area. Further details on the quality schemes for wine sector products are available on the following website: http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/quality/schemes/wines/index_en.htm The e-Bacchus database of the registered wine names is available on the following website: http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/markets/wine/e-bacchus/index.cfm?&language=EN 4.3 STATUS OF REGISTERED PRODUCTS IN GREECE At the time of the audit, there were 33 PDO and 116 PGI wines registered from Greece in the e-Bacchus database. Five registered names were selected to form part of this audit as a sample, in order to evaluate how the system of official controls works in Greece. The criteria used for this selection were, inter alia, the economic value and production volume, potential risks factors, the assessment of the multi-annual national control plan and annual reports, a representative selection of products and the geographical distribution of their production sites. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. 3 Findings 1. The relevant legislation relating to PDO/PGI wine sector products is the Joint Ministerial Decision (JMD) o 5833/155045/12.12.2013 as amended by JMD o 5066/117288/27.10.2015 (Official Journal 2322/B/27.10.2015).

Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Article 146 of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Article 90 (1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council in conjunction with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Findings

According to the Article 3 of the JMD No 5833/155045/12.12.2013, the CCA responsible for carrying out official controls to verify compliance with the legal requirements related to PDO/PGI wine sector products is the following:
The CCA is the Department of Wines and Spirits within the Directorate of Processing and Quality Control of Food of Plant Production (Directorate General for Sustainable Plant Production) of the MRDF.

A key responsibility of the CCA is the compilation and updating of the Register of Certified Operators for Producing PDO/PGI wine sector products at national level. The CCA stated that this register currently exists in an excel format and that it may become part of the wine register which will also include the digital application for wine production, stocks and processing / trading declarations. The digital application is currently in the testing phase. 4 7. The audit team reviewed the current electronic system at national and local level and noted that the vineyard register is in place and contains the harvest declarations from the vine growers. This electronic system will in the future contain the digital application for wine. At the time of the audit, information relating to wine production, including stocks, is obtained from each individual Directorate of Rural Economy and Veterinary Service of Regional Unities (DREV). 8. The CCA is responsible for the transmission of complaints relating to PDO/PGI wine sector products to the DREVs, and ensuring their follow up. DREVs can also directly receive complaints. 9. The Department of Wines and Spirits is tasked by the legislation to coordinate, inform and supervise the DREVs and the Regional Centres for Plant Protection and Quality Control (RCPPQCs) regarding official controls at all stages of production, bottling, labelling and distribution of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 10. The CCA stated that in 1996 the competence for official controls in the PDO/PGI wine sector products was delegated to DREVs. The above mentioned JMD came into force in 2013 and describes the specific tasks that the DREVs must undertake with regard to the certification of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 11. There are 61 DREVs, the inspectors of which undertake official controls of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 12. DREVs examine and approve operator requests for registration on the Register of Certified Operators for producing PDO/PGI wine sector products. In addition, the DREVs are responsible for compiling and updating the register at local level. They ensure compliance with the Product Specifications in order to carry out certification of PDO/PGI wine sector products and provide "quality control tapes for PDO wines" (these are paper strips which must be placed on bottles with PDO wine before placing on the market) and special code numbers to the operators for PGI wines. In addition, market controls at retail and wholesale are required to be carried out by DREV. Irregularities and infringements must be reported by DREVs to the CCA. However, the DREVs visited had not yet commenced such market controls. 13. The eight RCPPQCs are tasked with the coordination of the DREVs in their jurisdiction. The RCPPQCs draw up the annual programme of regular on-site inspections jointly with the competent DREVs. However the audit team was informed that such activities had not yet been implemented at the time of the audit (see paragraph 17). Conclusions on Competent Authorities 14. CAs are designated and their tasks are described in legislation. Coordination of controls by RCPPQCs is not implemented for the PDO/PGI wine sector products with a risk that relevant control requirements are not fulfilled. . 5 5.2.2 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 90 of Regulation (EU) No. 1306/2013. Articles 25 and 26 of Regulation (EC) No 607/2009. Findings Primary producers for PDO/PGI wine sector products 15. No on-site inspections at vineyards are undertaken by the relevant CAs. However, administrative cross-checks are carried out of the information on compulsory wine sector declarations (production and harvest declarations) against the information in the vineyard registers. These cross-checks are carried out for each wine producer and cover at least 5% of the grape growers delivering to the respective wine producer or, in the case of a wine-making operator with fewer than 100 growers, at least 5 growers. This cross checking gives some assurance of the quantity of grapes grown, the grape variety and that it was grown in the designated area. Annual Verification for PDO/PGI wine sector products 16. According to Article 25(1) of Regulation 607/2009, annual verification shall be conducted in MSs in accordance with the Product Specification and shall be carried out either through random checks based on risk analysis, sampling or systematically. In the case of random checks the MSs shall select the minimum number of operators to be subject to those checks. 17. The national legislation requires that in relation to PGI wines, at least 20% of applications for certifications have to be sampled and analysed as well as at least 20% of the total production quantity of the PGI wine in the relevant regional unit. Given that there is no coordination being undertaken by the RCPPQCs, the audit team could not determine whether or not these requirements were met. In the particular DREVs visited, the inspectors met stated that these requirements had not yet been met. 18. The annual verification is undertaken by DREVs as part of the certification process which includes administrative checks such as cross checking the compulsory declarations (production and harvest declarations) with the vineyard register. For PDO wines, the certification process consists of analytical and organoleptic tests as well as checking for compliance with the Product Specification. For PGI wines, the certification consists of compliance with the Product Specification. Analytical tests on certified PGI wines are carried out on a sample basis. 19. In relation to sampling, either RCPPQC staff in cooperation with DREV, or DREV staff if the RCPPQC is unable to do so, undertake the sampling for organoleptic and analytical testing of PDO/PGI wines. The accredited laboratories of the RCPPQC are used for analytical tests. Relating to organoleptic tests, these are done by the National 6 Inter-professional Organisation of Vine and Wine committee which is established within each defined production area of PDO wines. 20. In one DREV, it was noted that the method used for the determination of dry matter was not accredited. In the laboratory report there was no result for total sugar content which is a requirement of Article 26 of Regulation (EC) 607/2009. This was not noted by the CCA who is responsible for the supervision of the DREVs and the RCPPQCs. Official controls on the Market of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 21. The CAs responsible for PDO/PGI wine sector products selected for this audit confirmed that at the time of the audit, no market controls were being planned. Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 22. In relation to the PDO/PGI wine sector products selected for this audit, although the annual verification of PDO/PGI wine sector products is prescribed in national legislation, the relevant sampling is not always undertaken and the scope of laboratory testing did not always reflect the requirements of the Product Specifications. In addition, no market controls were being planned. 5.2.3 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Article 103(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013. Articles 25-26 of Regulation (EC) No 607/2009. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Findings Official controls of producers / processors 23. During this audit, the audit team visited the production sites of two PDO and three PGI wine sector products in three different regions. All inspections were undertaken by official control staff from the respective DREVs. In all site visits, it was noted that for the majority of inspections, no inspection reports were drawn up making it impossible to determine if all elements of the Product Specification were checked. 24. Where inspection reports had been issued by the DREVs, they contained very little detail of the site visit and the activities carried out and whether or not all elements of the Product Specification were checked. In addition, there was no documentation attached to the report to substantiate any checks that had taken place. 7 25. When non-compliances were detected, these were discussed orally with the operator along with the corrective actions required and no written record was created. Non- compliances were not reported to the CCA contrary to Article 3 of the JMD 5833/155045 of 12 December 2013. 26. At the time of the audit, limited documented procedures were in place to guide the DREV's inspectors on a common approach to official controls of PDO/PGI wine sector products. 27. Although the majority of inspectors met were knowledgeable on oenology, at the time of the observed inspections, there were no obvious guidelines or checklists used by the inspectors. Subsequently, the CCA stated that guidelines and checklists were provided by an implementing circular to the DREVs which were provided to the audit team. There was however no further explanation provided to the audit team as to why these guidance documents were not used by the inspectors observed. During two site visits the audit team requested traceability exercises to be performed. Although these were undertaken satisfactorily, the information of the producer, both in electronic and paper format, were fragmented and required a lot of effort and manpower to complete such traceability exercises. 28. The RCPPQCs visited had not implement a risk based approach to controls and neither was there any coordination of the DREVs in place. In addition, any communication between DREVs was informal and undertaken on an ad hoc basis. Controls on the Market: (visit to supermarket) 29. At the time of the audit, market controls of PDO/PGI wine sector products were not in place. The DREV inspector observed by the audit team had not undertaken any official controls relating to wine sector products on the market since 2013. The inspector had prepared for this observation exercise and had a listing of the key requirements for the labelling of wines. Conclusions on Procedures and Performances of Official Control Activities 30. In relation to the PDO/PGI wine sector products selected for this audit, procedures in terms of guidelines, checklists and reporting procedures were not used by the inspectors observed. The effectiveness of inspections, in particular the checking of each element of the Product Specification could not be assessed fully due to the lack of records and inspection reports. In addition, market controls were not in place. 5.2.4 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 607/2009. 8 Art 103 of Regulation (EC) No 1308/2013. Findings 31. The Law No 4235/2014 foresees administrative measures and administrative and penal provisions for non-conformities related to both food and wine. The CAs visited stated that, for the most part, non-compliances relating to PDO/PGI wine sector products which were detected during official controls were not documented and not reported to the CCA. Whether or not, the system functions in practice could not be assessed at the time of the audit due to no concrete examples being available. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures 32. A system is in place for enforcement measures to be applied in cases of non-compliance related to PDO/PGI wine sector products. However, as the actual system is only partially implemented, it is not possible to assess the effectiveness of the system. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Overall, there is a system of official controls in the area of PDO/PGI wine sector products with clearly designated CAs and relevant legislation in place. However, the effectiveness of the control system is weak. There is a lack of coordination of controls throughout the system which undermines the credibility of the quality schemes on PDO/PGI wine sector products in Greece. Moreover, guidelines and checklists provided by the CCA are not being used by the inspectors and laboratory reports were not always complete. Market controls are not in place.

Regulations (EC) Nos 852, 853 and 854 of 2004 2 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 LEGISLATION AND IMPLEMENTING MEASURES Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Point 2 of Chapter I, Section X, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Findings 1. The audit team was informed by BMEL that for the egg and egg products sector, the Länder CA follow the relevant EU and federal legislation. The federal level is responsible for policy and federal legislation in the area of food safety. The BMEL is responsible for drawing up legislative initiatives and general administrative regulations (Allgemeinen Verwaltungsvorschriften), as well as for issuing related statutory regulations (Rechtsverordnungen). The Länder CA informed the audit team that there is in place relevant legislation for the implementation of the federal law at Land level covering the scope of the audit and therefore there are no any additional implementing laws related specifically to the egg and egg products sector at Länder level.

Furthermore, various guidelines (federal and Länder) assist the Länder CA in controlling Food Business Operators (FBOs) and in implementing the requirements of the EU and federal requirements for the sector.

Due to the federal structure in Germany, there is no national multiannual control plan covering all control activities in Germany and each Land is responsible for developing and reviewing its own individual control plan for the implementation of official controls.

Regarding FBOs compliance with temperature requirements for eggs during storage and transport, the audit team was informed by the CCA that no federal legislation has been issued, therefore the FBOs should follow the relevant EU legislation (i.e. Article 2(3) of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008 and Point 2 of Chapter I, Section X, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

While a comprehensive review of German legislation was not carried out by the audit team, the federal and Länder laws and implementing measures (including guidelines), seen by the audit team during the audit were in line with EU requirements related to the audit scope. Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures

Germany has issued federal and Länder legislation and guidelines necessary to implement EU requirements relevant to eggs and egg products and, from a summary 3 analysis, these are in line with EU legislation.

National temperature requirements for storage facilities and for vehicles transporting eggs, in the context of Point 2 of Chapter I, Section X, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, have not been fixed in federal legislation 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Findings Structure and organisation

The structure of the CA and the allocation of responsibilities are described in the country profile of Germany available the Commission's website at:- http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=DE

Concerning the CA responsible for the official controls carried out in the egg/egg products production chain the competencies are distributed as follows: BMEL has almost exclusive competence for food and feed safety, animal health and animal welfare and is responsible for policy and for drawing up legislative initiatives in the area. The BMEL is also the CCA responsible for issuing federal legislation covering import controls of live animals and food of animal origin. BVL provides logistical and organisational support to the Länder and assists in the flow of information between federal and Länder level in the field of food safety and consumer protection. BVL is also the National Contact Point for the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) in Germany. The Länder are competent for the implementation of official controls and are responsible for ensuring that official controls comply with the legislation in the area of food safety. The federal government has no authority to instruct the Länder in these areas; however, it exercises supervision over the Länder to ensure that they implement federal laws correctly. At national level the BLE is responsible for granting and revoking authorisations for private control bodies (CBs) that carry out the control tasks and certify organic production. The competent Land authorities monitor the activities of these private CBs in accordance with a mutually agreed, harmonised and risk-oriented system. BLE is also the CCA responsible for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008 (marketing standards applicable to eggs). 4 Coordination

There are several types of coordination and communication between federal and Land level. The BMEL organises federal/Land consultations with representatives of the competent Land ministries to discuss legislative issues. With a view to achieve harmonised implementation at national level and serve as an interface between the federal and Land levels, the Länder have also developed co-ordination and communication structures (working groups).

Within the Länder Working Group on Consumer Protection (LAV), the Länder authorities responsible for consumer protection and veterinary matters work together. The responsibilities of the LAV include the topics of food and feed safety, animal health, animal diseases, veterinary medicinal products, animal welfare, relevant occupational law, and topics related to economic and regulatory aspects of consumer protection and nutrition. Both BMEL and BVL are permanent observers at these LAV meetings.
The audit team was provided with evidence in one of the Länder visited that topics related to eggs and eggs products were discussed during a relevant LAV meeting.
The audit team also gathered evidence of adequate cooperation between the different organisational levels of CA in the Länder visited. Training

Each Land is responsible for providing their official staff with the training needed to carry out official controls. To this end, each Land has its own training plans, through which training is provided each year in accordance with established priorities.

Principles for the planning, implementation, documentation and assessment of education and training measures for the official staff of the CA are set out in the quality management system (QMS) of the Land.
The audit verified that training arrangements were in place in order to ensure that staff performs their tasks effectively. Audit and verification

The federal government exercises supervision over the Länder to ensure that they implement federal laws correctly. The BMEL controls the lower-level bodies at federal level. These include, in particular the BVL and the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR).

The various Länder Ministries and Senate Administrations co-ordinate these activities within their respective Land. The local authorities are generally audited and subject to supervisory control in the context of technical supervision by provincial authorities (where applicable) or otherwise by the Land authorities/Ministries or Senate Administrations (i.e. the highest-level food monitoring and veterinary authorities). 5 19. The audit team saw evidence in each Land visited, that audits in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 have been carried out. The audit team was informed by the highest Land CA that no internal audits covering the egg and egg products sector have been carried out so far. In one of the Länder visited the audit team was informed and saw evidence of a state-wide audit regarding Salmonella in poultry carried out in 2013 during which also issues related to the handling of eggs in cases of positive Salmonella flocks were covered. Conclusions on competent authorities 20. The Länder CA responsible for the official control system covering the production of eggs and egg products are clearly designated. The Länder structure and organisation are adequate for the performance of their tasks. 21. In order to meet the requirement of Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Germany has put in place a system for ensuring co-ordination between the different Länder responsible for official controls for the sector audited. 22. A training system aimed at ensuring that official staff can execute their tasks effectively is in place. 23. Germany complies with the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 as an audit system has been established. 5.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The audit team was informed by the local CA in both Länder visited that there is a procedure in place for the registration of laying hen holdings and it was observed that 6 this procedure was applied as described. Official inspections are carried out on-site during the registration procedure in order to verify that the holdings comply with the relevant animal health, animal welfare, biosecurity and egg marketing requirements. 25. The CA allocates a 12-digit registration number to each holding, which is made up of the official municipality code (eight digits) and a four-digit holding number. 26. In order to be registered as organic, a holding has to be certified by one of the 16 private CBs operating nationwide in Germany who also grant a specific number to each holding. Registration of laying farms of poultry species other than Gallus gallus 27. The audit team was informed by the local CA that the registration procedure for laying poultry farms other than Gallus gallus (e.g. ducks, quails, etc.) is the same as for Gallus gallus laying hen farms with the exception that neither a code for marking the eggs nor an on-site visit is generally required in order to commence farming activities. 28. The audit team was provided with evidence of such a registration covering a quail farm visited. Registration of egg collectors 29. According to Article 1(c) of Regulation (EC) No 589/2008 collectors are defined as establishments registered in accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 to collect eggs from a producer for delivery to a packing centre, to a market selling exclusively to wholesalers whose undertakings are approved as packing centres, or to the food or non-food industry. 30. The Länder are responsible for establishing procedures for the registration of egg collectors since this type of activity is not explicitly mentioned in federal Law. 31. The audit team visited an establishment registered by the Land CA as an egg collector. The establishment was also approved as an egg packing centre and a liquid egg plant. During the visit it was noted that this establishment did not actually carry out activities which fall under the definition of an egg collector. At the time of the visit there were no documents available regarding the procedures followed for the registration of the establishment. Neither the CA nor the FBO could provide explanations about the procedure followed for its registration. 32. The audit team was provided, by the Land CA with a list containing information about registered egg collectors. The audit team noted that registered egg collectors are either standalone or are part of egg packing centres that carry out additionally egg collection activities. However in the latter case the additional activity of the egg collector is not reflected on the national list of approved establishments. Under Annex V to Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005 regarding the master list of approved establishments and the latest technical specifications published by the EU Commission (see link below), a collection 7 centre as defined in Regulation (EC) No 589/2008 and registered as a food business pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 can also pursue its activity on the basis of its inclusion on the list of approved establishments. https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/safety/docs/biosafety_fh_eu_food_establishmen ts-techspecs_en.pdf) 33. In another establishment visited that was approved as an egg packing centre and egg processing plant the FBO informed the audit team that as part of the normal egg packing activities they also collect eggs from laying farms which are then delivered, un-graded, to other egg packing centres for grading and packing. However the establishment had not been registered for this additional activity by the CA (see paragraph 71). Approval of establishments 34. The Länder are responsible for the approval of establishments (including egg products establishments and egg packing centres) where approval is compulsory. The CA informed the audit team that facilities used for the packing of eggs from poultry species other than Gallus gallus have to be registered, but not approved. This is not in line with Article 31(2) of Regulation 882/2004 and 4(2) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. The audit team was informed by the CA of the Länder visited that food business establishments are approved either by the local or provincial CA in accordance with the procedures laid down by these Länder. The audit team noted, in all establishments visited, that these approval procedures were in compliance with EU legislation. 35. The CCA informed the audit team that establishments processing shell eggs or unpasteurised liquid egg (i.e. unprocessed food) for the production of final products containing this ingredient (e.g. pasta) must also to be approved as egg processing plants, with the exception of bakeries which must be registered. Under federal law these types of establishment, can process or produce unpasteurised liquid egg only for their own use. The audit team noted that the majority of the approved establishments listed as egg products processing plants in both Länder are establishments which use shell eggs or unpasteurised egg for their own production of different types of food i.e. mass-caterers or pasta producers. The audit team saw evidence in one Land visited that egg packing centres are both approved and authorised under hygiene and egg marketing regulations respectively. 36. Once an establishment is approved by a CA then this is notified to the highest Land CA and then to BVL which publishes the up-to-date list on the internet, with a link to the relevant page of the European Commission. 37. This procedure is governed by federal law and BVL is the CCA that manages the national list. The list of approved establishments is publicly available on the website of BVL. 8 38. All establishments visited were approved by the local/ provincial CA for the activities that they perform and the approval documents were available to the audit team. 39. During a visit to an egg packing centre the audit team noted that in the specific establishment another two additional activities were carried out i.e. re-wrapping of already graded eggs and cold storage of egg products bought from other approved establishments. These additional activities were not indicated on the national list for the specific establishment. 40. The audit team visited two approved establishments where some discrepancies between the activities reported at Land level and those on the national list were noted by the audit team during the preparation of the audit. The establishments were approved by the local CA both as a liquid egg plant and egg packing centres. However, in the list of approved establishments published on the BVL website one was listed as egg products establishment (processing plant) and egg packing centre and the second one was additionally listed as egg products establishment (processing plant). This is not in compliance with the provisions of Article 31(2)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CCA attributed this to the fact that there is no clear definition in EU legis
