An overview of how control systems are organised in Hungary (based on information supplied by the national authorities) is provided in the Country Profile for Hungary at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=HU

The NFCSO with its central office in Budapest is the CCA in the scope of this audit. NFCSO is responsible for supporting the decision-making of the MoA and providing control plans, procedures and guidelines to CGO.
At central level coordinating tasks are shared between two directorates of NFCSO, DPPSC and FFSD.

At central level NFCSO DPPSC is responsible for coordination of inspection tasks in the field of primary production (except sprout establishments and establishments packing seeds for sprouting). Farmers, facilities producing/growing vegetables, fruit, seeds for sprouting, importers of seeds for sprouting are inspected at county level by CGO of DFCSPPSC or Department for Food Chain Safety and Agriculture (DFCSA).

At central level NFCSO FFSD is responsible for coordination of inspection tasks in the field of sprouts establishments and establishments of packing seeds for sprouting. 5 10. In Hungary there are 19 CGOs, one in each county. The CGO is headed by a government appointee and comprises fifteen specialised Directorates / Offices, three of which are involved in food controls ­ DFCSPPSC, DFCSA and Department for Public Health. 11. At local level, the administration consists of 198 district government offices (DGOs). Within these DGOs there are 82 district food chain safety and animal health units (DFCSAHU). On average each DFCSAHU is responsible for 2-3 DGOs. 12. At county (CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA) and/or local level (DFCSAHU) food engineers or veterinarians are responsible for the control of sprout-producers and packers of seeds for sprouting and to control sprouts and seeds for sprouting at retailers. 13. Official sampling of food for monitoring purpose is carried out by inspectors. Official laboratories perform analyses of official samples and assessment of test results. Official laboratories are designated by the CCA. 14. The CCA presented staff training files to the audit team. There were 5 regional training sessions about official controls on sprouting in 2016 and 240 inspectors from the CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSAs and District Government Offices took part in these trainings which were organised by NFCSO FFSD. Topics of the training were mainly about the regulation of sprouts but also considered the outcome of the last DG Health and Food Safety audits on sprouts. As for control of primary production, each year, there are two- day training sessions organised for plant inspectors. Microbiological safety issues in leafy green vegetable crops were addressed in 2015. The training was organized by NFCSO DPPSC with the participation of local inspectors of the CGO. 15. During official controls at sprouts and packer establishments, the CAs can gather information about suppliers of seeds, in particular through verification of traceability. The audit team noted that following such checks, CGO DFCSAHU had identified a number of producers of seeds for sprouting (see paragraphs 60, 65, 70 and 71). Based on the statement that the responsible divisions of NFCSO DPPSC and CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA were not aware of the existence of such producers, the audit team noted that the information had not been shared between the various bodies concerned resulting in such producers not being subject to official controls. This limited cooperation does not fulfil the requirements of Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls 16. The CAs in the context of this audit are designated at all stages of primary production as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and this gives a good basis for the implementation of official controls. However, limited coordination and cooperation between the government bodies involved results in some producers of seeds for sprouting not being subject to official controls. 6 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Food Establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Registration of Food Establishments 17. Primary producers can be registered in three different systems: Fruit and vegetable business operators including producers are registered in the fruit and vegetables distribution registration system; All FBOs throughout the food chain are registered in the Food-Chain Supervision Fee System; Farms receiving subsidies are registered by the Paying Agency. 18. For the purpose of inspection, at the beginning of each season the CCA requests data about produce/producers from the Paying Agency. As producers are also controlled for use of pesticides, the local inspectors in charge for control of primary production have a thorough knowledge of producers at their local level. 19. The audit team was informed by the CCA that there are around 600,000 registered primary producers in Hungary. The CCA estimated that this figure represents 90% of the entire primary producers of FNAO. Of these, 350 grow green leafy vegetables and/or soft fruits. 20. FBOs involved in the "sprout chain" (importers, distributers, retailers of seeds, internet sellers) are also registered. They have to submit an application for registration to the town clerk (as commercial authority) who notifies the CGO. Packers are registered at the CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA. 21. The audit team was informed that the NFCSO has launched a project to control e- commerce. This project is aimed at establishing a national system of official controls for such traders. Approval of Sprout-Producing Establishments 22. The audit team was informed that sprout-producing establishments have to be approved by CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA. The procedure is described in the rules on the registration and approval of food-processing establishments. The procedure starts with receiving an application for approval, which is followed by an inspection. If the FBO complies with the requirements of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 an approval is issued to the sprout-producing establishment. Once the approval is granted an FBO can start production and marketing of sprouts. 23. In one county, for administrative reasons, the formal approvals have not been granted. However, the facilities of FBOs who have applied for registration are regularly 7 inspected for compliance with EU legislation from the moment they apply and they are subject to systematic official controls (inspections and sampling). 24. According to the information provided by the CCA, there were nine establishments registered and approved for sprouting seeds. Two of them were suspended during this audit (see paragraph 67). Conclusions on Registration / Approval of Food Establishments 25. There is a system in place for registration of primary producers of FNAO and for registration and approval of sprout-producing establishments that enables the inspectors to identify FBOs for the purpose of official controls. However, in one county visited, while the approval of such establishments had not been formally issued, these were under official supervision in order to verify that they met the applicable requirements. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Articles 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings 26. The system of official controls is described in the Hungarian Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP), the current version of which covers the period 2013 to 2016. However, the audit team was informed by the CCA that the current version of the MANCP does not include a specific description of the control system for primary production of FNAO which will be part of the new MANCP. 27. The audit team was informed by the CCA that in 2013 NFCSO introduced an integrated approach to improve their Food Chain Monitoring Plan. A coordinating working group (headed by NFCSO Directorate for System Management and Supervision) has been set up to ensure that planning is in line with objectives, to carry out risk assessments, to identify priorities in the control system, to monitor the execution of the plan, and to coordinate the work of twelve Professional Panels which cover various aspects of food production and food safety. 28. One of the twelve Professional Panels is the Microbiological Hazards Professional Panel that is responsible for the preparation of the National Microbiological Control Plan. 29. Inspections are carried out using checklists. For primary producers of FNAO, except lettuce producers, these checklists are very generic. Not all points concerning microbiological risks are addressed and no samples at farms are foreseen. Moreover, inspections are mainly tailored to farms with pack houses (see paragraph 40). 30. The CAs informed the audit team that, in the counties visited, primary producers in the scope of the audit are inspected on an annual frequency, even if a set inspection frequency had not been established at national level at the time of the audit. 8 31. The audit team was informed that a new, more detailed, checklist is available since 2015. For the time being, the generic checklist is still being used for produce other than for lettuce. Lettuce is the first commodity subject to a more detailed plan for primary production controls because of the associated risk (see EFSA Risk Ranking). During the controls at lettuce farms, the inspectors use such a checklist (as a tool for a risk assessment) and based on the risk score, the CAs decide if samples are to be taken. In this early stage of implementation, a certain number of samples are taken irrespective of the outcome of such risk assessments. 32. The CCA informed the audit team that throughout Hungary there are 50 major producers of lettuce (more than 20 tons/year or more than 500,000 plants/year). In 2015, 20 inspections were performed and for the period April 2016 to March 2017, 100 inspections are planned in the five counties where those producers of lettuce are located. In the plan are included also 50 small producers. Specifically, in the two counties visited 35 inspections had been planned with six carried out at the time of the audit. 33. The audit team was informed by the CCA that the new checklist, in use for inspecting lettuce producers, will be extended to the other primary producers in the scope of the audit. Once a risk assessment has been concluded, frequencies of inspections will be defined for each category of product. 34. In all counties visited, at the time of the audit, official sampling at farm level is only undertaken for lettuce (see paragraph 31 and 32). Samples of other products in the scope of the audit are taken at retail level (county plans) unless there is a suspicion in which case inspectors can sample individual producers as required. 35. Ireland adopted national provisions to further define obligations contained in EU legislation through, inter alia, Statutory Instrument No. 112/2004, which empowers DAFM to enforce organic legislation, and Statutory Instrument No. 30/2009, which extends the validity of national requirements implemented before Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The audit team reviewed the implementing requirements and noted that they were in line with EU Regulations. Some of the requirements were noted to be stricter than those of the EU (e.g. triple withdrawal period instead of double for animals treated with antibiotics in some cases).

At the opening meeting, DAFM presented a draft version of a consolidated Statutory Instrument, detailing each type of infringement for all relevant organic legal requirements. It also set out a specific penalty regime for each infringement. DAFM stated that this was due to be signed into law by the Minister in a matter of weeks. 2 Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation and Provisions

According to the information provided by DAFM, all measures of national law necessary to implement legally binding EU acts relevant to this audit have been adopted in Ireland. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Articles 27(1), 27(4), 27(4)(a) and 27(14) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The country profile for Ireland is published on the DG Health and Food Safety website. It contains a description of the organisation of controls for organic production. The country profile for Ireland can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=IE

The CA designated for ensuring compliance with the requirements of EU Regulations is the Organic Unit of DAFM. The Organic Unit comprises staff of the two DAFM Divisions: The Agricultural Structures Division is charged with administering the sector at central level; Designated staff of Agricultural Environment and Structures Division provide technical support and co-ordinate organic controls; The regional inspectorates in the Agricultural Environment and Structures Division are responsible for the supervision of performance of CBs at operator level. Technical staff carry out controls of local markets; The Horticulture and Plant Health Division carries out inspections at retail level.

The main tasks and responsibilities of the Organic Unit are, inter alia: drafting proposals for legislation in order to further develop requirements in EU Regulations; approval, supervision and withdrawal of CBs; granting derogations for operators to apply exceptional production rules and other derogations; import controls of organic consignments arriving into Ireland from non-EU countries; 3 payments to operators eligible for receiving subsidies in the framework of the Organic Farming Scheme; application of administrative sanctions and monetary fines to operators;

There are six administrative staff in the Organic Unit assisted by two inspectors and one technical officer charged with, inter alia, organic controls of organic production. In addition, there are 30 technical officers who undertake controls at local markets and retailers. All DAFM staff met by the audit team were experienced in the area of organic production and were found to be knowledgeable for the tasks assigned. DAFM staff attend regular training on organic production and meetings, including the Committee on Organic Production held in Brussels. However, DAFM informed the audit team, that due to the limited resources, no dedicated staff member is allocated to supervisory activities in the area of processing.

The Irish Customs Service collaborates with DAFM in the controls of organic products imported from non-EU countries. At the time of the present audit, a new Memorandum of Understanding was being drafted to enhance the collaboration between DAFM and the Customs Service regarding import controls of organic products.

INAB, under the umbrella of the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment, is responsible for the accreditation and annual surveillance of CBs based in Ireland according to the International Standards Organisation (ISO) for guide ISO/IEC 17065:2012. INAB is also in charge of the accreditation of laboratories based in Ireland to ISO/IEC 17025:2005. DAFM and INAB signed an agreement in 2014 in order to enhance collaboration and the sharing of information on the results of supervisory activities of CBs carried out by both CAs.

The audit team reviewed a number of files (applications for derogations, supervision of CBs by DAFM, follow-up of notifications of irregularities by other Member States (MSs), communication of updates on the legislation to officials in charge of import controls, etc.) which showed good co-operation and communication between DAFM and INAB and also between DAFM and the CBs. DAFM meets regularly with CBs in a co-ordination committee in which control issues are discussed. An agreement is also in place and regular meetings are held with the Food Safety Authority, who is in charge of inspections of all operators in the framework of food safety controls. When non- compliant organic products are detected during food safety controls, this is notified to DAFM.

DAFM is responsible for granting payments to farmers in the framework of the Organic Farming Scheme, co-funded by the EU Commission and Ireland within the Rural Development programme. Subsidies are granted for land parcels, provided that operators manage the land and the livestock according to the requirements of the organic Regulations. DAFM receives information on the results of controls on the parcels which apply for subsidies directly from the CBs. In addition, DAFM carries out inspections to 5% of operators eligible for subsidies. When severe non-compliances are found, 4 amounts received in previous years must be repaid either partially or in full, depending on the severity and recurrence of the non-compliance. Evidence of these measures having been taken was shown to the audit team. Conclusions on Competent Authorities, Control Authorities and Control Bodies

A system of controls is in place in accordance with Article 27(4) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. CAs responsible for controls in organic production are designated with a clear distribution of tasks and responsibilities among the CAs and the delegated CBs. There is good communication and co-operation between the different CAs, and regular meetings are held between DAFM and the CBs. However, due to limited staff resources, the CA does not adequately supervise CBs controls in the area of processing which reduces the effectiveness of the system in place (see also conclusion no 23). 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Articles 5(2) and (3) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(c) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

At the time of the DG Health and Food Safety audit, there were five CBs approved for control and certification of organic products. Three of the CBs had headquarters in Ireland while the other two were based in other EU countries. Three CBs (hereinafter referred to as CB1, CB2 and CB3) were visited during the audit. The audit team carried out office audits at the headquarters of CB1 and CB2 and observed inspections carried out on operators under control of all three CBs.

DAFM is responsible for the approval of CBs. Accreditation by INAB or by an internationally recognised Accreditation Body is a prerequisite to obtaining and maintaining approval. At the time of the audit, all CBs were accredited to ISO/IEC 17065:2012. The documented procedure used by DAFM contains a checklist covering all requirements that CBs need to fulfil to be approved. Regarding reporting obligations by CBs, the audit team was shown examples of the information submitted monthly by CBs to DAFM. CBs notify DAFM of new operators under contract and the certificates issued and withdrawn during the previous four weeks. DAFM also stated that CBs comply with their obligation to submit an annual report before 31 March of each year.

For the delegation of controls, an agreement is signed between DAFM and the CBs. The agreement describes the specific tasks delegated to CBs as well as the conditions under which the tasks shall be implemented by CBs. Approval shall be withdrawn if CBs cease to fulfil their obligations, in line with Article 27(9) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 5 Temporary suspension of the approval for all activities is also foreseen where failure in the performance of the CB arises. The audit team was informed by the CA that one CB was suspended for three months in 2010. During this period, the CB was not allowed to take new clients, to carry out inspections or to issue any certificate.

DAFM is responsible for supervising the execution of delegated controls carried out by CBs. Supervision is carried out annually on the three CBs with headquarters based in Ireland taking into account the reports issued by INAB, in line with Articles 92c(1) and 92(e) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, when supervising the CBs with headquarters not based in Ireland, the reports issued by the Accreditation Bodies of the CBs not based in Ireland are not equally taken into account. Evidence of the exchange of information between DAFM and one Accreditation Body outside Ireland was presented, but it was noted by the audit team that the information shared was very limited.

Furthermore, as these CBs do not have a branch office in Ireland, the office audits are carried out at the home of the CBs´ inspectors, where all information necessary for supervision might not be available. Moreover, DAFM does not notify the result of the supervision to the CB headquarters, but only to the inspector. Therefore it cannot be ensured that the management of the CB is aware of any non-compliance and that effective corrective measures are taken as necessary.

Since 2014, DAFM carries out office audits at CBs on an annual basis. CBs follow documented procedures which describe the requirements to be checked and the methodology to be applied for documentary checks. However, DAFM failed to note some shortcomings identified by the audit team during the office audit carried out to CB1 and CB2 (e.g. inadequate selection of operators for additional visits, inconsistent and inadequate enforcement measures applied by CBs, no immediate notification of severe irregularities to DAFM, etc.). In addition, when shortcomings are detected by DAFM, these are not explicitly presented as non-compliance to the CBs and, therefore, no formal corrective action is systematically required. This is not in line with Articles 92c(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

In addition to office audits, DAFM carries out witness audits to observe the performance of the CBs´ inspectors. According to the information provided to the audit team, eight witness audits were carried out in 2015 at farm level. No witness audits were carried out to observe the performance of controls at processors. The inspections at processors by CBs observed by the audit team were overall superficial and not all relevant requirements were checked by inspectors (see finding 54). The failures in the performance of CBs were not identified by DAFM inspections described in paragraph

This lack of adequate supervision at processor level is not in line with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 20. In addition to the 5% of operators directly inspected by DAFM in the framework of the Organic Farming Scheme subsidies, DAFM also carries out direct inspections to 1-2% of registered operators, who are selected based on risk analysis. The outcome of these 6 inspections is compared with the outcome of the inspection previously carried out by CBs.

The audit team reviewed a number of reports issued by DAFM following witness audits and re-inspections. Several shortcomings were identified and the overall performance of inspectors was evaluated. The shortcomings were notified to the CBs concerned with a delay of several months. This delay in the communication of the results of supervision undermines its effectiveness, as it does not ensure that corrective action is taken by CBs in a reasonable time.

Moreover, corrective measures proposed consisted only in re-inspecting the operator where the supervision had taken place. No corrective measures were proposed by DAFM to or required from CBs to avoid the repetition of the shortcomings related to the performance of the inspectors. Some of the shortcomings described in the reports issued by DAFM were repeated during the inspections observed by the audit team (e.g. no identification of individual animals present on the fields, no measurements of stables in every inspection). The lack of corrective action to address the root cause of the problem detected does not fully ensure the effectiveness of the controls carried out by CBs. This is not in line with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of Control Bodies

There is a system of approval, annual supervision and withdrawal of CBs in place in Ireland, which includes the withdrawal of the CB's approval by the CA in case a CB fails to fulfil its obligations. Regular coordination and communication between CAs and CBs is established aiming at harmonising organic controls. The effectiveness of the CA's supervision of CBs is however reduced because the CA does not effectively supervise CBs' controls in the area of processing (due to staff shortage). The system is further weakened by the fact that the CA does not take all relevant information into account when supervising CBs located outside Ireland and that several systematic shortcomings in the performance of CBs related to the planning of controls and the enforcement of organic rules were overlooked by the CA during supervision of CBs. Inappropriate communication of such shortcomings by the CA to the CBs hampers timely implementation of appropriate corrective actions. 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 92(2) and 92(b) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings 7 24. According to DAFM, Ireland requires the registration of operators as indicated in Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Any operator who produces, prepares, stores, places organic products on the market or import/export from/to non-EU countries shall submit his undertaking to the control system. Subcontracted operators are also subject to the control system. The audit team reviewed the agreements for the delegation of tasks signed between DAFM and the CBs and noted that the requirement regarding operators who place products on the market was not explicitly included. The audit team noted that wholesalers dealing only with pre-packed and labelled feed were not subject to the control system. In addition, CBs did not adequately verify the activities carried out by traders dealing with pre-packed and labelled food, who were found by the audit team to trade products not included in the scope of their registration certification (see finding 64). This is not in line with the abovementioned Article 28(1). 25. Retailers fulfilling the conditions of Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are exempted from the control system. This means that retailers selling pre-packaged and labelled products directly to the consumer are exempted, provided that they do not produce, prepare or store other than in connection with the point of sale, or that they do not import such products or have not subcontracted any such activities. 26. DAFM is empowered to carry out inspections at market level to check compliance of organic products with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. DAFM stated that local markets are visited at least once a year. When organic products are found at unregistered operators, DAFM requires the operator to either submit his/her undertaking to the control system or to stop using the reference to organic production. The audit team was shown some examples of these actions having been taken recently. In 2016, DAFM has started inspecting also supermarkets and distribution centres. This is, in addition to the inspections carried out by CBs. 27. Since 2012, the Horticulture and Plant Health Division is responsible for inspections at retailers (which were previously inspected by technical staff of the Agricultural Environment and Structure Division). The fulfilment of conditions for the exemption of retailers from official controls is usually checked during these inspections. However, the audit team noted that the scope of these inspections focus on plant production only, and do not cover products of animal origin, providing information to the CA which is insufficient to satisfactorily assess whether retailers exempted under Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 (continue to) fulfil conditions for exemption. 28. Operators who propose to submit their undertakings to the control system apply directly to the CBs. The first planned inspection is usually carried out within two to three weeks of application. According to Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, CBs have to verify the declaration submitted by operators, including a full description of the units and the precautionary measures applied to reduce the risk of contamination with unauthorised products or substances, as required by Article 63(1) of the same Regulation. 8 29. After passing a successful inspection, operators are registered in the system and the relevant information is notified to DAFM. In the case of plant producers, the date of the application form is the reference starting date of the conversion period before the land can be considered to be in organic production. The information on new and suspended operators and the products certified and decertified is notified monthly to DAFM. This information is recorded in the register by DAFM who update the list of operators, which is kept publicly available on DAFM website. The list of operators can be found at: http://www.agriculture.gov.ie/media/migration/farmingsectors/organicfarming/Organic Operators251116.pdf 30. However, the list does not contain updated documentary evidence issued by CBs using the model set up in Annex XII to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, including at least the range or types of products certified. In addition, although the DAFM register is updated to reflect changes in the organic status of operators, the changes are not necessarily fed into the list kept on the website. This lack of complete information is not in line with Article 92(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 31. When operators change CB, they are obliged to notify their CB. The relevant elements of the operator's file and reports referred to in finding 28 must be transferred from the previous CB to the subsequent CB. In addition, the subsequent CB must carry out the first inspection 3 weeks after the transfer of the operator´s file. The new CB must send a notification to the CA immediately after receiving the application from new operators. The audit team checked several files managed by CB1 and noted that all requirements had been met. Conclusions On Registration of Operators 32. There is a system in plac
There are three pieces of national legislation relevant to the official control systems for PGI/ PDO/TSG.

Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 of the European Parliament and the Council on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs is mainly implemented through Section II 'Quality Policy' of the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation of Agricultural Products of the European Union (SG No 96/28 November 2006 in force since 01 January 2007 as amended 16 March 2016). This legislation sets out the procedures for authorisation of control bodies (CBs) to perform controls on compliance with the PDO/PGI/TSG Product Specifications and also describes the obligations of the CBs to the CAs.

The Ordinance No 16 of 2007 addresses the legal requirements for the preparation and submission of PDO/PGI/TSG applications to the European Commission. In addition, it describes the procedures for supervising the CBs, data entry and maintenance of databases relating to producers of PDO/PGI/TSG and CBs involved in their official control.

Ordinance No 6 of 2011 defines the main responsibilities of the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency (BFSA) and the specific requirements relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG as well as the measures to be taken when irregularities are found. Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation

Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. 3 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities1 Legal requirements Articles 36(1), 36(2), 37(1) and (3) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular Articles 4 and 6. Findings

The Ministry of Agriculture and Food (MAF) is responsible for implementing food quality policy and ensuring compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The MAF, together with the Directorate "Direct Payments and Quality Schemes" (DPQS) and the unit "Quality Schemes and Promotions" make up the national CA for PDO/PGI/TSG.
The official controls on the use of registered names in the marketplace is carried out by the BFSA and are undertaken as part of food safety inspections. Conclusions on Competent Authorities

CAs are designated for the verification of compliance of product specification prior to placing PDO/PGI/TSG on the market and the monitoring and use of registered names in line with Article 36 (EC) No 1151/2012. 5.2.2 Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 37(1), 39(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 5(2) (e) and (f) and 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

The verification of the conformity of a product with the corresponding Product Specification is carried out by CBs, accredited by an accreditation body as meeting the requirements of Standard EN ISO 17065:2012. Each CB is authorised by the MAF to undertake such control.

The supervision by the DPQS over the activity of the CBs includes examination of copies of checklists for each of the performed inspections and of the annual summary 1 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that due to restructuring at the Ministry of Agriculture and Food (in force from 9th of August 2016), the Unit "Quality schemes and promotions" has been moved from Directorate "Direct payments and quality schemes" (DPQS) to Directorate "Market measures and producers' organizations" (MMPO). 4 reports. Also, on-the-spot checks at producers' sites can be carried out by the CA in case of a serious non-compliance, found by the CBs. Coordinated actions between DPQS and the BFSA are taken to apply enforcement measures when necessary.

The procedure for authorising CBs to exercise the control on the compliance with the Product Specification is included in the national legislation: Section II of the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation and Chapter VI of Ordinance 16/2007. According to this law the CBs, when applying for permission from the Minister of Agriculture and Food to be approved, are required to present, amongst other documents, a notarised copy of the certificate of accreditation issued by the relevant accreditation body from the MS which verifies the CB's compliance with the requirements of Standard EN ISO/IEC 17065:2012.

There is a Standing Joint Consultative Commission on PDO/PGI/TSG at MAF, which together with DPQS, examines the application of the CB for approval and suggests to the Minister to grant approval or to issue a justified refusal. At the time of the audit, there are two CBs approved by the MAF, complying with the requirements to exercise control in the Republic of Bulgaria. These two CBs have been accredited by the Italian accreditation body. Conclusions on Control Bodies

The CA ensures that the CBs fulfil all requirements for approval, including accreditation to ISO 17065. The delegation of official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG to CBs is adequately supervised by the CAs as required by Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings Official controls of processors / producers of PDO/PGI/TSG

In compliance with the national legislation, the CBs carry out a comprehensive initial inspection of the producer to check the producer's readiness to comply with the PDO/PGI/TSG Product Specification.

In line with national Bulgarian law, the CB performs a mandatory annual inspection of all producers of PDO/PGI/TSG which is announced. The CB may carry out additional planned or unannounced inspections when non-compliances are found during the annual inspection. The CB sends the completed checklist after each inspection to the DPQS. Samples for analysis are usually taken and the results are sent to DPQS for information. 5 16. The CB may, in accordance with the relevant control plan of the product in question, not only perform an additional on-the-spot check, but also take samples for testing with a higher frequency. 17. The CB draws up an annual report of its overall control activity and submits the report to DPQS at MAF not later than 31 January of the following year. The annual report includes summarised information of the inspections, their results, prescribed measures, as well as summarised information on the produced quantities and export volumes of the products. Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market. 18. BFSA implements the official control over the use of names and symbols of registered PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs at the production and food trade establishments, following the requirements of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs, the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation and Ordinance No 6 of 2011 on the specific requirements of the official control on the use of PDO/PGI/TSG. 19. The control methods and techniques are set out in detail in the Procedure for official control of PDO/PGI/TSG at retail and wholesale level, which was approved by Order No 11-136/04.02.2014 of the executive director of BFSA. BFSA inspects the use of names, symbols and indications of PDO/PGI/TSG. In cases of doubt regarding the proper use of PDO/PGI/TSG, checks are made in the DOOR database. In the event of non compliances being found relating to non Bulgarian PDO/PGI/TSG, the BFSA notifies MAF who is responsible for overseeing the follow up. 20. The inspections at retail level on PDO/PGI/TSG are part of the official control on food safety and hygiene carried out by BFSA two times a year. In addition, thematic inspections may also be carried out, as well as ad hoc inspections to follow up complaints. 21. The official control inspections on PDO/PGI/TSG are scheduled in the Regional control plans of Food control departments at the Regional Food Safety Directorates and are carried out according to a procedure, approved by the Executive Director of BFSA. 22. BFSA submits an annual report by the end of March to MAF / DPQS on the performed inspections, detected irregularities and measures taken in respect of official controls on the use of protected denominations. DPSQ includes the information into the annual report of the Multiannual National Control Plan (MANCP). Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 23. There are clear procedures on the frequency of official controls to be undertaken for verification of compliance with the Product Specification and official controls on the 6 market, which are complied with. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 Findings Official controls of producers / processors of PDO/PGI/TSG 24. The CB has procedures in place, including a control plan for all products and checklists for specific products. The audit visited two TSG producers and three PGI producers and noted that for two out of the three products reviewed, the registration occurred in 2014. In addition, the particular operators visited, producing a product with a PGI, had changed the CB just before the audit took place. The new CB had received the documentation relating to the inspections undertaken by the previous CB from the CA. 25. In general, the CB inspectors met were competent and undertook annual inspections of producers of PGI/TSG as required. However, the CB inspectors had limited experience in identifying where the risks are highest in relation to particular products. 26. Each inspection commenced with a documentary check and only if this was in order, the inspector proceeded with sampling. During the observed control, the inspector noted a discrepancy in the amount of product at the last step of the process and brought this to the attention of the food business operator (FBO). The CB approves labelling prior to certification and in the event of a change of labelling. In addition, during labelling stocks were also checked by the inspector. 27. Organoleptic testing was undertaken by staff of the FBO for each batch and the results were recorded. The CB inspector also undertook organoleptic testing on the batch sampled during his inspection. Samples were sent to an accredited laboratory in Bulgaria for analysis of the parameters described in the Product Specification. In 2015, no non compliances were identified. 28. The audit team noted that there were specific elements of Product Specifications which were not routinely checked which is not in line with Article 36(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) No 1152/2012. 7 Official controls on the Market 29. The CA stated that non-Bulgarian PDO/PGI/TSG were only recently included in the official controls on the market. 30. A market control was observed by the audit team and it was noted that the two inspectors used two product lists: one, relating to Bulgarian produced PGI/TSG and the other listing EU MSs PDO/PGI/TSG which are distributed in Bulgaria. The labelling and packing requirements of the most commonly purchased PDO/PGI/TSG were also included in this list. This list was prepared by the BFSA headquarters. The inspectors had previously visited the same establishment in February and May 2016 and inspection reports were available. 31. Although no non-compliances were detected during any of these inspections, there was no specific documentary evidence about which details, apart from the name of the product, were checked. No information about the particular features of the product (weight, batch number producer) was recorded. 32. During discussions with the CA the difficulty of identifying whether or not the relevant producer was entitled to use PDO/PGI/TSG was described. This was particularly problematic when controlling non-Bulgarian PDO/PGI/TSG. The inspectors demonstrated an example of where the labelling of a non Bulgarian TSG included the details of the CB responsible for the official control of the product. This information allowed the inspectors to link the product with the producer through the website of the CB. However, such information is rarely available on the label. 33. The inspectors were not in a position to take photographs of product labels for checking against the registered names in the DOOR database back at the office. In these situations, inspectors relied only on their own notes taken during the inspection. 34. The Commission audit team was informed that for controls on the market, two BFSA inspectors undertake controls in their specific region, which are unannounced. A report is written on completion of the inspection and a copy is given to the FBO and another is retained by the CA. However, no documentary evidence of such procedures were made available. The audit team was informed that in the event of non-compliances being detected, a time frame is agreed for the corrective actions to be implemented. In addition, a follow up inspection would be undertaken to confirm that the problem was resolved. 35. The Quality Manager of the supermarket chain provided the audit team with a list of PDO/PGI/TSG which are marketed at their outlets. This list was unknown to the BFSA inspectors. 36. Discussions with regional BFSA inspectors confirmed that a control plan for market controls is prepared by the BFSA headquarters. The regional offices are required to report twice a year on inspections undertaken. In the Plovdiv regional office inspection staff were expected to undertake 20-30 inspections in a six month period. 8 Conclusions on Procedures and Performances of Official Control Activities 37. Official controls undertaken at producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG to verify compliance with the Product Specifications, did not always include verification of every element of the Product Specification. 5.2.5 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 38. At the time of the audit, no financial sanctions had been imposed at producer / processor level. However, the CB had procedures in place which defined a variety of categories of non-compliances including `severe non compliances' and the relevant corrective measures, including time limits for such actions to be implemented. The CB had an example of a severe non-compliance which had been reported to the CA within one day. In this situation, the BFSA was informed and undertook an inspection of the FBO who had to rectify a particular processing problem, but no financial penalty was imposed. The audit team reviewed the file relating to this non-compliance and considered it to be adequate. 39. A file relating to a non-compliance on the market was reviewed. In this case a market trader was instructed by BFSA to stop slicing a specific PDO/PGI/TSG. The Product Specification stated that the product could only be sliced in the region where it was produced. Follow up visits were undertaken by the BFSA inspectors to check that the slicing activity had been stopped and no financial sanction was imposed. 40. As every inspection report by the CB has to be submitted to the Ministry within one week of the inspection, a record of any non-compliances found is maintained by the Ministry enabling any trends to be noted in a timely manner. 41. Art. 25, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation prohibits the use of names, symbols and/or indications of agricultural products and foodstuffs with a PGI, PDO or a TSG, when: the names, symbols and/or indications are used on products, whose names are not registered in the European registers of agricultural products and foodstuffs with PDO/PGI/TSG; the names of the products are registered as PDO/PGI/TSG, but the products or foodstuffs do not comply with the specification; the names of the products are registered as PDO/PGI/TSG, but the products are not under control. 9 42. When the BFSA inspectors investigate irregularities identified at retail level, they trace the product back to identify the FBO responsible for placing the product on the market and capable of correcting the non-compliances. According to Article 25a, paragraph 3 of the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation, when performing official control, the BFSA may impose administrative measures, in line with the provisions of the Food Law in Bulgaria. 43. According to the Food Law, the marketing of foodstuffs, which are non-compliant with Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, may be restricted or prohibited. When needed, BFSA inspectors may impose sanctions on FBOs who do not comply with the PDO/PGI/TSG products legislation. Fines may be imposed and are set out in Article 65 of the Law on Implementation of the Common Market Organisation. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures 44. An adequate system is in place for effective enforcement measures to be applied in cases of non-compliance related to PDO/PGI/TSG. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Overall, there is a system of official controls in place in the area of PDO/PGI/TSG. The official controls of producers and processors are delegated to accredited CBs, which are supervised by the CCA. The CB inspectors were generally competent however some elements of Product Specifications were not always routinely controlled. Examples of enforcement in case of non-compliances detected at market level were shown

EU legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the most recently amended version. Full references to the EU acts quoted in this report are given in Annex 1. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 COUNTRY PROFILE DG Health and Food Safety has published a Country Profile for Greece, which describes in summary the control systems for food and feed, animal health, animal welfare and plant health as well as quality labelling and gives an overview of the state of play concerning recommendations from previous audits. The country profile for Greece can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=GR 4.2 EU QUALITY SCHEMES The EU quality schemes for PDO/PGI/TSG protect and promote quality agricultural products and foodstuffs and aim to ensure the protection of their names from, inter alia, misuse, evocation and imitation and help consumers by giving them information concerning the specific character of the products: PDO covers agricultural products and foodstuffs which are produced, processed and prepared in a given geographical area using recognised know-how. PGI covers agricultural products and foodstuffs closely linked to the geographical area. At least one of the stages of production, processing or preparation takes place in the area. 2 TSG highlights traditional character, either in the raw materials, composition or means of production. Further details on the quality schemes are available on the following website: http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/quality/schemes/index_en.htm 4.3 STATUS OF REGISTERED PRODUCTS IN GREECE At the time of the audit there were 29 PGI and 75 PDO from Greece registered on the Database of Origin and Registration (DOOR). In conjunction with DG AGRI, two registered geographical indications (names) were selected to form part of this audit as a sample, in order to evaluate how the system of official controls works in Greece. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Findings 1. text: Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 36(1), 36(2), 37(1) and (3) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular Articles 4 and 6. Findings

According to JMD No 261611/07.03.2007 as amended, the CAs in the context of this audit are as follows: 3 4. The CCA is the Directorate of Quality Systems, Organic Production and Geographical Indications of MRDF and is competent to monitor the implementation of EU legislation on PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs. 5. The ELGO-DIMITRA is responsible for carrying out official controls to verify compliance with the legal requirements related to PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs. This is an organisation operating under private law for public benefit under the supervision of the MRDF. 6. ELGO-DIMITRA is tasked with the certification of enterprises, undertaking official controls with the DREVs, ensuring conformity with Product Specifications and appropriate use of the registered names in the market place. In addition, it is responsible for establishing and maintaining a public register of certified enterprises and referring non-compliances to the Committee for the Examination of Infringements (CEIMRDF). 7. Further information on the authorities involved in official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs is available on: http://www.minagric.gr/index.php/en/farmer-menu-2/pdo-pgi-tsgproducts-menu Conclusions on Competent Authorities 8. The authorities are designated for the verification of compliance of product specification prior to placing PDO/PGI/TSGs on the market and the monitoring and use of registered names in line with Article 36 (EU) No 1151/2012. 5.2.2 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings Verification of compliance with product specification prior to placing a product on the market 9. At the level of primary producers, no targeted on-site inspections are undertaken by the CtrlA/relevant CAs apart from random, on the spot, inspections, in the area of PDO/PGI products of plant origin. 10. In order to initiate the verification prior to placing a product on the market, the operators submit an application to ELGO-DIMITRA, in order to be included in the ELGO- DIMITRA public Register of Approved Operators for PDO/PGI agricultural products and foodstuffs. 4 11. Once the application and all supporting documents are assessed and approved by ELGO-DIMITRA an official control at the operator's premises is scheduled and includes the verification of the conformity of a product with the corresponding Product Specification. If non-compliances are detected the operator is obliged to implement corrective actions in a specified time period to ensure registration. Assuming all is in order, the operator will be included in the ELGO-DIMITRA Register of Approved Operators. The details relating to making such an application and the register can be found on www.elgo.gr 12. ELGO­DIMITRA, in cooperation with the DREVs, carries out on site visits of producers for verification prior to placing the product on the market as well as for surveillance controls. These controls consist of checking production process, traceability and labelling in order to ensure product specification. 13. Operators are obliged to submit production information to ELGO-DIMITRA which enables the CA to have an overview of the sector. In addition, the information relating to primary production is available at the DREVs and this administrative information is useful to verify that primary producers are located within the demarcated areas. 14. To enable a more structured and systematic approach to the planning of official controls, ELGO-DIMITRA informed the audit team that since June 2016 an electronic risk assessment tool had been developed for PDO/PGI food of animal origin. It is anticipated that it would be extended to all other PDO/PGI by the end of 2017. Official controls on the market 15. ELGO-DIMITRA carries out market controls on a regular basis for all Greek PDO/PGI products. In addition, targeted market controls are carried out, following complaints received either from other Member States or non-EU countries or the CCA. Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 16. At the time of the audit, the planning of official controls was not fully based on a risk assessment of all PDO/PGI agricultural products and foodstuffs, although efforts have commenced to improve this situation. 5.2.3 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. 5 Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 Findings Official controls of producers / processors of PDO/PGI agricultural products and foodstuffs 17. The audit team observed official controls of two PDO products of non- animal origin. The inspections were undertaken by one ELGO-DIMITRA inspector and one DREV inspector in each case. A comprehensive preparation had been undertaken at the office prior to the onsite visits. The inspectors in both cases were knowledgeable and had been provided with detailed checklists. A template for the inspection report was also available. The inspectors also checked labelling, traceability and input output quantities. The audit team reviewed the inspection reports from previous inspections and noted that they were satisfactory. The inspectors had noted a number of non-compliances and these were handled in accordance with the written procedures from ELGO-DIMITRA. At the end of the inspection a report was prepared for the operator. Official controls on the Market 18. This official control of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs was undertaken by ELGO-DIMITRA. The inspectors undertake official controls in a wide variety of retail and wholesale establishments throughout the country. The control of PDO/PGI/TSG is included in their tasks. The main focus of the observed controls was related to national PDO/PGI products and products from other MSs and non-EU countries were not considered which is not in line with Article 36(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The inspector stated that the national legislation (Horizontal legislation on Certification of Rules for Marketing and Distribution of product and provisions of services, 31 July 2014) does not require the Union symbols to be visible on the stickers or showcase signs of bulk or unwrapped PDO/PGI/TSG products when displayed. This is not in line with Article 12(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. 19. The inspector reviewed a number of PDO/PGI products and prepared a report for the operator. Conclusions on Procedures and Performances of Official Control Activities 20. There are adequate procedures in place and on-site visits were adequately performed. However, according to national legislation it is not compulsory for the Union symbols to be displayed on the stickers printed by the weighing device for bulk/unwrapped products or on the showcase sign at retail level. This is not in line with EU requirements. In addition, market controls did not include PDO/PGI/TSGs from other MSs and non-EU countries except in the case of complaints. 6 5.2.4 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 21. In relation to agricultural products and foodstuffs the enforcement measures in place under the JMD 261611/2007 are the following: Withdrawal of Certification (Permanent or Temporary) Refusal to grant certification Withdrawal from the market, in cooperation with other Authorities Fines imposed by the Committee for the examination of infringements of MRDF. 22. These enforcement measures may be imposed following infringements found during controls or as a result of complaints reported to the relevant CCA. The audit team reviewed files, which followed up complaints and although they did not result in fines, the operator was required to withdraw and re-label the product. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures 23. Relevant legislation is in place for enforcement measures and implemented. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Overall, there is a system of official controls in place for PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs. Authorities involved in controls are clearly designated and relevant legislation is in place. Inspectors are provided with written guidelines and inspections observed were adequate and well-documented. However, the effectiveness of the control system in place is reduced as a more systematic risk-based approach to the planning of controls has only recently commenced. Moreover, market controls focus mainly on national products. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 25 November 2016 with the attendance of representatives of the different CAs. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main preliminary findings of the audit and a number of points were clarified. The CAs provisionally accepted the preliminary findings. 7 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The CAs are invited to provide details of the action taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (action plan), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. The CAs should: 1. Continue to develop the risk based approach for the planning of official controls to include all PDO/PGI/TSGs, as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 882/2004. Recommendation is based on conclusions No 16. Associated findings: No 14. 2. Ensure that the Union symbols are displayed in the same field of vision on the stickers printed by the weighing device for bulk/unwrapped products or on the showcase sign at retail level, in line with Article 12(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. District office Slaughterhouse 1 Cattle dealer 1 Sheep farmer 1 Assembly centre 1 Cattle farm 1 Pig point of sale 1 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules. 4 BACKGROUND The basic objectives for Union rules on identification of animals are the localisation and tracing of animals for veterinary purposes, which is of crucial importance for the control of infectious diseases. In the field of animal health, the systems for animal identification and registration serve as basic tools for disease surveillance, control and eradication. Additionally, they support certification for intra-Union trade or export and import of live animals. These systems are used in the public health sector for issues related to food hygiene, zoonoses and residues. 2 A new Animal Health Law (adopted at European Union (EU) level) will, together with consequential delegating and implementing acts, provide an opportunity to review the legal requirements for the animal identification and registration systems. In order to contribute to the future review of the rules on animal identification and registration, the Commission services has initiated a project on animal identification and registration. This project will critically evaluate the suitability of current EU requirements and the added value of current certification arrangements for intra-Union trade. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS The effective functioning of identification and registration systems depends on three main factors: the quality of data in the system, the capability of the system to provide users with relevant information from that pool of data and the Competent Authority's ability to monitor, review and improve the system. Therefore, the findings and conclusions of this audit have been organised under these three main headings. 5.1 QUALITY OF DATA Legal requirements Legislation sets: the maximum time limits for notifications of (various events for) both bovines and small ruminants. the minimum data requirements for all species, and requirements for the Competent Authority to carry out a minimum level of official controls on bovine and small ruminant holdings (farms, slaughterhouses, markets, assembly centres, etc.) to verify compliance with identification and registration requirements. These controls include, amongst other things, a reality check on the data entered into the database. For porcine species, there is no such requirement at EU level. Findings 1. The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development is the Central Competent Authority for animal identification and registration with responsibility for policy, legislation and general overview of controls. For routine controls related to animal identification and registration the District Veterinary Officer (DVO) is the Competent Authority. ARMA is delegated under Polish law to maintain, inter alia, the database of animals (bovine, ovine, caprine and porcine) and holdings and issuing passports. Full details are available in the country profile at : http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=PL An agreement, dated 15 April 2013, outlines the tasks and principles of cooperation between the VI and ARMA in relation to the identification and registration of farm animals in order to ensure the correct functioning of the system. 3 2. An extensive list of plausibility checks has been implemented to detect and prevent implausible data being recorded. The list was last reviewed in May 2015. 3. ARMA must be notified of both on and off movements for bovines, sheep, goats and pigs. Approximately 98% of compulsory event notifications, e.g. births and movements relating to bovines, ovines, caprines and pigs are made manually by producers. Nationally, a selection of standardised forms is available to make these notifications. Different forms were available for different events, e.g. every bovine birth required a separate form whereas movement of up to three bovines could be reported on a single form. In one district visited by audit team, a local template had been developed to notify ARMA of movements of multiple animals1. 4. Animal keepers including farmers, assembly centres, abattoirs and rendering plants can electronically notify events to the database via a platform (CKIRZ). This does not allow direct entry of data into the database and the information must subsequently be entered by ARMA staff. ARMA advised that <5% of stakeholders currently use this service. 5. Data can also be provided from animal keepers in the form of CD-ROMs or USB memory sticks. In one abattoir visited, the operator provided movement data for pigs to their district ARMA office on a fortnightly basis via a CD-ROM. The notification of movements of cattle to slaughterhouses within seven days (between 2013 ­ 2015) has increased from 72.9% to 89.1%. 6. All event notifications are checked at District ARMA offices prior to manual data entry. If discrepancies exist, ARMA advised that clarification is sought from producers. In the absence of a response, regional ARMA staff make the decision whether or not to perform an on-site control. Any financial penalties subsequent to such on-site controls by ARMA require an additional on-site visit by DVO as only they can impose financial sanctions. 7. For bovines, data provided by ARMA demonstrates improving compliance with producer notifications to the database. For example, between 2013 ­ 2015, notifications of birth within seven days have increased from 79.7% to 96.0%. Similarly, notifications of on- movements within seven days of the move taking place, has increased from 76.3% to 95.4%. 8. For movements of porcine, ovine, caprine and bovine animals, there is a requirement for two notifications to ARMA (one each from the consigning and receiving keeper). On a monthly basis, ARMA review coherence of data supplied to monitor, e.g. that on and off notifications for a particular animal(s) match and all required animal details have been provided. Lists of non-coherent data are generated and sent to relevant district ARMA offices for follow-up. Data provided by ARMA, demonstrated at 31/12/15, 4.82% of bovine notifications and 20.3% of porcine notifications were non-coherent. 1 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that specimen forms relating to animal events are posted on ARMA's internet page under the address: http://www.arimr.gov.pl/identyfikacja-i- rejestracjazwierzat/formularze-dotyczace-identyfikacji-i-rejestracji-zwierzat-gospodarskich.html. 4 Additionally, at 31/12/15, the location of 4.59% bovines, 4.67% ovines and 7.67% of caprines was unknown. 9. The number of bovine movements where the destination holding has not notified the arrival of bovines within 21 days has shown a slight increase over the past three years as indicated in table below. These animals are a subset of the non-coherent data in paragraph 8 above. The DVO were increasingly applying financial penalties to improve compliance with animal identification requirements. Figures provided by ARMA showed an approximate thirteen-fold increase in financial penalties between 2012 ­ 2014 for animal identification related issues. Holding numbers are allocated to farm buildings plus associated land. The land does not need to be contiguous and movement of animals between non-contiguous parcels of land within the holding does not require to be notified, irrespective of distances involved. Producers can have more than one holding number when there is more than one physical location where animals are kept - movement between these holdings must be notified. Additionally, holding numbers are allocated and registered to dealers with no premises or land where animals could be kept2. 11. The holding number takes the format: PL followed by a nine digit producer number suffixed by -001 / -002, etc. depending on the number of holdings registered by the producer. The same holding number is used for all bovines, small ruminants or pigs kept on a holding. 12. The database does not contain the geographic co-ordinates or equivalent geographic indication of the holding as required by Section D(1)(b) of the Annex to Regulation 21/2004 ( sheep and goats) and Article 1(d) of Decision 2000/678/EEC (pigs). 13. Since 2007, any request for the registration of a new holding must be accompanied by the land registry plot numbers associated with the holding. For 30% of holdings, the ARMA database contains a reference which can be used to identify the land associated with the holding. This information is held by the land registry and to access this information, GVI must contact ARMA who in turn contact the land registry i.e. there is no interoperability between the ARMA and land registry databases.

All holdings/herds with cattle, pigs, sheep, and goats in Denmark are recorded in the Central Husbandry Register (CHR). The CHR stores information required by national and EU legislation, e.g. a unique holding code, the address and the geographic coordinates of the holding, data on the owner and keeper of the herds present (name, address and contact numbers), animal species, number of animals of all species, allocation of ear tags and veterinary information.

Most events related to a change of holding/herd registration data must be notified to the CHR within seven days. Closing down of herds must be notified to the CHR within six months, closing down of slaughterhouses within seven days, common pastures within nine months and fairs within 14 months.

For bovines, all events (on and off herd movements, birth, death and slaughter) must be notified to the CHR within seven days as required by the EU legislation. No notification is required if the animal is moved within a "merged herd" (for more see point 40). 4 Furthermore, a derogation exists for animals moved to pastures (for more see points 42 and 43).

Average notification time (below seven days) has slightly improved during past five years for all types of notifications in cattle (figure 1). Figure 1: Average time for different types of notifications in cattle

For bovines, there is a timely update of the CHR with events (percentage provided for 2015 are shown in figure 2). Figures are lower for notifications of off-movements (85% made within seven days) but show improving trends (from 83% in 2010). The highest percentage of notifications made within first seven days is noted for notifications of slaughter (97% in 2015), mainly due to an electronic notification system and well- designed user interface, and interoperability of the CHR and internal systems in the slaughterhouses (for more see point 71). 5 Figure 2: Percentage of different type of notifications in cattle made within 7, 14, 21 and more than 21 days in 2015.

Since 2002, on-movements of pigs into holdings are notified and recorded into the CHR. Assembly centres notify both on- and off-movements of pigs. In instances of live pig consignments for EU trade directly dispatched from the holding, off-movements are notified.
For sheep, keepers must notify both on and off movements to the CHR, except movements between herds of the same owner, where only one notification is required.
All movements of pigs, sheep and goats must be notified to the CHR within seven days.

For sheep, pigs and goats, the timeliness of event notifications has improved, although it is not as good as for cattle: In 2015, 66 % of sheep movements were notified within seven days - an increase of 28% from 2010. However, the percentage of notifications exceeding 21 days remains still relatively high ­ up to 20 % (percentage of notifications is shown figure 3). Average notification time has shortened during past five years for movements in sheep from 36 days in 2010 to 13 days in 2015. 6 Figure 3: Percentage of movement notifications in sheep made within 7, 14, 21 and more than 21 days in 2010-2015. In 2015 notifications of pig movements within seven days account for 85% - an increase by 11% from 2010 (figure 4). Average notification time has shortened during past five years from 11 days in 2010 to 8 days in 2015. Figure 4: Percentage of movement notifications in pigs made within 7, 14, 21 and more than 21 days in 2010-2015.

In the cattle sector there is a large segment with large scale production driven by commercial farmers. Among the non-commercial farmers, the smaller segment of holdings with typically 10-20 beef cattle exists. The analysis of late notifications in cattle in 2015 (figures 5, 6 and 7) shows their higher proportion in a segment of smaller herds up to 50 heads. This segment accounts for 20 % of all notifications. There are no significant differences in a geographical distribution of late notifications or in their herd- type distribution. 7 Figure 5: Late notifications in cattle in 2015 broken down by herd size. Figure 6: Late notifications in cattle in 2015 broken down by regions. Figure 7: Late notifications in cattle in 2015 broken down by herd type. *Notifications made more than 14 days after event

In order to address the late notifications, in particular from holdings with smaller number of animals, the CA already took some measures, particularly aiming to raise awareness with the existing rules. Whenever a new herd is registered the CA sends a "welcome package" to the owner including a short introduction to the rules on identification and registration.

Since October 2012, all notifications of events on bovine holding to CHR must be done electronically with only exception for elderly farmers. In 2015 more than 95% of all notifications for cattle were submitted electronically. In sheep, the trend of electronic 8 notifications is very similar; the percentage of digital notifications increased from 60 % in 2012 to almost 90 % in 2015.

Once a year, every farmer is asked to confirm or correct the registered information in the CHR on his herds. This includes information on number of animals; name, address and contact number of owner and keeper; the veterinary clinic responsible for the herd; and the type of herd (e.g. dairy or beef cattle). Average time interval (in years) between updating of data on number of animals has decreased in recent years, e.g. for pigs from 0.5 year in 2012 to 0.2 year in 2015, for sheep from 0.8 to 0.4 and for goats from 0.9 to 0.4. This improvement is mainly due to the reminder system for the farmer to notify the changes and automatic database controls in place (for more see point 16). 5.1.2 Completeness and logical integrity

Completeness of data is checked at data entry level ­ for both electronic notifications and manual entry of data. After data are entered into the CHR, several checks apply to find missing, incorrect or non-coherent data.
The checks include plausibility checks on data regarding holdings, herds, movements of pigs, events on cattle and sheep/goats. Extensive list of plausibility checks is under continual review.

Internal checks for cattle are processed in the database control system called DYKO. The irregularities detected by internal checks on movement notifications (data mismatch, missing data) are timely presented to the owner electronically in the list of errors and on the herd list. The failure to correct them will then show up in the DYKO system and the automatic letter generated in the CHR is sent to the owner presenting all of the irregularities. If still no actions will be taken, the case will be handled by head office. Some potentially more serious irregularities are dealt with directly by the local veterinary control units (e.g. movements to/from herds under restrictions, movements without passport).

In 2015, 37,311 new cases were flagged by the internal checks and recorded in DYKO. The vast majority (30,897) related to movement notifications (data mismatch or missing data on departure or entry of animals into herds). 3,785 (10.19% of total) were dealt with directly by the local veterinary control units. In the same year, 37,140 cases were resolved; 3,235 by local veterinary control units. Furthermore, in 2015 2,227 cases were automatically closed by the system - all cases when more than one year elapsed since the case was transferred to the case worker. A high proportion of these automatically closed cases (32 %) fall under local veterinary control unit responsibility. Some of these internal checks are also risk criteria for selecting holdings for official controls (for more see point 28).

The total number of bovine movements where the destination holding has not notified the arrival (floating animals) has risen over the past three years as new floating animals are added each year (see table below). However, the number of new floating animals per 9 year has not risen as there is a constant supply of around 1,000 bovines per year. This is in most cases potentially affecting only forward traceability but the increasing trend is of some concern. This trend continues despite the CA activities to tackle this issue as part of the DYKO system. Authorisations granted by one MS should be accepted by other MSs where agricultural, plant health and environmental (including climatic) conditions are comparable. Under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, PPPs may only be marketed and used in a MS if they are authorised or have a parallel trade permit (PTP). When PPPs are authorised, the quantity of the each co-formulant and the quantity and specific source(s) of each active substance that must be included in the PPP are defined. PTPs are granted for a PPP that is authorised in one MS (MS of origin) and may be introduced, placed on the market or used in another MS (MS of introduction), if this other MS determines that the PPP is identical in composition to a PPP already authorised in its territory. Any deviation from these very detailed requirements means that the PPP does not comply with its condition of authorisation/PTP. Germany is allocated to the central zone with another twelve MS. 4.1. AUDIT SERIES This was the first of six audits planned in Member States to evaluate the authorisation system for PPPs. The overview reports of previous audit series on PPPs can be found on the DG Health and Food Safety website, http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/specialreports/index_en.htm. The most recent audit series, carried out in the period January 2012 ­ June 2014, had focused mainly on controls relating to the marketing and use of PPPs, but also covered some aspects of the authorisation process where weaknesses relating to the authorisation of PPPs were also identified. These included "delays with re-authorisations of PPPs under Directive 91/414/EEC, and with mutual recognitions under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. It was found that many authorised PPPs had not been evaluated to EU standards more than 15 years after the uniform principles for evaluation had been established.
