Legal Requirements Article 75(1) and, (2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on designation of CAs and co-ordinating national authority Findings 5.2.1. Designation of Competent Authorities:

text: The Plant Protection Act designates the CAs for the authorisation of PPPs. Three of these, the BVL, BfR and JKI are under the aegis of the FMFA, while the UBA is under the aegis of the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, Building and Nuclear Safety (FME). All CAs are funded directly from the federal budget and not from the fees received from applicants seeking for authorisation of PPPs or approval of active substances which go directly to the Federal Finance Ministry, rather than being ring-fenced within the four CAs. BVL is the CA responsible for co-ordinating the evaluation of active substances under the EU review process and the evaluation and -4- authorisation of PPPs. All four CAs conduct evaluations on both active substances and PPPs.

In the PPP authorisation process, BVL is responsible for evaluating the identity, physical, chemical and technical properties, and analysis methods (formulation), JKI is responsible for evaluation of efficacy, phyto-toxicity and ecotoxicology issues relating to honey bees and BfR is responsible for the evaluation of health risks, residue analysis procedures and maximum limits. Finally, UBA is responsible for the evaluation relating to environmental fate (E-fate) and ecotoxicology, with the exception of honey bees, but including other pollinators.

The Plant Protection Act requires BVL to make the decision on PPP authorisation, in consultation with JKI and BfR, and in agreement with UBA. The BVL and UBA interpretation of this requirement has resulted in shared competence in the area of risk management, resulting in decision making by consensus. BVL is solely responsible for granting emergency authorisations and PTPs, with no obligation to consult other CAs. Conclusions
CAs have been designated for all tasks relating to the evaluation and authorisation of PPPs. 5.2.2. Resources

BVL has 99 full time equivalents (FTEs) dealing with PPP related administration/co- ordination issues and evaluation work, of which 45 have a relevant university degree. Four FTE (two technical assistants and two degree holders) are responsible for evaluation in the area of responsibility of BVL (see paragraph 5). Beyond this, BVL were not able to quantify the FTE responsible for dealing with active substances as distinct from PPPs, or those having administration/co-ordination roles, as distinct from risk management.

BfR have 20 FTE dedicated to evaluating PPPs and approximately 12 FTE evaluating active substances (AS). Eighty percent of staff have a relevant university degree, with the remainder having a technical qualification. Relevant BfR staff dedicate an average of 40 % of their time to the evaluation of PPP applications. There is no specific training programme for evaluator staff, but they participate in relevant events, e.g. contributing to development of specific guidance in international fora, and participating in specific ad- hoc training on toxicology. Evaluations are conducted in teams and an in-house peer review system is used with the objective of ensuring consistently high quality work.

JKI have a total of 50 staff dealing with PPPs. On average, staff dedicate 25 % (range 10 - 60 %) of their time to evaluation work. This equates to twelve FTE responsible for efficacy (five technical assistants and seven degree holders) and 3.5 FTE responsible for ecotoxicology (two degree holders and 1.5 technical assistants). JKI stated that while there is no formal in-house training programme, staff participate in European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO) meetings and in-house training is -5- organised to disseminate new EPPO guidance to all staff. Work is organised by product type (herbicides, fungicides, insecticides etc.) to make the best use of staff expertise. The CA stated that there was an internal system for supervising the observance of legal deadlines and a staggered peer review process to ensure the quality of input for the evaluation of PPPs.

Within UBA, there are 13 FTE dedicated to ecotoxicology (11 degree holders), and 9.5 FTE (7.5 degree holders), dedicated to E-fate evaluations. UBA stated that, in general, staff dedicate two thirds of their time to evaluation work. UBA estimate that up to two years is required to train new staff. This is based on one-to-one training and a mentoring system where new staff are supervised by more experienced staff. Some UBA staff undertake relevant post-graduate courses and UBA also has a programme of in-house training using external experts. Systems are in place to monitor compliance with deadlines for completion of work and to assess the quality of work via an internal peer review process.

In all CAs, the scientific staff (degree holders) do the evaluation work, while the technical staff provide administrative support. BVL, BfR and JKI only employ permanent staff to conduct work in this area, whereas UBA employ both permanent and contract staff in an attempt to respond promptly to variations in workload.

There is no clear demarcation regarding risk management and risk assessment between BVL and UBA. As described in paragraph 6, the decision on authorisation of PPPs requires the agreement between BVL and UBA, which confers to both CAs risk management responsibilities. During the audit, the CAs informed the audit team that, as part of the risk assessment, UBA staff also propose risk mitigation measures. BVL stated that they are only responsible for risk management, with the exception of special areas such as the evaluation of physical-chemical data. Regulation (EC) 178/2002 laying down the general principles and requirements of food law, defines risk management as "the process, distinct from risk assessment, of weighing policy alternatives considering risk assessment and other factors and if need be, selecting appropriate prevention and control options" and the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) has published the working principles for risk analysis which states that "there should be a functional separation of risk assessment and risk management, in order to ensure the scientific integrity of the risk assessment, to avoid confusion over the functions to be performed by risk assessors and risk managers and to reduce any conflict of interest". (http://www.fao.org/docrep/006/y4800e/y4800e0o.htm#bm24) Conclusions
There are suitably qualified and trained staff in all CAs, capable of conducting evaluations to a high standard. -6- 5.2.3. Planning

BVL stated that, under national legislation, it is mandatory to accept all applications received. In 2013, BVL hired a consulting company to conduct a survey among known applicants to determine future resource requirements, based on a projected 100 applications per year. The assessment of the survey concluded that just five additional FTE in the scientific area would be required to process these applications and authorise the relevant PPPs in compliance with the prescribed deadlines, and that positions should be cut in the technical area. The other CAs used the BVL projections to determine their future resources needs. BVL have no formal process to engage with applicants to estimate future workloads and no official projections on the number of future applications, which would be critical information for future planning. BVL stated, in response to questions from the audit team, that they expect the number of applications to increase each year and to reach approximately 280 applications per year by 2021.

There are a number of reasons for the high, and increasing, number of applications. Mainly because, Germany is a relatively large PPP market in an EU context, so it attracts a high number of applications.

The number of applications will increase due to Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. This Article requires the re-authorisation of PPPs after the re-approval of each active substance in the product, rather than after the approval of the last active substance, as was previously the case under Directive 91/414/EEC. Therefore, PPPs containing two active substances must be re-evaluated twice as often and PPPs with three active substances must be re-evaluated three times more frequently under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 compared to Directive 91/414/EEC.

The high number of applications is accompanied by a relatively high evaluation workload for each product, for various reasons. Under both Directive 91/414/EEC and Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, active substances are reviewed at EU level, and when first approved or re-approved, PPPs containing these active substances must be evaluated/re-evaluated and authorised/re-authorised at MS level, in line with defined EU deadlines. MS may engage in voluntary work-sharing to reduce this evaluation workload. Voluntary work-sharing is a system MS can use, most commonly for re-evaluation and re-authorisation of existing PPPs. Under the system, each MS voluntarily agrees to evaluate a relatively small number of PPPs, share the evaluation reports, and re-authorise a larger pool of products based on their own evaluation reports, and those of the other participating MS. On the other hand, Germany has historically authorised all PPPs for ten years in line with national legislation, with a re-evaluation and re-authorisation needed to remain on the market. In order to satisfy the EU requirement of re-authorising the PPP following re-approval of the active substance, the German CAs stated that they conduct a brief review of the conditions of authorisation which had been granted under the re-evaluation conducted to National timelines with the objective of ensuring compliance with any additional requirements arising from the review of the active substance as required under the decision to approve the active substance at EU level. Germany performs complete reviews of the products at different points in time than in -7- the 27 other MS, meaning that the possibility to use voluntary work-sharing for evaluation work in conjunction with other MS is greatly reduced.

Looking forward, MS may conduct partial evaluations and/or combined evaluations in order to comply with the requirements of Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 (on renewal of authorisations) for PPPs with multiple active substances, in line with the "Guidance Document on the Renewal of Authorisations according to Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009" (SANCO/2010/13170 rev. 13). During the audit, BVL initially stated that it was their intention to harmonise their re-authorisation system with EU deadlines in future. However, BVL subsequently clarified that the Guidance is only applicable in case of active substances which had been approved under the Regulation (EC) 1107/2009. Therefore, for authorisations granted under Directive 91/414/EEC, which comprise the majority of authorised PPPs in Germany, and/or for PPPs containing more than one active substance, a full re-evaluation of the PPP focussing on the critical areas will be performed following approval of the first active substance. Other MS, considering the applicability of the guidance document also for active substances approved under Directive 91/414/EC, will only perform a partial evaluation at this point in time and a full re-evaluation once the last active substance contained in the PPP is re- approved. These differences in the interpretation of the Guidance Document would lead to impede the synchronisation to evaluate PPPs with other MSs. Therefore Germany will not be able to avail of voluntary work-sharing opportunities with other MS, which could greatly reduce the evaluation workload. BVL stated that at the time of the audit, no applications had yet been received for renewal of a PPP under Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Finally, all applications received in Germany are evaluated to satisfy NRs, in addition to EU requirements, which greatly increase the workload. This is even more relevant for PPPs which are already authorised in other MS of the same zone, where evaluation could be solely based on the evaluation completed in other MS according to uniform principles for the EU requirements. Due to the requirement to satisfy NRs, it is easier for applicants to submit additional studies for on-going applications to address them in cases where Germany is the zRMS rather than where Germany is cMS. Therefore applicants often apply to Germany as zRMS, which significantly increases the evaluation workload, compared to other authorisation systems, as summarised in Paragraph 23. Indeed, the audit team noted a number of applications where Germany was the zRMS and there were no cMS, where the product had been already authorised in other central zone MS to uniform principle standards.

In line with internal procedures, BVL implements a "first in first out" policy for managing applications, with exceptions only possible in cases of public interest. There is no fast-track system for relatively simple applications e.g. applications for extending the range of approved crops for an existing authorised PPP. There is no methodical approach and

Implementing powers under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, which entered into force on 14 June 2011, are laid down in the Rural and Fisheries Code and the Public Health Code. The CAs policy is to charge fees to facilitate full cost recovery as provided for under Article 74(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, except in specific cases, e.g. authorisation of PPPs for biological control. The fees for processing applications, which were last updated in 2012, are laid down in a Decree of the MAFF of 16 April 2012, and in ANSES opinion, do not fully reflect the actual costs involved.

Through amendments of the Rural and Fisheries Code, additional requirements have been introduced in France, which go beyond the minimum EU requirements. These include the total ban on all neonicotinoid PPPs, for all uses, from 2018, with derogations only possible until 2020, prohibition of chemical PPPs in public areas from January 2017 and prohibition of chemical PPP use by non-professionals from January 2019.

Two further Ministerial Decrees lay down restrictions going beyond the minimum EU requirements. A Ministerial Decree of 7 April 2010, as amended, restricts the general use of tank mixtures based on PPP classification and a Ministerial Decree of 28 November 2003, as amended, restricts the use of insecticides with a risk for honey bees, with derogations allowed following evaluation. Conclusion

National legislation within the scope of the audit is in place. Additional national legislation, going beyond the minimum EU requirements, restricts the range of authorised PPPs compared to other MS. 5.2. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES: DESIGNATION, RESOURCES AND PLANNING Legal Requirements Article 75(1) and, (2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on designation of CAs and co-ordinating national authority 4 Findings 5.2.1. Designation of Competent Authorities

The Rural and Fisheries Code allocates responsibilities for PPP authorisation between two CAs, the MAFF and ANSES. As of 1 July 2015, ANSES is the CA in charge of all aspects related to PPP authorisation, including risk assessment and decision making, as well as granting PTPs. ANSES is also responsible for the official product register. The responsibilities and structure of ANSES are set out in the Public Health Code.

Prior to 1 July 2015, the MAFF was responsible for granting PPP authorisations, based on ANSES evaluations. At present, the MAFF is the CA dealing with policy and legislation in the area of PPPs and processing requests for emergency authorisations. The Rural and Fisheries Code gives MAFF the right to request ANSES to review its decisions, where they believe this is justified. Conclusion
CAs have been designated for all tasks relating to the evaluation and authorisation of PPPs and granting PTPs. Allocation of responsibilities is clearly defined. 5.2.2. Resources
There are six MAFF staff dealing with PPP policy and five full time equivalents (FTEs) dealing with emergency use authorisations under Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

Within ANSES, 172 FTEs deal with PPPs. The majority of staff are permanent. Staff work in one of two Directorates, dealing with risk assessment, or risk management. Of the total staff, 42 FTEs are responsible for administrative tasks, including completeness checks, communication, IT support and secretariat. A further 13 FTEs are involved in decision making following evaluations, including legal advice. The risk management Directorate is solely responsible for determining the appropriate risk management measures, based on proposals by risk assessment colleagues.

One hundred and sixteen FTEs are involved in evaluations, of which 14 FTEs are contract staff recruited in 2015. Evaluators deal with both active substances and PPPs, but the proportion of time spent on each activity is not precisely quantified. Twenty one staff co-ordinate the evaluation of PPPs in the 5 evaluation units. There are 15 FTEs responsible for the evaluation of physical and chemical properties, 18 for residues and consumer risk assessment, 18 for toxicology, 12 for environmental fate, 18 for ecotoxicology and 14 for efficacy. Evaluators conclude on the risks associated with PPP use and propose risk mitigations measures.

Evaluator staff met by the audit team had relevant educational backgrounds and included chemists, veterinarians, toxicologists and agronomists. New staff receive on-the-job training covering regulatory issues and specific guidelines used in the evaluation process. New staff initially work under the supervision of a senior staff member. Management 5 estimates that it takes six months for new staff to be fully operational. On-going internal training takes place via meetings and discussions when new legislation enters into force or new work related guidelines become applicable.
ANSES is funded directly from central government and currently all fees received from applications for authorisations and PTPs are retained within ANSES.

ANSES management have identified a lack of staff as a constraint to meeting deadlines under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, but were unable to quantify the precise number of additional staff needed in all five evaluation units, as well as in the co-ordination unit. ANSES are unable to routinely employ additional staff due to restrictions on public sector recruitment, despite the fact that the fees allow for full cost recovery for this work. ANSES stated that the recruitment process, where permitted, can take up to one year. Conclusion
Staff are suitably qualified and trained, capable of conducting evaluations to a high standard. 5.2.3. Planning
Both MAFF and ANSES stated that the decision to have all authorisation related work in a single authority, under one roof, was taken with the intention of making the system more efficient.

ANSES use a customised IT system to track all applications. Management stated that the system allows for on-going compliance with the EU deadlines to be calculated. Within evaluation units, spread sheets are used to track files and monitor compliance with deadlines. ANSES management stated that from July 2015, they introduced measures to avoid delays, including appointing a dedicated co-ordinator to manage the workflow in each evaluation unit and give clear deadlines for all evaluation tasks, more streamlined work processes and dedicated planning meetings. Nevertheless, ANSES management estimate that compliance with EU deadlines will be achieved by the beginning of 2018, at the earliest.

ANSES stated that there is no restriction on the number of applications which are accepted, but in some cases applicants are requested to postpone application to help ANSES manage the workflow. In addition, they highlighted their commitment to active substance evaluation/re-evaluation work, which is particularly resource intensive. France acted as Rapporteur Member State (RMS) or co-RMS for 29 active substances in 2015, a significant increase on the 17 evaluated in 2013.

Consequently, while France accounts for 33 % of the PPP market in the southern zone, ANSES act as the zRMS for a considerably higher proportion of southern zone applications. They have, in conjunction with other southern zone MS, sought information from applicants regarding future applications under Article 43, so as to facilitate work- sharing among MS. All applications for new products under the zRMS and cMS streams must be notified six months pre-submission. There is no predictability regarding the 6 volume of MR applications. There is no other formal process to predict future volumes of work and therefore, while there is reasonable visibility over a six month period, there is no estimate of future workload over a 2-3 year period.

ANSES do not have precise data, but they estimate that cMS/MR applications are processed in 46 working days, whereas zRMS applications require 77 working days, so there are resource savings by using the cMS and MR streams, even allowing for the French practice of conducting evaluations on cMS/MR applications1. ANSES has data on the average time needed to conduct evaluations in each of the specialist evaluation areas, but given that this varies greatly depending on the levels of complexity of the different dossiers within each of the areas, this information does not allow the bottleneck in the evaluation process to be identified.

Prior to the Regulation, France conducted re-evaluations in line with EU requirements and, in addition, every ten years after PPP authorisation. This doubling of the evaluation workload is one of the reasons for the backlog of authorisation applications, but this double evaluation practice ceased with the entry into force of the Regulation. To comply with Article 43 of the Regulation (see Background), applicants are required to submit a full dossier within three months of re-approval of the active substance. In some cases, this is not possible e.g. residue trials take two years to complete, so the French authorities will allow applicants additional time to prepare and submit the dossier. Secondly, ANSES plans to conduct a re-evaluation for all substances contained in a PPP, where possible, taking into account the progress of the examination of the substances as part of the renewal of approval, in order to comply with the requirements of Article 43 for PPPs with multiple active substances. Both actions are in line with the "Guidance Document on the Renewal of Authorisations according to Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009" (SANCO/2010/13170 rev. 13).

ANSES operates a "first in first out" policy for managing applications, except for minor uses of national interest and PPPs for biological control, which have priority. They stated that a "risk-envelope" approach is taken when evaluating similar products as described in the Guidance Document (GD) SANCO/11244/2011 rev5 and also in the GD SANCO/13169/2010 rev. 9 on zonal evaluation and mutual recognition. The principle of this approach consists of conducting an evaluation on the "worst-case" scenario to cover a range of products, which avoids repetition of work.

Applicants frequently seek administrative changes to existing authorised PPPs e.g. change of company name, or authorisation to market an existing authorised PPP under a second trade name. Processing these types of applications does not require any technical evaluation work. There is a fast-track system to deal with these types of applications, and these are generally processed in one month. Biological PPPs are also fast-tracked through the evaluation process. 1 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that, in the case of MR, the additional work is based on checks, rather than evaluation work, which aims to ensure the suitability of conditions of use (management measures). 7 Conclusion

The difficulties seen with regard to long term planning and quantifying future workload coupled with the lack of data on key performance metrics can affect the capability of the system to ensure applications are, or will be, processed within legal deadlines. 5.2.4. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within Competent Authorities

Management stated that in all cases where applications for authorisation are refused, the Commission is informed as required by Article 36(3) of the Regulation. In cases of refusal based on efficacy, the Commission is not informed. In the case of refusal to grant a PPP authorisation, ANSES informs the applicants in writing, by official mail, stating the reasons. They also stated that all evaluation reports are uploaded to the common EU platform, CIRCABC, thus facilitating work-sharing with other MS.

France participates in southern zone co-ordination meetings established under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, which comprise four teleconferences and one face-to- face meeting per year. These meetings help to co-ordinate work-sharing among MS.

ANSES stated that meetings with the PPP industry are organised once a year. Pre- submission meetings do not take place routinely, but only in cases where ANSES believe these are justified following an in-depth analysis of the applications. ANSES pointed to the range of relevant information for applicants on their web-site. The PPP industry believes that the lack of routine pre-submission meetings limits the quality of dossiers, thus contributing to delays in the evaluation process. Conclusion

ANSES co-ordination and co-operation with other MS facilitates work-sharing in the southern zone. 5.3. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES: DESIGNATION, RESOURCES AND PLANNING. Legal Requirements Articles 75(1), (2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on Competent Authority. Findings 5.2.1. Designation of Competent Authorities:

The CA for authorisation of PPPs is laid down in the Law of 19 December 2014. The CA is the Minister of Agriculture, Viticulture and Consumer Protection, and the administrative tasks related to the application, as well as the co-ordination activities are delegated to the Plant Health department of ASTA.

The Luxembourg Law of 19 December 2014 established the Committee of Plant Protection Products. The CA may consult the Committee on issues relating to the authorisation of PPPs, although ASTA stated that all decisions were consulted with the Committee at the date of the audit. This Committee meets four times a year. Conclusions on the Designation of Competent Authorities
CAs have been designated for all tasks relating to the evaluation and authorisation of PPPs. 5.2.2. Resources

Within ASTA, there are 2.2 full time equivalent (FTEs) dedicated to tasks relating to the application for authorisation of PPPs. In total three staff are involved in these tasks. Although ASTA does not require specific qualifications for staff dealing with applications, one staff member holds a University degree in forestry and a master in plant protection, and one holds a Technical degree in horticulture. Minimum qualification is High School degree. ASTA stated that Luxembourg only processes applications based on Mutual Recognition (MR) of authorisations of PPPs, where only administrative tasks are required.

Members of staff participated in the training for Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) programme related to the authorisation of PPPs, and also in workshops. Members of staff routinely attend the Standing Committee for Plant, Animal, Food and Feed (PAFF). -4- 8. Applications received are allocated to one staff member who then remains responsible for the completion of the authorisation process. There is a "first in first out" policy for managing applications. 9. Staff is responsible for organising the workload and the activities needed to process the applications for authorisation of PPPs. ASTA uses databases to register the activities conducted related to applications of PPPs. Conclusions on Resources 10. Staff are suitably qualified to conduct administrative tasks relating to the management of applications for MR of authorisation of PPPs. 5.2.3. Planning 11. ASTA stated that they are legally obliged to accept all applications for authorisations/PTPs. However, due to the limited resources available (see paragraph 6), only applications for MR of authorisation of PPPs are processed. 12. Luxembourg grants authorisations for MR for a certain period of time, ranging from one to three years. In order to renew the authorisation, ASTA contacts the applicant who is required to submit only the latest information relating to the authorisation in the MS of origin. In addition, the CA requires that authorisations must be renewed every ten years from the first authorisation, when ASTA requires the applicant to submit all the documents and information as for first applications. Although provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 set out the responsibility of the applicant to inform the CA in case of relevant changes to the status of the authorisation, ASTA stated that the granting of authorisations for a defined period of time, ensures the proper update of the PPPs authorised in Luxembourg. This practice means that the administrative workload is increased. 13. ASTA provided an estimate of two days as the average time required to conduct the necessary administrative tasks for MR. ASTA estimates that processing applications for PTPs is shorter (one day). For modifications of existing authorisations or extensions of the validity period, the dedicated time range from 30 minutes to one day. For renewals of authorisation the time ranges from one to two days. According to this information and the number of applications received (see paragraph 27), in the worst case scenario, to cope with the average workload in the period 2013 to 2015, the minimum FTE required was 2.2, therefore the existing resources are sufficient. 14. Applications received are allocated to one of the staff who then remains responsible for the completion of the authorisation process. -5- Conclusions on Planning 15. Luxembourg only deals with applications for MR. Although the workload is increased by the policy of granting authorisation for short periods of time, the available resources are sufficient to deal efficiently with the number of applications received. 5.2.4. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within Competent Authorities 16. ASTA is the designated, national co-ordinating authority for communication with applicants, other MSs and the Commission. COMPETENT AUTHORITIES: DESIGNATION, RESOURCES AND PLANNING Legal Requirements Article 75(1) and, (2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on designation of CAs and co-ordinating national authority Findings 5.2.1. Designation of Competent Authorities

DGAV is the CA for all aspects relating to the evaluation, authorisation and placing on the market of PPPs under Decree law 31/2012. Within DGAV, the Pesticides Division of the Sanitary and Defence Directorate (DSMDS) is responsible for this task. The Ministry for Health is the CA for biocides, but DGAV is responsible for conducting evaluations on product type 8 (PT8) biocides. Conclusions
A CA has been designated for all tasks relating to the evaluation and authorisation of PPPs and granting PTPs. 5.2.2. Resources

The Pesticides Division of DSMDS has 27 full time equivalents (FTEs) dealing with PPPs, of which 17 are professional staff with a relevant university degree, and ten are administrative staff. All staff are permanent. Staff numbers have halved over the last 14 years.

Nine and a half FTE conduct evaluations on both actives substances and products relating to PPPs and biocides. It is estimated that evaluators spend 80 % of their time on PPPs. Two FTE are responsible for evaluations relating to physical and chemical properties, two for residues and consumer risk assessment, half an FTE for environmental fate and ecotoxicology, two for toxicology and three for efficacy. Evaluator staff are responsible for both risk assessment and risk management.

Among the evaluator staff, there are seven agronomists, two chemical engineers and a pharmacist. New staff receive specialist training/mentoring in their work area and many evaluator staff have worked in multiple specialist areas. This educational background, broad range of practical experience and specific on-the-job training gives staff an appreciation of the context in which PPPs are used, rather than considering applications in a purely theoretical manner.

Six and a half FTE professional staff are responsible for co-ordinating applications for authorisations, processing PTP applications and updating the official product register. 5 Ten administrative staff provide support dealing with issues such as invoices and completeness checks.

DGAV is funded directly from central government and currently all fees received from applications for authorisations and PTPs go directly to the Ministry of Finance, rather than being ring-fenced within the Pesticides Division.

Management within the Pesticides Division have identified a lack of staff, in both the co- ordination and evaluation areas. According to the management this acts as a significant constraint to meeting deadlines under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, but DGAV are unable to recruit staff due to restrictions on public sector recruitment. The lack of staff responsible for evaluation is relevant to Portugal's work as zRMS, while the lack of co- ordination staff is relevant for all types of applications.

Management within the Pesticides Division outlined two initiatives to secure additional staff. Firstly, they sought staff via lateral transfer from other public service organisations on two occasions in recent years, but with no success. Secondly, they have plans to outsource evaluation work to external experts, starting in 2017. These experts will be funded through application fees, 30 % of which will be retained in the Pesticides Division for this purpose, under the new Decree law on fees, expected to be signed into law in 2016. DGAV expect that this additional evaluation capacity will help to ensure greater compliance with deadlines when acting as zRMS. Conclusions

Staff are suitably qualified and trained, capable of conducting evaluations to a high standard. Their practical knowledge of agronomy is noteworthy, helping to ensure pragmatic, scientifically-sound decision making.

DGAV has identified limited resources as one of causes of non-compliance with legal deadlines. The proposal to outsource some evaluation work, if implemented, will increase capacity and should help to address deficiencies in the authorisation system when acting as zRMS. 5.2.3. Planning

The Pesticides Division use spreadsheets to track all applications. Management stated that they are unable to calculate compliance with the deadlines prescribed in the Regulation using this software. They had already identified this weakness, and stated that they have plans to move to a database management system in the future to allow for more comprehensive tracking of applications.

The Pesticides Division stated that there is no restriction on the number of applications which may be accepted. They have, in conjunction with other southern zone MS, sought information from applicants regarding future applications under Article 43 of the Regulation, so as to facilitate work-sharing among MS. All applications for new products 6 under the zRMS and cMS streams must be notified six months pre-submission. There is no predictability regarding the volume of MR applications. In summary, there is no formal process to predict total future workload over a 3-4 year period. The Pesticides Division have no data on the time taken to process applications under each of the different streams, so while there are significant resource savings by using the cMS and MR streams, these are not quantifiable using the current tracking system. In addition, they have no data on the time needed to conduct evaluations in each specialist area, and therefore, cannot identify the bottleneck in the evaluation process. This lack of forecasting and lack of data on key performance metrics means that, while the number of applications is expected to increase, mainly in connection with the requirements of Article 43, there are no clear projections regarding future workload, and the future resource requirements needed, to process these applications within legal deadlines.

To comply with Article 43 of the Regulation (see Background), applicants are required to submit a full dossier within three months of re-approval of the active substance. In some cases, this is not possible e.g. residue trials take two years to complete, so the Portuguese authorities will allow applicants additional time to prepare and submit the dossier. Secondly, DGAV plans to conduct combined evaluations, where possible, in order to comply with the requirements of Article 43 for PPPs with multiple active substances, in line with the "Guidance Document on the Renewal of Authorisations according to Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009" (SANCO/2010/13170 rev. 13).

On 1 January 2016, Portugal had a total of 322 PPPs currently awaiting re-authorisation. Management have established that the vast majority of these PPPs are on the market in other southern zone MS and will also require re-authorisation in these countries. Therefore, they are actively engaging with applicants to change these applications to MR applications, to facilitate re-authorisation by MR, and therefore avoid repetition of work already undertaken in another MS, and reduce the evaluation workload within Portugal.

Portugal generally operates a "first in first out" policy for managing applications. Exceptions are possible for PPPs that help to address critical crop/pest needs, which helps to reduce the number of emergency authorisations. A "risk-envelope" approach is routinely taken when evaluating similar products as described in the Guidance Document (GD) SANCO/11244/2011 rev5 and also in the GD SANCO/13169/2010 rev. 9 on zonal evaluation and mutual recognition. The principle of this approach consists of conducting an evaluation on the "worst-case" scenario to cover a range of products, which avoids repetition of work.

All staff involved in PPP evaluation and authorisation are based in Oeiras, about 20 km from Lisbon. All certificates granting authorisations and PTPs are signed by the General Director of DGAV, based in DGAV headquarters in Lisbon. All incoming and outgoing post relating to PPPs is addressed to, and issues from, DGAV in Lisbon. These administrative procedures take up to 3 weeks, a significant period in the context of a 120 day time limit to grant authorisations under the MR and cMS streams. Internal procedures mean that staff cannot define a period of time for accepting responses when seeking information/clarification from applicants and the audit team noted a number of 7 cases where responses from applicants were outstanding for a number of months. This leads to some applications exceeding legal deadlines, where the CA is awaiting a response from applicants.

Applicants frequently seek administrative changes to existing authorised PPPs e.g. change of company name, or authorisation to market an existing authorised PPP under a second trade name. Processing these types of applications does not require any technical evaluation work. There is no fast-track system to deal with these types of applications, with approval taking an average of over two years. Conclusions

While management have identified the lack of resources as a constraint to meet deadlines, limitations in the IT system and a lack of longer term planning mean that the true resource needs cannot be calculated.

The policies of systematically seeking out opportunities for more efficient work practices, e.g. using a "risk-envelope" approach and maximising the use of MR in addition to prioritising new/agronomically important PPPs could be considered as good practices.

Inefficient administrative processes relating to signing of certificates, corresponding with applicants and postal services contribute to delays in processing applications, and the failure to comply with legal deadlines. 5.2.4. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within Competent Authorities

DGAV management stated that in all cases where applications for authorisation are refused, the Commission is informed as required by Article 36(3) of the Regulation. They also stated that all evaluation reports are uploaded to the common EU platform, CIRCABC, thus facilitating access for other MS.

MS can engage in voluntary work-sharing, a system most commonly used for re- evaluation and re-authorisation of existing PPPs. Voluntary work-sharing precedes Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, and under this system, each MS voluntarily agrees to evaluate a relatively small number of PPPs, share the evaluation reports, and re- authorise a larger pool of products based on their own evaluation reports, and those of the other participating MS. While there have been some efforts at work-sharing in the southern zone, Portugal had a total of 322 PPPs awaiting re-authorisation on 1 January 2016, of which just 10 were formally part of work-sharing projects with other MS, meaning that 300 must be evaluated by Portugal. The vast majority of these PPPs are on the market in other MS and will also require re-authorisation in these countries.

Up to this point, Portugal has participated in southern zone co-ordination meetings established under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, which comprise four teleconferences and one face-to-face meeting per year. Active participation at this forum is critical to 8 facilitate work-sharing among MS. Due to financial constraints, DGAV will not participate in the face-to-face meeting in 2016, which will limit Portugal's ability to capitalise on the benefits of work-sharing. The Pesticides Division meets regularly with industry representative groups and individual applicants. Applicants met by the audit team expressed their frustration that the reasoning behind decisions relating to applications for authorisation were not always fully explained, as addressing negative decisions is more difficult without an understanding of the logic behind the decision. The CA stated that the policy of not providing more detailed explanations for negative decisions is due to the additional work involved. Conclusions

The CA communicates with both other MS and applicants in an open manner. Financial constraints threaten continued active participation at relevant fora, which are important to fully exploit the potential efficiencies resulting from the zonal authorisation system. 28. The DGAV stated that there have been no changes to the national plant protection organisation since the previous audit.

In summary, according to the provisions of the regulatory decree No 154/2005, the DGAV acts as the Single Authority for plant health. At regional level, the Regional Directorates for Agriculture and Fisheries (DRAPs) are responsible for the 5 implementation of phytosanitary legislation, including control of T. erytreae. The National Institute of Agrarian and Veterinary Research (INIAV) provides diagnostic support, including for the detection of citrus greening. Morphological identification of T. erytreae is carried out either by INIAV or by specially trained DRAP staff.

The audit team noted good cooperation between DGAV, DRAPs and INIAV concerning the exchange of information with respect to the situation of T. erytreae and citrus greening. 5.1.2 Legislation and guidelines

The DGAV informed the audit team that two official circulars had been issued at national level concerning T. erytreae: Circular No 3 of 9 March 2015 lays down the detection methods and the phytosanitary measures to be taken for isolated trees or trees grown in orchards and places of production of propagating material including nurseries and garden centres. In particular, the circular provides for treatments with plant protection products, severe pruning of infested trees, prohibition on the movement of host plants and plant material and intensive monitoring, including traps. Circular No 18 of 2 July 2015 intensified the measures to be taken within the infested and the buffer zones of the demarcated areas and banned the production and movement of host plants grown in nurseries located within the demarcated areas.

The DRAPs issued additional circulars that provided detailed information on the application of the national circulars, taking account of the specific conditions in each region. The circulars are part of the alert system addressed to fruit producers and nursery operators and specify the active substances for insecticide applications and cultural measures. In total, 41 circulars have been issued by the DRAPs in the North, Central and Algarve regions.

The DGAV informed the audit team that it had prepared a contingency plan for Candidatus Liberibacter spp. and its two vectors in consultation with the DRAPS and stakeholders (see also section 5.4.2 below). 5.1.3 Human resources and training

Overall, within the DRAPs mainly affected by T. erytreae (North region, Central region and Madeira) there are 30 inspectors whilst four more inspectors exercise their duties in Algarve. DGAV stated that the number of inspectors and their supervisors is in general insufficient to cover inspection needs and to carry out controls, across the wide range of duties which they perform.

Plant health inspectors have received training for monitoring the buffer zones within the demarcated areas and for carrying out visual inspections of traps and of plant material of 6 citrus. DGAV provided the audit team with a list and dates of training events delivered to plant health inspectors of DRAPs. 5.1.4 Registration of stakeholders and awareness raising campaign

The DRAPs operate a register of nurseries producing citrus propagating material and other hosts of T. erytreae. Citrus fruit producers are registered within their agricultural cooperatives and warehouses/packing stations in line with the provisions of the EU legislation.

Following the first finding of T. erytreae in mainland Portugal, the DGAV launched an awareness raising campaign for both T. erytreae and citrus greening. The DRAPs also provide a wide range of information targeting the public, municipal authorities and other stakeholders. This includes the use of leaflets, posters and technical bulletins; TV and radio broadcasts, and announcements in churches. The DGAV provided a list of training events delivered to citrus fruit growers, producers of citrus propagating material and nurseries.

All stakeholders met by the audit team had a high level of awareness of T. erytreae and citrus greening and were very collaborative with the competent authorities. All places of production of propagating material of citrus had a general supervising technician in charge of the technical management who was informed about the harmful organisms in question. Conclusion on organisational aspects of plant health controls

The diagnostic support for T. erytreae and citrus greening and the legislation in place provide the basis for the control measures to be applied against both harmful organisms. The information campaign addressed to the general public and registered citrus fruit and propagating material producers has increased the level of awareness about the importance of T. erytreae and citrus greening for Citrus culture. 5.2 SURVEYS FOR T. ERYTREAE AND CITRUS GREENING Legal requirements Article 16(1) and point 10.1 of Annex IV, A, II of Directive 2000/29/EC. ISPM 4 and ISPM 8 Findings

DGAV is the general coordinator of surveillance carried out for both T. erytreae and Candidatus Liberibacter spp. Surveys are based on an annual plan which is agreed between DGAV and the DRAPs. The plan indicates the minimum number of surveillance sites and samples to be taken. The DRAPS are responsible for organising and implementing the planned surveys in their region, and they select the survey locations, taking account of risk factors. 7 14. T. erytreae is not subject to diapause and in Portugal remains active during the winter period. Surveys in nurseries and garden centres take place throughout the year. They are risk based and from March to October are intensified in public and private gardens with isolated trees and in orchards located in areas which are still free from the pest. 15. Surveys are carried out through visual inspections of citrus trees and other host plants of T. erytreae (Fortunella, Poncirus, Casimiroa, Clausena, Murraya, Vepris, Zanthoxylum, Choisya) for characteristic suspicious symptoms of T. erytreae activity, as well as the actual presence of the insect. Given the scattered distribution of host plants in the North and Central regions, the surveys are carried out following a risk based approach, focusing on parishes in the buffer zones and parishes bordering demarcated areas. 16. Surveillance is also based on the visual inspection of yellow sticky traps placed in high- risk sites, and other geo-referenced locations throughout the different regions of the country. The Environmental Health Service (EHS), part of the larger competent authority HSE Public 1 Public Analyst's Laboratory (PAL) in Cork 1 Audit visits 1 1 GMO trial 2 Dublin Port; Waterford Port Food processor 1 Import point Seed establishment 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation, in particular Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. EU legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the latest amended version. Full references to the acts quoted in this report are given in Annex 1. 4 BACKGROUND This was the first audit carried out by the DG Health and Food Safety to Ireland on GMO issues. 4.1 COUNTRY PROFILE The DG Health and Food Safety has published a country profile for Ireland, which describes the control systems for food and feed safety, animal health, animal welfare and plant health including the organisation of official controls of GMOs. The country profile can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/fvo/country_profiles_en.cfm 4.2 AUTHORISED GMO PRODUCTS The list of the GM products authorised in the EU can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/dyna/gm_register/index_en.cfm The GM maize MON810 was authorised for placing on the market and use in food and feed and is the only one authorised for cultivation, on the basis of Commission Decision 98/294/EC. 4.3 PRODUCTION AND TRADE DATA There is no commercial cultivation of GM crops in Ireland. Some field trials with GMO plants have been carried out since 1997 and there is currently one trial authorised on GM potato. Ireland is a big producer of feed and it imports the majority of protein ingredients. Based on data provided by the CA - which does not distinguish between GMO and non-GMO products - Ireland imported some 738 000 t of soya bean in 2013 and 636 000 t in 2014. There were some 624 000 t of maize (grains) imported in 2013 and 591 000 t in 2014. The import of corn 2 gluten feed was 233 000 t in 2013 and 244 000 t in 2014. There was import of 264 000 t of rapeseed oilcake in 2013 and 190 000 t in 2014. Based on EUROSTAT data, the import of cotton oilcake was some 2 300 t in 2014 and no import in 2015. The trade of maize seed for sowing from other EU Member States was 309 t in 2014 and 404 t in 2015. Some 33 t of oilseed rape for sowing was brought into the country from other EU Member States in 2014 and 19 t in 2015. Only one lot of maize seed brought into Ireland in 2015 originate from a non-EU country. Regarding rice and rice products from China imported under the Combined Nomenclature codes listed in Commission Implementing Decision 2011/884/EU, there were not many direct imports. Between 2012 and 2015, 22 consignments arrived, however only four were accepted and imported because the rest were non-compliant and as such, were destroyed or re-exported (see 5.3.4 below). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Findings 1. The Irish GMOs (Deliberate Release) Regulations Statutory Instrument (S.I.) No. 500 of 2003 regulates deliberate release into the environment, the use of GMOs including field trials and placing products containing or consisting of GMOs on the market. The Irish authorities stated that the S.I. transposes Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has prepared a guidance document to provide assistance and guidance to users who wish to apply for consent to carry out a deliberate release of a GMO, for purposes other than placing on the market.

Article 4(4) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Findings

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) is the Central Competent Authority (CCA) for GMO in the area of food. It is responsible for enforcement and for technical advice. The Department of Health (DoH) is responsible for GM food policy development and legislation.

The FSAI is mainly a coordinating body for other agencies which perform control activities on its behalf based on Service Contracts. The Health Service Executive (HSE) is the CA for the implementation of official controls in GM food, in a small number of manufacturers and mainly at retail level, carried out through Environmental Health Service (EHS).

The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) is the CA for cultivation of GM crops and their coexistence with non GM crops and for GM presence in feed and seed. It is responsible for enforcement, policy and legislation.

The Department of the Environment, Community and Local Government is responsible for the policy and legislation and the EPA for enforcing legislation in relation to GMOs for deliberate release into the environment, including contained use and field trials.

The authorised laboratory for GM food analysis is the Public Analyst's Laboratory (PAL) in Cork. The Food and Environmental Research Agency (FERA) in the UK is the authorised laboratory for GM feed and seed analysis (see also section 5.3.6 below).

The FSAI informed the audit team that it organises at least one coordination meeting per year for all CAs responsible for controls on GMOs in relevant areas. There is also ongoing communication between all CAs on issues related to GMOs. 4 13. The representatives of the EHS and of the DAFM stated that they have regular meetings of inspectors and exchange of information at local, regional and national levels on GMOs related topics. 14. The audit team did not identify any cases where facilities or equipment needed for official controls were inadequate. Conclusions on designation and co-operation of Competent Authorities 15. CAs within the scope of the audit are clearly defined and tasks clearly allocated to ensure the appropriateness of controls. Effective cooperation takes place between and within the CAs which enables effective controls on GMOs. 5.2.2 Resources for performance of official controls Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 16. Environmental Health Officers of the local EHS carry out controls along the entire food chain from food manufacturers to retailers. They are also responsible for import controls on food of non-animal origin. EHS is organised nationwide in 32 geographical areas (local areas) grouped into four regional teams with a national management team. There are some 300 whole time equivalent staff and controls on GMO represent only a very small part of their duties. 17. Controls on feed are carried out by 11 Agricultural officers from DAFM Feedingstuffs Division who are assigned to control feed at import, at warehouses and manufacturers. Controls on seeds are carried out by DAFM officers at seed producers, processors and distributors. 18. Two inspectors of the EPA control the contained use of GMOs and deliberate release including field trials. 19. The EHS assess the training needs of staff on an annual basis and the DAFM training needs of staff are assessed via a performance management system. Staff from both CAs attend regular annual training programmes organised in-house and sometimes in cooperation with the FSAI. 20. The inspectors and laboratory staff met by the audit team had the necessary knowledge about GMOs and were prepared for their tasks. 5 Conclusions on resources for performance controls 21. The CAs Staff are overall appropriate to meet EU requirements for controls on GMOs. 5.2.3 Procedures for performance and reporting of control activities Legal requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 22. The FSAI issued Guidance Note 1 which provides guidance in relation to the official controls to be carried out on food business operators. GM foods are classified by the guidance under 'food legislation other than food hygiene'. FSAI also issued guidance for import controls on products of non-animal origin. In addition, a work programme of official controls is agreed with the HSE. 23. The EHS issued a protocol for inspection of food business operators under their supervision with related forms and checklists, which cover checks for GMOs. For each visit, a report is produced and entered into the Environmental Health Information System, which was put in place in 2013.The HSE also issued a guide for official controls and for the import control of food of non-animal origin carried out by Port Health Officers at Dublin seaport and airport. The EHS reports routinely to FSAI on the implementation of the Service Contract and an annual report is also submitted. 24. The DAFFM prepared Procedures Manuals for feed which include guidelines for import controls, including sampling. 25. The audit team reviewed some of the reports relevant to this audit, which were drawn up during or following inspections and sampling. The reviewed reports confirmed that the appropriate reporting system is in place which contribute to the effectiveness of the official controls on GMOs. Conclusions on procedures for performance and reporting of control activities 26. The CAs have created documented procedures for and report on controls carried out as required by Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, providing a satisfactory basis for the implementation of official controls on GMOs. 5.2.4 Planning of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Chapter I of Commission Recommendation 2004/787/EC. 6 Findings 27. The FSAI stated that GM food is not considered as a specific safety concern. In Guidance Note 1, controls on GMOs are included in official controls of food business operators but inspections and sampling activities related to GMOs are not carried out routinely, but only as deemed necessary. In practice, the operators' food safety management system is taken into account as well as the risk category of the premises and the history of compliance. 28. The National Sampling Group, consisting of representatives of the three PALs, FSAI and the EHS, prepares the annual national food sampling and analysis programme including all types of samples. The priority is to take samples as close as possible to the beginning of the food chain. After the sampling plan is agreed, the number of samples to be taken is allocated to the EHS local areas. Decisions are then taken at local level as to which types of sample will be taken and at what point in the food chain, taking into account the nature of the food businesses and their own sampling plans. Heads of the EHS local areas monitor the implementation of the plan. 29. The DAFM informed the audit team that controls on GMOs in feed mainly concern labelling and compared to contaminants and other undesirable substances, the risk is considered low. Detailed information on the scope of controls on feed is set out in their Animal Feed Controls Programme. The level of testing of imported feed for GMOs is set out in the "Feedingstuffs Inspection Plan". Sampling and analysis are targeted on whole grains and feed materials imported from non-EU countries that cultivate GM crops and where consignments are not labelled as GM or are labelled as non-GM. 30. Sampling of seeds is risk based taking into account the species where GM crops are cultivated ("risk crops", e.g. maize, oil seed rape, beet, soya bean), new point of origin, new or established crop or variety and previous check sample findings. 31. For the GMO field trials the EPA carries out controls of the implementation of the conduct of the trials taking into account the characteristics of the crop and the conditions of the consent. Conclusions on planning of official controls 32. Prioritisation of official controls is risk based, takes into account the operators' own controls in line with the Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, which enables an effective control system on GMOs. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Controls of the authorised deliberate release of GMOs Legal requirements Articles 4(1), 4(3), 4(5), 6, 8, 9, 10 and 31(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC. 7 Findings 33. The process of approval of field trials starts with the notifier submitting an application dossier to the EPA. The notifier is required to place a public notice of the proposed deliberate release in a newspaper within 14 days of submitting the application and forwards a copy of this to the EPA. Within the same deadline, the notifier sends a copy of the public notice to the site owner and the Local Authority where the proposed deliberate release is to be carried out. 34. The EPA examines the application (notification) for compliance with the requirements of the GMO deliberate release Regulations, S.I. 500 of 2003. In assessing the application, the EPA carries out extensive consultations with the FSAI, the National Advisory Committee on GMOs and other Government Departments. The EPA prepares an Inspector's Report with the proposed consent conditions taking into consideration comments received from the public and other CAs. The Board of the EPA makes a decision in favour (with or without conditions) or against (with reasons for the refusal). The EPA issues a decision and notifies all parties and publishes it on their website. The procedures take 90 days and can be extended for any consultation with the notifier. 35. The audit team checked the documentation for the authorisation of the proposed deliberate release for the recent GMO field trial and the procedure was in line with EU legislation. 36. Once the consent is granted the EPA carries out site inspections to ensure that the consent conditions are adhered to. This is done by the EPA inspector or by a certified professional agronomist hired by the EPA. Usually, three to four site visits are carried out during the growing season, at planting, mid growing season and at harvest time. The inspector also checks for the presence of volunteers of potato plants after the trial is completed. 37. At the time of the audit, there was one ongoing GMO field trial with a GM blight tolerant potato. The proposed period of deliberate release was from 2012 to 2016 with the trial completed in 2015. The post-trial monitoring for volunteers will continue until 2020 and the trial will be terminated when EPA is satisfied that the post-trial management and monitoring requirements have been met. 38. The EPA inspectors stated that the GM potato field trial was carried out in accordance with the consent conditions and no non-compliances were observed. 39. The audit team visited the GM potato field where the trial took place, interviewed the inspectors of the EPA and carried out a documentary check of the reports of controls carried out since the trial began. There were three types of on-site controls performed and reports produced for each inspection: 1) control visits carried out by a hired agricultural consultant, 2) inspections by the EPA inspectors and 3) the required bimonthly and end of year reports by the notifier. Since the beginning of the trial in 2012, the consultant carried out 11 and the EPA inspectors eight site visits and the 8 notifier produced 15 reports. No non-compliances were observed by the performers of these on-site controls. 40. The audit team checked also the weekly monitoring log of cultivation from 2012 to 2015 kept by the notifier. They monitored and reported on any damage to site fencing, on any berries or tubers outside site perimeter and on any tubers on the soil surface within the trial site. Nothing of risk was recorded in the log. Conclusions on controls of the deliberate release of the GMOs 41. An appropriate system for authorising the deliberate release of GMOs for trial purposes is in place in line with Article 6 of Directive 2001/18/EC. 42. There is a comprehensive control system in place regarding GMO field trials. These are controlled at an appropriate frequency and verifications carried out ensure that the conditions of the consent are met. 5.3.2 Controls of GMOs in seed Legal requirements Articles 4 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003. Articles 4(5) and 21 of Directive 2001/18/EC. Findings 43. The DAFM informed the audit team that an agreed voluntary protocol between the DAFM and the Seed Industry is implemented to control unintended presence of GMOs in conventional seed. The crops prone to GMO cross-contamination covered are maize and oilseed rape, which are commercially cultivated in Ireland, and beet and soybean imported for trial purposes. Each commercial seed lot or seed submitted for variety trials must be accompanied by a certificate of analysis for the presence of GMOs from a recognised laboratory. To facilitate random sampling of imported seed for analysis, the importer is required to give five working days advance notice of the import. 44. Seed is sampled randomly on a risk basis according to the International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) protocols by the DAFM officials. Seed is sent for testing to the FERA laboratory in the UK and is not marketed, distributed or planted in advance of test results becoming available. The target for sampling is some 5 % of commercial seed lots imported or moved to Ireland. The DAFM stated that the origin of the seed is generally other Member States and, very exceptionally, non-EU countries. In 2014 one maize sample was taken. Oilseed rape samples were not taken due to the very late seed delivery. In total, 70 seed lots of maize and 30 seed lots of oilseed rape were imported. In 2015, two samples of commercial maize and one sample of oilseed rape was taken (out of 79 and 34 lots imported respectively). In addition to this in 2014 and in 2015 two 9 samples each year were taken of each of these crops from seed submitted for variety trials. 45. The DAFM stated that no traces of GMO in seed were detected so far in commercial seed and, only in one case, in seed for trials. In a consignment of soya bean that was imported for commercial trialling purposes traces of GM material were identified in 2015. This seed was returned to the supplier in another Member State and its return was verified by the DAFM. 46. The audit team visited one seed company, reviewed the documents related to imported seed and observed seed sampling: The seed company has its own quality management system in place including a traceability system for each handled seed lot. Documents for the imported seeds lots included analytical reports attesting to the freedom of GMOs. The scope of testing varied very much in the reviewed analytical reports, from basic screening of the two GM elements (35S promotor and the NOS terminator) to full GM event specific analysis. The DAFM stated that they do not specify the scope of the analytical report which if done could improve the controls. The seed sampling demonstration observed was carried out appropriately by the DAFM officer who is ISTA accredited. Conclusions on controls of GMOs in seed and propagating material 47. Appropriate control measures are in place to verify that EU requirements regarding GMO presence in seeds are

Food Control Office Sealand/Funen Public 1 Audit visits Unintentional GMO release site 1 Food processor 1 Feed establishment 1 Seed establishment 1 1 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation, in particular Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. EU legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the latest amended version. Full references to the acts quoted in this report are given in Annex 1. 4 BACKGROUND This was the first audit carried out by the DG Health and Food Safety to Denmark on GMO issues. There was a previous audit DG(SANTE) 2015-7358 carried out in Denmark from 26 May 2015 to 4 June 2015 in order to evaluate the control systems for organic production and labelling of organic products which also covered GMO controls in organic feed and seed. 4.1 COUNTRY PROFILE The DG Health and Food Safety published a country profile for Denmark, which describes the control systems for food and feed safety, animal health, animal welfare and plant health including the organisation of official controls of GMOs. However, the latest country profile which can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=DK does not include the latest changes to the organisation of the control system, which changed as of June 2015, when the Ministry of Environment merged with the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries, to become the Ministry of Environment and Food of Denmark (MEFD). The reorganisation was completed on 30 September 2016. The current organisation of GMO controls is described in section 5.2 of this audit report. 4.2 AUTHORISED GMO PRODUCTS The list of the GM products authorised in the EU can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/dyna/gm_register/index_en.cfm The only GM crop authorised for cultivation in the EU is GM maize MON810, which was authorised for placing on the market and use in food and feed on the basis of Commission Decision 98/294/EC. 4.3 PRODUCTION AND TRADE DATA There is no commercial cultivation of GM crops in Denmark. Some field trials with GM plants have been carried out between 2011 and 2015 but at the time of the audit there were no active trials carried out. Denmark is a large producer of feed and imports the majority of protein ingredients. Based on data provided by the CA ­ which does not distinguish between GMO and non-GMO products 2 - Denmark imported in the period from 1 January 2014 to 6 September 2016 the commodities indicated in the table below. Table 1: Direct import of commodities to Denmark from 2014 to 2016 Commodity Volume (tonnes) Soya bean other than for sowing 8 458 Flour and meal of soya bean 418 Oilcake/pellets from soya bean oil 3 010 696 Rape seed (other than sowing) 1 295 Oilcake/pellets from rape 3 106 509 Oilcake/pellets from colza seeds 18 350 In addition to the imports in the table, negligible quantities were also imported of cotton seeds (18.6 t), corn gluten feed (0.3 t) and brewers grain (41.3 t). The vast majority of the imported volume commodities for feed (95 %) was oilcake/pellets from soya bean oil and oilcake/pellets from oilseed rape. The direct import of maize seeds for sowing in the period from 2014 to 2016 was very low (72.0 kg) and the same was the case for oilseed rape for sowing (2.6 t). Regarding rice and rice products from China imported under the Combined Nomenclature codes listed in Commission Implementing Decision 2011/884/EU, there were not many direct imports. From 2012 only three such consignments arrived, with a total weight of 44 t (see also chapter 5.3.5 below). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. Findings 1. The CAs informed the audit team that deliberate release of GMOs in Denmark is regulated by the Act on environment and gene technology No. 840 of 3 July 2015 and by the Act on cultivation of GM crops No. 695 of 9 June 2016. The Danish authorities stated that these two acts transpose Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council. They also stated that national legislation regarding plants, seed and propagating materials contains provisions on labelling of GM varieties. 3 2. The CAs stated that GMO cultivation is not currently taking place in Denmark and that they have opted for the restriction or prohibition of cultivation of GMO maize under Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council. The CA stated that in spite of the fact that no GM-crops have been marketed for cultivation, Denmark has a detailed regulation in place to secure co-existence between GM-crops and organic and conventional crops through two Administrative orders No. 177 of 28 February 2008 and No. 1559 of 11 December 2015. 3. The provisions of Commission Implementing Decision 2011/884/EU regarding rice and rice products from China are implemented by orders No. 141 of 22 February 2016 (for food) and No. 142 of 22 February 2016 (for feed). 4. National legislation also lays down provisions on sanctions and penalties applicable to infringements e.g. the legal basis for sanctions in cases of noncompliant food with respect to GMO are laid down in national order No. 641 of 13 May 2015 and for feed in order No. 722 of 14 June 2016. Conclusions on national legislation 5. National legislation is in place to implement the EU legislation relevant to the scope of this audit. 5.2 ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation and co-operation of Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 4(1), 4(2), 4(5) and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 4(4) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Findings 6. The MEFD has the overall responsibility for GMO policy, legislation and controls in all areas relevant to the scope of the audit. 7. Under the responsibility of the MEFD, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration (DVFA) is CA for controls on GMOs in food and conventional feed while the Danish AgriFish Agency (DAFA) is the CA for controls on GMO field trials and GMOs in seed and organic feed. The DVFA's laboratory in Ringsted is responsible for official GMO analysis of food, feed, seed and other plant material (see also section 5.3.7 below). A private control body carries out the official sampling of seed under the supervision of the DAFA. 8. The DAFA and the DVFA have written agreements in place concerning their cooperation on controls of organic food and feed (after primary production), organic 4 primary production, and import of food and feed including organic products. They have established a joint coordination group to discuss the division of competences as well as procedures. The group can also discuss the coordination of specific control cases and information sharing, if relevant for general considerations. The group meets once or twice a year, or on a need basis. Other authorities can be invited to the meetings depending on the agenda. 9. Within the DVFA there is a coordination group for GMO food control. Participants include the DVFA Chemistry and Food Quality Division (food and feed), the National Food Institute, the Technical University of Denmark, the DVFA laboratory and the DVFA food control offices (coordinators of GMO sampling). The group meets up to four times per year and discusses the control of GMOs in food products, especially the yearly sampling projects and results. 10. Within the DVFA there is also a coordination group for GMO feed control. Participants include the DVFA Chemistry and Food Quality Division (food and feed), the DVFA laboratory, the DVFA feed control offices and the DAFA (GMO control of organic feed). The group meets up to two times per year and discusses the control of GMOs in feed, including the yearly sampling projects and results. 11. Within the DAFA, the Environment and Biodiversity unit Plants Unit under the EU & Agriculture Department is responsible for GMO controls of field trials and seed, while the Administrative Area Control Unit under the Customers & Production Department is responsible for GMO controls of organic feed and seed. According to the DAFA, coordination of GMO controls in conventional and organic seed takes place on an informal basis. Conclusions on designation and co-operation of Competent Authorities 12. Designated CAs for GMO controls have a clear division of responsibilities and tasks. There are structures in place to ensure an effective co-operation between and within the CAs. 5.2.2 Resources for performance of official controls Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 13. The planned GMO controls for 2014, 2015 and 2016, until the time of the audit, were largely carried out as scheduled, while unforeseen tasks (e.g. follow-up of an unintended release of a GMO, see chapter 5.3.2) were also taken up effectively. This suggests that sufficient resources were available for these tasks. 5 14. Staff involved in GMO controls, are empowered to enter the premises of food, feed and seed business operators in order to carry out controls and to take samples. Where necessary, staff can impose corrective measures, impose administrative sanctions and refer serious infringements to the police. 15. The DAFA and the DVFA, have provided training pertinent to control tasks in general and, where necessary, on GMOs in particular. Samplers of seed, employed by a private control body, are required to be trained and certified according to international standards for the sampling of seed. DAFA staff responsible for the sampling of organic feed and seed have been trained by the DVFA. The DVFA samplers of food have started a training and certification programme on a voluntary basis.1 16. Staff of the DAFA and the DVFA interviewed by the audit team at central and local level, had the necessary knowledge to perform their tasks and had on-the-spot access to legislation and guidance relevant to GMO controls. Conclusions on resources for performance controls 17. Adequate resources have been made available to ensure that planned and unforeseen GMO controls are carried out. 5.2.3 Procedures for performance and reporting of control activities Legal requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 18. The DVFA has established written procedures and standardised reporting formats for controls of food and conventional feed. Control reports are stored in a database which is accessible on-line to control staff.2 19. The DAFA also has procedures in place for controls on the deliberate release of GMOs and the sampling of seed and organic feed. 20. The DVFA has written agreements (in so-called "sampling project plans") between the DVFA Chemistry and Food Quality Division and the DVFA laboratory, stipulating inter alia, test requirements and turnaround times. The DAFA has a written agreement only on financial matters with the DVFA laboratory. 1 In their response to the draft report the Competent authority noted that the DVFA samplers of food and feed are now enrolled in a training programme aiming at a nationwide inclusion of sampling in the ISO 17025 accreditation of the DVFA laboratory quality management system.
