text: In their response to the draft report the Competent authority noted that as regards control reports on food, these are made public on www.findsmiley.dk. 6 21. The audit team reviewed control reports which were drawn up following controls and sampling of food, feed and seed. The reports were comprehensive in relation to the scope of the control activity. Conclusions on procedures for performance and reporting of control activities 22. Documented procedures for the performance of GMO controls and reporting are in place. 5.2.4 Planning of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Chapter I of Commission Recommendation 2004/787/EC. Findings 23. The DVFA has a corporate policy on risk based controls. The GMO controls in food (except for rice and rice products from China) and conventional feed are consequently subject to a risk analysis. Annual control numbers are set by the DVFA at central level and distributed across the local offices. The selection of locations where a control is carried out and samples taken, is at the discretion of the local DVFA office. Individual food and feed business operator's control history is taken into consideration when planning controls. 24. Controls in food have focussed on the presence of GMOs in unlabelled products containing for example maize, soya bean, rice, linseed or papaya. The controls have shifted from large producers and retailers towards smaller food business operators. During four months of the year no sampling is scheduled in order to optimise the use of the laboratory's capacity for analysis of other type of samples (e.g. for seed potato production). This practice has, however, the potential to weaken the effectiveness of the controls because the representativeness of sampling is not fully achieved. 25. Controls on GMOs in conventional feed were mainly aimed at verifying the correctness of labelling, in feed labelled as non-GM and in GM labelled feed (absence of GMO which would be considered a labelling infringement), but also included checks for the presence of unauthorised GMOs in feed. 26. In previous years the controls on GMOs in organic feed had a strong focus on the imported raw materials from third countries. Only a small number of samples were taken from compound feed in Danish feed mills. Around 10 % of samples were taken of the domestically produced organic feed and feed products originating from Member States where the cultivation of GM crops takes place. However, the Danish CAs have started to implement their action plan in response to the shortcomings identified in Report DG(SANTE)/2015-7358 of the audit in order to evaluate the control systems for 7 organic production and labelling of organic products. This plan includes sampling in all stages of production, preparation and distribution of organic products. 27. Controls on GMOs in seed were planned after an unintended release of GM rape seed and only became fully effective in 2016. Sampling was based on a risk assessment and focussed on the larger seed businesses which cover the vast majority of trade and the GMO relevant crops (e.g. rape seed, maize and lucerne). However, a potential risk from smaller seed traders has not been taken into account, as focus has been on covering the largest volume of seed produced. 28. The DAFA unit responsible for organic production has not planned any sampling of organic seed. However, the DAFA unit responsible for conventional seed controls sampled 2 out of 30 seed samples from organic seed. 29. Controls on GM rice and rice products from China follow the applicable EU legislation (see chapter 5.3.5 below). 30. For GMO field trials under deliberate release into the environment, the DAFA planning of controls take into account the characteristics of the crop and the conditions of the consent. Conclusions on planning of official controls 31. The planning of GMO controls is generally risk based and fit for purpose. 32. The effectiveness of controls on seed is weakened due to the exclusion of smaller seed traders. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Controls of the authorised deliberate release of GMOs Legal requirements Articles 4(1) and 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Findings 33. The DAFA informed the audit team that there were three GMO field trials authorised since 2011 (GM maize, GM sugar beet and GM barley), but that at the time of the audit, there were no active GM field trials in place. 34. The CA performs official controls of trials two times during the growing season, at the time of sowing and harvesting. The consent holder must perform own checks and keep a monitoring log of cultivation and must report to the CA twice a year and produce a final report after the trial is completed. The consent holder is also obliged to monitor the volunteer plants for a period of four years after the last growing season of the trial or after the last GM plants are identified in the field and report the results to the DAFA. 8 The DAFA inspectors also carry out on-the-spot visits during the said monitoring period. 35. An authorised GM maize trial in 2011 has never been initiated and has ended with the consent holder's final report. A field trial with GM sugar beet from 2011 ended in 2015 with the production of the final report. The CA has derogated the consent holder from the regular post-trial monitoring because the risk has been considered low. 36. A GM spring barley field trial was approved in 2012 with a proposed period of deliberate release until 2016. However, the consent holder cultivated barley only in two growing seasons in 2012 and 2013. The consent holder produced the monitoring reports for the growing season 2014 and 2015 and produced a final report in June 2016. 37. In October 2016 the DAFA inspected the GM barley field trial site and found a small number (some 18) of barley plants along the rim of the trial plot. Plants were sampled for GMO analysis which was still ongoing at the time of the audit. The DAFA asked the Danish Centre for Food and Agriculture for scientific advice and was awaiting their recommendations for any further action. In any case, the trial plots are to be monitored for the next four years (until 2020) and treated according to the action plan. 38. The audit team checked the documentation for the controls of the GM barley field trial and noted that: The consent holder kept the monitoring log of cultivation for the 2012 and 2013 growing season as required. The final report indicated that a few barley seedlings had germinated in 2014, which were removed and destroyed. No volunteer plants were detected on the trial plot in 2015 and not in 2016 until June. Official field inspections were carried out by the CA at sowing and harvesting time of the trial. Conclusions on controls of the deliberate release of the GMOs 39. There is an adequate control system in place regarding GMO field trials which ensures that the conditions of authorisations are met and that any potential adverse effect on the environment is mitigated. 5.3.2 Controls of the unauthorised release of GMOs Legal requirements Articles 4(1) and 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Articles 4(2) and 16(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. 9 Findings 40. The DAFA informed the audit team that at the end of October 2015 they had received information from another Member State about the unintentional presence of GM oilseed rape OXY-235, which is not authorised in the EU, in a seed lot of conventional winter oilseed rape HRC-918. The DAFA was informed also that contaminated HRC-918 had been sown in late August 2015 in Denmark on three small trial plots (in total of approximately 126 m2) to assess the agronomic value of the variety. The DAFA immediately sought scientific advice from the Danish Centre for Food and Agriculture on the most appropriate measures to handle this situation. After visiting the site, in the beginning of November 2015, the DAFA issued an immediate enforcement notification to the company conducting the trials, ordering the immediate destruction of the plants in the three plots (spraying with glyphosate). Plots were thereafter to lie fallow and be monitored during the 2016 growing season. The DAFA was also informed by the trial performer that all the received seed of that variety had been sown. All plants from the three trial plots were sampled for GMO analysis before destruction and the results confirmed the presence of 0.20 to 0.39 % of OXY-235 plants on each of the three plots. The DAFA inspection of the site in December 2015 verified the destruction of the plants. 41. In May 2016 the DAFA issued an enforcement notification for the further treatment and monitoring of the affected trial plots. During the monitoring in 2016 no germinating oilseed rape was observed. At the end of August 2016 all three trial plots were steam treated under DAFA supervision to destroy remaining seed in the topsoil. However, the DAFA inspection in the middle of September confirmed that the steam treatment had not been 100 % effective because some oilseed rape seedlings occurred on one treated plot. Destruction of these plants with herbicide was carried out immediately and monitoring was continuing. At the time of the audit, the DAFA was developing an action plan for the future treatment (e.g. repeated steam treatment) and monitoring of the affected plots. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules, Official Journal L 165, 30.4.2004, pages 1 to 141, corrected and re-published in OJ L 191, 28.5.2004, pages 1 to 52. 2 2006/677/EC: Commission Decision of 29 September 2006 setting out the guidelines laying down criteria for the conduct of audits under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council on official controls to verify compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules. Official Journal L 278, 10.10.2006, pp15 to 23. 1 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation and, in particular Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Full EU legal references are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the latest amended version. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 PREVIOUS AUDITS Detailed information on the structure and organisation of the Estonia competent authorities can be found in the Country Profile for Estonia at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=EE DG Health and Food Safety has carried out numerous inspections and audits in Estonia, the reports of which can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/ audit_reports/index.cfm While the topic of the current audit has not been the specific objective of any previous audit, the subject has been considered within the scope of numerous sectorial audits carried out since 2006 as well as the general audit carried out in 2008-2009 (reference number DG(SANCO)/2009-8600). At the time of writing, there were no open recommendations to Estonia in relation to the application of Article 4(6). 4.2 CONTEXT: ARTICLE 4(6) OF REGULATION (EC) NO 882/2004 The requirements laid down in Article 4(6) of regulation (EC) No 882/2004, that: Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out, and shall take appropriate measures in the light of their results, to ensure that they are achieving the objectives of this Regulation. These audits shall be subject to independent scrutiny and shall be carried out in a transparent manner should be read together with the definition of Article 2(6) laid down in the same Regulation: "Audit" means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives. Further guidance on certain aspects of the requirement and definition is provided in Commission Decision 2006/677/EC. In particular, the guidelines in the Annex to this Decision provide information on aspects to be considered when ensuring that the audit process is systematic, transparent, independent and subject to independent scrutiny. In 2 addition, guiding principles in relation to compliance with planned arrangements, effective implementation of arrangements and their suitability to achieve objectives are provided. Guidance is also provided in relation to audit reporting, follow-up of the audit outcome, audit review and dissemination of best practice, resources and auditor competence. As reflected in the recitals of the decision: "The guidelines are not binding but serve to provide useful guidance to the Member States in the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004". The NAS Network is a network of officials (auditors) from national competent authorities, responsible for the performance of audits of official control systems as provided for by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Network meets regularly, under the chairmanship of, and facilitated by, DG Health and Food Safety to exchange experiences in implementing national audit systems on official control activities. During the course of these exchanges; discussions, workshops etc. good principles and practices are identified and agreed by the network. To enable dissemination of information the Network, working in plenary session and through sub-groups, consolidate agreed principles and good practices on specific topics into Network Reference Documents. In relation to NAS, at the time of this audit the NAS Network has produced the following Network Reference Documents: Risk Based Planning for Audits of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1 Independence and Independent Scrutiny - Feb 2014 ­ Version 1 Auditing Effectiveness of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1 Audit Evidence ­ October 2015 ­ Version 1 These documents may be used as reference documents; however, they do not constitute an audit standard and are not legally binding. The network document on risk-based planning for audits of official control systems clarifies what is the consensus of audit experts on the objectives of Article 4(6): The main objectives of audits as laid down in Article 4(6) are: To verify: CA's compliance with general and specific control requirements of feed and food law, plant health, animal health and welfare rules. Compliance of official controls with planned arrangements at a national level, which may include: Control plans of any kind (MANCP, business-, operational-, control-, monitoring- plan etc.) with the purpose of giving effect to legal requirements. Policies, strategies, procedures, guidelines. 3 To evaluate: Suitability of the planned arrangements in achieving the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Effectiveness and consistency of the implementation of planned arrangements i.e. the capability to deliver the planned outcomes. Whether enforcement measures are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. To identify: Areas for improvement in the CA control and management systems. Audits may also play a supportive role in risk identification and analysis. The network document "auditing effectiveness of official control systems" explains the audit experts' common understanding of the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004: Following from the definition of effectiveness, objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 have to be identified and they should be used as audit criteria. Within this document and for the purposes of assisting in auditing effectiveness according to Article 4(6), the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are considered to be, but not limited to: "To ensure high quality of official controls..." (from preamble 14) "...in verifying compliance with legal requirements" (from preamble 6, Article 1) Ensuring implies application of the PDCA cycle: Quality consists of: 4 Uniformity of controls and decisions (from preambles 12 and 14). Consistency of controls (from preamble 14). Effective risk-based targeting of controls (Article 3.1). Reliable detection of non-compliance. Turning non-compliance into compliance, when detected (Articles 54, 55). The network document "risk-based planning of audits on official controls" explains what is the audit experts' common understanding of the objectives of risk-based planning: The main objective of risk-based planning of audit programmes is to contribute to consumer safety, animal health and welfare, plant health and increase stakeholder confidence in effective and efficient use of resources. This is achieved by ensuring that: Audit universe(s) do not overlook any relevant areas; Planning processes are able to identify and categorise main risks appropriately; The whole process is subject to regular review; and Audit bodies (in case there are several) coordinate their planning processes. 4.3 METHODOLOGY The evaluation process consisted of: an initial desk study phase in which the relevant information already available in DG Health and Food Safety was collated and analysed. This included the Estonia Multi-Annual National Control Plan and associated Annual Reports, the Country Profile of Estonia and sectorial audit reports; examination of certain documentation provided by the CA prior to the audit; and meetings with the Competent Authorities i.e. Ministry of Rural Affairs, Ministry of Social Affairs, Ministry of Finance and Veterinary and Food Board. During these meetings, the audit team evaluated arrangements in place and verified their application through examination of a variety of evidence, including documentation of the programme development and for a number of audits. Observing the performance of individual auditors was not included in the scope of this audit as the audit team considered that the effectiveness of an individual audit can be better judged in the context of relevant DG Health and Food Safety sectorial audits. The evaluation focussed particularly on those elements, which the audit team considered essential to ensure the audit bodies can produce reliable audit results, with adequate coverage of official controls, to give assurance that the objectives of 882/2004 are being met: Responsibilities for the implementation of Article 4(6); Status and reporting lines of auditing bodies/units; Arrangements for independent scrutiny; 5 Procedures for the selection of auditors and management of auditor competence; Procedures for the development of audit programmes, with particular attention on how an adequate coverage of the audit/risk universe is ensured; Planning, conduct and reporting of audits, including the approach to auditing the suitability of arrangements in place for official controls to achieve the objectives of the Regulation; Follow-up of audit recommendations including the system in place for corrective action in cases where problems are identified during the audit activities; and How and to what extent transparency is ensured. In addition, the audit team gathered information on particular challenges faced by the CCA when implementing Article 4(6). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.1.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states, that "Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out......" Article 2(6) of the same Regulation defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." Article 4(3) of the Regulation states that "When a Member State confers the competence to carry out official controls on an authority or authorities other than a central competent authority, in particular those at regional or local level, efficient and effective coordination shall be ensured between all the competent authorities involved, including where appropriate in the field of environmental and health protection." In section 5.1 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Systematic' and, in particular, it states that "Where more than one audit programme is envisaged within a Member State, steps should be taken to ensure that such programmes are effectively coordinated, so as to ensure a seamless audit process across the relevant competent authorities. The audit programme(s) should also cover all relevant levels of the competent authority's hierarchy." In section 5.3 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Independence': "Audit bodies should be free from any commercial, financial, hierarchical, political or other pressures that might affect their judgment or the outcome of the audit process. The audit system, audit body and auditors should be independent of the activity being audited and free from bias and conflicts of interest. Auditors should not audit areas or activities for which they have direct responsibility. 6 All relevant competent authorities should introduce safeguards to ensure that responsibility and accountability for audit and control activities, such as the management and supervision of official control systems, are kept sufficiently distinct. Where the audit team makes recommendations for corrective and preventive action, the auditee should choose the methods to be applied for such action. Active audit team involvement in follow-up should be limited to assessing the suitability of the action plan and the effectiveness of the corrective and preventive action. Auditees should not be in a position to impede the audit programme, findings or conclusions. They should be consulted on the draft report and their comments should be considered by the audit body. Where appropriate, those comments should be taken into account in a transparent manner. The following points may help ensure that the audit process safeguards the independence of both the audit body and the audit team: -- a clear, documented mandate affording adequate power to conduct the audits should be provided, -- neither the audit body nor the audit team should be involved in managing or supervising the control systems being audited, -- for external audits, the audit body and audit team should be external to, and independent of, the organisational hierarchy of the auditee, -- for internal audits, the following general principles should apply to ensure the process is independent and transparent: -- the audit body and audit team should be appointed by top management, -- the audit body and/or the audit team should report to top management, -- a check should be carried out to ensure no conflict of interest exists for either the audit body or the audit team. Independent audit bodies should be external to or separate from the management of audited activities. Internal audit bodies should report to the most senior management within the organisational structure. Where technical expertise required for the audit is available only within a competent authority, measures should be taken to ensure the audit team remains independent. Where control activities are organised on a regional basis, technical specialists could be exchanged in order to ensure they are independent." 5.1.2 Findings 5.1.2.1 Responsibility for co-ordination of official controls 1. The distribution of control areas between the four main ministries is broadly described in Figure 2 above. 5.1.2.2 Responsibility for audits of official controls 5. Every ministry has its own internal audit unit (IAD), which is in charge of auditing also areas other than those falling within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. An external contractor is carrying out Article 4(6) audits on VFB, while other Competent Authorities under MoRA all have internal audit arrangements. 6. Each IAD is responsible for their own annual planning and the IAD of MoRA is in charge of overseeing that all of the main audit areas are covered over a 5-year period. 7. In practice ­ and taking into account the small size of the relevant audit units ­ this coordination is rather informal and consists mainly of meetings and personal contacts. 8. An important element of coordination is that all audit bodies work on the basis of a common legal basis (Auditors' activities Act and General rules for internal audit) and according to the International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF) of the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) (hereafter: IIA standard)3. This is to ensure high quality of audits and consistent approach across audit bodies. 9. Ministry of Finance plays an important role in coordination: it provides for an external assessment of other ministries' IAD and ensures that they all conform to the IIA standard. 10. The internal audit activities are reflected effectively and accurately in the Annual Report (on the implementation of multiannual national control plan), which gives a good overview across audit bodies and also detailed information on the main outcomes of each audit. 11. The audit team met four audit bodies: IADs of Ministry of Rural Affairs (MoRA), Ministry of Finance (MoF), Ministry of Social Affairs (MoSA) and the external contractor responsible for auditing the Veterinary and Food Board (VFB). All of these bodies had a good and consistent understanding of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requirements, in particular Article 4(6) and subsequent guidelines and network documents. The NAS Network is a network of officials (auditors) from national competent authorities, responsible for the performance of audits of official control systems as provided for by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Network meets regularly, under the chairmanship of, and facilitated by, DG SANTE Directorate F to exchange experiences in implementing national audit systems on official control activities. During the course of these exchanges; discussions, workshops etc. good principles and practices are identified and agreed by the network. To enable dissemination of information, the Network, working in plenary session and through sub-groups, facilitated by the DG SANTE Directorate F, consolidate agreed principles and good practices on specific topics into Network Reference Documents. In relation to National Audit System (NAS), at the time of this audit the NAS Network has produced the following Network Reference Documents: Risk Based Planning for Audits of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1 Independence and Independent Scrutiny - February 2014 ­ Version 1 Auditing Effectiveness of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1 Audit evidence - October 2015 ­ Version 1 These documents may be used as reference documents; however, they do not constitute an audit standard and are not legally binding. 4.3 METHODOLOGY The evaluation process of the current audit consisted of: an initial desk study phase in which the relevant information already available to the Commission Services was collated and analysed. This included the Polish Multi-Annual National Control Plan and associated Annual Reports, the Country Profile of Poland and DG SANTE Directorate F sector-specific audit reports; examination of certain documentation provided by the competent authorities prior to the audit; and meetings with the competent authorities responsible for audits under Article 4(6). 3 The audit team evaluated arrangements in place and verified their application through examination of a variety of evidence, including documentation of the audit programme development and its implementation. Observing the performance of individual auditors during audits was not included in the scope as the audit team considered that the effectiveness of an individual audit can be better judged by the sectoral Units' auditors in the context of relevant sector-specific audits. The evaluation focused particularly on those elements which the audit team considered essential to ensure the audit bodies can produce reliable audit results, with adequate coverage of official controls, to give assurance that the objectives of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 are being met: Responsibilities for the implementation of Article 4(6); Status and reporting lines of auditing bodies/units; Arrangements for independent scrutiny; Procedures for the selection of auditors and management of auditor competence; Procedures for the development of audit programmes, with particular attention on how an adequate coverage of the audit/risk universe is ensured; Planning, conduct and reporting of audits, including the approach to auditing the suitability of arrangements in place for official controls to achieve the objectives of the Regulation; Follow-up of audit recommendations including the system in place for corrective action in cases where problems are identified during the audit activities; and How and to what extent transparency is ensured. In addition, the audit team gathered information on particular challenges faced by the competent authorities when implementing Article 4(6). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements and other audit criteria Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states, that "Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out......" Article 2(6) of the same Regulation defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." 4 Article 4(3) of the Regulation states that "When a Member State confers the competence to carry out official controls on an authority or authorities other than a central competent authority, in particular those at regional or local level, efficient and effective coordination shall be ensured between all the competent authorities involved, including where appropriate in the field of environmental and health protection." Findings 1. Within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the Veterinary Inspection (VI) is responsible for official controls on animal health and welfare, food of animal origin, imports of live animals and products of animal origin, animal by-products, veterinary medicine products, residues and production of animal feed. The State Sanitary Inspection (SSI) is the competent authority responsible for official controls related to food hygiene, imports of food of plant origin and partially for animal by-products. The audit system within the context of official controls under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 comprises mainly two internal audit functions in the two aforementioned competent authorities: the Audit Department of the Control Office of GVI (GVI-CO) and the department for Food and Nutrition Safety of GSI (GSI-DFNS)

The CAs have established audit systems which are intended to achieve the objectives of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Responsibilities for carrying out audits on official controls have been clearly allocated, ensuring the proper functioning of the audit systems. 5.2 AUDIT ARRANGEMENTS 5.2.1 Independence Legal requirements and other audit criteria Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." In section 5.3 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on `independence', including: "Audit bodies should be free from any commercial, financial, hierarchical, political or other pressures that might affect their judgment or the outcome of the audit process. The audit system, audit body and auditors should be independent of the activity being audited and free from bias and conflicts of interest. Auditors should not audit areas or activities for which they have direct responsibility. All relevant competent authorities should introduce safeguards to ensure that responsibility and accountability for audit and control activities, such as the management and supervision of official control systems, are kept sufficiently distinct." In addition, the NAS Network Reference Document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny provides additional guidance to Member States on threats to independence and mitigating measures. Findings

The audit instructions of both authorities provide the basis for the independence of the audit system and of the auditors. Both instructions incorporate the definition of audit as provided in Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and in Decision 2006/677/EC.

GVI-CO, whose Director is the Chief Veterinary Officer's representative on matters relating to the Veterinary Inspection Audit, reports directly to the Chief Veterinary Officer. At the voivodship level each unit has at least one auditor that reports to the competent (voivodship) veterinary officer. Auditors at all levels are assigned exclusively to audit-specific activities (officials in GVI-CO perform verification activities as well) and are not involved in the organisation or performance of official controls. 6 9. All auditors in SSI are officials that are actively involved in the organisation and performance of official controls. The GSI-DFNS audit instruction provides for taking steps during the audit planning stage to ensure the independence of the audit teams. In this regard, auditors should not carry out audits of areas or activities for which they have direct responsibility. 10. The CAs discussed the challenge posed by the selection and sourcing of expertise while still ensuring the independence of the audit team (avoiding a "familiarity risk"). For GVI-CO the authority considers the centralisation of the audit function as a means of mitigating familiarity risk that could be faced by the auditors in the voivodship (regional) veterinary inspectorates (there is one auditor in most regions). In addition, the authority examines the option of establishing the administrative framework in such a way that an auditor can be assigned to audit in a different voivodship than the one he/she is working for. Conclusions on independence 11. The CAs have put in place arrangements to ensure the independence of the audit process at an organisational and individual auditor level contributing to the credibility and reliability of audit activities. 5.2.2 Independent scrutiny Legal requirements and other audit criteria Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that the audits "shall be subject to independent scrutiny". In section 5.4 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Independent Scrutiny of the Audit Process': "In order to check whether it is achieving its objectives, the audit process should be subject to scrutiny by an independent person or body. Such independent person or body should have sufficient authority, expertise and resources to carry out this task effectively. The approaches to independent scrutiny may vary, depending on the activity or the competent authority. Where a body or a committee has been established with a view to independent scrutiny of the audit process, one or more independent persons should be members of such body or committee. Such independent persons should have access to the audit process and be empowered to contribute fully to it. Action should be taken to remedy any shortcomings identified in the audit process by the independent person or body." Findings 12. Neither GVI-CO nor GSI-DFNS have any arrangements in place to perform independent scrutiny of the audit process contrary to the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 7 13. The competent authorities discussed some examples of external assessments that cover the audit functions within the context of administrative review and/or ISO assessments. However, the audit activities form a minor component of these assessments and focus rather on examining the administrative arrangements of the covered departments than the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on independent scrutiny 14. The competent authorities have not put in place arrangements to ensure the independent scrutiny of the audit process which means that they cannot avail of external inputs for promoting continuous improvement of the audit process to ensure that the audit process is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence Legal requirements and other audit criteria Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex to Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 8 Findings 15. Within the VI there are currently two auditors at the central level (GVI) and 23 in the VVI, with at least one auditor in each Voivodship Veterinary Inspectorate. Most have been trained to ISO 19011/2002 standard and training is also ongoing and may include attendance at BTSF sessions for auditing. In addition, practical audit exercises are carried out as part of the training of the auditors and knowledge is shared during the coordination meetings held at least twice per year (see finding 4). 16. The main selection criteria for auditors at both central and voivodship level require candidates to have been an official veterinarian with 4-5 years working experience as an official inspector. Aspects of personality and character are also considered as well as knowledge of a second language (preferably English). At the regional (voivodship) level the competent regional veterinary officers are responsible for the recruitment of the auditors. 17. GSI-DFNS: There are eight auditors at the central level, and 197 auditors at the regional level. Approximately 15% of the working time of auditors is dedicated to audit-related activities. All auditors are trained to ISO 9001:2009 and 19011/2002 standards, either directly or cascading. There is also an induction course in place to facilitate the integration of the newcomers in the auditor's role and tasks. 18. The internal auditors met during the audit demonstrated a sufficient level of audit expertise as regards knowledge of audit principles and techniques. 19. Audit instructions of both authorities foresee the possibility of using technical expertise when it is needed. 20. GVI-CO has not used external experts in their audits in the last three years. The central level audits are performed by two auditors and the regional (voivodship) audits are performed in most cases by one auditor. The competent authority acknowledged that there might be a potential compromise in the performance of the audit when the audit team consists of one auditor. 21. GSI-DFNS rarely uses external experts in their audits. Audits at all levels are performed by at least two auditors. In recent years there was a case of an audit in an official laboratory in which an external expert joined the audit team. Audits at official laboratories are generally carried out by experts from national reference laboratories. Conclusions on auditor competence 22. The members of staff involved in the audit process have sufficient auditing competence to perform their duties. The lack of sourcing of external expertise may limit the capability of the audit function to identify and properly assess technical deficiencies and underlying causes for deficiencies in the performance of the official controls, especially in particularly complicated areas of the official controls.

Article 2(6) of the same Regulation defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." 5.1.2 Findings 5.1.2.1 Responsibility for performance of official controls 1. For full details of the division of all relevant competences between all involved Competent Authorities, see the country profile for Austria at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=AT 4 2. In summary, official controls are organised as follows: The BMGF and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water Management (BMLFUW) are the main federal authorities in the areas of food and feed safety, animal health and plant health. The federal level is responsible for legislation on food and feed safety, animal health, animal welfare and plant health and coordinates the Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP: MIK ­ Mehrjähriger Integrierter Kontrollplan). Implementation of legislation falls either under the responsibility of the relevant competent Federal Ministers itself or the Länder. In the case of indirect administration, the federal level can issue instructions e.g. in the form of Decrees (e.g. animal health and food safety), which is not the case for direct administration (e.g. animal welfare). The Länder are in most sectors exclusively responsible for implementing legislation. The Länder are also responsible for the preparation of implementing provisions and the performance of controls on the use of PPPs. The responsibility of the federal level is limited to the preparation of the PPP framework law. There is no harmonised system for controls on the use of PPPs across the Länder. The relevant competent Federal Ministers are in charge of import controls, controls on the commercial production of feed and marketing of plant protection products. The competent body for providing scientific advice and laboratory services is the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES). The Federal Office for Food Safety (BAES) was established to enable the execution, as the authority of first instance, of laws for agricultural production such as for example for controls on the commercial production and marketing of seed and feedingstuffs and control on the marketing of PPPs. Controls are carried out by AGES staff which are permanently allocated to this task. At Länder level, control responsibilities are shared between the Veterinary Services, the Food Inspectorates and Plant Protection Services of the Länder. 5.1.2.2 Responsibility for audits of official controls Audit system for issues related to veterinary controls and food safety (ASVF) 3. For those areas where the national legislation entrusts the Länder with the responsibilities for controls, either through 'indirect' or 'direct' administrative functions, the Länder are also responsible for the organisation of audits, including food safety and veterinary controls. 4. In 2005 a nationwide audit system was established for food safety and in 2009 for all aspects of veterinary controls. 5 5. In 2010 the BMGF department "Koordination MIK und AGES" (Stabstelle) was entrusted with the independent scrutiny. At the time of the DG SANTE audit the Stabsstelle had the following tasks: Development and updating of the 'Orientierungsmatrix'. This is a table which provides, based on expert opinions, risk-based guidance for the preparation of the annual audit programmes by the audit bodies. Monitoring of the audit programme. Elaboration of and keeping up-dating the audit handbook. Preparation of the annual audit evaluation report. 6. The annual audit programme, audit procedures and checklists are developed by audit specific working groups which are, according to the BMGF, the audit bodies. In the case of food safety the working group for quality management (AG-QM), which is chaired by a representative from one of the Länder, is the audit body and in the case of veterinary controls it is the steering group (Steuerungsgruppe), chaired by a representative from the BMGF. 7. The representatives of the Länder are informed about the audit process at dedicated meetings several times a year. The audit system, the audit programme and any changes including procedures and checklists are endorsed by the joint conference of the heads of the food safety and veterinary departments of the Länder, with the exception of the 'Orientierungsmatrix' which is only brought to the attention of the joint conference. 8. The steering group is assisted by technical working groups, in particular with regard to the elaboration of sector specific audit check lists. 9. The Stabstelle is supported by the working group 'audits' (AG Audit) which consists of two nominated experts of the Länder from each of the sectors (veterinary and food safety), representatives from the BMLFUW and the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES) and the chairpersons of the two audit working groups. 10. The audits are performed by a pool of auditors from the Länder. 11. Auditors from several Länder and representatives of CAs met in two Länder stated that the ASVF has a high level of acceptance and also mentioned the good cooperation between the Stabstelle and the Länder. Use of PPPs 12. The DG SANTE audit visited two Länder and noted that one of these Länder did not have an audit system for official controls on the use of PPPs in place at all. The other Land carried out internal audits in relation to processes defined within their QM system, which covered the registration of PPP users, but no other aspect of PPP controls. The federal level does not have an overview of the audit activities of the Länder with regard to controls on the use of PPPs. 6 Control areas at federal level 13. The activities of the BMGF, which for most control areas issues instructions and guidelines and monitors the implementation of controls, are not subject to any audit. 14. The BMGF performs annual audits at frontier posts with the aim of verifying that import controls are carried out in compliance with EU provisions. These types of audits follow detailed checklists covering the border control facilities, control procedures and controls. In 2014 an external audit by an expert from another MS was carried out, which followed the same checklists. Given that BMGF issues instructions also for import controls, there is a risk of self-review and in particular if the audits would cover aspects of 'suitability of the planned arrangements'. 15. For control areas for which the BAES is responsible, the AGES was entrusted with the organisation of internal audits. Until 2015 AGES performed internal audits in the context of the accreditation to ISO 17020 which covered these sectors. As a result of the revision of the ISO 17020 AGES could not renew the accreditation to this standard. This, together with changes concerning the organisation of BAES triggered the establishment of the new audit system. This new audit system was, at the time of the DG SANTE audit, not yet fully operational, but audit arrangements were in an advanced stage of development. It was planned to carry out the first audits in the second semester 2016. Conclusions 16. Responsibility for auditing official controls are clearly allocated, with two exceptions: Auditing arrangements are not defined for controls on the use of plant protection products falling under the scope of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004. The activities of the BMGF which are directly related to official controls including the planning of controls, monitoring the implementation of controls and issuing instructions for controls are not subject to any audits. 17. An audit system for feed controls at federal level was in an advanced stage of preparation but had not yet been implemented. 5.2 AUDIT ARRANGEMENTS 5.2.1 Independence 5.2.1.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." 7 In section 5.3 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on `independence', including: "Audit bodies should be free from any commercial, financial, hierarchical, political or other pressures that might affect their judgment or the outcome of the audit process. The audit system, audit body and auditors should be independent of the activity being audited and free from bias and conflicts of interest. Auditors should not audit areas or activities for which they have direct responsibility. All relevant competent authorities should introduce safeguards to ensure that responsibility and accountability for audit and control activities, such as the management and supervision of official control systems, are kept sufficiently distinct." In addition, the NAS Network Reference Document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny provides additional guidance to Member States on threats to independence and mitigating measures. 5.2.1.2 Findings 18. The two working groups (AG-QM and Steering Groups) have been mandated by the joint conference of the provincial heads of the veterinary and food safety services to act as audit bodies. 19. The audit documents including the audit handbook have been approved by the joint conference of the heads of the provincial veterinary and food safety services. The audit handbook defines the conditions that auditors have to fulfil, inter alia, independence of the auditors. According to the audit arrangements auditors are not allowed to perform audits in the Land where they are employed. 20. All auditors met showed a clear understanding of potential risks related to impartiality and conflicts of interests. They stated that the Austrian public service law provides guarantees regarding impartiality and conflict of interest. All auditors met confirmed that their management supports and respects their work as independent auditors for the ASVF. 21. The audit system operated by AGES in relation to controls carried out by BAES is based on a service level agreement and arrangements had been put in place to ensure the independence of the audit body and the auditors. 22. The AGES auditors are not involved in BAES control activities, although BAES is using staff employed by AGES for the performance of the controls. 23. The AGES is a private, state-owned company and BAES cannot give instructions to AGES. 24. In the case of the veterinary audits and AGES audits the auditors have to sign a declaration that they are free from interest of conflicts and are impartial. Although this is not based on legal provisions, it was considered by the steering group and AGES as a 8 useful instrument to remind auditors prior to the start of the audit to check whether there are potential threats regarding this matter. 25. In the case of audits of import controls at frontier posts, the auditor who is working at the BMGF, is also involved in the organisation of the import control system including drafting import control procedures and instructions. Although this has an advantage when auditing compliance with planned arrangements, there would be a risk of 'self- review' when auditing the suitability of the planned arrangements. However, 'suitability' was not covered by the audit system for import controls at the time of the DG SANTE audit. Conclusions 26. Sufficient arrangements are in place to ensure independence of the audit bodies and the auditors. Auditors demonstrated a good understanding of threats to impartiality and of conflict of interests. 5.2.2 Independent scrutiny 5.2.2.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that the audits "shall be subject to independent scrutiny". In section 5.4 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on the `Independent Scrutiny of the Audit Process': "In order to check whether it is achieving its objectives, the audit process should be subject to scrutiny by an independent person or body. Such independent person or body should have sufficient authority, expertise and resources to carry out this task effectively. The approaches to independent scrutiny may vary, depending on the activity or the competent authority. Designation of Competent Authorities

There are two CAs involved in the PPP authorisation process, MAPAMA and MSSSI. Within MAPAMA, there are two General Directorates dealing with PPPs, DGSPA and the General Directorate of Quality and Environmental Evaluation and Nature 2 In their response to the draft report, the Competent Authority noted that the General Directorate for the Treasury is under the aegis of the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness of the Government of Spain. 3 In their response to the draft report, the Competent Authority MSSSI noted that direct assigned revenue of fees and charges could contribute to compliance with the provisions of Article 75(3) of the Regulation to ensure that CA have a sufficient number of suitable qualified and experienced staff so that the obligations laid down in the Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 are carried out efficiently and effectively. 5 (DGCEAMN). DGSPA is responsible for the overall co-ordination of the process, communication with applicants, compiling the Draft Registration Reports (DRRs), maintaining the official product register and dealing with PTPs and emergency authorisation applications. DGCEAMN is responsible for classifying and labelling checks of all PPPs for their environmental properties, and for conducting an environmental evaluation on MR applications. The General Directorate for Public Health, Quality and Innovation (DGSPCI) of the MSSSI is responsible for evaluations linked to toxicology and Operator Exposure (OpEx) in all cases, except for risk management measures related to re-authorisations that are not evaluated under Regulation 1107/2009, in which case DGSPA is responsible for evaluating OpEx.

INIA is a unit under the aegis of the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness and contributes to the authorisation processes under two different frameworks. Under specific management commissions awarded by MAPAMA, INIA conducts different type of evaluations for applications received under the Directive 91/414/EEC, and under Royal Decree 971/2014 INIA has been designated as the Independent Assessment Body to conduct evaluations under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 relating to zRMS and cMS applications in the areas for which it is responsible, i.e. product identity, physical and chemical properties, analytical methods, residues, environmental fate, ecotoxicology and efficacy. Tragsatec is a public, state-owned company regulated by Royal Legislative Decree 3/2011, which DGSPA have appointed to conduct evaluations covering all these areas by specific management commissions, except analytical methods, for all other types of applications, and in these cases, DGSPA is responsible for evaluation of analytical methods.

DGSPA are responsible for risk management in all areas based on the evaluation conducted, and risk management measures proposed, by DGSPCI, DGCEAMN, INIA or Tragsatec. DGSPA can legally amend or overrule the risk mitigation measures deemed appropriate by these entities in their risk assessments. DGSPA stated that DGSPCI and DGCEAMN recommendations are always accepted and included in the proposals for authorisation of the products. Therefore, in practice, there is no clear separation of risk assessment and risk management, which could be considered as a best practice to ensure the scientific integrity of the risk assessment and to reduce any conflict of interest.

DGSPCI and DGCEAMN are jointly responsible for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 on the classification, labelling and packaging (CLP) relating to PPPs. Conclusions on designation of Competent Authorities
CAs have been designated for all tasks relating to the evaluation and authorisation of PPPs and granting PTPs. Allocation of responsibilities is clearly defined. 6 5.2.2. Resources

Within MAPAMA, in the area of responsibilities for the authorisation of PPPs, there are 5.75 full time equivalent (FTE) in the DGSPA and one FTE in DGCEAMN. Both Directorates outsource much of their evaluation work to Tragsatec, which allocates nine and three FTE to work for each of the Directorates respectively.

Nineteen FTE work in the area of toxicology, of which four work in MSSSI, and 15 in Tragsatec. Four FTE deal with OpEx, with one FTE in MSSSI and three in Tragsatec. All MSSSI staff are permanent, whereas approximately 40% of Tragsatec staff are permanent. MSSSI stated that they are ultimately responsible for the outcome of the evaluation, and therefore MSSSI staff review all work conducted by Tragsatec. MSSSI highlighted that this review procedure requires almost full dedication from their staff.

In INIA, a total of 25 FTE work on PPPs and on active substances. These comprise 2 FTE responsible for overall management of the process and 23 FTE responsible for evaluation, of which four are responsible for physical/chemical properties and analytical methods, five for residues, five for e fate, five for ecotoxicology and four for efficacy. Approximately 75% of INIA staff are on three year non-renewable contracts. This leads to very high levels of staff turnover and the consequent loss of expertise, leading to increased training and supervision requirements. INIA management emphasised that the evaluation of PPPs is a complex process and the effectiveness of work is undermined by both the high proportion of staff on short term contracts and resultant high staff turnover rates.

In all cases, management identified the lack of staff as a constraint to meeting deadlines under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, and estimated that staff numbers would need to be doubled to meet the deadlines in the Regulation. The authorities are unable to employ additional staff due to restrictions on public sector recruitment, despite the fact that Article 74 of the Regulation provides for the possibility of MS to recover the costs associated with the work they carry out in implementing the Regulation by means of fees or charges. They added that there is a brain drain of experienced staff to the private sector due to better career prospects.

Management of the evaluation authorities stated that staff have relevant educational backgrounds and included chemists, pharmacists, veterinarians, agronomists, biologists, medical doctors, environmental scientist and toxicologists. New staff receive on-the-job training covering regulatory issues and specific guidelines used in the evaluation process. MSSSI management estimates that it takes at least one year for new staff to be fully operational, and this requires the diversion of experienced staff to train new colleagues, which also contributes to delays in PPP assessments. In contrast, DGCEAMN estimates that it takes one month and a half for new staff to be fully operational. On-going internal training takes place via meetings and discussions when new legislation enters into force or new work related guidelines become applicable. 7 Conclusions on resources
Evaluator staff are suitably qualified and trained, and therefore are capable of conducting evaluations to a high standard.

The high staff turnover levels, particularly for junior staff, and short term contract staff significantly impairs the efficiency of the authorisation process compromising the capacity of the CAs to comply with the legal deadlines, and in the future may compromise the requirement for CA to have sufficient number of suitable qualified and experienced staff to carry out the obligations of the Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. 5.2.3. Planning

DGSPA use a customised database to track all applications. This system can show the percentage compliance with the deadlines laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, but cannot identify in what areas, or why, delays occurred. Neither DGCEAMN nor MSSSI have an effective system of tracking applications to monitor compliance with their respective deadlines, within the overall evaluation and authorisation process4. INIA have introduced a tracking and recording system, which is operational since mid-2016.
