text: Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 36(1), 36(2), 37(1) and (3) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular Articles 4 and 6. Findings

The Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection (Bundesministerium der Justiz und für Verbraucherschutz; BMJV) has general competence in the area of intellectual property, which also encompasses the protection of geographical indications (PGI and PDO) of agricultural products and foodstuffs in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The BMEL also provides expertise on these issues.
The BMEL has competence as regards traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012.

Based on the distribution of competences enshrined in the German Constitution (Grundgesetz), the Länder have competence as regards the official control of indications in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 (PDO/PGI/TSG) (producer and market controls) and Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act (for PDO/PGI) and Section 4 of the Food Specialities Act (for TSG).
The three Länder visited provided details of the relevant local CAs which are in place.
Market controls are mainly performed as a part of food safety inspections by the competent local-level food monitoring authorities.

A Länder working group for PDO/PGI/TSG (LAG Geoschutzkontrollen) was instituted in 2012 based on a decision to that effect by the Official Conference of Agriculture Ministers (ACK- Amtschefkonferenz der Landwirtschaftsministerien der Länder und des Bundes). This working group is chaired by a participating Land. The chairmanship 4 rotates. The BMEL, the BMJV and the German customs administration are permanent observers. The objective of this working group is to harmonise the controls at producers/ processors and the market controls relating to PDO/PGI/TSG. It also participates in the drafting of the Multi Annual National Control Plan and on annual reporting by the Länder and the federal level and it promotes coordination between the Länder.
In all the regions visited there were sufficient staff to undertake official controls and all staff met in the context of this audit were adequately trained. Conclusions on Competent Authorities
The CAs are designated for the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG and are adequately staffed. 5.2.2 Control Bodies

Control bodies, (CBs), in addition to being accredited, must also make an application to be approved in each Länder in which they wish to operate. Some Länder grant approval for a limited period, while in others there are no time limitations. As part of the approval process, the CBs agree to submit regular reports of their activities to the CA and to conform to specific control requirements. Once approved by the Länder, the CBs are authorised to enter into contracts with producers/processors and carry out official controls on behalf of the CA.

Each producer/processor may choose the CB of its choice as long as the CB has been approved in the relevant Länder. To ensure a harmonised approach to controls regardless of which CB is chosen by the producer/processor, the CA draws up a `Control Concept'. This is a document in which the control procedure for each specific PDO/PGI/TSG is described. It describes the following items that should be checked; the control contract, the control procedure, which refers to the risk category, the annual control of the register of producers / processors which should be undertaken by the Producer Group (PG), the on the spot controls and the risk basis for the selection of smaller producers/processors. The existence of the 'Control Concept' is considered a good practice as it ensures all CBs operate to the same standard.

The CA produces a checklist based on the relevant Product Specification which contains the minimum requirements that must be checked by the CBs. The checklist also includes the requirement to check the mass balance at the producer/processor level.

The CA supervises the CBs in an appropriate manner. An annual meeting takes place between the CA and CB and additional meetings may take place if required. The CBs are required to inform the CA of their planned inspections. This enables the CA to participate in a shadow audit of the CB inspector from time to time. Shadow audits are undertaken in approximately 1% of a CBs inspections. 5 15. Approved CBs may undertake official controls on all PDO/PGI/TSG. However, some CBs choose to specialise in one specific area of expertise. Conclusions on Control Bodies 16. Where the CAs delegate certain official control tasks to CBs, it is ensured that they fulfil all requirements for approval, including accreditation. The preparation of a 'Control Concept' document by the CAs is considered a good practice and ensures a harmonised approach to CBs activities. There is adequate supervision of the CB by the CA. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 17. In Land No 1 and Land No 2 the official controls of producers / processors are delegated to CBs. The CB controls the larger producer/processors once every year. The frequency of inspection on small producer/processors is less than once per year. Generally a minimum of 10% of small producers are checked each year on a rotating basis, depending on the product and the complexity of the Product Specification. 18. The tasks of the PGs vary depending on the Land. In Land No 1, the PG is required to carry out a full on-site inspection each year on all its participant members. In Land 2 the PG uses other control mechanisms. Either approach ensures all operators are subject to some control each year although it is not an official control. It should be noted that every PG is subject to an annual official control by the CB each year. This control is an office based audit in which all the records of all the members of the PG are reviewed. Based on this paper review, a decision is made on which operators in the PG are to be subject to control by the CB in that particular year. 19. In Land No 3, official controls are undertaken by the CA. There is a risk categorisation of producers/processors based on their turnover, which classifies all producers/processors into two risk categories. The higher the turnover, the higher the frequency of inspection. Each producer/processor is subject to at least one annual inspection, the larger ones are inspected twice per year. 20. In general, the majority of producer/processors are subject to an annual inspection. There may be some exceptions to this frequency, in relation to smaller operators who are controlled less frequently. 6 Verification of compliance with product specification prior to placing a product on the market 21. In Land No 1, the audit team observed, two verification of compliance audits. One was undertaken at an arable farm and one at a livestock farm. In Land No 2, the audit team observed a verification audit which was being undertaken at the producer/processor for the first time. 22. In each of these situations where the CB has a contract with a PG ( and not directly with producer/processor) not all of the operators would be subject to a verification of compliance control prior to placing the product on the market. Producers/processors in a PG that were producing the product before registration are not necessarily immediately controlled once registration is granted. New producers which join the PG and begin production after registration of the product are subject to a first verification of compliance. 23. However, the PG is obliged to undertake an unofficial or own control of all producer/processors on its register. In addition, the CB performs an official control on the PG, in which a documentary check is undertaken for all producer/processors. This exercise can help the CB identify producer/processors to be chosen for official controls. 24. In the Land No 3, the audit team was shown the original inspection documents to illustrate that the verification of compliance prior to placing the product on the market was undertaken after the relevant PDO/PGI/TSG had been registered. Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market. 25. In all Länder visited the market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG are undertaken by the local level food safety inspectors. These market controls are focussed on food safety issues and PDO/PGI/TSG is a relatively low priority. There was no systematic risk based approach to market controls in place which is not in compliance with Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. 26. At the time of the audit, a new risk based approach towards market controls had been developed in Land No 2 and was in the process of being implemented. The approach included the development of a risk categorisation for each product based on five headings; market relevance, ease of falsification, economical gain in the event of falsification, probability of detection and inspection history of the operator. This leads to three risk categorisations; low, medium, and high risk. 27. In Land No 3, although no systematic risk based approach to market controls was in place, as part of a targeted food safety campaign focussing on allergens in the hospitality sector and mass catering establishments, the correct use of the designated name relating to two PDOs from other Member States was also assessed in the framework of mutual administrative assistance. Of the 717 catering establishments controlled, 63 were found to have incorrectly stated that PDO/PGI/TSG products had been used when this was not the case. 7 28. The audit team was informed that all Länder visited are participants in the Länder working group for PDO/PGI/TSG (Paragraph No 8) one of whose aims is to address the issue of market controls. Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 29. Official controls for verification of compliance prior to placing on the market of PDO/PGI/TSG are adequately planned and implemented on a risk based approach. 30. There was no systematic risk based approach to market controls in place at the time of the audit which fails to ensure that PDO/PGI/TSG on the market are in compliance with the requirements of the legislation. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 Findings 31. The audit team observed inspections at seven producers / processors in three Länder and one market control. In all cases there were inspection histories available, which had been carried out at reasonable intervals and the reports reviewed by the audit team were considered satisfactory. 32. In Land No 1, the audit team observed four inspections. In Land No 2, three inspections were observed. In these two Länder, official controls were delegated to CBs. In Land No 3, one inspection was observed which was carried out for the CA by a food inspector in the framework of administrative mutual assistance. 33. In Land No 1, the four inspections observed were undertaken by CB inspectors, using the relevant CB checklists. The inspectors generally verified the relevant documents to confirm the information provided by the producer/processor. 34. In Land No 2, the audit team observed two inspections where the CB inspectors used the checklist provided by the CA and which contained all the relevant elements in the Product Specification. At the first inspection, the inspector undertook a mass balance calculation and also checked labelling. Inspection reports from the three previous years 8 were reviewed and were considered satisfactory by the audit team. In the second inspection, the inspector undertook the first verification of compliance with the Product Specification and detected some non-compliances. 35. In Land No 3, official controls were carried out for the CA by a food inspector in the framework of administrative mutual assistance. There was a consistent inspection history and the inspection reports reviewed by the audit team were considered satisfactory. A review of labelling at this producer/processor confirmed that the labelling used was in compliance with the requirements. However, there was no control of the number of labels used and the producer/processor confirmed that they do not keep any such records. In addition, the inspectors do not perform a mass balance exercise as part of their official control. 36. In Land No 3 each year a private accredited laboratory undertakes an unannounced sampling exercise at each PDO/PGI/TSG producer/processor to check the integrity of what is being produced. This laboratory also checked the PDO/PGI/TSG labelling. The audit team considered this annual, unannounced sampling exercise as a good practice. In general, the results of laboratory analyses from the products chosen during the unannounced sampling exercises were in compliance with the requirements of the Product Specification. In addition, the official accredited laboratory examines PDO/PGI/TSG products as part of risk-orientated sampling in the field of food monitoring. Ifs results reveal non-compliances the food monitoring authorities forward the report to the CA. Official controls on the Market 37. The audit team observed an official control of a large sized supermarket. The inspector took samples of two PDO/PGI, as per the instructions given in the recently implemented risk based market controls plan. The samples taken were dispatched for laboratory analysis, focussing on PDO/PGI/TSG specification compliance, abusive practices and labelling. 38. The inspector took some of the samples from the delicatessen counter and advised the operator on how to improve the display and labelling of PDO/PGI/TSG. A pre-prepared information sheet was provided to the operator, which had contact details of CA offices, should any further issues arise. Afterwards the inspector provided some examples where market controls had detected non-compliances relating to PDO/PGI/TSG at a farmers' market and a restaurant. The audit team reviewed these files and noted sanctions had been applied which were considered dissuasive. Specific examples of Good Practice observed during the audit 39. In those Länder where the CAs delegate the official controls of producers/ processors of PDO/PGI/TSG; the existence of a 'Control Concept' for each Product Specification is a 9 sound approach to ensure harmonisation of the standards applied by every CB. This significantly reduces concerns relating to consistency. 40. The practice of a Land CA contracting an accredited laboratory to undertake, annual unannounced sampling of all producer/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG ensures the integrity of the PDO/PGI/TSG and is more reliable than visual controls of the commercial presentation of the PDO/PGI/TSG on the market. 41. The development and implementation of a risk based methodology for official controls on the market was demonstrated during this audit. Although this is in the early stages of implementation, it contains all the relevant risk factors and its' application is pragmatic. 5.2.5 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities 42. In Land No 1 and 2, the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG producers/processors were announced to ensure the relevant staff members were available to meet the CB inspector. A checklist was filled in by the inspector as the inspection was undertaken and a copy of this was given to the producer/processor at the end of the inspection. 43. In Land No 3, official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG producers/processors were undertaken on the same day and by the same inspectors as the food safety inspections. Each

The relevant national legislation for PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs is Government Decision No. 152/2015, establishing measures for the implementation of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs.

The relevant national legislation for GI spirit drinks is Government Decision No 276/2014 establishing measures for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation

Relevant national measures are in place to implement EU Regulations relating to official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities Legal requirements Articles 36(1), 36(2), 37(1) and (3) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular Articles 4 and 6. Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings
The MARD is the CCA responsible for carrying out official controls to verify compliance with the legal requirements related to PDO/PGI of agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI of spirit drinks.

The principal tasks include implementation of the national procedure of registration and assessment of documentation in order to obtain protection of PDO/PGI/TSG of agricultural products and foodstuffs and GI of spirit drinks. 4 6. In addition, MARD has responsibility for the control and monitoring of the activities of CBs. The MARD website provides a list of agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks, along with the address of product associations, and the names of the CB to which official controls have been delegated. http://www.madr.ro/industrie-alimentara/sisteme-de-calitate-europene-si-indicatii- geografice/informatii-utile.html http://www.madr.ro/industrie-alimentara/sisteme-de-calitate-europene-si-indicatii- geografice/dosare-tehnice-indicatii-geografice-ig-2017.html Conclusions on Competent Authorities 7. The CAs are designated for the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks. 5.2.2 Control Bodies Legal requirements Articles 39(1), 39(2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 5(2)(e), 5(2)(f) and 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. 8. The official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG, agricultural products and foodstuffs, are delegated to CBs. All CBs are required to be accredited according to International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) 17065. In addition to being accredited, the CBs are required to be approved by MARD. 9. The CBs undertake the verification prior to placing the product on the market as well as subsequent routine controls once the product is on the market. 10. The MARD is responsible for the supervision of CBs. The supervision consists of an annual office audit carried out by Directorate of Inspections at MARD at the office of the CB. Documentary checks are carried out to ensure that inspections are undertaken at all producers/processors and that all producers/processors have been subject to sampling. 11. The CA confirmed that they do not undertake any shadow audits of the CB inspectors as part of their supervisory activities. A representative of MARD may occasionally attend the RENAR accreditation audit of a CB as an observer. An accreditation audit occurs once every four years for each CB. However, as no judgement is made by the CA in these observation roles, it cannot be considered to be part of the supervisory activity of the CB. 5 12. Once the office audit is completed, a report is issued and submitted to the General Directorate for Food Industry and Commerce. This report forms the basis for the annual approval of the CB. The certification of a CB is only issued when all requirements have been met. At the time of the audit there were no examples of corrective actions being necessary. 13. The audit team reviewed a number of the reports prepared by the CA relating to the CB office audits. These mainly describe the findings that the CBs have observed during producers/processor inspections during the previous year. However, the CA does not evaluate the activities of the CB. 14. The fact that the CA does not carry out any witness audits of the CB inspectors at the operator level does not permit the CA to evaluate the effectiveness of inspections carried out by CBs. This lack of supervisory activities by the CA is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted some systematic shortcomings in the inspections carried out by the CBs (see paras 33, 34 and 35). Such shortcoming could only be detected through carrying out such witness inspections. Conclusions on Control Bodies 15. The CA delegates certain official control tasks to CBs which are accredited to ISO17065. Supervision of the CBs by the CA is not fully effective as the supervisory process does not include witness inspections, which is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings 16. Given the relatively small number of producers/processors of PDO/PGI agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks in Romania the approach taken has been to subject all producers/processors to an annual official control. At the time of the audit the official controls for agriproducts and foodstuffs were delegated to CBs whereas official controls of spirit drinks were undertaken by the CA. The CCA confirmed that all annual official controls at producers/processor level for both types of registered names are announced. 6 This is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which states that official controls shall be carried out without prior warning. 17. An annual official control consisting of an on-site inspection as well as official sampling of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs is undertaken annually by the CB. The samples are dispatched to an accredited laboratory where they are analysed for physical- chemical parameters as well as organoleptic testing. Once this task is completed, the CB issues an overview report to the Producer Group (PG). The PG is made up of producers/processors working with the same product and is responsible for ensuring that all PG members comply with the Product Specification. At the time of the audit, there had been no instances of non-compliances being recorded. Once the results of the inspection and the laboratory analysis are known to be compliant, the certification of the producers/ processor can be issued for a one year period. 18. In relation to spirit drinks, the annual official control at producers/processors did not include the checking of all elements of the technical file and neither did it include, sampling, for laboratory analysis. This could not ensure compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. 19. At the time of the audit, there were no risk based market controls in place which is not in line with Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Verification of compliance with product specification and specifications in the technical file prior to placing a product on the market 20. The audit team noted that an inspection history was available from inspectors and producers/processors for all products immediately following their registration by the Commission. This fulfils the requirement to undertake a verification of compliance prior to placing the product on the market for the first time as a PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks. Official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG on the market. 21. At the time of the audit, the CA confirmed that there were no risk based market controls in place in Romania. However, the NACP undertakes investigations of ad-hoc consumer complaints as they arise. A number of case studies were described by the NACP which illustrated their competence to investigate and to sanction where appropriate. One complicated investigation related to a registered name from a non-EU country. The NACP had received a complaint that coffee which was not the genuine article had been traded in Romania. The NACP successfully identified the source of the problem and implemented the relevant enforcement measures. 7 Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls 22. There is a system in place whereby producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks are subject to regular annual official controls. 23. All annual official controls of producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks are announced which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 24. The lack of official sampling and laboratory analysis of spirit drinks means that the requirements of Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 are not met. 25. Routine risk based market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks were not included in the prioritisation of official controls at the time of the audit. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings Controls at Visited Premises 26. The audit team visited two producers of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and three producers of GI spirit drinks. In all cases, a series of inspection reports were available which illustrated that all producers/processors were subject to an annual official control. The audit team was informed that all inspections at operators whether carried out by CAs (spirit drinks) or CBs (agriproducts and foodstuffs) are announced. The CA stated that this approach ensured that inspections take place at the time of processing and that all relevant documents are prepared by the operators. 8 Agriproducts and Foodstuffs ­ Controls Undertaken by CBs 27. The audit team observed two inspections undertaken by two different CB inspectors at two separate producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs. The inspectors were provided with a checklist by the CB. 28. It was noted that raw materials were accepted on the basis of a general declaration by the supplier, that the raw materials complied with the requirements of the Product Specification. As an example, the CB never raised a non-compliance regarding the absence of labelling of a specific raw material. This acceptance signifies a lack of control measures. 29. The audit team reviewed past inspection reports and noted that two traceability exercises had been undertaken in a competent manner. These exercises included all the quantities of raw materials used for specific batches of product. 30. During each official control, the CB inspector takes samples of the finished product and sends them for analysis to an accredited laboratory. Up to the time of the audit no non- compliances had been detected. 31. The audit team visited an agricultural fair and met two producers of protected names who were selling their produce. The audit team confirmed that the producers were certified and complied with all relevant labelling requirements. Spirit Drinks ­ Controls Undertaken by Regional CAs 32. The audit team noted that inspectors from the County Directorates for Agriculture were not provided with a checklist. The inspectors relied on their own experience and also referred to the Technical File. 33. In practice, this approach did not ensure that all the details of the Technical Files are verified. As an example, in the case of one spirit drink producer visited, the raw materials should have been stored in a wooden tank, however, a plastic tank was in use. In addition, inspections were limited to verify the conditions seen on the day of the inspection, rather than confirming the systematic compliance of the operator with all the requirements of the Technical Files. This approach limits the effectiveness of the control and is not in line with Article 22(1) of Regulation No 110/2008. 34. In the spirit drink producers visited, although the operators kept records as regards the production, as well as purchase and sales records, no verification of the information in these were made by the inspectors. The inspectors stated that such controls were undertaken by the revenue authorities. 9 35. The proof that the raw material came from the defined / delineated area was verified by documentary checks of the delivery dockets of the incoming goods. However, this verification was only carried out for the products processed on the day of the inspection. The systematic compliance of the operator for a given period was not confirmed, even if the relevant documents were present. 5.2.5 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities 36. The CB inspectors were provided with checklists and were required to take samples of the finished products for analysis at an accredited laboratory. The inspectors from the regional CAs did not use a checklist and did not take any samples for laboratory analysis. 37. In all cases, reports on official controls were provided to the operator in a timely manner. Conclusions on Procedures and Performances of Official Control Activities 38. Although official controls are undertaken at an agreed frequency at producers/processors, the inspections are announced, superficial and do not always include each element of the Product Specification/Technical Files. Consequently, this approach does not provide the necessary level of assurance that producers/processors are fully compliant. 5.2.6 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 Findings 39. The Romanian legislative framework categorises the wilful infringement of industrial property rights as a criminal offence. According to Article 90 of the Law on Trademarks and Geographical Indications, infringements related to GIs are liable to a term of imprisonment ranging from three months to three years, and a fine from RON 50,000 to 150,000. The NACP described how one protected name from a non-EU country had been successfully investigated and sanctions applied (see section 21). 10 40. The Geographical Indications for wines or spirits benefit from additional protection as it is not necessary to prove that the consumers were misled or that unfair competition activities were carried out. 41. In the case of non-compliances detected by CBs or regional CAs, a number of sanctions are available depending on the situation. The failure of the producer/processor to rectify a non-compliance by an agreed date can result in the suspension of a certificate. The suspension may apply to a single producer/processor or to a whole group. The withdrawal of certification can occur when the PG can no longer meet the requirements for certification. At the time of the audit, there had been no examples of such actions being implemented in the context of this audit. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures 42. Enforcement measures are available for implementation when required. At the time of the audit no sanctions had been implemented against producers/processors. One example of an ad-hoc market sanction being implemented was described and considered satisfactory.

OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Overall there is a system of official controls in place whereby producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG of agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks are subject to regular inspections. The inspection reports reviewed by the audit team illustrated that not all elements of the Product Specifications/Technical Files were verified during regular inspections. The inspections observed by the audit team also confirmed this shortcoming. At the time of the audit, there were no risk based market controls in place, although product specific co

The country profile of Hungary describes the structure of the competent authorities and the organisation of official controls on animal welfare during transport. It is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=HU

A previous audit to Hungary on animal welfare during transport (report DG(SANCO) 2011/6045) identified shortcomings on vehicle approvals (suitability of watering devices, ventilation systems), controls to verify journey times and use of satellite navigation systems and temperature data on a risk basis, controls of space allowances and ventilation above animals, and verification of the effectiveness of controls. It made recommendations to address them and enhance the control systems in place. The Hungarian authorities took a number of measures at central level between 2011 and 2017 aimed at improving the system of controls and addressing these recommendations.

In addition, NÉBIH issued a number of updated guidelines on animal welfare during long journeys to transporters and county offices throughout 2016. This was in response to the Zuchtvieh judgement1 and to problems reported at the border with Turkey. They required that: a. Operators' planning of long journeys and district officials' verification of them should take into account conditions in the non-EU leg of the journey. Where there are no resting places in the non-EU country, stocking density should be decreased by 20%, and appropriate drinkers and back-up portable watering equipment should be carried in vehicles; b. Where temperatures on the route exceed 30, the space allowances for animals must be increased by at least 30 %; 1 Judgement of the European Court of Justice (Fifth Chamber) of 23 April 2015 ­ Case C424/13 3 c. In order to provide adequate ventilation the minimum internal height of the vehicle must be at least 20 cm higher than the withers of the highest animal; d. Drivers must check more frequently on animal conditions and use fans when vehicles are at a standstill in heat. Whenever possible, vehicles transporting animals should be parked in the shade; e. Checks on journey planning should take into account the border crossing between Bulgaria and Turkey, the opening hours of the Turkish veterinary services, and reflect at least the minimum time of six and a half hours to cross the border; f. Written confirmation of a control post booking and declarations concerning how the provision of food, water and bedding throughout the journey will be achieved as well as a written contingency plan on how drivers can react to potential emergency situations should be supplied by organisers; g. Journey logs must have all relevant information submitted including the border as a transit point and the name of the final destination.

The County offices provide training for district offices mainly on certification of animals but also on welfare issues. During 2016 NÉBIH required all counties to give training on animal welfare requirements to those district official veterinarians dispatching consignments for long journeys. NÉBIH supplied training materials (including the elements in paragraph 3 a-g above) and all officials were trained by December 2016.

Most officials at district level did not take into account the training or instructions regarding the time taken to cross the border at Turkey and the working hours of Turkish veterinary authorities there, in their verification of journey log planning (see paragraphs 26 to 28 below). This resulted in incorrect journey planning and animals subjected to routinely longer journey times.

Staff at district level generally did not know how to check certain requirements requested by NÉBIH, e.g. approving vehicle deck surface areas and suitability of drinkers or analysis of retrospective satellite navigation system or temperature records from long journeys (see paragraphs 10, 11, 12, 26 27 and 28 below). This is despite training and guidance from both central and county level. This lack of knowledge or competence in carrying out tasks at district level is not in compliance with Article 6 of Regulation 882/2004.

There is no verification of the district level work due to budgetary constraints, though a framework for doing so is in place. The district levels could not demonstrate adherence to documented procedures and this was not known to higher levels. This is not in compliance with Article 8 of Regulation 882/2004. District officials at times took decisions based on discussions with transporters rather than confirming themselves that requirements are met or following NÉBIH guidance. 4 Conclusions on Official Controls

There has been inadequate progress in rectifying the deficiencies reported during the Commission audit to Hungary DG(SANCO) 2011/6045 on animal welfare during transport. Actions taken by the Hungarian authorities to rectify the deficiencies were ineffective as the same deficiencies were found at district level in 2017.

Official controls at district level do not ensure transporter's compliance. This together with the absence of verification in a number of key areas might cause unnecessary pain or suffering to animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 18 and 26 and Chapters II, III and VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings

Vehicle approval renewals are subject to the same process as new vehicles. There is extensive written guidance available for consultation for district official veterinarians (OVs) who approve vehicles for long journeys. This includes specific guidance on suitability of drinkers but not on measuring vehicle space allowances. There is no systematic training for OVs, but some have taken part in Better Training for Safer Food courses and meetings between counties and districts allow dissemination of this information. A note from NÉBIH also draws attention to the need for accurate vehicle deck areas to calculate appropriate stocking densities and to verify the suitability of drinking devices for the species of animals being transported.

The audit team reviewed vehicle approval certificates. All but one of them were inaccurate with regard to the calculation of deck surface area: many listed only an overall area for multi-deck vehicles, or the same deck surface areas for multi-deck trucks, including those with goose-neck decks at the front. This is not in compliance with the requirements necessary to correctly issue the vehicle certificate in Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 and the specifications required to be completed in the certificate listed in Annex III Chapter IV of Regulation 1/2005. District officials relied upon the figures provided by vehicle manufacturers' which were not always accurate.

Vehicle drinking devices were not physically verified at the time of approval by the district OVs. They assumed vehicle manufacturers' would fit suitable drinkers for the species that the vehicles was listed as being capable of transporting. This is not in compliance with Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 or in line with NÉBIH guidance. Vehicles approval certificates were issued for different species and ages of animals which would require different non-compatible drinking systems e.g. horses, rabbits, 5 calves and pigs on one certificate and would lead to some animals being unable to drink during rest stops due to the unsuitability of drinkers.

Increased space allowances for animals of up to and beyond 20% was indicated in journey logs for two of the three transporters met. They were based on the deck surface area indicated in the vehicle approval certificate. The exception was one of the bigger exporter/transporters visited where the district OV indicated using discretion to allow exports to take place at almost normal stocking densities (+10%) - disregarding the guidance from NÉBIH.

Officials at district level did not recognise the physical limitations imposed by vehicle design height restrictions and the carriage of two decks of average height large adult cattle. There was a recent instruction issued (see also paragraph 3c above) but no clear practical guidance (vehicle and animal schematics) from NÉBIH on this. Adequate headspace and therefore ventilation was not ensured when large adult cattle (over 500kg) were transported e.g. the guidance from NÉBIH for 20cm space requirement above the withers of large bulls on two decks (which must be stacked in some way) on conventional trucks would require a minimum2 vehicle height of over 4.8m. i.e. it is not possible to load large adult cattle on two decks in conventional livestock vehicles while providing adequate headspace. This is not in compliance with Annex I, Chapter II, point 1 (1.2) of Regulation 1/2005 and NÉBIH guidance. For the most-modern, modified two- deck vehicles, and for other smaller categories of cattle this was satisfactory.

The audit team observed a number of good practices at one large transporter/exporter. The company was working closely with a non-governmental animal welfare organisation (NGO) to redesign new vehicles to include a number of modifications to improve the transport of animals for long journeys: e.g. additional ventilation, sealed deck/wall junctions, lowered floors to increase ventilation, additional access points and modified drinkers and partitions. The company also used the NGO's experience and literature to train all their drivers and it reported a very positive outcome. The company also developed a useful mobile phone application for their drivers for working out stocking densities, listing legislative requirements and logistical information (contacts and language phrases). The operator accepted operating with lower profits per animal transported in order to improve animal welfare and indicated they were frustrated that inconsistent enforcement allows lower standard operators to gain market share and drive down prices to the detriment of animal welfare standards in Europe.

According to NÉBIH instructions, fitness for transport is to be checked at the moment of loading for all consignments destined to non-EU countries. Loading checklists require the district officials to sign that the criteria listed in paragraph 3 of this report (a, b, c, f 2 This is calculated taking into account: the animals height, normally at least 1.5 to 1.6 m multiplied by two, plus twice the ventilation requirement 20cm and the height of the first vehicle deck off the ground (1.1 to 1.2m) and the thickness of the floors of decks two and three (+24 cm). 6 and g) are complied with before a journey starts. All checklists seen were completed as satisfactory by the OVs.

The poor implementation of vehicle approval requirements (surface area and drinkers) and problems with ventilation and space above large animals' heads would negate the usefulness and veracity of certain aspects of these checks. On the other hand, the very low percentage of unfit animals reported from the non-compliances detected during controls at the Bulgarian border (see annex) points to the positive outcome of systematic controls on the physical fitness of animals for loading and transport. Systematic checking fitness at the moment of loading can be considered a good practice and goes beyond the requirements of Article 15 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 which does not require carrying out systematic checks at the moment of loading.

The vehicles seen by the audit team during the audit were in good condition. As required by the NÉBIH instructions they also carried additional portable drinkers. None of the vehicles seen was equipped with cooling equipment for the livestock.

Long distance transport of animals at temperatures above 30°C is permitted by NÉBIH. All satellite navigation records examined for journeys to Turkey in summer demonstrated that the temperature inside the vehicles consistently exceeded 30 °C for certain parts of journeys. Taking into account the limitations of transporting animals for long journeys in vehicles incapable of regulating internal temperatures to comply with the range of temperature requirements as laid down in Annex I, Chapter VI, point 3 (3.1) of Regulation 1/2005, this is not in compliance with Article 3 (c) of the same Regulation. NÉBIH has asked the counties and districts to focus on mitigating the associated risks by: increasing space for the animals, giving more headspace and ensuring realistic journey planning to take account of the typical delays entering Turkey. Conclusions on transport conditions

NÉBIH guidelines together with supervision of loadings at the time of departure have had an impact on reducing risks regarding fitness to travel and space allowances. The supervision of loadings is a good practice going beyond EU requirements.

The poor standard for approval leads to a risk of inadequate space allowances and unsuitable drinking devices, during long journeys and thus to welfare problems for the animals transported. The inadequate measuring of deck floor surface areas and assessment of drinking devices at the time of approving the vehicle leads to incorrect calculations on stocking densities ­ as they are based on the deck surface area indicated in the vehicle approval certificate. Therefore, reductions in stocking density indicated in most journey logs for summer consignments are often inaccurate.

The requirements for adequate headspace and therefore ventilation provision for large adult cattle in two-tier vehicles is not respected causing unnecessary suffering to these animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. The actions 7 proposed in response to previous DG SANTE recommendations on these issues were not effective as they have not been properly implemented at district level.

The absence of cooling equipment for livestock in approved lorries implies that they will not be able to maintain the animals at the temperature range specified in Regulation 1/2005 during long journeys with regular external temperatures over 30°C, which will result in causing unnecessary pain and suffering. The actions proposed in response to previous DG SANTE recommendations on these issues were not effective as they have not been properly implemented at district level.

The liaison between one large exporter/transporter and an animal welfare NGO led to the development of innovative vehicle designs and an intensive driver/company training programme which should lead to better conditions for animals transported by the operator. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 19, 25 and 26 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings
The audit team saw evidence that control post bookings were routinely sought and provided during pre-transport planning controls.

NÉBIH request transporters to return all journey logs after the journey and districts do follow up on non-returned documents. The NÉBIH animal welfare control plan requires counties to report monthly the checks of satellite navigation systems and temperature records for two consignments a month. NÉBIH also gave counties specific TRACES certificate numbers during the summer to review. Districts did not report any non- compliances to NÉBIH from the reviews of journey logs, navigation systems data and temperature records.

The audit team reviewed returned journey logs, navigation systems data and temperature records. Journey plans (section 1 of the journey log) were not always completed to the final place of destination, nor was the border crossing to Kapikule indicated as a stopping point in many. Operators planning journeys and OVs tasked with verifying the planning had not taken on board the NÉBIH guidance on the time to cross the border or the opening hours of border authorities.

Satellite navigation systems records showed that many journeys were taking far longer than the planning indicated in the journey logs. Despite the availability of clear navigation records, there were no records of actions taken to compare journey planning with the reality given by this data. None of these irregularities had been noted nor had any remedial action had been taken by the district officials in these cases. Effective 8 verification of journey planning required in Articles 14 and 15 of Regulation 1/2005 was not in place and journeys which were not in compliance with the limits for journey times laid down in Annex I, Chapter V of Regulation 1/2005 were permitted.

Reports of non-compliances by Hungarian transporters have been regularly communicated in TRACES from the Bulgarian competent authorities at the border with Turkey to NÉBIH and the district authorities (see table in annex). Almost all the non- compliances were noted in the TRACES category "Other". The lack of further categorisation of non-compliances listed in TRACES as "Other" has made it difficult for the receiving authorities to follow up on these cases; though attempts were made by some district offices.

Additional information recently received from the Bulgarian authorities indicates that the majority of the notifications labelled as "Other" in TRACES concerned consignments which were likely to exceed journey times once they had left the Bulgaria

Visit to a transporter involved in the transport of live animals to non-EU countries 1 Visit to the body responsible for the testing and approval of livestock vehicles for long journeys 1 Visit to an assembly centre from where consignments of cattle depart to non-EU countries and meeting with a transporter 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation and in particular Article 28 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations, and Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules. EU legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex 1 and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND Enforcement of animal welfare requirements during transport remains a challenge. There have been several reports to the Commission of long delays of live animal transports at the EU land border with Turkey. After a sudden drop in exports to Turkey between 2012 and 2013 this trade has been increasing significantly in recent years. The number of live ruminants exported to Turkey in 2016 (more than 290,000) has surpassed the numbers for 2011 (more than 280,000). In response to these reports, complaints from non-governmental organisations and following a meeting with national contact points, the Commission services wrote to all Member States in June 2016 urging them to improve official controls in this area. 2 The letter emphasised the importance of proper planning of long distance journeys, with particular focus on: adequate contingency planning; temperature requirements; and the provision of sufficient water, feed and bedding for the duration of these long journeys. To follow up on this issue, DG Health and Food Safety planned a series of audits for 2017 and 2018 to identify activities that are suitable and effective in improving animal welfare during long distance transport to non-EU countries. The Commission will share the outcomes from these audits with all Member States in order to help with the uniform application of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This audit to the Netherlands is the first of the series. Long journey exports from the Netherlands in 2015-2016 amounted to approximately 1,127 ­ 1,115 of these were cattle and 12 were sheep and goats. Most of these exports were to Russia: 71% of live cattle consignments in 2016 and approximately 51% for 2015. The last exports of live cattle from the Netherlands to Turkey were in March 2015. After that date, there was no longer an agreed health certificate for Turkey and therefore this activity was suspended. The system for official controls on animal welfare during transport is the same regardless of the destination country. According to data recorded in the Commission's Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES), the majority of transporters involved in 2016 long journey exports from the Netherlands were from Hungary (36%), the Netherlands (35%) and Poland (24%). The remaining transporters were from five other Member States. Of these consignments 91% were checked against animal welfare requirements somewhere along the journey. These checks didn't reveal any animal welfare incidents. A previous audit to the Netherlands (report reference nr: DG(SANCO) 2010/8400) concluded that the competent authority carried out extensive controls on the protection of animals during transport, had a dedicated office for issues related to animal welfare during transport. Auditors from DG Health and Food Safety and national experts from other Member States have identified good practices on official controls on transport during this, and later1, visits to the Netherlands. The country profile of the Netherlands describes the structure of the competent authorities and the organisation of official controls on animal welfare during transport. It is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 1 See also the overview report DG(SANCO)2014-7350 on Study visits to improve Member State controls on animal welfare during transport 3 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 DESCRIPTION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 11, 14, 15, 17 and 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 3, 4, and 5 of Directive 96/93/EC. Findings 1. The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs assigned the inspection and approval of means of transport for the purposes of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 to the RDW. This body is also responsible for licensing vehicles and vehicle parts, registration, information provision and issuing vehicle certificates of approval.

text: Drivers' certificates of competence are issued by the Dutch Driving Test Organisation (Centraal Bureau Rijvaardigheidsbewijzen ­ CBR).

The NVWA has centralised the task to perform pre-screening checks on the journey plans that are submitted by the operators. This pre-screening activity includes administrative checks on documents submitted for issuing animal health export certificates. The Remote Certification Department (Certificeren Op Afstand ­ COA), another centralised Unit within the NVWA, is carrying out the pre-screening administrative checks for animal health export certificates for cattle to Russia as part of a pilot project.
Retrospective checks of these journeys are performed by NVWA's Livestock Transport Bureau (IBD).

The table below summarises the activities carried out by the Dutch competent authorities on the transport of animals over long journeys to non-EU countries: Necessary certification NVWA: Transporter authorisation Driver's certificate of competence. before a journey can be CBR: Vehicle approval certificates for long journeys. planned RDW: Planning a Journey (done by the organiser and submitted electronically to the NVWA) Evaluation of the NVWA: Journey plan and relevant documents. organiser's request to COA: export animals Animal health documentation for pilot project on exports of cattle to Russia. 4 Prior to departure NVWA: Vehicle inspection; Inspection for fitness for transport and transport Retrospective checks IBD: conditions; Signing animal health certification; Communication of NVWA: Stamping the journey log. issues with other countries and actors Returned journey logs; Returned Satellite Navigation System (SNS) data. National Contact Point for issues related to animal welfare during transport (NCP). Trade National Contact Point for issues related to animal health.

Documented procedures are available for the authorisation of transporters, vehicle approval, animal health certification for export including the principles of Directive 96/93/EC, evaluation of journey plans, inspection prior to departure and retrospective checks. These procedures are detailed enough and suitable in achieving the objectives of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 18 and 26 and Chapters II, III and VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings

Fitness for transport is mandatorily checked by the NVWA at the moment of loading for 100% of consignments destined to non-EU countries2. The NVWA uses this opportunity to carry out controls on the vehicles' conditions at the same time. The NVWA stated that its intention in carrying out these checks is to provide additional assurances on the good conditions in which animals are exported from the Netherlands (see also Paragraph 4 of the Background and Finding 20). This is considered a good practice and goes beyond the requirements of Article 15 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. 2 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that "as of 1 June 2017, it is no longer our standard policy to check 100% of transports for intra EU trade and exports at the moment of loading. For animals for which individual identification with digital eartags is in place, checks may take place within 24 hours before departure. Certain animal categories are exempted and still need to be checked at the time of loading. These include unweaned calves and lambs, sows and piglets for slaughter, horses for slaughter and end-of-career milking cows. For long journeys, the vehicle needs to be present at the time of inspection." 5 8. The validity and correctness of the transporters' authorisations and the vehicles' approval certificates are verified as part of the NVWA's pre-screening administrative checks that are performed prior to scheduling the mandatory official on-site inspection at loading. Additionally, the NVWA checks drivers' certificates of competence during the on-site inspection and confirms that the vehicle(s) and driver (s) present are the same that were indicated in the planning and checked at pre-screening (Article 14(1)(a)(i) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005). 9. Regarding the vehicle's conditions: the full range of checks carried out by the RDW for a new vehicle approval is also performed when renewing the 5-year approval (Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005); the Dutch certificates of approval currently do not distinguish which vehicles are appropriate for weaned and which are appropriate for unweaned animals, contrarily to what is required by Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005). The NVWA indicated that it intends to split the vehicle approval on this basis: one approval for "calves younger than 2 months" and another for "calves over 2 months" (similarly, one for "lambs and kids younger than 6 weeks" and another for "lambs and kids over 6 weeks). This was supposed to start after 1 January 2017, but has been delayed; the new start date is 1 July 2017; the stocking density (Point 2.1 Chapter III, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005) is checked during loading; the presence of an official at 100% of loadings also allows the NVWA to check: o maintenance conditions of the vehicle and space above the animals (Points 1.1. and 1.2 of Chapter II, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005); o appropriate bedding for the animals and suitability of the vehicle's drinking devices for the species and categories of animals that are to be transported (Points 1.2 and 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005). 10. Regarding temperature: the temperature at the place of departure has to be taken into consideration during the mandatory on-site inspection at the time of loading; checks are not carried out on the predicted temperatures at the place of destination when evaluating the journey plan. These checks had been suggested by the Commission in its letter to all Chief Veterinary Officers (CVOs) of 28 June 2016; the IBD carries out retrospective checks on temperature records when the transporter submits these with the SNS data (see also Finding 16). 11. Since there were very little issues concerning transport conditions in live animal exports, the audit team also reviewed several examples of communication of these issues regarding intra-EU consignments of live animals (Article 26 of Regulation (EC) No 6 1/2005). In these examples the Netherlands was both on the receiving side and on the notifying side with the other Member States. These communications have generally resulted in investigations from both sides and mainly concerned: stocking densities of pigs and their fitness for transport; poor welfare of poultry arriving at slaughterhouses. Conclusions on transport conditions 12. The Dutch policy to carry out inspections of 100% of consignments at the moment of loading enables the competent authority to verify a much wider number of requirements in addition to the animals' fitness for transport. The official verification, at the moment of loading, on the adequacy of the vehicles, bedding, handling, space allowances and ventilation, in addition to fitness for transport, contribute to prevent causing unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to animals during long distance transport by road. This high frequency and type of checks at loading is considered a good practice and it goes beyond the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 under which it is not mandatory to carry out systematic checks at the moment of loading. 13. The current system for certification of approved vehicles does not sufficiently distinguish the types of vehicle appropriate for weaned and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. The risk of unweaned animals being transported in these unsuitable vehicles is sufficiently mitigated in the Netherlands by systematic controls at the moment of loading. However, this shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, where the suitability of the vehicles may not be systematically verified at the moment of loading as in the Netherlands. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 19, 25 and 26 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings 14. It is part of the national animal welfare ambition to reduce as much as possible the number of hours of transport for animals (maximum of 8hours or 500km). In addition the Netherlands currently does not allow the transport of cattle, sheep and goats for slaughter to non-EU countries. Therefore, in the case of these species, only breeding animals may be exported. Exceptions are made for EU-harmonised export certificates. 15. Regarding the organiser's plans to rest the animals during the journey and provide them with feed and water (Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): 3 Judgement of the European Court of Justice (Fifth Chamber) of 23 April 2015 ­ Case C424/13. 7 the journey plan has to be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country, as indicated by the Zuchtvieh judgement3. This is checked as part of the pre-screening administrative checks that are performed prior to scheduling the mandatory official on-site inspection at loading; a detailed route map (from a specific internet site identified as being the closest to reality for vehicles transporting live animals) including all the planned stops, and booking confirmation of the control post(s) and, if applicable, of the livestock vessel(s) has to be submitted with the journey plan, as additional evidence of proper planning of the journey. This information is used at the pre-screening stage to check that the journey plan is realistic and satisfies the requirements of Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, and has been identified as good practice; the NVWA indicated that the most common gaps detected during these pre-screening administrative checks are incomplete journey plans and missing proof that the livestock vessel for the sea part of the journey, where applicable, was confirmed; the procedure for validating journey plans involving a livestock vessel did not include a check on the vessel's approval certificate (Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005). This was identified by the audit team when reviewing a specific case. The NVWA solved the immediate problem by contacting the National Contact Point of the Member State that had authorised the vessel and informed the audit team that the instructions would be amended to include also this verification; one of the transporters met by the audit team indicated that, when transporting animals from other Member States to Turkey, his journey plans take into account at least six hours for controls at the Turkish border. 16. Regarding retrospective checks to verify the travelling and resting times to provide water, feed and rest to the animals: for journeys departing from the Netherlands, 100% of journey logs are requested to be returned, and are checked; 10% of SNS data are also requested and checked (Articles 15(1) and 15(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 respectively); if it makes any findings during checks on the completed journey log the IBD indicated that, depending on the type of finding, it then asks for the SNS data for that journey; the audit team saw samples of requests to foreign transporters to return completed journey logs and SNS data: o Failure to return the journey log or SNS data within the stipulated deadline is followed by a maximum of two reminders to the transporter after which a letter is sent to the NCP of that country requesting that the SNS data is provided, and the transporter is also put in copy (Dutch transporters are instead subject to an administrative fine of up to 1,500); o In 2016 the German and Polish NCPs were contacted to obtain SNS data once and twelve times respectively. The NVWA indicated that both NCPs collaborated on these requests, and obtained and provided the requested data. the checks on both the returned journey log and the SNS data detected non- compliances, and were well targeted and comprehensive. The NVWA indicated that 8 journey log information and SNS data is often only provided for the EU part of the journeys and that, due to legal uncertainty, it does not take action to obtain the missing information concerning the non-EU parts. Conclusions on resting 17. The system in place provides satisfactory assurances that there are planned arrangements to provide feed, water and rest to the animals until the final place of destination in the non-EU country to prevent causing unnecessary suffering to animals during long distance transport by road. The high number of retrospective checks, supported by the communication between NCPs, provides additional assurances that these planned arrangements are fulfilled for the EU part of the journey. 5.4 UNEXPECTED DELAYS AT THE EU BORDER Legal requirements Articles 3 and 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 3, 4, and 5 of Directive 96/93/EC. Findings 18. Unless there is an EU-harmonised export health certificate, it is the policy of the Ministry of Economic Affairs to authorise the export of live ruminants only to those countries with which a template health certificate has been agreed upon. The declarations to be made in these health certificates are agreed between the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the importing country(ies) thus avoiding that consignments of live animals are blocked at the EU border due to insufficient or inadequate animal health assurances. Recommendation based on conclusion 18. Associated finding: 15, 3rd bullet.
