DGAL is the central competent authority for animal welfare on transport while district (département) level authorities are responsible for implementation, under the coordination of the regional level.

The table below summarises the activities carried out by the French competent authorities on the transport of animals over long journeys to non-EU countries: Necessary certification District level : Transporter authorisation; before a journey can be Driver's certificate of competence; planned Vehicle approval. Planning a Journey Done by the organiser and submitted to the district Evaluation of the District level : Journey plan and relevant documents; organiser's request to export animals Animal health documentation. Prior to departure District level : Stamping the journey log; Signing animal health certification; Inspection for fitness for transport; Vehicle inspection. Retrospective checks District level : Returned journey logs; Returned satellite navigation system data. Communication of The National Contact Point for issues related to animal welfare issues with other during transport at the DGAL and/or the districts. countries and actors

DGAL created a working group in 2017 on long journey transports comprising relevant professionals (e.g. traders, organisers, and transporters), technical institutes, animal protection associations, other administrations, private veterinarians and control service officials. This working group aims for participants to exchange views on the state of play of French livestock exports and the problems associated with very long journeys in order to arrive at proposals for best practices. The group met for the first time in September 2017 and drafted an action plan identifying six focus areas of work: precise identification of responsibilities for all involved, improve journey planning and its reliability, develop contingency planning, improve official controls, strengthen the training of operators, and ensure proper transport by sea. This action plan included some preliminary details and estimated deadlines for completion of each work area. 4 5. DGAL annually organises a 3-day national training session on animal welfare during transport for officials involved, and evidence of this was provided to the audit team for the years of 2014 to 2016. For 2017 two 3-day national training sessions are programmed. The first session was in May and covered the overall methodology for official checks and their follow up and respective records. The second is scheduled for November and will go more in depth into particular control tools (satellite navigation data, tachographs, etc.) and specific types of checks (at loading, retrospective). 6. With the increase in live animal exports seen since 2015 DGAL organised 10 additional 1-day regional training sessions between May 2016 and March 2017 specifically targeting long journey transports for export. In total over 100 officials attended this additional training. The districts met during this audit indicated that they considered these additional regional training sessions as being good and useful. 7. DGAL produced detailed procedures (with information and instructions) for the districts on how to implement the requirements of Reg. 1/2005 correctly and consistently. The procedures cover the selected points of relevance for this audit, namely: authorisation of transporters, approval of means of transport, issuing of veterinary certificates, checks on planning of journeys, controls prior to departure and retrospective checks on journeys. 8. Some requirements from these procedures that are considered good practices are: The requirement for transporters to provide updated and detailed contingency plans that drivers must have with them during the journey; That the satellite navigation system in livestock vehicles must be able to provide the information on the location of the vehicle not only through the geographic coordinates but also with explicit location names, addresses or references such as of the road travelled. 9. The procedures are revised and updated periodically. For example in September 2011 DGAL issued an extensive procedure covering all the checks related to the journey logs, such as planning before the journey, verification during transport, and retrospective checks on returned journey logs. Subsequent to the letter to the CVOs of June 2016 DGAL issued a separate procedure (numbered 2016-643) containing the additional suggestions from that letter. As part of its review and update process DGAL plans to revoke that separate procedure 2016-643 by incorporating its requirements into the 2011 procedure (expected to be finalised in the first trimester of 2018). 10. The audit team saw several requirements from DGAL procedures that had not been operationally implemented. While in some cases this was because those particular requirements were recent additions to the procedures (see also the 1st and 2nd bullets of paragraph 13) several other requirements had not been implemented even though the relevant procedure has been in place for several years (see also paragraph 25). 5 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, and 18 and Chapters II, III and VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings 11. Fitness for transport is confirmed by authorised private vets within the last 24h prior to departure of cattle, in line with requirements (Art. 15 of Reg. 1/2005). 12. The validity and correctness of the transporters' authorisations, the vehicles' approvals and the drivers' certificates of competence are verified by the districts when the application for the journey is received, also in line with requirements (Art. 14(1)(a)(i) of Reg. 1/2005). 13. Regarding the vehicle's conditions: The DGAL procedure concerning approval of vehicles (Art. 18 of Reg. 1/2005) was updated in May 2017. Since none of the districts met had approved or renewed an approval of a vehicle for long journeys since May 2017 the districts described how they performed the most recent approvals prior to this update. As described they would adequately verify the requirements concerning deck surface areas, ventilation, and most structures and facilities of the vehicles. However, they would not have ensured adequate verification of the requirements for satellite navigation systems (Chapter VI of Annex I to Reg. 1/2005). The May 2017 update includes additional provisions that can ensure this correct verification Vehicle approval certificates issued indicate species but not categories of animals, contrary to what is required by Chapter IV Annex III of Reg. 1/2005, so for example, they do not indicate that vehicles are appropriate for unweaned animals. Therefore unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animal, with the biggest risk being their inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Annex I, Chapter VI, point 2.2 of Reg. 1/2005). The template forms associated with the approval procedure were updated in June 2017 and now clearly state that the category of animals must be indicated in the application form and in the certificate of approval; the stocking density (Point 2.1 Chapter III, Annex I of Reg. 1/2005) is checked during the administrative checks. 14. The DGAL procedure covering all the checks related to the journey logs (see also paragraph 9) also refers to checks at time of loading during which the handling of the animals and vehicle conditions could be verified in line with requirements (Article 15(1) and Annex I, Chapters III and VI of Reg. 1/2005). However, it does not require the performance of checks at time of loading. In this regard: 6 DGAL informed the audit team that checks at the moment of loading is something that is under study as there are difficulties with having official staff available to perform them; For 2016 two of the districts met had not planned nor performed any such check and were the departure point for a total of 69 export consignments; Another district, departure point for 55 export consignments, programmed and performed one check at time of loading in 2016. This check was of a multi-vehicle consignment and reported compliance of vehicles and of handling of the animals but detected that the journey time that had been indicated by the organiser in the journey plan was underestimated. This occurred because after loading the first vehicle the driver waited for the other vehicles to also load, in order to travel together, and these loading and waiting times had not been included in the journey planning. The consignment left with the journey plans, submitted to and already stamped by the district, unchanged, contrary to the requirements of Art. 14(1)(b) of Reg. 1/2005. The district sent a formal notification to the transporter informing them about the results of the check and indicating corrective action required for future journeys. 15. Regarding temperatures: All three districts met informed the audit team that they perform checks on the predicted temperatures for the journey when evaluating the journey plan. The DGAL procedure 2016-643 of August 2016 indicates that if the weather prediction for the journeys exceeds 30°C the districts should not stamp the journey log as satisfactory without additional guarantees from the organiser about the vehicle's capabilities to maintain the internal temperature within the required limits. The districts stated that they had started these checks before August 2016 as a consequence of DGAL previously raising awareness on this issue (see also paragraph 19); One district informed the audit team that in 2016 it had stopped some consignments from leaving on the originally planned date because of high temperatures expected along the journey. Conclusions on transport conditions 16. Up to 2017, the system for approval, and certifying vehicles, did not sufficiently distinguish the types of vehicle appropriate for different categories of animals, nor adequately verify the satellite navigation systems' compliance with requirements. The 2017 update of relevant procedures correctly addresses both the categories of animals and satellite navigation verification. 17. The administrative checks in place adequately verify the presence and validity of relevant transporter, drivers and vehicle certificates, as well as the respect of maximum stocking densities. Those checks together with the confirmation of the animals' fitness for transport and postponement of departure of consignments when high temperatures are expected along the journey help prevent unnecessary suffering to the animals. 7 18. The absence of checks at the moment of loading prevent the competent authorities from having adequate confirmation of the handling at loading and maintenance conditions of vehicles leaving from France for export. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings 19. Proper planning of long journeys is essential to ensure the respect of time limits and rest periods for animals on long journeys. DGAL distributed information to help with this, namely: In 2015 to all districts about the possible impact of high temperatures on live animal transports requesting particular care be given to this; In July 2016 to industry associations about the temperature limits within which exports of live animals can be performed and of the difficulties, and necessary care, with such transports in summer, namely if travelling by road to Turkey; In August 2016 to all districts with the separate procedure 2016-643 (see also paragraphs 9, and 15 2nd bullet); In July 2017 with a reminder to all districts that the procedure 2016-643 was still of relevance. 20. Regarding the organiser's plans to rest the animals during the journey and provide them with feed and water (Art. 14 of Reg. 1/2005) the districts: require the journey plans to be until the final place of destination even if it is a non- EU country, in line with the European Court of Justice ruling of 23 April 2015 in Case C-424/13; check the plausibility of the proposed journey plan using an online route planner, with proper consideration of the speeds achievable by a heavy vehicle; take drivers social hours requirements into account in some way by requiring organisers to provide certificates of competence for two drivers when journeys exceed 8h. 21. Procedure 2016-643 includes the working hours and expected time needed to go through Turkish border controls as well as requiring that these be taken into account when evaluating the journey planning. However the districts were not aware of the working hours and the usual time needed to go through checks at that border. This has a significant negative impact on the capacity of the districts to correctly evaluate the feasibility of the journey times indicated in the planning of journeys to Turkey. 8 22. The DGAL procedure for planning of official checks on transport prescribes annually retrospective checks of at least 5% of journey logs issued by the districts, with a minimum of five retrospective checks. National data, provided by the districts to DGAL, for 2016 indicates a much higher percentage (approximately 30%) of retrospective checks. DGAL stated that some districts carry out checks on almost 100% of journey logs but that the depth of the checks performed by different districts appears to vary significantly. 23. Regarding retrospective checks to verify the travelling and resting times to provide water, feed and rest to the animals (Art. 15 of Reg. 1/2005): Two of the districts met informed the audit team that they had performed the required 5% minimum retrospective checks of journey logs but could not provide the corresponding records. The other district informed that because of lack of human resources it had been unable to carry out these checks in due time; The three districts stated that it was difficult to obtain the return of journey logs from the transporters and that up to 2016 no system was in place to attempt to ensure this return. For 2017 a system to obtain the journey logs was being designed and would be implemented; Two districts informed the audit team that when attempting in 2017 (in preparation for this audit) to obtain satellite navigation data and temperature registers for consignments exported to Turkey during 2016 almost none had been received. One district stated that it received one set of satellite navigation for a consignment but that the data provided was impossible to analyse; In 2016 one animal died during the journey in each of four consignments leaving from France for export. None of the districts from which the consignments originated had targeted these as journey logs to be investigated; Until October 2017 two of districts met had not yet implemented a system with identified c

The BFSA is the Single Authority in the sense of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The Border Control Directorate (BCD) is a specialised unit within the BFSA, responsible for import controls, including those for plant health. 3 2. For plant health purposes, the BCD is made up of nine departments, one of which is based in the BFSA's headquarters and deals with the policy and organisation of plant health import controls. The remaining eight departments are based at inspection posts located at points of entry, and are responsible for the implementation of controls. 3. Two other directorates of the BFSA are also directly involved with plant health, the Plant Protection and Quality Control of Fresh Fruits and Vegetables Directorate and the Central Laboratory for Plant Quarantine (CLPQ). The two departments support border phytosanitary control activities by providing training, methodological guidelines and work instructions, as well as monitoring programmes for control and observation of harmful organisms. The CLPQ is also responsible for providing diagnostic support to inspectors (see section 5.1.5 below). 4. The Regional Food Safety Directorates (RFSDs) are involved with import controls in so far as they are responsible for performing inspections at approved places of inspection (see section 5.1.2 below). 5.1.2 Staffing provisions and power of inspectors 5. The BFSA stated that there are 36 staff working on plant health within the BCD, two of whom work at the BFSA's headquarters on policy and organisation, and the remaining 34 are inspectors working at the eight permanently staffed inspection posts. In addition, 81 inspectors working regionally within the RFSDs are responsible for carrying out checks at approved places of inspection. These RFSD staff work full time as plant health inspectors, but unlike the BCD plant health inspectors, also cover inland controls including the plant passport regime and export certification. 6. All inspectors are required to hold a higher education degree in the field of Agricultural Sciences, specialised in "Plant Protection", this is provided for in Article 4 of Ordinance No. 8 of 27 February 2015 on Phytosanitary Control. Upon recruitment, inspectors undergo a two-week induction programme based around the work instructions for import controls, this includes training on pest and disease detection which is delivered by the CLPQ. After induction, all inspectors are required to attend annual refresher training courses organised by the BFSA. 7. The audit team confirmed with inspectors met during the audit, that they had undergone training as described by the BFSA. However, the audit team noted that two inspectors at Sofia Airport, who had recently completed their induction training, did not carry out an effective inspection of basil (see section 5.4.4 below). All other staff met by the audit team appeared to be fully technically competent. 8. Two staff at Sofia Airport, responsible for performing import checks for plant health, are not technically competent and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, at least to perform plant health checks, which is not in line with Article 1 of Directive 98/22/EC, in particular Point 2 of the Annex to that Directive. 4 9. The BFSA stated that they have issued official work instructions (see section 5.1.3 below) to ensure that, if followed, controls are performed appropriately and in line with Directive 2000/29/EC. However, at least in the case of sampling (see section 5.1.3) and dealing with soil attached to imported produce (see section 5.1.6 below), staff were generally not aware of these work instructions. The lack of awareness of official work instructions means that staff are not necessarily able to ensure the proper application of the Directive, and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, which is not in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 10. The BFSA stated that inspectors have all legal powers necessary to enforce import controls, including the power to control the movement of consignments or have them destroyed or re-exported. This was confirmed by the audit team, based on observations made of import checks being carried out which led to non-compliances being identified and action taken as a result (see section 5.5.1 below). 11. Inspectors have the legal basis to apply import controls to non-regulated articles and take action against non-regulated harmful organisms, where it is considered necessary based on phytosanitary risk. This is in line with Article 13(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC and the objective of Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.1.3 Working instructions and internal communication 12. The BFSA stated that inspectors are issued with work instructions covering all of the tasks relevant to import controls. These work instructions consist of methodological guidelines and the so-called "monitoring programmes" which have been set up for the monitoring of the territory and trade for specific harmful organisms or of specific commodities. 13. For commodities within the scope of EU emergency measures, inspectors are required to follow the specific provisions in the legislation as they relate to import controls (e.g. sampling of imported citrus fruits from South Africa or Uruguay). 14. A summary of the sampling rates for different commodities is provided in Table 2 below. Table 2: Sample sizes for different commodities, as specified in work instructions: Commodity Lot Size Sample size Plants intended for planting, other 1 - 100 All units* in lot than seed 101 ­ 3 000 20% and not less than 100 units 3001 ­ 10 000 10% and not less than 150 units Ware potatoes (from all non-EU 2% and no less than 200 units countries except Egypt**) >10 000 <30 tonnes 200 tubers (from 5 sacks) 30 ­ 50 tonnes 200 tubers (from 5 sacks) 50 ­ 200 tonnes 200 tubers (from 1 sack/10 tonnes) >200 tonnes 1 tuber per tonne 5 Commodity Lot Size Sample size <5 packages All packages Other produce (fruits, vegetables 5 ­ 20 packages 20 % of packages and cut flowers) 20 ­ 100 packages 5 packages 100 ­ 500 packages 20 packages >500 packages 4% of packages * In the case of plants for planting, other than seed, the sampling unit is defined as a single plant. **The Single Authority stated that sampling of imported ware potatoes from Egypt is carried out directly in line with the provisions of Decision 2011/787/EU. 15. The audit team noted that, if applied, the sampling rates in the work instructions would, according to ISPM 31, provide an appropriate probability of detecting harmful organisms in small and large lots of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, and plants intended for planting. However, for mid-sized lots, the sample size would, in many cases, provide a confidence level significantly below 80% of detecting even a 5% level of infestation and this reduced level of confidence was not justified based on risk. The work instructions on sampling do not therefore provide for a sample which is large enough to be considered as representative, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 16. The audit team noted that the work instructions on sampling are not generally applied in practice in the case of fruit, vegetables and cut flowers. All inspectors met by the audit team, other than those at Sofia Airport who followed the work instructions on sampling, stated that they sample 200 individual fruit, vegetables or stems, selected at random from 10 boxes, which is not in line with the work instructions. 17. The audit team observed an inspection of citrus from Turkey and noted that: the lot consisted of 2 200 boxes, each weighing 10 kilograms; the BCD inspectors selected 10 boxes from five different pallets and inspected 20 fruit from each box; according to the work instructions, the sample size should have been 88 boxes. The sample size taken in this case was therefore lower than that provided in the work instructions, which already provides for too low a confidence level. The sample was not therefore representative of the lot, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 18. The BFSA informed the audit team that changes to legislation, or to the scope of import controls, are rapidly communicated to BCD inspectors via email and additionally during refresher training courses. The audit team was able to confirm, through observation, that this was the case at the inspection posts visited during the audit. 19. Whilst observing an inspection of cut basil (Ocimum sp.) from Israel, inspectors stated that they were unaware of any interceptions having been notified on this trade elsewhere in the EU. In fact, at the time of the audit, basil was the second most frequently 6 intercepted commodity from Israel which in turn was the non-EU country with the fourth highest number of interceptions for harmful organisms in the EU1. These inspectors did not have available information on interceptions made by other Member States. This is not in line with Point 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.4 Planning of official controls 20. The audit team visited four of the eight main inspection posts in Bulgaria and, based on the number of consignments containing regulated articles, it appeared staffing provisions were sufficient to enable appropriate checks to be carried out. At Kapitan Andreevo inspection post, which the BCD stated was the busiest land border crossing point in the EU and the second busiest in the world, there were 13 BCD inspectors responsible for plant health import controls. In order to provide 24-hour coverage, the BCD explained that a shift system is in operation and that a minimum of three inspectors are on duty at any time. The BCD stated that, on average, there were 30 consignments requiring plant health checks during a 12-hour shift. Therefore, including rest breaks, an inspector has to complete the checks of approximately one consignment per hour. The BFSA stated that Kapitan Andreevo has the highest workload per inspector of any inspection post in Bulgaria. 21. The BFSA stated that in order to identify new or unusual trades of unknown risk, inspectors regularly check shipping manifests to identify consignments of interest and alert the Customs Service of those they wish to inspect. This includes regulated articles from new origins and new trades of non-regulated articles. This practice was described by inspectors at all of the inspection posts visited by the audit team. In practice, this was most often put into effect for WPM (see section 5.5.1 below). 5.1.5 Laboratories and technical support 22. The CLPQ is a Directorate within the BFSA and the BFSA stated that the laboratory performs the tasks of a National Reference Laboratory for plant health. There are also six regional laboratories in Bulgaria, however, the BFSA stated that all official diagnoses must be undertaken by the CLPQ. The CLPQ stated that they were not yet accredited under any international standards. 23. The CLPQ described the methods used for diagnoses of samples received in relation to import controls. Morphological methods are relied upon for entomological samples, and molecular methods (polymerase chain reaction techniques) together with serological tests (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay and immunofluorescence) are also available, in particular for the identification of pathogens. 24. During 2016, the CLPQ stated that they received 355 samples related to import controls, of which 130 were from consignments of seed, 155 of plants for planting and 70 of other 1 https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/plant/docs/ph_biosec_trade-non-eu_alert-list_201603-201702.pdf 7 plants and plants products, mainly ware potatoes. As a result of the laboratory analyses carried out on these samples, four diagnoses of harmful organisms were made, one of plum pox virus and three of ring rot in ware potatoes. The CLPQ explained to the audit team that the testing carried out for harmful organisms was systematic and that analyses would be undertaken whether or not symptoms were observed. 5.1.6 Verification procedures and audit 25. The BFSA explained that they have a specialist team working on internal audit and verification in the Verification of Official Control General Directorate, which is responsible for carrying out audits of all official control activities, including plant health import controls. It audits each inspection post annually to ensure that all relevant legislation and work instructions are complied with. The competent authorities for plant health have been described in detail in the previous audit reports and the Country Profile for Poland, which is available at http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=PL . Since the previous audit there have been no changes in the designation of the Polish Competent Authorities. SPHSIS is the single competent authority for plant health which comprises of the Main Inspectorate of Plant Health and Seed Inspection (MIPHSI) and the Voivodeship Inspectorates (VIPHSI) whose organisational structures include field and border units. 5.1.2 Staffing provisions

At the time of the audit there were some 2,300 staff of SPHSIS of which 878 carry out plant health surveys. During the interviews carried out by the audit team, staff resources were not mentioned as a problem or limiting factor for carrying out potato surveillance and controls following ring rot or brown rot outbreaks. Representatives of the VIPHSIs visited, stated that in order to overcome temporary problems with implementing increased plant health controls the tasks and personnel can be redeployed between different field units of a VIPHSI. 5.1.3 Training and working instructions

Since the previous audit there have been no major changes in the designation and organisation of training events addressed to employees of both SPHSIS and VIPHSI. Apart from the training events scheduled for the newly employed staff, the managers 6 and the field unit managers of the Voivodeship inspectorates, employees also participate in the Better Training for Safer Food courses organised at EU level.

For emerging needs such as the implementation of the proposed new "export" regime (RSPP programme), SPHSIS intends during 2017 to organise 34 training sessions addressed to 796 plant health inspection staff.

MIPHSI sets the overall goals of inspection and issues work instructions and technical guidelines including the methods, rates and densities for sampling of tubers and surface or waste water. Operating procedures provide inter alia, standardised forms with codes and serial numbers of samples to be taken for laboratory analysis.
Most inspectors met by the audit team were aware of relevant plant health requirements and competent to carry out their tasks. 5.1.4 Legal powers of inspectors and sanctions

As already mentioned in the 2014-7204 audit report, inspectors have legal powers to access plants, plant products and other objects at all stages in the production and marketing chain. Since the last audit, no significant changes have been made regarding the enforcement of plant health legislation at regional level. Tasks related to checks of potatoes at transport are carried out in collaboration with the Police or the Road Transport Inspectorate.

VIPHSI inspectors may be assisted by police officers when undertaking controls in market places; usually they are asked to assist where cooperation with inspectors is refused. Since the last audit, there have been no changes in the sanctions and fines imposed on parties involved in illegal movement of potatoes. Operators have the right to appeal to the MIPHSI and request further investigation and examination of their case by the state court. 5.1.5 Work planning and record keeping

Since the previous audit there have been no changes in work planning and record keeping. MIPHSI sets the overall goals for the inspection and prepares the annual work plan. VIPHSI draw up working plans for field units. Inspection, sampling and testing records are kept in a national database. 5.1.6 Cooperation and communication with stakeholders

Following the first brown rot outbreak in Poland in December 2014, SPHSIS launched an information campaign and conducted consultation meetings with operators of the potato production and marketing sectors. The campaign included the publication of numerous articles in the press and the MIPHSI website http://piorin.gov.pl/ , radio/television broadcasting where discussions focusing on ring rot, brown rot and other potato diseases took place. 7 11. During 2016, SPHSIS experts and consultants participated in 36 potato conferences, fairs and exhibition events organised by different institutions where they delivered presentations on potato issues. Overall, 1,785 training sessions of which 302 for potato ring rot, 210 for potato brown rot and 661 for both potato bacteria were attended by nearly 42,500 participants. In 2017, 488 external training events will be delivered to ca. 11,900 operators of the potato production sector including growers, packers and wholesalers. 12. All training sessions and consultation meetings were accompanied by information material on the presented topics. A wide range of leaflets, posters and other information material has been distributed to farmers and are available in local VIPHSI offices. The leaflet on the requirements for the movement of Polish potatoes to other EU Member States has been printed in eight EU official languages. 5.1.7 Laboratories 13. Since the previous audit there have been no substantial changes in the general organisation and structure of official laboratory network in Poland. 5.1.8 Relevant national legislation and rules 14. The EU legislation regarding ring rot and brown rot is transposed by national acts and regulations. Since the previous audit, substantial changes regarding the implementing legislation for the control of quarantine harmful organisms of potato have been adopted or are under preparation. Order 16/2015 sets out the rules to be followed during the movement of potatoes in Poland and other Member States. Following the first finding of brown rot, MIPHSI adopted Order 1/2016 "Programme to control the presence, eradicate and contain Cms and Rs in Poland" with surveillance and control measures. Taking into account the recommendations of the previous audit report, Order 1/2016 provides for the inspection and surveillance to be carried out also in small scale farmers. In addition, it provides for the notification of Cms or Rs findings where contamination could involve other Member States and the prohibition of planting for the production of seed following ring rot findings in a place of production, even on newly acquired land. 15. MARD introduced certain changes in the order for the subsidy rates provided for the compensation of producers who are subject to measures implemented for the control of Cms and the reimbursement of cost of testing potato tubers intended for planting. Necessary conditions are the participation of producers in the integrated plant production system and the use of certified or tested material for potato production. In addition, MARD launched a public consultation on the draft regulation dated 26 April 2017, setting out detailed procedures to control and prevent the spread of Cms through the movement of contaminated or probably contaminated material. The regulation aims at more precise implementation of Directive 93/85/EEC and includes the necessary and sufficient conditions for the establishment of places of production free from ring rot in 8 line with the proposed RSPP programme. The regulation was adopted and entered into force on 10th May 2017. 5.1.9 Registration/approval of establishments 16. As already mentioned in the 2014-7204 audit report, all producers of seed potatoes, ware potatoes to be marketed and potato wholesalers, packers and processors have to be registered. A list of registered entities is kept in the Voivodeship inspectorates and compliance is monitored through regular market controls. Overall, by the end of January 2017, there were 49,978 registered entities of which 46,423 in seed and ware potato production, 4,268 distributors and 305 potato importers. The competent authorities for plant health have been described in detail in the previous audit reports and in the Country Profile for the Netherlands, which is available at http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL. Since the previous audit there have been no changes in the designation of the Dutch Competent Authorities. NVWA is the single competent authority in charge of export inspection and certification for plant health. It functions as an executing agency of the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

Among NVWA competences are the supervision and auditing of official inspection bodies, the development of inspection protocols and the validation of test methods, the organisation of surveys and the handling of outbreaks. Phytosanitary policy issues, international multilateral and bilateral representation and research funding remain within the competence of the Ministry. The activities related to controls in the production sector of Rosa have been assigned to NVWA and delegated to the Netherlands Inspection Service for Horticulture ­ Naktuinbouw.

Naktuinbouw is an official independent non-profit foundation, which, together with the Dutch General Inspection Service (Agriculture), the Flower Bulb Inspection Service and the Quality Control Bureau (fresh fruit and vegetables, cut flowers and potted plants/ornamentals), comprise the four Agricultural Inspection bodies in the Netherlands. Naktuinbouw is an agency authorised to carry out inspections for the quality of propagating material and to provide certification according to instructions received from the NVWA. It operates on long-term agreement under the financial supervision of the Ministry and the responsibility / technical supervision of NVWA. Its main activities are the implementation of marketing and plant health directives on propagating material used in horticulture and the provision of routine and supplementary inspection and diagnostic support in case of emergencies. Specific plant health tasks assigned to Naktuinbouw include the surveillance and inspections carried out in propagating material for the implementation of the plant passport regime. An additional task is that of surveying, sampling and laboratory testing for the detection of certain regulated harmful organisms. Handling of findings or outbreaks and enforcement of specific measures is the responsibility of the NVWA, which issues statutory notices to inform the producers and impose appropriate measures. 4 5.1.2 Staffing provisions

NVWA employs around 2,470 staff: approximately 150 are responsible for plant health. Naktuinbouw has around 285 staff, of which 60 are full time inspectors specialised in the horticultural sector with a focus on propagating material (seed and planting materials), quality supervision and phytosanitary controls. A large proportion the resources are devoted to the production industry in horticulture. During the course of actions following-up the outbreak of Rsr1 examined by the audit team, staff resources were not a significant problem or a limiting factor for controlling propagating material or flowers of Rosa. 5.1.3 Training and working instructions for the control of Rsr1 in Rosa

In September 2015, NVWA following technical advice provided by its laboratory and its risk assessor, prepared specific surveying instructions for the inspection and sampling of Rosa, Gerbera (which, depending of the R. solanacearum strain, can also be a host plant) and black nightshade (S. nigrum) weeds growing in glasshouses. Three senior inspectors accompanied by newly appointed staff carried out visual inspections and sampling of water and plants grown in glasshouses under suspicion for the detection of Rsr1.

In January 2016, a meeting was organised for NVWA inspectors prior to a general survey at the places of production of Rosa which at that time were not affected by or involved with the Rsr1 outbreaks. The audit team met NVWA and Naktuinbouw inspectors and noted that they were competent for carrying out their tasks. Senior inspectors had provided on- the-job training to others. 5.1.4 Relevant national legislation ­ legal powers of inspectors and sanctions

The national plant health law, in particular article 2 "Decision to combat harmful organisms" and article 3 "Scheme for import, export and movement of plants" provide the legal basis for implementing decisions for affected places of production for the eradication of Rsr1 and the prohibition of movement of contaminated material. Articles 10 and 11 of the national plant health law enable the organisation and carrying out of surveys and monitoring for the detection of harmful organisms.

text: Both NVWA and Naktuinbouw inspectors have the necessary legal power to access the premises of places of production including propagators and growers and carry out phytosanitary controls. 5.1.5 Laboratories

Since the previous audit there have been no changes in the general organisation and structure of official laboratory network in the Netherlands. Diagnostic tests for handling plant health outbreaks in horticulture are carried out by the official laboratory of 5 NVWA. In the case of Rsr1 in Rosa, routine diagnostic support with isolation and PCR tests was provided by the laboratory of Naktuinbouw whilst further laboratory analyses and pathogenicity tests were carried out by NVWA. In total about 4,800 samples of plants and water were analysed in the course of the outbreak (see also section 5.2.2).

Both laboratories carried out extensive research on the genetic diversity of Rsr1 from Rosa and its relatedness to other Rsr1 isolates of worldwide origin. Additionally experiments on the virulence were conducted in the NVWA laboratory by using various inoculation methods on two varieties of Rosa as well as on tomato, tobacco, eggplant and sweet pepper. Results proved that all species were susceptible to Rsr1 from Rosa and after stem inoculation at 24°C showed symptoms of infection.

Laboratory support is also provided to producers by private laboratories, which may analyse additional samples upon request. In cases when Rsr1 was detected or suspected, these laboratories ensured that NVWA was notified. 5.1.6 Registration/approval of establishments

The registration of producers of plant propagating material in the Netherlands with Naktuinbouw is obligatory. Currently there are fifteen registered producers of Rosa propagating material. There is no legal obligation for the registration of Rosa growers. Most of these are members of the Dutch association of horticulture entrepreneurs. Trace back and forward of Rosa plants, which were infected by Rsr1 and which had been used for the production of propagating material, was carried out by the NVWA and extracted from the requested trade data from administration of the infected breeders and propagators. 5.1.7 Cooperation and communication with stakeholders for the control of Rsr1

Following the Rsr1 outbreaks, NVWA together with glasshouse producers' organisations, breeders, propagators and growers organised seven meetings in order to provide information to Rosa and Anthurium cut flower producers. The growers attending included those that had been affected by the disease with the purpose of achieving a common understanding between NVWA and producers' organisations about the severity of the measures that had to be taken.

An ad hoc joint research project of ca. 1.5 million euro was launched with the participation of Naktuinbouw and the Universities of Wageningen and Utrecht and the Dutch General Inspection Service. The project includes a risk assessment for Rsr1 spread and focuses on its epidemiology, the development of early, reliable, fast and affordable diagnostic methods including early detection and final verification of Rsr1 infection and the implementation of advanced hygiene protocols in Rosa production. This is 80% funded by the Ministry and 20% by the private sector.

The audit team met representatives of producers' organisations and noted that: 6 They were highly aware of the situation and expressed their concerns as the Rsr1 outbreaks had led to bankruptcy of four companies in the sector; They had provided information about their members and were permanently updated by the competent authorities about the monitoring and eradication of Rsr1; They had provided clonal links between growers and propagators who often had purchased downstream propagating material (bud wood) from healthy looking flower producing plants of Rosa.

Information about Rsr1 and the measures to be taken is available on the website of NVWA: https://www.nvwa.nl/onderwerpen/ralstonia-solanacearum-in-snijbloemen. Several press releases in newspapers and articles in dedicated journals have been addressed to Rosa producers. LTOglaskracht, the Dutch association of horticulture entrepreneurs, in collaboration with NVWA, elaborated and published leaflets with guidelines with mandatory hygiene measures for the prevention of Rsr1 in places of production of Rosa. Conclusions on organisational aspects of plant health controls

The competent authorities are well structured with competent staff and a significant laboratory capacity to deal with the emergency situation of handling the Rsr1 outbreaks. The high level of awareness observed in the rose production sector facilitated the adoption of stringent measures for the eradication of the disease. 5.2 CONTROL OF RSR1 Legal requirements Article 16(1) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. Findings 5.2.1 Organisation of official controls for the eradication of Rsr1

Following the suspicion about the presence of Rsr1 in roses and potentially emerging outbreaks in mid-August 2015, NVWA set up a technical advice team of risk management experts for issuing specific inspection and sampling instructions for plants and water, tracing back and forward of the disease and communicating with stakeholders. The team comprised experts of NVWA and Naktuinbouw and provided technical advice for the management of the outbreaks and elaborated specific follow up actions to be taken in the places of production of propagators and growers aiming at the ultimate eradication of Rsr1. In September 2015, a technical task force supported by the NVWA incident management centre was established to manage the surveillance and eradication operations. 7 19. As there was no previous experience of Rsr1 presence in Rosa, it was unclear if the severity in the expression of symptoms would vary according to the rose varieties and the specific growing conditions in the glasshouses. The audit team received two diagrams with the general control strategy and the course of actions to be taken in case of suspected symptomatic / non-symptomatic and confirmed Rsr1 outbreaks in places of production of propagators and growers. Figures 1 and 2 below show the diagrams with different options and follow-up measures together with the necessary monitoring and intensive sampling to be carried out for the eradication of the disease and the re- establishment of crops for the production of propagating material and cut flower stems. 20. The actions referred to in Figure 1 for places of production of propagating material (including plants for planting) include: In case of suspicion due to symptomatic presence of Rsr1 or recent deliveries of plants from a contaminated source, the entire place of production is blocked. All plant lots under suspicion and drain water must be sampled and tested; All plant lots found infected including plants that might have been in contact with drain water from contaminated lots must be destroyed; All other plant lots in the same place of production are subject to intensive sampling and testing (99% probability to detect 0.1% infection). This in practice means that every single plant within the same variety of small lots must be sampled. Subsamples from up to 200 plants can be combined in one sample for analysis. 21. The measures can be lifted when all contaminated plant lots have been removed and destroyed and all remaining plant lots under suspicion have been tested negative. The glasshouses and all equipment including tools and machinery must be disinfected and samples of irrigation and drain water must be tested and found negative. Production of propagating material may resume following water sampling after disinfection. Sales may resume following a second sampling of drain water confirming Rsr1 absence. Monitoring of drain water by sampling and testing is subsequently continued every six weeks for a total period of nine months after eradication. 22. The actions referred to in Figure 2 for places of production of cut flowers (including those growers where stems are used for producing bud wood) include: In case of suspicion drain water and all plant lots must be sampled and tested (200 plants / lot); cut flowers can be traded but no bud wood can be delivered for propagation; In case of infection no cut flowers can be traded and no bud wood can be delivered for propagation. All infected plant lots or plants of other lots growing in the same gutter have to be destroyed. Cut flowers from other plant lots can be delivered. 8 Figure 1. The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Spain are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for the country (http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=ES)

In summary the central competent authority (CCA), the Single Authority in terms of Council Directive 2000/29/EU, is the Directorate-General of Health and Agricultural Production of MAPAMA. Its Sub-directorate General for Forestry, Plant Health and Hygiene is charged with issues related to outbreaks of harmful organisms at national level, such as coordination, information exchange, international representation. The Sub-directorate General for Health Agreements and Border Controls is responsible for import controls, including inspections related to Xf at the phytosanitary border inspection posts.

Sixteen of the autonomous communities (AC) of Spain are included in the EU plant health regime. Each AC has a plant health service under the relevant ministry/department of the regional government, which is the CA for plant health at AC level (ACCA). Some ACs have provincial plant health services as well. ACCAs are responsible for the control of harmful organism outbreaks, including implementation of the measures of the Decision, except the provisions related to controls at the border inspection posts.

In forest areas the AC's forestry and environmental authorities are responsible for the implementation of the measures related to Xf, including visual inspections and sampling as appropriate. 4 5. In the Balearic Islands AC, two directorates-general of the regional government deal with issues related to Xf. The Directorate General of Agriculture and Livestock (Agriculture Department) is responsible for the management of plant health and the Directorate General of Environment and Biodiversity (Forestry Health Department), is responsible for forestry issues. The local governments of the Islands and the municipalities are also responsible for the implementation of certain measures. 5.1.2 National and regional legislation 6. After the initial outbreak was detected, national and regional decrees were adopted to ensure the application of the Decision. 7. MAPAMA Decision APM/21/2017 of 20 January establishes specific measures for prevention in relation to Xf, including a prohibition of transporting specified plants intended for planting from the Balearic Islands. 8. The Regional Minister of Environment, Agriculture and Fisheries of the Balearic Islands issued several resolutions related to the Xf outbreak. The Resolution of 25 November 2016 declares the existence of Xf in the Balearic Islands and adopts phytosanitary measures to eradicate and control it; 25 January 2017 declares the entire territory of the Balearic Islands as DA for Xf and adopts precautionary protective measures to prevent the spread from the islands; 10 February 2017 bans the exit from the territory of Ibiza of all specified plants to the rest of the territory of the Balearic Islands; 14 February 2017 establishes a management and coordination group to deal with issues related to Xf outbreak in the Balearic Islands. 5.1.3 Contingency plan, action plan 9. The Spanish national contingency plan for Xf is in place since 2015. It was elaborated by the MAPAMA with the help of experts and in collaboration with the ACCAs. The plan is kept continuously under review. 10. The structure of the plan is in line with the relevant provisions of the Decision. It defines clearly the roles and responsibilities at national and AC level and regulates the application of the necessary measures in agricultural, forest and other areas, including the communication within the CAs, with professional operators and the public, training and minimum resources available and how to mobilise additional resources. 11. The plan includes survey, diagnostic and eradication protocols. The survey protocol takes into account the 2015 Commission guidelines for Xf surveys. It defines the following areas, which are considered as national priorities during the surveys: Nurseries and garden centres in general; Areas (fruit, horticultural plantations, forests, parks, gardens, public roads etc.) established 2-4 years ago with plants from DAs and from non-EU countries, where Xf is present; Nurseries and garden centres on transport routes from DAs; The Valencia coastline; Agricultural crops of particular economic importance for Spain with the following minimum annual inspection rates: olives, citrus, almonds, plums and cherries - 1 per 10,000 ha; vines, apricots, peaches, nectarines - 1 per 15,000 ha and oaks 1 - per 5 50,000 ha with at least one sample per inspection. However, the audit team is not convinced that these minimum annual inspection rates are sufficient for the detection of a possible infection, taking into account the presence of these crops in different parts of Spain; Vector insects collected from the main agricultural crops. Sweeping and direct catch is recommended but not the use of sticky traps. The survey protocol also describes the main symptoms, defines the method and timing of the visual inspections and sampling of symptomatic and asymptomatic plants. 12. The diagnostic protocol states that the samples have to be analysed by laboratories, approved by the ACCAs, using two different methods described in the diagnostic protocol (PM 7/24(2)) of the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO). In the case of positive or dubious results, the samples must be re-tested by the National Reference Laboratory (NRL). 13. The eradication protocol describes in detail the measures which need to be implemented in the case of an outbreak, such as demarcation, specific surveys, removal of plants, tracing back and forward, movement restrictions and controls and good agricultural practices. The audit team noted that the listed measures are in line with relevant provisions of the Decision. 14. The national contingency plan also states that ACs can prepare their own contingency plans, which may adapt the national measures to their specific conditions. It requests the elaboration of an action plan in the AC after an outbreak is detected. 15. In each of the three ACs, visited by the audit team, there is an Xf contingency plan in place, which were elaborated after the assessment of the regional risk of Xf. The regional plans follow the structure and information content of the national contingency plan and in addition contain numerous specific provisions, relevant for the region. They also take into consideration the specificities of the production structure, landscape, environment, public administration, stakeholders in the AC. Consequently the survey priorities, especially the inspection frequencies in agricultural areas and nurseries are different (see chapter 5.2.1). 16. The ACCA of the Balearic Islands elaborated the first version of its Xf action plan in December 2016, which had already been modified three times prior to the audit. The action plan contains a detailed description of the outbreak situation and the measures implemented, including surveys in the DA and updates on the removal of the infected plants. The plan also highlights the main elements of the control strategy as follows: Surveys and removal of infected plants in line with provisions of the Decision; Protection of places with plants of specific cultural, social or scientific value; Technical advice to and involvement of stakeholders and private persons, including the establishment of a permanent information point; Study the potential vectors of Xf in the Balearic Islands; Develop a code of good agricultural practices; Specific role of the regional steering and coordination group. 5.1.4 Communication and cooperation within the plant health services and with other authorities involved in controls 17. The main national level co-ordination forum for activities related to outbreaks, surveys and implementation of EU emergency measures on outbreaks is the National Plant 6 Health Committee (CFN). This is chaired by the head of MAPAMA Directorate General of Health and Agricultural Production and is composed of representatives from all ACCAs. The CFN meets at least quarterly, its activity is supported by 13 expert working groups, dealing with specific production sectors. Since the Xf outbreak was detected the Committee has dealt with Xf issues during each of its meetings, including assessment of reports about the spread and controls, discussion on proposals for legislation and implementation of controls. The audit team was informed that CFN will play a crucial role in establishing the priorities and in the implementation of a coordinated approach throughout Spain. 18. MAPAMA ensures the continuous distribution of all relevant information they receive to the ACCAs and to the Commission services. It coordinates issues related to Xf at national level with the relevant authorities. MAPAMA plays a key role in the work of the CFN. 19. Plant Health Services in the three ACs visited made specific attempts to coordinate the work of all relevant authorities involved concerning Xf surveys and concerning the implementation of the control measures as appropriate. In each AC visited, there was good cooperation with the forestry and environmental services for the proper implementation of the surveys. 20. In the AC Balearic Islands a management and coordination group was established in February 2017 to deal with Xf issues. It is composed of representatives of the relevant authorities at regional and island level, including forest and environmental services, municipalities, airport and port authorities and the Civil Guard. The audit team noted that the Agriculture Department of the Balearic Islands maintains close working relations with all relevant authorities and plays a strong advisory and coordination role related to their activities to control the outbreak. (see also chapters 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4). 21. The audit team was informed that at national and AC level, resources were mobilised and deployed to deal with the extra burden derived from the outbreak. However, the audit team considers that these resources are not sufficient for the full implementation of the measures required by the Decision (see chapters 5.1.6, 5.2.2, 5.3 and 5.4). 5.1.5 Information and publicity, awareness raising, related to Xf 22. There is a high level of engagement with stakeholders and the general public about Xf through multichannel awareness raising measures (websites, posters, flyers, social media, e-mail bulletins and direct communication) at central and AC level; 23. The MAPAMA website contains detailed information about the pathogen, the state of play of the outbreaks in the EU and in the Spanish DA and about the measures

Law 43/2002 on Plant Health and Royal Decree 58/2005, establish protection measures against the introduction and spread within the national territory and the territory of the EU of organisms harmful to plants and plant products.

Royal Decree 1190/1998 of 12 June 1998 regulates the national programmes for the eradication or control of harmful organisms of plants that are not yet established on the national territory. 5.1.2 Competent Authorities

The ACCAs are responsible for the implementation of plant health legislation. The Single Authority, within the meaning of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC is the MAPAMA. Plant health control activities are supervised by the Sub-directorate General for Plant and Forestry Health and Hygiene. Information on the structure and responsibilities of the plant health services can be found in the country profile: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=ES.

The audit team noted that, overall there has been an effective exchange of information between the MAPAMA and the ACCAs on CLs in general and the outbreak in Cantabria. The ACCA of Cantabria had bilateral communications on the CLs outbreak with the ACCA of neighbouring Castilla y León.

In this context, staff of the ACCA of Cantabria expressed concerns that staff shortages could jeopardise the necessary follow-up on the CLs outbreaks. In order to address the concerns, the ACCA sought to employ a private contractor for inspection activities and to involve District inspectors in surveillance tasks.
All plant health staff met during the audit exhibited adequate knowledge and technical competence with regard to the biology, identification and epidemiology of CLs. 5.1.3 Laboratories
The National Reference Laboratory for bacterial plant diseases is the Institute for Agricultural Research in Valencia. The ACCAs have their own laboratories for routine analysis.
The presence of CLs in potatoes had been detected by the plant heath laboratory of Cantabria. The National Reference Laboratory confirmed the presence of CLs and determined its haplotype.

The plant health laboratory of Cantabria had been closed for budgetary reasons on 31st December 2016. The ACCA informed the audit team that, in the light of the CLs outbreak, new funds had been made available and that the laboratory would re- 4 open by June 2017. However, it was not clear when the laboratory would be fully operational, considering inter alia that staff would need to be recruited and materials purchased.

The ACCA of Castilla y León confirmed to the audit team that it has adequate laboratory capacity for identifying potential vectors and detecting CLs in potatoes and vectors. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls

A legal framework, a clear division of responsibilities, communication between the competent authorities, competent staff and analytical capability underpin a coordinated and effective response to the outbreak of CLs.

The implementation of future control measures is at risk of being delayed if the plant health laboratory in Cantabria is not operational during the forthcoming potato growing season and if sufficient inspection staff is not made available. 5.2 PEST CONTROL Legal requirements Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC. Findings 5.2.1 Control plans

The MAPAMA has established a national contingency plan for CLs and its vectors (April 2017). The objective of the plan is to inform ACCAs how to prevent the introduction of zebra chip and how to act in case of an outbreak in order to contain the disease. The plan contains background information on the legal basis for taking action, the competent authorities involved, background information on the harmful organism, instructions on how to detect and identify CLs and its vectors, measures for eradication and guidance for extension to stakeholders, internal communication, training, evaluation and review of measures taken. The plan has been sent to all ACCAs.

text: The ACCA of Cantabria has adopted a plan for the suppression of CLs haplotype E and its vectors in Cantabria (April 2017). The plan's main objective is to identify the source of CLs and its vectors in potatoes. Other objectives are raising awareness, to reduce the incidence of CLs in potatoes and to prevent future introductions of CLs in the potato production system. In addition to background information on CLs, the plan contains planned action with regard to surveillance, controls on the movement of plant material, measures on infected places of production and measures on other places of production, evaluation and review of actions taken. 5 15. The ACCA of Castilla y León has adopted a plan for phytosanitary controls in potatoes (11 May 2017), which also covers CLs. The plan includes extension activities to raise stakeholder awareness, training off staff and surveillance of potatoes and vectors. 5.2.2 Pest identification and distribution 16. According to information provided by the ACCA, there are 32 registered producers of ware potatoes in Cantabria, all of whom are located in the municipality of Valderredible. Due to the geographical and climatological circumstances, potatoes are not commercially grown in other parts of the AC, with the exception of one producer of basic seed. 17. The AC of Castilla y León borders Valderredible and has enclaves within the territory of the municipality. Producers must notify to the ACCA of Cantabria the fields where potatoes are grown in the territory Cantabria. The obligation to notify does not apply to fields cultivated in another AC. 18. In October 2016, the ACCA took samples from potatoes in the warehouses of eight producers, in order to be examined for the presence of potato ring rot (Clavibacter michiganensis) and brown rot (Ralstonia solanacearum). Visual symptoms of zebra chip were observed in the samples of six producers. The ACCA laboratory detected the presence of CLs. The NRL subsequently confirmed the presence of CLs and established its haplotype by the end of November 2016. 19. In March 2017, the ACCA took six additional samples, one from a place of production already sampled and confirmed infected and five from other places of production. The previously sampled place was re-confirmed as infected. From the other five, four appeared to be infected. 20. In summary, out of 32 places of production, 13 were sampled and 10 were confirmed infected with CLs haplotype E. The 10 infected places of production are located in 3 different zones within the municipality. 21. At the infected places of production the ACCA identified the plots on which potatoes had been grown in 2016. A week prior to the audit the ACCA discovered that one of the potato plots of an infected place of production is located in the territory of Castilla y León. The ACCA of Castilla y León had not been aware of this until the meeting with the audit team. The ACCA of Cantabria explained that staff shortages and other activities going on at the same time had prevented an earlier communication (see also section 5.1.2). 22. According to the producers and plant health inspectors interviewed by the audit team, there had been no visible symptoms of disease in the growing crops and there had been no measurable economic damage to harvested potatoes. The infection rate in the samples from infected places of production was 0.5%. 6 23. The affected producers grew different potato varieties (Agria, Baraka and Spunta), from certified seed as well as from farm-saved seed. Certified seed originated from the Netherlands, Spain and the UK. The fact that ware potatoes became infected regardless of variety and certification, suggests that seed potatoes are not the most likely source of the outbreak. 24. At the time of the audit there was no information available on the presence of potential vectors in the area. The number of insecticide treatments on infected farms had been minor. Combined with the low infection rate in sampled potatoes, this suggests that there may be no vectors present that can efficiently transmit CLs from infected to healthy potato plants, or that the population of such vectors remains low for unknown reasons. 25. Regarding potential host plants of CLs, other than potato, according to the ACCA there is no commercial cultivation of carrots, celery or parsnips in the municipality of Valderredible. There are, however, wild Apiaceae and Solanaceae (e.g. Anthriscus sylvestris and Solanum nigrum) present in the area. 26. The audit team noted that the initial investigation has generally followed the aspects listed in ISPM 9 section 2.3.1. 5.2.3 Containment and eradiation 27. Although the MAPAMA has stated in the notification to the EC that the aim of the control measures is eradication, the feasibility of eradication has not been established as advised by ISPM 9 section 2.4. 28. The ACCA issued the following instructions for the infected places of production: do not grow potatoes on infected plots; destroy volunteer potatoes in those plots; destroy all farm-saved seed; place potatoes on the market for human or animal consumption only. In the forthcoming season producers shall use certified seed and must apply insecticides for vector control. These containment measures provide additional assurances that CLs does not spread to other EU MS, as required by Article 16.2 of Council Directive 2000/29. 29. The ACCA had verified on-the-spot and through documentary checks that farm- saved-seed was destroyed. The allocation of plots and use of certified seed would be verified in the forthcoming growing season. 30. According to the ACCA and producers interviewed by the audit team, potatoes from Valderredible are marketed in Spain only. The production is relatively small scale and partly sold under a regional brand name. Potato sales are required to be recorded in a farm register. The ACCA confirmed that it had verified the records of affected producers. There had been no direct sales to customers in other EU Member States. The ACCA considered it unlikely that potatoes from Valderredible would end up in other EU Member States, and even if they did, being ware potatoes or potatoes for processing there would be a negligible risk of CLs being transmitted. 7 31. Considering the high incidence of CLs, several of the non-sampled 19 places of production in Valderredible are likely to be infected. The ACCA declared that it did not have the resources to take samples at all places. Lacking the evidence of the presence of CLs, the ACCA did not impose measures on those producers. However, given the epidemiological situation there is reason to impose similar measures on producers with an, as of yet, unknown status. Moreover, since potato stocks would be eliminated by the start of the new growing season, the sampling opportunity was lost. 32. Given the fact that the ACCA of Castilla y León had not been aware of the presence of an infected plot on their territory, it had not been in the position to take measures to address the situation. 5.2.4 Surveillance 33. Prior to the finding of CLs, the ACCA of Cantabria had not conducted any surveys for the presence of CLs and its potential vectors. According to their action plan for the 2017 growing season, there will be visual checks of growing crops, vector traps will be set in the three different infection zones and checked every week, potential other host plants will be identified and sampled (number not determined) and a minimum of six potato samples will be checked for CLs symptoms (standard samples to be collected in the framework of potato ring rot and brown rot surveillance). This number of potato samples is too small for eradication purposes, considering that based on current data, approximately 24 out of 32 places of production could be expected to be infected. Moreover, the sample size of 200 tubers is too small if the potatoes are only visually inspected and the incidence of visual symptoms is 0.5%. 34. Three plots of carrots and three plots of leeks were tested for CLs in Castilla y León in 2016. Carrots and leeks are grown in areas at a distance from the Cantabria. No CLs was detected. The 2017 potato control plan of the ACCA of Castilla y León foresees visual inspection of potato crops, sampling of potatoes in warehouses and trapping of vectors. In total 830 lots of seed potatoes and 150 lots of ware potatoes are scheduled to be sampled. Special attention will be paid to a seed producer who is based in Castilla y León and cultivates fields in Cantabria. All fields will be visually inspected and eight samples will be taken. With regard to the trapping of vectors, the number of traps was undetermined. The ACCA would look out for Bactericera cockerelli and Trioza apicalis. Whith regard to CLs in potatoes it would be relevant to pay attention to Bactericera trigonica, B. tremblayi and B. nigricornis as well. The ACCAs of Cantabria and Castilla y León confirmed that relevant vectors, if trapped, would be tested for the presence of CLs. 35. The MAPAMA provided information regarding surveillance in other ACs in Spain. The Canary Islands have conducted several surveys since 2013 in carrots. In 2016, Asturias included checks for CLs in the Epitrix papa surveillance programme for 8 potatoes, Galicia carried out visual inspections for CLs on all potato samples collected for other purposes and Valencia did the same in the framework of the potato ring rot and brown rot surveillance. No findings were reported. For 2017, the ACs of Andalucia, Galicia, Catalonia and Murcia have plans to check potato tubers for symptoms of CLs. As all surveillance plans are based on visual examination, while only symptomatic plants will be tested for the presence of CLs, the question whether potatoes can carry the bacterium without expressing symptoms may remain unanswered. 36. With regard to vector surveillance, AC Valencia has 1,114 fixed points for traps. In 21,000 analysed traps no potential carriers for CLs were found. The AC Canary Islands trapped Bactericera trigonica in carrot plots. According to the information provided, this vector stays in the carrot crop and not seek refuge in other crops. AC Murcia and Castilla la Mancha are planning to survey for vectors in 2017. 37. The MAPAMA and the ACCAs have not substantiated that the surveys planned and those already carried out in some of the ACs, are representative for the concerned ACs, together representative for Spain, and designed and executed in a way to provide an adequate statistical confidence necessary for the results to be meaningful for regulatory purposes, as advised by ISPM9. 5.2.5 Communication with stakeholders 38. Both the ACCA of Cantabria and Castilla y León prepared leaflets about CLs and distributed those among stakeholders. The topic was also raised during meetings with producers and processors. 39. The producers and operators of warehouses visited by the audit team had a basic knowledge of CLs. 5.2.6 Research 40. Published literature indicates that CLs haplotype E is known to be present on mainland Spain since at least 2013 (see section 4.2), though data suggest with a low incidence. This raises the question why, in the absence of an eradication program, there have been no reports of large scale zebra chip outbreaks causing economic damage and why recently its presence was officially detected. 41. There are several related questions, important for taking informed decisions on control measures, to which the planned surveillance programmes may not give the answer. For example: what is the mode of action of the bacterium in the potato plant and to what extent does CLs have the capacity to cause economic damage; are there non-symptomatic infected plants which can transmit the disease; can the bacterium survive in potato seed and express itself in the following crop; and how effective are vectors in transmitting the bacterium. 9 42. Whilst the ACCAs are responsible for the control of CLs within their territories, whose activities mainly focus on surveillance, the audit team did not observe a coordinated research effort concerning above questions which are pertinent to ISPM 9 section 2.4.1and 3.2.3.
