Provided they meet the definition of "feed business" and "feed business operator" laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council 1 4 BACKGROUND This is the first time that official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production in the EU have been specifically audited by the Commission in Greece. Feed additives and their mixtures (premixtures) are the essential ingredients in modern compound feed manufacture and their use is steadily increasing. In the EU in 2016, the annual consumption of minerals, feed additives and vitamins was approximately 5.4 million tonnes (compared to 4.6 million tonnes in 2014 and 4.7 million tonnes in 2015).2 A substantial quantity of feed additives and ingredients for their production is sourced from non-EU countries and it is important to be able to demonstrate that such imports do not contain undesirable substances. From 2010 to the end of 2017, there were 79 notifications issued for feed additives under the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) for the presence of non-authorised genetically modified organisms (GMOs) (26), dioxins (21), heavy metals (17), veterinary medicinal products (5), microbiological contaminants (3) and other non-specified hazards (7). Most of these were for imported feed additives and ingredients for their production. Thus proper traceability of those substances/products is a vital prerequisite for effective control. In Greece, there are 2 feed additive manufacturers (1 approved and 1 registered), 54 premixture manufacturers (31 approved and 14 registered). Of the 32 approved additive and premixture manufacturers, 22 feed business operators (FeBOs) are also approved as traders. There are also 51 importers (24 approved and 27 registered) and 343 traders (133 approved and 210 registered). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant articles or sections of the legislation cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings in this section of the report. In addition, a table is included as an Annex II to this report summarising the main legal requirements related to the specific provisions and measures laid down in the body of EU legislation pertaining to the control of feed additives. 5.1 STRUCTURE OF THE SYSTEM FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON FEED ADDITIVES AND INGREDIENTS FOR THEIR PRODUCTION 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. The organisation of official controls on FeBOs is described in the Commission services' country profile for Greece.3

In the feed area, the DFP is the central competent authority responsible for incorporation of EU legislation into national law, planning and supervision of the implementation of 2 Source: European Feed Manufacturers' Federation

Available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/index.cfm?co_id=GR 2 the National Annual Control Programme for Feed, coordination of work of feed inspectors and laboratories involved in the official controls, preparation and maintenance of guidelines/instructions for feed inspectors, approval of FeBOs according to Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and keeping and updating the list of FeBOs. The DFP is also the national contact point for feed-related RASFF notifications. Feed inspectors at the Directorates of Rural Economy and Veterinary Services (DREVS) of the Ministry of Interior are responsible for the implementation of the official controls. 3. Based on Joint Ministerial Decree 323306/2007, each of the 61 DREVS appoints one main feed inspector and at least one substitute feed inspector. Feed inspectors can carry out controls tasks other than feed controls.

In 2015 and 2016, the DFP organised seven two-day training sessions where all feed inspectors participated. The training included relevant legislative requirements and simulation exercises of official controls on-the-spot. The control of feed additives and premixtures was covered as well including hazard analyses and critical control points (HACCP), labelling and traceability. The audit team interviewed inspectors who had participated in the training and noted that they were not aware of some particular requirements on feed labelling (see finding 28). Between 2013 and 2017, 27 feed inspectors participated in several Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) trainings on different topics (feed law, HACCP/feed HACCP and contaminants in food and feed). The BTSF training included official control of feed additives/premixtures. BTSF training materials are available to all feed inspectors through the intranet of the DFP.

There are currently 53 officials who are undergoing a comprehensive training programme on the requirements of feed control. These new feed inspectors will finish their training at the beginning of 2019 and will start to carry out official controls on-the- spot soon thereafter. They will be responsible for the official inspection of low risk category establishments at first.

Greece has national legislation for the verification of the effectiveness of official controls. The DFP plans an annual verification programme in the feed sector. Verification can be done either on-the-spot (in case of higher risk) or by documentary check (in case of lower risk); 8 DREVS each year are covered by this verification plan. Since 2016, 21 DREVS have been checked. Common weaknesses/deficiencies identified to date have been: lack of resources in certain DREVS and absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP-plans. The audit team noted that no follow-up of the recommendations made in the reports of these verification inspections or documentary assessments have been carried out as yet. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators

Ministerial Decision 340668/2008 gives supplementary measures for the harmonised implementation of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 related to the registration, approval and listing of FeBOs. There is a detailed approval/registration procedure including an 3 instruction for documentary and on-the-spot checks before approval, in accordance with the requirements of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.
The list of approved or registered FEBOs is regularly updated and published on the DFP website, in accordance with Article 9(3) and Article 19(1)(2)(7) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The registration decision on the FeBO is issued by the relevant DREVS after a documentary and on-the-spot control (required by Ministerial decision - see finding 7). The approval decision is made by the DFP after a documentary check and an obligatory on-the-spot control carried out by a feed inspector of the relevant DREVS. All establishments visited were registered and, when necessary, approved as required by Articles 9 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and the associated documentation was available. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production

The system in place ensures clear designation of competent authorities and adequate distribution of relevant tasks and responsibilities. The system for registration and approval of feed business operators complies with relevant EU legislation and supports the effective implementation of official controls.

The competent authority has put appropriate training arrangements in place to support feed inspectors in carrying out their duties competently. However, there was evidence that the training on legislative requirements for labelling checks had not been effective. 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL FEED CONTROLS 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 Planning of inspections

For the planning and harmonised implementation of official inspections, the DFP has developed a procedure (feed manual) which takes into account a range of primary data (e.g. type of business, volume of production, number of production lines, characteristics of product, etc.) in combination with weighting coefficients related to HACCP, traceability and results of previous inspections. Based on this input, the risk category and related inspection frequency of FeBOs is established. Before 2018, the calculated inspection frequencies in some instances were unachievably high. To remedy the situation, the DFP revised the inspection frequencies and since 2018 the minimum inspection frequency of high risk category establishments (all approved FeBOs) is once every year, for medium risk category establishments once every three years and for low risk category establishments once every six years. The audit team noted that FeBOs` 4 past records as regards compliance with feed law and the reliability of their own checks are included in the risk assessment as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Participation of FeBOs in private certification schemes does not influence the frequency of official controls.

The audit team reviewed the feed manual (see finding 12) and noted that it contains several checklists developed by the DFP to ensure the uniformity of the conduct of the official inspections of FeBOs manufacturing feed materials, feed additives and/or premixtures and compound feeds. The checklists seen include matters of relevance for the premises (e.g., hygiene, building and equipment, staff), potential contamination/cross-contamination with undesirable substances, processed animal proteins, GMOs and the adequacy/review of FeBOs' HACCP systems.
The DFP has prepared a comprehensive guidance document on the requirements for controls on labelling . 5.2.1.2 Implementation of inspections

In the regions visited, 70-90% of the inspections planned for 2018 had been carried out to date. The audit team noted that in most of the cases inspectors followed the instructions in the feed manual, and previous years' inspection reports were available.

All of the FeBOs visited had implemented a HACCP-based system. Detailed assessment criteria for certain aspects of HACCP-based procedures are described in the feed manual. In most cases inspectors met could demonstrate sufficient assessment of the adequacy of the HACCP-based procedures. However in two cases inspectors stated that they had never carried out assessment of FeBO`s HACCP so far and they could not demonstrate sufficient knowledge to do during the visit of the audit team. Also the absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP plans was identified as a common deficiency in the internal audits of the DREVS carried out by the central competent authority and the audit team noted that these had not been followed-up (see finding 6).

The DFP explained that FeBOs have to carry out tests for checking the homogeneity of mixing generally every year, however the DFP has not provided FeBOs with guidance on the methods which can be used to assess homogeneity of mixing. If the test results of the previous years are adequate and it is clearly described in the FeBOs' HACCP systems, the homogeneity test can be carried out every two years. However, three manufacturers visited carried out the homogeneity test less frequently. This was spotted and documented only in one DFP inspection report seen by the audit team. Generally, the inspectors were able to adequately evaluate the results of the homogeneity test.

The audit team noted that testing for carry-over of feed additives is generally part of FeBOs' HACCP plans and is performed regularly. This is in line with the requirements of Article 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Generally, the inspectors were able to adequately evaluate the results of these tests. 5 19. FeBOs are required to ensure that the feed, including feed additives and premixtures, they import satisfies the requirements of the relevant Union requirements in accordance with Article 23(1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team reviewed the available documents and noted that FeBOs have put the necessary arrangements in place to ensure that the imported feed additives/premixtures fulfil relevant Union legislative requirements. The audit team also noted that these arrangements are not normally checked during inspections. 20. There is an official instruction on the checks to ensure measuring devices used for weighing feed ingredients are calibrated. The audit team randomly checked calibration records in the FeBOs visited. All checked devices had been calibrated and the due date of the calibration was clearly labelled on the devices. The feed inspectors met informed the audit team that they checked these labels during official inspections. This is in line with the requirements of Point 3(a) of Annex II "FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 21. The audit team also checked documentation/labelling of imported feed additives from third countries and noted that all but one fulfilled the relevant authorisation requirements laid down in Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. The one exception was an amino acid at a trading company. In this case the labelling and other available documents did not contain information about the bacterial strain used in the production of this amino acid. 5.2.1.3 Traceability 22. Verification of FeBO's traceability systems is part of the approval/registration procedure and is also an obligatory requirement of official inspections. During the audit, the feed inspectors demonstrated sufficient knowledge and understanding related to the assessment of FeBOs' traceability systems. In the establishments visited, the inspectors could successfully carry out verification of FeBOs' traceability systems. This is in compliance with the requirements laid down by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 23. Generally, documents related to FeBOs' traceability systems (e.g. product specifications, recipes, production sheets, labels, results of laboratory analysis, delivery documents, etc.) were available, allowing for comprehensive traceability of feed additives and premixtures. This is in line with the requirements of point (2)(b)(i) and (iii) of Annex II "RECORD-KEEPING" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The feed inspectors met were aware of how to use the relevant documents to control FeBOs' traceability systems. 24. The feed manual contains instructions and checklists as regards controls on retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final products manufactured). The audit team randomly checked some of these samples, and in the majority of the cases these had been appropriately taken, labelled and kept under control in dedicated storage places. However, in several cases retained samples of ingredients and/or final products were not available, and, if taken, had not been sealed properly. 6 This is neither in line with the requirements of the feed manual nor the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "QUALITY CONTROL" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Previous inspection reports in the establishments visited did not mention this non-compliance. 5.2.1.4 Labelling 25. Labels of official samples sent to the DFP laboratories for analysis have to be assessed by the laboratory staff. If the labelling is not adequate, they inform the relevant feed inspector who issues an official order to the FeBO for corrective action. The audit team visited a compound feed producer where samples had been taken and the laboratory had identified some inadequacies with the labels. The laboratory had informed the feed inspector and the feed inspector had instructed the FeBO to modify the labels. The operator had made the requested modification. 26. In addition, verification that labels of feed additives and premixtures comply with legislative requirements is part of the routine official inspections as required by Article 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The feed manual gives detailed instructions on the labelling check and includes relevant requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. 27. The audit team noted that in the FeBOs visited, labels had been checked during previous inspections with no non-compliances having been identified. At the time of the audit, the audit team identified numerous and significant shortcomings in labelling in the majority of the establishments visited. Examples of non-compliances included: Complete and complementary feed was labelled as compound feed which is not in line with the requirements of Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. The instructions for proper use indicating the purpose for which the feed was intended were missing on some of the labels seen. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 17(1)(b) and point 4 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. The identification numbers of feed additives were missing on the labels of feed additives and/or premixtures, which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. The use of certain premixtures containing vitamin A in accordance with the labelled instruction would lead to the established maximum levels of vitamin A in complete feed being exceeded, which is contrary to the requirements laid down in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2015/724. The exceedance of the maximum permitted levels for vitamin A can adversely affect public health (Question No EFSA-Q-2006-121). Vitamin A content in different types of complete feed exceeded the maximum limit established by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2015/724. 28. Generally, the feed inspectors met were aware of the guidance on labelling controls (see finding 14) but, in several cases, despite the training they received (see finding 4) 7 inspectors were not able to follow it and thus could not adequately assess the correctness of the labelling. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections 29. Inspections on hygiene and traceability at FeBOs are generally carried out as required and adequately verify operators' fulfilment of relevant legislative requirements. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by the absence of assessment of FeBOs' HACCP plans which had been identified by the central competent authority and by overlooking the requirement for FeBOs to take and appropriately store retained samples. 30. The ANSVSA is the regulatory and supervisory authority for veterinary and food safety matters. The ANSVSA organises and controls the public, sanitary, veterinary and food safety activities. The authority is also responsible for the Institute for Diagnoses and Animal Health (the national reference laboratory for animal health) and the Institute for Hygiene and Veterinary Public Health (the national reference laboratory for products of animal origin).

The Government Ordinance No. 42/2004 is the basis for import controls of live animals and products of animal origin. In this act, the ANSVSA is the designated competent authority for import controls of live animals and commercial consignments of products of animal origin and non-commercial pets. NSVFSA Order No. 145/2007 establishes national procedures on import, export and transit for monitoring and surveillance of foodstuffs of non-animal from third country origin.

The Government Emergency Ordinance No. 71/2017 established a new structure of the competent authority. The new organisation of the competent authorities and their functional responsibilities took effect in June 2018. Since then BIPs/DPEs/DPIs are under the direct responsibility of the County Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Directorates instead of the central competent authority. Details of the role of County Directorates in the framework of import controls are still being finalised and these changes are not yet reflected in the country profile for Romania. The ANSVSA stated 4 that at present it is premature to gauge the impact of the reorganisation, because it has only been in force for three months and the effects are not yet quantifiable.

The ANSVSA informed the audit team that, whilst the national law designating Customs as the responsible authority for controls on personal luggage is still only at a draft stage, in practice Customs are detaining prohibited products of animal origin in personal luggage and BIPs are seizing and destroying products of animal origin identified in personal luggage. Customs, as part of the financial administration of Romania, stated that they carry out controls at the borders based on the State Border Law Government Ordinance No. 105/2001.

The authorities dealing with import controls are the ANSVSA and Customs. Their area of competences are summarised in the following table: Area of competence ANSVSA Customs X X Live animals X X Food for human X X consumption of animal origin X X Food for human X X consumption of non-animal origin Products of animal origin not intended for human consumption Feed of non-animal origin 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between competent authorities

Two formal agreements, established at central level, are in place on the cooperation between the ANSVSA and the General Customs Directorate. In addition, agreements on cooperation at local level between BIP/DPE staff and Customs were in place at all places visited.

The audit team noted that there is a good co-operation between Customs and the ANSVSA at central and regional level, and Customs and BIPs/DPEs at local level, which is in line with Articles 4 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.3 Resources and training of staff

The audit team noted that the authorities involved in import controls had a good knowledge of the import requirements and procedures and control staff receive training to maintain their knowledge. This is in line with the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5 9. The BIP/DPE staff have participated in Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) seminars on import controls in recent years. The competent authority stated that the knowledge obtained from BTSF trainings is shared with all the staff at BIPs/DPEs. 10. In 2017, the ANSVSA provided to all staff at road BIPs training on the disinfection of empty livestock vehicles to meet the control requirements laid down in Commission Implementing Decision 2013/426/EU. 11. The audit team noted that the BIP/DPE staff had also participated in the training on the use of Customs IT systems: the Import Controls System (ICS) and the New Computerised Transit System (NCTS). 5.1.4 Administrative provisions for implementation of EU rules and planning 12. In accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the ANSVSA has developed detailed documented procedures for the performance of import controls. These include instructions for sampling and analyses of products of non-animal origin in line with the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014. 13. Lists of DPEs and DPIs are published on the ANSVSA website as required in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014. The ANSVSA stated that these lists would be reviewed and updated in due course to reflect the applicable legislation.1 5.1.5 Use of TRACES 14. The audit team noted that in general, the staff use the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) correctly and without undue delay. This is in line with the requirements of Article 3(2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC. In the cases verified, with the exception of information on exit of transit consignments, all relevant information was recorded in TRACES, including details on laboratory testing. 15. The DPE staff also use TRACES to record results of import controls on products of non- animal origin subject to special import conditions although this is not an EU legal requirement. The audit team considered this to be a good practice. 16. Customs have access to TRACES to verify the validity of the common veterinary entry documents (CVEDs) and common entry documents (CEDs). 5.1.6 Use of other databases 17. Customs use the Information Systems ICS and NCTS. Customs use the integrated Tariff of the EU (TARIC) system where consignments subject to import controls are flagged based on the Combined Nomenclature code (CN code). Based on this system, Customs can only release relevant consignments for import into the EU if accompanied by a valid CVED or CED. The project `Single Window' is in a pilot phase. 1 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that the published lists of DPEs and DPIs have been updated since October 2018 to reflect the applicable legislation. 6 18. In line with Article 7 of Commission Regulation (EC) 136/2004 the BIP and DPE staff have access to and use the Customs databases ICS and NCTS. The audit team noted that the BIP staff used the information available, e.g. in case the exit of consignments in transit had not been confirmed by a Romanian exit BIP. In such cases, the BIP staff of the entry BIP can verify in the NCTS database if the consignment has left the EU territory within the statutory 30 days. 5.1.7 Enforcement measures 19. The ANSVSA has the legal authority to enforce EU import legislation. The ANSVSA stated that provisions for sanctions are laid down in national Ordinance No 984/2005, following the requirements laid down in Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/8004. During the audit, the ANSVSA did not present any information on any sanctions applied.2 5.1.8 Verification mechanisms 20. In line with the requirement of Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 the ANSVSA planned yearly visits to nine BIPs/DPEs from 2016 till 2018. The ANSVSA visited five BIPs/DPEs in 2017 and another five in 2018. Detailed reports from these supervisory visits were made available to the audit team and with the exception of the findings related to facilities and equipment, the majority of shortcomings identified by the audit team were reflected in these reports. The ANSVSA stated that the supervisory visits had led to an improvement in import controls. Following the reorganisation (see paragraph No 3) there is no specific verification procedure yet defined for BIPs, DPEs and DPIs that takes into account the changes in the competent authority organisation and responsibilities. Conclusions on the structure of the system for import controls 21. The organisation of the competent authorities and their functional responsibilities changed in June 2018. Since then BIPs/DPEs/DPIs are under the direct responsibility of the County Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Directorates instead of ANSVSA at central authority level. 22. It is too early to gauge the impact of this change on the effectiveness of the control system for imports. Nevertheless, the audit team considers that the framework in which official controls on imports are conducted is adequate, being supported by documented procedures, information technology systems and relevant training for staff. 23. The ANSVSA had verified and documented in detail the performance of BIPs/DPEs in recent years (prior to the reattribution of responsibilities), which had contributed to improvement in the conduct of official import controls. Future arrangements for supervision are as yet undefined. 2 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority provided information on fines applied during the period 2008-2016 in three of the four BIPs visited. 7 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTED GOODS 5.2.1 Pre-notifications and systems to endure the presentation of imported consignments for controls 24. Importers or their agents send an application for inspection to the ANSVSA staff in BIPs and DPEs prior to arrival of consignments. The importers or their agents use part I of the CVED to notify consignments of products of animal origin or part I of the CED for products of non-animal origin. Following the applications and pre-notification, appointments are made for the identity and physical checks - if applicable. 25. The staff in BIP/DPE Constana North stated that in agreement with Customs, unloading of containers of products subject to import controls are authorised by BIP/DPE. For this purpose, the BIP/DPE staff receive shipping manifests and information on the containers to be unloaded. Records of such authorisations were not kept at this BIP/DPE. 5.2.2 Transhipment procedures 26. The ANSVSA stated that no transhipment has taken place at the BIP Constana North, although instructions are available. 5.2.3 Transit procedures 27. In the period 2016-2017, respectively 644 and 871 consignments of products of animal origin for human consumption were subject to transit procedures in Romania. The ANSVSA stated that no transit had taken place at the BIP Constana North. 28. Procedures to verify consignments in transit entering Romania were in place in the BIPs and in line with Article 11 of Directive 97/78/EC. For the consignments verified by the audit team, the BIP staff could demonstrate that these transit procedures were correctly implemented. There were no cases where the BIPs had refused consignments transiting by road through the EU. 29. The audit team noted in TRACES that in 2017 a high number of consignments (99) in transit through EU territory and exiting via the road BIP Albia were not confirmed as having left the EU. The audit team noted that this issue was identified by the ANSVSA during their supervisory visits of the BIPs in 2017. Consequently, corrective action was taken. The BIP staff could demonstrate for a randomly selected number of cases, by using the NCTS system, that these consignments had left EU territory. 30. The Customs procedure allows transit of any products, including products of animal origin through the EU over a period of maximum 45 days instead of 30 days. The ANSVSA stated that in this respect the agreement with Customs would be reviewed.3 3 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that this would be reviewed by the end of July 2019. 8 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks 31. Procedures are in place in the BIPs/DPEs for documentary, identity and physical checks, including laboratory sampling. For controls of products of animal origin, a checklist for such controls was in use at the BIPs visited. 5.2.4.1 Checks on live animals 32. The number of live animals imported into the EU through Romania is low. In the period 2016-2017, only 12 commercial consignments of live animals arrived at the BIP Albia road, including two consignments of re-imported live pigs. All consignments were subject to documentary, identity and physical checks in line with the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Directive 91/496/EEC. 33. As at present there are no EU requirements for re-import of live animals, the BIP staff sought advice from the ANSVSA on the re-import of two consignments of live pigs which were rejected entry at the border of Moldova. Both consignments were re- imported following similar principles as for re-import of products of animal origin. One consignment of live pigs was sent for immediate slaughter; the pigs of the second consignment were euthanised and sent for destruction. 5.2.4.2 Checks on products of animal origin including sampling 34. All consignments of products of animal origin are subject to documentary and identity checks, which is in most cases a full identity check. Physical checks are included where relevant for sampling for laboratory testing. For 20 consignments verified, the ANSVSA could demonstrate that the requirements of Article 4 of Directive 97/78/EC were correctly implemented. 35. The audit team noted that the ANSVSA did not have procedures in place for handling of waste resulting from official controls. The 15kg meat present in one BIP visited could not be traced to its original consignment.4 36. In line with Article 1(2) of, and Annex II to, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, the ANSVSA has developed an annual monitoring plan for imports of food and feed of animal origin for each BIP in order to detect potential hazards to humans, animals and environment. In 2016, 2017 and 2018 all consignments sampled for laboratory analysis, had favourable test results. After the first semester the ANSVSA issued corrigenda to the BIP monitoring plans to ensure that all planned samples could be taken. The audit team noted that at one BIP visited the sampling was limited to consignments with destination Romania only. The organisation and responsibilities for import controls and the designated competent authorities in line with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are described in the country profile for Germany (see section 4).

The main responsibility for the overall legislative policy for the imports of animals and products of animal- and non-animal origin lies with the BMEL and its subordinated authorities. For some of the legal acts related to environmental and industrial contaminants, the Federal Ministry for Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (Bundesministerium für Umwelt, Naturschutz und nukleare Sicherheit ­ BMU)1 is also involved.
The Länder in Germany are responsible for the planning and implementation of official controls on imports of animals and goods. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between competent authorities

Provisions requiring cooperation between the veterinary and sanitary authorities and Customs are included in the national Food and Feed Code (§ 55), the Animal Health Act (§ 29) and the Animal Welfare Act (§ 14). A project group within the Import and Transit working group (AGED) of the Länder Working Group on Consumer Protection has worked together with the Customs Administration to produce a draft `administrative agreement on cooperation between the competent supervisory authorities in the Länder and the German Customs Administration pursuant to Regulation (EU) No 576/2013'. The agreement governs cooperation between the competent Land authorities and the German Customs Administration on controls on pet dogs, cats and ferrets brought into the EU from third countries via entry points in Germany, pursuant to Article 34 of Regulation (EC) No 576/2013. The administrative agreement is pending signature by the General Customs Directorate and the Länder. It will enter into force on the first day of the month following its signature by all the parties.

Meetings of AGED are organised at the national level twice a year where representatives from the Customs, the Länder, the Animal Health and Food unit of BMEL and BVL 1 The previous name of the BMU as described in the country profile was the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, Building and Nuclear Safety (Bundesministerium für Umwelt, Naturschutz, Bau und nukleare Sicherheit) 4 participate. Each Land presides over these meetings for two years. Minutes were available and demonstrated that issues pertinent to this audit were discussed.

The competent authorities stated that they communicate on an ad hoc basis with Customs when necessary. Regular meetings have also been organised at BIPs/DPEs/DPIs (two to three times a year) and minutes thereof were presented to the audit team. 5.1.3 Resources and training of staff

Officials in the visited places were knowledgeable and well acquainted with the procedures and the legal requirements for imported goods and animals. Evidence was available that they had participated regularly in Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) sessions and in various training courses organised at the national or local level particularly for, or relevant to, imports of animals and products of animal and non- animal origin, in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The competent authorities stated that in-house training courses are organised for newcomers. The training starts after recruitment and continues until the officials are capable of performing the job appropriately. The period depends on the background and the experience of the new employee and varies from a few weeks to a few months.

The staff at the visited entry points have access to the information in the Technical Information System for Consumer Protection and Food (Fachinformationssystem Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit) where the updates of the legislation, the reports from the working groups, the guidance, the presentations and the materials from BTSF sessions, etc. are uploaded. The system is managed by BVL.

The BIP officials have access to a commercial veterinary legislation database at the visited BIPs which enables quick access to the amendments and consolidated texts of the legal acts. 5.1.4 Administrative provisions for implementation of EU rules and planning

National legal acts, a general manual for import controls, detailed guidelines and instructions have been developed for performing official controls on imported and transited consignments, in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Non-harmonised species (including experimental animals) under Article 1 of Directive 92/65/EEC that could pose an animal or public health risk according to the national Animal Health Act need to have an import authorisation issued by a designated competent authority in each Land where BIPs are located. The audit team saw evidence that the procedure had been implemented.

Research and diagnostic samples are imported with a preliminary authorisation issued by the designated competent authority in each Land where BIPs were located, in compliance with Article 27(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. 5 14. The general manual for import controls contains links to different applications and Commission guidance allowing staff to have quick and direct access to these documents. 5.1.5 Use of TRACES and other databases 15. With a few exceptions in 2017 due to an IT breakdown, consignments of animals and products of animal origin imported into Germany were entered into TRACES as required by Article 3(2) of Decision 2004/292/EC at the BIPs visited. 16. At the port visited by the audit team, in addition to TRACES, three national IT systems are in use by the competent authority: COACH ­ a system for imported and transited consignments of animals and products of animal origin that interfaces with TRACES; COACH manifest system; COPER ­ a system for imported products of non-animal origin which is not connected with TRACES and from which the information has to be manually introduced into TRACES. 17. Products of non-animal origin are recorded in TRACES although not required by Union legislation. This significantly improves the traceability of such consignments and is considered a good practice. 18. The IT system required under Article 6(1) of the Union Customs Code for the largely automated clearance and monitoring, in accordance with customs legislation, of cross- border goods traffic by the Customs Authority is called the Automated Tariff and Local Customs Processing System (ATLAS). The audit team reviewed Customs' checks performed for two consignments of animal origin. The customs authorities are informed about consignments of animals and goods subject to import controls at BIPs or DPE/DPIs via an electronic system on the basis of their customs tariff codes. The system also flags whether a common veterinary entry document (CVED) or common entry document (CED) is required. Such flagged consignments can be cleared by Customs only after the required checks have been completed in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The New Computerised Transit System is incorporated in ATLAS. 5.1.6 Verification mechanisms 19. National guidance has been developed which sets out tools and procedures for internal audits. The document for verifying the effectiveness of official controls has also been developed in line with Article 8(3)(a)of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 20. The Länder are responsible for the above verification and for carrying out audits on the implementation of import controls. The frequency is decided by each Land. In two of the visited entry points the planned frequency was respected, reports were available and where non-compliances were identified, action had been taken. However, neither verification of the effectiveness of official controls nor supervision visits had been performed in recent years at the third entry point. 6 21. The competent authority stated that regular meetings have been organised at all entry points where significant/repeated errors in checks were discussed. The audit team saw minutes of such meetings at one of the BIPs visited. Conclusions on the structure of the system for import controls 22. The staff had a good understanding of the relevant EU import controls legislation and procedures and were supported by guidance, detailed instructions and IT infrastructure. There is an adequate framework of official controls in place which contributes to efficient coordination and cooperation within and between the designated competent authorities and to effective planning and consistent implementation of controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTED ANIMALS AND GOODS 5.2.1 Pre-notifications and systems to ensure the presentation of imported consignments for controls 23. In the majority of files checked, the importers had sent pre-notifications from the importers in a timely manner, using Part I of the Common veterinary entry document (CVED) and Common entry document (CED) in line with: Article 3(1)(a) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Article 1(1) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 for animals; Article 3(3) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 2(1) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 for products of animal origin; Article 17(1), second indent, of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and Article 7(1) and 7(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 for products of non-animal origin. 24. In the few cases where consignments have not been pre-notified by operators, the BIP staff identifies such consignments through manifest checks carried out in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 and Article 6 of Commission Regulation (EC) 136/2004, or it receives such information from Customs. 25. Manifest checks are also carried out for products of non-animal origin at the port using the COACH manifest system. At the airports visited this was is done manually. Even though not required by the legislation this is considered a good practice. 26. The audit team noted that the system in place for the organisation and conduct of manifest checks at the port (COACH manifest system) is efficient. 27. Evidence was available that warning letters had been sent to the importers when notifications had not been sent to the BIP/DPE staff prior to arrival of consignments subject to import checks. Occasionally fines had been imposed (see also finding 46). 7 5.2.2 Transit procedure 28. No transits (as described in Article 11 of Directive 97/78/EC) were registered in TRACES for the last three years via the visited BIPs. The audit team verified with the Customs the number of transits for 2017 at one entry point and no such instances were registered. 5.2.3 Documentary, identity and physical checks 5.2.3.1 Checks on live animals 29. Two of the three BIPs visited were approved for imports of the category 'Other animals'. The audit team checked different aspects of the documentation available for 50 such consignments which included, for example, ornamental aquatic animals, fish, racing pigeons, insects, experimental animals, etc. 30. With some exceptions, the checks were performed in accordance with Union and/or national legislation, for example those concerning the importation of racing pigeons, captive birds, experimental animals, insects and ornamental aquatic animals. However in four consignments of live fish out of 17 checked, the number of fish declared in Part I of the CVED differed substantially from that in the certificate and this had not been detected by the BIP staff. 31. The competent authorities issued authorisations for imports of birds (threatened with extinction) for conservation programmes, under the derogation of Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 139/2013. The audit team checked 18 consignments. All of them were destined to an approved quarantine facility. 5.2.3.2 Checks on products of animal origin including sampling 32. In general imported products of animal origin were accompanied by the correct model certificates, and originated from approved establishments and third countries listed in the relevant EU legislation. The audit team checked different aspects of the documents for 64 consignments in the three BIPs visited and with a few exceptions, the checks were seen to have been implemented correctly. 33. For example, a consignment of camel milk was imported with the required heat treatment marked in the certificate corresponding to the third country of origin as set out in Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 605/2010. The organisation of, and responsibilities for official controls on business operators producing and trading PAP are included in the wider scope of controls of the ABP chain. These controls are largely described in the country profile for Ireland, available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=IE

The SAT Division and the Milk and Meat Hygiene (MMH)/ABP Division of DAFM is responsible for the policy, legislation and planning of official controls in the area of ABP, including the specific subject of this audit.

Within DAFM, the delivery of official controls in ABP plants and operators is carried out by 16 Regional Veterinary Offices (RVOs). From an administrative point of view, eight RVOs belong to the northern macro-region and the other eight to the southern one.

The SAT Division and MMH/ABP Division are also responsible for the coordination with other divisions at central level operating in common areas of official controls (i.e., the Veterinary Public Health Inspection Service, the National Disease Control Centre and Veterinary International, the Trade and Veterinary Certification Division and the DAFM Laboratories) and with the aforementioned RVOs. This coordination is ensured thorough regular meetings organised by the MMH/ABP Division.

The allocation and distribution of various responsibilities within DAFM in the area of official controls within the scope of the audit and the coordination activities demonstrated during the audit are generally in line with the relevant requirements laid down by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The SAT Division is also responsible for ensuring appropriate training for DAFM officials. From 2013 to date various training sessions have been organised for all staff on topics which are relevant to the subject of this audit. There were two training sessions on rendering plants, one in 2014 (16 participants) and the other in 2018 (38 participants). A training session on the use of TRACES was organised in 2017 (25 participants).

Further training has been provided by Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF), in particular: "Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) principles and 4 techniques" in 2014 (11 participants), ABP (7 participants between 2013 and 2016) and TRACES (11 participants between 2015 and 2016). 5.1.2 Registration, approval and authorisation of ABP plants and operators Legal requirements Articles 23, 24, 44 and 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Article 32(5) and Chapter II of Annex XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Section D of Chapter IV, Section A of Chapter III and Section A of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Findings

ABP plants and operators are listed in publicly available lists. On-line registration forms are directly accessible to the public on the DAFM website. Answers to frequently asked questions are also available on-line to facilitate the required registration and to clarify relevant provisions to business operators wishing to handle, trade or transport ABP and derived products, including PAP.
All ABP plants and operators visited by the audit team, and their suppliers or clients, were registered or approved as required by Articles 23 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

However, in some cases, the audit team noted that the approval and registration certificates issued by DAFM did not reflect the actual products manufactured or handled, contrary to what is required by Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and did not follow the technical specifications as required by Article 32(5) in conjunction with point (3), Chapter II of Annex XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In particular, in a Category 3 processing plant visited, several processing lines were in operation. One was producing poultry PAP and another, mammalian PAP (containing also protein of ruminant origin). In the approval document, the list of products manufactured included only "poultry PAP", whereas mammalian PAP was described as "mixed offal meal". Moreover, in the aforementioned list, the wording "blood products" was used instead of "bloodmeal". The same inaccurate details were included in the relevant list of ABP plants. In another case, the registration certificate of a haulier visited, carrying only Category 3 PAP, referred to "meat and bone meal (MBM)" instead of PAP.

In the same Category 3 processing plant visited, a production line for Category 3 poultry blood has been in operation since November 2017. According to the business operator and from what was described in the relevant part of the operator's HACCP plan, the resulting poultry bloodmeal (a type of PAP) was being dispatched to another Member State to be used for the manufacturing of pet food and feed for aquaculture. However, the audit team noted that the competent authority had not yet given the relevant authorisation for the production of PAP to be used in aquaculture, which is necessary when a processing plant also processes ABP of ruminant origin, as laid down in Article 5 7 in conjunction with point (c) of Section D, Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

The audit team noticed that the above-mentioned Category 3 processing plant was not yet listed as producing PAP to be used in aquaculture, contrary to the relevant requirements laid down in Section A, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation 999/2001. In this regard, the audit team acknowledged the fact that the Irish competent authorities have not yet fully implemented the technical specifications for food, ABP and feed establishments and operators which were endorsed at the meeting of the Standing Committee for Plants, Animals and Food on 29 March 2017. 5.1.3 Planning of official controls Legal requirements Articles 4(3) and 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Article 32 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Articles 3, 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings 5.1.3.1 Planning of inspections

Between 2011 and 2015, the SAT Division carried out a comprehensive risk analysis to determine the frequency of inspections of ABP plants and operators. This analysis included: a) a risk assessment step where the potential national significance of ceasing carrying out relevant official controls was evaluated; b) a risk management step, where factors like the type and number of operators, the average size/volumes of ABP handled and the number of non-compliances found for the type of operator, were taken into account, and c) an operator selection based on the cumulative calculation derived from the previous steps.

On the basis of such risk analysis the following frequencies of inspections were decided for the type of ABP plants and operators in the scope of this audit: a) processing plants: twice per year; b) storage plants of PAP: twice per year and, c) transporters: 20% per year. The audit team noted that traders were not yet included in the system of official control, contrary to what is required by Articles 4(3) and 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, though only two such traders of ABP and derived products were in operation at the time of the audit, and only one of these was dealing with PAP and MBM. During the closing meeting, the audit team was informed of steps already taken by DAFM to address this issue (see finding 19).

Before the beginning of each year, an inspection list is prepared by MMH/ABP Division, and forwarded to SAT Division for selection of ABP plants/Operators for inspection based on the frequencies calculated (see finding 14). At this stage, further factors are considered, including results of inspections in the previous year in that type 6 of plant and the results of individual inspections. The list of inspections is subsequently sent to each RVO where the inspections are allocated to the veterinary inspectors.

The planning of inspections in 2016 and 2017 largely followed the frequencies determined through the risk classification described in finding 14, although the planned number of inspections for hauliers was less than the expected 20% (about 15% in 2016 and 11% in 2017, assuming that the current number of hauliers, about 420, was in operation also in 2016 and in 2017). Representatives of the SAT Division explained that this was due to some resource constraints. The audit team noted that the shortfall was mitigated by the fact that the frequency of inspections planned for some hauliers deemed to be more risky, e.g. those registered as transporting more than one category of ABP, was higher than expected (approximately once per year). 5.1.3.2 Sampling programme

As part of routine official controls in Category 3 processing plants, monthly samples are taken to verify that PAP complies with relevant microbiological criteria and three samples per year are taken for the quantification of insoluble impurities in rendered fat destined for animal feed. In 2017, 853 samples of feed were also planned to detect the presence of unauthorised protein of animal origin. Out of these, 293 samples of feed material were planned to detect the presence of terrestrial animal bones.

Official samples to determine the level of glyceroltriheptanoate (GTH) in Category 1 MBM (in Ireland there are no Category 2 processing plants) are planned on a quarterly basis in Category 1 processing plants. 5.1.3.3 Procedures and instructions

A comprehensive set of standard operating procedures (SOPs), checklists, circulars, etc. are available for officials carrying out all types of official controls in the area audited. These also include the "DAFM standard", specific to types of business plants/operators (e.g. processing plants, storage plants, hauliers, etc.), where a comprehensive summary of all applicable ABP requirements is included. All these documents are available on- line from DAFM's website, mainly through two information technology applications (AFIT and Ezone). The audit team noted that no specific DAFM standard had been prepared for traders of ABP and derived products, although a draft copy of such a document was shown to the audit team during the closing meeting.

Circulars Nos SAT/2017/05 and SAT/2017/04 specifically clarify the conditions on the basis of which export of ruminant PAP is allowed. SOP SAT/01/2017 specifies and clarifies the condition for transport and dispatch of MBM/PAP. 5.1.4 Conclusions on the system of official controls

With the exception of (the very few) traders, the system of official controls covering producers, storage facilities and transporters of PAP is characterised by a relatively high frequency of inspections, is based on risk criteria, and supported by a comprehensive set 7 of procedures. A relatively high number of samples are also planned to verify that PAP to be used in feed are in line with relevant microbiological criteria and are free from non-authorised proteins of animal origin. However, insufficient attention has been paid to ensuring that processing plants producing PAP to be used in aquaculture and also processing ABP of ruminant origin on the same site are authorised by the competent authorities and inaccuracies identified in the certificates of approval and registration of some ABP plants and operators (also reflected in the relevant publicly available list) could undermine the overall reliability of relevant information available. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Articles 8, 17(1), 20, 21, 31, 32 and Annexes IV, VIII, IX, X, XV and XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The first NAP was adopted in November 2012 and covered the period 2013-2017. It is available at the NFCSO web site.

The MoA, in cooperation with the NFCSO, acting as the CA, started the review of the NAP in autumn 2017. The review is led by the MoA and the NFCSO, with the support of the Plant Protection Committee (PPC), which is the responsible body for the NAP. The PPC includes several non-governmental organisations (the Chamber, Grain Producer's Association ­ Hungary, Greenpeace Hungary, National Agricultural Research and Innovation Centre, Plant Protection Institute of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Hungarian Crop Protection Association, Hungarian Association of Traders of Plant Protection Products and Fertilisers, Hungarian Beekeeper's Association), and representatives of other relevant CAs responsible for public health, nature conservation and environment protection, who are permanent members of the PPC.

During the last quarter of 2017, the responsible authorities had gathered information on the current situation of the areas covered by the NAP to provide the PCC with information on the implementation of the plan. However, the CA stated that there are no annual reports, and it is not foreseen to draft a report following the review of first NAP. The MoA and NFCSO stated that the indicators for targets included in the NAP would be under evaluation until summer 2018. The PPC has the responsibility for the amendment of the NAP. The CA indicated that it was planned to finalise the draft of the revised NAP and make it available to the public through the PPC, and by publishing it on the website of the MoA. The CA stated that two weeks would be allocated for the public consultation of the revised NAP. The revised NAP is expected to be adopted by the end of 2018.

The NAP 2013-2017 established two main objectives: To maintain an adequate level of plant health in Hungary by applying the minimum amount of PPPs; Reduction of risks to human health and the environment arising from PPP use and from pest management programs, and minimising risk by establishing appropriate risks mitigating measures. This latter objective is further developed by risk mitigation measures with regard to different aspects, including the following: 5 o reduction of operators' exposure to prevent health risks and pesticide poisonings; o reduction of risks for consumers; o reduction of the pollution of soil, surface and ground waters, and air; o protection of non-target organisms and mitigation of related risks; o substitution of PPPs of concern; o promotion of use of low-risk PPPs; o support of environmental-friendly PPP; o suppression of unnecessary treatments or high-dose treatments; o fight against the placing on the market and use of illegal PPPs; o reduction of waste generated and reduction of damage to the environment caused by the use of PPP; o mitigation of risk factors associated with aerial spraying in order to achieve safe use of PPPs by using this technique; o promotion of IPM, biological control, non-chemical alternatives and organic farming; o establishment of an independent advisory network with regard to PPP use.

In order to achieve these objectives, the NAP set out a number of measures, including specific actions to be taken and indicators to demonstrate progress. However, in the majority of cases, there were no quantifiable targets, but rather statements of intention for reduction/increasing, with no reference to a quantifiable goal. Some examples are listed below, as follows: Measure 5.2. on the marketing of PPPs: Several sub-objectives were set, including marketing of PPPs only by a trained and qualified person, providing advice to end users at the time of purchase, and decrease in the number of MRL exceedances that are caused due to lack of knowledge of PPP operators. Although this measure established some information to be gathered, such as the number and results of official controls carried out on the marketing and use of PPPs, and the number of certificates of competence issued, there were no targets set allowing for evaluation of the progress. Measure 5.3. on PPP use by trained operators: The objective was that PPP applications shall be performed only by persons having adequate qualification and knowledge. The information to be gathered for this measure included the number of offences found during official controls or the number of poisoning cases caused by PPPs. However, no quantifiable targets to be achieved had been set for this measure. Measure 5.3.2. on aerial spraying: The objective was to decrease the risk posed by drift. However, the related indicative information included the number of derogations granted for aerial spraying and the number of cases, where damages were found due to drift, with no quantifiable targets either in the area affected or in the number of cases. 6 Measure 5.3.6. on organic farming: The objective was to increase the number of producers and area dedicated to organic production, but no quantifiable targets had been set. Measure 5.4.3. on reduction of risks associated to PAE: The objective was that PAE shall be subject to inspection, and the related indicator was the number of PAE having passed the test. However, the NAP did not quantify the number of tested PAE items to be achieved. Measure 5.6.2. on PPP monitoring programme: The objective was to mitigate environmental and human health risks, posed by PPPs, and to perform targeted monitoring of which active substances are contained in PPPs. Again, there was no specific target to achieve, such as the number of controls and ratio of cases where pesticide residues were found.

Regarding the use of PPPs containing active substances of particular concern, the CAs had not established a list of substances that may fall under such consideration in Hungary and consequently, targets have not been defined for the reduction of use of such substances, as required by Article 4 (1) of SUD. The CAs stated that there was no harmonised definition or criteria at EU level to decide what substances should be considered as substances of particular concern. In the view of the CAs, new data requirements for the renewal of active substances approvals and PPP authorisations are strict enough to identify those products, which should be withdrawn from the market. However, the conclusions on the assessments of active substances are only available for those substances, included in the renewal programme each year. In addition, the EU has agreed on certain active substances, which are considered as candidates for substitution, which could have been subject to particular surveillance. However, the CAs have not focused on these substances either. Conclusion on NAP

The NAP did not establish clear targets and measures to reduce the risks and impacts of pesticide use on human health and the environment. This approach does not meet the requirements of Article 4 of the SUD. Moreover, this makes it more difficult to use the NAP as a tool to conclude on the current situation and evaluate the progress achieved.

Although steps for the review of the NAP had been initiated, at the time of the audit the review had not been concluded within the timeline of five years set in Article 4(2) of SUD. 7 4.2. TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION OF OPERATORS Legal Requirements Article 5 of Directive 2009/128/EC on training and certification Article 6 of Directive 2009/128/EC on pesticide sales Findings

The Hungarian Decree 43/2010 on plant protection lays down the requirements with regard to training and qualification of operators, involved in distribution, transport, storage and use of PPPs. Operators must hold a certificate of competence, depending on the activities they are involved in, as well as the category of PPPs to be handled. As part of the authorisation process, PPPs are classified into the following three groups: Category I PPPs are the most demanding in terms of qualification required for more hazardous products, Category II PPP other professional products not falling in the previous category, and PPPs for non-professional use are classified as Category III.

Purchase and use of a Category I PPPs must be prescribed and supervised by an expert registered as member of the Chamber. It is required that a contract binds the expert with the professional user for the whole growing season. The expert must hold a higher degree of qualification in the area of plant protection, meeting one of the following three criteria: a) a university degree in plant health, agricultural engineering, environmental management or garden engineering, where the education comprises at least 600 hours related to PPPs and it finishes with a final exam; b) a university degree as agricultural engineer, nursery engineer, biologist, forest engineer, including university graduates in other areas of natural science, and where they had completed a minimum of 24 weeks of consultations with a qualified plant health expert, or the qualification includes a diploma as a certified plant protection professional engineer, meeting the requirements listed under point a) above; c) a qualification recognised by the Minister responsible for food chain supervision as equivalent to the qualifications referred to in points a) and b) above.

Marketing, purchase and use of a category II PPP is allowed for: a) operators qualified as plant protection, horticulture or soil management technicians; b) workers qualified and trained in plant protection and storage of toxic substances/products; c) operators who have passed an exam in plant protection subject in a university or college course; d) individuals who have finished at least primary school, are at least 18 years old and have successfully passed an exam after having attending an 80-hour "Basic plant protection course". The syllabus of this basic training is approved by the MoA.
