BACKGROUND In the period January 2012 ­ June 2016, two audit series in the area of pesticides were performed, both of which focused on the control systems for the marketing and use of PPPs. In addition, some SUD related aspects were covered. Audits were performed in 25 MS, of which five MS were visited in both occasions. The outcomes are summarised in the following two Overview Reports: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=79 and http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=109. In order to assess the level of implementation of SUD, the Commission took the following actions: Evaluation of MS NAPs, which was finalised in early 2015 and then presented to MS in September the same year, identifying common weaknesses and good practices with regard to NAPs; A web-based questionnaire, that was sent to all 28 MS in December 2016 to obtain an overview of the progress made by MS with regard to SUD implementation and implementation of their NAPs; Fact-finding audits in the period March to June 2017, when six MS were visited, including Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Denmark, Sweden and Poland. 3 Based on the results of these actions, the Commission submitted a report to the European Parliament and the Council on MS NAPs and on progress in the implementation of SUD. The report was published on 10 October 2017 on the DG Health and Food Safety web-site: https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/plant/docs/pesticides_sup_report-overview_en.pdf. This report was discussed at the AGRIFISH Council meeting on 6 November 2017 and at the Agriculture and Rural Development (AGRI) Committee of the European Parliament on 13 November 2017. This report was complemented by an Overview Report, which provides more details on the state of place with regard to SUD implementation in individual MS, including good practices identified and the main obstacles encountered by MS: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=114. The NAPs are the means by which MS establish targets and actions to achieve the objective of SUD, and they can be seen to represent a significant step towards the sustainable use of pesticides. The report to the European Parliament and the Council states, however, that despite the substantial progress made by MS, there are significant gaps in many areas of their NAPs, for example in relation to aerial spraying, information to the public, the gathering of information regarding poisoning cases and measures to protect the aquatic environment. IPM is a cornerstone of SUD, and it is therefore of particular concern that MS have not yet set clear targets and ensured their implementation, including for the more widespread use of land management techniques such as crop rotation. According to the report, MS need to improve the quality of their plans, primarily by establishing specific and measurable targets and indicators for a long term strategy for the reduction of risks and impacts from pesticide use. These improvements should be included in the revised action plans, which would allow MS to continuously monitor progress with implementation and adjust strategy as necessary. The Commission wrote to all 28 MS in October 2017, specifying the omissions in either the NAPs or their implementation, to remind them of their obligations and the importance of fully implementing SUD. France provided additional information and explanations requested in a letter dated on 11 January 2018, and in particular, it provided information on water protection measures and aerial spraying. In the case of France, several issues had been identified by DG Health and Food Safety, and these were included in the scope of the present audit. In order to facilitate MS and relevant Commission services in their better understanding of SUD provisions, exchange of information on MS NAP and SUD implementation and further on-going activities, on 10 October 2017 DG Health and Food Safety launched an SUD web- portal: https://ec.europa.eu/food/plant/pesticides/sustainable_use_pesticides_en. Building on the series of six fact-finding visits to Member States in 2017, the Commission will continue evaluating NAPs and monitoring implementation of SUD by MS through its audits, other actions and follow-up activities to ensure that the objectives of SUD are being achieved. This was the third audit in a series of four audits to be undertaken by the Commission in 2018 regarding the implementation of SUD. During their visit to Brittany, on 6 June 2018, the mission team met a number of people associated with a petition submitted to the European Parliament (EP Petition No 0328/2016 4 on the exposure of agricultural workers to pesticides). The issues are being examined outside of the scope of the audit and will be the subject of a separate assessment and report to the Commissioner. An update will be provided to the Committee on Petitions of the European Parliament. 3.3. COUNTRY PROFILE AND STATISTICS DG Health and Food Safety has published a country profile for France, which can be found on the web-site of DG Health and Food Safety (http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=FR). This summarises the control systems for food and feed, animal health and welfare, and plant health, and gives an overview on the implementation of recommendations of audit reports. In terms of utilised agricultural area (UAA), France has the largest area of any MS, with more than 29 million hectares (ha) and is also the fourth largest MS in terms of forest area with 17.6 million ha. According to the information provided by the MAA, in 2015 the area dedicated to organic farming was almost 1.65 million ha representing 5.7% of the total UAA. According to the latest available data (2014) of the statistical office of the European Union (Eurostat), France was the second largest MS in terms of sales of PPPs. In 2016, a total of 73 600 tonnes of active substances contained within PPPs were placed on the market in France. The main land uses are cereals, oilseed crops, and protein crops with more than 12.88 million ha, permanent pasture with more than 9.33 million ha, fodder crops with 4.74 million ha, vineyards with 0.78 million ha, vegetables, horticulture and flowers with 0.35 million ha and fruit trees with 0.21 million ha. The agricultural sector has a significant importance in both regions visited during the audit. According to 2016 data provided by the Regional Directorates for Food, Agriculture and Forestry (DRAAF) offices: In Grand Est, the UAA is 3 million ha, of which 1.37 million ha are dedicated to cereals, 768 000 ha to permanent grassland, 347 000 ha to oil crops, 332 000 ha to fodder crops, 136 000 to industrial crops (sugar beet and potatoes), 51 000 to protein crops and 48 000 ha to vineyards. The forest area in Grand Est covers 2 million ha. In Bretagne, the UAA is 1.71 million ha, of which 570 000 ha are dedicated to cereals, 440 000 ha to temporary grassland, 330 000 to fodder crops, 192 000 to permanent grassland, 42 000 to rapeseed and 21 000 to vegetables. Bretagne is the main region for the production of cauliflowers, artichoke and tomatoes in France. The area devoted to forestry is 550 000 ha. 5 4. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 4.1. NATIONAL ACTION PLAN Legal Requirements Article 4 of Directive 2009/128/EC on National Action Plans Findings 1. The first NAP in France was launched on 10 September 2008 and was entitled "Ecophyto-2018" (Ecophyto 1). The plan reflected the objective set by the President of the Republic to reduce the use of pesticides by 50% within ten years. This objective reflected the outcome of the consultation process for the Law on Environment 2009-967 which was adopted on 3 August 2009, and sets out the same objective. Ecophyto 1 comprised 114 specific measures grouped into eight focus areas with a specific annual budget of 41 million. Focus 1: Evaluation of progress on reduction of pesticide use as measured by the number of dosage units (NODU) (see paragraph 11). Focus 2: Determination and general dissemination of agricultural systems and methods that reduce the use of PPPs, through the involvement of research, development and knowledge transfer bodies. The approach taken was first to communicate known techniques for the more effective use of PPPs. Focus 3: Innovation in the design and development of low-pesticide alternatives and cropping systems. Focus 4: Training for the safe use and for the reduction in the use of PPPs. Focus 5: Reinforcement of monitoring networks for pests and diseases, and for undesired effects of pesticide use. Improving and updating information given to farmers on the current state of crop diseases and pests would help users adapt practices and to reduce use. Focus 6: To take into account the specific conditions of overseas departments. Focus 7: Ensuring reduced and safe use of PPPs in non-agricultural areas. Focus 8: Organisation of national monitoring of progress of the plan and its roll-out in the regions, plus communication on the reduced use of PPPs.

In 2014, a thorough and independent assessment on the implementation of Ecophyto 1 was undertaken by a member of the French Parliament. The report on the assessment noted that the conditions required for meeting the objective of reducing PPPs use had been created, but not on a sufficiently large scale. The report made 68 recommendations for improving the plan (http://agriculture.gouv.fr/rapport-de-dominique-potier-pesticides- et-agro-ecologie-les-champs-du-possible).

A new plan (Ecophyto 2) was developed on the basis of these recommendations. This was published on 20 October 2015 (http://agriculture.gouv.fr/sites/minagri/files/151022_ecophyto.pdf). As had been the case for Ecophyto 1, the preparation of the plan involved consultation with stakeholders 6 and the public. While the Ministry of Agriculture was responsible for Ecophyto 1, in the case of Ecophyto 2, it was decided that the plan should be steered jointly by the Ministers responsible for Agriculture and the Environment, and greater emphasis should be given to the role of the Regions. The co-ordination and co-operation between CAs was enhanced by the decision to allocate responsibility for areas of work to units of both the MAA and MTES. This joint steering approach has improved the ownership of the projects and has facilitated the co-operation between departments. In the case of the Regions, the joint steering of the programmes is carried out by both DRAAF and DREAL. During the audit, the CAs showed a consistent approach and undertaking of their responsibilities, and the different departments were working in a co-ordinated way.

The annual budget specifically devoted to the implementation of the plan rose from 41 million in Ecophyto 1 to 71 million in Ecophyto 2, of which 30 million is allocated to the Regions and managed by the Water Agencies, and 41 million is managed by the AFB. The audit team requested information on the sources to finance the plan and the CA indicated that Ecophyto plans are financed by a levy, known as the "diverse pollution levy" collected by the Water Agency of Artois-Picardie (http://redevancephyto.developpement-durable.gouv.fr/). This levy is included in the sale price of PPPs and is based on the hazardous properties of the PPP. Therefore, the levy encourages the use of less polluting products, and it ranges from 0.90/Kg for the least hazardous products to 5.10/Kg for the most toxic products. A total of 181 million is collected annually on average, of which 41 million is used to fund Ecophyto and 140 million is used to fund actions of the Water Agencies to promote changes in agricultural practices. The total spend on these actions by the Water Agencies is 250 million per year.

There are other sources of funding which are not specifically dedicated to Ecophyto, but which contribute to the objectives of the plans. For example, in the area of research, while the direct funding from Ecophyto has amounted to 15 million since 2009, the total financing of projects which have been "labelled" as Ecophyto has reached 52 million. Other examples are a tax for monitoring the adverse effects of pesticides (phytopharmacovigilance), the budget dedicated to agro-environmental and climate measures and to conversion to organic farming under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and water protection actions by the Water Agencies. The CAs estimated that the overall total annual budget dedicated to actions related to the current Ecophyto plan exceeds 300 million.

In Ecophyto 2, the target of a 50% reduction in the agricultural use of PPPs within ten years was renewed with a two-phase timeframe, without negatively impacting on farm incomes, as measured by the NODU indicator. The first phase aims for a 25% reduction by 2020 through mainstreaming and optimising currently available techniques. The second phase targets a 50% reduction by 2025. When they enquired about the technical background used to set these figures, the audit team was informed that the decision on setting the targets had been driven by political directions of the Government after periods of consultation with the stakeholders rather than by technical assessments, both for the 7 first and second Ecophyto plans. The CAs stated that such a reduction will depend on far-reaching changes to production systems and will required the widespread adoption of scientific and technical advances, some of which have yet to be developed. The audit team requested the Directorate-General for Food (DGAL) to clarify the baseline year or period to be used to determine the compliance with the targets; however the CA informed the audit team that no decision had been formally taken in this regard.

Ecophyto 2 continued certain structural actions from the first plan, including the demonstration farm network (DEPHY) for experimental and reference systems aimed at reducing pesticide inputs. Other measures include the training and certification system (Certiphyto), information sharing tools, such as crop health bulletins and the integrated pest management portal (EcophytoPIC).

The Ecophyto 2 is structured into six priority areas, which aim to: Bring about change in practices and systems. This includes actions that were already included in the first plan, such as Certiphyto, the DEPHY network of 3 000 demonstration farms, the EcophytoPIC web portal and the plant health bulletin system with more than 19 000 plots being monitored by 4 000 technical staff. In addition, two new actions were introduced: the "30 000 farms" scheme to roll-out the proven practices developed across the DEPHY network to reduce the use of PPPs, and the Certificates of Savings of PPP (CEPP). Since the previous audit carried out in April 2013, Romania has adopted new national legislation to facilitate implementation of certain requirements contained in the EU Regulations on the production and labelling of organic products. The new legislative acts related to organic production are as follows: Ministerial Order 895/2016 on measures to strengthen the supervision of CBs by the CA; 2 An amendment to Order No 1253/2013 which provides for the exemption from control of retailers who sell organic products packaged and labelled directly to the final consumer; Government Emergency Ordinance No 34/2000 related to fees to be paid by CBs for the approval by the CA; Article 8 of Government Emergency Ordinance No 34/2000 related to conditions for direct payment of subsidies for organic operators.

Based on a review of this legislation, the audit team noted that some provisions contained in Article 9 of Ministerial Order No 895/2016 are not fully in line with Articles 65(4) and 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 9 of Ministerial Order No 895/2016 stipulates that the CBs must carry out additional random unannounced visits to at least 10% of operators under contract (Article 92c(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 stipulates that 10% of the total inspections carried out by the CB must be unannounced). The quantity of product is one of the criteria that must be taken into account for the evaluation of risk for additional visits according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 while Article 9 of Ministerial Order 895/2016 does not mention this. Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation and Provisions

National laws necessary to implement legally binding EU acts relevant to this audit have been adopted by the CA. However, one national legislative act includes some legal requirements that are not fully in line with EU organic regulations which may result in the implementation of some organic requirements by the CCA or CBs that are not in line with EU organic rules. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 27(1), 27(4), 27(4)(a), 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The country profile for Romania, published on the DG Health and Food Safety website, contains a description of the organisation of controls for organic production. The country profile for Romania can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=RO.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) is the CCA responsible for the official control on organic production. Within the Ministry the Directorate for 3 Monitoring, Inspections, Verification and Control (DMIVC), Department of Technical Inspections in Organic Farming is responsible for the control and supervision of CBs as well as for communication with the Agency for Payments and Intervention in Agriculture (APIA). The General Directorate for Agricultural Policies and Strategies (DGPAS), Department for Organic Farming and Processing Products is responsible for approval and withdrawal of approval of CBs, granting derogations (in accordance with the provisions of Articles 36, 37 and 39 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) and managing the seed database.

Both the DGPAS and the DMIVC, are represented in the County Directorates for Agriculture (DAJ) in the 41 Counties Offices and in the Municipality of Bucharest. The DAJs are in charge of annual registration of organic operators, of supervising CBs according to audit topics drawn up by MARD, of carrying out controls on 5% of operators (the list is established by MARD according to risk analysis) and on operators with more than 50 ha and for the control of the full chain in organic production, including market controls at retail level.
The control and certification of organic production is delegated to 13 CBs designated and supervised by the CCA in accordance with Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

The National Sanitary Veterinary and Food Safety Authority is the CA responsible for import control and the release into circulation in the EU of organic consignments from non-EU countries through the designated border inspection posts.

The Romanian Accreditation Body (RENAR) is the national accreditation body. It is responsible for the accreditation of CBs according to the International Organisation for Standardization (ISO)IEC 17065 standard. Five out of 13 CBs operating in Romania are accredited by accreditation bodies in other MSs.

The APIA is the National Paying Agency responsible for granting subsidies to eligible organic farmers, based on their compliance with organic requirements. The MARD sends relevant data regarding organic farming to the APIA. The MARD has signed a protocol on the basis of which MARD informs APIA about infringements in organic farming in line with Article 92(6) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The audit team noted that when serious non-compliances were detected by the CBs which lead to de- certification of land, the CCA informs APIA and APIA imposes sanctions.

The CCA informs RENAR of its supervisory activities. CCA supervision reports are sent to RENAR. The audit team reviewed the exchange of information between the CCA and RENAR concerning CCA supervisory activities, and noted that supervision reports on CBs are regularly sent to RENAR.

The CCA also receives a monthly report of the activities carried out by the DAJs on organic operators. The audit team noted that DAJs submit organic activity reports on a monthly basis to the CCA. 4 13. The CBs have procedures in place for certification of operators who move between CBs. The audit team reviewed one file related to transfer of operators and noted that not all relevant information related to the operators concerned was exchanged between the CBs involved. The CB just informed the other CB that the relevant operator had irregularities and was no longer covered by that CB as the certification was not renewed. This is not in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that the previous CB must hand over all the relevant elements of the control file and reports referred in Article 63(2) to the subsequent CB. 14. The audit team reviewed examples of the exchange of information between the CBs, the CCA, the APIA, RENAR and DAJs. The audit team noted that overall there is a good communication between the CAs and the CBs and other interested parties in line with Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Competent Authorities and Control Bodies 15. A system of control is in place in accordance with EU provisions. CAs are designated with a clear division of responsibilities and tasks between CAs and CBs. There is good communication between the CAs and the CBs and other involved parties which includes the regular exchange of relevant information on the results of controls. However, in cases where operators change their CB, the exchange of information between the two CBs involved does not cover all relevant elements of the control file. 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Article 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92c of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings 16. At the time of the audit, there were 13 CBs in Romania approved for the control and certification of organic products. 17. The CCA is responsible for the approval and withdrawing approval of CBs. Accreditation by an accreditation body is a prerequisite in order to obtain and maintain approval. CBs must be accredited to ISO/IEC 17065:2012. In line with Ministerial Order No 895/2016, approval of CBs may be withdrawn if CBs are no longer accredited or if they cease to fulfil their obligations, in accordance with Article 27(9) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Approval of CBs by the CCA is valid for one year. 18. The CCA supervises the execution of delegated controls carried out by CBs. Supervision is carried out once a year, and covers all areas of the CBs' activities. It 5 includes an office audit at the CB headquarters and witness audits in the field. The audit team acknowledge the considerable efforts made by the CCA to strengthen the control and supervision over CBs since the 2013 report. Order No 895/2016 gives the CCA a legislative tool to supervise CBs and to carry out direct control on organic operators. This legislation describes in detail the main points the CCA is required to verify during CB supervision visits / inspections. The CCA supervision audits of CBs are based on the provisions of this ministerial order which covers the relevant requirements on EU organic regulations. 19. The audit team reviewed two CCA office audits to CBs carried out in 2017 and 2018. It was confirmed that all organic requirements described in Order No 895/2016 were checked by the CCA and when irregularities were identified, an action plan with specific deadlines was requested of the CB. The audit team noted that, as results of an office audit in one CB, major non-compliances (e.g. not timely investigation of a series of OFIS notifications in 2016, granting authorisations for the purchase and use of untreated conventional seeds 2-6 months after the sowing of crops, etc) were detected and the CCA asked the CB to take measures to solve the non-compliances. The action taken by the CCA was a written warning in line with Order No 895/2016. The CB replied to the audit report with three letters: the first was an action plan to address the audit findings and recommendations, the second summarised the measures taken by the CB following the direct controls of operators in 2016 (i.e. replacement of the CB manager, more inspectors were contracted, new sampling practices, trainings, etc.) and the third contained a list of new staff in 2017. The action plan provided by the CB in response to the 2017 audit report was mostly a commitment to address the non- compliances without providing concrete actions and a timetable for this. The CCA accepted this action plan and explained that the implementation of actions proposed would be followed-up in the next office audit. 20. The CCA informed the audit team that, as result of their supervisory activity, the sanctions applied to CBs included one withdrawal of approval in 2016 and one in 2017. 21. As part of the supervision by the CCA of the CBs, the DAJs carry out inspections on a minimum of 5% of operators registered with each CB with the aim of checking the effectiveness of controls carried out by the CBs. The CCA informed the audit team that these operators are selected by the CCA based on risk (operators with past non- compliance as well as operators under suspicion or the subject of complaints). The DAJs also carried out controls on all registered operators with more than 50 hectares (ha). 22. The CCA also organised campaigns to carry out additional controls on operators considered to be on high risk, mainly operators with farms with a large number of hectares (ha) and operators sending products outside Romania. During the campaign of 2016/17, 47 operators were selected for controls. Major non-compliances were detected in a significant number of these. The audit team reviewed four files relating to 6 controls carried out by the DAJs on organic operators. Inspection reports of such inspection were comprehensive and well documented. In cases where major irregularities were identified measures were taken and sanction imposed (Overall in 2017 the sanctions applied by the DAJs to operators consisted of five written warning and one order to pay fines). 23. RENAR does not notify the CCA of the results of the accreditation audits carried out on CBs. So, this information is not taken into account by the CCA for their supervisory task which is not in line to Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, the CCA does not require the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedure which is not in line to Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This may reduce the effectiveness of supervision as any deficiency related to the CBs' risk analysis may only be detected post factum. 24. CBs provide an annual report to the CCA on control activities carried out at all operators under their control. In addition, CBs inform the CCA on a weekly basis of irregularities. 25. Training is organised by the CB visited which ensures that inspectors, including newcomers, acquire and maintain the necessary knowledge on organic production. Training records for CB inspectors reviewed by the audit team were complete and up to date. 26. New inspectors do not carry out inspections on their own until they have undergone theoretical and practical training, and have accompanied senior inspectors on inspections. Each inspector is required sign a declaration that no conflict of interest exists as well as an undertaking to respect all information obtained as confidential. 27. The CBs have a recruitment policy whereby all new inspectors agree to be trained and accompany a senior inspector on a number of inspections prior to undertaking inspections on his/her own. In addition, a new inspector must undertake his/her first inspections in the company of a senior inspector. 7 Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs 28. CBs are accredited and approved in accordance with national and EU rules. CBs are generally subject to effective annual supervision by the CCA which includes office and witness audits. However, the CCA neither takes into account the reports of the accreditation body audits nor requires the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedures in advance of annual supervision which may undermine the effectiveness of the CCA supervision. Since the previous audit, and in order to address recommendations Nos 1 and 4 from audit report 2014-7098, previous non-compliances are now factored into the risk assessment calculation. The audit team thoroughly reviewed the approach to risk assessment and noted a number of contradictions. The CB met has a highly complex approach to calculate the score to allocate an operator to a specific risk category which requires 20 criteria to be addressed. Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 specifies three criteria which have to be taken into account for the risk assessment. These are (i) results of previous controls, (ii) the quantity of products concerned and (iii) the risk for exchange of products. The audit team noted two out of these three criteria were not included in the approach used by the CB visited. 6 20. Each of the 20 criteria is reviewed separately by the CB when it performs the risk assessment of each operator. In relation to the first of these criteria, previous non- compliances, the following approach is used. The number of points attributed to an operator when a non-compliant result is confirmed with regard to unauthorised substances is 25 points. These 25 points remain on the record of the operator for the purpose of calculating the risk categorisation of the operator for the subsequent five years. A similar approach for carrying over risk points is applied when complaints from other CBs are received relating to a specific operator. If this occurs, an additional 10-30 risk points could be added to the risk categorisation score regardless of whether or not the complaint is upheld. 21. The second criterion, the quantity of products produced by the operator is only indirectly considered. One of the 20 criteria refers to the size of the operator's holding which only applies to primary producers. As an example, a holding the size of 1000 ha receives one risk point. This approach does not factor in the type of production, whether it is vineyard, tillage, or pasture and how such different production activities give rise to different quantities. The risk assessment criteria make no reference to the quantity of product produced for any other activity. 22. Regarding the third risk criteria, that associated with exchange of products (organic and non-organic), at mixed operators, a risk score of two points is allocated. 23. The CB stated that there were five other criteria which indirectly assessed the issue of quantity. However, the audit team noted that all of these criteria would only add one or two points per criteria. This would not ensure that such significant risks are taken into account in a proportionate manner. 24. The handling of other risk criteria also raised concerns for the audit team. Examples include the situation where more points are allocated to operators who have a greater number of species of animals on their land than those with a single species. This leads to a situation where an operator with 1000 cattle gets one point however an operator with two goats and two sheep got more points. The audit team also noted that when an operator complied with the requirement to obtain a derogation for the use of non-organic seed, an additional risk point was added. 25. One operator can have many activities which are controlled and certified by the CB. However the risk assessment is carried out at the level of the operator, not at the level of the activity. Each activity is subject to one annual control and if the operator is a medium risk, one additional control is imposed. The CB explained that the activity with highest risk involved e.g. mixed operation would receive the additional control. 26. One operator visited during the audit is certified for nine activities and categorised as medium risk. According to the CB procedure, each activity is subject to an annual control. The operator is subject to one additional control due to the fact that he is categorised as a medium risk. The CB stated that for this additional control, the processing activity would be selected as it is the activity carrying the highest risk due to 7 the fact of having parallel production. However, the audit team noted that at least one other activity of this operator also involves parallel production. However, this activity would not be chosen as, at the level of activity, there is a random approach to selection. 27. In relation to a new operator, the CB does not allocate a risk categorisation during the first year. One example reviewed illustrated an operator signed a contract on 17 March 2016 and was visited by the CB on 31 March 2016, however this operator would remain uncategorised for a full year. In the event of an operator being categorised as high risk this would result in a situation where no additional inspections or sampling would be undertaken during that first year. Although the CB inspectors were knowledgeable, there was a lack of guidance relating to the interpretation of the PDO/PGI/TSG legislation and its application in practice. This resulted in a number of deficiencies being overlooked by the inspectors. 5.2.5 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 33. Articles 10 and 12 of the National Framework Order No 1073 of 13 September 2017 on Quality Schemes for Agricultural Products and Foodstuff stipulate that the breaches of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 are punishable by fines. 34. Article 16 of the same Order states that if a violation is committed with intent or gross negligence, the penalty may rise to imprisonment for up to 2 years. 35. The CA stated that when the DVFA inspectors come across businesses that do not meet the requirements, they will sanction the business in question. There are four types of sanctions: warning, injunction, prohibition order (ban), and administrative fines. Finally the DVFA can file a police report in case of repeating non-compliances or serious non- compliances. Furthermore, the DVFA can withdraw a registration or approval, meaning that the establishment will no longer be allowed to operate. The DVFA conducts follow- up inspections within two months of any sanction, to ensure that the businesses have rectified the circumstances behind the non-compliance as quickly as possible. 36. In relation to CBs, the handling of non-compliances is as follows: in accordance with point 3.2.7 of the contract between the DVFA and the CB and in accordance with Article 5(2)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the CB communicates the results of the controls carried out to the CA on a regular basis and whenever the CA so requests. If the results of the controls indicate non-compliance or point to the likelihood of non- compliance, the CB shall immediately inform the CA. The relevant local CA is the first contact point for the CB with regard to the notification of non-compliances with PDO/PGI/TSG. 8 37. The CA provided a number of case studies which illustrated the types of non- compliances the CA had dealt with in recent years. Examples include: Restaurant menus stating that a certain PDO/PGI/TSG was used on a menu and on further investigation it was proven that the relevant PDO/PGI/TSG was not available in the restaurant. An ad- hoc investigation by the CA on a Danish company marketing a product which was an evocation of another MS's PDO/PGI/TSG was reviewed by the audit team. The producer stopped selling the product after having been contacted by the CA. A Producer group of a Danish PGI informed the CA that the relevant PGI was being marketed by another producer who was not being controlled by any CB. In all cases, the follow up by the CA was satisfactory. 38. The audit team noted that non-compliances relating to packing and Union symbol issues detected during official controls at Producers/Processors were categorised as minor non- compliances. Even where there were multiple cases or recurrence of such non- compliances they were still considered a minor non-compliance with the sanction being a "reprimand" which permits PDO/PGI/TSG to remain on the market. This approach is not in line with Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures 39. A system for enforcement is in place. However, there is evidence that the sanctions imposed have not remedied some of the long-standing non-compliances. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Overall, there is a system of official controls in place for PDO/PGI/TSG. The CA has been designated for official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG at Producers/Processors and at market level. However, official controls on PDO/PGI/TSG have not yet been fully implemented and, at the time of the audit, market controls were at a preliminary stage. The supervision of the CBs by the CA is not yet fully implemented as not all elements of controls have been defined. A system for enforcement is in place. However, there is evidence that the sanctions imposed have not remedied some of the long-standing non-compliances. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 31 January 2018 with the attendance of representatives of DVFA. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main preliminary findings of the audit and a number of points were clarified. 9 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The CA is invited to provide details of the action taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (action plan), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. The CA should: 1. Ensure that CBs are subject to appropriate supervision by the CA and 2. appropriate coordination between CA and CBs is in place in line with Articles 3. 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 15, 32. 4. Associated findings No 13, 14, 25, 27-31. Ensure that official controls cover the monitoring of the use of registered names to describe products place on the market in line with Article 36(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 23. Associated findings No 19. Ensure that all elements of Product Specifications are checked during official controls, and in particular: The compliance of labelling with Article 12(3) and 23(2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 and That a calculation of the input/output is performed (Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 668/2014). Recommendation is based on conclusion No 32. Associated findings No 27. Ensure that enforcement measures imposed are sufficiently dissuasive to reduce the risk of non-compliant PDO/PGI/TSG reaching the market. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 39. Associated findings No 38.
Ensure that official controls at the producers/processors of agricultural products and foodstuffs include verification of every element of the Product

Specification as required by Article 37 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012, and 3. in particular that the origin of feed is verified, as required by Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 664/2014. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 41 Associated findings No 32 and 33. Ensure that inspections and audits of Control Bodies delegated with official controls are organised as necessary, in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Czech Moravian Breeding Corporation operates the central database for pigs on behalf of the Ministry of Agriculture. The Czech Republic has a derogation5 for persons keeping a single pig for own consumption which excludes these holdings from the requirement to be registered in the central database. All other holdings must be registered in the database. 2. In 2017, the domestic pig population in the Czech Republic was 1 490 775 pigs kept on 2378 registered holdings.

Following confirmation of ASF, the competent authority issued a Decree requiring all single pig holdings in Part I to be registered. The authorities prohibited the keeping of 5 Commission Decision 2006/80/EC 4 pigs in unregistered holdings within the fenced area and required their slaughter by 1 December 2017. Following the redefinition of Part II on 1 February 2018, it was prohibited to keep pigs in unregistered holdings in Part II from 12/03/18.

The competent authority confirmed that during census of domestic pigs in fenced area (autumn 2017) and census within current Part II, almost a quarter of the forty seven non- registered holdings were identified with more than one pig. Based on the census of holdings and taking into consideration the above mentioned fact controls of farms were performed, and in case of deficiencies found, sanctions were imposed. They had imposed sanctions on the eight holdings so identified in 2017.6

The authority provided the number of pig holdings and pigs in Part I and Part II at 02/03/18 as: Registered holdings Part I Part II Number of pigs 80 34 Non-registered holdings 103 Number of pigs 68,793 24 573 30 892

Decree No. 136/2004 details the requirements for identification of animals, their registration and the registration of holdings. For breeding pigs, identification is by a unique alphanumeric number applied as a tag to left ear. For fattening pigs, identification has to be applied before pigs leave holding of birth with an ear tag in left ear or a tattoo in left ear or left side of body. This identification consists of a four digit code which permits identification of holding of origin. The audit team confirmed this mark was recorded in database allowing correlation of holding registration number with identification mark as required by Article 3 of Directive 2008/71/EC.
The audit team saw that the central database for pigs includes details of holding number, name and address of keeper and the mark which is applied as an eartag or tattoo to pigs7.

Holding registers were available on the three holdings visited by the audit team. These registers followed a national template and recorded number of pigs present and dates of events e.g. date of movement on / off and slaughter for own consumption. In both the large commercial farm and one of the smaller holdings visited, entries to holding registers recorded that more than one pig (between 2 - 8 pigs) had moved to non- registered holdings in single movement events. The ultimate destination of these pigs 6 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities added that: "Currently [July 2018], based on the Extraordinary Veterinary Measures (EVM) adopted, keeping of pigs in non-registered holdings in Part II (infected area) is forbidden". 7 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities indicated that the central database has a data field "statutes of holding infections" ("statuty nákaz chovu") where sanitary information can be inserted. 5 was not clear e.g. the large commercial farm had name and address of person they sold pigs to but competent authority considered these persons were acting as an agent and supplying pigs onwards. These were not always local transactions, in one case, the person buying the pigs lived 50 km from the large commercial holding.8 5.1.2 Movement restrictions
Notification of movements of pigs and number of pigs present on a registered holding must be notified to the central database on a monthly basis.

All movements of pigs out of Part II to a slaughterhouse must be accompanied by a veterinary certificate and food chain information. The veterinary certificate is issued by a private veterinarian and countersigned by an official veterinarian who certifies compliance with Decree No. SVS/2018/017168-Z (Extraordinary measure for domestic pigs which outlines Decision 2014/709/EU requirements) and that the holding performs testing for ASF (see point 65). Outside of Part II, there is no official requirement for movement certification to accompany pigs.

The food chain information accompanying consignments of pigs from ASF restricted areas did not include information on the regional animal health status where the holding of origin was located i.e. which ASF restricted area pigs originated from. The Competent authority indicated that this information is provided to the slaughterhouse operators by means of veterinary certification. 5.1.3 Biosecurity and wild boar management Legal requirements Article 15 and 16 of Directive 2002/60/EC; the ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 7). Findings

There are 5 815 hunting grounds in the Czech Republic of which 51 are in Part II and 315 in Part I. Prior to the reduction in size of Part II on 01/02/18, there were 100 hunting grounds in Part II and 266 in Part I.

The density of the wild boar population in the Czech Republic is shown below (per 100km²). 8 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities added that: "The above mentioned deficiency was solved by the EVM Reg.No. (C.j.) SVS(SVA) /2018/039334-G, which stipulates for all the pig farmers on the whole territory of CZ the obligation to keep an accurate and updated record concerning the sale of pigs from registered holdings, including the final destination of the pigs." 6 0-0 101-200 1-100 201-300 301-400 more than 400

The wild boar population is estimated by a combination of methods e.g. hunters walk through grounds and count sightings, photo-traps, counting hoof tracks and estimating population based on hunting bag statistics. The authorities confirmed they only use an estimate based on hunting bag and estimate current wild boar population to be in excess of 500 000.
The audit team received the national hunting bag, for the previous five years: Year 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 Hunting bag 152,468 169,483 186,148 160,164 225,000

A reliable estimate of the wild boar density in the 52km² fenced area, prior to confirmation of the first case, can be deducted from a combination of 241 found dead, 157 hunted by police and 242 hunted by trained hunters. This density of more than 12 wild boar / km² is greater than the original estimate of 2 ­ 3 wild boar / km².

Act no. 449/2001 is the principal legislation on game management. The authorities indicated they plan to amend this Act to better regulate management of wild boar populations. Currently, no strategy for non-disruptive and gradual reduction of wild boar populations is in place as required by the ASF Strategy for the Eastern Part of the EU9.

In the country there is no closed season for hunting wild boar. The authorities do not set a hunting quota. Hunting grounds with more than 1 000 hectares of forest area require a 9 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities noted that pending an amendment to the Hunting Act, guidance authorising exceptions from banned hunting practices have been issued and that the wild boar hunting season has been fully opened, with no limits on the basis of age or sex at any time in the year. Furthermore, SVS has requested Government to introduce a bounty system throughout the country to incentivise hunting. 7 hunting plan though the number of wild boar to be hunted is set by the hunting ground managers.

Following confirmation of first case of ASF in wild boar, the competent authority introduced a number of Extraordinary Veterinary Measures to control biosecurity and wild boar management. In Part II these requirements include: Group hunting (all species) is prohibited All hunted and found dead wild boar are tested for ASF and disposed of in a rendering establishment; Only trained hunters permitted to hunt / trap wild boar; No feeding of wild boar ­ only baiting allowed across the national territory. However, in fenced area, crops were left unharvested over winter and feed was provided to discourage movement of wild boar; Entry by unauthorised persons prohibited.

The authorities implemented a comprehensive awareness campaign for all groups impacted by ASF including hunters, farmers and members of the public e.g. State Veterinary Administration website regularly updated, biosecurity guide for farmers distributed, TV and radio publicity, information provided on noticeboards at municipality level and training for hunters was provided.

Training of hunters from Part II began in July 2017 and was delivered by Regional Veterinary Administration of Zlin. Training included biosecurity advice on e.g. protective clothing, handling carcases, testing procedures for ASF and identification of carcases. Training was compulsory for those wanting to hunt in Part II and 1,105 hunters followed the training. In one hunting ground visited in Part II, nine out of 16 hunting ground members had attended training and certificates were available to demonstrate attendance.

Within Part II, the authorities established a fenced area from July 2017 to prevent migration of wild boar from a 52km² area in which the vast majority of positive wild boar had been confirmed. The entire perimeter was enclosed by an odour fence (repellent to wild boar) which is reinforced, in parts, with an electric fence.

The audit team visited two hunting grounds. In Part I, hunters estimated their hunting ground had two to three hundred wild boars present and during the previous 23 months, 112 wild boars had been shot. Hunter further confirmed that it was not their intention to decrease wild boar population and in 2016 ­ 2017 hunting season, no wild boar sows were hunted. Records of hunting date, type of wild boar (sow, boar, piglet), weight and identification number were available. Identification is by a plastic tag with a unique serial number attached to carcase. In Part I, hunters are responsible for sampling all hunted wild boar for ASF, delivering samples to local veterinary office and holding carcase until ASF test results are available. A standardised submission form must be 8 completed and accompany all samples to laboratory. The form includes, inter alia, hunting ground and hunter details and description of wild boar (sex, weight and age). Chill storage was available in hunting ground (Part I) visited by audit team for carcase storage pending laboratory results. Hunter confirmed carcases were eviscerated and offal buried in the field which is not in compliance with the ASF Strategy for the Eastern Part of the EU10.

In Part II, all hunted wild boars are sent for rendering. Hunters are required to place the carcase in a plastic bag and transport it to a designated collection point for transportation to rendering plant in addition to disinfecting the site where the wild boar was shot. An official samples the carcase at rendering plant and submits samples to laboratory for ASF testing.

In the collection point visited by audit team, a storage bin for carcases was not clean and had traces of blood on it. Notwithstanding, carcases are meant to be delivered to collection points in a sealed plastic bag and the bin had undergone a cleaning process as evidenced by the presence of disinfectant in the bin. A supply of disinfectant was available on-site.

To incentivise hunting in Part II, the competent authorities have introduced financial rewards. For wild boar up to 50kg, there is a payment of 194 euro and above 50kg, there is a payment of 310 euro. In addition and to compensate for all carcases being rendered, an additional fee of 39 euro, 78 euro and 125 euro is paid for, respectively, piglets, one year old and adult sows disposed of in the rendering plant. 5.1.4 Biosecurity measures applied on pig holdings Legal requirements Articles 15 of Directive 2002/60/EC; the ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 7) Findings

The Emergency Veterinary Measure SVS/2018/017168-Z on ASF, was issued by the Regional Veterinary Administration for the Region of Zlin and came into force on 1 February 2018. It updates previous legislation by amending the municipalities in Part II and outlines measures required in accordance with the ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU including: Prevent contact between domestic pigs and feral pigs; Use disinfectants at entrance to holding / stables; Use dedicated protective clothing when looking after pigs; 10 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities noted that outside of Part II there are no ASF positive cases and that in Part I and the intensive hunting area, all hunted wild boar are tested for ASF. All tests were negative. 9 Ban feeding grass and using straw as bedding for pigs.

The competent authority has a control plan specifying the number of planned and non- planned official inspections to be performed on pig holdings across the Czech Republic. In 2017, 105 planned and 463 non-planned inspections were performed. In 2017, all registered pig holdings in Part I (62) and Part II (102) were subject to official controls for biosecurity - only 2 of these holdings were recorded with deficiencies.

Commercial farm visited had a stock-proof perimeter fence and a single point of entry for personnel and vehicles. A disinfectant barrier using a disinfectant approved by the competent authority was used at the entrance. Vehicles used for transport of live animals, feed, animal by-products and manure did not enter the site. Instructions for staff working on site were available which prohibited them from, inter alia, hunting, keeping pigs and taking meat products into the site.

In one small registered holding visited, a disinfection barrier was in place at entrance to stable using an approved disinfectant. Holding had recently been approved and herd owner confirmed advice on biosecurity and clinical signs of ASF had been provided during the approval process. In a second small registered holding, records confirmed pigs were sold to non-registered holdings ­ in two instances, two pigs were recorded as moving to a non-registered holding. Conclusions on preventive measures

The competent authorities have directed extensive resource to dealing with ASF and successfully limited the spread of ASF within the wild boar population and prevented its spread to the domestic pig population.
The central database for pigs has the functionalities necessary for traceability of pigs.

The fact that holdings with more than one pig are not registered, and consequently are not under official control represent a weak point in the control system. Outside of Part I and II, these non-registered holdings are unknown in terms of number and location. This, along with incomplete holding registers, will represent a challenge in tracing pigs and containment of disease in the event of an outbreak. 11

The biosecurity measures implemented on registered farms reduce the likelihood of introduction and spread of infection. 11 In their comments to the draft report the Competent Authorities added that: "CZ has a derogation (from Commission Decision 2006/80/EC) for persons keeping a single pig for own consumption (see 5.1.1 point 1. of the Report). Keeping more than one pig in a non-registered holding is in contradiction to the CZ legislation. In case of such a finding the SVA orders the keeper an immediate remedy including eventual sanctions." 10 5.2 EARLY DETECTION AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements Articles 4, 14, 15, and 18 of Directive 2002/60/EC, Commission Decision 2003/422/EC; articles 4 to 10 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; the ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4). 5.2.1 Surveillance in wild boar
All wild boars found dead in the country (including those killed in road traffic accidents) must be reported to the competent authority and are tested for ASF.

In Part II, an incentive of 194 euro is paid for each found dead wild boar reported. Once notified, a Regional Veterinary Administration officer attends the location where dead wild boar are found and ensures they are transported to rendering establishment (placed in a sealed plastic bag, area where carcase found disinfected, geo-coordinates recorded and carcases taken to collection point) where the carcases are officially sampled for ASF before disposal.
All hunted and trapped wild boar from Part II have their cadastral area

The Agricultural Registers and Information Board (ARIB) database contains a list of all registered pig holdings in Estonia. Currently, there are 157 holdings and the competent authority confirmed approximately 50 of them were non-commercial (backyard holdings). All movements of pigs must be notified to the authorities 48 hours in advance of movement.

All herd owners are required to maintain a holding register which can be kept in electronic or paper format. This must be updated within 3 days of a movement event and kept for 3 years. The register must include e.g. the number of animals present on the holding and an up to date record of movements. Holding registers examined by audit 3 team contained the information required by Article 4(1) of Council Directive 2008/71/EC.

All farm to farm movements must be recorded in ARIB within 7 days of the movement and these movements must be accompanied by a veterinary certificate (Form 7E). This certificate confirms, inter alia, the pigs are clinically healthy, eligible for transport and there are no movement restrictions related to infectious disease.

Currently, there is no requirement to notify and record movements of pigs to slaughter in the ARIB database. The authorities plan to introduce a requirement for the notification by both herd owner and slaughterhouse operator of movements of pigs to slaughter during 2019. This information will be entered into the national database. At present, the herd owner must inform the regional veterinary office and slaughterhouse of such movements in advance by e.g. e-mail.

The competent authority confirmed that all pigs slaughtered in Estonia are marked with an oval health mark. This means that all pigs originating in Estonia and moving to slaughter must meet the requirements of Article 3 or Article 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU. To comply with this, movement of pigs to slaughter within Estonia are accompanied by either a veterinary certificate 9T or originate on a farm officially listed as having high biosecurity standards.

Form 9T includes consignor and consignee details, number of pigs in consignment, transport details (including route), details of ASF testing performed and includes a statement that following slaughter of animals and processing of meat, there are no further restrictions on its marketing.

The Regulation of the Ministry of Agriculture No. 179 of 2004 (as amended), on the rules for the control of ASF and classical swine fever, specifies the biosecurity measures required on pig holdings. The competent authority has established a procedure for official veterinarians to perform a biosecurity inspection on all pig holdings twice per annum with an interval of at least 4 months between visits. Decree No. 130 of 18 October 2016 (as amended) provides a standardised worksheet for these inspections which cover, inter alia, the need for a biosecurity plan, controlled access of people and vehicles through disinfectant barriers and the requirement for the holding to be fenced. Holdings visited by audit team had completed biosecurity checklists which meet the requirements of Article 3(3)(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU.

The authorities approve and maintain a list of pig holdings with higher biosecurity on their website. To be included on this list, the herd owner must apply to the authorities who carry out an on-site inspection. If satisfactory, the authority issues a unique Decision for the holding which allows them to dispatch pigs to slaughter without a veterinary certificate 9T.

VFB Decree 177 of 29/12/17 requires all holdings to submit samples from the first two dead pigs, older than 60 days, for ASF testing on a weekly basis. The ASF National 4 Reference Laboratory in Tartu is the only laboratory performing diagnostic tests for ASF.

Holdings reviewed by audit team had records to demonstrate weekly submission of samples from dead pigs for ASF testing in conformity with ASF Strategy for the EU. In one county, turnaround time between sample submission and reporting of test results was 1 ­ 2 days. In two other counties visited, turnaround time within the reference laboratory was usually one day but in some cases it took an additional 4 ­ 7 days to transport the samples to the laboratory. Sampling is performed by the herd owner and the regional veterinary office despatches samples to the laboratory. The authorities confirmed that samples are sent to the laboratory using a bus service and the frequency of bus service impacted directly on sample delivery.

Between 2016 and October 2018, twenty two consignments of live pigs were dispatched from areas listed in Part II of the Annex to Decision 2014/709/EU in Estonia to areas listed in Part II of the Annex of another Member State.

The audit team reviewed the file for a consignment of live pigs which had been sent from Estonia to Lithuania. The following documents were available, reviewed by audit team and met the requirements of Article 3(4) of Decision 2014/709/EU: initial application from herd owner for the movement; risk assessment against spread of ASF performed by the competent authority and acceptance of this and the transport route by Member State of transit and destination; letter of notification of movement to Commission; an emergency plan in the event of transport failure; official inspection reports performed at least twice per annum with a minimum 4 month interval between inspections and serology results for ASF; certificate for this consignment which included the statement that "Pigs in compliance with Article 3 of Decision 2014/709/EU

In two counties visited by the audit team, authorised veterinarians performed the bi- annual sampling for ASF. There is no national guidance available for them to assist in the interpretation of Chapter IV of the Annex to Decision 2003/422/EC (ASF Diagnostic manual) and no official supervision of their performance. In a third county visited, the official county veterinarian selected pigs to be sampled and oversaw holding employee taking the samples.

On another holding visited, the team noted that pigs were moved to slaughter 4 days after a consignment of pigs were introduced from an area listed in Part II. This holding did not fully comply with the requirements necessary to avoid a standstill period e.g. the implementation of the biosecurity plan was checked every 6 months rather than every 3 months as required by both Article 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU and the authorities staff guidance. 5 15. The authorities confirmed that they do not require all holdings on the high biosecurity list to observe the 30 day standstill required for movement to slaughter ­ contrary to what is required by Article 11(3) of Decision 2014/709/EU. 16. The inspection template used during the twice per annum annum biosecurity checks has no specific section to check on residency / standstill periods. 17. The audit team reviewed a selection of holdings in ARIB, both commercial and non- commercial, and confirmed the timely recording of farm to farm movements. The authority confirmed there was no field for entering sanitary information as required by Article 1 (1)(e) of Commission Decision 2000/678/EC. 18. The competent authority has documented procedures for the movement of live pigs within and from Estonia. The instructions include the requirement to monitor common biosecurity plans, at least every 3 months, when no standstill period is applied. 5.1.2 Control of fresh meat, meat preparations and meat products from domestic pig Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) 178/2002; Directive 2002/60/EC; Directive 2002/99/EC; Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU; Annex II, sections I and III of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004; Articles 4(6) and 5 Regulation (EC) No 854/2004; Annex III, section I, Chapter IV, Points 3 and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Findings 19. The authorities have established a system which enables all domestic pigs slaughtered in Estonia to be marked with an oval health mark (see finding 5). This permits the despatch of fresh pig meat / pig meat preparations to other Member States and third countries. 20. The system depends on pigs being accompanied to slaughterhouse with a Form 9T (see finding 6) or to be listed as a holding with a high level of biosecurity (see finding 8) in order to apply the oval health mark and comply with Article 11(3) or (4) of Decision 2014/709/EU. 21. It is compulsory to notify all home slaughter of pigs to the authorities. An official veterinarian certifies ante mortem and post mortem examination has been performed and confirms there are no signs of ASF. This meets the requirements of the ASF Strategy for the EU. The backyard holding visited had veterinary certificates to prove these examinations had taken place. 5.1.3 Control of carcases, fresh meat, meat preparations and meat products from feral pigs Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) 178/2002; Articles 15 and 16 of Directive 2002/60/EC; Directive 2002/99/EC; Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU; Annex III, section IV of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004; Articles 4(6) and 5 Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. 6 Findings 22. The VFB is the authority responsible for controls on animal health in wild animals. The Regulation of the Minister of Agriculture No. 179 of 23.11.2004 outlines the general rules for hunters. These rules include the requirement to notify VFB about hunted and found dead wild boar, the requirement to take samples from all hunted wild boar, dressing of carcases in a dedicated area and the need to clean and disinfect all footwear and equipment immediately after hunting. 23. The Environmental Board sets the hunting quota for wild boar and recommends an equal number of male and female wild boars are hunted ­ the quota is a minimum number which can be exceeded. The VFB confirmed that wild boar densities (see annex 2) have decreased since the first cases of ASF in 2014. They attribute this to mortality caused by infection with ASF and an increase in the number of female wild boar hunted. 24. In one hunting ground visited, records for 2017 confirmed 13 out of a total of 25 wild boar hunted were female. In one county visited with 15 hunting clubs, 47 out of a total of 173 hunted wild boars in 2018 within the county (to November) were female. The authorities pay a fee of 100 Euro for each female wild boar hunted. 25. All wild boar hunted in Estonia, from areas listed in Part II of the annex to Decision 2014/709/EU, are tested for ASF. The traceability of the carcase and correlation of samples is achieved by the use of a unique hunting permit number (The Environmental Board issues one permit for each wild boar included in the hunting quota). 26. In the hunting ground visited, the audit team confirmed the satisfactory use of hunting permit numbers for the traceability of ASF samples and laboratory results. In general, the audit team considered the turnaround time between sampling wild boar and receipt of test results as acceptable. In addition, the hunting ground visited had chill storage and satisfactory facilities for dressing wild boar. 27. All wild boar carcases and fresh meat is restricted to the territory of Estonia. The authorities confirmed that wild boar hunted Part I are marked with a triangular health mark and can move throughout the territory of Estonia. Wild boars hunted in Part II are marked with a square health mark and are restricted within Estonia to the area listed in Part II of the annex to Decision 2014/709/EU. 28. The audit team visited a game handling establishment. It sourced wild boar directly from hunters, who deliver the carcases accompanied by a copy of the laboratory report for ASF testing and a hunter's declaration. These documents are linked by the hunting permit number. The hunters declaration contains statements relating to, inter alia, behaviour pre-hunting and findings from inspection of viscera as required by Chapter II (4), Section IV of Annex III of Regulation 853/2004. 7 5.1.4 Control of ABPs of domestic and feral pigs Legal requirements Articles 2 and 7 of Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU. Findings 29. The competent authority has established and funds a national network of containers for collection of ABPs and ASF positive wild boar carcases from hunting grounds. This has been in operation since 2016. When a positive carcase is identified, the county veterinary office instructs the hunting club to dispose of carcase in container and at the same time, arranges for container to be collected by rendering establishment. 30. The audit team selected two positive wild boar carcases to review controls over their disposal. An ABP movement document to rendering establishment and an invoice from the rendering establishment sent to VFB for the container containing positive wild boar, were available. The authorities confirmed they correlate these two documents to verify correct disposal of positive cases. They further confirmed there is no direct official supervision of disposal of positive wild boar carcases from hunting grounds. 31. At the time of mission, Estonia had no areas listed in Part III of Annex to Decision 2014/709/EU. Consequently, there was no prohibition on the dispatch of consignments of ABPs from porcine animals. Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions 32. The ARIB database is used by the competent authorities to record movements of pigs between holdings and can be used for tracing these animals. However, movements of pigs to slaughter are not recorded making it more difficult for the authorities to carry out forward tracing. The absence of a field to record sanitary information makes e.g. routine verification of movement restrictions difficult. 33. Movement controls for live pigs within Estonia allows pig meat from Part II to be dispatched to other Member States and third countries. However, there are weak points regarding how pigs should be selected for ASF sampling and on the application of standstill requirements. These may increase the risk of spread of ASF infection. 34. The fact that veterinary authorities correctly controlled the movement of pigs from Part II in Estonia to Part II in other Member States reduces the risk of ASF spreading to other countries through movement of live animals. 35. The surveillance implemented for domestic pigs, with holdings regularly submitting samples from dead pigs for ASF testing, contributes to the early detection of ASF. The delays observed in transporting some samples to the laboratory may weaken this early detection and delay measures to control the spread of ASF. 36. The authorities have implemented a system capable of sampling and testing all hunted and found dead wild boar for ASF. This gives confidence that they will likely detect 8 future cases promptly. The traceability system used for wild boar carcases should ensure that this meat is confined to the national market. 5.2 MEASURES IN CASE OF SUSPICION/CONFIRMATION OF ASF IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Articles 4-5 and 8-11 of Directive 2002/60/EC; Decision 2003/422/EC. Findings 37. The Animal Disease Control Act requires the veterinary authorities to be notified of suspicion of certain infectious diseases including ASF. 38. The number of ASF suspicions in domestic pigs notified to competent authority were as follows: 2016 2017 2018 (to October) Suspicion Suspicion Confirmation Suspicion Confirmation Suspicion Confirmation of ASF 7 6 4 3 1 0 39. In one Regional office, the audit team reviewed an ASF outbreak file for a commercial farm with more than 6,000 pigs at the time of the outbreak. The documentation confirmed the herd owner made the notification following an increased mortality. On the same day as notification, officials from the county VFB office visited the holding, took samples and delivered them to the national reference laboratory for ASF testing. A movement restriction notice on animals, people and vehicles was served, a preliminary epidemiological enquiry completed, checks made on disinfectant barriers and a census completed. 40. Protection and surveillance zones were defined at central level using ARIB database. This database has the capability to display details of neighbouring pig farms corresponding to the specific filters applied. In this outbreak there were no other pig holdings within the 3 and 10 km protection / surveillance zones. 41. ASF was confirmed the day after initial notification. Depopulation of infected premises began the following day and was completed within six days. The Estonian contingency plan for ASF lists suitable disinfectants, their required concentrations and the necessary contact times. Cleansing and disinfection of the infected premises followed the requirements of Article 12 of Directive 2002/60/EC. 42. Repopulation of the pig holding, following the disease outbreak, began more than 40 days after completion of cleansing and disinfection with a total repopulation. A sample of these pigs was then subjected to a serological examination for ASF with negative results in accordance with Article 13 of Directive 2002/60/EC. 9 Conclusions on measures in case of suspicion/confirmation of ASF in domestic pigs 43.
