Order No 131 of the State Chief Food and Veterinary Inspector establishes guidance and instruction for official staff to ensure food business operators comply with the laws and regulations corresponding to the consignments from the areas listed in Parts III, II and I of Decision 2014/709/EU, as well as from the ASF free areas.

When live pigs are despatched from areas listed in Part II or Part III of the Annex to Decision 2014/709/EU, this is carried out in accordance with the derogations provided for in Article 3, Article 3b and Article 4 of the Decision. The competent authority has established a system of holding approval and establishment approval.

Holdings wishing to use the derogations outlined in Articles 3,3b and 4 of the Decision must first apply to the territorial structural unit for authorisation. This requires an on- site inspection with report of findings and the issue of a permit to authorise movement of pigs. This movement authorisation can be valid for 3 months (holding using Article 3b derogation), 6 months (holding using Article 3 derogation) or can be for a one off movement. Each renewal of movement permit requires an on- site inspection from the territorial structural unit.
At the time of issue of movement authorisation, the herd owner signs an affidavit to respect 30 day residency and standstill requirements.
Approved holdings are listed on the Food and Veterinary Service's website. The audit team visited a slaughterhouse in Part II- they confirmed that its suppliers were all approved holdings.

To move pigs to slaughter using Article 3b derogation, the slaughterhouse operator applies via the Agricultural Data Centre (ADC) database to move the pigs. The official veterinarian in the slaughterhouse assesses the application e.g. checks holding status, ASF regionalisation status and food chain information prior to authorising the individual movement event. 4 8. Once movement is authorised, the slaughterhouse operator generates two movement documents from ADC database. One of them accompanies pigs to slaughterhouse and the other one is retained at holding of origin. 9. The audit team visited a holding using Article 3b derogation and noted: The permit to move pigs from this holding to slaughterhouses was issued quarterly (five separate movement permits were available as the holding supplied five different abattoirs and each movement permit requires a route plan). The holding is inspected at least four times per annum by the territorial structural unit who, inter alia, review biosecurity plans. The common biosecurity plan (breeding holding and fattening unit) is not approved in advance by competent authority, which is not in line with Article 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU. There is official sampling for ASF, as required by Article 3b(b). The official veterinarian confirmed they select pigs to be sampled to ensure sick pigs and samples from all age groups and stables within holding are included. In addition, the business operator carries out regular surveillance for ASF. Records of post mortem examinations and sampling / test results for ASF were available with samples taken throughout the month e.g. 19 samples tested in January, 14 in February and 14 in March (2018). The audit team noted delays of up to 10 days between sampling and test results being available. The authorities confirmed this was due to the business operator collecting samples over a number of days before submitting them for laboratory testing. The audit team reviewed movements of pigs into this herd for the period January to March 2018 and confirmed all pigs originated from a single, separate breeding holding. For holdings using the derogation provided by Article 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU, the authorities confirmed they did not carry out a complete risk assessment related to the risk mitigation measures in place in both the breeding holding and the holding of dispatch. This is not in compliance with Article 3b(d) of Decision 2014/709/EU. 10. On the large commercial pig holdings visited, business operators had recently made significant investments in biosecurity e.g. enhanced disinfection points for transport vehicles and hygiene sluices for staff. 5.1.2 Control of fresh meat, meat preparations and meat products from domestic pig Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) 178/2002; Directive 2002/60/EC; Directive 2002/99/EC; Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU; Annex II, sections I and III of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004; Articles 4(6) and 5 Regulation (EC) No 854/2004; Annex III, section I, Chapter IV, Points 3 and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5 Findings 11. The authorities have provided guidance for officials on the approval of slaughterhouses, cutting plants and meat processing establishments under article 12 of Decision 2014/709/EU (Order 131, Section VI). At the slaughterhouse visited, the audit team saw the pre-approval inspection report. The report confirmed that the authorities had evaluated the operator's procedures which specified, inter alia, that pigs could only be slaughtered from Part II if the holdings complied with Article 3 or 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU. In addition, the operator had a policy to slaughter pigs from Part II on a separate day from pigs originating in Part I and the free area. 12. The authorities carry out four official inspections each year to each slaughterhouse, which include an assessment of traceability and application of measures related to ASF - the reports for slaughterhouse visited showed compliance. The audit team selected a consignment of pigs presented for slaughter and the operator demonstrated their ability to forward trace carcases. 13. The audit team reviewed conformity with the 30 day standstill requirement in a random selection of pig herds, supplying the slaughterhouse visited, and found them all compliant. In one consignment, pigs had moved to the slaughterhouse despite pig movements in to the consigning herd within the previous 30 days. The authorities explained this was one of the two holdings in the country using Article 3(1)(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU which permits the competent authority to define production units within a holding. 14. The audit team visited an operator producing minced meat, meat preparations and meat products. The procedures in place indicated the food business operator only accepted meat eligible for the EU market. For a product selected by the audit team, the operator demonstrated an adequate internal traceability system. 15. The competent authority performs one detailed official check on traceability per annum in all cutting plants and processing establishments in Latvia. This is in addition to traceability forming part of the inspection they carry out in all processing establishments at a minimum frequency of three times per annum. The recent official reports on traceability, for processing establishment visited, confirmed the reliability of their system. One report recorded a national health marked carcase (beef) being detected & rejected which confirms the implementation of operator's procedures. 16. The ADC database stores individual slaughter numbers for pigs which allows their tracing back to the holding of origin. Both competent authority and food business operator can access this information. 17. The authorities confirmed there is no routine post-mortem inspection for home slaughtered pigs on non-commercial holdings. On the non-commercial holding visited by audit team, the herd owner indicated they would inform the authorities of any 6 abnormalities observed during slaughter. Findings 18. Food and Veterinary Service is the authority responsible for controls on animal health in both domestic and wild animals. At the time of audit, their responsibility for wild boar mainly included the receipt and processing of surveillance samples from hunters and supervision of stored wild boar carcases awaiting test results. 19. The State Forest Service is the authority responsible for hunting controls and collection of wildlife population data. Order No. 77 of 7 May 2015 outlines national biosecurity measures for hunters. These include rules on disposal of animal by-products derived from wild boar, use of disinfectants in hunting grounds and the requirement to sample hunted wild boar for ASF testing. In order to strengthen biosecurity in hunting grounds, the competent authority confirmed the Regulation of the Cabinet of Ministers No. 226 was published on 19 April 2018. The Regulation will be monitored and controlled by the Food and Veterinary Service in co-operation with the State Forest Service. The authorities estimate that seventy percent of hunting grounds have primary processing facilities (including access to chills) with the remainder of hunting grounds using home storage for carcases awaiting ASF test results. In hunting ground visited by audit team, facilities for dressing wild boar, chill storage and a dedicated pit for disposal of animal by-products were available. 22. State Forestry Service has a control plan in place which requires each hunting ground to be inspected at least once per year. A standardised checklist is used which does not allow for a detailed assessment of effectiveness of measures applied e.g. biosecurity. During the most recent inspection of the hunting ground visited (Part II), there was no indication on the checklist that biosecurity was evaluated. 23. All wild boars found dead, across the country, are tested for ASF. 24. All wild boars hunted in Part II and Part III are tested for ASF. Samples are taken by hunters who deliver them to a territorial structural unit and generally get the results by e- mail. A standardised sample submission form must be completed by hunters and includes, inter alia, the unique identification number allocated to carcase, geographical co-ordinates for place of shooting, name of hunter, address where carcase is stored and a declaration from hunter to confirm they will store carcase until test results are available. A fee of 30 euro is paid to hunters for sampling and an additional 50 euro if sample is from a female wild boar. The audit team observed there was a quick turnaround for test results and hunters / hunter representatives met were satisfied with service provided. 25. In one territorial unit visited, the competent authority confirmed they had no plan to perform official controls in hunting grounds. Instead, their inspections were mostly reactive e.g. to a positive ASF test result in hunted wild boar or a request to organise a driven hunt which requires a joint inspection and approval by the territorial unit and the Forest Service. 26. For carcases with positive results to ASF, the territorial structural unit seizes and destroys the carcase, supervises cleansing and disinfection of storage area and pays hunter 50 euro compensation for loss of carcase. In one territorial unit visited, the authorities confirmed there had been two instances when positive ASF results had been notified by the laboratory and carcases were not available for seizure and destruction. At closing meeting, officials confirmed sanctions had been taken against these two hunters. 27. In hunting ground visited (Part II), hunting leader confirmed members lived both locally and in Riga (free area). Hunting leader confirmed in 2017 -18 hunting season approximately 50 wild boar were shot and all were used for own consumption by all hunters. Therefore, some wild boar meat left Part II and hunting leader was not aware this was prohibited. This movement of wild boar carcases / fresh wild boar meat from Part II is not in accordance with Article 15(1)(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU. 28. The authorities confirmed there is one game handling establishment processing wild boar carcases in Latvia (Part II) with the remainder of wild boar carcases used for "own 8 consumption" by the hunters. The establishment processed 108 wild boar carcases in 2017 and 15 wild boar carcases to April 2018. The carcases arrive at the establishment with a hunter declaration confirming e.g. initial examination of carcase by trained hunter, date, time and place of hunting and generally fulfils the requirements of Annex III, Section IV, Chapter II of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 29. Wild boar carcases in this game handling establishment are only sourced from the free area. The food business operator and official veterinarian confirm this using the Food and Veterinary Service's interactive map for ASF regionalisation. The official veterinarian performs post mortem examination and samples carcase for trichinella. On receipt of negative trichinella result, oval health mark is applied to wild boar carcase. This is not in compliance with Article 15(1)(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU which prohibits consignments of fresh meat of feral pigs from the areas listed in the Annex being dispatched to other Member States or to other areas in the territory of the same Member State. This risk is mitigated by the fact that all carcases despatched from this game handling establishment are heat treated. 5.1.4 Control of ABPs of domestic and feral pigs Legal requirements Articles 2 and 7 of Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU. Findings 30. For domestic pigs, there is a proforma for the movement of ABPs from Part III. The staff at the territorial structural unit visited explained that currently there is only one company responsible for collection and processing ABPs from part III. All the trucks had Global Positioning System (GPS), had an authorised route within Part III, and were sealed at a designated exit point where they were also disinfected. Full EU legal references are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the latest amended version. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 PREVIOUS DG SANTE AUDITS Detailed information on the structure and organisation of the Greek competent authorities can be found in the country profile for Greece at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=GR DG SANTE has carried out numerous inspections and audits in Greece, the reports of which can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm While the topic of the current audit has not been the specific objective of any previous audit, the subject has been considered within the scope of numerous sectoral audits carried out since 2006. At the time of writing, there was one open recommendation (recommendation 2012- 6285-13 in relation to controls on pesticides) to Greece in relation to the application of Article 4(6). 4.2 CONTEXT: ARTICLE 4(6) OF REGULATION (EC) NO 882/2004 The requirements laid down in Article 4(6) of regulation (EC) No 882/2004, that: Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out, and shall take appropriate measures in the light of their results, to ensure that they are achieving the objectives of this Regulation. These audits shall be subject to independent scrutiny and shall be carried out in a transparent manner should be read together with the definition of Article 2(6) laid down in the same Regulation: "Audit" means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives. Further guidance on certain aspects of the requirement and definition is provided in Commission Decision 2006/677/EC. In particular the guidelines in the Annex to this Decision provide information on aspects to be considered when ensuring that the audit 2 process is systematic, transparent, independent and subject to independent scrutiny. In addition, guiding principles in relation to compliance with planned arrangements, effective implementation of arrangements and their suitability to achieve objectives are provided. Guidance is also provided in relation to audit reporting, follow-up of the audit outcome, audit review and dissemination of best practice, resources and auditor competence. As reflected in the recitals of the decision: "The guidelines are not binding but serve to provide useful guidance to the Member States in the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004". The NAS Network is a network of officials (auditors) from MS CA, responsible for the performance of audits of official control systems as provided for by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The Network meets regularly, under the chairmanship of, and facilitated by, DG SANTE to exchange experiences in implementing national audit systems on official control activities. During the course of these exchanges; discussions, workshops etc. good principles and practices are identified and agreed by the network. To enable dissemination of information the Network, working in plenary session and through sub- groups, and facilitated by DG SANTE, consolidates agreed principles and good practices on specific topics into Network Reference Documents. At the time of this audit in Greece the NAS Network has produced the following Network Reference Documents: Risk Based Planning for Audits of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1; Independence and Independent Scrutiny - Feb 2014 ­ Version 1; Auditing Effectiveness of Official Control Systems - February 2014 - Version 1; Audit evidence, October 2015 - version 1; Root cause analysis, November 2016 ­ version 1. These documents may be used as reference documents; however, they do not constitute an audit standard and are not legally binding. The network document on risk-based planning for audits of official control systems clarifies what is the consensus of audit experts on the objectives of Article 4(6): "The main objectives of audits as laid down in Article 4(6) are: To verify: CA's compliance with general and specific control requirements of feed and food law, plant health, animal health and welfare rules. Compliance of official controls with planned arrangements at a national level, which may include: Control plans of any kind (MANCP, business-, operational-, control-, monitoring- plan etc.) with the purpose of giving effect to legal requirements. Policies, strategies, procedures, guidelines. 3 To evaluate: Suitability of the planned arrangements in achieving the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Effectiveness and consistency of the implementation of planned arrangements i.e. the capability to deliver the planned outcomes. Whether enforcement measures are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. To identify: Areas for improvement in the CA control and management systems. Audits may also play a supportive role in risk identification and analysis." The network document "auditing effectiveness of official control systems" explains the audit experts' common understanding of the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004: "Following from the definition of effectiveness, objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 have to be identified and they should be used as audit criteria. Within this document and for the purposes of assisting in auditing effectiveness according to Article 4(6), the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are considered to be, but not limited to: "To ensure high quality of official controls..." (from preamble 14) "...in verifying compliance with legal requirements" (from preamble 6, Article 1) Ensuring implies application of the PDCA cycle: Quality consists of: Uniformity of controls and decisions (from preambles 12 and 14). 4 Consistency of controls (from preamble 14). Effective risk-based targeting of controls (Article 3.1). Reliable detection of non-compliance. Turning non-compliance into compliance, when detected (Articles 54, 55)." 4.3 METHODOLOGY The evaluation process of the current DG SANTE audit consisted of: an initial desk study phase in which the relevant information already available in DG SANTE was collated and analysed. This included the Greek Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) and associated Annual Reports, the country profile for Greece and sectoral audit reports; examination of certain documentation provided by the CA prior to the audit; and meetings with the services responsible for carrying out audits under Article 4(6). The DG SANTE audit team evaluated arrangements in place and verified their application through examination of a variety of evidence, including documentation of the audit programme development and its implementation. Observing the performance of individual auditors during audits was not included in the scope as the DG SANTE audit team considered that the effectiveness of an individual audit can be better judged by DG SANTE's sectoral Units' auditors in the context of relevant sectoral audits. The evaluation focussed particularly on those elements which the audit team considered essential to ensure the audit services can produce reliable audit results, with adequate coverage of official controls, to give assurance that the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 are being met: Responsibilities for the implementation of Article 4(6); Status and reporting lines of auditing bodies/units; Arrangements for independent scrutiny; Procedures for the selection of auditors and management of auditor competence; Procedures for the development of audit programmes, with particular attention on how an adequate coverage of the audit/risk universe is ensured; Planning, conduct and reporting of audits, including the approach to auditing the suitability of arrangements in place for official controls to achieve the objectives of the Regulation; Follow-up of audit recommendations including the system in place for corrective action in cases where problems are identified during the audit activities; and How and to what extent transparency is ensured. In addition, the audit team gathered information on particular challenges faced by the CA when implementing Article 4(6). 5 5 OVERVIEW OF MAIN FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES 5.1.1 Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states, that "Competent authorities shall carry out internal audits or may have external audits carried out......" text: The Ministry of Rural Development and Food (MRDF) is responsible for the organisation of controls in the areas of animal health, animal welfare, feed, import, animal by-products, fishery and live bivalve mollusc, primary production and food safety until the first stage of processing. It is mainly responsible for policy co-ordination (including issuance of circulars, checklists and guidelines), while the implementation of controls is decentralised to services at regional level (13 administrative regions and regional units).

The Helenic Food Authority (EFET) is responsible for controls of processed food after the first stage of processing, food hygiene and food contact material and, since 2017, it has also responsibility for milk collection centres and egg and honey packaging.

Food for special nutritional purposes is within the competence of the National Organisation for Medicines, and bottled water is within the competence of the departments of the Ministry of Health. Neither of them was included in the scope of this audit. 5.1.2.2 Responsibility for audits of official controls

Presidential Decree 223/2000 on the "Organization of Hellenic Food Safety Authority" established EFET's audit service the Department for the Quality Assurance of Provided Services (DQAPS). The Department carries out audits in relation to requirements of Standard ISO 9001:2008 and Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Within the MRDF there are two audit services: 6 a. The Directorate of Agronomic Controls and Audits (DACA) has been established by Presidential Decree 97/2017. It carries out special investigations (complaints, special investigations in relation to fraud and disciplinary measures) which was at the time of this DG SANTE audit a major task. It also is responsible for carrying out internal inspection of agricultural, animal and fisheries policy and is responsible for organising internal audits in relation to Regulation (EC) 882/2004. b. Joint Ministerial Decision 11935/134642/24-10-2014 establishes the procedural framework for the internal audits system for the areas of pesticide residue controls and controls on the marketing and use of plant protection products (PPP). It was last modified by the Joint Ministerial Decision 1201/18604/2-2-2018 which in particular established new rules for the selection of members of the Audit Committee which is considered to be the audit body once the system is implemented. At the time of the DG SANTE audit the Committee had not yet been set up.

The Director of DACA oversees four departments. The heads of the department have no staff working for them and are entrusted with the performance of investigations and audits within their areas of responsibility. Regarding Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in particular the following are within the responsibility of the departments: i. Veterinary Department: animal health, animal welfare, food of animal origin (first level of processing), slaughterhouses, live bivalve molluscs, fishery and import controls in relation to live animals and food of animal origin. ii. Department of Agriculture: primary production, genetically modified organisms, organic farming, food of non-animal origin (until first stage of processing) and imports of food of non-animal origin. iii. The Department of Animals: feed and feed imports, organic feed, organic products of animal origin. iv. The Department of Fishery covers audits in relation to fisheries policy, but has no responsibilities in relation to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The internal audit system of the DACA was not fully operational at the time of the DG SANTE audit and, so far, had only carried four pilot audits (two in relation to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) in 2017.

According to the MRDF the internal audit system for PPP is planned to be operational by the end of 2019. The fact that the audit arrangements had not yet been put in place did not allow the DG SANTE audit team to evaluate the audit arrangements. Conclusions

Responsibility for auditing of official controls has been clearly allocated, but so far only 7 EFET has put internal audit arrangements in place and carries out audits. Audit systems of MRDF are at an early stage of development and, therefore, cannot provide assurance that official controls are carried out as intended and that instructions or guidelines given to staff carrying out the controls are followed. 5.2 AUDIT ARRANGEMENTS 5.2.1 Independence 5.2.1.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 defines "audit" as "a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related results comply with planned arrangements and whether these arrangements are implemented effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives." In section 5.3 of the Annex of Decision 2006/677/EC further guidance is provided to Member States on `independence', including: "Audit services should be free from any commercial, financial, hierarchical, political or other pressures that might affect their judgment or the outcome of the audit process. The audit system, audit service and auditors should be independent of the activity being audited and free from bias and conflicts of interest. Auditors should not audit areas or activities for which they have direct responsibility. All relevant competent authorities should introduce safeguards to ensure that responsibility and accountability for audit and control activities, such as the management and supervision of official control systems, are kept sufficiently distinct." In addition, the NAS Network Reference Document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny provides additional guidance to Member States on threats to independence and mitigating measures. 5.2.1.2 Findings
DQAPS reports directly to the President of EFET as provided for in Article 7 of Presidential Decree 223/200.

DQAPS stated that it is equipped with sufficient resources in order to perform its tasks including a sufficient travel budget. DQAPS stated that reason for not achieving the full implement multi-annual audit programme was not a lack of resources, but had other reasons (see section 5.2.4).

DQAPS procedures contain some general requirements regarding the independence of auditors, but do not specify details. 8 14. DACA reports directly to the Minister of MRDF as laid down in Presidential Decree 97/2017. 15. DACA stated that the travel budget for 2018 was 1400 Euro and the budget allocated for the first three months of 2018 had to be completely spent before the additional funding is made available. The Director of DACA stated that this amount did only allow performance of even one full audit per year per department and that the administrative rules put additional burdens on the audit body regarding the planning and performance of audits. For example, for the animal by-product pilot audit of 2017 the RU of Attica was selected as the budget available to the audit service was not sufficient in order to visit the RU initially planned for. DACA stated that also the number of staff was not sufficient in order to perform its tasks independently. 16. DACA carries out specific investigations. According to the Director of DACA the State Secretary may ask at any time to carry out any kind of investigation or controls and that the workload (which cannot be planned) may affect the implementation of the audit programme. The DG SANTE audit team noted that no specific arrangements are in place to ensure that no potential conflict of interests may arise from additional tasks given to the audit service. 17. In the absence of a clearly defined audit universe and methodology for the identification of risk-based audit priorities (see section 5.2.4), DACA based its multi-annual audit programme solely on suggestions from the relevant Directorates of the MRDF which are involved in controls (issuance of circulars and supervision of controls) and may be subject to internal audits by DACA. 18. DQAPS and MRDF referred to the following public sector law regarding the independence of the auditors and experts potentially used by the internal audit teams: a. General rules concerning independence, objectivity, confidentiality and impartiality are laid down in Ministerial Decision No 12932/2006, Article 23. b. Law 3528/2007 (Civil Servants Code) establishes legal provisions for the avoidance of conflict of interests for staff involved in official controls. 19. Both CAs stated that technical experts used for internal audits will not be allowed to perform audits in regions where they are employed. This is not contained in the DACA's procedures, but is specified in the DQAPS procedure (E003.8). 20. The Heads of the audit services and the auditors met by the audit team had a good understanding of potential risks concerning independence and impartiality. Conclusions 21. Although procedures are not detailed, the arrangements put in place by EFET ensure sufficient independence of the audit function and process, as well as of individual 9 auditors, to safeguard the credibility and reliability of audit results. 22. The independence of DACA is compromised by several factors including a limited travel budget which is not adequate to ensure that the audit service can perform audits in all Regions of Greece based on risk-based planning. Furthermore, the independence of the audit service is undermined by a lack of arrangements for the avoidance of conflicts of interest which may arise from special investigations/controls and a planning process which solely relies on contributions from the relevant Directorates of MRDF. 23. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the latest amended version. 3.2 INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures (ISPMs) are issued by the International Plant Protection Convention of which all EU Member States are members. Those of particular relevance to this audit are listed in Annex 2 to this report. 4 BACKGROUND The audit was carried out as part of a series, aimed at evaluating Member States' controls at import of plants, plant products and other objects for the purposes of plant health. It forms part of a wider project on this topic, the objectives of which are to ensure the correct and uniform application of EU plant health legislation, to identify examples of good practice being applied by Member States, and to help inform the development of new measures and guidelines for import controls in the EU. This was the tenth audit carried out by the Commission services in Germany on plant health related topics since 2003, and the third related to plant health import controls. The previous audit on that topic was carried out in April 2008 (Ref: DG(SANCO)/2008/7909), as part of a general audit. Further information on DG Health and Food Safety, including audit reports and its work programme, are available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. Unless otherwise stated, statistical data in this and the following chapters was provided by the JKI. 4.1 IMPORTS OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS Approximately 40 000 consignments of regulated plants and plant products are imported into Germany each year. The majority of these are cut flowers (mainly roses (Rosa sp.)) and fruit and vegetables (mainly mangoes (Mangifera sp.), aubergines (Solanum melongena) and leaves of basil (Ocimim sp.). There are a further 60 000 consignments imported each year, 2 which contain wood packaging material included in the Commodity Risk List (see section 5.1.5 below). There are 84 designated points of entry in Germany for regulated plants and plant products however, Frankfurt airport and the port of Hamburg are the two main points of entry for such consignments and both were visited during this audit. 4.2 INTERCEPTIONS The Europhyt ­ Interceptions annual reports published by DG Health and Food Safety1, provide a detailed analysis of the interceptions notified by all Member States and Switzerland each year. According to the report for 2016, the latest published at the time of this audit, Germany accounted for 14.3% of all interceptions notified in Europhyt, the EU's rapid alert system for plant health, and 7.6% of all interceptions of harmful organisms that year. As detailed in Table 1 below, Germany notified a total of 5 564 interceptions between 2013 and 2017. A further 1 733 interceptions were notified in the first five months of 2018. The majority of the interceptions were for reasons other than the presence of harmful organisms, including the lack of, or incomplete, phytosanitary certificates or the presence of prohibited items. The Country Profile for Germany published by DG Health and Food Safety2 provides a detailed description of the organisation of the official controls for plant health relevant to this audit. In summary: The Federal Ministry for Food and Agriculture (Bundesministerium für Ernährung und Landwirtschaft - BMEL) acts as part of the national plant protection organisation; The Institute of National and International Plant Health of the Julius Kühn Institute (JKI) acts as the Single Authority, within the meaning of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The tasks of the JKI are established in Article 57(2) of the Plant Protection Act; it plays an advisory and coordination role on matters relating to plant health, including the provision of information on new and emerging risks, training and guidance for use by inspectors. Further information is available on the JKI's website: https://www.julius-kuehn.de/en/; The 16 Land Plant Protection Services (Pflanzenschutzdienste der Länder - LPPS) are competent for plant health at Land level, and are responsible for the implementation of official plant health controls in their respective territories. In some Länder (e.g. in North Rhine Westphalia) the State Forestry Service (Landesbetrieb Wald und Holz) is responsible for plant health activities in the forestry sector, including the control of wood and wood packaging material imported from non-EU countries; The Federal Customs service (Bundeszollverwaltung) is responsible, inter alia, for monitoring compliance with customs legislation. It is also involved in the identification and supervision of consignments declared to contain regulated articles, including those imported by post or passenger baggage, until the required plant health controls have been completed; Diagnostic and technical support for the plant health checks is provided by laboratories of the LPPS. The JKI acts as the national reference laboratory for plant health, and includes specialised laboratories such as entomology, mycology and bacteriology to assist the work of the institutes, and on request, the LPPS.

text: The authorities responsible for plant health have been designated in line with Article 1 and 2 of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.1.2 National legislation relating to import controls for plant health

The JKI informed the audit team that Directive 2000/29/EC is transposed by the Federal Plant Protection Act (Pflanzenschutzgesetz) and the Plant Health Order (Pflanzenbeschau-verordnung). The Plant Health Order contains specific provisions on 2 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=DE 5 new harmful organisms and sets obligations for the Länder for import and outbreak controls (see section 5.5.3 below). The Annexes to Directive 2000/29/EC are directly applicable; no implementing act is required. Similarly, Commission decisions on emergency measures are directly applicable in Germany.
Article 10 of the Plant Health Order transposes the provisions of Article 13b(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC concerning exemptions for small quantities (see section 5.3.4 below).

The BMEL stated that the Plant Protection Act provides the necessary legal powers to perform import controls for plant health and to take any necessary measures including the power to control the movement of consignments or to require their destruction or re- export. This was confirmed by the audit team during their site visits and review of documents relating to the interception of consignments (see section 5.6 below).

The BMEL informed the audit team that requirements for charging fees for import checks are harmonised at national level, however it is the responsibility of individual Lander to establish the level of fees for their import checks. The fees are published by the Lander; the method for their calculation has been communicated to the European Commission in line with Article 13d (3) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The Federal Ministry of Finance and the customs authorities it appoints are involved in monitoring compliance with plant protection regulations during import, export and transit in accordance with Article 61 of the Plant Protection Act. To this end, they can intercept affected consignments, communicate their suspicion of a violation of plant protection provisions and share information obtained during customs formalities with the relevant authorities, and present these consignments to the relevant plant protection authorities.

The responsible official bodies in charge of inspection posts, have the authority to carry out their duties in line with Article 1, and Point 1, first indent, of the Annex, to Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.3 Staffing provisions and training

The BMEL informed the audit team that there is a total of 197 full-time equivalent (f.t.e.) plant health inspectors in Germany, of which, 81.5 f.t.e. are responsible for import controls for plant health.

In Hesse, there is a total of 21 inspection staff based at Frankfurt airport, which provide cover in a three-shift pattern. At Hamburg port there are 7.4 f.t.e. inspectors who perform import and export plant health checks. As noted in section 5.4.4 below, this number is not sufficient to ensure that appropriate checks can be carried out for all consignments of regulated plants, at peak times. 6 11. All of the staff responsible for performing plant checks have at least a university or third level qualification, which is complemented by training provided by the LPPS and the JKI. 12. The LPPS are primarily responsible for providing training for their inspectors, and this varies by Länder, but typically comprises of a period of on-the-job training for new recruits, followed by three to four one-to-two day training courses annually, covering all aspects of plant health controls, including surveillance, plant passports and import controls. In North Rhine Westphalia, Hesse and Hamburg, the LPPS informed the audit team that they also hold weekly meetings with inspectors to provide an update on new legislation and risks, and to enable the informal exchange of information between staff. 13. The JKI, together with the LPPS, also provides training for inspectors, including annual workshops, which are held in February and March, and involve 100 to 120 inspectors. LPPS inspectors should attend these at least once every two years. 14. The JKI also provides specific training for inspectors on the use of Europhyt- interceptions, and occasional training following significant amendments to the Compendium (see section 5.1.5 below). The JKI stated that it is organising a first training on the use of TRACES3, in 2019. 15. Meetings are also held in May each year between the JKI and senior inspectors to exchange experience and discuss proposed changes to controls at national and EU level. The JKI also informed the audit team that it organises bilateral and multilateral meetings and visits, to enable the exchange of experience with other Member States, including visits to points of entry. 16. The system of training ensures that the staff responsible for performing plant health checks are appropriately qualified to do so, in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC, and have the necessary technical competence, especially in the detection of harmful organisms, required by Article 1, and Point 2, first indent, of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.4 Laboratory and technical support 17. Inspectors performing checks at points of entry and places of destination make an initial identification of suspected harmful organisms, which enables a preliminary decision to be taken on whether there is a non-compliance, and if so, the action that should be taken, pending confirmation by the relevant laboratory. It was noted that the inspection posts at Frankfurt airport and Hamburg port had access to appropriate laboratory facilities and equipment for that purpose, including Berlese funnels and mesh cages for samples of suspected fruit flies. 18. The JKI acts as the national reference laboratory for plant health. It informed the audit team that most LPPS have established their own laboratories to provide diagnostic and 3 https://ec.europa.eu/food/animals/traces_en 7 technical support for plant health controls. The laboratories are either already accredited to ISO Standard 17025 with flexible scopes for analytical methods, or are in the process of being so. 19. The audit team visited the LPPS laboratories in North Rhine Westphalia and Hamburg and noted that both had a high-level of expertise and facilities for performing analysis of samples from imported consignments. Both laboratories had appropriate record keeping and procedures in place for handling samples suspected of being infested with harmful organisms. 20. The specialists met by the audit team stated that they used only internationally recognised diagnostic protocols for the identification of harmful organisms, including fruit flies. 21. The JKI is responsible for performing preliminary pest risk analysis on request by the LPPS to support decision making following a finding of a new harmful organism, either in imported consignments, or in the field. The JKI informed the audit team that it had carried out assessments for 88 such assessments since 2012. Further details are available on the JKI website: http://pflanzengesundheit.jki.bund.de/index.php?menuid=57. 22. The official bodies responsible for performing plant health checks have expertise in the identification of harmful organisms, or access to such expertise, in line with the Article 1, and the third point of Item 1 in the Annex, to Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.5 Working instructions and internal communication 23. The JKI informed the audit team that a range of information and guidelines relating to import controls have been provided at federal level to assist inspectors performing import checks, which are published on the JKI plant health portal4. The main guidance document is the Compendium on plant health controls in Germany (Kompendium zur Pflanzengesundheitskontrolle in Deutschland, hereafter, 'the Compendium'). Additional, specific guidance is issued as required, either by email or as a specific guidance document. 24. The Plant Health and Horticulture Department of the EAB has been designated by the Ministry of Rural Affairs as the Single Authority for plant health in the sense of Article 1(4) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The EAB is responsible for the policy and co-ordination of plant health import controls, including the preparation of written guidelines and providing training and technical advice to inspection staff.

The implementation of plant health import controls is carried out at 16 inspection posts at points of entry under the competence of the regional county centres of Harju, Lääne- Viru, Ida-Viru, Pärnu, Võru and Põlva.

The Agricultural Research Centre provides diagnostic services to the EAB and is responsible for carrying out analysis of all samples collected during plant health import checks. The laboratory of plant health and microbiology is accredited according to ISO 17025. The EAB stated that the Agricultural Research Centre generally carries out a preliminary diagnosis based on PCR testing methods, and these are systematically followed up with full DNA sequencing to confirm the species. The DNA sequencing is carried out under contract by a third party laboratory. 5.1.2 National legislation relating to import controls for plant health

Transposition of EU plant health legislation is the task of the Ministry of Rural Affairs. The provisions of Council Directive 2000/29/EC have been transposed through the Plant Protection Act (RT I 2004, 32, 226 adopted on 21 April 2004) and implemented by ministerial regulations. Decrees of the Director General of the EAB provide the regulatory basis with specific orders that have to be implemented by plant health inspectors at the inspection posts and county centres.

Inspectors have most of the legal powers necessary to enforce import controls, including the power to control the movement of consignments or have them destroyed or re- exported. This was confirmed by the audit team during visits to inspection posts and when reviewing documents concerning intercepted consignments (see section 5.6 below).

However, the EAB stated that there is no legal basis for inspectors to carry out plant health checks of non-regulated articles and therefore such checks are not carried out (see also section 5.3.7 below). The absence of a legal basis is not in line with Article 13(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The EAB also stated that there is no legal basis for inspectors to target or take action against non-regulated harmful organisms, even if they were 2 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=EE 4 considered to present a phytosanitary risk. Estonia does not have the necessary legal basis to take the measures necessary to prevent the introduction of non-regulated harmful organisms, which is not in line with the objective of the second subparagraph of Article 16(2) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC. The Agricultural Board stated that in both cases, the lack of legal basis was an issue of transposition, and they recognised it as an omission, and stated that this would be remedied with the implementation of the new plant health regime3, due to come into force in December 2019. 5.1.3 Staffing provisions and training

text: At the central level, nine officials of the Plant Health and Horticulture Department of the EAB are responsible for plant health import control activities. Other tasks include the evaluation of the effectiveness of the control system and the cooperation and exchange of information with other institutions, official control bodies of other countries and international organisations. At the 16 inspection posts, 18 inspectors are responsible for carrying out plant health import checks. The same staff also carry out pre-export checks and issue phytosanitary certificates as required, and in some cases perform import checks under marketing standards regulations4.

In the 15 county centres, 20 plant health inspectors are responsible for tasks other than import controls. The EAB stated that these staff undergo the same training as inspectors based at inspection posts at points of entry so that, if necessary, they can be temporarily redeployed and assigned to inspection tasks.

All inspectors are required to hold a university or a higher education technical degree in Agronomy. Upon recruitment, staff responsible for performing plant health import checks undergo an induction course and follow a four-month training plan. All inspectors must also attend annual refresher training, (last organised in April 2017) aimed at ensuring consistency of implementation, sharing experience and covering new or recent changes to legislation. At the time of the audit, plant health inspectors had also received training on the latest version of the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES), and had participated in Better Training for Safer Food courses organised by the EC.
Inspectors are competent and appropriately qualified to carry out proper checks, in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.1.4 Working instructions and internal communication

The Plant Health and Horticultural Department has issued an inspection manual for carrying out import checks, with up-to-date work instructions (last updated on 18/01/2018). Additional guidance based on ISPMs and the EPPO Global Database for performing import checks is provided in the training material for inspectors during their induction and refresher training. The EAB stated that the sampling methodology set out 3 https://ec.europa.eu/food/plant/plant_health_biosecurity/legislation/new_eu_rules_en 4 https://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/fruit-and-vegetables/marketing-standards_en 5 in the inspection manual is based on the EU Vademecum (harmonised import plant health inspection procedures).

The EAB has also issued datasheets for specific plants and plant products, with detailed information on the special requirements of Annex IV, part A, section I of Directive 2000/29/EC and the derogations provided for specific commodities for import, in particular wood from the USA. The guidance documents issued to inspectors cover the full scope and range of import controls.
Inspectors have access to written, up-to-date work instructions in line with Article 1, and Point 1 of the Annex, to Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.5 Planning of official controls

Planning of import controls is based on the notification of import and request for plant health inspection submitted by importers or their import agents. All companies importing plants and plant products or their import agents, need to be registered in the EAB's database which is accessible by inspectors operating in the inspection posts and the county centres. In order to plan official controls, inspectors take into consideration the type of business and the commodities imported by companies, the results of any previous risk analysis and the history of compliance of a particular trade.

The EAB does not implement reduced frequency of checks, all regulated articles are subject to documentary, identity and plant health checks. The inspection posts of Muuga, Narva and Luhumaa operate either in shifts or according to a continuous time- schedule. Other inspection posts operate only in response to advance notification of import by stakeholders. 5.1.6 Verification procedures and audit

Plant health inspectors' work is subject to assessment by the chief specialist of the EAB and the lead inspector of the relevant inspection post. This includes on-the-spot control of inspectors to ensure that all relevant legislation and inspection instructions are complied with. Assessments are carried out annually for two years following the assignment of tasks and at least once every three years thereafter.

The EAB stated that a system is in place to ensure that inspectors from one point of entry carry out shifts in another on a rotational basis to gain additional experience and to ensure the consistency of applied controls. The audit team confirmed this with inspectors met during visits to inspection posts. Conclusions on organisation of plant health import controls

The organisation of plant health controls in Estonia is generally in line with EU requirements and it provides considerable assurance that all consignments of regulated articles are subjected to import checks carried out by trained and competent staff. This is reinforced by the detailed induction process for new staff, comprehensive work 6 instructions, regular training and supervision.

The lack of legal basis to take measures against non-regulated harmful organisms or to carry out checks of non-regulated articles means that the programme of plant health checks cannot quickly be adapted to respond to new or emerging plant health risks. 5.2 COOPERATION AND COMMUNICATION WITH CUSTOMS SERVICE AND STAKEHOLDERS Legal requirements Article 6 of Directive 2004/103/EC. text: There is a bilateral cooperation agreement between the EAB and the Tax and Customs Board which was revised in 2015. The agreement contains information about commodities subject to plant health checks and import requirements for wood and WPM. The cooperation agreement includes provisions concerning the exchange of information between the two services, which includes allowing the EAB inspectors access to the Customs database and to information about imports of regulated and non- regulated articles including WPM through TARIC codes.

Regular meetings between the two services take place both at central, and local level within inspection posts. Information on new legislation or changes to existing legislation related to plant health import controls, is regularly provided to the Customs services through training events carried out every three years (last took place in 2016). In particular, any changes to the list of regulated articles are shared in advance of the amendments coming into force.

The Customs Service informed the audit team that they have included information on plant health regulations in their internal manual of procedures, which is regularly updated, and that new procedures and instructions are always prepared in close cooperation with the EAB and communicated to the responsible Customs officers. They also stated that there is good cooperation with the EAB which provides clarification and additional information when needed.

Customs are responsible for controlling courier and postal imports and carrying out checks of passengers and private vehicles entering through Tallinn airport and road border crossings, for the presence of regulated or prohibited plants and plant products (see also sections 5.3.4 and 5.3.5 below). Customs also carry out checks of WPM found during their own controls. WPM which does not carry the ISPM 15 mark or which is suspected of carrying harmful organisms is referred to the EAB for further action (see also section 5.5.1 below). 7 24. The audit team noted that there was very good cooperation at both national and local level between the plant health and Customs services. This ensures that consignments of regulated articles are kept under Customs supervision until plant health checks have been completed, in line with Article 13(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.2.2 Stakeholders 25. The EAB publishes information related to plant health import controls on their website, including updates to legislation or the scope of import controls, as well as information on new and emerging threats from specific harmful organisms. During 2016 and 2017, the EAB organised training events for the use of TRACES and ad hoc training events for the import of WPM used in the transport of specified commodities originating in China. Plant health import related information and guidelines for using TRACES are available to operators on the website of the EAB. Information for passengers and the general public is also provided through the Estonian Association of Touring Companies and on the webpage of the Tax and Customs Board and the internet: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EGRps6Us8Fs&feature=youtu.be . The audit team confirmed that the information available on the EAB website is up-to-date. Conclusions on cooperation and communication with Customs Service and stakeholders 26. The good cooperation between the plant health and Customs services, which is based on a national agreement, ensures effective supervision and control of imported consignments, in line with EU legislation. This is supported by the effective communication with stakeholders. 5.3 IMPORT PROCEDURES Legal requirements Articles 4, 13(1), 13(3), 13b(1) and (3), 13c(1)(c)(ii) and 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC. Directive 2004/103/EC. Findings 5.3.1 Notification of import 27. There is a legal requirement for advance notification of import of regulated articles, which must be made to relevant inspection posts 24 hours prior to arrival of the consignment. The advance notification of import also serves as an application of the operators for plant health inspection. Details of the consignment need to be provided, including the number of the accompanying phytosanitary certificate and the estimated time of arrival for inspection. The phytosanitary certificate (or a copy) and the bill of lading must be submitted with the pre-notification. 8 28. The EAB informed the audit team that the advance notification can be delivered either through TRACES (in place since 2014) or via email. Due to differences between the data that private stakeholders are obliged to submit and the data required by TRACES, where time allows, inspectors insert import data arriving by email from operators into TRACES during the documentary check. The EAB stated that approximately 30% of advance notifications are submitted online through TRACES, which has been in use in the inspection posts of Narva and Luhamaa since November 2017. At the time of the audit, whilst still in transition, the use of TRACES by private stakeholders was not obligatory. The EAB stated that, as there is no option for the inclusion of pre- notifications in the national database, their intention is to make notifications by TRACES mandatory from mid-2019. 29. Findings DG Health and Food Safety has published a country profile for Spain1 which provides a detailed description of the organisation of the official controls for GMO of relevance to this audit. In Summary:

Within the Ministry of Health, Social Services and Equality (MSSSI), the Spanish Agency for Consumer Affairs, Food Safety and Nutrition (AECOSAN) is the central competent authority (CCA) responsible for the coordination of food safety controls, including GMO in food, excluding import controls. Also within the MSSSI, the Sub- directorate General for Foreign Health (SGSE) is responsible for the control of food imports, including GMO in food.
MAPA's Sub-directorate General for Means of Livestock Production is responsible for coordinating GMO controls in feed, other than imports.
The Sub-directorate General for Health Agreements and Border Controls (SGASCF) is responsible for controls of feed imports including GMO in feed.
The ACs are responsible for the implementation of controls regarding GM food and feed other than at import.

The Inter-ministerial Council on GMOs is responsible for authorisation and deliberate release of GMO into the environment under Part B of Directive 2001/18/EC in connection with the entry in the national catalogue of genetically modified plant varieties.

Within MAPA the Spanish Plant Variety Office (OEVV) is responsible for coordination of controls for GMO presence in conventional seeds. Furthermore, it is responsible for controls on GMO release into the environment under Part B of Directive 2001/18/EC for the purpose of variety registration of GM crops in the national catalogue. 1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=ES 5 13. MAPA's Sub-directorate General for Quality and Organic Farming (SGCDAE) is responsible for the control of the presence of GMOs in organic products, other than at import. Within the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness, the Sub- directorate General for Inspection, Certification and Technical Assistance in Foreign Trade is responsible for import data and for controls on the presence of GMOs in import. 15. Laboratorio Arbitral Agroalimentario (LAA) together with Centro National de Alimentación (CNA) are the two national reference laboratories (NRL) appointed under article 33 of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004 and Regulation (EC) No. 1981/2006. The two NRLs jointly co-ordinate the activities of official GMO laboratories in Spain and provide training for inspectors and staff of official laboratories. They participate in proficiency tests and also organise comparative tests and transfer information from the EU Reference Laboratory for GM food and feed to the Spanish official GMO laboratories (see also section 5.3.7 below). 16. The CA's stated that the planning of controls is coordinated between and within authorities through various mechanisms such as joint meetings to prepare control plans, information exchanges via emails and telephone. Coordination of the implementation of control activities takes place centrally within each AC. 17. Findings 19. Except for import controls, the operational implementation of official controls in Spain is the responsibility of the 17 autonomous communities and the two autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. 6 20. The staff met by the audit team, responsible for carrying out official control of GMOs, had the necessary qualifications and knowledge to perform their duties. Central CAs and CAs of ACs generally have access to appropriate analytical capacity. In certain cases, the scope of laboratory analysis is limited and does not cover all pending and known unauthorised GMOs (see also section 5.3.7 below). Findings 23. The CAs of the ACs visited developed written procedures for the implementation of official controls, which include instructions for inspections, sampling manuals, checklists and other forms. Controls on GMOs are part of general inspections carried out at food and feed business operators and instructions in relation to GMO controls are included in the general food and feed control guidelines. 24. The audit team noted that an inspection report is drawn up follows each GMO control and control results are systematically reported by the regional/district services to the CAs. Chapter I of Commission Recommendation 2004/787/EC. Findings 27. The Spanish Multi-annual National Control Plan, known in Spain as the National Plan for Official Control of the Food chain (PNCOCA), is updated on an annual basis and the latest version, covering 2016-2020, was submitted to the Commission in January 2016. It was prepared jointly by MSSSI and MAPA with significant input from each AC and the two autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. The control plan includes GMO controls of food, feed and deliberate release. Each AC prepares a regional control plan based on the PNCOCA. 28. Within the PNCOCA, four programmes provide the framework for control on food. Programme III.1 on 'Control of food establishments' (which includes traceability and labelling requirements); programme III.2 on 'HACCP control of food establishments' (including a sampling plan); programme III.5 on 'Control on food information and materials in contact with food to the final consumer'; and programme III.9 on 'Control of biotechnological foods'. The audit was conducted through data and document review, meetings with veterinary, hunting and agriculture officials, the authority responsible for the protection of the Danube Delta biosphere, pig keepers and hunters. Full legal references are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND ASF was first detected in Romania in domestic pigs during July 2017, on two holdings located in the county of Satu Mare in the north-eastern part of the country, close to the borders with Hungary and Ukraine. No further outbreaks were reported until 2018 when three 2 further outbreaks were confirmed in the same county during January and March. The first confirmed case of ASF in wild boar was reported in the same area during May 2018. The next outbreak occurred on the other side of the country, in the county of Tulcea close to the border with Ukraine early in June 2018. The disease spread rapidly in the area during that month, with 199 outbreaks of ASF being reported in domestic pigs and five cases in wild boar also being confirmed. The first outbreaks occurred within the Danube Delta Biosphere Reservation, one of the widest and most important wetland areas in Europe, that covers an area of approximately 58 000 km2. The veterinary authorities linked the introduction of the disease in this area to the migration of wild boar across the Danube. The disease continued to spread with an additional 350 outbreaks being reported in Tulcea during July and August. Outbreaks were also confirmed in the neighbouring counties of Braila and Constana, which reported 46 and 61 outbreaks respectively in domestic pigs during the same period. The outbreaks in Braila county included a group of three commercial farms under common ownership, which lost approximately 140 000 pigs. Towards the end of August the first case of ASF in wild boar was confirmed in Constana ­ no cases had been confirmed in Braila county at the time of the audit. At the start of October, the veterinary authorities reported that 246 localities in 13 counties were affected by the disease. By that time there had been 999 confirmed outbreaks in domestic pigs and 90 confirmed cases in wild boar. Additional background information on the epidemiological context in Romania and the organisation and function of the veterinary authorities can be found in the following audit reports: DG(SANTE) 2017-6118 ­ evaluation of the programme for the surveillance and emergency preparedness in relation to African swine fever; http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/act_getPDF.cfm?PDF_ID=13292 DG(SANTE) 2018-6477 ­ evaluation of the application of animal health control measures relating to classical swine fever; http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/act_getPDF.cfm?PDF_ID=13715 An overview of how control systems are organised in Romania, based on information supplied by them, is provided in the Country Profile for Romania and is available at the following link: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=RO 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS The effective control and eradication of epizootic disease depends on the correct application of measures to: 1. Prevent the introduction of disease to healthy animals. 3 2. Detect new cases as early as possible. 3. Control disease outbreaks by segregating and removing infected and in-contact animals. 4. Contain potentially infected animals, their products and other possible sources of contamination within known affected areas. 5. Coordinate the activities of the veterinary authorities internally and with those of other authorities and agencies. Findings Note: Information on the system in place in Romania for the registration of domestic pig holdings, domestic pig identification and movement controls can be found in the following audit reports: DG(SANTE) 2017-6118 and DG(SANTE) 2018-6477. 5.1.1 Domestic pigs 1. NSVFSA Order 20/195/2018 of 20 March 2018 introduced new biosecurity rules on domestic pig holdings. Three levels of biosecurity are defined according to the size and the five types of holding defined in Order 300/2017 of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (see Annex to this report). These rules meet the minimum requirements established in Commission Implementing Decision 2013/764/EU and are broadly in line with the recommendations made in the African Swine Fever Strategy for the EU (SANTE/7113/2015 Rev 9). 4 2. A transitional period of six months (ending in September 2018) was granted to allow non-commercial with commercial activities come into compliance with these requirements. 3. The veterinary authorities carried out a preliminary study in 18 counties at highest risk of ASF introduction to assess the impact and feasibility of implementing the new biosecurity rules. Key findings and conclusions reported include: a. A lack of awareness of the new biosecurity requirements among pig keepers, particularly on non-commercial holdings that have infrequent contact with veterinarians; b. The National Committee for Special Emergency Situations decided in August 2018 to adopt a national plan for the eradication of ASF in wild boar in Romania. A copy of this plan was submitted to the Commission.

Each hunting ground is under the supervision of the zonal veterinarian. At the start of the hunting season each hunting association signs a protocol undertaking to comply with veterinary requirements. These include: a. The duty to notify the veterinary authorities whenever wild boar are found dead or present with abnormal clinical signs; b. Ban on feeding, except for the purposes of baiting; c. Regular patrols with collection and removal of wild boar carcases; d. The provision of facilities for the evisceration of carcases and for the secure cold storage of meat and animal by-products; 6 e. The collection of samples (by an official veterinarian or a trained hunting technician) from wild boar found dead or shot (as required).

Neither the veterinary authorities nor the hunting authorities carry out on-the-spot official controls to verify whether and how the hunting associations are applying these biosecurity requirements (see also paragraph 26).

The veterinary authorities are taking measures to reduce the wild boar population. The aim is to achieve a maximum wild boar population density of 0,5 head/km2 (across the entire territory of Romania). In order to achieve this goal the following measures are applied: a. The hunting period for female wild boars has been extended to cover the entire period from June to January; b. An additional 'intervention' quota of 28 000 head of wild board above the approved harvest quota (see above). This quota was to be executed during a 90 day period from the end of August; c. Bounties have been introduced (see paragraph 23) which incentivise the hunting of breeding females; d. Intensive hunting of wild boar and predator species is carried out by authorised hunters along the borders with Ukraine and the Moldova; e. Arrangements have been made with the Danube Delta biosphere authorities to undertake targeted hunting to reduce the populations of wild boar and predator species.

The measures mentioned above, that were recently introduced in the Programme for the control and eradication of ASF to manage the wild boar population, are largely in line with the African Swine Fever Strategy for the EU (SANTE/7113/2015 - Rev 9). 7 Conclusions on disease prevention

New biosecurity rules applicable to all domestic pig holdings complement the controls already applied to commercial farms. They also provide a basis for implementing disease prevention measures on non-commercial holdings that are proportionate to the animal health risks that they face and the activities that they undertake. Non-commercial holdings that engage in local trading activities present the greatest risk of disease spread and are also the most challenging to regulate.

The measures that were recently introduced in the Programme for the control and eradication of ASF to manage the wild boar population and to improve biosecurity within hunting areas are broadly in line with the African Swine Fever Strategy for the EU (SANTE/7113/2015 - Rev 9) and should reduce the likely spread and persistence of ASF. However, the lack of on-the-spot official controls calls into question the effectiveness of the measures in practice. 5.2 EARLY DETECTION Legal requirements Council Directive 2002/60/EC, particularly Articles 3, 4, 14, 15, 16 & 18 and Annex IV Commission Decision 2003/422/EC Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, particularly Article 4 In addition to the above legal requirements, reference is also made to the African Swine Fever Strategy for the EU (SANTE/7113/2015 - Rev 9), which includes guidelines on: Laboratory tests for disease screening purposes Enhanced passive surveillance in domestic pigs and wild boar Awareness campaigns Findings 5.2.1 Domestic pigs

text: The second and third "strategic" objectives relate to improving procedures and are, as such, operational rather than strategic objectives. There is no link between the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect these objectives. Article 42 (2) (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

In addition, these are not measureable objectives on what Germany wants to achieve for animal welfare. There are no specific strategic objectives indicated in relation to animal welfare outcomes e.g. reduce incidence of tail docking by x%, improve FPD levels by x%, decrease lameness levels in cattle by x % through official controls and related actions in the MANCP such as training, targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues, liaison with sector to set agreed targets etc. For instance, considering the amount of resources devoted to the development and drafting of an Action Plan on tail docking of pigs there is no mention of it as either a strategic or an operational objective (with measureable targets) in the MANCP nor any meaningful reporting on its implementation in either the annual report on the MANCP, or in the report to the Commission on official controls on farms required by Commission Decision 2006/778.

The omission of the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs from the MANCP objectives is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 42 (1) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which require that MANCPs should be regularly updated and adjusted in the light of various developments and factors.

Documentation related to the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs is included in the QMS documentation of the Land (Federal State) visited but only for information purposes. Previously there had been animal welfare objectives set in the Land visited, such as, on group housing of sows where the local level (Kreis - district or county) were asked to carry out specific controls. However, currently as there is no legal spur for such a focus, there are no specific objectives set for animal welfare controls at Land level, nor were any specific reports received at Land level on local level objectives or activities.

In 2018, a project on monitoring animal welfare in larger slaughterhouses was initiated in the Land visited which included joint controls between the supervising Land level and the local level. In addition, two farmer meetings and three training events on animal welfare were also held at local level in the reporting year. Nevertheless, there was no report of any of these actions in the Land report to BMEL on actions taken to improve official controls under Decision 2006/778 or regarding broader strategic actions in relation to MANCP objectives.

Animal welfare controls are largely driven, in the Land visited, by cross compliance requirements and then left to the local level to ensure any other relevant findings are reported and investigated5. For every farm, receiving payments, approximately 200 criteria are used in a statistical analysis to determine its risk profile. Inspection frequency and farm selection are derived from national database information and biannually updated. The basic target of 1% inspections on premises subject to controls is increased in several sectors e.g. statistical analysis identified that higher number of cows correlated with higher risk ­ whereas there was an inverse correlation with numbers of sheep and goats (lower risk with higher numbers).

However, for sectors not covered by cross compliance requirements there is no binding framework, in the Land visited, for the planning of inspections on the basis of risk. There is voluntary guidance but the local level decide e.g. laying hens, broilers where no Land is associated with the holding. For poultry farms, sending animals for slaughter such as broilers and turkeys, on farm ante-mortem inspection means there is less need for targeted checks in these sectors and less risk due to regular official veterinary presence on farms. Additional animal welfare inspections were carried out on poultry farms and reported by local level to Land level (as a result of ante-mortem inspections and avian influenza animal health monitoring).

The Land level verifies how controls are implemented at local level through, amongst other means, periodic audits of the quality management system. However, as animal welfare is only one element in the scope of these audits, their impact is limited.

Procedures for controls laid down in the Handbook are (with the exception noted in Finding 5 above) generally very detailed.
