The QMS, of the Land visited, indicates that the Handbook should be followed (and a binding legal decree Erlass to this effect was in place) but officials at each level are not clear on the specific tasks of Official Veterinarians (OVs) in relation to the assessment of cumulative daily mortality rates (CDMR). This is defined in the Handbook as both an on farm task during ante-mortem controls and a slaughterhouse task.

The OV at the slaughterhouse visited did not specifically check the plausibility of CDMR as this had already been checked at the ante-mortem check. The on farm inspection report did not indicate that the specific target for CDMR was monitored. The Handbook requires the slaughterhouse OV to verify if the CDMR exceeds the limit calculated by the formula (1.0 % + 0.06 % x number of days of life) x 1.5 and the plausibility of the daily mortality rates. Directive 2007/43/EC Article 3(1) and Annex III (1) require this data to be sent and the official veterinarian to supervise the assessment of this data for flocks with stocking densities above 33kg/m2.

LAV AGT has not started to work on the requirements of Article 9 (1) (d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to ensure that the reliability and results of own controls that have been performed by the operators, or by a third party at their request, including, where appropriate, private quality assurance schemes, are taken into account in the planning and performance of official controls. This Article enters into force on 14 December 2019. Conclusions on management of official controls

The competent authorities' approach to the setting of objectives and the planning and reporting of official controls is mainly operational "business as usual" with no targets, indicators or measurement of progress, nor any prioritisation of controls or allocation of resources and as such is insufficient to bring measureable change.

The omission of the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs from the MANCP and the Handbook, illustrates the need to reinforce the planning, execution and reporting of official controls to include important objectives that should be implemented according to established principles of quality management systems i.e. objectives should be Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART).

In contrast to the above, planning of cross compliance controls is well formulated on a demonstrable risk profiling (including severity, recurrence etc.) basis using a wide range of risk indicators that effectively target official resources to inspecting the potentially worst offenders in order to meet the objective of safeguarding European Community funds.

Procedures for inspections are generally comprehensive but the omission of instructions on the Action Plan on pigs means that no progress in this area is being made yet as no 5 effective controls to implement the plan are being carried out.

Ante-mortem inspection of poultry on farm provides additional reassurance of health and welfare standards above the requirements of Directive 2007/43, including a check on the specific legal requirements for production data. However, this caused confusion in the division of competencies between OVs on farm and at slaughter and resulted in the legal requirement to verify this data at the slaughterhouse not being followed according to existing instructions or legal requirements. 5.2 REPORTING OF CONTROLS Under the current EU requirements, the Member States submit three different types of reports addressing animal welfare: a report on the implementation of the MANCP; a report on inspections carried to verify compliance with Directive 2007/43/EC (the "Broiler Directive") and a report of inspections of production sites on which certain animals are kept for farming purposes, as required by Commission Decision 2006/778/EC. There may also be internal or national requirements for other reports which the competent authority has to satisfy. These reports have slightly different purposes and therefore, their contents are different. However, they share one common objective for these reports: to describe whether the Member States' animal welfare objectives were achieved during the reporting period. Legal requirements Article 44(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Commission Decision 2006/778 and Article 7(2) of Directive 2007/43/EC Findings

The BMEL and the BVL provide the Commission with an annual report (most recently for 2018) on the implementation of the MANCP as required under Article 44 (1) of Regulation 882/2004 which consists mainly of the results of inspections as required by Decision 2006/778 and the report on transport required under Regulation 1/2005. There is no report for broilers as required under Directive 2007/43.

The annual report on the MANCP gives statistics on compliance for each of the areas covered by Decision 2006/778 and Article 27 of Regulation 1/2005. Nonetheless, it does not indicate whether the actions taken are contributing to improvements, whether compliance/detection is improving/decreasing and whether the activities are suitable to reach the objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, including enforcement action and its results as required under Article 44 (1) (d) of Regulation EC No 882/2004.

There are output indicators such as the quantity of inspections and non-compliances detected per inspection but these do not give an outcome for animal welfare. The outputs are not linked to the existing strategic objectives.

The annual report on the MANCP indicates that the QM and audit systems and the independent audit do not yet sufficiently take into account the effectiveness of official 6 controls and that Länder do not currently have a documented system to ensure the effectiveness of official controls.

The reports sent to the Commission by Germany on Decision 2006/778 give only a collation of non-compliances with no analysis at any level of the significance of the findings or the root causes or any influencing factors. text: The instruments used to implement the objectives of the policy are: the legislation (mainly the Regulation on Animal Keepers - Besluit houders van dieren), encouraging Quality Assurance Systems (QAS) and market concepts, incentivising the sector on specific animal welfare aspects, good practice guides, subsidies schemes, facilitating research and providing information.

The objectives for animal welfare in the 2015-2018 Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) include: a. To increase compliance, with a target of 80% compliance or better from the result of inspections. b. To include a random selection of farms for comparison of their compliance results with the risk chosen farms.

The report on the implementation of the MANCP in 2017 indicates that: a. For pigs, 350 production sites were inspected with an overall compliance rate of 70%. For calves the compliance rate was 60%, and the report concluded that this level of compliance was "moderate". For broilers, the compliance rate was 45% and the report concluded that this was unsatisfactory. b. The results do not give a representative picture of compliance within the sector as the inspections were conducted with other controls: for the purpose of cross compliance; for a project; in response to a notification from a third party. The report does not provide any indication of how the results from the inspections of the randomly selected farms compare with the results from the farms chosen on the basis of risk. 4 The MANCP network reference document "Developing Objectives and Indicators" states that the underlying principle behind these requirements and guidelines is that we cannot manage our control systems without setting clear objectives and monitoring progress towards those objectives. A strategic objective is a long- term objective, setting out what an official control system and its priorities intend to achieve. Strategic objectives usually relate to outcomes and impacts. Objectives should be Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART). 3 5. The Ministry of Agriculture Nature and Food Quality (Ministerie van Landbouw, Natuur en Voedselkwaliteit - NLV) (hereafter "the Ministry") set the work of the NVWA in a framework letter. The Framework letter describes the political and policy priorities of the Ministry and the NVWA then incorporates these into its annual plan. The plan describes annually specific, in particular risk based controls, but controls are fairly stable from year to year, in particular those to meet inspection requirements of EU legislation. The priorities for 2020 on animal welfare are pet animals (trade and breeding) and farm animals, and there have been exchanges between officials in the Ministry and the NVWA on how these are best incorporated into the annual plan. Regarding farm animals the priorities include: A focus on calf mortality, to be broadened to other young animals; A further commitment to ensure farmers carry out a risk assessment in relation to tail-docking of pigs and, To increase the visibility of the work of the NVWA in the holdings, within the framework of risk controlled surveillance, by communicating more on the controls and their findings. 6. The NVWA develops these priorities using a strategical, tactical and operational approach. On animal welfare the tactical "Team Expertise Dier" develops tactics which may include operational inspection divisions carrying out checks of farms. Regional NVWA teams carry out controls on farms and the organisation of these teams varies, depending on the sector. The NVWA motto for controls is "gentle as possible, tough where needed". More information is available at http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 7. The NVWA do an integral analysis of the production chain to support their decisions on the best approach to achieve better compliance, for example: Regarding a problem with high mortality in calves, the NVWA concluded in the evaluation of a project on this issue that inspections of all farms with high calf mortality would not be achievable. The NVWA therefore developed an approach to increase awareness of the problem ("insight into the problem"). This involved presenting the data not only to representatives of the dairy farmers where most deaths occurred, but also to engage with representatives of the dairy farmers where calves are born, and the dairy processors who are an important driver in the sector. The NVWA is also considering how to reward farmers who achieve a low mortality. The NVWA noticed a similar problem with an increased mortality in kid goats, and decided that checks of farms were not necessary as they already had sufficient data to discuss the problem with the sector and request corrective measures. In 2018, the NVWA carried out reactive checks in 30% of the 2747 farm notifications from public and farm consultants and in 84% of the 121 notifications from dairy companies. The NVWA have started a project "enhanced supervision"(5) 4 in order to find a way to identify these farms at an earlier stage. The French requirements for rearing pigs generally follow the intent and wording of the Directives with no additional requirements, which would be necessary to achieve their objectives. 2. Guidance for inspectors and the related inspection checklist only require the provision of enrichment material to sows and gilts in groups. DGAL are aware of this error and plan to take graduated enforcement measures to rectify it (see also paragraphs 48 and 49 of this report). Sanctions and enforcement

Enforcement action to rectify non-compliances detected during official controls ranges from verbal and written warnings, administrative fines, up to judicial proceedings. In 2017 and 2018 the CA carried out approximately 350 animal welfare inspections on pig premises with non-compliances detected in approximately two thirds. Administrative action has been taken to follow up the majority of non-compliances with financial penalties imposed for recalcitrant or non-cooperative offenders. Financial sanctions imposed in the major pig producing area have ranged from EUR 300 to over EUR 10 000 together with reductions in cross compliance payments. More detail on the types of non-compliances can be found in the official controls section of this report.

Guidance for inspectors on administrative sanctions and the follow up actions required is given in DGAL Technical instruction 2015-103. The enforcement section of the inspection vademecum is being revised to reflect changes in the way non-compliances are administered by the CA. This is as a result of an initiative of the CA in the main pig producing area which has achieved more consistent follow up and more effective rectification of non-compliances.

Enforcement action was taken in the Prefectures visited and followed up effectively in one of them. Lack of resources meant that follow up visits had not been carried out in the second Prefecture to assess progress with planned rectification measures. 3 Strategy for prevention of tail docking and avoidance of routine tail docking

The National Animal Welfare Strategy 2016-2020 defines a coordinated approach to animal welfare with themes of knowledge sharing, including progress reports, promotion of innovation, shared stakeholder responsibility, and encourages the development of practical methods for more responsible production.

It has five objectives: training; information; support; sanctions and innovation and has funded a working/steering group to implement the Action Plan on tail-docking on pigs. This group includes representatives from central and local authorities, pig sector associations, veterinarians, chambers of agriculture, scientific/technical research institutes, the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety (ANSES) and the French national inter-professional pig organisation (INAPORC), bringing together all representatives in the pig sector.

The Action Plan for the prevention of tail biting and avoidance of routine tail docking (paragraphs 14 to 34 below) is being implemented in accordance with the general principles of the Animal Welfare Strategy with active participation from all stakeholders and a high awareness of ongoing activities.

The central competent authority estimates that the incidence of tail docking in France is over 99%. This is routine tail docking. The CA does not yet enforce the legal requirements in Point 8 of Chapter I, Annex I, of the Pig Directive to take measures to prevent tail-biting and other vices by improving inadequate environmental conditions or management systems.

Data on the frequency of tail biting/tail lesions in pigs was not systematically collected on farms or slaughterhouses before June 2019 (though farms are now collecting sample records of single houses per category of pigs) and is not known with any certainty.

Farmers, veterinary practitioners and officials reported that in general tail biting outbreaks/lesions in docked pigs on farm are only sporadic events. In the slaughterhouse visited, tail lesions were recorded in 0.38% of pigs slaughtered and five warnings were issued and followed up by the CA in 2019 (See also section 5.3 of this report).

A study in 2016 to record the incidence of tail lesions at slaughter (3) was conducted by the French Pig Institute (IFIP) on 18,000 carcases in two slaughterhouses. For docked pigs with short tails it found severe lesions (recorded as 3 or 4 on scale of 0-4) in 1.3% and 0.9% respectively of carcasses. 63% had mild tail lesions. 44% of the batches inspected on farms had at least one severe lesion. In tail docked pigs, worse results were found as tail length increased. Most studies indicate that slaughterhouse findings seriously underestimate the on farm incidence due to the healing of previous bites/lesions and the authors of this study indicate that about 25% of tails showed some signs of healed lesions (deformation or healing of bitten tails).

In the fattening farms visited, tail biting incidents were estimated on the first farm at between 1 to 2%. The second farm had trialled rearing pigs with intact tails with mixed success: initial batches were successful but later trials resulted in tail biting outbreaks where 15% of pigs (3) https://www.ifip.asso.fr/sites/default/files/pdf-documentations/jrp_2018_courboulay.pdf 4 suffered serious lesions. However, apart from adding rope as additional enrichment, no risk assessment was done before the trial and no other improvement measures were put in place. Action Plan

The CCA drafted the Action Plan in October 2018 in coordination with the pig sector and other stakeholders. The CCA coordinates inputs from and leads regular meetings with the pig sector, research, NGOs, veterinary associations and official services. It has also co-funded the development of tools to assist the sector.

The Action Plan has been divided into five sections with respective deadlines: drafting clear compliance criteria with the legal requirements related to risks for tail biting, risk assessment, recording of ear/tail lesions on farm, actions involving private veterinarians, and enforcement through official controls. Compliance criteria

Initial compliance criteria were drafted in 2018 for the provision of water, enrichment material and light and technical guidance notes (fiches) elaborated in agreement with the pig sector. The working group intends to finalise compliance criteria (if needed) for the remaining legal requirements for cleanliness, thermal comfort and air quality, health status, competition for food and space and diet before the end of summer 2019. See also Annex 2 to this report.

Further changes are also being made on the basis of feedback from the sector and official services on the evaluation of measureable animal and resource based indicators and the results of official controls. Problems with the provision of water have already been noted by the authorities and further details on the provision of enrichment material are being drafted which will lead to revision of both of these fiches which were not yet finalised at the time of the audit.

Guidance for inspectors and the related inspection checklist only require the provision of enrichment material to sows and gilts in groups. DGAL are aware of this error and plan to take graduated enforcement measures to rectify it (see also paragraphs 48 and 49 of this report).

The agreed compliance criteria will be adopted by the sector and incorporated into the Guide to Good Hygiene Practices on pig farms. There is no deadline set for updating the Guides and this process can take years to implement.

DGAL's vademecum providing guidance on carrying out official controls on pig farms is being updated to take into account the agreed compliance criteria and is scheduled for completion by the end of summer 2019. This will then become the compulsory standard for the CA and the sector. Risk assessment

DGAL has a two stage approach to risk assessment: educate and train farmers and then enforce corrective measures on the recalcitrant minority. It has worked with the sector which has decided to introduce mandatory risk assessment.

The pig sector has funded and created a farm animal welfare monitoring tool BEEP (bien être en élevage de porcs). It includes 15 indicators for farmer self-assessment on 5 themes: 5 accommodation, health, behaviour, feed and watering. The indicators are mostly animal based and address the main points of Commission Recommendation (EU) 336/2016. It includes individual and group assessment of 4 animal houses during each rearing phase from weaning to fattening. BEEP will be utilised on paper initially and once its use is evaluated by the end of 2019 it will be incorporated as a mandatory requirement in the sector's production standard le porc français in 2020. It will then migrate to a mobile platform (App) which will include training and enable centralisation of data so that farmers can compare their farm rating against national averages. Introductory training has already been given to a pilot group of 50 farmers and further training will be given through cascade. There is no provision made for applying this monitoring tool for sows and gilts or piglets, the latter category being relevant for addressing tail biting risks at an early age. It has not been decided if this data will be available to the CA or how the BEEP assessment will be taken into account during official controls (4) as this is the only form of mandatory risk assessment being considered.

DGAL and INAPORC have funded a French version of the German SchwIP tail-biting intervention programme (Schwanzbeiß Interventions Programm) which will be available to veterinarians and technicians by end 2019. The programme is not intended for routine use on farms but to help identify risks for tail-biting in problematic farms. It is not clear how the tool will be utilised: by whom (5), and at what frequency, nor how farms are defined as "problematic" or by whom. The sector wish to collate data on the outcomes to gain an overview of the common problems/solutions found. Recording of ear/tail lesions on farm

The pig sector distributed in May 2019 a sheet for recording evidence of tail and ear lesions on farms which requires farmers to record incidence and severity of bites in one house for each category of pigs throughout the rearing period. It includes space to record any changes to environmental conditions on farm. Whilst this is progress, registering data from only one house in farms that have two or more houses would not provide an overview of the farm situation in relation to evidence of tail biting. This would not satisfy the requirement for evidence described in paragraph two of Point 8 of Chapter I, Annex I, of the Pig Directive. Monitoring sheets can be easily integrated into basic farm management procedures as every house already has a management/health monitoring sheet. This would give a representative picture of the situation on holdings, where biting problems may vary from location, or type of housing/ climate, over the whole premises within the different categories. There is information provided to the sector in the IFIP brochure "Pain Prevention in Pigs" (Prévenir la douleur chez le Porc") which gives suggestions on how to address risks for tail biting and improve certain environmental conditions.

Enforcement through official controls See section on official controls. Additional findings on the Action Plan
There has been a wide distribution of information on actions to reduce tail biting from DGAL and the pig sector.

There are no intervention levels for tail biting defined to establish when farmers should/can start trials on keeping pigs with intact tails. It is notable that some Member States have already set intervention levels for when these should start. The only mention of rearing small groups of pigs with intact tails as "control groups" within existing premises is one sentence in the fiche for recording evidence of tail/ear biting which states: "If few bites have been observed for six months, have you thought of contacting your technician or veterinarian in order to set up a `whole tail' trial?". As there is no definition of what is "few bites" and no threshold has been set for any move to rearing pigs with intact tails, this will at present only be on a voluntary basis whereas the legal requirements of paragraph 2 Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to the Pig Directive clearly state that routine tail docking is prohibited. The staff working document accompanying Commission Recommendation (EU) 336/2016 also states in Point 9 that "When tail-biting has stopped, then some batches (1-2 litters) of undocked tails should be trialled ­ with a view to stopping the docking of tails."

Trials for rearing pigs with intact tails are ongoing within France (44 since 2015) and the results are now being collated and shared in a standard reporting format and within one coordinating body's database (Coop de France) which should result in better knowledge sharing and more consistent comparative analysis. The protocol for running/monitoring trials does not mention maximising all the management and environmental factors in the system to be assessed before starting the trial. 7 31. There are no proposals for dealing with the trade in tail docked pigs, including from other Member States. Some Member States are working together to draft proposals to deal with this issue which will require close cooperation to ensure the provisions of the Directive are complied with. 32. DGAL proposes to upgrade the collection of data in slaughterhouses by the end of 2020 to enable the collation of better data on the frequency and type of tail lesions in pigs. See also paragraph 60. 33. The pig sector intends to propose a farmer training initiative at the end of 2019 involving the existing training given by SNGTV but adding additional elements relating to BEEP, the recording of tail/ear lesions etc. resulting in at least one trained animal welfare officer on each pig holding. Conclusions on implementing measures 34. DGAL has worked with stakeholders to implement an Action Plan on tail docking as part of the overall animal welfare strategy. It has taken actions to develop criteria for certain legal requirements that are related to tail biting risk factors on tail docking of pigs to enable inspectors and farmers to make a judgement on whether individual farms comply with EU requirements but these have not yet been implemented. Tail docking is still routinely carried out and the CA is not yet enforcing the corresponding legal requirements. 35. The relatively high levels of lesions detected during a survey in two slaughterhouses indicate serious animal welfare problems in a significant number of French farms and a need for an enforcement strategy aiming at improved compliance with minimum requirements as well as serious improvement measures to reduce the incidence of tail biting. 36. The sector has started to record evidence of tail/ear biting lesions. However, procedures for the assessment of lesions are incomplete. Farm risk assessment tools are still being developed and there is no robust framework in the Action Plan for improvement measures or when farms should transition to rearing pigs with intact tails. These last three components need to be put in place quickly in order to start making tangible progress to improve compliance with the Directive. In addition, the extended CA deadlines (end 2022 to 2024) mean that without a focus on shortening deadlines and sufficient priority, full compliance with legal requirements will not be reached within the next four years. 37. text: BACKGROUND In 2014, the European Parliament published a study indicating extremely low implementation of the Pig Directive in relation to tail docking. In 2016, the Commission published Commission Recommendation (EU) 2016/336 which recommends at EU level best practices aimed at reducing the need for tail docking and an 4 Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 laying down specific rules for the organisation of official controls on products of animal origin intended for human consumption (OJ L 139, 30.4.2004, p. 206)

Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on official controls performed to ensure the verification of compliance with feed and food law, animal health and animal welfare rules (OJ L 165, 30.4.2004, p. 1)

Commission Recommendation (EU) 2016/336 of 8 March 2016 (OJ L 62, 9.3.2016, p. 20) on the application of Council Directive 2008/120/EC laying down minimum standards for the protection of pigs and the provision of enrichment materials to pigs (C (2016)1345 final)

Commission Staff Working Document on best practices with a view to the prevention of routine tail-docking and the provision of enrichment materials to pigs (C (2016)1345 final). 2 accompanying Staff Working Document on best practices with a view to the prevention of routine tail docking and the provision of enrichment materials to pigs. One of the Commission services' main priorities on animal welfare is to ensure higher standards of implementation and enforcement of EU legislation. With this in mind, the Commission services have implemented a three-year project (2017 to 2019) on reducing the systematic tail docking of piglets. The Pig Directive and Directive 98/58/EC lay down the minimum standards for the protection of pigs confined for rearing and fattening. The Commission has taken measures to improve the application of these Directives, taking into account the Recommendation and accompanying Commission Staff Working Document, including requesting Member States to draft and implement Action Plans to ensure compliance with these requirements by the end of 2018. The Hungarian pig sector has approximately 23,500 pig farms (4,500 breeding and 19,000 fattening holdings). The 226,300 sows produce an estimated 4.2 million pigs annually. Although 10 % of breeding animals are reared with intact tails and some of their offspring are also reared this way, it is estimated that of the remaining commercial pigs born and travelling into Hungary from Germany, Denmark, The Netherlands and Slovakia, 95-97% are tail docked. There is little demand for undocked pigs in Hungary. This is a major obstacle to getting greater efforts to avoid tail docking. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 IMPLEMENTING MEASURES Legal requirements Points 4 and 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to Directive 2008/120/EC and Directive 98/58/EC (as stated below). Findings 1. The Hungarian Animal Welfare Act No. 1998. XXVIII (Magyar Állatvédelmi Törvény) and

The identification system for pigs and the Agency for Restructuring and Modernisation of Agriculture (ARMA) database are described in reports from previous Commission audits related to this area, i.e. DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, DG(SANTE)/2016-6114- MR and DG(SANTE)/2014-7294-MR.

In response to Recommendation No 3 from report DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, i.e., "To improve the accuracy and quality of the tools for the traceability of pigs, in order for them to be effective tools for animal health controls", Poland proposed a public procurement procedure for the design and development of a new database, i.e. "e-IRZ Plus". ARMA informed the audit team that a tender process had been opened in 2017 and then cancelled. A decision was taken during 2018 to modify the existing database and create "IRZ Plus". This modification improved electronic data exchange with livestock owners. However, it did not improve the functionality for adding animal health information and official veterinarians still have limited direct access to statistical data on the database, both of which would support planning and implementation of official disease control programmes. The audit team was told that "IRZ Plus" could still become a reality in the future if funding was to become available. The system currently maintained by ARMA was never designed as a system to contain information on animal health (its main task is to cover the whereabouts and movements of animals -- Article 3(2) of the Law of 2 April 2004 on the animal identification and registration system). The DEPiRZ (Producer Register and Animal Registration System Department) issues various statistics required by the GVI. In addition, the Agency made available the application platform and the `IW SIRZ' browser, which are tools allowing an overview and analysis of data from the IRZ database. 4 3. As described in previous reports, the GVI maintains its own separate database ("Vetlink") which includes animal health information and is used to support District Veterinary Offices (DVOs) to manage disease control programmes including ASF. There is limited access to data on Vetlink from areas outside the region in which holdings are located. The GVI have plans to expand the capabilities of the system. 4. All movements of pigs should be notified to and included in the ARMA database. Movements must be notified within 2 days in ASF restricted area (areas subject to restrictions due to ASF as listed in the Annex of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU - Parts I, II and III) and within 7 days in the ASF free area. 5. Figures for the number of pig holdings and pigs in Poland: Data from the Central Data Base of 01/01/2017 01/01/2018 01/01/2019 ARMA 13,742,322 13,565,913 12,501,622 Number of pigs 227,190 202,850 164,576 Number of pig holdings 6. Figures for the size of pig herds in Poland on 1st January 2019: The size of Number Number the pig herd of herds of pigs 328,901 1 ­ 10 74,516 11 ­ 20 (2.6%) 21 ­ 50 (45%) 51 ­ 100 436,573 101 ­ 1,000 29,483 Over 1,000 973,064 Total (18%) 939,226 30,263 4,378,397 (18%) 5,445,461 13,286 12,501,622 (8%) 15,071 (9%) 1,987 (1%) 164,576 7. Although the number of pig holdings has decreased by about 19% between the start of 2018 and 2019, the decrease is far more dramatic in the areas affected by ASF where a combination of voluntary opting out and compulsory orders to stop keeping pigs has resulted in falls of up to 80% in the number of holdings at DVO/Poviat level. For example, one DVO visited had 1,376 pig holdings in January 2018 which had reduced to 269 by 30 March 2019. 8. The high number of visits to holdings in the ASF affected area has provided an up-to- date picture of pig numbers on holdings. This has allowed a cross check with the information on the central database and the removal of many holdings that no longer 5 keep pigs which has also contributed considerably to the reduced numbers of pig holdings. (A similar exercise has not taken place in the ASF free area and therefore the accuracy of pig holding information in the database would be lower.) 9. The GVI has prepared guidelines from the Chief Veterinary Officer (dated 16 September 2016) concerning rules on the movement of pigs, pig meat and pig meat products, from holdings and establishments situated in the ASF affected area and in the protection or surveillance zones related to outbreaks of ASF. 10. The Chief Veterinary Officer's guidelines are largely based on the requirements of Decision 2014/709. All movements of live pigs under derogations are based on Article 3.2 of Decision 2014/709 which requires amongst other requirements, the testing of a representative number of pigs from the holding for ASF in the 7 days prior to movement. The option in Article 3.3 which allows the movement of pigs from a holding based on testing a representative number of pigs from the holding twice a year for ASF (plus compliance with several other requirements) has not been implemented in Poland. The guidelines state that "this option is not recommended by the Chief Veterinary Officer and its application is conditional on individual cases only after a detailed risk analysis has been carried out". 11. All movements of pigs from holdings in the ASF restricted area must be accompanied by a movement permit (issued by DVOs) and a veterinary certificate which can be issued by either official or "appointed" (authorised) private veterinarians. 12. The audit team visited two large pig holdings where testing for ASF was carried out frequently (generally, weekly testing in one and fortnightly in the other) with fatteners being sent for slaughter to Article 12 approved slaughterhouses within 7 days of sampling. The relevant standards for sampling procedures were observed as set out in Decision 2014/709/EU. 13. According to the competent authority, the movement of live pigs from Parts II & III in Poland to similar areas in other Member States has never taken place. 5.1.1.1 Biosecurity on pig holdings 14. The eradication plan for ASF in wild boar in Poland approved by Commission Implementing Decision 2014/442/EU sets out three categories of farm, i.e. commercial, non-commercial and outdoor (similar to the categories in the EU strategy for ASF, (SANTE/7113/2015, Rev 10). Holdings are not categorised on the ARMA database and the same biosecurity requirements apply to all three categories with the exception of outdoor farms where some additional requirements apply related to double fencing and the provision of additional disinfection mats. Therefore, it is not possible to provide figures for how many of each of the three categories exist in Poland. 15. The EU strategy for ASF states that "Outdoor keeping of pigs is banned" in the areas covered by Decision 2014/709/EU and sets out higher biosecurity requirements for commercial holdings compared to non-commercial ones, e.g., stock-proof fencing and 6 the requirement for a "Biosecurity plan approved/recommended by veterinary services according to the profile of farm...". Neither measure is applied in Poland because the competent authority regards the EU strategy for ASF as optional guidance. 16. The GVI has a target to visit all pig holdings in the ASF restricted area at least twice per year to check on compliance with biosecurity rules and a comprehensive check-list is used for these checks. 17. DVOs produce annual reports on how many such visits are carried out and the main non-compliances detected. They do not confirm the extent to which the target of twice annual visits was achieved, e.g. percentage of holdings visited twice. The reports do not include data on the number of holdings that should have been inspected and the reasons why inspections did not take place as planned. The competent authority did say that many holdings on the list may not have pigs when contacted to arrange a visit but records viewed by the audit team in DVOs did not include this information. 18. During 2018, the GVI carried out 38,641 official controls for biosecurity on pig holdings in the 6 provinces affected by ASF. 4,561 holdings were issued with a decision ordering action to address biosecurity issues and 4,148 received a decision to suspend keeping of pigs. 19. The audit team was provided with evidence that the ASF expert group had received summary data related to checks on biosecurity on holdings and had assessed the main non-compliances with a view to providing advice on future approaches. 20. Since April 2018, biosecurity rules have also applied to pig holdings in the free area which are generally similar to those in the restricted areas but with some exceptions, such as there being no requirement to place disinfected mats at the entrance of holdings, just at the entrance to pig houses. The GVI has set a range of target dates for when all holdings should be inspected at least once. This date is linked to the number of pig holdings at DVO level, with a longer period allowed for DVO's with more holdings, e.g. DVO with over 2,000 pig holdings have up to November 2021 to complete the inspections (although the central competent authority did state that was the maximum period and it could be shorter). 39,000 inspections on biosecurity on holdings in the free area were carried out between April ­ end of 2018 with 21% being recorded as non-compliant. 21. At one of the holdings visited during the audit which had 1 sow to produce pigs for own consumption, no births had been recorded in the herd register during 2017 or 2018 although numerous pigs had been home slaughtered. The owner had obtained semen from a neighbouring farm. Neither of these issues was recorded in the recent biosecurity reports for the holding. 7 5.1.2 Control of fresh meat, meat preparations/products from domestic pigs Legal requirements Directive 2002/60/EC Directive 2002/99/EC Commission implementing Decision 2014/709/EU Findings 22. The GVI has established a system which enables all domestic pigs slaughtered in Poland to be marked with either an oval health mark or a round mark if destined for the national market in accordance with Article 4(7)(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU. The system relies on the documentation accompanying pigs to slaughter. 23. A pentagonal mark has also been issued for use when movement is confined to Part III although the central competent authority believes that this mark has not been used as the GVI pays for all certification and pre-movement testing which increases the value of the pig at slaughter as it can be sold on a wider national market and not confined to Part III. 24. The GVI maintains a list of establishments approved under Article 12 of Decision 2014/709/EU. 25. The audit team visited two slaughterhouses, both in Part II, which received pigs from different areas, including Part III. The movement documents examined by the audit team were in compliance with the relevant requirements of Decision 2014/709/EU with the exception of Article 4.3 which requires that "the pigs are transported for immediate slaughter directly, without stopping or unloading, to a slaughterhouse...". Many of the consignments had passed through "collection points" which is specifically allowed under current national law. According to the competent authority, pigs from smaller holdings would be taken to "collection points" by their owner and reloaded onto larger lorries and then taken to the slaughterhouse. 26. The audit team visited a meat processing establishment in Part II which receives fresh pig meat with oval and round health marks. Due to a commercial decision, all products leave with a round mark and are confined to the national market. Therefore no channelling is required. 27. National rules require that slaughter for own consumption has to be notified to the DVO 24 hours prior the slaughter in the ASF restricted area and pigs have to pass post mortem examination. Ante-mortem inspection is also required in Parts II & III and a laboratory test for ASF is required in Part III (also applies in Parts I & II, if any abnormalities detected during ante or post mortem examination). The competent authority considers that the compliance level for notification of home slaughter is high as the GVI pays for the inspections/test. The audit team saw evidence that home slaughtering was subjected to inspection at holdings visited during the audit. 8 5.1.3 Control of carcases, fresh meat, meat preparations/products from wild boar Legal requirements Articles 15 and 16 of Directive 2002/60/EC Directive 2002/99/EC Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU Findings 28. There is no farming of wild boar in Poland and therefore no trade in live wild boar. 29. All wild boars hunted in Poland in the ASF restricted area are tested for ASF (as are those in the free area if there is a suspicion of ASF). A system is in place for the appropriate traceability of carcases (individual tags for carcases can be traced back to the DVO in which the hunting ground is located) and correlation of samples. 30. The audit visited a game collection centre in Part I where wild boar carcases from Part I are stored after they receive a negative result for ASF (was previously stored in a "carcase collection centre" ­ see finding 31). The centre was also used to store wild boar carcases from the free area and the carcases from Part I and the free area were destined for a game processing establishment in the free area. Based on discussions with the operator of the game collection centre, only about 5-10% of hunted wild boar carcasses were sent to game processing establishments with the rest being consumed locally. Although the risks are minimal, Article 15.1(b) of Decision 2014/709/EU does not allow wild boar carcases from a free area to enter Part I and then return to the free area as no derogation exists in the Decision unlike for example carcases from wild boar shot in Part I which can leave Part I if tested with negative result for ASF. 31. There are 4,831 hunting grounds in Poland. 1,167 are located in the ASF restricted area and 3,664 in the free area. Poland has established "carcase collection centres" which serve several hunting grounds where facilities such as dressing areas and refrigerated storage are available. Official Veterinarians visit regularly to collect samples and examine carcases when required (e.g. in Parts II & III) and report on the implementation of biosecurity measures at these locations. 32. Provided they meet the definition of "feed business" and "feed business operator" laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council 1 4 BACKGROUND This is the first time that official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production in the EU have been specifically audited by the Commission in Ireland. Feed additives and their mixtures (premixtures) are the essential ingredients in modern compound feed manufacture and their use is steadily increasing. In the EU in 2016, the annual consumption of minerals, feed additives and vitamins was approximately 5.4 million tonnes (compared to 4.6 million tonnes in 2014 and 4.7 million tonnes in 2015).2 A substantial quantity of feed additives and ingredients for their production is sourced from non-EU countries and it is important to be able to demonstrate that such imports do not contain undesirable substances. From 2010 to the end of 2017, there were 79 notifications issued for feed additives under the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) for the presence of non-authorised genetically modified organisms (GMOs) (26), dioxins (21), heavy metals (17), veterinary medicinal products (5), microbiological contaminants (3) and other non-specified hazards (7). Most of these were for imported feed additives and ingredients for their production. Thus proper traceability of those substances/products is a vital prerequisite for effective control. In Ireland, there is one approved feed additive manufacturer and 15 approved premixture manufacturers. There are also 45 approved importers of which 31 operators have also other activities (trader, producer). There are 66 approved wholesalers of which 29 have also other activities (importer, producer). The total number of the compound feed producers is 85 (82 approved, 3 registered). 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant articles or sections of the legislation cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings in this section of the report. In addition, a table is included as an Annex II to this report summarising the main legal requirements related to the specific provisions and measures laid down in the body of EU legislation pertaining to the control of feed additives. 5.1 STRUCTURE OF THE SYSTEM FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON FEED ADDITIVES AND INGREDIENTS FOR THEIR PRODUCTION 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. The organisation of official controls on feed business operators (FeBOs) is described in the Commission services' country profile for Ireland.3

Within the DAFM the Animal Feed Control Group (AFCG) is responsible for the planning of official controls including announced audits, unannounced inspections and 2 Source: European Feed Manufacturers' Federation

Available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/index.cfm?co_id=IE 2 sampling. The AFCG is also responsible for managing and communicating feed-related RASFF notifications. 3. The implementation of the unannounced official controls is the task of Regional Supervisory Agriculture Officials (local inspectors). Local inspectors, under the supervision of District Superintendents, are responsible for carrying out announced audits (in-depth on-the-spot checks) of FeBOs. Approximately 35 audits were carried out yearly in the last few years focusing mainly on feed manufacturers including feed additive manufacturers.

Based on the national implementing regulation (Statutory Instrument 432 of 2009) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, the Feed, Fertiliser, Grain and Poultry Division is responsible for the registration/approval and listing of FeBOs.

Every year DAFM organises a one to two days training for all staff involved in feed controls. During this training participants are informed on new legislative developments, review the work of the previous year and discuss planned controls for the current year. The training provides an open forum for staff to raise and discuss issues they have come across in the course of their work. In addition to general topics, the training also focuses on targeted control areas. Between 2014 and 2018, these targeted areas were control of hazard analyses and critical control points (HACCP), labelling, hygiene, official feed sampling and follow-up and close out of infringements. The audit team assessed the training materials pertaining to official feed sampling and follow-up of infringements and these adequately addressed the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 and Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Between 2014 and 2018, 23 Better Training for Safer Food trainings on different topics (feed law/animal nutrition, HACCP/feed HACCP import controls and RASFF) were attended by different feed inspectors. The information provided in these training courses was disseminated to other feed inspectors. The training materials are available on the shared drive of the DAFM.

The AFCG coordinates communication, collaboration, and cooperation between the different divisions of the DAFM, between the DAFM and other agencies, competent authorities and industrial groups/associations in the feed sector, Irish governmental authorities and competent authorities of the United Kingdom. Examples include the Food Safety Authority of Ireland, the Food Standards Agency of the United Kingdom, the Sea Fisheries Protection Agency, etc. A comprehensive Memorandum of Understanding describes the distribution of the different tasks and responsibilities between the different DAFM divisions. Generally it is in line with the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators

There is a procedure in place for the registration/approval of FeBOs which is described in the country profile of Ireland (see finding 1). The procedure is supported by a 3 guidance document and checklists for the harmonised implementation of the approval/registration procedure. The Feed, Fertiliser, Grain and Poultry Division had developed clear instructions for documentary and on-the-spot checks before approval, in accordance with the requirements of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. National legislation (see finding 4) gives the power to the competent authority to suspend/withdraw the approval and/or registration of a FeBO in case of serious infringements (see finding 43) which is in line with the requirements of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The decision to register a FeBO is issued by DAFM and details of the registration (company name, address, activity, registration number, etc.) are recorded in the central database (Inspection System for Animal Feed). The approval decision is made by the DAFM after an obligatory on-the-spot control carried out by a local feed inspector. All establishments visited were registered and, when necessary, approved as required by Articles 9 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and the associated documentation was available.

The list of approved or registered FeBOs is regularly updated and published on the DAFM website, in accordance with Article 9(3) and Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production

There is a clear system in place for designation of competent authorities and adequate distribution of relevant tasks and responsibilities. The system for registration and approval of feed business operators complies with relevant EU legislation and supports the effective implementation of official controls.

There is a comprehensive communication and coordination system in place within and between different relevant competent authorities. The central competent authority has put appropriate training arrangements in place to support feed inspectors in carrying out their duties competently. 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL FEED CONTROLS 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 Planning of inspections

The planning of feed inspections is carried out on a risk basis taking into account the identified risks associated with the business activity and an individual risk assessment of FeBOs within each activity. Factors taken into consideration in the individual FeBO risk evaluation include: scale and range of operation(s); previous inspection/audit results; reliability and results of FeBO own controls; results from previous years' sampling; and any information that might indicate potential non-compliance. This approach is in line 4 with the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted that participation in private certification schemes does not influence the risk assessment and the derived frequency of official controls.

Based on the risk assessment associated with the business activity(ies) and the individual risk assessment of the FeBO, the minimum inspection frequency relating to low risk operators (e.g. registered retailers, traders) is every five years. The highest inspection frequency relates to high risk operators (e.g. approved compound feed manufacturers, premix manufacturers, etc.) and is once every three months.

The Feedingstuffs Annual Inspection Programme of Ireland is elaborated by the AFCG annually in wide consultation with other divisions of DAFM and other authorities. The programme provides information on the following: scope and criteria for controls; overview of inspection activities; type and number of inspections; type and number of samples and analyses; analytical methods, tolerances and designated testing laboratories and risk assessment for determining control activities. The programme is implemented through inspections of premises and sampling of feedingstuffs at all stages of the feed chain, including importation, storage, manufacture, trade and use at farm level.

The DAFM has developed a set of guidance documents to ensure the uniformity of the official inspections of all types of FeBOs. Checklists have been developed by the DAFM based on the guidance documents. The audit team reviewed the sets of the guidance documents and the checklists. These include matters of relevance for the premises (e.g., hygiene, cleanliness of building and equipment), the adequacy/review of the FeBO's HACCP systems, review of the FeBO's approval/registration including registration/approval of suppliers and the review of traceability and the FeBO's own- sampling programme. The documents reviewed by the audit team were adequate for checking the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The DAFM has prepared a comprehensive guidance document on the requirements for controls on labelling of different types of feeds including feed additives, premixtures, mineral mixtures and other compound feeds. The audit team reviewed these documents and noted that these are well prepared and adequate for checking the requirements of Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Articles 15 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. 5.2.1.2 Implementation of inspections
Between 2013 and 2018, an average of 1180 inspections were carried out annually.

All establishments but one visited, had been inspected with the planned frequency (see finding 14). Local inspectors met always used the centrally prepared checklists during their previous inspections and the previous years' inspection reports were available. All manufacturers and some other types of FeBOs visited were audited by the District Superintendents in the last four years. Detailed audit reports were available. 5 20. All of the FeBOs visited had implemented HACCP-based systems. Detailed assessment criteria for HACCP-based procedures are described in the guidance/checklists (see finding 16). Local inspectors and District Superintendents met could demonstrate sufficient assessment of the adequacy of the HACCP-based procedures. This is in line with the requirements of Article 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 21. There is an official advice for FeBOs to carry out tests on mixing homogeneity at least once every year. All relevant FeBOs visited carried out these tests and local inspectors were able to adequately evaluate the results of the homogeneity test. The audit team noted that testing for carry-over of feed additives was generally part of FeBOs' HACCP plans and was performed regularly (once or twice per year). Local inspectors met carried out inspections on records of carry-over tests and were able to adequately evaluate the results of these tests. Thus, the requirements laid down by Point 3 of Annex II "PRODUCTION" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 were adequately addressed by the official controls. 22. Evidence was seen that local inspectors had checked calibration of measuring devices (scales) during inspections. The audit team randomly checked calibration records at some of the FeBOs visited. All checked devices had been calibrated and the due date of the calibration was clearly labelled on the devices. This is in line with the requirements of Point 3(a) of Annex II "FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 5.2.1.3 Traceability 23. Verification of the FeBO's traceability systems is part of the approval/registration procedure and is also part of inspections and audits. In the guidance documents (see finding 16), there is a step-by-step procedure for verification of product traceability in different types of establishments. During the audit, local inspectors and District Superintendents met used this procedure and demonstrated sufficient knowledge and understanding related to the evaluation of FeBOs' traceability systems. In the establishments visited, local inspectors could successfully carry out assessment on the effectiveness of FeBOs' traceability system. This is in compliance with the requirements laid down by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 24. Documents related to FeBOs' traceability systems (e.g. product specifications, recipes, production sheets, labels, results of laboratory analysis, delivery documents, etc.) were available on-the-spot, allowing for comprehensive traceability of feed additives and premixtures. This is in line with the requirements of point (2)(b)(i) and (iii) of Annex II "RECORD-KEEPING" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Local inspectors and District Superintendents met were aware of how to use the relevant documents to control FeBOs' traceability systems. 25. Relevant guidance documents (see finding 16) contain instructions on controls of retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final 6 products manufactured). The audit team checked some of these samples randomly, and all of these had been appropriately taken, labelled and kept under control in dedicated storage places. These retained samples from feed additives and premixtures were kept at least for six months or until the end of the shelf-life of the products produced with these ingredients. Retained samples of compound feeds were kept at least for three months or until the end of the shelf-life of the produced products. The samples had not been sealed properly except at one FeBO visited. In two compound feed producers visited, retained samples were not taken from amino acids used for production. This is not in line with the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "QUALITY CONTROL" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Previous inspection reports in these establishments did not mention this non- compliance. 5.2.1.4 Labelling 26. The label of the sampled feed is attached to the official feed samples which had been sent to the feed headquarters (see finding 38). All labels are checked by the feed headquarters staff. If an incorrect label is identified, this is notified to the FeBO requesting corrective action(s). The FeBO must respond and correct the label within six weeks. The response of the FeBO is recorded in the central database. The audit team saw some examples for correction of labels requested by the feed headquarters. These examples were in line with the described procedure. 27. In addition, verification that labels of feed additives and premixtures comply with legislative requirements is part of the inspections and audits as required by Article 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The centrally prepared guidance (see finding 17) gives detailed instructions on the labelling checks and includes relevant requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. 28. The audit team also checked documentation/labelling of imported feed additives and noted that generally these products fulfilled the relevant authorisation requirements laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Some exceptions were identified relating to amino acids (no information on the bacterial strain used). The competent authority had overlooked these non-compliances during previous official inspections. 29. The audit team noted that, at the FeBOs visited, the labelling control focused on the final products but not on feed additives, premixtures used during the production. At the time of the audit, the audit team identified numerous shortcomings relating to labelling of feed additives/premixtures used as ingredients for production and some shortcomings relating to the labelling of premixtures and complementary feeds produced in the majority of the establishments visited. Most labelling shortcomings related to products originating from outside Ireland and these had been overlooked during previous inspections. A substantial quantity of feed additives and ingredients for their production is sourced from third countries and it is important to be able to demonstrate that such imports do not contain undesirable substances. From 2010 to the end of 2017, there were 79 notifications issued for feed additives under the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) for the presence of non-authorised genetically modified organisms (GMOs) (26), dioxins (21), heavy metals (17), veterinary medicinal products (5), microbiological contaminants (3) and other non-specified hazards (7). Most of these were for imported feed additives and ingredients for their production. Thus proper traceability of those substances/products is a vital prerequisite for effective control. In Lithuania, there is one approved feed additive manufacturer and 3 approved premixture manufacturers. There are 48 approved importers and 182 traders trading feed additives and/or premixtures. The total number of the compound feed producers is 59 (out of which 19 are approved, 40 registered). This is the first time that official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production in the EU have been specifically audited by the Commission in Lithuania. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. As of December 2019, a new structure of territorial SFVS is planned: 10 territorial departments will be created, with the task to coordinate the responsibilities of several different territorial units.

The National Food and Veterinary Risk Assessment Institute is the national reference laboratory for feed analyses. This institute is also responsible for the drafting of feed monitoring sampling plan and performance and evaluation of results of laboratory analyses. In 2019, the SFVS organised training courses for local inspectors in three different administrative parts of Lithuania. During these courses local inspectors received information/presentations on labelling requirements, and in particular those relevant to feed additives, cross-contamination and carry-over of coccidiostats, differentiation between premixtures and complementary feeds, implementation of Hazard Analyses Critical Control Points (HACCP) audits (comprehensive assessment). The audit team assessed these training materials and concluded that these adequately addressed the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003, Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 and Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In the previous years, several central and local inspectors participated in Better Training for Safer Food trainings on different topics (feed law/animal nutrition, HACCP/feed HACCP, RASFF). The information provided in these training courses was disseminated to other feed inspectors. The training materials are available to the local inspectors.

To raise awareness of the operators of the requirements in the feed sector, in 2019 the SFVS gave a presentation at a feed workshop organised by the main feed operators` association in Lithuania. The presentation highlighted different risks of various feed ingredients, the labelling requirements applicable to feeds including feed additives and the main weak points in performance of FeBOs identified during previous official controls. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators

There is a procedure in place for the registration/approval of FeBOs which is described in the country profile of Lithuania (see finding 1). The procedure is supported by a guidance document and checklists (national order number 3D-606 and 3D-607) for the harmonised implementation of the approval/registration procedure. There is a clear instruction on documentary and on-the-spot checks to be carried out before the approval, in accordance with the requirements of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The two national orders give the power to the competent authority to suspend/withdraw the approval and/or registration of a FeBO in case of serious infringements, recurrent 6 deficiencies and if a FeBO does not operate for more than a year (except the case of reconstruction or repair), which is in line with the requirements of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

Concerning registration, the territorial SFVS considers the application submitted and, if no concerns are raised, assigns a registration number to the entity in accordance with the procedure laid down in the national order No 3D-606 (see finding 8). Whenever required, the territorial SFVS performs an on-the-spot inspection and issues an inspection report. The decision on registration is taken by the head of the territorial SFVS and the newly registered FeBO is added to the publicly available registered feed operators list (see finding 12).

When approval is necessary, the territorial SFVS examines whether the documents presented are in compliance with the relevant requirements laid down by Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Then, normally an on-the-spot inspection is carried out and an inspection report is issued. An on-the-spot inspection is not compulsory when the FeBO does not produce and/or store feed at its premises, but only places it on the market (so called paper traders). The head of the territorial SFVS evaluates the inspection report and documents submitted, makes a decision on the approval of the FeBO and adds it to the register of approved FeBOs.

The audit team assessed the implementation of the approval procedure in one recently approved FeBO. The territorial SFVS granted a conditional approval for three months. During this period, the operator produced a very small amount of product and did not place it on the market. Two and a half months after the end of the conditional approval period the FeBO started commercial activity and the local inspector carried out another on-the-spot inspection (on HACCP, delivery and storage of the final product). Based on the outcome of the second on-the-spot inspection, the FeBOs got full approval. The audit team noted that the competent authority did not prolong the conditional approval (which lapsed at the end of three month period) and did not carry out the required inspection within this time. This led to a few months' gap in the approval status of the operator (between the date of expiry of the conditional approval and the date of granting the full approval following the second on-site inspection).

All establishments visited were registered and, when necessary, approved as required by Articles 9, 10 and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and the associated documentation was available. The list of approved or registered FeBOs is regularly updated and published on the Ministry of Agriculture website, in accordance with Article 9(3) and Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The planning of feed inspections takes into account the risks associated with the business activity, outcome of the previous official controls, any complaints and RASFF notifications in relation to the FeBO and the reliability of the FeBO`s own-controls system based on HACCP principles. Based on these four risk factors, each territorial SFVS has to carry out an annual individual risk assessment of all relevant FeBOs. The central SFVS prepared a comprehensive guidance document to harmonise the individual risk assessments by different territorial SFVS. This approach to planning of inspections is in line with the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted that participation in private certification schemes does not influence the risk assessment or frequency of official controls on certified FeBOs.

Based on the individual risk assessment of the FeBO, the minimum routine inspection frequency relating to very low risk operators (e.g. feed operators involved in retail trade of pet food) is every six years. The highest routine inspection frequency relates to high risk operators (e.g. approved compound feed manufacturers, premix manufacturers, etc.) and is once every year. In addition to the planned routine inspections, there are also targeted (non-routine) inspections. These non-routine inspections relate to consumer complaints, recalls, RASFF notifications or other ad hoc identified risks.

The SFVS has developed a comprehensive set of guidance documents including checklists to ensure the uniformity of the official inspections of all types of FeBOs. The audit team reviewed the guidance document and those checklists which were updated on

June 2019. These documents covered matters of relevance for the premises (e.g. hygiene, cleanliness of buildings and equipment), the adequacy of the FeBO's HACCP systems, review of the FeBO's approval/registration including registration/approval of the suppliers, review of traceability and FeBO's own-sampling programme. The documents also contain information and questions on the official inspection of labelling requirements including labelling of feed additives and premixtures. The documents reviewed by the audit team were adequate to support the inspectors in verifying compliance with the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003, Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 and Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. 8 18. Before 2018, official audits of FeBO`s HACCP system were planned centrally and were not part of the routine inspections. Since 2018, the system has been changed and the HACCP audits have become a part of the routine inspections. Since 2018 audits have not been carried out in the feed sector. 5.2.1.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF INSPECTIONS

The average number of inspections carried out annually on feed additive and premixture manufacturers was around ten in each of the last three years, which was always higher than the number of planned inspections (three to four). In general, the routine inspection frequency of traders and importers of feed additives and premixtures is once every two to four years. The number of implemented official inspections has varied in the last three years (between 50 to 100 inspections per year). Planned official inspections of traders and importers were achieved in the last three years. Routine inspections are unannounced.

All establishments visited had been inspected with the planned frequency (see finding 16). Local inspectors met always used the centrally prepared guidance/checklists; the previous years' inspection reports were available. For one establishment affected by a RASFF notification, the territorial SFVS took this notification into account in the individual risk assessment and increased the inspection frequency for the following year (see findings 15 and 16).

Local inspectors met could demonstrate sufficient knowledge on official controls related to hygiene and maintenance of facilities and equipment, which is in line with the requirements of Annex II "FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

All of the FeBOs visited had implemented HACCP-based systems. Detailed assessment criteria for HACCP-based procedures are described in the guidance/checklists (see finding 17). However, the local inspectors met could not demonstrate sufficient knowledge to assess the adequacy of the HACCP-based procedures, in particular hazard analysis of feed additives. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

All of the FeBOs visited, where tests on homogeneity of mixing and on carry-over of coccidiostats were relevant, included relevant tests their HACCP plans and carried out such tests regularly. The audit team noted that these tests, as described in the FeBOs' procedures, were not fit for purpose in a number of operators visited. However the local inspectors met were not able to adequately evaluate the methods and the results of testing and assess compliance with the requirements laid down in Point 3 of Annex II section "PRODUCTION" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The audit team saw evidence that local inspectors had adequately checked the calibration of measuring devices (scales) during inspections, which is in line with the 9 requirements of Point 3(a) of Annex II "FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT" of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

This inspection group comprises one inspector from the central level and two-three inspectors from different territorial SFVS.
