The FAVV/AFSCA is in the process of a reorganisation, resulting in the provincial division being dismantled and several local control units being merged, creating a total of nine local units. A separate chain of command will be established concerning imports from third countries, but the FAVV/AFSCA stated that this change would have no impact on the audit.

The FAVV/AFSCA stated they would review the country profile in order to reflect the reorganisation and the responsibilities of the competent authorities on the implementation of official controls on imports of animals and goods of animal and non- animal origin.

The FAVV/AFSCA is responsible for import controls of animals, goods of animal and non-animal origin. Customs are responsible for controls on accompanying pet animals at airport entry points and on passengers' luggage. In case of irregularities, when needed, Customs contact the FAVV/AFSCA for advice and follow-up and/or the Federal Public 4 Service - Health, Food Chain Safety and Environment (FPS HSFCE), which has the competence for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). The area of competences of the authorities dealing with import controls is summarised in the following table: Areas of competence FAVV/AFSCA Customs Other authorities Animals X X Food for human consumption of X animal origin X Accompanying pet Food for human consumption of X animals at airport non-animal origin entry points Goods of animal origin not X intended for human consumption X X Feed of non-animal origin X Passengers' luggage, including (postal) parcels X FPS HSFCE/regional authorities X Luggage controls of passengers at airports 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between competent authorities

A protocol on cooperation between the FAVV/AFSCA and Customs was established in 2007. This protocol was reviewed in 2018 and lays down the general provisions and areas of cooperation between both authorities. The annexes to the protocol contain more details on the tasks and competences of each authority. The annexes do not contain details on controls of travellers' luggage for pet food and certain animal-by-products. The FAVV/AFSCA and Customs committed to update the annexes in this respect.

Biannual meetings between the FAVV/AFSCA and Customs take place at central level. At local level, cooperation platforms are established and meetings are held on a regular basis. When needed, ad-hoc meetings are organised in addition to the regular meetings. Records of these various meetings were made available to the audit team.

Customs stated that they organised together with other competent authorities' common targeted actions covered by specific control legislation. Regarding import controls for example, an annual action "OPSON" is organised at Antwerp and Zeebrugge ports and in the Belgian airports, targeting commercial consignments; and on a regular basis the action "BACON" is organised in the airports passengers' terminal targeting travellers' luggage. These actions target any product subject to import controls, e.g. animals, 5 plants, products of animal and non-animal origin, and medicinal products; including species subject to the CITES trade rules, etc.
The FAVV/AFSCA stated that cooperation protocols are also established with other competent authorities such as the FPS HSFCE.

The audit team noted that there is a good cooperation within the FAVV/AFSCA, between the FAVV/AFSCA and Customs at central, regional and BIP/DPE level, which is in line with Article 4 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.3 Resources and training of staff

The FAVV/AFSCA explained that an internal procedure outlines the organisation of the training of new inspectors performing official (import) controls or inspectors returning after a long period of absence, which includes on-the-job training under the guidance of a coach.

Import controls are often performed by inspectors who are not permanent employees, but independent veterinarians, bio-engineers, industrial engineers, bachelors and masters graduates who are contracted in for this purpose (known as 'belast met opdracht' (BMO)). In addition to the conditions mentioned in paragraph 9, the independent veterinarians/graduates are required to follow 50 training hours over a period of three years with a minimum of 12 training hours per year to maintain their competences. The training must be validated by the FAVV/AFSCA.

The FAVV/AFSCA plans a yearly training programme to fulfil training needs on specific topics for its staff. The audit team received from the FAVV/AFSCA a list with topics for training related to import controls which was provided in the period 2017- 2018. The list included phytopathology at imports, invasive alien species, import controls on animal-by-products and risks related to exposure to fumigation gases. Training on customs procedures was planned in this period, but was not given due to lack of resources. The FAVV/AFSCA provided evidence of BIP staff participating in these training sessions. This is in line with the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. BIP/DPE staff also participated in a number of Better Training for Safer Food sessions related to import controls.

The inspectors and Customs officials dealing with import controls interviewed by the audit team had good knowledge of the import procedures. BIP/DPE staff consulted their hierarchy and Customs consulted the FAVV/AFSCA when advice was needed. 5.1.4 Legislative and administrative provisions for the implementation of EU rules and planning

The FAVV/AFSCA has a quality management system in place which is accredited following the standard NBN EN ISO/IEC 17020 (conformity assessment ­ requirements for the operation of various types of bodies performing inspection) and certified following the standard NBN EN ISO 9001 (quality management systems ­ requirements). All official import controls carried out under the responsibility of the 6 FAVV/AFSCA in all border inspection posts, DPEs and DPIs are executed following the documented procedures and instructions prescribed by the quality management system implemented by DG Control of the FAVV/AFSCA. Examples of procedures for import, execution of the sampling plan, technical sheets on specific import conditions, import of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin were made available to the audit team.

In line with Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the management system contains procedures for import controls of animals and products of animal origin which are both harmonised and non-harmonised at EU level, goods subject to specific import conditions, transhipment, transit and ship supply.

The FAVV/AFSCA has procedures in place regarding enforcement measures and sanctions, in line with Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. A typical enforcement measure is the Proces Verbaal ­ an official (infringement) report addressed to the operators containing a decision related to deficiencies identified, action to be taken and options to appeal the decision taken. The audit team received examples of Proces Verbaal issued at the BIPs, but also Proces Verbaal issued at destination in the case of consignments imported under the channelling procedure (Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC).

The procedures and related documents are available on the intranet site of the FAVV/AFSCA for the control staff, and the audit team observed that the FAVV/AFSCA staff was familiar with the procedures in place.

Examples of actions initiated by Customs were also provided. For example, for a rejected consignment of food of non-animal origin which was not destroyed within the deadline given by the FAVV/AFSCA, Customs drafted a Proces Verbaal for their hierarchy's approval, containing details of the case and proposing administrative sanctions in addition to the destruction of the goods.

The FAVV/AFSCA has designed in line with Article 1(2) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, as part of the national control plan, an annual monitoring plan for BIPS/DPEs/DPIs to detect potential hazards to humans, animals and the environment during import controls. Different requirements are taken into account for the establishment of the national control plan, for example the analyses fixed by legislation and the analysis determined by a risk analysis (severity of adverse effects, the estimated prevalence in the population, and potential contamination or spread).

Since the DG(SANCO)2011-8920 audit and its recommendation No 8, the Belgian competent authorities have improved the implementation rate of the annual monitoring plan to detect potential hazards to humans, animals and the environment during import controls. 7 Conclusions on structure of the system for import controls

There is an adequate framework of official controls in place, implemented by well- trained staff and supported by a quality management system, detailed procedures, guidance documents and information technology system. This framework contributes to efficient coordination and cooperation within and between the designated competent authorities, and consistent implementation of controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTED GOODS 5.2.1 Notification prior to arrival and systems to ensure the presentation of consignment for import controls

A well-established system is in place for operators to notify consignments before arrival in the BIPs/DPEs to the FAVV/AFSCA. The importer or its representative must use the Trace Control and Expert System (TRACES) to notify the arrival of animals and goods of animal origin by completing part 1 of the Common Veterinary Entry Document, in line with Article 1(1) of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 and Article 2(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 respectively. Although not an EU legal requirement, goods of non- animal origin subject to special import conditions must also be notified in TRACES by completing part 1 of the Common Entry Document, which the audit team considered to be a good practice. Of the files selected for review by the audit team, only a few consignments were not notified before their arrival at the BIPs. This did not negatively impact the organisation of the import controls.

The FAVV/AFSCA, in cooperation with Customs, verifies on a regular basis the manifests of ships and planes to ensure that products and animals are presented for import controls, which is in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 respectively. At one port visited, the BIP staff provided evidence of the follow-up of one consignment notified for import controls, which was not presented for the identity and physical checks. The follow-up was done in cooperation with Customs and the authorities of the Member State of destination. 5.2.2 Transhipment procedures
The FAVV/AFSCA implemented the procedures in place to verify transhipments, in line with Article 9 of Directive 97/78/EC. The audit team reviewed the implementation of transhipment procedures

The country profile for Denmark describes the organisation and responsibilities for import controls and the competent authorities designated in accordance with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see section 4 above). The DVFA stated that changes in the organisation and responsibilities of the competent authorities are expected to take effect as of 1 October 2019, but these will not have a significant impact on the organisation and responsibilities for import controls(1).

The DVFA is responsible for import controls on animals, products of animal origin, food and feed of non-animal origin, controls of facilities approved for carrying out import controls, and housing of animals and storage of goods intended for import. The Danish Agricultural Agency performs phytosanitary checks on imported goods, where relevant. The BIPs and DPEs fall under the responsibility of the local Food/Veterinary Inspection Units of the DVFA, a part of whose staff are assigned to perform the import controls. Each BIP has a lead border veterinarian responsible for the performance of import controls and the BIP facilities. The staff assigned to the BIP/DPE are responsible for checking imported consignments, whereas the local DVFA staff are responsible for checks of the facilities and equipment. The DVFA has conferred responsibility on Customs to carry out checks on non-commercial pets (dogs, cats and ferrets), travellers' personal luggage and postal parcels. The DVFA is responsible for the supervision of controls on travellers' personal luggage and postal parcels and for issuing sanctions.

The DVFA staff taking samples of goods are accredited by the Danish Accreditation Body (DANAK) to do so. These inspectors are accredited by the Danish Accreditation body to perform accredited inspection tasks such as weighing, measuring, sampling, inspection and tally. The BIP staff stated that they witness the sampling of the liquid fish oil and that they prepare the samples to be sent for laboratory analysis in line with the appropriate DVFA sampling plan and/or project.

Following recommendation No 1 of the audit report DG(SANTE)/2016-8870 regarding the evaluation of the official control system on special import conditions, the organisation of import controls on products of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions has been re-structured to enable the documentary checks on these products to take place at DPEs situated at the border (rather than inland as was previously the case). For this purpose the administrative offices of the BIPs are shared with the DPE staff. All BIPs are privately owned and a written agreement is in place between the BIP operator and the DVFA for each BIP.

The DVFA stated that it has access to an adequate laboratory network for testing in accordance with Article 4(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The DVFA confirmed that all laboratories testing official samples of consignments intended for import are accredited in line with Article 12 of the aforesaid Regulation with the exception of the Danish Technical University. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between competent authorities

The DVFA and Customs operate under a cooperation agreement, last updated in May 2019, which sets out the framework conditions for constructive and effective cooperation. The agreement covers cooperation in the following areas: veterinary checks on imported animals and goods of animal origin, food and feed of non-animal origin, illegal fishing (illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing), as well as organic produce, wine, and market surveillance. The cooperation agreement between the DVFA and Customs is renewed every two years. A joint steering committee meets before the renewal date to discuss the cooperation and revise/update/renew the agreement. A contact group, composed of heads of unit and administrators, meets 1-2 times a year to ensure ongoing coordination, share information and discuss cases of mutual interest. The audit team reviewed the minutes of these meetings. An additional annual meeting is planned to address identified risks in the veterinary/sanitary fields so that Customs may take account of them in their planning. BIP staff meet with their Customs colleagues regularly. The audit team saw the minutes of such meetings.

The DVFA has provided Customs with written instructions on how to carry out controls on non-commercial pet animals, products of animal origin and certain products of non- animal origin. These are published on Customs' intranet site.

The DVFA together with Customs have planned for 2020 a joint campaign on checks of travellers' personal luggage. 5 9. The DVFA has concluded an agreement with a private laboratory, accredited to the ISO 17025 standard, for analysing official samples of imported bivalve molluscs, echinoderms, tunicates and marine snails for various algae toxins. Official samples to be tested for radioactive substances are analysed at the Danish Technical University. All other official samples are analysed at the DVFA's two in-house laboratories. 10. Since BIP and DPE staff are drawn from local DVFA Food/Veterinary Inspection Units, there is close communication and cooperation between the border staff and the local units, of which the audit team saw evidence. Information on non-compliance or repeat offenders is communicated to local inspection units to enable them to follow up with the importer during their routine checks. 11. The audit team noted good cooperation between the DVFA staff at local and central level and with the port and airport authorities. 12. The communication and cooperation between competent authorities is in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.3 Resources and training of staff 13. Staff at the BIPs, DPEs and Customs offices visited have been appropriately trained on import requirements and procedures, in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 14. The DVFA requires all BIP staff to undergo mandatory training before being assigned to work in a BIP. For products of animal origin and animals, the DVFA organises annual training for its BIP staff on a variety of relevant topics. For products of non-animal origin, a training course was held in the autumn of 2018 targeting both DPE staff and those working in local DVFA inspection units responsible for carrying our checks on DPIs and control points. 15. According to point 3.4 of the cooperation agreement between the DVFA and Customs, the training of Customs officials is coordinated with the DVFA. The DVFA has provided training which has included instructions on how to read a common veterinary entry document (CVED) and common entry document (CED) in order to determine whether a consignment can be released for free circulation. 16. The audit team examined the content of training courses and individual training records. All staff met had been appropriately trained and participated in training regularly (annual DVFA courses, Better Training for Safer Food, etc.). Furthermore, the staff interviewed were knowledgeable and well-acquainted with the procedures and legal requirements for imported goods and animals. 5.1.4 Legislative and administrative provisions for the implementation of EU rules and planning 17. In accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the DVFA has issued a number of written procedures by means of executive orders, circulars, instructions and 6 guidance on the various official controls associated with imports of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin. Whilst the executive orders are directed to the public transposing the provisions set out in Union legislation, where applicable, the circulars and instructions are addressed to the DVFA staff. The DVFA have published the administrative provisions related to import controls on their database. The DVFA provided to the audit team copies of the main executive orders, circulars, instructions and guidance. 18. The conditions for import of non-harmonised food of animal origin are laid down in Order no 406 of 9 April 2019 on veterinary control of food: the importer has to apply to the DVFA for an import permit. The conditions for products of animal origin not intended for human consumption are laid down in Order 134 of 6 February 2019: import is only possible after securing permission from the DVFA prior to import. Non- harmonised products of animal origin must be sent to the place of destination following the channelling procedure set out in Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. 19. In response to recommendation No 4 of audit report DG(SANTE)/2016-8870 regarding the evaluation of the official control system on special import conditions, the DVFA has issued a guideline on channelled consignments and use of the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES), which sets out when channelling of consignments applies and how to enter relevant data in TRACES to confirm that channelled consignments have arrived at their destination. The guideline on channelling entered into force on 1 January 2018. 20. The DVFA has the legal authority to enforce EU import legislation and has provisions for sanctions in place, in line with Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/8004 for animals and products of animal origin. The local DVFA units are responsible for imposing sanctions. The DVFA stated that during the period 2017 till recently no sanctions have been applied related to import controls, other than the seizure, rejection, and/or destruction of non-compliant consignments. 21. A well-developed information technology system is in place ensuring that the frequency of physical checks on consignments of goods of animal origin for which import requirements are harmonised at EU level are carried out in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 2, 3 and 4 of Commission Decision 94/360/EEC, and on consignments of goods subject to special import conditions, in line with Article 8(2) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and Article 9(5) of Regulation No 884/2004. 22. Each BIP has developed its own manual of procedures for official controls of each import category for which it is approved so that the procedures are adapted to the local situation. These manuals are published on the DVFA intranet. The audit team saw evidence of local procedures being implemented at several sites visited. 23. No control on the consistency of the manuals issued at the different BIPs has been undertaken by the DVFA. However, BIP staff are encouraged to access BIP manuals issued at other BIPs and the DVFA stated that it is continuously working towards consistency between the different BIPs. For this purpose, working groups have been 7 established where specific topics are reviewed and these topics are discussed at annual training days. Where relevant, existing circulars or guidelines are revised and/or new ones are drawn up. 24. The DVFA has set up a knowledge exchange group in order to establish standard operating procedures for products subject to special import conditions, including kitchenware from China. These procedures are expected to be in place in the first quarter of 2020. In addition, the scope of the group includes exchange of experiences, discussions of cases and other procedures in relation to import of products of animal origin and non-animal origin. 25. The DVFA has developed annual monitoring plans for categories of products of animal origin intended for import and their related potential hazards, in line with Article 1(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and point 1 of Annex II to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. The plans comprise test parameters such as residues, microorganisms/their toxins and metabolites, and other substances posing a risk to animal or public health. 26. The DVFA has also established a sampling plan for categories of goods of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions taking into account the parameters and frequency of sampling laid down in relevant Union legislation. The plan is updated whenever there is an amendment to the applicable Union acts. 27. The DVFA has not established a sampling plan for animals intended for import due to an absence of eligible ungulates for import other than registered equidae in recent years. The organisation and responsibilities for import controls and the competent authorities designated in accordance with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, are described in the country profile for Finland (see section 4). Since 1 January 2019 the competent authority for the import controls of live animals and products of animal origin (as well as hay and straw) and feed of non-animal origin within the scope of the audit has changed from the Finish Food Safety Authority, EVIRA, to the Finnish Food Authority (FFA). The latter is a merger of EVIRA, the Finnish Agency for Rural Affairs and a part of the Centre for Information and Communication Technology Services under the National Land Survey of Finland.

Customs is responsible for the import controls of food of non-animal origin (defined in the Finnish Food Act 23/2006) and composite products listed in Annex II of Commission Decision 2007/275/EC, which are not subject to veterinary checks under Article 6(1)(b) of the aforesaid Decision.

The controls on the travellers' personal luggage, postal parcels and empty livestock vehicles, and the identity checks required for consignments in transit exiting the EU and for the supplies of cross border means of sea transport are performed by Customs. These Customs responsibilities are set out in the following national legal acts: For empty livestock vehicles - §12 of Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (MAF) Decree 1121/2014; For travellers' personal luggage, including postal parcels - §9 of MAF Decree 1121/2014; and For identity checks (seal checks only) of transited consignments and of the supply of cross border means of sea transport - Chapter 2 Section 9 of MAF Decree 1370/2004. 4 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between competent authorities

Cooperation between the FFA and Customs for the import controls of live animals and products of animal origin is laid down in national legislation (MAF statute 1192/1996). Customs has an appointed contact person for the FFA. The audit team noted the good cooperation and communication between the FFA and Customs, which is in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Regular meetings between the authorities responsible for the import controls are organised at the central level, the minutes of which were reviewed by the audit team. Three co-operative groups involving the relevant competent authorities have been established to strengthen the controls in Finland: Imports of food, feed and plants: this group consists of representatives of the FFA, Customs and MAF. Meetings are organised every two months; Illegal imports and intra-EU trade of dogs and cats: this group consists of representatives from the FFA - border control section, Customs, police, tax authorities and the relevant regional administrative agencies. Meetings are organised annually and whenever necessary; and Measures for preventing the introduction and spread of African swine fever: this group consists of representatives from the MAF, the FFA, Customs and the Finnish Border Guards. Meetings are organised every two months.
Every two weeks meetings take place between the FFA (central level) and the BIP staff to discuss import requirements, current issues and other topics e.g. resources and training needs.
Annual meetings are organised between the MAF and the FFA with the stakeholders for the coordination of the import controls on feed. 5.1.3 Resources and training of staff
Staff at the visited BIPs and at the Customs Electronic Centre have been appropriately trained, which is in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

BIP staff have participated in Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) sessions related to import controls and/or in the one-day training sessions organised by the FFA once a year. Staff who had participated in BTSF courses disseminated the information received during these courses at the FFA training days. Information and training materials are made available on the FFA's Intranet.

Customs organise five-day training sessions once a year for their staff, during which the FFA also gives presentations. Specific training is also organised for all Customs staff performing physical checks, including sampling of food of non-animal origin.
Newcomers to the FFA and Customs receive on-the-job training. 5 5.1.4 Legislative and administrative provisions for the implementation of EU rules and planning

Instructions for the performance of official import controls at the BIPs are made available to staff by the FFA in line with the requirements of Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, although they have not been updated since 2014 (some not since 2009). Guidance for official controls on returning empty livestock vehicles at entry points and imports of pet animals was updated in 2018. The competent authority stated that instructions will be updated and, where necessary, new guidance for import controls will be developed in line with Regulation (EU) 2017/625. BIP staff have access to relevant legislation and regularly receive the latest information regarding importation rules by the MAF via email. The Product Safety Unit of Customs as well as the FFA regularly send up-to-date information to Customs officials.
The FFA issues import permits for non-harmonised animals under Council Directive 92/65/EEC.
Customs has developed and published Guidance for the performance of official import controls for consignments of food of non-animal origin.

Administrative sanctions for infringements relating to imports of animals and goods of animal origin are set down in the Fees Decree ­ MAF Decree 1425/2016. They include an hourly fee collection for consignments that require a longer inspection time (e.g. when consignments are detained and additional documents are required, or the importer requests the BIP staff to upload the Common Veterinary Entry Document (CVED) in the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES)). The audit team saw evidence of such fines imposed.

No sanctions for infringement of the requirements for imports of goods of non-animal origin are incorporated in Customs legislation. Customs stated that a draft legal act of the national import controls has been developed in which the fees and sanctions are included.

Annual monitoring plans have been developed for the controls of imported products of animal origin in line with Article 1(2) and point 1 of Annex II to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. They comprise test parameters such as residues, microorganisms/their toxins and metabolites, and other substances dangerous to animal or public health. The minimum sampling frequency was set out for each BIP. 6 Conclusions on structure of the system for import controls

The responsibilities of the competent authorities for the official import controls are clearly defined. Good cooperation based on regular meetings and communication between the Finnish Food Authority and Customs underpins the correct implementation of the official controls at the entry points.

The competent authorities have put suitable arrangements in place to ensure staff are trained and are kept up-to-date in their area of competence. Staff have been provided with relevant legal acts, documented procedures and instructions to support their work, although in some cases these procedures and instructions are out-of-date. There is a monitoring plan in place which aims to support officials in identifying suitable consignments of goods for testing. The administrative framework, therefore, contributes to ensuring that the official import controls are largely carried out to a consistent standard. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTED GOODS 5.2.1 Notification prior to arrival and systems to ensure the presentation of consignments for import controls

In general, the consignments of animals and goods are notified by the operators to the authorities prior to arrival in line with the relevant legislation. The team noted that some consignments of goods were notified on the day of arrival, on which the competent authorities commented that this did not cause any problem for the organisation of the official import controls. Concerning horses, before the arrival of the consignment arrangements are agreed by e-mail. The TRACES notification is made on the day of arrival by the border veterinarian (for which a fee is charged). For more details on food of non-animal origin see section 5.2.4.3.
The audit team observed that, based on national legislation, the inspection fee is doubled when animals and goods of animal origin are not notified prior to arrival.

Since 2014 the BIP staff no longer have access to the ship and aircraft manifests, in order to use these manifests as information source to verify if all animals and goods requiring veterinary checks are presented for these checks, which is contrary to the requirements of Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 and Article 6 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, respectively. Customs have developed a system to identify consignments subject to veterinary import controls and forward all such consignments of animals and goods of animal origin to the BIPs, if these had not already been notified to the veterinary authorities by the importers. The audit team saw evidence of forwarded cases. 7 5.2.2 Transhipment

The FFA confirmed that no transshipment of consignments of animals and goods of animal origin had taken place for the period 2017 up to the time of the audit. 5.2.3 Transit and supply of cross border means of sea transport
The FFA confirmed that there had been no transits of animals in the period 2017 up to the time of the audit.

All consignments of products of animal origin in transit are subject to documentary and identity checks at the entry BIP, which is in line with Article 11(2)(b) of Directive 97/78/EC. The records verified demonstrated that consignments came from third countries whose products are not prohibited entry into the EU and were accompanied with the correct model certificates, in accordance with Article 11(1)(a) of Directive 97/78/EC.

The exit from the Union of the consignments in transit is checked by Customs and the BIP staff register the time of exit in TRACES. The audit team reviewed records of exiting consignments and found that all of them exited Finland within the 30-day deadline following their departure from the entry BIP, which is in line with Article 11(2)(c) of Directive 97/78/EC.

The documentary checks of the supplies of cross border means of sea transport are performed by BIP staff and the identity checks (seal checks) are performed by Customs. BIP staff receive the results of the controls carried out by Customs, and together with the results of documentary checks, form the basis for the BIP staff signing the CVEDs.

Regarding all records of supplies of cross border means of sea transport checked by the audit team, the certificate referred to in Article 1(3) of Decision 2000/571/EC, of which the model is laid down in the Annex to that Decision, was used and the arrival of the respective consignments within the deadline of 30 days was confirmed, which is in line with Article 2 of that Decision. 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks 5.2.4.1 Checks on animals

The majority of the animal species imported into Finland are dogs, horses, ornamental fish and non-harmonised species (insects, snakes, etc.). Two consignments of ungulates had been imported since the beginning of 2017.

The organisation of, and responsibilities for, official controls on business operators producing and trading PAP are included in the wider scope of controls of the ABP chain. These controls are largely described in the country profile for Spain, available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=ES

Generally, at central (federal) level, the General Secretariat of Agriculture and Food of the MAPA is responsible for the ABP sector, except for the control of food establishments producing ABP which is the responsibility of the Ministry of Health, 3 Consumption and Social Welfare. The main tasks of the General Secretariat of Agriculture and Food in the ABP sector are: coordination of official control programmes, preparation of national guidance/instructions/legislation, representation of Spain at the relevant technical meetings in the EU, negotiating bilateral trade agreements and certificates with third countries and maintaining and updating the relevant list of business operators.

Generally, the Autonomous Communities (Regions) are responsible for the implementation of official controls in the ABP sector. Each Region designates the department(s) responsible for the official control of the ABP sector. The official control is structured on two levels (regional and local) in both Regions visited.

Communication and cooperation between central and regional level is well established. There are different National Committees (expert working groups) with the representatives of each central and each regional competent authority. Committees ­ relevant to the control of ABP and PAP - carry out five-six meetings annually. The aim of the meetings is to ensure the harmonised implementation of the different legislative requirements.

Generally, twice per year, there is a meeting between the central authorities and the representatives of the ABP business operators. The main purpose of the meeting is to share/exchange information between stakeholders and competent authorities. In 2017, when Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 was modified and the export of PAP containing ruminant protein was permitted, this meeting provided the opportunity to highlight this point.

In both Regions visited there are several coordination/cooperation meetings/committees. During these meetings local inspectors and regional officers share information and practices on the implementation of different legislative requirements in the ABP sector. Also in both Regions visited local inspectors had participated in special ABP training courses (sometimes these were on-line) and training on the relevant feed ban requirements.
Central, regional and local inspectors had participated in Better Training for Safer Food courses on the official control of ABP and/or feed sector.

In 2016, the internal audit unit of one Region visited audited the implementation of the feed and the ABP official control programmes. The objective of the audit was to check whether the control programmes designed by the Region followed the requirements of the centrally prepared guidance and that local inspectors implemented the programmes as required. The internal audit identified some weak points (risk assessment, coordination, training, transparency, reporting, effectiveness of official controls and official laboratories) in the implementation of official controls. In 2018, this internal audit was followed up and all recommendations were closed except for one relating to the designation of official laboratories. In the other Region visited an internal audit on the ABP sector had not been carried out in the last five years. 4 9. The allocation and distribution of various responsibilities at central, regional and local levels in the area of official controls within the scope of the audit, the competence of staff and the cooperation and coordination activities demonstrated during the audit satisfy the relevant requirements laid down by Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.1.2 Registration, approval and authorisation of ABP plants and operators Legal requirements Articles 23, 24, 44 and 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Article 32(5) and Chapter II of Annex XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Section D of Chapter IV, Section A of Chapter III and Section A of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Findings 10. The list of approved and registered ABP plants and operators is available on the MAPA website. The update of the list is managed at central level based on the information provided by the Regions. The publicly available lists are updated at least once annually; the last update was in February 2019. There is an internal IT system which contains detailed information on ABP operators. Lists of the ABP operators are updated in this system automatically when any changes have been recorded (change of name, address, activity etc.) These lists are only available for the Spanish competent authorities. All operators visited by the auditor, and their suppliers or clients, were registered or approved and were listed in publicly available lists of ABP plants and operators, as required by Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. One transporter visited was registered to transport Category 1 and 3 ABP in its registration document and also in the internal IT system in July 2018. However, the information in the registration documents (and internal IT system) does not match the data on the publicly available list as the latter indicates that it is only registered to transport Category 1 ABP. 11. Listing of ABP processing plants authorised to produce feed materials for aquaculture, and compound feed manufacturers authorised to produce feed with PAP for aquaculture animals, is the responsibility of the central competent authority. Each Region has to communicate the list of APB processing plants and compound feed manufacturers to the MAPA. These lists are available on the MAPA website. The auditor visited one processing plant producing PAP for aquaculture. The plant has two processing lines, of which one was authorised by the Region for the production of PAP for aquaculture animals. However, the information in the authorisation documents does not match the data on the publicly available list which indicates that both lines were authorised for production of PAP for aquaculture. 12. There are several listed processing plants officially authorised to produce PAP for aquaculture. Two of these processing plants produce pig PAP using processing method 4. This is not in line with the requirements of point B, section I, Chapter II, Annex X to 5 Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authorities did not detect this problem during the authorisation process. 13. Based on Royal Decree 578/2014 only slaughterhouses which do not slaughter ruminants and cutting plants which do not debone and cut up ruminants are authorised as food establishments to deliver raw materials (Category 3 ABP) for production of non- ruminant PAP. This national requirement is stricter than the requirements of Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Article 7 of the above- mentioned Royal Decree contains detailed information on the requirement for transporters transporting PAP and compound feed with PAP for aquaculture animals. There is a centrally prepared procedure (see finding 22) on the inspection of transporters transporting ABP as raw materials from authorised slaughterhouses and/or cutting plants to authorised ABP processing plants for the production of non-ruminant PAP for aquaculture. 14. The auditor visited a registered Category 3 ABP and PAP transporter. The company transported Category 3 ABP in Spain and PAP in both Spain and another Member State. The registration document referred to a Regional Order and did not mention Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 but it is generally in line with the legal requirements. 15. In Spain there is very limited number of organic fertiliser/soil improver (OF/SI) manufacturers who use PAP or MBM for its production (four PAP, one MBM, one MBM and PAP). Based on Royal Decree 506/2013, all OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM is subject to pre-authorisation before being placed on the market. All authorised OF/SI is entered in the Register of Fertiliser Products (nine products with PAP, two MBM, two MBM and PAP). The package size of all OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM cannot be bigger than 50kg. These OF/SI do not contain any mixing component to make it unpalatable because there is no authorised mixing component in Spain. This is in line with the requirements of points 2 and 4 of Section 1, Chapter II Annex XI of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. 5.1.3 Planning of official controls Legal requirements Articles 4(3) and 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Article 32 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Articles 3, 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings 5.1.3.1 Planning of inspections 16. In Spain the planning of official controls (inspection and sampling) in the ABP sector is covered by two multiannual national control programmes (the animal nutrition control programme and the ABP control programme). The central competent authority prepares 6 a set of guidance documents to support the implementation of the national control programmes including the risk assessment of operators in the ABP sector. Both Regions visited used these guidance documents to design their own annual risk-based official inspection programme. The risk assessment used to determine the operators to be inspected in the annual programmes included the activity of the operator, size of the establishment, type of production or transported products, implementation of an own- control system and the results of previous official controls. This is generally in line with the requirements of Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 17. The planned inspection frequency of the different types of operators was different in the two Regions visited. The minimum inspection frequency of Category 3 ABP plants is two times per year; storage plants are inspected once every 2-3 in one and once every 5- 6 years in the other Region visited. Generally, the inspection of ABP transporters is a low priority. In one region visited the minimum inspection frequency is once every 6-7 years and 3% of the total number of transporters in the other region visited every year. 5.1.3.2 Sampling programme 18. Spain has an annual sampling plan to detect animal proteins and/or particles in feedingstuffs. Around 900 samples were taken in 2017 and in 2018. In 2017, four samples of feed for ruminants were found with unlabelled presence of fishmeal. In 2018, 11 official samples identified presence of ruminant protein in fishmeal and two feed for aquaculture results were found positive with Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for presence of ruminant protein. All consignments of unlabelled/contaminated fishmeal were sent for pet food production. At the feed producer where the two positive PCR cases were identified, the competent authority requested a change in the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) plan (including PCR test) and a recall of the contaminated feed. After an official investigation the source of the contamination was identified. The auditor reviewed the official investigation and it was adequate. 19. There is a sampling plan for the detection of concentration of Glyceroltriheptanoate (GTH). In 2017 and 2018, 62 and 40 samples, respectively, were taken from MBM in Spain. In 2017, six samples contained a lower concentration of GTH than the legal requirement (250mg/ fat kg). These MBM batches were reprocessed, and the competent authority checked that the GTH concentration/dosage of the operator was adequate. There is also a sampling plan for the detection of GTH in PAP. In 2017 and 2018, 17 and 48 samples, respectively, were taken from PAP. The minimum detection limit of the GTH is 50mg/ fat per kg using accredited laboratory analyses. These analyses did not detect GTH in PAP. 20. There is an annual microbiological sampling programme for feed materials in Spain. Every year approximately 600 samples are taken for microbiological analyses including Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and a Clostridium perfringens test for PAP. 21. In both Regions visited the planned number of samples was taken in 2017 and 2018 for the detection of animal proteins and for the detection of GTH in MBM and for the 7 control of Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and Clostridium perfringens contamination of PAP. 5.1.3.3 Procedures and instructions 22. The central competent authority has prepared a procedure for the inspection of Category 3 ABP processing plants producing feed materials. Point 5 of this document contains a detailed description of the requirements for the commercial document accompanying ABP and/or derived product to its destination. It is clearly mentioned in bullet point two that if the ABP and/or derived product is intended for use in feed, the commercial document has to contain information on species and sub-category as described in Article 10 of Regulation (EC) 1069/2009. Point 9 contains detailed information on the transport requirements for ABP intended for use in the production of feed for aquaculture animals as set down in Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 23. The central competent authority has prepared a procedure for the notification of intra- EU trade of PAP and MBM in the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES). Point 3 of this procedure describes the obligation of the Spanish competent authorities to inform the competent authority of Member State of origin of the arrival of each consignment. Based on this procedure the Spanish competent authorities have two options of how to inform the competent authority of origin. The first is via TRACES, which is the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; the second is to send back the fourth copy of the commercial document from the receiver business to the producer business based on point 2 of Chapter III, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. With the second option the information exchange is carried out between business operators which cannot replace the obligatory information exchange between competent authorities as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 24. The central competent authority has prepared guidance on the authorisation of the 30 day validation of processing method 7 based on the requirements of point G, Chapter III,

To ensure that official checks on the validation process verify compliance with the requirements laid down in Section 2 of Chapter I to Annex XVI to Regulation (EC) No 142/2011, in particular, in points 1, 3(b) and 4 with respect to the critical parameters to be checked and monitored for the continuous process and to alterations made to the process. Recommendation based on conclusion: 23 Associated finding: 15

To ensure that arrangements are put in place for listing approved or registered ABP establishments, plants and operators, keeping the lists up-to-date and making them available to other Member States and to the public as required by Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 24 Associated finding: 20

The competent authorities involved in the planning and implementation of the residue monitoring plan and in follow-up of non-compliances are described in detail in the country profile for Austria. 5.1.2. Planning of residue monitoring Legal Requirements Articles 3, 5 and 7 of Directive 96/23/EC; Articles 3, 8 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Commission Regulation (EU) No 37/2010; Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 of the European Parliament and of the Council; Commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006; Council Regulation (EEC) No 315/93; Article 4 of Commission Decision 2002/657/EC. Findings

The planning process of the residue monitoring plan is initiated and finalised in a timely manner. In the case of the residue monitoring plan for animals, an interim plan for January-March is prepared and once all non-compliant results from the previous year are available these are taken into account and the residue monitoring plan for March- December is sent to the Provincial Veterinary Services (Landesveterinärbehörden - PVS). The residue monitoring plan for food (milk, eggs, honey) covers the whole calendar year and is implemented as of January by the Provincial Food Authorities (Landeslebensmittelbehörden, PFA).

For planning, the competent authority takes into account recommendations made by the European Commission and the European Union Reference Laboratories and the availability of analytical methods. All important risk factors such as previous non- compliant results, animal numbers and slaughter volumes per species at Länder- and establishment level, membership in governmental animal health services and the use of veterinary medicinal products (e.g. antimicrobial substances) in food-producing animals are considered annually. This is in line with Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 2 4. The plan aims to ensure that multiple sampling from the same mammal or poultry farm is avoided as required by point 2.3.3.1. of the Annex to Commission Decision 98/179/EC, except for cases where non-compliances have been found, as these are again sampled in the following year, which supports risk-based planning (see finding No 3). 5. The 2018 residue monitoring plan included all of the required and highly desirable substance groups for almost all species and commodities as laid down in Annex II to Directive 96/23/EC. Caprine and ovine milk are covered for substance groups A6, B1, B2a, B2e, B2f and in the 2019 residue monitoring plan also for substance groups B3a, B3b, B3c and B3d. Group B3f substances for hen eggs include fipronil. Quail eggs, of which around 2 million are produced, are planned to be included in the 2019 residue monitoring plan for the required substances in line with the requirements of the Annex to Directive 97/747/EC. 6. Detection levels for all analyte/matrix combinations in the residue monitoring plan are at or below the required Maximum Residue Limit (MRL), Minimum Required Performance Limit or Maximum Level including those for dihydrostreptomycin, enrofloxacin, florfenicol, gentamycin, lincomycin and oxytetracycline, thus recommendation No 1 of the 2011 report has been addressed. 7. The number of samples calculated in the residue monitoring plan for all domestic species and commodities are based on national production as required in the Annex to Directive 97/747/EC and slaughter data including animals (bovines, ovines and caprines) sent from other EU Member States for slaughter for human consumption in Austria, as required by Annex IV to Directive 96/23/EC. 8. Residue monitoring plan samples from farmed game were planned to be taken from farmed cervidae such as red or fallow deer and wild boar in line with point 2.3.3.1 of Commission Decision 98/179/EC, which requires considering the species when selecting targeted samples from animal carcasses at primary processing establishments. 9. The planning spreads samples over the year or in key production periods for all species and commodities in line with the requirements laid down in point 2.1. of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. Conclusion on the planning of residue monitoring 10. The planning of residue monitoring is timely, comprehensive, takes relevant risk factors into account and contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.3. Implementation of the residue monitoring plan Legal Requirements Articles 3, 4, 10 and 12 of Directive 96/23/EC; Articles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Commission Decision 97/747/EC; Commission Decision 98/179/EC; Commission Directive 2002/63/EC; Commission Regulation (EU) No 589/2014; Commission Regulation (EC) No 333/2007; Commission Regulation (EC) No 401/2006; Article 69 of Directive 2001/82/EC; Annex I, Part A III, point 8(b) to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council; Annex II, Section III, point 3(c) to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council; Article 5 and Annex I, Section I, chapter IIA, point 1 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 3 of the European Parliament and of the Council; Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/262. Findings 11. The residue monitoring plan for animals is implemented by the PVS, by official staff from the District Veterinary Services (Bezirksveterinärdienst) in the event of sampling on farm and by authorised veterinarians at slaughterhouses. These are private veterinarians that are authorised for this official control task and an administrative process is in place to ensure that no potential conflict of interest exists for them. The residue monitoring plan for food is implemented by the PFA and all sampling is carried out by official food inspectors. 12. In line with the requirements of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, staff have been provided with and follow detailed instructions on how to carry out their work, and how to take targeted and suspect samples as required in point 2 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. 13. The implementation of the residue monitoring plan is monitored at provincial and national level. The respective department at the Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs, Health and Consumer Protection (Bundesministerium für Arbeit, Soziales, Gesundheit- und Konsumentenschutz, BMASGK) verifies if samples have been collected as planned and sends reminders to the provinces in case adjustments are required. Sample targets for the 2017 and 2018 residue monitoring plans were met as planned at national level and in the two provinces visited by the audit team. 14. Sampling is carried out without prior warning and spread over the whole calendar year by PVS and PFA staff, which is in line with the requirements of point 2.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC and Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The slaughterhouse operator and the farmer owning the animal receive a copy of the sampling report, and milk, egg or honey producers can request a copy, which indicates which animals/products have been sampled. 15. Samples are taken using appropriate sampling materials. These are in the case of the PVS purchased by the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (Österreichische Agentur für Gesundheit und Ernährungssicherheit, AGES) and in the case of the PFA of the two provinces visited by the audit team, by themselves. In these provinces, samples were adequately sealed in tamper-proof bags, frozen (for tissue samples) and transported in line with point 2.6 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. 16. Representatives of Department IX/B/12 of the BMASGK informed the audit team that under the national audit system implemented according to Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, internal audits carried out in 2017 covered the implementation of Directive 96/23/EC in three Länder. In addition, a system is in place which enables the BMASGK to monitor each Land with regards to the implementation rate of the residue monitoring plan, the percentages of questionnaires submitted in relation to non- compliances found or the percentage of sample analysis completed. 17. Clear instructions exist enabling suspect samples to be taken during any inspection, if there is a suspicion of the presence of residues. This is in line with the requirements of Article 24 of Directive 96/23/EC. In total 596 suspect samples were collected in 2017 from almost all animal species/commodities. 18. In both Länder visited, multiple sampling from the same producer was largely avoided. However, in one Land visited by the audit team, several samples were taken at the same 4 aquaculture farm both in 2017 and 2018 despite the fact that other farms could have been sampled. This is not in line with the requirements of point 2.3.3.1. of the Annex to Commission Decision 98/179/EC. Furthermore, samples taken for substance Group B were not taken from fish ready to be placed on the market. The responsible staff from the BMASGK took immediate action during the audit, issuing a decree which requires all Länder to avoid multiple sampling of the same producer, including aquaculture farms, and to take fish samples to be analysed for substance Group B preferably from fish ready to be placed on the market. Conclusion on the implementation of the residue monitoring plan 19. The residue monitoring plan is implemented in accordance with planned arrangements and thus contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.4. Follow-up of non-compliant results Legal Requirements Articles 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 23, 24, 27 and 28 of Directive 96/23/EC; Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings 20. In line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, officials have been provided with instructions including detailed templates on how to carry out follow-up of non- compliant results. 21. The audit team evaluated in-depth five follow-up investigations of non-compliant samples taken in 2017 and 2018 (alpha-boldenone in urine of a male fattening calf, marbofloxacin in bovine muscle, metamizol in ovine muscle, leuco-crystal violet in trout and penicillin in milk). The audit team noted that in line with the requirements of Articles 16 to 19 and Article 23 of Directive 96/23/EC: all follow-up activities had been initiated in a timely manner; investigations on farms were thoroughly carried out and generally in accordance with the comprehensive national instructions; follow-up samples had been taken and included also sampling on farms from which animals with non-compliant results had originated; the root cause of the residues could be identified in three out of the five cases; comprehensive recording of the follow-up activities was undertaken, albeit not always as completely detailed as provided for in the national templates; administrative fines (where applicable) had been imposed in order to create a dissuasive effect, as provided for in Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 22. In accordance with Article 16(1)(b) of Directive 96/23/EC, non-compliant results had been communicated to other Member States concerned in case the slaughtered animals originated from these Member States, but not always to the Commission. 23. The officials met informed the audit team that it was agreed with the representatives of the provinces to start a follow-up investigation based on screening results, because it had paid off to check the suspect farm when the screening test result was available and thus to have the possibility to act immediately. When the non-compliant result is confirmed, the official veterinarian carries out the control on the farm again. 5 Conclusion on follow-up of non-compliant results 24. Appropriate procedures for follow-up investigations are in place and the respective follow-up of non-compliant results has been implemented in an effective and timely manner. 5.1.5. Laboratories Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Article 14 of Directive 96/23/EC; Articles 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Decision 2002/657/EC; Regulation (EU) No 589/2014; Regulation (EC) No 333/2007; Regulation (EC) No 401/2006; Article 100 of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625. Findings 25. The laboratory network comprises five NRLs which are also conducting the analysis of all residue monitoring plan samples. Four NRLs belong to the AGES. These are the Institute for Food Safety Vienna, Department for veterinary medicines, hormones and contaminants (Institut für Lebensmittelsicherheit Wien, Abteilung Tierarzneimittel, Hormone und Kontaminanten , THKS), responsible for the following substance Groups: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, B 1, B2a, B2b, B2d, B2e, B2f; the Institute for Food Safety in Innsbruck, Department for pesticide and food analysis (Institut für Lebensmittelsicherheit in Innsbruck, Abteilung Pestizid- und Lebensmittelanalytik), responsible for the Groups B2c, B2f, B3a, B3b, B3e, B3f; the Institute for Animal Nutrition and Feed in Linz, Department for analyses of elements (Institut für Tierernährung und Futtermittel in Linz, Abteilung Elementanalytik), responsible for substance Group B3c; and the Institute for Food Safety in Linz, Department for analysis of contaminants (Institut für Lebensmittelsicherheit in Linz, Abteilung Kontaminantenanalytik), responsible for Group B 3d. The fifth NRL is the Environment Agency Austria (Umweltbundesamt GmbH) in Vienna, responsible for substances B3a (dioxins and PCBs). 26. Each of these laboratories is solely responsible for the analysis of the residue monitoring plan samples within the substance groups highlighted above, thus in the context of the residue monitoring plan they do not need to exercise an NRL function. However, the AGES THKS regularly organises proficiency tests with regards to the five plate "Screening Test for Antibiotic Residues" for Group B1, conducted in the context of the microbiological analysis of meat, in four provincial AGES laboratories responsible for analysis of suspect samples. (see findings 37 and 38). 27. All network laboratories are accredited according to International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 17025:2005 by the accreditation body "Akkreditierung Austria", a member of the European co-operation for accreditation. AGES laboratories have a common quality management system in place. The accreditation is valid until 2020 and the last surveillance audit took place in October 2018. 5.1.5.1. The AGES-THKS laboratory 28. The national turnaround time for sample analysis is 28 days. It is monitored and the audit team was informed that it was met at a rate of 90% for the residue monitoring plan samples during 2017 and 2018. For substances with a limited analyte stability like Group A2 (thyrostats) and Group B1 (beta-lactam antimicrobials), the turnaround time 6 was largely met ensuring the analytes' stability and sample integrity in line with the requirements laid down in part 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. 29. The audit team found that the laboratory facilities and equipment are adequate to meet its obligations as an NRL as required by Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 30. The laboratory has accredited and appropriate methods in place for the analysis of residue monitoring plan samples. The audit team examined two confirmatory methods and one screening method. 31. The audit team was informed by staff met from the AGES THKS that, in contrast to past practice, flexible scope accreditation is no longer offered by the Austrian accreditation body. Therefore, with the fixed accreditation approach the scope of accreditation may only be modified annually. The wait time to receive accreditation might pose challenges with the entry into force of Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires that only accredited methods may be used for official control purposes. 32. To ensure a high level of quality control, the laboratory ranks all used methods according to risk, based on which they define quality assurance measures and a five- year proficiency test participation plan. In the last three years AGES-THKS participated annually in more than 40 proficiency tests covering different analytes, matrices and instruments. If results were unsatisfactory, the cause was identified and shortcomings were rectified. 33. The standard operating procedure for sample reception and handling ensured that required conditions (temperature, amount, packing) were met, and if not, that the respective sampler was informed and a replacement sample was taken. The way in which samples are handled ensures sample traceability and analyte stability in line with the requirements laid down in part 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. 34. Methods are validated according to an in-house validation procedure, which is based on requirements laid down in Decision 2002/657/EC. The samples are required to be spiked at three concentration levels with six repetitions as required in point 3.1.2.2 of the aforementioned decision, thus recommendation No 4 of the 2011 audit report has been addressed. However, one parameter, the within-laboratory reproducibility, is not part of the formalised validation plan, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in point 3.1.2.3 of the Annex I to Commission decision 2002/657/EC. Nonetheless, the competent authority can have confidence in the reliability of the result given the other quality assurance measures in place as outlined below. This was verified by the audit team on-the-spot when assessing the validation of the confirmatory methods for gestagens (A3) and macrolides (B1). 35.
