text: BACKGROUND The Commission carried out a series of audits in 2007 ­ 2010 to check the implementation of the European Union (EU) legislation in the area of food additives in 18 MS. Bulgaria was audited as part of this series (ref. DG(SANCO) 2010-8584). The results of this series of audits were published in an overview report (ref. DG (SANCO)/2010-6204 ­ MR Final) which is available at the link below: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=13 The Commission also carried out a series of fact-finding missions on controls on food additives and smoke flavourings from January to December 2015. Six MS were visited, not including Bulgaria. The results of this series of audits were published in an overview report (ref. DG (SANTE) 2016-8978) which is available at the link below: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=115 Both overview reports concluded that these controls were, at the time, not a priority issue for the CAs and, as a consequence, controls were either not performed or were ineffective. As a follow-up to the series of fact-finding missions the Commission services organised meetings with experts to support the MS in addressing problematic issues associated with official controls on FIAs. The Commission continues to offer Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) on FIAs and has identified opportunities for MS to support the implementation of EU legislation on FIAs. 2 The aim of this new audit series is to evaluate whether EU and national legislation on FIAs is appropriately implemented and enforced in a uniform way and that FIAs produced, imported and used on the EU market are subject to adequate official controls.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 NATIONAL MEASURES Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU Findings 1. The Bulgarian Law on Food, Article 12 regulates that FBOs, applying for registration and approval of establishments, have to submit a list of food groups that are to be produced or traded. Ordinance No 1 describes that FBOs have to attach technical specifications, including ingredients to be used for each product to the application. Through this, the CA has a good overview of the production, trade and use of FIAs. The register of FBOs is published on the internet. 2. Ordinance No 4 of 3 February 2015 on the requirements applicable to food additives is the basic national legislation implementing the directly applicable EU FIA-related legislation. There are no specific additional requirements to EU legislation concerning FIAs in the Bulgarian food legislation. 3. The audit team was informed that all food industry associations have organised a number of fora and training seminars to familiarise FBOs with the use of FIAs and how to work with the EU database on food additives. Staff of BFSA participates occasionally in these meetings. In 2016 BFSA organised a conference on FIAs. Trainings with FBOs and CA staff were organised in the region of Plovdiv. 4. There is a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in place since 26/08/2015 which sets out a procedure to carry out inspections at manufacturers of FIAs and at producers of Food of Non Animal Origin (FNAO) containing FIAs. BFSA informed the audit team that this SOP is also used at producers of Food of Animal Origin. Conclusions on national measures 5. Correct implementation of the requirements related to FIAs is supported by detailed knowledge of the FBOs concerned, a specific control procedure and information available to FBOs. This facilitates the uniformity of controls and assists official staff in verifying compliance. 3 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008, Article 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 Findings

Detailed information on the structure and organisation of the Bulgarian competent authorities can be found in the country profile for Bulgaria at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=BG
BFSA is the central CA responsible for official controls on foodstuffs within the scope of the audit.

In 2011 a major reorganisation took place to merge several control organisations into one, the BFSA, which controls the whole food production chain from farm to fork, including retail, catering and advertising.
Bulgaria participates at European level at the relevant working groups and in the Codex Alimentarius Committee and in European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) meetings on food additives.

Controls in establishments in relation to FIAs are carried out by the 28 RFSDs of BFSA. The planning of inspections at RFSD level is based on the national document: "Instruction on the implementation of the Multiannual National Plan for the control of raw materials and food, food additives and food contact materials". It sets out the principles for official controls, the frequency of inspections according to the risk assessment of the establishments, and the activities for planning, distribution and reporting of control activities.
The Executive Director of the BFSA can issue orders for thematic inspections in a certain period that can include FIAs.

Between 2016 and beginning of 2019 BFSA staff participated in 15 BTSF training sessions on FIAs. The participants have to disseminate the content of the trainings to their colleagues during internal meetings. The audit team received evidence of these cascade trainings.
The inspectors met during the audit showed good knowledge regarding FIAs.
As a result of a recommendation in a national audit report, a rotation system was implemented, so inspectors rotate to control other FBOs every year.

In 2016 an internal audit on controls on FIAs was carried out. Findings were that the controls were not effective to assess the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 and reports were not drawn up in line with the SOP (see paragraph 4). An 4 action plan was drafted and a follow-up was carried out in 2017. The report concluded that there were significant improvements in compliance with the SOP and in the effectiveness of the controls.

The CA informed the audit team about the activities regarding the monitoring of the consumption and use of food additives, as required by Article 27 of Regulation (EC) 1333/2008 and the monitoring of the consumption and use of flavourings as required by Article 20 of Regulation (EC) 1334/2008. Currently, no monitoring in these areas has been carried out by the National Centre for Public Health and Analyses, a research institute under the Ministry of Health, responsible for these activities. Conclusions on Competent Authority
BFSA is designated for official controls of FIAs at all levels of the food chain. It has sufficient and suitably qualified staff to perform official controls on FIAs.

Bulgaria does not comply with the requirements of Article 27 of Regulation (EC) 1333/2008 and Article 20 of Regulation (EC) 1334/2008. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OF FBOS PROVIDING OR USING FIAS 5.3.1 Organisation and implementation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Findings

The audit team observed four inspections at FBOs producing, importing, mixing, repacking and/or distributing FIAs and four inspections at FBOs using FIAs in their products. In cases where FIAs were checked as part of the inspection, one or more products were selected and examined.

Controls on FIAs were based also on the present SOP (see paragraph 4) and focused mainly on the following: use of FIAs on the basis of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 and No 1334/2008, the quantity of additives in mixtures, and the calculation to determine that the FIAs in the final product do not exceed the maximum limit, the method for weighing additives (calibration of scales and verification of the weighing process), compliance with the purity criteria in Regulation (EC) No 231/2012 including checks of the technical data sheets and analyses for both pure substances and mixtures, 5 storage of additives, labelling, including allergen labelling, shelf life, and, own check sampling and analysis programmes.

All FBOs visited were in the risk category "medium" which results in an inspection frequency of at least three times a year. In all establishments visited this frequency was met. The frequency can be higher in case of non-compliances and complaints. The audit team was informed by the CA that at least once a year FIAs are included in the inspection. This is in line with the reports provided to the audit team at the establishments visited.

In seven out of eight establishments visited, no non-compliances concerning FIAs were detected by the inspectors or the audit team. Only in one establishment, a non- compliance concerning FIAs was detected by the inspectors. A flavouring substance, present in one of the ingredients, was not mentioned on the label of the final product. The FBO acknowledged the mistake and could immediately correct the non-compliance as the labels were printed when the batch was produced. Another FIA, present as anti- caking agent in a raising agent, was also not indicated on the label of the final product. The FBO and the inspectors agreed that in this case the carry-over principle applies (Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008) and therefore labelling is not required.

The audit team noted inconsistencies in the comprehensiveness of the observed inspections. Sometimes all ingredients of a final product were checked for the presence of FIAs, and sometimes only the ingredients that were clearly labelled as FIAs. The specifications of additives, as laid down in Commission Regulation (EU) No 231/2012, were sometimes checked, sometimes not, independent of the type of establishment.

The SOP for controls on FIAs indicates that food additives and flavourings mentioned in the specifications of the final product should be checked. It does not mention other ingredients that could contain FIAs, not being indicated in the specifications of the final product. The SOP also does not clearly indicate when it is necessary to check the specifications of additives. 5.3.1.1 Sampling

Sampling is planned at central level and performed at regional level. Foodstuffs are analysed for a determined group of FIAs, for example, colouring agents, preservatives or sweeteners. Samples are taken mostly in retail. The RFSD quarterly reports to central level about the sampling results and measures taken. 6 Table 2 Year Samples tested for colouring Samples tested for preservatives agents and sweeteners 2017 29 110 2018 75 50 2019 (plan) 64 43 All samples analysed complied with the FIA legislation, including labelling. 5.3.2 Measures in case of non-compliance Legal requirements Article 54 and Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The Food Law is the legal framework which enables the authorities to take actions to impose measures in the event of non-compliances. More details can be found in the country profile of Bulgaria, page 17-20.

Two cases of measures taken in connection to non-compliances were presented to the audit team. One case, from 2016, concerned boza, a fermented wheat drink, containing the sweetener cyclamate, three times above the legal limit. As the analytical result was available after the "best before" date of the product had passed, the product was no longer on the market. The FBO was fined a 1 000 Bulgarian lev. A follow-up sampling was carried out and the product was found to be compliant.

The second case concerned an olive oil containing a colouring, not allowed for use in olive oil. The product was withdrawn from the market. As this caused a lot of costs to the company, the CA concluded that it was not proportionate to give a fine. 5.3.3 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) and Administrative Assistance and Cooperation (AAC) system Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2015/1918 Findings

The audit team was presented with a RASFF case concerning undeclared content of sulphite in a food supplement originating from China. Adequate and timely measures were taken to prevent further placing on the market of this product. After relabelling with added text that the product contained sulphites, the stock was released. 7 30. The audit team was informed that the AAC system has not been used by Bulgaria for FIA related issues. 5.3.4 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over production, marketing and use of FIA 31. Sometimes the CA has discussions with FBOs regarding the categorisation of the produce according to part D of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Until the time of the audit, these discussions always ended in an agreement in good harmony. For example, there was a discussion if Bulgarian Easter bread is bread (category 7.1) or fine bakery ware (7.2). It was agreed with the FBOs that it was fine bakery ware. Conclusions on official controls of FBOs providing or using FIAs 32. There is a system of official controls in place supported by procedures and applied as required by performing inspections and sampling. Adequate enforcement measures are in place and used when required. RASFF notifications are followed up satisfactorily. The approach followed by the inspectors is not clearly guided by the present SOP which leads to inconsistencies as to what is required to be checked during official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Official controls consist of sampling and analysis of products destined for the final consumer for FIAs and of on-the-spot controls to verify their correct as well as the labelling requirements. Official controls are supported by procedures which allow the inspectors to fulfil the requirement for a formal verification of the proper use of FIAs. Information from FBO organisations on FIAs provides additional support at achieving compliance with the legal requirements. A system of national enforcement measures is in place. Some shortcomings were noted in the Standard Operating Procedure for official controls of FIAs, leading to unclarity for inspectors as regards complete checks on ingredients and on purity criteria. This, in turn, affects the consistency of the official controls to some extent. Bulgaria does not comply with Article 27 of Regulation (EC) 1333/2008 and Article 20 of Regulation (EC) 1334/2008, concerning a monitoring programme of food additive and flavouring intake. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 20 March with representatives of the CCAs. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The CAs made some minor comments on the findings and conclusions 8 8 RECOMMENDATIONS 1. The CA should set up and implement a monitoring programme of food 2. additive and flavouring intake in line with the requirements of Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 and Article 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008. Recommendation based on conclusion: 18 Associated finding: 16 The CA should ensure that the approach followed by official staff when carrying out controls on FIAs is adequately and correctly described in the relevant SOP, in order to avoid possible misinterpretation of what is required to be checked during official controls and to ensure consistency of official controls, as required by Article 4.4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 32 Associated findings: 23, 24.

The CAs should ensure that the approach followed by official staff regarding purity criteria is consistent and that this is adequately and correctly described in the relevant guide, in order to avoid possible misinterpretation of what is required to be checked during official controls. Recommendation based on conclusions: 70

The CCA should provide the necessary guidance and tools to regional and local authorities to ensure that controls over compliance with the applicable EU legislation on FIA at the level of the FBOs, and with particular attention to the FIA users, are carried out in a consistent manner at all levels, in accordance with article 4, point 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions: 77 Associated findings: 44, 46, 49, 50, 51

To take further measures aimed at verifying that owners/keepers of horses 2. meet the obligations of Articles 11, 12, 27 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 and, mainly, concerning timely identification, the notification of animals which are permanently brought in Belgium from another countries, the change in their status (from food producing animals to animals which are excluded from slaughter for human consumption), and/or the death of the animals, in order to provide reasonable assurance that the information contained in the CED is up-to-date and reflects the status of the horses kept in the country. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 95, 96 and 98. Associated findings Nos 28, 62, 63, 68, 79, 87, 88, 89, 92 and 93. To take measures aimed at verifying that, when horses eligible for slaughter for human consumption are treated with medicinal products, the obligations 3. laid down in Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 concerning the medication records in the passport and the transmission of relevant information to the PIB and/or to the CED are met; in particular: - in case of non-permitted treatments, the exclusion of the animal from the food chain should be recorded and the information transmitted to the relevant authorities and/or PIB; - when permitted treatments are given (Article 37(6) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262), they are properly registered in the relevant section of the passport. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 149, 150 and 152. Associated findings Nos 64, 67, 75, 124, 144, 145 and 146. To ensure that when carcases of death animals are disposed or processed in rendering plants, there are measures in place to protect the transponder from subsequent fraudulent use as required by Article 34 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. In particular, the system in place should provide guarantees that the transponder code implanted on the animal corresponds with the transponder code destroyed or disposed. Recommendation based on conclusion No 97. Associated finding No 62.

The CA should ensure that the repeated deficiency concerning the washing of poultry carcases before post-mortem inspection shall be remedied in order to allow the officials to reject poultry carcases showing faecal contamination in line with point 1(s), Chapter V, Section II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and that FBOs respect, during slaughter, points 5 and 6, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 preventing the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 21 and 29. Associated findings Nos 9, 27 and 28.

The CA should ensure that all birds are to undergo post mortem - inspection in accordance with point 1, Part B, Chapter V, Section IV of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No 21. Associated finding set out in paragraph No 9.

The CA should ensure that they have qualified and experienced staff to carry out official controls efficiently and effectively in line with point 2(c) of Article 4 to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 so that staff can detect non-compliances with specific hygiene requirements set out in Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, in particular on production hygiene and maintenance of cold chain, and take actions when needed. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 21, 29 and 32. Associated findings Nos 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 27, 30 and 31.

The CA should take measures to ensure that the EU requirements concerning in particular production hygiene and maintenance of the cold chain in the establishments, are enforced as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 21 and 29. Associated findings Nos 9, 10, 11, 15 and 27. _______________________

The competent authority should ensure that the criteria for the risk 2. assessment of food producing establishments, as required by Article 3 of 3. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (since 14/12/2019 Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625), based upon which the frequency of the inspection of an establishment is established, are reliable and correctly reflect the real conditions of the inspected food producing establishments, by: envisaging the introduction in the formula of a "corrective factor" to take into account particular non-conformities identified during previous inspections; ensuring that the official veterinarians correctly evaluate any non- conformities and categorise them by relevance and gravity. Recommendation based on conclusion No 65. Associated findings Nos 43 and 60. The competent authority should ensure official controls identify relevant non-compliances and that the action plans presented by food business operators to correct any non-compliances are evaluated and verified within the specified deadlines, as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 ( since 14/12/2019 Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625). The competent authority should ensure that a system of supervision is established of the performance of official staff that are carrying out official controls, as required by Article 12.2 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 32. Associated findings Nos 27 and 29.

The directly applicable EU legislation is supplemented by national provisions.

All relevant legislation has been brought within a single framework, Act XLVI of September 2008. According to this act the main priority of the food chain official control is the protection of human health, plant and animal health and national economy.

The development of a Guide on GAP for fruit and vegetable production, including information to prevent microbiological contamination for primary producers, is still under development as was the case during the previous audit. Conclusion on Relevant National Legislation and Guidelines

There is national legislation in place complementing the directly applicable EU legislation. No progress was observed since the last audit regarding the development of a Guide of GAP for fruit and vegetable. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation of Competent Authorities and Resources for Official Controls Legal requirements Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 4 Findings Designation of CAs

An overview of how control systems are organised in Hungary (based on information supplied by the national authorities) is provided in the Country Profile for Hungary at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=HU.
Official laboratories are designated according to the Act XLVI of September 2008. They are part of the CCA and perform analyses of official samples.
The NFCSO is the CCA within the scope of this audit. NFCSO is responsible for supporting the decision-making of the MoA and providing control plans, procedures and guidelines to local level.

At central level coordinating tasks are shared between two directorates of NFCSO: NFCSO DPPSCA, responsible for coordination of inspection tasks in the field of primary production (except sprout establishments and establishments packing seeds for sprouting); NFCSO FFSD, responsible for coordination of inspection tasks in the field of sprouts-producing establishments, establishments of packing seeds for sprouting, FNAO processing establishments (including freezing, pre-cut and canned plants).

There are 19 County Government Offices CGOs, one in each county; at local level, the administration consists of 174 District Government Offices (DGOs). Staff professional management and funding are under the responsibility of the Prime Minister's Office.
CGO Department of Food Chain Safety and Land-Registry / Department of Public Health and Food Chain Safety (DFCSLR/DPHFCS) are the local CAs in charge of approval of sprout-producing establishments.

DGO of Plant Protection and Soil Conservation Unit (PPSCU) are the local CAs in charge of implementing official control at primary production excluding sprout- producing establishments (farmers, facilities producing/growing vegetables, fruit, seeds for sprouting and importers of seeds for sprouting). The inspectors are generally plant protection specialists.

Within the DGOs there are 82 District Food Chain Safety and Animal Health Units (DFCSAHU). On average each DFCSAHU is responsible for 2-3 DGOs. DGO DFCSAHU are the local CAs in charge of implementing official control plan at FNAO processing establishments, sprout-producing establishments and establishments packing seeds for sprouting. The inspectors are generally food technologist or veterinarians. Training

Guidelines and checklists for official controls are produced at central level, are used all over Hungary and their use is part of annual training. The CCA informed the audit team that such training is compulsory for all the inspectors involved in official controls.

The CCA presented, to the audit team, staff training files concerning EU legislation for sprouts and seeds for sprouting, microbiological safety in primary production, 5 microbiological sampling, Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) risk in FNAO production, These trainings are provided regularly and are attended by local staff. Resources

The CAs informed the audit team that due to shortages in resources the official control plan cannot be fully implemented and official inspection reports are not systematically uploaded in the central IT system (see points 34, 45, 51, 52 and 117). This limits the availability of information that would be relevant for future control planning and supervision purposes.

Although the CAs suggested shortages in staff, the CCA informed the audit team that the official controls in FNAO processing plants are also performed by the CCA in addition to those of the DGOs (see points 50, 51, 52, 89, 93 and 95) and in most cases without notification to the local authorities (DGO). Similarly, DGOs at local level, as required by official procedures and work instructions, carry out their official controls and upload their data to the central IT system but to which the CCA has no access.

In addition, the inspectors involved in official controls on FNAO perform a low number of inspections per year in this sector and this makes it hard for them to gain and maintain the required expertise. Moreover, moving the implementation of controls for FNAO processing establishments from CGO to DGO results in further lowering the number of inspections in such establishments (processing and sprout-producing establishments) for every individual inspector. This further limits the possibility to gain practical experience in controlling this type of establishments. Conclusions on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls

The CAs are designated for all stages of FNAO production and this gives a good basis for the implementation of official controls. However, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, limited coordination and cooperation between CAs results in inefficient use of resources and information, thus impacting on the effectiveness of the official control system.

Contrary to what is required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 4(2)(c), the provision of a sufficient number of qualified staff is not ensured, thus weakening the system of official controls. 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Food Establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 6 Findings Registration of Food Establishments Primary producers
They can be registered in different official databases. For the purpose of planning official controls, data about produce/producers are taken from the Hungarian State Treasury.

At central level, NFCSO DPPSCA has completed the list of primary producers of FNAO under official control regarding microbiological risk. The primary producers included in the list are 153 growers of leafy green vegetables and 1,066 growers of soft fruits. At the time of the audit, other primary produces in the scope of the audit were controlled at retailer level as part of the annual official microbiological monitoring plan (see paragraph 5.2.5). FBOs involved in the "sprout chain"

Importers, distributers, seed retailers and internet sellers are registered. They have to submit an application for registration with the DGO. Packers are registered at the DGO. The CCA informed the audit team that at the time of the audit there were no importers of seeds for sprouting from third countries.

The audit team was also informed that the NFCSO has since the last audit (DG SANTE 2016/8327) a project to control e-commerce. This project is aimed at establishing a national system of official controls for such traders. Producers of seeds for sprouting

At the time of the audit there were six producers of seeds for sprouting. The DGOs in charge of sprout-producing establishments and packers of seeds for sprouting informed the CCA in charge of primary production of FNAO (including seeds for sprouting) of these producers. In addition, during the audit the CCA in charge of primary production of FNAO informed the audit team and NFCSO FFSD (CCA in charge of sprout- producing establishments) that two of them ceased the production. FNAO processing establishments

Registration of FNAO processing establishments is kept at local level by the DGO DFCSAHUs which are responsible for the registration of FNAO processing establishments (including freezing, pre-cut and canning plants). Approval of Sprout-Producing Establishments

The procedure for approval of sprout-producing establishments starts with the application for approval by the operator followed by an official control on-the-spot. The CGO DFCSLR/DPHFCS issues approvals ­ according to act No XLVI of 2008, the requirements of Annex I in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 ­ for sprouts producing establishments. Approvals can be withdrawn by the CGO if conditions are no longer considered satisfactory.

According to the information provided by the CCA, at the time of this audit there were seven registered and approved sprout-producing establishments. The audit team verified 7 the approval files of the sprout-producing establishments and noticed that one FBO produced as a registered establishment until 30/04/2019. However, the registration was done in consideration of the requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 after an inspection. Conclusion on Registration / Approval of Food Establishments

There is a system in place for registration of producers and processors of FNAO and for registration and approval of sprout-producing establishments, which enables the inspectors to identify FBOs for the purpose of official controls. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Articles 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The Structure and the Organizational and Operational Rules of NFCSO had been changed on 1st January 2019, and all the procedural changes have to be reflected by the new Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP), which is planned to be issued this year.

For the time being, the system of official controls is described in the Hungarian MANCP, the current version of which covers the period 2017 to 2020. However, the audit team was informed by the CCA that the current version of the MANCP does not include a specific description of the control system for primary production of FNAO which will be part of the new MANCP.

The plan for official controls (inspections and sampling) produced by NFCSO at central level is sent to the local GCO and DGO for evaluation before publication and implemented at local level. The plan covers the period April/year ­ March/year + 1. Primary Production

In all counties visited, at the time of the audit, official samples at farm level were taken for lettuce and soft fruits. Samples of other products in the scope of the audit are taken at retail level (county plans) unless there is a suspicion in which case inspectors can sample individual producers as appropriate.

Based on the opinion of EFSA3, for official inspections at farm level, the CCA decided to focus on the two most risky crops: leafy green vegetables and soft fruits. In order to optimize the resources, with regard to the leafy green vegetables the CCA decided to include in the official controls the producers with a surface greater than 3 hectares. On that basis, the CCA allocate a number of inspections and official samples to each county following the criteria defined above. At local level, the producers to be inspected are chosen by the CAs. 3 Scientific Opinion on the risk posed by pathogens in food of non-animal origin. BACKGROUND 3.1. LEGAL CONTEXT The 2006 Thematic Strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides led to a new legislative framework for the approval and use of pesticides. This includes a strict framework for the approval of active substances and the authorisation of plant protection products (PPPs) by MSs, introduced by Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 of the European Parliament and the Council, adopted on 21 October 2009. This Regulation requires that active substances be approved, and PPPs to be authorised, only if they are shown to have no harmful effects on human and animal health, and no unacceptable effects on the environment. It also requires that PPPs be applied according to the authorised conditions of use. The SUD was adopted on the same date (21 October 2009) as part of the above mentioned Thematic Strategy. Article 4 of SUD requires MSs to adopt NAPs to set out quantitative objectives, targets, measures and timetables to reduce risks and impacts of pesticide use and to encourage the development and introduction of IPM and of alternative approaches or techniques in order to reduce dependency on the use of pesticides. In addition, the NAPs shall also include indicators to monitor the use of PPP containing active substances of particular concern, especially if alternatives are available. NAPs shall be reviewed at least every five years and any substantial changes shall be reported to the Commission without undue delay. The SUD also identifies specific measures that MSs are required to include in their NAPs for proper implementation. The main actions relate to training of users, advisors and distributors, inspection of PAE, the prohibition of aerial spraying, limiting pesticide use in sensitive areas, and information and awareness-raising about pesticide risks. The Italian Legislative Decree No 193 of 6 November 2007 designates the CAs for the implementation, among others, of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on official controls. The organisation of the control system for pesticide residues involves the Ministry of Health (MOH), the Health Regional Authorities and the Local Health Authorities.

The MOH also provides guidance for the implementation of the control plan programme and is responsible for the communication of the results to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). It also monitors the performance of the official laboratories by setting annual performance indicators.
The Local Health Authorities assess the risk to consumers when MRLs are exceeded. The MOH supports local authorities when conducting such risk assessments.

The MOH manages the national Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF). Regional Health Authorities are responsible for communicating the information to the MOH, who takes the final decision on issuing RASFF notifications. 3 5. In the opening meeting of this audit, both the MOH and the Regional Authorities stated that Regional authorities are the CA for the designation of official laboratories to conduct the analyses in their respective regions. 6. The audit team visited two regions within the scope of this audit, Lombardia and Emilia- Romagna. In Lombardia, the CA is the Directorate General for Welfare, and within this Directorate General, the Prevention Unit is in charge of controls of pesticide residues in food of plant origin and the Veterinary Unit is in charge of controls of pesticide residues in food of animal origin. The Directorate General for Welfare is responsible for the planning of official controls and provides guidelines, procedures and manuals on official controls to the local health authorities. 7. In Emilia-Romagna, the CA is the Directorate General for Caring, Health and Welfare. Within this Directorate General, the Veterinary Health and Food Hygiene is the regional CA for food safety. It is responsible, among others, for the planning of official controls, including controls of pesticide residues. It also provides guidelines, procedures, and manuals on official controls to Local Health Units. 5.1.2. Designation of national reference laboratories and official control laboratories 8. The MOH, by decision notes of 7 March 2007 and of 13 November 2006 respectively, has designated the following NRLs in the area of pesticide residues. ISS as the NRL for fruits and vegetables, for single residue methods and for food of animal origin; Experimental Zooprofilatic Institute of Piemonte, Liguria and Valle d'Aosta (IZSPLV) as NRL for the testing of pesticide residues in cereals and feed. 9. OFLs are designated by each regional CA. There are 24 designated OFLs involving 26 laboratory sites in Italy which are all accredited to EN ISO IEC 17025. The list of designated OFLs is included in the annual NCPPR for pesticide residue testing issued by the MOH. OFLs fall under one of the following public laboratory networks: Laboratories of the Local Health Authorities; Laboratories of the Prevention Environment Regional Agencies (ARPA); Laboratories of the Experimental Zooprofilatic Institute (IZS). 10. In Lombardia, the Prevention Unit of DG Welfare is the CA responsible for the designation and monitoring of OFLs for food of non-animal origin. There are two designated OFLs, referred to as the regional reference laboratories for pesticide residue testing of FNAO: The laboratory of the Health Protection Agency (Agenzia di Tutela della Salute ATS) of Milan Metropolitan City; The laboratory of the ATS of Bergamo. 11. The Prevention Unit stated that OFLs must comply with defined requirements in order to be designated as an OFL, such as holding accreditation of analytical methods; to 4 demonstrate sufficient investment capacity to upgrade equipment/resources when required by new regulation, including EU legislation; to have sufficient resources/knowledge to carry out the analyses for the whole region; and to report to the MOH through the specific IT system in accordance with relevant procedures and time schedule. 12. In Emilia Romagna the following laboratories are designated for official controls: the Agenzia Regionale per la Prevenzione, l'Ambiente e l'Energia (ARPAE) and the Istituto Zooprofibattico Sperimentale Lombardia e Emilia-Romagna (IZSLER). Pesticide residue testing of food of non-animal origin is carried out by ARPAE. 13. In both visited regions, the CAs stated that once the laboratory has been designated, it is sufficient to demonstrate that the accreditation of the OFLs are maintained and there are no further supervision activities. The CAs have not established and/or agreed specific requirements for the laboratories to comply with, such as maximum turn-around time for the analyses, the capacity to analyse all analytes included in the coordinated control plan of the European Union, or mandatory participation in EURL PTs. These requirements are not expressly included by EN ISO IEC 17025 and therefore are not covered during accreditation audits. This is not in line with Article 4(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The accreditation body ACCREDIA stated that SANTE/11813/2017 guidance is taken into account for accreditation of laboratories conducting pesticide residue analysis. 14. During the audit, it was revealed that OFLs from different region had contacted both of the visited laboratories seeking assistance to carry out the analysis. In 2018, the laboratory of Milan received and analysed samples from an OFL of another region. However, the competent authority of that other region had not been directly involved in the allocation of samples to other laboratories of the network, despite designation of OFLs is a competence of the Regional authorities. Monitoring of NRL/OFL 15. The MOH monitors the performance of OFLs and informs regional CAs in case underperformance of OFLs. The MOH is the competent authority for the establishment of essential "levels of assistance" and has implemented different assessment tools, such as the assessment of compliance with the reporting obligations of the Regions to the State, and the "level of assistance" grid, which is used to assess the healthcare services provided by the regional health systems1. Regarding the reporting obligations, indicators have been set for the analytical work. In the case of pesticide residue analyses, the Region is eligible to additional healthcare funding when analyses cover at least 70% of the active substances provided for by the applicable Commission Implementing Regulation, even though the mandate arising from the Regulation requires that all analytes listed shall be analysed. 1 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that the National Programme issued by Directorate- General for Hygiene, Food Safety and Nutrition in Note No 47313 of 13 December 2018 states that the Regions must ensure that, in any event, 100 % of what is laid down in that national programme is carried out. 5 16. The MOH provided the audit team with the assessment related to the controls conducted in 2018. For all the Italian regions, the conclusion was that performance of the laboratories was insufficient due to the low percentage of analytes included in the scope of analysis. Nevertheless, laboratories in these regions continue to be designated, and requested to undertake analysis, for which they do not have the necessary capacity. Monitoring by NRLs 17. The NRLs organise an annual workshop in which OFLs and the MOH participate. At these meetings, performance of the laboratories which participated in European Proficiency Tests (EUPTs) is discussed, as well as the results of the proficiency tests on olive oil organised by ISS as NRL for pesticides in Food of Animal Origin and Commodities of High Fat Content in collaboration with the International Olive Council, and results of other national proficiency tests. In these meetings, other issues related to OFLs' control activities and the revision of SANTE/11813/2017 guidance document on quality control and method validation procedures document are discussed. The presentations are disseminated to all participants. The NRLs does not conduct specific audits or other supervision activities. 5.1.3. Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities 18. There were documented procedures in place for the planning and operation of the sampling plan. Based on the general figures for sampling allocated to the Regions in the National Plan, the visited regions have prepared a plan for each of the administrative areas in which their regions are divided. The local health authorities, in co-ordination with the laboratories set the specific plan detailing the type of product to be sampled, the timing and the inspector, and the type of operator. 19. Ministerial Decree of 23 July 2003 lays down the sampling methods for pesticide residue analyses for foods of animal and plant origin. In addition, ISS has issued guidelines for sampling taking into account the requirements of Commission Directive 2002/63/EC of 11 July 2002 establishing Community methods of sampling for the official control of pesticide residues in and on products of plant and animal origin. There are standardised sampling reports. 20. There are procedures in place for results exceeding the MRL. Local Health Authorities are responsible for conducting the risk assessment, and results are duly communicated to the Ministry of Health who also advises the local health authorities for conducting the risk assessment. 5.1.4. Co-ordination and co-operation between and within competent authorities 21. Based on the general figures for sampling allocated to the Regions in the National Plan, the visited regions have prepared a plan for each of the administrative areas in which their regions are divided. The local health authorities, in co-ordination with the laboratories set the specific plan detailing the type of product to be sampled, the timing and the type of operator. 6 22. The local authorities are responsible for both conducting the sampling and enforcement measures in case of non-compliances arising from the analysis. In both visited regions examples of non-compliances were reviewed, where in case the origin of the non- compliant product was from a different area, the responsible local health authority is reported for further actions. 23. The follow-up of MRL breaches included adequate communication between services at central, regional and local levels and if appropriate, follow-up activities are reported through the RASFF notification system managed by the MOH. 5.1.5. Prioritisation of Controls 24. The MOH stated that the NCPPR is planned as a random sampling programme and this highlights the main commodities and active substances involved in previous non- compliances. The Regional CAs of the visited regions transferred the general guidance of the NCPPR to the regional control plan. This includes food from certain origin, and previous non-compliances of operators and commodities. For example the NCPPR 2019 identifies the non-compliances found for both the national and the EU community plan in the previous year, including the active substance and the commodity and for the national plan, the country of origin of the product and the province/region where the product was sampled. Despite the NCPPR includes information on the previous non- compliances, the CAs stated that the plan to assess dietary consume exposure of the EU Coordinated Community Plan is implemented through random sampling. Conclusions on Organisation of Official Controls 25. The CAs are clearly designated, but the designation of OFLs does not establish binding instructions on the methodology, time span and scope of laboratory analysis necessary for the effective implementation of the NCPPR. 26. The performance´s assessment of designated laboratories by the MOH does not remedy the lack of capacities for analysing all required analytes. The designation of laboratories which do not have the necessary capability to complete the requested analyses has a negative impact on the effectiveness of the NCPPR. 7 5.2. Pesticide residue control programmes Legal Requirements Articles 26 to 31 of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2016/662 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2017/660 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2018/555 Findings General information 27. Ministerial Decree of 23 December 1992 lays down the National plan for pesticide residues, and allocates the number of samples per category group to be sampled and analysed by each Region. This is the base for Regions to determine the annual sampling plan. The MOH stated that this Ministerial Decree takes into account the specificities of Italian agriculture and the population's eating habits. The total number of samples for pesticide residues to be taken annually according to this Ministerial Decree is fixed to a minimum of 6725 for food of plant origin and 2031 for food of animal origin. 28. Annually, the MOH issues the programme for pesticide residues which is the base for the EU community plan. This annual document specifies the number of samples broken down by region, the type of products to be sampled, the range of pesticide residues to be checked in the various products. The plan for 2019 comprises 794 samples for food of plant origin and 152 for food of animal origin. 29. In general, the number samples actually taken was larger than those foreseen in the plan. The EFSA report on EU pesticide residue controls for 2017 noted that in Italy 18.7 samples were taken per 100,000 inhabitants, compared to a mean value of 17.1 samples per 100,000 inhabitants for all reporting countries. 30. The Italian report for pesticide residue monitoring plan of 2017, showed that 11 497 samples (6 593 of fruit and vegetables) were analysed of which 109 exceeded MRLs taking into account measurement uncertainty. This means 0.9 % of the samples. After validation by the Regional authorities, the results are communicated to the MOH through dedicated IT software and the MOH informs EFSA. 31. The samples are analysed in 26 designated laboratories. The Italian annual plan to implement the EU Community plan in Italy for 2018 included all active substances detailed in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/555. However, this requirement is not satisfied due to the limited number of analytes which can be analysed by OFLs. The MOH annually assesses the capabilities of all the laboratories of the network to conduct analysis according to the EU list of active substances. In 2018 only four laboratories were able to analyse more than 80% of the listed analytes for some 8 commodities. The percentages varied depending on the commodity, ranging for fruits and vegetables from 27% to 89%, for oil from 14% to 90%, for baby foods from 5% to 89% and for food of animal origin from 24% to 91%. This is not in line with Articles 1 and 2(2) of the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 555/2018. The same problem regarding low scope is highlighted by the MOH in previous assessment reports. Despite the exercise of collecting and assessing this information on laboratories performance, this has not triggered actions to address the shortcomings. 32. The National plan for the implementation of the EU Coordinated plan describes that samples are to be taken from harvest points and cooperatives, general markets, wholesalers, supermarkets and hypermarkets, and imports. The sampling should cover primary production, processed products, and imported food as well as products for export. Regions and local health authorities are responsible for transferring these general lines into their specific areas of responsibility. 33. In Lombardia region, the audit team visited the Local Health Authority of the area of Milan. In this case, more relevance is given to distribution rather than production, and sampling focused on central markets rather than final retailer shops to allow for better subsequent enforcement action to be taken in case of non-compliance. Those of particular relevance to this audit are listed in Annex 2 to this report. 4 BACKGROUND The audit was carried out as part of a series, aimed at evaluating Member States' controls at import of plants, plant products and other objects for the purposes of plant health. It forms part of a wider project on this topic, the objectives of which are to ensure the correct and uniform application of EU plant health legislation, to identify examples of good practice being applied by Member States, and to help inform the development of new measures and guidelines for import controls in the EU. The previous audit on import controls of plant and plant products in Spain was carried out in September 2012 (Ref: DG(SANCO)/2012/6313). Further information on DG Health and Food Safety, including audit reports and its work programme, are available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. Unless otherwise stated, statistical data in this and the following chapters was provided by the Sub-directorate General of Sanitary Agreements and Border Controls. 4.1 IMPORTS OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS Approximately 44,000 consignments of regulated plants and plant products are imported into Spain each year, whilst during the last import period 2018 the amount of consignments with regulated plants and plant products was almost doubled (ca. 80,800 consignments). The majority of these for the last three import periods were mainly citrus (ca. 22,600 consignments), other fruits (including mangoes ca. 32,600 consignments), vegetables (mainly peppers, aubergines and tomatoes ca. 76,500 consignments) cut flowers (ca. 21,000 consignments) and plants for planting including regulated seeds (ca. 14,000 consignments). text: The EU legislation relevant to import controls has been transposed. The competent authority provided the audit team with a table of correspondence on the relevant EU and Spanish legislation. Directive 2000/29/EC is transposed by Law 43/2002 and Royal Decree 58/2005. The Annexes to Directive 2000/29/EC are directly applicable; no implementing act or specific provisions on new harmful organisms are required.

The Sub-directorate informed the audit team that the impending amendment to Directive 2000/29/EC regulating the inclusion of additional products in Annex VB3 would not have any significant impact on inspection activities as those products were already undergoing physical checks at higher frequencies during 2018 i.e. grapes 12%, strawberries 7%, raspberries 9%, avocados 9% and papaya 6% and no additional measures were necessary to implement import controls on these new trades.

Article 12.3 of the Royal Decree 58/2005 transposes the provisions of Article 13b(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC concerning exemptions for small quantities (see section 5.3.4 below). Articles 10 and 11 of Law 43/2002 provide the necessary legal powers to perform import controls for plant health and to take any necessary measures including the power to control the movement of consignments or to require their destruction or re- export. This was confirmed by the audit team during their site visits and review of documents relating to the interception of consignments (see section 5.6 below).

The requirements for charging fees for import checks are harmonised at national level, with Article 67 of Law 43/2002. The method for their calculation has been communicated to the European Commission in line with Article 13d(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

Articles 10 and 12 of the Royal Decree stipulate that the Customs service is responsible for controlling the import of regulated articles. Article 69 of Law 43/2002 authorises the MAPA to collect the fees for the import checks for plant health, in line with Article 13d(6) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The Sub-directorate service informed the audit team 3 Directive 2019/523/EU was adopted on 21 March 2019 5 that in order for any administrative action to be initiated for the import of plants and plant products the inspection fees are collected at the time of submitting an application.

The responsible official bodies in charge of inspection posts, have the authority to carry out their duties in line with Article 1, and Point 1, first indent, of the Annex, to Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.3 Staffing provisions and training

The Sub-directorate informed the audit team that there is a total of 82 plant health inspectors in Spain assigned with both import and export controls under the supervision of seven more regional co-ordinators liaising with the MAPA. They also have other tasks: they carry out the survey on surfaces and crop yields (ESYRCE), and can be part of the jury of forced expropriation.

In Madrid, there is a total of nine f.t.e. inspection staff and a regional coordinator based at Barajas airport. The service is covered 24 hours a day and seven days/week by the shifts of the inspectors. At Barcelona port and airport there are eight f.t.e. inspectors and a regional coordinator who depending on the number of registered applications carry out both import and export plant health checks. Similarly in Valencia port there are a total of eight f.t.e. inspection staff and a regional coordinator who perform import and export plant health checks. During the interviews carried out by the audit team at Barajas airport, lack of human resources was mentioned as a problem or limiting factor for carrying out import controls.

All of the staff responsible for performing plant checks have at least a university (or other third level) qualification, which is complemented by training provided by the Sub- directorate. The Sub-directorate is primarily responsible for providing continuous training for its inspectors which typically comprises of a period of on-the-job training for new recruits, followed by two three-to-four day refresh and online training courses annually, covering all aspects of plant health controls, including administrative and on- the-spot checks.

New developments in legislation are also communicated to inspectors through a common electronic work space created for exchanging experience regarding emerging risks and the interception cases recorded in different points of entry. The Sub-directorate informed the audit team that for the harmonization of procedures they also hold annual meetings with the regional coordinators. The meetings allow for the provision of updates on new legislation and risks and enable the informal exchange of information between staff.

The Sub-directorate also provides specific training for inspectors on the use of Europhyt-interceptions, and occasional training following significant amendments to the CEXVEG, the IT database system for the registration and administration of plant health controls at import (see section 5.1.5 below). text: BACKGROUND 4.1 PREVIOUS AUDITS AND COUNTRY PROFILE This was the second audit on the topic, carried out in Spain. The previous audit was carried out in October 2016 (Ref.: DG(SANTE) 2016-8797). 2 The reports of all previous audits are available on the Directorate-General's website: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. The Directorate-General has also published a country profile for Spain2, which provides a detailed description of the official control systems for plant health, which are of relevance to this audit. 4.2 TRIOZA ERYTREAE AND CANDIDATUS LIBERIBACTER SPP. The African citrus psyllid, Trioza erytreae, is a harmful organism, listed in Annex I, Part A, Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC. The psyllid may, if present in large numbers, have a significant impact on citrus production, however it is its role as a vector of the bacteria Ca. Liberibacter spp., the causal agent of HLB that is of primary concern. T. erytreae is widespread in sub-Saharan Africa, including the islands of Mauritius, Reunion and St Helena, and is also known to be present in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. It was found in Madeira in 1994 and in the Canary Islands in 2002. The psyllid was found for the first time in continental Europe in August 2014 in Galicia and later, in January 2015, in northern Portugal. T. erytreae is not subject to diapause, and therefore remains active throughout the winter period. It is though known to be sensitive to hot, dry weather, with significant mortality above 30oC. The data sheet for T. erytreae3 issued by EPPO provides detailed information on the biology of the psyllid and means for its control. HLB is regarded as one of the most destructive diseases of citrus worldwide; it is caused by one of three species of the bacteria Ca. Liberibacter: africanus, asiaticus and americanus. T. erytreae is known to act as a vector for the first of these. The Asian citrus psyllid D. citri is also a harmful organism, listed in Annex I, Part A, Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC, and is known to act as a vector for Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus. The data sheet for HLB issued by CABI4 provides a detailed overview of the disease. Neither HLB nor D. citri have been found in Europe. 4.3 PRODUCTION OF HOST PLANTS OF T. ERYTREAE The most important host for T. erytreae is Citrus spp.. Spain is the fifth largest producer of such fruit in the world, with a total area planted with citrus of approximately 300 000 ha5, the majority of which is concentrated in Valencia and Andalucía. There is no commercial citrus production in Galicia where there is the equivalent of only 280 ha of citrus (based on the average planting density of 400 trees/hectare found in commercial orchards). Citrus production in the Canary Islands follows a similar pattern. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Council Directive 2000/29/EC Commission Directive 93/50/EEC. Findings 5.1.1 Competent authorities 1. MAPA stated that the structure and organisation of the competent authorities for plant health in Spain are as described in the Country Profile and previous audit reports. In summary: MAPA is the Single Authority for plant health. Its responsibilities include the co- ordination of the activities of the ACPHS, at the political level through the Sectoral Council for Agriculture and Rural Development, and at operational level, through the National Phytosanitary Committee. The National 5 Phytosanitary Committeeinter alia oversees the development and approval of national control measures, legislation and contingency plans relating to plant health including those for T. erytreae, HLB and D. citri; The ACPHS have exclusive competence and responsibility for the implementation of official controls including surveys, in their respective Communities. The ACPHS of Galicia has delegated the implementation of certain surveys and control measures for T. erytreae, HLB and D. citri to be carried out under their supervision by public state-owned companies, in particular TRAGSATEC (Tecnologías y Servicios Agrarios), which is a subsidiary of the TRAGSA Group6. 5.1.2 Legislation 2. The report of the previous audit provides a detailed description of the legislation and action plans that were in place at that time, which included the following: Royal Decree 23/2016 of 22 of January 2016 (hereafter `Royal Decree') established the national programs for the control and eradication of T. erytreae and the prevention of D. citri and Ca. Liberibacter spp., (see section 5.3 below). The National Contingency Plan for T. erytreae was published in April 2015 and revised in October 2016. The revised plan is available on MAPA's dedicated webpage for T. erytreae7; The National Contingency Plans for D. citri and HLB were both published in July 2015, and are available on the above webpage. 3. MAPA informed the audit team that there have been no changes to the Royal Decree since the time of the previous audit, although an amendment has been drafted to transpose the provisions of Item 10.1 of Annex IV Part A Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC, concerning the conditions for the production and movement of host plants other than in Pest Free Areas, introduced by Commission Implementing Directive (EU) 2017/1279. At the time of the audit Article 6 of the Royal Decree, which prohibits the movement of host plants and plant products, except fruits and seeds, within and from demarcated areas was in force. 4. The Canary Islands and Galicia have adopted specific legislation to define the demarcated areas for T. erytreae and the control measures to be taken in those areas. The report of the previous audit provides a detailed description of the regional legislation in place at that time. 5. The ACPHS of Galicia informed the audit team that the following legislation had been adopted since the previous audit:

See http://www.tragsa.es/es/Paginas/default.aspx for further information on TRAGSA and its activities 7 https://www.mapa.gob.es/es/agricultura/temas/sanidad-vegetal/tryoza-erytreae/ 6 Resolution of 1 June 2017, of the Directorate-General for Livestock, Agriculture and Agri-Food Industries, extending the areas demarcated for the presence of the quarantine pest Trioza erytreae Del Guercio or African citrus psyllid in the Autonomous Community of Galicia. The demarcation has not been updated either by legislation or other measures, despite the continuing spread of the pest (see section 5.2.2 below); The Work Plan for the eradication and control of T. erytreae in Galicia, which establishes the survey and control measures for the pest, has been updated annually since the previous audit. The latest version was published in May 2019. The regional legislation and Work Plan, is available on the Xunta da Galicia website8. 6. The ACPHS of the Canary Islands informed the audit team that there had been no change to the legislation concerning T. erytreae since the previous audit: Order of the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Food of 16 September 2002, declared the presence of T. erytreae in the islands of Tenerife and La Gomera and established temporary urgent measures for its control, including a prohibition on the movement of plants of the family Rutaceae (including Citrus spp.) from those islands9.

MAPA informed the audit team that in light of the potential impact of T. erytreae and HLB, a number of Autonomous Communities had developed their own contingency plans for those pests: Andalucía adopted the Andalusian Plan of Phytosanitary Surveillance in Citrus in 2015. This established a survey programme and a contingency plan for the control and eradication of T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB; The Community of Valencia adopted their Autonomic Contingency Plan for T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB in June 201610; Catalonia has provided guidelines for T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB for the Citrus sector, aimed at raising awareness of the pests.

The comprehensive national and regional legislation and action plans provide a clear legal basis for the implementation of appropriate control measures aimed at eradicating T. erytreae, or inhibiting its spread in those areas in which it is already present, and ensuring the effective eradication of any occurrences of D. citri and HLB, in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 8 https://mediorural.xunta.gal/areas/agricultura/sanidade_vexetal/organismos_nocivos_de_corentena/trioza_e rytreae/

BACKGROUND The 2012 report concluded that, whilst sampling was carried out in line with planned arrangements and staff ware properly trained to undertake this task, the overall effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan was weakened by several factors. These included risk-related deficiencies in the planning process, prior publication of sampling and analysis details, uneven distribution of sampling throughout the year and the failure to carry out all of the planned analyses due to shortcomings in laboratory capability and/or capacity. The six audit report recommendations were largely satisfactorily addressed. 5. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS EU legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant provisions of the EU legal acts cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings. In addition, a table is included as an Annex II to this report specifying the EU legal requirements pertaining to each chapter of this report. 5.1. Residue monitoring 5.1.1. Competent authorities 1. The competent authorities involved in the planning, implementation of the residue monitoring plan and follow-up of non-compliances are described in detail in the country profile for Bulgaria (3). In brief: The BFSA within the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Forestry (MAFF) is the national competent authority responsible for the residue monitoring plan, hereafter the National Monitoring Program for the Control of Residues (NMPCR). The Food Control Directorate (FCD) within the BFSA, is the main service responsible for developing of the NMPCR, drawing up the instructions, as well as for the supervision of its implementation and reporting results to the European Food Safety Authority. In particular, the FCD is responsible for allocating samples to regions with an initial breakdown of sample numbers into substance group/matrix/commodity combinations, for monitoring progress of the NMPCR implementation and the overall supervision of follow-up investigations of non- compliant results. The NMPCR is developed under the provisions of national legislation (5) and prepared annually by a working group (task force) enacted in December of each calendar year by the BFSA director's order. The working group has a task to prepare the annual NMPCR, which is presented by the BFSA Director (6) for the approval by the Minister for Agriculture, Food and Forestry before 25 March of each calendar year. The NMPCR operates from April of the current calendar year until the end of March of the next calendar year. 3. The working group usually comprises specialists from the FCD, the Border Control Directorate (BCD), the Animal Health and Welfare, and Feed Control Directorate, the Control of Veterinary Medicinal Products Directorate (CVMPD), and the CLVSEE. 4. The working group acts in accordance with the BFSA Organisational Rules and Procedures and in line with EU rules (7) taking into consideration some risk criteria such as national production volumes of various commodities, information on the most frequently used veterinary medicinal products and their quantities sold in Bulgaria, information on coccidiostats used in production of feed for poultry and the number of non-compliant results found in the previous years. The opinion from an independent Risk Assessment Centre (created under the MAFF in 2016) is sought when necessary.

Whilst relevant risk factors regarding coccidiostats in poultry and eggs are taken into account, the information on the use of feed additives was not documented until the time of audit but this is going to change for the 2021 NMPCR. Copies of the 2018 and 2019 annual plans from two different RFSDs were provided to the audit team. The results of the food business operators` self-monitoring (own-checks) have not been taken into account during the planning process of the NMPCR. 9. With regard to scope and content of the NMPCR the audit team noted: a) the plan includes all relevant commodities except for farmed pheasants which are reared in small quantities for hunting or for release into the wild. There are no processing units in Bulgaria and efforts to identify foreign laboratories for testing feed samples was so far unsuccessful. No farm water samples have been considered for inclusion in the plan. b) the plan largely meets the sampling levels and frequencies laid down in EU law (9) and samples are divided over substance groups according to the prescribed breakdown. However, for milk and eggs 300 samples in total are collected from bovine and ovine milk and from hen and quail eggs, respectively. This is not in line with the EU requirements (10) as milk samples from other animal species (ovine, caprine) and egg samples from other poultry species must be included in the sampling plan as additional samples; c) the plan covers all of the substance groups required except for horses, for which in 2018 and 2019 testing for substance groups B3a, B3b and B3d was not included although required (11). Testing for these substance groups was resumed in 2020; d) matrices tested are largely in line with the recommendations of European Union Reference Laboratories (EURLs) except for 17-oestradiol and 17-testosterone (A3) in pigs (urine) and nitroimidazoles (A6) in poultry (muscle). The BFSA Executive Director issues annually an order setting deadlines for drafting the residue monitoring plans and deadlines for reporting on their implementation. In line with the established deadlines, by the end of March of each calendar year the FCD of the BFSA distributes the NMPCR to the RFSDs. Annex VI to this document establishes, for each commodity, the number of samples to be collected per region, based on its regional production and livestock numbers. 12. Based on this general document each RFSD develops its own regional plan that, once approved at regional level, is sent back to the FCD for information. The designated BFSA officers at regional level allocate samples to sampling points, coordinate its implementation and report these activities to the central level. Farms are selected by official veterinarians working at the Animal Health departments at municipal level based on their local information on animal health status, the type of farming and fattening systems. In each region, sampling is distributed to slaughterhouses based on their production volumes. 13. text: BACKGROUND Controls on residues and contaminants and the use of veterinary medicinal products in Germany were previously audited by the Commission in 2012 (DG(SANCO)2012/6530 MR-Final (2)), hereafter referred to as the 2012 report. That report concluded that the system of residue monitoring was in compliance with EU legislation. However, the overall effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan was slightly compromised by weaknesses in its implementation, use of food chain information and the conduct of internal audits. All four recommendations made in that audit report were satisfactorily addressed.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS EU legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant provisions of the EU legal acts cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings. 5.1. Residue monitoring 5.1.1. Competent authorities 1. At federal level the BMEL is the central competent authority with the overall responsibility for residues of veterinary medicinal products. In line with the EU legal requirements (3), the central competent authority is responsible for the co- ordination of the residue monitoring plan. Unit 115 of the BVL carries out specific tasks regarding the preparation of the National Residue Control Plan (Nationaler Rückstandskontrollplan, (hereafter referred to as residue control plan), collects and analyses the results of the Länder, summarises the data, reports them to the European Commission and publishes the reports. The responsibility for the organisation and supervision of the implementation of the plan at regional level lies primarily with the competent authorities in the 16 Länder. In Bavaria, the residue control plan is implemented by the BY StMUV in cooperation with the 7 regional competent authorities and the BY LGL. In Thuringia, the residue control plan is implemented by the TMASGFF in cooperation (2) https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3060 (3) Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 2 with the TLV. In both Länder the Veterinary and Food Supervisory Offices at district level are responsible for sampling. The competent authorities and the distribution of responsibilities have been described in more detail in the country profile for Germany (4). 5.1.2. Planning of residue monitoring 2. In line with the EU legal requirements (5), the planning process of the residue control plan as well as the relevant operational procedures are available to the staff. The plan is laid down in a comprehensive document created by the BVL in cooperation with other bodies involved in its planning and implementation (6). The document also provides instructions regarding factors to be taken into account by the Länder when preparing their residue control plans such as the risk-criteria and procedures to consider for sampling. 3. Each September, under the leadership of Unit 115, a working meeting is organised in which representatives of all the Länder, the BMEL, the Federal Institute for Risk- Assessment (Bundesinstitut für Risikobewertung), the BVL and its NRL agree the following year´s plan. Relevant factors are taken into account and discussed including: non-compliances of previous year´s residue control plans, the outcome of controls on the use of veterinary medicines or notifications within the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed notifications (RASFF), which is in line with EU requirements (7). Furthermore, annual production/slaughter data are taken into account as required (8). Finally, recommendations from the European Union reference laboratories (EURLs) were also generally taken into account, as evident in table 11 of the 2020 residue monitoring plan document. 4. The BVL breaks down the plan to the Länder level, which subsequently distribute them to the district level for sampling. Each Land then places its final plan in a federal database, the Consumer Protection and Food Safety Technical Information System (Fachinformationssystem Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit) which is accessible to the BVL. 5. The 2019 federal residue monitoring plan included all relevant species and commodities, covered all of the substance groups required and complied with the sampling levels and frequencies laid down in EU law (9).
The risk-based distribution of samples to the 16 Länder is based on their respective production volumes for all commodities and animal species, which is in line with EU requirements (10).

For aquaculture finfish, sampling distribution in the two Länder audited, took into account the counties` aquaculture production volumes and covered the main commercially produced species like trout, carp and other fresh-water fish. Aquaculture samples to be analysed for Group A substances, were planned to be taken at farm level from all stages of farming, in line with EU requirements (11).
