In 2019 aquaculture samples were planned for collection during two months only and sampling of slaughtered pigs was not foreseen during 8 weeks at the end of the calendar year during which 15% of annual pig production were slaughtered. This shortcoming was addressed by the competent authority of Thuringia during the audit, thus ensuring that all future samples from these commodities are spread over the year, in line with the EU legal requirements (12) . Conclusion on planning of residue monitoring 9. The planning of residue monitoring is timely, comprehensive, takes relevant risk factors into account and contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.3. Implementation of the residue monitoring plan 10. In line with EU legal requirements (13), clear instructions for the implementation of the plan and for sampling were available to staff at both Länder 11. Sampling is conducted by official staff, unforeseen and unexpected by operators as required in the relevant EU legislation (14).
Procedures are in place to ensure that official staff are free from any conflict of interest when performing official controls. This is in line with EU requirements (15).

In line with EU legal requirements (16), the validity and integrity of samples is ensured as each sample is identified and packed in appropriate tamper-proof bag accompanied by a standardised sample report. Samples are transported as frozen or refrigerated to ensure the stability of the analytes. Procedures were in place in both Länder audited to ensure that samples reach the respective laboratories within the established time limits.
Evidence was provided that animals sent from other EU Member States for direct slaughter to Germany are sampled under the German residue control plan in line with EU requirements (17).

To facilitate coordination by the central competent authority the Länder are required to provide the BVL with their overall sampling results every six months and also at the annual working meeting (see finding No 3).

The 2019 national residue monitoring plan was implemented as foreseen with a slight undersampling of farmed and wild game (93 % and 85 % of planned samples taken, respectively) (18). The competent authority provided documentary evidence during the audit on how to rectify this shortcoming for 2021 plan, thus ensuring in future that all samples for these commodities are taken as planned.

Conclusions on implementation of residue monitoring 18. The residue monitoring plan is implemented in accordance with planned arrangements and thus contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.4. Other residue monitoring programmes Findings

In addition to the residue monitoring plan, a number of other official national residue monitoring programmes have been implemented in Germany. These include inter alia: a requirement under the German Regulation on Monitoring of Food of Animal Origin for at least 2% of all commercially slaughtered calves and at least 0.5% of all other commercially slaughtered ungulates to be tested for residues of antimicrobials using the three-plate microbial growth inhibition test. Any screened positive results under this programme are subject to qualitative and quantitative confirmation by instrumental methods to identify and confirm the substance detected; a national monitoring plan for food, cosmetics and medical devices to generate representative data on the presence of, inter alia, pesticides, heavy metals, mycotoxins etc. (20);

In Bavaria several additional Land-specific residue monitoring programmes had been in place. Testing for residues and contaminants performed in the context of other residue monitoring programmes and the operation of self-monitoring for residues contributes positively to ensuring food safety. When a sample taken within the residue control plan is confirmed as non-compliant, the BVL, the Länder, the State Office (Landesämter) and district (Kreise) concerned are informed by the respective laboratory. text: The organisation of official controls on feed business operators (FeBOs) is described in the Commission services' country profile for Austria.

In short, the Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Regions and Tourism is responsible for issuing general instructions and deciding policy in relation to feedingstuffs. The BAES is the competent authority for the implementation of official feed controls in FeBOs other than primary producers, including registration and approval of FeBOs and taking legal decisions. It is also responsible for import controls on feed of non-animal origin at points of entry. The AGES is a public scientific and technical advisory agency, carrying out risk assessments and providing consumer information, scientific advice and laboratory services. The AGES is also involved in the organisation of training courses. The district Administrative Authorities implement official controls on farms (primary producers). There is a clear designation of roles and responsibilities related to the organisation and implementation of official feed controls. These arrangements ensure that the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are met.

Feed inspectors need to participate in an initial training including on relevant legislative requirements, and practical training on implementation of official inspections and sampling. During the practical training, the new feed inspectors need to participate in at least 10 joint inspections (first as an observer, later as a lead inspector) of different FeBOs accompanied by experienced inspectors. In addition, there is a comprehensive yearly training plan for each inspector to maintain and improve their theoretical and practical knowledge on feed controls. The feed inspectors interviewed participated in training courses, including those organised under the Commission's Better Training for Safer Food initiative. The Commission auditor noted that staff regularly received training, including in the areas referred to in Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(4) of that Regulation.

Inspectors of the Administrative Authorities (farm inspectors) were trained on the legal requirements (e.g. sampling) which are relevant during implementation of their feed controls. 5.1.2 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FEED BUSINESS OPERATORS
The system of registration and approval of establishments and intermediaries is described in detail in part 2.4 of the country profile for Austria (see finding 1).

In short, registration and approval procedures (placing on the market) are the responsibility of the BAES. Such procedures require FeBOs to complete relevant application forms (available on the BAES website), stating what they intend to do, and provide further supporting documentation (e.g. HACCP-based procedures, own control 3 systems, etc.) for assessment. This technical assessment is performed by the AGES, which informs the BAES as to whether an approval is necessary and the specific information that needs to be provided by the FeBO. When all necessary information and documentation has been submitted, a comprehensive onsite inspection is scheduled for the FeBO. This is followed by granting approval to the FeBO.

There is one publicly available list of FeBOs on the BAES website: where details of both registered and approved FeBOs are available. All feed-related activities are clearly shown on the list, which is updated automatically on a daily basis. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 19(3) and (7) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.
All of the operators included in the programme of this audit were registered or approved in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 9 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The Commission auditor assessed the complete approval documentation of one recently approved FeBO. The approval procedure followed the requirements of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed hygiene

The structure of the competent authority is clear and there is a well-established system of registration and approval of feed business operators. This, combined with a robust training programme, contributes to the effective planning and implementation of official controls on feed hygiene. 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON FEED HYGIENE 5.2.1 INSPECTIONS 5.2.1.1 Planning of inspections

The planning of official controls was fine-tuned based on the recommendations of the previous DG SANTE audits (see chapter 4). In summary, the planning of official controls is based on a number of primary (operating activities) and secondary factors (e.g., type of production, tonnage, third countries' import/exports, use of genetically modified organisms, reliability of operators' own controls, operators' past records, and feed labelling-related information) to which a weighting is given to categorise establishments in three risk levels. This categorisation affects the frequency of inspections to be performed at the FeBOs (e.g., feed material manufacturers are to be inspected from one inspection per year to one every 5 years; compound feed producers from one inspection per year to five per two years). During each inspection, the primary and secondary factors are routinely checked and, if necessary, changed by the inspector directly in the database. This procedure gives updated information on activities and other relevant details of approved and registered FeBOs. The planning of official 4 inspections is thus risk based and in line with the requirements of Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.
The AGES is responsible for the preparation of annual risk-based planning of FeBOs and primary producers (farms).

BAES provided documentation on projects devoted to verification of cross- contamination with components with established maximum allowed levels for certain categories of animals in feed for non-target animal species, verification of labelling requirements of feeds, online marketing and verification of potential use of ethoxyquin (a feed additive for which authorisation was suspended by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/962). The Commission auditor assessed the provided documents and noted that the aims of these projects were to verify that selected operators/products comply with relevant parts of the legislation.

Planning of official controls on primary producers is also risk-based. In general, inspectors of the district Administrative Authorities perform official inspections on 3% of the farms yearly. 60-70% of these farm inspections include official sampling. The inspection plan for agricultural holdings contains clearly the name and other relevant details of the farms to be visited including instruction on the sampling.

The BAES stated that official controls (inspection and sampling) are always carried out without prior notice being given to the operator. This is in line with the requirements of Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

To facilitate harmonisation of the control activities, the BAES prepared a set of guidance documents and checklists, which are consistently used for official feed controls. These were made available to the Commission auditor who noted that whilst these are not detailed they are nevertheless adequate to verify relevant requirements laid down by Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, and Articles 4-6, 8-20, 22-24 of, and Annexes I-VIII to, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.1.2 Implementation of inspections

BAES feed inspectors carry out inspections of FeBOs. In the last three years, 75-85% of the planned inspections were carried out. The BAES explained that the main reason of this relatively poor performance was the lack of availability of resources. On average, 690 inspections were carried out yearly.

The Commission auditor observed documentation of official controls of nine establishments included in the audit programme. The inspection frequency of all nine FeBOs assessed was in line with the risk-based planning. The Commission auditor saw that the feed inspectors had used the relevant guidance documents and checklists during the inspections. 5 19. The inspections scrutinised by the Commission auditor covered registration/approval, pre-requisites of HACCP (e.g. cleaning, pest control), identification of ingredients, intermediate and final products (relating to traceability) and general hygiene of facilities and equipment. These inspections also checked the availability of documentation relating to the FeBO`s HACCP-plan and own control system (e.g., hazard analyses, critical control points, corrective measures, monitoring plans and results for undesirable substances and/or microbiological contaminants, homogeneity and cross-contamination tests) but not their adequacy since BAES inspectors do not carry out a comprehensive assessment of these documents. Instead, they forward part or all of the documentation to the AGES for further assessment. AGES' experts assess the documents (not necessarily all of them) and report to the BAES any non-compliances identified. Such arrangements considerably complicate the verification by the competent authorities that FeBOs implement the requirements laid down in Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 20. Where relevant, the Commission auditor scrutinised the assessment by the feed inspectors of hazard analyses, and tests on efficiency of mixing (homogeneity) and cross-contamination with coccidiostats. The auditor noted that in three of the nine FeBOs scrutinised, the hazard analyses were incomplete (they were either very general and/or several potential hazards were missing or not assessed) even if these operators were regularly controlled during the previous years (see finding 18). At one operator where the cross-contamination test was discussed, the BAES inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties to adequately carry out the assessment of the relevant documents. In principle, these assessments are carried out by the AGES, not by the BAES officials on-the-spot. The AGES officials stated that they had have never assessed the requested documents before, however they did demonstrate good knowledge of the assessment criteria. 21. In the documentation of the cross-contamination tests seen, the method of sampling, which is an essential element of related assessment, was not described, which complicates the assessment of the said testing. While the AGES officials interviewed did identify this as a non-compliance during the interview with the Commission auditor, the BAES inspection report seen did not contain the corresponding finding. The assessment of cross-contamination tests is not part of the BAES inspections. 22. Where relevant, the AGES officials assessed the tests for mixing efficiency (homogeneity) adequately. The assessment of homogeneity tests is not part of the BAES inspections. 23. The verification of operators' traceability systems, which operators are obliged to have in place by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, is part of the audits. The audit guidance and checklist contained adequate information on official control of compliance with the traceability requirements. The inspectors interviewed demonstrated adequate knowledge on the subject. 6 24. The guidance documents seen contained adequate instructions for controls of retained samples (i.e. those to be taken and kept by FeBOs from ingredients and final products manufactured). The audit reports seen by the Commission auditor contained information on official controls of retained samples in FeBOs. Feed inspectors interviewed demonstrated good knowledge on the practical implementation of such controls. This was in line with the requirements of point 4 of Annex II "Quality Control" to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 25. The Commission auditor noted that audits normally include a thorough control of establishments' scales and metering devices in the form of a check of documented and traceable procedures for testing/calibration, as required by part 3(a) of section "Facilities and Equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit reports observed by the Commission auditor and the feed inspectors interviewed demonstrated suitability of verification of establishments' controls on this aspect. 26. In Austria, there are 42 feed importers but only three of these import feed regularly. Specific instruction on official inspection of feed importers was not prepared. Documentation of the feed importer assessed contained product specifications and laboratory analyses reports. Before each import, the labels and the composition of the imported feeds with the transport documents are assessed by the AGES. The BAES' inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties to verify, based on the documentation available, whether the imported feed satisfies the requirements laid down in Article 23(1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 27. In general, verification of whether operators meet the legislative labelling requirements is carried out in conjunction with official sampling. Official feed samples are always accompanied with the sampled feed's label. The AGES officials randomly chose 50% of these labels and carry out a comprehensive assessment of these. In addition, there is currently a special project on labelling controls of feed marketing via the internet (see finding 13). 28. The Commission auditor requested several labels from the FeBOs included in the audit programme. Some of these labels were inaccurate (e.g., the safety instruction was missing on a label of a feed additive, the type of the feed was not mentioned on a compound feed). AGES officials interviewed were able to identify these inaccuracies. 29. Control on hygiene, facilities and equipment is part of the official inspections. The inspectors interviewed demonstrated adequate knowledge of official controls of FeBOs' hygiene, facilities and equipment laid down in Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections 30. The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. Notwithstanding that the inspections largely adequately address 7 pertinent legal requirements on feed hygiene, the lack of a comprehensive assessment of the appropriateness of the FeBOs' HACCP plans and own-check programmes weakens the effectiveness of the system. 5.2.2 SAMPLING 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling 31. Information on planning of official sampling is available in the report DG(SANTE) 2018-6313 (see point 4). In short, the national sampling plan prepared by the AGES includes undesirable substances as referred to in Directive 2002/32/EC, pesticide residues as referred to in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005, unauthorised substances (for example, veterinary medicinal products and prohibited animal proteins), prohibited materials as referred to in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009, genetically modified organisms, etc. Sampling covers the whole feed chain, i.e. both primary and non-primary FeBOs. 32. text: BACKGROUND The protection of the welfare of laying hens is among the sustainable farming practices necessary to achieve the objective of the Commission's Farm to Fork Strategy1 to ensure sustainable food production. In 2012, the EU banned the use of conventional cages for laying hens. The currently authorised laying systems provide these hens with more space and with a nest, perches and litter to satisfy their behavioural needs. Commercial laying hens are kept in enriched cages or in non-cage systems. Directive 1999/74/EC establishes the legal requirements for those 1 https://ec.europa.eu/food/farm2fork_en 5 farming systems while a European Food Safety Authority report2 defines a cage as "a system which is operated without the human keepers entering it". At present, the only EU-wide compulsory system of labelling on animal welfare applies to table eggs. The labelling includes a code which reflects the production methods (enriched cages (i.e. caged hens) or non-cage systems (i.e. barn, free range and organic)). Directive 1999/74/EC does not cover the protection of chicks, pullets or breeders. For these birds, Directive 98/58/EC applies. Regardless of the housing systems in use, producers and authorities have to assess the effectiveness of the protection of the hens (e.g. by considering the incidence of injurious pecking, the use of beak trimming, the expression of normal behaviour by the hens or the results of post-mortem inspections, etc.). Animal mutilations are in principle prohibited, but Member States may authorise beak trimming under certain conditions to prevent feather pecking and cannibalism. Animal health restrictions (e.g. due to seasonal avian influenza risk) may affect the accessibility to open-air runs used in free-range farms and potentially compromise certain welfare aspects while the biosecurity measures present specific challenges in some non-cage systems (e.g. prevention of contact of hens with migrating wild birds). According to the data communicated to the Commission by the Member States3, half of the laying hens in the Union live in cage-free conditions. 2 https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/197 3 https://ec.europa.eu/info/sites/info/files/food-farming-fisheries/farming/documents/eggs-dashboard_en.pdf 6 There is a wide variation in the proportions of laying hen systems among the Member States. In 2020, Italy reported a total population of 41 047 911 laying hens (11% of the EU hens) with 58.1% of them kept in cage-free conditions. According to industry data the number of laying hens kept in cages in Italy has decreased by 20.5% between 2016 and 2020. Member States have to perform their official controls based on a MANCP produced coherently and strategically by a single body through coordination across all competent authorities responsible for official controls. The Italian country profile, describing responsibilities for drawing up and updating the MANCP and the organisation of the competent authority, is available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=IT There has not been any recent Commission audit in Italy related specifically to the welfare of laying hens. The last Commission audit in Italy covering certain related aspects was a generic audit on organic production and labelling which took place in 2018 (report DG(SANTE)/2018-6401-MR4).

MAIN CONCLUSIONS 1. There is a system in place to ensure the welfare of laying hens throughout their life cycle and in all production systems, with the exception of the requirement that nests are a separate space. This creates the risk that hens are disturbed or attacked by other hens while laying eggs. 2. The CCA is strengthening its control system through the recent development of an extensive risk-categorisation database, ClassyFarm. This database collects a wide range of data that will inform the authorities of the animal welfare conditions in 4 https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=4079 7 laying hen farms at national, regional and local level, enabling them to better target their controls. Farmers will be able to access similar information to compare their performance against average trends. 3. The CCA has updated the inspection checklist for laying hen farms to support ClassyFarm. This document provides brief guidance to the inspectors, defines open norms and uses resource-based and animal-based indicators to verify compliance with EU requirements. It provides official veterinarians with a robust methodology to ensure more effectively the welfare of laying hens in farms. 4. The new inspection checklist for laying hen farms covers all animal welfare provisions, but is inconsistent with a previous instruction requiring that nests must guarantee tranquillity to the hens to lay eggs. As a consequence, there are reduced assurances that official controls are appropriate and consistent in verifying that nests satisfy the hens' ethological need to lay eggs. 5. In addition to the documented procedures and ClassyFarm, the competent authorities are supported by a centralised farm register. This database helps to verify the stocking density on farm and that forced moulting is not practised.

Assurances that stocking densities are complied with in laying hen farms are weakened by potentially incorrect information held in the centralised farm register concerning the number of birds present in the farms and maximum permitted capacity. The CCA is aware of this weakness and regularly monitors the data, requesting controls to be carried out.

The competent authorities perform a high number of animal welfare controls, in line with the planned arrangements, in laying hen farms from all types of production systems, and hatcheries and breeder and pullet farms. Nevertheless, the CCA has missed the opportunity to set animal welfare objectives in its MANCP.

Although a significant proportion of laying hen farms are inspected annually, the analysis of the results of official controls has, to date, been limited to monitoring compliance. With the development of ClassyFarm, the competent authorities have an opportunity to perform a less superficial analysis of controls carried out.

The authorities are not using animal-based indicators at slaughterhouses receiving spent laying hens although there is an in-field awareness of these indicators. Using and collecting indicators at slaughterhouse level could contribute to the ClassyFarm system and provide the authorities with an even better picture of the welfare of laying hens in Italy.

There are alternatives for reducing the culling of male day-old chicks, with approximately 10% of the individuals sent for fattening and a minor percentage of eggs undergoing in-ovo sexing. Their use is limited by the low demand. 8 6 FINDINGS ON THE FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS The strengths of the framework are the intensive ongoing work on a comprehensive risk assessment database that also provides an oversight of the animal welfare situation in laying hen farms, the high number of animal welfare inspections on laying hen farms and the introduction of animal based indicators in the control system. The weaknesses is that the maximum capacities and hens kept on farm, recorded in the national database may not be correct or kept up to date. The audit reports concluded that due to the non-compliances the plant health risk of the spread of Xf by natural means and/or human assistance within and out of the DAs of Italy is not appropriately managed. Any open recommendation of the previous audit reports was followed-up during this audit in the light of the provisions of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATIONAL ASPECTS OF THE PLANT HEALTH CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4 to 5, 11 to 14, 28 to 33 and 37(1) ­ (4)(d) to 42 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 25 and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 in its entirety and in particular Annex IV of it. Findings 5.1.1 Competent authorities 1. The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Italy are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Italy (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=IT). In summary: The regions and in particular the RPS, as part of the regional administration, implement the plant health controls. MIPAAF is responsible for the national plant health policy and for the coordination of the regions' work. The National Phytosanitary Committee (NPC), composed of representatives of the central and regional phytosanitary services, is the forum where plant health issues beyond regional competence and interest are discussed. NPC provides guidance to the regions on plant health controls.

In Apulia, the Command Units of Forest, Environment and Agri-food of the Carabinieri (CUFAA) are responsible for the controls on the movement of plants and for the enforcement of the mandatory insect vector control. The Xf surveillance within and outside the DAs and some plant removals are carried out by the Regional Agency for Irrigation and Forestry (ARIF). In Tuscany, all official activities related to Xf controls are implemented by the RPS. For plant removal, chemical and mechanical vector controls, the RPS contracts business operators. 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

The following national legislation is relevant in the context of the audit: · Legislative Decree No 19 of 2 February 2021 adapts the national legislation to the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and repeals Legislative Decree No 214 of 19 August 2005; 5 · The implementing legislation of this legislative decree was under elaboration at the time of the audit, including a new decree which will replace Ministerial decree of 13 February 2018 on emergency measures for prevention, control and the eradication of Xf in the territory of the Italian Republic; · Ministerial Decree of 6 June 2019 defines the areas free from Xf in the territory of the Republic; · Inter-ministerial Decree No 2484 of 6 March 2020, adopted an extraordinary plan for the regeneration of the olive sector in Apulia, and established financial support to the olive oil supply chain in the areas affected by Xf and to the related research, monitoring and laboratory tests.

MIPAAF stated that Legislative Decree No 19 of 2021 establishes an enhanced framework for phytosanitary controls in Italy, in particular concerning that: · The coordinated and timely management of phytosanitary emergencies is a legal requirement; · The NPC is entitled to make decisions, the implementation of which are mandatory for the regions; · The Research Centre on Plant Protection and Certification of the Council for Agricultural Research and Economics (CREA-DC) is nominated as National Reference Institute for Plant Health; · The laboratory of CREA-DC is nominated as national reference laboratory for plant health and the national network of plant health laboratories is established; · An audit system is established for plant health activities at central and regional level; · Timely addressing staffing and training needs is a legal requirement and the corresponding financial provisions are established.

In Apulia, in particular the following regional legislation applies for the Xf controls: · Regional Law No 14 of 4 June 2007 on protection of monumental olive trees; · Regional Law No 4 of 29 March 2017 on the management of Xf ; · Regional Council Resolution No 548 of 21 April 2020 and Regional Council Resolution No 538 of 6 April 2021 publishes the 2020 and 2021 Xf action plan, respectively; · Regional decree No 35 of 29 April 2021 establishes the DAs Monopoli, Polignano a Mare and Canosa di Puglia and amends the borders of the DA Salento in line with the minimum requirements of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201.

In Tuscany, the most relevant regional legislation is as follows: · Regional Executive Decree No 7809 of 6 June 2017 establishes measures to be applied in the case of Xf emergency; · Regional Government Resolution No 66 of 8 February 2021 publishes the action plan for 2021 for the eradication of the outbreak of Xf in the territory of Monte Argentario; 6 · Regional Executive Decree No 2227 of 16 February 2021 updates the delimitation of the DA for Xf subsp. multiplex. 5.1.3 Cooperation, documented control procedures

There is up- and downstream information flow between MIPAAF and the regions mainly by e-mails and official letters. MIPAAF provides guidance for the regions in the form of non-mandatory recommendations. The NPS and its working groups can also make non- mandatory recommendations to the regions. The audit team was informed that in 2020- 2021 the NPS regularly dealt with issues related to the Xf controls. MIPAAF provided assistance to regions for the Xf surveys in nurseries and other areas in the form of technical notes (see section 5.2).

In Apulia and Tuscany, a wide range of manuals and guidelines assist RPS inspectors during Xf controls. For the management of ad-hoc cases and specific situations, meetings and oral and e-mail communication is used. The audit team checked some of these documents.

In Apulia, Xf controls are carried out by ARIF and CUFAA based on cooperation agreements with RPS, which are regularly adapted to the changes in EU legislation and outbreak situation. There is continuous communication between RPS, ARIF and CUFAA for the daily management of Xf controls. ARIF carries out the surveillance and plant removal according to a detailed RPS manual, which is updated regularly. ARIF exchanges information with the RPS within a common IT system and database. Due to legal reasons it is not possible to link the RPS and CUFAA databases on Xf controls. However, CUFAA provides regular reports and on request additional information about their activities. 5.1.4 Technical support

The RPS of Apulia and Tuscany operate sophisticated IT systems with tailor-made applications for Xf controls. Detailed information about each inspection related to Xf surveys, eradication or containment and movement controls is recorded at the time of the action with mobile devices and all information is uploaded to the relevant RPS database. All territorial aspects of the surveys, including the exact geographical coordinates of the sampled plants are recorded, which provides clear reference to any follow-up. The IT systems provide detailed, real-time information about the state of play of the controls and facilitates the implementation and planning of the relevant actions. 5.1.5 Laboratories and diagnostic support

The laboratory of CREA-DC is the national reference laboratory for plant health and works as EU reference laboratory for bacteriology. MIPAAF technical note of 5 February 2018 lists 37 laboratories, which are designated for the initial analysis of plant and insect samples for Xf. These are laboratories of the RPS or of universities or research institutions.

The CREA-DC laboratory is accredited to ISO 17025 and the scope was recently extended to Xf analysis on olive samples by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The 7 laboratory has actively participated in international proficiency tests for Xf analysis with molecular methods, and contributed to the establishment of the Xf test protocol of the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO).

CREA-DC stated that the designated regional laboratories use one or more of the methods listed in Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 2020/1201, in about 80% of the cases real-time PCR according to the protocol of Harper et al., 2010. Insect samples are tested with loop- mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP). However, the CA did not present documents, which supported this statement.

CREA-DC is legally obliged to provide technical assistance and training to the authorised regional laboratories, including checking the proficiency of their work. The audit team noted that CREA-DC has not yet organised any proficiency test for Xf analysis with methods listed in Annex IV of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 for the regional laboratories. The laboratory did not have detailed information about the technical details of the methods for Xf detection used by the designated laboratories of the regions and about their actual test performance.

The audit team noted that: · The national reference laboratory has limited activities in supervising, coordinating, and assisting activities of the designated regional laboratories and has not organised tests to prove the proficiency of the work carried out by the regional laboratories in Xf testing. This is not in line with provisions of Article 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; · Based on the information provided, the CAs cannot confirm that the regional laboratories other than those of Apulia and Tuscany carry out Xf tests with methods listed in Annex IV of Regulation (EU 2020/1201; · The majority of regional laboratories involved in testing samples from outside the DAs have not participated in any proficiency test for Xf identifica

The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Portugal are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Portugal (http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=PT). Since the previous audit a minor change took place in the organisation of PWN control responsibilities allocated to the ICNF. In summary, the four different competent authorities involved in the control of PWN in continental Portugal are: · The DGAV is designated as the Single Authority for plant health in line with Article 4 of the OCR. In close collaboration with the Regional Directorates for Agriculture and Fisheries (DRAPs), DGAV is responsible for the approval and supervision of companies or operators authorised to carry out heat treatment. The DGAV accompanies 5% of the inspections carried out at operators by the ICNF and approves its proposals for suspension or restart of their operations (see section 5.6 below); · Since 1 March 2019, ICNF is responsible for the inspections carried out for the registration and the follow-up supervision of manufacturers of wood packaging material (WPM), beehives and nests. The ICNF has a new organisational structure based on one central and five new regional directorates (DRCNF) with a territorial delimited scope of action and remains responsible for the development and implementation of control measures for PWN. Contracted operators, under the direction and supervision of the regional and central services of ICNF, carry out the felling of dead trees, trees in poor health or trees affected by fire or storms (hereafter referred to as "dead trees or declining trees") and the recovery/disposal of wood material and debris, where such action is not taken by the tree owners. · The National Republican Guard (Guarda Nacional Republicana ­ GNR) performs road controls to verify that susceptible material moving from the infested zone into the buffer zone, and from demarcated areas of Portugal to other Member States, complies with the requirements of Decision 2012/535/EU; · The Authority for Food and Economic Security (Autoridade de Segurança Alimentar e Económica ­ ASAE) is structured in three regional units north, central and south and performs inspections at all kinds of commercial establishments including wholesalers and retailers of wood and WPM to verify that any susceptible material present complies with the requirements of Decision 2012/535/EU.

The latest contract with a private company covering a three-year period for felling and removal of dead and declining trees from different forest sites, including sites within the buffer zone expired in August 2021. At the time of the audit, certain operators were still finalising the felling and removal activities of susceptible material within the framework of their obligations resulting from the contract. The ICNF stated that since 1st September 4 2021, there is no contract in place and the sum of EUR 210 000 necessary to cover the felling operations to be carried out by the private contractor by the end of December 2021, had to be allocated from the State General Budget. A tender for a new three-year contract starting in the beginning of 2022, was under preparation, for the felling and removal of dead or declining coniferous trees and the operations carried out for the elimination of plants affected by other pests like Xylella fastidiosa. The new contract will, as for the recently expired one, include provisions for the destruction of trees found infested with PWN in private areas within the buffer zone and areas adjacent to the buffer zone, when private owners take no action. 5.1.2 Relevant national legislation

The audit report DG(SANTE)/2017-6167 provides a detailed description of the national and regional legislation relating to the control of PWN in Portugal. There have been no significant changes in the national legislation since, other than Order No. 9364/2018 of 8th October4 allocating new tasks to ICNF and Decree-Law No. 43/2019 of 29th March5 establishing its new organisation (see also section 5.1.1 above).

Order No. 9364/2018 establishes the terms for the official registration, supervision and controls of WPM manufacturers and other operators producing and marking WPM, within the scope of applying the Decree-Law No. 95/2011 of 8th August, laying down control measures for PWN in continental Portugal. Decree-Law No. 43/2019 strengthens plant protection by creating within the new decentralised structure of the ICNF a Forest Protection Division in each DRCNF, with powers of controlling harmful organisms and reinforcing the surveillance, inspection and protection of plants through the Portuguese territory. 5.1.3 Action plans

Since the previous audit, the ICNF continued to implement the two action plans elaborated for control of PWN: · The National multi-annual action plan for the control of pinewood nematode 2018 ­ 2022 (hereafter, multi-annual action plan). This plan establishes the objectives, strategy, measures and actions for the containment of PWN6 as required by Article 9 of Decision 2012/535/EU. It gives priority to the surveillance, monitoring and removal of trees from high risk areas for dispersion of PWN within the buffer zone and the 5km wide area immediately adjacent to the buffer zone (hereafter referred to as "the adjacent area"), where the multi-annual action plan foresees that all declining trees are identified and felled; 4 https://dre.pt/home/-/dre/116607521/details/maximized 5 https://dre.pt/home/-/dre/121712773/details/maximized 6 http://www2.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/prag-doe/resource/doc/divul/fitonoticias/Fitonoticias16-2018.pdf 5 · The intervention priorities of the Specific Action Plan against PWN in the 2017 fire-affected areas of the Portuguese buffer zone (hereafter `specific action plan'), were revised and adjusted for the 2019-2020 period. The ICNF presented the intervention priorities of this plan and gave instructions for the identification, monitoring and disposal of susceptible trees to its regional directorates. In line with the amendment of Decision 2012/535/EU and the derogation provided to Portugal, a total of 1 038 518 trees were identified and felled from 1st April 2018 until 31 March 2020, of which 525 330 were eliminated in maximum priority, 332 205 in areas with very high priority and 180 983 in areas with high intervention priority. The implementation of the specific action plan is detailed in section 5.4 below. 5.1.4 Staffing and training

There had been no changes to the staff resources of the DGAV since the previous audit. Two inspectors from DGAV are responsible for the authorisation and registration facilities for heat-treating WPM and bark.

The ICNF informed the audit team that since the previous audit, more staff were involved at national and regional level in PWN controls. During the 2019-2021 period, 28 plant health inspectors or "technicians" were assigned to the control of PWN, and staff numbers doubled when compared to 2018 where only 14 technicians were assigned. However, a substantial proportion of technicians' duties includes new inspection tasks for the registration and the follow-up supervision of operators producing and marking WPM resulting from the recent reorganisation of ICNF, resulting in approximately 17 full-time equivalent staff allocated to PWN control actions in the forest.

The ICNF informed the audit team that the total number of "operational technicians", also known as "forest rangers" increased from 27 in 2018 to 57 in 2021. Of them, four at central level and 26 at regional level carry out controls for the PWN in the buffer zone and the adjacent area. The actions taken by the remaining 27 forest rangers for the control of PWN is below 25% of their time. Approximately. 3.14 million ha of the buffer zone and the adjacent area, have to be covered by 16 teams each composed of two forest rangers dedicating a weighted average of ca. 70% of their time to the PWN programme. This includes the identification and sampling of declining trees and the supervision of the felling activities.

The audit team noted that despite their motivation, the assignment of additional tasks to forest rangers did not allow them to keep up with all their PWN related duties in the territory where they are responsible (see also section 5.2 below). The ICNF stated that the movement restrictions and the emergency confinement imposed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulted in additional constraints in surveying efforts when compared to the pre-COVID-19 period.

The DGAV informed the audit team that between 2019 and 2021 they had organised and provided numerous courses and training events to inspectors of the regional services of 6 ICNF, DRAP North and Centre and to technical staff working in private operators, responsible for the heat treatment of wood and WPM. The training of 13 new plant health inspectors of ICNF, was completed in 2021.

The ICNF informed the audit team that between 2019 and 2021 it had organised two on the spot and remote training courses on the methodology of forest pest surveillance and monitoring in collaboration with the National Institute of Agrarian and Veterinary Research (INIAV). More than 200 technicians, plant health inspectors and forest rangers attended these courses. One of the trainings delivered included practical components on the installation of traps.

In line with a module on the PWN prevention, control, policing and law enforcement, updates and refresher training courses are provided to GNR officers and forest guards. Given the importance of these controls, training courses on PWN are now the subject of a whole module in their induction training. The most recent courses were delivered in March and October 2020.

The audit team noted that most staff from the different authorities met during the audit were knowledgeable and familiar with the guidelines and procedures when carrying out their tasks. 5.1.5 Documented control procedures

The DGAV and the ICNF informed the audit team that since the previous audit they revised the manuals with guidelines and work instructions on the following subjects: · In 2019, the DGAV revised the "Technical requirements for the heat treatment of coniferous bark ­ hot steam coniferous system" and set up the conditions under which bark can be shipped in bulk through maritime transport; · In 2020, the DGAV revised the "Technical requirements and procedures for the manufacturing and the effectiveness of heat treatment for wood and WPM" with additional details described in the "Manual of procedures for the official supervision system of economic operators"; · Following the updates of the two informative notes about the "Application of plant protection products in coniferous wood" and the "Installation of traps to reduce the risk of PWN dispersion and its vector" already in place since 2018, the ICNF published in its website7 a new edition of "Good phytosanitary practices in pine trees" launched by Centro PINUS in collaboration with INIAV. 5.1.6 Laboratories

The previous audit reports on PWN provide a detailed description of the laboratories involved in the analysis of samples taken during the surveys for PWN and felling 7 http://www2.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/prag-doe/divulg 7 activities, and the handling of those samples. The system for handling samples had not changed and the additional laboratory capacity already in place since the previous audit minimises the delays for the analysis of samples at peak times, which remains at approx. 1 800 samples per month.

The ICNF confirmed that any positive results are communicated on a weekly basis to the regional services, and where appropriate, the work plans for the contracted operators are adapted. 5.1.7 Awareness campaigns

The DGAV informed the audit team that the information and awareness raising activities aimed at stakeholders and the general public, which were detailed in the previous reports, continued during 2019-2021. The most recent audit series concerning controls on the marketing and use of PPPs was carried out in the period January 2015 to June 2016. The overview report of the series (DG(SANTE) 2016-6004 - MR) concluded that control systems on users and retailers were satisfactory. On the other hand, there were significant weaknesses in controlling that the products placed on the market complied with the stringent conditions of their authorisation or parallel trade permit. In the majority of MS, the risks associated with larger, higher-risk operators, specifically, importers, manufacturers and re-packers of PPPs, had not been sufficiently considered in the planning of controls. Consequently, the frequency and scope of controls at these operators was generally insufficient. Controls at these specialist operators were further weakened by the lack of specific training for inspectors and insufficient formulation analysis programmes. Finally, the majority of MS did not conduct controls on PPPs intended for use in other MS or in non- EU countries, a significant weakness that could be easily exploited to place non-compliant products on the market. Malta was not included in the most recent audit series concerning controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, and consequently the most recent audit of Malta dealing with this topic was from 3 to 6 October 2005 (DG(SANCO)/7671/2005 - MR). 5. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1. ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE MARKETING AND USE OF PLANT PROTECTION PRODUCTS Legal requirements Articles 4 to 6, 9 to 14, 28 to 33 and 37 to 42 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Article 28(2)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 Article 291(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union Findings 5.1.1. Competent authorities 1. The CAs responsible for planning and implementing official controls are described in the country profile; however there have been some changes since it was last updated. The CAs responsible for official controls on the importation and the marketing and use of PPPs are clearly defined and designated in line with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In summary: · Technical Regulations Division (TRD) within the MCCAA is the main CA within the scope of this audit. It is responsible for authorisation of PPPs, controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, training and certifying all professional users and distributors and controls on residues of PPPs in the food and feed in Malta; 3 · ARPA conducts controls on PPPs users in receipt of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) payments on behalf of MCCAA; · Department of Customs within the Ministry of Finance and Employment (MFIN) is responsible for controls on imports of PPPs, including those imported via post or in passenger luggage.

The following national legislation is relevant in the context of the audit: · Pesticides Control Act from 2001 is the framework act that, among other things, defines MCCAA as the main CA for the authorisation and control of the marketing and use of PPPs; · S.L 430.07 of the Laws of Malta (LN 284 of 2011) implements provisions of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009; · S.L 430.08 of the Laws of Malta (LN 489 of 2011) implements the provisions of Directive (EC) 2009/128 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework for Community action to achieve the sustainable use of pesticides; · Other relevant legislation has also been developed such as SL430.02 on residues of PPPs in food and feed and SL430.04 on sampling methods for residue controls in food and feed.
There are cooperation agreements (Memoranda of Understanding) developed between MCCAA and ARPA and between MCCAA and Customs.

The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between MCCAA and ARPA is signed for four year periods, with the current version covering 2019-2023. It covers among other things reporting and data exchange, obligations for both authorities, including the scope of controls covered by ARPA and the status of follow-up actions undertaken by MCCAA in response to non-compliances reported by ARPA. It also obliges MCCAA to provide ARPA with any updates in national legislation and the list of authorised PPPs.

The MoU between MCCAA and Customs covers a five year period, with the current version effective from 2019. It is not a PPP specific agreement and covers various aspects of MCCAA and Customs cooperation activities.

There are sufficient suitably qualified and experienced staff at the disposal of TRD for controls on the marketing of PPP: · Five scientists within the Regulatory Affairs Directorate provide support on legal interpretations and guidance on information published by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA); · Sixteen staff (including one senior administrative officer, four enforcement officers and 11 inspectors) in the Enforcement Directorate are responsible for data collection during 4 the inspections. The audit team was informed by the CA, that these staff spend approximately 20% of their time working on PPP controls; · Three scientists under a Senior Manager of PPPs develop the strategy for risk-based controls and conduct follow-up inspections if needed (see details of control procedure in paragraphs 45-49); · Three inspectors at the Market Surveillance Unit accompany the scientists described above on follow-up inspections.

Each of the 11 inspectors in the Enforcement Directorate of TRD has to undertake a three day introductory training course upon taking up their duties. On the job training is primarily used for any updates. There is no specific educational requirement for inspectors, but the majority have a secondary-level education.

Since ARPA conduct controls on the use of PPPs as a part of cross compliance checks under CAP, there is no ARPA staff specifically dedicated to controls on the use of PPPs. In line with the MoU between MCCAA and ARPA, it is the MCCAA's responsibility to ensure that ARPA staff have up to date information at their disposal and that its field inspectors are sufficiently trained on all technical aspects to conduct controls on the use of PPPs.

There is an internal audit team of four auditors within MCCAA. The most recent audit conducted by an external auditor was in 2020. It covered among other things the PPP authorisation procedure and residue controls. No audits have been conducted to date on the other aspects of marketing and use controls, either by the internal audit team or by an external auditor.

Malta has three ports handling freight and one passenger only port that could be used to import PPPs from outside the EU. Controls by Customs are based on their own risk assessment. The audit team was provided with examples from 2019 and 2021 when illegal imports were discovered during these controls. Conclusions on the competent authorities

All relevant CAs and their responsibilities are clearly defined, with coordination and cooperation paths established between CAs, thereby providing a solid foundation for official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs.

Comprehensive national legislation and well-trained staff provides a solid basis for implementation of official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs. 5 5.1.2. Planning of official controls Findings
There is no manufacturing or repackaging of PPPs in Malta. The controls on the marketing are solely focused on the distributors of PPPs.

At the time of the audit there were some 137 operators in Malta marketing PPPs, of which 67 were selling PPPs for professional users. The CAs consider 59 (88%) of these as small scale and 8 (12%) as large scale. According to the data provided by the CAs, just 70 of the 137 operators (51%) actually sold PPPs in 2020.

The standard control frequency for official controls of marketing of PPPs by TRD is one inspection every two years. If non-compliances are identified, a follow-up inspection is carried out and these business operators will also be automatically inspected the following year. There is no differentiation based on scale, i.e. the same control frequency is applied to all operators marketing PPPs.

An electronic information system to manage official controls on marketing was developed within MCCAA, the ICO system. The system was launched at the end of 2019 and is now the primary tool used by TRD to manage official control implementation in Malta. The system provides inspectors with a checklist, which they have to follow during the inspections, and is also the main tool for senior managers to supervise and verify the whole inspection process.

At the time of the audit there were some 6 228 CAP beneficiaries registered in Malta. Even though requested by the audit team, the CA was not able to provide an information to the audit team, on how many of those use PPPs. The audit team was informed by the CA that there are 4000 certificates issued for professional users to purchase and use PPPs in line with the requirements of Article 5 of the SUD. This 4000 comprised both new certificates issued following the completion of initial training and certificates issued following the expiry of the initial certificate. In addition, there are 62 operators certified by TRD as service providers for the application of PPPs in non-agricultural areas.

The CA stated that these service providers are currently not covered by any official controls unless they are also CAP beneficiaries. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires that official controls have to be performed at all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency.

There are no up-to-date list(s) at the disposal of TRD of all possible professional users of PPP, contrary to what is required by Article 10(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Given the high number of farmers/land owners in Malta (approximately 11 400 in 2005 audit report DG(SANCO)/7671/2005), the CA acknowledge during the audit that it is possible 6 that a significant proportion of professional users of PPPs are not known to the TRD, are not trained and certified as professional users, and are not subject to official controls. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The standard control frequency for the official controls of users of PPPs by ARPA is 1- 1.5% of CAP beneficiaries per year. If non-compliances are identified, these operators are prioritised for inspection in the following year. The audit team was provided with the checklist used for official controls, which is included as an Annex to the MoU. The information covered by the checklist is primarily included in order to ensure that all data necessary to draft the annual report under Article 68 of the Regulation (EC) 1107/2009 can be produced and submitted to the European Commission efficiently.

The MCCAA is the CA responsible for enforcing PPP legislation in the area of use and for ensuring that professional users of PPPs are certified as required by Article 5(2) of SUD. Representatives of ARPA informed the audit team that the primary goal of their controls is to verify implementation of cross compliance rules. Therefore, their only enforcement action in the case of non-compliances is applying a deduction to CAP payments.

The audit team noted that TRD does not communicate the results of official controls on PPP residues in domestic food and feed to ARPA to facilitate their planning of controls at user level. This is not in line with the Article 4(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires to ensure efficient and effective coordination between all authorities involved. In 2020, some 10% of samples taken from domestically grown products had exceedances of maximum residue limits (MRLs), while in 2019, the exceedance rate was almost 15%. According to the European Food Safety Authority report "The 2019 European Union report on pesticide residues in food" (https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/6491) the average level of MRL exceedances in the EU for products of EU origin was 2.7%. The CA informed the audit team that information on MRL exceedances is not communicated to ARPA because court decisions are required to confirm these breaches and define penalties. The court proceedings are pending in most of the cases, with some dating back to 2016. There is no investigation undertaken by TRD of the root cause of the MRL exceedances at users of PPPs.

The CA has not conducted formulation analysis since the last European Commission audit on PPPs in 2005. The CA informed the audit team that it had planned to take 24 samples for formulation analysis in 2021. According to their volume based risk analysis, the targeted PPPs would contain one of the following active substances - cypermethrin, deltamethrin, metaldehyde or sulphur. However, as Malta has not yet designated an official laboratory for formulation analysis, the implementation of this part of the official control plan in 2021 had not yet started at the time of this audit (see also section 5.1.4).

Customs selects specific consignments of PPPs authorised for use in Malta for control at the point of entry into Malta. Controls on commercial imports always include 7 documentary checks. When PPPs are declared, the list of authorised PPPs in Malta, published on the MCCAA website, is consulted. In the case of any doubts or suspicion, consultations with TRD take place before consignments are cleared by customs. The audit team was provided with several pieces of evidence of when such communication between Customs and TRD took place.

As far as passenger luggage control is concerned, controls are based on random selection by Customs at the ports. In the case of any suspicion, TRD is always consulted prior to the release of consignments. The audit team was also provided with examples of such communication between Customs and TRD.

The CAs confirmed that inspectors are instructed to perform official controls without prior notice as required by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, except where such notice is necessary and duly justified for the official control to be carried out. The audit team was informed by the TRD that follow-up inspections and incident investigation inspections are always conducted unannounced. The inspectors met by the audit team confirmed that controls are undertaken without prior notice. Conclusions on planning of official controls

The CAs consider most of the relevant risks and have defined control frequencies for controls on the marketing and use of PPPs. However, the absence of up to date list(s) of all professional users of PPPs and the lack of control at some users, such as service providers for the application of PPPs in non-agricultural use areas, reduces the efficiency of controls on the use of PPPs.
The lack of exchange of some official control data between TRD and ARPA further reduces the effectiveness and efficiency of the official control.
Official controls are performed without prior notice and in a consistent manner thereby contributing to the effectiveness of the control system. 5.1.3. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

The CAs confirmed that all aspects of the planning and implementation of controls on the marketing and use of PPPs are undertaken by the CAs, rather than being delegated to other bodies or natural persons in accordance with the conditions provided for in Articles 29 and 30 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on delegation of certain tasks
All aspects of the planning and implementation are undertaken by the CAs. 8 5.1.4. Laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls Findings

There is no laboratory for formulation analysis for PPPs designated by the CA in Malta, and no samples for formulation analysis have been taken at least since the last European Commission audit in 2005. This is not in line with the Article 5(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requiring CAs to have access to adequate laboratory capacity for analysis, testing and diagnosis.

The audit team was provided with documentation for a tendering process, which was published in July 2021, in order to identify and designate a laboratory(ies) for formulation analysis. However, there was no interest from any laboratories in EU MSs, and therefore the tender had to be republished in September 2021. Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls

The absence of a designated laboratory for PPP formulation analyses limits the scope of official controls. Consequently, the CA cannot confirm that PPPs placed on the market are compliant with the authorisation requirements. 5.2. IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE

The NVWA is the designated competent authority for the implementation of the SNCPs.

The Netherlands created an Animal Health Fund to help monitor and combat animal diseases and to prevent and reduce welfare problems. The responsibility and tasks under the Animal Health Fund are split between: the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality, responsible for policy; the NVWA, responsible for veterinary supervision of monitoring and control; and the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland), responsible for some administrative support tasks, such as managing contracts for delegated controls, checking payment requests and issuing payments under the fund, including for the SNCPs.

Poultry producers, of both egg and meat sectors, can enrol in a private quality scheme called IKB. The NVWA informed that around 90-95% of the poultry holdings (including breeding flocks) are enrolled in this scheme, and that this will namely require those holdings to undergo a yearly IKB inspection. That IKB inspection includes hygiene requirements such as annual water testing, and swabs for verification of effectiveness of cleaning and disinfection. 1 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2019.5926 4 4. Additional details on organisation of SNCP official controls are included in section 5.2.1 of this report, and on the overall organisation of the control systems in the Netherlands are described in the country profile, which is available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 5. National legislation obliges feed manufacturers and suppliers to monitor feed materials and compound feed for the presence of Salmonella at a given frequency. 6. In case of positive test results of samples taken by a feed producer or supplier, serotyping must be carried out by an accredited laboratory. If Salmonella enteritidis, Salmonella typhimurium, Salmonella hadar, Salmonella infantis, Salmonella virchow or Salmonella java is present, the feed producer or supplier has to notify the NVWA and the farmer(s) concerned. The feed manufacturer or supplier shall inform the competent authority of the measures taken and collaborate with the competent authority on action taken in order to avoid risks posed by a feed which they supply or have supplied. Laboratory analysis results are reported in a private database and are made available to the authorities for trend analysis. 7. From 2017 to 2019 the NVWA did not perform official sampling of feed materials nor compound feed. The number of samples, and results, from feed producers and suppliers during that same time period was: Year Samples Positive Salmonella spp Positive for a notifiable Salmonella 2017 11 642 6 1 (S. typhimurium) 2018 3 543 5 0 2019 7 879 34 1 (S. typhimurium) 8. The NVWA carries out controls over feed producers and suppliers via a combination of inspections and audits. To select which operators to control it gives priority to those it has not visited for over 3 years, or are newly registered. 9. From 2017 to 2019, the NVWA performed 564 inspections and 309 audits to feed producers/suppliers. These reported very few non-compliances in relation to salmonella, including one case in 2018 of non-verification of salmonella in feed, another of lack of an hazard analysis and critical control points plan; and in 2018 and 2019 of lack of a risk analysis of incoming feed materials. 10. The SNCPs do not require Salmonella vaccination. Nevertheless, farmers may use authorised Salmonella vaccines on a voluntary basis and vaccination of breeding and laying hens is subsided by the government. This vaccination goes beyond requirements for laying hens, Article 3(3) of Regulation 1177/2006, which requires vaccination only when prevalence of Salmonella in the country is above 10 %. 5 11. Ten different vaccines with S. enteritidis and S. typhimurium strains (five of them with live attenuated strains) are authorised in the Netherlands. They are intended for oral vaccination and provide protection against one or both Salmonella serovars. 12. The NVWA provided the following data on the number of vaccinated flocks, for which a subsidy was requested. Poultry No of No of flocks No of birds No of doses Age Year flocks vaccinated vaccinated administered type 1082 (% ) 690 088 2 070 264 1302 43 (3.9) 1 164 423 3 493 269 Breeders Adult 2017 1699 61 (4.7) 1 049 781 3 149 343 Layers Adult 2018 2686 47 (2.8) 25 732 021 77 196 063 2019 2812 1 184 (44.1) 24 184 452 72 553 356 2017 2547 1 078 (38.3) 23 979 286 71 937 858 2018 1 028 (40.4) 2019 13. Vaccination uptake is not recorded in a database available to the NVWA or the laboratories. Information on if a flock is vaccinated is sent to the laboratories in the sampling form, completed by the samplers after checking the farmer's records. 14. Flocks vaccinated with one particular live attenuated vaccine will sometimes give "false" Salmonella enteritidis positive results. This happens because the test also detects the vaccination strain not only a wild-type strain that could cause disease. If Salmonella enteritidis is detected in a flock vaccinated with this vaccine, the isolate is tested in a designated laboratory with a differentiating method (vaccine vs. wild-type strain, as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation 1177/2006) validated in Germany but not yet for the Netherlands. The designated laboratory performing this test is in the latest stages to obtain the certification for the Netherlands. 15. When S. enteritidis or S. typhimurium is detected in a flock vaccinated with any of the other four authorised live attenuated vaccines (either at own or official sampling), the results are considered positive and no further differentiating test is officially considered. Although the manufacturers of these vaccines provide a differentiating method, as required, the NVWA does not use them within the SNCP. 16. The vaccination schedules, described for two laying hen holdings, were solely during the rearing period, in line with Article 3 of Regulation 1177/2006. The audit team confirmed compliance with vaccination rules on records reviewed, and that when rearing flocks are moved to another holding they are duly accompanied by production documents, listing all vaccinations done and Salmonella test results. 6 Conclusions on preventive measures 17. The preventive measures in place are in line with the approved SNCPs and are suitable for reducing the risk of introducing Salmonella in poultry populations. 5.2 MONITORING AND SAMPLING SCHEME 5.2.1 General points in relation to SNCPs Legal requirements Articles 3 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. The approved Salmonella national control programmes. Articles 5(4), 8(2), 12(4), 13(4), 16(6), 28(1), 29 and 32 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 18. National legislation is in place for all SNCPs. Article 81c of the Dutch legislation `Gezondheids- en welzijnswet voor dieren' is the basis for implementation of Regulation 2160/2003 and the underlying poultry population specific Regulations. Articles 15, 17, 19 to 22, 24 and 32, of that national legislation provide the basis for the prevention of transmission of contagious animal diseases and eradication measures. Articles 83 to 92 cover compensation payments. Monitoring and eradication regulations are adopted in the Dutch legislation `Regeling preventie, bestrijding en monitoring besmettelijke dierziekten en zoonosen en TSE's', in particular articles 95 to 98p. 19. National legislation (entitled `Besluit zoönosen') designates as relevant six Salmonella serovars: Salmonella enteritidis, typhimurium, infantis, hadar, virchow and java. The designation of Salmonella java as a relevant serovar goes beyond EU requirements, and applies only in broilers, and in breeding flocks for the meat line. 20. For the egg production chain, the NVWA delegated some SNCP tasks to The Netherlands Controlling Authority for Dairy and Eggs (COKZ, Controle Orgaan Kwaliteits Zaken) to perform the supervision. 21. The NVWA also delegated all the routine official sampling of the four relevant poultry populations (breeding flocks of Gallus gallus, laying hens, turkeys and broiler flocks) to C-Mark. 22. AVINED (a poultry industry body) manages the central database, called KIPnet, where all Salmonella sampling results, from both official and operator sampling, must be registered. 7 23. The NVWA provided data showing that since 2018 the sampling frequencies implemented for all four relevant poultry populations respected EU requirements, for both routine official and operator sampling. 24. The NVWA delegations of certain official control tasks to both COKZ and C-Mark are generally in line with the relevant requirements of Regulation 2017/625, which effectively address the recommendation in report DG(SANCO) 2013-6696 about the accreditation and impartiality of delegated control bodies. The noted exception is for COKZ in relation to the requirement in its' Article 29(a) for a `precise description' of controls (see also paragraphs 79 and 80). 25. Laboratories analysing operator and/or official monitoring samples within the SNCPs must enter the results into the KIPnet database. Operator samples are identified as `regular' and samples taken by C-Mark and COKZ are identified as `official'. This effectively addressed the recommendation in report DG(SANCO) 2013-6696 to ensure this distinction. 26. National legislation (Article 100(2) of `Gezondheids ­ en Welzijnswet voor dieren') requires any laboratory that examines samples and detects a designated animal disease, such as the six designated serovars of Salmonella, to report it to the NVWA as soon as possible. 27. Registration of a positive Salmonella test result (from official or operator sampling) in KIPnet generates an automatic alert that is sent to the NVWA Incident and crisis Centre. If, for some reason, positive results cannot be entered in the database they must be reported by telephone or e-mail. 28. Slaughterhouses are obliged to assess food chain information prior to accepting animals for slaughter. The NVWA supervises this by also assessing the food chain information and takes action if necessary. 5.2.2 Laboratories Legal requirements Articles 37, 38, 39 and 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 11 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Findings 29. The National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu) is the designated national reference laboratory (NRL) in the Netherlands. It is also the EU reference laboratory for Salmonella, although both are kept operationally separated. 8 30. Official and operator samples within the SNCP for detection and serotyping of Salmonella are all analysed in designated laboratories as required by Art. 12(1) of Reg. 2160/2003. 31. The NVWA designated 15 laboratories in the Netherlands, and a further seven laboratories in other Member States, to carry out testing for detection of Salmonella. For serotyping Salmonella it designated 12 laboratories in the Netherlands and a further two laboratories in other Member States. The NVWA updates the list of designated laboratories regularly. 32. The laboratory designations include the information prescribed by EU requirements. In some cases, the audit team noticed that the designation letter still refers to the previous ISO reference instead of the most recent update. Nevertheless, the designations clearly state that the laboratory should use the most current methods. In addition, the NVWA communicated with all laboratories confirming that all but one designated laboratory for this method is operating under the latest update, ISO 6579-1. 33. The NVWA has well established procedures for the designation of laboratories within the SNCP. NVWA takes into account, for each laboratory, the NRL assessments of standard operating procedures and at least two satisfactory proficiency tests for each method. NVWA also requires that all laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025 and have the relevant ISO certifications for each method included in the designation, in line with the required by Article 12 of Regulation 2160/2003. 34. The Dutch Council for Accreditation accredits the laboratories established in the Netherlands. If the laboratory is established in another Member State the accreditation must be granted by an European Accreditation recognised organisation. 35. However, the NVWA does not have records that designated laboratories for the Dutch SNCPs, located outside the Netherlands, are also designated as an official laboratory by the competent authorities of that Member State. This is not in line with Art. 37(2) of Reg. 2017/625. The NVWA informed that it is planning to send a letter, and to organise a meeting, with all the designated laboratories to improve communication and to address this (as well as the reported in paragraph 43 below). 36. All laboratories need to participate quarterly in proficiency tests for the methods covered by their designation (detection and/or serotyping) in order to maintain the designation. This proficiency testing is organised by a designated body. The laboratories send the results for each round of tests to the NRL for assessment. The NVWA considers the proficiency unsatisfactory when there are two or more incorrect results out of five for each round. In case of unsatisfactory results in one proficiency test round, the NRL contacts the relevant laboratory requesting explanations for the results and if necessary gives advice for improvement. 37. The NRL summarises the results quarterly and sends a report, including the trend analysis over 1-2 years, to the laboratories and to the NVWA.
