Laying hens farms using alternatives system (free- range) Others 3 A hatchery, a farm of pullets and a farm of breeders 2 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of European Union (EU) legislation and, in particular Articles 116, 117, and 119 of the OCR. The Annex 1 provides full legal references. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND The protection of the welfare of laying hens is among the sustainable farming practices necessary to achieve the objectives of the Commission's Farm to Fork Strategy1. In 2012, the EU banned the use of conventional cages for laying hens. From then, cages used for laying hens must provide the birds with an enriched environment, including more space; a nest; perches and litter for allowing the satisfaction of their behavioural needs. Commercial laying hens may be kept either in enriched cages or in non-cage systems. The Directive 1999/74/EC establishes the legal requirements for those laying systems while the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) report2 defined the cage as "a system which is operated without the human keepers entering it". At present, the only EU-wide compulsory system of labelling on animal welfare applies to table eggs. The labelling includes a code, which reflects the production methods (enriched cages (i.e. caged hens) or non-cage systems (i.e. barn, free-range and organic)). Directive 1999/74/EC does not cover the protection of chicks, pullets or breeders. For these, Directive 98/58/EC applies. Regardless of the housing systems in use, producers and authorities have to assess the effectiveness of the protection of the hens (e.g. they may consider the incidence of injurious pecking, the use of beak trimming, the expression of normal behaviour by the hens or the results of the post-mortem inspection, etc.). Animal mutilations are in principle prohibited, but Member States may authorise beak trimming under certain conditions in order to prevent feather pecking and cannibalism. Animal health restrictions (e.g. due to seasonal avian influenza risk) may affect the accessibility to open-air runs used in free-range farms and potentially compromise certain welfare aspects while the 1 https://ec.europa.eu/food/farm2fork_en 2 https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/197 3 biosecurity measures present specific challenges in some non-cage systems (e.g. prevention of contact of hens with migrating wild birds). According to the data communicated to the Commission by the Member States3, half of the laying hens in the Union live in cage-free conditions. There is a wide variation in proportions of laying systems among the Member States. Laying hens in the EU 2020 Free- Range Barn 12% Organic 34% 6% Cage 48% In 2020, Poland reported a total population of 50 150 219 laying hens (13.5% of the EU hens) 80 % of which were kept in caged conditions, 14 % in barn system, 4 % in free-range system, and approximately 1 % in organic production systems. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/info/sites/info/files/food-farming-fisheries/farming/documents/eggs-dashboard_en.pdf 4 Member States have to perform their official controls based on a MANCP. A designated single body shall coordinate the preparation of the MANCP across all competent authorities responsible for the official controls and ensure it is coherent. GIW is the designated single body, which is also responsible for collecting the information on the implementation of the MANCP in view of submitting the annual report and of its review and update as necessary. 5 MAIN CONCLUSIONS 1. The competent authority has adequate level of staff competence contributing to the quality of the controls but it should be strengthened with further training and verification. 2. There is appropriate allocation of resources for the performance of the official controls, resulting in a high proportion of farms being inspected.

text: The system includes a range of procedures and checklists, provided by the central level. Those are consistent among different voivodeships and facilitate consistency of controls through the country.

The system lacks appropriate and dedicated training and procedures for the official controls (animal welfare) on breeder and pullet farms and on hatcheries. As a result, the competent authorities do not control systematically and effectively animal welfare on those areas (e.g. beak trimming in hatcheries and pullet farms, killing of day old chicks).

There is an incomplete methodology for risk-based planning of official controls (does not take into account all relevant risks). Moreover, in the regions visited whilst there is a high proportion of laying hens farms checked every year, there was no evidence that those farms are inspected on a risk basis (with the exception of a district area). This may have implications on the efficient allocation and use of resources (meaning that perhaps controls could be better streamlined and targeted).

As regards verification activities, there are relevant procedures (not sufficiently detailed though) and a regular implementation of supervisions of official controls. However, in some areas, supervisions have not detected significant shortcomings in the performance of the official controls, which presents a missed opportunity for the competent authority to improve the official control system.

As regards the deficiencies on specific requirements on animal welfare on laying hens the most important are: the registration of laying hens farms (not updated, missing, mistaken in some cases), the deficient evaluation in some cases of the stocking density requirements in 5 the farms, and the deficient evaluation of the requirements for the nests' floor in caged hens farms. 6 FINDINGS ON FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS The key strength of the system is that it establishes a high number (and proportion) of official controls on AW in laying hens farms. In addition, official veterinarians are competent and knowledgeable and documented procedures accurately reflect legal requirements. Federal Public Service for Health, Food Chain Safety and the Environment (FPS-HSFCE) Competent Federal 1 Federal Agency for the Security of the Food Authorities chain (FASFC). 1 Customs (Federal Public Service Finance) Regional 2 Competent authority of the Flemish Region Competent authority of the Walloon Region Diagnostic Centre for Plants of the Research Laboratories Reference Laboratory 2 Institute for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Laboratory of the Walloon Agricultural Research Centre (CRA-W) Plant health control sites BCPs Airports 2 Bierset (Liège) Zaventem (Brussels) Seaports 1 Antwerp CPs 1 Facility in the area of the village of Meer Meetings with stakeholders 3 1 1 Airport of Bierset (Liège) 1 Seaport of Antwerp 1 Airport of Zaventem (Brussels) The scope of the audit included the organisation and implementation of import controls, in particular checks on plants and plant products, parcel couriers, passenger luggage and the competent authorities' cooperation with reference laboratories and Customs Service and other stakeholders. Also included, was a desktop assessment of facilities at the border control posts (BCPs) and control points (CPs), in line with the requirements set out in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. 3 LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation and, in particular Articles 116, 117 and 119 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and in agreement with the NPPO. 3.1 RELEVANT EU LEGAL ACTS AND INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 establishes rules to determine the phytosanitary risks posed by any pests, and measures to reduce those risks to an acceptable level. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 establishes the uniform conditions for the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 including those pests, plants and plant products and other objects that are subject to phytosanitary certification. Regulation (EU) 2017/625 provides for harmonised rules for official controls and other official activities to verify compliance with the EU rules on plant health, and minimum requirements for BCPs and CPs. Full legal references to the relevant EU legal acts are listed in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures (ISPMs) are issued by the International Plant Protection Convention of which all EU MS are members. The references to international standards quoted in the report are listed in Annex 2. 4 BACKGROUND This audit was the eighth of the series, aimed at evaluating the correct and consistent application by the MS of the EU legal requirements and to identify examples of good practice on controls on imported plants, plant products and other objects. This is the fifth series of audits on import controls for plant health, the most recent of which took place in 2017-2018. An overview report was published in 2019 and is available at https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/overview_reports/act_getPDF.cfm?PDF_ID=1474. This project runs in parallel with another, which covers the implementation of the official 2 controls requirements under Regulation (EU) 2017/625 for import controls other than those concerning plant health. Further information on the DG Health and Food Safety's Health and Food Audits and Analysis Directorate, including audit reports and its work programme, is available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits_analysis_en. 4.1 PREVIOUS RELEVANT AUDITS This is the fifth audit of Belgium focussed specifically on import controls of plants and plant products. A previous audit was carried out in 2015: DG(SANTE)/ 2015-7602. Audit reports, together with the comments and action plans submitted by the competent authorities (CAs), are available on the European Commission website: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. 4.2 IMPORT DATA In 2021, a total of 94 037 consignments of plants, plant products and other objects were inspected through the BCPs and CPs of Belgium. More than 35 500 of these imports were of cut flowers, of which roses (Rosa spp.) were mainly imported from Kenya (21 482) and Ethiopia (6 296), while carnations (Dianthus spp.) were imported from Colombia (1 582) and Kenya (1 515). Large amounts of fruits were also imported, including avocados (Persea americana) (3 174) from Mexico (1 140) and Colombia (514), citrus fruits (2 200) from Argentina (367), Zimbabwe (290) and South Africa (273), aubergines (Solanum melongena) (1 062) from Uganda (624) and Mexico (213), tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) (812) from Senegal (539) and Spain (Canary Islands, 264), papaya (727) and kiwi (487). Rooted cuttings (1 480) were imported from Israel (527), Costa Rica (399), Ethiopia (193) and Uganda (192). Seeds for sowing (721) were imported from a considerable number of countries, including; Guatemala (101), Chile (69), United States of America (65), Costa Rica (47) and China (45). 4.3 INTERCEPTION DATA In the period between 2020 and 2021, the CAs of Belgium have notified 1 475 interceptions of consignments of plants and plant products. Of these interceptions, 940 were for non- compliances regarding documentary checks and 245 for the presence of harmful organisms, including 135 interceptions of consignments with fruit flies, 98 with white flies and 24 with false codling moth (Thaumatotibia leucotreta). The other interceptions were due to other reasons such as incorrect declarations or prohibited commodities. 3 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATIONAL ASPECTS OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS FOR PLANT HEALTH Legal requirements Articles 4 to 6 and 9(1), Articles 12(2),(3), 28 to 33 and 37(1) ­ (4)(d) to 42, Articles 79, 82(1), 83, 84(1), 85(1) and Article 100, of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Article 2(a) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2125; Article 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/127, Point 6, Annex III to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. text: The FPS­HSFCE is responsible for policy matters and is the designated contact point for international organisations. The FASFC is responsible for the implementation of EU control measures related to quarantine pests. The central directorates of the FASFC plan and coordinate plant health controls, which are implemented by the BCPs and the LCUs.

There are seven BCPs designated in Belgium for imports of plant, plant products and other objects; the airports of Brussels (Zaventem), Liège (Bierset), Oostende and Charleroi and the seaports of Antwerp, Gent and Zeebrugge. At these facilities, documentary controls are generally performed at the main offices, while identity and physical checks are carried out at inspection centres (ICs). In addition, identity and physical checks can be conducted at the 68 designated CPs.

Implementation of official controls is performed by 58 specialists, of which six are inspectors, 25 controllers and 27 self-employed staff (independent engineers or veterinarian staff on assignment by the CAs). Besides checks on plant and plant products, the BCP staff also carry out import controls on food and feed of non-animal origin, food contact materials and marketing standards for fruit and vegetables. 4 5. Plant and plant product checks at CPs and the BCPs of Gent seaport and Charleroi airport are carried out by staff working within the primary plant production sector of the LCUs. These staff also perform marketing standard controls on fresh fruit and vegetables. 6. Controllers have a bachelor degree or more than 10 years of experience in import controls, while inspectors have a masters degree. Training is provided by the CAs on a regular basis and is compulsory for all staff. The CA provided examples of agendas and training material given at these sessions outlining the aspects covered. Newly recruited personnel have to follow at least one month of training supervised by a senior plant health inspector and a further assessment before they are allowed to perform checks on their own. 7. Customs is responsible for conducting checks on personal luggage, postal and courier services providers. There is close cooperation between the FASFC and Customs regarding checks on plant and plant products, which is laid down in a memorandum of understanding signed in 2018. A coordination body of FASFC and Customs meets at least once a year to enhance coordination. 5.1.2Audits and verification of procedures 8. An independent body of the CA plans and executes external and internal multi annual audit programmes following procedures developed in accordance with Commission Notice 2021/C 66/02 and the ISO 19011 standard. Audit series are implemented following requirements of the integrated quality management system of the CAs (ISO 9001, 17020 and 17025) and Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 as part of the control system of the Federal Internal Audits Department. According to the information provided by the auditing body, at least two sectors of the audit universe are in the scope of plant health import controls. The audit team was provided with an overview report of two of these audits, conducted after the entry into force of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 9. The CA stated that verification of import control procedures is implemented by the LCUs as part of the ISO management system. The verification of procedures is applicable to all staff members carrying out inspections and include the verification of an import file, preferably a file of a non-compliant consignment, and an in situ supervision of an import check. Following these requirements, senior inspectors conduct verification of procedures on each of the staff posted at the BCPs/CPs by reviewing at least two files per staff member and year. This system of verification of procedures is also part of the training of new staff. The audit team confirmed implementation of verification procedures with members of staff during the visits to all BCPs. This practice is in line with the requirements of Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.1.3Planning of official controls 10. Planning of controls on goods listed under Articles 72 and 73 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is based on operators submitting the CHED-PP part 1 via TRACES in advance of the consignment arriving. Pre-notification of 24 hours for the seaports and 4 hours for the airports is required. The audit team noted that some flexibility is given to operators. Documentary checks on commercial consignments of regulated goods are carried out at 5 the offices of the BCPs, while identity and physical controls are conducted by the plant health officers at designated ICs or CPs. When operators make a customs declaration for plants and plant products, as per the combined nomenclature codes listed in part A and B of Annex IX to Regulation (EU) 2019/2072, they are informed by the customs declaration system that for these consignments the submission of a CHED-PP is required. Customs has reading access to TRACES and verifies that checks are completed by FASFC with a validated CHED-PP, before clearance into free circulation is permitted. Brussels airport manages a perishable management application in parallel to TRACES. Liège airport authorities are evaluating if this IT system could be implemented, and the audit team was informed by the CA that it may also be implemented at other BCPs. This software, provides real time information of the situation of each consignment and commodity to official staff and operators and helps planning inspections. The implementation of these support IT systems, can be considered as a good practice. 11. The CAs aim to inspect 100% of the consignments of Article 72 commodities unless subject to reduced frequency in accordance with Commission Regulation (EC) No 1756/2004. Each BCP maintains a database in order to achieve compliance with the minimum level of inspection demanded by the above Regulation. The same database is used to ensure compliance with the minimum 1% identity and physical inspection level for Article 73 commodities. 12. The CA performs controls of WPM listed under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/127, which is inspected at the BCPs at a rate of 15%, in line with the requirements of this Regulation. The CA stated that the wood packing material (WPM) monitoring plan is based on two pillars. Firstly, controls of WPM present in consignments subject to official control by FASFC at the BCP. Secondly, the CAs conduct checks on operators selected by the number of imported consignments of WPM imported from a list of combined nomenclature codes, when imported from; Canada, China, Democratic Republic of Korea, India, Japan, Mexico, Republic of Korea, Taiwan, USA and Vietnam, where the presence of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus and Anoplophora glabripennis is known. These checks are performed by the LCUs and target the WPM present at the operator during the visit, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2125, which requires that these physical checks shall be carried out on consignments selected in accordance with the provisions of Article 4(1) of the same Regulation. 13. The CA provided a copy of the plans for sampling for latent infection for 2021 and 2022. The plans are produced annually and indicate the number of latent samples to be taken for a list of commodities and countries of origin, in line with the requirements of point 6 of

It concluded that the number of new positives detected in the DAs indicate that the plant health risk of spreading Xf exists. Although in Apulia, the delays in plant removals were reduced significantly, they were still considerable and together with the less efficient vector controls this created a pronounced plant health risk for the spread of the disease. In Tuscany only the positive tested plants were removed (with delays) from the IZs. The presence of the bacterium together with the weak movement controls meant that there was a risk for spreading of Xf from the DA. Further information on the work carried out by the DG Health and Food Safety in relation to audits, and its work programme, is available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits_analysis_en 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATIONAL ASPECTS OF CONTROLS FOR XYLELLA FASTIDIOSA Legal requirements Articles 4 to 5, 11 to 14, 28 to 33 and 37(1) ­ (4)(d) to 42 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 25 and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 in its entirety and Annex IV for the diagnostic support. Findings 5.1.1 Competent authorities 1. The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Italy are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Italy (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=IT) and in the relevant sections of the previous audit reports. There were no changes in the responsibilities since the 2021 audit. In summary: The RPS implements the plant health controls in the region. MIPAAF is responsible for the national plant health policy and for the coordination of the regions' activities. The National Phytosanitary Committee (NPC), composed of representatives of MIPAAF and the regions, is the forum where issues beyond regional competence are discussed. NPC provides advice and guidance to the regions.

The Command Units of Forest, Environment and Agri-food of the Carabinieri (CUFAA) are responsible for the controls on the movement of plants for planting and for the enforcement of the insect vector controls. In Apulia the Regional Agency for Irrigation and Forestry (ARIF) carries out the Xf surveillance within and outside the DAs and completes the plant removals if the owner does not act. In Lazio and Tuscany, contract agents and business operators assist the surveys, plant removals and vector controls. 5 5.1.2 National and regional legislation

At national level, Legislative Decree No 19 of 2 February 2021 adapts the legislation to the provisions of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031 and 2017/625. Ministerial Decree of 24 January 2022 repealed Ministerial Decree of 13 February 2018, which introduced the specific national emergency measures on Xf. Consequently, at the time of the audit no measures are applied beyond the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. Ministerial Decree of 24 January 2022 also published the Italian National Contingency Plan for Xf (see section 5.3).

In Apulia, the legal framework for Xf controls is established by the Regional Law No 4 of 29 March 2017 on the management of Xf outbreak and Regional Law No 14 of 4 June 2017 on protection of monumental olive trees. In Tuscany, Regional Executive Decree No 7809 of 6 June 2017 establishes measures to be applied in the case of an Xf emergency (see further details in sections 5.3 and 5.4). In Lazio, the regional action plan was approved on 14 June 2022 by Regional Committee No 422. 5.1.3 Procedures for the quality and consistency of controls

A series of national technical notes assist the Xf controls by the regions, including a MIPAAF note on inspections and sampling in nurseries. The Research Centre on Plant Protection and Certification of the Council for Agricultural Research and Economics (CREA-DC), which is the national reference institute for plant protection elaborated a specific card on Xf surveys for the regions.

A working group of the NPC prepared the national technical procedure for the diagnosis of Xf, including details of sampling and laboratory analysis. The proposal of the working group will be distributed to the regions as a recommendation after the NPC approves it.

In the regions with outbreaks the RPSs elaborated a range of manuals and guidance documents for the inspectors and service providers and mobilised additional resources for the controls. Since the 2021 audit: · In Apulia, the RPS updated the monitoring and sampling procedures for Xf and published them as executive document no 31 of 13/05/2022. Accordingly, the RPS updated the operational guidelines for ARIF. The regional IT system and database was also updated, which provides real-time information about the state of play of the controls for analytical and management purposes. The number of staff involved in Xf controls, and the financial resources were significantly increased both in 2021 and 2022, which had a positive impact on the controls (see sections 5.5 and 5.6); · In Lazio, after the detection of the outbreak, the RPS mobilised quickly the resources necessary for the comprehensive controls. The available databases and IT tools were successfully used for the planning and implementation of the eradication measures (see section 5.7); 6 · In Tuscany, external resources were involved for the surveys, plant removals and vector treatment. The RPS maintained cooperation with neighbouring universities for the identification of host plants and vectors for epidemiological studies. The IT system and database provides real-time information about the state of play of the implemented measures for planning and management purposes (see section 5.8). 5.1.4 Diagnostic support

The audit paid particular attention on the implementation of the provisions of Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires that after 29 April 2022 the designated official plant health laboratories shall operate according to the provisions of the standard EN ISO/IEC 17025. The activity of the national reference laboratory (NRL) on ensuring the proficiency of the designated official laboratories in testing plant and vector samples for Xf was also checked.

The laboratory of CREA-DC is the national reference laboratory (NRL) for plant health and acts as EU reference laboratory for bacteriology. It is accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. The scope of accreditation was recently extended to Xf analysis on olive samples with real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR). At the time of the audit 31 laboratories, belonging to the RPSs or universities and research institutions, had been designated by MIPAAF for the analysis of official plant and insect samples for the detection of Xf.

The NRL has elaborated a national technical procedure for Xf laboratory tests with methods required by the EU legislation. The NPPO expects that the NPC formally approves the document in the months after the audit, which will then become mandatory for the designated laboratories.

In 2021-2022 the NRL organized a proficiency test for the designated laboratories. Each of the 31 laboratories, designated by MIPAAF for Xf analysis, participated. The NRL stated that: · The scope included testing the presence of Xf subspecies pauca and multiplex in a matrix of DNA extracts of plant samples of Lavandula sp., Olea europaea, Prunus dulcis, Salvia rosmarinus and Vitis vinifera. · The laboratories were asked to analyse the samples with the method(s) they commonly used for Xf detection. Each laboratory used at least one of the molecular methods listed in Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 2020/1201; · The performance of 29 laboratories was assessed as fully satisfactory. Two laboratories had issues with the detection of Xf subspecies multiplex in the DNA extract of lavender plants. The NRL recommended corrective actions, which have already been implemented by the two laboratories.

The audit team noted that the proficiency test did not include the assessment of the DNA extraction part of the procedure and therefore may not provide comprehensive assessment on the performance of the laboratories. The NRL plans to organise further proficiency tests, which will cover the entire scope of the molecular tests. 7 13. The NRL stated that: · At the time of the audit nine designated laboratories were accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025 with a scope of analysis of Xf or other bacteria with molecular methods; · Several designated laboratories are at various stages of the accreditation process. The NRL supports the preparation and application for accreditation with training and technical assistance (e.g., by providing reference material). 14. In Apulia, the initial Xf tests are carried out by the same five laboratories, referred to by the 2021 audit report. Only one of the laboratories is accredited. For quality control, the Laboratory of the Institute for Sustainable Protection of Plants of the National Research Council in Bari retests a given percentage of the negative samples of the other regional laboratories. In Lazio the initial and confirmatory tests are carried out by the laboratory of the University of Tuscia, which is in the process of accreditation to ISO/EN 17025. In Tuscany, the RPS laboratory is responsible for the initial and confirmatory tests and for subspecies identification. The audit team noted that the laboratory is accredited to ISO/EN 17025 with a scope including Xf analysis with molecular methods. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of Xf controls 15. text: The NPA under the MARD is the competent authority (CA) for plant health in the meaning of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which is responsible for national plant health policy, coordination of tasks, control verification procedures, documented procedures, staff training and representation at EU level.

There are 41 regional county phytosanitary offices (CPOs), under the responsibility of the NPA, who are responsible for the implementation of the EU system of plant passports, registration of operators and authorisation of professional operators, maintenance of the regional databases and the recruitment of staff. There are approximately three staff working in each region. The CPOs are also responsible for the 3 verification of compliance of plant health aspects with the relevant EU requirements for marketing of plant propagating material and for export certification, import controls of plants, plant products and other objects. The CA stated that staff have not received specific training on the system of plant passporting since before Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and current implementing EU legislation on plant passports came into force (see paragraphs 15, 16, 19, 20, 28, 29, 30, 33 and 36). 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

According to the CA the following legislation is relevant in the context of this audit1: · Order No. 136 of 31 August 2000 is the basic plant health legislation giving rise to the legal powers to the CA and its officials. · Judgment No. 563 of the Government of Romania of 6 June 2007 approving the implementing rules for the Government Ordinance No. 136/2000. This law includes the provisions for the designation of the NPA of the MARD the CA for plant health controls. · Order No. 580 of 13 July 2007 on the registration procedure for producers and importers. · Order No. 583 of 13 July 2007 on establishing a degree of standardisation for plant passports to be used for movement of certain plants, plant products or other objects within the Community and establishment detailed procedures for issuing plant passports, conditions and procedures details to replace them.

The CA stated that certain elements of the Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council and their implementing acts establishing specific requirements on plant passporting will be incorporated into national legislation but noted that these EU Regulations are directly applicable in Romania. See also section 5.7 on enforcement of actions. 5.1.3 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

The CA provided the audit team with a copy of the documented procedures dated 2007, which were prepared by the NPA. This document outlines the general tasks and responsibilities necessary for the inspectors to carry out their plant health duties including templates of relevant forms for use by the operator and CA. The audit team 1 Link to national legislation https://www.madr.ro/protectia-plantelor-si-carantina-fitosanitara/legislatie- nationala-fitosanitar.html 4 noted that the guidelines are based on repealed EU plant health legislation and do not include guidance for the implementation of any of the provisions on plant passporting established by Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and its implementing acts. This is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA stated that an up-to-date version of this document is being prepared and will reflect the new requirements of the plant health and official controls legislation, however no draft was available.

The CA stated that there is a system of internal audits in place in Romania in accordance with the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, covering also plant health controls. No audits have been carried out in the area of official controls on plant passports nor could they indicate when they intend to cover this subject.

The CA stated that they do not have control verification procedures in place to ensure consistency of the implementation of the system of plant passporting among the 41 CPOs. This is not in line with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the control system related to plant passports

The structure, responsibilities and legal powers of the CA are defined in national legislation. However, the lack of up-to-date documented procedures and control verification procedures and staff training does not ensure that the system of plant passports is implemented in a consistent manner and in line with EU requirements. 5.2 REGISTRATION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS Legal requirements Articles 65 to 68 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Findings 5.2.1 Official registration

According to the CA all operators that are involved in the production, collective warehousing, dispatch centres and importers of plants, plant products and other objects are obliged to register. Operators register directly with their respective CPO with their information being kept on a local county database. The data submitted by the operators, is verified by the CPO prior to being officially registered. Following approval, all professional operators receive a certificate of registration. However, the CA could not confirm that all operators are registered given that they do not know the number of operators selling through distance contracts (see also paragraph 12 and 38). This is not in line with Article 65(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Furthermore, the CA informed the audit team that there is no central register and that it does not have direct 5 access to the 41 local county databases. The CA stated that there are advanced plans to have a centralised register but did not provide a date by when this new system will be operational.

Professional operators are required to submit an update of their registration data of the preceding year to the CA by the 30 April each year. Once submitted, the CA verifies the data by way of a visit to the operator after which the operator's certificate of registration is endorsed for another year. In the examples examined by the audit team, most of these updates were submitted after the 30 April. The CA stated that this was because the operators had not planted all their crops at this stage yet. This is not fully in line with the requirements of Article 66(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.2.2 Application of exemptions provided for in EU law

The CA stated that they apply Article 65(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, however they have not exempt operators on the grounds of trading `small quantities', which has not been defined in national legislation. Nevertheless, the CA specifically exclude garden centres and retail outlets that sell directly to the final consumer from registration without the application of `small quantity' criteria. Furthermore, the CA stated they understood that operators selling though distance contracts are not exempt from registration but were unable to register them due to a lack of resources. This is not fully in line with Article 65(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on the registration of professional operators

There is a system in place for the registration of professional operators as required by EU Regulations. However, Romania provides no guarantees that all operators selling through distance contracts are registered. This may result in the movement of plants without a valid plant passport within the EU. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures

In Romania, there is only one authorised operator and 1 552 registered operators, which are defined by the CA as 804 producers, 503 importers and 245 exporters. The CA stated they issue the vast majority of plant passports (see paragraph 26). Furthermore, 6 the CA stated, there has been no initiative to encourage registered operators to become authorised. Thus, the competent authority have failed to embrace the concept of Article 84(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and the guidance provided for in recital no. 45 of the same Regulation, has not been considered. Recital no. 45 states that plant passports should generally be issued by the authorised professional operator and gives rise to authorising them to issue plant passports under the supervision of the CA. This is currently not the case in Romania.

According to the CA, the NPA is the authority responsible for the authorising of professional operators. The procedure for authorisation consists of the professional operator sending an email to the NPA, followed by an inspection by the CPO. It was noted that there is no formal documented procedure established for the authorisation of professional operators.

The CA stated that compliance of authorised operators with Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is verified without the assistance of formal work instructions. Furthermore, the CA does not verify the obligations of the authorised operator to identify and monitor the points of its production process, and the requirements concerning the movement of plants, plant products and other objects, as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The CA stated that it determines informally the extent to which professional operators fulfil the criteria, by way of regular day-to-day interaction with the operator (see paragraph 11, 14, 18, 19, 22, 23). In addition, the competent authority has not made available technical guidance on the criteria to be fulfilled in the examinations to professional operators possibly interested in applying for authorisation which is not in line with Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827.

The website2 of the NPA contains information on the biology of relevant pests, symptoms of pest damage, information on best practices mostly meets the criteria of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. However, information on the establishment and content of an effective plan to be followed in case of any suspected occurrence or finding of regulated pests has not been made available to the authorised professional operators contrary to Article 2(1)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions

The CA are required to carry out official controls on professional and authorised operators at least once per year in order to verify compliance with EU requirements. During the site visits, the audit team learnt that inspectors plan controls on operators based on the biology of the pest or around the growing season of the plant. During the site visits the inspector examined the crop closely for the presence of pests and recorded their findings on official inspection forms. Copies of these inspection reports were 2 https://www.anfdf.ro/sanatate/ghid/ghiduri.html 7 provided to the audit team (see also paragraph 23). In addition, the inspectors frequently visit operators upon request, to carry out official controls on new consignments when they arrive or when notified of the suspected presence of a pest. Many of these new consignments include regulated goods from other MS that are accompanied by a plant passport. Some of these operators were visited at least once a week. The CA stated that this is something they always did since before the new EU requirements came into force. The audit team observed that a risk assessment is not always applied to these controls. Data such as, species, type of plant produced, origin, growing cycles or history of compliance is not taken into account and therefore do not justify these increased level of checks as required by Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66. The option for reduced frequency controls as provided for in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 is not applied in Romania.

As part of these controls the CA stated, they also carry out checks on compliance with the format of the plant passport. However, the CA did not identify plant passports which were not issued in accordance with Article 83 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 as provided for in Articles 1 and 2 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313. Issues such as the absence of a border line, the background colour being determined by the colour of the packaging, the absence of the EU flag, the word `plant passport' not placed where it should be. In some cases, the plant passport had the EU flag and word plant passport cut off, due to the potential issues with printer used etc (refer also to paragraph 28 and 29). Furthermore, it was noted by the audit team that the CA has not reported any plant passport non-compliances since the new EU plant passport Regulations came into force. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports
The CA has not fully embraced the concept of the new system of plant passporting with the objective of placing greater responsibility on professional operators.

There is a system of authorisation of professional operators to issue plant passports in Romania, however the CA do not make professional operators aware of all the necessary criteria for professional operators authorised to issue plant passports. Furthermore, the CA does not verify the criteria to be fulfilled by professional operators authorised to issue plant passports. This presents a risk where in the event of an increase in the number of authorised operators, plant passports would be issued by operators that are not qualified to do so thus, increasing the phytosanitary risk of plants moved within the EU. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 8 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators

The authorised operator visited showed the audit team detailed records of the examinations carried out during the growing season in line with the EU requirements. This entails checks for the presence and symptoms of quarantine pests at the appropriate times of the year, complemented by inspections and sampling by the CA. These checks are recorded, and records are kept for at least three years. The operator visited demonstrated a good level of knowledge of relevant pests and the EU plant passport requirements demonstrating that they had the competence to issue plant passports. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators

The CA stated that it conducts examinations and verifications at operators at least once a year (see also paragraph 19). During the site visits the following observations were made: a. Controls performed by the CA are carried out without a formal risk-based plan in place. However, according to the CA controls are carried out during the growing season of the plant or based on the biology of the relevant pest. The inspector stated that there are at least two visual inspections carried out on each crop during the growing season which may result in sampling for laboratory analysis in the event of suspicion of the presence of a pest. This is not fully in line with the obligations of the CA to perform examinations as per Article 87(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, where a CA shall carry out examinations at authorised operators for inspections, sampling and testing in the event of a suspicion or presence of a pest or when carrying out an examination in the immediate vicinity. b. The inspectors met were found to be knowledgeable of plants, regulated pests, kept records of activities of each visit and demonstrated meticulous examinations of the plants. c. It was noted by the audit team that there were no checks on verification of examinations performed by the authorised operator, no checks on the format of the plant passport (see paragraph 19), no checks to ensure the operator complies with the conditions of authorisation to issue plant passports (paragraph 19) or checks on obligations o

The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Ireland are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Ireland (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/IE).

DAFM is the competent authority (CA) for plant health in the meaning of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. There are four divisions within the DAFM responsible for official controls in the context of this audit: · Horticulture and Plant Health Division (HPHD) ­ official controls on all nurseries and traders, except for the forestry sector; · Forestry Inspectorate Division (FID) ­ official controls on all nurseries and traders of forest material; · Import Control Operations Division (ICOD) - official controls of plants for planting and plant products at import; · Crop Evaluation and Certification Division (CECD) - official controls of plants for planting and plant products subject to certification schemes.
There is no delegation of official control tasks by the CA to any other control body in Ireland.

Among the staff available, HPHD has 9 assistant agricultural inspectors, FID 7 field inspectors and ICOD 2 inspectors (including 1 forestry inspector) and 16 assistant agricultural inspectors that are directly involved in official controls on compliance with PP requirements.

The audit team was informed by the NPPO that there have been major changes in the staff numbers within the DAFM since 2019 with regard to the official controls on plant health. In addition, due to Brexit some staff were reallocated from plant health related activities within the DAFM exclusively for pre-export activities due to the increased need for pre-export inspections on products exported to the United Kingdom. This has resulted in delays in establishing the national legal framework for plant health matters 3 under Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Consequently, this also resulted in delays in developing and implementing a national system for PPs (see also section 5.1.3). 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

The following legislation developed is relevant in the context of the audit: · Statutory Instrument S.I. No 459 of 2020 is the framework national law for the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. It includes among other things provisions for the implementation of EU requirements on the registration of professional operators, authorisation of professional operators to issue PP and for the official controls on plant health matters. It also provides the legal basis for enforcement. · Statutory Instrument S.I. No. 310 of 2021 requires pre-notification on arrival of plant species and plant products of economic, environmental, and social importance to Ireland. This allows DAFM to organise the official inspections on the plants and plant products with higher focus on those operators who receive listed plants and plants products from other EU MS. 5.1.3 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

text: The CA provided the audit team with five standard operating procedures (SOP) adopted by HPHD and relevant in the context of this audit. These SOPs cover specific aspects of plant health inspections including registration of professional operators, authorisation of professional operators to issue PPs and verification and inspection of PPs. The audit team noted that while most SOPs for plant passport inspections were adopted in April 2020, the revised versions of these SOPs were adopted in 2022. The audit team also noted that one of the SOPs focusing on verification of the examinations done by the authorised operator was only adopted in September 2022 and was not yet implemented in practice at the time of the audit.

Updated Technical Guidance that also includes PP aspects was made available to the operators by FID in November 2021. The audit team noted that specific SOPs for the inspectors on the authorisation of professional operators to issue PP, on official controls of authorised professional operators and on general forest health inspections were adopted between August-October 2022 and their implementation only started shortly prior to or during the audit.1

The SOP on official procedures for the issuance of PP to replace phytosanitary certificates for imports of certain plants, plant products and other objects was adopted by the ICOD on 15 September 2022. 1 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that these delays in implementation of plant passport controls were caused by the extra need to allocate staff for tasks related to the preparation for BREXIT between August 2018 to the end of the transition period for the UK to leave the EU on the 31st December 2020, as well as during implementation of the first year of BREXIT requirements in 2021. However good progress has been made since 2021. 4 10. The audit team noted that some aspects of the PP system as established in EU legislation are not adequately addressed in the SOPs or technical guidance. The SOPs do not include specific guidance for the development and verification for replacing a PP for the horticulture sector and in the case of both the horticulture and forestry sectors, they do not include the requirements to verify the appropriateness of operators' examinations as required by Articles 92(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 11. Staff met during the audit had received training on PP matters and were generally aware of the context of SOPs developed. 12. The audit team was provided with sufficient evidence on the internal coordination within the DAFM on plant health matters. These included minutes of the monthly Plant Health Risk meetings and quarterly meetings of the Emerging Plant Pests Review Group. The audit team observed that some of these minutes also covered aspects of the PP system. The audit team was also provided with examples of Pest Risk Assessment protocols developed by the CAs. 13. The audit team noted that no written records are required to be drawn up on PP controls contrary to what is required by Article 13(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see also details in section 5.3.2). 14. There have been no internal audits undertaken yet on PP matters and there are no formal control verification procedures established, contrary to the requirements of Articles 6 and 12(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625) respectively. The DAFM informed the audit team that an internal audit on the implementation of the PP system is planned for 2024- 2025. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the control system related to plant passports 15. Recently developed procedures form a good but not complete basis for the official controls on PPs in Ireland. 16. Due to the incomplete guidance provided to the inspectors on the application of the PP system, the CA cannot always ensure the appropriateness and effectiveness of the official controls on the PP system. This conclusion is further supported by the lack of internal audits and formal control verification procedures in place on PP matters. Consequently, these deficiencies compromise the reliability of the system of PPs issuance in Ireland. 5.2 REGISTRATION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS Legal requirements Articles 65 to 68 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 5 Findings 5.2.1 Official registration 17. There is a system established for the registration of professional operators as required by Article 65 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. There are two parallel registers available, one for the forestry sector managed by FID and one for the horticulture sector managed by HPHD. The audit team was provided with a demonstration of the planned electronic register combining both registers. The audit team was informed that this register was in the very last stage of pre-launch testing and would be implemented shortly after the end of the audit. 18. The audit team observed that there is no duplication of the registration of the same company in two registers. One operator can only be registered once by the CA as required by the Article 65(2). 19. The audit team observed that the registration procedure follows the requirements of Article 66 (1)(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and the information in the official register can be made available as required by Article 68 of the same Regulation. 20. The audit team observed that the requirements of Article 66(5) of the Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 for the operators to notify the CA of annual updates are not implemented consistently and no clear guidance has been provided to the operators. During the site visits to the operators the audit team noted that all operators met had some updates on their annual activities such as commodity types, general or species of plants, but none of them were required to submit any updates by the 30 April of each year contrary to requirements of the abovementioned Article 66(5). According to the data provided by the CA, less than 2% of the registered operators have provided the annual updates in line with EU requirements for 2022. At the time of the audit some 1 573 professional operators were registered by the CAs in Ireland. 21. As highlighted under point 6 in section 5.1.2 there is a requirement in the national legislation to pre-notify the CA about the trade of high-risk plants from other EU MS. This contributes to the prioritisation of official plant health controls at registered professional operators. 5.2.2 Application of exemptions provided for in EU law 22. Ireland has opted not to use derogations provided under Article 65(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, except for the supply of small quantities of seed. However, small quantities of seeds are not defined in the national legislation or in any of the technical guidance or SOPs available to operators and inspectors. 6 Conclusions on the registration of professional operators 23. There is a system in place for the registration of professional operators as required by EU legislation. However, the lack of enforcement of the requirement for operators to provide annual updates reduces the possibilities for the CA to implement the risk based official controls as required by Article 9(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures 24. The registered professional operators must submit an application form to the HPHD for the horticulture sector and to FID for the forestry sector. The authorisation procedure is divided into a two-stage process with stage 1 being the documentary check, primarily on the compliance with the requirements of Article 1 (a)(b)(d) and (f) of the Regulation (EU) 2019/827 and stage 2 being the actual on-the-spot verification of the operators' compliance with the other requirements of the same Article. 25. The applicants' knowledge of the EU quarantine pests and the best practices to prevent their spread is verified via an online test that each applicant must pass. Separate tests are available for the operators in the horticulture and forestry sector. 26. Once the administrative checks are completed, an on-the-spot inspection is conducted prior to the finalisation of the pre-authorisation assessment of compliance. An inspection report is completed and attached to the operator's file in the CA database. The audit team was provided with an inspection report that included among other things verification of the traceability systems in place at the operator and verification of compliance with the requirements of Article 1 (c) and (e) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. Once completed, the certificate of authorisation is issued, and the operator is informed by the CA. 27. The CA provided evidence to the audit team that training materials and guidance documents have been made available to the professional operators. This also included information on quarantine pests and PZ pests, including links on the CA website to the EPPO Global Pest Database and EFSA's survey sheets for priority pests. This is in line with what is required by the Article 2(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2019/827. 7 28. At the time of the audit, some 169 professional operators were authorised to issue PPs in Ireland, also for the movement of plants and plant products within and into the PZs. 29. The audit team noted that the vast majority of professional operators had been authorised to issue PPs less than a year before the audit. All authorised professional operators visited by the audit team were in business and had distributed plants for planting and plant products subject to PP prior to their formal authorisation, without PP or with PP not complying with the layout established by Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 (see also point 47 in Section 5.5.2). 2 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions 30. According to the CA, official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions should be conducted at least once a year according to the SOPs developed. However, no written records are kept of the official control activities by HPHD with regard to PP, contrary to the requirements in Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Therefore, the audit team was not provided with evidence that these activities were performed and at the frequency established by the Article 92(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. For the forestry sector, FID stated, that no such supervision activities had yet been undertaken, as authorisation of professional operators to issue PPs started only in February 2022. 31. The audit team was provided with some evidence of the official controls conducted with a focus on PPs at the authorised operators in the horticulture sector, but these were inspection visits conducted during stage 2 of the authorisation process. 32. There are no procedures developed yet for the implementation of the requirements of Article 91 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 with regard to pest risk management plans. Consequently, an option to conduct official controls with a reduced frequency at professional operators authorised to issue PPs has not yet been applied. 33. As already highlighted under point 10 above, the SOPs developed for the supervision and verification of professional operators for issuing PP do not include all elements of the PP system, in particular regarding the requirement to verify appropriateness of operators' own examinations. Therefore, official inspections do not fully cover the scope foreseen by Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. This was confirmed during the official controls observed by the audit team at the operators visited. 2 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that these delays in implementation of plant passport controls, including authorization of operators to issue plant passports, were caused by the extra need to allocate staff for tasks related to the preparation for BREXIT between August 2018 to the end of the transition period for the UK to leave the EU on the 31st December 2020, as well as during implementation of the first year of BREXIT requirements in 2021. 8 Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports 34. There is a system in place for the authorisation of professional operators to issue PPs as required by EU legislation, although it is not fully in line with EU requirements. Therefore, the system to verify operators' compliance with the established requirements can only provide some but not full assurance to the CA on operators' compliance to issue PPs. 35. The delays in the introduction of a system for the authorisation of PPs and lack of evidence on the verification and supervision of authorised operators by the CA compromises the reliability of the PPs issued by the operators. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators 36. In the food producing sector, the collection of Category 1 and Category 2 material mostly takes place directly from operators generating such materials. Collection of ABP originating from on-farm slaughter and of fallen animals (Category 1 and Category 2 material) takes place directly from the farms via six dedicated intermediary plants. 3 From these intermediary plants the concessionaire transports the collected Category 1 and Category 2 material to the Category 1 processing plant where the Category 1 and the Category 2 materials (mixed) are processed using Method 1 ­ the pressure sterilisation. The concession does not cover the digestive tract content and the manure (Category 2 material). These products are collected separately and disposed on arable lands, landfills or send to biogas plants by farmers and other operators. ABP consisting of the Category 3 material from meat producing sector are collected, mostly, directly from slaughterhouses and meat processing establishments by the operator of the Category 3 processing plant. The Category 3 material which consists of former foodstuffs from the retail sector, butcher shops, meat and fish processing food establishments, household waste and the catering waste (except from means of transport operating internationally) is collected by intermediate plants for transformation in biogas plants or composting in composting plants. Certain amount of Category 3 material, originating from slaughterhouses and/or cutting plants, is collected by pet food operators for production of raw/processed pet food or dog chews. The Category 3 material of milk origin which originates from dairy approved establishments is placed on the market as feed material destined for agricultural holdings authorised for use of milk, milk-based and milk-derived products for feeding farmed animals. Centrifuge and separator sludge from dairy establishments are either processed as Category 3 material in ABP processing plants, transformed in biogas plants or disposed of on the land. The meat-and-bone meal (MBM), resulting from processing of Category 1 material, is destined for incineration in incineration plants and/or co-incineration in cement factories in other Member States. Category 1 fat is destined for production of biodiesel (in other Member States). Processed animal proteins (PAP) resulting from mixed Category 3 material of different species are destined for production of pet food (mostly in other Member States). In recent years, some part of PAP of poultry origin was used for production of feed for aquaculture. The Category 3 fat goes for production of feed for farm animals and pet food, and the amount in excess is destined for technical purposes, mainly the production of biodiesel (in other Member States). According to the information presented by the AFSVSPP, the country avails of sufficient ABP processing and transformation capacity, well exceeding current needs and allowing to process high quantities of ABP in case of sudden outbreaks of epizootic animal diseases. While the national finances the collection, processing and destruction of fallen stock, resulting in a free of charge service for animal keepers, other business operators must pay for the collection, processing and destruction of ABP in proportion to the collected amounts. Since the collection of fallen animals covers the entire territory of the country, no areas of Slovenia are permanently designated as remote for the purpose of ABP collection and disposal. However, foreseeing changeable and unexpected situations, the domestic legislation defines 4 conditions limiting the operator's access for collection of ABP and describes the procedure allowing, if necessary, for exceptional burial on the spot. 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS The specific provisions of the legal acts relevant to each section of this report are cited in Annex II and are referred to in the individual findings of the report. 5.1 Structural elements of the official control system 1. An overview of how the control system is organised is described in the country profile for Slovenia, which is available here: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=SI

In summary, there are four competent authorities involved in the system of official controls on ABP and DP: the AFSVSPP, the Ministry of the Environment and Spatial Planning (MESP), the Inspectorate of the Republic of Slovenia for Agriculture, Forestry, Hunting and Fisheries (IRSAFHF) and the Financial Administration of the Republic of Slovenia (FARS). Of these four authorities, the AFSVSPP is the authority competent for the areas within the scope of this audit as it, solely, covers almost the entire chain of ABP and DP.

The AFSVSSP is responsible for policy-making, coordination, management of the approval and registration process and the maintenance of lists of ABP operators, plant and establishments, and for carrying out ABP/DP official controls, except in areas covered by MESP, IRSAFHF and FARS.

The AFSVSPP inspectors from ten Regional Offices carry out official controls along the ABP chain, covering establishments and plants producing food of animal origin (slaughterhouses, cutting and meat processing plants and dairy establishments), retailers (including butcher shops), farms and regular ABP establishments, plants and operators.
The MASP is responsible for approving the incineration and co-incineration plants, incinerating also ABP and DP, following the environmental legislation requirements.

The FARS is responsible for collecting the products of animal origin confiscated from the personal luggage of passengers travelling internationally and the subsequent notification to the Veterinary Hygiene Service of the National Veterinary Institute, which in turn collects such materials on the request of the competent Customs Authorities.
The IRSAFHF is responsible for controls on placing on the market and use of ABP/DP as OF/SI on arable land and pastureland.

The National Veterinary Institute, and in particular its Veterinary Hygiene Service, collects fallen animals (fallen stock). This organisation, however, does not perform official controls along the ABP chain.

The audit team noted that the competent authorities are clearly designated and that all staff have the necessary legal powers to carry out control activities. This is in line with the requirements of Article 4(1) and Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5 10. Distribution of the AFSVSPP responsibilities is clearly established and all staff interviewed were aware of their roles and tasks. This complies with the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) and Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 11. The audit team obtained evidence of past training provided to staff and noted that most of the AFSVSPP staff carrying out ABP controls had received the training required to perform their tasks competently, in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 12. The AVSVSPP has developed for its staff guidance documents specific to the type of operation inspected and the official control checklists. These concern the approval, registration and authorisation process, and inspections (including sampling), often on a particular type of establishment, plant or operator handling and/or generating ABP ad DP. 13. As required by Article 5(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for the samples collected during official controls on ABP, the competent authority avails of designated official laboratories with a sufficient examination capacity. Designated laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, with the relevant methods in their scope of accreditation, except for Glyceroltriheptanoate ­ GTH, for which, the accreditation process is envisaged to be completed in 2023. 14. The internal audit system covers official controls on ABP and DP. The AFSVSPP representative stated that controls on ABP/DP were of a lower priority than controls in other areas. Hence, at least since 2015, no internal audits have been carried out in relation to ABP and DP. Conclusions on the structural elements of the official control system 15. The competent authorities avail of trained and, mostly, experienced staff, supported by a set of operating procedures and with access to an adequate laboratory capacity. This gives the competent authorities a good basis for implementing official controls along the chain of ABP and DP. 5.2 Official controls along the ABP chain 5.2.1 Registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators 16. Domestic legislation establishes rules for the registration and approval of ABP operators, establishments and plants. Application forms are available for operators applying for registration or approval. The AFSVSPP Regional Offices carry out the approval process and issue the approval decision. The audit team noted that the approval steps in place are in line with the requirements of Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 17. The audit team examined several approval files and associated records and noted that the approvals granted for the first time to ABP operators followed appropriately the approval steps. However, in two out of the three processing plants visited and operating under the full approval, the audit team noted that even though the operators made significant changes to the processing treatment subsequently to receiving the original approval, the 6 required validation of the altered ABP processing treatment and the validation checks thereof by the plants' operators and the competent authority, respectively, had not been carried out, in particular: a. in one plant, the operator using the processing method 7 for processing Category 3 material has changed the processing equipment, the processing parameters and the system for processing from batch to continuous, and b. in another plant, also applying the method 7 for processing of Category 3 material, the operator has modified the processing machinery by installing a new cooker. The absence of checks by the competent authority on the operator's validation procedures, in case of any significant alterations are made to the processing treatment, such as modifications of the machinery, is not in line with requirements of Section 2(4) in Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The AFSVSPP representatives explained that the above-mentioned deficiencies resulted from some misinterpretation of the approval requirements for already approved and operating plants. The authority undertook to expand the existing approval procedure by including instructions referring to the above situations. 18. AFSVSPP maintains the list of registered and approved ABP plants, establishments and operators and has a system in place for keeping these lists up-to-date. The audit team noted that, in line with requirements of Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the AFSVSPP: a. makes the lists publicly available by publishing them on its website (1), b. keeps the lists up-to-date, and c. ensures that the format of published lists follows the requirements of the Technical specifications (2) published by the European Commission. 19. The published lists accurately reflected the ABP operators in activity in the regions visited. Conclusions on registration, approval and listing 20. Although the national rules for approval of establishments are in line with EU requirements, they lack clarity with respect to the competent authority actions when significant alterations are made to the process in already approved ABP processing plants. This resulted in the absence of required operator's validation of the so modified processing treatment and validation checks thereof by the competent authority. text: BACKGROUND It is important that the official controls performed on animals and goods entering the EU provide adequate guarantees that they meet the requirements of EU agri-food chain legislation (4). The rules on official controls, including those on animals and goods entering the EU, are laid down in the OCR. Consignments of animals and goods listed in Article 47(1) of the OCR must be subject to official controls at the BCP of first arrival into the EU. EU Member States (hereafter `Member States') are required to designate BCPs in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 59 of the OCR. In addition, pursuant to Article 3(14) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, Member States are required to inform the Commission of any changes in the infrastructure or operation of a BCP, or of an inspection centre within that post, if such changes necessitate an update to the information previously provided to the Commission in accordance with Article 59(2) of the OCR. Lists of the designated BCPs in each Member State are available on the European Commission webpages (5). (4) Cf. Article 1(2) and (3) of the OCR. The organisation of the competent authorities responsible for official controls on animals and goods entering the EU is as described in the county profile. In summary: · The Policies on Agri-food Chain Directorate within the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Forestry (MAFF) is responsible for policy matters relating to the agri-food chain, and for coordinating implementation of policy. The Directorate also acts as the national contact point for the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed information system `iRASFF' (see section 5.1.5 below); · The Bulgarian Food Safety Agency (BFSA) under the MAFF is responsible for the implementation of official controls, including the official controls on animals and goods entering the EU; · The BFSA Border Control Directorate consists of nine departments, eight of which are the individual BCPs. The ninth, the Organisation and Management of Border Control Department, is responsible for coordinating and supervising the implementation of official controls at the BCPs. It is also responsible for issuing guidelines and instructions for performing the controls; · The BFSA has 28 Regional Food Safety Directorates (RFSDs), which form the BFSA's territorial administrative units; · The BFSA's Directorate-General for Verification of Official Controls (DGVOC), which reports directly to the Executive Director of the BFSA, is responsible for planning and performing internal audits and verification checks (see section 5.1.6 below). 2. The National Customs Agency under the Ministry of Finance (hereafter `Customs'), cooperates with the BFSA in their implementation of official controls, based on two instructions detailed in section 5.1.2 below. 3. The areas of competence of the authorities involved in official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are summarised in the following table: Area of competence BFSA Customs Animals (LA) Products of animal origin and composite products (POA-HC) Germinal products, animal by-products, derived products, hay and straw (POA-NHC) Personal consignments (Regulation (EU) No 2019/2122) 4 Area of competence BFSA Customs Non-commercial movement of pet animals (Regulation (EU) No 577/2013) Food of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at BCPs (3) (PNAO-HC(food)) Feed of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at BCPs (3) (PNAO-NHC(feed)) Food contact materials (4) (PNAO-NHC(other) 4. The competent authorities responsible for the organisation and performance of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU at BCPs have been designated in line with Article 4(1) of the OCR.

The BFSA informed the audit team that the increase in the number of consignments of goods entering the EU through BCPs in Bulgaria in 2021, noted in section 4 above, did not necessitate the allocation of additional staff resources for the BCPs.

There is a network of 19 laboratories, including national reference laboratories, which the BFSA stated have been designated in accordance with Article 37 of the OCR for the analysis of samples taken during official controls, including those on animals and goods entering the EU. The BFSA has published a list of the designated laboratories (7), all of which are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between authorities

The BFSA informed the audit team that the cooperation and communication with Customs is based on two agreements, which have been in place since 2012. Neither of the agreements had been updated to include references to the OCR and its implementing and delegated acts. The BFSA informed the team that it was in the process of updating both at the time of the audit.

The agreements include procedures for carrying out joint actions and the exchange of information relevant to official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. An information system has been developed based on the agreements, to automate the exchange of information between the BFSA and Customs on consignments of animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU, which is detailed in section 5.1.5 below.
The BSFA also has access to other information systems at port and airport BCPs such as Customs' and operators' manifests, as detailed in section 5.1.5 below.

The audit team noted that, based on documented evidence provided by the BFSA and Customs, the authorities cooperate for the official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR.
