The audit team also noted that there are mechanisms in place that, based on evidence obtained during the audit, ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between the BFSA at central level and the staff performing official controls at the BCPs, which is in line with Article 4(2) of the OCR. 5.1.3 Training of staff 12. The BFSA stated that BCP staff performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU must be appropriately qualified, which is ensured by having minimum education requirements as a pre-condition for employment, and the provision of post- employment internal and external training courses, including those provided by the Commission-funded Better Training for Safer Food Initiative (8), and on-the-job training delivered by experienced official veterinarians. 13. All controls on animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU at BCPs are carried out by official veterinarians, and therefore Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1081 establishing the rules on specific training requirements for staff other than veterinarians performing certain physical checks at border control posts is not applicable. 14. Documentary evidence was provided to the audit team confirming that appropriate internal and external training had been provided to BCP staff responsible for performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. The audit team noted that the competent authorities ensure that staff performing those official controls are adequately trained, in accordance with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place 15. The BFSA stated that, with limited exceptions, it did not have documented procedures in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU, including on transhipped consignments, consignments in transit and channelling of consignments, which is not in line with article 12(1) of the OCR. 16. The limited exceptions concern a documented procedure for the use of TRACES-NT in the case of unsatisfactory laboratory results for certain consignments of goods of animal origin, and a standard operating procedure for the sampling of food of animal origin, the latter of which the audit team noted had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR. 17. In contrast to finding 15, the BFSA has documented procedures in place for official controls on food of non-animal origin entering the EU, for the onward transportation and transfer to control points of consignments of food and feed of non-animal origin, and for the exchange of information in iRASFF, which is in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. A further procedure concerning the action to take for non-compliant consignments of (8) https://btsfacademy.eu/training/ 6 food of non-animal origin and food contact materials had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR. 18. The BFSA also stated there are no documented arrangements in place for the implementation of measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR, which is not in line with Article 12(1) and Article 64(3)(d) of the OCR. 19. The BFSA Border Control Directorate stated that it develops an annual risk-based monitoring plan for official controls on products of animal origin for human consumption entering the EU, as part of its National Monitoring Programme for the Control of Residues of Veterinary Medicinal Products and Environmental Contaminants in Live Animals and Products of Animal Origin 2021 (hereafter `National Monitoring Programme'). The monitoring plan does not include products of animal origin which are not intended for human consumption, or hazards other than residues and histamine. The BFSA informed the audit team that it has established a working group to review the scope of the monitoring plan for 2022, which it expects to be finalised by 31 March 2022. 20. The competent authorities informed the audit team that the organisation of official controls is broadly as described in the country profile for Spain. In summary, the competent authorities comprise: · The Ministry of Health (MS - Ministerio de Sanidad), which has principal responsibility for food safety, and through its Subdirectorate-General for External Health, for the official controls on food of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU; · The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (MAPA - Ministerio de Agricultura, Pesca y Alimentación), which has principal responsibility for the official controls on live animals, goods of animal origin not intended for human consumption and feed of non-animal origin entering the EU. 2. The Spanish Tax Administration Agency (Agencia Tributaria) and its designated customs offices (hereafter `Customs') cooperate with the competent authorities in their implementation of official controls of animals and goods entering the EU, based on cooperation agreements detailed in section 5.1.2 below. In the event that Customs identify any suspected non-compliance with EU requirements during their activities, they detain the consignment and notify the relevant competent authority. Customs may require that such consignments be destroyed at the expense and risk of the person responsible for the consignment. 3. The areas of competence of the authorities involved in official controls on animals and goods entering the Union are summarised in the following table: Area of competence MS MAPA Customs Animals (LA) (a) Products of animal origin and composite products (POA-HC) (b) Germinal products, animal by-products, derived products, hay and straw (POA-NHC) Personal consignments (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122) Non-commercial movement of pet animals (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 577/2013) 4 Area of competence MS MAPA Customs Food of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control posts (2) (PNAO-HC(food)) Feed of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control posts (2) (PNAO-NHC(feed)) Food contact materials (3) (PNAO-NHC(other)) Key: (a) Including live insects, live terrestrial snails, live fish, molluscs and crustaceans intended for direct human consumption or processing and molluscs for relaying. (b) Animal by-products for the pharmaceutical, cosmetic or medical device industry and for the control of catering waste from cross-border means of transport. 4. The competent authorities responsible for the organisation and performance of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Spain have been designated in line with Article 4(1) of the OCR. 5. The Ministry of Territorial Policy (MPT - Ministerio de Política Territorial y Función Pública) has administrative responsibility for staff responsible for performing official controls at BCPs on animals and goods entering the EU. The MPT informed the audit team that, in anticipation of additional responsibilities resulting from the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the EU, and in response to changes in trade noted in section 4 above, the total number of full-time equivalent staff at BCPs increased from 156 in 2019, to 239 in 2022. Of particular note, the staff at the BCPs Madrid Airport and Bilbao Port, which were visited by the audit team, increased from 22 to 29 and from 4 to 9 respectively during that period, while the number of staff at the BCP Algeciras Port increased from 23 to 35.

The audit team noted, based on the evidence obtained during the audit, that there are mechanisms in place which ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between and within authorities for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Spain, in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR. 5.1.3 Training of staff

The competent authorities informed the audit team that staff performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU at BCPs must be suitably qualified and experienced in line with Article 5(2) of the OCR, which is ensured by established pre- conditions for employment, including educational and professional experience, and the provision of regular internal and external training. The training provided to such staff since 2019 included courses provided by the Commission-funded Better Training for Safer Food Initiative (10), and on-the-job training delivered by experienced officials and external experts including from the Spanish Food Safety and Nutrition Agency (Agencia Española de Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutrición).
The MS informed the audit team that it is also developing an e-learning course for newly recruited staff, which it plans to launch in 2023.

The competent authorities provided documentary evidence that confirmed the fulfilment of the pre-entry educational and working experience requirements for officials performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, and that internal and external training had been provided to BCP staff responsible for such controls, which is in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. The audit team also noted during their visits to the BCPs, that recently recruited staff had been provided with training as detailed above.

The MS stated that technical staff assist official veterinarians in the performance of official controls within its area of competence, and that those staff receive training in line with the obligations and requirements laid down in Articles 2 and 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1081. MAPA stated that all official controls within its area of competence, are carried out by official veterinarians only, and therefore that Regulation is not applicable. MAPA and the MS have issued a range of guidelines and documented procedures for performing official controls on consignments of animals and products of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU through BCPs in Spain.
The audit team noted that, with two exceptions, the guidelines and documented procedures had been updated where appropriate, in particular following the introduction of the OCR.

The two exceptions concerned the MS protocol for performing physical checks on food of animal origin and the protocol for sampling on food of animal origin for laboratory testing, which were issued in 2011 and 2015 respectively, which had not been updated in line with Article 12(2) of the OCR.

The audit team also noted that the guidance for the selection of items or packages provided in those two protocols was not in line with the percentage of items or packages in a consignment of products of animal origin and the maximum number of items or packages specified in point 4 (b) of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. Similarly, the guidance for the selection of items or packages for the performance of identity checks of products of animal origin, was not in line with Article 3(3) of the same Regulation (See also finding 64).

The MS develops a risk-based Annual Surveillance Plan for goods for human use or consumption from third countries, which establishes a schedule with an estimate of the number of samples and analyses to be carried out, based on data from iRASFF and the results of controls carried out in the previous year. The sampling frequencies in the Monitoring Plan are entered into a specific information technology system of the MS (`SISAEX') that identifies those consignments that should be checked at the BCPs in accordance with the Monitoring Plan. The plan is updated in the event that new hazards are identified as a result of the surveillance.

MAPA establishes an annual sampling plan for products of animal origin not intended for human consumption. The annual sampling plan is based on a risk assessment, which takes account of notifications in the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed information system (`iRASFF') and the results of controls of goods entering the EU through BCPs in Spain in the previous year. The resulting sampling frequencies for each product and hazard are listed in Excel tables, for use by the BCPs.

The competent authorities informed the audit team that the organisation of official controls is broadly as described in the country profile for Ireland. In summary, the competent authorities comprise: · The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), which has overall responsibility for the enforcement of food safety legislation in Ireland, apart from at the level of primary production. The FSAI manages its responsibility through service contract arrangements with other competent authorities, including the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) and the Health Service Executive (HSE); · DAFM, which is the competent authority for the official controls on animals and goods of animal origin, feed of non-animal origin and pesticide residues in food of non-animal origin listed in Annexes I and II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793, entering the EU. The Import Controls Operations Division of DAFM is responsible for the implementation of those official controls at the four BCPs. Staff from that Division also perform controls on pet animals entering Ireland and checks on catering waste from international means of transport, arriving at those four locations; and · The Environmental Health Service (EHS) of the HSE which is responsible for the official controls on food of non-animal origin (with the exception of controls for pesticide residues), and goods not intended for human consumption, such as food contact materials, entering the EU. 2. The Office of the Revenue Commissioners and its designated customs offices (hereafter `Customs') cooperate with the competent authorities in their implementation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, based on cooperation agreements detailed in section 5.1.2 below. If Customs identify any suspected non-compliance with EU requirements during their activities, they detain the consignment and notify the relevant competent authority. 3. The competent authorities informed the audit team that, as a result of the UK's withdrawal from the EU, there was a need for a substantial increase in the number of staff at BCPs. The total number of full-time equivalent DAFM posts at the BCPs was increased since 2019 from 15 to 243 at the time of the audit, while the EHS posts increased from 9 to 123. Customs also noted that they had recruited 900 additional staff since 2019 in response to the increased number of customs declarations following the UK's withdrawal from the EU.

All authorities noted that there was a shift to 24 hour/7 days a week operation at that time which, together with other factors, adversely affected both the recruitment and retention of staff at BCPs. DAFM noted for instance that 53 of the 243 allocated posts were vacant at the time of the audit, and that a recruitment process was underway.

text: The organisation of official controls of feed business operators (FeBOs) is described in the Commission services' country profile for Bulgaria (2).

In short, the BFSA under the Ministry of Agriculture is the competent authority performing official controls on feed safety and feed hygiene. Within the BFSA, the main Directorate responsible for feed control is the Feed Control and Animal By-products Directorate. This Directorate manages, controls and coordinates the activities of the Regional Food Safety Directorates (RFSDs) in the feed (1) Available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=2984 (2) Available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=BG 2 sector. These arrangements ensure that the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are met.

The staff performing the official controls receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training. The BFSA has developed a procedure for introductory training of newly appointed employees who receive initial training during the first six months after the appointment. After the initial training, all of the inspectors undergo regular trainings organised by the BFSA. In the last three years, training events covered topics related to the implementation of feed legislation (e.g., on HACCP control, official sampling, labelling, etc.). The RFSDs visited provided evidence that their feed inspectors had attended the pertinent training events. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators

The system of registration and approval of establishments and intermediaries is described in detail in part 2.4 of the country profile (see finding 1). The BFSA was seen to have provided adequate standard operating procedures (SOPs) for this purpose, addressed to the RFSDs.

The audit team examined SOP 4 (approval of FeBOs) and SOP 6 (registration of FeBOs) and saw that both SOPs provided detailed instructions on the various steps of approval and/or registration of FeBOs including the relevant requirements laid down in Articles 9, 10, 23 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

Lists of FeBOs, which are updated twice per month, are publicly available (3) and include FeBOs' activities. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 19(3) and (7) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

All of the operators selected by the audit team were registered in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed hygiene

The structure of the competent authority is clear and there is a well-established system of registration and approval of feed business operators. This is underpinned by the provision of appropriate guidance and procedures by the central competent authority and the regular training of feed inspectors. These elements contribute to the effective planning of official controls and should facilitate their effective implementation. 5.2 Planning and implementation of official controls on feed hygiene 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 Planning of inspections

The Feed Control Framework Plan includes planning of inspections (routine official control) and audits (comprehensive official controls on written procedures and functioning of the HACCP- (3) Available at: https://www.bfsa.bg/bg/Object/site_register/view/8/%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B B%20%D0%BD%D0%B0 3 system) all along the feed chain. Each RFSD develops its Regional Feed Control Framework Plan based on risk analysis and assessment. The BFSA submits harmonised risk assessment criteria to the RFSDs. The assessment criteria are based on an equation converting the risk criteria into numeric values, which provide the basis for establishing the frequencies of inspections, audits and sampling. These criteria for risk assessment and planning of official inspections in the feed sector take account of the requirements laid down in Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In general, the planned inspection frequencies of different types of FeBOs vary between twice per year to once every three years (excluding primary producers). The RFSDs carry out official controls (inspections and collecting of samples) in the form of unannounced visits. This is in line with the requirements of Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The audit team noted that the RFSDs carry out audits in form of announced visits with, in general, two weeks' notice. The audit team pointed out that while prior notice can be justified in rare cases (remote locations, irregular working hours, etc.), systematic provision of prior notice is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team noted that the number of the audits was around 20% of the total number of official inspections which partly mitigates the effect of arranging official controls with prior notice.

To facilitate harmonisation of control activities, the BFSA has prepared a set of guidance documents and checklists. The audit team reviewed several guidance documents and checklists. These documents covered matters of relevance for the premises (e.g., hygiene, cleanliness of buildings and equipment), the adequacy of the FeBOs' HACCP systems, review of the FeBOs' approval/registration, review of traceability and the FeBOs' own-sampling programme. These documents also contain information and checklists on the official inspection of labelling requirements. The documents reviewed by the audit team were suitable to support the inspectors in verifying compliance with the relevant requirements laid down by Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, and Articles 4-6, 8-20, 22-24 of, Annexes I- VIII to, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009, Article 18 of Regulations (EC) No 178/2002 and Articles 12(1), 37-39 and137-140 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.1.2 Implementation of inspections
In 2019-2021, 92-95% of the planned inspections were implemented.

The audit team examined documentation pertaining to official controls carried out in seven establishments in three different regions. Inspection and/or audit reports were available in all cases. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In all of the establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection/audit reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in five of the seven establishments. In general, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was deficient or very generic without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assessment. This issue was not reflected in any of the inspection/audit reports seen and operators were thus, unaware that there was a problem. Having said this, some of the inspectors did correctly identify these deficiencies during the interviews. 4 16. In one establishment visited the FeBO's own control plan specified a target level of contamination with heavy metals and mycotoxins in incoming feed materials (cereals) which was below the relevant legal limits for such materials. The audit team observed laboratory reports for own controls where the contamination levels exceeded the operators' specified limits (but complied with the legal limits). The operator had not noted the exceedance of its own specifications and had not taken any actions (questioning the utility of the operators' specifications and the purpose of its own controls). None of the official control reports mentioned the issue. 17. Verification of establishments' tests on homogeneity of mixing required by part 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, forms part of the inspections, when applicable. In short, the FVS under the Ministry of Agriculture is the central competent authority for the system of official controls on feed safety and feed hygiene. The staff performing the official controls receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training. After the initial training, all of the inspectors undergo regular trainings organised by the FVS. The FVS annual inspection plan includes planning of inspections (compliance checks of a product, service, process or enterprise with regulatory requirements) and audits (systematic and independent checks that the planned measures are implemented effectively) all along the feed chain. Fixed and variable criteria of risk assessment are used to determine the frequency of inspections/audits. The fixed risk criteria are the activity of the FeBO and composition/type of the feed produced. The variable risk criteria include reliability of FeBOs own check, results of previous inspections, and participation in private certification schemes. The inspection plan is developed in cooperation with the FVS Information Analysis and Emergency Response Division, which is responsible for the monitoring of fraudulent and deceptive activities. This approach is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In general, the planned inspection frequencies of different types of FeBOs vary between three per year to once every two years (excluding primary producers). Official controls are unannounced. This is in line with the requirements of Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

These farms may produce mountain cheese aged at least 60 days from raw milk that does not comply with the raw milk criteria of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 as regards plate count (PC) and somatic cell count (SCC). The same applies to milk products obtained in connection with the manufacture of cheeses used for the production of mountain butter and "mese" milk products, again under certain conditions which ensure that the purpose of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 is met. d. Derogations are in place regarding primary producers' direct supply of small amounts (up to 2500 litres/year) of colostrum to the final consumer, or to local retail establishments (article 71) and raw milk (up to 70 litres/week) to final consumer (article 77), provided that relevant general and specific requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004, are met. These derogations are in line with Article 1.2(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Article 1.3(c) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2204. e. "Local retail establishments" are defined as establishments directly supplying consumers, located in the county in which the producer's establishment is located, or in a neighbouring county. f. Producers who intend to supply consumers with small quantities of raw milk, must notify the CAB for special registration. g. Specific provisions are included in respect of record keeping by FBO of the amounts of colostrum supplied to final consumers and/or local retail and of raw milk supplied to final consumers. This activity does not require a notification to the CAB for specific registration. FBOs are also obliged to provide labelling/written information to consumers about the untreated nature of the products, and of the precautionary 4 measures to be taken. h. Article 77 allows for derogation to supply small amounts of raw milk (up to 70 litres/week) directly at the farm to the final consumer provided the requirements of points 2-4 and 6-8 of Part A, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and the specific hygiene requirements of points 3-4 of Part I, Part II and Part III of Chapter I of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) 853/2004 are adhered to. 6. LIVSFS 2009:13, SFA's rules on reporting and other certain duties of competent authorities (Livsmedelsverkets föreskrifter om rapportering och vissa andra skyldigheter för kontrollmyndigheter) establishes the national rapid alert system. 7. The specific procedures for the performance of official controls in the dairy sector are described in the relevant sections of the report. 8. The competent authorities have established comprehensive guidelines and documents to support the CAs and FBOs in their work. These are available on the SFAs and SBAs webpages (https://www.livsmedelsverket.se, https://www.jordbruksverket.se). The SFAs website "kontroll-wiki" (https://kontrollwiki.livsmedelsverket.se/) includes training material and several guidelines. The dairy industry has developed several guidelines and has consulted the SFA when developing them. For example, guidelines for the dairy industry from the Federation of Swedish Farmers (Lantbrukarnas Riksförbund, LRF) cover requirements for pre-requisites, HACCP, microbiological criteria, traceability, and laboratories and analytics. They are approved by, and available on the website of, the SFA. 9. The Swedish translation of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in respect of raw milk sampling on holdings is incorrect as it suggests holdings may be randomly selected, meaning some holdings might not be sampled at all. The SFA advised the CABs to use the English version of the Regulation regarding this point. 5 Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures 10. Legislative and administrative measures covering the dairy sector are in place and national rules provide certain derogations regarding mountain dairies for production of milk products produced with traditional methods and intended for sale in small quantities directly to the consumers and for direct supply of raw milk and colostrum. 11. Legislation and policies provide officials with the appropriate power to take enforcement actions in cases of non-compliance detected during official controls. 12. The CAs have established a comprehensive set of guidelines and instructions that support the CAs in their control tasks. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 13. The SBA is the CCA for animal health, animal by-products (ABPs) and feed, and coordinates, advises and supports controls on animal health (including on the use of medicinal products on-farm) and welfare, and is responsible for legislating those areas. 14. The SFA is as CCA responsible for governance, guidance, and legislation regarding food safety. The CAs are responsible for planning the official controls of FBOs under their responsibility. The SFA is also responsible for the approval of food establishments. SFA staff carries out inspections and audits of dairy establishments and cold stores, except for the municipalities of Stockholm and Gothenburg, which are responsible for the controls within their own jurisdiction. The SFA inspectors are also responsible for the controls of ABPs generated in food processing establishments. Controls of ABPs had not been included in the annual control plans of dairy establishments until 2021, when ABPs were included in the operative control plan under "basic controls"(baskontroller) for all types of establishments controlled by SFA handling more than 20 kg of ABPs/week. The control area ABP is included in the control plan at least every third year. 15. Within the SFA the Science Division is responsible for risk and benefit assessment, biology and chemistry. The Control division is responsible for the controls of the food industry, border controls, and control support. The Governance and Guidance Division manages controls and is also responsible for EU coordination, and export. The Strategic and Support Division covers communication, legal affairs, IT and service evaluation. It is among other tasks responsible for crisis management and human resources. 16. SFA inspectors operate in teams responsible for 5 geographical areas and one team responsible for border controls. The SFA has local offices in 16 locations of the country 6 but not all of them are fully equipped. 17. The regional CA comprises the CABs, which are responsible for the controls on primary production, including controls of premises and equipment, hygiene, raw milk quality in primary production, etc. They also carry out controls on animal welfare, use of veterinary drugs and ABP controls (plants, transport). The CABs report annually on their control activities to the SFA. As CABs organise their control responsibilities in primary production and tasks under their responsibility independently, the 3 CABs reviewed by the audit team were all organised slightly differently. 18. The Administrative Procedure Act (SFS 2017:900, Förvaltningslag), contains provisions to ensure the CAs impartiality, and regulates potential conflict of interest, and requires the CAs to co-operate with other CAs within their area of responsibility. 19. Several structures and groups have been established to allow co-ordination and exchange of information within and between the SFA, SBA and the CABs: a. SFA organises monthly assessment meetings for the heads of inspection teams to discuss control situations encountered, and their assessments. Dairy topics were, however, discussed relatively seldom. b. The "Reference Group for Food and Feed" under the "Group 28", comprising representatives from the CABs, meet representatives from the SFA Governance and Guidance Division, from the SVA and from SBA monthly for information and guidance on different topics related to the primary production of food and feed. c. The "Group 28" CAB network comprises members of all 28 counties. Minutes of the meetings were available. Various topics are discussed regularly, including general matters (resources, competencies, audits), and specific food and feed ones. d. The SBA and SFA organise, together with the CAB network for veterinary matters and animal welfare ("Group 28") bi-annual meetings to exchange information on relevant developments on management level. e. The SFA organises specific meetings (bedömningsmöte) to discuss the judging of audit and inspection outcomes and classification of findings. f. A specific milk support group within SFA's Control Division in organises regular meetings to discuss dairy control topics. The group meets several times annually and minutes are available. The group has a specific question and answers session on their web link. g. The SFA and the two municipalities Stockholm and Gothenburg organise meetings together to discuss food control matters. Minutes of the meetings were available. 20. However, at county level, there is little co-ordination between the SFA inspectors and CAB inspectors regarding controls of the dairy sector. Both CAs are carrying out controls over the sector, with clearly defined different responsibilities which interface regarding control of raw milk. For example, dairy holdings that also have a small dairy on the site are visited by the CAB inspectors for primary production and the SFA inspectors visit the dairy processing plant. When the audit team asked the SFA responsible for such plants 7 about the raw milk quality, the inspector stated this was the responsibility of the CAB. 21. SFA, SBA and the CABs organise regular training for inspection staff. Introduction material and guidance documents are available to new staff, who start by joint inspections and audits with experienced colleagues. The support group "Milk" introduces the new SFA staff to dairy controls and audits. 22. An e-learning package called CAB Days 2020 (Länsstyrelsedagarna 2020), consisting of 14 different presentations with focus on primary production and its official controls, including control of milk production. The package covers the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004, contains frequently asked questions and addresses controls topics with frequent non compliances. It comprises the control of veterinary medical products, traceability, sampling by primary producers and the national legislation about direct deliveries of small quantities of raw milk and colostrum. 23. In September 2019 a web-meeting was organised for all CAB, to deal with frequently asked questions regarding the raw milk criteria laid down in Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, and their control. 24. Several SFA, CAB staff members and municipal authorities have participated in Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) courses relevant for the controls on the dairy sector. 25. The CAs can take enforcement measures and impose penalties (see paragraph 4) and enforcement actions have been taken by different CAs over the years (see paragraph 102). 26. The CAs use several IT tools to plan and document their controls. For example, the CABs use "PRIMÖR" and "PLATINA" to plan and collect information on risk-based controls on primary production. The tools allow them access data of the primary producers in their county. The SFA uses "360" and the "PIMLO" (Planering inom och mellan Lagstiftningsomrade) and can access data on national level regarding approved dairy establishments. Regarding raw milk ­ an interfacing control area between SFA and CABs ­ access to each other's databases would be useful. However, the law on data protection prevents different CAs from accessing data available in IT tools of the other CA. 8 Conclusions on Competent authorities 27. The responsibilities for the controls on milk and dairy products are clearly designated. 28. Provisions are in place to exclude potential conflicts of interest. 29. Training programmes and information available are adequate to enable inspection staff to carry out the controls effectively, and to keep their knowledge up-to-date. 30. Several fora and structures within and between different CAs enable exchange of general information but such structures are not mirrored at county and local level between the SFA and CABs although both CAs control tasks interface regarding are involved in control of raw milk and this would contribute to effective and efficient coordination and cooperation between the CAs in line with Article 5.5 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.3 REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 31. The SFA is the CA for approval of dairy establishments, whereas the municipal authorities are the CA for food businesses that only need to be registered. The SFA's website contains general information on registration and approval, including information on small quantities. 32. A FBO must apply to SFA for approval using a standard form, and a specific appendix for dairy plants; if all information required is included, the SFA carries out at pre-approval inspection. If the FBO passes the inspection, the plant is approved and can start production. The possibility of a conditional approval exists but is seldom used. The CA has to carry out an additional inspection within 3 months to check how the FBOs HACCP is working. Reports of these inspections were available. T

text: INTRODUCTION The audit of the official control system for residues of veterinary medicinal products, pesticides and contaminants in live animals and animal products was conducted from 15 to 25 November 2022 as part of the European Commission's Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety's 2022 work programme. The audit team comprised two auditors from the Commission. The audit was conducted as a hybrid exercise with a mixture of remote meetings (by videoconference) and on-site visits. An opening meeting (by videoconference) was held on 15 November 2022 with representatives of the central competent authority (Food and Veterinary Service (FVS) of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food) and the national laboratory carrying out testing under Residue Control Plan (RCP) (the Institute of Food Safety, Animal Health and Environment (BIOR). In this meeting the objectives, itinerary and the reporting procedures for the audit were confirmed. During the on-site component, the audit team was accompanied by representatives from the FVS and visited three Territorial Structural Units (TSUs) of the FVS, and the BIOR.

OBJECTIVES OF THE AUDIT The objective of the audit was to evaluate the planning and implementation of monitoring of residues of veterinary medicinal products, pesticides and contaminants in live animals and animal products in the context of preventing, eliminating, or reducing to acceptable levels the risk to humans and animals either directly or through the environment. The principal audit criteria against which fulfilment of the above objective was assessed comprised: · Annexes I-IV to Council Directive 96/23/EC (1), and (1) Although Directive 96/23/EC is no longer in force, having been repealed by Article 146 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Article 150 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requires competent authorities to continue to perform official controls necessary to detect the presence of the substances and groups of residues listed in Annex I to Directive 96/23/EC, in accordance with Annexes II, III and IV to that Directive until 14 December 2022. iii · Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council. A full list of relevant European Union (EU) requirements is set out in Annex II. The audit focused on the legal and administrative measures in place in Latvia to implement the relevant EU requirements and on the performance of the competent authority in meeting these requirements during the period 2019 to 2022. text: BACKGROUND The Commission services last audited the implementation of official controls on residues and contaminants, and the use of veterinary medicinal products, in Latvia in 2013 (3). The report of that audit made four recommendations, all of which were closed due to actions taken.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1. Competent authorities 1. The organisation of the official control system for residues of veterinary medicinal products, pesticides and contaminants in live animals and animal products is described in the Commission services' country profile for Latvia (4). 2. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food is responsible for drawing up legislation and policy development. The FVS is responsible for the planning and implementation of the RCP. Authorised inspectors from the 11 TSUs are responsible for carrying-out sampling under the RCP and follow-up of non-compliant results. These arrangements are in line with EU requirements (5). Planning of residue control programme 3. National legislation (6) sets rules for the control of residues in live animals and animal products, which are further explained in a `Procedure for determining the number of samples/tests for laboratory examination' (7). 4. In October of each calendar year the responsible person of the FVS starts the preparation of the draft RCP for the following year, which is then transferred to other FVS departments and experts, for consultation. 5. The planning methodology does not include the identification of risks. It is purely based on production volumes or the numbers of registered establishments. This absence of risk-based planning is neither in line with pertinent EU requirements (8) nor with national legal requirements (9) which stipulate that the quantity and range of veterinary medicinal products distributed in Latvia in the previous calendar year, and the residues of such substances in animals, feed, products, and water shall be considered. The competent authority had no information on the sale of veterinary medicinal products in Latvia (10).

Whilst the RCPs for 2019 to 2022 that were submitted to the European Commission indicated that non-compliant results from previous years were taken into account to increase the sample numbers (especially for eggs), this was not the case in practice. For certain substance groups with a relatively high number of non-compliant results (e.g. for salinomycin and toltrazuril in eggs), neither the sample numbers for coccidiostats nor the frequency of testing for these particular substances had been changed. Furthermore, egg production increased year by year.

To establish the number of the RCP samples, the following data sources are used: · the annual Agricultural Reports of the Ministry of Agriculture (11), · public information on slaughtered animals on the website of the Agricultural Data Centre (12), · information on the number of establishments registered in the FVS database.

While in line with EU requirements (13), the national legal requirements (14) and the related procedure (15) both indicate that Latvian and other Member States products of animal origin shall be sampled. This was not enforced. Planned sample numbers for bovine, ovine and porcine animals and poultry were based solely on the number of animals of Latvian origin slaughtered, without considering the number of animals traded/moved into Latvia for slaughter. Following the consultation with other FVS departments, the calculated sample numbers are allocated to the 11 TSUs. With the exception of samples to be taken at slaughterhouses, for which production figures per establishment are available, the samples for all other commodities are allocated based on the number of establishments registered in the FVS database (16), in relation to the territory covered by the TSU. For milk, while production figures and the number of dairy cows would be available, it is only the number of farms which is considered in the distribution of samples.

The BIOR is consulted on the preliminary monthly breakdown of samples to be taken and analysed. It also proposes new substances to be included in the plan. In 2019, 27 antibiotic substances were newly introduced, following the first results of a scientific project it conducted related to antimicrobial resistance.

Following the changes to the draft plan after the comments received from the TSUs and from experts of the central office, the RCP is officially approved by order of the State Chief Food and Veterinary Inspector. For the 2022 plan this occurred on 14 January 2022 (17). The approved RCP is sent to the TSUs via the Document Management System (DMS). The plan for a given year contains specific guidelines for sampling.

The audit team observed that the sample numbers planned for 2019-2021 were with one exception in line with the relevant EU requirements (18) including those concerning the testing of 70% of the milk and egg samples for compounds from specific substance groups (19). Across all the commodities, the range of the analytes covered within the substance groups was generally broad.

The audit team noted that, in general, sampling is, at the planning stage, spread over the year for those commodities produced throughout the entire year, and is seasonal for honey and game. This is in line with applicable EU legal requirements (20).

The selection of holdings to be sampled is within the competence of each TSU office, which decides on the farms and establishments to be sampled. Sampling was assigned well in advance to farms and establishments randomly chosen from those planned for various routine inspections during the month. Production volumes, previous non- compliant test results, the outcome of previous routine inspections on farms, quality parameters of raw milk, change of activity type of the operators/farms, etc., are factors which are not considered in the planning, however. This is not in line with applicable EU requirements (21). Conclusions on planning of residue monitoring

Implementation of the residue control plan 17. As required by EU legislation (22), written procedures are available to the staff responsible for sampling. In line with EU rules (21)(23) the national legal requirements (24) cover measures to ensure that sampling is targeted, unforeseen and unexpected. It is indicated in the text which risk factors the sampling officer should consider when choosing the animal or group of animals to be sampled, including the possible use of veterinary medicines, the state of health of the animal and its behaviour. 18. Methodological guidelines exist for the sampling of products of animal origin in general, and for cow's milk, blood, and urine samples. They include the requirement for a targeted selection of the animals to be sampled and describe how samples should be taken, the equipment to be used as well as the storage and transport of samples.

In the three TSUs visited, sampling was in most of the cases examined neither targeted nor performed without prior notice being given to the operator. Most of the samples were taken randomly by food inspectors (at slaughterhouses and from honey) and by veterinary inspectors (for eggs, milk, fish). This is not in line with EU requirements (25).

While national procedures clearly state that, in line with applicable EU legal requirements (26), RCP samples can only be taken by trained and authorised sampling officers, this was not always the case. In one TSU, samples were regularly taken by official veterinarians engaged in ante- and post-mortem inspection at slaughter. Whilst these veterinarians were likely capable of carrying out the sampling correctly, they had not been trained for the task. This is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (27).

Contrary to applicable EU requirements (21), the choice of animals to be sampled was not risk-based but random with no justification given. For aquaculture finfish, sampling was carried out exclusively at processing plants on fish ready to be placed on the market and not at all stages of production, as required by EU legislation, which stipulates that, for Group A (illegal) substances, samples must be taken from fish at all stages of farming (28).

The audit team noted that, in two visited TSUs, sometimes it happened that a single sample taken was registered in the records as several individual samples that were originally planned. Therefore, the number of samples actually collected was lower than the number indicated in the plan.

Sampling procedures for all commodities ensure that samples can be traced back to the farm of origin, which is in line with pertinent legal requirements (29). (22) Articles 9 and 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. (23) Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In line with legal requirements (30), after sampling, the inspector draws up a sampling report, which must accompany the sample to the laboratory. The samples are transported to the laboratory or a collection point by sampling inspector.

The audit team noted that the central level of the FVS provides the TSUs with necessary and suitable materials and equipment for sampling. The inspector packages the samples in suitable containers and seals the package. While the seals and sealing presented to the auditors did not ensure a fully tamper-proof packaging, as required in EU legislation (31), all samples in transport remain under the custody of officials or testing laboratory (see also finding 43).

The audit team scrutinised several sampling and laboratory reports and saw that most of the samples had arrived at the laboratory either on the day of sampling or very soon thereafter. Upon receipt of the samples, the laboratory divides them into two equivalent sub-samples to ensure compliance with relevant EU legal requirements (32).

The audit team noted that although sample turnaround times are not monitored by the FVS, the numerous examples seen demonstrated that samples were tested promptly, thus minimising the effect of any time-dependent analyte instability.

During the last three years, several internal audits on official controls in different sectors, including those on residues, were carried out. Findings were related to the citation of outdated legal references in certain documents. In some cases, it was found that the statements of compliance of the analytical test results did not comply with the requirements laid down in internal procedures. Corrective actions were taken within the deadlines. This procedure can be considered as satisfying relevant EU legal requirements (33). Conclusions on implementation of the RCP

In general, the RCP is implemented as planned. The majority of samples however, are taken with prior notice being given to the operators and in many cases are selected randomly, rather than being targeted as required by EU legislation and national legal requirements. Collectively these shortcomings in implementation weaken the effectiveness of residues controls. 5.4. Other residue testing programmes

In addition to the RCP, residues testing is carried out under: a) the programme `For laboratory control of products of the poultry sector' (34) - control of heavy metals in poultry and eggs. b) the programme `For control of foodstuffs for export' (35) ­ to verify operator compliance with criteria laid down by the importing countries.

Latvian legislation (36) lays down specific requirements for the self-control of residues in raw milk. In accordance with the procedures, results are submitted to the Agricultural Data Centre. Follow-up of non-compliant results 34. In line with EU legislation (37), the guidelines for actions to be taken by sampling officers in the case of non-compliant results are provided in a compulsory instruction (38). This was recently updated and contains detailed instructions on the follow-up measures to be put in place after the detection of a non-compliant result. These include on-farm inspections, follow-up sampling, movement controls and fines. 35. In the case of non-compliant results, the laboratory records the results in a dedicated database. Results are assessed by the sampling officers who took the samples. In accordance with the compulsory instruction, the veterinary inspectors and food inspectors prepare and send a statement of compliance of the test results to the central office of the competent authority. 36. In the three TSUs visited, there were delays in the identification of non-compliances. In one case (up to one year after having received the result), the non-compliance (chloramphenicol) was overlooked by the inspector in charge. It was discovered by the central competent authority in the framework of result collection and transmission to the European Food Safety Authority. In the other cases, the delays occurred when the inspector in charge was absent. In none of the TSUs visited was the evaluation of test results regularly supervised. 37. Out of the non-compliant results detected between 2019 and 2022 (to date), the auditors evaluated 12 files from five different TSUs. The following observations were made: a. sample submission to the laboratory, completion of analyses and transmission of test results were timely; b. the assessment of the results was, in some cases, performed with delays ranging from four days to four weeks, while the instructions indicate that this task should be performed within a maximum of three days from receipt of the result; c. in the chloramphenicol case mentioned above, no follow-up measure was deemed to be necessary given that a year had elapsed before it was identified; d. the operators were in nearly all cases immediately informed of the non-compliant result and for the follow-up inspections, in some cases, prior notice was given to the animal holding/food business operator. This is not in line with applicable EU requirements (39); e. follow-up investigations were undertaken in most of the cases very promptly. The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Czechia are described in sections 1 and 2.11 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Czechia (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/CZ). In summary: the CISTA is the competent authority (CA) for plant health in the meaning of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Amongst its other tasks, the CISTA's Section of Seed, Planting Material and Plant Health is responsible for the coordination and implementation of the plant passport system including the registration and authorisation of professional operators. Its seven regional departments are responsible for control of professional operators. 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

According to the CA the following legal acts are relevant in the context of the audit: · The Plant Health Law No. 326/2004 includes details for registration and authorisation of professional operators, and requirements regarding the plant passport system. · The Implementing Decree No. 5/2020 further specifies the authorisation for issuance of plant passports. 5.1.3 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

Coordination meetings are organised twice a year with the participation of the regional plant health coordinators to ensure uniform and harmonised interpretation and application of the EU requirements. Regular trainings are provided for the inspectors on plant health topics, including the plant passport system. The training material and the minutes of the coordination meetings are available on the internal workspace of the CISTA, as well as the video records of these trainings and meetings.

The CISTA developed a checklist that shall be used by the inspectors during their official controls for plant passports to verify whether the authorised operators comply with EU requirements. The checklist contains the elements listed in Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The CISTA issued a collection of guidelines, containing detailed documented procedures for inspectors on plant health matters, including the plant passport system. The procedures regarding the content of the plant passports contain some differences from the requirements of Article 83(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. For commodities originating in Czechia intended for the domestic market, the CISTA does not require that plant passports issued by authorised operators contain the code of the MS of origin. 3 5. The Audit and Quality Management Department of the CISTA carries out internal audits as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The latest audit that covered specific parts of the plant health regulation, including the registration of professional operators and the implementation of the plant passport system, was carried out in 2023. This audit did not identify shortcomings. 6. The CISTA verifies the implementation of legal requirements by their inspectors in the form of supervised plant health specific inspections. The reports provided by the CISTA identified weaknesses and contained recommendations. The checklist mentioned in finding 4 was developed to prevent further occurrence of some shortcomings related to official controls on authorised operators. 7. The website and the Plant Health Portal of the CISTA contain comprehensive information for operators about the implementation of the plant passport requirements. They also function as the platform for technical guidance on the criteria to be fulfilled by authorised operators in their examinations relating to the issuance of plant passports. All elements required by Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 are accessible for professional operators. The CISTA makes available templates for professional operators for recording examinations, for identification and monitoring of critical points of their production process, to prepare their action plan and pest risk management plan. In addition, the CISTA prepared detailed manuals for authorised operators to support them to carry out their examinations. 8. A specific e-learning platform with comprehensive training material is developed for operators who request authorisation for issuance of plant passports. The e-learning course is finished with the completion of a test. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the control system related to plant passports 9. The official procedures provide an appropriate basis for the CA to implement controls consistently. The training system and the information shared by the CA ensure that authorised operators have access to the necessary information to meet their legal obligations. 10. Minor inconsistencies in the application of some plant passport requirements mean that Czechia does not implement all the rules in line with the requirements established by EU legislation. 5.2 REGISTRATION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS Legal requirements Articles 65 to 68 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 4 Findings 5.2.1 Official registration 11. Professional operators request their registration from the CISTA. The official register is based on the unique business registration number, this ensures that professional operators are registered only once as required by Article 65(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. A standard application form which contains all elements listed in Article 66(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is available at the website of the CISTA. Where relevant, registered operators can use the same form to request authorisation for issuing plant passports. The list of registered operators is published on the website of the CISTA (https://eagri.cz/public/app/eagriapp/ro/Prehled/). 5.2.2 Application of exemptions provided for in EU law 12. Professional operators who supply small quantities of plants, plant products and other objects exclusively and directly to final users by means other than sales through distance contract are not required to be registered. The "small quantity" is not formally defined in the national legislation or in any of the official guidelines, but in Czechia it is considered that sales directly to final consumers always constitutes small quantities. Conclusions on the registration of professional operators 13. There is a system in place for the registration of professional operators as required by EU legislation. The registration procedure and the proper application of the exceptions provide the CA with up-to-date information on the operators subject to official controls. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures 14. At the time of the audit, Czechia had 5 140 registered operators of which 1 176 were authorised to issue plant passports, and 27 of them also authorised to issue plant passports into PZs. 15. Authorisation may be carried out together with the registration. Before the authorisation is granted, operators shall participate in an e-learning course providing general and technical guidance which is finished with the completion of a test. Operators shall pass 5 the test within 30 days from the date of receiving an invitation to take the online test. However, the test only contains questions regarding the general knowledge concerning plant passports and related issues and is not adequate to verify whether operators possess the knowledge required by EU law (see also finding 16). 16. Before the authorisation is granted, phytosanitary inspectors carry out an official control at the operators' premises to verify: · that an effective plan to be followed in case of any suspected occurrence or finding of regulated pests is available, · that they possess or have access to the necessary equipment and facilities for the performance of the required examinations of the plant, plant product or other object, and also possess the capacity to take the measures to prevent the spread of regulated pests, · that a contact person responsible for the communication with the competent authority is appointed, · that systems and procedures are in place to fulfil obligations concerning traceability. The CA does not sufficiently verify whether operators possess the necessary knowledge concerning the signs, symptoms, and the means to prevent the spread of regulated pests, and to carry out the examinations as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions 17. Inspectors of the CISTA carry out official controls on authorised operators at least once per year to verify compliance with the relevant EU requirements. The controls include the examination of plants required to be accompanied by plant passports present at the operators' premises. Sampling and testing are done in case of the suspected presence of regulated pests. The audit team observed that the controls are carried out at appropriate times with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of relevant pests or signs or symptoms thereof. In addition, in the case of plants for planting subject to EU Marketing Directives, examinations during the growing period by official inspectors are sometimes combined with the official controls (see also section 5.4.2). 18. The CISTA may decide to reduce the frequency of official controls to one in every two years. Based on the application and the pest risk management plan of authorised operators, phytosanitary inspectors carry out an on-site control to verify if the plan is effective and complies with Article 91(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Authorised operators tailor the template recommended by the CISTA to prepare their pest risk management plan. The application of reduced frequency of official controls is in line with Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66. 6 19. During the official controls observed by the audit team, the inspectors used the checklist developed by the CISTA (see finding 4) to verify whether authorised operators comply with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The audit team noted the following: · The inspectors asked all questions listed in the checklist. · In general, authorised operators used the templates recommended by the CISTA for recording examinations, for identification and monitoring of critical points of their production process, to prepare their action plan and pest risk management plan. · In the case of plants for planting of fruit trees and seed potatoes, inspectors accepted that the operator records only the official examinations as own controls or did not record any examinations. Consequently, inspectors did not consistently verify if authorised operators carry out meticulous examination to show that their plants, plant products and other objects fulfil the EU requirements, and whether the results of these examinations have been recorded and stored for at least three years, as required by Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. · Although there was a related question in their checklist, phytosanitary inspectors did not consistently verify whether authorised operators possess the necessary knowledge to carry out such examinations as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports 20. There is a system in place for the authorisation and supervision of professional operators to issue plant passports which has all the elements required by EU legislation. 21. The compliance with EU requirements by professional operators who applied to issue plant passport is not appropriately verified during the authorisation procedure and the annual official controls. Therefore, there is a risk that plant passports are issued by professional operators who do not possess the necessary knowledge to carry out examinations, potentially increasing the phytosanitary risks of plants moved within the EU. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 7 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators 22. In general, authorised operators or their employee, who passed the test required for authorisation, carry out examinations of plants for regulated pests. Based on the records provided to the audit team, the examinations were carried out at appropriate times with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of relevant pests or signs or symptoms thereof. However, as mentioned under finding 19, the audit team met authorised operators who did not carry out and record these examinations contrary to Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators 23. The CISTA explained that the CA carries out the examinations when the presence of regulated pests is suspected or where they shall be carried out in the immediate vicinity of the operators' premises by. Examinations for seeds falling under EU marketing legislation and subject to quality certification are carried out by official or authorised seed inspectors. In the case of seed potatoes, examinations in the field are carried out by official seed inspectors. The examination of plants present at the operators' premises is part of the annual official control. 24. The inspectors met were aware of the EU requirements and the regulated pests. The audit team noted that these examinations are done in line with the documented procedures of the CISTA at appropriate time with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of pests, their signs or symptoms. However, verification of the examinations carried out by authorised operators was not consistently done by the inspectors, contrary to Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 19). 5.4.3 Examinations in relation to the protected zones 25. There were no PZs designated in Czechia at the time of the audit, however, plants are moved from Czechia into PZs of other MS. There are BZs designated in line with point 9(d) of Annex X of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 from where host plants of Erwinia amylovora are moved to PZs. The CA carries out two inspections every year in the places of production in the BZs. In both cases, the inspectors examine the host plants of Erwinia amylovora in the place of production. During the second examination, samples are taken to test for the latent infection of Erwinia amylovora. Additional examinations are carried out in the 500 m vicinity of the places of production. If the pest is detected, the symptomatic plants are destroyed and the issuance of plant passports for PZ is prohibited. 8 Conclusions on examinations for the issuance of plant passports 26. The CA carries out examinations of plants of operators authorised to issue plant passports. However, phytosanitary inspectors do not always verify whether authorised operators carry out the examinations required by EU law. As a result, they cannot be sure that the operators meet their responsibility regarding plant health safety. 5.5 ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS, INCLUDING RECORD KEEPING Legal requirements Articles 69, 70 and 87 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 in its entirety Regulation (EU) 2019/827 in its entirety Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.5.1 Issuance of plant passports by competent authorities 27. The CA issues less than ten plant passports a year, since almost all operators who are required to do so, are authorised. 28. Plants and plant products introduced from third countries and required to be accompanied by plant passports are transferred from the border control post to the premises of registered operators in Czechia with a copy of the CHEDPP. This procedure is not in line with the requirements of Article 94 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. In such cases phytosanitary certificates shall be replaced either by a plant passport or by a certified copy of the phytosanitary certificate at the point of entry or at places designated according to EU law to carry out import inspections. Such consignments were not released by Czechia to other MS during 2022 and 2023. 5.5.2 Issuance of plant passports by authorised operators 29. Practically all plant passports, including those combined with certification labels, are issued by authorised operators in Czechia under the supervision of the CA. In line with EU requirements, the application of the term "trade unit" in Article 2(8) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 is not limited, it can be one plant or even a whole consignment with any combination of species and origins, provided that the traceability is guaranteed. The traceability code can be any kind of code used by the authorised operator to identify each trade unit. 30. The plant passports provided to the audit team during the on-site visits were clearly legible, easily visible, unchangeable, and durable and their content and format were largely compliant with Article 83(1) to (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. text: BACKGROUND It is important that the official controls performed on animals and goods entering the EU provide adequate guarantees that they meet the requirements of EU agri-food chain legislation (4). The rules on official controls, including those on animals and goods entering the EU, are laid down in the OCR. Consignments of animals and goods listed in Article 47(1) of the OCR must be subject to official controls at the BCP of first arrival into the EU. EU Member States (hereafter Member States) are required to designate BCPs in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 59 of the OCR. In addition, pursuant to Article 3(14) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, Member States are required to inform the Commission of any changes in the infrastructure or operation of a BCP, or of an inspection centre within that post, if such changes necessitate an update to the information previously provided to the Commission in accordance with Article 59(2) of the OCR. Lists of the designated BCPs in each Member State are available on the European Commission webpages (5). The Commission services carry out regular audits of Member States' implementation of (4) Cf. The Commission maintains country profiles for Member States, which provide an overview of the organisation of the official control systems, based on information provided by the competent authorities. The country profile for Portugal is available at the following link: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/PT. Unless stated otherwise, data cited in this report were provided by the competent authorities. DG(SANTE) 2018-6329): https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/4021 3 5 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. The competent authorities stated that the organisation of official controls is as described in the Commission's country profile. In summary: · The Directorate-General for Food and Veterinary (Direcão-Geral de Alimentacão e Veterinária ­ DGAV) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food (Ministero da Agricultura e Alimentacão) is the central competent authority for the official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. The DGAV Central Services are responsible for planning and coordinating the implementation of those official controls; · The official controls on animals, goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin are implemented by the relevant Regional Food and Veterinary Directorates of DGAV (Direção de Serviços de Alimentação e Veterinária da Região - DSAVR) or Autonomous Region (Azores and Madeira), while those on food of non-animal origin and food contact materials are implemented by the relevant Regional Directorates of Agriculture and Fisheries (Direçõa Regionais de Agricultura e Pescas ­ DRAP), or Autonomous Regions (AR); · The Customs Authority of the Ministry of Finance (Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira - hereafter `Customs') is responsible for official controls at points of entry on passengers' personal luggage and postal and courier services. 2. The areas of competence of the authorities involved in official controls on animals and goods entering the Union are summarised in the following table: Area of competence Competent authority Animals (LA) DGAV Products of animal origin and composite products (POA-HC) DSAVR/AR Germinal products, animal by-products, derived products, hay and straw DGAV (POA-NHC) DSAVR/AR Personal consignments (Regulation (EU) No 2019/2122) Non-commercial movement of pet animals (Regulation (EU) No DGAV 577/2013) DSAVR/AR Food of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control posts (2) (PNAO-HC(food)) Customs Feed of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control DGAV posts (2) (PNAO-NHC(feed)) DSAVR/AR DGAV DRAP/AR DGAV DSAVR/AR 4 Area of competence Competent authority Food contact materials (3) (PNAO-NHC(other)) DGAV DRAP/AR 3. The DGAV informed the audit team that they considered that, at the time of the audit, there was a sufficient number of suitably qualified staff at central level and at the BCPs for the performance of official controls. 4. The DGAV stated that it has designated official laboratories, in accordance with Article 37(1) of the OCR, to perform the analysis of samples, including those taken during official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Portugal. The laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025 in line with Article 37(4) of the OCR and each of the methods they use is included in the scope of their accreditation, in accordance with Article 37(5) of the OCR. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between authorities

The audit team found that, based on the evidence obtained during the audit, there are mechanisms in place which ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between and within authorities for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Portugal, which is in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR. 5.1.3 Training of staff

The DGAV central services and regional services provided documented evidence to the audit team, which confirmed that staff responsible for performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU had received appropriate training for their area of competence, which is in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place

The DGAV Central Services have issued and kept up-to-date comprehensive documented procedures, arrangements and instructions for staff for the performance of official controls on animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the EU through BCPs in Portugal. The audit team noted that those include arrangements for the implementation of the measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR. The audit team further noted that the documented procedures include the subject areas for control procedures set out in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, which is in line with Article 12(1) and (2) of the OCR.

The DGAV Central Services also develop and implement annual risk-based monitoring plans for the purpose of carrying out laboratory tests to detect hazards in in goods of animal origin entering the EU, in line with Article 4(5) and point 5 of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. 5 9. The DGAV informed the audit team that the flow of goods and the risk they represent, and the results of monitoring and notifications from the EU Agri-Food Fraud Network `iRASFF' from previous years, are taken into account during the development of the monitoring plans. Annual sampling plans, based on the monitoring plans, are established for each BCP and adapted to the flow and nature of goods entering the BCPs. 10. The DGAV informed the audit team that the shortcomings in the implementation of the monitoring plan for microbiological criteria in products of animal origin intended for human consumption was due to a lack of imports of the target commodities. 5.1.5 Use of the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) and other information systems 12. The use of TRACES-NT is mandatory for the official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Portugal, including for the prior notification of arrival of consignments (see also section 5.2.1 below). Certifying officers at BCPs avail of the use of Common Health Entry Documents (CHEDs) in an electronic format as provided for in Article 41 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715.
