Hazardous to humans, animals or the environment 6 13. Animals and goods entering the EU that require official controls at BCPs are identified in the Customs databases. The placing and handling of such consignments under a customs procedure is subject to the presentation of a finalised CHED by the operator responsible for the consignment, in line with Article 57 of the OCR, through the EU Customs Single Window Certificate Exchange Programme (EU-SW-CERTEX). 14. DSAVR staff at BCPs have access to the Customs' SDS system (Sistema Integrado de Meios de Transporte e das Mercadorias) as well as other computerised information systems necessary for the handling and exchange of data on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU, for example cargo manifests, which is in line with Article 64(3)(f) of the OCR. 15. The BCP staff performing official controls are responsible for submitting notifications to iRASFF, which are checked and validated by the National Contact Point before being transmitted to the EU contact point as necessary. 5.1.6 Audits of competent authorities and control verification procedures 16. Internal audits are carried out by the DGAV's Audit Unit, based on a multi-annual risk- based internal audit programme. The audit team noted that the internal audits are based on documented procedures that include measures to address any shortcomings identified during the audit, within a specified deadline, which is in line with Article 6(1) of the OCR. The Audit Unit provided documented evidence that it had carried out audits relevant to the official controls on consignments of animal and goods entering the EU, at central level in 2020, and at regional level each year, in line with its audit programme. 17. The DGAV provided evidence to the audit team that they have control verification procedures in place at central and regional level, to ensure that official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are consistent and effective, and that corrective actions are taken in cases where the verification procedures identify shortcomings, including the updating of relevant documented procedures as appropriate, which in line with Article 12(2) and (3) of the OCR. 18. The control verification procedures also include checks on the continued compliance of BCPs, including inspections centres thereof, and control points with minimum requirements. In the case of BCPs designated for live animals and products of animal origin, the assessment of the BCPs is carried out annually by the head of the BCP. In the case of products of non-animal origin, a compliance check is carried out regularly, and in any case, at least every two years, in accordance with the control plan on the importation of food of non-animal origin. The DGAV provided documented evidence that such checks had been carried out, and in line with the planned frequency. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU 19. There is a comprehensive system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the Union though BCPs in Portugal, which is 7 supported by suitably qualified and experienced staff, detailed documented procedures, information technology systems and good cooperation and communication within and between the competent authorities. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU 20. In summary: · The Agriculture and Food Board (AFB), which is an agency of the Ministry of Rural Affairs (MRA), is the competent authority for the official controls on animals, goods of animal origin, food and feed of non-animal origin and food contact materials entering the EU through BCPs in Estonia. The Border Control Department (BCD) of the AFB is responsible for the organisation, co-ordination and performance of those official controls; · The Tax and Customs Board of the Ministry of Finance (hereafter Customs) is responsible for official controls at points of entry on non-commercial pet animals, passengers' personal luggage and postal and courier services. 2. The areas of competence of the authorities involved in official controls on animals and goods entering the Union are summarised in the following table: Area of competence Competent authority Competent authority AFB Animals (LA) AFB Products of animal origin and composite products AFB (POA-HC) Customs Germinal products, animal by-products, derived products, hay and straw (POA-NHC) Personal consignments (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122) 4 Area of competence Competent authority Competent authority Customs Non-commercial movement of pet animals AFB (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No AFB 577/2013) AFB Food of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control posts (2) (PNAO-HC(food)) Feed of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control posts (2) (PNAO- NHC(feed)) Food contact materials (3) (PNAO-NHC(other)) 3. The AFB informed the audit team that at the time of the audit there were a total of 36 staff in the BCD, including 19 official veterinarians, 16 plant health officers and 1 food technologist. The AFB stated that while staff resources at BCPs are sufficient and in line with those planned by the heads of BCPs, it considered that additional staff are required at central BCD level. 4. The AFB has designated the National Centre for Laboratory Research and Risk Assessment and the Radiation Protection and Radiation Monitoring Office of the Environmental Board as official laboratories in accordance with Article 37(1) of the OCR, to perform the analysis of samples, including those taken during official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. The laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025 in line with Article 37(4) of the OCR by the Estonian Accreditation Centre, the scope of which includes each of the methods used, in accordance with Article 37(5) of the OCR. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between authorities 5. The AFB and Customs cooperate based on a formal agreement which sets out the principles of cooperation and communication at national and BCP level regarding the official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, including provisions for the exchange of information between the authorities and reciprocal access to data.
The AFB stated that regular meetings are held between the AFB, MRA and BCD, that include the planning and implementation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU.

Customs informed the audit team that the Estonian Customs Tariff information system identifies those animals and goods subject to official controls at BCPs. The customs import declaration processing system Impulss, which is linked to TRACES through the EU Customs Single Window Certificates Exchange System, enables the automatic verification that consignments subject to official controls at BCPs have been notified by operators and that the required controls have been completed before they may be placed under a customs procedure. 5 8. In addition, Customs cooperate with the AFB through a risk processing information system which enables the identification and control of consignments of other goods at BCPs, based on a risk assessment. 9. The audit team found that, based on the evidence obtained during the audit, there are mechanisms in place which ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between and within authorities for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Estonia, which is in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR 5.1.3 Training of staff 10. The AFB stated that official controls on animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin, including food contact materials, entering the EU through BCPs in Estonia are performed by official veterinarians. 11. Training is provided to both BCP staff and Customs' officials in accordance with an annual plan drafted by the BCD. The AFB provided evidence to the audit team which confirmed that BCP staff performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are trained in accordance with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place 12. The AFB has issued documented procedures including a checklist, for the performance of documentary, identity, and physical checks on consignments of animals and goods which the audit team noted were in line with the requirements of Articles 2, 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. 13. The audit team noted however, that the competent authority did not have documented control procedures for the performance of certain official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, including on, inter alia, the frequency of identity and physical checks on goods of animal and non-animal origin, consignments in transit, channelling of consignments, and arrangements in place for the implementation of the measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR. 14. In response to the audit team's findings, the AFB provided updated documentary procedures for BCPs for the performance of those official controls, copies of which were provided to the audit team. 15. The AFB develops an annual risk-based monitoring plan for the purpose of carrying out laboratory tests to detect hazards, in line with Article 4(5) and point 5 of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The monitoring plan takes into account the current flows of goods and the risk they represent, and the results of monitoring and RASFF notifications from previous years. 16. The AFB provided data on the number of samples planned, taken and analysed from consignments of goods of animal origin entering the EU through BCPs in 2022, which are summarised in the following table: 6 No of No of No of No of samples Percentage samples samples samples with sampled planned taken analysed unfavourable results Products of animal origin, intended for human consumption (POA-HC) Microbiological 41 5 5 0 Residues (8), 31 30 30 0 Pathogenic organisms (9) 21 19 19 1 Other hazardous substances (10) 8 1 1 0 Total 99 53 53 1 Products of animal origin, not intended for human consumption (POA-NHC) Microbiological 8 4 4 0 Residues 0 0 0 0 Pathogenic organisms 0 0 0 0 Other substances dangerous to humans, 0 0 0 0 animals or the environment Total 8 4 4 0 17. The AFB stated that the shortfalls in the implementation of the monitoring plan in 2022, in particular those for microbiological criteria were due to reduced flows of the targeted goods. 18. The AFB stated that no consignments of ungulates other than registered equidae have entered the EU through BCPs in Estonia and therefore no sampling, as referred to in Article 4(3) and point 3 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, was undertaken. 5.1.5 Use of the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) and other information systems 19. The use of TRACES-NT is mandatory for the official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Estonia, including for the prior notification of arrival of consignments (see also section 5.2.1 below). The AFB has contingency arrangements in place, in line with Article 46 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715, in the event that TRACES-NT is not available. 20. The AFB informed the audit team that its certifying officers at BCPs avail of the use of CHEDs in an electronic format as provided for in Article 41 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. (8) Groups A, B(1), B(2) and B(3) in Annex I to Directive 96/23/EC (9) Dangerous to humans, animals or the environment (10) Hazardous to humans, animals or the environment 7 21. The placing and handling of consignments of animals and goods that require official controls at BCPs under a customs procedure, is subject to the presentation of a finalised CHED by the operator responsible for the consignment, in line with Article 57 of the OCR. 22. BCP staff have access to the customs declaration system in order to confirm that consignments subject to control at BCPs have been correctly declared. Staff at the BCP Muuga port also have access to the computerised information system of the container terminal and the national electronic maritime information system. 23. The BCP staff performing official controls are responsible for submitting initial notifications to iRASFF, which are checked and validated by the National Contact Point in the Food Department of the AFB before being transmitted to the EU contact point as necessary. The AFB has guidelines in place for the use of iRASFF. 5.1.6 Audits of competent authorities and control verification procedures 24. The MRA informed the audit team that it develops and implements a risk based multi- annual program for internal audits. The last audit of relevance to official controls on animals and goods entering the EU was carried out in 2017, with a focus on the activities of Customs in relation to entry of pet animals. In 2023, two audits are planned, one of which will be on plant health and will include the official controls on plants, plant products and other objects entering the EU. The second audit will be on the activities of the Tax and Customs Board. 25. The AFB has in place a documented procedure for the planning and performance of control verification procedures referred to in Article 12 of the OCR and their follow-up as part of a multi-annual national control plan. The procedure includes an annual assessment of BCPs which are carried out by the BCD. 26. A report is issued summarising the findings of each verification control together with recommendations to address and shortcomings identified. The competent authorities provided copies of the reports of control verification procedures carried out in 2022. The audit team noted that a deadline for completion of corrective actions was specified in each case and that the procedures and reports had identified similar findings to those of this Commission audit. The audit team noted though that the recommendations for corrective action did not address the lack of, or need to update, related documented procedures. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU 27. There is a well-functioning system of official controls in place for animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Estonia, supported by suitable qualified and experienced staff, information technology systems and cooperation and communication within and between authorities.

text: In their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of June 2019, the CCA provided Circular 170258/20.7.2011 outlining the tasks and responsibilities of the Regional Units 3 and Regional Veterinary Directorates for official controls on the protection of animals during transport.

According to Circular 170258/20.7.2011, Regional Units must plan their official controls for the next year so that the controls cover 5% of animals transported in their jurisdiction in the current year i.e. movements within Greece and between Member States, departing, transiting and arriving in each Regional Units' jurisdiction.

This established control frequency of 5%, for the purposes of Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, includes checks at all stages of a journey, in line with Article 21(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Circular 170258/20.7.2011 also provides a risk assessment, in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, that the Regional Units must use to plan their official controls. While most Regional Units can use this risk assessment to determine at which stages of the journey to carry out the controls, the risk assessment obliges some specific Regional Units to perform official controls at ports and/or on the road (roadside checks); Five Regional Units from two different Regional Veterinary Directorates must carry out roadside checks.

According to Circular 170258/20.7.2011, the Regional Veterinary Directorates must supervise the Regional Units to verify the implementation of the official control system on the protection of animals during transport, including the frequency of the controls planned.

Additionally, Circular 170258/20.7.2011 requires: · Regional Units to forward their official control plans of the next year to their Regional Veterinary Directorate by 30 December of the current year; · The Regional Veterinary Directorates to forward the Regional Units' control plans to the CCA by 31 January of the control year; · The Regional Units to submit quarterly reports of the official controls carried out to their Regional Veterinary Directorate within established deadlines.

In their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of June 2019, the CCA provided a copy of the "Written procedures on the implementation of the protection of animals during transport" (hereafter "old Handbook"). This documented procedure for official controls, required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, on the protection of animals at all stages during transport, had last been updated and circulated to all Regional Veterinary Directorates in November 2016.

In their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of August 2021, the CCA indicated that it intended to produce a new Handbook for official controls on the protection of animals during transport in the second half of 2022, with the intention of: · including new requirements arising from Regulation (EU) 2017/625; · providing more detailed instructions for quality controls of journey logs and a dedicated template. 4 The CCA distributed the new Handbook to the Regional Veterinary Directorates on 31 January 2023 (Circular 232/32048).

According to both the old and new Handbooks, when carrying out a control during a journey, official veterinarians must also inspect the animals and the means of transport for compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that when Regional Units plan and perform roadside checks, the CCA's expectation is that they are also planning to and inspecting the means of transport.

In their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of June 2019, the CCA did not provide sufficient evidence that all Regional Units were planning their official controls on animal welfare during transport at the control frequency of 5% established in Circular 170258/20.7.2011.

Concerning the five Regional Units that must plan and perform roadside checks, in their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of June 2019, the CCA provided data on the number of controls carried out by three of those Regional Units in the first 6 months of 2019 and provided 2018 reports from their respective Regional Veterinary Directorates. These demonstrate that the three Regional Units did not carry out all their planned controls and one also did not plan to perform any controls for certain years.: · One of the Regional Units did not carry out roadside checks in 2017, the first quarter of 2018 and the first 6 months of 2019. The May 2018 report of the relevant Regional Veterinary Directorate also indicates that this Regional Unit had not planned to perform roadside checks in 2017 and 2018. · According to the June 2018 report of the relevant Regional Veterinary Directorate, a second Regional Unit had planned to perform one roadside check in 2017 and 2018 but did not carry out this check in 2017 nor in the first quarter of 2018. This Regional Unit also did not carry out roadside checks in the first 6 months of 2019. · A third Regional Unit carried out 10 roadside checks in the first 6 months of 2019. The May 2018 report of the relevant Regional Veterinary Directorate also indicates that this Regional Unit had planned to carry out five roadside checks in 2017 but carried out only three, and had planned to carry out three roadside checks in 2018 but had not carried these out in the first quarter of that year. A follow-up in September 2018, reports that the Regional Unit had neither carried out roadside checks in the second quarter of 2018. The CCA did not provide any relevant documents or data concerning the remaining two Regional Units.

In their reply to the Commission's questionnaire of August 2021, the CCA provided Circular 2543/349457 on the organisation of official controls on the protection of animals during transport, that was sent on14 December 2020 to all Regional Units and Regional Veterinary Directorates. This circular: 5 · reminds Regional Units and Regional Veterinary Directorates of their tasks and responsibilities described in Circular 170258/20.7.2011; · shifts to the Regional Units the task of submitting the annual control plans to the CCA, extending the deadline for this to 31 March of the control year; · clarifies that Regional Veterinary Directorates are to cooperate and coordinate with the Regional Units to verify that they perform the planned number of controls and to send information on the Regional Units' performance to the central competent authority.

The Directorate of Animal Welfare, Veterinary Medicinal Products and Veterinary Applications within the Veterinary Directorate-General of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food is the central competent authority (hereafter: competent authority) responsible for supervision and the coordination of delivering official controls of the welfare rules for farmed fish at all relevant stages of production. The local competent authorities of the regions deliver the official controls at farms and other establishments.

The national veterinary legislation sets, among others, the hygiene requirements for the foundation and operation of aquaculture establishments, regulates fish health and welfare and requirements up to the placement of safe products in the market. The approval of establishments as well as transporters of live fish is a task assigned to local veterinary competent authorities.

The competent authority has considered the Recommendation concerning Farmed Fish and formally ratified it. They have not incorporated it in the national legislation and therefore they did not issue further legal text. However, the inspection checklist includes a question about scientific protocols or guidance (including a reference to the Recommendation) used in the fish farm. In addition, parts of the Recommendation have been elaborated in the guidelines developed (paragraph 4). Those guidelines have been disseminated in the local competent authorities to be considered during the preparation and performance of official controls in fish farms. In addition, further reference to the Recommendation is made in the national guidance (paragraph 17). Other parts of the Recommendation are included in Presidential decree 28/2009.

The competent authority has developed a policy for farmed fish that identifies the need to examine the applied practices in the production with a focus on welfare in transport and slaughter. It aims to develop methodologies to enhance the existing legislation and also to contribute to the preparation of future legislation. In that context, with the support of the academia, they have participated in various projects on the application of alternative methods for fishing and slaughtering of fish. In addition, the competent authority coordinated the production of Guidelines on water quality and handling for the welfare of farmed vertebrate fish. The guidelines were produced in 2020 voluntarily under the EU Platform on Animal Welfare. These guidelines on water quality and on handling aim to be of use for aquaculture operators and the relevant competent authorities. They include factors and parameters that are common across species. The guidelines adopt and embed the Council of Europe Recommendation concerning farmed fish. 4 5. The competent authority considers the training of personnel crucial to enhance the welfare practices in farmed fish sector. In cooperation with academia, they have designed and implemented training for staff involved in fish farming as well training for official inspectors - the most recent ones in 2022 and 2023. 6. In the context of the project titled `Development of expertise for the review and update of the multi annual strategic plan for the development of aquaculture 2021-2027', the competent authority has identified the relevance and importance of fish welfare in the context of aquaculture development. Various research works exploring welfare issues are ongoing under this project. 5.1.2 Planning, methodology and delivery of the official controls Findings 7. The competent authority has made available to the local competent authorities a written procedure that defines the methodology for risk-based planning of the official controls. The methodology considers farmed fish as a stand-alone area, and it includes a separate tab for numerical calculation of the risk of each aquaculture establishment. Among other factors, the methodology lists the production size, the past record of official controls (existence of non-compliances), the likelihood of extreme weather temperatures, time elapsed since last official control, the turnover rate and competence of staff and the existence of certification under a quality assurance scheme. According to the methodology the farmed fish presents low risk related relating to animal welfare. 8. The local competent authorities perform official controls on animal welfare at fish farms in the context of fish health inspections. They use a joint checklist that includes fish health checks as well as a part dedicated to fish welfare. That part covers the use of scientifically proven protocols or guidelines to ensure welfare, the use of welfare indicators, the methods of stunning and killing of fish. In addition, it includes the verification of requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 for example vehicle transport authorisation and transporter licence. Apart from the part referring to live fish transport, the other points covered by the checklist do not relate to specific legal requirements and are thus not enforceable. 9. The manual for animal welfare checks during transport (second version, 2023), includes in Chapter 16 specific guidelines for fish transport that assist the inspectors in their work. It includes guidelines for the evaluation of transport vehicles before approval as well as during routine inspections, for example the assessment of fitness of fish to be transported, the loading practices etc. 10. One of the regions has prepared a comprehensive checklist that covers the inspection of essential elements of the system applied in a fish farm as well as different process steps. This checklist includes training requirements, monitoring of indicators and keeping of records, implementation of corrective actions, assessment of the environmental conditions (e.g. density, light, protective nets), feeding practices, stunning and killing. It goes beyond 5 legal requirements but is very informative on whether and how the fish farm addresses welfare of the fish. 11. Although the competent authority suggests a risk-based system for selecting fish farms for animal welfare official controls, this methodology was followed only in one of the three regions visited. In two regions visited there are annual inspections of farms including transport processes and vehicles, and in another region visited, there are official controls every three years as the farmed fish is ranked as of low risk compared to other sectors in that region. 12. The transport operation examined during the on-the-spot part of the study, was equipped with insulated water tanks and a system to monitor water temperature, oxygen and pH. They were also equipped with an alarm system for oxygen and with backup systems to supply oxygen in case of need. for pumping the oxygen into the water tanks. 13. Immersion in ice and water mix (ice slurry) to provoke thermal shock (hypothermia) and asphyxia is the killing method used in practice and does not include a stunning step. Electric stunning is a requirement under the organic standard (see paragraph 21) and is also used on a voluntary basis on ongoing experimental scale by some companies in cooperation with research institutes. It has been trialled with a view to anaesthetising fish rapidly and directly after they are pumped from cages prior to killing via immersion in ice baths. This technology, which is used for Atlantic salmon and on a small scale for rainbow trout and carp, is regarded as being in line with EU animal welfare objectives as using it guarantees immediate stunning prior to killing. However, the parameters that ensure proper anaesthesia for different species and different size of fish are not yet well known, indicating that more research needs to be done in that area. Electrical stunning presents a risk to operators and requires a significant amount of investment, as it must be done in the sea, on board modified vessels that reach the cages of fish. This means that the method might be of severe financial burden for small and medium size operators. 14. According to the competent authority, the most critical steps in the process concerning elevated risk to fish welfare are lack of or inadequate feeding, vaccination, exhaustion of breeding stock, improper stunning, handling during selection, stocking density (especially relating to reduced oxygen levels as well as difficulties in reaching feed), impact of parasitic diseases. 5.2 OTHER MEASURES TO PROTECT THE WELFARE OF FARMED FISH 5.2.1 Research and emerging technologies ­ Other initiatives Findings 15. As mentioned earlier in the report (paragraph 13) there are ongoing projects managed by academia in cooperation with fish farming companies related to stunning and slaughtering of fish based on alternative methods and electric stunning. This has led to the production 6 and optimisation of pumping systems, electric stunning and killing of fish on board vessels. The results have led to the production of documented procedures that instruct operators how to perform relevant tasks, and aspects to be considered with regards to protecting staff safety, optimising quality and yield of product, and ensuring adequate levels of welfare with reduced stress of fish. For example, it describes how to collect and pump the fish so that crowding and injuries are prevented. 16. The main objective of the research for alternative methods for fishing (stunning and slaughtering) is to optimise fish welfare. It aims to develop a biosensor to monitor fish cortisol levels based on a non-intervention method to evaluate the level of stress. The wider goal is to deploy the biosensor in assessing the stress of fish at different production steps including breeding and fattening. 17. The association of farmed fish producers has published a guidance document titled Mediterranean Fish Welfare: Guide to good practices and assessment indicators. The competent authority adopted the guide and disseminated it to all relevant competent authorities. Published in 2020, its main objectives are to describe current scientific data and ethical practices on animal welfare with particular focus on the needs of European sea bass and gilthead sea bream in different production phases, in relation to improving their welfare. It includes operational and laboratory welfare indicators and lists their advantages and disadvantages. It covers different production systems, production phases and husbandry practices. 18. In the case of Pagrus major farms the companies have installed tents to protect the cages from intense sunlight as it is proven that direct sunlight enhances the aggressive behaviour of the fish. However, as the farmers stated during the visit, this feature reduces the possibility to observe the fish. This highlights the complexity of welfare issues in the aquaculture sector. 19. During the visit, representatives from the fish farming companies as well as the association of farmed fish producers discussed the main indicators they are using that are relevant to welfare. They mainly monitor and assess mortality as well as a wide range of other parameters including density and environmental indicators (water temperature, oxygen etc). They also widely deploy observations of fish behaviour during handling and especially feeding to assess the welfare status of fish. A representative commented on the importance of monitoring the acute/dramatic change of indicators, especially mortality to trigger alerts on welfare or health status. 20. In one company visited, the quality department has developed an advanced indicator system to monitor deficiencies of received fish in the packing plant. This includes indicators of haematomas and similar issues that affect the quality and yield of the production. The association of farmed fish producers has also developed comprehensive photographic guidance to evaluate those deficiencies, including in addition to haematomas, a range of morphological deviations (injuries, absence of gills covers, malformed fish etc). Monitoring some of those indicators is a potentially good practice as 7 a useful tool not only to minimise quality defects, as but also for monitoring welfare as these parameters could also relate to welfare. At this stage however there is not adequate scientific evidence to suggest sufficient baseline levels within which welfare can be considered satisfactory. 5.2.2 Quality assurance schemes and fish farmers' own checks Findings 21. The competent authorities specified three quality schemes that include welfare requirements used in Greece within their applied scope. Those are an international standard applied in farmed fish, an international standard specifically for organic farmed fish and a national standard developed by the association of farmed fish producers. All three are promoting the welfare of farmed fish, they are accredited, and they are applied on a voluntary basis. They include sections with requirements relating to welfare of fish at the different stages of production. The standards include some specific requirements but mostly generic and open requirements. For example, requirements for the humane slaughter of fish, reduction of stress during handling and transport processes, training for staff involved in the production of fish, monitoring of health, requirements relating to feeding and quality of feeding stuff etc. They also include some specific requirements. · The international standard has established risk assessment for fish welfare as a major requirement. It is asking to conduct a risk assessment for fish welfare at all stages of production from the hatchery to stunning and killing of fish and to document/monitor proposed actions to mitigate those risks. The study team considers this as a potentially good practice if consistently applied in the farmed fish sector. · The organic standard requires that live fish must be supplied with enough oxygen during transport and when kept in cages. A transport density of 1 kg of fish per 8 litres of water may not be exceeded. The water must be changed at the latest after 6 hours of transport and must be of the same temperature. The transport duration is maximum 10 hours. In addition, slaughtering of fish shall be carried out by means of incision of gills or immediate evisceration. Prior to this, fish must be stunned by means of concussion, or electrocution. The standard sets requirements for density at farm for other species (e.g. for salmon) but not for sea bass and sea bream. · The national standard includes a section for welfare. It requires documented procedures and records to demonstrate protection of fish at all production stages, monitoring and control of fish mortality, monitoring of feeding quality and quantity, feed withdrawal times, the establishment and use of practices to reduce fish stress during handling processes etc. Twenty-one (out of twenty- two) members of the association are certified under the standard. This represents a total of 80% of the national production certified. The representatives of the association indicated that they plan to embed specific 8 requirements included in their published guidelines (paragraph 17) in the new version of the standard. 22. Representatives of competent authorities as well as operators met during the study indicated that the use of private quality schemes has been proven to be useful to enter markets and the companies have benefited in their operations by consistently applying documented procedures and standardising their processes. 5.3 CHALLENGES FACED 23. Local competent authorities indicated that their main challenges are the difficulty to perform official controls, as reaching farms in the sea depends on weather conditions and the long travel distance. The specialised knowledge required for fish welfare inspection presents a challenge for official inspectors dealing with controls of various sectors. In addition, the open/generic legal requirements combined with gaps in the available knowledge relating to scientifically established baselines on fish welfare limit the capacity to enforce. 24. The representatives of the producers' association and the academic institute as well as representatives from the producers met, also described the challenges they face concerning fish welfare. Primarily, the lack of available scientific knowledge limits the use of indicators to protect productivity/efficiency as it is not clear which levels are sufficient to ensure acceptable conditions for welfare. They also commented that the market of farmed fish is price-driven and the competition with non-EU producers is hard to follow. This is due to increased cost for EU producers to comply with EU standards not applicable to non-EU producers (namely, in addition to welfare, feed and management of animals by product requirements). In that respect, they commented that the current requirements for labelling do not support the fish produced in the EU. In addition, they questioned whether there are welfare standards applicable to wild caught fish. They would welcome the introduction of new legislation, but strictly on a species-specific basis, scientifically based, and applicable to both EU and non-EU producing countries that place products on the European market. As the current knowledge is not sufficient to support specific indicators/descriptive requirements, they suggest the introduction of qualitative/open requirements such as the obligation to keep staff trained and up to date on welfare issues, and specific tools such as the obligatory use of root cause analysis tools and reporting on welfare issues. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The report finds that there is a system for official controls on the welfare of farmed fish in Greece. There are documented procedures supporting the official controls on fish farms and good knowledge of farmed fish welfare matters by both the central competent authority and industry. Official controls cover animal welfare in the context of fish health inspections. However, they have a reduced impact on welfare (apart from the 9 requirements for transport vehicles) as there are no legally enforceable requirements specific to fish welfare. Industry processes have several arrangements, established by joint efforts with the state, research institutes and the industry. This includes a national accredited private quality scheme, a guide to good practices on fish welfare linked to the certification scheme and a wide range of indicators already in use. Although indicators might cover welfare, they are predominantly used to ensure quality and efficiency of production. There is ongoing academic research determining welfare in sea bass and sea bream and other species farmed in the country to provide stakeholders with guidance and baselines for corresponding indicators. This, (the absence of welfare related baselines on indicators), is the main challenge that both competent authorities and operators face, and advances would help fish farmers in managing fish welfare in their farms. The study identified a good practice in a private quality assurance scheme that requires a documented risk assessment methodology to mitigate risks for animal welfare throughout the processes from hatchery to stunning and killing of fish, if applied consistently by the operators. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting took place on 20 September 2023 with representatives of the Commission and competent authorities at which the main findings of the fact-finding study were presented.

The organisational aspects of plant health controls in Sweden are described in section 1 of the DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Sweden (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/SE).

SBA, and specifically its Plant and Control Department is the competent authority (CA) for plant health in the meaning of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. That in- cludes among other things the responsibility to keep and update of the register of profes- sional operators as required by Article 65 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, to authorise professional operators to issue plant passports and undertake official controls over the authorised operators as required by Articles 89 and 92 of the same Regulation.

The following Units of the Plant and Control Department of SBA are involved in the official activities falling under the scope of this audit: a. Plant Regulations Unit, which has a plant health team of 11 staff in the central of- fice and in two regional offices. It is responsible for the registration of profession- al operators, for the authorisation of operators to issue plant passports and to de- velop guidelines both for officials and for the authorised operators on plant pass- port matters. b. Plant Control Unit, which has a plant health team of 13 staff in the central office and in three regional offices. They are primarily responsible for the official con- trols at the operators authorised to issue plant passports. Specific official control guidelines are also drafted by the Unit. c. Seed Unit, however, their role is limited to official controls on compliance with EU marketing Directives1 for plants and plant products, which may include some plant health related activities, such as verification of compliance with regard to the regulated non-quarantine pests, as established by the Directives. 1 https://food.ec.europa.eu/plants/plant-reproductive-material/legislation/eu-marketing-requirements_en 3 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

The most relevant national legislation in the context of this audit is the Plant Health Law (2022:725) and the Plant Health Ordinance (2022:795), which designates SBA as the CA for plant health matters in Sweden, including on matters related to plant passports, and gives SBA empowerments related to plant health including plant passports. It also establishes the framework principles for the registration of professional operators. There are other secondary legislative acts about fees related to official controls including those related to plant passports. There is also national legislation to transpose EU marketing Directives into Swedish national legislation, which also include some aspects of plant passports such as provisions with regard to the issuance of combined labels, as provided under Article 83(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.1.3 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

The audit team was provided with evidence that written records in paper format are drawn up on plant passport related official controls, as required by Article 13(1) of Reg- ulation (EU) 2017/625. In addition, checklists and inspection guidelines are used in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The following inspection guidelines and checklists of the Plant Regulations Unit were made available to the inspectors: a. Procedure for the registration and processing of applications for the authorisation of operators to issue plant passports (latest version from 2023), b. Guidance for the control of operators authorised to issue plant passports (latest version from 2023), c. Specific inspection guidelines for the official control of operators: for nurseries, greenhouses, and seed producers, d. Checklist to conduct official controls on plant passports at authorised operators.

There is a system developed for internal audits within SBA as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The last internal audit on plant passport matters was under- taken in 2021. Several recommendations were made by the internal audit team, includ- ing to update information regarding the pests on the website of the SBA.

The audit team observed that inspectors met during the site visits to the professional operators had received training on plant passport matters and were aware of the context of the inspection guidelines developed. This was reflected in the consistency in the per- formance of the official controls on plant passport matters at the operators visited. It is in line with Article 5(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Based on the number of official controls conducted in 2022 and 2023, where the planned targets for the plant passport controls were met, the audit team could conclude, that the 4 SBA has access to sufficient staff for plant passport controls as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the control system related to plant passports

The clear delineation of tasks and close cooperation within SBA, combined with the level of resources available and well-developed documented control procedures, pro- vides a sound basis for the consistent implementation of the legislation on plant pass- ports. 5.2 REGISTRATION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS Legal requirements Articles 65 to 68 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Findings 5.2.1 Official registration

There is a system established for the registration of professional operators as required by Article 65 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The registration is done electronically using the application form available on the SBA website. All operators are registered in the database named VAKT (Register över aktörer inom växtområdet), where data required under Article 66(2) of the same Regulation are kept.

Separate registration numbers can be allocated for facilities of the same professional operators at different locations, which is not fully in line with Article 65(2) of Regula- tion (EU) 2016/2031. However, the audit team observed that this shortcoming had no negative impact on the effectiveness of the official controls at the operators visited. The SBA explained, that although separate registration numbers are allocated to facilities at different locations, technically the operators are registered only once in the SBA data- base, as the elementary contact information for the professional operator is retrieved on- ly once through their national corporate identity number directly from the Swedish Tax Agency.
The audit team was provided evidence that all traders selling through distance contracts must be registered, except those who deliver to the final consumer without third party involvement.

There is a system implemented for the operators to notify the CA of annual updates as required by Article 66 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. It currently requires operators to provide updates on the changes in the location of their operations such as the size and 5 the location of the production area and cultivated or traded commodity types. However, it does not require them to provide updates on other criteria required by Article 66(2)(e) of the same Regulation e.g., species and families of the plants and plant products. The SBA stated that the level of details provided in annual updates is sufficient for them to plan risk based annual plant health control plans at registered operators. In addition, the SBA stated that according to their legal interpretation it is sufficient if data on one of the criteria required by Article 66(2)(e) is collected. The audit team was given an example of the annual letters sent by the SBA to every registered professional operator to remind them about their obligation to provide annual updates of their activities for the forthcom- ing cultivation year by the 30 of April.

The audit team was provided evidence on the application of enforcement measures es- tablished against operators failing to provide up to date information on the plant health register. This included a fine of 300 SEK imposed to several operators in 2023. 5.2.2 Application of exemptions provided for in EU law

Sweden opted to use derogations provided under Article 65(3)(a)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 on the exclusive supply to final consumers of small quantities of plants, plant products and seeds. In the implementing guidelines there are no small quantities defined except for seed. For plants and plant products all operators exclusively selling to final consumers are exempted. Conclusions on the registration of professional operators

The SBA has accurate and fit for purpose up-to-date information in electronic format on all relevant operators and their activities, thereby providing a solid basis for planning and implementing efficient and effective controls. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures

In Sweden, all plant passports are issued by professional operators. As of 12 February 2024, there were 311 operators authorised to issue plant passports, including 49 opera- tors authorised to issue plant passports for trade into protected zones. Two thirds of the authorised operators have nurseries cultivating primarily ornamental plants, and 48 of the operators were engaged in distant sales. 6 19. In order to be authorised to issue plant passports in accordance with Article 89(1) (a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, an operator has to complete SBA's online course and suc- cessfully pass the final test. 20. Once the online course has been completed and users have received training certificates, the operator is required to prepare and submit to the SBA an effective plan to be fol- lowed in case of any suspected presence or finding of EU quarantine pests or pests under EU emergency measures, as required by Article 1(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. The plan must include information covered by Article 1(c)(e)(f) of the same Regulation. The audit team observed that the template to draft such a plan was made available to opera- tors on the SBA website as required by Article 2(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. 21. The audit team was informed by the SBA that its legal interpretation of the requirements of Article 1(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 means the plan referred to in the Article is only required for operators first authorised to issue plant passports after 14 December 2020, the date of application of Regulation (EU) 2019/827. Therefore, the plan is not re- quired for operators re-authorised to issue plant passports under the umbrella of Regula- tion (EU) 2016/2031 between 14 December 2019 and 14 December 2020. According to the data provided by the SBA, approximately 60% of operators authorised to issue plant passports were authorised prior to 14 December 2020. 22. The audit team noted that compliance of professional operators with the requirements of Article 1(b)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, such as competence to conduct plant health examinations and to apply best practices and measures to prevent the presence and spread of plant pests, is not verified during the authorisation process. This is not in line with Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 23. For compliance with Article 2 (a)(b)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, SBA has provided operators some information on their website, mainly for priority pests and for some EU quarantine pests such as regulated potato pests. For other pests, links to the EPPO global database were made available (information is in English only). The CA has not provided operators information on modalities of visual inspections as required by Article (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 and information on best practices and measures to prevent pest presences as required by Article (2)(c) of the same Regulation. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions 24. According to the data provided by the SBA, the minimum frequency of one official in- spection by SBA per authorised operator was met in 2022 and 2023. According to the data provided by SBA, some 324 inspections were undertaken in 2022 and 313 inspec- tions in 2023 (as of 1 November 2023). This is in line with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 25. The inspections on plant passport matters observed by the audit team followed estab- lished guidelines and checklists and focused mainly on the verification of compliance with the requirements on the content and format of plant passports and the availability of 7 staff who participated in e-training. These controls adequately assessed compliance with the established requirements. 26. Each of the observed inspections was complemented by official inspections of the health status of the plants present at the operators' facilities. According to the instructions for inspectors, samples must be taken in cases where the presence of regulated pests is sus- pected. In 2022, 16 samples were taken with 6 samples testing positive for Bemisia tabaci and 1 for Phytophthora ramorum. In 2023, 5 samples were taken, as of 1 No- vember 2023, and 1 tested positive for Bemisia tabaci. See details on enforcement ac- tions in section 5.7. 27. As inspection guidelines and checklists do not require verification of the authorised op- erators' compliance with the requirements of Articles 87 and 90 on the appropriateness of authorised operators' examinations and obligation to keep records on examinations, compliance with these requirements was not included in any of the observed inspections. This is not in line with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports: 28. The system of authorisation of professional operators to issue plant passports follows rules established in EU legislation. However, the CA has neither provided authorised operators with the information needed to carry out meticulous inspections independent- ly and at critical points, nor has it required them to keep records of such inspections. Moreover, there is no requirement in the guidelines for the CA to verify compliance to the abovementioned criteria. These shortcomings increase the risk that operators do not carry out their inspections meticulously, and that they place plants on the market, in- fested with regulated pests. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators 29. Operators met by the audit team stated that they check their plants constantly as they go about their work, even though formally not required to do so by the SBA. However, as operators visited had never documented this activity, as required by Article 87(3)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, the audit team could not verify that authorised operators conduct meticulous examinations in line with Article 87(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 prior to issuing plant passports. In addition, only one of the operators met by 8 the audit team had defined their critical points and the list of pests for monitoring pur- poses as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. No records are kept on monitoring by authorised operators. The reason for not undertaking this task is the lack of specific requirements and official controls by the SBA as stated in point 27 in section 5.3.2. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators 30. The SBA carries out their annual control at authorised operators, taking into account the production cycle and the nature of the plants and plant products produced, as well as the possibility of detecting the presence of relevant pests or signs or symptoms thereof as required by Article 1 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66. Where relevant, the inspectors added information about the production cycles in the inspection report, which can be used for the planning of future inspections. The audit team was provided with an example of such additional information at operators visited. 31. As already stated under point 27 in section 5.3.2, the SBA does not verify the examina- tions carried out by authorised operators. 5.4.3 Examinations in relation to the protected zones 32. Sweden has established a protected zone status for Cryphonectria parasitica and Be- misia tabaci in certain plants and plant products and for Leptinotarsa decemlineata in some parts of Sweden. As stated under point 18 of section 5.3.1, there are 49 profession- al operators authorised to issue plant passports for trade into protected zones in Sweden and in other MSs. 33. According to the SBA, it conducts additional inspections at those authorised operators trading plants and plant products to the protected zones following the specific require- ments for each protected zone established in Annex X of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072. Controls are risk based. For example, plants of Euphorbia pulcherrima receive controls by the SBA in August/September as this is the period dur- ing which the risk of introduction of Bemisia tabaci into their premises is at the highest. 34. The audit team was informed that regarding the protected zones for Erwinia amylovora established in other MSs, there are six nurseries in Sweden who have signed up to send host plants for Erwinia amylovora to these protected zones. Awareness and prevention 25. In Belgium regional environmental authorities are the competent authorities for wildlife manage- ment including wildlife health and biodiversity: a) Agentschap Natuur en Bos in Flanders, b) (Département de la Nature et des Forêts) in Wallonia, c) (Leefmilieu Brussel) in Brussels. 26. Regional environmental authorities provide information on their website for the public on HPAI risks and what to do when they find a dead wild bird or animal. There is a citizens' magazine where regional environmental authorities can communicate information on appropriate precau- tions. 27. Members of the public can report wildlife carcasses through a free national hotline in Belgium, with an additional regional hotline available for Wallonia. They will be advised whether the car- cass should be sent for testing (if it qualifies for surveillance testing). If the carcass is found on municipal land and qualifies for surveillance testing then the regional environmental authority will be involved in the dispatch fo the carcasses to the NRL. The municipalities are responsible for disposal of the remaining carcass (if any) or of a carcass found on their land if it is not qualified 8 for surveillance testing. They are also responsible for providing the appropriate protective measures such as PPE to their staff handling the carcass. If the carcass is found on private land the regional environmental authority will also dispatch it to the NRL if it qualified for surveillance testing. If it does not, then the owner must dispose of the carcass with no other intervention by the authorities and is responsible for appropriate PPE. There is no communication to people that have found a wildlife carcass in the case of it testing positive for HPAI. 28. In Belgium there are several wildlife sanctuaries and rehabilitation centres. Regional authorities are also responsible for these wildlife rehabilitation centrrs and provide derogations to these cen- tres in order for them to capture, transport, temporarily accommodate (rehabilitate) endemic wild- life species (i.e. species listed on the Soortenbesluit in Flanders, Natuurordonnantie for Brussels Capital Region). Some can host up to 4,000 birds and small mammals (rabbits, foxes, squirrels) annually, and keep young animals for several months. Injured, sick or distressed wild animals found by the public are consistently directed towards these centres. Flanders has legislation in place to recognize wildlife rehabilitation centres. A significant proportion of their staff are volun- teers. PPE and training on its use is the responsibility of the employer i.e. the wildlife rehabilitation centres. The biosecurity, with respect to inter-animal transmission, is the responsibility of the re- gional environmental authorities.

Monitoring & early detection 29. The environmental authorities have not carried out a specific risk assessment or developed a risk mitigation policy for the potential effects of Avian Influenza on wildlife and biodiversity. Scientific risk assessments are performed from RAG-V-EZ or the FASFC. However, the Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO), an independent research institute of the Flemish government, closely follows up the outbreaks of Avian Influenza in the Flanders (in collaboration with ANB). 30. The HPAI epidemiological situation elsewhere in Europe is monitored by veterinary services at federal level and by the regional environmental authorities through information disseminated by neighbouring countries and European bodies. These include, for example, the website of the EU reference laboratory, EFSA's quarterly reports and dashboard (https://hpai.efsa.aus.vet/), information disseminated by the European Commission and Member States via mail and at PAFF meetings, initiatives such as bird flu radar (https://app.bto.org/mmt/avian_influenza_map/avian_influenza_map.jsp), following webinars and conferences with HPAI topics. 31. In 2006, in response to the risks associated with the introduction of zoonotic H5N1 viruses from Asia by migratory birds, Belgian veterinary authorities conducted a risk assessment regarding high-risk zones and wetlands for migratory waterfowl. As a result of this evaluation, so-called "sensitive natural areas" were identified. These are wetlands where large numbers of waterfowl reside, with high numbers of migratory waterfowl passing through, resting, and foraging each year. Because of the change in epidemiological evidence regarding HPAI virus, a new evaluation should be carried out to identify sensitive natural areas. In these areas, FASFC imposes specific measures on poultry establishments and specific attention is given by the regional environmental authorities 9 to the surveillance in wild birds. The visit team saw evidence of several poultry and livestock farms located directly under the paths of wild migratory birds close to wetlands. 32. In areas where hunting of waterfowl or other animals is permitted (Wallonia and Flanders), regional environmental authorities may impose measures to either ban hunting or enforce stricter regulations in case of HPAI presence in the area. For example, in 2022, this was the case at three locations in Wallonia, where a high infection rate of HPAI was detected in pheasants and ducks that had been released for hunting. 33. For birds released for hunting, responsibilities for managing HPAI risks are divided between the veterinary and the regional environmental services. Until their release, these birds are considered captive birds; once released, they are considered as wild birds. Often, these birds are imported from another member state (France). They are not included in the active surveillance whereas there have been three HPAI outbreaks in Wallonia involving thousands of these birds. As these birds can further infect other wildlife upon their release, a risk assessment for better managing possible HPAI risks to exposed humans, other wildlife and poultry, appropriate measures and a clear division of responsibilities may be important to consider. The practice is banned in the regions of Flanders and Brussels. 34. There is wastewater surveillance for monitoring influenza in some stations in Wallonia but not targeting HPAI.

Actions and guidance regarding initial response to HPAI cases 35. Regional environmental services are communicating with the NRL and veterinary authorities in the context of positive wildlife samples. The authorities in their comments to the draft report stated that the regional environmental authorities communicate the necessary information on the findings received from the NRL towards the FASFC, the concerned municipalities, the other regional environmental authorities and respective regional health authorities. The team however did not see an established communication channel for timely warning to public health authorities in the event of wildlife deaths due to HPAI. 36. Regional environmental authorities are currently members of the joint structure RAG-V-EZ that is established with the FASFC to assess and manage HPAI risks. Their participation in such a multisectoral structure facilitates the flow of information regarding the HPAI risks during outbreaks in farms. III. Human health 1. Awareness and prevention 37. The national competent authority for public health is the Federal Public Service of health at Federal level and at regional level the Department Zorg for Flanders, the Agence pour une vie de qualité for Wallonia and Vivalis for Brussels. 38. There is the RMG (multidisciplinary, with federal and regional health authorities and designated scientific experts including epidemiologists) that meets and communicates on an ad hoc basis 10 regarding the management of Avian Influenza risks for public health, such as guidance for PPE for health professionals. Communication flows from the RMG to both primary and secondary care sectors, with the primary care sector receiving information through federal public health entities. 39. There is also the RAG at federal level that is composed of designated scientists (bringing in additional specialists from specific areas depending on the subject) that carries out risk assessments and issues recommendations on a scientific basis. It was created (in place since 2008) to be independent and is an advisory body. 40. Another working group with risk assessment output of advisory nature is the RAG-V-EZ which has a more veterinary focus and was described under the animal health section. In 2023 it issued an opinion on the zoonotic risks of Avian Influenza virus infections in mammals with its recommendations summarised in an FAQ format, publicly available on the FASFC website4. In this context the group was requested to provide advice in the first case of mammal infection in a farm (ferrets in 2023). However, the study team found that although the advice of RAG-V-EZ is in the public domain, relevant at-risk groups such as private and local government veterinarians were not aware of their existence. Hence authorities could consider improving the visibility and communication channels of the RAG-V-EZ to allow its advice to reach relevant professional groups at operational level. 41. As both RAG and Rag-V-EZ groups have competencies in zoonotic diseases there seems to be an overlap in some aspects of their scope (e.g. occupational health). Further clarification of scopes and relevant processes would enhance the clarity of the necessary advice and communication channels. 42. The Superior Health Council of Belgium issues annual guidelines for seasonal influenza vaccination, identifying priority groups based on risk factors. These groups typically include individuals at higher risk of complications, such as pregnant women, people aged 65 and over, those with chronic conditions, and healthcare personnel. 43. The Council has not specifically included poultry workers and veterinarians in the priority groups for the national strategy for seasonal flu, citing a lack of clear evidence to support their inclusion. The recommended prioritisation was nevertheless requested by the RAG-V-EZ, also in line with the HSC opinion on zoonotic Avian Influenza, by the time of the audit. 44. Occupational health services are based at federal level and have limited involvement in ensuring appropriate PPE use at workplaces with high risk of HPAI exposure. The RAG-V-EZ has provided advice in relation to appropriate protective equipment, and precautions to reduce spillover risks from zoonotic avian influenza for people exposed to potentially infected animals. The responsibility for the PPE supply and use lies with the employer. Subcontracting firms undertaking culling, cleaning and disinfection on infected farms are providing their staff with PPE and training on appropriate use. Some of these firms can be based in a different Member State. Compliance with relevant occupational health requirements in this case, lies with the Member State where the firm is based. The team saw evidence of mostly appropriate PPE and correct use from staff of 4 https://favv-afsca.be/nl/themas/dieren/dierengezondheid/dierziekten/vogelgriep (in Dutch) 11 these firms although it also saw evidence of no mask wearing during depopulation of infected farms. 45. While there is no vaccination program specifically for Avian Influenza, there is a strategic stockpile of Avian Influenza vaccines (Bavarian). The Belgian Task Force Therapeutics Viral Diseases has evaluated antiviral agents like oseltamivir (Tamiflu®) and baloxavir (Xofluza®) for potential stockpiling in preparation for influenza pandemic. 46. There is no generalized awareness campaign directed at the public concerning Avian Influenza spillover risks from birds and mammals. Health authorities have determined that such a campaign could lead to unnecessary panic and potentially undermine public trust in health guidance. This has been agreed upon multiple times as a consensus among Belgian health authorities. Information on the zoonotic risks of HPAI can be found nevertheless the website of FASFC and environmental authorities. 2. Monitoring & early detection 47. The laboratory of respiratory pathogens at Viral Diseases of Sciensano acts as the National Influ- enza Centre in Belgium and is officially recognized by the WHO and ECDC. Overall, Sciensano is ISO 17025 accredited for more than 100 different test procedures. In 2012, several laboratories, including the laboratory of respiratory viruses, obtained the ISO 15189 accreditation for different test methods. 48. It is coordinating the national surveillances programs for influenza including influenza like illness (ILI) (since 2007) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infections surveillance (SARI) (since 2010) thereby testing for influenza (typing and subtyping) and 16 other respiratory viruses. 49. Samples from the sentinel networks of the above surveillance programs (hospitals, general practi- tioners, nursing homes) and from external laboratories/hospitals are submitted to a series of tests: identification and typing for influenza A and B, subtyping influenza A (for H1, H3, N1 and N2), determination of influenza B lineage (Yamagata, Victoria) and subtyping for H5Nx, H7Nx, H9Nx for suspected cases of avian flu (by qPCR, but WGS has been also implemented) and swine influ- enza is performed on samples that test negative for seasonal influenza virus and if there is any indication of a zoonotic event. Results are shared with the RAG and with ECDC weekly. 50. A subset of influenza positive clinical samples is sequenced at the laboratory to characterize cir- culating strains to detect mutations in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes which might be associated with severe clinical outcomes. A subset of samples is isolated and fur- ther characterized (e.g. hemagglutination inhibition test and sero-neutralisation). Results are shared with RAG and ECDC weekly. The Centre notifies ECDC (through the European surveil- lance portal for infectious diseases, Epipulse) of confirmed cases within 24 hours of laboratory diagnosis. Results are also shared with WHO and ECDC twice a year. 51. The Centre shares data with the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System Collaborating Centres for Reference and Research on Influenza. It is also responsible for uploading 12 genetic sequencing data on influenza virus in the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID).

OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE This follow-up audit took place in Italy from 13 to 25 October 2024 and was undertaken as part of the Directorate General for Health and Food Safety's planned 2024 work programme. The audit team comprised two auditors from the said Directorate General. iv The audit was performed as a hybrid audit, using a combination of remote videoconferences and on-site meetings. The remote part was carried out on 13 and 14 October and the on-site part between 16 and 25 October. Representatives of the central competent authority, the Directorate-General for Animal Health and Veterinary Medicinal Products of the Ministry of Health, accompanied the audit team throughout the audit. The objective of this follow-up audit was to evaluate the implementation of the action plan proposed by the Italian authorities after the Commission audit DG(SANTE)2022-7586 in 2022 to evaluate the application of measures for the control of avian influenza, The audit also evaluated the control by the authorities of the subsequent epidemics of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). The scope of the audit included the nine recommendations raised in the previous audit report and the authorities' actions to control subsequent epidemics of the disease. The previous audit concluded that the competent authorities had not addressed satisfactorily some important structural and organisational shortcomings that undermined the capacity of the animal health emergency preparedness system, notably in Veneto and Lombardy, to respond rapidly and effectively to the previous (2021/22) HPAI epizootic. The audit team conducted the audit through data and document review, interviews with officials and other parties concerned and system verifications via videoconference and visits on the spot at local, regional and central level. In pursuit of these objectives, the audit team carried out the following visits and meetings: Visits / meetings No. Description Central competent authority 3 Including opening and final meeting Regional/local competent authority 5 Livestock Establishments 4 Poultry establishments infected in the last HPAI seasons Laboratory 2 National Reference Centre for Epidemiology, regional official laboratory 1. LEGAL BASIS The audit was carried out under the general provisions of EU legislation and, in particular, Articles 116, 117 and 119 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Full legal references to EU legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex 1 and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 5 2 BACKGROUND The 2021/22 HPAI epidemic season was the largest observed in Europe with an unprecedented geographical extent reaching from Svalbard islands to South Portugal and Ukraine, affecting 37 European countries1. During the season 2022/23, the number of HPAI outbreaks in poultry decreased. However, as in the 2021/22 epidemic, outbreaks declined briefly in April with the departure of the winter migratory birds, but the number of cases rose again between May and June. According to EFSA, this increase may have been linked to the wild bird chicks hatching in breeding colonies during summer, as these chicks are highly susceptible to HPAI H5N1. The surge of outbreaks in seabirds did not coincide with a rise in poultry cases. The 2023/2024 epidemic year had the lowest number of cases in poultry and wild birds since 2019/2020. This drop maybe due to several factor e.g., immunity in wild birds from previous infections; reduction in certain wild bird populations; decreased environmental contamination; or changes in viral genotypes. Further investigation is needed to confirm these causes. As in past epizootics, migratory wild birds played a key role spreading the HPAI virus to the poultry population during 2022-2024. 1 https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/avian-influenza#published-on-this-topic 6 The graphics below illustrate the number of poultry outbreaks (figure (a)) and the number of wild bird outbreaks in Europe (figure (b)) since Oct 2019: Number of wild bird and poultry outbreaks in Europe since Oct 2019 (Source- EFSA) Italy has several provinces with high poultry density, making them particularly vulnerable to HPAI in past epidemics. During audited period, most outbreaks occurred in Veneto (31 in domestic birds) and Lombardy (nine). For more information see maps 1 to 4 in Annex II. From 2021 to 2024, the number of poultry farms and birds kept on those in Veneto and Lombardy declined, including in the provinces with the highest farm densities. Turkey populations in these areas have been a recurring concern during epidemics. Between September 2022 and 8 October 2024, Italy notified 324 HPAI events to the Commission's Animal Disease Information System (ADIS). These included 49 poultry farm outbreaks, one case in a captive bird establishment, and 274 cases in wild birds. Poultry outbreaks decreased from 31 in 2022 to three in 2024. Meanwhile, wild bird cases rose sharply, from 47 in 2022 to 227 in 2023, with eight more cases detected in 2024. Seabirds accounted for 169 out of 193 cases (87.56%) in 2023. 7 The 2022/23 epidemic had two waves: the first wave in September to December 2022 (30 outbreaks) and the spring wave in March to July 2023 (11 outbreaks). Between November 2023 and February 2024, Italy detected six HPAI outbreaks, five in commercial farms and one in a small backyard flock. 3 MAIN FINDINGS 3.1 FINDINGS ON PREVENTION Biosecurity 1. The previous Commission audit report, DG(SANTE)2022-7586 (hereafter "the previous report"), identified weaknesses in the poultry farms' biosecurity measures. These measures did not adequately address the risks associated with high-density poultry establishments and environmental contamination from wild birds.
