text: The characteristics of the 2021/2022 outbreaks highlight the high risk of environmental infection along wild bird migratory routes. The poultry industry's failure to adapt its disease prevention measures, combined with inadequate verification by the competent authorities left these critical risk factors insufficiently addressed.
After the previous audit, Italian authorities amended national legislation and adopted a new Ministerial Decree in May 2023 to strengthen biosecurity in poultry farms.

The Decree focuses on high-density poultry areas to improve biosecurity and reduce the risk of disease transmission. It sets clear guidelines for the new poultry farms, requiring sufficient spacing to limit infection spread. These requirements align with rules already in place in Lombardy since July 2020. The legislation also mandates measures to minimise environmental contamination from dust emissions caused by ventilation systems. It requires stricter cleaning and disinfection practices, including automated vehicle disinfection systems (disinfection arcs), and hygienic loops at entry points.

The Decree requires monitoring and reporting systems to detect abnormal production data and mortality. Farmers must report these issues to private veterinarians and authorities. New farms have been required compliance with the new biosecurity measures since 1 July 2023. Existing registered farms must comply by 1 July 2024, one year after the Decree came into force.

The Decree sets new criteria to identify high-risk areas for HPAI introduction (Zone A) and spread (Zone B). To mitigate these risks, it bans new free-range turkey farms, the conversion of existing farms to this system, and specific restocking practices for turkey farms. Regional authorities, together with the Regional Veterinary Epidemiological Observatories and the National Reference Laboratory (NRL), regularly assess risks to adjust the zones and ensure that enhanced biosecurity measures are implemented where needed (see map 5 in Annex II for details).

The legislation requires breeders and animal professionals to complete compulsory training to make them aware and ensure they implement biosecurity measures correctly. It also mandates regular inspections of poultry farms, with at least 10% inspected annually. Some regions, like Veneto, have opted for more intensive surveillance, inspecting 50% of 8 turkey flocks in high-risk zones. For future years, the authorities will determine the minimum sample size for inspections in collaboration with the NRL and the regions, based on the epidemiological situation, the risk category of each farm, and progress in biosecurity compliance.

Regional authorities apply pre-defined risk criteria to select poultry farms for inspection, e.g., poultry density, proximity to waterbodies, bird movements, and the type of farm. Inspectors use tailored checklists for different categories of poultry farms to guide their inspections. Inspection results are recorded in the "ClassyFarm" system, part of the veterinary portal Vetinfo.it. Farms are ranked by risk levels, which authorities use to prioritise official inspections. This aligns with the requirements set out in Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 regarding risk-based controls.

The Ministry of Health, in collaboration with regional authorities and research institutes, is developing an automated system to optimise poultry farm inspections based on risk level. From 2025, the system will allocate 60% of inspections in regional plans to the highest-risk establishments, with a further 35% allocated at the discretion of regional authorities. This will ensure comprehensive coverage, with the remaining 5% allocated randomly. Regional authorities will also retain the flexibility to inspect a higher proportion of establishments, as is already the case in Veneto for turkey flocks.

The regional and local authorities presented evidence of various training sessions and campaigns to farmers aimed at raising awareness about biosecurity. They also provided a summary of the controls carried out, which shows a satisfactory level of implementation of official controls in regions affected by recent epidemics.

In 2023, Lombardy reported 847 inspections on 706 farms (out of 1,729). Inspectors found 68 establishments partially non-compliant with biosecurity rules. Both in Veneto and Lombardy, local authorities conducted inspections in accordance with their annual plans. The inspections highlighted a concerning trend of increased non-compliance with biosecurity rules among poultry establishments over the past two years. This trend is partly attributed to the new, stricter biosecurity requirements and one-year transitional period for their implementation, which ended on 1 July 2024.

In addition to the planned inspections, local authorities have introduced additional inspections prior to restocking turkey establishments, particularly in high-risk areas during HPAI high-risk periods. This selective requirement ensures that only establishments meeting biosecurity standards are allowed to restock.

The central epidemiological laboratory, in cooperation with authorities and industry, redefined and started implementing the "homogeneous areas" concept for the fattening turkey sector. The concept aims to prevent the rapid spread of infection in Zone B during high-risk periods by avoiding areas with high-risk age categories of turkeys (older than 14 weeks) and implementing a strict timely coordinated all-in-all-out farming system. Initially, the concept is being implemented in macro-areas of the region of Veneto, where the risk is the highest. The authorities plan to expand the implementation to the region of Lombardy in the coming years.

The Regional Working Group for Poultry Biosafety in Veneto was established in 2022 to address the region's biosecurity needs. The group's main goals are to develop and 9 implement effective guidelines for biosecurity measures and avian influenza control in the region. In 2022, the group organized training sessions on the use of the national "ClassyFarm" system and new checklists, and later conducted a course on key biosecurity issues to promote a harmonized approach. Group members also contributed to the development of new biosecurity measures, including specific restocking practices for turkey establishments and minimum distances between establishments, which were previously identified as critical issues.

The actions described above demonstrate the authorities' commitment to adapting disease prevention measures to mitigate the impact of critical risk factors, as required by Article 10(1)(b) and (c), (4), and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The audit team visited poultry farms. They were in good condition and had recently been inspected by authorities to assess compliance with biosecurity measures. The outcome of the authorities' inspection was favourable. The owners also confirmed that their staff had received training on preventive measures against HPAI, which included guidance from integrated company and /or company veterinarians.

The audit team identified some weaknesses in business operator procedures and official veterinary controls. Specifically, disinfection procedures for vehicles entering establishments lacked necessary details, e.g., absence of a list of disinfectants used, their dilution, and minimum contact time to kill the HPAI virus. The audit team observed that some establishments were applying disinfectants in shorter contact times than recommended in technical specifications. There were also shortcomings regarding pest control management, such as the absence of procedures to deal with an increased presence of rodents close to poultry houses or the adherence to predetermined visit plans even when an ad-hoc visit had been recommended by the pest control operator. These deficiencies, that were not detected in any official controls, are not in line with the requirements set out in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (4)(a)(ii), (4)(b)(i), 4(b) (ii) and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 ­ on responsibilities on disease prevention and biosecurity, and Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 ­ on general obligations of the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls. Early detection Wild birds

Italy's national surveillance plan covers poultry, game bird farms, and wild birds. The plan includes a passive surveillance system that involves testing wild birds found dead throughout the year, with a focus on high-risk areas such as wetlands, intensive poultry industries, and migratory flyways. Enhanced passive surveillance is also conducted in specific areas, including the Po River Delta, where there are high concentrations of wild birds, as well as in locations where active surveillance is not feasible due to restrictions on hunting.

In September 2022, the Italian Ministry of Health asked regions at high risk (Veneto, Lombardy, Piedmont, Lazio, Umbria, and Emilia-Romagna) to implement an active surveillance plan for wild, hunted migratory birds (Anatidae) and live decoys. The plan ran during the hunting season, from late September to the end of January. As of 2024, the 10 Italian national surveillance plan for wild birds combines both passive and active surveillance, covering hunted and live-captured wild birds.

Recently, regional epidemiological observatories have worked closely with authorities to identify areas at higher risk of avian influenza. They have focused on improving early detection of HPAI in wild birds, following Articles 4(1)(b) and 10(2) of, and Annex II (Section 4) to Regulation (EU) 2020/689 and thus address the recommendation from the previous audit. By considering wildlife habitat, bird migration patterns, and poultry farm density, the observatories helped regions focus their surveillance efforts. They also worked with bird migration experts to gather data on wild bird movements. This has allowed regions to design and implement tailored surveillance plans, including both passive and active methods, in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Regional and local authorities worked with hunting associations and rescue centres to improve avian influenza surveillance. Hunters received training to collect cloacal swabs from hunted Anatidae, and agreements with these associations allowed testing of shot birds. In Lombardy, 1,504 birds were tested during the 2022/23 epidemic season and 1,993 during 2023/24. The tests showed avian influenza virus positivity rates of 5.26% and 5.21%, respectively. Positive samples appeared throughout the hunting season, with higher rates at the start (September-October) than at the end (January). Veneto reported similar findings from comparable sampling activities. Both regions designed their plans to minimise the burden on hunters collecting samples. Although this approach increased the workload for veterinary services; it led to a higher number of collected samples, improving surveillance outcomes.

Regional authorities partnered with provincial police and park rangers to improve passive surveillance. They distributed brochures to raise public awareness about HPAI. The central authority supported these efforts by providing guidelines on handling mass mortality in wild birds, conducting HPAI testing and ensuring biosecurity in rescue centres. Both Veneto and Lombardy have prioritised strengthening passive surveillance through targeted campaigns and meetings with stakeholders, such as fishing lakes and waterbodies owners and managers. This focus increased the number of samples collected in 2023 (details can be found in Graphs 1 in Annex II).

Wild bird surveillance data provides an early warning for outbreaks in farmed poultry, particularly in Zones A and B. To stay prepared, Italian authorities and experts regularly review EFSA epidemiological reports and monitor the situation in neighbouring countries. This helps them to anticipate high-risk periods and prepare, even with limited domestic data.

The Central Crisis Unit activates when positive cases or worsening epidemiological trends are detected, particularly in neighbouring countries. In consultation with the Reference Centre for Avian Influenza, this unit advises regional authorities on preventive measures and enhanced surveillance. For example, in September 2022, authorities issued directives for Zones A and B. These included keeping birds indoors, increasing passive surveillance of wild birds, and restricting the stocking of fattening turkeys in high-risk areas of Lombardy and Veneto. Enhanced surveillance measures for domestic birds included pre- 11 movement checks and sampling/testing within 48 hours before dispatch. Authorities and experts monitored the epidemiological situation in wild birds throughout the 2022/23 high-risk season and adjusted measures as needed.

Over the past two seasons, most samples collected through passive and active surveillance originated from regions previously heavily affected by HPAI. Active surveillance generally followed established guidelines, with peak sampling activity during the winter months of 2022 and 2023 (refer to Graph 1 and 2 in Annex II for more information). However, during the 2022/23 HPAI season, active surveillance contributed minimally to early disease detection. This was due to a delayed start, with the bulk of samples only being collected from January 2023 onward. In contrast, the 2023/2024 season showed significant improvements, with active surveillance detecting a higher percentage of positive samples (up to 12%) in the Veneto and Lombardy regions as early as September/October 2023.

The data highlight variability in the timeliness of confirming HPAI outbreaks in wild birds. In 2022, laboratory confirmation of 12 out of 47 outbreaks occurred within 24 hours, while nine took more than two weeks. This trend was consistent in 2023, with 11 outbreaks confirmed within 24 hours, 124 within one week, and 14 taking longer than two weeks to confirm. In 2024, three out of eight outbreaks were confirmed within one week, while the remaining cases experienced delays of up to 50 days. Delays in confirming outbreaks from rescue centres were a particular challenge, as these centres rely on volunteers and experience high staff turnover, requiring ongoing attention from authorities.

The effectiveness of Italy's early detection system has varied across regions and epidemic seasons. For instance, during the 2022/23 season, Veneto's system failed to detect the disease in wild birds until after it had spread to domestic birds. In contrast, Lombardy's system performed well, detecting the disease in wild birds before any outbreaks occurred in domestic birds, which is a significant improvement from the 2021 season, when the first detection of H5N1 HPAI virus in domestic poultry in Lombardy occurred after detection in wild animals. The 2023/24 season saw further gains, with Veneto detecting the disease in wild birds before it spread to domestic birds, and Lombardy experiencing no outbreaks in domestic birds. This is line with the objectives for surveillance in wild birds as laid down in Annex II (Section 2) to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

In early October 2024, an HPAI outbreak was detected in poultry in the Emilia-Romagna region, with no corresponding outbreaks in wild birds in the surrounding area. The authorities responded by introducing additional preventive measures on poultry establishments in high-risk areas (Zones A and B) in the region. The delay in detection of the disease in wild birds was attributed to the insufficient sensitivity of the passive surveillance system at that time, as well as the delayed start of the hunting season (and therefore active surveillance) due to a legal dispute. This case highlights the need for adequate application of early warning system described in finding 24, and for improvement in the region of Emilia-Romagna's surveillance system, which falls short of the requirements set out in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, Articles 4(1)(b) and 10(2) of, and Annex II (Section 4) to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. 12 29. In 2022/23 and 2023/24 seasons, experts sequenced the complete genome of 238 A(H5N1) viruses isolated from domestic and wild birds in Italy. The genetic analysis revealed a high degree of genetic diversity among these viruses. The CCA stated that, as a consequence of the implementation of the OCR there have not been any changes in the national legislation. 2 2. Act XLVI of 2008 on the Food Chain and its Official Control defines the official tasks of the CA responsible for food chain control (e.g., approval/registration of food business operators (FBOs), official controls, sampling and enforcement). Government Decree 383/2016 determines which level of CA is responsible for different tasks (central, county or district level). 3. MA Decree 20/2021 on the production and placing on the market of foodstuffs and materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs contains detailed rules on the approval procedure for food producing establishments. 4. Joint MA-Ministry of Social and Labour Affairs Decree No 16/2008 on the testing of raw milk regulates the requirements for laboratory testing and control procedures for the placing on the market of raw milk of all animal species. However, the audit team noted that the Decree allows milk collection centres (MCCs) to test raw bulk milk for raw milk quality criteria instead of testing milk samples received from single dairy holdings, as required by Chapter I.3 of Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5. MA Decree 4/1998 on the acceptable levels of microbiological contamination in foodstuffs sets requirements for foodstuffs, providing for microbiological tests and recommended limits for the internal quality control of production for milk and dairy products. 6. Direct supply of small quantities of food is regulated by MA Decree 60/2023 on the hygiene conditions for the production and sale of small, local and marginal quantities of food. Raw milk and dairy products (in quantities not exceeding 200 Kg of dairy products or 500 litres/day, respectively) may be sold if the dairy herd is certified as free of tuberculosis and brucellosis by an official veterinary certificate (which is valid for 1 year) Moreover, the words "raw milk that can be consumed after boiling" or "produced with raw milk" must be clearly displayed at the point of sale. 7. There is no national legislation regarding the implementation of Article 10.2 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 with regard to flexibility rules (traditional methods and/or regions with special geographical restraints). 8. The legal basis for enforcement of regulatory requirements is provided by the Act XLVI/2008 on the food chain and official control and by the Government Decree 194/2008 on the method and level of fines for the supervision of the Food Chain. The sanctions range from administrative sanctions to withdrawal of approval. Official guidance on enforcement was available. Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures 9. National legislation and administrative measures covering the dairy sector have been enacted and are in line with relevant EU legislation, except for sampling and testing provisions in relation to the quality criteria of raw milk in collection centres. 3 10. Legislation and policies provide officials with appropriate powers and to take enforcement actions when non-compliances are detected during official controls. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 11. A general description of the CAs and of their responsibilities can be found in the country profile for Hungary, available at the link: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country/profile/details/HU 12. Overall responsibility for the organisation and operation of official controls throughout the whole food chain in Hungary is shared as follows: a. NFCSO, which reports to MA, is the CCA responsible for the policy for the whole food chain, and for supervising the control activities at county and local level in the areas of feed, animal health and welfare, border controls, food safety and quality, and the registration/marketing/control of veterinary medicinal products (VMPs). The NFCSO is also the national contact point for the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF); b. CGOs direct, supervise and coordinate the work of the district offices and collect the data required for the reports. Based on the Government Decree 22/2012, CGOs carry out their official duties through the IT systems operated by NFCSO, implement the control and sampling plans, collect data, keep records and report to NFCSO. They also implement actions based on the recommendations made in internal controls/audits/specialised audits, and carry out inspections and other activities in accordance with the available procedures and guidelines issued by the NFCSO; c. as from 1 January 2024, the administrative supervision of CGOs has been transferred to the Ministry of Public Administration and Regional Development. However, NFCSO still maintains the technical supervision in its areas of competence; d. at local level, there are 197 DGOs, of which 81 have a Food Chain Safety and Animal Health Unit (FCSAH). Each FCSAH unit covers 2-3 DGOs on average and carries out all official controls on the food chain, animal health and welfare, feed and food hygiene/safety/quality and VMPs. 13. NFCSO operates a national network of laboratories: NFCSO Food Chain Safety Laboratory Directorate performs, among other tasks, analyses on milk and dairy 4 products, foreign water content in milk and dairy products, residual substances and chemical elements in foodstuffs of animal origin, and microbiological analyses in foodstuffs. NFCSO is also responsible for the approval and registration of private food and feed testing laboratories. 14. Private veterinarians carry out mandatory animal health tests and sampling. According to Government Decree No 113/2006 on the powers and detailed rules relating to the operation of the approved veterinarians, a three-parties contract (NFCSO-CGO- approved veterinarian) regulates the tasks performed by the approved veterinarian. 15. NFCSO operates the IT Food Chain Control Information System (FELIR), in which all FBOs are registered, and the Electronic Examination and Control System (EÜER) database, which contains all records related to official controls. 16. Coordination and flow of information between the CCA, the CGOs and FCSAHs is ensured by regular CGO reports to the CCA on the supervision of DGOs official controls (i.e., through the data uploaded in the EÜER database by the CGOs). The audit team noted that there was no feedback from the DGOs to CGOs of follow-up controls on non-compliances with SCC and PC at holding level, and in some cases follow-up visits had not been carried out (see paragraphs 47 and 49). 17. Official controls in the milk sector shall be carried out only by qualified staff (veterinarians, or agricultural or food engineers). Whilst CGOs and NFCSO are responsible for training their newly recruited staff continuous training is mandatory for all staff, who have to collect a minimum number of training points each year. 18. No specific training for the dairy sector has been provided in recent years as there have been no legislative changes in this sector. However, the findings regarding dairy inspectors' knowledge on HACCP-based procedures indicates there is a need for specific training on this topic (see paragraph 62). 19. The NFCSO intranet (for central and county/district staff) provides an update of legislative provisions relevant for the activities. 20. The CAs currently experience shortage of qualified staff, as a number of staff left the service in 2022. This issue had been dealt with, partially by sharing responsibilities between CGOs and DGOs, and by prioritising tasks (i.e., follow-up of corrective actions requested to the FBOs postponed to the following annual inspection). 21. Some weaknesses in relation to the technical knowledge of the CA staff were noted by the audit team during the official controls of the milk processing establishments, in particular 6 regarding the control over the FBOs' procedures in relation to pasteurisation of milk (see paragraphs 62, 65 and 66). Conclusions on competent authorities 22. The CAs responsible for the official control system over the production of milk and 5 dairy products are clearly designated and their structure and organisation are adequate for the performance of their tasks. 23. The CA has taken mitigating actions to cope with shortages of official staff and to maintain an appropriate level and effectiveness of official controls. 24. Communication flows and cooperation between the different levels of the CAs involved in the dairy sector are generally established and effective. However, follow-up of non- compliances regarding certain raw milk criteria was not adequately followed-up by the CGOs. 25. The general training system in place, aimed at ensuring that official staff carry out their tasks adequately, does not include specific training on official controls in the dairy sector. No such training has been carried out in recent years. The official staff met was not fully knowledgeable in the technical matters pertaining to the dairy sector. 5.3 REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 26. The approval procedure is regulated by Ministerial Decree 20/2021 "on the production and placing on the market of foodstuffs and materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs". The procedure in place is in line with Article 148 of the OCR and covers both conditional and full approvals. 27. The approval of milk processing establishments, MCCs and cold stores (CS) is the responsibility of the CGOs. The approval is issued by the CGO, with the approval number being issued by NFCSO: approved activities, maximum production capacity and specific conditions that the FBO must meet are included in the approval decision. The approval of MCCs is issued by the CGO. 28. The list of approved food establishments is available at: https://portal.nebih.gov.hu/documents/10182/567630931/enged_2024_01_11.pdf/. There are currently 108 milk processing establishments, 60 MCCs and 37 CS, which are also approved for storing dairy products. 29. Dairy holdings must be registered and are given a unique holding code, as primary food- producing businesses in accordance with the procedure regulated by a Circular. The 6 registration is carried out by the CGOs. The list of registered dairy holdings is available at: https://portal.nebih.gov.hu/documents/10182/567630931/Tejtermgazd_2023_10_27.pdf/ . 30. The MA Regulation 60/2023 provides for a specific registration for FBOs involved in direct sale and supply of small quantities of primary products and processed products of animal origin to the final consumer and other retail establishments. Holdings selling raw milk to final consumers must be registered for this purpose. The complete list of operators registered for direct sale of such products was available at CCA level. Details of which products are manufactured are available at CGO level. 31. Conditions for approval are reviewed by the CAs during the inspections of all dairy processing establishments and MCCs. Documented evidence of such activities was provided to the audit team during the visits. 32. All establishments visited had a valid approval, and documented evidence was provided that changes had been appropriately included in the approval files. 33. The audit team noted the following shortcomings regarding approval and registration: a. One FBO that also stored and traded, in small quantities, chilled dairy products and some other foodstuffs obtained in other establishments2; b. Another FBO had received consignments of raw milk from another milk processing establishment. The FBO was not able to explain if the consignment came directly from milk producing holdings, or from an intermediate storage of the other milk processing establishment. In the latter case the establishment sending the raw milk is required to have the activity of collection centre included in its approval, in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 148 of the OCR. The CAs committed to investigate the situation and report the outcome to the audit team; c. Transport companies delivering foodstuffs (including raw milk) must be registered. The control checklists seen by the audit team did not have a specific section for verification of the means of transport, indicating that official controls do not cover transport means. In one case, the audit team could verify that the registration of the transport company in the specific register/database (FELIR) was not requested by the processing dairy when signing the contract with the transport company. The FELIR registration number of that company could not be retrieved for the audit team. Conclusions on registration and approval of food business establishments

In addition to Regulation (EU) 2020/689, the animal health requirements are regulated by FVN Regulation 12/2008 (II.14) and MA Decree 56/2019 (XII.12). All bovine animals older than 12 months are subjected to the intradermal tuberculin and brucellosis tests; controls are also performed in the cases of abortions reported in the holdings (Q- fever and brucellosis). The CCA stated that, in recent years, 4-7 outbreaks of bovine tuberculosis (MTBC) have been identified per year, mainly in free-range, grazing beef herds. 38. Three abortions had occurred in 2022 in the dairy cattle holding (with 376 milking cows) visited by the audit team. The contracted private veterinarian stated that the cause was Q-fever. This resulted in vaccination of the herd and slaughter of positive animals. All eligible animals had been tested for tuberculosis and brucellosis with favourable results. 5.4.2 Hygiene on milk and colostrum production holdings 5.4.2 Hygiene on milk and colostrum production holdings 39. In the 2023 annual national control plan for animal holdings drafted by the CCA, it was planned to inspect 3 310 animal holdings (all species) during that year. This number does not include "ad hoc" inspections for new registrations, follow-ups, etc. The 3 310 holdings were distributed among CGOs based on their own risk rate, and calculated taking into account the number of outbreaks, number of animal holdings (large and small) and the number of non-compliances detected in previous years. 8 40. Irrespective of the above risk-based selection, inspections on milk producing holdings have to be carried out by the DGOs at a minimum frequency of once every 3 years, for milk hygiene checks using specific checklists. 41. No cases of positive results for residues of inhibitory substances in the milk had been recorded in recent years on the dairy holding visited by the audit team. The stock of VMPs was properly kept and recorded. The animals currently under treatment with VMPs, present in the premises, were visually identified, segregated and milked at the end of the milking session. The structure and cleanliness of the milk storage room was satisfactory, whilst the milking parlour was in need of some maintenance (this is already planned by the owner). 42. Law On the Supervision of the Handling of Food of 19 February 1998 (as amended) defines the official tasks of the CA responsible for official control of foodstuffs.

Direct supply of small quantities of raw cow and goat milk is regulated by Republic of Latvia Cabinet Regulation No 73 of 19 February 2019. Small quantities are defined as up to 1000 kg and 600 kg weekly production of cow and goat milk, respectively. Such raw milk can be sold directly to the consumer and retail within a radius of 300 km. A permit from the FVS is required for this and the sales must be documented. The milk must be sold within 48 hours of the first milking, and labelled as "Raw cow milk" or "Raw goat milk" and "Boil before consumption". The audit team visited a dairy holding which had the TSU permit to sell small quantities of raw cow milk in bottles directly to the final consumer, in line with the above-mentioned national requirements.

An overview of how control systems are organised in Latvia is provided in the Multi- annual National Control Plan (MANCP) of Latvia which can be found under the 'Mem- ber State Links' tab on the following web page: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country/profile/details/LV
FVS (under the supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture) is the CCA, with overall re- sponsibilities for food and veterinary controls. It consists of the central office and the TSUs.

Within the central office: · The Food Surveillance Department (FSD) plans, organises and co-ordinates offi- cial controls on compliance with requirements laid down in legislation governing food of animal and non-animal origin, and compliance of food products with consumer safety and quality criteria. It also approves establishments; drafts guidelines, instructions, and procedures; evaluates inspection and sampling re- 3 sults; carries out the audits of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) systems at establishments of food of animal origin; and organises the follow-up of corrective actions. · The Veterinary Surveillance Department (VSD) covers areas including preven- tion and eradication of animal infectious diseases, official controls on production of primary products of animal origin, animal welfare and protection, control of animal identification and movement and holding registration. It also, provides training for veterinary inspectors and supervises the performance of TSUs.
The regular official controls of dairy establishments and holdings are carried out by food inspectors and veterinary inspectors, respectively, placed in the 11 TSUs.

The FSD food control system and VSD veterinary control system have been accredited in accordance with ISO 17020 by the Latvian Accreditation Body (LATAK) since 2007 and 2009, respectively. These accreditations include the TSUs.
Within this quality management system, several documented procedures (work instruc- tions, guidance, checklists, etc.) are available for the official controls.

According to the data provided by FVS, there is a total of 232 inspectors (including food inspectors and veterinary inspectors) at the TSUs. Out of these staff, 43 food inspectors are responsible for official controls in the food sector (including dairy establishments) and 69 veterinary inspectors for the supervision of holdings (including dairy holdings).

FVS has established a centrally managed training system for its staff. FVS prepares a training plan every year, for which leading experts in their field plan the necessary train- ing for inspectors. The training plan can be supplemented with additional training, if necessary.

Evidence was provided to the audit team of staff participation in training sessions in all the TSUs visited. The audit team noted that some staff also participate in relevant train- ing events organised by the European Commission under the Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF) programme.
The official staff interviewed had a good knowledge of the tasks that they are required to carry out and the applicable EU and national legislation.
At central level, FVS has two senior dairy technical experts, who support the work of food inspectors carrying out official controls in the dairy sector.

Official controls are supported by electronic databases (e.g. iPVD and DVS). The iPVD database contains general information on all the establishments that are registered or ap- proved by FVS. All inspection reports are stored in this database. The information stored in the database is used for the planning of inspections (risk-based controls) and supervi- sion by FVS over the work of TSUs. The DVS database is used for document manage- ment purposes (e.g. electronic correspondence between FVS central level and TSUs). 4 Conclusions on competent authorities
The structure and organisation of the CA is adequate for the performance of the control tasks related to milk and dairy products.
The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures and training) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently.

There is a training system in place, aimed at ensuring that official staff carry out their tasks adequately. 5.3 REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. FVS informed the audit team that colostrum is not collected and used in the production of dairy products in Latvia.

Official controls of dairy holdings are carried out by veterinary inspectors of the TSUs. The selection of holdings for inspection is risk-based. The dairy holdings targeted for a planned inspection in 2023 were selected based on at least two non-compliant PC and/or SCC results in 2022. Furthermore, inspections on milk hygiene are often combined with other inspections (e.g. cross-compliance, animal welfare, animal health or use of veteri- nary medicinal products (VMPs)). Holdings registered for direct sale of raw milk or dairy products made with raw milk are inspected at least once a year.
The checklist used for official controls of dairy holdings was comprehensive and con- tained relevant points of the legal requirements.

According to the data provided by FVS, 1 441 on-site and 740 documentary checks were carried out in dairy holdings in 2023 (including bovine, ovine and caprine holdings) and in addition, 118 and 97 dairy holdings were subject to cross-compliance checks in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

The audit team visited one bovine dairy holding which was subject to regular (at least once a year) official controls by the veterinary inspector of the TSU, as the farm was registered for direct sale of raw milk to the final consumer. The stock of VMPs was properly kept and recorded. The animals currently under treatment with VMPs, present in the premises, were visually identified, segregated and milked separately. In addition, their ear-tag numbers were flagged in the IT system of the farm. Conclusion on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings

Republic of Latvia Cabinet Regulation No 597 of 6 September 2016 provides the legal basis and the details of implementation for quality control of raw milk in accordance with Part III of Chapter I, Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 (see paragraph 5).

A highly developed database on raw milk quality (hereinafter ­ database) has been es- tablished in the Agricultural Data Centre, which is an institution under direct administra- tive supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture. All laboratory tests for raw milk, sam- pled in the framework of the obligatory sampling scheme and required follow-up sam- pling, and the results of same are recorded in the database. The information in the data- base, including warnings and bans of the sale of raw milk to the establishments, is ac- cessible to the CA and to the milk purchasers (dairy establishments and collection cen- tres) and enables them to check the quality of raw milk from the holdings producing raw milk for sale to the dairy industry.

The national legislation is in line with the EU requirements and requires sampling of raw milk at dairy holdings at least twice a month for PC and SCC and at least once a month for residues of inhibitory substances.

Two milk quality control laboratories are designated by FVS, in accordance with Cabi- net Regulation No 404 of 3 June 2008 Recognition of raw milk quality control laborato- ries and supervisory arrangements, to analyse and certify the quality of raw milk.

According to the information provided by FVS, these laboratories are accredited and use the reference methods or alternative methods, validated against the reference method for the PC and SCC. The raw milk laboratory, examined by the audit team, provided evi- dence that the laboratory had regularly participated in proficiency testing for PC and SCC with satisfactory results.

On behalf of the "purchaser" (usually the dairy processing establishment or the milk collection centre buying the milk directly from the dairy holding), raw milk samples are taken by the truck drivers who are trained by the purchaser. Certificates of training were available, and evidence was seen that these training certificates had been verified by the TSU food inspector during official controls. In addition, the audit team was informed that the food inspector routinely accompanies the truck driver in order to observe and verify the milk collection and sampling at the dairy holding. 7 39. After receiving the test results of the raw milk sample from the designated laboratory, the Data Centre calculates the geometric average values of the PC and SCC and records them in the database. 40. Republic of Latvia Cabinet Regulation No 597 also lays down the rules for when the criteria for raw milk is exceeded: if the geometric average of PC and/or SCC exceeds the criteria laid down in point 3 of Part III of Chapter I, Section IX of Annex III to Regula- tion (EC) No 853/2004, the Data Centre records a warning in the database, which sets a 3-month deadline for the producer to remedy the non-compliance in question, and also informs the purchaser and the producer of this electronically. 41. If the established non-compliance has not been rectified within the set 3-month period, the veterinary inspector can then temporarily prohibit the marketing of raw milk from the producer in question. 42. If the presence of inhibitors is detected in the raw milk (in any laboratory sample), the purchaser should immediately discontinue the use of raw milk for processing and take a repeat sample to confirm the presence of inhibitors. If the outcome of this repeat sample is positive, the Data Centre will then inform FVS electronically. The veterinary inspec- tor can then prohibit the marketing of the milk, inform the producer and the processing establishment and register the prohibition in the database. 43. In order for the sale of raw milk or the use of raw milk for processing to resume, the producer should submit an application to the TSU requesting an inspection of the hold- ing for the purpose of lifting the prohibition. The veterinary inspector will then perform an inspection of the holding and take an official sample which will be sent to the labora- tory for analyses. If the results of the analyses are compliant with the requirements, the prohibition is lifted and this is recorded in the database by the veterinary inspector. 44. FVS presented the audit team with several examples of when warning or prohibition was imposed and registered in the database. In general, the procedure laid down in the na- tional legislation had been followed. 45. Bulk raw milk in raw milk trucks is routinely tested for inhibitors upon arrival at pro- cessing establishments, using commercial rapid kits. Evidence was available that posi- tive results were notified to the TSUs for follow-up, and that the contaminated milk was either sent to a biogas plant or alternatively back to the farm of origin as an animal by- product. 46. The raw milk quality of the holdings visited, delivering milk to the collection centre and the dairy processing establishments, was adequate and the system in place was adhered to in the multiple examples examined by the audit team. 47. Some of the dairy establishments visited received raw milk from neighbouring member states. Contracts were in place with the foreign company selling the milk, which includ- ed the provision that the quality of raw milk fulfils the requirements laid down in Annex 8 III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Nevertheless, the receiving establishments had no data on the raw milk quality of the individual foreign dairy holdings. 48. text: An overview of how control systems are organised in Italy is provided in the Multi- annual National Control Plan (MANCP) of Italy, which can be found under the 'Member State Links' tab on the following web page: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/IT (3) TRACES (currently named TRACES-NT) is the European Commission's online platform for animal and plant health certification required for the importation of animals, animal products, food and feed of non- animal origin and plants into the European Union, and the intra-EU trade and EU exports of animals and cer- tain animal products. 3 2. In the Ministry of Health, Office 2 of the Directorate-General for Food Hygiene, Food Safety and Nutrition is the central division responsible for policy, legislation and general planning of official controls in the area of ABP and DP (including petfood). 3. Office 7 of the Directorate-General for Animal Health is responsible for coordinating the implementation of feed legislation and for planning official controls on feed. As petfood is regulated by both ABP and feed legislation, Office 7 is involved in the overall frame- work of official controls, including in relation to official sampling. 4. At regional level, the responsibility for controls on ABP and DP is assigned to the re- gional veterinary services (RVS) which are part of the regional public health services. RVS tasks include planning, coordination and verification of the control activities of the local competent authorities. 5. Responsibility for the planning and execution of official controls lies with the local health units (ASL) based on the instructions provided by the regions and the Ministry of Health. In each ASL, staff in charge of ABP (including petfood) usually have other re- sponsibilities, mainly (but not only) in relation to livestock hygiene and animal welfare. 6. The audit team noted that the competent authorities in charge of official controls on ABP and DP are clearly designated and that staff have the necessary legal powers to car- ry out control activities. This is in line with the requirements of Article 4(1) and Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 7. Distribution of responsibilities within competent authorities is clearly established and all staff interviewed were aware of their roles and tasks. This fulfils the requirements of Ar- ticle 4(2)(a) and Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 8. As required by Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, staff have access to guidelines and checklists that support the approval and registration of ABP plants and operators, as well as the execution of official controls on ABP plants and food business operators where ABP are produced. 9. The audit team noted that staff involved in official controls had received training which should allow them to perform their tasks competently, in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10. As required by Article 5(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for the analyses carried out on samples taken during official controls, competent authorities avail of designated offi- cial laboratories with a sufficient examination capacity that are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. Based on the analytical reports reviewed, the audit team verified that the methods used for analyses of official samples were included in the respective scopes of accreditation of the official laboratories (see finding 33). 11. Representatives of the ASL met during the audit stated that they experienced difficulties in meeting the planned minimum frequency of inspections on ABP and DP due to limi- tations in the number of staff available (see finding 26). All of the plants visited by the 4 audit team had been controlled, although sometimes with a reduced frequency of inspec- tions. The RVS and ASL representatives met explained that recruitment of new staff was ongoing, in particular to offset the retirement of staff. Therefore, the current level of staff can be considered as broadly meeting the provisions of Article 5(1)(e) of Regula- tion (EU) 2017/625. 12. The RVS receive information on the number of controls carried out by the ASL and the volume of ABP and DP produced in the regions. Each RVS monitors the performance of the ASL placed under their remit. One of the RVS visited was in the process of develop- ing an IT system to monitor more closely the implementation of official controls on ABP and DP, while in another RVS such a system was already in place. As part of this supervisory process, the RVS audits the performance of the ASL. The audit team ob- tained evidence that when RVS audits identified issues in the performance ASL, these were followed-up in due time and actions were taken to address them. 13. The internal audit system operated required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 covers official controls on ABP and DP. As part of this system, the Ministry of Health at central level audits the RVS and ASL. The audit team received evidence of follow-up on recommendations made during past internal audits on ABP and DP. Conclusions on the structural elements of the official control system 14. The structural elements of the official control system on ABP and DP are in place. They provide a sound basis for the implementation of official controls on petfood. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ALONG THE ABP AND DP CHAIN FOR THE PRODUCTION OF PETFOOD 5.2.1 Registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators 15. All of the ABP plants visited (petfood plants and processing plants) were approved in accordance with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The audit team noted that the approval documentation reflected the activities carried out by the operators. 16. The audit team also examined the records of a selection of recent plant approvals and noted that the steps and assessments required by Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 were followed during the approval process. In particular, the ASL carried out on-the-spot inspections prior to recommending approval of the plants in question. 17. The ASL manage approval and registration requests from operators. The audit team saw documentary evidence that, during the approval process the ASL assessed operator compliance with all of the requirements applicable to the activities for which approval was requested. The two RVS visited by the audit team have issued application templates (for registration and approval), specified the lists of documents to be attached to such applications and use standardised inspection forms designed for the various steps of the approval process. 5 18. Based on information provided by the ASL, the RVS are responsible for assigning the approval and registration numbers to the plants and for entering the names of the ap- proved and registered ABP operators in the national lists. 19. The audit team noted that the national list of approved and registered petfood plants published on the Ministry of Health website did not contain information on the product types placed on the market, contrary to the Commission technical specifications (4) and the requirements of Article 20a(a) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. 20. The list of Italian petfood plants on the Commission's Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES NT) was not up to date; 125 plants were listed vs. 184 on the website of the Ministry of Health. Thus, the requirements of Article 20a(b) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are not met. 21. Based on the review of documents submitted by the Ministry of Health, the audit team noted that, in several regions, petfood plants that had stopped their activities for a long while were still present on the published list of petfood plants, despite several reminders sent by the Ministry of Health to RVS to ensure the timely removal of inactive operators from the national lists. Therefore, it cannot be considered that the list of petfood plant is kept up-to-date as required by Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Conclusions on registration, approval, and listing 22. There are arrangements in place for the registration, approval, and listing which should provide assurances that the operators active along the chain of petfood production are known and thus facilitate the implementation of official controls throughout this supply chain. However, the fact that the registration/approval data are not kept up to date (as evidenced by the disparity between the data in the national list and TRACES-NT), weakens an otherwise satisfactory system for approval and registration. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls 23. At national level, instructions and guidelines from the Ministry of Health are available and cover planning of official controls (inspections and sampling). 24. Both RVS visited issued instructions to ASL to plan their annual official controls. In turn, the ASL met developed tools to organise official controls at their level. 25. The frequency of inspections of approved ABP plants is based on a risk analysis carried out by the ASL. The minimum number of inspections to be carried out on an annual ba- sis directly derives from the risk category of the plants (low, medium or high risk). 26. The RVS and ASL visited followed the national rules for risk categorisation for planning their controls. However, due to limitation in resources available, one of the RVS visited had planned only 10% of the required number of inspections for approved ABP plants in 2024. Despite this 90% reduction in the frequency of inspections, all of the approved 4 https://ec.europa.eu/food/document/download/cf578ce7-3e32-4eb9-93de-6e5a4fac9089_en 6 petfood plants and processing plants (involved in the petfood chain) were included in the planning arrangements and were inspected. 27. In addition to inspections, audits are planned and carried out by ASL at approved ABP plants with a minimum frequency of 1 audit every 2 years. Audits cover the operators' system of own-checks, including Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) based procedures. 28. There is a 3-year national official feed sampling plan that is updated annually, and which covers feed and includes provisions for the sampling of petfood, in particular for the de- tection of Salmonella (113 samples per year) and glycerol tri-heptanoate in Category 1, 2 and 3 derived products (25 samples per year). The Ministry of Health allocates a number of samples to each RVS, which, in turn, allocates a number of samples to each ASL (tak- ing into account the production of feed in the geographical area controlled by the ASL). Conclusions on planning of official controls 29. Planning of official controls takes account of risk criteria, covers all operators acting along the petfood production chain and should provide assurances that the sector is ad- equately controlled. 5.2.3 Implementation of official controls 30. The ASL visited used RVS templates (see finding 24) to record their inspections of ap- proved and registered ABP operators. 31. The outcome of official controls is recorded and notified to the operators. The inspection records reviewed by the audit team contained all the elements required by Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 32. The audit team noted that inspections carried out in ABP plants are usually unan- nounced, in line with the requirements of Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 33. The audit team noted that official samples were taken by ASL staff in accordance with the annual control plan. Based on the review of several analytical reports, the audit team noted that samples were analysed by official laboratories that were accredited, using methods included in their scope of accreditation. 5.2.3.1 Official controls on collection and transport of ABP and DP 34. The audit team noted that ASL carry out controls on the collection and transport of ABP and DP to be used in petfood. In particular, ASL staff in charge of the approved petfood plants visited, reviewed, during their inspections, the commercial documentation ac- companying the ABP used for the production of petfood. Notwithstanding, the audit team saw that the official controls did not identify a number of shortcomings which were identified by the audit team in the visited facilities. These are described in the find- ings below. 7 35. In both of the raw petfood plants, the operators had received (and accepted) incomplete commercial documents for incoming Category 3 materials. These documents did not contain information demonstrating that, as required by Article 35(aa)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the ABP consisted of exclusively Category 3 material of the sub- categories defined in Article 10(a),(b)(i) and/or (ii) of the said Regulation, which are the only sub-categories allowed for the production of raw petfood in the EU. 36. The internal procedures of both operators did not mention any restrictions on the sub- categories of Category 3 material that could be used for production of raw petfood. 37. In one of the raw petfood plants, some raw materials of animal origin were not accom- panied by any ABP commercial documentation, contrary to the requirements of Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The operator stated that such raw materials were considered food and, in its opinion, ABP documentation was not necessary. How- ever, by definition, in accordance with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, these raw materials are ABP and must be accompanied by ABP commercial documents. 38. The incompleteness and absence of commercial documentation for ABP dispatched from food establishments (such as slaughterhouses and cutting plants) is also an indica- tion that official controls at food business operators where these ABP originate have not effectively verified compliance with ABP requirements. 5.2.3.2 Official controls in ABP plants 39. text: Available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/3939 2 5. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant articles or sections of the legislation cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings in this section of the report. In addition, a table is included in Annex II to this report summarising the main legal requirements related to the specific provisions and measures laid down in the body of EU legislation related to controls on feed hygiene. 5.1 Structure of the system for official controls on feed hygiene 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. An overview of how control systems are organised in Denmark is provided in the Multi-annual National Control Plan (MANCP) of Denmark which can be found under the 'Member State Links' tab on the following web page: [https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/DK]

In short, the DVFA is the main competent authority in the feed sector. Local inspectors in different Food Inspection Units (FIU) of the DVFA carry out official inspections relating to feed hygiene, Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP), traceability, mixing homogeneity, cross-contamination etc. at FeBOs, including manufacturers of medicated feed. Official controls on primary producers (inspection and sampling) are performed by the Agency for Green Transition and Aquatic Environment on behalf of the DVFA.

Veterinary inspectors of the DVFA are responsible for controls on the use of medicated feed at farm level. DVFA prepared a guidance and checklist to help the harmonised implementation of such controls.

To facilitate the harmonisation of control activities, the DVFA has prepared a set of guidance documents and checklists. The audit team reviewed several of these and found that these documents covered matters of relevance for the premises (e.g. hygiene, cleanliness of buildings and equipment), adequacy of FeBOs' HACCP systems, review of FeBOs' approval/registration, checks on traceability and on FeBOs' own-check programmes. These documents also contain information and checklists on the official inspection of labelling requirements. The documents reviewed by the audit team were seen to be suitable to support the inspectors in verification of FeBOs' compliance with the relevant requirements laid down in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, Articles 4-6, 8-20, 22-24 of, Annexes I-VIII to, Regulation (EC) No 767/2009, Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 5-10, 16 of, Annexes I, III and V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4, and Articles 12(1), 37-39 and 137-140 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 3 5. The DFVA has also prepared guidance on the assessment of testing methods and test results of FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination. Whilst this guidance contained relevant information, some key elements (e.g. acceptance levels of homogeneity tests, criteria of adequate sampling techniques), which are necessary for a comprehensive assessment of these tests, were not described. Local feed inspectors carry out a comprehensive assessment of the FeBOs' tests on homogeneity of mixing and, in particular, on cross contamination. If the inspector needs assistance for the evaluation of the FeBO's homogeneity and/or cross- contamination samples, the inspector can issue a preliminary control report and consult with the DVFA Food and Feed Safety Division and the Chemistry and Food Quality Division before issuing the final control report. 6. The staff performing the official controls receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training. In the past three years these training events have covered topics related to the implementation of feed legislation (e.g. on approval/registration, HACCP control, official sampling, labelling, etc.). Central DVFA officials also provided training to local inspectors on the conduct of official controls on the manufacture and use of veterinary medicinal products in medicated feed. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. DVFA confirmed that specific feed training, for food inspectors implementing official inspections in food establishments manufacturing and supplying by-product to the feed chain, had not been provided. 7. DVFA has a written procedure in place on the recruitment of new employees. New staff members must be qualified for the type of control they are performing. All new employees have to participate in a series of e-learning courses regarding the role and obligations of being a civil servant. 5.1.2 Registration/approval of feed business operators 8. The system of registration and approval of establishments and intermediaries is described in the MANCP of Denmark (see finding 1). The DVFA is responsible for the registration and approval of FeBOs including operators manufacturing and/or placing on the market of medicated feed. 9. The audit team noted that the DVFA had prepared adequate instructions on the approval and registration of FeBOs. Based on checks of documentation and on-the- spot inspection carried out by local inspectors, of the relevant FIU, the DVFA issues the approval certificate to the FeBO in question. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 9, 10, 23 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 10. The DVFA maintains and updates the lists of the approved and registered FeBOs and is responsible for publishing these lists on the internet. The lists are updated automatically each day. The audit team noted that the lists contain relevant information on FeBOs dealing with medicated feed. This is in line with the 4 requirements laid down in Article 19(3) and (7) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. 11. All of the operators visited by the audit team were registered or approved in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed hygiene 12. The structure of the competent authority is clearly defined and there is a well- established system for registration and approval of feed business operators, underpinned by the provision of largely appropriate guidance, procedures, and regular training to feed inspectors. These elements contribute to the effective planning of official controls and should facilitate their effective implementation. 5.2 Planning and implementation of official controls on feed hygiene 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 Planning of inspections 13. The DVFA has a risk-based planning approach for its official inspections. In principle there are three types of inspections (basic, in-depth, follow up). Basic inspections include four control activities. These are: approval visit, samples-based inspections, frequency-based inspections and targeted inspections. In-depth inspections can be incident-based or campaign inspections. After injunction or prohibition orders are issued, follow-up inspections are performed. The frequency-based inspection is calculated based on an individual assessment of FeBOs. This assessment is based on different risk factors e.g. the type of activity(s) registered, the risk of products produced, results of previous official controls. The final score is based on a mathematical formula which converts the risk factors into numerical values and provides the risk points for each of the FeBOs (scores range from 1 to 87) which determines the standard inspection frequency for each FeBO. The standard inspection frequency varies between once every 2 years (low score) to four times per year (high score). Those FeBOs, which have demonstrated satisfactory compliance (no sanctions in the last 12 month), are inspected under a reduced inspection frequency. FeBOs in the very low risk group (below 21 points) are covered by sample-based inspections. FeBOs dealing with medicated feed are also included in the risk-based planning (high risk). The above-described approach is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9 (1) to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 14. In 2023 and 2024, DVFA planned and carried out three campaign inspections. The objectives of these campaign were: traceability, own check-HACCP at trade and contamination during transport of feed. 15. Before January 2022, the Danish Medicines Agency was responsible for the authorisation of FeBOs manufacturing and/or placing on the market medicated feeds. 5 At that time there were 16 medicated feed manufacturers and several distributors authorised in Denmark. At the end of January, the Danish Medicines Agency withdrew the authorisation of all FeBOs manufacturing and/or placing on the market medicated feeds, and informed these operators, that the DVFA was the new authority responsible for the authorisation of these activities. 16. The DVFA requested these manufacturers to declare that they meet the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/4 (on medicated feed), as required by Article 15 of said Regulation. One of the 16 medicated feed manufacturers submitted the declaration expressing its intention to continue the production of medicated feed. All of the remaining 15 only produced Zinc-oxide-containing feed and after the ban of manufacturing Zinc-oxide as a medicated feed (June 2022) they chose not to produce medicated feed and did not request the renewal of their authorisations. None of the authorised medicated feed distributors requested the renewal of their authorisation. The renewal procedure was in line with the requirements of Article 15 of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. 5.2.1.2 Implementation of inspections 17. In 2021-2023, official feed inspectors implemented all planned inspections. 18. In general, DVFA inspectors carry out their official controls (inspection and sampling) without prior notifications (unannounced controls). Announced controls are carried out when it is necessary to inform the business in advance (48 hours' notice), because the purpose of the control requires certain employees to be present at the business at the time of the control (e.g. investigation of complaints) This is in line with the requirements of Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 19. The last internal audit related to the feed area was carried out in 2019. The objective of the audit was to check documented procedures relating to approval/registration of FeBOs. The internal audit team mainly focused on planning, case processing, data registration and documentation in the control system and on the quality assurance and cooperation of different departments/units. The internal audit team issued three recommendations, relating to issues with (i) quality assurance, (ii) planning of inspections of food businesses providing by-products to the feed chain and (iii) procedures of approval of FeBOs. The next internal audit relating to the feed area is planned to take place in 2028. The audit team reviewed the internal audit procedure and, in general, considered it to be in line with the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 20. DVFA implements a quality supervision system to evaluate feed sector inspections. The head of the FIU and/or a highly experienced colleague carries out joint inspections with local feed inspectors. There is a dedicated check list relating to the implementation of these joint inspections. During the inspection the supervisor shadows the inspection procedure and prepares an assessment on the performance of 6 the feed inspector. Supervised inspections to evaluate the performance of each feed inspector should be performed every three years. The supervisor interviewed during the audit identified only minor shortcomings during joint inspections in recent years. 21. The audit team examined documentary records of the official controls carried out in five establishments in different regions. Inspection reports were available in all cases, and they contained the information required by Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 22. In two compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team reviewed the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. In one establishment, the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plan and the HACCP principles on the critical control point were correct. The audit team could identify some minor shortcomings, and during the audit interview the feed inspector correctly assessed these shortcomings. In the other establishment, the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plan was very generic. Several hazards were grouped and assessed together, although the severity and the probability of these hazards were very different (for example several different types of cereals and relevant hazards were assessed as a single group). The operator's monitoring procedure described in its own HACCP system did not reflect the procedure implemented by the operator. The above shortcomings in the implementation of Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) 183/2005 identified by the audit team were overlooked during previous official inspections. 23. In the two food establishments manufacturing and suppling a by-product to the feed chain, the feed part of operators' HACCP systems were deficient. HACCP documents did not consider any production steps relating to feed production or the procedures for the collection and storage of retained samples. These are not in line with the requirements of Article 7(1) and point 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. HACCP documents did not contain descriptions of the requirements for labelling of feed materials manufactured and several of these requirements were not communicated to the buyers (feed material, compulsory declarations) which is not in line with the requirements of Articles 15 and 16 of Regulations (EC) 767/2009. These deficiencies were not identified in previous inspection reports. 24. Verification of establishments' tests on homogeneity of mixing (required by point 3 of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) is included in the scope of the inspections, when applicable. In three compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team reviewed the operators' documentation on the related homogeneity testing and interviewed the inspectors who usually control those establishments. In one establishment visited, several results of mixing homogeneity tests were unacceptable in the previous 9 months, but the FeBO did not implement any corrective actions. In another establishment, the number of the samples collected was lower than necessary to implement an adequate test. The feed inspectors met indicated 7 that they had experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the mixing homogeneity tests. 25. Verification of establishments' tests to assess the measures taken to minimise cross- contamination, required by point 2 of section "Facilities and equipment" and point 3 of section "Production" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, forms part of the inspections, when applicable. In one establishment visited, the analytical results of the testing laboratory were higher than the maximum limit described in Section VII,
