text: An overview of how control systems are organised in Austria is provided in the Multi- annual National Control Plan (MANCP) of Austria which can be found under the 'Member State Links' tab on the following web page: [https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits- analysis/country/profile/details/AT] (1) Available at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/4418 2 2. The Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, Regions and Water Management is responsible for issuing general instructions and deciding policy in relation to feed- ingstuffs. The BAES is the competent authority for the implementation of official feed controls on FeBOs other than primary producers, including registration and approval of FeBOs, and taking legal decisions. The AGES is a public scientific and technical advisory agency, carrying out risk assessments and providing consumer information, scientific advice and laboratory services. BAES inspectors are responsible for the im- plementation of comprehensive official inspections on FeBOs' HACCP-based proce- dures. The Ministry of Social Affairs, Health Care and Consumer Protection is respon- sible for issuing national legislation and general instructions in relation to official con- trols on medicated feed. The BASG is the competent authority responsible for the im- plementation of official controls on FeBOs manufacturing and placing on the market medicated feed. 3. There is a clear designation of roles and responsibilities related to the organisation and implementation of official feed controls, including medicated feed. These arrange- ments ensure that the requirements laid down in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are met. 4. BAES staff performing the official controls on FeBOs' HACCP-based procedures received appropriate training in the last three years. BASG officials have a good knowledge of requirements on manufacturing and use of veterinary medicated prod- ucts including medicated feed, and of official controls thereof. This is in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed hygiene 5. The structure of the competent authority is clear, and inspectors participate in regular trainings on feed, including on the assessment of FeBOs' HACCP-based procedures, and on the implementation of official controls on medicated feed. These elements fa- cilitate the effective implementation of official controls on feed, including medicated feed. 3 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL INSPECTIONS ON HACCP 5.2.1 Planning of inspections 6. BAES has a risk-based planning approach to official inspections (further details on this approach can be found in the 2021 audit report, see section 5.2.1.1 of that report). Since the beginning of 2024, the official control plan contains 5-7 comprehensive in- spections of FeBO`s HACCP systems at feed manufacturers, importers, high risk cate- gory distributors and transporters. At the beginning of 2024, there were 120 of these FeBOs in Austria. BAES inspectors choose which FeBO will be subject to the com- prehensive inspection. Based on the existing resources and the above planning, the in- spection cycle of HACCP systems of all relevant FeBOs is approximately 17-20 years(2). 7. To facilitate the harmonisation of control activities on HACCP systems, BAES has prepared a set of documents including a comprehensive checklist. The Commission auditor reviewed these documents and noted that they were suitable to support the in- spectors in verifying compliance with the relevant requirements laid down in Article 6 and Annex II to Regulation (EC) 183/2005. 8. BAES inspectors carry out their comprehensive inspections of HACCP systems in the form of announced visits. BAES inspectors send pre-notification to the relevant FeBOs two weeks before the on-the-spot visit. With the pre-notification, BAES in- spectors inform the FeBOs about the objective and the timeline of the comprehensive inspection and request several documents (e.g. Standard Operational Plans (SOPs), work instructions, organisation charts, blueprints, list of facilities/equipment) to be as- sessed before the on-the-spot visit. The competent authority stated that the prior notifi- cation is necessary because, in several cases, relevant workers/managers of the busi- nesses are not continuously present in the facilities. This approach is in line with the requirements of Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.2 Implementation of inspections 9. In 2024, BAES inspectors carried out two comprehensive inspections on FeBOs HACCP systems until the time of this audit. 10. The Commission auditor examined documentation from official controls carried out in six feed establishments in different regions. Inspection reports were available in all cases and contained information required by Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The Austrian competent authority noted in its answer to the draft report: "Due to the different establishment categories and the different workload per establishment category (manufacturers, non-manufacturers), this is currently not foreseeable and has so far been estimated for all establishments with an estimated unit value. An assessment will be carried out for the further planning of inspections, whereby it is assumed that the inspection cycle will be reduced." 4 11. All operators visited by the auditor were approved in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9 and 10 of Regulation (EC) 183/2005. 12. In five establishments visited, the Commission auditor scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the opera- tors' HACCP plans. Additionally, in each establishment, the auditor requested the BAES inspectors to carry out a comprehensive assessment of two potential feed safety risks described in operator`s HACCP documentation. BAES inspectors were able to carry out adequate assessment of these risks. During their assessment, BAES inspectors used the checklist and other relevant documentation established to im- plement the controls in a harmonised way (see finding 7). Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official inspections on HACCP 13. Since the previous audit in 2021, the Austrian competent authority has developed and started to implement a new procedure on official inspection of FeBO`s HACCP sys- tems. The new procedure is effective in ensuring adequate official controls on this as- pect. 5.3 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MANUFACTURING AND PLACING ON THE MARKET OF MEDICATED FEED 5.3.1 Planning of official controls 14. BASG is the competent authority responsible for approval and official controls on manufacturing and placing on the market of medicated feed, excluding the final us- ers (farmers). 15. Before July 2022, there was one medicated feed manufacturer in Austria. This estab- lishment declared that it meets the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/4, (as it is required by Article 15 of this Regulation) and expressed its interest to continue the production of medicated feed. At the time of this audit, this establishment was the sole medicated feed manufacturer in Austria. 16. BAES maintains and updates the lists of approved and registered FeBOs and is re- sponsible for publishing the lists on the internet, as required by Article 19 of Regula- tion (EC) 183/2005. BASG is expected to inform BAES on any changes relating to operators dealing with medicated feed. The Commission auditor noted that the list of approved FeBOs did not contain relevant information on the sole FeBO dealing with medicated feed. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2019/4 (3).

The Austrian competent authority noted in its answer to the draft report: "In order to ensure that in future all relevant information concerning medicated feed manufacturers is transmitted from the BASG to the BAES, the following passage was inserted in the associated SOP SVA_I09 "Preparing Notices and Manufacturing Authori- sations": "In the event of a Manufacturing Authorisation being issued for the production of medicated feed, the BAES must be informed of this by email baes@baes.gv.at when the License is issued"." 5 17. The Austrian Veterinary Medicines Act contains instructions on implementation of Regulation (EU) 2019/4 (Article 72, Section IV special provisions for medicated feed) including requirements on prescriptions and labelling of medicated feed. These instructions are in line with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. The Com- mission auditor noted that the template form for prescription of medicated feed is not included in the Austrian legislation. 18. BASG prepared a set of guidance documents and checklists to facilitate the harmo- nised implementation of official controls on manufacturing and placing on the mar- ket of medicated feed. The Commission auditor reviewed these documents and not- ed that they are suitable to support the inspectors in verifying compliance with the relevant requirements laid down in Articles 5-10, 16-17 of, and Annexes I, III, IV and V to, Regulation (EU) 2019/4. 19. The planned inspection frequency of medicated feed manufacturers is at least once every three years. Since 2021, no official feed samples from medicated feed were planned to be collected. At the time of this audit, there was only one establishment manufacturing medicated feed in Austria (see finding 15) and there were no other types of FeBOs dealing with medicated feed. 20. The central competent authority stated that expired medicated feed and intermediate products are considered as hazardous waste and are collected and disposed of by au- thorised hazardous waste disposal companies. This is in line with the requirements of Article 18 to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. 5.3.2 Implementation of official controls 21. The Commission auditor scrutinised the documentation concerning manufacturing of medicated feed in the one establishment approved in Austria. In general, prescrip- tions, recipes and labels of medicated feed were available. However, the auditor not- ed that the reviewed prescriptions did not contain information on diagnosed disease to be treated, inclusion rate of active substances and any warnings necessary to en- sure the proper use. These information items are required to be included in the pre- scriptions by points 5, 8 and 13 of Annex V of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. The heading of the prescriptions reviewed referred to the repealed European legislation (which is no longer applicable) and did not contain the unique number required by point 2 of the above-mentioned Regulation. These deficiencies were overlooked during previ- ous official controls. 22. The Commission auditor assessed the labels of medicated feed and noted that they contained all relevant information required by Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. 23. In the one operator visited by the Commission auditor, only one type of active sub- stance was used for production of medicated feed and only for one species. There was a dedicated line for manufacturing of medicated feed, and it was not used for production of any other feed. Therefore, there was no need to perform cross contam- 6 ination tests. While the homogeneity test was also not preformed, the concentration of the active substance was checked from all produced batches by an external labor- atory accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. There were deviations between the concen- tration of the active substance in the different batches, but these deviations were al- ways lower than 20% which is the requirement of Annex IV of Regulation (EU) No 2019/4. 24. Regarding the collection and disposal of expired medicated feed, the Commission auditor reviewed the documentation in the one establishment visited and noted that the FeBO`s procedure on the management and disposal of hazardous waste was in line with the requirements (see finding 20). Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official controls on medicated feed 25. The Austrian competent authority has an adequate system in place to plan and imple- ment official inspections on manufacturing and placing on the market of medicated feed. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by the use of inappropriate prescriptions for the production of medicated feed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION In Austria, the competent authorities have put in place an adequate system to carry out official controls on feed business operators, including those manufacturing and placing on the market medicated feed. The actions taken by the competent authority to address (open) Recommendation 1 of the 2021 audit were effective and have led to a significant improvement in the official controls on feed business operators' HACCP based procedures. This recommendation can therefore be closed due to action taken. Whilst official inspections on manufacturing of medicated feed are regularly performed, they are not effective in verifying operator's procedures to comply with requirements on prescriptions, weakening an otherwise well-performing system. 7 CLOSING MEETING, A closing meeting was held on 11 October 2024 with representatives of the Austrian competent authorities. The auditor presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The competent authorities did not express any disagreement with those. 7 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below. With regard to those non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authorities are nevertheless, requested to address these. The effectiveness of actions taken to address such non-compliance will be assessed in future audits on this topic. 1 To ensure that official controls consistently check prescriptions of medicated feeds to de- termine their compliance with the relevant legal requirements. The principal audit criteria against which fulfilment of the above objective was assessed are listed in Annex 2 to this report. The scope of the audit included official controls on the following categories of animals and goods referred to in Article 47(1) of the OCR: · animals; · products of animal origin, germinal products, animal by-products, hay and straw and composite products (hereafter `goods of animal origin'); · products of non-animal origin subject to temporary increase of official controls or emergency measures (3) (hereafter `goods of non-animal origin'), and · food contact materials whose entry into the EU is subject to conditions set out in Commission Regulation (EU) No 284/2011 (hereafter `food contact materials'). The scope excluded official controls: · carried out at any location other than BCPs, control points and approved warehouses (e.g., at travellers' points of entry); · pertaining to protective measures against pests of plants, and · pertaining to organic production and labelling of organic and in-conversion products. 4 BACKGROUND It is important that the official controls performed on animals and goods entering the EU en- sure that they meet the requirements of EU agri-food chain legislation (4). The rules on official controls, including those on animals and goods entering the EU, are laid down in the OCR. Consignments of the categories of animals and goods listed in Article 47(1) of the OCR must be subject to official controls at the BCP of first arrival into the EU. EU Member States (hereafter Member States) are required to designate BCPs in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 59 of the OCR. In addition, pursuant to Article 3(14) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, Member States are required to inform the Commission of any changes in the infrastructure or operation of a BCP, or of an inspection centre within that post, if such changes necessitate an update to the information previously provided to the Commission in accordance with Article 59(2) of the OCR. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. The organisation of official controls is as described in the MANCP. In summary: · The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration (DVFA), which is an agency of the Ministry of Environment and Food, is responsible for food and feed safety, animal health and animal welfare. Staff of the Food Inspection Units of the DVFA are re- sponsible for the official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark. · The Danish Customs Agency (hereafter `Customs') assists the DVFA in the perfor- mance of official controls on non-commercial pet animals and goods in passengers' luggage or sent by postal or courier services. 2. The areas of competence of the authorities involved in official controls on animals and goods entering the EU are summarised in the following table: Area of competence (8) Competent authority Animals (LA) Products of animal origin and composite products (POA-HC) DVFA Germinal products, animal by-products, derived products, hay and straw DVFA (POA-NHC) DVFA Personal consignments (9) Non-commercial movement of pet animals (10) DVFA/Customs Food of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control DVFA/Customs posts (3) (PNAO-HC(food)) Feed of non-animal origin subject to mandatory checks at border control DVFA posts (3) (PNAO-NHC(feed)) Food contact materials (PNAO-NHC(other)) DVFA DVFA (9) Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122. The DVFA informed the audit team that, at the time of the audit, there was a sufficient number of suitably qualified staff at the BCPs for the performance of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. 4. The DVFA has designated laboratories in accordance with Article 37(1) of the OCR, to perform the analysis of samples, including those taken during official controls on ani- mals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark. The DVFA informed the audit team that the laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025 in line with Article 37(4) of the OCR and that each of the methods they use is included in the scope of their accreditation, in accordance with Article 37(5) of the OCR. 5.1.2 Communication and cooperation between authorities 5. The audit team found, based on evidence obtained during the audit, that there are mecha- nisms in place which ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between and with- in authorities, and in particular with Customs, for the conduct of official controls on ani- mals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark, which is in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR. 5.1.3 Training of staff

The DVFA provided documented evidence to the audit team which confirmed that staff responsible for performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU at BCPs and control points had received training for their area of competence, which is in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place

The DVFA has issued documented procedures in the form of a manual, for the perfor- mance of official controls on goods of animal origin entering the EU. The DVFA in- formed the audit team that there are no documented procedures for the official controls on animals entering the EU, other than a locally issued work instruction at the BCP Co- penhagen airport, and no specific documented procedures for the implementation of measures in case of suspicion of non-compliance, confirmed non-compliance or risk, re- ferred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR.

The audit team noted therefore, that the documented procedures do not include all of the subject areas set out in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, which is not in line with Arti- cle 12(1) of that regulation. The audit team found related shortcomings in the implemen- tation of measures in case of non-compliance, as detailed in section 5.2.5 (findings 36 and 44 to 46) below.

The DVFA develops and implements an annual risk-based monitoring plan for the pur- pose of carrying out laboratory tests to detect hazards in goods of animal origin entering the EU, in line with Article 4(5) and point 5 of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The monitoring plan for food of animal origin takes into account notifications of the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), risks asso- 5 ciated with each type of product, results of audits by the Commission services in third countries and the availability of adequate laboratory methods. The monitoring plan takes into account the relevant parts of the multi-annual national control plans for residues and contaminants.

The sampling of consignments as part of the monitoring plan is based on specific sam- pling projects, which are developed by interdisciplinary groups that comprise of repre- sentatives from various DVFA Divisions, in particular the International Trade Division, and relevant laboratories and officials responsible for performing the controls. Each sampling project is described in a manual that includes instructions for performing the sampling.

Animals and goods entering the EU that require official controls at BCPs are identified in the Customs information system. The placing and handling of such consignments under a customs procedure is subject to the presentation of a finalised CHED by the operator responsible for the consignment, which is in line with Article 57 of the OCR. Customs have read-only access to TRACES NT to confirm the presented CHED and the decision made by the DVFA on the consignment.

The DVFA informed the audit team that BCP staff performing official controls are pro- vided with relevant information from Customs on request. DVFA staff at the port BCPs Aarhus and Copenhagen also have access to the terminal booking system `PIC', which is used to control the movement of containers and enables staff to identify and hold con- tainers for inspection.

The DVFA stated that BCP staff have access to manifests when provided by operators on a voluntary basis, or on request when the DVFA suspect the presence of goods that are subject to official controls at BCPs. The audit team noted that undermines their ability to ensure that, for each consignment of the categories of animals and goods referred to in Article 47(1) of the OCR, the operator responsible for the consignment has given prior notification of arrival of those consignments in TRACES NT, in line with Article 56(1) and (3) of the OCR.

In the event that non-compliances are identified during the official controls, the BCP staff forward relevant information, if applicable, to the National Contact Point for the RASFF, which creates the notification in the electronic system iRASFF, and transmits it to the EU contact point as necessary. 5.1.6 Audits of competent authorities and control verification procedures

Internal audits of the DVFA are carried out based on a five-year multi-annual risk-based internal audit programme. The audits are performed by the Internal Audit Unit in the DVFA Centre for International Cooperation, which reports directly to the Director- General of the DVFA.

The Internal Audit Unit informed the audit team that based on the outcome of their risk- assessment and annual reviews, no internal audits on topics related to the scope of this audit were planned for the period 2022 to 2026.

The audit team noted that the internal audits carried out by the DVFA are based on doc- umented procedures that include measures to address any shortcomings identified during the audit, within a specified deadline, which is in line with Article 6(1) of the OCR.

The DVFA provided evidence to the audit team that they have control verification pro- cedures in place at BCP level to ensure that official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are consistent and effective. The procedures include 7 measures to ensure that corrective actions are taken at BCP level in case shortcomings are identified, which is in line with Article 12(2) of the OCR.

The audit team noted that the outcome of the control verifications may be discussed within experience exchange groups held between BCPs and the central International Trade Division which is responsible for documented procedures. However, they are not systematically shared with that Division, which thereby risks compromising the review of documented procedures required by Article 12(3) of the OCR.

As detailed in section 5.3 below, the DVFA carries out controls to verify the compliance of BCPs and control points with the relevant EU requirements for the categories of ani- mals and goods for which they had been designated. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU

There is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non- animal origin entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark, which is supported by suitably qualified and experienced staff, and good cooperation and communication within and between the authorities.

The EFSA scientific opinion on the risk posed by pathogens in food of non-animal origin uses the term VTEC- Verocytotoxin-producing Escherichia coli, while the term STEC is used in the EFSA Scientific Opinion on the risk posed by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) and other pathogenic bacteria in seeds and sprouted seeds. The term STEC is also used in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. IV 1 INTRODUCTION This audit took place in Italy from 28 May 2025 to 13 June 2025 and was part of the planned work programme of the European Commission's Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety (DG Health and Food Safety). It included a remote meeting via videoconference and on-site visits. The audit team comprised two auditors from DG Health and Food Safety accompanied by a national expert from a Member State. A remote opening meeting was held on 28 May with staff of Ministry of Health (MoH ­ the designated central competent authority ­ CCA), representatives of regional and local competent authorities (CAs) and representative from the official laboratories. At this meeting, the objectives and itinerary for the audit were confirmed by the audit team and the control systems were described by the authorities. This meeting was followed by the on-the-spot part from 3 to 13 June. A representative of the CCA accompanied the auditors for the duration of the audit.

OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE The objectives of the audit were to: · Evaluate the system of official controls in the area of food hygiene to prevent microbiological contamination in food of non-animal origin (FNAO). · Evaluate the system of official controls regarding traceability of sprouts and seeds intended for sprouting, including applicable microbiological criteria and the approval of sprout-producing establishments. · Verify the implementation and enforcement of guarantees and corrective actions submitted in response to recommendations from the previous DG Health and Food Safety audit report on 2021 (2). In terms of scope, the audit team reviewed the official controls for food hygiene to prevent microbiological contamination in FNAO, including seeds intended for sprouting and sprouts. This covered a review of the planning and implementation of official controls, control procedures and sampling performance. The implementation of official controls over food business operators' (FBOs) obligations included: cultivation of vegetables (consumed raw), cut fruits and vegetables and sprout-producing establishments. In pursuit of these objectives, the following sites were visited: (2) Ref. text: BACKGROUND FNAO is consumed in a variety of forms and is a major component of most meals. These food types have the potential to be associated with large disease outbreaks in the EU. In particular: · May 2011: a major outbreak of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) O104:H4 in sprouted seeds. 4 000 people were reported ill, and the outbreak resulted in the deaths of 56 people. · 2012: a major outbreak of Norovirus in frozen strawberries from China. 11 000 people (mainly children) were reported ill and with symptoms. · 2018-2020: a major outbreak of Hepatitis A in frozen strawberries, most likely from Egypt. 65 people were reported ill and with symptoms. · 2023: a major outbreak of Salmonella linked to the consumption of sprouted seeds with 509 confirmed human cases in nine EU/European Economic Area countries. The focus of the outbreak was located in the northern European countries with 94 cases in Finland, 110 cases in Sweden and 257 cases in Norway. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) concluded in a scientific opinion that the top-ranking food/pathogen combination was leafy greens eaten raw and Salmonella spp., followed by (in equal rank) bulb and stem vegetables and Salmonella spp., tomatoes and Salmonella spp., melons and Salmonella spp., and fresh pods, legumes or grain and pathogenic Escherichia coli (E. coli). More details can be found at: http://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/doc/3025.pdf. 2 In view of the number of large outbreaks and the high number of Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) notifications concerning products of non-animal origin, DG Health and Food Safety decided to undertake an audit series in Member States on FNAO. This was the third audit to Italy on this topic. The previous took place on 2015 and 2021.

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 RELEVANT NATIONAL LEGISLATION Legal requirements Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU; Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings 1. The relevant national legislation has not been changed since the previous audit in 2021. 2. The Legislative Decree 2/2/2021 No 27 lays out provisions for the adaptation of national legislation to the Regulation (EU) 2017/625 on official controls. Guides to Good Agricultural Practices and to Good Hygiene Practices 3. MoH has issued several guides related to the scope of this audit, taking into account also EFSA opinions 3. In addition to the guidance documents already in place and described in the previous audit report, new guidelines have been issued. These were distributed to the regions, with instructions to adopt the guidelines and use the checklists they contain. The aim was to ensure comprehensive official control activities in the FNAO sector. The new guidelines include: · Guidelines for official controls of sprout-producing establishments and seeds for sprouting. · Guidelines for official controls of FBOs regarding primary production of FNAO. · Guidelines for official control of FBOs regarding food establishments (including FNAO). Conclusions on relevant national legislation 4. The existing legal framework at national level enables CAs to put in place official controls in the area of food hygiene to prevent microbiological contamination in FNAO at all stage of production, processing and distribution. 3 EFSA Panel on Biological Hazards (BIOHAZ) Panel; Scientific Opinion on the risk posed by pathogens in food of non-animal origin. Part 1 (outbreak data analysis and risk ranking of food/pathogen combinations). EFSA Journal 2013;11(1):3025. [138 pp.] doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2013.3025. Available online: www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/ 3 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings 5. MoH, regions, autonomous provinces of Trento and Bolzano, and local health units (Aziende Sanitarie Locali ­ ASL) are the designated CAs for food safety, in accordance with the Legislative Decree No 27 of 2 February 2021. Regions and ASLs have responsibility, within their territories, for planning, coordination, guidance, authorisation and verification of controls, along the entire production chain, from farm to fork.

Carabinieri Health Protection Unit (Carabinieri per la tutela della salute ­ NAS) is a special department of the Carabinieri with the authority of judicial police. The NAS carry out controls and investigations on its own initiative or at request of MoH, including health inspections of FBOs, verification of self-control systems, sampling of products and examination of authorisation documents.

Implementation of the official controls is under the responsibility of regions. Their main role is to provide guidance and training to staff on official control activities at local level. The operational implementation of controls is handled at local level by ASLs, and more specifically within ASL, the department of Food Hygiene and Nutrition Services (SIAN).

MoH, departments of health of regions, and SIANs are responsible for official controls at all stages of production, including pre- and during harvest primary production. Therefore, their area of responsibility covers possible sources of microbiological contamination such as irrigation, fertilisers, staff health, hand washing facilities, toilets and presence of animals.

Additional information can be found at the Italian multi-annual control plan (https://www.salute.gov.it/portale/pianoControlloNazionalePluriennale2023/homePCNP2023.j sp) and at the country profile within the EU Commission website (https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/IT).
Nonetheless, the audit team observed shortcomings in the cooperation between ASL, region and MoH (see paragraphs 18, 20, 30, 32, 42 and 57). Official staff and Training

There are specific rules in place regarding the hiring of staff at CAs. Regarding SIANs, the eligible profiles for staff conducting official controls are medical doctors, veterinarians, technician of the prevention, or biologist. Other profiles such as agronomist or food technologist are not eligible.

The staff of SIAN units cover a wide range of activities, and official controls include, among others, FBOs such as restaurants, catering facilities, and controls of food contact material, and 4 additives. Official controls of primary production of FNAO are a small part of the allocated tasks. In one of the ASLs visited, CAs indicated that official controls of primary producers had been allocated to a dedicated team of inspectors to build up expertise.

Regions are responsible for planning and organising training of staff, both for regions and their ASLs. Regarding specific training on primary production of FNAO, the audit team observed significant differences in the visited regions. In Veneto, since the previous audit, specific courses on official controls of primary production have been organised every year. The courses included an on-site component to conduct inspections on production farms, and attendees were subject to a written test at the end of the course to assess the acquired capacities of staff.

Opposite to this situation, in Sicily or Campania, no training has taken place regarding official controls in primary production of FNAO. In Sicily, the first training in the matter is planned for September 2025. As seen in paragraphs 42, 44 and 46, both regions had started to conduct inspections at primary production including microbiological risks in October 2024 (Campania) and from May 2025 in Sicily. This absence of training for staff is not in line with the Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and calls into question the effectiveness of the implementation of the action plan submitted to address recommendation No 6 of the DG (SANTE) 2021-7175 audit report.

During official inspections witnessed by the audit team, inspectors and their supervisors overlooked some critical deficiencies (e.g., risk of cross-contamination, lack of hygiene and staff misconduct). Official staff acknowledged that these deficiencies represent a risk for food safety (see paragraphs 47, 53, 59 and 62). Audit / Supervision

There are several layers of audits carried out. MoH, annually carries out sectorial internal audits to regions including the placing on the market of FNAO. In the case of regions, they may carry out audits to assess the organisation and functioning of SIANs. In this regard, MoH have identified that some regions have not carried out internal audits due to the lack of internal auditors (for example Emilia Romagna, or Sicily).
MoH may carry out also internal audits in addition to the annual plan, for example to assess the response of the Regions following RASFF notifications.

Examples of planned audit reports were provided to the audit team: Friuli Venezia Giulia in November 2021, Sicily in 2022, Lombardy in June 2023 and Sardinia in May 2024. In general, the main shortcomings identified were lack of internal audits by regions due to the lack of auditors; failure to use the checklists proposed by MoH for official controls in primary production; insufficient training of staff; low number of inspections on primary production level and difficulties of inspectors in identifying non-compliances. However, the audit team could not find evidence that regions had implemented measures to address key non- compliances identified by MoH during its internal audits (see paragraphs 13, 14, 42, 47, 53, 59 and 62). 5 19. The audit team was provided with examples of audits carried out by MoH related to RASFF notifications, such as draft reports for audits carried out in Sicily in November 2024 and in Emilia Romagna in February 2025. In addition to the shortcomings mentioned in the previous point, weaknesses were also identified in the management of a RASFF notification related to Salmonella in cherry tomatoes: the report highlights that regional CAs did not take measures to manage the emergency situation. 20. Despite several RASFF notifications on seeds for sprouting (4) mentioning both FBOs placing seeds for sprouting on the market and farms producing seeds for sprouting, none of them were included by the Italian CAs in the national list of FBOs producing seeds for sprouting. MoH informed the audit team that this was due to poor cooperation between local and central CAs. This is not in line with Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 21. Regarding supervision activities, in all visited regions, regional CAs do monitor the implementation of the official control plan. Regions require that ASLs provide information on the actual number of controls carried out to oversight the actual compliance with the activities planned. This applies to the sampling programme and to inspections to FBOs. 22. CAs of Veneto and Emilia Romagna informed the audit team that supervision activities are in place to evaluate the performance of inspectors, based on witnessing on-site official controls by a senior inspector. Emilia-Romagna region provided the audit team with examples of such supervisions. However, such a system of on-the-spot supervision, was unable to identify shortcomings in the implementation of official controls (see paragraphs 47, 53, 59 and 62). Conclusions on competent authorities 23. CAs are designated for all stages of FNAO production and for sprout-producing establishments. This provides a good basis for the implementation of the official controls system. 24. The level of training provided to staff performing official controls on FNAO varies significantly between regions. While some regions offer thorough and specialised training to cover new areas of official controls for Cas, other provides little to no training. This disparity in training levels compromise the effectiveness of official controls in several regions. 25. Shortcomings in collaboration and coordination between ASL, regional level and MoH have prevented a major non-compliance, such as the absence of registration of producers of seeds for sprouting, from being resolved in a timely manner, thus weakening the official controls system. 26. MoH has implemented an internal audit system which covers the official controls in FNAO. This has allowed to identify organisational problems and shortcomings which, if addressed (and it was not the case) by regional CAs, could allow to improve the effectiveness of official controls in the area of concern. 27. In some regions, the lack of a supervisory system to assess, on-the-spot, the performance of (4) European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, European Food Safety Authority, 2025. ISBN 978-92- 9498-782-2; doi: 10.2900/7051610; Catalogue number TQ-01-25-013-EN-N 6 staff during official controls and, in regions where such a system exists, the failure to identify shortcomings in official controls, has a negative impact on the effectiveness of the implementation and enforcement of EU legislation. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Registration and approval of food business operators Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004; Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013; Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings Registration Primary Producers (farms) 28. All FBOs in Italy are required to be registered, and this includes any type of primary producer. They are required to submit a notification of initial activity to the municipality where they are located. The municipality notifies to the competent ASL the new registered activities and their updates. The ASLs keep registers of FBOs within their territory. 29. However, these registers do not include relevant information on the crops being grown. Different strategies have been followed by the regional CAs to overcome the lack of detailed information in the register: · In some cases, regional CAs have got access to the data bases of the Chambers of Commerce. These databases only provide for general activity groups, which in the case of primary production comprises permanent crops and other general activities such as "cereals", or "horticulture". · In Sicily, there are 53 000 farms dedicated to primary production of FNAO, including permanent and non-permanent crops. The regional CAs of Sicily indicated that 8 000 farms were dedicated to horticulture. In Campania, CAs indicated that there were 39 000 farms of non-permanent crops. These systems do not provide enough information to CAs to identify growers producing crops with a higher microbiological risk. Therefore, recommendations No 4 and 5 of the DG(SANTE) 2021-7175 audit report have not been addressed. · In other cases, as for example in Veneto and Emilia Romagna, CAs have an agreement with the Department of Agriculture which provides accurate information on the type of crops grown in the farms. The information provided is updated around every 18 months. CAs of Veneto indicated that this frequency of exchanges will be increased to every six months. The information of the register of the Department of Agriculture indicates the type of crop except for seeds for sprouting, which are not identified as such. 7 30. Regarding seeds for sprouting, the current available registers do not provide information on the farms producing this type of product. To overcome this lack of information, one local SIAN has requested to a FBO placing seeds for sprouting in the market the list of farms supplying seeds for sprouting located in the territory under the remit of the SIAN. FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS 5.1 ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU 5.1.1 Competent authorities involved 1. The organisation of official controls is described in the MANCP of Finland. In summary: · Within the Finnish Food Authority (Ruokavirasto ­ FFA), which operates under the guidance of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry: o the Veterinary Border Control and Intra-Union Trade Section is responsible for official controls on consignments of animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU through BCPs in Finland; and o the Feed Section is responsible for official controls on consignments of goods of non-animal origin not intended for human consumption entering the EU. · The Finnish Customs (Tulli ­ hereafter `Customs') are responsible for official controls on: o consignments of goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption and food contact materials entering the EU; o consignments of goods of animal origin in transit exiting the EU through BCPs in Finland; o consignments of composite products exempted from official controls at BCPs; and o official controls at points of entry on goods which form part of passengers' personal luggage or sent by postal or courier services and on non-commercial pet animals. 2. Based on evidence obtained during the audit, the audit team found that there are mechanisms in place to ensure communication and cooperation between and within authorities responsible for conducting official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Finland, which is in line with Articles 4(2) and 75(1) of the OCR. 5.1.3 Training of staff

The competent authorities provided evidence to the audit team, which confirmed that staff responsible for performing official controls on animals and goods entering the EU had received appropriate training for their area of competence, which is in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of the OCR. 5.1.4 Documented procedures and arrangements in place

The competent authorities have, in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR, issued documented procedures and instructions for the performance of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU. The audit team noted that the FFA has in addition a repository of EU legislation to supplement its documented procedures.

The competent authorities stated that arrangements are in place for the implementation of the measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR in line with Article 64(3)(d) of the OCR.

Regulation (EU) 2017/625 contains general provisions for the implementation of the official controls for plant health. Full legal references for the relevant EU legal acts are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND 4.1 CLAVIBACTER SEPEDONICUS IN THE EU AND IN LITHUANIA C. sepedonicus is a Union quarantine pest, the cause of potato ring rot. Positive findings are detected in several MS every year, but more than 80% of the outbreaks are in Poland. Since 2020, with its annual 15 to 39 positive findings, Lithuania has the second highest number of outbreaks in the EU. Based on the annual survey reports of Lithuania, the annual number of positive lots follows a four to six year periodic cycle. Within the last 20 years, the highest number of outbreaks was reported in 2006 with 110 positive findings. The lowest number of annual outbreaks (12) was reported both in 2004 and in 2013. Lithuania is not listed as a highly infected area in Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Further information on the pest is available from the website of the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organisation (EPPO): https://gd.eppo.int/ . 4.2 POTATO PRODUCTION AND TRADE After the accession of Lithuania to the EU in 2004, the declared potato cultivation area significantly decreased from ca. 79 000 ha to ca. 16 000 ha in 2014. Since then, after a moderate decrease until 2018, it is between 9 000 and 11 000 ha annually. Since the previous audit in 2018, the number of seed potato producers decreased from five to two. The registration requirements were changed in 2018, and the SPS registers farmers producing potatoes on fields above one hectare in the phytosanitary register. Earlier, the limit had been five hectares. As a result, the number of registered ware potato producers increased by some 50% during the recent years. At the same time, ware potato production on small fields is decreasing. However, it is still significant, small scale non-registered operators produced ware potatoes on almost 40% of the total production area in 2023 (see table 1). The National Payment Agency under the Ministry of Agriculture (NPA) provides the annual data of producers who request subsidies to the SPS. This includes farmers producing potatoes in fields below one hectare. However, the number of those non-registered producers who do not request subsidy from the NPA and their corresponding cultivation areas are not known. There is a strong tradition among farmers in Lithuania of planting ware potatoes or farm saved tubers of undetermined plant health status. 2 Movement of potatoes from Lithuania to other MS is not significant. text: In summary: the SPS is the CA for plant health in the meaning of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, within which the Phytosanitary Division coordinates and supervises the plant health activities of the regional divisions. In each county the regional division of the SPS is responsible for the implementation of the plant health controls. 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

The relevant national legal acts on registration of operators and supervision of their activities, on methods of sampling, on official measures against the spread of potato ring rot and on compensation of losses due to phytosanitary measures are listed and explained in detail in the report of the previous audit (DG(SANTE) 2018-6489). The legal acts are up to date, their requirements are in line with EU legislation. 5.1.3 Procedures for the quality and consistency of controls

The annual phytosanitary inspection plan is prepared by the regional divisions and approved by the director of the SPS. The plan contains the data of each operator to control that year, including all seed potato producers, all operators involved in C. sepedonicus outbreaks and at least 25% of the registered ware potato producers. The CA conducts official controls on every operator listed in the plan and take samples for testing where applicable. Inspectors use standardised official documents and questionnaires which are available in the specific IT system of the SPS.

In the ten counties, 79 officials are involved in the surveys for C. sepedonicus. The SPS organises regular trainings for its staff on plant health matters, including the requirements for C. sepedonicus. In order to increase impartiality in each county, at least 5% of official controls are carried out by inspectors of other regional divisions. Inspectors met by the audit team were knowledgeable and well trained.

The SPS carries out internal audits on its regional divisions as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The latest general audit including plant health topics was carried out in 2022 in County Kaunas. Shortcomings regarding official activities for C. sepedonicus were not reported. In addition, the SPS verifies the implementation of plant health requirements by its officials. The report provided contains proposals to improve and harmonise the implementation of official measures. 4 7. Where the CAs establish non-compliances, the operator receives an official warning containing the consequences of further non-compliances or shall pay a penalty of 30- 300. In 2023 and 2024, 23 such warnings were issued for various non-compliances. In the case of repeated infringements, operators shall pay a penalty of 50-550. Only 50% of the penalty shall be paid if it is paid within 14 days. In the last two years, penalties of 15, 25, 50 and 300 were imposed in six cases. However, such penalties are not effective, proportionate and dissuasive when producers knowingly break official eradication measures of an outbreak, such as by planting potatoes in infected or potentially infected fields or by planting uncertified tubers in other sites of a DA (see also finding 30). The applied penalties are not in line with Article 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The situation did not change since 2018 when the CA had already been recommended to implement dissuasive sanctions in case of infringements with regard to the application of phytosanitary measures. An amendment of the Phytosanitary Act was in public consultation in the beginning of 2025 and this was intended to increase sanctions. 5.1.4 Laboratories 8. The national reference laboratory is the Phytosanitary Research Laboratory (PRL), which is a division of the SPS and the only laboratory testing official samples for C. sepedonicus in Lithuania. The PRL is accredited according to ISO 17025:2018 including techniques, methods and equipment used for the analysis for C. sepedonicus. The SPS organised a proficiency test for the detection of C. sepedonicus in 2023 with the participation of the PRL and official laboratories of Latvia and Estonia. The comparison test included five different test methods listed in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2022/1194 and the PRL achieved 100% confirming result. 9. The PRL use the methods for detection and identification tests listed in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. The first detection test is the immunofluorescence test. In the case of a positive result, the TaqMan® Real-time PCR (Massart et al. (2014) test is used for confirmation. In the case of an inconsistent result, the TaqMan® Real-time PCR (Gudmestad et al. (2009) as adapted by Vreeburg et al. (2018)) test is used to confirm or refute the result. In the case of a positive first detection test result, the PRL informs the CA about the suspected presence of C. sepedonicus in the form of an interim report. The interim and the final test results are provided to the CAs without delay via the IT system of the SPS. 10. The PRL stated that they are able to test 80 laboratory samples for C. sepedonicus a week. Frequently laboratory tests are started only two to three weeks after sampling. However, these delays do not pose phytosanitary risk because inspectors always prohibit the movement of sampled lots. When the sample flow is less intense, i.e., up to 80 laboratory samples per week, tests are started on the same or the following working day after receiving the sample. 5 Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls 11. The controls are carried out by designated authorities based on EU and national legislation. Regular audits, detailed procedures and appropriate laboratory background provide a good basis for the proper implementation of EU law. 12. The penalties applied are not effective and dissuasive to prevent the infringement of official measures which decreases the chance of successful eradication of outbreaks. 5.2 SURVEYS OUTSIDE THE DEMARCATED AREAS Legal requirements Article 19 and 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Findings 13. Based on the annual phytosanitary inspection plan, 100% of seed potato producers and at least 25% of registered ware potato producers are inspected annually. Since 2018, all growers producing potatoes on fields larger than 1 ha are obliged to be registered. Five to eight samples are planned to be collected in every region from non-registered producers. Every summer, the regional divisions of the SPS receive the data of producers who receive subsidies from the NPA. The CAs prioritise those non- registered producers who increased their potato production above 1 ha or produce potatoes on fields close to 1 ha. 14. Samples are taken mostly from storage facilities, but operators may request the samples to be taken from the field prior to harvest. Inspectors collect 200 tubers from ten places in the lot for laboratory testing. The samples taken appropriately reflect the potato lots investigated. Systematic visual inspection of the growing crops and of lots in store is carried out in case of seed potatoes. 15. All seed potato lots are sampled and tested for C. sepedonicus before official certification and placing on the market. When seed potato growers produce ware potatoes too, all ware potato lots are sampled as well. At least one lot is sampled of other ware potato producers. Based on national legislation, inspectors always prohibit the movement of sampled potato lots pending the results of laboratory tests. 16. In recent years, the number of non-registered producers decreased, however it is still significant, covering some 40% of the total ware potato production area. The number of samples taken from these producers only slightly increased after the audit in 2018. Table 2 below contains the number of samples and the positive results from 2023 in case of registered and non-registered ware potato producers. Only ten percent of the samples were taken from non-registered operators, but 15 percent of these samples were infected by C. sepedonicus, proportionally higher than in the case of registered 6 producers. This difference is similar in most of the years since 2016. Despite the high number of positive samples, the CA decreased the number of samples taken and in the period since 2014, the lowest number of samples were taken from 2022-2024 (see table 3). The design of the annual phytosanitary inspection plan and the number of samples taken did not take into account appropriately the risk that C. sepedonicus occurs in the area covered by each survey contrary to Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The number and origin of the samples were not based on the particular potato production system of Lithuania, contrary to Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Table 2. Outbreaks were reported from all regions of Lithuania during the last decade. Beside the fields of registered producers, the presence of C. sepedonicus was regularly detected on fields cultivated by non-registered producers. Hence the pest is present in productions sites which are not under official supervision (see table 3). These areas function as reservoirs for C. sepedonicus. The territory of Lithuania meets the criteria for "highly infected area" under Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. 18. The majority of outbreaks were detected in fields where producers planted tubers of undetermined plant health status, such as farm saved tubers and ware potatoes which are not tested for the presence of C. sepedonicus. The CAs carry out appropriate surveys on fields of and potato lots produced by registered operators. However, the risk from areas which are not under official supervision is not taken into account appropriately during the annual surveys, as places of production cultivated by non-registered producers who typically plant tubers of undetermined plant health status function as a reservoir for C. sepedonicus and contribute to the spread of the pest. The likelihood that the presence of C. sepedonicus in Lithuania is much higher than detected is significant. 5.3 MEASURES IN CASE OF SUSPICION OF THE PRESENCE Legal requirements Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. Findings 20. The SPS ensures that samples taken by inspectors for the purpose of annual surveys are subject to detection tests in line with Article (1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1194. In all cases when the first detection test had a positive result, the PRL provided the information about the suspected presence of the pest without delay, in the form of an interim report. 21. During the visit of the DA of six outbreaks, the audit team noted the following: 8 · Official controls were carried out without delay when the CAs received the interim report.
