The organisational aspects of controls on plant health in Italy are described in its country profile and its Multi-Annual National Control Programme, both of which are published at https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/IT.

The CAs for planning and implementing surveys and contingency plans are clearly designated as required by Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The National Plant Health Service is the CA for plant health in the context of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031 and (EU) 2017/625. It has three components as follows: · The central competent authority is Office 5 of the Directorate-General of Rural Development of the MAFF. It transposes EU legislation and issues decrees and technical standards, which the RPSs must follow, 1 https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/98998dd99125401f9f19c91369385918 3 · The 21 RPSs are the CAs in the regions and Autonomous Provinces. In the context of this audit, they are responsible for conducting surveys, · CREA-DC is the National Reference Institute for Plant Protection ­ its role is to provide scientific support to the National Plant Health Service.

The National Plant Health Committee (NPC) is the technical body of the National Plant Health Service. It comprises the Director of the central competent authority, the heads of the 21 RPSs and the head of CREA-DC. The NPC meets monthly. It has a series of Working Groups, including the National Technical Working Group for the National Plant Survey Programme. This Working Group, which was first established in 2015, meets quarterly, and comprises representatives from the MAFF, the RPSs and CREA-DC.

The MAFF is responsible for planning and coordinating the implementation of the multi- annual and annual survey programmes. It has a contract in place with CREA-DC, under which CREA-DC is delegated responsibility for drafting these survey programmes, monitoring their implementation and collating the resultant data. It has also delegated operational responsibility for developing contingency plans to CREA-DC. For statistically based surveys, CREA-DC drafts the annual survey programme. For risk-based surveys, the 21 RPSs each propose the number of surveys they plan to conduct for each pest. CREA-DC then compiles this data into the national programme. In both cases, the National Technical Working Group for the National Plant Survey Programme is consulted. The NPC then reviews and approves both (statistically-based and risk-based) survey programmes, and on this basis, the MAFF approves the programmes.

The MAFF explained that this system was established to give the regions autonomy while also ensuring that MAFF and CREA-DC could review and analyse their proposals and seek changes to the numbers and types of surveys if required. It was envisaged that this process would result in a survey programme for Union quarantine pests and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests that would be risk-based with surveys carried out in all appropriate locations based on sound scientific and technical principles as required by Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

At the time of the audit in September 2025, the 21 RPSs had 426 phytosanitary inspectors, 59 phytosanitary agents and 694 phytosanitary assistants dealing with plant health related tasks. Phytosanitary inspectors and agents are permanent staff. RPSs can hire phytosanitary assistants on short term contracts to undertake specific tasks, and these staff are not subject to the restrictions on employing permanent staff. One third of all phytosanitary assistants work in Puglia, where they are heavily involved in survey activities relating to the X. fastidiosa outbreaks identified.

All three RPSs met by the audit team stated that they have insufficient staff in the plant health area as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to implement all legally required tasks, given the number of operators, areas of host plants and relevant phytosanitary risks in their regions. Sicily explained that due to the regions' financial constraints, there are severe restrictions on the numbers of public servants, making it very 4 difficult to employ permanent staff. It tried to recruit phytosanitary assistants in 2023, but a court ruling arising from a legal challenge meant that it was unable to progress with the planned recruitment of these staff. The RPSs in both Calabria and Lazio explained that they have insufficient staff as plant health tasks are not considered a high priority in terms of recruiting and allocating staff within the public administration. None of the three RPSs met by the audit team had examined the possibility to delegate survey work as permitted under Article 31 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

At central level, both the MAFF and CREA-DC stated that they do not have sufficient staff to plan and oversee the implementation of surveys and to prepare contingency plans. They attributed the delays in drafting contingency plans (findings 70 and 71) and deficiencies in surveys as described below to these staff shortages.

The three RPSs met by the audit team stated that they propose survey numbers for risk- based surveys for all Union quarantine pests (including priority pests) and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests based on available resources, rather than phytosanitary risks. The MAFF acknowledged that the majority of RPSs follow this same approach. The MAFF and CREA-DC stated that they do not have the human resources to critically analyse the survey proposals of the RPSs (in terms of numbers of planned surveys, locations for surveys and survey methodology) as foreseen under the structures described in findings 4 and 5, with the result that the proposals of the RPSs are aggregated to form the multi-annual and annual survey programmes, without any analysis to determine if the resultant national programmes comply with Article 22(2) (for Union quarantine pests) and Article 24(1) (for priority pests) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

Phytosanitary inspectors must have a relevant university degree, must complete 120 hours specific in-house training on plant health and successfully pass the associated exam. Phytosanitary agents do not require a relevant university degree but must complete the 120 hours training course and pass the exam. Phytosanitary assistants receive training relevant to the specific tasks they complete. The audit team concluded, based on observing surveys, that all three categories of staff have received sufficient training to enable them to perform surveys in a consistent manner as required by Article 5(4)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In the context of surveys, the CAs do not have appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment to perform surveys efficiently and effectively as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The National Plant Health Service uses the Monitoring of Harmful Pests (MORGANA) IT system to plan and record surveys, to send samples to laboratories, and to manage the resultant data. Sixteen of the 21 RPSs input survey data directly into MORGANA, while the remaining five use their own systems and transfer relevant data into MORGANA periodically throughout the year. The MAFF explained that deficiencies in MORGANA make it very difficult to extract data from the system. As a practical example, the MAFF are unable to monitor the implementation of surveys on an ongoing basis to check progress towards annual targets or to check that 5 surveys are being done at the appropriate times of the year as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 due to these deficiencies.

In the context of implementing surveys at field level (as distinct from planning surveys), there are procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, quality and consistency of surveys as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. CREA-DC has drawn up a series of Official Technical Survey Sheets (OTSSs) for individual harmful organisms or groups of related pests. These documents provide technical information to staff conducting surveys such as the biology and the regulatory status of the pest and detailed instructions for visual examinations and sampling and diagnostic methods. The MAFF confirmed that these are legally binding on the RPSs, i.e. surveys must be conducted in line with these documents. The OTSSs are complemented by a series of seven "Operational Indications" documents. These are based on decisions of the National Technical Working Group for the National Plant Survey Programme, are drafted by CREA-DC and are circulated to all RPSs. They provide practical information for implementing surveys such as details on the types of traps to use. Finally, contingency plans (for the four pests where they are finalised) provide guidance on surveys.

While work is ongoing to establish a system, MAFF does not have an operational programme of internal audits at national level, and does not conduct such audits, in the plant health area as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The MAFF has designated five different CREA-DC laboratories as National Reference Laboratories (NRLs) in the area of plant health in line with Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Three CREA-DC laboratories in Rome are the NRLs for bacteriology, virology and mycology. Two CREA-DC laboratories in Florence are the NRLs for entomology and nematology. The 21 RPSs have designated a total of 45 official laboratories under Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for testing samples taken under the annual survey programmes. The MAFF stated that it is satisfied that it has adequate laboratory capacity for the current annual survey programmes on priority pests, as required by Article 5(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and added that there is sufficient capacity in the laboratory network to handle an increase in survey (and hence sampling and testing) work. It explained that: · Six of the 45 designated official laboratories have accreditation as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 for all categories of pests (but not all pests) and avail of the derogation permitted under Article 41 of the same Regulation for pests/methodologies for which they are not accredited, · Eighteen have accreditation as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 for some types of pests and avail of the derogations permitted under Article 40(1)(b) and Article 41 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in accordance with Article 3(c) of Regulation (EU) 2021/1353, for pests/methodologies for which they are not accredited, 6 · Twenty-one are not accredited for any pests and avail of the derogation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, · In all cases where the presence of a Union quarantine pest is suspected, confirmatory diagnosis is carried out by an official laboratory accredited for that pest, or where appropriate, by the relevant NRL, · There is a national network of plant health laboratories which meets monthly and is a useful forum to share information among laboratories.

The RPSs conduct an assessment prior to designating laboratories that avail of the derogation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to verify that the laboratories comply with the conditions of the derogation, including if they have a quality assurance system as required by Article 40(1)(b)(iv). The 21 laboratories that avail of the derogation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 participate regularly in proficiency tests as required by Article 40(1)(b)(iii).

CREA-DC stated that none of the official laboratories (including NRLs) designated by the CAs are accredited for testing 11 of the 20 priority pests. These pests are Agrilus anxius Gory (A. anxius), Agrilus planipennis Fairmaire (A. planipennis), A. ludens, Anthonomus eugenii Cano (A. eugenii), Aromia bungii (Faldermann), Bactericera cockerelli (Sulc.) (B. cockerelli), Conotrachelus nenuphar (Herbst) (C. nenuphar), Dendrolimus sibiricus Tschetverikov (D. sibiricus), R. pomonella, S. frugiperda and Thaumatotibia leucotreta (Meyrick) (T. leucotreta).

CREA-DC highlighted that it is difficult to obtain biological reference material for approximately 90 pests surveyed under the multi-annual survey programme, which poses a challenge for laboratories designated to conduct testing under the programme. These include the priority pests A. anxius, A. planipennis, A. ludens, A. eugenii, B. cockerelli, Bactrocera zonata, C. nenuphar, D. sibiricus, R. pomonella, S. frugiperda and T. leucotreta. 7 Conclusions on Competent Authorities

The system for planning the multi-annual and annual survey programmes, as currently in operation, does not ensure that the resultant plans comprise a sufficient number of risk- based surveys, to be carried out in all appropriate locations, and based on sound scientific and technical principles, to ensure the timely detection of any outbreaks of these pests.

At an operational level, there is clear, legally binding guidance for the planning and implementation of surveys, but deficiencies in the IT system used means that the central competent authority is unable to monitor the implementation of surveys by the regions.

The absence of a system of internal audits in the area of plant health means the CAs do not avail of an important tool to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of their official controls and other official activities.

The available laboratory capacity is sufficient to support the survey programmes, with the majority of laboratories availing of the derogations from the requirement for accreditation. 5.2 SURVEY PROGRAMMES Legal requirements Articles 22, 23 and 24 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1702

Ensure that the scope of the accreditation of the official laboratories include those methods of laboratory analysis, test or diagnosis required to be used by the laboratory for analyses, tests or diagnoses of those pests included in the multi-annual survey programme, in line with Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 14. Associated findings No. 4.

Ensure that a statistically based annual survey programme based on the level of risk is established and implemented for Xylella fastidiosa, as required by Article 2(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. Ensure that this annual survey takes into account the European Food Safety Authority Guidelines for statistically sound and risk-based surveys of this pest in the survey design and the sampling scheme for all parts of Croatia, in line with Article 2(4) of the above EU Regulation. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 40. Associated findings Nos. 21, 23 and 34.

Ensure that surveys for the presence of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus are annually carried out on vectors in line Article 2(1) of Implementing Decision 2012/535/EU. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 40. Associated findings Nos. 30, 35 and 36

Ensure that the CAs regularly review and, where appropriate, update their contingency plans in line with Article 25(4) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031, and consult all relevant stakeholders in the process of keeping up to date the contingency plans in line with Article 25(1) of the same EU Regulation. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 46. Associated findings Nos. 43 and 45.

The organisational aspects of controls on plant health in Austria are described in the Multi-Annual National Control Programme for Austria at: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/AT.

The CAs for surveys and contingency plans are clearly designated as required by Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · The BMLUK is responsible for international relations and the overall coordination of the CAs. It also leads the Steering Committee, which is a technical forum for the harmonised implementation of plant health requirements in the nine Federal States. 1https://efsa.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/filtergallery/index.html?appid=fe5cb24504f74af7839012586d61587b 3 · The AGES is responsible for technical coordination and for laboratory analysis in the field of plant health, except for forestry pests. · The BFW is responsible for technical coordination and laboratory analysis for forestry pests. As a CA, the BFW also carries out surveys for B. xylophilus in forests on behalf of the RPS in three Federal States. · The Federal States are directly responsible for plant health regulation and its implementation, except for trade and forestry related matters. The nine RPS are also responsible for the development of their own contingency and survey plans. · The Steering Committee was established to facilitate the consistent implementation of the plant health regulations in Austria. Its members are technical experts and officials of the BMLUK, the AGES, the BFW and the nine RPS. The Committee prepares, amongst others, the contingency plans which are accepted and used by all Federal States.

There is efficient and effective co-ordination and co-operation between the CAs responsible for planning and implementing surveys as required by Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This includes biannual coordination meetings with the participation of each CA, national and regional training and harmonised national and regional procedures. 5.1.2 Relevant national and regional legislation

The Plant Protection Act of 2018 establishes the roles and responsibilities in the plant health area and implementing provisions for Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and 2016/2031. The Plant Protection Regulation 2019 includes details for plant health related official controls and other official activities. Each Federal State adopted regional legal acts for the implementation of EU plant health requirements. This is in line with Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires that CAs have the legal powers to perform official controls and other official activities. The CAs have the legal power to gain access to the premises of, and documents kept by, operators to be able to accomplish their tasks properly. This is in line with indent (h) of the same point of this Article. 5.1.3 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

There are procedures in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness, and the impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls and other official activities as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The most important procedure is the "Guidance Agriculture". It contains information about and guidance for inspection and sampling for all Union quarantine pests listed in Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 (pests listed in groups in the Annex are also presented as a group of pests in the Guidance). Another guideline was prepared for the RPS to harmonise the development of their regional surveillance strategies. 4 6. Each CA met by the audit team explained that they have a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Inspectors and technical experts met by the audit team were knowledgeable, experienced and trained. Based on the interviews and visits, the audit team concluded that the CAs have appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 7. The CAs have developed and implemented training programmes for staff involved in planning and conducting surveys as required by Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team received detailed programmes and structures for basic and refresher trainings provided to the RPS inspectors by the AGES and the BFW. The training programmes contain appropriate information on plant health surveys, so providing a solid basis for the implementation of survey programmes. 8. There is an internal audit system as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit programme for 2023-2028 of the AGES contains one plant health related audit in each Federal State. Besides the chosen plant health topic, such as risk-based planning or outbreak management, general requirements of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are also assessed. The audit reports provided contain a detailed description of findings, recommendations and the corrective actions done by the audited RPS. 5.1.4 Laboratories and Testing 9. The AGES is designated as the National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for pests of plants, in compliance with Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The AGES is listed in Article 1 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/530 as the European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) for pests of plants (insects and mites) as a member of a consortium. All nine Federal States designated the AGES as the official laboratory for pests of plants in line with Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Where another official laboratory carries out only the initial analysis, all positive test results are confirmed by the AGES. 10. The BFW functions as an official laboratory for pests of forest plants. In cooperation with the AGES, it also functions as NRL for the analysis of B. xylophilus. While there was adequate coordination and cooperation between the BFW laboratory and the CAs, and the laboratory tests were performed adequately, the BFW laboratory is not designated as an official laboratory in writing with a detailed description of its tasks. Contrary to Article 37(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no detailed written description of · the tasks that the laboratory carries out as an official laboratory, · the conditions under which it carries out those tasks and 5 · the arrangements necessary to ensure efficient and effective coordination and collaboration between the laboratory and the competent authorities.2 11. The laboratory of the RPS of Styria is designated as the official laboratory for Styria for the analysis of certain potato pests, in line with Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 12. The AGES and the RPS laboratory of Styria are accredited in accordance with the standard EN ISO/IEC 17025, as required by Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The scope of the accreditation of the RPS laboratory of Styria includes all methods of laboratory analysis used. According to the information provided to the audit team, for most samples of Union quarantine pests, the AGES uses an accredited test method in line with the requirements of Article 37(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In the absence of an accredited method, the derogation under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2021/1353 is applied. 13. The BFW laboratory does not operate in accordance with the standard EN ISO/IEC 17025 and is not accredited in accordance with that standard, contrary to Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/6253. Nevertheless, the laboratory uses the test methods required by EU legislation, it participates regularly in proficiency tests for the respective methods with satisfactory results, and it has a quality assurance system in place. · The derogation from the mandatory accreditation provided by Article 40(1)(b) is not applicable because the BFW also tests samples taken during official controls. The CAs are clearly designated as required by Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The DG Health and Food Safety country profile for Italy and the Multi-Annual National Control Programme for Italy, both of which are published at https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country/profile/details/IT provide some information on the organisational aspects of controls on GMOs in Italy.

The MH is the central competent authority (CCA) for GMOs in animal feed. It is responsible for developing the National Control Plan on Animal Nutrition (NCPAN) and for collating the results of its implementation. Regional Directorates for Health are responsible for developing regional plans based on the NCPAN. Local Health Units (ASLs) determine which operators to control in line with the frequencies in the national and regional plans. They carry out official inspections and sampling relating to GMOs in feed on the internal market. Controls on feed at Border Control Posts (BCPs) are conducted by the MH.

The MH is also the CCA for GMOs in food. It is responsible for general policy, coordination, and developing the National Control Plan. The Regional Directorates for Health are responsible for developing regional plans based on the national plan. ASLs carry out sampling relating to GMOs in food on the internal market. Controls on food at BCPs are conducted by the MH.

The MAFF is the CCA for seeds. Official controls on conventional seeds to verify the absence of GMOs are conducted by: · CREA-DC and the ICQRF at operators that package and distribute seeds. The ICQRF also draws up the annual control programme for GMOs in seeds, · Customs at entry points. (In some regions, this is done in cooperation with the Regional Plant Health Services, so that in reality the staff of the Plant Health 3 Services actually do the controls). These cooperation agreements are at regional level, with no CCA having an overview of the system throughout Italy.

The MEES is designated as the CCA for Directive 2001/18/EC as required by Article 4(4) of that Directive, and therefore is responsible for examining notifications for field trials of GMOs under this Directive. The agricultural authorities of the respective regions are responsible for conducting controls to verify if operators conduct trials in line with the conditions of authorisation.
There are over 20 laboratories responsible for analysing GMOs in food, feed and seeds as described in findings 59 and 63.

The MH is responsible for contact with the Commission in the context of Article 4(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and is the designated national RASFF single contact point, including for GMOs in food and feed, in line with Article 50(1) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002.

The MEES stated that Directive 2001/18/EC has been transposed into national legislation by Decree No. 224 of 8 July 2003 as required by Article 291 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. It added that all subsequent amendments to the Directive have also been transposed. 5.1.2 Procedures for quality and consistency of official controls

There are procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in the context of controls on trials and sampling food. The MEES has developed a checklist for controls on GM trials and the MH has devised clear guidance and report templates for sampling foods for GM analysis. Both Ministries stated that these documents are used by all regions. Finally, all regions log all food samples taken for GMO analysis in a database managed by the NRL for food and feed.

There are insufficient procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls in the areas of feed and seed contrary to Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The MH has developed detailed checklists for conducting official controls on feed operators. The NCPAN provides sampling guidelines and sampling report templates based on the requirements laid down in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. All controls on feed operators are recorded in a harmonised manner in the Veterinary Information system for food safety (SINVSA), a national Information Technology (IT) system used by all regions. However, the checklists used for controls on feed mills do not include any specific references to controls relating to labelling and traceability of feeds containing GMOs, or the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds. Consequently, the MH could provide no documentary evidence that these requirements are systematically controlled during inspections at feed business 4 operators. The guidance/instructions for taking seed samples for GMO analysis is deficient in a number of areas as described in findings 38 and 40. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on GMOs
The CAs and their roles are clearly defined, thereby providing a solid basis on which to plan official controls.

The procedures and arrangements on which controls on trials and food are based provide a sound basis for ensuring the consistent implementation of legislation on GMOs in these areas. Deficiencies in the checklists used by inspectors in the feed area mean that there is no documentary evidence that controls relating to labelling, traceability and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds are performed.

Sampling of seed lots, which forms the basis of the control system for seeds, is not performed consistently due to significant deficiencies in the procedures provided to inspectors, which compromises the reliability of the control system on seeds. 5.2 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Articles 4(5) and 21 of Directive 2001/18/EC Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 Findings

The MH does not take account of all identified risks when planning official controls in the feed area as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Official controls on feed business operators are based on the NCPAN. The current NCPAN covers the period 2024-2026. The RVSs develop regional inspection plans based on the NCPAN allocating the regional workload between the ASLs.

Under the NCPAN for the period 2021-2023, 549 feed samples were planned for GMO analysis each year. Under the NCPAN for the period 2024-2026, this has been reduced to 380 samples per year. The MH explained that under the 2021-2023 plan, 389 samples were tested for authorised GMOs only, with the remaining 160 samples tested for unauthorised GMOs only. Under the 2024-2026 plan, all samples of conventional feed are being tested for both authorised and unauthorised events, with organic samples (which typically comprise about 10-12% of samples) being tested for unauthorised 5 GMOs only. This approach of analysing organic feed samples for unauthorised events only is sufficient to meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, but it is not sufficient to meet the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003, as authorised GM events may be present at levels greater than 0.9%, (which requires the feed to be labelled as GM, and its marketing as conventional feed), but this non-compliance would not be detected if the analysis is only for unauthorised events.

The NCPAN requires that all samples for GM analysis should contain at least one feed material derived from soya, maize, cotton, rapeseed, sugar beet, potato, rice or flax. It adds that at least 50% of samples should be feed materials stating that the detection of GMOs is more reliable and effective in these samples in comparison to compound feed samples.

These targets comprise both monitoring samples (taken at random) and surveillance samples (taken based on identified risks). Under the 2024-2026 plan, 320 samples are allocated equally to all 19 regions (16 samples each) and two autonomous provinces (8 each) for monitoring purposes and just 60 samples taken on the basis of specific risks. The 320 samples are taken at all types of operators whereas the risk-based samples are taken at producers of feed materials and manufacturers of compound feeds as the MH considers that these are the highest risk operators.

The NCPAN requires that at least 3% of imported feed consignments are sampled and analysed, but there are no specific targets for sampling and analysis related to GMOs, with one exception. The BCPs are instructed to sample all consignments of linseed from Canada and wheat from the United States of America (USA) due to previous detections of unauthorised GM events in these commodities from these countries. The NCPAN notes the low numbers of controls on imported feed materials in previous years and the risks associated with these products, given that GM crops are grown in many of the countries of origin. However, it does not establish targets for sampling and analysis for these materials, either at the point of entry, or during controls on the internal market. Given that Italy imports six to seven million tonnes of maize and maize derived products and about 2.5 million tonnes of soya and soya derived products each year, the failure to prioritise the sampling and analysis of imported feed materials for GMOs linked to the country of origin is not in line with Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires official controls to be carried out on a risk basis.

The NCPAN requires at least one annual control at all approved feed mills and at least one control every two years at all registered feed mills. Registered producers and retailers are also scheduled for at least one control every two years. The NCPAN recommends that labelling and traceability of feeds containing GMOs and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds is checked during these controls.

Italy has had a series of national control plans for GMOs in food since 2006. The current plan covers 2023-2027. The national target is to sample at least 1% of relevant (e.g. 6 containing maize, soya, linseed, rapeseed) imported food consignments. This equates to about 60 samples per year. In addition to this general guidance, the MH has instructed the BCPs to take a sample from all consignments of linseed from Canada and wheat from the USA. The national plan also includes 628 samples (mainly in foods containing maize and soya, but also rice, rape, cotton, potato, papaya and linseed) from the internal market. The plan specifies that at least 60% of the samples should be raw materials or processing intermediates. These numbers were identical under the previous plan covering up to 2022. All food samples are tested for both authorised and non-authorised events.

Samples are allocated per region based on the number of imported consignments (for imports) and the number of food business establishments (for internal market samples). Each region then allocates its quota of samples per ASL.

The MH is satisfied that there are no foods marketed in Italy containing GMO so there are no planned controls to determine if the operators comply with labelling requirements for GMO containing foods, i.e. Articles 12 and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003, as these obligations are not relevant.

The MAFF explained that in line with a Ministerial Decree of 27 November 2003, 20% of maize and soya seed lots placed on the Italian market are sampled and analysed for GMOs each year. Sampled seed lots can only be marketed following a negative analysis result. Operators are obliged to notify the ICQRF of all maize and soya seed lots brought into their premises intended for marketing in Italy (regardless of origin). The ICQRF plans to sample 400 seed lots per year, and CREA-DC plans to sample 500 seed lots to achieve the 20% target.

While maize and soya are the two most widely grown crops in Italy which have been subject to genetic modification, the MAFF acknowledged that the sampling and analysis programme for GMOs in seeds has not been reviewed, and revised as necessary, since its inception in 2003 to reflect all identified risks as required by Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Therefore, the programme does not meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, as other seeds which may be subject to GM modification, e.g. tomato, are not included in the scope of the control programme. 7 Conclusions on the planning of official controls
The planned official controls for GMOs in food are risk based and are fit for purpose.

The planned official controls for GMOs in feed fail to address risks related to imported feed materials and organic feed, thereby weakening the assurance that animal feed marketed in Italy complies with legislation on GMOs.

Official controls on seeds are based on an outdated plan that does not reflect all known risks, thereby failing to provide sufficient assurance that seeds sown in Italy are free from GMOs. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Controls on the deliberate release of GMOs, other than placing on the market (field trials) Legal requirements Articles 4(1), 4(3), 4(5), 6, 8, 9, 10 and 31(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Findings

The MEES received four requests for deliberate releases of GMO under part B of Directive 2001/18/EC (i.e. field trials) in 2024. These requests related to rice resistant to rice blast, two trials for vines resistant to downy mildew, and one trial for tomatoes resistant to Orobanche spp. The Ministry granted authorisation in all four cases, but only one of the trials was undertaken in 2024.

In all cases the applicants submitted a notification together with a Summary Notification Information Format (SNIF) form in line with Article 6(1) of Directive 2001/18/EC and the notifications contained all information as required by Article 6(2) of the Directive. The MEES stated that in all cases it requests the Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA) to conduct an assessment to satisfy the requirements of Article 4(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC. The audit team examined two of the files and noted that in both cases, the Ministry responded to the notifier within 90 days of receipt of the notification (including any time taken seeking further information and time taken for the public consultation) indicating that the proposed release could proceed, which is in line with Article 6(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC.

The Ministry stated that there are arrangements in place for public consultation regarding proposed deliberate releases, and that information is made available to the public on all field trials via its website in line with Article 9(1) and (2) of Directive 2001/18/EC. The MEES has established a public register 8 https://bch.mase.gov.it/index.php/it/?view=article&id=435:registro-publico-relativo- alla-localizzazione-di-emissioni-di-ogm-nell-ambiente-2&catid=15 where the location of GMO trials are recorded as required by Article 31(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC. In line with national legislation, the precise Global Positioning System (GPS) co-ordinates of trials are published.

In the case of the one trial completed in 2024, the agricultural authorities of Lombardy conducted controls to verify that the trial had been conducted in line with the conditions of authorisation, and it plans to conduct further controls following the conclusion of the trial, as required by Article 4(5) of the Directive 2001/18/EC. The CA completed written records of all official controls (using a standard inspection template annexed to a National Decree of 8 November 2017) and provided a copy to the operator as required by Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.3.2 Controls on GMOs in seed and propagating material Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 Article 9 of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625 Artic

The competent authority should complete documented procedures so that they provide sufficient information and detailed instructions for staff, as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, to carry out official controls at the port, including inspections carried out according to Articles 19 and 20 of Regulation (EC) 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 2 Associated findings: 5 and 17

The competent authority should take measures to ensure that inspections: · for the purpose of granting a certificate of approval or renewals of such approvals, and · on the loading of livestock vessels; are performed by a team of inspectors including at least an official veterinarian and a maritime expert, as required by Article 9 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/372 and Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/842. Recommendation based on conclusion 3. Associated findings: 9, 10, 14 and 47.

The competent authority should take measures to carry out official controls by an official veterinarian on board a livestock vessel during the entire first voyage following the approval of the livestock vessel and prior to the renewal of such approval, as required by Article 10(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/372. Recommendation based on conclusion 3. Associated findings: 10 and 21.

Full legal references are provided in Annex 1. Legal acts quoted in this report refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. 4 BACKGROUND The export of live animals by sea from Member States to non-EU countries is an economically significant trade. However, it is also a sensitive area, as incidents involving livestock vessels have repeatedly drawn public attention due to severe animal welfare issues. High-profile cases in recent years have shown the suffering that can occur when animals are transported under poor conditions or experience long delays at sea. Historically, audits of Member States have identified weaknesses in animal welfare standards during these transports. These shortcomings have sometimes involved inadequate checks on the vessels, poor journey planning, and insufficient contingency measures. To strengthen the welfare of animals during sea transport, the EU adopted new rules in 2023. These include an Implementing Regulation that sets out uniform conditions for official controls at exit points and during loading onto livestock vessels. Additionally, a Delegated Regulation introduced more detailed requirements for the approval of livestock vessels. These changes aim to address past problems and ensure a higher level of protection for animals transported by sea. This series of audits intends to check the measures taken by Member States since they were previously audited, and to verify the implementation of the new requirements introduced by the 2023 Regulations2.

This means that the system is well set up and capable of ensuring compliance with animal welfare legislation. 2. Some shortcomings reduce the effectiveness of official controls and compromise guarantees of animal welfare during sea transport. Some contingency plans lacked risk analysis, failing to address key welfare risks (e.g. extreme heat, engine failure).

With regards to the competence of the official veterinarian that accompanied the vessel, the audit team noted 11 during sea very good knowledge of the animal welfare implications during sea transport transport as well as comprehensive measures he had taken to monitor the status of the animals and of the surrounding environment to ensure a high level of animal protection. 10. This discrepancy was communicated to the THETIS-EU administrator team in the European Maritime Safety Agency so that they provide proper guidance to support a seamless process across the EU and enhance compliance with Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2023/372.

FINDINGS ON OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE PROTECTION OF ANIMALS DURING TRANSPORT BY LIVESTOCK VESSEL TO NON-EU COUNTRIES The strengths are the systematic and consistent use of the animal welfare module of THETIS-EU to record the results of official controls. In addition, maritime experts provide solid technical input, and some good practices were noted, such as cooperation with Israeli authorities on arrival checks. The weaknesses relate mainly to some contingency plans and the enforcement in relation to some non-compliances. Some contingency plans fail to address key animal welfare risks (heat stress, engine failure, etc.), and enforcement of these shortcomings has been insufficient. Overall, while technical competence and the use of recording systems are strong, enforcement and the evaluation of contingency plans remain weak points and compromise the guarantees of animal welfare during sea transport. 7.1 ARRANGEMENTS TO CARE FOR THE ANIMALS 11. Despite the split of responsibilities, both Departments cooperate and coordinate the ABP policy overlap- ping their areas of competence. 6 FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. The specific provisions of the legal acts relevant to each section of this report are cited in Annex II and are referred to in the individual findings of the report 6.1 Recommendation No.1 on conditions for granting approval for ABP plants

This recommendation of the 2021 audit report required the competent authority to ensure that, when granting approval for ABP processing plants, the operator meets all of the infra- structure and equipment requirements for a plant and, in particular, has put in place appropri- ate own checks and HACCP-based procedures, including validation of the processing plant.

To address this recommendation, NFCSO planned the following corrective actions: a. To deliver a training focusing on practical aspects related to controls on operators, plants and establishments acting in the ABP sector. b. To carry out a cross-check of approved ABP facilities to verify if these comply with the legal requirements, infrastructural provisions and with the required own checks con- trols. Cross-checks would cover the control reports of authorities from county and dis- trict level, as applicable. To carry out internal audits (complementary to cross-checks), covering verification of official controls on ABP plants and operators. Audits would verify if official controls accurately assessed operators' documentation and the results of operators' own checks. Moreover, audits would check if the resulting controls reports provided a reliable pic- ture of the activities of those establishments such as the collection, identification, transport, traceability, placing on the market, handling, the use and disposal of ABP and DP. NFCSO set the deadline for completing these actions on 31 December 2023.

NFCSO presented evidence demonstrating that it satisfactorily delivered corrective actions aiming at addressing recommendation No.1, namely: NFCSO organised 26 training sessions covering official controls in meat producing estab- lishments, authorisation process for ABP operators, sampling methods, and some other ABP- related aspects. NFCSO, distributed the training materials to all participants and also made them available online. a. In six counties (regions), NFCSO carried out cross-checks to verify the methods used for the authorisation and effectiveness of inspection on ABP establishments. b. In three counties and one district, NFCSO carried out internal audits covering ABP- related activities in meat producing establishments and of ABP operators. c. NFCSO analysed outcomes of these cross-checks internal audits and together with their results communicated them to all CGOs.

The audit team noted that CGO officials carry out approval of ABP plants and, every five years repeat this process (as re-approval) to verify if operators continuously comply with ap- plicable requirements. Approval and re-approval follow the same regime as regular, risk- based planned inspections, with exception that: a. contrary to planned inspections, the number of documents subjected to verification (e.g. commercial documents, results of laboratory analyses, etc.) is usually higher, and b. HACCP-based procedures are subjected to complete checks (full assessment), unlike during planned inspections, when checks usually cover randomly selected elements, (e.g. operator' sampling programme, calibration, etc).

While some assessments during approval/re-approval process properly concluded on operators' compliance with some of the applicable requirements (e.g. general layout of the plant, pest control programme, calibration), other assessments were incorrect and concluded on satisfactory compliance even though they should not. In ABP plants visited, incorrect as- sessments concerned: a. An arrangement for monitoring processing/treatment parameters; the system lacked continuous recording devices for processing parameters and adequate size reduction steps to ensure that particles size met EU requirements. b. HACCP-based procedures; these were either absent or were incomplete because they were missing identification of hazards and risk assessment, identification of potential 7 critical control points, information on established critical limits and ways of their moni- toring and applicable corrective actions. The operator own-check programme for sampling and testing on microbiological standards for: i. digestion residues missed one set of samples, namely samples that should be col- lected during/or immediately after the transformation process ­ contrary to re- quirements laid down in point 1(a) in Section 3 of Chapter III in Annex V to Regu- lation (EU) No 142/2011; ii. manufacture of raw petfood entirely lacked a sampling programme to verify com- pliance with microbiological standards (Salmonella) and hygienic criterion (Enter- obacteriaceae) ­ contrary to requirements laid down in point 6 in Chapter II of An- nex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; iii. production of processed animal proteins of pig origin, relied on the analysis of one instead of five samples ­ contrary to requirements laid down in Chapter I of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Besides the above, the audit team noted that official controls did not perform validation checks laid down in point 4 of Section 2 in Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. Consequently, an operator resumed its processing activity without validating the processing plant despite significant alterations were made to the process (i.e. modification of the machinery and change of the processing system).
The audit team noted that ABP operators with the above-mentioned deficiencies received their approvals/re-approvals allowing commencing or continuation of their operations.

The CGOs' officials accompanying the audit team initiated corrective actions aiming at removing the above-mentioned non-compliances in visited ABP plants. Conclusions on corrective actions to address recommendation No.1

The competent authority delivered the planned corrective actions, and the approval/re-approval process experienced some improvements. However, it cannot yet be ensured that approval/re- approval is granted only for those operators, which meet the respective requirements. There- fore, the recommendation No.1, is only partially addressed and requires further actions. 6.2 Recommendation No.2 on planning official controls
This recommendation of the 2021 audit report required the competent authority to ensure that all types of operators acting along the entire chain of ABP and DP are subject to official con- trols.

To address this recommendation, NFCSO planned to put in place a new software for risk assessment of operators, plants and establishments. The software would include all types of ABP-related activities listed in Article 24 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009 and allow for planning controls on all of them according to the pre-set criteria. 8 NFCSO set the deadline for completing the action on autumn 2022.

NFCSO presented evidence demonstrating that it satisfactorily delivered corrective actions aiming at addressing recommendation No.2, namely: a. has put in place a new software for selecting of ABP operators, plants and establish- ments following the risk-based assessment, b. the software allows to plan official controls based on pre-set criteria, which match these listed in Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625, and c. the list of ABP operators used by the software for risk-based selection matches with those listed in Article 24 of Regulation (EC) o 1069/2009.

The audit team verified the list of ABP operators selected for official controls in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and noted that the corresponding annual control programmes contained all kinds of ABP operators. The actions taken by NFSCO to address recommendation No.2 on shortcomings in the risk- based planning of official controls, have achieved their planned effect. This recommendation of the 2021 audit report required the competent authority to ensure that official controls accurately assess operators' documentation and the results of operators' own checks and that the resulting reports provide a reliable picture of the activities of those estab- lishments generating, collecting, handling and processing ABP, so that the risk-based plan- ning of official controls is improved.

To address this recommendation, NFCSO has planned to combine the corrective action for recommendations No.1 (cross-check verifications of approved ABP plants) with newly estab- lished internal (multiannual) audit plan covering verification of official controls on ABP plants and operators (see finding 3). NFCSO presented evidence demonstrating that it satisfactorily delivered corrective actions aiming at addressing recommendation No.3, namely cross-checks and internal audits ­ ac- tions implemented to address also recommendation No.1 (see finding 4).
